#2. Hasan Minhaj Thinks America’s Greatest Accomplishment Is Cereal

This is Amused Bouche, SAVEUR’s food questionnaire that explores the culinary curiosities of some of our favorite people. This interview series dives deep into their food routines, including dinner party strategies, cherished cookbooks, and the memorable bites they’d hop on a flight for.

Comedian and actor Hasan Minhaj is known for quippy questions, biting comebacks, and colorful commentary, but his most delightful soundbites are about food. During a recent  hour-long chat, he named a wide range of favorites, including bananas and oranges (“they come prepackaged and are great for traveling”); macaroni and cheese (“I love every category and version of it, from the box of Kraft to anyone’s Thanksgiving mac ’n’ cheese”); and dal chawal (specifically his mom’s version of the lentils and rice dish, “pure comfort food and my love language”).

These are the best-of-the-best bites for Minhaj, which is coincidentally the name of his new movie—Best of the Best, streaming now on Netflix—that he cowrote and produced with Prashanth Venkataramanujam and stars in as a professor and former dancer. The film pays homage to real-life Bollywood competitions, following collegiate dancers Maya and Anjali (played by Maitreyi Ramakrishnan and Priyanka Kedia, respectively), whose characters were inspired by “deeply passionate college kids in the biggest world that a lot of people have never heard of.”

Fiery passion is at the center of Minhaj’s life, especially when it comes to actual spice. “Some people want to drive at 85, some like a nice even 65, and some take it five miles below the limit,” he explains in a speedy analogy. “My spice level? I want to feel things in all caps. Life is to be lived. So I’m like, ‘Give it to me!’ Give me the full robustness of flavor that’s possible. I am a maximalist and love it all!”

His other spice of life is chai, “a form of commiseration, community, and love in Indian households—and an entry point to gossiping.” He loves that everyone does chai differently (he and his wife, Beena, prefer a more ginger-forward profile, while his parents like it sweeter). That’s why he became an investor and partner in the New York City-based Kolkata Chai in 2024, working with brothers Ani and Ayan Sanyal to expand the reach of a drink so engrained in their lives and culture. “It’s a welcome change to a lot of people’s only chai experience being at Starbucks in Middle America. It’s really amazing how you can change the complete perspective of an entire culture because of a drink that people can explore and make their own.”

Read on for Minhaj’s answers to our Amused Bouche questionnaire—it’s no surprise they’re chock-full of equally heartwarming and appetizing soundbites.

If you could only eat one thing 24/7/365, what would it be?

America is celebrating its 250th-year anniversary, and I think as a country, America’s greatest accomplishment is what we brought to cereal. I have been caught many a time red-handed with my full paw inside of some Golden Grahams, going to town. I will kill half a box, straight up, no milk. It is a snacking cereal. I’ll be watching a prestige drama and stress-eating Golden Grahams. Sometimes I’ll even drizzle honey over a bowl. I’ll also do the same with Honey Bunches of Oats. There’s a Montagues-and-Capulets debate here of blue box or orange box. I’m a blue box guy, because I love the almonds, extra crunch, and sweetness. It was my granola mix before I started eating granola, and it’s like trail mix without dastardly raisins coming in and f—ing shit up!

What’s the first thing you learned how to cook?

A strawberry Toaster Strudel, one of my all-time favorites. I popped it in the toaster as a kid, and it was an eye-opening experience. When I came home from elementary school, it felt like I was a master chef making myself this crisp little strudel cake and frosting it. I felt like a confectionery master. It was incredible. I toasted it on a level three and would sometimes pop it up and flip it midway through.

I actually didn’t hit my growth spurt until much later in high school, so I was quite undersized and malnourished-looking when I was younger. I was bullied a lot. My mother would make me eat three hard-boiled eggs on the way to school. And I hated hard-boiled eggs. Now that I’m a parent of small children, I understand the efficacy of hard-boiled eggs. But now I will pan-fry hard-boiled eggs, because really my hatred of them came from texture and temperature issues. But if you cut them in half and fry them yolk side down, there’s a crispness that makes it turn into a crunchy, almost taco-like topping that you can put on top of bread and butter.

It’s a really delicious, warm-and-gooey snack that I started making when I tried to give my daughter a hard-boiled egg and she immediately spit it out. I’m like, “Yeah, the cycle of torture continues! There needs to be a better way! Let me figure out a way to make this delicious.” The secret was making a quesadilla as the on-ramp she needs to get eggs in her. It was an experiment I worked backward from, kind of like writing a joke, telling a story, or working on a screenplay. My daughter loves quesadillas but hates eggs, so by making it into crunchiness that would blend right in, it wouldn’t feel like a squishy thing that I’m force-feeding her.

Growing up, we were never allowed to order dessert from restaurants. It is my greatest joy to order dessert from restaurants. I’ll tell the missus to order whatever she wants. Sometimes she’ll be indecisive. She always wants the chocolate lava cake, but she’ll be eyeing a berry tart. It’s a distant second, but I’ll take the bullet and order both for us to share. Sometimes when I do it, I’ll look over my shoulder to be like, “Are mom and dad going to find out?” But now I’m dad. We’re mom and dad!

I do not cook from cookbooks, but I will cook from YouTube Shorts. There’s just something about the looping nature of it breaking down the recipe. It’s tickling something in my mind and letting me know, “Hey, it’s not that hard. You can totally do it! You’ll get to completion, and it’s going to look pretty good.” And then as soon as doubt kicks in, the video starts playing again and snaps me out of it. It’s like the feeling of playing a song that you love over and over again, like “This Is How We Do It” by Montell Jordan. Play it again! “Men in Black”—play it again! I want to listen to it again, and that’s the feeling I get when I search “chicken tinga recipe” on YouTube Shorts.

Is there a cooking disaster that made you swear off a dish forever?

My wife does most of the cooking, but I want to put on the record that I try. I do cook, but a lot of the reaction is like, “Oh, you tried. I appreciate the effort. And that’s great for you. Why don’t you enjoy the omelet that you’ve made?” But I think I make a great soft-scramble, and what I bring to the breakfast table is pretty solid. I used to burn all of my food because I got impatient and cranked up the heat too fast. I learned you can’t bring microwave energy to a stove. Once I understood that foundational element in not burning your eggs, it was a huge unlock. Then I got to experience the full variety of eggs that aren’t charred.

Which nostalgic foods from childhood bring you the most comfort?

Dal chalwal: just lentils and rice. It has always been the first thing my mom makes for me when I get home to Sacramento, from college until now. It’s this beautiful gesture of love that I’m eating dal chawal with my mother, and her grandchildren are eating it with her at the same time. It’s pure comfort food and my love language.

When you’re playing dinner-party DJ, what’s spinning?

It’s a seasonal thing. Beena is really the entertainer and has been an incredible host since we met. For a holiday party, she’ll queue up a Pentatonix holiday playlist. Thematic, but a little left of center and unexpected.

What is your biggest entertaining flex to impress guests?

Beena loves a theme. We host Halloween on our block every year and call it Boo Bash. We go all out with a Halloween-themed live band, fog machines on the dance floor—aka the driveway—children’s face painting, bounce house, fake blood as drinks in IV bags. Her level of joy and imagination is unparalleled. She’s incredible. I add pizzazz, but I’m like, “Go off, queen!” She is the show. She’s the show creator, and I’m the showrunner.

Tell me about a meal so good you would hop on a flight to relive it.

My grandparents on both sides of my family have passed away, but I’m lucky enough that I was raised by my grandmother on my mother’s side from third to fifth grade. There’s a specific memory of when my grandmother made biryani. When the lid came off the pot and the steam and aroma of all the flavors escaped for the first time, she would put a ladle in and scoop it out for me, with meat that is so tender because it’s been cooking for so long. That’s the feeling that I would chase and book a flight immediately for, but it’s just a feeling. A feeling of love from it taking all day to make biriyani and that she loved me enough to put in that time and energy. Goat biriyani especially was a special-occasion dish, like when a cousin was getting married, and I associate it with being with family and something happy happening. In Hindi you call it ghar kha khana, the food from home. Biryani is the crème de la crème and the chef’s kiss of Indian cuisine for me. Especially my grandmother’s.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

#3. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#4. Air Fryer Pumpkin Donut Holes

If you’re ready to jump into fall baking, but your kitchen is still running at 80°, these air fryer pumpkin donut holes are the perfect treat. Baked in tiny silicone liners and rolled in cinnamon sugar, these poppable, bite-sized donut holes promise to leave you with sticky fingertips and an extra dose of fall vibes. Baking in an air fryer is like baking in a tiny high-powered convection oven—so while it’s similar to regular baking, there are a few things to be aware of.

Every air fryer bakes differently:Every oven also bakes differently, but due to the smaller size and high convection power of an air fryer, the differences are often more pronounced. In testing these donut holes, I found that timings could vary a lot, depending on which brand and model of air fryer I was using. “Hot spots” can vary too. Because of this, I often test cooking a smaller batch or even just a single sample of something, just to see how the air fryer behaves before I try making a full-sized batch.

Drop the temperature by 25°:Because the extra air power creates additional heat and browning, a good rule of thumb is to set the air fryer 25° lower than you would a conventional oven. This ensures that the baked goods don’t brown too heavily on the outside before the inside is baked.

Decrease the time by 25%:Even with the decreased temperatures, air fryers tend to bake faster than a conventional oven. Specifics will vary by recipe, but in general, you can expect to decrease the time by about 25%.

Make ahead & storage:These donut holes are best on the day they’re made, but if you have leftovers, they can be stored in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. The cinnamon sugar mixture will dissolve and sort of melt into the donuts over time, but they’ll still taste great.

#5. These are the Best Hybrid Pans for Home Cooks, Tested for Performance and Durability

Tested by Katie Bandurski, Nicole Doster and Marisa Hillman

We tested all the combo clad pans we could get our hands on to find the best hybrid cookware for every home chef.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Stainless steel, nonstick, ceramic, cast iron—these days, you can find dozens of different materials by simply walking down the cookware aisle. But the best hybrid cookware is something entirely different. Instead of settling for a single material, this type combines the best traits of all these options into a single pan.

According to cookware expert Alycia Johnson, Vice President of Merchandising at Sur La Table, this Frankenstein-ed result is the main reason hybrid cookware is so popular. She likens hybrid cookware to a cronut, in that it combines two things to create something even better.

“Hybrid cookware combines the benefits of multiple cookware materials and technologies in a single pan,” says Alycia. “It most often combines the durability and cooking performance of stainless steel with the convenience of a nonstick cooking surface. The result is cookware designed to offer the versatility of stainless steel while making everyday cooking and cleanup easier.”

While hybrid cookware is relatively new to the cookware scene, its usefulness is undeniable. From Gordon Ramsey’s recommendations to budget-friendly finds, our team at Taste of Home just had to see which options make up the best hybrid cookware. After trying eight popular brands, here’s what we found.

As the original hybrid cookware brand, it’s no surprise that our pick for the overall best hybrid pan is none other than HexClad. This Gordon Ramsay-backed cookware claims to combine the best parts of stainless steel, cast iron and nonstick pans all in one. And, according to testing data from three different editors, it delivers on this promise—and has been for years.

While we love the orignal HexClad pan, that’s not all the brand has to offer. In fact, Deputy Editor Katie Bandurski has spent the past two years reviewing HexClad gear ranging from pans to pots to knives. “I first tried the Dutch oven and was instantly hooked,” she explains. “Then I ordered a three-piece skillet set, which is now my go-to cookware. I love that I can pull out my stainless steel turner and not have to worry about nicking the coating like I do with ceramic.”

While pricey, we find that it’s worth the splurge—especially with HexClad’s generous lifetime warranty. It’s also the most heat-resistant option we’ve tried with a temperature rating of up to 900ºF. HexClad pans heat evenly, remain nonstick through years of use and can perform almost any cooking task you throw at them.

In our full HexClad cookware review, Katie details her experience using the pans over the course of several years. As of June 2026, she notes that most of her skillets have held up like a dream, with only the small one developing a noticeable scratch in the coating.

“They still perform beautifully for nonstick searing and high-heat cooking. Maintenance has been pretty simple, too. Occasionally, I need to scrub off some burnt-on marks with coarse salt, but it lifts away very easily,” she raves. “I’m still so pleased with this purchase and the pans’ longevity. I tell all my friends/family who are getting married to add HexClad to their registry!”

Size(s) Available: 7, 8, 10, 12 and 14 inches| Lid Included: No | Oven Safe: Up to 900ºF | Metal Utensil-Friendly: Yes | Features: Aluminum core, diamond dust-infused nonstick coating, patented

GreenPan is one of our favorite kitchenware brands. Over the years, we’ve tried several top sellers from the brand’s myriad cookware and appliance categories. While some of our favorite picks include a handsome  ice cream maker and a hosting-friendly raclette grill, GreenPan’s Spectra hybrid cookware line might just be our favorite of all the brand’s offerings.

In our full review, we cover the ins and outs of these hybrid pans. Much like HexClad kitchenware, they are resistant to high heat and come with a slick, PFAS-free nonstick coating. The rivetless interior is also a huge bonus, as it prevents gunky buildup. Where these pans really shine in comparison to the rest, though, is their luxe look. The polished stainless steel exterior and raised star-shaped pattern looks ultra-professional.

“So far, I’ve been impressed with how quickly the pans heat up and how effortlessly food slides off,” says tester Nicole Doster. “Cleanup is quick and easy, too. Plus, the stainless steel finish looks luxe on my stovetop.”

While we haven’t yet put GreenPan’s Spectra line through the same paces as HexClad, we’ve tested the brand’s ceramic cookware extensively at Taste of Home. In fact, after testing over 17 brands, we rated the GreenPan Valencia pan as our top pick for the best ceramic cookware. So far, we’re just as impressed with this set, especially given that it uses the same Thermolon 9G nonstick technology as GreenPan’s ceramic cookware.

Size(s) Available: 8 and 10 inch | Lid Included: No | Oven Safe: Up to 850ºF | Metal Utensil-Friendly: Yes | Features: Thermolon 9G nonstick ceramic technology, 3-ply stainless steel, aluminum core

Made with non-toxic ceramic covered by a stainless steel grid, the OXO hybrid frying pan is ideal for searing, braising and sauteing. While HexClad is still our top pick for longevity seeing as we have yet to test this version longterm, the early results indicate a similarly impressive performance.

Like similar options, it features a hybrid construction with a nonstick surface and a stainless steel grid pattern. The exterior is composed of a solid stainless steel layer, which helps the pan heat evenly. While OXO uses non-toxic ceramic as its nonstick layer, this particular coating is diamond-infused and safe for use with metal utensils.

In our review, I detail its performance as I work my way through a breakfast plate. My egg cooked quickly and efficiently, even getting a layer of crispy lacy goodness on the edges. Flipping it was surprisingly simple, too. A quick turn with my nylon spatula was all it took to release the egg. There was nary a speck of egg white stuck anywhere. It also produced some of the crispiest hash browns I’ve ever enjoyed!

While it’s still a bit pricey, it’s also nearly half the price of our top pick, making it a solid mid-price option for folks who want to try out their first hybrid pan. Plus, unlike our budget option, this one is oven-safe up to 850ºF!

Size(s) Available: 8, 10 and 12 inch | Lid Included: No | Oven Safe: Up to 850ºF | Metal Utensil-Friendly: Yes | Features: Pouring rim, aluminum core, dishwasher safe

Folks on the hunt of a budget hybrid pan should look no further than Walmart. The Beautiful by Drew Barrymore hybrid pan offers comparable performance to the pricier pans on this list, but at less than $30. For those wanting to try out their first hybrid pan, that’s a total steal. Plus, it comes with a lid!

“I was surprised by how well this pan worked given its low price point,” says tester Marisa Hillman. “If I were to stock a rental home, I’d buy a set of Beautiful by Drew cookware. It’s incredibly affordable and I’m really impressed by the quality. It heats up quickly, cooks evenly and is very easy to clean.”

While we were overall impressed by this inexpensive pan’s performance, it’s worth noting that it offers the lowest heat resistance of all the options we tested. While most of the combo clad pans we tried were oven-safe up to at least 850ºF, this one can’t handle more than 500ºF (or 350ºF if you’re using the lid).

Additionally, this is one of the smaller options we tested at only 10 inches. Unfortunately, the brand has yet to release any additional sizes, though we’re hoping that changes. That said, for the price point, we’re willing to overlook these marks against it thanks to its overall performance.

“When I cook, I’m generally cooking for six people in a much larger pan,” says Marisa. “This was perfect for eggs and pancakes for one. If I was just cooking for myself or myself plus one, I’d definitely break it out on a regular basis!”

Size(s) Available: 10 inch | Lid Included: Yes | Oven Safe: Up to 500ºF (or 350ºF for the lid) | Metal Utensil-Friendly: Yes | Features: Gold accents, dishwasher-safe

Hunting down a new set of pans, but don’t want to fuss with stainless steel or nonstick? This pair of Circulon hybrid pans offers the best of both worlds: a solid sear and easy cleanup, no sticking or questionable coatings required!

“As someone who struggles cooking on stainless steel, this hybrid pan is a great way to get the best of both worlds: tough and long-lasting like stainless but easy to cook on like nonstick,” says tester Amanda Oliver. While we wish this pair of pans offered a higher temperature resistance—they’re only oven-friendly up to 500ºF—we still found the performance impressive at such a low price point.

Amanda also notes that this might be her new favorite set of pans. Both perform better than the T-Fal nonstick pans she’s used to. So far, everything she has made has cooked evenly and easily with little to no sticking. As someone who wishes she could use stainless but finds it difficult, this pair of pans made a big impression!

“I thoroughly enjoyed cooking with this pan. Even with scrambled eggs—which I usually have issues with egg pieces sticking to pans or uneven browning—the food cooked evenly and quickly,” raves Amanda. “It required little effort on my part to get good results.”

For the price, we’re incredibly happy with the pans’ performance. Plus, you get two for the price of one, making this a good option for a full kitchen upgrade. That said, these pans aren’t available as singles. If you prefer having only one pan on hand, we recommend grabbing one of the other options.

Size(s) Available: 8 and 10.25 inch | Lid Included: No | Oven Safe: Up to 500ºF | Metal Utensil-Friendly: Yes | Features: Circular hybrid pattern, two pans included, brushed stainless steel exterior

While we love that our top budget pick comes with a lid, it also has a few drawbacks that come hand-in-hand with a lower price point. That’s why we advise anyone who wants to grab something comparable—albeit a bit more robust—to snag the Zwilling Peak hybrid frying pan. Not only does this top-tier pick come with a clear lid for added versatility, but it’s also impressively heat-resistant and slick.

“I still love my cast iron, but it’s heavy and takes a little work to maintain that nonstick surface,” says tester and home cook Paul Rankin. “The Zwilling gives me excellent food release right away, without the extra steps.”

While the nonstick properties are the main attraction, the included lid is the true star of the show. It fits securely, and the glass makes it easy to check progress without opening the pan. And, most importantly, the pan performs a lot like stainless steel, without the added stress during cleanup.

“I tried my best to make something stick to this pan, and I couldn’t,” raves Paul. “Fried eggs, steak and chicken all released incredibly easily, yet I was still able to get a great sear.”

The deeper-than-average sides ended up being especially useful. They make the skillet feel almost like a cross between a traditional frying pan and a shallow sauté pan, so it’s useful for more than simply frying eggs or searing meat. Paul comfortably used it for larger, saucier dishes such as pasta and risotto as well.

“The deeper sides were an unexpected bonus. There’s enough room to move beyond eggs and steaks and comfortably cook bulkier dishes like pasta or risotto,“ he says. “Cleanup was almost laughably easy. Even after searing meat, everything basically slid off the cooking surface with a quick wipe.”

Size(s) Available: 8, 9.5, 10, 12 inches | Lid Included: Yes | Oven Safe: Up to 500ºF | Metal Utensil-Friendly: Yes | Features: Deep sides, clear tempered glass lid

According to cookware expert Alycia Johnson, Vice President of Merchandising at Sur La Table, hybrid cookware makes up a unique category of cookware in that the materials differ from pan to pan. Typically, hybrid pans combine a nonstick material such as ceramic with stainless steel ridges. This offers many of the benefits of both stainless steel and nonstick cookware in one singular pan.

“Hybrid cookware gets its performance from a combination of materials and surface design,” says Alycia. “Many pans feature a textured cooking surface with raised stainless steel elements and recessed areas containing a nonstick coating. The stainless-steel helps create a durable cooking surface, while the nonstick components help release food more easily.”

She notes that depending on the pan’s construction, additional layers of conductive materials such as aluminum help distribute heat evenly.

“Together, these features allow home cooks to tackle a variety of techniques, from browning proteins and sautéing vegetables to preparing delicate foods that might stick to traditional stainless steel,” she says. “It brings together the best of two worlds so you can sear your proteins to a beautiful golden brown and slide a delicate omelet right onto the plate without a hitch. No compromise required.”

Overall, the biggest benefit of a hybrid pan is versatility. Alycia explains that hybrid cookware bridges the gap between traditional stainless steel and nonstick. It offers a more forgiving cooking surface without sacrificing the ability to achieve a good sear. As a bonus, a single hybrid pan can often handle a wide range of everyday tasks.

“Depending on the construction and coating, durability and easier cleanup can be added advantages,” she says. “For home cooks who want cookware that performs well across daily cooking needs, hybrid cookware can be a smart investment that delivers both searing power and nonstick performance.”

To find the right cookware for you, Alycia advises that you consider what you cook most often. If you frequently sear meats, look for cookware designed to withstand higher-heat cooking and provide higher heat retention. For folks who cook a lot of eggs, fish, or other delicate foods, the type and quality of the nonstick surface is extra important.

“Shoppers should also consider compatibility with your stovetop, whether it is oven-safe, and what temperatures it can withstand. Understanding how to clean and maintain the pan will help extend its performance and lifespan,” she explains. “Look for hybrid cookware with sturdy construction, high-quality materials and a trusted nonstick coating. A good pan should feel solid but not too heavy, heat evenly and have a comfortable, secure handle.”

Ultimately, the best hybrid cookware should strike a balance. It should offer the durability and performance of stainless steel, plus the ease and convenience of nonstick.

Alycia notes that hybrid cookware is a versatile addition to your kitchen rather than a replacement for every pan. Therefore, we chose to focus testing on hybrid cookware’s purported strengths. To do this, we created a testing criteria based closely on our tests for nonstick, ceramic and stainless steel cookware.

Tests centered on several cooking tasks, including browning, searing, deglazing, tossing stir fries and, of course, making eggs. Our testers used the pans over the course of two months in their day-to-day cooking tasks. We also consulted cookware expert Alycia Johnson to get her take on the most important features to look for.

“While [hybrid cookware] offers benefits from both stainless steel and nonstick cookware, understanding its capabilities and limitations is key to getting the most out of it,” says Alycia.

She also notes that the best way to use hybrid pans is to first read your cookware manual. To ensure we gathered accurate data, we treated the pans based on each manufacturer’s included instructions. This is especially important when it comes to heat levels, utensils, and cleaning methods.

Hybrid cookware usually combines a nonstick material like ceramic with raised stainless steel ridges. This creates a pan that is durable, nonstick, typically safe for metal utensils and offers amazing searing power.

Unlike other types of cookware, “hybrid cookware” is a term that encompasses several different materials and constructions. cookware expert Alycia Johnson notes that the term “hybrid cookware” covers a lot of different options. When shopping, it’s important to look beyond the term “hybrid.” Instead, pay attention to the specific materials, construction and coating used. This will be different from pan-to-pan.

Some hybrid pans will have you lightly season the pan with olive oil or another type of fat. This will depend on the materials used, so be sure to read your product manual prior to use. Some, like HexClad pans, suggest seasoning the pan once when you receive it. You’ll also want to do this anytime you do a deep clean.

To date, our team at Taste of Home has tried hundreds of products in the kitchen, home and lifestyle space. Our cookware experience spans everything from new releases to reputable ceramic cookware brands like Caraway, GreenPan, Alva and more. To find the best hybrid pans for every home cook, we tried out nine different options in our own homes. We put them through the paces by searing, steaming and sautéing over the course of several months. After all that testing, only seven of them stood up to our rigorous standards.

#6. Where Chef Eric Sze Eats on His Day Off in NYC

Award-winning Taiwanese chef Eric Sze takes Eater on a food tour of NYC

Chef Eric Sze, the owner of NYC’s Wenwen, shows us the bakeries, pizzerias, and restaurants he visits weekly for everything from simple baguette sandwiches to oversized wontons.

Sze starts his day off with a sandwich at Bakeri; his go-to order is honey, apple, and brie layered on a crunchy baguette. Then he heads to The Meat Hook, Wenwen’s meat supplier, to get a specialty cut of steak and dry-aged short ribs for dinner. Next, he grabs a whole, crispy, NY-style pie at Chrissy’s Pizza (chef Chris Hansell has been perfecting this pie for years). The jalapeño and garlic pie has perfect proportions of each ingredient, all on a doughy, yeasted crust.

For his final stop, Sze goes to Maxi’s Noodle 2 in Flushing for the nostalgic Chinese food he’s craved since leaving Taiwan. Owner Maxi Lau-O’Keefe teaches him how to make her iconic wontons, filled with shrimp and pork before being expertly folded. After being humbled by the complex folding process, Sze settles in for a soup full of thin noodles made with duck eggs and those classic wontons, alongside beef soup.

Watch the most recent episode of Chef’s Day Off to see how chef Eric Sze spends his day off at his favorite restaurants, bakeries, and butcher shops around New York City.

#7. Victoria Beckham’s Second Gap Collection Is Full of Posh Cold-Weather Essentials

The drop includes high-rise jeans, merino turtlenecks, and car coats designed to last.

Victoria Beckham is considered the ultimate It Brit by many, but she clearly has a soft spot for the All-American wares at Gap. Following her sold-out debut capsule with the brand, the duo is back for round two: a fall/winter 2026 collection full of transitional and cold-weather must-haves, imbued with the designer’s posh spirit.

“With this second collection, we wanted to build on the foundations of our first capsule, exploring new ways to bring our two distinct design identities together,” Beckham tells ELLE exclusively.

After setting the stage with “wardrobe building blocks” in the first drop, Beckham’s latest offering continues that ethos with new additions, both in color and cut. In true Beckham fashion, the color palette is equally as muted as the debut and draws its deep burgundy and butter yellow hues from works in the Doris and Donald Fisher Collection at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art.

Highlights of the collection are prime for layering season: high-rise straight-leg jeans, merino turtlenecks, and wool-cashmere three-quarter zip-ups. Naturally, there’s a substantial outerwear offering, too, including oversize parkas and satin bombers, latch-collar denim jackets, and a particularly elevated wool-blend Chesterfield coat. Perfect for wearing under those heftier pieces are the CashSoft pullovers, Gap’s wallet-friendly alternative to cashmere.

“Working with Gap has felt like such a natural partnership because we share a belief in creating timeless, considered pieces designed to last,” Beckham said. “Gap has an iconic place in American fashion, with a rich heritage of creating wardrobe essentials, and it has been a real honor to bring my own design perspective to that legacy.”

Gap x Victoria Beckham will be available to shop on gap.com and in select Gap stores globally starting October 23.

#8. Kate Berlant Is Very Serious About Being Ridiculous

The comedian and actress talks to Bazaar about doing stand-up in her teens, John Early, and her new HBO comedy special, Parmesan

Kate Berlant stumbled into her first stand-up routine during her ninth-grade play. Having forgotten the lyrics to a song—which, she admits, she had never memorized—she came up with a solution: improvise a series of gestures through the entire song instead of singing a word. “It was improvised, and it killed,” Berlant tells me from her home studio in Los Angeles. “That was my first time doing something that felt like stand-up, but I’ve been the class clown forever.”

The routine could have come straight out of one of her zany stand-up specials or on-screen performances. Berlant, 39, brings a natural theatricality to her comedy, often spiraling into improvisational digressions and dispensing with the traditional punch line. Her absurdist style gained a following at comedy clubs in the 2010s, leading to her first special, Cinnamon in the Wind, an almost entirely off-the-cuff performance filmed in 2019 and released in 2022. That same year, Berlant teamed up with her longtime friend John Early to produce the sketch-comedy hour Would It Kill You to Laugh?, where the two comedians play fictionalized, famous versions of themselves. In 2022, she staged a one-woman, meta-fictional, absurd comedy show, KATE, at the Connelly Theater. This year, she starred in Early’s campy full-length melodrama film Maddie’s Secret. Her second stand-up special, Parmesan, out October 19, takes a more deliberate approach. Filmed at Los Angeles’s Plaza Nightclub, the almost entirely scripted monologue reflects on stand-up comedy itself, the end of the world, coming out to her father, and her overwhelming (and relatable) addiction to her phone.

“You are humiliated [to join in on] the structure of social media,” she jokes. “And then you realize, ‘Oh, this is just what the world is now.’ ” Berlant gives her screen time a lot of thought in her special because, like the rest of us, she can’t stop scrolling through the endless reels. Only recently, she says, has she allowed herself to post clips of her stand-up, despite how vulnerable it makes her feel. On my call with Berlant this month, she tells me she just ended a six-week social-media cleanse, an attempt to find some peace of mind away from the feed. When asked what she’d been doing instead, she says: “I’m on the RealReal!” More earnestly, she adds, “You look out a window, you stare at the wall, and it’s incredible.” Like any of us, Berlant is grappling with screen time and its horrors.

“There is no balance,” Berlant insists. “Carl Jung talked about how balance is not achievable and not a goal to strive for. It’s not possible! I go on these social-media cleanses, as I call them. I think, ‘I’m not returning again. I’m done!’ I really believe it. Now, I’ve relapsed so hard. I thought, when the special comes out, I’m not going to read the comments, and I’m not going to engage. How embarrassing! I’m going to be, as I say in the special, tied off on my couch, [mainlining social media] just directly into the veins!”

Phones and social media come up several times on our call, but Berlant is grateful to have grown up—and started doing comedy—before they took over our lives. “Live performance was the only thing that mattered,” she says. “The only thing that mattered was, can you go up on stage and make people laugh?”

An only child, Berlant entertained herself by filming pretend talk shows in her bedroom. By 17, she was performing stand-up at her high school, the Archer School for Girls in Los Angeles. At the time, she was obsessed with “the guys,” as she calls them: Steve Martin and (“Cover your ears,” she interjects) Woody Allen. Her then-boyfriend burned the Stella Shorts—the comedy series by Michael Showalter, Michael Ian Black, and David Wain—onto a DVD that she carried like a talisman until she lost it in a cab many years later. Before graduating, she was sneaking into the Laugh Factory to perform sets.

Berlant moved to New York to attend Bard College, then transferred after her freshman year to New York University, where she earned bachelor’s and master’s degrees in performing arts. But her real education took place in front of small audiences across the city, where she spent years honing her theatrical, absurdist brand of comedy at open mics.

“I was the most hungry and pounding the pavement and sacrificing myself on the altar of comedy,” Berlant says. “For years, I did so many shows every week, taking the subway to do as many as I could in a night and doing horrific shows in the basement of Maui Taco in Times Square for six people in folding chairs.”

Two encounters encouraged Berlant early on. While living in New York, she often returned to Los Angeles to perform. On one visit, she ended up on a bill with Sarah Silverman at Upright Citizens Brigade. “She was aware that it was a big deal for me to be on a bill with her, even just like a little $5 show, and she watched my set and was really complimentary,” Berlant recalls. Soon after, she shared a bill with Maria Bamford at What’s Up, Tiger Lily?, a long-running underground stand-up comedy show at Gower Gulch. After seeing Berlant’s set, Bamford wrote down her own address and invited Berlant to a small party there.

Still, Berlant remembers those first years as being driven almost exclusively by her personal desire to succeed on stage, with little community within the industry. “I did it alone,” she says. “I was a lone wolf. I was friends with a lot of people and friendly with a lot of comedians, but there wasn’t somebody I was, like, going to shows with. I was doing it entirely alone.”

That changed when she met John Early at a comedy show in 2012, and he subsequently messaged her on Facebook. Soon after, they collaborated on “Family Dinner,” a bizarre eight-minute sketch in which they played suburban parents, casting three children to complete the happy family.

“John and I, when we met, had this uncanny shared language,” Berlant says. “Even though we had such radically different upbringings and our families are so different, and there’s so much difference between us, we had such a shared language.”

The two have been creatively inseparable ever since, sharing a thorny sense of humor and an uncanny physicality. In 2017, they released 555, a five-part Vimeo series taking aim at fame and Hollywood. And after countless stage performances together, the two dropped the absurd sketch special Would It Kill You to Laugh?, earning a Primetime Emmy Award nomination for Outstanding Writing for a Variety Special.

In Maddie’s Secret, Early’s hysterical, Sirkian feature debut about a food influencer with an eating disorder, Early plays the titular character in drag, while Berlant plays her obsessive best friend, Deena Michaels. From the get-go, Berlant felt everything click. “The first thing we shot was me and John in the break room with the towels over our shoulders, and Showgirls was the primary reference, and I thought, ‘This IS Showgirls. We are moving like that.’ ” This role—one of Berlant’s six on-screen appearances in 2026—only affirmed Berlant’s true ambition.

“The goal is to be an actress,” Berlant says. “I don’t want to be a touring comedian who sometimes pops into the frame. I want Sandra Hüller’s career. I want Olivia Colman’s career. I want to be Jesse Plemons. I want to be up for whatever Jesse Plemons is up for. I don’t know why I’m pulling him off the top. I should pull Sandra. One of the most aspirational performances in films for me is Toni Erdmann [starring Hüller]; being able to pull off anything that approaches that movie would be an accomplishment.”

Parmesan is the “most conventional stand-up that I’ve ever done,” Berlant says. She wrote almost all the material ahead of time in a black notebook she brings onstage, openly consulting it and flipping through its pages throughout the show. This gives the show a diaristic quality, fitting for someone who has kept a journal since she was five. It also provides a framework for her digressions, allowing her to dip into personal musings about everything from the moon to polyamory.

“It allowed me to go into these non sequiturs and the chaotic style,” she says. “It was a reminder to myself that it didn’t have to be done or perfect, or I could still bring [something new] on stage.… The notebook kept me tied to this idea: You can cross anything out, you can add anything; this is alive, this is moving, this is changing, and it will change. There was a genuine mania to my stage persona generally. I thought it was chaotic and frenetic and fast moving and propulsive.”

Berlant plays with the line between performer and persona in her comedy. Throughout Parmesan, Berlant oscillates between personal anecdotes and theatrical asides. She discusses her father’s Alzheimer’s and repeatedly coming out to him as queer, then shifts into physical comedy, whether in a theatrical skit or flipping frantically through the notebook. Even the ending becomes an opportunity to test the conventions of stand-up: After discussing her distaste for a closer, she forgoes a final punchline and stays on stage, watching the audience file out of the theater.

“I typically have a lot of trouble leaving the stage,” she says. “I think why sometimes it feels hard to post on Instagram is it’s hard to just humiliate yourself into the predetermined structure of how things go. Jerome Hagai, one of my oldest best friends, came to the show and was like, ‘You need a big closer.’ Then, a couple of days later, I tried staying on stage, and it made me laugh. I loved how it looked. I thought it looked so ridiculous. It was a final joke and a visual joke. And it was sweet. People were so delighted. It was really cute to me.”

Ironically, the special takes its title from an Instagram joke. Berlant recalls finding a pasta recipe whose creator asked people to type “Parmesan” to get the full instructions. In the special, she describes her embarrassment at seeing friends and acquaintances so publicly chomping at the bit to get the recipe (“Have some social-media hygiene,” she quips) before admitting that she, too, left a comment. Then, clear as day, she saw Succession’s Sarah Snook comment for the recipe: “Even she’s in hell!”

#9. I Tried Gap x Victoria Beckham’s New Collection, and It’s About to Take Over My Fall and Winter Wardrobe

Shopping for a new season is my weakness, but fall shopping? Now that’s a different story. Maybe I’m biased (ahem, I do live in New York City), but fall is hands down the chicest season of the four. The wool, the cashmere, the coats—I’m already putting outfits together in my head. And don’t even get me started on the excuse to stock up on cozy sweaters, luxe knits, layering pieces, and great denim. Right on cue, Gap and Victoria Beckham are back with their much-anticipated Fall/Winter 2026 collaboration, and let’s just say, it’s right up my alley (and I have a feeling you’ll love it, too).

Their first collaboration this spring sold out in a flash, so expectations are high for round two. The 37-piece collection puts a high-fashion spin on everyday staples, with elevated details across everything from bomber jackets and parkas to zip-up sweaters, trouser shorts, cargo pants, and more. I love that the designs are understated but still have personality. They have that cool, slightly dressed-up look I always associate with London style—which feels pretty fitting!

Gap invited me to preview and try on the collection ahead of its launch, so I got to handpick a few pieces to put to the test. I went with the Denim Shirt Jacket, Merino Turtleneck Sweaters, Oversized Parka Jacket, Oversized Satin Bomber Jacket, and Wool-Cashmere Zip Sweater. Safe to say, my cold-weather wardrobe is off to a good start! Everything fit so well, too.

For reference, I’m an XS and usually shop petite sizing as a 4’11” gal, but even the oversized styles felt roomy without swallowing me whole and left plenty of space for layering. The tops and sweaters felt luxe and buttery-soft, while the bomber and parka were warm and well-insulated without feeling too bulky. The only bummer? The new jeans weren’t available in petite sizing, so I couldn’t try those on. Keep scrolling to see how everything looked on me.

As you can see, everything feels tailored without being too structured, with a cool, sophisticated feel throughout. Think high necklines (funnel necks are having a moment!) and cinched waists that give each piece a little extra shape. The color palette is also so good, with all the fall neutrals we know and love mixed with pops of color like yellow and burgundy that fit right in.

Honestly, I’d buy everything I picked out—which probably isn’t the best news for my bank account! But you can really feel the quality in the materials, and I love that the collection delivers a luxury feel at a range of price points, from $28 to $368. #10. Adrian Danchig-Waring Bid Farewell to New York City Ballet With a Post-Show Rave

How do you measure a storied ballet career? You can look at time spent in the ranks, shaped by rigorous training and its corresponding toll on the body. Or repertoire: the historic roles a dancer has come to define in their own way, along with the new commissions they’ve breathed into being. You can consider the reverberation of influence, both on younger dancers and the company itself. And then there’s an energetic quality, at times radiating light and other times shining it—with or without pulsing strobes—on others.

All of these facets were front of mind on Sunday when the New York City Ballet principal Adrian Danchig-Waring took his final bow with the company, beside a heap of ribbon-tied white roses. Ever since the California native moved into the dorms at the School of American Ballet, its sister institution, in 2001, and joined NYCB two years later, he has been a quietly majestic interpreter of George Balanchine’s canon. Along the way, Danchig-Waring has been equally engaged with today’s dancemakers, both in the studio and in his role as the artistic director of the New York Choreographic Institute.

To sign off, Danchig-Waring didn’t just curate a matinee program with needle-moving classics alongside 21st-century works that reflect his love of process. Rather, fitting for an artist with an expansive sense of the medium’s possibilities, he also gathered his friends for a post-show tropical rave at Performance Space in the East Village. The double whammy meant the usually subdued attire inside the Lincoln Center theater was peppered with disco brights (the comedian-poet Alok Vaid-Menon), buttercream suiting (the playwright Jeremy O. Harris), and Carmen Miranda-esque fruit appliqués (the filmmaker and producer Drew Denny).

“Dancing for me has never been about the solo—it’s about the collective experience of bringing these works to life,” Danchig-Waring said ahead of the show, referring to the four pieces he chose for Sunday’s send-off. The bookends were two of Balanchine’s Black and White ballets—The Four Temperaments (1946) and Agon (1957)—with their pioneering pelvis tilts and flexed wrists, made all the more legible in stripped-back leotards and tights. “These are dances that resonate with me on a cellular level,” he said. “I feel simultaneously at ease inside of their complexity and totally electrified.” He danced the cool-headed Phlegmatic variation in Four Ts and delivered a crystalline pas de deux with Unity Phelan in Agon, to effusive applause. He also singled out two dancers making their debuts in Sunday’s Agon: the soloists Dominika Afanasenkov and David Gabriel. “As I’m stepping off that stage, I want to witness people who are just arriving. I want to roll out the red carpet for them.”

The middle two dances represented the flipside of Danchig-Waring’s identity, as a collaborator alongside choreographers in the present moment. One was Lar Lubovitch’s duet Each in Their Own Time, originally created with Danchig-Waring and Joseph Gordon as part of a 2021 Fall for Dance festival commission, and later added to the NYCB rep with fellow principal Taylor Stanley joining Danchig-Waring. On Sunday, the two men slipped back into their blousy white shirts and pants, taking turns in limpid call-and-response solos before reuniting in a series of looped-arm gestures.

The other piece, Once With You, was a gift from the choreographer Pam Tanowitz: a new quartet for Danchig-Waring alongside Phelan, Mira Nadon, and Indiana Woodward. “He didn’t want it to be a solo—he wanted to be dancing with friends, which was great because choreographically that’s much more interesting to me,” said Tanowitz, whose work is in dialogue with seminal figures like Balanchine and Merce Cunningham. Danchig-Waring is attuned to her layered process, describing how she has a “series of tools that move ideas—musical, spatial, architectural, mathematical, or intellectual—into the body,” he said.

The costume-design duo Reid & Harriet, known for their longtime partnership with Tanowitz, worked their usual magic. The women wore maroon unitards with subtle puffed sleeves, while Danchig-Waring’s tank unitard featured two faces in profile, each hugging a side of his waist. “It’s me and Pam—isn’t that cute?” the dancer said of the electric blue silhouettes, which even illustrated a wisp of her messy low bun. The wraparound effect reminded him of the knit back warmer he wears in rehearsal—a nod to the cataclysmic spinal injury he suffered in late 2024 before returning to the stage last fall.

The kind of dancer who arranges his swan song with such care—down to the specially requested black-and-white confetti and the prop lute from Balanchine’s Apollo, which Danchig-Waring’s husband, the art adviser Thomas Rom, brought onstage as a parting salute—would naturally take the same approach to the after-party. “I can find ecstasy in this type of dance on the stage,” Danchig-Waring said of the uptown performance, “but the true ecstatic is in the club.” Hence the kaleidoscopic rave the couple threw for a crowd that ranged from nine-year-old nephews to silver-haired patrons.

On the fourth floor of Performance Space, where Rom serves as the board chair, the elevator opened onto an abstracted video projection of Danchig-Waring in motion. Down the hallway inside the black box theater, a light installation by Studio GUMGUM glowed like radioactive flora. The DJ Illich, stationed behind a thicket of fronds, unspooled an introductory mix of warm, ambient tracks, as guests stopped by the bar for Heavensake cocktails and the night’s signature Disco Eclipse, with mezcal and edible black glitter. On a side table lay Spanish-style fans decorated with photos of Danchig-Waring and lime green earplugs that read “Full Volume.” Later on, as a remixed “Jolene” rang out, boxes of pizza moved in, custom-stamped with the words “Final Bow Full Belly” and the leaping man of the hour.

“Adrian had this idea that usually when dancers retire at the end of the season, their bodies are aching and they’ll go to the beach,” Rom said. The couple’s schedules didn’t accommodate an immediate departure—“so we said, what if the after-party is your tropical holiday and it starts now?” Rom’s own take on their Disco Tropicalia moodboard involved one-of-a-kind pants by the Moroccan label Maison ARTC, layered Chinese and Japanese kimonos, and platform boots. Back out on the dance floor, Danchig-Waring started the night in a floral Dries Van Noten button-down, Issey Miyake tank top, and Maison ARTC pants—sewn from hand-painted French curtains, with roses and cherubs—before changing into a green silk Dries top and reflective Rick Owens shorts; two pairs of Micromega sunglasses capped off the looks. As a circle widened around Danchig-Waring grooving with his mom, the artist Matthew Placek said, “The apple doesn’t fall far!”

As for the happy throng of guests, the dress code was wide open to interpretation, from paillettes to pink marabou. Yvonne Force Villareal, the cofounder of Art Production Fund, wore a leopard-print bodysuit and headband; the curator Samantha Ozer laced up burgundy pants, while the artist Julie Mehretu stuck to classic black leather. The NYCB contingent included Taylor Stanley in a black knit tank, Unity Phelan in a triangle top and nude mesh, and Mira Nadon in a leotard plucked from the Reid & Harriet costume archives. The designers themselves, Harriet Jung and Reid Bartleme, raided their own archive, unearthing diamante-studded mesh and ombré rayon fringe, respectively. Bartleme’s top was a 2025 costume experiment for Kyle Abraham’s 2x4 that didn’t move forward, he explained, but under the strobes, it was definitely in motion.

“Adrian goes so hard on the dance floor, it only feels appropriate that he would host a disco and get everyone all dressed up in crazy, colorful outfits,” said Nadon, before heading back into the scrum. Meanwhile, Lar Lubovitch was slipping out early, with a morning flight to catch, but paused to reflect on the ceremony of the evening. “I feel very honored and humbled for Adrian to show my work on his final night of dance,” said the choreographer, whose own many-act career includes a namesake company founded in 1968, Broadway dances for Into the Woods and The Red Shoes, and a full-length Othello co-commissioned by American Ballet Theatre and San Francisco Ballet. “Adrian is a major artist, and he understands dance creation, in the sense of how to be pliable and to experiment and to find new ways to feel about dance.”

It harked back to something Danchig-Waring said earlier in the night: “It’s definitely not a retirement energy.” All the efforts that, until now, have fueled a performance-ready instrument are finding new pathways, including a yet-to-be-announced slate of New York Choreographic Institute projects. “I’m thinking of it as a rewiring,” he said, “and that energizes me.”

Gilbert Bolden III, Mira Nadon, Phil Chan

Thomas Rom, Marcella Ciacci, Adrian Danchig Waring

Yvonne Force Villareal, Slobodan Randjelovic, Christopher Cronson, Marcella Ciacci

#12. 12 Dishes and Drinks Everyone Should Try in Mexico City

Mexico City is a colossal, beautifully overwhelming metropolis and an absolute paradise for those who live to eat. Across thousands of restaurants, markets, street stalls, bakeries and fondas, food from every corner of the country converges. So deciding where (and what) to eat can feel daunting.

I’ve spent over a decade writing about Mexico’s food scene, along with popping up on TV shows to talk about it occasionally. My favorite way to navigate it all is still right here on the ground with my food tours. Sidestepping the obvious spots and encouraging travelers to go deeper into the food culture here constantly reminds me of the fascinating nature of how we chilangos eat.

To me, that means having the flexibility to move between completely different culinary worlds. We can spend lunchtime standing on a crowded sidewalk, leaning over a taco drenched in salsa and lime juice, then dress up that same evening for a multicourse dinner at a dimly lit restaurant. We’re fiercely loyal to the neighborhood places that have fed us for years and know our names, but we remain insatiably curious about the next opening or dish worth crossing town for.

That same flexibility shapes the city’s food. CDMX knows exactly how to pull tradition into modernity without losing its spirit. These 12 spots offer a taste of the city’s versatility: dishes and bites deeply rooted in history but shaped by the wonderfully chaotic, ever-evolving way we eat today.

Adolfo Prieto 1364 B, Tlacoquemecatl del Valle, Benito Juárez +52 55 5559 6358

I remember being dragged out of bed early on a weekend as a teenager to have breakfast here. Although I was still drowsy, the smell of the wood-fired stoves, the café de olla (traditional “pot coffee”) bubbling away, and sounds of the older musicians playing classic tunes on their guitars were enough to bring me around. I was fully awake by the time a plate of refried beans with scrambled eggs and a stack of warm tortillas made it to the table. It’s the kind of humble combination you’d find in almost any Mexican home. At Fonda Margarita, these eggs, which are cooked over a wood fire and enriched with lard, take on a different life. Getting here early is a requirement, as they open around 6:30 a.m. and by 10 a.m., all the food is gone.

C. Chilpancingo 35, Colonia Condesa, +52 55 5264 4976

Few breakfast menus are complete without chilaquiles. What started as a way to use up day-old tortillas is now one of the country’s quintessential breakfasts: triangles of tortillas, deep-fried until crisp, then bathed in salsa. At Chilpa in leafy Condesa, several salsas are available, from a red, tomato-based version to the bright, tangy tomatillo number, all with different spice levels. Pile on your choice of cecina, shredded chicken, or fried eggs. Crema, grated cheese, and chopped onion are standard, making it easy to order a different version every visit.

If you asked my Mexican grandma what breakfast looks like, she’d say coffee and a pan dulce—more often than not that would mean a concha. The quintessential Mexican pastry makes an appearance in virtually every bakery in town, from the most traditional versions made with a combination of lard and shortening to the tender butter-forward renditions found in most modern bakeries. At Panadería Gala, a speakeasy-style bakery, the extra-bouncy conchas get an extra layer of indulgence when topped with a white or dark chocolate ganache quenelle.

The Margarita may be known worldwide as the quintessential Mexican cocktail. Legend has it that the iconic drink was first conceived in Ensenada, Baja California, and its ties to coast and borderlands are still strong. But chilangos tend to save it for specific occasions and places such as a beach vacation, a favorite cantina, or a particular restaurant where we know they’ll make a killer one. At Despacho Margarita, the classic shaken version gets a new life, alongside spicy and frozen variations. In the slushy machine there are usually two flavors: a classic tequila and lime version and a seasonal mezcal-based one that changes monthly, with unique flavors such as nopal and shiso or raspberry and cayenne pepper.

Cantinas have long been places to gather over good food and several rounds of drinks. In these laid-back establishments, both are given equal importance. At Covadonga, a cantina without background music, generations mix at the tables, from the young and cool to sixty-somethings who come to play dominoes (available on request).

Banderas have been a popular order here from the beginning: three shot glasses lined up, one with tequila, another with lime juice, and a third with sangrita, a red-hued blend of tomato and fruit juices. Together they mimic the three colors of the Mexican flag (hence the name). They’re not meant to be knocked back but rather sipped slowly, alternating between glasses.

There’s a certain type of stand you’ll see repeatedly throughout the city centered around a large, round comal, usually fired with charcoal, with a bucket of corn masa and, more often than not, two women working side by side. Gorditas, quesadillas, and sopes are all on the menu, but the tlacoyo may be the most emblematic of central Mexico and Mexico City.

Football-shaped and stuffed with your choice of fava bean purée, requesón (a soft cheese similar to ricotta), or refried beans, tlacoyos are typically topped with cactus salad for a tangy contrast, grated queso fresco, and red or green salsa, depending on your preference. They're the kind of morning or afternoon snack you might grab during errands or before wandering into the adjacent market.

Petén 248 y, Avenida Universidad, Narvarte Poniente, Benito Juárez+52 55 5536 3060

The idea of stacking meat on a rotating spit was brought to Puebla by Lebanese immigrants. Once it reached Mexico City, it evolved into one of the city’s great late-night bites: the taco al pastor. At El Vilsito, a garage by day that moonlights as one of the city’s best taquerías, they take the pastor one step further, turning it into the most Chilango version possible by making it into a torta. A warm, lightly toasted telera gets a smear of refried beans, avocado, onion, tomato, and freshly shaved pastor, all finished with melted cheese.

Calle Versalles 113, Casa Versalles, Juárez+52 55 8568 7397

You can’t talk about Mexico City without talking about its obsession with seafood. It may seem strange for a city far from the coast, but seafood from both of Mexico’s coastlines makes its way here through the second-largest seafood market in the world (surpassed only by Tokyo’s Toyosu) before being distributed across the rest of the country.

At Taller de Ostiones, clams, barnacles, and tuna arrive three times a week by air from Baja California Sur, alongside sustainably farmed oysters. Those bivalves pair perfectly with a house-made sauce that’s rich, briny, deeply umami, and slightly spicy.

Mexico City runs on fondas and street food. These casual eateries serve homestyle food that’s quick, affordable, and feels like a warm hug. Stepping inside a fonda means being a part of a daily ritual known as comida corrida, where a meal typically unfolds in four acts: a steaming bowl of soup or broth to start, followed by your choice of rice or pasta. Next comes the main course, which at some places, like Nuevo Tehuacán, is what dictates the price of the meal; meatballs in chipotle, pork with tomatillo and purslane, and chicken in peanut sauce are classics. Everything is washed down with a pitcher of freshly made agua fresca and finished with a sweet treat like a cup of gelatin. Look around, and you’ll see schoolchildren sitting elbow to elbow with office workers all savoring the comfort of one of the city’s most democratic meals.

Mostly homemade, flan is a staple of casual Mexican cooking, but it’s one of those desserts that look deceptively simple. Getting the texture just right (silky, firm, not overly sweet) is way harder than it seems, which may be why the best versions are often found in homes. Siembra may be a temple dedicated to heirloom corn masa, tacos, and antojitos, but its flan has all the right qualifications to receive just as much attention.

Fernando Montes de Oca 89, Cuauhtémoc, Colonia Condesa+52 55 5286 1258

Ice cream parlors used to be an almost daily afternoon ritual for families and couples alike. Nevería Roxy was one of the early ones, and its 1950s-diner palate of teal and red has barely changed, even in the newer locations. Alongside the classic milk- and cream-based flavors, sundaes, floats, and banana splits, you’ll find nieves.

The word literally translates to “snow,” and the closest comparison might be a sorbet, though the texture tends to be a little coarser and the flavors typically center around seasonal fruits. Mamey, an endemic fruit, may have a short season, but Roxy keeps its nieve de mamey year-round. With a faintly nutty flavor reminiscent of baked sweet potato, it’s become a local favorite. And thanks to mamey’s lush, natural creaminess, it’s easy to forget there’s no dairy in the cup.

Avenida 5 de Mayo 39, Centro Histórico de la Ciudad+52 55 5521 1787

Stepping into Dulcería de Celaya feels more like entering a 19th-century jewelry store than a candy shop. Founded in 1874, this Centro Histórico institution still retains its original art nouveau interior, complete with French mirrors, tiled floors, and hand-carved oak cabinets, all filled with traditional sweets made in-house. Among the colorful sweet treats are candied lime skins stuffed with shredded sweetened coconut. The peel is candied and tender and, unlike fresh lime rind, is not bitter, so you can go ahead and bite into the whole thing at once.

Recommendations on where to dine, shop, and stay, wherever you’re headed next.
