#13. 11 Types of Vinegar: A Guide to Cooking With Them and More

There are an awful lot of vinegars in the world—which ones you cook with depends entirely on your favorite flavors and what you’re making. Maybe you favor red wine vinegar for the punchy tang it brings to salad dressing. Or you can’t imagine a bowl of white rice without the gentle acidity of seasoned rice vinegar running through it. Perhaps you fall asleep at night dreaming of bowls of vanilla ice cream covered in ripe summer strawberries dripping with balsamic vinegar.

Whether you’re the kind of cook who has a favorite vinegar for every occasion or simply grabs whichever bottle is closest to the stove, it pays to know what you’re working with. You can often substitute one vinegar for another, but it's worth being strategic. “Each vinegar contributes its own flavor and character rather than just adding acidity,” says Sathish Kumar, the head chef of Indienne in New York and Chicago.

So which bottles deserve a spot in your pantry? We’re breaking down 11 types of vinegar, what to use them for, and substitutions that work in a pinch.

Vinegar starts with alcohol, which bacteria convert into acetic acid. The starting ingredient—wine, apples, rice, malted barley, or sugarcane, for example—helps determine the flavor, as do the fermentation and aging processes. That's how you get everything from the crisp, fruity tang of apple cider vinegar to the rich, savory complexity of Chinese black vinegar.

There are countless varieties of vinegar; these are just the ones we reach for most often.

Apple cider vinegar starts with—you guessed it—apples. The fruit is fermented first into hard cider and then into vinegar. The result is bright, fruity, and pleasantly tart, with enough character to stand up to bold ingredients. It’s also the subject of some debatable health claims.

We like it in salad dressings, quick-pickled onions, and anything that could use a little fruitiness. It's a natural partner for pork and chicken, particularly in apple-cider braises, and its acidity cuts through the richness of cheeseburger fried rice or braised collard greens. And not for nothing, it makes a heck of a pie.

White wine vinegar is the closest everyday substitute, though Champagne vinegar or unseasoned rice vinegar can also work when you want a lighter touch.

Clear, inexpensive, and unapologetically sharp, distilled white vinegar is the pantry's most straightforward source of acidity. Made by fermenting distilled alcohol, often derived from grains, it has a relatively neutral flavor that lets other ingredients shine.

Tom Carlin, the chef of Burl in Evanston, Illinois, likes adding a dash to braises at the end of cooking. It brightens them “without changing the flavor at all,” he says. That same clean tang makes distilled white vinegar a natural choice for classic dill pickles. It’s also a great base for homemade flavored vinegars, especially those infused with chiles, herbs, or spices.

In many cooked dishes and dressings, you can substitute rice, apple cider, or white wine vinegar. Each will bring its own flavor to the party, so taste as you go.

Red wine vinegar is bold, fruity, and assertive. You can’t dress a classic Greek salad or splash oysters with mignonette without it. Like white wine vinegar, it begins with wine that undergoes a second fermentation, but the red wine base gives it a more robust fruit flavor.

Red wine vinegar brings welcome acidity to BA’s Best Gazpacho, coq au vin, a pot of hearty lentils, and rich meat marinades. If you're making a vinaigrette for a salad loaded with tomatoes, olives, or cheese, this is a good bottle to reach for.

You can use white wine or apple cider vinegar in its place, but Chicago-based Sifr culinary director Sahil Sethi favors sherry vinegar. He says its nutty, aged character gives it a depth that mirrors red wine vinegar’s body and acidity.

Fermented from white wine, white wine vinegar has a lighter, more delicate flavor than red wine vinegar. Its gently fruity acidity makes it particularly useful when you want to brighten a dish without overpowering it.

Reach for it to use in salad dressings, seafood marinades, braised chicken, brothy steamed mussels, or a buttery pan sauce like beurre blanc. Conor Dalton, head chef at Smyth in Chicago, calls white wine vinegar “the most versatile” option and likes infusing it with herbs, such as lemon verbena, to sharpen creamy sauces for shrimp and balance richer preparations.

Champagne vinegar is an especially good substitute. Sherry, apple cider, and unseasoned rice vinegars can also stand in, depending on the dish.

Light, fruity, and delicately tangy, Champagne vinegar is typically made from wines produced using the same grape varieties as Champagne, such as Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. That doesn’t mean it’s necessarily made from Champagne wine, nor does it enjoy the same strict regional protections. Its subtle fruit and floral notes give it a gentler flavor than many white wine vinegars, though it isn’t necessarily less acidic. Some producers age Champagne vinegar in barrels to develop a rounder, more complex flavor. It’s a particularly good choice when a more assertive vinegar might steal the show.

Sethi calls Champagne vinegar his favorite for salad dressing, thanks to its subtle fruitiness. Try it in a vinaigrette for tender greens, drizzled over seafood, or in a dressing for spring vegetables. It can bring a little lift to richer dishes, too, without contributing much competing flavor.

White wine vinegar, though slightly more assertive, is the most straightforward substitute. Unseasoned rice vinegar also works when a mild flavor is the primary goal.

If red wine vinegar is bright and brash, sherry vinegar is its smoother, more nuanced cousin. Made from sherry wine and aged in wooden barrels, this amber-hued vinegar develops a rounded acidity with nutty, sometimes caramel-like notes.

That complexity makes sherry vinegar especially good at finishing sauces, dressing roasted vegetables, and brightening stews. Try it in a classic leeks vinaigrette, braised chicken escabèche, or a glaze for ribeye. Dalton also likes using it to deglaze a pan or brighten a sauce at the end of cooking.

Vinagre de Jerez comes from the area around Jerez, Spain, and must age in wooden barrels for at least 6 months. It’s worth keeping a bottle around if you like a vinegar with a little more depth, but red or white wine vinegar works in many of the same applications. Malt vinegar has a more robust flavor, but can contribute some of the same woody, caramel undertones.

Dark, rich, and sweet-tart, balsamic vinegar can be a finishing touch or an essential ingredient, depending on the bottle. Traditional balsamic vinegar, made in Modena or Reggio Emilia, Italy, starts with cooked grape must (freshly crushed grape juice), and ages in wooden barrels for at least 12 years. The result is intensely concentrated, syrupy, and complex.

The balsamic vinegar you’re more likely to find at the supermarket is different. Commonly made by combining grape must with wine vinegar, it's generally thinner, tangier, and far less expensive than traditional balsamic. That’s not a bad thing: It's the kind we reach for when making balsamic dressing, roasting brussels sprouts with honey and garlic, or adding sweet-tart depth to Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta.

For a thicker finishing sauce, you can also simmer everyday balsamic into a balsamic reduction, concentrating its sweetness and acidity. Save especially good aged balsamic for drizzling over Parmesan, ripe tomatoes, or even strawberries and vanilla ice cream.

Made with grape must processed to minimize browning, white balsamic is paler, lighter, and fruitier than traditional dark balsamic. Use it to brighten a melon salad, dress roasted peppers, bring a little sweetness to a pan sauce without turning everything brown, or to make a sweet-and-tangy custard for a fruit tart.

Both varieties of balsamic are tricky to substitute because their sweetness is as important as their acidity. For dressings or cooked sauces, try sherry or apple cider vinegar with a little honey or brown sugar. It won't have the same depth, but it'll get you closer to the sweet-tart balance.

Mild, gently sweet, and endlessly versatile, rice vinegar is a staple in Japanese, Korean, Chinese, and Vietnamese cooking, among other cuisines. It's made by fermenting rice into alcohol and then vinegar, though its flavor and production vary by region.

At the grocery store, you’ll usually encounter two kinds: seasoned and unseasoned.

“Unseasoned rice vinegar has a clean, mild acidity with a subtle sweetness,” says Jae Seong Ha, head chef at Jeong Yuk Jeom restaurant in New York. That makes it a natural fit for Korean dressings, marinades, and pickled vegetables. We also like it in this Crispy Rice Salad with Spicy Tahini Dressing, tomato-basil salad, Salt and Pepper Fish, and miso-caramel glazed salmon.

Seasoned rice vinegar contains added sugar and salt, making it especially convenient for sushi rice and certain dressings.

Wondering about rice wine vinegar? “The terms ‘rice vinegar’ and ‘rice wine vinegar’ are used interchangeably,” Ha says. “When shopping, I pay more attention to the ingredient list and whether the vinegar is seasoned or unseasoned.”

To substitute unseasoned rice vinegar, try Champagne or white wine vinegar. If you need seasoned rice vinegar, start with unseasoned and add a little sugar and salt to taste. You can do the same with another mild vinegar in a pinch.

Dark, earthy, and deeply savory, black vinegar brings considerably more than acidity to a dish. There are several styles, including Chinkiang vinegar from China, but they’re generally made from fermented grains, such as rice, wheat, or sorghum.

“It has a little sweetness, a malty character, and more fermentation flavor” than milder rice vinegar, says Cheng Lin, chef-owner of Shota Omakase in Brooklyn. He likes it with dumplings, noodles, “and other dishes where you want the vinegar to have a stronger presence.”

Try black vinegar in dipping sauces for scallion pancakes, splashed into a cabbage stir-fry or Black Vinegar Chicken With Radishes, or whisked into a punchy dressing. A little goes a long way.

There’s no substitute for black vinegar's complex, distinctive flavor. If you’re in a pinch, Lin suggests combining balsamic and unseasoned rice vinegar. “It won’t be exactly the same, but it gives you some of that darker, sweeter, aged character.”

If you’ve eaten fish and chips, you’ve probably tasted malt vinegar. Made from malted barley, it can range from amber to dark brown, and has a sweet, nutty tang and a toasted flavor.

It’s hard to beat on french fries, but we'd happily splash it over roasted or steamed potatoes, or stir it into mayonnaise for dipping sweet potato wedges too. Malt vinegar can also lend depth to Sweet-and-Sour Tomato Chutney and other sauces. Reduce it with chiles and molasses for a sticky glaze for roast chicken, or use it in a tangy lamb chop marinade.

For fried foods, a squeeze of lemon will provide a similar bright finish, though not malt vinegar’s toasty flavor. Apple cider or sherry vinegar is a reasonable stand-in for sauces and glazes.

Made from fermented sugarcane juice, cane vinegar is a staple in many Filipino kitchens—and important in many other cuisines, too, but the category is broad. Sukang maasim is an all-purpose white (clear) cane vinegar, while sukang Iloko is a darker variety hailing from the country’s north, often made from clay-aged sugarcane wine (basi).

Its flavor varies by producer and region, but it generally offers a clean, sometimes subtly sweet acidity. It’s a key ingredient in Philippine adobo, often balanced with soy sauce and aromatics like black pepper and bay leaf. Kumar also points to cane vinegar’s importance in Northern Indian pickling traditions, including sirka pyaaz, tangy onions commonly served alongside kebabs. It also works well in dipping sauces or infused with chiles for a spicy, tangy condiment.

If you can't find cane vinegar, try unseasoned rice vinegar or apple cider vinegar, depending on the dish. Neither is an exact match, but both can provide the acidity you need. Coconut vinegar is another popular option in regions that favor cane vinegar, and can also work well in similar applications.

The world of vinegars is vast. Other varieties include honey vinegar, made from mead and vaguely similar to white balsamic; akazu, a beautifully layered red vinegar that comes from aged sake lees; and roasty-toasty beer vinegar, a good swap for malt vinegar.

Coconut vinegar, made from fermented coconut sap, is another versatile option, especially in Filipino and South Asian cooking. Kumar says its flavor is “distinctive and slightly funky” and that it works well in dipping sauces, marinades, and rich, savory dishes.

Unseasoned rice vinegar and Champagne vinegar are good choices when you want acidity without an overpowering flavor. White wine vinegar is another versatile option. Distilled white vinegar has a neutral flavor, but a sharpness that can make it aggressive in some dishes.

Can you substitute one type of vinegar for another?

Usually, yes. Red and white wine vinegars can often stand in for each other, though red wine vinegar has a bolder flavor. Apple cider vinegar works well in place of white wine vinegar, while unseasoned rice vinegar is a good choice when you want something milder. Balsamic and black vinegars have more distinctive flavors and are harder to replace. For home canning and shelf-stable pickling, follow a tested recipe and use vinegar with the specified acidity rather than making substitutions based on taste alone.

Which vinegar is best for salad dressing?

You know that old saying: The limit does not exist. And a simple vinaigrette is a great way to taste the nuances of a new-to-you vinegar.

That said, red wine, white wine, Champagne, and sherry vinegars are all commonly used in Western-style salad dressings. Red wine vinegar works particularly well with bold ingredients like tomatoes and olives, while Champagne and white wine vinegars complement delicate greens. Reach for sherry vinegar when you want something a little richer and nuttier.

Most commercially produced vinegars don't need refrigeration. “Vinegar is actually very easy to take care of,” Lin says. He recommends storing bottles tightly closed in a cool, dark cabinet away from sunlight and heat. Some vinegars may become cloudy or develop harmless sediment over time, but that doesn't necessarily mean they've spoiled. Homemade infused vinegars may require refrigeration.

What are the essential vinegars to keep in your pantry?

The answer depends on what you cook. One way to cover your bases is with something mild and versatile, like unseasoned rice vinegar; something fruity, like red wine or apple cider vinegar; and something distinctive, like sherry or balsamic.

But if chicken adobo is in heavy rotation, you’re going to want a steady supply of cane vinegar. Love fish and chips? Don't skip the malt. Whatever your pleasure, there’s no wrong way to take an acid trip.

#14. Lay’s Turned Thanksgiving Dinner Into Chips—And Somehow, They Actually Work

Turkey and scalloped potatoes just landed in the snack aisle.

Lay’s is betting big on America’s biggest food holiday this year. Just in time for Thanksgiving, the company is releasing new limited-edition flavors inspired by two of the dinner table’s biggest stars: turkey and potatoes.

Beginning in late October, fans can pick up Lay’s Cheddar Scalloped-Style Potatoes and Lay’s Roasted Holiday Turkey. And before you clutch your pearls over the more ambitious of those flavors, hear me out. They’re pretty damn good.

The Cheddar Scalloped-Style Potatoes chips aren’t a huge leap for Lay’s considering we’re starting with potatoes anyway. These go hard on the cheddar, while a sprinkling of parsley helps bring them surprisingly close to the dish they’re trying to emulate. They deliver that creamy, comforting flavor without being nearly as indulgent as actual scalloped potatoes. I’d call these a win.

The Roasted Holiday Turkey chips, however, had me a little uneasy. That disappeared after the first crunch. To me, they taste more like stuffing and gravy than an actual bite of turkey, but in this case, I’m not mad about it. Thyme, onion powder, and pepper come through strongest, reminding me of the sides that usually share the plate with the bird.

And Lay’s isn’t stopping there. On November 8, the brand is bringing Canadian favorite Maple Bacon to the U.S. for the first time. In fact, it’s shaping up to be a very Lay-tastic holiday season, as in late November, it’s embracing its sweeter side with Lay’s Wavy Milk Chocolate and Wavy Dubai-Style Dark Chocolate. #16. The History of This Must-Try Cheese Goes Back Nearly 1,000 Years

An authentic wheel of Grana Padano carries a signature brand burned into its rind—so you know that if you see a diamond pattern and the cheese’s name, it must have been produced in the Valle Padana (Po River Valley) of Northern Italy according to strict rules with roots in a 12th-century Cistercian monastery. At the time, the region surrounding the city of Milan was primarily soggy marshland. The monks who built the monastery—Chiaravalle Abbey—were followers of the Rule of Saint Benedict, which, along with devotion to prayer, mandated that they practice agriculture with a focus on responsible, sustainable use of land. They first figured out how to turn the marshy landscape into arable fields so they could grow high-quality feed for dairy cattle. Since milk (and fresh cheese) didn’t last long, the next challenge for the monks was how to preserve this nutritious, valuable food source to nourish themselves and their community.

The method they developed—heating the milk in copper cauldrons, adding rennet (a coagulating enzyme), cutting the curds into tiny pieces, and molding, salting, and aging the cheese—remains largely unchanged today. By producing the first iteration of what is now known around the world as Grana Padano, the monks of Chiaravalle Abbey earned the distinction of operating the world’s first cheese dairy.

Easy to like, portable, and a good source of protein, the cheese became an emblematic food, enjoyed by Italians at all levels of society through the Renaissance and into the modern era. Its iconic name, meanwhile, developed over time. The monks called it “caseus vetus”—Latin for “old cheese”—but since the peasants didn’t know Latin, they referred to it as “grana” for its distinctive grainy texture. As production spread well beyond the monastery, each province had its own grana: Cheese made in Milan was “grana Milanese,” and “grana Mantovano” was from Mantua.

It wasn’t until 1954 that the Italian government codified the name Grana Padano to unite the different varieties of grana cheese under a single wider geographical indication and that the Grana Padano Protection Consortium was established. In 1996, Grana Padano was awarded the European Union’s Protected Designation of Origin (PDO) designation. Today the consortium incorporates 134 member dairies, who together produced over 6 million wheels of cheese in 2025. In addition to safeguarding the name, the organization is also responsible for the global promotion of Grana Padano PDO and governs every detail of production to ensure that each wheel meets the strict standards established under the PDO.

The specifications start with the cows’ diet: All fresh forage and at least 75 percent of dry fodder (such as hay) must be grown within the cheese production area. Raw milk must be collected within 24 hours of milking and be partially skimmed, allowing for natural separation of the cream. After a natural whey starter is introduced to the copper (or copper-lined) milk vat, calves’ rennet is added for coagulation. The cheese is then broken into rice-size curds using a spino, which resembles a large whisk, and packed into round molds, where it sits for at least 36 hours. The wheels are immersed in brine for anywhere from 14 days to a month and aged for at least nine months and up to 24 months or longer. Wheels aged over 20 months can be labeled Riserva.

Bite into a chunk of Grana Padano PDO, and you taste the sweetness of fresh milk coupled with a savory hint of toasted nuts. Riservas may be flakier and more crystalline in texture than younger versions of the cheese but never dry or crumbly, and they must still have a delicate flavor. Grana Padano PDO is an exceptionally versatile cheese, equally delicious on a cheese board, wrapped with a slice of Prosciutto di Parma PDO and drizzled with aged balsamic for a sophisticated appetizer, as a filling for ravioli, or grated over soup or pasta.

It’s good for you, too. Lactose- and gluten-free, Grana Padano PDO is low in fat and an excellent source of protein, calcium, and vitamin B12. A 30-gram piece (just over one ounce) has as much nutrition as a pint of milk, making it a beneficial as well as tasty solution to the “afternoon slump” for both kids and adults. Whoever you share Grana Padano PDO with, be sure to tell them what they have in common with Italians from more than 1,000 years ago—that they’re savoring a taste of European culinary history.

Head to DistinctlyDeliciouslyEuropean.eu to learn more about Prosciutto di Parma PDO and Grana Padano PDO.

The monks called it “caseus vetus”—Latin for “old cheese”—but since the peasants didn’t know Latin, they referred to it as “grana” for its distinctive grainy texture. As production spread well beyond the monastery, each province had its own grana: Cheese made in Milan was “grana Milanese,” and “grana Mantovano” was from Mantua.

It wasn’t until 1954 that the Italian government codified the name Grana Padano to unite the different varieties of grana cheese under a single wider geographical indication and that the Grana Padano Protection Consortium was established. In 1996, Grana Padano was awarded the European Union’s Protected Designation of Origin (PDO) designation. Today the consortium incorporates 134 member dairies, who together produced over 6 million wheels of cheese in 2025. In addition to safeguarding the name, the organization is also responsible for the global promotion of Grana Padano PDO and governs every detail of production to ensure that each wheel meets the strict standards established under the PDO.

The specifications start with the cows’ diet: All fresh forage and at least 75 percent of dry fodder (such as hay) must be grown within the cheese production area. Raw milk must be collected within 24 hours of milking and be partially skimmed, allowing for natural separation of the cream. After a natural whey starter is introduced to the copper (or copper-lined) milk vat, calves’ rennet is added for coagulation. The cheese is then broken into rice-size curds using a spino, which resembles a large whisk, and packed into round molds, where it sits for at least 36 hours. The wheels are immersed in brine for anywhere from 14 days to a month and aged for at least nine months and up to 24 months or longer. Wheels aged over 20 months can be labeled Riserva.

Bite into a chunk of Grana Padano PDO, and you taste the sweetness of fresh milk coupled with a savory hint of toasted nuts. Riservas may be flakier and more crystalline in texture than younger versions of the cheese but never dry or crumbly, and they must still have a delicate flavor. Grana Padano PDO is an exceptionally versatile cheese, equally delicious on a cheese board, wrapped with a slice of Prosciutto di Parma PDO and drizzled with aged balsamic for a sophisticated appetizer, as a filling for ravioli, or grated over soup or pasta.

It’s good for you, too. Lactose- and gluten-free, Grana Padano PDO is low in fat and an excellent source of protein, calcium, and vitamin B12. A 30-gram piece (just over one ounce) has as much nutrition as a pint of milk, making it a beneficial as well as tasty solution to the “afternoon slump” for both kids and adults. Whoever you share Grana Padano PDO with, be sure to tell them what they have in common with Italians from more than 1,000 years ago—that they’re savoring a taste of European culinary history.

Head to DistinctlyDeliciouslyEuropean.eu to learn more about Prosciutto di Parma PDO and Grana Padano PDO.

#17. The Best Gifts for Martini Lovers (Besides an Ice-Cold Martini)

From a martini lover to my brethren: 27 gifts that hit that brisk, briny spot, whether you like gin or vodka, shaken or stirred, twist or olives

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Ah, a perfectly made martini. When in the right mood, is there anything better than its bracing crispness? Then there’s the saline hit of the brine, should you take yours dirty, and the yield of an olive’s flesh between one’s teeth while your dining or drinking companion commiserates, flirts, or reveals gossip as juicy as your vodka- or gin-soaked Castelvetrano. (If you’re a twist person, respect, but we’re different.)

Sipping on an icy martini really conveys a feeling of glamour and mystery— there’s really no other cocktail that quite embodies elegance and timelessness that same way, nor that hits quite the same (did I mention they’re very strong?). No wonder a martini is the drink of choice for everyone from James Bond to Jay Gatsby to Brian Griffin from Family Guy (yeah, the dog). In fact, the martini is the second most popular drink in America after the margarita, with some bars in New York making more than 1,000 martinis each night.

Once considered an old man drink by Gen Xers and millennials, the martini’s popularity has been majorly revived in recent years, and being a martini-lover has become something of a personality trait. In my early 20s, when I discovered the appeal of the dirty martini, it quickly became my go-to drink at the San Francisco dive bars that occupied that time of my life in the late aughts — I was fine with well vodka as long as the martini was extra, extra dirty (some drinkers, as you’ve likely noticed, revel in saying “filthy” to their bartender). Nowadays, my taste is a bit more dignified and I’ll call my spirit (Tito’s, Belvedere, or Ketel One, depending on my mood) and ask for my drink with only a whisper of brine and, instead, a couple of extra olives. This is the thing about becoming a martini person: This simple drink suddenly becomes a blank slate for your micro-preferences, in the same way espresso does for coffee snobs.

Martinis are having a reawakening, no doubt, and there’s an unprecedented array of martini-centric bar gear, accoutrements, and even merch out there, from jewelry to martini-specific insulated tumblers to high-end olive brine. If you’re hunting for the best gifts for martini lovers, look no further — I’ve skipped the corny stuff and reached straight for the top shelf.

The gear you need to make a perfect homemade martini depends on that (frankly worn out) adage: shaken or stirred? The truth is that most bartenders will recommend stirred, but most people in casual bar settings are fine with shaken, and may even prefer it if they like each sip icy. If you’re making martinis at home (or know someone who likes to), a great cocktail kit sets the stage for a better drink.

This classic Williams Sonoma set is top of the line; yes, it includes everything you need for a Ritz-caliber martini, but will also come in handy for any other cocktail your recipient wishes to whip up.

For something a bit more affordable but still luxe-feeling, this stirred martini cocktail kit from Barfly comes with an etched 24-ounce mixing glass as well as copper tools that make handsome additions to a bar cart.

On the more whimsical side, this best-selling set from Mark & Graham nests into a cute boat, so it’s ornamental even when not in use. If you know anyone with a yacht, well, perfect gift for them.. and we’re not jealous at all, but maybe they should extend an invitation for us to all drink martinis on the deck.

There is an argument to be (convincingly) made that “soggy, splintered, deflated” “bottom-shelf bulk olives”actually make the best brine — the cheapo Manzanilla and Queen olives that culturally preceded the now ubiquitously trendy Castelvetrano. To be real with you, I adore all olives — the fancy newcomers and artisanal beauties but also the Mezzettas that have been living in the door of my parents’ fridge for my entire life. That being said, this is a story about gifts, and the thing about gifts is that a good one should feel a little bit special, curated, lesser-seen, harder-to-acquire, thoughtful, more premium than what you’d typically buy for yourself.

I recently became a big fan of Quincy olives; the olive-to-brine ratio is specifically formulated to make 14 dirty martinis with no waste (of fruit or liquid). The brine itself is just the right level of salty and umami; I’ve made a few friends dirty martinis with it recently and they all commented on how excellent their drinks came out. The recipe is right on the label, so it’s foolproof.

Another great brand for both brine and olives is Filthy; a friend of mine who works at a high-end Hollywood cocktail bar said that Filthy brine is the fave of both staff and customers. Filthy also makes standalone brine as well as a variety of stuffed olives; some dirty-martini-drinkers really love a blue-cheese-stuffed olive for a more creamy, complex experience, and they are a smart offering for a host gift or housewarming present.

Cocktail glasses have never been more personality-forward than in the present, with elegance, eccentricity, and whimsy all equally playing into the current renaissance of Very Interesting Glassware. Half the fun of drinking a martini is doing so from a smart, snazzy glass, whether minimalist or over-the-top decorative. I am addicted to collecting cocktail glasses and so have a half-dozen different options at home, should a guest arrive or the need for a martini strike. In recent years, restaurants and bars have begun thinking outside the box in terms of how to serve a martini; the only hard rule in my book (and that of many others) is that the glass should have a stem or at least a foot to help it stay cool as long as possible.

Here are a few special-looking martini glasses that have caught my eye recently…

Cocktail napkins and picks are truly underrated gifts — they’re small, easy to transport and store, and in that category of home goods that feels a little frivolous to buy for yourself but that is well-appreciated in ownership. I like these jeweled Joanna Buchanan cocktail picks for the martini-sipping diva in your life or the Archer stainless steel picks for a more Don Draper type.

Plutonia Blue is a New York City-based artist and jewelry designer whose sterling silver cocktail picks are dripping with iridescent keshi pearls. According to the designer, the string of pearls was first envisioned as the “the tresses of a woman dining alone (one of my favorite pastimes, how scandalous!).”

Founded by New York-based caterer Stephanie Nass, the brand Chefanie is behind these entertaining-ready olive napkins.

Another cocktail napkin I’m a bit obsessed with right now: this set of Polo Bear napkins from Ralph Lauren Home — they’re preppy (which I am decidedly not) but I appreciate that they seem self-aware. No, they aren’t emblazoned with any martini-specific imagery, but something about them does feel perfect for being the resting surface for an ice-cold Belvedere martini.

Being a martini drinker is now akin to being a huge fan of the Philadelphia Eagles or something; it no longer seems to be enough to just really like martinis. One must make it known that martinis are one’s thing. The market is abundant with ways to do so, from jewelry to hats to phone cases to sweaters.

Attention: true martini lunatics only! This section is for you.

Brümate is known for its functional, colorful water bottles, coolers, and other vessels — and for a martini-lover who needs to take one on the go (perhaps to the beach, a picnic, or the upcoming Wicker movie) and keep it chilled, there’s the MargTini, a tumbler made specifically for transporting cocktails. It has a splash-proof lid and slip-proof base, is made of double-walled steel so it doesn’t get condensation on the outside, and it keeps your drink cold for 12 hours. As one gin-drinking reviewer notes, “It even fits in the cupholder on the golf cart.”

I did a double take at the sight of this wildly lifelike handcrafted candle that uses gel wax for its doppelgänger of a frosty ‘tini, complete with extra olives. A fun accent piece that you’ll probably want to keep around instead of burn — but should you want to light it, its made with premium unscented wax.

I’m not advocating spending $565 on what’s essentially jewelry for your handbag, but I will note that if you’re, as noted above, a true martini freak, you should probably be made aware of the popular Loewe olive bag charm.

A slightly more reasonably priced option would be Chloe’s martini bag charm, although purists like myself may raise an eyebrow at the lime wheel on the side of the glass. Not a classic martini garnish; just saying!

If the trompe l’oeil candle above didn’t do it for ya because it’s unscented, I present this alternative: a candle from Rewined that “captures [a dirty martini’s] essence with the crisp, briny hint of olive and the fresh, piney aroma of juniper pays homage to the gin at the heart of this storied drink — rounded out with a touch of amber, evoking the luxurious ambiance of a high-end cocktail lounge.” Alluring! It has an 80-hour burn time for many evenings spent in the aura of a dirty martini right in your very living room.

For the martini-drinker who has it all — the cocktail picks, the carefully selected olive — we must ask: Do they have their very own signature cocktail? If not, another great gift option remains. Wonderbly will customize and print a cocktail book for your recipient of choice that includes 29 recipes for both classic and newfangled cocktails, but most importantly, its main attraction is a drink named for your friend and formulated specifically with their tastes in mind. Might we suggested a drink that includes gin or vodka, a touch of vermouth, and perhaps some olive juice? Just an idea.

#18. Cartier’s Most Coveted New Watch Invites You to Take Your Time

You’re going to want to soak up every detail

The history of the Baignoire is one of reinvention. When Cartier introduced its distinctive oval watch in 1958, the shape was already a departure from the typical round and rectangular cases of the era. Nearly seven decades later, that same silhouette remains one of the house’s most recognizable designs, endlessly inviting reinterpretation.

Over the years, Cartier has played with the Baignoire’s proportions, materials, colors, straps, and settings, continually finding new ways to make an unconventional shape feel of-the-moment. Its iterations have ranged from an 18-karat-gold style punctuated with diamond polka dots to pavé bezels contrasted with rich croc straps and monochromatic models featuring color-matched dials slipped over lithe ribbons of leather. Its oval construction and slender feel have charmed generations of fashionably zeitgeisty stars, from Lauren Bacall and Catherine Deneuve to Kendall Jenner and Elle Fanning.

The Baignoire’s latest incarnation transforms the diminutive watch into a sculptural gold cuff punctuated by the geometric peaks of Clou de Paris, a motif that has been part of Cartier’s vocabulary since the 1920s and a defining element of its Clash de Cartier collection, which combines contrasting aspects of different designs. In the new Baignoire, each geometric prism is shaped by hand to follow the elegant lines of the band and case, creating a tactile surface that catches the light from every angle. The collision between two of the house’s most recognizable signatures lends the watch a new sense of volume and dimension.

At just over 24 millimeters at its widest point, the Baignoire’s visual impact is all the more surprising. Available in solid 18-karat gold or set with round diamonds, each version brings its own touch of novelty. In the latter, the dial is punctuated by 100 brilliant-cut diamonds, while additional stones illuminate the case and cuff, amplifying the interplay between the geometric Clou de Paris surface and the sparkle of the gems.

Worn solo, the Baignoire offers a subtle infusion of texture; stacked with Clash bracelets, it takes on a more substantial presence. It is less about telling time than making a statement—a small object with an outsized ability to change the feeling of what you’re wearing, whether it’s a T-shirt and denim or a little black cocktail dress.

It’s a reminder that timelessness, in jewelry, isn’t confined to demure strings of pearls or heirloom pendants. The longevity of a motif or design often lies in its ability to evolve and find new life in different forms in different eras, which is why the Baignoire has never lost its luster and continues to shine.

#20. Why You Should Always Read the Label on Your Cleaning Spray

Until I started reviewing kitchen gear five years ago, I rarely read product manuals or user guides. I’m sure that’s due in large part to my ADHD, as my brain tends to move more quickly than step-by-step instructions allow. Plus, I like to figure things out on my own, thank you very much!

But my rogue, DIY, quick-start method hasn’t always worked out in my favor. I inadvertently killed my first Dyson stick vacuum (that I saved for months to buy) because I failed to educate myself on proper filter maintenance. And I’ve owned my car for a decade and still have no clue what a couple of the buttons actually do.

While user error can make for a funny punchline, it can also get expensive. For example, it might seem silly to read the manual for a nonstick frying pan or enameled cast-iron Dutch oven, but that’s where you’d learn that putting it in the dishwasher or using metal utensils can destroy or degrade the cooking surface.

In the case of cleaning products, the stakes can be even higher—especially in this era of, er, less restrictive food safety regulations.

Before you get to the instructions on the back of a cleaning spray bottle, you need to pay close attention to what’s on the front, because not all kitchen cleaning sprays (no, not even all all-purpose cleaning sprays) are created equally.

Though they might have some very minimal, naturally occurring disinfecting properties from ingredients like vinegar or essential oils, basic cleaning sprays like Mrs. Meyer’s and Aunt Fannie’s have one job—and that is to clean the surfaces in your kitchen. And by “clean,” I mean they contain surfactants, which help to dislodge grease and gunk so you can more easily wipe away a mess.

Mrs. Meyer’s Clean Day All-Purpose Cleaner Spray

Aunt Fannie’s All-Purpose Cleaning Vinegar Spray

But simply removing discernible debris won’t leave you with a germ-free countertop, which is why you also need a disinfectant to kill bacteria and viruses (not to be confused with a sanitizer, which only kills bacteria). And if you want to ensure your counters are so clean you could eat off of them, I recommend using both. If you spray a disinfecting solution on top of a spill, it’s not disinfecting the counter underneath the spill—it’s sanitizing the surface of whatever is stuck to your counter.

Here’s the real kicker, and the reason it’s important to read the instructions on the back of your disinfecting (or sanitizing) spray: In order for the product to kill the number of germs the label claims, it needs to sit on the surface in question for anywhere from about two to 10 minutes. This period is called the “dwell time” or “contact time,” and the product needs to remain visibly wet for however long it takes to be truly effective.

For example, Lysol's All-Purpose Cleaner (which is truly all-purpose when used properly), is a sanitizer at 10 seconds, but it only "kills 99.9% of viruses and bacteria" as the front of the label claims, if it’s left to sit for 10 minutes. The little asterisks after that claim lead you to the back label, which details the dwell time along with the common bacteria and viruses it kills.

All-Purpose Cleaner Spray, Lemon Breeze Scent, 32 oz.

“Use as directed” shows up four times in the online product description for Clorox’s Multi-Surface Disinfecting Mist, which also claims to kill 99.9% of viruses and bacteria. It even has a specific instruction for kitchens (to rinse off of any food-prep surfaces after a 10-minute dwell time).

The moral of the story? Use your cleaning products as directed, which unfortunately does require reading the fine print on the label. While you’re at it, you might want to consider replacing your microfiber cleaning cloths after a 2010 study found that microfiber becomes less effective at removing contaminants from surfaces the more it gets used.

#21. Brown Butter Banana Bread

If there's anything better than freshly baked banana bread, it's this toasty, nutty brown butter banana bread. Browning the butter gives the classic loaf an extra layer of flavor—and the scent is irresistible.

Brown butter gives our back-pocket banana bread a little more oomph in this new-fashioned recipe. Although brown butter isn’t exactly new (the French have used beurre noisette for centuries), it’s picked up within the past decade in the States. When butter melts down and cooks further, the milk solids toast and turn golden brown, deepening the flavor into something wonderfully nutty. You’ll smell it in the air as the brown butter banana bread bakes in the oven—it’s so good, you’ll want to turn it into a candle.

Baked with bananas and toasted walnuts, this version is pure heaven and totally steps up the classic banana bread recipe.

Place the cubed butter in a small heavy saucepan. Cook the butter over medium heat until it’s golden brown, 5 to 7 minutes, stirring constantly to evenly cook the milk solids. Immediately pour the butter into a bowl to stop the cooking process and to let it cool slightly.

Editor’s Tip: If you’ve never browned butter before, know that it feels like it takes forever to turn. Then when it does, it happens instantly. It’s going to foam up at some point, too, but keep stirring and scraping the bottom so you can keep an eye on the milk solids.

Preheat the oven to 350°F. In a large bowl, whisk together the all-purpose flour, sugar, baking soda and salt. In another bowl, stir together the eggs, mashed bananas, cooled brown butter, buttermilk and vanilla extract. Add the banana mixture to the flour mixture, stirring just until they’re combined. If you’re using walnuts, fold them in now.

Pour the batter into a greased or parchment-lined 9×5-inch loaf pan. Bake until a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean, about 1 hour. Cool the loaf in the pan for 15 minutes so it can finish setting up its crumb structure, then remove it from the pan and onto a wire rack.

Editor’s Tip: If your banana bread’s top is browning too much while the inside is still raw, lower the oven’s temperature to 325° and cover the pan with aluminum foil.

Allow the brown butter banana bread to cool completely to room temperature, then transfer it to an airtight container or wrap it tightly in a few layers of storage wrap. Keep the loaf at room temperature for up to three days or in the fridge for up to five days.

Yes, you can freeze brown butter banana bread. Allow the loaf to cool completely to room temperature, then wrap it tightly in two layers of storage wrap followed by a layer of aluminum foil. It feels excessive, but this keeps the moisture locked in and prevents freezer burn. Freeze for up to two months, then thaw the loaf at room temperature for a few hours.

You can quickly ripen bananas using your oven. It’s my favorite trick when I need ripe bananas like, now—not in two days! Place the unpeeled bananas on a baking sheet and into a 250ºF oven until the skin turns brown and the flesh becomes soft and super sweet, about 15 minutes. Let them cool before using.

If your banana bread is gummy, there may be a few culprits at play. The first is whether you used two bananas instead of measuring out 1 cup of mashed bananas. Since bananas vary in size, you might have added too much to the batter, and too much moisture will make your banana bread gummy. Always follow the exact measurement rather than the suggested number of bananas.

Also, make sure you’re mixing enough, but not too much. Undermixing won’t develop the gluten and create a strong crumb structure for your loaf. Overmixing will lead to excessive gluten development, causing your bread to sink after baking. Mix the batter just until no flour streaks remain.

Lastly, let your banana bread cool completely before cutting into it. I know, this is the hardest part! But the cool-off period is important because the loaf is still developing its crumb structure, even after coming out of the oven. Let the loaf cool in its pan for 10 minutes, then remove it to a wire rack to cool off completely. Leaving the loaf in its pan will trap moisture and make it gummy.

Yes, you can bake brown butter banana bread in a different-sized pan. Instead of a 9×5-inch loaf, divide the batter evenly between three greased 5-3/4 x 3-inch mini loaf pans, or one 8-inch square pan. Start checking for doneness around the 40-minute mark.

#23. Is An Apple A Day Actually Good For You? A Dietitian Weighs In

The classic snack supports your health—but with a few caveats.

An old proverb says one apple a day keeps the doctor away, but does nutrition science back that up? For most people, yes: An apple is a healthy way to add fruit to your diet and help you meet the recommended daily amount. But a few caveats—like apple variety, washing, and digestive sensitivity—are worth keeping in mind.

Current dietary guidelines recommend two servings of fruit per day, and since an apple is about one serving, it can help you meet those needs. But most types of apples are high in fiber and natural sugar, so eating too many could mean problems for your gut health, according to Lauren Manaker, M.S., R.D.N.

Let’s dig into the science to learn how to safely add apples to our diets.

“Apples offer a range of health benefits, including supporting heart health, supporting immune function, and reducing inflammation,” Manaker says. She credits vitamin C with supporting the immune system and flavonoids, a type of antioxidant, with helping lower the risk of heart disease.

While nutrient content varies by apple type, a medium Golden Delicious is mostly water. A single apple contains roughly 96 calories, 23 grams of carbs (17 of which come from sugar), and about four grams of fiber. That fiber, especially soluble fiber like pectin, can help regulate blood sugar and support gut health.

“Eating an apple every day can be incredibly healthy, as apples are a nutrient-dense fruit full of fiber, vitamins, and antioxidants,” Manaker says. “Since most people don't eat the recommended servings of fruits and veggies daily, making a habit of having an apple a day can be a good thing.”

Just don't forget to wash them. “Eating unwashed apples may pose a risk of pesticide exposure, so washing them thoroughly is recommended,” she notes. Apples often appear on lists of produce with higher pesticide residues, such as the Environmental Working Group's Dirty Dozen. Of course, washing is recommended for all produce, and conventional (versus organic) apples still provide nutritional benefits.

“While apples are healthy, over-consuming them in excessive amounts could lead to excess calorie intake or digestive issues due to their high fiber and natural sugar content,” Manaker says.

For most people, it's hard to overdo it enough to cause harm. However, she cautions that too much fiber and natural sugars could cause mild discomfort for those with IBS or more sensitive stomachs, and people managing blood sugar may want to pair apples with protein or fat.

One apple per day is a healthy choice for most people, but rotate fruits, wash produce, and adjust portions if apples trigger digestive symptoms. Your doctor—and your gut—will thank you.

Lauren Manaker M.S., R.D.N., L.D., C.L.E.C. is a registered dietitian based in South Carolina. She earned a bachelor's degree in Food Science and Human Nutrition at the University of Florida before going on to complete her master's and dietetic internship at Rush University Medical Center. Manaker received the Emerging Professional in Women’s Health Award from the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics in 2018 and provides her expert advice at CNN, Women’s Health Magazine, SHAPE, The Oprah Magazine, and Cooking Light.

#24. Baltimore Yat Gaw Mein

Yat gaw mein, also known as Baltimore yak or dirty yak, is Baltimore carryout comfort food at its finest. A Chinese American remix of Beijing’s zha jiang mian, the dish dates back to the late 19th century, when Chinese immigrants started settling in the city. Setting up shop in traditionally Black and working-class neighborhoods, Chinese cooks adapted their recipes to locally available ingredients, swapping fermented pastes for a simpler, soy-based gravy. Over time, something new emerged: savory wheat noodles, stir-fried with shrimp, beef, and vegetables and punctuated with a hard-boiled egg. Today you can find the beloved dish at counter spots around town like Jimmy’s Carryout, Danny’s, and Pimlico Chinese Carry Out.

In this at-home version from Steve Chu, the chef behind Baltimore’s Ekiben, smoky wok-charred noodles are tossed with umami-packed soy sauce and oyster sauce, rich fat, and sweet caramelized onions. What makes the dish “dirty” is the flavor that develops when soy sauce, sugar, and aromatics scorch against the hot metal of the wok, creating deep savory notes balanced by subtle sweetness. Be sure to keep the wok on high heat and stir frequently, since this allows the wok hei—which translates to “the breath of a wok” and refers to that elusive smokiness—to work its magic. The finishing squeeze of ketchup might sound unusual, but it delivers the acidic punch that makes the dish complete.

#25. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

#28. Millennial Side Parts Are Angel-Approved on the Victoria’s Secret Runway

In the center-part versus side-part debate, the Angels have landed on a verdict

Bombshell blowouts returned to the Victoria’s Secret runway this year, thanks to legendary hairdresser Guido Palau and his team. Models like Barbara Palvin and Rosie Huntington-Whiteley were spotted backstage wearing rollers for hours before the show, a tried-and-true technique for creating bouncy, voluminous waves. But amid the excitement of the show's return with OG Angels like Adriana Lima and Alessandra Ambrosio, we also noticed a nostalgic beauty trend taking hold: more than a dozen models wore deep side parts, the kind synonymous with millennials, the early aughts, and VS runways of years past.

It wasn’t just the models wearing deep side parts or bangs at this year’s live Los Angeles show. Megan Thee Stallion’s showstopping performance was elevated by her Bombshell blowout, complete with a bang styled over one eye—a classic, sultry look perfect for an artist making hot-girl history on the runway. Tate McRae also wore her golden waves flipped over to one side, which lent incredible movement as she performed her new single “Housewife.”

A debate has raged for years between side parts and center parts, with Gen Z favoring the latter. They claim it makes you look more youthful—but the Angels prove this theory wrong. Ultimately, a side-parted blowout is meant to be touched, tousled, and tossed. You should be able to throw it to one side, then the other, without your hair looking out of place. That’s what makes a Bombshell blowout so signature to the Victoria’s Secret runway. A center-parted blowout tends to be more rigid and structured—with such a meticulous part, you can’t fluff it, zhuzh it, or mess it up.

There’s no wrong or right way to part your hair. Even supermodels like Alex Consani and Adriana Lima preferred a center part on last night’s runway. But many others, including Ashley Graham, Caroline Trentini, and Paloma Elsesser, proved that the millennial side part—much like the glitz and glam of the Victoria’s Secret show—will never go out of style.

SU: Like a takeout one. And then when you feel your oil is hot enough, you plunge the tip of the chopstick into the oil, and then you watch the part that's submerged.

SU: Yeah. You watch the part of the chopstick that's submerged, and you should see, right where it meets the oil, you should see little bubbles forming. And that is an indication of how hot your oil is. If there are no bubbles or just very few small lazy bubbles, that means your oil is not hot enough. If there's a stream of bubbles that immediately rises and they lazily, blub, blub, blub, blub, that means your oil is kind of at the right temperature. And then if you have very rapid boiling and they're violently hissing against the side of the chopstick, that means your oil is a bit too hot.

JS: And this is just the moisture from the wood coming out, essentially?

SU: Yes, I think so. So that's the part about frying. And when you're ready to fry also, I think part of it is setting yourself up for the post-fry part.

SU: Exactly. That's a good point, Jesse, it does go so fast. And I think having that setup really helps. So, I almost always use a wire rack that's set inside a rimmed baking sheet, like a half sheet tray. And I have something, either it's tongs or a spider, or a slotted spoon so I can fish out my fried food and move it to the wire rack. I never place it on paper towels.

SU: Because I think it just steams up, because-

SU: It gets soggy. You're putting this paper towel on a platter or a plate, and when the fried food makes contact, yes, the oil tends to get absorbed, but then it's steaming up beneath the surface because there's no air circulating. So I almost never put fried food on a plate with a paper towel.

JS: Sure, sure, sure. I've seen people put paper towels under the wire rack.

JS: I don't really know what that's about.

SU: ... but it's not sucking the oil out of that fried food because it's now suspended over the wire rack.

JS: It's just depleting Earth's resources.

JS: Okay, okay. So we're set up for frying.

JS: How do you scoop the batter in? How do you avoid sploshing hot oil everywhere? What is your technique?

SU: I know it's scary to get your hand close to the pot of oil, but actually the closer you can possibly get to the pan and the surface of the oil, the less dangerous it is. If you plop your, in this case, the fritters from up high, let's say chest height into the oil, that's going to fall and splash. Think of somebody diving into a pool, it's going to splash oil on you. Whereas, if you think of instead of a, I don't know, like a hippo entering the water. And you just gently glide the fritter into the oil, it's less likely to splash and splatter. So, I use an ice cream scoop to portion the batter, because I think that leads to consistent fritters and they all fry evenly. I've also made it with measuring cup, like a quarter or one third measuring cup, and it's worked perfectly fine. But I like the scoop because the spring-loaded action lets you drop the batter in quicker.

SU: And then I hold the batter as close to the surface of the oil as I feel comfortable and I just let it go gently.

JS: And what about overloading the pan? I know this is a big thing people preach about frying is don't overload the fryer.

SU: Yes. I think that's a valid concern. I think it's overloading or not is a matter of how big your pan is, obviously. The larger your pan and the more oil you have, the more you can fit in there. I would say think about deep-frying the same way as you would when you're sauteing something. You're looking for something to get color. You're looking to give these things enough space to float around, be surrounded with the oil and have the moisture evaporate. Same as you would in a skillet when you're sauteing chicken breast, for instance. You don't want to crowd things to the point where they don't have space to move and there's too much steam builds up. I would say have the pan about three-quarters full. That's a good gauge.

JS: Sure. Okay. So you have your fritters frying.

SU: This one, these fritters in general, because they have a lot of sugar. They have the sugar from the apples, they have the sugar from the syrup, so they will brown quite rapidly.

SU: They are quite dark. And in shaping the fritters, I also found it very helpful to... After I put the oil, I found it very helpful to go in with the back of the scoop that I use, for instance, and just squish the batter down a little bit because then that flattens the fritter.

SU: And it helps things cook a bit more evenly.

SU: Think of it like when you're grilling a burger, and you know how when you grill or cook the burger and the center tends to rise?

SU: Yes. And then to prevent that you dimple the middle.

SU: So think of that as the same way. By pressing down on the center of the fritter, you even everything out and things fry quicker and more evenly. This one, I would say push it a little past golden brown to a deep golden. And this rule applies, what I'm about to say next applies to anything that you're frying. I always use the bubbles around the fried food as an indication to know when to take things out. Because the more bubbles there are around the food that's in the oil, the more moisture there is. And when you're frying, you're really trying to drive away that surface moisture. And when the bubbles start to slow down or become really lazy, that's when you know that enough moisture has been driven off of the surface of whatever you dropped in to be crispy.

SU: So when there's less bubbles, pull that thing out.

JS: And then the dreaded question, what do you do with the oil? When you're done, can I reuse it?

I get rid of whatever's in the sieve, little bits and bobs and apple pieces sometimes. And then you can reuse the oil once, for sure. You might have to top it off with fresh oil, and then after that I would get rid of it. Whatever you do, don't put oil down your sink or in the toilet.

SU: That's true. Don't do that. The best way to dispose cold oil is to put it in something else, like a clean used milk jug, for instance, or a bottle.

SU: Yes, or it's original container. And then seal it tightly and put it in the trash. Never pour oil down your sink.

#31. The Best Culinary Resorts in the United States

Where to go to rest, relax, recharge, and eat well while doing it

At some hotels, food is an afterthought: Breakfast buffets are bland, in-room mini bars are stocked with generic snacks, and lobby bars are lackluster. But other resorts understand that we don’t simply factor food into an itinerary; many people plan their entire trip around eating, hoping to get to the heart of local cuisine and dine at the area’s best restaurants without ever leaving the property.

These culinary resorts will help you build an entire vacation around great meals. If you want to get your hands dirty, resorts on working farms have guests harvesting produce that will end up on their dinner plates that night, and some properties send visitors off on fishing and foraging expeditions to find their own meals. Other spots keep it more low-key with award-winning restaurants, special wine tastings, and wellness-minded retreats serving homegrown juices. No matter how you want to engage with the food that will power your trip, these 10 culinary resorts are the best places in the U.S. to have a truly delicious stay.

Acura has always done things its own way. We believe the best experiences are created through intentional choices, thoughtful craftsmanship, and the confidence to pursue a different approach. This spirit is reflected in our philosophy of Precision Crafted Performance. Learn more.

Made up of 65 freestanding cottages, Wildflower Farms gives guests a taste of farm life — albeit an incredibly chic version. Guests can start the day with a complimentary tour of the 6-acre farm and a visit to feed the resort’s Icelandic sheep and chicken, then pick up a few eggs to bring over to the on-site restaurant Clay for an incredibly fresh breakfast. Other food-focused activities include suiting up in beekeeping gear to learn how to make honey, taking a guided foraging walk, or stirring up a cocktail using ingredients grown on-site in a class hosted in the resort’s cooking school barn.

Clay serves breakfast, lunch, and dinner in a cozy dining room that centers a massive wood-burning fireplace. The menu changes seasonally to feature lamb and pork raised just steps from the kitchen, plus a selection of the 14,000 pounds of fruit, vegetables, and herbs that the farm produces annually. The beverage program also has local roots: Wine director Vanessa Price has built a 7,000-bottle cellar that shines a light on New York’s often-overlooked Finger Lakes and North Fork wine regions, and ingredients like carrot eau de vie show up in martinis.

With just four cabins situated on 3,800 acres of working ranch, Quercus is a small culinary resort that punches well above its weight. Chiara Visconti di Modrone and her husband Angelos Pervanas originally launched Quercus as a regenerative farming project an hour outside Atlanta before teaming up with acclaimed Atlanta restaurateurs to morph it into a full-scale culinary escape. Now the all-inclusive experience features private saunas and cold plunge pools, holistic wellness consultations, and activities like horse training or kayaking in the Flint River.

Guests are encouraged to kick off their visit with a garden tour so they understand the property’s commitment to biodynamic farming principles and recognize the rare varieties of turmeric and uncommon peppers that will later appear on their plates. The resort offers three meals per day, along with snacks like beef jerky and gochujang okra chips stocked in each room. Each meal can be enjoyed in the restaurant spaces on the property or delivered in a wicker picnic basket through the resort’s charming take on room service. Uberto is the pinnacle of Quercus’s culinary experiences, a 10-plus course tasting menu helmed by chef Ryan Smith, whose Atlanta restaurant Staplehouse earned a Michelin star. The menu changes with the seasons, but mainstays like clarified curry made with lemongrass and galangal from the farm’s tropical greenhouse showcase an essential truth: Chefs spend all week in the kitchen and fermentation lab crafting each dish, but the garden has been working on dinner all year.

Mii Amo is an adults-only wellness resort tucked into the red rocks of Sedona’s Boynton Canyon vortex, which is supposedly one of the most powerful hubs for spiritual and healing energy in the area. It has everything one would expect at a luxury wellness retreat: lodging in one of 23 cozy casitas, a daily credit to book treatments at the 40,000-square-foot spa, an array of sound baths and meditations, and guided hikes and mountain bike rides through the canyon.

But unlike some other wellness resorts, Mii Amo has a top-notch culinary program as well. During all-inclusive stays ranging from three to 10 nights, guests get three meals per day at the on-site restaurant, Hummingbird, along with unlimited juice bar visits to pick up protein-packed smoothies, ginger shots, and sleep tonics. While menus are rooted in seasonal produce from the chef’s garden, the resort doesn’t believe in total restriction so sweet treats, alcohol, and caviar are available to add a little indulgence to your stay. Book one of the weekly nutrition classes or juicing demonstrations to learn how to recreate the nourishing fare served at Mii Amo after returning home.

On a hillside in the Catskills, Susan Manning and Doug Doetsch built a cidery, farm-to-table restaurant, and hotel on the same land that Doetsch’s family has farmed for five generations. Eight Shaker-inspired, apartment-style accommodations are built into two 19th-century historic buildings and each has views of the nearby Delaware River and the cidery on which the resort is centered.

The 12-acre orchard features rows upon rows of trees bearing 60 different varieties of apples and pears. The resort offers weekend tours of the orchard, plus cider tastings. Cider-maker Joshua Hinchman turns the fruit into an ever-expanding portfolio of traditional cider, while also experimenting with other beverages like fortified apple wines and cyser, a type of mead. All tastings are hosted in a barn that was built into the hillside using reclaimed wood that once supported the original Tappan Zee Bridge, and the structure is also passive house-certified, making it the world’s first cidery to receive that energy efficiency designation. Apples find their way onto executive chef and culinary director Edwyn Ferrari’s menu as well, so digging into custardy cider posset at the end of a meal in the resort’s restaurant feels full circle.

This Healdsburg hotel is the flagship property from Appellation, a hotel collection co-founded by chef Charlie Palmer and Christopher Hunsberger, who spent more than 35 years working for Four Seasons Hotels and Resorts. As a self-described culinary hotel, the 108-room resort set lofty expectations for itself, but Appellation Healdsburg delivers with three restaurants, a packed schedule of food-focused activities, and a premier location in the heart of Sonoma County.

Folia Bar & Kitchen is the resort’s premium restaurant, and it offers a three-course menu of local ingredients from purveyors like Hog Island Oyster Co. and Sonoma Bee Company. For guests who want to try their hand in the kitchen, the resort offers a variety of hands-on cooking classes, some of which are taught by Palmer himself. Since the hotel counts hundreds of wineries as neighbors, it invites a different winemaker to the property every Friday to host a guided tasting. But when it’s time to venture off the property, guests can also book with the concierge to get special access to Sonoma County producers like Knights Bridge Winery, Bricoleur Vineyards, and Dry Creek Vineyard for behind-the-scenes tours and tastings.

Los Poblanos is a historic inn dating back to 1932 where lavender grows in wide, fragrant rows and fruit trees line the paths between buildings. The property was designed by seminal architect John Gaw Meem in classic Santa Fe style with pitched tin roofs that nod to the site’s history as a dairy farm and the original 1934 hand-painted grain silos still stand on site.

Though it no longer produces dairy or serves as the headquarters of a larger ranch, a 25-acre organic farm is the heart of the property. Guests can take a formal tour of the greenhouses or wander the resort’s gardens, orchards, and cottonwood trees, which are fed by community-managed irrigation systems called acequias that are older than the state itself. All that benefits Campo, the property’s signature restaurant, where the flavors of the Rio Grande Valley appear on every plate. In addition to homegrown produce, the restaurant sources meat and other ingredients from local purveyors including Native American Beef, a program that supports Indigenous cattle producers who faced hurdles competing in the commercial meat industry. Don’t miss the Farm Shop with lavender-scented products, hot sauce from the garden’s peppers, and the estate’s handcrafted gin, which is produced in the resort’s distillery just down the road in downtown Albuquerque.

The Ojai Valley Inn has long been lauded as a wellness escape thanks to its 31,000-square-foot spa and location at the center of the hippie enclave of Ojai, but the resort is also a culinary destination in its own right. With six restaurants and bars on the property, options range from a casual pub serving quintessential burgers and local beer to a renowned four-course tasting menu at Olivella, where guests will eat dessert drizzled in honey from the resort’s apiary and order wine from the 10,000-bottle cellar.

In addition to the restaurants and bars, the resort recently poured $20 million into an epicurean center called the Farmhouse, where culinary ambassador and beloved California chef and restaurateur Nancy Silverton curates a slate of cookbook talks, cooking classes, and special tasting menu dinners with visiting chefs and buzzy winemakers. It’s also the site of the annual Ojai Food & Wine festival, held in March, which brings renowned chefs from around the world to the peaceful valley.

For travelers looking to be spoiled for choice, look no further than the Grand Hotel. Abundance is wrapped into every aspect of the resort, from its 660-foot porch that offers views of the idyllic car-free island to 388 Victorian-style guest rooms dressed up in maximalist candy-colored decor.

The property is not lacking in options on the food front either: It has 13 different bars and restaurants. The elegant main dining room serves breakfast, lunch, and dinner, but the peak time to visit is for nightly live entertainment from the Grand Hotel Orchestra and a five-course menu that rotates every three days to highlight a different type of cuisine. Other restaurants are just as grand; the Woods Restaurant serves cozy Bavarian dishes in a dining room that feels like a lodge with a roaring fireplace, while the Jockey Club serves seafood towers and steakhouse classics in a room outfitted in saddle leather. More casual picks are also available like Detroit-style pies at Mackinac Island Pizza Company or old-school sundaes made with scoops of Guernsey Farms Dairy ice cream at Sadie’s Ice Cream Parlor.

When visitors check into one of the rustic cabins at Windy Hill Farm and Preserve, a retreat and upland preserve in the foothills of the Great Smoky Mountains, there are plenty of ways to get involved in cultivating the food that will eventually end up on their plates. The all-inclusive experience features activities like beekeeping demonstrations, bourbon tastings, and cooking classes hosted by executive chef Ben Warwick, and every evening ends with an opportunity to make s’mores around a campfire. The resort has also recently launched themed dinners that offer built-in lessons on the surrounding Appalachian region. The first in the series is called Watershed, which tells the story of how water flows from the highlands surrounding the resort to the Gulf in 10 delicious courses.

But some of the most popular ways to spend a day on the 650 acres of rolling hills are more hands-on. Guests who opt to go crappie fishing on the Tennessee River will cast their reels in search of the native fish, and those who get lucky can have their catch cleaned and cooked at Wilder, the hotel’s restaurant. Quail hunting is also popular. Each hunt begins with a hearty breakfast at Wilder before guests head out with professional guides and sporting dogs. Proceeds from the hunting operation are used to fund large-scale land conservation and native habitat restoration.

Hidden Pond is a retreat where the quintessential clapboard cottages are as beloved as the property’s farm-to-table restaurant. Many of the accommodations were recently redesigned, and part of the revamp included outfitting the in-unit kitchens with top-of-the-line Breville appliances. However, you may not even bother firing up the appliances once you try the fresh-baked pastries delivered to each room by picnic basket, and dig into the menu at the on-site restaurant Earth.

The restaurant is popular with locals as well as hotel guests, and the menu is built around produce pulled from the resort’s organic garden. Summer brings heirloom tomatoes and micro basil while cooler months stock pumpkins and root vegetables like celeriac. It’s all paired with fresh-caught lobster and other local seafood, so you’ll also get a taste of the Atlantic that inspired the trip to Maine in the first place.

#32. More Than 1.5 Million Pounds of Meat Recalled—Here’s What You Need to Throw Out

Time to check your refrigerator for recalled meats like hot dogs, chicken sausage, bacon and deli products sold under several brand names.

A package of chicken sausage can settle the question of what to make for dinner in a hurry. But before you put one to work this week, check the label. A nationwide recall includes chicken sausage, hot dogs, bacon, deli meats and other refrigerator staples sold under several brand names.

Kayem Foods, based in Chelsea, Massachusetts, is recalling approximately 1,584,361 pounds of ready-to-eat meat and poultry products, according to an October 17 USDA announcement. The products were shipped to retailers and foodservice locations nationwide and in Hong Kong.

Here’s what to check before you make your next meal.

The products may have been stored at improper temperatures. According to the USDA’s Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS), Kayem received a customer complaint on Oct. 1 about products arriving warm. The company investigated and found that a warehouse cooler had not consistently kept the products at a safe temperature.

In Kayem’s announcement, the company attributed the problem to a cooling system malfunction at one of its warehouses. Kayem says it has now corrected the issue.

As of the USDA’s October 17 announcement, there were no confirmed reports of illness linked to the recalled products.

The products went to stores and foodservice locations across the country, but the USDA notice does not name specific locations. It says retail distribution lists will be posted on the agency’s recall website when available.

Kayem’s consumer product list includes items sold under these brands:

Examples include Kayem Fenway Franks, Al Fresco fully cooked chicken sausages and chicken meatballs, McKenzie bacon and turkey breast and Triple M ham. Check the product details carefully. A brand name alone does not establish whether a package is recalled.

The USDA says the recalled products were produced approximately March 31 through Oct. 7, 2026. That’s the production window, not a range of best-by dates to look for on your package.

Start by checking for one of these establishment numbers inside the USDA inspection mark:

Then match your product’s brand, description, UPC and applicable date or lot information against the USDA’s complete product list. Package sizes and identifying details vary, so there isn’t one date or code that covers everything.

The USDA also provides product label images to help you identify recalled packages. If you bought meat slices at a deli counter and no longer have the original label information, ask the store whether your purchase was included.

Do not eat the recalled products. The USDA advises throwing them away or returning them to the store.

For help identifying a product or questions about the recall, contact Kayem Foods Customer Service at 800-426-6100, Monday through Friday, 7:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern, or email [email protected].

If you’re concerned about an illness after eating one of the recalled products, contact a healthcare provider.
