#34. 5 Cookbooks That Go Deep on a Single Ingredient

If you’ve ever been starstruck by a perfect Cinderella pumpkin or a stately stalk of Brussels sprouts, you likely understand the appeal of a book focused on a single fruit or vegetable. While books like this aren’t always long, they typically go deep, with the fervor of an author who is fully obsessed.

One charming example, The Core of an Onion: Peeling the Rarest Common Food by Mark Kurlansky, melds authority with a dose of irreverence. First published in 2023, it’s a slim 200 pages, but the writer (who’s also written nonfiction books dedicated to oysters, salt, and cod) packs a lot in. “Onions have a way of taking on unexpected significance,” he posits. The first section covers the allium’s history and cultural impact. (Did you know that ancient Egyptians tied them to mummies’ feet as a preservative?) Kurlansky then offers loosely structured recipes for breads, sauces, and more, all centering the humble bulb.

Elevating a perhaps overlooked ingredient is a core tenet of single-­subject cookbookery. In The Compleat Squash: A Passionate Grower’s Guide to Pumpkins, Squash, and Gourds, a canonical 2004 ode to members of the Cucurbitaceae ­family, master ­gardener Amy Goldman Fowler’s passion is abundantly evident. “Sometimes I don’t know where pumpkins begin and I end,” she writes, before segueing into a series of squash and gourd portraits, each showing an individual specimen more striking than the last. Fowler shares recipes too, in addition to breed spotlights, resources for seed ­buying, and advice on growing your own.

Some such tomes aim to introduce the reader to the joys of less ubiquitous ingredients. Lane Selman and Margarett Waterbury’s Radicchio: A Celebration of the Beloved Italian Vegetable tells the “human and natural history” of the bitter chicory, along with instructions for how to grow it and cook with it. Selman is the founder of the Culinary Breeding Network, an initiative that rallies scientists, farmers, and chefs to geek out over new produce varieties. The book gets weird in the best way possible, with profiles of Italian growers and recipes including gnocchi with radicchio pesto, radicchio with prosciutto ­gratin, and chocolate–radicchio cake (why not?).

Radicchio reads almost like a community cookbook, and that’s intentional. Selman’s inspiration to pursue the topic was the sheer lack of writing on this oddball vegetable: “All of these people that we’ve met on our way down the rabbit hole needed to be included,” she says. “They’re the ones who have given us all this information. Sometimes it takes a village.”

Other single-subject cookbooks showcase pantry ­staples that are rarely in the spotlight. Anna Hezel’s Little Book of Olives: A Guide to Cooking, Eating, and Drinking for the Brine-Inclined presents recipes including cantaloupe and crushed-olive panzanella, Castelvetrano and pistachio pesto, and a whole chapter of olive desserts, plus shopping tips and a breakdown of varieties. The book’s retro aesthetic lends ­gravitas to an ingredient often relegated to garnish status.

Finally, some books exist more to dazzle than to inform, as is the case with pop artist Ed Ruscha and River Café chef Ruthie Rogers’s 2025 release Squeeze Me: Lemon Recipes & Art. In the pair’s high-gloss love letter to the lemon, pop art–coded photos with cheeky captions and a suite of minimalist recipes—such as lemon–­mascarpone tart and limoncello—make this ode to the simple citrus equally at home on a coffee table or the kitchen shelf.

While styles and forms vary, these books serve a ­common goal: to illuminate the sometimes surprising pleasures of a particular fruit or vegetable. That they manage to do so in such delightful fashion is proof that, once in a while, ­working with less really is more.

#35. Pecan Pie Cheesecake

Ditch the same old Thanksgiving desserts and try this fun twist on classic pecan pie this year. Cheesecake makes basically everything better, and that’s especially true for this dish. This recipe takes the classic pie to new heights by introducing an extra creamy base and a sweet, sticky pecan topping that we’d add to practically anything. Whether you’re a classic cheesecake lover at heart or are simply looking to go beyond pies this season, this pecan pie cheesecake will be the star at any holiday spread.

Once your cheesecake is done, turn off the heat, prop open the oven door, and let the cheesecake cool in the oven for around 1 hour. Then, remove the aluminum foil and refrigerate the cheesecake in the pan until firm, at least 5 hours and up to overnight. Serve it right away, or wrap it in plastic wrap and keep it refrigerated for up to 5 days. We recommend not topping the cheesecake until you’re ready to serve, but if you’re storing prepared cheesecake, be prepared that the topping will change texture.

#36. Rafael Pavarotti on His Groundbreaking Fashion Photography Exhibition

The Brazilian photographer’s work is on view at Musée des Arts Décoratifs.

Once you know his name, you can recognize a Rafael Pavarotti photo instantly. His vivid colors, high contrast, and surreal texture have marked his work with Chanel, Dior, Rihanna, Beyoncé, and Harry Styles, among others. His striking and unique visual images are uncompromising and unabashedly bold: no color too bright, no silhouette too over-the-top, and no pose too statuesque, all inspired by his own Afro-Indigenous Brazilian culture. And now, over 200 of his prints are on display in his very first solo exhibition, at the Musée des Arts Décoratifs in Paris.

Born in 1993 in the Amazon rainforest in Pará, Pavarotti taught himself photography at age 12 after borrowing his father’s Kodak camera. The exhibition, presented in partnership with Brazilian luxury group Iguatemi, uses this as an entry point and showcases some of his earliest photographs from his hometown, as well as his first professional shots of models from when he moved to Rio de Janeiro at the age of 16. He then moved to São Paulo and London, before setting his roots down in Paris. Today, it’s easy to see his global influence in fashion photography and beyond.

“Colour has always been central to my understanding of the world,” he tells ELLE. “Growing up in the Amazon, colour was never separate from life. In my photography, it is deeply connected to memory, presence, and the ability of an image to preserve something beyond the moment in which it was created.” His images draw from his real-life experience: “My family, my friends, my community, and the people who have walked beside me remain among my greatest sources of inspiration,” he says. “The Amazon also continues to exist within my work as a source of energy, memory, and orientation.”

When it comes down to lensing some of the most iconic celebrities of our time, the photographer says, “For me, photography has always been about seeing another person fully. Every portrait is an exchange that requires trust, attention, and openness.”

Beyond that, Pavarotti’s work is in many ways deeply personal and seeks to show the beauty of the underrepresented. He made history in 2022 with his British Vogue cover featuring nine Black models. “I want people to encounter images that remain open, that continue to exist in their minds after they have seen them,” he adds. “Photography has the power to expand how we see ourselves and the world around us, and to create space for new forms of visibility and recognition. For me, it is the opportunity to contribute to a visual culture where more people can recognize themselves.”

“Rafael Pavarotti: Photographer” is open at the Musée des Arts Décoratifs in Paris until May 2, 2027.

#37. An Inside Look at Miley Cyrus’s Noir Hollywood Bowl Looks

The pop star’s longtime stylist, Bradley Kenneth, details the curation of her all-Saint Laurent show wardrobe

It’s a rare occurrence to see Miley Cyrus on stage these days. While the Grammy-winning superstar spent the early years of her career touring the world in blonde wigs, she’s slowly stepped away from the traditional concert tour. In recent years, she’s opted for more intimate settings, like her Spotify Billions Club performance, which she held at Maxim’s restaurant in Paris last June, or her surprise pop-up sets at Bemelmans Bar and 3 Dollar Bill in New York City. In fact, after the release of her ninth studio album, Something Beautiful, she even went on to say she had “no desire” to do another large headlining tour due to the difficulties it poses for her mental health and sobriety journey. “I do have the physical ability, and I have the opportunities to tour,” she told Good Morning America. “I wish I had the desire, but I don’t.”

So, when Cyrus announced that she would be taking the stage at the Hollywood Bowl amphitheater in Los Angeles for two nights only, it was no surprise that she brought her all—and an arsenal of knockout looks from Saint Laurent by Anthony Vaccarello—to make it happen.

For the sold-out shows, Cyrus teamed up with her longtime stylist, Bradley Kenneth, to create a sleek, rock ‘n’ roll-inspired display that perfectly encapsulate her new Bass Persuades era. That consisted of pieces like a black leather newsboy cap and a floor-length fur coat. In other moments, she wore a chiffon cape romper and knee-high leather boots.

“There’s an effortless confidence to Saint Laurent that really resonates with Miley,” Kenneth said in an exclusive interview with Harper’s Bazaar. “This era has really been about stripping back the fashion and putting the music first. Miley is in such a beautiful place in her life right now. She’s happy, self-assured, and confident, and she wanted the fashion to reflect that without overpowering her.”

Ahead, Kenneth speaks about curating the collection of chic, all-black looks that Cyrus wore for her Hollywood Bowl shows. Plus, he opens up about her love affair with Saint Laurent, her constant evolution, and where her fashion stands today.

You have long styled Cyrus in looks from Saint Laurent by Anthony Vaccarello. Why do his designs resonate so strongly with you both? What is it about the brand that pulls her in?

Anthony is brilliant in the way he can make something minimal feel incredibly elevated. His ability to work with textures and silhouettes in a way that never feels overpowering, but always remains cool and chic, is something I’ve always loved about his designs.

There’s an effortless confidence to Saint Laurent that really resonates with Miley. The clothes feel timeless and modern while still maintaining that sexy, rock ‘n’ roll attitude that’s always been part of her DNA. Especially in this era, when we’re intentionally stripping things back, his designs feel like such a natural fit. They have a strong point of view without ever taking away from the woman wearing them.

Additionally, how does it feel to have this special moment arrive right as Vaccarello has announced his departure from Saint Laurent? Does it feel like a swan song in a way?

Anthony has created such an incredible legacy at Saint Laurent, and Miley and I have shared so many special moments wearing his designs over the years. I’ve always admired his ability to make something feel elevated while still maintaining that effortless, cool sophistication.

In a way, it does feel like a beautiful full-circle moment. The Hollywood Bowl looks really represent where Miley is creatively right now, and Anthony’s designs captured that so perfectly. It’s special to celebrate this chapter of his work while also celebrating a new chapter in Miley’s evolution. I’m excited to see what he does next.

How would you describe the style aesthetic of the Bass Persuades era? How did that inform the looks you curated for the Hollywood Bowl shows?

This era has really been about stripping back the fashion and putting the music first. Miley is in such a beautiful place in her life right now. She’s happy, self-assured, and confident, and she wanted the fashion to reflect that without overpowering her. The idea was to keep things minimal, chic, and effortless, allowing who she is today to be the focal point.

For the Hollywood Bowl, we wanted to carry that same philosophy onto the stage. The Saint Laurent looks played with strong tailoring, sheer elements, leather, and fur, but everything was kept relatively simple. There was a sense of ease to the wardrobe that felt really important.

The clothes still needed to have an impact, especially in a venue as iconic as the Hollywood Bowl, but ultimately we wanted Miley to shine through. It was about creating a wardrobe that felt elevated and sophisticated, but still unmistakably her.

How does the fashion of Bass differ from the fashion of Something Beautiful? For that era, you and Cyrus leaned a lot into archival and I know Thierry Mugler’s 1995 couture show was a key influence as well. Were there any touchpoints that inspired this era?

Something Beautiful was such a fashion-forward era. We really embraced the fantasy of fashion through incredible archival pieces, couture, and dramatic silhouettes. Thierry Mugler’s 1995 couture collection was a huge influence, and the fashion played such an important role in defining the visual identity of that project.

One thing I’ve always loved about Miley is that with every new era, she tends to do the opposite of what you might expect. She never wants to repeat herself, and I think that’s what makes each chapter feel so distinct.

With Bass Persuades, we almost went in the complete opposite direction. After an era where the fashion was such a major part of the storytelling, Miley wanted to pull everything back and let the music and who she is today take center stage.

We were inspired by effortless, chic style and that classic rock ‘n’ roll attitude where the clothes feel lived-in and natural. There’s something so cool about the simplicity of throwing on your favorite jeans and a tank top and not needing anything else. That was really the spirit we wanted to capture.

It’s still very much a considered fashion direction, but there’s a certain confidence in knowing when to hold back. Sometimes the most powerful statement is the simplest one.

You’ve long worked as Cyrus’s stylist. What is the best part of getting to collaborate with her?

Having worked with Miley for so long, I’ve been lucky enough to see so many different versions of her through her creative process and each era of her career. There’s always something new, but she also has this incredible ability to reference different parts of herself from the past and reinterpret them in a completely fresh way.

She is constantly evolving, which definitely keeps me on my toes! My job has always been to meet her where she is creatively and help bring that vision to life through fashion.

These concert looks, like Cyrus’s press shots for Bass Persuades, center around an all-black aesthetic. What was the intention behind this achromatic palette?

I think there’s something incredibly chic and timeless about black. It allows you to focus on the silhouette, the textures, and ultimately the person wearing the clothes.

Because this era has been so much about stripping things back, the palette felt like a natural extension of that idea. We didn’t want the fashion to feel distracting or overly complicated. Miley wanted to keep things minimal and let her presence and the music really be the focus.

What I love about Anthony’s designs is that even within such a simple palette, there’s so much depth. The contrast between sheer fabrics, leather, tailoring, and fur creates interest without needing a lot of color or embellishment.

There’s a confidence in that simplicity that feels really reflective of where Miley is right now.

What was the most challenging look to put together for this show? Was there one that was also particularly rewarding?

I think the challenge with a show like this was actually the simplicity of the wardrobe. When you’re working with such minimal looks, every detail becomes that much more important. The fit, the proportions, the way the fabric moves, everything has to be just right because there’s nothing to hide behind.

We also had to make sure everything worked for a live performance and felt comfortable and effortless on Miley.

One of my favorite looks was the opening look with the sheer black tank, high-waisted tailored trousers, and floor-length fur coat. It’s such a simple silhouette, but there’s something incredibly powerful about it. I love that it makes such a strong statement without feeling overdone.

Ultimately, the most rewarding part was seeing Miley bring everything to life. The whole intention of this era was to let her shine, and seeing her onstage, completely confident and comfortable in who she is, was exactly what we wanted the fashion to reflect.

#38. Where The Wild Things Are: Tactically Tinged Fashion Takes to the Water—and the Woods—in Maine

I spend summers in Maine, where I was born and raised. Despite this, a yearly aspiration, or yearly delusion, possesses me each June when I’m staring into my Manhattan closet and choosing what to pack. I think, I might wear that cotton dress, or I should really pack those sandals. I won’t and I shouldn’t. Because I’m often outside, in wildly shifty weather—a half century in Maine prepared me to expect the best and the worst, often in quick, cycling succession—I know that neither will ever touch my body. But restriction can promote innovation. As a result, I’ve developed a summer style based on practicality and foresight and to which I also have a deep emotional attachment, because it pays homage to the clothing habits of my childhood. I’m layering my old self over my new.

ROCK THE BOAT Model Ana Beatriz Cortes (left) is ready for anything in her weatherproof Tory Burch boots. Balenciaga shirt and skirt; balenciaga​.com. Meanwhile, model Betsy Gaghan is a bright spot on a gray day in Loewe; loewe​.com.

Take one recent late-summer day. Invited to attend a party on an uninhabited island a mile offshore, I looked out the window and saw morning sunshine and blue skies and thought HAHAHAHA, then opened the old sea chest where I keep the fashionable multipurpose gear required to survive a typical summer day on a Maine island.

SHOULDER SEASON Gaghan—pairing her tactical Sacai hat and Miu Miu boots with a ladylike Dolce & Gabbana jacket and dress (select Dolce & Gabbana boutiques)—watches on as Good points out some fowl play.

HIT ME WITH YOUR BEST SHOT Cortes’s pastel Lii windbreaker and pants (lii-studio​.com) add a touch of softness to the often harsh conditions. Isabel Marant jacket; isabelmarant​.com. Loro Piana boots.

First, I snapped on an old Speedo, because the ocean acts like battery acid on bathing suits and ponying up for a new one is roughly as sensible as tying hundreds of dollars around a rock and throwing it into the harbor. (As I yanked the straps over my shoulders, I received a text report that it was currently hailing on the island.)

THROUGH THE TALL GRASS Model Sunday Rose’s vibrant Louis Vuitton look (select Louis Vuitton boutiques) is a beacon in the fog.

GUIDE PATH In a studious Celine look (celine​.com), Sunday Rose takes to ornithology like a bird to the wing. Artemas Quibble belt.

GEARHEADS In their glittering beaded Miu Miu trapper hats (miumiu​.com), Sunday Rose and Cortes offer a highly embellished take on an outdoor staple.

Next, I put on a hand-​me-​down T-shirt I got from my friend John, which has holes so perfectly placed that my teen son, a Rick Owens fanatic, regularly comments on its accidental genius. Over it, a Helly Hansen long underwear shirt featuring modernist racing stripes down the sleeves, to provide a bit of visual architecture. Over it, an Icelandic sweater from the ’60s with a funnel-​shaped boatneck high enough to shield me from the elements, nearly to the chin.

Gaghan goes on the march in a Sacai shirt and shorts. Sportmax necklace.

Gaghan plays the field in Phoebe Philo overalls.

Sunday Rose, in Burberry (us.burberry.com), always has her binoculars at the ready.

Cortes is ready to steer the ship in an Etro coat and hat.

Because the sweater is boxy, I tied a Patagonia hooded Micro Puff jacket around my waist like a cummerbund, which could serve as an extra layer if needed. Then I pulled on some bright-​pink-​and-​blue running tights, and over the tights, a pair of men’s madras Bermuda shorts.

On my feet, I put a pair of wool socks and shin-high white fishing boots. I packed an extra pair of wool socks in case one wasn’t enough.

FIT TO PRINT Sunday Rose’s and Gaghan’s rugged Miu Miu hiking boots add another dimension to their sweet, power-clashing sets. Sunday Rose wears a Prada top and N21 by Alessandro dell’Acqua skirt. Gaghan in Prada.

STAR TURN Chanel; select Chanel boutiques.

PILING ON One can never have too many layers on an unpredictable Maine day. Loewe sweater; loewe​.com.

Finally, I randomly grabbed one of the two matching foul-weather jackets I inherited from my parents, who, in the ’80s, thought it best to spend summers sailing northward to even colder places, like Cape Breton. The zipper is broken but the Velcro works, and there’s still a safety whistle attached to the hood, to be used in case my dinghy, which I planned to row solo to the island, capsized—which it nearly did, because the wind whipped up—and I needed a rescue.

In my bag I stashed a ski hat, for when it got cold, and a baseball cap, for when it got sunny, because it would get both, sometimes simultaneously.

POSTCARDS FROM THE EDGE Even from beneath a blanket of fog, it’s hard to miss Gaghan’s and Cortes’s dreamy silhouettes. Gaghan wears a Michael Kors Collection jacket; michaelkors​.com. Chloé dress. Cortes wears a Chloé jacket and skirt; chloe​.com.

After battling through a half mile of waves in my dinghy, I arrived at the party. I immediately found myself helping fend a bigger boat off the rocky shore, which meant my boots swamped with ocean water, the insoles chilly sopping sponges now. I would have to go barefoot for the rest of the day, which was fine—by the end of summer my feet have toughened up. Still, once they thawed later that night, I’d find deep slices under my toes that already looked infected. I should have packed a pair of rubber clogs, not just extra socks. Every day in Maine is a learning opportunity.

PEEP ME Sunday Rose wears a Burberry coat and jacket. Nocs Provisions binoculars.

SNAP TO IT  Cortes wears an Isabel Marant jacket. Lii windbreaker.

Then another squall blew through, just rain and wind this time, no hail, and I flipped my dinghy over so that underprepared people could shelter beneath it. My dinghy counted as part of my outfit, the ultimate foul-weather gear, which I was happy to let others borrow.

For the rest of the day, the weather alternated between sunny and stormy, and then it was 6 p.m., and it felt more like fall than summer, but when it’s cold like this the water is paradoxically warm and welcoming, especially after many piña coladas, and so that’s when we went swimming.

PARKING IT Sunday Rose wears a Prada top and belt. N21 by Alessandro dell’Acqua skirt. Miu Miu boots. Maria La Rosa socks. Gaghan in a Prada top and skirt. Miu Miu boots. Nocs Provisions binoculars.

THE WATER’S FINE Cortes (left) in Balenciaga. Gaghan in Loewe.

IN THE THICK OF IT Gaghan wears a Michael Kors Collection jacket and Chloé dress. Cortes in Chloé.

Finally, the wind seemed to permanently lie down, though storm clouds still haunted the horizon, forcing the sunset to squeeze beneath them, its rays condensed into a lurid, painterly slash. I rowed home through the Technicolor reflection and reached the dock just after nightfall. I forgot a flashlight, which I could have tied around my waist with a rope. Next time I’ll add it to my outfit, because my layers are always accruing, in response to the wind, the rain, the waves, the dark.

THROUGH THE LOOKING GLASSES Birder Amy Geier.

FIELD DAY Gaghan in Phoebe Philo overalls and a COS top. Bottega Veneta hat and Tory Burch shoes. Nocs Provisions binoculars.

EYE SPY Cortes wears an Etro coat and hat. Lii windbreaker.

In this story: hair, Dre Demry-Sanders; makeup, Homa Safar.

Produced by Petty Cash. Visuals Editor: Paige Viti.

#39. Sources Reveal How Val Chmerkovskiy’s Suspension from ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Went Down and If an HR Complaint Was Involved

Val Chmerkovskiy has been suspended from Dancing With the Stars due to the inappropriate “Oscar Slap” comment he made toward Carrie Ann Inaba after her criticism of Jenna Johnson’s routine last week. And the vibes backstage on DWTS have been understandably tense.

One source tells TMZ that “Carrie Ann was so heated over Val's remarks, she raised the issue with BBC Productions' HR department.” Meanwhile, another insider “would not confirm whether Carrie complained” and insists that BBC “launched the investigation after seeing the joke.”

Either way, BBC Studios released a statement confirming Val’s suspension over the weekend, telling Deadline, “The well-being of everyone who works on Dancing with the Stars is non-negotiable. Val’s social media post was inappropriate and does not reflect the values or standards expected of anyone connected with the show. As a result, he will not participate in next week’s show.”

Val has since apologized, saying in part that “I made a poor decision to reference a meme to ‘keep my wife’s name’ out of the conversation, without stopping to think through what else that reference could imply, which was genuinely never my intention. Carrie Ann certainly didn’t deserve to get caught in the middle of my bad judgment, and I hate that she was.”

Val’s celebrity partner, Jenna Dewan, will be dancing with Alan Bersten during Tuesday’s Dedication Night show, with Val expected to be back in the ballroom next week. Per TMZ, it’s unclear if he’s being paid for the week he’s missing due to his suspension.

#40. Our Best Thanksgiving Yet

If you listen in on Test Kitchen conversations, you’ll hear the editors say that Thanksgiving is our Super Bowl, our World Cup, and our Fashion Week. For food people, it’s the culmination of a year’s worth of prep, planning, brainstorming, and, as my colleague Hana Asbrink describes, Post-it Note–filled recipe scrums. But I wouldn’t call it stressful.

We look forward to basking in the day’s many gravy-soaked superlatives. We delight in stories that showcase celebrating family, friendship, and community while giving guidance for making the most of the holiday season. Of course, it’s a busy time, but it also brings so much joy.

I revel in the little tasks that make the day feel even more special, like sorting my china patterns and silverware, checking napkins for grease stains, and sending table linens to the cleaners for some extra TLC.

I’ve never really bought into Thanksgiving Day angst. I find the shopping stress and pressure-packed meal planning to be exaggerated myths perpetuated by pop culture. After all, the mac and cheese, potatoes, pies, and pound cakes are similar to the celebratory dishes that punctuate the year’s other holidays.

Of course, traditions vary between cultures and communities. What makes a classic Thanksgiving recipe is a matter of heritage, geography, and nostalgia. But even tradition can use a little zhuzh. New recipes, such as our Cranberry Meringue Pie and A Beautiful Cabbage Galette can add excitement—and practicality—to the holiday.

The Bon Appétit Test Kitchen has created 18 dishes, including breakfasts and variations for sides and salads to complement your family staples. We even asked five sommeliers for their recommendations for the best wines to pour on the big day.

These all add up to the best Thanksgiving ever.

Two in five American college students are food insecure. This California-based advocacy group champions food security and better educational outcomes through a network of campus food programs. swipehunger.org

People nationwide waste about 300 million pounds of food during Thanksgiving. This network of organizations collects surplus food before it ends up in landfills, providing meals to scores of people in need. feedingamerica.org

This DC-based nonprofit supports access to meals for school-age children who are experiencing hunger. It also helps during nonacademic periods, such as school holiday breaks. nokidhungry.org

#41. These Resorts Offer a Real Taste of American Regional Cuisine

No more generic resort food. These culinary-savvy properties bring a distinct sense of place to the all-inclusive experience.

American resorts are once again having a moment — and it’s not pickleball partisans driving the trend. A new generation of travelers, beset with decision fatigue in their daily lives, are embracing the all-inclusive stay where activities, amenities, and dining are all on the menu and usually just a short walk from their rooms.

Fortunately, stress-free no longer needs to mean bland or generic when it comes to cuisine and culture. Resorts have begun forging deep culinary connections to their surroundings, far beyond merely offering a few regionally specific cocktails or themed burger toppings.

Onsite farms, creameries, and distilleries provide fresh ingredients with true terroir, as well as a new category of resort activity: food-and-drink-focused tours and workshops to fill the time between morning yoga and an afternoon poolside nap.

Some resort restaurants, like Clay at Wildflower Farms in New York’s Hudson Valley and Sierra Mar at the Post Ranch Inn in Big Sur, California, have become destinations in themselves, where star chefs take diners deep into a region’s foodways.

These resorts leave visitors not just relaxed but also satisfied, having truly experienced — and tasted — a particular place.

Acura has always done things its own way. We believe the best experiences are created through intentional choices, thoughtful craftsmanship, and the confidence to pursue a different approach. This spirit is reflected in our philosophy of Precision Crafted Performance. Learn more.

By the time you get to Hawks Cay Resort in the middle of the Florida Keys, the blue vistas of the Overseas Highway will have made mainland worries seem very far away. The 60-acre resort on Duck Key offers a spa, five pools (including a saltwater lagoon), and soon a full water park. Also making a splash is Salt + Ash, the resort’s flagship live-fire restaurant from Florida native, Top Chef winner, and former Eater Miami Chef of the Year Jeremy Ford. Of course, fish and seafood from the surrounding waters feature prominently. But Florida flavors shine through in other ways too: Much of the produce on the menu comes from Ford’s Farm, strategically located between Miami Beach and the Keys. That might mean homegrown lychees in a uniquely local take on conch salad, or heirloom tomatoes just hours off the vine accompanying crisp-fried spear-caught fish.

Many resorts lay claim to a signature dish or cocktail. But the Tides Inn, situated on a quiet tributary of the Chesapeake Bay about 3 hours’ drive from Washington, D.C., has something few resorts, if any, can boast: its own oyster. Cultivated near the property by resident ecologist Will Smiley and served exclusively at the resort’s Salt & Meadow restaurant, the Widgeon oyster provides guests with an intimate connection to the estuary it calls home. To taste it is to taste the tides and the weather. “Our oyster changes salinity as the season changes, and as the weather changes,” says executive chef Kyle Perkins. He further notes that the freshwater influx with a heavy rainfall can quickly, if temporarily, change how much of a salty punch a Widgeon possesses. Beyond bivalves, Perkins sources everything from beef to blackberries from the region. Along with activities from lawn games and pickleball to kayaking, guests can even help themselves to the harvest: Those blackberries, a thornless variety, grow in abundance on the property, giving many children a first foraging experience.

Though it’s only about a 90-minute drive from the concrete canyons of Manhattan, Auberge Collection’s Wildflower Farms feels a world away. The Hudson Valley property’s 65 cabins, cottages, and suites feature floor-to-ceiling windows framing arcadian views. Thistle, an Auberge Spa, makes use of local botanicals and blooms in its treatments, while the on-site farm provides more than 14,000 pounds of produce annually for the restaurant, Clay. “The Hudson Valley is unique in the array of locally grown ingredients available,” says farm director Will Conway, noting that the resort’s culinary reach extends beyond its 140 acres. The menu is resolutely seasonal; even a dish like ricotta meatballs provides a changing taste of what is coming from nearby producers, with the protein shifting from pork to lamb depending on the time of year.

The Kohler name is, for most people, synonymous with kitchen and bath fixtures. But the company is also a serious player in hospitality, most notably with Kohler, Wisconsin, its sprawling resort in the town where the company is headquartered, two and a half hours from Chicago. Along with golf, a legendary spa, and outdoor activities like canoeing, hiking, hunting, and fishing, Kohler, Wisconsin, puts a strong emphasis on dining with Midwestern ingredients and hospitality. Among the on-site options is River Wildlife, a log cabin restaurant offering regional specialties like walleye, pheasant, and duck. The Wisconsin Room, meanwhile, combines steakhouse fare with Wisconsin supper club favorites like a “Not So Lazy” Susan, which includes deviled eggs, chicken liver mousse, and pickled vegetables in a nod to the classic relish tray. Regional cocktails like a brandy Old Fashioned and a grasshopper (de rigeur after dinner) leave no doubt where you are.

This resort three and a half hours northwest of Denver is big — about twice the size of Manhattan big. That leaves plenty of room for culinary operations that include a distillery, a bakery, and a greenhouse. Brush Creek Ranch’s herd of American wagyu cattle is raised using Japanese methods, which minimize stress in the name of producing superior marbling for added tenderness. You may not run into a steer getting a facial in one of the resort’s two spas, but rest assured, these animals are living their best lives. The ranch’s goats, meanwhile, don’t just assist with yoga classes: Some provide milk for the property’s Medicine Bow Creamery and its range of excellent cheeses. It all comes together at the Cheyenne Club restaurant, where meals and most beverages — like many of the resort’s activities, ranging from horseback riding and hiking to fly-fishing and standup paddleboard yoga — are included in the room rate.

At Castle Hot Springs, everything comes back to the water. The 130-year-old resort in the Bradshaw Mountains, about an hour north of Phoenix, was Arizona’s first spa retreat; families like the Rockefellers and Astors would come to soak in the spring-fed pools first discovered by Native American people thousands of years before. Along with a full roster of wellness and outdoor activities, the resort grows 35 types of citrus and features a 3-acre farm, irrigated by the same mineral-rich water that fills the pools. “Everything tastes a little bit better because it’s already pre-seasoned for me,” said executive chef Chris Knouse. To get a taste of “the farm on a plate,” Knouse recommends the lunchtime “farmer’s hummus,” which comes with that day’s harvest as a crudités assortment. At dinner, Harvest restaurant offers a tasting menu where dishes like cavatelli with corn, zucchini, tatsoi, and cherry tomatoes offer a deeper dive into what the Sonoran Desert can produce.

Arguably the only thing more beautiful than Post Ranch Inn is the drive there. It is, after all, located along what might be the most picturesque stretch of road in the entire country: Highway 1 in Big Sur. On a cliff overlooking the Pacific Ocean, the resort offers guests access to a spa and three pools, as well as activities like forest meditation and stargazing. Of Post Ranch Inn’s 100 acres, 90 are kept wild, and just over one is dedicated to a chef’s garden, which supplies the resort’s restaurant Sierra Mar. On this patch of land, chef Reylon Agustin and his team grow everything from apples and tomatoes to herbs and specialty ingredients like celtuce. From the surrounding forests come wild mushrooms, while nearby waters provide treasured ingredients like abalone for Sierra Mar, which is housed in a glass and wood pavilion that feels like it’s hovering over the cliff’s edge. Augustin knows well enough not to try to compete with the view. Instead, dishes like abalone congee and Grimaud Farms guinea hen with sunchokes and stone fruit highlight local ingredients to “complement the experience” of being in such a singular place.

#43. A Chef’s Guide to the Best Restaurants in Asheville, North Carolina

By Meherwan Irani as told to Jamie Feldmar

Part of what gives me so much joy about eating in Asheville is recognizing that we’re all part of a very integrated ecosystem. It feels like every restaurant I love is either run by an alum of one of the places I’ve been involved in, or by people that I’ve worked side by side with at hurricane-relief events, or by someone I know I’m going to see at the farmers market.

That’s what makes Asheville special. The folks that come in from out of town are lucky that there’s a virtuous cycle of talent here to keep the pipeline full. It’s so cool to see the evolution of this place, even if we locals don’t always realize how good we have it.It’s almost funny how not a big deal eating out here is. It’s so laid-back. We take it for granted that it’s going to be a great restaurant—of course it is! Having said that, the sheer range of restaurants is incredible. Given how small our town actually is, I sometimes find myself thinking, How lucky are we?

A hallmark of most of the restaurants I love is their connection to nearby farms. At my last count, there were more than a dozen farmers markets happening in Asheville, and there are probably more than twice as many local farms within an hour of here. Most people know the farmers by name, and nobody is precious about it. So when you go to a restaurant, they’ll just say, “It’s Evan’s greens tonight,” and everybody knows who Evan is.

The last thing is that whether it’s an Indian restaurant or a Filipino restaurant or Italian or Spanish, I love the Southern throughline in all of the dishes and hospitality here. That doesn’t mean there’s cornbread or okra in every dish; it’s honoring the fact that we all chose to open Indian or Italian restaurants here in Appalachia, so let’s not divorce the two from each other.

Let’s find a way to make it feel holistic. We do that really well. I was worried after the pandemic and Hurricane Helene that Asheville might not bounce back, but we have. I know that this place is going to continue to trailblaze for years to come.

20 Battery Park Avenue, Floor 1(828) 271-9808

Luminosa is hands down my wife, Molly, and my favorite date- night restaurant. It checks every box so beautifully. It’s intimate, but also a showstopper. It’s visually exciting to be in there, and yet [the design] doesn’t detract from the food, which they describe as “hyper-local Italian.” In the two years that they’ve been open, they’ve picked up a Michelin Green Star and a Michelin Bib Gourmand, and they deserve it. Everything about it just feels very intentional. The food is brilliantly delicious and the menu changes a lot—which sometimes drives me crazy, but it works here, because I know there’s going to be something fun and new every time I go. Their style of service and hospitality is so old-fashioned it almost borders on being antiquated, but I love it. It’s a small town at the end of the day, and everybody touches your table.

One word: respect. Katie Button and her crew have been at the top of their game for so long, you almost forget that continuing to win the championship is really hard to do. But they execute at the exact same incredibly high level as they did the first time I walked in years ago. I go there because what they do is incredible, and it’s always good to be reminded of how well they represent the tapas side of Spanish cuisine. It’s also a really exciting restaurant to be in—there’s an energy and a vibe because of the open kitchen, and it feels so intimate and fun. It’s always packed—they’re a victim of their own success—but even if I’m just going in for a glass of sherry and a plate of jamón ibérico, it’s worth pulling whatever favors I must to get in.

701 Haywood Road, Suite 102(828) 552-3880

This is a true only-in-Asheville pick, a chest-swelling-with-pride kind of choice. The chef, Silver Iocovozzi, worked with me at [two of Irani’s erstwhile restaurants] MG Road and Buxton Hall, and now they get to showcase their own cuisine, Filipino. Neng Jr.’s feels like the kind of restaurant that this city is built for. It’s so tiny and so intimate, with maybe 12 seats, so you’re packed in and you really feel like you’re eating dinner at Silver’s house. The food feels so personal—it’s brilliant and fun and totally them, with flavor profiles that remind me of Indian street food in some ways, full of fermentation and funk.

First of all, this space was converted into a restaurant without doing much to disguise the fact that it used to be a house. You’re dining on the front porch or in the side yard or in the living room, but somehow it manages to make you feel like you’re in a small village in Provence. The food has a French focus, as well as an Americana element. They win all kinds of awards for their wine program, deservedly so. Leo’s is hard to describe. It feels like this rustic little bistro where you might order something as simple as a grilled cheese sandwich and tomato soup, but when it shows up, you realize this could actually be the best grilled cheese and tomato soup you’ve ever had in your life. It’s totally unique and transportive, and it’s become my go-to spontaneous dinner recommendation for friends visiting from out of town.

I’m going to throw it back a little to one of the first places that really popped in West Asheville. Ten or 15 years ago, The Admiral was essentially a dive bar in a cinder-block building next to a gas station where probably 80 percent of Asheville’s pot deals went down. There, a young chef named Elliot Moss [ed note: later Irani’s partner at Buxton Hall] was putting out gastropub food that was blowing people’s minds. After service, they’d push all the tables to the side to clear room for these legendary dance parties. Now the neighborhood isn’t as sketchy, Elliot is long gone, and they no longer push the tables aside, but the food has not lost an inch. When you’re eating, you can just feel that it’s world-class cuisine, and reservations are hard to get, so it still feels special to get to go to The Admiral.

The best way I can describe chef Matt Dawes’s food, or at least my experience of it, is that it’s elevated British pub cuisine with a French influence and a Southern twist. The menu swings from steak frites au poivre to the best shepherd’s pie you’ve ever had to a pitch-perfect Welsh rarebit (it’s also the first place I had Welsh rabbit). The restaurant is located maybe 30 feet from the railroad tracks, next to a dirt field and one of the noisiest outdoor breweries in Asheville, but don’t let that deter you. It’s one of the most reliable and satisfying restaurants in the city.

This is a newcomer to the scene. Chef Ashleigh Shanti Santi, a James Beard Award–winner and prominent Top Chef contestant, has been a passionate advocate for Black Southern foodways. Good Hot Fish is exactly what it sounds like: a fish counter with amazing hot fish sandwiches and seafood, plus the perfect sides. All of the fish she serves comes from local waterways. There’s fried catfish and Gulf shrimp burgers and fish dip with fried saltines. It’s literally just a counter with a few stools against the wall, but the technique is immaculate. The sandwiches are served on squishy white bread with buttermilk tartare sauce, and it delivers on its promise of being the best damn hot fish sandwich you’ve ever had.

I have to give a shout-out here to one of the OGs. To call All Souls just great pizza does it a disservice; you need to understand the backstory. David Bauer, was one of the first bread gurus/savants of Asheville. Farm and Sparrow, his bakery, helped usher in the modern renaissance of heirloom grains and bread that you now see everywhere. He grew his own grain, milled his own flour, and made these amazing breads. Then he helped open All Souls, which makes pizza using stone-ground heirloom grains, in a style I can only describe as Carolina pizza. It’s our own thing, with our own grains, cooked in a wood-fired oven with toppings that come from within 50 miles or so. It’s in a building that was a diner for decades in West Asheville, next to a big old field where you can spread out a picnic blanket if the restaurant is full. All Souls is a classic example of doing one thing, doing it well, and not being too uptight about it, which is everything I love about Asheville.

244 Short Coxe Avenue, #110(828) 505-1003

I have to include two bakeries here. Mother serves a full lunch and dinner menu, so it’s a little more on the restaurant side of things. It’s again in a weird part of Asheville, sandwiched between a sauna and a tire shop, with garage doors that open to a front patio that looks like a loading ramp for trucks. And yet, like so many places here, it’s totally transportive. You feel like you’re eating in Europe somehow. Their jambon-beurre sandwich is the closest I’ve had to Fauchon’s in Paris, and their pumpernickel bread is divine. It feels like a restaurant run by a group of passionate friends that care deeply about food and hospitality, who all got together to open a little place as a gift to the community, because that’s exactly what it is.

I would describe Owl as a bakery with Southern sensibilities and French technique. I’d put the lamination on their croissants up against anything in Stockholm. They’re known for their almond rose croissants, cardamom buns, and squirrel bread [a seed-and-nut loaf], and if you don’t get there right at 8 a.m. they’re going to be sold out. Sometimes I look at the people lining up, and I want to shake each and every one of them and yell, “Do you have any idea how good you have it right now?!” I actually have to resist doing that as I see them gabbing away over their morning pastries and lattes without a care in the world, not recognizing that the rest of us have to schlep around the world God knows how many times to find anything even close to this good in terms of quality and execution. And that’s just life in Asheville.

It’s an honorable mention, because I haven’t stepped foot in the restaurant for 17 years, but I get takeout from Rocky’s almost every Sunday, when I host a men’s group at my house where we discuss things like “How do you actually define electro music?” and play Crocodile, a weird Canadian board game. In the very crowded field of hot fried chicken, Rocky’s stands at the top, because their chicken is actually melt-your-face hot, not “oh-look-how-cute” Nashville hot. Beginners should get the medium. The hot is for veterans, and the extra hot is something the CIA should use to extract information. The crust is thin and it has the perfect amount of crunch, and the seasoning goes all the way through. But most importantly, every week we get the same order, and never once in 17 years have they messed up that order. I feel like a highly underrated aspect of a great restaurant is doing exactly the same thing 52 weeks out of the year, and I have mad respect for Rocky’s.

Meherwan Irani, of Chai Pani and Spicewalla, shares his go-to places to eat and drink in his adopted hometown.

By Meherwan Irani as told to Jamie Feldmar

By Meherwan Irani as told to Jamie Feldmar

Part of what gives me so much joy about eating in Asheville is recognizing that we’re all part of a very integrated ecosystem. It feels like every restaurant I love is either run by an alum of one of the places I’ve been involved in, or by people that I’ve worked side by side with at hurricane-relief events, or by someone I know I’m going to see at the farmers market.

That’s what makes Asheville special. The folks that come in from out of town are lucky that there’s a virtuous cycle of talent here to keep the pipeline full. It’s so cool to see the evolution of this place, even if we locals don’t always realize how good we have it.It’s almost funny how not a big deal eating out here is. It’s so laid-back. We take it for granted that it’s going to be a great restaurant—of course it is! Having said that, the sheer range of restaurants is incredible. Given how small our town actually is, I sometimes find myself thinking, How lucky are we?

A hallmark of most of the restaurants I love is their connection to nearby farms. At my last count, there were more than a dozen farmers markets happening in Asheville, and there are probably more than twice as many local farms within an hour of here. Most people know the farmers by name, and nobody is precious about it. So when you go to a restaurant, they’ll just say, “It’s Evan’s greens tonight,” and everybody knows who Evan is.

The last thing is that whether it’s an Indian restaurant or a Filipino restaurant or Italian or Spanish, I love the Southern throughline in all of the dishes and hospitality here. That doesn’t mean there’s cornbread or okra in every dish; it’s honoring the fact that we all chose to open Indian or Italian restaurants here in Appalachia, so let’s not divorce the two from each other.

Let’s find a way to make it feel holistic. We do that really well. I was worried after the pandemic and Hurricane Helene that Asheville might not bounce back, but we have. I know that this place is going to continue to trailblaze for years to come.

20 Battery Park Avenue, Floor 1(828) 271-9808

Luminosa is hands down my wife, Molly, and my favorite date- night restaurant. It checks every box so beautifully. It’s intimate, but also a showstopper. It’s visually exciting to be in there, and yet [the design] doesn’t detract from the food, which they describe as “hyper-local Italian.” In the two years that they’ve been open, they’ve picked up a Michelin Green Star and a Michelin Bib Gourmand, and they deserve it. Everything about it just feels very intentional. The food is brilliantly delicious and the menu changes a lot—which sometimes drives me crazy, but it works here, because I know there’s going to be something fun and new every time I go. Their style of service and hospitality is so old-fashioned it almost borders on being antiquated, but I love it. It’s a small town at the end of the day, and everybody touches your table.

One word: respect. Katie Button and her crew have been at the top of their game for so long, you almost forget that continuing to win the championship is really hard to do. But they execute at the exact same incredibly high level as they did the first time I walked in years ago. I go there because what they do is incredible, and it’s always good to be reminded of how well they represent the tapas side of Spanish cuisine. It’s also a really exciting restaurant to be in—there’s an energy and a vibe because of the open kitchen, and it feels so intimate and fun. It’s always packed—they’re a victim of their own success—but even if I’m just going in for a glass of sherry and a plate of jamón ibérico, it’s worth pulling whatever favors I must to get in.

701 Haywood Road, Suite 102(828) 552-3880

#44. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#46. Are We in a Reading Monoculture?

BookTok promised us endless discovery. So why does everyone seem to be reading the same thing?

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Maybe you were by a pool this summer, or on a beach, or on a train headed to either of the above. As though in a particularly on-the-nose Black Mirror episode, you looked left, looked right, and there were the season’s ubiquitous books: Strangers, Famesick, or Yesteryear. The hardcovers multiplied, like Tribbles, across your timeline. Your book club was reading them, and your friend’s book club was too. The library hold list was longer than the waitlist for a kidney transplant.

It’s become a truism that we no longer live in a monoculture. Save for events like the Super Bowl and the VMAs, there are few cultural events that unite us anymore. The kinds of movies that once seemed predestined to be blockbusters fail to attract an audience. “Must-see TV” seems as conceptually distant as cave painting. Lots of people have apparently never heard the No. 1 song in the country (Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas”) and the ones who have probably aren’t listening to Music, Fashion, Film. But the literary landscape, at least lately, feels like a throwback to a time when consensus coalesced around just a few cultural products.

I enjoyed all of the aforementioned titles (I even interviewed debut novelist Caro Claire Burke about Yesteryear), so this isn’t to say that any of the above are undeserving of their massive success. But as the take machine ground all three titles into its jaws, I found myself thinking: Where were the weird, fringe authors, the obscure titles BookTok and Bookstagram and book Substack (BookStack?) were supposed to introduce us to?

The internet promised us endless variety, but precious few titles seem to penetrate the collective consciousness these days. According to Publishers Weekly, over 600,000 books were released by traditional publishers last year, to say nothing of the countless small-press and independent publishers. Why did fewer and fewer feel anointed?

To find out, I consulted a self-convened panel of writers and readers. First, I turned to Maris Kreizman, the essayist, critic, and author of I Want to Burn This Place Down. We found ourselves commiserating over the fact that book coverage is not what it used to be. Every time I find a great used book, I told her, it’s a gut punch to open to the first few pages and see the reviews from publications that either no longer exist or no longer publish a book review supplement. That has a trickle-down effect, Kreizman says. “With book criticism completely falling apart, there are fewer ways, even for TikTokers, to find out about new books.”

Book review sections also used to provide a sense of curation. “I don’t know how a book becomes The Book, but I do know that when it does, everybody’s ready to talk about it. Everybody’s ready to get on the train,” Kreizman says. “So it’s really not about discovery anymore. It’s about, ‘What’s the book that people are talking about and should we then cover it?’”

Lincoln Michel, who is the author of titles including Metallic Realms and a book critic himself, notes that “it’s easier to get clicks online for an article that is about a topic related to a book, something like tradwives or affairs, than for a traditional review.”

Kreizman also points to the fact that the book publishing industry, like so many others, has been squeezed by corporate consolidation. As a result, “You have the same sales teams trying to sell these huge lists of books from across the company and they need help prioritizing,” she says. “It’s now a time when you could be published by the Big Five and still be a total underdog. It doesn’t get you anything anymore, really.”

Book publishing, “like many culture industries, has kind of a blockbuster model, and it’s become more and more that way over recent decades,” says Michel. “The publishers are kept afloat by a few titles that sell massively, and everything else is kind of throwing something against the wall and hoping it sticks….In a certain way, it’s the story of the entire American economy, where everything is increasingly K-shaped, where a handful of people amass more and more of the money and attention. And one thing publishers will tell you is the midlist has kind of disappeared.”

Even “old-new books,” as an essay in the latest issue of n+1 calls them, tend to follow that K-shaped path. Certain once-undersung authors go posthumously or late-in-life viral (see: Eve Babitz, Nancy Lemann, and more recently Barbara Trapido) in a move that parallels debut novelists’ path to success in 2026, combined with the satisfaction of someone being rescued from the well of obscurity. But even these reissues, intended to fill in the gaps in literary history, have their yawning blind spots. (According to the n+1 story, one of the most popular reissuers has only published one book by a Black American author in the past decade.)

But it’s not entirely a publisher problem, or a media problem. It’s also a reader problem. The same sense of cultural FOMO that leads us to wait on endless Ticketmaster queues or line up for a new fashion collaboration drop is also driving the rise of books that demand to be discussed, whether it’s Burden’s bruising experiences with infidelity and divorce or Dunham’s divulgent mix of Hollywood insider goss and personal revelations. “I think as much as reading is a solitary activity, in one way, it’s also a very communal one,” Michel, who has a Substack newsletter called Counter Craft, says. “You want to read what your friends are reading. Even if you hate it. In my literary Substack circles, the most recent Rachel Cusk book [Life of M] got a lot of disparate reactions. There were people who were hating the book and some who were loving it, but you’re more likely to read it, even if you think you’re going to dislike it, because you get to be part of the conversation.”

Ochuko Akpovbovbo, a brand consultant and the writer of the Substack newsletter As Seen On, underscores the importance of the discourse when it comes to attracting readers. “For Gen Z women, [these books] tap into bigger conversations that were already happening, that were already big on TikTok.” The platform, she says, lends itself to “How many buzzwords can you attach to a book? And is it going to be something that people are going to have personal experience with, thoughts on, disagreements about, hot takes? You could really sit down as a publisher and try to reverse-engineer the success of a book in that way. A book that could have thrived on its nuance in those long reviews in The New York Times isn’t the same kind of book that can really thrive on BookTok.”

Writing in Dazed, Natalie Beecroft posits that another factor is “making us all read the same thing”—AI chatbots. As a bookseller, she is finding that customers are increasingly coming in with ChatGPT-sourced recommendations, and others in her profession are reporting the same. The problem, she writes, is that “the reading choices that AI vomits out pander to commercial interests using algorithms which reward whatever is already popular,” she writes. “ChatGPT can’t find the indie titles, small presses, and debut authors that deserve attention. Due to algorithmic bias, it is far less likely to recommend books by authors of color or translated fiction.”

There’s also the fact that readers, like everyone else, are increasingly time-poor. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, Americans over age 15 had a little over five hours of leisure time per week in 2025; an average of 16 minutes per week was spent reading for pleasure. Even bibliophiles may find that their appetite is bigger than their proverbial plate. When pressed for time, those who still have time to read at all may opt for the lowest-hanging fruit.

Akpovbovbo carves out the time to read 15 to 20 books per month, and posts a monthly reading roundup on As Seen On; she also hosts a regular book club feature on the platform with fellow Substack writer Pandora Sykes. (Most recently, they discussed Kathryn Stockett’s The Calamity Club.) “When you read a certain amount of books a month, you’ll go broke if you try to get all the recent releases,” she tells me. “Thankfully, I get sent a lot of those, but it’s simply not enough. And then you get more curious and you can’t read 10 ‘sad girl lit’ books in a row. I think over time, my reading scope has definitely widened.” That said, “I’m never going to avoid the noise of a really big book.” She read all three of the summer’s big blockbusters. (“I loved Famesick. I thought Yesteryear was okay. Strangers was really fun.”)

She thinks about the landscape right now as a series of layers. At the top are “books with massive budgets that are being spammed and sent to every bookish creator there is. But beneath that, and for people who are really interested in reading or really interested in appearing to read, you definitely see a rejection of the very popular books. You see people wanting to be like, ‘I’m reading a lot of translated fiction,’ or ‘I’m reading a lot of really weird subversive fiction that you might not get but I get,’ or ‘I’m reading a lot of queer literature,’ or ‘I’m reading a lot of classics that are not getting air.’ Maybe because I’m really deep into that world, I see a lot of that stratification. I see a lot of that variety. But the machine of getting books into the hands of creators is so massive right now that when a publisher has a big budget for a book, you really feel it.”

So how can readers break out of the Matrix? For those lucky enough to live close to a great independent bookstore, there are good old-fashioned staff recommendations. But there’s also a growing number of Bookstagrammers and newsletter writers catering to readers who seek something more obscure. Writer and critic Molly Young has been doing this for years, vaulting little-known titles back into the conversation. (She was talking about Trapido’s Brother of the More Famous Jack, now freshly reissued by NYRB Classics, back in 2018.) I’m also partial to my former colleague Emily Coleman’s recently launched Substack, Favorable Margins, in which she features a mix of old and new releases—think Diana Vreeland nestling next to Zoe Dubno.

In addition to recommending the work of Sykes, Akpovbovbo cites Nic Marna’s newsletter Milking It and Martha Adams’s Martha’s Monthly as sources for finding off-the-beaten-path ideas. (A casual poll of ELLE editors included Books Are Magic, The Strand, fellow ELLE staffers, and the influencer Jack Edwards as their go-tos for finding new titles to add to their TBRs.)

With “taste” becoming such a single-minded obsession among everyone from tech bros to fragrance heads, soon, reading the “big books” might be passé. And uncovering more niche, even semi-forgotten authors could be a status signal, proclaiming that you’ve tapped out of the monoculture. But take heart in the fact that no matter what you’re reading, it will be obscure to someone. Jokes Michel, “My corner of literary Substack talks about completely different books, to the point that when my wife was reading Strangers, I was like, ‘What is that?’ I hadn’t heard of it.”

#47. Chicken Pot Pie Casserole

Chicken pot pie is a warm, hearty crowd-pleaser. But for all the comfort it delivers, it can be a difficult dinner dish, with hours of work required to make the perfect pie crust. So, we came up with the perfect solution: chicken pot pie casserole. Classic chicken pot pie filling is baked into a stress-free casserole, topped with buttery biscuits (my favorite store-bought hack) for that tantalizing golden-brown finish. In a little more than an hour, you’ll have a crowd-pleasing weeknight dinner on your hands—no pie crust required.

This casserole is all about ease. After preheating the oven to 375º, melt butter in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add your diced carrots, celery, onion, thyme, and salt to the skillet, and cook until softened. This should take around 5 to 7 minutes—make sure you are stirring often! Once softened, add the flour and stir to fully coat the vegetables.

After cooking for a couple of minutes more, add the milk, broth, mustard, garlic powder, and even more salt. Whisk to combine, then increase the heat to bring the mixture to a boil. Once boiling, immediately reduce the heat to medium so the mixture can simmer. Let simmer, stirring often, until it has visibly thickened. This should take around 3 to 5 minutes. Once thickened, fold in the chicken and peas. Give it a taste, and add more salt as needed.

Once your mixture is to your liking, transfer it to a baking dish. Grab your biscuits, separate them, then arrange them on top of the filling. Give the entire dish a good sprinkle of salt and pepper, then bake.

Bake until the filling is bubbling, and the biscuits are golden and risen. This should take around 22 to 25 minutes, but depending on the size of your biscuits, they may need longer in the oven. Once done, let the casserole cool for around 5 minutes before serving.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

If you have any leftovers, store them in the fridge in an airtight container for around 3 days. Keep in mind that as time goes on, the biscuits will start to lean more on the soggy side. For the crispiest biscuit topping possible, enjoy this casserole the day of, or separate the biscuits after cooking.

#49. Want to Know What Ivy Wolk Thinks About the Massachusetts Lesbian Bar?

In honor of her Broadway debut in Downstate, the actor tells Cosmopolitan about the power of live theater, her spiritual connection to maligned women, and why she’s a tech optimist.

Within the span of 12 hours, comedian and actor Ivy Wolk posted these things on her Instagram: an AI-generated video of an animated wooden paddle spanking a woman with a wooden paddle; a video of comedian Nick Viagas’s mother asking people to “see my large disabled son on tour”; a video edition of her monthly advice column “Born Sexy Yesterday” for the Julie morning-after pill; a photo of Newt Gingrich’s wife “Cally” (in bright blue) posing awkwardly with a U.S. ambassador-at-large (also in bright blue); a clip from the show English Teacher in which Ivy played a high school student; a shot of the marquee for her latest acting project, the Broadway play Downstate; and no fewer than four pictures of a police horse outside the aforementioned Broadway theater. “Bitch it’s a horse outside of Downstate rn” she wrote. “When you’re a machine of the carceral state but you’re also a horse,” she said in another.

It’s no accident that a collection of Instagram Stories on a random day sums up Ivy’s unique résumé and singular point of view: brainy, absurd, charming, occasionally abrasive, very online, and thoroughly booked. Ivy’s internet isn’t just a vehicle for bald promotion; it’s an artistic medium. This year, the media, as well as iconic, equally polarizing stars like Sandra Bernhard and Courtney Love, caught on to what Ivy’s online fans and haters have known for years: When she posts (or talks or acts or writes), we pay attention.

Her name is Effie, and she is a bratty, steadfast girl who works at Staples in Southern Illinois. One of her coworkers is a registered sex offender, and she drives him to and from their job every day, and they have a volatile, funny relationship. The play is a chamber drama, and it all takes place over the course of one day in a house where the coworker lives with other sex offenders. Effie is the kind of a girl who is just bored after work and wants to go somewhere, even if it’s in the house of four, you know, messy pedophiles.

I think this show is going to be the zeitgeist-y ticket of the season. I also hope that my inclusion in this cast will get young people who know me from the internet or stand-up comedy or TV out to come and, like, sit their asses down for two and a half hours and just fucking pay attention. There’s a misconception that Gen Z are not good, attentive audiences or they’re not interested in being audiences of live performance, and I think that’s just not true.

I’ve always wanted to do theater. It’s what made me fall in love with performance as a craft. I grew up in a children’s musical theater conservatory. I’m very accepting of lowbrow culture in all other facets of art, but theater is the one thing that I’m very pretentious about.

Primarily, I’m a stand-up comedian and the immediacy of the form is really important to me. It’s why I use the internet the way that I do—posting constantly, very quickly—it feels very intimate. That’s what I love for art to feel like. Theater provides this immediacy and sort of acceleration of response. I want to hear people gasping in the audience. I want to hear people laughing. I want to see where people pull back. That’s something that you don’t really get from film.

It’s the fullest extent of what it is that I want to do. I think that my ideas are interesting—ergo people should hear what I have to say. But I also think that the work I can do is interesting, and I like being a conduit for somebody else’s vision. I don’t ever really view myself as an extension of a TV network or movie studio. I’m not a product for them to move around and place. I am an autonomous person with thoughts and ideas, and that comes from being a comedian. Some people make a choice to just be a performer and then disappear in the interim. I think, especially for people of my generation, that schism is fear-based. But I’m not fearful of people knowing what I have to say or what I think. What I’m offering on the internet is a very uncurated-seeming sense of self, and there’s not much pretense. Most people cling to the idea of privacy as a big thing, but I am private when I insist that I want to be private. It doesn’t have to be so bifurcated for me.

All the press about me is like, “A lot of people on Twitter are saying you’re a nasty bitch and you’re everywhere. Care to comment?” And yet, even if people expressed disdain for it or judgment, they could not ignore me. I think people find me, for better and for worse, very sticky and attractive, not always in a good way.

I’ve been labeled annoying since I was a very little girl. I have this high voice, and it sort of hits above other people’s vocal registers, so even at school, when everybody was talking, the teacher was like, “Ivy, be quiet.” Because you could just hear me over everybody. I’m very intense about the things that I like and care about. I have a thorough perspective on my own self and my own work and my own taste. I always have, since I was a very small child.

Around the time I was 13, I started posting publicly on the internet and pretty much immediately the general response was like, “Who the fuck are you? You’re so loud. Why is this what you think is funny? Why is this what you think is interesting?” Which was the same shit that I faced at school and at summer camp. And yet, even if people expressed disdain for it, they could not ignore me. Today, regardless of who was paying attention, I would be posting myself on the internet willy-nilly. I do it because I like connecting with people and using the internet as an artistic medium.

Yeah, they have to pretend that they’re stoked on tech so that we’re not so scared when the robots are breaking down our doors. But I am kind of a tech optimist. People are letting the phone serve them anything, and they’re feeling, like, beholden to the phone. You have to make the phone serve you. You have to make the world in the phone look how you want it to look, and you look at your phone and you see stuff that is funny and interesting and provocative and that makes you happy. You just have to train an algorithm. But it’s totally possible to not feel like you’re in a pit of shit at all times.

I am so down to talk about it. It’s interesting fodder that did not need to spread as far and wide as it did. It was like a circus article—“Look at the monkeys in the zoo”—which, of course, is fun, and there’s gossip and cattiness and it brought us all together on the internet for a week. But that community is so insular. There would be no way anybody who is not a part of that Western Massachusetts bar-going, mask-wearing community would have any interaction with these people—it’s so silly.

But also my big question, really, which is also silly, was: Which disabilities do you guys even have? Does every person at this bar have some sort of disability that if they take a mask off, they will immediately burst into flames? None of these people are being forthright about what they actually need protection from. It’s just that the mask wearers want to keep things exactly as they are. People want to feel safe. People want to feel like their communities are not being infringed upon. People want to feel like they can show up on Saturday night and see that everybody is wearing a mask because that’s what they’ve come to expect. Because the world outside this bar is so hectic. I have empathy for that, but also I would never be in a room with any of those people. Our lives don’t coincide.

At this point, the dossier is so long of anything that I could have said that would impede or prevent a career. I mean, I’ll probably never be in a Marvel movie, but am I interested in being in a Marvel movie? No, not really. Most of the filmmakers and directors and writers I’ve worked with are people who are similar to me in their senses of humor and references. They’re people who make work that is irascible and provocative and punchy, and that’s the kind of stuff that I make.

There was a moment where call-out culture hit the entire internet and people at the helm were responding to it. But these days, most people at the helm in Hollywood are not kowtowing to public pressure like that. I think everybody has realized that that is futile. And firing somebody from a movie for a tweet that they made 15 years ago is not what’s going to make the country feel like a more hospitable place to live. It’s deeper structural issues that are oppressing us.

People think that they give a shit about these things, but then they actually don’t. They’re not actually paying attention. That’s not a name that’s on people’s lips. He’s a nice, normal guy. I’ll say it: He’s a chiller. I find him to be normal and professional and pleasant. I think people can be different from what they once were. I don’t think anybody is so permanent.

People think that I am whatever I tweeted. That my entire being and my entire personality and all of my values can be encapsulated in one post on the internet. But life is long and things mutate and people move and people shift and you have awakenings and things startle you and you figure shit out. The fact that people still hold me to standards online that they held me to when I was, like, 14 years old is crazy to me. So I would never do that to another person. It’s a major tenet of my politics as an abolitionist, as an empathy-first leftist, that we actually have to meet people where they’re at and hope that against all odds, people’s hearts are intrinsically good and that people only want the best for one another.

It’s not literally like I’m sitting in front of a shrine of Elizabeth Taylor and pushing my crystals around. It’s more that it’s my heritage. They’re women whose fucking faces and output are seared into my brain. Who experienced the same shit as me. It’s like all of this knowledge that they’ve accrued flows through me. It’s intellectual. It’s emotional. It’s spiritual. It’s so deeply entrenched.

I read a lot about fame studies, celebrity studies, media theory, postmodern theory. I’m trying to understand and intellectualize using myself as the case study, so I am hitting the fucking books. I know so many young celebrities who pass off all the shit that they’re undergoing as frivolous or only acknowledge it with a sense of irony, like, “Isn’t this so stupid?” And it’s like…but you’re still here and you’re still doing it and this is still your life. Find out what motivates you toward this and become more intelligent and interesting.

I’m not interested in presenting as easygoing or simple. I guess the central thesis is that I’ve never done anything for anybody’s comfortability. Instead of trying to figure out how to make people comfortable, I try to figure out how I can be smarter.
