#50. Make-Ahead Mashed Potatoes

Thanksgiving dinner can feel like a game of Tetris, but this make-ahead mashed potato recipe gives you one less thing to juggle. It lets you prepare the potatoes up to two days in advance, then reheat them just before serving without sacrificing their rich flavor or velvety texture.

The secret is in the technique: Simmer whole, skin-on Yukon Gold potatoes to keep them from absorbing excess water, then pass them through a potato ricer with plenty of butter. Adding the butter before the warm milk and cream coats the potato starches in fat, helping the mash stay smooth and creamy even after refrigeration. A little sour cream adds a welcome tang.

For extra flavor, try adding roasted garlic, finely grated Parmesan, or infusing the milk and cream, as we do in BA’s Best Mashed Potatoes, with bay leaves, thyme, or rosemary.

How far in advance can you make mashed potatoes?

Up to two days. Let the finished mashed potatoes cool slightly, then cover and refrigerate promptly. Need a longer head start? Learn how to freeze mashed potatoes.

How do you reheat mashed potatoes without making them gummy?

Gently warm them in a saucepan over medium-low heat with the additional milk and cream to restore the proper consistency. Stir often but gently to prevent scorching without overworking the potatoes, which can turn them gluey.

The potatoes may have absorbed too much water during cooking. For this recipe, simmer them whole, with the skins on, until very tender but not falling apart. Drain well and let them dry in the warm pot before ricing. Add the warm milk and cream gradually, stopping when the potatoes reach your desired consistency.

No. Leaving the skins on while boiling helps prevent waterlogging, and most of the peels will stay behind in the ricer. Clear out the collected skins between batches to prevent clogging. If you prefer to peel the potatoes yourself, do so after cooking, while they’re still warm.

Can you make mashed potatoes without a ricer?

A food mill fitted with a fine disk is your best alternative. A potato masher will produce a less uniform texture and requires peeling the potatoes first. Avoid a food processor or blender, which can overwork the starches and make the potatoes gluey.

OXO Good Grips Stainless Steel Potato Ricer

Rubbermaid Brilliance Glass Food Storage Containers

Place 4 lb. medium Yukon Gold potatoes, scrubbed, in a large pot and pour in cold water to cover by 1". Add a large handful of kosher salt (water should taste briny, like the ocean) and bring to a boil. Reduce heat and simmer until potatoes are very tender but not crumbly, 30–40 minutes. Drain and return potatoes to warm pot to dry (off heat).

Meanwhile, heat ⅔ cup heavy cream and ⅔ cup whole milk in a small saucepan over medium until just about to simmer. Reduce heat to low and keep warm until ready to add to potatoes.

Pass hot potatoes and 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) unsalted butter, cut into pieces, through ricer into a large bowl (this will help combine them quickly; most of the skins should stay behind, but pick out any small pieces that get through if you want); season generously with salt. Mix with a potato masher until butter is melted and combined.

Gradually add half of the warm cream mixture to mashed potatoes, folding with a spatula until combined, followed by ½ cup sour cream. Gradually add remaining cream mixture until you reach your desired consistency (the potatoes will thicken slightly as they sit). Taste and season with salt and freshly ground black pepper as desired.

Transfer mashed potatoes to a baking dish or other shallow container, let them cool until the potatoes stop steaming, then cover and chill up to 2 days.

To serve, transfer refrigerated potatoes to a small pot and add ⅓ cup heavy cream and ⅓ cup whole milk; reheat over medium-low, stirring often (but gently) to prevent scorching.

#51. Enjoy Fishing, Foraging, and Focaccia-Making at These U.S. Resorts

Guests today expect more than a Michelin-starred restaurant. They want to get into the kitchen and out in the field.

Plenty of resorts across the country have excellent restaurants, but travelers seeking more should explore the hands-on side of culinary resort experiences. From New York’s Hudson Valley to the South Texas Coast, adventurous food lovers can partake in workshops and experiences that get them out of the dining room and into the kitchen, garden, farm, or ocean. Whether you’re looking to forage or fish, these excursions will introduce you to local people, ingredients, and techniques, and ultimately offer a true taste of the destination.

At these properties, it’s less about what’s on your plate and more about how it got there. Big Sur is the perfect place to forage for edible botanicals and aromatics, and on Chesapeake Bay, harvesting and shucking oysters is woven into the community’s cultural fabric. Those wanting to escape the hustle and bustle of New York City can head up to the Hudson Valley for focaccia-making, while a desert oasis on the outskirts of Scottsdale, Arizona, teaches you how to craft pasta like a pro.

No matter your level of expertise, these resort experiences are designed to connect curious travelers with an impressive network of chefs, farmers, ecologists, mixologists, and bakers. For a vacation that will also quench your thirst for knowledge, head to these exciting culinary resorts.

Acura has always done things its own way. We believe the best experiences are created through intentional choices, thoughtful craftsmanship, and the confidence to pursue a different approach. This spirit is reflected in our philosophy of Precision Crafted Performance. Learn more.

Head down to the South Texas Coast for a true catch-to-table culinary experience. Local guides at La Pesca Lodge take guests to prime spots throughout Baffin Bay, offering everything from fly-fishing and wading to drifting and sight casting. Though you’re welcome to bring your own gear, the lodge provides spinning rods, lures, and live bait if needed.

Expect to reel in an array of speckled trout, redfish, flounder, and black drum. Your catch will be cleaned and bagged for you to take back to the lodge, where chefs transform your bounty into ceviche, grilled fillets, and more. Just remember that you’ll need to purchase your own Texas fishing license in advance. Those more interested in old-fashioned hunting can partake in dove, duck, or nilgai shoots.

The Andaz Scottsdale Resort & Bungalows is a retro, palm-tree-lined oasis with a premier spa, unique art collection, and the on-site restaurant Weft & Warp. Every Thursday, guests can beat the desert heat with a hands-on pasta class in the restaurant for $65.

You’ll learn a variety of techniques while crafting a few different pasta shapes. You might make agnolotti filled with a chive and shrimp paste; and you will also learn simpler pastas, like classic linguine or fettuccine. Once you’re done, enjoy your finished product with an optional wine pairing on the patio. If you’ve got dessert on the brain, book the Sweet Escape truffle-making workshop (hosted every Friday) and elevate your pastry skills by learning the basics of chocolate tempering.

Virginia’s Tides Inn gives travelers the chance to live like a Chesapeake waterman for the day. This signature activity pairs guests with a resident ecologist who takes you out to oyster cages via boat for an educational experience that’s all about shellfish. You’ll haul up your own oyster cages and sort through the very best bivalves, all while learning about the region’s longstanding history with oystering and the positive impact it has on the local ecosystem. Oysters harvested during the excursion need to be refrigerated for at least 24 hours, so when you return to the inn, enjoy a shucking how-to with the previous day’s haul while sipping on local wine and beer. The Chesapeake Gold experience is a similar outing, but includes a visit to one of the inn’s very own oyster farms, meaning you get to consume the same ones you collect. Once back at the inn, enjoy them both raw, grilled, and topped with your favorite seasonings.

Located in the foothills of Tennessee’s Great Smoky Mountains, Blackberry Farm is a working estate that maintains a strong connection to Appalachian agriculture. A twice-daily farmstead tour is available all year long, giving guests an in-depth look at the heirloom gardens, heritage livestock pasture, and dairy barn. These manicured, bright green gardens create a scenic backdrop to your itinerary, which includes sampling of farmstead cheeses, cured meats, preserves, and a rotating seasonal beverage. Those wanting a more formal culinary experience can book a three-hour artisan cooking demo with a three-course educational lunch and a glass of wine to pair.

Located about an hour and 20 minutes away from Phoenix, Castle Hot Springs is a picturesque desert resort with a thriving agricultural operation. The 3-acre garden yields more than 150 seasonal fruits, veggies, herbs, and flowers, supporting a dynamic farm-to-table ethos across the resort’s Relais & Châteaux-approved restaurant, Harvest.

Start your day with a one-hour farm tour, tasting your way through a variety of crops as you learn about the fertile soils supported by the area’s natural geothermal hot springs. In the afternoon, test your skills with a hands-on mixology class using produce and botanicals straight from the property grounds.

Ready to hard-launch your sourdough baking era? Learn the basics with Ashley Napoli, also known as the Focaccia Flourist, at the Hudson Valley’s Wildflower Farms. This Auberge Collection property is about 90 miles away from New York City, which makes it an easy escape for city dwellers needing to touch some grass.

The focaccia workshop costs $168 per person and starts by teaching you how to care for and maintain a living sourdough starter. You then knead, arrange, and shape your loaf, topping it with herbs, onions, florals, olives, and anything you’d like before baking. This particular workshop is being offered every Sunday and Tuesday through the end of October, but the resort typically hosts some version of a focaccia class throughout the year.

In Big Sur, towering redwood forest meets dramatic, bluff-lined coast, creating a diverse ecosystem brimming with unique plant life. The serene 54-room Alila Ventana Big Sur is a wellness-focused resort that spans 160 acres of lush, open meadows, tree-lined trails, and shaded ravines, creating the ideal conditions for a plethora of fungi and botanicals.

Every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, the hotel hosts a complimentary foragers hike for guests, who will learn all about wild-food harvesting and spotting secret ingredients hidden within the local terrain. There’s also a year-round Foragers Cocktail class ($99), a more in-depth experience that begins with an outdoor search for various herbs and aromatics, and culminates in a mixology lesson where you craft small-batch bitters for a custom cocktail.

#54. What Goes Into Making Real-Deal Prosciutto di Parma PDO

There are precious few food products that have been enjoyed for as much of human history as Prosciutto di Parma. The signature silky texture and buttery, sweet-savory flavor of the “King of Hams” is recognized around the world as the result of carefully controlled production methods, dedication to quality, and traditions continued for centuries.

The history of Prosciutto di Parma reaches back more than 2,000 years, to Roman times, when the art of preserving pork through salting and natural drying was already well established in the Po Valley. As early as the 3rd century BC, Cato the Elder described methods for curing pork legs with salt and allowing them to dry and mature. Today, Prosciutto di Parma is produced exclusively in a strictly defined area of northern Italy, in the province of Parma in the Emilia-Romagna region, where local know-how combines with distinctive climatic conditions. Humid breezes from the Tyrrhenian Sea become drier as they flow over the Apennines and down onto the hills. Prosciutto producers discovered that this created an ideal environment for dry aging, and they built storerooms with tall windows that could be opened and closed as necessary, allowing the air to circulate through the racks of hams for gradual drying.

The specifics of aging, like every step in the process, are governed by a consortium—the Consorzio del Prosciutto di Parma—that was founded in 1963 to protect the authenticity of the product. In 1996, Prosciutto di Parma obtained the European Union’s Protected Designation of Origin (PDO). These have a red and yellow seal to show that a product is made in a certain geographical area using time-honored, traditional methods. Grana Padano, a nutty, aged hard cheese also from Northern Italy that’s often paired with Prosciutto di Parma on a charcuterie plate, was awarded a PDO the same year.

Grana Padano PDO and Prosciutto di Parma PDO also share the distinction of being fire-branded—a sign for consumers that you are buying the real thing. Only Parma hams that meet the PDO’s specifications can receive the five-pronged Ducal Crown that signifies a true Prosciutto di Parma.

Well before that brand is applied, production starts with the pigs. Which breeds, where they can be bred and raised (in 11 Italian regions), and what they are fed (a list that also includes whey from local cheesemakers) are all precisely detailed. Within the 28th day from birth, the piglets receive a breeder tattoo that will also appear on the final product along with the crown brand. The fresh pork (hind legs only) sent to prosciutto producers must weigh between 26 pounds and 40 pounds, with a set amount of fat coverage. After they arrive at the production facility, the legs are trimmed to form the characteristic rounded shape, chilled to a precise temperature, and salted by hand with sea salt, which joins the pork as the only two ingredients that go into the making of Prosciutto di Parma PDO.

Following a resting period of at least 90 days, the hams are washed then hung in windowed storerooms to dry slowly. The next step is called sugnatura: The parts of the ham not covered by rind are rubbed with sugna—a mixture of pork fat, salt, and pepper—to keep the meat from drying too quickly. For final aging, the hams hang in cool, dimly lit cellars. From start to finish, the process cannot last less than 14 months (many producers continue aging for 24, 30, or even 36 months and beyond). The last step before inspection may be the most fascinating: The hams are tested using a needle made from horse bone, selected because the bone is able to absorb the aroma and quickly shed it. By inserting the needle into different parts of the cured meat and smelling it, experts can determine if a whole ham leg has the qualifications to be named Prosciutto di Parma PDO.

The Consorzio, which started with 23 producers, now numbers 125, and in 2025 they turned out 6.75 million Prosciutto di Parma PDO hams. Beyond its economic significance to the region, the “King of Hams” is a cultural icon and a tourism magnet. The annual Parma Ham Festival is held in September, and there’s even an entire museum dedicated to the region’s signature product—with a tasting room, of course.

However you experience the exceptional flavor and texture of Prosciutto di Parma—on a visit to the museum or from your local specialty store—look for the crown and PDO seal, and take a moment to remember that you are tasting a distinctly delicious slice of history.

Centuries of knowledge and tradition are key to producing the “King of Hams.”

There are precious few food products that have been enjoyed for as much of human history as Prosciutto di Parma. The signature silky texture and buttery, sweet-savory flavor of the “King of Hams” is recognized around the world as the result of carefully controlled production methods, dedication to quality, and traditions continued for centuries.

The history of Prosciutto di Parma reaches back more than 2,000 years, to Roman times, when the art of preserving pork through salting and natural drying was already well established in the Po Valley. As early as the 3rd century BC, Cato the Elder described methods for curing pork legs with salt and allowing them to dry and mature. Today, Prosciutto di Parma is produced exclusively in a strictly defined area of northern Italy, in the province of Parma in the Emilia-Romagna region, where local know-how combines with distinctive climatic conditions. Humid breezes from the Tyrrhenian Sea become drier as they flow over the Apennines and down onto the hills. Prosciutto producers discovered that this created an ideal environment for dry aging, and they built storerooms with tall windows that could be opened and closed as necessary, allowing the air to circulate through the racks of hams for gradual drying.

The specifics of aging, like every step in the process, are governed by a consortium—the Consorzio del Prosciutto di Parma—that was founded in 1963 to protect the authenticity of the product. In 1996, Prosciutto di Parma obtained the European Union’s Protected Designation of Origin (PDO). These have a red and yellow seal to show that a product is made in a certain geographical area using time-honored, traditional methods. Grana Padano, a nutty, aged hard cheese also from Northern Italy that’s often paired with Prosciutto di Parma on a charcuterie plate, was awarded a PDO the same year.

Grana Padano PDO and Prosciutto di Parma PDO also share the distinction of being fire-branded—a sign for consumers that you are buying the real thing. Only Parma hams that meet the PDO’s specifications can receive the five-pronged Ducal Crown that signifies a true Prosciutto di Parma.

Well before that brand is applied, production starts with the pigs. Which breeds, where they can be bred and raised (in 11 Italian regions), and what they are fed (a list that also includes whey from local cheesemakers) are all precisely detailed. Within the 28th day from birth, the piglets receive a breeder tattoo that will also appear on the final product along with the crown brand. The fresh pork (hind legs only) sent to prosciutto producers must weigh between 26 pounds and 40 pounds, with a set amount of fat coverage. After they arrive at the production facility, the legs are trimmed to form the characteristic rounded shape, chilled to a precise temperature, and salted by hand with sea salt, which joins the pork as the only two ingredients that go into the making of Prosciutto di Parma PDO.

Following a resting period of at least 90 days, the hams are washed then hung in windowed storerooms to dry slowly. The next step is called sugnatura: The parts of the ham not covered by rind are rubbed with sugna—a mixture of pork fat, salt, and pepper—to keep the meat from drying too quickly. For final aging, the hams hang in cool, dimly lit cellars. From start to finish, the process cannot last less than 14 months (many producers continue aging for 24, 30, or even 36 months and beyond). The last step before inspection may be the most fascinating: The hams are tested using a needle made from horse bone, selected because the bone is able to absorb the aroma and quickly shed it. By inserting the needle into different parts of the cured meat and smelling it, experts can determine if a whole ham leg has the qualifications to be named Prosciutto di Parma PDO.

The Consorzio, which started with 23 producers, now numbers 125, and in 2025 they turned out 6.75 million Prosciutto di Parma PDO hams. Beyond its economic significance to the region, the “King of Hams” is a cultural icon and a tourism magnet. The annual Parma Ham Festival is held in September, and there’s even an entire museum dedicated to the region’s signature product—with a tasting room, of course.

However you experience the exceptional flavor and texture of Prosciutto di Parma—on a visit to the museum or from your local specialty store—look for the crown and PDO seal, and take a moment to remember that you are tasting a distinctly delicious slice of history.

Deeper than crimson and more interesting than brown.

Burgundy has become fashion’s latest fixation. Deeper than crimson, more interesting than brown, and infinitely more wearable than the fleeting “It” shades of seasons past, this wine-soaked hue is autumn’s firm favorite.

Sitting somewhere between cherry and oxblood, burgundy takes its name from the red wines of France’s Burgundy region (what’s not to love?). It’s luxurious without being loud, and, crucially, easy to style. Even those of us who rarely stray from head-to-toe black can dabble in the shade without feeling out of our depth.

From high-shine leather and liquid satin to plush, cocooning knitwear, burgundy has infiltrated every corner of our fall wardrobes. Across the catwalks, designers made the strongest case for burgundy with slews of the shade seen across Elie Saab, Max Mara, and Julien Dossena. Elsewhere, Balenciaga proved that the wine-tinged hue can perform just as well as any neutral, opening the show with all-black looks before quickly introducing the moody hue.

If you’re tempted to introduce this jewel-toned shade into your wardrobe, the best place to start is with a dress. Whether you’re drawn to velvet, silk, or knitted textures, minis or maxis, a burgundy dress will carry you into the depths of autumn with ease. Year after year, it’s a hue that’s never fallen out of favor, making it a stylish (and sensible) investment to make this season—and a piece you’ll reach for time and time again.

Here are the most stylish ways to wear one now.

Try a plush burgundy velvet midi dress layered under a black wool overcoat, balancing feminine flourishes with oversized outerwear. When styling it, the dress carries enough impact, so keep your accessories minimal—a delicate pair of strappy heels and a small shoulder bag are enough to complete the look.

A deep burgundy satin dress is a natural staple for any transitional wardrobe. For ultimate versatility, a long-sleeve dress will see you through any autumnal occasion, from dinner dates to after-work drinks, and will add more coverage to fend off that evening chill. Finish with coordinating wine-tinged mules and a croc-embossed bag.

For an easy daytime look, a ruffled smock dress with a leather jacket is the perfect pairing. Add slouchy black leather accessories—a Loewe Flamenco shoulder bag and ballet flats—to contrast the frills.

Lean into the richness of the hue with a full monochrome look. A burgundy maxi knit dress will work exceptionally hard in your wardrobe and is surprisingly simple to style, too. The pearl-button front of this Nobody’s Child number is like an accessory in itself, so keep things polished with a sleek pair of brown leather boots and some delicate huggies.

#56. 1.5 Million Pounds Of Hot Dogs, Sausage & Meat Products Recalled Due To Temperature Abuse

Check your fridge and freezer before your next cookout.

Over 1.5 million pounds of meat and poultry products are being recalled because they were stored at improper temperatures.

Kayem Foods Inc. is recalling approximately 1,584,361 pounds of ready-to-eat products sold under various brand names. The affected products were produced between March 31, 2026, and October 7, 2026, and bear the establishment numbers EST. M/P 7839, EST. P 20935A, or EST. M 9520.

Recognizable products include Kayem Old Tyme Beef & Pork Franks, Kayem Fenway Franks, Genoa Hot Ham, Al Fresco Chicken Breakfast Sausage, McKenzie Cob Smoked Bacon, and many more meat and poultry products. A full list of product labels and UPC codes can be found here.

The firm shipped the affected products to retail and foodservice locations nationwide.

The recall began after a retail customer reported receiving products at warm temperatures on October 1. An investigation found that meat and poultry products had been stored in a warehouse cooler that experienced temperature deviations. Kayem says the problem was caused by a malfunction in the warehouse cooling system.

Temperature matters when storing perishable food. According to FoodSafety.gov, refrigerators should remain at 40°F or below and freezers at 0°F or below. Bacteria can grow rapidly in the “Danger Zone” between 40°F and 140°F, which is why perishable foods generally shouldn’t remain in that temperature range for more than two hours.

No illnesses have been reported in connection with the recall. Consumers should not eat the affected products and should instead throw them away or return them to the place of purchase. Anyone concerned about a possible illness should contact a healthcare provider.

#57. Victoria Beckham’s Second Gap Collection Reimagines Fall’s Essential Layers

Earlier this year, when designer Victoria Beckham released her inaugural collection for Gap, it sold out almost as fast as it landed. Shoppers vied to get their hands on the iconic brand’s heritage denim, button-downs, khakis, and hoodies, all reworked with the sharp tailoring and sleek silhouettes Beckham is known for.

On October 23, Gap and Victoria Beckham are returning with the second collection that carries that same signature polish into pieces for the colder months ahead, this time building upon it with cozy knits and statement outerwear. “I wanted to explore proportion, silhouette and color, balancing structure with an elevated sense of ease,” Beckham shares with Vogue. “I was inspired by the idea of taking Gap’s familiar wardrobe staples and reinterpreting them through my own design lens.”

The collaboration was always meant to be a multi-season partnership, and this second chapter really leans into the evolution of the line, with layering leading the way. Among the 37 pieces, you’ll find simple button-front turtlenecks, oversized half-zips and chunky ribbed zip-ups in cashmere, merino and Gap’s CashSoft, all designed with roomy proportions and plenty of texture. The outerwear includes a selection of high-necked parkas that cinch at the waist, plus cropped bombers in deep green and burgundy.

The color palette of jammy reds and emerald greens suits the season, but also have a close tie to Gap’s hometown of San Francisco. “The color palette draws inspiration from the works in the Doris and Donald Fisher Collection at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art,” Beckham shares. Their art selection is peppered with Alexander Calder mobiles, Ellsworth Kelly canvases, and Gerhard Richter paintings, works that offer plenty of reference material, naturally.

“Victoria often starts with art when she’s designing, and the Doris and Donald Fisher Collection at SFMOMA gave us a natural place to begin. Works by Claes Oldenburg, Cy Twombly and Agnes Martin inspired the rich browns and deep greens you see throughout the collection,” president and CEO of Gap Mark Breitbard tells Vogue. “It’s meaningful to see our founders’ love of art come through in a way that feels authentic to both Gap and Victoria.”

Pieces made for winter nights in and out complete the lineup, with cozy sweats, including the signature Gap logo hoodie, and a high-neck black dress in the mix. There are also deep green corduroys and belted wide-leg trousers in olive and burgundy, all very fitting for holiday dressing.

And then there are the jeans, of course, which Beckham reworked with her own point of view. She included a ’90s-inspired high-rise straight leg, a staple in her personal wardrobe, and a baggier drawstring style, expanding on Gap’s denim offering, which has been on a hot streak since the release of viral Hailey Bieber jean. There’s a crisp white T-shirt and button-down to pair with them.

Prices range from $118 for a merino turtleneck to $368 for outerwear, a little higher in price range than the first, with most of the denim landing around $120. But, if the first chapter is any indication, shoppers will move fast on this, too, so consider this your cue to set that alarm.

Gap x Victoria Beckham launches October 23 at select Gap stores and on Gap.com.

#60. How This Snack Brand Gained 929k Followers by Mocking Influencers

In Person of Interest we talk to the people catching our eye right now about their projects past and present. Next up, we chat with Jay, who cofounded popcorn brand Daadi Snacks with his family but has become internet-famous for his anti-influencer videos.

There’s a standard playbook that most consumer product good (CPG) companies use when launching their company into the marketplace. They might make a few cute reels or TikToks showing the behind-the-scenes process, maybe host an in-person pop-up or two, but most importantly, they send thousands of dollars of product to influencers to help get the word out.

Jay (who prefers to keep his last name off the internet), the 30-something cofounder of Daadi Snacks, decided to burn that playbook to the ground when launching his family’s popcorn company.

Instead of sucking up to influencers, he started calling them out for their over-the-top and ridiculous antics. Parodying their annoying parlance, by opening each video with an “OHMYGODYOUGUYS” or a nasally “Come with me…” before skewering his latest victim, such as the American tourist upset that baristas in Italy refuse to mimic her Dunkin’ coffee order.

With this strategy, Daadi Snacks has amassed 929,000 followers and counting, which has turned Jay into the very thing he spends his time making fun of: an influencer. Or is he a content creator? Surprising for someone who never even had an Instagram account until 2022.

But unlike the folks he skewers, Jay likes to use his powers for good, aiming to be “the Keith Lee of New York City” and shining a light on spots that don’t tend to get attention. We called him up to speak about how his family started Daadi Snacks, the impact of his anti-influencer reels, and if it really has helped him sell any popcorn at the end of the day.

How did your family get into the snack business?

My grandma made this popcorn for our family growing up for as long as I can remember. We had floated the idea of commercializing it and turning it into an actual product, but it was more just like an idea than anything else. When COVID hit, I was working remotely, and we were just looking for ways to stay in touch with my grandparents, my mom, my uncles. I brought it up to them. “Why don't we use this time inside to actually start working on this?” My family worked on the recipe. I thought about marketing, branding, and promotion. When things started to normalize in 2021 and 2022, we spent two years iterating on what we wanted our first two flavors to be.

There's no denying that social media is an important part of growing brands, especially CPG brands. Did you think you'd need to work with influencers to get the brand out there?

I didn't get on Instagram until 2022! I never had one before then. There was one specific well-known food influencer—I've made a video about them—and I think I had a pretty terrible interaction with them. So I just thought, why don't I just start posting and stop relying on other people to shout us out? That's how I kind of landed on that.

Having lived in New York City for so long and observing the way it's changed over the last ten years, I had a longer-term vision. If I can build my own platform to market our snacks and our business, why can't I use that to try to be like the Keith Lee of New York City? Not to the extent of what he's done, but just promoting places that typically don't get promoted. Places that have been around for 30 or 40 years, whose storefront isn't super aesthetic, with Gen Z fonts. I thought that would be really cool.

You have never reached out to or responded to influencers for collabs?

Correct. I have not reached out or responded. And honestly, it's been the other way—influencers have reached out to us for samples or collabs.

When did you post your first reel skewering influencers? Was there one particular video that really launched everything?

I want to say that was around springtime last March, if my memory serves me. Before that, sales were slow but steadily growing. We were doing pop-up events to get the word out. Then in June we had hundreds and hundreds of orders come in within like two days (I don't even know the exact number), which was just crazy.

I think the inflection point was when I made a video naming who it was that influenced me to start posting videos about not liking influencer culture. When I did that and people heard the story, that's when we went from around 70,000 to over 130,000 or 140,000 followers in a week or two.

Why do you think people are so engaged and responsive to what you're doing?

In New York City it just feels like there's this need for some degree of counterculture. It's been so overwhelming in terms of the growth of these NYC-based influencers with millions of followers, just drowning in brand deals. I think people have felt the need to push back on it for a while.

You nail that restaurant influencer voice so well. Why do you think these accounts are as successful as they are, even if you punch holes in what they're doing?

I think for a lot of the NYC influencers, their content doesn't connect super well with people who actually live here—but it can connect really well with people who aspire to live here. There was this article about how this has been a very mechanical way of repurposing the whole Carrie Bradshaw thing, selling people on a manicured, aspirational idea of being a West Village girl. New York doesn't need influencers to find great food.

You've accidentally become a content creator/influencer. Do you think there's a difference between the two, or are they one and the same?

To me, an influencer’s content basically just revolves around a perpetual cycle of brand deals, which they then market to their viewers, which then propels them to get more brand deals, and so on. Honestly, I feel like because we've been on this ridiculous post-COVID run. Beauty brands have so much money, and a lot of these CPG brands have scaled so fast—it's just been unchecked. People haven't had to put in the effort.

I make it a point to never go anywhere that DMs me and asks me to review their stuff. It's crazy some of the stuff you get offered once you build any kind of following. But I've never taken PR, never taken free stuff. I'm very clear about where I stand on all that.

When do you decide to make a response video? Is it just a gut thing, like something's annoyed you enough?

I'm very opinionated, and I legitimately feel like I'm right. I pick up my phone, stop everything I'm doing, and record my 30-second video in my office chair in the same crappy apartment lighting.

#61. Steal my Food Itinerary: A SoCal Beach Dive Bar Crawl

In my opinion, this is the best way to celebrate your birthday.

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Do birthdays matter? Not really. But they are, at the very least, an excuse to do something you might not usually do as a middle-aged father of two. On this most recent occasion, my birthday was a reason to drag an assortment of friendship flotsam across the Los Angeles coastline, working our way down through a selection of Southern California beach dive bars. (It also marks the second time I’ve used my assignments for Eater and Punch to rationalize, or maybe subsidize, a birthday bar crawl.) I truly believe that these old, salt-crusted pubs are an essential, last-remaining stronghold of our regional culture, and that they demand both our respect and our money.

This crawl took place on a Saturday in September, filled with drinks and snacks (but mostly bites of bar burgers), working our way from Santa Monica to Manhattan Beach before wandering inland for dinner in Torrance, home to some of the best Japanese food in the United States.

The plan was to start relatively early, enjoying as much sunlit ocean breeze as we could, while also allowing me to get a normal amount of sleep at the end of the night before waking up at traditional dad hours. The great thing about a bar crawl is that it allows people to jump on and off as they see fit. I’m also a sucker for a brisk itinerary, moving quickly from place to place: the key is to not care who shows up when and where, simply telling someone to add the necessary ETAs to the group chat as applicable.

Opened in 1959, and a roughly 8-minute walk from the beach, Chez Jay has remained a staple and a refuge in a city that has been rapidly pricing out old neighborhood bars and restaurants. It is a place to drink a martini or a beer, where the only rules are that you “take no pictures, and throw your peanut shells on the floor.” (I broke one of the rules.) The kitchen was not open yet, but the peanuts were plentiful and the pours were heavy. The red booths and red checkerboard tablecloths evoke an old Italian restaurant, though it is certainly more of a steak-and-seafood kind of place to have dinner. It started strong, with six people showing up, including my dad and stepmom.

Hinano Cafe has been operating on a busy stretch of Venice Beach since 1962. This perpetually packed place has become an iconic surfer hang serving beer and burgers (no full liquor license here) — and like a true surfer bar, it serves breakfast from 8 a.m. until noon. Our group swelled with more friends at our second location, where pitchers of beer were poured in a standing-room-only setting, alongside board-short-wearing day drinkers who were far too young and attractive for us to stay any longer than it took for this gaggle of graying dads to order and split a hamburger. At $12.50, this perfectly acceptable bar burger on a sesame seed bun was a pleasant enough edible intermezzo. I’d prefer to come back again at another time, like maybe 1975.

We had now crossed to the other side of the marina — something of a traffic dividing line in Los Angeles County — and settled into a perfect little three-bar-crawl that exists on a 0.2-mile stretch of this hidden, working-class LA beach community. The sun was starting to drop and the ocean breeze was relaxing our shoulders (although that also may have just been the drinks). We sauntered into Prince O’ Whales, which has been serving drinks under this name for over five decades, with another 18 years before under a different one (“The Bowsprit”). There are two indoor bars, though one was closed for the afternoon. Our bartender was the kind of grumpy you look for in a sailor’s saloon, and the room was crowded with some rather loud folks watching college football. (It turns out I’m getting old.) We took our drinks to the back patio, a serene little patch of cement, brick, faded paint and sun-withered wood. There was also a ping-pong table, and this round was highlighted by exactly the kind of late-summer weather that makes people live by the beach in Southern California.

After walking for about 90 seconds, we made it to a place known as “the smallest dive bar in Los Angeles.” It would feel like a California-themed yokocho in Tokyo if it weren’t so perfectly lived in, lined with old wood that feels like you’re drinking in the bowels of a turn-of-the-century vessel crossing the Atlantic. A drunk, nonthreatening stranger joined our group and asked a lot of questions. I ordered a vodka-soda and they gave me a gin and tonic, so I ordered a gin martini. It came with a “sidecar” that was, incredibly, just a rocks glass with a splash of rapidly warming gin in it. I curiously wandered into the adjoining Italian restaurant and was convinced by some very friendly women to order some food. I told them to pick their favorite dish and near the end of my martini, a foil container of steaming hot ravioli was dropped at our table. If my wife divorces me, I could see myself paying rent on one of these barstools, living out my twilight years and wondering where it all went wrong.

Looking back at my iPhone photo timestamps, I am incredibly impressed that we were able to have a round of martinis and a plate of ravioli in 26 minutes. We soldiered on, with an even shorter walk to our next location: the classic old surf bar and restaurant, The Shack. It feels almost set-decorated, with the perfect amount of wear and tear. This place was significantly more spacious and we found room at the bar, where we ordered the Shack Burger for all to try, as well as some wings. The signature burger comes, miraculously, with a butterflied Louisiana hot link on it, operating like juicier, snappier, spicier bacon. I, meanwhile, remained impressed with my ability to have five drinks (or was it six?) — a skill that rarely gets tested anymore.

Nearing its 100th year of operation (though not always as a bar — it opened during Prohibition), this could easily have been the last stop of the tour, the flagship bar you build a crawl around. Known among my friends as “the best dive bar burger in LA County,” this proud, defiant establishment has stood the test of time, surviving rapidly escalating real estate prices to remain the great neighborhood dive it has always been. It feels like a sacred escape from the rest of this wealthy beach community. The whole place seems to be made of wood and beer signs; there is one line for ordering and another for the bathroom; and every single patron — whether gray-haired in Hawaiian shirts or tatted-up bikers — seems to know how lucky they are to be there. There is a small grill behind the bar in the corner, under a yellow sign proudly proclaiming “no fries.” The cheeseburger is an exercise in simple chargrilled perfection, its meat sourced from the butcher shop next door, all served in a basket with a bag of potato chips. The menu also claims to have a teriyaki chicken sandwich, though I’ve never seen one there. I wished we could have stayed longer, or to have eaten a whole burger instead of just two bites, but such is the nature of a crawl. We quickly made our way out, calling our next restaurant to let them know we were running about 20 minutes late for our reservation.

Stop 7: Torihei — Torrance – sometime not long after 8 p.m.

We did a decent job of snacking rather than eating on our beach dive crawl, so after we settled into a long table adorned with sake and beer, there was perhaps no more comforting bite of food in the world than Torihei’s simmered slab of daikon radish, served in dashi and blanketed in katsuobushi (smoked, dried skipjack tuna flakes). It warmed my chest. This classic standby izakaya specializes in yakitori (grilled chicken skewers) and oden (simmered ingredients in broth). We sipped beers and crunched tender chicken cartilage alongside grilled chicken meatballs before finishing the night with some soborodon (a ground chicken and rice bowl).

I was home, showered, and in bed before 11:15. I think we nailed it.

#63. These Immersive Coffee Tours Follow the Beans From Tree to Cup

Travelers who can’t go a day without press-and-go espresso pods or a ­meditative pour-over ritual, rejoice! Coffee tourism is on the rise, and, thanks to expert tour operators with access to the best farms and baristas, your next visit to Latin America, East Africa, or Southeast Asia can be as caffeinated as you want. That could entail lingering with like-minded locals in cafés or stomping on the very soil in which these prized beans grow. If you’re eager to geek out on the whats and hows of it all, immersive education is always on the table—and in the cup.

In the Antioquia region, a custom itinerary with True Colombia Travel balances exclusive access to three of the country’s best producers with myriad adventures (like coffee in a village where locals still get around on horseback). Enthusiasts will marvel at coffee trees on volcanic slopes and learn about fermentation techniques. A visit to Café Cocondo Orgánico, where coffee is cross-­pollinated with mango, avocado, orange, and soursop trees, is especially thrilling.

Known for high-quality ­arabica and robusta beans, this East African nation is paradise for those who crave a brightly flavored brew. Arusha Coffee Lodge by Elewana is conveniently located between Mount Kilimanjaro and the Ngorongoro Conservation Area. It’s also surrounded by 100 acres of coffee trees. Hotel guests can tour the roasting facilities and sample as much of the final product as they’d like. Don’t miss the day’s rotating selection of java-flavored treats, which might include nutty cakes, tiramisu, or scones.

Every year, Augusto Carneiro—founder of Nossa Familia Coffee in Portland, Oregon—leads tours of Guatemala City’s third-wave scene. Travelers start by sharing breakfast with the owners of the trendy café Coffee District, then help with the harvest at a farm partway up Volcán de Agua. Later, they head to Finca San Jerónimo Miramar in the Atitlán region to learn about grafting arabica plants onto robusta roots. There are also many sorts of excursions, from a hike on Acatenango mountain to swimming in Lake Atitlán.

#64. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#68. Contact Sport: How Much Eye Contact Is Too much?

You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s bewildering new Elizabeth Holmes documentary, had its surprise world premiere at the Telluride Film Festival on September 6. But it was the film’s first teaser trailer, released the same day, that got the wider public talking. In it, Fielder and the disgraced biotech entrepreneur—then just weeks away from entering prison for fraud—are seen in a beach house, seated very close together.

“I can promise you that. I don’t have anything to deceive you on. Of course I’m not deceiving you,” Holmes says. “I’m engaging with you as a human being. Why would I deceive you? There’s no reason for me to do that.”

“Okay. Alright. Okay, good chat,” comes Fielder’s reply. Then, after a few beats: “You’re being real right now?”

All the while, the two are engaged in a staring contest like two territorial bald eagles locked in a death spiral. The clip, which runs just over a minute, has racked up 8.5 million views.

Watching the teaser for the first time, I was among the many people who simply couldn’t get past their penetrating gazes. I grew up going to Texas cotillion, where I was taught that good eye contact was an important part of Southern charm. Yet what I witnessed in that scene was almost aggressively unpleasant.

So, what was the difference? The answer, according to etiquette expert and author Elaine Swann, was a matter of duration, in part. “The golden rule I share with my clients when it comes to eye contact is to always use it in moderation,” she says. “Look at the person, but don’t stare too deeply, because then you can come off as creepy. But don’t look away for too long, because you may be perceived as elusive.”

Like most social signals, the conventions around eye contact have evolutionary underpinnings. Research has shown that mutual eye contact can trigger everything from an elevated heartbeat to arousal—but if it goes on for too long (that is, beyond 3.2 seconds, per a 2015 study), the contact shifts from being engaging to potentially threatening, and suggesting a fight for dominance.

“If a person holds eye contact without breaking it for an uncomfortable amount of time, it might reveal a couple of things,” Swann says. “They might lack social awareness and not recognize that their long gaze is impacting someone negatively.” At other times, however, “they may be intentionally using that long stare to intimidate an individual or assert power over them.”

A central question of Fielder and Oppenheim’s film is whether Holmes is really as guileless as she seems, or in fact a master manipulator. On one hand, the project at large leaves that call to the viewer. On the other, perhaps the very first teaser tells you everything you need to know.

#70. Chicago’s Most Exciting New Restaurant Is Cooking From 900-Year-Old Recipes

An interview with the chef behind Muhājir

Now Open is a yearlong series celebrating some of 2026’s most exciting new restaurants. Throughout the year, we’ll check in with teams in Chicago, New York City, and Washington, D.C., to hear what it’s really like behind the scenes of a buzzy opening. Then, we’ll host exclusive meals at these restaurants as part of Dinner Party, presented by Capital One. Read along for challenges, candid reflections, and advice from the proprietors behind some of the country’s hottest new openings.

Zubair Mohajir is one of Chicago’s most prolific new chefs and restaurateurs, behind such openings as Lilac Tiger, Mariela, Mirra, Sarima, and most recently, Muhājir, a restaurant that traces historical spice routes to tell the story of global migration. I talked to Mohajir about how the opening is going, how he thinks about collaboration across his different projects, and why Muhājir is finally the restaurant that feels like home.

Zubair Mohajir: Muhājir is such a personal story for me, because my last name is Mohajir, and the meaning of “muhājir” in Arabic and Urdu is “one who migrates.” When the partition [of India and Pakistan] happened, the Muslims that were moved from India to Pakistan were named Muhājirs because they were migrated. In my family, we always wondered why that was our last name. When I started cooking [after working in finance], it really started to settle in. Our late maternal grandfather was obsessed with mapping where this family name came from. It comes from Southern Basra, Iraq, and that was so mind-blowing for me because it’s one of the biggest spice roads.

At Coach House for the past five years, I’ve been exploring ancient recipes in southern Spain and southern Portugal. [They] bring in pre-Crusade Muslim, Christian, Jewish [influences] that are also affected by the Southeast Asian traders coming on the spice road that shoots through the Mediterranean and hits North Africa and the Iberian Peninsula. I’m just obsessed with history and it started to become very evident for me that I really wanted to feed people, but with the context of where the food came from.

At Muhājir, it’s all about riding the spice road that runs from Portugal through the Mediterranean, through the Levantine [region], and then hits out of Basra, Iraq, into the Persian Gulf, and the first landmass it comes across is southern India, where I’m from. We’re all muhājirs — you know, all of our families came from somewhere, and that really has been the driving force for me.

I’d never cooked on live fire, but we’re cooks, and it was going back to core things. I remember growing up in my grandmother’s house back home in India, and it’s not like there were gas stoves everywhere. When I decided that I was going to do Muhājir, it became so obvious to me that it couldn’t just be a sauté pan on a stove. The story that we wanted to tell had to be told through wood fire.

We do a duck that is inspired by a 927-year-old recipe we found from southern Spain that is influenced by Roman garums, Muslim origins, and Jewish origins. We do this duck “experience,” where we take a whole duck, butcher it, and have the crown dry-aging for seven days. We take the wings and make a jus [and] take the legs and make a confit. We blast that duck crown over the fire when we start service every day, and then it gets finished in the brasa. If you’re sitting in the restaurant, you can see the ducks hanging over the fire.

When we present it, we have this beautiful ornate Turkish platter. There’s black raspberry achaar, the duck jus in a saucier, the duck rice next to it, the duck skin cut in these beautiful medallions on top almost like duck chicharrón, and then we’re also presenting the duck breast itself that has a very crispy skin. The top of that duck breast is the spice mix from that exact recipe that’s more than 900 years old, with cumin, coriander, cardamom, toasted pine nuts, red wine vinegar, and fish sauce. It’s a story of cross-cultural collaboration.

Bobo’s really inspired by Jacob Dela Cruz, who’s my partner here. We built Sarima together, and it became very important to me to highlight his upbringing and his background as well. He was one who said, “You should name the restaurant Muhājir.” His point was that we’re all immigrants. I was like, “That’s such a simple statement, but such a profound statement.” It was kind of vice versa when we were talking about the bar: Jacob’s father is an amazing person and his name is Bho, and “bobo” in Tagalog means “silly” or “stupid,” as a term of endearment. We always say that as Spice Road-driven and transformative the food experience at Muhājir is, we still like to have fun.

If people are early for their reservation, we take them back to Bobo, or they stop by after dinner. You can’t get to Bobo without walking through the restaurant, so the spaces contribute to each other. If you came to Bobo, you might be like, “I want to eat there.” And if you come straight to Muhājir and see people walking back constantly, you might be like, “What’s happening back there?”

I wouldn’t say it’s easier [than my other restaurants], but now I don’t freak out. I’ve created a methodical way of approaching issues or problems head-on and figuring it out as a group or with the people that support us. We don’t have investors who are private equity firms; our investors are our guests. When it comes to managing expectations and navigating obstacles, you get better with repetition.

I’m living a dream. Sometimes, when you’re building restaurants with others, you’re not necessarily in the kitchen. [At Mirra, I] was like, “I’m helping create and build this concept, but that’s [chef Rishi Kumar’s] kitchen to run.” Here, it’s the home that I’ve been yearning for and working toward my whole career. I plan to be old in this place. Things have been so crazy and wild and amazing, but slowly, every day, I sit more and more in that moment where I’m like, “This is home.”

This interview has been edited and condensed.

#71. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

#72. Slow-Cooker Birria Tacos

Recipe by Ericka Sanchez, La Habra, California

Nothing tops slow-cooker birria tacos. This comfort food is cheesy, crispy, crunchy and dunked into a warm bowl of rich, umami-packed consommé.

If you’re new to the concept of birria, allow me to introduce you to the Mexican gift that is quesabirria, or cheesy birria tacos. Half taco, half quesadilla and 100% delicious, they’re the kind of midnight snack or after-work meal that will quickly earn repeat status in your recipe repertoire.

The only problem? Making traditional birria can be quite labor-intensive because the beef needs to simmer for hours on end. That’s where this slow-cooker version comes in. If you don’t have the time or patience for the traditional hours-long process, this recipe delivers all that comforting goodness in a fraction of the time.

With a few store-bought spices, a handful of fresh ingredients, and about 30 minutes of prep time, you’ll have the best-ever birria ready to dominate taco night. The only decision left is whether you’ll serve them with cervezas or margaritas.

In a large bowl, combine the chiles and hot water, and let them stand for 30 minutes.

Editor’s Tip: Rehydrating the peppers breathes new life into the dried chiles. You’ll know they’re ready when they’ve softened and plumped up.

Add the chiles and the soaking liquid to a blender, along with half an onion, the tomatoes, garlic, bouillon granules, peppercorns, thyme, oregano and cumin. Puree the mixture until smooth, then strain it through a fine-mesh sieve to eliminate any chunky pieces.

Editor’s Tip: You’re going for a silky consommé, not a chunky salsa, so the sieve is important. But if you don’t have one, a regular mesh strainer will also work. Just use the back of a spoon to press as much of the sauce through as possible. No sauce spared on our watch!

In a large skillet, heat the oil over medium-high heat, then add the chuck roast. Sear it until a nice golden brown crust has formed, about two to three minutes per side.

Editor’s Tip: Searing is the handy step that turns making birria beef from an all-day affair into a slow-cooker cinch—without sacrificing flavor.

Transfer the roast to the slow cooker. Add the bay leaves and remaining onion half. Add the strained sauce, and stir to combine. Cook the beef, covered, on low until it’s tender, five to six hours.

Editor’s Tip: You’ll know your beef is ready when your kitchen smells like a taqueria and the chuck pulls apart easily with a fork.

Remove and discard the onion pieces and bay leaves. Transfer the meat to a cutting board. Shred it with two forks before returning it to the slow cooker.

Working one at a time, dip a tortilla into the cooking liquid, coating it thoroughly. Place the tortilla onto a griddle, comal or cast-iron skillet over medium heat. Sprinkle it with cheese if desired, and cook it until the cheese melts. Top it with beef, and fold the tortilla over to form a taco. Serve tacos with your desired toppings and a side of the cooking liquid.

Editor’s Tip: For authentic texture, cook the folded tortilla until crisp and golden on both sides.

Store the birria beef filling in an airtight container in the fridge for up to four days. You can store the beef in the consommé cooking liquid, but keep it separate from the tortillas and toppings.

If you’re prepping birria tacos the day before a party or game, make the slow-cooked beef as directed and return the shredded beef to the cooking liquid. Keep it in the fridge until about an hour before you’re ready to fry up the tacos. Reheat the filling in the slow cooker until it reaches 165°F, or reheat it in the microwave or on the stovetop. Keep the tortillas in a sealed bag so they don’t go stale, and prep any toppings and herbs in individual containers so you can set up your taco bar at the very last minute.

You can freeze slow-cooked birria beef for up to three months. Transfer the beef and some of the consommé to a freezer-safe container and seal it tightly. Be sure to label it; a frozen pint of taco meat can look an awful lot like Bolognese or chili.

We wouldn’t recommend freezing fully assembled, cooked tacos, which can turn soggy and lose their signature crispness. Your best bet is to keep the beef and cooking liquid separate from the tortillas, cheese and toppings, then assemble and sear your tacos when you’re ready for round two.

We like to make slow-cooker birria with boneless chuck roast. It produces plenty of flavor-packed fat for the cooking liquid, and saves you the hassle of removing the meat from the bones. Plus, it becomes fork-tender after a few hours in the slow cooker.

That said, you can absolutely use a bone-in chuck roast or beef short ribs. The only cuts we wouldn’t suggest are especially lean ones like sirloin or tenderloin. They can dry out during the low-and-slow cooking process.

For 3 to 4 pounds of meat, plan on roughly six to eight hours on the low setting on your slow cooker. It may be ready closer to the six-hour mark since you’ll be quartering the chuck roast first. Either way, we highly recommend giving your meat the ol’ fork test toward the end to see how it’s doing. Once the beef pulls apart easily, you’re good to go. Slow-cooker birria tacos will save you a ton of time, but the last thing you want to do is overcook your meat and dry it out.

Most people are strictly divided when it comes to flour or corn tortillas for tacos, but in the case of birria tacos, you really want to lean into corn. They’re the traditional choice, and they crisp up beautifully once dipped in the rich, chile-stained fat from the m. Flour tortillas don’t have the same texture—and trust us, that crispy exterior is the whole point.

#74. The 15 Cookbooks We’re Most Looking Forward to This Fall

Fall cookbook season is upon us, and in advance of the holidays and cooler nights, that means big-name releases from restaurant-world heavyweights (ahem, Eric Ripert and Kwame Onwuachi) along with topic-based books delving into underrepresented cuisines (Basque, Taiwanese, and plant-based Ghanaian, to name a few) and even specific courses. There’s plenty to choose from this year, which is why we’re presenting a special supersize fall cookbook preview, with 15 of the titles we’re most looking forward to.

Ghanaian author Afia Amoako has amassed hundreds of thousands of followers on social media, where her account @eatwithafia highlights Ghanaian and West African cultural traditions and recipes through a plant-based lens. In her lush, colorful debut cookbook, Amoako builds a deeply researched archive of a cuisine that’s often passed down only orally, and we all benefit from her efforts: More than half of the recipes are traditional and unmodified, not modern interpretations, creating an essential record of Ghanaian foodways. Recipes include classics such as jollof rice and okra stew, plus “roadside snacks” like ofam (a sweet plantain-based snacking cake) and drinks including iced Moringa milk tea. (Avery, Aug. 18)

Pim Techamuanvivit is a legend. A former food blogger turned chef of several Michelin-starred Thai restaurants in San Francisco and Bangkok, she is uniquely poised to help guide home cooks interested in understanding the nuances of Thai cuisine. Teaming up with fellow food writing superstar Andrea Nguyen, Techamuanvivit created more than 100 new recipes covering an expansive range of Thai flavors and techniques, including chapters dedicated to “Grilled, Roasted, Simmered, and Steamed” dishes, along with “Stir-Fried and Deep Fried” delights, plus soups, curries, noodles, and more. (Ten Speed Press, Aug. 25)

Ali Stoner, aka the delightfully named @rovinghaggis on social media, is a Glasgow-born, Melbourne-based home cook and former Masterchef Australia contestant who tackles the flavors of her heritage in her debut cookbook (the title is Scottish slang for a simple, comforting meal). There are plenty of hearty breakfasts and handheld “savouries” (tattie scones and bacon pieces, “wee tongue sandwiches,” and chicken Balmoral sausage rolls), plus sweet puddings (try the Tipsy Laird trifle), soups, and breads. It’s refreshing to see modern Scottish cuisine given the spotlight, especially in such an approachable, home-cook-friendly fashion—with moody, evocative photos, to boot. (Mitchell Beazley, Sept. 10)

PBS host and Mexico City native Pati Jinich is back with a new cookbook (following 2021’s Treasures of the Mexican Table). This time she focuses on the cuisines of the borderlands between Mexico and the U.S. (or, as she prefers to call it, “la frontera”). What that translates to is thoughtfully researched dishes that go far beyond Tex-Mex, including skirt steak and shrimp hot pot, seafood fried rice with asparagus and mushrooms, and smashburger tacos with poblano peppers. Throughout, she intersperses personal stories of growing up between two cultures and challenges readers to think beyond the confines of a single place. (Harvest, Sept. 15)

Enrique Salmón is a Rarámuri (Tarahumara) scholar at Cal State University, East Bay, and an expert in the connection between Indigenous foodways and land-management practices and climate change. In his second cookbook, he explores the concept of “kincentricity,” an Indigenous worldview emphasizing the interconnectedness of all living beings and our responsibility to be good stewards of the planet we share. After a comprehensive introduction, Salmón dives into the history, harvesting, and cooking methods of more than 50 Indigenous ingredients, ranging from huckleberries to black walnuts to wild onions. The result is as much an ethnography as it is a cookbook, from an author with the lived experience to guide the newly kincentric-curious. (Rizzoli, Sept. 15)

In his second cookbook, Kwame Onwuachi, the Bronx-raised chef behind Tatiana in New York and Dōgon in Washington, D.C., promises personal recipes “about how I really eat” at any and all hours of the day. What that translates to is big, bold dishes that aren’t afraid to mash up cultures and cuisines, like Red Stew Chicken Parm and Drunken Noodles Alla Vodka. (“That’s not a thing! Well, it wasn’t a thing, but now it is,” he explains.) There are chapters dedicated to sandwiches, the “Holy Grail of the Bronx” (aka New York Chinese food), and “Goddamn Veggie Sides,” which should give you some indication of the verve and voice behind this raucous collection. (Knopf, Sept. 22)

Dona Murad is the Bahrain-born owner of New York’s beloved Librae, a self-described “third culture bakery” that draws equally from SWANA flavors and Danish technique. With recipes for pastries like rose and pistachio croissants, za’atar and labneh morning buns, and loomi and lemon curd babka, her debut book is aimed at home bakers who revel in a project, but Murad walks readers of all levels through techniques like lamination with a steady, gentle hand. And with step-by-step photos throughout (plus plenty of beginner-friendly bakes), you’ll be turning out pastries that inspire lines down the block, just like Librae, in no time. (Quadrille, Sept. 22)

In his ninth book, Eric Ripert, the celebrity chef and owner of New York’s fine-dining temple Le Bernadin, draws on his travels to Buddhist monasteries across Korea and Japan to put together 75-plus recipes designed to emphasize the joy and mindfulness that cooking with plants can bring. The recipes here hopscotch across Asian, European, and Latin cultures, in chapters introduced by “guiding principles” like gratitude, intention, and joy. That translates to recipes like Radish & Turnip Carpaccio With Yuzu Kosho Vinaigrette, Tamales Rojos, and Seared Tofu With Chili Crisp, among others. Through it all, the boundlessly enthusiastic Ripert encourages home cooks to consider cooking itself as a meditative act and to enjoy the process of nourishing ourselves in both body and spirit. (Random House, Oct. 6)

The crew behind the acclaimed Montreal wine bar Mon Lapin—namely co-chefs Marc-Olivier Frappier and Jessica Noël, along with sommelier Vanya Filipovic and coauthor Mireille Silcoff—team up for a cookbook that’s every bit as chic and vibey as the restaurant that inspired it. With chapters like “What Is a Wine Bar Anyway?” and “Every Vegetable Is a Summer Vegetable in Quebec,” their collective voice shines through, and recipes like White Asparagus Soldiers with Good Anchovies and Eggplant-and-Cantaloupe Ceviche belie a deep understanding of quality ingredients and elegant presentation. As to be expected, there’s plenty of wine writing throughout, making this a must for future dinner parties. (Phaidon, Oct. 7)

Award-winning New York-based pastry chef Caroline Schiff (formerly of Gage & Tollner) makes her cookbook debut with this bright, cheerful baking book, which encourages readers to consider making and eating some form of sweet treat as a daily ritual. Yes, there are a few advanced-level pastries (such as Hazelnut Roche Profiteroles with Glossy Chocolate Sauce), but most of the recipes are approachable and friendly, as outlined in chapters like “Bake Once, Snack All Week” (snacking cakes) and “Little Bakes Just for You (and Maybe a Friend)”. With a section dedicated entirely to doughs, toppings, and crumbs, Schiff equips bakers of all levels with the confidence they need to make dessert a regular part of their day. (Abrams, Oct. 13)

Ernesto’s chef Ryan Bartlow is American, but he spent years living and cooking at the three Michelin-starred Akelarre in San Sebastián, Spain. Despite his fine-dining bona fides, though, what Bartlow really fell for during his time abroad was the rustic, humble side of Basque cooking, codified, as he writes, “on farms, in fishing ports and cider houses.” In his handsome debut with coauthor Laurie Woolever, Bartlow champions recipes with simple ingredients, like a classic tortilla de patatas, callos de Madrileña (a smoky, spicy tripe stew), and a lush crème caramel, along with pintxos and cocktails. This is a book fully steeped in a sense of place, including helpful guides to the Basque language and Basque-Spanish drinking culture, and a travel guide to the region itself, with gorgeous photographs. (Abrams, Oct. 13)

Eric Sze, the chef behind 886 and Wenwen in New York, teams up with veteran food writer Elyse Inamine for a voicey, intimate, and delightfully neon-soaked exploration of the foods of Taiwan, where he was born and raised. The first half of the book focuses on Taiwanese dishes as they’re presented in Taiwan itself, while the second half is more experimental, covering the fusion-y (a term the chef embraces) recipes Sze has perfected cooking at his New York pop-ups and restaurants, such as Mochi Gnocchi with Chili Oil Pumpkin purée and Beef Noodle Soup Ragu). Shot colorfully on location, this is a book brimming with personality—and a sneakily impressive amount of research—on every page. (Hardie Grant, Oct. 20)

Siberia-born, London-based academic and food writer Alissa Timoshkina is the author of two previous cookbooks on Eastern European foodways, though she’s perhaps best known as the founder of #CookForUkraine, a global fundraising campaign supporting humanitarian relief. It’s fitting, then, that her latest title is focused on humble-yet-mighty soups and stews from across a borderless collection of Ukrainian, Jewish, Tatar, Hungarian, Polish, Slovak, and Roma traditions. Organized into “Soups & Broths,” “Stews & Grains,” “Dumplings & Pasta,” and “Sweet Comfort,” the chapters highlight the myriad ways in which foods eaten with a spoon have the power to soothe, surprise, and connect people across cultures and conflicts. (Quadrille, Oct. 20)

Fuchsia Dunlop, who graduated from culinary school in Sichuan Province, is one of the West’s foremost experts in Chinese cuisine, guiding home cooks with a knowledgeable and compassionate hand. The author of several renowned cookbooks on the topic, she’s back with a strikingly illustrated new volume, focused on the five taste sensations (sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and pungent) that a Chinese cook strives to balance harmoniously within a dish. Instead of a dogmatic approach to traditional dishes, she encourages cooks to apply Chinese seasonings and flavoring techniques to “whatever ingredients you have on hand,” assuring readers that “the ways of the Chinese kitchen travel well.” (W.W. Norton, Oct. 20)
