#75. Heated Rivalry Season 2: Everything We Know So Far

Good news has arrived for Heated Rivalry fans. The steamy HBO Max and Crave show, based on the six-book series Game Changers by Rachel Reid, is officially returning for a second season.

“Watching our show become an international phenomenon has been extraordinary,” series creator Jacob Tierney and executive producer Brendan Brady said in a statement. “We’re profoundly grateful to everyone that has been on this journey with us. Being renewed for a second season so early is a true honor, and we can’t wait to bring you even more of what you love.”

Yes, HBO Max announced the news in December 2025. The streamer posted a video on Instagram with series stars Hudson Williams and Connor Storrie opening up a gift box with a hockey puck that says “Heated Rivalry” on one side and “Season 2” on the other. The video is captioned, “The game’s not over. Season 2 of #HeatedRivalry is coming to HBO Max.”

Justin Stockman, vice president of content and programming at Bell Media, said in a statement: “Heated Rivalry represents the very best of what Canadian creators can deliver: rich characters, compelling drama, and a world audiences want to live in. The response has been extraordinary, and seeing the series now traveling internationally is an incredible milestone.”

While the exact season 2 plot is still under wraps, Storrie hinted that it’ll be based on Rachel Reid’s sixth Game Changers book, The Long Game. “Start reading The Long Game if you want to spoil it for yourselves,” he said.

The novel continues to follow hockey rivals-turned-lovers Shane Hollander (Williams) and Ilya Rozanov (Storrie), who are still keeping their romance a secret—10 years in. A decade of hiding is a challenge for them both, but going public could sabotage their careers. “It’s time for them to decide what’s most important—hockey or love,” the book’s synopsis reads.

The season 1 finale ended with Shane and Ilya confessing their love to one another at Shane’s cottage before being accidentally outed when Shane’s dad swings by for his phone charger. After an emotional afternoon with his parents, the two young men start figuring out how they can have a future together in Canada and perhaps even come out someday.

In an interview with Variety after the season 1 finale, showrunner Jacob Tierney commented on the episode, plans for season 2, and how the series leaned more into romance than sex toward the end.

“There’s quite a bit of sex in The Long Game,” said Tierney. “But I think it functions differently in the second book, and that’s just what I want to do. The journey of this show, no matter how long it goes on for, will always be centered around the relationship between Shane and Ilya. Sex will always be a big part of it, like it is with any romantic relationship. But it’s really about continuing that progress of what happens after that first blush of love, what happens after you decide you’re in love and how do you sustain it?”

He continued, “That’s a very adult question: ‘We love each other, and now what? Does that mean everything’s easy?’ No, it does not. There’s loads of challenges that get thrown Shane and Ilya’s way. Beyond what’s in the books, I really don’t have an agenda besides that I love this couple and I love these characters, and I want to just hang out with them more and watch them grow more and watch them become better for each other.”

He also said that Kip and Scott’s characters will be back since their story overlaps with Ilya and Shane’s throughout Reid’s books.

Tierney shared more information about season 2 at BookCon on April 18, 2026.

“Long Game is…so long and it’s so gamey, like eating venison,” Tierney told attendees. “It really is different, and the challenge, from an adaptation standpoint, is you’re in much more serious territory. There’s still lots of flirting, and there’s lots of sex, but it’s this kind of danger. This kind of ‘hotel room, adolescent sex’ stuff is largely gone.”

He also revealed characters from Reid’s novel Role Model would be part of the season: Ottawa Centaurs forward (and Ilya’s new teammate) Troy Barrett and the team’s social media manager, Harris Drover, who have their own love story in the book.

“It’s very ‘grumpy sunshine.’ It’s very ‘apple orchard,’” he said. “It can drift into things that you want, but Troy is a really damaged guy. And Troy is quite damaged on the show. I would say we’re digging into that even harder.”

Entertainment Weekly revealed the logline for season 2 that day: “The Long Game picks up 10 years into their relationship. Shane and Ilya’s love remains a secret, but Ilya has parted ways with his Boston team to play for the Ottawa Centaurs so that he can be closer to Shane. The pair have also launched their charity organization, which they spoke about at the famous cottage. While they are seeing each other more than ever, the potential price of going public with their romance weighs heavily on the couple, especially as Ilya wants them to come out of hiding much sooner than originally planned.”

Ilya’s friendship with Svetlana Vetrova (Ksenia Daniela Kharlamova) will also receive more attention in season 2.

Speaking at an October 2026 fan event in Brooklyn, Tierney explained that Svetlana gives Ilya someone to confide in, even when he isn't being entirely truthful about his feelings.

“This happens a lot in season 2, where he’s lying, but at least he’s saying something out loud,” Tierney said, per E!. “It’s so interesting to have to watch him call her and be like, ‘I’m fine. I love it here.’ You’re like, ‘OK, well, you’re not.’”

On October 18, Kharlamova spoke to E! at the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show about returning to set with the show’s growing ensemble. “It’s awesome,” she said of the new cast members. “It’s changed it for the better. It’s like having more friends there.”

Williams and Storrie will reprise their roles as Shane and Ilya, respectively, in Heated Rivalry season 2.

Crave and HBO Max revealed on August 7 that Justice Smith (Now You See Me: Now You Don’t) and Charlie Gillespie (One Night Only, Splitsville) will play the roles of Harris Drover and Troy Barrett, respectively.

“Rachel Reid has given us two beautifully layered characters in Harris and Troy who you can’t help but root for,” Tierney and Brady said in a joint statement. “From the start of the casting process, we knew we were looking for actors who could create something truly special together and bring that same depth and heart to the screen.”

“Justice and Charlie do exactly that,” they added. “They immediately connected with the vulnerability and resilience at the core of these characters, bringing an instinctive understanding of who Harris and Troy are.”

Justice’s casting led to some backlash from fans of the show, which he later addressed on Instagram.

“I have to say I am moved by the support and love I’m getting from fans in my dms, fans who have welcomed me with open arms and who already feel a responsibility to protect me,” he wrote in a text post shared to his Story. “I am honored to play a character that you all care about deeply and I promise that I will take good care of him if you give me the chance. I am beyond excited for the experience.”

Reid subtly addressed the drama on Instagram. “Thinking about all the people last summer who told me the casting for llya and Shane was wrong and bad…” she captioned an Instagram Story.

More casting announcements arrived on August 7. Deadline revealed that Emily Hampshire (Schitt’s Creek), Edvin Ryding (The Young Royals, 28 Years Later), Robert Naylor (Mile End Kicks), Sabrina Jalees (Black Mirror), and drag queen Priyanka (Drag Brunch Saved My Life, Meet Me Next Christmas) will be joining the cast for the next season.

According to the outlet, “Hampshire will play Vanessa, Ryding is Luca Haas, Jalees is Farah Jalali and Priyanka portrays Tarek.” Naylor, meanwhile, will play Wyatt Hayes in the series, a starting goaltender for the Ottawa Centaurs and a fan favorite character in the Game Changers book series.

Deadline reported on August 25 that Daniel Diemer and Shaheen Jafargholi will star in season 2 as Ryan Price and Fabian Salah. Ryan and Fabian are the leads of Reid’s Tough Guy, the third novel in the Game Changers book series.

“Fabian and Ryan each bring a distinctive energy to the world Rachel Reid has created,” Tierney and Brady said in a statement. “They are bold, complicated, and deeply compelling characters, and finding actors who could really take on all of those different sides was so important to us.”

The statement continued, “Daniel and Shaheen bring such confidence and emotional honesty to the roles. We can’t wait for audiences to see what they do with Fabian and Ryan and how they make these characters their own.”

Jafargholi shared the news of his casting to Instagram and captioned the post, “gag it.”

On September 1, Deadline reported that François Arnaud, Robbie G.K., Sophie Nélisse, Ksenia Daniela Kharlamova, Christina Chang, Dylan Walsh, Callan Potter, Benjamin Roy, and Kamilla Kowal would be returning for Heated Rivalry season 2.

Two days later, on September 3, Deadline reported three more additions to the season 2 cast. Kevin Zegers will play Coach Wiebe, Paul Gross will appear as Commissioner Roger Crowell, and Milla Jovovich will take on the role of Dr. Galina Molchalina.

On September 17, Deadline reported that six new cast members would be joining the cast of season 2. The Handmaid’s Tale alum Brendan Morgan will play Zane Boodram. Michelle Mylett (Letterkenny) will star as Lisa. Lauren Chan (The Devil Wears Prada 2) will play Gen. Other additions include Gerry Dee (Animal Control) as Coach Cooper and Nick Stahl (Terminator 3) as Curtis Barrett.

David Tomlinson (Fellow Travelers, Silent Night, Deadly Night) also joins the cast of season 2 and will play Cody Kent, which will be a name change of the character of Dallas Kent in the Game Changers book series.

The singer would like to. At the Palm Springs International Film Festival, she told Variety, “Oh, I’m so in [to do music]. Book me. Get me booked!”

A day later at the Critics Choice Awards, Variety asked Arnaud about Cyrus’s interest. “I think we might get a little bit bigger budget for season 2, but I don’t know if we get Miley budget,” he admitted, before adding, “I think if she sees the show, she might give us a discount.”

In a February 2026 interview with GQ, Williams spoke about his hopes for his character Shane’s growth in season 2. “I want to see what Shane looks like when he comes into himself and moves away from fear and stifling of his emotions,” he said.

Williams also reflected more broadly on how he chooses projects at this stage of his career. “It starts with the script, and comes down to the director/creator,” he said. “No actor can turn shit writing into something great. And at the end of the day, a subpar director can butcher a good performance—and even a good script if they’re really bad—by fumbling the movie at so many points along the way.”

In September 2026, Williams admitted that getting back into character was initially difficult for him and Storrie.

“He [Storrie] worked through day one. I worked day two of shooting,” he said during a TIFF Q&A. “And he came back—and I don’t think he’d mind if I said that—but he was like, ‘It was sort of weird. They were all so good that I was like am I good? Am I in it? Am I doing the thing? Am I doing like an impression of Ilya?’ And we were talking about this before we even started shooting. And I was like, it’s weird that our memory of playing season 1 isn’t just our true memory of showing up and doing the scenes. It’s having watched them cut together. It’s fan reactions. Our memory isn’t ours. It’s everyone’s, which is—it’s been abstracted and twisted, and it’s become this weird amalgamation of a memory.”

Williams went in confident that he could recapture Shane on his first day of shooting. That wasn’t what happened. He had been shooting with some extras who were fans. He suddenly thought to himself, “Oh god, oh god, am I doing a Shane expression? Okay, and I was like, Oh, I’m losing it, I’m losing it.”

He and Storrie compared their experiences and found it became much easier to play their roles in the days that followed.

“After our first day ones, it came back, thankfully, because Jacob does a really good job of making the set feel as tiny as it was in season 1,” he explained. “It’s all the same crew, which is really great. But it was surreal to step into it.”

Tierney and Brady spoke with Gayle King on CBS Mornings on Feb. 26, 2026, and said that the second season of Heated Rivalry is currently being written, with filming set to begin in August 2026.

“There will be more Heated Rivalry on your TVs, like, truly, as soon as humanly possible,” Tierney said. Brady added, “like the best parts of this show,” and that fans should “enjoy the yearn.”

On May 29, Tierney accepted the Showrunner Award at the third Critics Choice Celebration of LGBTQ+ Cinema & Television in Los Angeles via video, seemingly offering an update in his speech.

“Thank you so much to the Critics Choice Association for this amazing and unexpected honor,” said Tierney. “I’m so, so grateful, and I’m so sorry that I cannot be there to celebrate with all of you in person and accept this. I’m working very hard on season 2 to get it out to people as soon as possible. I genuinely wish I could be there. I’m so moved by this.”

Tierney also discussed season 2 during a BookCon panel in New York in April 2026, when he confirmed that Heated Rivalry is slated to return in spring 2027. He also shared more about his approach to adapting Reid’s The Long Game for the screen.

“I want to dig deeper,” Tierney said, per People. “Because everything in her book, there is the foundation of a very real and understandable queer relationship. And I didn’t want to shy away from it. I wanted to dig into it.”

#76. 6 Foods & Drinks You Should Stop Buying After 30, According To A Dietitian

Despite the paralyzing fear I had about turning 30 for years leading up to it, I was pretty relieved once I actually hit the milestone. I felt older, wiser, and more settled. The only downside to the new decade (other than the quarterly Botox bills)? Realizing my metabolism wasn’t quite as speedy as it once was.

Let’s face it: As much as I’d love to still eat as I did in high school, my body feels it differently now. When I drink too much, I feel the hangover for days; overly processed foods make my joints ache; and dairy just doesn’t sit right the way it did at 21 when I was pounding pizza slices at 2 a.m. And those are just the immediate effects. There are a lot of long-term consequences related to diet, too!

So, I tapped an expert on the subject, registered dietitian Lauren Manaker, to help me round up the food and drinks that no one (not me, you, your parents, your besties, anyone!) should be eating after the age of 30—minus, of course, a few caveats and the understanding that most things in moderation are OK* from time to time!

*You can pry the Diet Coke from my cold, dead hands!

Here are six things you should stop buying, eating, and drinking once you hit the big 3-0.

I’m not saying you have to bow out of happy hours the second you turn 30 (I mean that as someone just a year away from that milestone), but you might want to invest in higher-quality bottles—if only to ward off worse hangovers.

Manaker also points out that it's a good age to start reevaluating your relationship with alcohol and potentially cutting back. “Sure, a glass of wine or a cocktail here and there can be part of a balanced lifestyle, but as we age, our bodies process alcohol less efficiently,” she tells Delish. “This means those hangovers hit harder and last longer (ugh). Alcohol can also negatively impact sleep, which can impact mood, focus, and more. Moderation is key if you choose to drink alcohol. Your liver (and your morning self) will thank you.”

Even if you’ve graduated from late-night study sessions fueled by Red Bull to workouts motivated by Alani, as Manaker points out, “your 30-something body isn't as forgiving” when it comes to processing these ingredients. These drinks are packed with caffeine and sugar, and aren't nearly as beneficial as they might seem.

They can “spike your energy temporarily but leave you crashing hard later. Over time, they can mess with your heart health, blood pressure, and even your sleep quality,” she explains. “If you need a pick-me-up, try a cup of tea instead; it’s gentler on your system. Or if you like the idea of a canned energy drink sans the loads of added sugar, plus some extra benefits, an option like Bloom Nutrition Sparkling Energy is a nice choice.”

Like with alcohol, moderation is key when it comes to sweets, but candies like gummy bears are just a bad idea in general. As Manaker puts it, they’re “pure sugar.”

“While gummy bears might have been a fun snack in your teens, they’re not doing your 30-something self any favors. Excess sugar can lead to energy crashes, weight gain, and more,” she says. “Plus, gummy bears don’t offer any real nutrients, so they’re just taking up space that could be filled with something more nourishing.”

A dietitian-approved alternative? Fresh fruit or a square of dark chocolate. If you really can't shake the gummy bear craving, try something with less added sugar and gut-health-supporting fiber, like Smartsweets.

While what I'm about to say isn't a free pass to go wild on actual sugar, artificial sweeteners aren’t the holy grail solution you probably thought once upon a time—in fact, you should steer clear as best you can. They can impact your gut health and more!

According to a study presented at Nutrition 2025, an annual meeting of the American Society for Nutrition, there is a significant link between drinking artificially sweetened beverages and an increased risk of diabetes. The whole study took place over a 30-year time period and found that those who consumed diet bevvys and drinks sweetened by saccharin were more than twice as likely to develop type 2. Since you probably haven't been throwing back diet sodas and eating sugar-free pudding since birth, now is the perfect time to reevaluate your relationship with artificial sweeteners—ya know, before you hit that 30-year mark yourself.

As a Diet Coke stan, this one hurts. “Don't hate me,” Manaker jokes. “But if you're focused on bone health, drinking tons of [Diet Coke] might not be doing you any favors.” She explains that sodas, in particular, contain phosphoric acid, which can interfere with calcium absorption and might even weaken your bones. It also has zero nutritional value.

“To tame my Diet Coke cravings, I drink OLIPOP Vintage Cola,” she says. “It is free from phosphoric acid and contains nothing artificial. Plus, it contains prebiotic fiber to help support gut health—OG Diet Coke could never!”

Frozen meals are the GOAT in college and right out of school because they’re easy and cheap, but let’s face it: they’re not the healthiest—even if the packaging tries to convince you otherwise. While there are some decent frozen options out there, a lot of the frozen aisle contains products with high sodium and little nutritional value. If you're really craving pizza rolls that badly, it might be time to go all Nara Smith and make your own from scratch.

The newest bra, which is estimated to be worth $50 million, was covered in 4,410 natural diamonds and designed by Jacob & Co. founder Jacob Arabo. During the show, Jenner was supported by her beau, Timothée Chalamet, as well as her mom, Kris, who cheered her on as she walked the runway. Her sister, Kendall, was notably absent from the runway, despite having walked in three previous VS shows since 2015.

Not to mention, the remote control added a super fun element with my partner! I would definitely recommend this to anyone looking to explore anal play."

"The shorter end stays in place very well, even when things get quite slippery. Both of us had to be a little slow removing it because it's a little larger, but it isn't uncomfortable to insert or to keep in. It's just the right size to stay put in pretty much all the positions you can think of and for as long as you want to use it."

The best sex toy for you and your partner really depends on what you're hoping to get out of it. More clitoral stimulation during penetration? Something you can both feel? A remote-controlled vibrator that lets one of you call the shots?

External vibrators, like bullets and wands, can be great for clitoral stimulation, while dual-action toys offer a combination of internal and external sensations. And if you're interested in hands-free play, wearable vibrators and couples rings might be more your speed.

You'll also want to think about the practical stuff: size, shape, vibration settings, and whether you actually want to deal with an app or remote. Stick with nonporous, body-safe materials, and make sure whatever you choose is easy to clean.

Bringing up sex toys with a partner can feel a little awkward, especially if you've never used them together before. But you don't need to make it a whole serious relationship summit. Instead, try framing it as something fun you want to explore together, rather than something that's missing from your sex life.

"A toy is supposed to add to the fun—not become a referendum on anyone’s sexual abilities," Rowntree says. In other words, wanting to bring a vibrator into bed doesn't mean your partner isn't doing it for you. Sometimes you just want a little extra stimulation.

You can start by talking about what sounds hot to both of you, browsing toys together, or suggesting something you already own and love. And if your partner isn't into it? That's a boundary worth respecting. The goal is to find something you're both genuinely excited about, not convince someone to do something they're uncomfortable with.

You can bring a vibrator into foreplay, use a finger vibe during oral sex, try a wearable toy during penetration, or hand your partner the remote and see where things go. As long as everyone involved is comfortable and consenting, you've got options.

A little prep goes a long way, though. Make sure your toy is charged, read the manufacturer's instructions, and grab some lube if you need it. Just double-check compatibility first: Silicone-based lubes can damage some silicone toys, so water-based lube is generally the safer bet unless the manufacturer says otherwise.

You'll also want to keep things clean. "If you’re sharing a toy between partners, clean it thoroughly between users or use a new condom or barrier on the toy," Rowntree advises. The same goes for switching between anal and vaginal use: Clean the toy or change the barrier first.

#80. The 38 Best Restaurants in Rome, According to a Best-Selling Local Cookbook Author

Where to eat in Rome, including the best pizza, pasta, wine bars, and more

Roman cuisine is a reflection of the city itself — layered, deeply rooted in tradition, and full of contrasts. After years of eating my way through Rome, I’ve found the best meals are shaped as much by history as the hands that prepare them. Family-run trattorias have served the city’s defining dishes for generations: cacio e pepe, carbonara, roasted lamb, and offal-based specialties, many of which trace their origins to Rome’s historic slaughterhouse economy. While these places remain essential, a wave of neo-trattorias constantly reinterprets the classics, and the broader dining scene continues to shift too. The influence of Rome’s immigrant communities and cuisines, from Ethiopian to Venezuelan, is stronger than ever.

Rome in February and March can feel like a damp intermission which pivots quickly toward spring. One day you’re ducking into bars to escape the downpour and the next you’re scanning patios for a table in the sun. If recent years are any indication, high season now revs up well before Holy Week, and by late March the city is already moving at full tilt. This is the narrow stretch to lean into artichokes simmered with the first peas, favas, and lettuce into vignarola, Rome’s definitive spring stew. Blink and you’ll miss it.

Eating and drinking well in Rome isn’t just about knowing where to go; it’s about knowing how to navigate the city’s idiosyncratic dining culture. Travelers often book tables months in advance, making last-minute reservations tough. While online booking is becoming more common, many places still rely on the phone, and it’s best to call at the very start or very end of service, when the staff actually has time to pick up. Plan ahead — but leave some room for spontaneity too.

We update this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing dining scene in Rome. Our write-ups include insider tips from our experienced writers and editors, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in euros), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

New to the map in October 2026: In San Giovanni, Beppe e I Suoi Formaggi has moved beyond its former Ghetto shop, with a larger space where Beppe Giovale’s selection of Italian and French cheeses shares the table with dishes like tajarin with alpine butter. Near the Pyramid of Gaius Cestius, third-generation family-run Taverna Cestia serves Roman classics, seafood, and wood-fired pizza alongside a thoughtful wine list. In Prati-adjacent Della Vittoria, Vetro pairs natural wines with small plates that borrow freely from Roman and wider European traditions, making it as appealing for dinner as for a drink.

Katie Parla is a Rome-based food and beverage journalist, culinary guide, and New York Times best-selling cookbook author. Her latest cookbook, Rome, is available now.

Where to eat in Rome, including the best pizza, pasta, wine bars, and more

Plan ahead — but leave some room for spontaneity too.

We update this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing dining scene in Rome. Our write-ups include insider tips from our experienced writers and editors, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in euros), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

New to the map in October 2026: In San Giovanni, Beppe e I Suoi Formaggi has moved beyond its former Ghetto shop, with a larger space where Beppe Giovale’s selection of Italian and French cheeses shares the table with dishes like tajarin with alpine butter. Near the Pyramid of Gaius Cestius, third-generation family-run Taverna Cestia serves Roman classics, seafood, and wood-fired pizza alongside a thoughtful wine list. In Prati-adjacent Della Vittoria, Vetro pairs natural wines with small plates that borrow freely from Roman and wider European traditions, making it as appealing for dinner as for a drink.

Katie Parla is a Rome-based food and beverage journalist, culinary guide, and New York Times best-selling cookbook author. Her latest cookbook, Rome, is available now.

Vetro’s sidewalk crowd can look like the cigarette-rolling Olympics, with drinkers claiming improvised seats and lingering over glasses of wine and beer. Inside, high-tops and tables offer a more settled way to explore a menu whose ingredients often speak Roman, while its sensibility ranges across Europe. Gildas and eggs with mayonnaise join tongue with sweet potatoes and piquillo peppers, while baccalà mantecato goes by brandade and comes with marinated zucchini and isot pepper. Order a few snacks and small plates, and suddenly staying for dinner becomes an appealing proposition. Set in a former alimentari on Viale Carso, the bar pairs its neighborhood hangout atmosphere with a thoughtful natural wine selection spanning Italy, Spain, and southern France, including wines served sfuso (on tap).

Vibe check: Stay outside for the people-watching; claim a table inside to work your way through the food menu.

Colombian chef Roy Caceres is a veteran of Roman fine dining. His landmark, Michelin-starred restaurant, Metamorfosi, didn’t survive the pandemic, but his signature dishes have found a place at Orma (an anagram of Roma) just a few blocks southeast of the Galleria Borghese. Orma is home to a number of distinct concepts: The bistrot is a power-lunch spot set on a shaded terrace, the cocktail bar specializes in tropical fruit- and herb-forward drinks, and the restaurant offers tasting menus and a la carte dishes that blend Caceres’s Colombian heritage with Italian flavors and ingredients. Fans of the chef’s Uovo 65° Carbonara (a soft-cooked egg floating in Parmigiano-Reggiano foam, served with a side of puffed pasta and tender strips of guanciale) will find it in the bistrot, while the restaurant serves his renowned lacquered eel with pickled onions.

Best for: The business lunch is a great deal for anyone into fine dining but not keen to linger.

A short walk from the Trevi Fountain, this friendly trattoria has been serving satisfying dishes from Emilia-Romagna, a region in northeastern Italy, since 1931; the current owners took the helm in 1967. The menu is rich in egg-based house-made pastas like tortelli di zucca (pumpkin pasta with butter and sage) and tagliatelle alla bolognese (long strands of fresh, egg-based pasta dressed with a rich meat sauce). Save room for meaty mains including bollito misto (assorted simmered meats) and fried liver.

Must-try dishes: Tortellini in brodo and the bollito misto.

Just 100 feet from Rome’s most intact ancient monument, Armando al Pantheon champions local food traditions. For more than five decades, the Gargioli family has been dutifully producing Roman classics like fettuccine con le rigaglie di pollo (fettuccine with chicken innards) and coda alla vaccinara (oxtail braised in tomato and celery). Among the seasonal side dishes, look for puntarelle (Catalonian chicory) with anchovy sauce and carciofi alla romana (simmered artichokes) in the cooler months. Save room for the torta antica Roma, a ricotta and strawberry jam pie. The lovingly curated wine list gets better every year.

Know before you go: Book online exactly one month ahead to secure a spot — it fills up fast.

Moriondo e Gariglio is a time capsule with a cocoa perfume. Founded in Turin by cousins Agostino Moriondo and Francesco Gariglio, former chocolatiers to the Savoy royal household, the chocolate shop followed the court to Rome in the late 19th century and eventually settled on Via del Piè di Marmo, a couple of minutes from the Pantheon. Glass counters hold more than 80 chocolates and bonbons, all made by hand. In autumn, locals stock up on the shop’s cult marrons glacés, sold whole or blended into a paste, while spring brings elaborately engineered Easter eggs with surprises hidden inside. A small box is an easy souvenir. A kilo feels like joining a noble Roman ritual.

Know before you go: Chocolate production winds down in the warm months, which see the arrival of pâte de fruits in their place.

After Settimio al Pellegrino, a cult favorite featured on Anthony Bourdain’s Parts Unknown, shuttered in 2022, Leonardo Vignoli and Maria Pia Cicconi (of Cesare al Casaletto fame) resurrected the restaurant. They’ve retained the institution’s signature tiled floors, midcentury furniture, and infamous doorbell required for customers to gain access. The trattoria near Campo dei Fiori serves a succinct menu, including minestra con broccoli e arzilla (romanesco and skate soup) and former chef-owner Teresa Zazza’s legendary pan-fried meatballs.

Best for: A dinner (or weekend lunch) when you’re ready to drink from the incredibly affordable wine list.

If Roman restaurants have become known for brusque, no-nonsense service, Hosteria Grappolo d’Oro did not get the message. Affable servers circulate through the dining rooms beneath exposed wooden beams, delivering pure versions of cucina romana classics like toothsome tonnarelli cacio e pepe and tender roasted suckling lamb.

Best for: The 36 euro, four-course Roman tasting menu is one of Rome’s best deals.

Open for: All dayPrice range: $In the southwest corner of one of Rome’s most touristy squares, Forno Campo de’ Fiori bakes sweet and savory Roman specialties like jam tarts and flatbreads. Look for pizza alla pala (long slabs baked directly in a deep electric deck oven), which is sold in slices by weight; the unctuous toppings and crispy bases make a surprisingly balanced pair. An annex across the alley on Vicolo del Gallo stays open during the main bakery’s afternoon break, from 2:30 to 4:45 p.m.

Must-try dish: The pizza con mortadella is one of the best bites in town.

Culinary power couple Francesca Barreca and Marco Baccannelli reopened their landmark restaurant Mazzo after a five year hiatus, and this time around, a relatively central location in San Lorenzo makes it considerably more accessible to many residents. The dining room has also grown from a single 12-seat communal table to full-fledged restaurant seating complete with a massive porthole peering into the brightly lit kitchen. Just like the original, the new Mazzo plays with nostalgic forms in dishes like wagon wheel pasta with braised beef and onions, which joins Barreca and Baccannelli’s classics like fried tripe with grated pecorino Romano in a pool of tomato sauce, a retooling of Rome’s signature offal dish, trippa alla romana.

Must-try dishes: The fried tripe, and the wagon wheels with an oniony braised beef sauce.

The Camerucci family’s well-loved trattoria is not actually in Monti, but rather the adjacent multicultural Esquilino district near Stazione Termini. The cuisine is heavily Marchigiano — from the Italian region of Le Marche — so expect lots of game like braised rabbit and roasted duck, meat-filled fried olives, and fresh pasta like the legendary raviolo filled with a runny egg yolk and dressed with butter and sage.

Must-try dish: The runny-yolk raviolo is not to be missed.

Founded in the Historic Center in 2004 by Rome’s premier baking family, Salumeria Roscioli does triple duty as a deli, wine bar, and restaurant. Though the menu is extensive, the real stars are the cheeses (burrata with semi-dried tomatoes is spectacular), cured meats (Culaccia and mortadella with Parmigiano-Reggiano are both stellar), and pasta classics (get the gricia, cacio e pepe, amatriciana, or carbonara). If you dine at lunch or on the early side at dinner, the bread basket will include warm bread from nearby Antico Forno Roscioli. The wine list is wide-ranging, and don’t miss the distilled spirits before closing out the meal.

Vibe check: Request a table upstairs or outside to avoid getting seated in the basement.

For two centuries, Rome’s Jewish community was confined to a walled ghetto along the Tiber River. The squalid buildings are long gone, but a historic ghetto-era bakery survives on what has become the transformed neighborhood’s main thoroughfare. The pizza ebraica — a sort of fruit cake studded with nuts, raisins, and candied fruits — is an easy specialty to eat on the go, but it’s worth seeking out a bench to get messy with a slice of ricotta and sour cherry tart. Also try the amaretti and biscotti made with heaps of cinnamon and a generous smattering of whole almonds.

Must-try dish: The ricotta and sour-cherry tart — grab it before it sells out.

Via Prenestina has been a hub for Ethiopian and Eritrean community and cuisine in Rome for decades, and Mrgda, situated on this wide avenue at the edge of Pigneto, is a standout example. Partake of the free-flowing tej, a heady, honey-fermented wine that pairs perfectly with dishes like richly spiced legumes, aromatic vegetables, tender braised chicken, and deeply seasoned raw beef. Each bite is scooped up with Mrgda’s ethereal, naturally leavened injera, which has a balanced tang.

Know before you go: There is a vegan restaurant from the same owners, Mrgda Vegano, just a few blocks away.

Routinely named among the best places to drink in Europe, this long-established craft beer pub in Trastevere pours around a dozen draft beers from Italy, the U.S., Belgium, Germany, and the U.K., in addition to a small but well-curated assortment of bottles. The staff is passionate and knowledgeable, and can guide you to the right choice for your palate. It’s worth waiting for the few tables on the street outside, set up during the pandemic, which offer a front row seat to Trastevere’s lively nightlife.

Best for: Drinking vintage sour beers from Italy and beyond, 365 days a year (it’s even open on holidays).

Open for: Dinner, with lunch Wednesday to Sunday

L’Elementare has multiple locations around Rome, but the Trastevere outpost is the one that stands out service-wise. The focus is Roman pizza tonda: thin, nearly rimless, crisp and chewy at the edges. It’s baked longer than a Neapolitan pie, lending structural integrity that prevents slices from collapsing under disappointing tip sag. Start with molten supplì ar telefono, fried bricks of lasagna, and fried parcels of tonnarelli cacio e pepe.

Know before you go: There are several locations, so double check you are booking the Trastevere address, and be warned that although they post all day hours Wednesday to Sunday, the kitchen actually does close from 3:30ish to around 6:45.

Trapizzino is a small street food chain with locations throughout Italy (and an outpost in New York). The concept is based on the trapizzino, a combination of the popular triangular tramezzino sandwich with long, slowly leavened pizza dough, invented by pizzaiolo Stefano Callegari in 2008. Callegari fills his tricornered creations with Roman classics like oxtail simmered with tomato and celery, chicken cacciatore, and tripe cooked with tomato, each going for just 5 euros.

Know before you go: Visit the Trastevere branch for table service and a full bar with Lazio wines.

The cool, windowless inner sanctum at number 10 on Via del Moro in Trastevere only has a handful of tables lining two walls, and they fill up quickly with 90-minute reservation slots beginning at 6 p.m. The interior design evokes the Orient Express with wooden accents and overhead racks above the seating, and the bartenders’ wardrobe and glassware are a throwback to the last century too. The menu of bottled classic cocktails, Champagne, and non-alcoholic drinks provides an oasis of refinement in the heart of Rome’s rowdy nightlife district.

Know before you go: Reservations are essential — book online for this hidden cocktail bar experience.

Latteria Trastevere is a wine bar and bistro in Rome’s nightlife epicenter focused on natural vino, cheeses, and cured meats culled from tiny, sought-after producers across Italy. There are some hot dishes too, and Sardinian owner Antonio Cossu brings in island specialties like sa fregola (pearl couscous) with crab and bottles from Barbagia, one of Sardinia’s most delicious wine regions. As a bonus, Latteria is open nearly every day of the year.

Must-try pairing: The Sardinian prosciutto and wines from small producers from the Barbagia.

Few restaurants in Rome are as deeply tied to the city’s culinary identity as Sora Lella. Founded in 1959 by Elena Fabrizi — actor, cook, and icon — this trattoria in a medieval tower on the Tiber Island has long been a standard bearer for the hearty cucina romana. While there was a period when the restaurant seemed to coast on its reputation, the third generation has brought it back to top form. Today, Sora Lella is once again a satisfying place to experience traditional Roman dishes executed with care. The wine list leans local, highlighting Lazio’s underappreciated labels. With its rustic wood-paneled dining rooms and medieval tower setting, Sora Lella is a nostalgic but enduring pillar of Roman dining.

Must-try dish: Go in spring for the coratella d’abbacchio (sauteed sucking lamb offal) with artichokes, or try the coda alla vaccinara (oxtail stewed in a rich tomato and celery sauce).

L’Antidoto sits on a cobbled Trastevere side street, far from the crowds queuing outside tourist-packed trattorie. What started as a simple natural wine bar in 2020 has evolved into one of the most compelling dining experiences in the city with the arrival of chef Mirko Pelosi in 2024. Pelosi’s training in France, Norway, and Scotland gives him a worldly sensibility, which he puts to work aging fish, fermenting vegetables, and sourcing spices from across continents. Each dish is rooted in ingredients, driven by technique, and free from ego. The menu changes constantly, but expect dishes like mahi mahi confit, chard, tendons, and grapes. In a Roman dining landscape crowded with derivative plates and copycat concepts, Pelosi’s food is a revelation.

Know before you go: Two hungry people definitely can — and should — order everything on the menu.

A short walk from the Colosseum, Tempio di Iside is an elegant fish restaurant known for its crudi (raw dishes) like fish carpaccio, sea urchin roe, langoustines, and oysters. The pasta with sweet red shrimp, cherry tomatoes, and fresh pecorino is excellent (and proof there are valid exceptions to the “no cheese with seafood” rule), as are the spaghetti with clams, whole roasted fish, and pasta with spiny lobster. Book ahead, especially to secure an outdoor table for dinner in the summer, and expect to pay a premium for access to some of the freshest fish around.

Know before you go: Book ahead for a coveted outdoor table in summer.

Located in the sprawling Centocelle district in eastern Rome, Menabò Vino e Cucina offers a veritable tour of Italian regional comfort food. Rigatoni is served with oniony braised beef in the style of Naples, while pasta with chickpeas and mussels evoke the coastal south. Meanwhile, unctuous local classics like pasta alla gricia get punched up with fresh, seasonal twists such as grapes or figs. As the name promises, wine shares the stage with the kitchen’s creations, and the list is populated primarily by naturally and traditionally made wines.

Know before you go: The menu is always changing and the wine list is consistently outstanding.

After a career working in Roman gourmet temples like Salumeria Roscioli, Pasquale Borriello struck out on his own in 2022. His small shop in Trastevere near the church of San Francesco a Ripa has a few high-top tables where you can sip natural wine or craft beer alongside Italy’s greatest cheeses. All the big names are on the menu — Parmigiano-Reggiano, gorgonzola, and mozzarella di bufala among them — but Borriello favors the smallest and most artisanal producers of these famous styles. In addition to formaggio, Forme sells cured meats, sandwiches, and pantry items like jars of obscure marinated vegetables.

Best for: Sit at a high-top table and try blue cheese from celebrated affineur Andrea Magi.

Marco Radicioni trained with Rome’s gelato maestro Claudio Torcè, embracing his sensibility of all-natural flavors, meticulous sourcing, and restrained sweetness. Since launching his own gelateria, Radicioni has grown into a maestro in his own right, churning some of the most exquisite gelato in Italy. His newest location in Monteverde Vecchio serves more than just Otaleg’s rich and creamy gelato made from the world’s best pistachios and chocolates. There are specialty coffee and artisanal pastries, too, which have transformed Otaleg into a point of reference for third-wave coffee drinkers.

Know before you go: Try the Monteverde location for gelato and coffee; Trastevere for pure gelato bliss.

A few minutes from the Circo Massimo, Pizzarium alum and Bonci protégé Alessandro Ruver runs a tiny laboratorio where pizza in teglia gets the kind of focus usually reserved for restaurant menus. The daily lineup of trays features long-fermented dough that bakes up light, crisp, and audibly crunchy. Pizzas get named with a sense of humor, and topped with ingredients from small farms in central Italy. The Ragùver is loaded with slow-cooked meat sauce and Parmigiano-Reggiano, reminiscent of Sunday sauce.

Know before you go: Like most Roman slice joints, you eat standing at a few outdoor high tops, so don’t wear yourself out too much wandering the nearby Colosseum and Forum before stopping by.

Santo Palato is chef Sarah Cicolini’s neotrattoria in Rome’s Appio Latino district, a residential area just beyond the city walls near San Giovanni in Laterano. When it first opened in 2017, the trattoria quickly became a pilgrimage spot for those craving a bold, updated take on Roman cooking. The new, larger location, which opened in the spring, stays true to that original spirit, serving deeply satisfying dishes like tender trippa, an ethereal chicken gizzard frittata, and the yolkiest carbonara around. With a bigger kitchen, Cicolini now has the space to turn out fresh pasta and a wider range of braised, grilled, and smoked meats. Diners can watch it all unfold through large windows that separate the kitchen from the dining room, bringing the action right into view.

Know before you go: The communal table near the entrance is available for walk-ins. Book well in advance if you’d rather sit anywhere else.

After nearly two decades in Rome’s historic Ghetto, cheesemaker Beppe Giovale closed his original shop at the end of 2025 and resurfaced in San Giovanni with a brighter, roomier version. The Via Gallia location still revolves around a refrigerated counter filled with more than 100 mostly raw-milk cheeses, including selections from Giovale’s family dairy in Piedmont and small producers throughout Italy and France. But there is now a real kitchen and around 20 seats, allowing the menu to venture beyond cheese and butter tastings into dishes like tajarin with alpine butter and tongue with bell peppers and salsa verde. For shopping only, Giovale maintains a small stall at boxes 227 and 228 in the Mercato Trionfale; the Ghetto location has closed.

Must-try dishes: A selection of cheeses made by Beppe and his family, accompanied by the smoked salted butter.

Located in Testaccio, Rome’s undisputed offal capital, Piatto Romano focuses on classics like rigatoni con la pajata (pasta with milk-fed veal intestines cooked in tomato sauce) and fettuccine con le rigaglie di pollo (fettuccine with chicken innards). There are plenty of pescatarian options as well, like the outstanding cod baked with onions, pine nuts, apricots, and prunes, and pan-fried anchovies spiked with vinegar and chile pepper, and the vegetable dishes are incredible.

Must-try dishes: Vegetable sides like the braised zucchini greens and foraged greens salad are showstoppers.

Open for: Breakfast, lunch, and some Friday evenings

The Testaccio neighborhood market is the best place in central Rome to shop for seasonal produce, meat, fish, and baked goods all in one place. Get there in the morning to see it in full swing (it’s open Monday through Saturday until 2 p.m. and occasional evenings). Visit Da Artenio (Box 90) for takeaway pizza slices and pizzette, little pizzas topped with tomato sauce, potatoes, or onions. Don’t miss the essential Mordi e Vai (Box 15), where the Esposito family prepares sandwiches filled with offal and meat based on generations-old recipes, including disappearing historic dishes like alesso di scottona (simmered brisket). Nearby Da Corrado (Box 18) sells natural wines, artisan cheeses, and a handful of hot dishes — including incredible soups — while Casa Manco (Box 22) serves naturally leavened pizza by weight and Sicché (Box 37) specializes in Tuscany-inspired soups, sandwiches, and salads.

Must-try shops: Hit Mordi e Vai for offal sandwiches and Da Corrado for cheese, soup, and wine.

Founded in 1967 by Amatrice native Gioacchino Salvi, Taverna Cestia sits across from the ancient pyramidal tomb of Gaius Cestius that gives the restaurant its name. Now run by third-generation restaurateur and sommelier Valerio Salvi, the trattoria covers a lot of ground without losing focus. Roman staples like tonnarelli cacio e pepe and grilled abbacchio share the menu with locally caught seafood, seasonal vegetables, and thin, crisp Roman pizzas from the wood-fired oven. The sprawling dining room and outdoor tables attract families and large groups, while the unusually thoughtful wine list favors small producers and natural wines.

Must-try dishes: This very Roman trattoria serves a very Neapolitan dessert: babà. The rum-soaked pastry can be cloying and sodden elsewhere; here, it’s spectacular, with just the right balance of booze, sweetness, and airy crumb.

The sign teetering on the roof might read “Cafè Du Parc” in the most appealing mid-century font ever, but this kiosk at the nexus of the Aventino, Ostiense, and Testaccio districts now has new ownership and a new name, Mostro. It opens early for specialty coffee, cruises through the afternoon with restrained momentum, then pivots into low key drinking with draft cocktails and natural wines that attract locals who aren’t phased by the flurry of trams and buses that careen over the adjacent cobblestones. The vibe stays casual and the soundtrack vacillates between staff playlists and vinyl on the turntables by the bar.

Know before you go: This is largely an outdoor stop, so dress for the weather, and aim for earlier hours if you want a calmer moment with your drink before the aperitivo crowd clocks in.

Following careers in fine dining in Italy and abroad, Leonardo Vignoli and Maria Pia Cicconi went back to basics with Cesare al Casaletto, a straightforward trattoria the husband-and-wife duo took over in 2009. The menu features Roman classics with a few restrained twists, like fried gnocchi served on a pool of cacio e pepe sauce. The pasta alla gricia has achieved cult status, the suckling lamb mains are exceptional, and the beverage list spotlights stunningly affordable natural wines from Italy, France, and Slovenia.

If you take public transit: Take tram 8 for easy access, and stroll back to the center through Villa Pamphili park after lunch.

Pizzaiolo Sami El Sabawy first made a name in the Roman pizza world at the iconic slice joint Pizzarium (also on this list). But it’s the thin crust, wood-fired personal pizzas he makes today that attract diners to Torpignattara in eastern Rome. Named after the Roman phrase meaning “to do something continuously,” A Rota lives up to its name; once you try the impeccably crisp pizza and golden fritti, like supplì and battered squash blossoms, you’ll keep coming back for more. El Sabawy specializes in a hyper-thin, low-hydration dough that he rolls out with a pin before baking at a lower temperature for longer than its Neapolitan counterpart. The result is a shatteringly crisp base, sturdy enough to support both classic and creative toppings without losing its integrity. The traditional margherita is a lesson in balance, with bright tomato sauce, fior di latte, and fragrant basil, but don’t skip Sami’s specials, like April’s stuffed pizza filled with chard, potato, Parmigiano-Reggiano, and ham.

Must-try dish: Try the classic margherita to understand Sami’s style, then go for the seasonal special.

Located a short distance from Stazione Trastevere, C’è Pasta… e Pasta (translation: “There’s pasta… and pasta”) serves delicious kosher meals to eat in or take away. Order at the counter and don’t miss Roman Jewish classics like carciofi alla giudia (fried artichokes), filetti di baccala (battered fried cod), aliciotti con l’indivia (layered anchovy and frisee casserole), and concia (fried and marinated zucchini). As the name promises, they also serve pasta dishes and sell fresh pasta to cook at home.

Must-try dishes: The Roman Jewish concia and baccala are particularly special.

Bruno Persiani, an Umbrian transplant to the Italian capital, opened this homey trattoria in southern Trastevere in 1968 to serve a mix of dishes from Umbria and Rome. Tavernaccia is now run by Persiani’s daughters and Sardinian son-in-law, who throws in a few of his own regional specialties like suckling pig cooked in the wood-fired oven. The fresh pastas are excellent (especially Sunday’s lasagna, which sells out fast), and the wood oven-roasted brisket is otherworldly. Organic and natural wines from Italy and Slovenia round out the wine list. The service is patient and unbelievably kind — far from the norm in the Italian capital, so don’t get used to it.

Must-try dishes: Order whatever was made in the wood fired oven that day, whether it’s brisket, lasagna, or eggplant parm.

Nearly a decade in, Trattoria Pennestri is still one of Rome’s smartest answers to the question “where do I eat Roman food near the center but away from the tourists?” The room is relaxed and the cooking is grounded in the classics, but the kitchen knows exactly when a twist is worth making, like rigatoni con la pajata brightened with a measured hit of collatura (anchovy elixir) that elevates the sweetly lactic, milk-filled calf intestines with a savory note. The accessibly-priced wine list leans heavily toward small producers, with a strong showing from Lazio and central Italy.

Know before you go: Book ahead, especially on weekends, and ask the staff to steer you through the wine list.

Stecca is the Roman debut of Abruzzese chef Franco Franciosi of Mammaròssa in Avezzano, in partnership with Flavio De Maio of Rome’s Flavio al Velavevodetto. In a low-lit Garbatella space fitted with austere, Nordic-inspired design, the two turn the dining room into a kind of multisensory stage where Abruzzo’s mountain flavors meet Roman cooking. The menu shifts constantly and leans comforting: rigatoni with meat roll sauce; perfectly roasted lamb chops with puntarelle; a creamy soup of chickpeas, chestnuts, and dried figs. It’s all paired with excellent naturally leavened bread and a serious central Italy-leaning wine list

Know before you go: There are a handful of bar seats, ideal for solo diners.

After nearly 30 years at the helm of Rome’s first Thai restaurant, Beijing-born chef Ge Jing Hua opened Sinosteria in 2020 to serve a blend of Chinese regional cuisines featuring dishes like Beijing-style tripe with chile oil and cilantro, and Shandong-inspired squid with peppers, ginger, and bamboo. There are also signature creations like basmati rice with coconut milk, shrimp, capers, and oregano from Pantelleria. The front of house is expertly managed by Ge’s gregarious sommelier son Jun, whose natural wine list and coffee menu are outstanding.

Must-try pairing: Ask Jun to recommend a natural wine or tea.

Trecca is, for lack of a better term, a neo-trattoria. It delivers everything a Roman trattoria should: an informal setting, rigorously seasonal comfort food, and an offal-forward menu. But there’s also a natural wine list, an Instagram page, and two young brothers at the helm. Manuel and Nicolò Trecastelli lean into Rome’s powerful flavors and rich ingredients. Their carbonara and amatriciana are as loaded with pepper-spiked guanciale as any in the city, and tomato and vinegar are employed in the meaty mains to offset their unctuousness.

Must-try dish: Try the pajata in any and every way the restaurant serves it.

At Da Michele, two generations of the Pignotta family have perfected an incredibly high-level wine and seafood experience, presented without pretense. Since opening in the residential San Paolo district in 1991, this spot has become a neighborhood institution, drawing back regulars with its consistently fresh catch from local fish markets in Fiumicino and Anzio, and attracting wine connoisseurs from across the city eager to taste through the exceptional cellar. Pair mineral-driven white wines from across Europe — including older vintages — with al dente linguine with telline (wedge clams) and fried or roasted fish.

Must-try pairing: Pair linguine with telline or roasted fish with older vintage white Burgundy from the cellar.

Pizza Nader in the Roma 70 neighborhood — an area in the southern part of town once home to emperor Nerva’s grain reserves — is worth the detour. This unassuming shop might look like your standard Roman pizza al taglio joint, but step inside and you’ll find a level of care and precision that sets it apart. Sacks of stone milled flour from Le Marche, Campania, and Sicily crowd the entrance, where I ate a delightful supplì on a visit last month while waiting for a slice of pizza adorned with pecorino, black pepper, and guanciale. Owner Nader Abdelkader praises the dedication of the farmers and millers that make the flour for his deeply flavored pizzas and the dozen types of naturally leavened pane that he bakes.

Must-try dish: Don’t miss the legendary kebab, a favorite of regulars.

#82. Baked Potatoes on the Grill

Making baked potatoes on the grill means fluffy, tender spuds with buttery skins—all without turning on the oven.

When you already have your grill fired up for steaks or chicken, there’s no need to turn on the oven for a baked potato side. These grilled baked potatoes take just a few minutes to prep, and turn out fluffy and tender inside with buttery skins. Once they’re on the grill, you’re free to focus on the rest of the meal. Serve this grilled side dish with classic toppings like sour cream and chives, or set out a few options and let everyone build their perfect potato.

Making baked potatoes on the grill is just as easy as cooking them in the oven. Scrub and pierce the potatoes, then brush them with melted butter, season with salt and pepper (or any other seasoning you like), and wrap them in foil. Place the foil-wrapped potatoes over indirect medium heat, cover the grill and cook the potatoes until they’re tender.

Set up the grill for indirect cooking. For a gas grill, preheat the burners on one side to medium and leave the other side off. For a charcoal grill, arrange the coals on one side, leaving the other side empty. Close the lid and let the grill preheat to about 350°F.

Scrub the potatoes well and pierce each one several times with a fork or sharp paring knife. Place each potato on a 12-inch square of heavy-duty foil. Brush them with melted butter, then season them with salt and pepper. Fold the foil around the potatoes and seal the packets tightly.

Editor’s Tip: A pastry brush makes it easy to coat each potato evenly, but you can also use your fingers to rub the butter over the skin.

Place the foil-wrapped potatoes over indirect heat, away from the burners or coals. Cover the grill and cook the potatoes for 45 to 50 minutes, or until the potatoes are tender when pierced with a fork. Carefully open the foil packets to allow the steam to escape.

Let the potatoes cool, then remove them from the foil and transfer them to an airtight container. Refrigerate them for up to four days.

Reheat individual potatoes in the microwave or warm them in a 350° oven until they’re heated through. For crispier skin, reheat them in an air fryer or directly on the grill.

Yes! To freeze baked potatoes off the grill, unwrap the potatoes and let them cool completely, then rewrap them tightly in foil or storage wrap and place them in a freezer-safe bag or container. Freeze them for up to three months.

When you’re ready to enjoy the potatoes, thaw them overnight in the refrigerator, then reheat them in a 350° oven until they’re heated through. For crispier skin, finish them on the grill or in an air fryer for a few minutes.

Russet potatoes are your best bet for grilled baked potatoes. We like large Russets because they make a hearty side and hold up well on the grill. Their high starch content gives you that classic fluffy baked-potato center. Try to choose potatoes that are about the same size so they cook at roughly the same rate.

Baked potatoes take about 45 minutes on the grill. Larger potatoes may need a little extra time, while smaller ones can cook more quickly. Start checking at the 45-minute mark by piercing a potato with a fork; it should slide easily into the center when the potato is done.

Whether you choose the oven or grill, baked potatoes take about the same amount of time to cook. Potatoes on the grill take about 45 to 50 minutes, while oven-baked potatoes may take up to an hour. So there’s not much difference in cooking time. The grill does have one big advantage in warm weather, though: You can make baked potatoes outside without heating up the kitchen.

The topping possibilities for grilled baked potatoes are endless! Keep it classic with butter, sour cream, shredded cheddar, bacon and chives, or turn them into a substantial meal by topping them with chili, pulled pork, broccoli and cheese, or sauteed veggies. For a Tex-Mex twist, try your favorite salsa, sliced avocado or guacamole, and green onions. You can also set out a variety of toppings and let everyone build their own loaded baked potato.

#83. 5 Quick Dishes Our Editors Make With Marinated Artichokes

Each month in Well Stocked, our staff shares unfussy recipe ideas that you can call upon any day of the week. Because yes, our editors love to cook, but sometimes we need to get dinner on the table 12 minutes ago. That’s when we look to pantry and fridge staples that can quickly morph into delicious meals. This month, it’s all about marinated artichokes.

Oh, the artichoke: an aloof green globe, made up of scale-like leaves and a fuzzy interior. But the flavor? So vegetal, so buttery. As a member of the thistle family, the raw vegetable takes a fair amount of trimming and coaxing (including removing the spiky part aptly known as the choke) before it’s good to go. And after you’ve wrestled it into submission, there’s not a ton to show for all that effort.

Which is part of the appeal of marinated artichokes—the kind you get in a jar. Tender, tangy, and genuinely ready to eat, they’re a shortcut worth taking, adding a bright hit of acidity and a satisfying meaty texture to all kinds of dishes. Toss them into a pantry-friendly pasta with speckles of salty pancetta. Mix them into a no-cook antipasto salad. Even nestle them into an unhinged sandwich. Read on for five smart ways our editors put them to work.

A last-minute galette happens to be my specialty, and marinated artichokes are the perfect addition. You could make this full recipe, which involves a simple cream cheese filling, those ’chokes, and asparagus, plus a vinaigrette-dressed arugula topping. But you could also just toss the artichokes with whatever other veg you have in the fridge and a couple spoonfuls of marinade, maybe some grated parm if you have it, into a rolled out puff pastry crust. —Rebecca Firkser, Test Kitchen editor

My team knows my love for a good potato salad, as I sing its virtues all the time. Marinated artichokes are a killer ingredient to add to a French- or German-style potato salad that’s heavy on the vinaigrette: Add chopped marinated artichokes and their brine to just-cooked potatoes, which will hungrily drink up the juice. Standard marinated artichokes are fine; grilled marinated artichokes (like the jarred ones at Trader Joe’s) are even better. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food editor

It’s saved my butt many times: antipasto pantry pasta. (Antipantry pasta? Hm. No.) I raid my cupboard for salty-savory-oily things like olives, capers, roasted peppers, sun-dried tomatoes, chickpeas, and, of course, marinated artichokes. Mix everything in a bowl while the pasta boils. Throw in some mozzarella if there’s any around. Takes 15 minutes tops and always hits the spot. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

My fanciest 20-minute dinner involves a couple of sheet-pan fish fillets surrounded by frilly burnished artichoke hearts. I’ll simply brush some of the marinating juices over salmon or whatever flaky white fish my seafood share provided that week, then save the rest for a finishing drizzle. The drained artichokes go right on the same pan. Then it goes into the oven for about 15 minutes and dinner’s ready. For what it’s worth, those crispy ’chokes are also great for a vegetarian Italian-style deli sandwich. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO & cooking

My bakery days taught me many things, chief among them that ricotta deserves a little fluffing. I loosely follow this recipe and whip it until smooth, then pile it onto pan-fried toast with sizzled artichokes and capers (two dependable ingredients always stationed in my pantry). I like to top the toasts with an herb salad: usually basil and dill dressed in the brine from the artichoke jar. Let no drop go to waste. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

#84. Our 20 Favorite Rosh Hashana Recipes

Rosh Hashana marks the beginning of the Jewish New Year and the first of the High Holy Days that take place each autumn. For many, it’s a time of year to pause, reflect, and take stock of life’s simple pleasures. Family and friends gather to celebrate over generous shared meals made up of dishes that reflect the season and traditions passed down through generations. From slow braises and hearty sides to crisp fall desserts and plenty of challah, the food served during Rosh Hashana is an important part of the celebration. Here are some of our favorite recipes.

“On the red carpet of Rosh Hashana desserts, honey cake has a far smaller fan base than some of its glittering apple counterparts,” writes baker Ellen Gray. “Yet honey cakes are iconic, tethered to the High Holidays as a symbol of hope for a sweet New Year.” Here, Gray upgrades her grandma Minnie’s Rosh Hashana cake with a splash of cream soda and a slick of dark chocolate icing. Get the recipe >

Rings of fresh apple are dipped into a lightly sweet batter, fried until crisp and golden, and tossed in vanilla sugar while still warm. The result is a simple fall treat with a tender center and a fragrant, crackly coating. Get the recipe >

Beef and an assortment of root vegetables slowly braise together in this hearty, gently sweet stew. The long cooking time allows the meat and vegetables to soak up the flavors of the rich braising liquid. Get the recipe >

Instead of one large loaf, braided challah dough is shaped into individual knots before baking, giving each piece a soft, fluffy center and beautifully golden crust. Serve them alongside a holiday meal, or pull them apart and eat them warm with morning coffee or afternoon tea. Get the recipe >

This savory take on classic noodle kugel combines egg noodles with caramelized onions, eggs, and plenty of black pepper. Baked until set and lightly browned on top, it makes a comforting addition to any table. Get the recipe >

New York City chef Elyssa Heller shares her mom’s secrets to a richly flavored matzo ball soup, including roasting the chicken bones separately and adding lots of parsnip to the stock. Get the recipe >

Lightly sweetened dough is filled with a fragrant mixture of date syrup and pistachios before being rolled and baked until golden and crisp around the edges. A drizzle of rosewater-infused honey adds a floral finish to these bite-size pastries. Get the recipe >

Chicken roasts alongside sweet apricots and tart currants, which soften and mingle with the savory pan juices as they cook. The combination of tender meat and jewel-like dried fruit makes for a festive main course with a pleasing balance of sweet and savory flavors. Get the recipe >

Apples are roasted with honey and butter until tender and lightly caramelized, then tossed with their cooking juices, French apple brandy, and toasted sesame seeds and served warm with crème fraîche for a simple but memorable dessert. Get the recipe >

Whole smaller fish like branzino or porgy are coated in a mixture of herbs and spices and fried until deeply golden and crisp, letting the aromatic crust lock in the tender, flaky flesh. A garlicky parsley-and-chile rub adds brightness and heat, while lemon brings a fresh, citrusy finish to balance out this impressive centerpiece. Get the recipe >

Sweet, crisp carrots, bitter radicchio, and crunchy pistachios come together in this colorful salad that’s sweetened with dates and brightened with citrus and punchy balsamic vinegar. Get the recipe >

This dessert splits the difference between cake and pie, with a buttery, pie crust surrounding Granny Smith apples, raisins, and walnuts. Honey and warm spices flavor the filling, while pieces of dough scattered over the top bake into a rustic streusel-like finish. Get the recipe >

Raspberries do double duty here: a few spoonfuls of raspberry jam are added to the chocolate filling, and a raspberry syrup is used to lacquer the final loaf. Get the recipe >

Beans, barley, potatoes, and beef simmer slowly together overnight, allowing their flavors to deepen and mingle. The result is a hearty, deeply savory stew with tender meat, creamy beans, and a rich broth. For a faster version, the dish can be braised on the stovetop in just a few hours. Get the recipe >

Made with French miel de lavande from Provence, this simple custard combines milk, egg yolks, sugar, and honey, then is churned until firm. The honey gives the ice cream its distinctive floral aroma and flavor. If you’re unable to find miel de lavande, regular honey and dried lavender make a suitable substitute. Get the recipe >

Cooked carrots are blended until silky smooth and brightened with orange juice and a gentle hit of fresh ginger. The resulting purée is sweet, citrusy, and warmly spiced, making it an elegant accompaniment to a holiday spread or autumn table. Get the recipe >

Perfumed with warm spices including cinnamon, allspice, and ginger, then finished with a brighly flavored orange glaze, this dessert is a classic at Jewish holiday tables. Get the recipe >

Tender cabbage leaves are wrapped around a savory filling of beef and rice, then nestled into a rich tomato sauce to braise. As the rolls cook, the cabbage softens and the filling takes on the sweet, savory flavors of the sauce seasoned with cayenne, paprika, raisins, and honey. Get the recipe >

After a quick blanch, the sprouts are halved and broiled with olive oil and smoked paprika until caramelized. Lemon juice and zest plus white wine vinegar add acidity, while grated horseradish and pomegranate seeds bring heat and bursts of tartness. Get the recipe >

#85. All About Romain Gavras, Emily Ratajkowski’s Boyfriend

In February 2026, Emily Ratajkowski went Instagram official with French director Romain Gavras. This isn’t Gavras’s first public relationship, though. He dated Dua Lipa in 2023, with the pair first sparking dating rumors that March when they were photographed holding hands while leaving the Saint Laurent show during Paris Fashion Week.

They went red carpet official at the Cannes Film Festival that May and ultimately ended their relationship in December 2023. (Lipa is now married to Callum Turner.)

In November 2025, Gavras was photographed kissing Ratajkowski, beginning their public love story. Here’s what we know about the French filmmaker and his romances, past and present.

Forty-five-year-old Gavras was born in Paris, and the Onassis Foundation states that he’s the son of Greek-French film director Costa-Gavras, so directing runs in the family. His most recent big works include Sacrifice (2025) and Netflix’s Athena (2022), but he is also known for directing several popular music videos, including the video for M.I.A.’s “Bad Girls,” winner of a 2012 MTV Video Music Award. In 2017, he was nominated for Best Music Video for Jamie XX’s “Gosh (Version 2)” at the award show again. He was additionally nominated for a Grammy Award in 2013, for directing Jay-Z, Kanye West, and Frank Ocean’s “No Church in the Wild.” Gavras has headed a number of ad campaigns, too, including Louis Vuitton’s “Coeur Battant,” Dior’s “J’adore: The New Absolu,” and Powerade’s “The Corner,” per his IMDb page.

On Nov. 10, 2025, Gavras and Emily Ratajkowski were photographed in New York City, marking their first public appearance together. The two were seen holding hands and kissing during a nighttime walk.

Yes, on Feb. 19, 2026, she posted photos with him, going Instagram official with their romance:

Yes. In September 2026, Ratajkowski and Gavras stepped out together in Rome, where they shared a kiss while walking through the city. Gavras also kept his arm around Ratajkowski as the pair walked together.

For the outing, Ratajkowski wore a fitted black halter minidress, white sneakers, and black sunglasses. She carried a small black shoulder bag and wore her hair down. Gavras paired an olive-green short-sleeve shirt with loose white pants, sneakers, a white baseball cap, and black sunglasses.

In October 2026, Ratajkowski and Gavras made their red carpet debut at the Academy Museum Gala. They posed for photos together, and Gavras had his arm around his partner’s waist.

Ratajkowski wore a bright red gown with gathered detailing at the waist and styled her hair in loose waves. Gavras opted for a classic black suit with a white shirt and black tie.

Gavras dated singer Rita Ora from 2020 to early 2021.

In March 2021, a spokesperson for Gavras told the Daily Mail, “Rita and Romain split up months ago because of difficulties with their respective work commitments. They remain close friends.”

While they were dating, yes. Lipa celebrated Gavras’s 42nd birthday on July 4, 2023, with an Instagram tribute. “joyeux anniversaireeeee bébé 💞,” she wrote in French. Her message translates to: “happy birthday baby.” The post has since been taken down.

In December 2023, breakup reports first came out.

Neither Gavras nor Lipa has commented on the alleged breakup. In January 2024, Lipa spoke about being single to Rolling Stone. “Dating, I think overall, is just a little confusing,” she said. “It’s either through friends of friends or people you trust where you can meet new people, because [dating] is not really so straightforward when you are, I guess, a public person.”

She also touched on experiencing a breakup with no animosity, though she didn’t reveal whom it was with: “I think I’ve had breakups in my life where I felt like the only kind of breakup you could have was when things just ended really badly,” she said. “Things ending in a nice way was such a new thing.… It taught me a lot.”

#88. Chicken Marsala Casserole

When you’re hungry for something that’s comforting, cozy, and a little luxe feeling too, chicken Marsala is a truly excellent option. The pan sauce has plenty of mushrooms, fortified Marsala wine, and a splash of cream, because why not? It’s a fantastic dinner, easy enough for a weeknight and special enough for date night. This Italian-American recipe is such a crowd-pleaser that we have reimagined it with orzo, as a slow-cooker meal, and as a gnocchi and chicken soup too. Now it’s time for chicken Marsala’s casserole moment. There's still a rich mushroom-Marsala sauce and plenty of chicken, but now there’s al dente pasta and lots of melty Swiss cheese, creating a rich, shareable dinner that everyone will reach for.

The cheese:Melted Swiss gives this casserole an almost French onion soup-like flavor. If you can’t buy a block of Swiss cheese, pick up 8 ounces of sliced Swiss cheese from your deli counter and coarsely chop it. A mix of low-moisture mozzarella and white cheddar would work here too.

The chicken:A rotisserie chicken will usually yield 3 ½ to 4 ½ cups of cooked meat. Picking up a whole cooked chicken is a great option here, but definitely not the only one. If you cook chicken for another meal–roasting a whole chicken or chicken thighs or breasts—cooking an extra 1 1⁄2 to 2 pounds of chicken will yield enough cooked meat for this recipe. If you have 4 cups of cooked penne or rigatoni, you can add the cooled cooked pasta to the baking dish in step 2 along with the chicken.

The garnish:Now, a casserole as delicious as this doesn’t need a garnish per se, but some chopped parsley adds a fresh finish, and a little bit of freshly grated Parmesan would add more cheesy, umami notes.

Storage:This casserole can be prepared through step 5. Cover with foil and refrigerate for up to 24 hours. Take the casserole out of the fridge while the oven is preheating. Bake, covered, for 25 to 30 minutes, until the sauce is bubbling, then bake uncovered for 10 to 15 minutes, until the cheese has melted and is browning in spots. You can cook the casserole 4 days ahead; store in an airtight container and refrigerate. Any leftovers should last about the same time.
