I was also surprised to rank Litehouse Ranch lower on this list. I tend to prefer refrigerated salad dressings sold in the produce section rather than shelf-stable options in the grocery store aisles. I have purchased other varieties of Litehouse products in the past and liked the taste, but this ranch dressing didn’t have the flavor punch I was hoping for.

Selling for $3.99 per 13-ounce jar, this ranch comes out to about 30 cents per ounce, which is on the higher end compared to other options on the market. I did like that this was the only product sold in a glass jar with a screw top, rather than in a plastic container or a squeeze bottle.

Bottom Line: Litehouse Ranch needs more herbs and seasonings to really be considered a contender in the jam-packed ranch dressing space.

I’ve always had good luck with Ken’s products. The dressings are typically sold in large, 16-ounce bottles with a respectable price point. This ranch retails at my local store for $3.29, which comes out to about 21 cents an ounce. Ultimately, both the price and flavor of this dressing were middle-of-the-road. I did like the velvety texture of the dressing, so I might keep it on hand when making recipes that call for ranch, rather than just using it on a basic salad or as a dip.

Bottom Line: Ken’s Steak House offers a diverse line of salad dressings, but its ranch wasn’t a standout in this ranking.

Tuscan Garden is a product line from Aldi, and a 16-ounce bottle of its ranch dressing sells for a bargain at $1.99. That comes out to about 12 cents an ounce and is one of the most budget-friendly options in this ranked list. This ranch skews a little sweeter than others I tasted and has a muted vinegar tang. Depending on your palate, this could be right up your alley or not your thing.

Bottom Line: While this might not become my go-to ranch dressing, it will certainly be on my radar whenever I’m entertaining a crowd and need to save on groceries.

Marie’s is another refrigerated ranch dressing option. The Creamy Ranch comes in a 12-ounce screw-top plastic jar for $3.99, or about 33 cents per ounce. Refrigerated dressings tend to cost more than shelf-stable dressings.

Sour cream is listed in the ingredients, which sets this ranch apart from others I tested. It resulted in more of a dip consistency rather than an easy-to-drizzle dressing for a salad. I did enjoy the rich, thick texture of this dressing, but I also felt the sour cream slightly muted the vinegar’s tang.

Bottom Line: This would be my choice for a ranch to serve as a dip or a spread rather than drizzled on a salad.

The tiny but mighty bottle of Classic Ranch Dressing from Kraft was the biggest surprise of this taste test. At only $1.00 for an 8-ounce container, this ranch was the least expensive of the bunch. I presumed that the big brand name and the low price point might mean a lower-quality product, and I was proven wrong. Just looking at this dressing, you can see more specks of herbs and spices than in other brands. It also has a delightful tang that I have mentioned missing in other products. Given the fact that it is also such a deal, I was blown away.

Bottom Line: If you want the best-tasting ranch dressing on a budget, look no further than Kraft.

I wasn’t surprised when the Marzetti Classic Ranch ranked quite high on this list. The Marzetti brand is one I reach for over and over again with consistently delicious results. This 13-ounce refrigerated jar retails for $3.99.

The flavor profile was the perfect balance of herbaceous and zesty, all while having the ideal texture and thickness for a dressing. It perfectly hovers that line between feeling substantial enough for a veggie tray and still having the ability to drizzle over a salad. This brand uses real buttermilk in its recipe, and it is the second ingredient after oil. I think that leads to the tartness and richness I have come to love in a great ranch dressing.

Bottom Line: Marzetti makes the best of the refrigerated ranch dressing options.

It’s no surprise that the best ranch on this list was awarded to the brand that started it all, Hidden Valley Ranch. What began as one cowboy’s signature recipe in the 1950’s has transformed into an iconic American staple. I purchased an 8-ounce bottle for $2.49, or about 31 cents an ounce, which is an average price for a bottle of ranch.

The classic flavor settled right into the perfect ranch balance of creamy, tangy and savory, with an ideal drizzling consistency. I also like how Hidden Valley Ranch offers a variety of products so you can make ranch for different needs. If you want to make a more homemade version of this legendary dressing, you can purchase a spice blend packet and mix it with mayonnaise and buttermilk or grab some sour cream and cream cheese and whip up a Loaded Hidden Valley Ranch Dip.

Bottom Line: I’d say go straight to the source! Hidden Valley Ranch created the legendary ranch flavor, and it continues to be the best today.

Which is your favorite brand? Let us know in the comments below!

#91. An Insider’s Guide to the Best Coffee Shops in Bogotá

As the world’s third-largest coffee producer, Colombia generated 1.81 billion pounds of green coffee in 2025. Although most visitors to the country associate its bean production with the Eje Cafetero—the departments Caldas, Quindío, and Risaralda—the growing regions here extend far beyond it. Ironically, for decades, the best beans largely went abroad. To this day, Colombia exports more than 90 percent of its coffee crop.

As a result, what’s traditionally consumed within the country is largely the beloved tinto, so named for the dark undertones in red wine (vino tinto). Don’t get me wrong: I love a tinto. Typically made with commodity-quality beans, this potent cup is brewed in a metal pot or filtered through cloth and sweetened with panela (unrefined cane sugar). A tinto evokes a sense of nostalgia and the camaraderie of gathering at the street corner with friends on a leisurely Sunday afternoon. You can never go wrong, because they all taste the same.

In recent years, there has been a movement to drink locally, thanks to a new generation of roasters who are paving the way to showcase the diversity of Colombia’s coffee beans. One of the unique aspects of the country's terrain is its dramatic elevation changes—coffee is cultivated from roughly 4,000 to more than 6,500 feet above sea level. This includes the volcanic mountains of Nariño near the Ecuadorian border, all the way to the misty slopes of Huila, where coffee farms climb the foothills of the Central and Eastern Andes.

The same terrain also allows for an extraordinary range of fruit to flourish, from the tangy lulo and citrusy-sweet passion fruit to the juicy guava and the tart tomate de árbol. All that fruit grown alongside coffee plants, in addition to topography ranging from snowcapped peaks to Caribbean coastline, brings out distinct flavor profiles.

Although I have always loved the taste of coffee, I never quite appreciated the nuances of what I was drinking until I moved to Colombia three years ago. Bogotá has been a large part of that education. The high-altitude capital has become a hub for specialty cafés. Roasters here find distinct ways to serve beans from around the country, from carefully prepared pour-overs to cold brews infused with orange or tamarind. Visiting the city’s cafés can often feel like traveling through Colombia one cup at a time, with single-origin brews offering inspiration on what regions to explore next.

Earthy interiors with terra-cotta tones and smooth concrete open onto a welcoming sun-filled, plant-lined courtyard in this design-forward oasis. With locations in two of the city’s trendiest neighborhoods, El Nogal and Quinta Camacho, Tropicália works with small Colombian producers and rotates its coffees every three months or so. What makes its coffee particularly interesting is the supplier list, which ranges from small producers and women-led farms to competition-grade selections and, more recently, experimental, wild-processed coffees that push flavor in new directions. Each filter coffee comes with tasting notes that help you understand the flavors in your cup. Don’t leave without trying the cold brew tamarindo, where the fruit’s tartness plays against the bitterness of the coffee. Pair your drinks with Tropicália’s popular avocado toast, served with a tangy mango pico de gallo and a poached egg.

One of my favorite things about Bogotá? When I ask for a coffee recommendation, I know I’ll always get a good one. That’s how I stumbled upon Lohas Café by specialty exporter Lohas Beans, a company that has worked with Colombian producers for over a decade. Tucked inside a colonial redbrick house, this minimalist coffee bar offers the intimacy of stopping by someone’s home for a cup. The café specializes in competition-level coffees, including limited lots sourced from producers in southern Colombia’s Huila region. Filter coffees are a highlight, but order a cappuccino or latte to experience one of Lohas’s curious signatures: milk that is frozen to remove much of its water, resulting in a richer cup that pairs beautifully with the selection of coffees.

Cl 93b #13–91Cra. 9 #79A–23 Primer Piso, Chapinero+57 317 720 5538

With locations in Chicó and El Nogal, Azahar Café is a great place to visit when you can’t decide on just one coffee. Order the Cata de Café, a tasting of three coffees from its current rotation. One of the unique aspects of Azahar is its close long-term relationships with producers, ensuring that farmers are consistently paid above-market prices. Pair the top-notch cold brew with one of the delicious flaky almond croissants made in-house. The café also has an outpost at Bogotá’s El Dorado airport for one last cup before leaving the city.

Cl. 119b #5–43, Usaquén, Bogotá+57 3225112476

Libertario Coffee Roasters is the kind of coffee shop that feels effortlessly cool, with elegant interiors and an extensive menu for curious drinkers. With multiple locations across the city, it has a range of coffees in its rotation at any given moment, from balanced and fruit-forward to experimental and rare. I’m generally partial to the filter coffees, but for something more unexpected, order the Bruma, which pairs the cold brew with citrusy yuzu, rose petals, and rosemary. They have an all-day menu spanning pastries and brunch to sandwiches and bowls. Try the torta de almojábana, a play on the beloved cheese bread.

Varietale takes its name seriously, with an impressive collection of coffees ranging from familiar chocolatey and caramel-forward varieties to limited auction lots. The fun is figuring out how you want to drink them: Choose from nine filter methods, including V60, Chemex, and French press, and let the enthusiastic baristas guide you toward the one that best suits your beans. Despite all that geekery, Varietale feels refreshingly unpretentious at all its locations throughout the city. It has the spirit of an old-school cantina, where meeting a friend for a tinto was reason enough to get together.

Cra. 11B #96–54Carrera 5 # 71–45 Local 104Carrera 9 # 78–31+57 3202973150

If you like having options, Café 18 is the place to linger. Between its Chicó, El Nogal, and Rosales locations, the café typically offers around 15 Colombian coffees, with at least five varieties available at any given time. Some of the beans are sourced through Colombian coffee auctions held across the country, giving the café access to distinctive lots from producers. One of my favorite parts of visiting is ordering a filter coffee and watching it being prepared in front of me.

Cra. 6a #117–26, Usaquén, Bogotá, Cundinamarca

Colo Coffee has several locations across Bogotá, but I’d make a point of visiting its sprawling Usaquén café. The space unfolds around trees far older than its walls, with trunks cutting through the floors and coffee planters surrounding the interior. It’s the kind of place where you can easily lose track of time, especially since the coffee shop doubles as a roastery and serves a full menu. Grab a table near the roasting area and pair your coffee with carimañolas, crisp yuca fritters filled with cheese and served with spicy suero costeño, a tangy fermented cream from Colombia’s Caribbean coast. Before leaving, pick up one of Colo’s canned cold brews to go.

Calle 120 A # 3A–47Calle 70a # 5–71+57 321938 4156

Catación Pública is as much a classroom as it is a café. Founder Jaime Duque spent 17 years at Colombia’s National Federation of Coffee Growers before opening a space devoted to understanding what happens between farm and cup. At its original Usaquén café and newer Rosales outpost, you can taste Colombian coffees spanning different varieties and filter brewing methods. Alternatively, you can go deeper through hands-on experiences. The Rosales space mirrors that approach, with a sleek, laboratory-like interior centered around a deep-green coffee bar. I’d book the recently launched 75-minute roasting workshop, where you start with green coffee and watch the beans transform every two minutes as you roast them yourself. At the end, brew your coffee in a French press and leave with a 12-ounce bag of your own roast.

Cl. 12b #2–85, La Candelaria+57 3157307016

Located in La Candelaria, Bogotá’s oldest neighborhood, Jaguar Coffee sits inside a remodeled 200-year-old home. The café unfolds like a maze, with intimate lounge spaces and a bar where you can learn about the coffee cupping process or watch your order being prepared. Founder Mario Patiño has spent more than a decade building Jaguar and now works with some 170 coffee growers across the country. Beyond the café, Jaguar extends the experience to its farm in Silvania, about 30 miles outside Bogotá. Opt for a day trip or stay the night, and you can follow the journey from plant to cup and learn about the cultivation process.

#92. The 38 Best Restaurants in Tokyo, According to a Local Expert

Where to eat in Tokyo, including sushi, ramen, and yakitori, as recommended by a local food writer and shochu advisor.

Restaurants in Tokyo are known for shokunin, the people who focus on a single skill to the point of obsession. These chefs dedicate their lives to the smallest details of a cuisine: the optimal temperature for the oil when frying tempura, the perfect texture for sushi rice, the ideal sear on grilled unagi. This long-term commitment separates Tokyo from the other great dining cities in the world, and it has fostered a lot of continuity in the restaurant scene; some of the earliest restaurants in Tokyo also served sushi, tempura, and unagi, along with soba, sukiyaki, and other specialties still represented in restaurants today. Though Tokyo is infamous for a few highly regarded spots that are impossible to get into without an introduction by a regular, visitors will find more than enough to love across the massive dining metropolis.

We update this list quarterly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing Tokyo dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips from our experienced writers and editors, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in yen), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

New to the map in October 2026: The tea master at Chokeikyo offers traditional, modern, and even cocktail options. The handroll sushi bar reaches new heights thanks to legendary nori from the revered shop Yamamoto Noriten. The baton has been passed to a new chef at Sezanne and it continues to shine. Finally, yet another pizza spot at Bulgari Bar for a metropolis spoiled with top pizzerias.

Yukari Sakamoto is the author of Food Sake Tokyo and offers guided tours to markets in Tokyo. She is a graduate of the French Culinary Institute, a sommelier, and a shochu advisor.

Where to eat in Tokyo, including sushi, ramen, and yakitori, as recommended by a local food writer and shochu advisor.

We update this list quarterly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing Tokyo dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips from our experienced writers and editors, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in yen), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

New to the map in October 2026: The tea master at Chokeikyo offers traditional, modern, and even cocktail options. The handroll sushi bar reaches new heights thanks to legendary nori from the revered shop Yamamoto Noriten. The baton has been passed to a new chef at Sezanne and it continues to shine. Finally, yet another pizza spot at Bulgari Bar for a metropolis spoiled with top pizzerias.

Yukari Sakamoto is the author of Food Sake Tokyo and offers guided tours to markets in Tokyo. She is a graduate of the French Culinary Institute, a sommelier, and a shochu advisor.

This spacious warehouse is a sister shop to the original Koffee Mameya Kakeru, a popular boutique in Omotesando. The cafe specializes in flights of coffee, which might include a pour over, an espresso, a latte, and one or more mocktails, all showcasing different expressions of the same bean. You can also order drinks a la carte, including spiked coffee cocktails in the evening. The interior is sleek, with contrasting wooden chairs and a U-shaped limestone counter, and the knowledgeable staff wear white lab coats and bowties — though they’re perfectly friendly.

Know before you go: Reservations are required.

Former New York City architect Shinji Mizutani opened Tanikoretani in the Kiyosumi Shirakawa neighborhood with his brother, Tomoji. Vegetables shine at this hipster izakaya, including in dishes like mizu nasu eggplant sashimi, mountain vegetable tempura, and wafu ratatouille. There are also classic sake-friendly plates like seasonal sashimi, karaage fried chicken, and potato salad. The best plan is probably to opt for the omakase, and leave it to the brothers to create a menu for you.

Best for: An early dinner following a late afternoon visit to Kiyosumi Teien, one of Tokyo’s traditional gardens, just a short walk from the restaurant.

Yamariki in Morishita, an older part of Tokyo, is a shinise restaurant, meaning that it dates back one-hundred years. The signature dish, nikomi offal stew, is simmered in Hatcho miso, zarame sugar, red wine, and bouquet garni; Yamariki’s version is said to be one of the top three nikomi in Tokyo. There is also a colorful selection of vegetable dishes including tsukemono pickles, rainbow crudite with miso for dipping, and a hearty salad with an anchovy dressing. Be sure to inquire into any seasonal dishes like tempura of spring mountain vegetables. Sake, beer, and shochu are all on the menu, but Yamariki is also known for a short list of wines that pairs well with its cuisine.

Know before you go: Yamariki also serves yakiton, grilled pork skewers with interesting cuts like tongue, heart, liver, stomach, and harami skirt steak.

You’ll find dozens of shops lining this street in the Tsukishima neighborhood all serving monjayaki, a local dish similar to Osaka’s okonomiyaki. The setup at every shop is essentially the same: Diners select fillings such as mentaiko (spicy pollack roe), mochi, and cheese, and cook the monja themselves on a large iron plate set into each table with the help of a tiny spatula. The trick is to spread the mixture out thin and wait for it to crisp up (the staff will gladly show first timers the proper technique). Paired with an icy mug of beer, it’s a fun meal.

Know before you go: The street is blocked off at night for pedestrians, letting visitors peruse the shops and giving the whole scene a festive atmosphere.

In Juzo Itami’s movie Tampopo, there’s a scene in which a cook surreptitiously makes omurice, a soft omelet over ketchup-stained rice, for Tampopo’s son Tabo. Diners can experience the version of the dish that was specifically developed for the movie at Taimeiken in the historic Nihonbashi district, a short walk from Tokyo Station. The third-generation chef, Hiroshi Modegi, now helms the kitchen at this iconic restaurant, which also serves other kinds of yoshoku (Western dishes adapted to the Japanese palate) like katsu. The first floor is walk-in only and quite popular, while the second floor is more formal and takes reservations.

Must-try dish: At lunchtime on the first floor, order the small portions of borscht soup and coleslaw for only 100 yen each.

Manhattan has more handroll bars than Tokyo. But the nori specialty shop Yamamoto Noriten, in business since 1849, has started to close that gap, recently opening an imported concept worth your attention: a counter for temaki, DIY hand rolls. Iron Chef Kimio Nonaga has curated a dozen fillings including tuna sashimi, soy sauce-marinated egg yolk, grilled eel, and caviar. A small brick of roasting charcoal warms the nori that is presented in a wooden box.

Know before you go: The casual counter is behind a large noren curtain in the retail shop.

On the 40th floor of the Bvlgari Hotel Tokyo, Il Ristorante - Niko Romito’s long dining room, decorated in carnelian orange and boasting a vaulted ceiling, feels like a chapel to haute cuisine. Chef Mauro Aloisio’s modern Italian takes advantage of seasonal seafood like amberjack sashimi or the collagen-rich kue longtooth grouper steamed and smoked with sakura chips, while the wagyu beef tongue is braised until it falls apart under a beetroot sauce.

Know before you go: Niko Romito is in a hotel so it’s open all-year long, including on holidays (it was a lifesaver for me over the New Year holidays when most of Tokyo was closed). For a shorter meal, head up to the Bulgari Bar on the 45th floor for pizza by Pier Daniel Seu, each paired with a bespoke cocktail.

Chef Steve Lancaster is the new chef at Sézanne, formerly the number one restaurant in the world. Though he is new to Japan, Lancaster worked with Japanese seafood for seven years while cooking at Poise in Singapore. Glass shrimp, uni, monkfish liver, and scallops are highlights on his menu at the Four Seasons Hotel Tokyo at Marunouchi. Many components in the dishes are fermented or include Japanese pantry staples like mirin, soy sauce, or koji on the French menu. The sommelier’s thoughtful pairings of wine and unique sakes, including a sweet kijoshu sake, are a highlight.

Know before you go: Substitutions are not accommodated for allergies, so do check when making a reservation.

Part of the ritual of riding a shinkansen (bullet train) is enjoying a bento and green tea (or sake if you like), while taking in the view. Located inside of Tokyo Station, Ekibenya Matsuri offers about 170 regional ekiben (“eki” for station and “ben” short for bento box) brought in from throughout Japan, an excellent chance to enjoy a range of regional Japanese flavors. The colorful selection includes rice topped with sashimi, wagyu beef, or yakitori grilled chicken skewers, and there is even a gyutan beef tongue bento that contains a warming device activated by a pull-string, allowing you to enjoy a hot meal on your journey.

Know before you go: The shop opens at 5:30 a.m. for anyone catching an early train.

Shabusen’s simple menu is sukiyaki or shabu shabu with thin slices of marbled wagyu beef, sliced by staff into thin sheets, or pork with vegetables. Seated at a casual counter, each diner gets their own hot pot to cook their own meal — think New York diner meets high-end hot pot. Once cooked, the meat and vegetables are dipped into a nutty sesame dressing, tart ponzu, or, in the case of sukiyaki, a raw egg. Aficionados of mingei, or traditional folk crafts, will cherish the tableware and noren curtain at the entryway.

Best for: Top-quality sukiyaki and shabu shabu, but in a quicker and more accessible format.

Torigin Honten, sandwiched between two buildings on a dark narrow pedestrian alley in the heart of Ginza, specializes in yakitori and kamameshi rice cooked with ingredients like ground chicken, bamboo shoots, salmon, shrimp, or sansai mountain vegetables in a personal-size rice pot. There are also chicken and vegetable skewers, grilled over Kishu bincho charcoal.

Know before you go: Across the alley there’s a restaurant called New Torigin that serves a similar menu; it’s not quite as good, but can be a serviceable backup if lines at Torigin Honten get long.

For his contemporary French cuisine, chef Guillaume Bracaval sources 95 percent of his ingredients locally. Set in the Four Seasons Hotel Tokyo at Otemachi, Michelin-starred Est features a variety of tasting menus, including items such as monkfish with house-made yuzu kosho, kombu-cured flounder, corn flan gazpacho, and pickled zucchini with tomato paste and nasturtiums. Wine aficionados will want to explore the Japanese bottle list, which is a study on unique grapes like muscat bailey A and fruity koshu, though the sommeliers can also include sake as beverage pairings. The meal finishes with sweets by pastry chef Michele Abbatemarco, including friandises utilizing honeys from various regions of Japan.

Best for: Est offers a fabulous vegetable-focused menu, a great primer on Japan’s wide variety of produce.

Tori paitan (creamy chicken broth for ramen) is rich and comforting, like grandma’s chicken soup. The broth clings to the thin straight noodles as one slurps. At Kagari, seasonal and colorful vegetables such as watermelon radish, snap peas, and kabocha squash top the dish and rotate throughout the year. Use the side dish of grated ginger and fried garlic, along with a bottle of vinegar from the counter, to brighten up and adjust the umami-rich soup to your liking.

Know before you go: The main Ginza shop is on a quiet pedestrian back street, but the sister shop at the Roppongi Hills complex isn’t as crowded.

Music and cocktails intersect at Bar Meijiu, where Keisuke Matsumoto crafts bespoke cocktails to suit each customer’s whims. After a quick conversation about flavors and vibes — Are you in the mood for something fruity or sparkling? Or perhaps something caffeinated made with house-roasted beans? — Matsumoto works like an alchemist in a compact booth at the heart of the space to concoct the ideal beverage. The non-alcoholic drinks are also worth a try.

Vibe check: While serving customers, Matsumoto also spins items from his record collection, which includes a variety of genres but mainly jazz.

Apartment and retail complex Azabudai Hills opened in the heart of the city in 2023 with more than 100 food shops and restaurants, along with the Teamlab Borderless museum. There’s a meal here for everyone, including two-Michelin-starred Florilège and a second location of Sushi Saito, giving diners a chance at a seat despite the fierce competition for reservations at the original. Other standouts include Arabica Kyoto for coffee, Kawamura for tonkatsu, Pelican Café for ham katsu sandos, Sembikiya fruit parlor for over-the-top parfaits, Shogun Burger for wagyu burgers, and Sobamae Yamato for soba and sake-friendly small plates.

Best for: Finding something for everyone, at any time during the day.

At Tenko, vegetables and seasonal seafood from Tokyo Bay are battered and fried into tempura, a specialty of Tokyo. The restaurant is on the quiet backstreets of Kagurazaka in a former geisha teahouse. Second-generation chef Hitoshi Arai is a master at creating delicate and lacy tempura, serving each one as it comes out of the oil, and it’s worth trying some of the tempura with salt instead of dipping sauce to preserve the crispy covering.

Vibe check: Part of the experience is listening to the tempura as it bubbles in the hot oil.

Open for: Dinner, with the addition of lunch of Saturdays

The former geisha district of Kagurazaka is worth exploring at any time, but especially as evening falls on the atmospheric narrow alleys. Even more so if you’ve booked yourself into Ishikawa for an extended, multicourse kaiseki dinner. Hideki Ishikawa’s impeccable cuisine, superb quality ingredients, and gracious welcome have won him three well-deserved Michelin stars and a host of admirers around the world.

Know before you go: Chef Ishikawa used to work at a tableware company so dining here is a delight for the palate and the eyes.

Owner Kentaro Nakahara sources the finest wagyu and knows all the best cuts to grill over the charcoal burners set into your tabletop at Sumibiyakiniku Nakahara. Besides his seven-item yakiniku (grilled meat) tasting menu, don’t miss the beef “prosciutto,” the tartare, or his self-styled legendary grilled tongue. Yakiniku is always fun, but it’s rarely as chic, clean, and smoke-free — both from cigarettes and the grills — as it is here.

Know before you go: If you want to try that legendary grilled tongue, you must reserve it in advance.

Kaiseki, Japan’s ineffable, hyper-seasonal traditional cuisine, always tastes best in its hometown, Kyoto. This can be attributed to the water, which is softer than in Tokyo. Chef Yoshihiro Murata gets around this by shipping water from the ancient capital to the Akasaka branch of his renowned Kikunoi to ensure his dashi soup stock is always perfect. In this tranquil, secluded setting, it’s almost possible to imagine you have left the metropolis far behind.

Know before you go: Lunch is more affordable than dinner, and the menu includes several seasonal dishes served on beautiful dishware.

The historic Japanese confectionery shop has been making wagashi sweets for the Imperial court since the early 16th century. The flagship Akasaka shop is a glorious sanctuary with a cafe, retail shop, and museum, all designed by celebrated architect Hiroshi Naito. Capturing the fleeting moments of the season is at the heart of wagashi, so the menu changes monthly; in summertime the kakigori shaved ice is topped with sake, apricots, or matcha.

Know before you go: The gallery exhibition in the basement always offers something informative, such as hand-drawn prints of Toraya’s wagashi over the centuries.

Chef Daisuke Nomura serves modern shojin ryori — vegetarian Buddhist cuisine — strategically locating his restaurant Sougo in the Roppongi district to appeal to the younger, international crowd who live and work in the neighborhood. The menu includes a myriad of vegetables from land and sea, along with traditional shojin ingredients like fu (wheat gluten) and yuba (soy milk skin). Diners wanting to learn more about Japanese food can take classes at Tokyo Cook, a cooking school located within the restaurant.

Must-try dish: The signature sesame tofu, fried or grilled to bring out a silky texture.

Bricolage offers work by a dream team of prestigious chefs. Soups and salads come from chef Shinobu Namae of three-Michelin-starred L’Effervescence; baker Ayumu Iwanaga of Le Sucré-Coeur in Osaka contributes sourdough, baguettes, and pastries; and Kenji Kojima of Fuglen provides the coffee. Stop by for tartines and sandwiches, served on vintage blue and white dishes. Bricolage also has an outpost at Shibuya Station’s Tokyu Food Show for takeaway.

Know before you go: Take advantage of the outdoor seating, a rarity in Tokyo.

Second-generation chef Daisuke Shimazaki serves traditional Edomae sushi at Sushi Yuu, located in a quiet residential area not far from the busy Roppongi district. While some high-end sushiya can feel stiflingly formal, more like a library or a church than a convivial restaurant, chef Shimazaki puts all of his customers at ease (in English, Russian, or Italian, as well as Japanese). The meal starts off with small seasonal bites such as grilled Pacific mackerel and simmered yellowtail before the parade of nigirizushi.

Best for: Sushi Yuu is particularly famous for tuna, which Shimazaki sources from one of Toyosu Market’s top tuna vendors.

Sake aficionados flock to Marie Chiba’s Eureka sake bar. The impressive sake list includes labels like Senkin, Aramasa, and Raifuku. Pair a glass with sake-friendly small plates like a smoked jammy egg covered in squid ink mayonnaise, blue cheese ham katsu, and crab cream croquettes. As a sake sommelier, Chiba can expertly recommend pairings, and will warm up some sake to draw out different expressions.

Know before you go: There are only a dozen counter seats so be sure to book in advance, or walk in and hope to get a tachinomi (spot for standing and drinking).

Yoshihiro Narisawa worked under Paul Bocuse, Frédy Girardet, and Joël Robuchon. But at his namesake restaurant, he fuses French haute cuisine with a profound understanding of Japanese ingredients that has resulted in a style uniquely his own. Serving brilliant left-field dishes such as soil soup (yes, really) and Okinawan sea snake broth, alongside superb langoustine and wagyu beef, he more than merits his two Michelin stars and spot on the Asia’s 50 Best Restaurants list.

Know before you go: Chef Narisawa and his team are flexible to accommodate dietary restrictions.

Butagumi, serving tonkatsu (breaded deep-fried pork), is set in a romantic 60-year-old, two-story, freestanding traditional house. Here, you dine on premium cutlets — made from your choice of a couple dozen regional heirloom breeds from around Japan — cooked a beautiful golden-brown and served with a pyramid of finely slivered cabbage and thick, house-made Worcestershire-style sauce.

Know before you go: Butagumi has a second shop in the nearby Roppongi Hills complex in the Metro Hat level basement two.

Nao Motohashi is one of only a handful of female chefs in Japan listed in both the Michelin and Gault & Millau guides. She and her sommelier husband, Ken, are warm hosts at their Aoyama restaurant, which is located in a former house. Diners enjoy an aperitif and appetizers on the first-floor lounge before moving upstairs to the main dining room overlooking an open kitchen. Highlights on the vegetable-forward menu include pickled tomatoes in a rose and hibiscus sauce, scallops with butterbur, and duck with slightly bitter spring mountain vegetables. The signature cheesecake ice cream pairs wonderfully with a warm sake.

Must-try drinks: The non-alcoholic program is exciting, with house-made beverages such as grilled mandarin oranges with jasmine; burnt honey juice; and an apple, whey, and pomegranate drink.

Grillmaster Takashi Imai’s namesake yakitoriya is large, sleek, and contemporary. All the seats look in on his spacious open kitchen, so you can watch him in action over the main charcoal pit. Besides his excellent chicken skewers, Imai usually offers a list of premium meats, such as French pigeon, and a serious selection of grilled vegetables from his second grill.

Know before you go: There’s also a substantial list of natural wine to pair with your skewers.

Chef Zaiyu Hasegawa’s decision to move Den from its iconic Jimbocho address has paid off in spades. At the new location, the chef can see each diner’s face and may adjust service or the size of dishes accordingly. The cooking remains innovative and satisfying, incorporating audacious, humorous ideas into Japan’s highly formalized kaiseki tradition. Expect foie gras in your appetizer and unique personalized front of house service from the chef’s wife, Emi, and her team.

Must-try dish: The signature Dentucky Fried Chicken.

Chef Yuki Motokura left a traditional Japanese kitchen to open Pizza Marumo. Motokura defines his pies as neither Neapolitan nor Roman, but as Tokyo-style. The charred pizza dough has the texture of freshly grilled mochi rice cakes, a comfort food for many Japanese diners. The extensive menu includes wagyu carpaccio, oven-roasted vegetables, and a long list of pizzas. The restaurant covers classic pizzas, as well as unique Japanese-style renditions incorporating umami-rich ingredients like katsuobushi (smoked skipjack tuna flakes), shaved kombu (kelp), shiitake mushrooms, or almost cheesy, soy-marinated tofu.

Know before you go: Marumo is popular, so be sure to book a reservation via the restaurant’s website.

Fresh, house-made tofu is the specialty at Tofu Shokudo, a temple to soy. Try set meals like a spicy Korean-style soup of soy milk, soft oboro tofu, and pork, or the tofu gozen set featuring nine types of soybean and tofu dishes. The bare bones wooden interior feels like a busy cafeteria packed with diners enjoying the many expressions including cheesy, fluffy, soft, firm, and spongey when deep-fried.

Know before you go: Diners start queuing before the doors open for lunch. The take-away window offerings include doughnuts made from okara tofu lees, fresh and fried tofu, and silky soymilk skin called yuba.

There’s no shortage of soba specialists in Tokyo, but few manage to create noodles quite as flavorful and satisfying as those at Tamawarai. Each batch is made from scratch — the dough mixed, rolled, and cut by hand — and much of it with buckwheat the restaurant helps to grow. The side dishes, such as soba miso and the wonderfully creamy yuba (soy milk skin), are prepared with equal care.

Know before you go: Tamawarai doesn’t accept reservations, so expect to stand in line for up to an hour.

No visit to Tokyo is complete without exploring a depachiku — the food halls found on the basement levels of major department stores. Isetan in Shinjuku can’t be beat for gourmet glamor, with local wagashi (Japanese confections) arranged alongside the patisseries of Sadaharu Aoki, Jean-Paul Hévin, and Pierre Hermé.

Know before you go: Take a bento or light meal up to the rooftop garden.

Just minutes from Shinjuku Station, L’ambre, which opened in 1950, allows customers to step back in time to an old-school kissaten. The cafe sports a high ceiling, red velvet seats, and classical music, providing the perfect atmosphere for enjoying coffee drinks, pizza toast, tuna and egg sandos, and a selection of cakes. Retro menu items include coffee jelly topped with ice cream and whipped cream, as well as a bright-green melon soda float.

Diners sit around a C-shaped counter in this basement eatery to watch as Mai Nagamatsu shaves smoked and dried katsuo filets into delicate flakes called katsuobushi, and serves them over a bowl of rice. Katsuobushi is rich in natural umami, and sits at the heart of Japanese cuisine, so it’s a rare and precious opportunity to try it shaved a la minute. The set menu uses the skipjack tuna (also called bonito) flakes in each component from miso soup to a garnish made with chili oil.

Know before you go: Be sure to make a reservation through Katsuo Shokudo’s website and bypass the queue of diners hoping to get a coveted counter seat.

The serene Tea Bar Chokeikyo by Sakurai exalts the tea experience. Umami-rich gyokuro is steeped three times, the last time with thin slices of fresh peach. Star anise, cardamom, cloves, and cinnamon are freshly ground and warmed up in a Turkish ibrik over hot sand before being whisked into matcha. Come later in the day for tea cocktails like hojicha mojito or white tea with shiso gin fizz.

Know before you go: It’s easier to get seats here in Daikanyama than at the popular Sakurai Tea Japanese Experience in Aoyama. Chokeikyo is down the street from the hip Tsutaya bookstore.

Udatsu is the rare high-end sushiya that can accommodate vegetarians with a special menu. Both courses, vegetable and seafood, are satisfying: Chef Hisashi Udatsu incorporates texture and umami for the delicate vegetable sushi, frying some vegetables and simmering others in kombu kelp dashi. The seafood neta include two types of uni served over fried nori, five types of tuna in a large futomaki roll, and classics like kohada, vinegared gizzard shad.

Know before you go: The vegetarian sushi course must be reserved two days in advance. The restaurant has branches in Los Angeles and Hong Kong also offering vegetarian sushi.

Blossom Afternoon Tea at the Park Hyatt Tokyo’s Peak Lounge & Bar is a parade of savory and sweet bites. Seared yellowtail, snow crab, and smoked duck are followed by chef Julien Perrinet’s whimsical pastries, where seasonal fruits like chestnuts, pears, strawberries, mandarins, and yuzu shine. For the finale, a trolley laden with small bites including madeleines and canelés is rolled up tableside. There is also a wide selection of British and Japanese teas, hojicha and matcha lattes, and more to sip while taking in the view from the glass atrium 41 floors above Tokyo.

Know before you go: Afternoon teas at luxury hotels in Tokyo are popular with locals. Be sure to book in advance.

#93. Self-Care Gifts for Wellness-Focused Foodies (2026)

Shopping for the wellness-minded people in your life can be surprisingly intimidating. They already have their rituals, their favorite powders, and the matcha whisk they swear by. But the right gift can make those habits feel even more special. And during a season that leans heavily into indulgence and nonstop plans, a present that helps someone slow down and reset can go a long way.

Whether they unwind with a candlelit face mask, start every morning with a revitalizing smoothie, or simply enjoy sipping a sparkling beverage out of a pretty tinted coupe, your giftee will love these thoughtful, useful self-care gifts. Consider them little moments of calm that can become part of their wellness routine all year long.

As far as making matcha at home goes, it doesn’t get much better than Rocky’s. The newer brand, which founder Rocky Xu started in 2022, has that cool kid aesthetic from their apparel to their tea accessories. It’s perfect for the matcha lover in your life who wants to level up their morning ritual and do it in style.

Flamingo Estate practically wrote the handbook on luxurious indulgence. Lighting one of their herbaceous candles, washing my hands with their rosemary clary sage soap, or spooning some of their raw, unfiltered wildflower honey into tea makes me feel like all my troubles are so far (or at least farther) away. With a selection of the brand’s most beautiful products, The Garden Tour gift set lets someone you love experience that same little escape.

If you know someone switching to nontoxic cookware, this is exactly the gift they’re looking for. Made In’s CeramiClad pan is PFAS-free and sturdier than most ceramic nonstick pans we’ve tested thanks to its 5-ply stainless-clad base. It’s senior commerce writer Emily Farris’s go-to for eggs, and a great gift for anyone rethinking their cookware.

For new parents, friends in older buildings, or anyone trying to drink more water, this is a practical but thoughtful gift. The NSF-tested Rorra system filters out lead, forever chemicals, microplastics, and over 50 other contaminants while serving as a chic countertop reminder to stay hydrated.

This Brooklyn-based tea brand, which sells whole-leaf teas in biodegradable plant-based sachets, is worth grabbing off the shelf for the packaging alone. But their delightfully fragrant teas, conveniently sold as a bundle of two of the brand's best sellers here, could make a tea lover out of anyone.

If you have a friend who loves a DIY kitchen project (or refuses to buy store-bought anything), this is a wildly good gift. Nama’s machine makes nut or oat milk in under a minute. No more additives; just nuts, water, maybe a touch of sweetener, and voilà, they’ll have fresh alt-milk for smoothies, coffee, and cereal with a touch of a button.

Our team has a lot of Owala fans. They all swear by the brand’s functional-but-cute products, whether the cult-followed FreeSip water bottle or the SmoothSip coffee mug. My colleague Alaina Chou says, “I became immediately hooked and quickly abandoned all of my other water bottles. The cute butter yellow color, the satisfying click of the spout cover as it pops open, the joy of sipping through a straw—I loved it all, and found this was the first water bottle I’d owned that actually encouraged me, a person who is perennially underhydrated, to drink water throughout the day.” I’m sold!

For loved ones who don’t want one more powder in their routine, Plant People’s WonderHydrate Electrolyte Gummies are a fun, travel-friendly alternative. They taste like lychee candy, support hydration and recovery, and are easy to toss into a bag. A pouch makes a great stocking stuffer for wellness lovers and frequent travelers.

Few things feel more “wellness” than a smoothie loaded with greens, fruit, seeds, and healthy fats. If someone in your life needs a blender upgrade, this is the one. The Ascent X2, one of our Gear of the Year winners, has a powerful 2.2-hp motor that is so powerful it can even turn raw ingredients into hot soup in six minutes. Yes, it’s a splurge, but with a 10-year warranty, it’s the kind of gift they’ll use for years to come.

Ghia’s nonalcoholic aperitif is floral and bright and comes in a bottle worthy of being front and center on your bar cart. Unwind in style with the Ghia Cocktail Box, which comes complete with everything from a bottle of Ghia to a fancy pour spout to a handmade Totem Glass designed in collaboration with Sophie Lou Jacobsen. And if you’d rather take your Ghia to the outdoors, picnic with Le Fizz, the brand’s newest aperitif with a refreshing tart strawberry and orange blossom flavor. Le Fizz is meant to be shared, and this set comes with two bottles and four Ghia spritz tumblers.

Buffing Bar Miniature Collection: Volume II

Soft Services buffing bars are the kind of body care product you didn't know you needed until you use it. The exfoliating bars are made of superfine sanding crystals compressed within a moisturizing base, and after just a use or two, which means you'll get exfoliating and moisturizing all in one. This is a Bon Appétit gift guide after all, so I'm here to talk about the brand's most recent collection of gourmand-inclined dessert-inspired scents (think affogato l'orange and cocoa delight). They're packaged quite perfectly for gift-giving in a gift set of four mini bars that are just as exciting to unwrap as an (edible) holiday treat.

Whether you’re drinking a cosmopolitan or your favorite N/A beverage, the Our Place Party Coupes will make the experience that much more luxurious. They’re stackable and dishwasher-safe, perfect for the friend who loves to host but hates cleaning up. Pro tip: They also make a very good vessel for an ice cream sundae, granita, or parfait.

The only thing more indulgent than a few bars of chocolate is one aromatically infused with pure essential oils, like mint leaf, blood orange, and bergamot. Spring & Mulberry chocolate is notoriously good for gifting—the packaging is beautiful, and the brand uses the best of ingredients from direct-trade single-origin cacao and organic dates.

Fellow, one of our favorite design-centric coffee gear brands, has finally released a five-piece matcha set. And true to Fellow fashion, it’s both gorgeous and functional. The set includes everything needed for a proper matcha ritual, from bamboo whisk to sifter, in four stunning colors. It’s the perfect gift for the person in your life who actually (or aspires to) delight in the ritual of making matcha at home.

Ilém's finishing olive oils are more akin to artwork than something we'd usually cook with. One is infused with heirloom damask roses, while the other boasts ceremonial-grade matcha from Uji. Both are meant to be used just before serving to keep the fragrance intact. But the real art are the bottles with a sculptural dramatic red topper and beautiful embossed labels.

Raw manuka honey is something of a wellness buzz (get it?) term these days. It promises to support immune function, boost digestion, and make your skin glow. If any of that intrigues you, perhaps add a Manukora manuka honey kit to your cart this season. It comes with raw manuka sourced from New Zealand, travel-pack honey sticks to stick to your routine, a wood dose spoon, a guidebook, and a few more bee-you-tiful perks.

There are few better gifts than a well-stocked pantry and this grocery bundle from Cap Beauty is a very good place to start. It comes with the brand's magic spice, which makes practically everything from chicken to veggies taste better (it boasts a blend of green garlic, coriander, Persian lime, and CAP Himalayan pink salt), a bag of CAPNOLA, a matcha-spiked granola with gluten-free oats, buckwheat groats, and puffed rice that I could eat all in one sitting; a jar of coconut butter, and a tin of matcha. I'd happily receive this bundle once a month.

Chugging a greens powder isn't everyone's idea of a good time—even if the possible benefits doing so brings is. For those folks, getting your vitamins via a fun-to-eat, tasty gummy will be a real gift. Grüns aims to support your energy, gut function, and cognitive health with whole-food ingredients like apples, beets, kale, spinach, cabbage, spirulina, and so much more.

Algae Cooking Club broke onto the scene in 2023 with a sustainable neutral oil made from algae. The brand—a favorite of Daniel Humm, chef-owner of Michelin-starred Eleven Madison Park—is now back with a very buzzy collab with model and creator Nara Smith. It’s a roasted garlic oil that packs in all the allium flavor without having to endure sticky, stinky garlic fingers. Plus, it’s steeped with yuzu, miso, and scallion for added flavor. It’s flavorful, adorable on the counter, and perfect for the home cook who loves trying cool new ingredients.

Alice mushroom chocolates are the ideal gift for someone who loves to try every single wellness trend. The brand is delivering the supposedly magical powers of functional mushrooms (no, not the kind you put in risotto, and no, not the psychedelic kind) in the form of organic dark chocolate. One of the varieties is chocolate bites for “deep sleep” with ingredients like chamomile and L-theanine. Our editors tested them over a few months and were shockingly pleased with the results.

#94. Toasted Meringue Hazelnut Blondies

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Lightly coat a 9x9" pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Line pan with parchment paper, leaving overhang on two sides. Toast 2 cups blanched hazelnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown and fragrant, 15–18 minutes. Let sit until cool enough to handle, then coarsely chop; set aside.

Cook 1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring often, until butter foams, then browns (do not burn), 7–9 minutes. Remove from heat.

Whisk 2 large eggs, room temperature, 1 large egg yolk, room temperature, 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, ¼ cup (packed; 50 g) light brown sugar, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¾ tsp. instant espresso powder (if using) in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium-high speed until mixture is pale and doubled in volume, 6–9 minutes (mixture will form an unbroken ribbon when whisk is lifted from bowl).

Reduce speed to low and with motor running, gradually pour in brown butter in a thin, continuous stream; beat until incorporated, about 2 minutes. Remove bowl from mixer and gently fold in 1½ cups (187 g) all-purpose flour with a rubber spatula, scraping down sides and bottom of bowl, until no large, dry streaks of flour remain. Scrape batter into prepared pan; smooth surface. Top with reserved hazelnuts and press in gently to adhere (surface will be smothered with nuts).

Bake blondie until edges are golden brown and center is just set, 35–45 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let blondie cool in pan. Using parchment paper to help, lift blondie out of pan and transfer to rack.

Meanwhile, combine 3 large egg whites and 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar in the clean bowl of stand mixer and set over a saucepan of just simmering water (make sure bottom of bowl does not touch water). Heat, whisking constantly, until sugar is dissolved and an instant-read thermometer registers 170°.

Fit bowl onto mixer fitted with clean whisk attachment. Beat egg white mixture until thick and glossy and mixture is barely lukewarm, 8–10 minutes. Add 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt; fold in with a rubber spatula just to combine. Taste meringue and season with more kosher salt if needed

Peel away parchment paper from blondie and transfer to a heatproof platter. Using an offset spatula, spread meringue evenly over blondie, covering from edge to edge. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue until deep golden brown. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Using a long knife and wiping off with a damp kitchen towel between cuts, slice blondie into 9 squares.

Do Ahead: Blondie can be baked 24 hours ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#95. Kylie Jenner and Timothée Chalamet’s Complete Relationship Timeline

Beauty mogul Kylie Jenner and actor Timothée Chalamet sparked a romance in 2023, shortly after Jenner split with the father of her two children, Travis Scott. She and Scott had an on-again-off-again relationship for a few years and now co-parent their daughter, Stormi, and son Aire.

While Chalamet and Jenner are an unexpected couple to fans, they’ve been together for years. Chalamet even gave Jenner a public declaration of love at the 2026 Critics Choice Awards, saying in his acceptance speech, “I’ll just say thank you to my partner of three years. Thank you for our foundation. I love you. I couldn’t do this without you. Thank you from the bottom of my heart.”

Here’s everything we know about their love story so far.

On January 25, Jenner and Chalamet were seen enjoying one another’s company at Paris Fashion Week during the Jean Paul Gaultier show. This was allegedly their first meeting, and a video of them laughing together surfaced on social media once rumors started circulating that they were more than friends.

TMZ released pics of Jenner’s black Range Rover parked outside Chalamet’s Beverly Hills home amid rumors the two stars were dating.

On April 14, a source told People that the pair had been “hanging out and getting to know each other.”

A few days later, another source told Entertainment Tonight that they were officially dating, but things were “not serious.”

“They are keeping things casual at this point,” the insider explained. “It’s not serious, but Kylie is enjoying hanging out with Timothée and seeing where it goes. They added, “Kylie decided she didn’t want to make things public with Timothée this past weekend at Coachella and really just wanted to chill and have fun with her friends.”

Another insider told People that the two “hang out every week,” but it’s “not serious.”

“She is getting to know him,” the source added. “Kylie is having fun. After years of back and forth with Travis [Scott, her ex-boyfriend and father of her two children], she just wants to date without any pressure.”

In May, a source told Entertainment Tonight that the new couple was trying to keep thing quiet. They're “casually seeing each other but are trying to keep it low-key,” the source said.

“They are becoming more comfortable with each other, but Kylie wants to take things day by day and see where it goes,” they added. “Her family thinks it’s great that Kylie is doing her thing, and they are supportive.”

The source continued, “Timothée loves that Kylie is such a hands-on mom and a boss. He appreciates her confidence and thinks she’s incredibly beautiful.”

Jenner’s ex Travis Scott was also reportedly disturbed by their connection.

“Travis is not thrilled about Kylie moving on, but they are still cordial and focused on co-parenting and being the best parents they can be,” the insider said.

In late May, Jenner’s black Range Rover SVA was seen outside Timothée Chalamet’s mansion in Beverly Hills, California. It stopped off early in the morning then left with a security detail.

On Thursday, June 1, the couple was seen outside Chalamet’s Beverly Hills home and then out for lunch wearing matching tie-dye shirts.

In July, Scott seemed to comment on Jenner’s relationship with Chalamet on his new album Utopia. On a track called “Meltdown,” Scott appears to make a reference to Chalamet’s role in the new movie Wonka, a take on the classic novel Willy Wonka and the Chocolate Factory. He raps:

Following false early August tabloid breakup rumors, TMZ and Entertainment Tonight both reported that Jenner and Chalamet’s romance was still going strong.

A source told Entertainment Tonight on August 16, “Kylie and Timothée are still seeing each other when they can. Kylie’s busy with work and traveling a lot, but they make time for each other when it works and both like each other. They’re keeping things low key and chill for now, but get along great and have fun together.”

On September 4, Jenner and Chalamet made their public debut at Beyoncé’s concert. They were filmed keeping close to each other and talking during the show.

TMZ obtained video of them kissing there in the first PDA sighting.

Just a few days later, on Friday, September 8, the new couple was seen at a New York Fashion Week dinner for the launch of Haider Ackermann’s beauty collaboration with Augustinus Bader, Vogue reported. Jenner was Chalamet’s plus one. Also attending were Jared Leto, Oscar Isaac, Sofia Coppola, and Amelia Gray Hamlin. In a video on TikTok, Jenner is sitting beside Chalamet.

The couple went on to attend the US Open together. They were seen kissing there on September 10.

On September 19, a source spoke to Entertainment Tonight about how Jenner feels really comfortable dating Chalamet. The insider explained that Jenner and Chalamet went public at Beyoncé’s concert on September 4 “because she is confident and secure in their relationship. [She] feels like she can be herself with him [and] really likes that.”

Jenner and Chalamet “also connect on a deep level,” the source said, adding that “Timothée is also a family man, and they relate to each other about that. Kylie’s friends and family think Timothée is great and love seeing her happy.”

On September 21, ELLE Mexico captured photos of Jenner at Prada’s fashion show with her Timothée Chalamet lockscreen visible on her iPhone. Although it was likely unintentional, it marked the first little hint Jenner gave herself of Chalamet’s place in her life.

And on September 25, Chalamet and Jenner were photographed together again, this time in Paris. The pair was seen holding hands while exiting a car at Folderol Wine Bar for Rosalía’s birthday party. Both had black outfits on.

Chalamet touched on his relationship with Jenner in an interview with GQ.

He started by discussing the fan interest in him and his love life: “I can’t say that this stuff doesn’t matter, because my intense fandom has led me to where I am.”

But he also “bristles at the suggestion that he might not be entitled to a wholly private life,” GQ’s reporter Daniel Riley wrote. Riley then gently suggested that “if he really wanted to be left alone he might not spend time with one of the four most followed people on Instagram,” referring to Jenner.

Chalamet nodded at the comment, laughed, and replied, “This reminds me of that recent South Park episode with the Worldwide Privacy Tour [which was a parody of Meghan Markle and Prince Harry, and had their characters traveling around the world, demanding privacy]. Sometimes, people are going to be hella confused when you say you’re trying to live a private life.”

On October 25, WSJ. Magazine published an interview with Jenner. The outlet wrote that Jenner was not ready to speak about her relationship with Chalamet, but she did give her opinion on his film Dune as a sci-fi fan. “I do love that movie,” she said.

Chalamet and Jenner kicked off the month together by both attending the WSJ. Magazine Innovator Awards on November 1 in New York City. Jenner was honored with the Brand award, while Chalamet presented the Film award to director Martin Scorsese.

The couple matched in dark ensembles and sat next to each other during the dinner portion of the event. Photographers captured one shot of them at the table:

After the successful show, Jenner was seen going to the after-party in a black ensemble to show her own support for Chalamet.

At the end of the month, Jenner secretly traveled to London to support Chalamet at the premiere of Wonka. She attended the after-party, Entertainment Tonight reported, with an eyewitness saying Jenner was seen at The Corinthia Hotel, “just steps away from” Chalamet.

Chalamet, meanwhile, is “in awe of everything she is accomplishing [and] especially thinks she is an amazing mom.”

“You went to Beyoncé. That is documented, I will say that,” Horowitz joked.

He laughed, “That’s right. That was great. Hard to be present.”

He then commented more on the concert, saying, “I was actually surprised. I’m not, like, Beyhive-level, but I thought I knew way more [songs]. But I guess I know some of the more basic hits.”

On Friday, January 5, Chalamet was seen driving Jenner’s Range Rover in Los Angeles, stopping on Sunset Boulevard at the Supreme clothing store. The actor was wearing a brown sweatshirt set from Pakistani streetwear label Rastah and matching shoes. His other accessories included a black baseball cap and gold neck chain.

Jenner and Chalamet attended the Golden Globes together. While the couple opted not to walk the red carpet together, they sat side-by-side during the ceremony. They were filmed kissing at one point. Fans speculated that Jenner told Chalamet she loved him in the footage based off her lip movements.

The couple was also photographed being affectionate during the broadcast:

Sources spoke to Entertainment Tonight and People about how serious Jenner and Chalamet are. A source told People: “They’re both real with each other, and things have been easy and fun. Timothée reminds Kylie to live in a very ‘present’ way, and she really likes that about him. They both push each other to be better people, and that’s a constant thing in their relationship.”

The source said of their current dynamic: “[They] are super serious and very involved with each other’s day-to-day lives, family on both sides included. On Kylie’s side, Kris [Jenner] and Kim [Kardashian] are especially supportive and think there’s so much potential.” On Chalamet’s side, “his family also sees how happy she makes him. They’re definitely beyond the ‘just having fun’ point of the relationship. Everyone on both sides sees definite potential for something real here.”

That evening, Chalamet shut down rumors sparked at the Golden Globes that he and Jenner had drama with Selena Gomez. Fans speculated that Gomez had told Taylor Swift that Jenner blocked her from taking a photo with Chalamet.

Chalamet spoke to a TMZ reporter who followed him and asked repeatedly about the drama. Chalamet said that “yeah, of course” he and Gomez were cool. When asked if Jenner and Gomez had any “beef,” he said “no,” adding that the three stars, “we’re all good.”

Jenner briefly addressed fan theories that dating Chalamet changed her style in an interview with The New York Times. “I don’t know how I feel about that,” she responded. “I just don’t want to talk about personal things.” She avoided discussing him otherwise.

On May 29, a source told Entertainment Tonight that Chalamet and Jenner are still dating even though they hadn’t been seen together recently. “Kylie and Timothée are still seeing each other and happy,” the insider shared. “They don’t need to try to make things work and it just comes naturally to them. One source told People that Jenner and Chalamet were spotted on a double date at New York City’s Tatiana by Kwame Onwuachi on Thursday, May 23. A second source told the outlet that Jenner and Chalamet “are very low-key when it comes to their relationship and like to keep it that way.”

On June 28, Jenner and Chalamet were photographed at TCL Chinese Theatre, having a movie night. Both wore black masks as they walked alongside each other. Chalamet was in an all-black outfit, while Jenner wore a white strapless top with black pants. It marked their first sighting in months. See the photo here.

Sources spoke to People and Entertainment Tonight about Jenner and Chalamet’s relationship.

People’s source said on July 2, “Things are great with Timothée. Kylie is happy. They are both busy, but making time to see each other, especially on the weekends. He’s been working in NYC. She’s visited him, and he’s also been back to L.A. some weekends. They’re making it work.”

On July 15, Entertainment Tonight published the lengthy intel its source shared. “Kylie and Timothée like to do low-key date nights and keep their relationship under the radar in order to feel some sense of normalcy,” they began. “They both want to have a mature relationship where they aren't constantly in the public eye. Jenner briefly addressed why she doesn’t like talking about Chalamet in her British Vogue interview. “Privacy is so important to me in life,” she said, noting this is in part because the reality star hasn’t had much of it in her life. “It feels so good.” She revealed she has been able to see Chalamet in New York City unnoticed with the help of a baseball cap. “There’s an angle that you can do where they can’t see your face, and I wear a mask,” she said.

The reporter said, “You have a lot of supporters in here, I know you also brought your partner in crime, Kylie, here, too. What’s it like to have her supporting you on a night like this?”

On April 18, a source told People that the couple is now “very serious” after they faced a more challenging start to the year.

“With the awards season and premieres, earlier this year was intense for their relationship,” the insider explained. “But they are making it work. Kylie is truly his biggest fan. She would clear her schedule to attend awards and premieres with him. She couldn’t be more supportive of his career.”

On May 21, a source spoke to Entertainment Tonight about Jenner’s hope for a serious, long-term future with Chalamet. “Kylie thinks Timothée is so great with her kids, and she has told her closest friends that she would love to have another baby with him some day,” the insider said.

Jenner liked her boyfriend’s Instagram about his Marty Supreme trailer, which he shared on August 12. On October 6, Jenner joined Chalamet at the New York Film Festival premiere of his upcoming film Marty Supreme. NYFF’s social media account shared a photo of the couple backstage. The couple later attended the premiere’s after-party at the Waverly Inn, wearing matching black leather outfits.

Two days later, they went to a baseball game between the New York Yankees and the Toronto Blue Jays at Yankee Stadium. For the rare public date night, Jenner wore a black and navy-blue Marty Supreme hoodie, and he wore a black and navy Yankees bomber jacket.

In an interview with Vogue, Chalamet commented on his relationship by not commenting about it. “And I don’t say that with any fear, I just don’t have anything to say,” he told the magazine.

He did discuss both marriage and children, starting with noting the relationship status of his Dune co-stars, saying, “Zendaya is engaged. Anya [Tayor-Joy] is married.”

The actor said he watched an interview with a friend where a childfree person was “bragging about not having kids and how much time it afforded them to do other stuff.” He said their reaction was “like, holy shit. Oh my God. Bleak.”

Which he joked meant that fatherhood “could be on the radar.”

Daily Mail claimed Chalamet and Jenner had split after a month out of the spotlight. Jenner hopped onto Instagram to like her boyfriend’s recent posts in response.

A second source added, “Timothée talked about Kylie all the time while filming Marty Supreme. She even flew out to visit him on set in NYC. They also met up in London while he was shooting Dune. They’re really in love.”

A source told People that Chalamet would spend Thanksgiving break with Jenner after several months filming.

The couple plans to celebrate “with her family next week in L.A., but he’s also spending time with his family before he has to return to the Dune set.”

The source continued, “He started filming in Budapest, in July, and they’ve seen each other as much as they can. Kylie’s been flying back and forth every few weeks. Despite the distance, they’ve stayed close. They’ve been making it work.”

The couple attended the Los Angeles premiere of Chalamet’s new film, Marty Supreme in custom matching orange Chrome Hearts looks. Chalamet wore a leather suit, Timberland boots, and a black ping-pong paddle side bag. Jenner wore a long gown with side cutouts, a plunging neckline, and pumps.

A source told People on New Year’s Eve that the couple intends to spend the holiday together and also has a “trip planned.” The insider explained, “They are making their careers work and making their relationship work at the same time."

The insider added: “It’s been special for Kylie to have Timothée in Los Angeles more in December. She traveled to Budapest several times in the fall when he was busy working. They spent a lot of time apart, but the past few weeks have made up for it. Still, it’s not the easiest relationship. They are both incredibly focused on their careers and ambitious. She’s running a massive business and raising her kids. He’s super focused on being the best at what he does.”

Jenner “loves [his work ethic],” the source continued, adding that she would “never date anyone who just sits around. [They’re] grateful for what they have.”

Jenner joined Chalamet at the Palm Springs International Film Festival Awards on January 3 and at the Critics Choice Awards a day later.

The Marty Supreme star won Best Actor at the Critics Choice Awards and thanked Jenner at the end of his speech. He offered rare public remarks on their relationship, telling her and the crowd, “And lastly, I’ll just say thank you to my partner of three years. Thank you for our foundation. I love you. I couldn’t do this without you. Thank you from the bottom of my heart.” She seemed to mouth “I love you” in response from her seat:

The next weekend, Chalamet won Best Performance by a Male Actor in a Motion Picture – Musical or Comedy at the Golden Globes. He paid tribute to Jenner again in his acceptance speech, saying, “For my parents, for my partner, I love you.”

A day later, he soft-launched their relationship on Instagram. Jenner’s hand appears holding his Golden Globe trophy in the photo:

Jenner joined Chalamet at the Oscars, where he was nominated for Best Actor. The two were seated together during the ceremony and were photographed holding hands and staying close throughout the night.

They later attended the Vanity Fair Oscar Party, where they posed together on the red carpet. Jenner wore a custom McQueen dress with a cut-out, while Chalamet changed into a white Chrome Hearts suit. The pair continued to show PDA, with Chalamet placing his hand on Jenner’s waist and kissing her cheek.

Jenner and Chalamet appeared to give separate glimpses into the same tropical getaway. On March 30, both posted Instagram photo dumps within hours of each other, featuring similar scenery, including white sand beaches and clear turquoise water.

Jenner captioned her post simply, “heaven,” sharing several bikini photos, along with moments of her relaxing in the sun and unwinding indoors.

The insider added that the couple recently “went away on a double vacation” with Kendall Jenner and Jacob Elordi for a “staycation” in Malibu.

Chalamet was seen driving up to Bird Streets Club, where Jenner was reportedly already inside with some friends. The actor pulled his SUV into a private garage, wearing a baseball cap low. Later, Anastasia Karanikolaou, Jake Shane, Mandana Bolourchi, and Jesse Jo Stark were spotted at the venue.

#97. 8 Fall 2026 Coat Trends Worth Investing In

Cooler temperatures swept through New York City this past weekend, which means one thing: coat season is here. And what better excuse than to refresh your outerwear wardrobe? After all, when temperatures drop, your coat becomes the look. And if you’re anything like us, we’re itching to wear a coat that makes a statement.

Strong outerwear anchored the fall 2026 collections. Toggle coats appeared in both familiar neutrals and bold color stories, fastened with leather or woven rope, at Dries Van Noten, Louis Vuitton, and Polo Ralph Lauren. Elsewhere, the shearling—a perennial favorite—returned in sculpted form with a cinched waist, offering a fresh take on cold-weather dressing at Loewe and Bottega Veneta.

Equally noteworthy were the robe coats (belts optional) at Colleen Allen and Calvin Klein, cut in soft shapes for a natural drape. The funnel-neck coat remained a key style for the season, too iterated on in midi and maxi lengths at Gucci and Tory Burch. On the more maximalist side of the spectrum, we saw a steady supply of animal print options, along with jacquard and fur-trimmed takes, for a sense of emboldened everyday glamour.

This season’s outerwear trends have you, expectedly, covered, whether you’re replacing an old faithful, working in a statement piece, or channeling a bit of both.

The toggle coat might be a classic, but it’s been a minute since we talked about it. Its return has been swift this season, as seen at Dries Van Noten and Polo Ralph Lauren, with unexpected toggle closures and fresh crops.

A little shearling was to be expected, and this season’s option get a more structured look. Peplums, or otherwise slightly contoured waists, give it fresh shape.

Crafted in rich velvets and lightweight wools, the house coat appeared on numerous runways in drapey, flowing silhouettes. The epitome of elegant ease.

Animal print isn’t going anywhere anytime soon. Whether it’s leopard, fawn, or cheetah, the runways made a strong case for the pattern in every spot and stripe imaginable.

A timeless option that gets a fresh feel in bold color and swingy cuts. We love it with a funnel-neck closure, too.

Faux fur-trimmed jackets, on the sleeves and hems, brought whimsy (plus a little drama) to the collections. We love them styled with denim, as seen at Conner Ives.

Richly detailed with subtle lustre, the jacquard coat is both a fabulous evening option and a luxurious statement for day—team with denim and flats for contrast. Spotted at Dior, Kallmeyer, Dries Van Noten, and Tory Burch.

Winter isn’t complete without a faux fur coat—choose a longer style for maximum warmth.
