#98. I Ate My Way Through Edinburgh For A Weekend & Had One Of The Best Meals Of My Life

I found plenty to love before I even made it to the Michelin star.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

I love traveling, but I usually like having someone there to experience everything with me. Every once in a while, though, I need a few days where I can move completely at my own pace.

I have some Scottish roots, and when I got the opportunity to take myself to Edinburgh for a long weekend, the answer was pretty easy. I wanted to walk as much of the city as possible, get a little lost, see the sights, and, most importantly, eat extremely well along the way.

With only a few days to work with, I squeezed in everything from Scottish classics I’d never tried before to an old favorite and, for my final dinner, a Michelin-starred tasting menu that I’ll never forget.

Here’s everything I ate and drank along the way.

Nothing says “welcome to Scotland” like getting off a plane and immediately finding an almond croissant of epic proportions.

Cobbled Roastery was my first food stop, and I wasn’t looking for anything complicated. The croissant had a flaky shell that shattered everywhere the second I tore into it. It was aggressively almond-y in the best way, covered with powdered sugar, and after an overnight flight, it did exactly what I needed.

Dishoom and I already had history. I first went in London and loved it enough to return for breakfast on the same trip, so in Edinburgh I did what any adventurous food writer would do and ordered basically the exact same things again.

That consisted of their vegetable samosas and some Chicken Ruby with a healthy side of jasmine rice. The samosas were crisp and packed with warmly spiced peas and potatoes, while the Chicken Ruby was exactly as rich and silky as I remembered it. I had zero regrets about repeating myself.

Later that day, I joined Eating Europe’s Old Town Food & Drinks Tour, which was my crash course in some of the Scottish foods I probably wouldn’t have known to order on my own.

First up was Cullen skink at The Doric, a Scottish soup made with smoked haddock, potatoes, and cream. I’ll admit, a bowl of creamy fish soup didn’t immediately sound like something I needed in my life, but this won me over. The smoke came through first, then the creaminess, while the haddock was much subtler than I expected. It tasted more like a really good potato soup that happened to have smoked fish in it than a bowl screaming “SEAFOOD!” at me.

I knew what haggis was in the broadest sense, but then I actually Googled the ingredients and briefly wished I hadn’t.

Thankfully, eating it was a much better experience than reading about it. Arcade serves theirs as little fried bon bons with whisky marmalade and crispy kale, and the texture immediately reminded me of arancini with that crunchy outside and soft, savory inside. The filling was super meaty without tasting remotely as intimidating as the ingredient list sounds, and my skepticism quickly turned into borderline plate-licking.

By dinner at BABA inside the Kimpton Charlotte Square Hotel, I had reached the part of the trip where ordering one thing felt unnecessarily restrictive, so I went with the Best of BABA and let the table fill up.

This was also where I remembered how aggressively I love a good dip. I kept going back to the muhammara with the warm pita, and somehow haggis made another appearance on one of the skewers (we’re dating now). And I couldn’t remember the last time I’d deliberately ordered pork neck, if ever, but it was gone very quickly.

Then there was the mandarin crème brulée. The top had that satisfying crack, with smooth, citrusy custard underneath, and photographic proof of a completely scraped-clean dish was 100 percent necessary.

A brief interruption from all the eating for one of my favorite moments of the trip.

I grabbed a Cold Town lager, sat outside at Kick Ass, and looked straight out at Edinburgh Castle right there in the distance. Just me, my Scottish beer, and a lot of people watching. Not every moment needs to be more complicated than that.

By my second night, I wanted to go classic: fish and chips.

Herbie More’s did it with panko-crusted haddock, tartare sauce, fries, and mushy peas. The fish had that ideal contrast of a super-crisp outside and flaky interior, and I was embarrassingly happy about the mushy peas. I love peas enough that I regularly put them in pasta at home, although admittedly I usually stop short of mushing them first.

I only meant to stop for coffee until I saw a sausage roll sitting in the bakery case—which is generally how these things happen.

The pastry was buttery and flaky enough to leave evidence all over the plate, while the pork filling had leeks and potato worked through it. It tasted like something somebody had actually made that morning rather than something pulled from a plastic package and reheated.

87-91A Henderson Street, Leith, Edinburgh EH6 6ED

I saved my most ambitious meal for last. Heron in Leith has a Michelin star, and for roughly three hours—longer than some Avengers movies—I was taken through course after course, each paired with wine and presented with such precision that I almost felt guilty disturbing the plate.

The squid was one of my early favorites, but the venison was probably the course I kept thinking about afterward. It was rich, really well cooked, and one of those dishes I was genuinely bummed to finish.

And I will always find room for dessert. One of the final bowls got the same treatment as that crème brulée at BABA: spoon around the edges, spoon across the bottom, and leave nothing to investigate.

It was probably one of the best meals I’ve ever eaten, and as a final dinner, I couldn’t have planned much better.

More than anything, I loved that I got to experience the city through food without feeling like I was eating the same version of “Scottish food” for three straight days. And for someone who doesn’t usually seek out solo travel, eating my way through Edinburgh turned out to be a pretty convincing argument for doing it more often.

#99. 20 Solo Date Ideas Worth Your Time

Your own company deserves a reservation, too.

Taking yourself on a date sounds straightforward until your “solo date” becomes buying toothpaste, answering emails at a café, or squeezing in your usual workout. Useful? Sure. Romantic and self-nurturing? Eh, not quite. I think we can aim higher. You wouldn’t be thrilled if a romantic interest invited you out just to accompany them on errands, so you deserve to give yourself the same consideration.

Research shows that choosing to spend time alone can support relaxation and reduce stress. “It’s so easy to spend all of our time tuning out from ourselves,” says Emma Johnson, LMSW. “A solo date can help us check in with ourselves. To enjoy being in our bodies and the present.”

And yes, solo means solo. Your best friend, your partner, and even your dog need to sit this one out. Being around people at a class or concert is fine, but actually bringing a companion defeats the purpose. Make a plan. Put your phone away. Choose something because it delights you, intrigues you, or gives you a chance to discover what you like when nobody else gets a vote. Give yourself the attention you’d want from a great date.

Whether you’re single or partnered, learning to enjoy your own company deserves time on your calendar. Here are 20 ways to make that time yours.

Take a page out of Dua Lipa’s book and get your hands into some clay. Book a beginner pottery session and give yourself permission to make something slightly lopsided. You’re here to enjoy the process, not launch a ceramics business. A mug you made yourself is a cute souvenir of the afternoon—even if it holds approximately three sips of coffee.

Spend an evening appreciating the human form without wondering whether it’s going to text you back. A figure drawing session gives you something to focus on beyond your notifications, and you don’t have to be good at drawing to enjoy it.

You know that thing where you’re reading the wall text and your companion is already three galleries ahead? Not today. Pick an exhibition you actually want to see, linger over whatever catches your attention, and skip whatever doesn’t. You can spend 20 minutes with one painting or devote an afternoon to ancient jewelry. Your ticket, your itinerary.

Make a reservation for one at a tasting room or settle into a bar that offers flights, then try something beyond your usual order. Ask about the differences and notice what you actually enjoy, even if your tasting notes are mostly “yes,” “no,” and “tastes like there’s still dirt in this.” An alcohol-free tasting works, too. The date is about exploring your palate, not how much you can drink.

Set aside an afternoon to browse antique shops or a vintage market with no shopping list and no urgent need for a nightstand. Follow your curiosity toward strange paintings, old postcards, or the glassware you’d use at your imaginary country house. Buying something is optional. The fun is discovering what you’re drawn to when you don’t have to defend it to anyone else.

Give your lunch an actual occasion. Bring a blanket, something you’re excited to eat, and a book if you’d like one, then find a comfortable spot in the park. A sandwich eaten between meetings doesn’t quite qualify; a leisurely lunch you planned just for yourself absolutely does. Stay long enough to taste your food, watch the clouds, and remember that being outside doesn’t have to involve a step count.

Buy a ticket to an artist you love without waiting for a friend to share your enthusiasm—or your budget. You’re going to be scream-singing the entire time anyway, so consider this a kindness to someone else’s ears. Once the music starts, you have somewhere to put all that excitement. You can also stay for the encore without negotiating with someone who wants to beat traffic.

That restaurant you keep saving on Instagram? Book it. Request a table for one or grab a seat at the bar, order what sounds good, and resist spending the entire meal pretending to be busy on your phone. My friend sets aside time for what she calls, “Meg’s Mondays.” Where she takes herself out every Monday by checking a new place off of her never ending “Wants To Go” Goggle Maps list. An important tip: don’t forget to make room for dessert. Chocolate cake tastes even better when you don’t have to share it.

Rent a kayak, surfboard, paddleboard, or a really good floatie and do a water sign’s equivalent to touching grass or forest-bathing. Go solo but do it safely. Choose calm water and an established rental outfitter, wear a properly fitted life jacket when necessary, and check conditions before heading out. Let someone know you're going out and return time. If you’re new to water activities, book an introductory session rather than figuring it out offshore.

Instead of streaming the latest blockbuster from your sofa, or rewatching Off Campus for the fifth time, buy a ticket to the film, play, musical, or comedy show IRL. Going alone just means no compromises over the genre, the showtime, or whether subtitles are “too much work.” Get your preferred snack and enjoy having nothing to do but watch. Afterward, give yourself a minute to decide what you thought before consulting everyone else’s reviews.

Walking to the pharmacy is an errand. Choosing a neighborhood you’ve wanted to explore and giving yourself an hour to wander is a date. Pick a scenic route, leave the fitness tracker out of it, and notice the things you usually rush past: an elaborate front door, a tiny garden, a bakery with a very convincing window display. You’re allowed to stop. In fact, that’s sort of the point.

If cooking usually means assembling whatever will expire first, change the game. Choose a dish you’re excited about, put on music, and set the table like someone you’re into is coming over. That someone is: you. Light the candle, use the nice plate, and sit down to eat without a laptop beside your fork. This can be a three-course production or excellent buttered noodles. The care is what makes it a date.

Sign up for a beginner class because you’re curious about the movement, the music, or what it might feel like to channel your sexy side. Treat it as a chance to play, rather than another fitness obligation. You don’t have to perform for anyone or emerge capable of hanging upside down. Follow your instructor’s lead, laugh when something feels awkward, and notice which moments make you feel most like yourself.

Who says you need a player two? Find an arcade with games you can play solo and spend an afternoon indulging your fun side. Try to beat your own score at skee-ball, shoot some hoops, or finally master that racing game without anyone asking when it’s their turn. If you win tickets, pick yourself a prize. You’ll appreciate it more knowing you earned it yourself.

Yes, smashing things is an unusual date idea. But going solo also means you can bring whatever you’re angry about without having to explain it—or worry about alarming the person you’re trying to flirt with. Book a private session, suit up in the required protective gear, and follow the venue’s rules as you take a swing at the designated breakables. No pressure to look cute or keep your composure. This date can handle a little rage.

Book a class devoted to something you’ve always wanted to make: pizza, fresh pasta, dumplings, the pastry you usually buy three of. You get an activity, something delicious, and an instructor to help when your dough develops an attitude. Check the format before booking so you know whether you’ll have your own station or work in a group. Yes, Chef—arriving alone still counts, even if you chat with the person beside you.

Everyone’s wearing headphones, and different channels mean your neighbors might be dancing to entirely different songs. Excellent conditions for following your own taste. Pick the station you like, switch whenever you feel like it, and dance without worrying whether your friends are enjoying the DJ. You don’t need a designated dance partner to have a good night.

If it fits your budget, book one night somewhere you’d enjoy waking up. That might mean a hotel across town or a nearby destination you’ve been meaning to visit. Choose one outing to look forward to, then leave space for a leisurely dinner, a long bath, or reading in bed. Or take this date one step further and book a trip with a little more miles.

Give yourself an unhurried hour in a bookstore and browse beyond the section you usually head toward. Read the opening pages of a novel, flip through a photography book, or investigate an interest you haven’t made time for yet. You don’t have to choose anything impressive—or buy anything at all. If a book catches your attention, take it to a nearby café and extend the date over a pastry.

Book a massage, facial, or day pass to a spa and clear your schedule so you can enjoy it. Arrive with time to settle in, linger in the relaxation lounge, and put your phone on DND. You get to spend a few hours being cared for without being responsible for anything or anyone else. Honestly, a pretty dreamy date.

#100. Sweater Weather Spritz

Recipe by Christine Rukavena, Milwaukee, Wisconsin

The Sweater Weather spritz is what happens when your Aperol spritz goes apple-picking and turns into a bubbly drink built for flannel season.

I’m a die-hard Aperol spritz enthusiast. But the minute Chicagoans put away the patio umbrellas and pull out the parkas, I feel like folks start giving me the side-eye when I reach for the Prosecco and bright orange Aperol bottle. Like white pants, are spritzes supposed to be retired after Labor Day? Not on my watch. I say it’s time for swimsuits to meet snowsuits with this apple cider Aperol spritz, which we affectionately named Sweater Weather spritz.

This fall-themed spritz keeps the bittersweet orange sparkle I can’t quit and includes a pour of crisp, chilled apple cider, so it tastes less like a beach vacation and more like an afternoon of corn mazes. Apple cider softens Aperol’s bitter edge, and a splash of soda keeps things bright and bubbly. It’s made for Friendsgiving, bonfire nights, football Sundays or any evening that calls for a cozy blanket and bubbly sip.

Best of all, it’s just as simple to make as its summery sister cocktail. No shaker, no muddler, no simmering syrup on the stove while your guests hover in the kitchen. Just pour four ingredients into a wine glass and give it a gentle stir.

Fill a wine glass with ice and add the chilled Prosecco, apple cider, Aperol and soda. Give it a gentle stir to combine, just enough to swirl the cider and Aperol through the bubbles.

Editor’s Tip: You can always skip the ice if you pre-chilled your ingredients ahead of time.

If you like, tuck a sprig of fresh rosemary and a few apple slices into the glass. Serve your spritz right away while it’s cold and fizzy.

Editor’s Tip: If rosemary feels too woodsy and wintry for you, swap in mint to add a fresh, cooling finish.

Like bubbly Champagne cocktails, this spritz is best enjoyed the minute you mix it because those bubbles wait for no one. If you have leftover Prosecco, seal the bottle with a sparkling wine stopper and refrigerate it for a day or two. Keep opened apple cider in the fridge for about a week.

You can stir together the apple cider and Aperol up to a day ahead and stash it, covered, in the fridge. When guests arrive, pour the cider mixture into glasses and top each one with chilled Prosecco and soda so every spritz stays perky and fizzy.

You can make an apple cider spritz with or without soda. We like it because it adds a little extra sparkle and sweetness, but the drink holds up just fine without it. Skip it for a more cider-forward, slightly less sweet spritz, which is my move when my cider is already on the sugary side.

You can make an apple cider spritz with any type of spirit. Try Campari for a bolder, more bitter version that’ll speak to the Negroni lovers in the crowd, or go with an orange liqueur like Cointreau to lean into citrus and omit any bitterness at all. For a zero-proof option, a nonalcoholic bitter aperitivo will add the same gorgeous color and bittersweet bite without any alcohol. If you’re feeling experimental, steer away from the classic orange flavor profile found in many spritz recipes and try bourbon or brandy.

If you want to experiment and create your own spritz recipe, look for cozy fall flavors from orchard fruits and warm baking-type spices. Apple, pear and cranberry all shine next to sparkling wine, and a touch of ginger, cinnamon or maple adds instant sweater-weather warmth. For garnishes, woodsy herbs like rosemary and thyme are your best friends.

#101. The Best Apples for Baking

Not every apple is cut out for the oven. The best apples for baking—whether you’re making BA’s Best Apple Pie, a Buttery German Apple Cake, or Suspiciously Cheesy Apple Crumb Bars—have firm flesh that softens when cooked without turning to mush. A good balance of sweetness and acidity helps too. Granny Smith, Pink Lady, Braeburn, Honeycrisp, Golden Delicious, Jonagold, Mutsu, and Winesap are among our favorites.

But say you’re at the farmers market and none of those varieties is in sight. Don’t panic. Cookbook author and former BA food editor Claire Saffitz has a simple trick for finding a worthy substitute: Press your thumb against the apple. If it’s firm enough that you don’t leave an indent, you’re probably in good shape.

Softer apples—those that yield to the pressure of your thumb—are higher in water content and more likely to lose their shape or get soft and mushy when cooked. Save them for applesauce or apple butter, where a little breakdown is exactly the point. For more on why those apples listed above top our list of apple picks, read on.

Whether you’re making a classic apple pie or one with a cheddar-laced crust, the fruit you pick matters.

Granny Smith apples have long been a go-to for baking thanks to their pronounced tartness, firm texture, and year-round availability. Their bright, citrus-like acidity balances the sugar in pies and other desserts, like Gourmet’s classic Apple Strudel, and has made them a favorite among professional bakers for decades.

But they’re not everyone’s first choice anymore. During recipe development for BA Bake Club, senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic found that Granny Smiths repeatedly turned mushy in baked desserts, including their Apple-Cranberry Tarte Tatin and Caramel Apple Monkey Bread. Switching to Honeycrisp produced desserts in which the fruit held its shape—and offered more complex flavor. Granny Smith remains a classic, but if you want distinct pieces of tender fruit, another apple may be a better bet.

Pink Lady apples strike an ideal balance of sweet, tart, and tannic notes. They hold their shape in the oven and are relatively slow to oxidize, so the slices won’t brown as quickly while you’re assembling your dessert. Their bright flavor and relatively wide availability make them our first choice for BA’s Best Apple Pie.

Pink Lady is also a favorite of Christa Campbell of Rainbow Orchards in Camino, California, where they bake plenty of pies. “They keep that divine sweet-tart flavor,” she says, “and have the perfect oh-so-soft crunch and juiciness when baked.”

This superbly crisp apple has a concentrated taste and bakes up juicy but not mushy. Braeburns have pronounced sweetness balanced by tartness, and their flavor becomes richer, almost spicy, in the oven.

They release relatively little liquid during baking, which makes them particularly good for a crumb-topped apple pie: Less excess moisture means less risk of a runny filling or soggy crust. They’re equally at home beneath the streusel topping of Saffitz’s Yeasted Apple Coffee Cake, where their concentrated flavor can stand up to plenty of cinnamon.

Use a mix of apples with the skins on for this colorful Fall Fruit Galette.

Honeycrisps are the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen’s desert island apple. With their shatteringly crisp texture, juicy sweetness, and ability to hold their shape, they are as appealing baked as they are eaten out of hand.

The catch? Honeycrisps can be expensive. Shilpa suggests saving them for recipes that showcase the fruit, like Apple Dumplings, an Apple-Walnut Upside-Down Cake, or old-fashioned baked apples. For recipes where the apples are sliced or chopped and cooked down with sugar and spices, she recommends sticking to “something cheaper and just as effective.”

Golden Delicious apples might not be the most exciting choice for snacking, but their mild flavor becomes sweet, tart, and honeyed in the oven. They soften more than some of the other varieties on this list, making them a good option when you want a tender filling rather than distinct, firm slices.

Freshness is key: Older Golden Delicious apples can become mealy. They’re also less acidic than other varieties on this list, so pair them with a tarter variety or add an extra tablespoon of lemon juice to your pie filling. Their relatively thin skins make them a good candidate for leaving unpeeled in a rustic apple galette.

Tart with a honeyed sweetness, Jonagolds hold up exceptionally well in the oven. Related to Golden Delicious, they have a similarly mellow flavor but a firmer texture, making them excellent for pies and other baked desserts where you want recognizable pieces of apple.

The downside is their short window of peak quality. Jonagolds don’t store particularly well, so look for them early in the fall, especially at farmers markets and orchards. If you find good ones, put them to work in a Naked Apple Tart when they’re at their best.

Firm apples stay suspended in batter better than softer, wetter apples. Try your favorites in this Dutch Apple Snacking Cake.

Also known as Crispin, Mutsu apples are juicy, crunchy, and on the sweeter side. A cross between Golden Delicious and Indo apples, they have a similar flavor to Golden Delicious but a firmer texture that holds up particularly well during cooking.

They’re a great choice for pies, tarts, and other desserts, like Shilpa’s Glazed Apple Pie Fritters, where you want tender apple pieces that don’t disappear.

Winesap apples bring intense, full-bodied flavor with deep cider-like notes, and are equally suited to cooking, eating fresh, and making cider. They resist breaking down during cooking, adding complexity to baked desserts while keeping their shape.

Their assertive flavor makes them especially good in recipes with other fruits like an Apple-Rhubarb Crumble, or strongly flavored ingredients like a puff-pastry apple tart with almonds, maple syrup, and brandy.

Can you use the same apples for pie, cake, and crisp?

Generally, yes. Firm, flavorful apples work well in a range of baked desserts, but the ideal variety depends on the texture you want. For pies and tarts with distinct slices, prioritize apples that hold their shape. In cakes, crisps, and cobblers, a slightly softer apple can work well too.

Which apples should you avoid for baking?

Soft or mealy apples are less suited to desserts where you want the fruit to retain its shape. McIntosh, for example, tends to break down readily when cooked, making it better suited to applesauce or apple butter. But if you’re making a dessert where a softer filling is welcome, that tendency isn’t necessarily a drawback.

Do you need to peel apples before baking?

Not always. Leaving the skins on can add color and texture, especially in rustic desserts. For a more uniform filling, peeling is usually preferable. It ultimately depends on the recipe and whether you enjoy the texture of cooked apple skins.

#104. How Amanda Seyfried Mastered the Elizabeth Holmes Voice

“If you’re playing somebody who’s real, the further away you get from yourself—the more indulgent—the farther you fall into the character.”

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

This story was originally published on Mar. 3, 2022, for the premiere of The Dropout on Hulu. Later that year, Amanda Seyfried won an Emmy Award for her portrayal of Elizabeth Holmes. It has been republished in light of You Can See Everything, a new documentary on Holmes, released on Oct. 16, 2026.

From the moment Amanda Seyfried first appears in The Dropout as teenage Elizabeth Holmes, she is already using a version of “the voice.” She speaks in a lower tone, pursing her lips and tensing her cheeks to tighten up her vowels, adding in awkward pauses here and there. But there’s a scene in the third episode, where she gives herself a pep talk in the bathroom after a tense argument with her boyfriend and business partner Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani, that’s particularly startling. Shaken and disheveled with green juice staining her white shirt, grown-up Elizabeth, now the CEO of biotech startup Theranos, recites a business pitch in the mirror to hype herself up. Her voice grows deeper and deeper each time she repeats it.

“Here at Theranos, we are developing new technology,” she says, sinking to lower depths. “This is…an inspiring…step…forward.”

It’s terrifying. It’s amazing. Whatever it is, it’s a freakishly accurate impression of Holmes’s gruff baritone. Seyfried has lent her angelic voice to high notes in Mamma Mia! and even higher ones in Les Misérables; she also spoke breathily in Mean Girls. So how did she prepare for The Dropout?

The training included voice lessons, which she takes regularly. Now she only does them twice a week, but she still keeps up with them on Zoom.

“I worked with my voice coach to make it a safe space for me to explore the depth,” the actress tells ELLE. “But I knew I was never going to get that low because I sit naturally a little above average on the scale of frequency. And so I was just going to do what’s deep for me and hope that the audience is already with me, because that’s episode three, when she really starts trying it on. And yes, there are different levels depending on what she’s doing, and who she’s speaking to.”

Seyfried approached Holmes’s voice like an accent. “But the thing about the voice is that it’s actually more, for me, an accent. It’s the way her mouth moves—it moves differently than mine,” she explains before seamlessly switching into her Holmes voice to say: “We speak differently.” Then she’s back to speaking as Amanda: “Like, her mouth is shaped differently.”

Before filming began, Seyfried would send videos to the director, Michael Showalter, of her practicing her accent work at home at her farm in the Catskills. She’d be “throwing hay out to the horses, as if I’m doing a TED Talk about selling hay.” She rehearsed endlessly “until it became muscle memory.”

Seyfried adds, “And then, when I got the accent, when the accent started to feel comfortable, we would work on the depth a little bit, but the depth would be in the moment. It wasn’t like I trained my voice to go lower. I just know how low I can go. And with projection, with the accent, and with deepening it and breathing a certain way, it all coincides on a good day.”

People working on The Dropout weren’t too shocked by Seyfried’s Elizabeth voice, she says, because she was always speaking with it, and their filming schedule was gradual. What did shock them, though, was her wardrobe transformation in episode 3 as she ditched her frumpy button-downs and ill-fitting trousers for a sleeker all-black outfit. “The thing I remember about being on set is the reaction when I walked out for the first time with the Elizabeth 2.0 look, which is the turtleneck, the red lip, and the hair pulled back. That was the thing that turned heads.”

The change was a thrill for Seyfried, too. “It felt incredible, because you need those layers. If you’re playing somebody who’s real, the further away you get from yourself—the more indulgent—the farther you fall into the character.”

The show explores how Holmes’s deep voice and obsession with black turtlenecks are more than just quirks; they’re proof of how she manipulated her image and her presence to be seen (and respected) as a young CEO, especially when most of her peers and advisers were men.

“She needed to be taken seriously,” Seyfried says. “And everybody knows that in the world of men, they’re naturally commanding in a lot of ways, which is why we take on these deeper voices or more projection in order to be heard, to be seen, to be understood, to be coveted. You learn that there are certain things that you can do to gain speed.”

She adds: “And she was also this petite woman who was very smart and very charismatic and knew her way around these guys in this world because she studied. She studied Steve Jobs for her whole adolescence...she was studying the way he spoke, the rhythm. She sounds a lot like public speakers in her rhythm; she sounds a lot like Obama at times. That’s not a coincidence.”

Holmes’s black turtleneck, blazer, pants, and messy bun ensemble became a uniform—something she could put on easily and look serious and put-together, without having to worry about what to wear every day. “And that was all to project this commanding presence, to project this power,” Seyfried says. “Which I get—I totally get all of it.” Holmes, a #GirlBoss icon of the early 2010s, would go on to wield that power to scam Silicon Valley, the health care industry, and everyday citizens with Theranos’s failed blood-testing technology. (Early this year, she was found guilty on four charges in her criminal fraud trial.)

Everyday professional women, though, can also understand the pressures of looking a certain way to be taken seriously at work. Seyfried says Dropout showrunner Liz Meriwether has felt it too. “She has a lot of stories about that and trying to feel like she fits in...and command the attention of a lot of people [and] be the boss.”

This image manipulation wasn’t all Holmes’s idea. The show posits that Sunny also had a hand in molding how the young entrepreneur presented herself. Seyfried’s co-star Naveen Andrews, who plays Balwani, tells ELLE that they portrayed Elizabeth and Sunny’s relationship as “fundamentally imbalanced—it opens the door to all sorts of toxic behaviors that one party might practice on the other. And it goes both ways, it seems.”

As for the show, Seyfried is excited, but bracing herself for how it—and perhaps her performance—will be received. Though, if the tweets rolling in are any indication, she doesn’t have much to worry about. “I’m on pins and needles,” she says. “Are people going to watch it? I’ve never been a part of something this…” she takes a brief pause. “I’ve never been the center of something so stressful. And wonderful.”

#106. The Best MacBook Deals We're Watching on Amazon

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

Considering Apple’s recent price hikes, up to $900 off a MacBook is nothing to sneeze at.

If there’s one Apple product line where the recent price hikes hit the hardest, it’s the MacBook. Rising RAM and storage costs have pushed laptop prices up across the board, which makes scoring a new MacBook on sale all the more mission critical.

While we expect the deepest discounts on Apple tech to come once Black Friday sales start to ramp up early next month, plenty of models are quietly on sale on Amazon right now if you can’t wait that long. In fact, a handful of these laptops are cheaper than they were during October Prime Day a couple weeks ago.

Of course, not all MacBooks were created equal. While the standard MacBook Air is great for most, those who are planning on running hardcore software might be benefit from a beefed-up MacBook Pro (at 20 percent off, it’s the steepest deal right now). And if budget is your primary concern, we’re of the opinion that the MacBook Neo is a worthy buy, even at full price.

The MacBook Air packs Apple’s M5 chip into a fanless, 2.7-pound frame that handles heavy multitasking and light video editing without breaking a sweat. Base storage doubled to 512 GB this year—a great upgrade for storing more apps, photos, and files—and the 13.6-inch Liquid Retina display is sharp and vivid. You also get a 12 MP Center Stage camera that’s great on video calls, WiFi 7 for fast downloads, and up to 18 hours of battery, enough for a busy workday and then some. It won’t replace a MacBook Pro for serious creative work or gaming, but for school, business, and general use, it’s the one to get.

Step up to the MacBook Pro and you get a 14.2-inch Liquid Retina XDR display with 120Hz ProMotion, up to 24 hours of battery, three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI, an SD card slot, and up to 2 TB of storage. Why go Pro over the Air? The GPU is fast, which makes a difference when editing video, working with high-res photos, or gaming, and the XDR screen is significantly brighter. If your daily workload has started becoming too much for the Air to handle, this is where you should look next. If you want the biggest, most powerful model possible, souped-up MacBook Pros are up to $900 off.

The MacBook Neo is Apple’s most affordable laptop, even with the recent price hike from $599 to $699. Although this model is not technically on sale (we’re holding out hope for a Black Friday deal), it’s still an easy recommendation for anyone looking for their first Mac. It runs on Apple’s A18 Pro chip and is surprisingly quick for browsing, sending email, and streaming video. The 13-inch Liquid Retina display looks great for the price, and the battery lasts a solid 16 hours. It also comes in four fun colors, with the yellow-green citrus being a fan favorite.

There are some trade-offs with going with Apple’s budget model, including storage that starts at 256 GB, just 8 GB of RAM, and no keyboard backlight. You also get only two USB-C ports, so getting a USB-C hub is a must if you plan to connect a lot of accessories. Spending an extra $100 gets you a Neo with 512 GB of storage and a Touch ID sensor for quick unlocking. For students or anyone who mostly sends emails and browses the Web, the Neo is hard to beat.

#107. The 10 Most Outrageous Dishes At NHL Arenas This Season

Come for the hockey, stay for the sandwich stuffed with pierogies, mozzarella sticks, and waffle fries.

If there’s one thing Heated Rivalry has taught me, it’s that you don’t necessarily have to care about hockey to get really interested in hockey players. And with hockey romance trending on TV and in books, you can bet NHL arenas will be even more packed than usual this season. From die-hard fans to newcomers to the sport, hockey games can be just as much about the food as they are about the action on the ice. After all, you’re going to need something to keep your hands occupied if a fight breaks out.

Here are some of the tastiest and most outrageous new bites being served at arenas throughout North America this season. If the boy aquarium doesn’t intrigue you, these dishes certainly will.

Minnesota Wild fans can head to Section 115 to try a wild trending dessert that people can’t seem to get enough of. The Butter Dipped Ice Cream Cone features vanilla ice cream dipped in—yes, butter—and topped with salt, all served in a waffle cone.

Washington Capitals fans can find the Joia Burger, which takes the classic to new heights. The double Wagyu burger comes topped with American cheese, lettuce, tomato, onion, pickles, and Joia sauce, all on a toasted bun.

Edmonton Oilers fans can take Canadian cuisine to the next level with Cheddar Dust Poutine, available at several eateries throughout Rogers Place. Crispy French fries are dusted in cheese powder and topped with cheese curds, gravy, and green onions. You can find it at the Downtown Grill, Jasper Ave Eatery, Coventry Homes Club, and Play Alberta Club.

If you’re catching a Pittsburgh Penguins game with a crew, the Ultimate Penguinator will more than meet your needs. You won’t go home hungry.

New Jersey Devils fans may not think popcorn sounds like the most exciting option, but this is one you’ll definitely want to get your hands on. San Jose Sharks fans can take a bite out of the K-Chomp Dog, which features spicy Louisiana sausage, pepper jack cheese, Korean BBQ sauce, and vibrant blue Takis.

Chicago Blackhawks fans can find these mighty handhelds in Corona Beach Section 306. Both Chicken and Beef Tortas are available with your choice of spiced chicken or beef, plus shredded lettuce, tomatoes, creamy refried beans, sour cream, and queso fresco on a soft telera roll. Housemade tortilla chips and salsa come on the side to round out the meal.

Cleveland Monsters fans can dig into the Kickin Birria Eggrolls, packed with slow-simmered shredded beef and Chihuahua cheese inside a crispy fried wrapper. They’re topped with cilantro and white onions and served with a lime wedge and consommé for dipping.

St. Louis Blues fans can forget the nachos and push aside the fries because Loaded Potato Wedges are taking center stage. The hearty dish features hand-cut potato wedges topped with cheese sauce, sour cream, bacon, and chives for a comforting twist on classic game-day eats.

Ottawa Senators fans can dig into the SenSational Burger, a filling twist on a classic Canadian dish. The burger features braised Canadian bison, poutine gravy, cheese curds, and smashed crispy potato tots, all piled onto an artisan burger bun baked on-site.

After helping lead the Knicks to their first championship in over 50 years, this is how KAT is keeping himself focused.

KARL-ANTHONY TOWNS had one helluva summer. Add that to a career featuring six All-Star appearances and three All-NBA selections, and it’s fair to wonder where else the former first overall pick has to go. Ahead of the 2026 season opener, we caught up with the man called KAT on what’s keeping him motivated, focused, and confident heading into the new season.

Towns is a long-time fan of Dove products, noting his sister introduced him to the deodorant when he was young, so when the opportunity to partner with Dove Men+Care presented itself, it was a natural fit. Of the Plant-Powered Body Wash line that he’s leading the campaign for, this bourbon-and-vanilla scented option is his favorite. On game days, the 7-footer says that he showers three or four times throughout the day, so using something soothing in there helps:. “That moment in the shower is especially important because I don't know where the madness the rest of the day has [in store] for me, but I know in that moment, that’s my moment,” he says.

You can find him blasting anything from Mac Miller to Burna Boy out of this speaker.

Towns is a huge fan of English muffins, pointing to their versatility in both caloric needs and bulking. “Probably everyone right now wants me to gain weight,” he says. Whether it’s pre-game, postgame, or for help bulking up, he rides for Stone and Skillet above the rest.

When Towns was in Minnesota, his coach Ryan Saunders gifted the entire team a copy of this book. He’s read it three times since, discovering new takeaways every time he revisits it. “I'm such a different person than I was the first time I read the book.”

How does the book land now that he’s helped the Knicks win their first title in 53 years? He’s learned that it’s not about the rings, but the friends you made along the way—or something like that. “It's very crazy how far you go to chase something and realize that the journey was actually the reward the whole time.”

#109. What’s the Difference Between Apple Juice and Apple Cider?

Apple cider gets all the attention in fall, but what sets it apart from ordinary apple juice?

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Apple season is a big deal in Oregon, and cider is one of my favorite things about it. Of course apple pies and crisps and tarts are wonderful, but there’s something especially cozy about freshly pressed cider with its cloudy appearance and robust apple flavor. We have a few apple trees on our property—although calling them our trees might be a little generous. The deer seem to have a stronger claim to the fruit, and have been remarkably unwilling to share. Fortunately, our neighbors have a more productive relationship with apples (and fences). Every fall, they turn their harvest into fresh apple cider, which they generously share with us. It’s a pretty nice arrangement.

We were enjoying some of our neighbors’ delicious hot cider recently when my son asked me what makes apple cider different from apple juice. It’s a good question, considering both are made by pressing apples, and the answer isn’t quite as straightforward as the labels might suggest.

If you’ve ever had cider fresh from the orchard, you’ve probably noticed that it looks and tastes different from the apple juice you buy at the grocery store. Apple cider is usually cloudy, with a fuller apple flavor and sometimes a little tartness. Depending on the types of apples used, one batch can taste quite different from the next, with some leaning sweeter and others having a sharper, more tart flavor.

The difference generally comes down to processing. Both drinks begin with apples that are crushed and pressed for their juice, but apple cider is typically left unfiltered or only lightly filtered. Apple juice usually goes through additional filtering, which removes the fine apple particles responsible for cider’s cloudy appearance. That’s why most commercial apple juice is clear and golden, while fresh cider tends to look as though it came straight from the press. The additional processing gives commercial apple juice its familiar clear appearance and helps manufacturers produce a consistent product year-round.

The distinction isn’t quite as clear-cut as it might seem, though. While apple cider is commonly less filtered than apple juice, there’s no legal requirement that one must be cloudy and the other clear. That’s why you’ll occasionally come across unfiltered apple juice—or cider that’s been processed much like ordinary juice. And outside the United States, the terminology changes again. Order cider in England, for instance, and you’ll be served the alcoholic version that Americans call hard cider.

There’s one other difference worth checking before you buy fresh apple cider: whether it’s been pasteurized. Some orchard-pressed ciders are sold unpasteurized, which means they haven’t been heat-treated to kill potentially harmful bacteria. The FDA advises that children, pregnant people, older adults and people with weakened immune systems avoid unpasteurized juice and cider. If you’re buying directly from a farm or orchard, it’s worth asking how the cider was pasteurized.

Generally speaking, yes. In most recipes, you can substitute apple juice for apple cider, or vice versa, without making any other adjustments. Both bring apple flavor, sweetness and a little acidity, though the proportions can vary depending on the apples and how the drink was made.

I’d pay closer attention to recipes that depend on a pronounced apple flavor. Apple cider doughnuts are a good example. Many recipes call for simmering apple cider until it’s reduced, which concentrates the flavor before it goes into the batter. You can do the same thing with apple juice, although the flavor of the finished doughnuts will depend on what you started with. The same applies to apple cakes, muffins and other baked goods that call for apple cider. In most cases, either will work, but when apple flavor is the point, I’d reach for cider.

I also love cooking with apple cider, especially when pork is involved. A splash in a roasting pan or a slow braise adds sweetness and acidity, both of which work beautifully with richer cuts of pork. Apple juice can do the same job, though I’d be sure to taste the sauce before serving. If it’s sweeter than you’d like, a little lemon juice or apple cider vinegar can bring it back into balance.

If you’re making a drink like mulled cider, the difference isn’t quite as important. Apple juice takes perfectly well to cinnamon, cloves, orange peel and a gentle simmer on the stove. Fresh cider will generally give you a fuller apple flavor, but either makes a perfectly cozy fall drink.

Ultimately, you should choose based on what you’re making and what’s available. For everyday cooking and baking, there’s rarely a compelling reason to make a special trip for one if you already have the other. But when fresh cider is in season, it’s definitely worth enjoying. Especially when someone has been generous enough to do all the pressing for you.

A source from People also enters the chat, saying that Billy’s 2024 divorce from his ex Firerose “put him down” and “Liz is perfect for him to move on. And she won’t put up with any nonsense.”

Not to be outdone, yet another insider chats to Page Six, saying, “She’s been waiting a long time for romance. I think she likes the whole cowboy thing. Liz’s friends think it must be a joke or madness, but they aren’t saying it to her. Elton may not understand this relationship and is a bit bemused by it. But for all his faults, Elton is really loyal to Liz.”

At last, Billy Ray goes onto Apple Music Country’s The Ty Bentli Show (via EW and People) and chats about meeting Elizabeth on set of their film, saying, “We did very few scenes together, but the couple times we were in the same scene there was a chemistry. We just laughed and it was at a time I wasn’t laughing a lot, and I found it the oddest thing.”

He adds that they lost touch until Elizabeth randomly reached out: “A friend reached out, I didn’t even know the number, and it’s like, ‘Hey, it looks like life might be a little bit tough and just wanted you to know I’m in your corner. You’ve got a friend in your corner.’ So, I text back, I go, ‘Who is this?’ And it’s like, ‘Elizabeth Hurley.’ Of all the people to reach out to me in that second that maybe I needed most… this friend who made me laugh.”

He continues, “It’s just been beautiful, and again, no expectations of where we go from here other than her and her son. I do love him a lot, and it’s great that God brought them into my life when he did. It’s just a good thing. It’s been a long time since I’ve been this happy.”

Oh, and amid the world reeling from their relationship reveal, Elizabeth shares a photo from her and Billy Ray’s weekend in Tennessee, where they appear to have spent their time posing by random trees and riding around in trucks with concerned-looking dogs and American flags.

Elizabeth makes an appearance at the Breast Cancer Research Foundation’s 2025 Hot Pink Party, and says, “I have to go back to England tomorrow, but Billy will come to England soon.” She adds, “We are very happy. We both love country music. We both love the country, and we both love our kids. We’re happy together.”

By the end of the month, these two go red-carpet official!

Elizabeth and Billy Ray continue on their summer of love tour, this time walking the red carpet at the Royal Academy Dance fundraiser in London. They wore slightly coordinating looks, with Elizabeth going for a tight white dress, while Billy Ray was in all black.

Elizabeth shares a pic of herself under a rainbow on IG and captions it with (you guessed it) the lyrics to “Over the Rainbow.” Which, according to Billy Ray, is ~their song.~

“Thank you 🙏🏼 for sharing our song 🎵 in such a sweet… beautiful… and truly wholesome way!!!!” he comments in response. “You are one of a kind young lady!!! Truly an original. ♥️♥️♥️♥️”

According to the source for the Daily Mail, Billy Ray is working on new “love songs” inspired by his “muse.” As the insider claims, “His next album will include songs that are about Elizabeth for sure. He is definitely smitten with his new love and she has become his muse.”

Oh, and apparently: “He is very happy with Elizabeth. She is motivating him in a very big way. The songs are all about how she ‘heals’ him and how sexy she is.” Love that for him.

Then the couple has a cute night out in London for the premiere of The Inheritance.

Another red carpet date night—this time for the 2025 National Television Awards!

Another month, another red carpet date night, this time for the CMAs.

Elizabeth and Billy attend the Olivier Awards alongside Elizabeth’s son Damian.

While chatting with Page Six, Elizabeth says she and Billy share a love for the country life. “Funnily enough, [Billy’s] farm in Tennessee is very similar to my farm here in Gloucestershire, so in a way it kind of feels normal,” she says.

Billy and Elizabeth attend London’s Air Ambulance Charity Black and White Gala, looking quite dashing.

Later in the month, they provide some insight into their relationship to People, with Elizabeth saying, “We split our time between Billy's farm in Tennessee and my country house in England, with brief forays into Nashville and London. We both love the countryside, where I’m usually wielding power tools in the garden whilst Billy strums his guitar under a tree. We obsessively watch birds of prey and light lots of bonfires. It’s bliss.”

Of their connection, Billy then adds, “There was something in the opposites of us, I think, that maybe not only got other people's attention but even our own. And I’ve never seen anybody that, in some ways, has more in common with the insanity that I have lived through in this crazy show business. Then mix in other personal, good things and tragedies—she’s like me.”

During an appearance on the SheerLuxe podcast, Elizabeth says “there are a lot more similarities than you’d think” between her and Billy. “We have the same hair. Identical hair. Apart from his beard, we’re actually like twins,” she jokes.

Then, after just about a year and a half together, Elizabeth sparks engagement rumors when she slides a pic of herself wearing what looks like a diamond rock on her left ring finger into an Instagram photo dump.

A few days later, Billy Ray posts about his new single, “Party’s in the Back,” on Instagram, concluding his caption with, “I’m so excited for the show this weekend teaming up with NASCAR in Phoenix !!! Kinda has a ring 💍 to it.” Hmm...

Soon after that, a source for Page Six reportedly confirmed the engagement.

Neither Billy nor Elizabeth has confirmed anything yet for themselves, but perhaps the big reveal is happening this weekend!

#112. 39 Food Gifts We’re Giving (and Secretly Hoping to Get) in 2026

It’s never too early to get a head start on holiday gifting. After all, getting your shopping done now means you can focus on the important things once the holidays actually roll around—you know, like spending time with family, cooking a festive feast, and enjoying plenty of mulled cider and wine. If you’re in need of gifts for the food people in your life, look no further. These are the 27 gifts we’re planning to give (or hoping to receive) this year.

A handmade mug is a little luxury they’ll use every day (and think of you when they do!). Tailor your pick to your giftee’s caffeine preferences to make it feel more personal: opt for an oversized mug for the friend who needs drip coffee on an IV, or a more petite cup for the cappuccino drinker.

Cookbooks make for great gifts, and lucky for you, we’ve spent all year cooking through dozens of them to find the best ones. These are a few favorites from our quarterly best new releases roundups, like Yotam Ottolenghi’s latest collection of weeknight-friendly recipes and Roxana Jullapat’s ode to morning baking.

Obsessed With the Best: 100+ Methodically Perfected Recipes Based on 20+ Head-to-Head Tests

Ohana Style: Food from Hawai'i, for Your Family

No. 1 Best Indian Cookbook in the World: At-Home Recipes from the Streets, Truck Stops, Villages, and Palaces of India

Hello, Home Cooking: Do-Able Dishes for Every Day

Morning Baker: Recipes and Rituals for Breakfast and Beyond

These cheery yellow kitchen scissors aren’t just fun to look at—they’re super practical, too. The shears come equipped with a bottle opener, a nutcracker, and a lid opener, and the blades separate for easy cleaning, plus the bright color makes them easy to spot amidst all your other cooking tools.

That aunt who always insists on baking the pies for Thanksgiving? Get her a handmade walnut rolling pin she’ll use for years to come. These French-style pins come in a marbled cardboard case that’s perfect for gifting. Their handleless design makes them comfortable to grip and easy to maneuver, and allows you to get a nuanced feel for your dough as you roll.

Get the friend who nerds out on coffee roasting and fermentation processes a subscription to Podium Coffee Club’s Platinum tier, which sources its monthly beans from award-winning roasters across the country. The Platinum tier is focused on rare coffee varietals made using experimental techniques, so it’s perfect for someone who likes an expressive, unique roast.

If you’re the kind of person who’s always ordering the fun new seasonal pour-over option at your local craft coffee shop, or who hunts down rare bean varietals like it’s your job, Podium Coffee Club’s Podium Platinum is the coffee subscription for you. Founded in 2023, Podium is a relatively new kid on the block in the world of coffee subs. The concept? A subscription service that solely sends out coffees that have stood on the podium (hence the name) at a major US coffee competition. The brand’s Podium Platinum subscription focuses on coffees that are unique and experimental in some way, be it flavor-wise, varietal-wise, or through the processing technique used.

Testers: Noah Kaufman, senior commerce editor, and Alaina Chou, commerce writer In the two months we’ve tested this service, we’ve received two bags of coffee that have lived up to that claim. The first bag was a light roast from Royal Flamingo Coffee, a micro-roaster based in Columbus, Ohio. The beans, grown in Colombia, were made using the Black Honey process and mossto lactic fermentation, which you can read more about on Podium’s website. The notes of blueberries, white chocolate, and florals definitely came through in the brewed coffee in both smell and taste, though not too aggressively. We quite enjoyed this one.

The next coffee hailed from Wonderstate Coffee in Wisconsin and claimed notes of gummy bear, melon, and cooked berries. That might seem like a crazy flavor profile for a bag of coffee, but the brewed stuff was subtle and highly drinkable.

The bottom line: This is a great coffee subscription to get if you’re looking to explore, nerd out on coffee-making processes, or discover award-winning roasters from across the country. Note that Podium also offers a less expensive Podium Gold subscription option, which does not get you the same unique selection that the Platinum offers.

We all know someone who finishes every dish with flaky salt. Get them this pack of tins from Jacobsen Salt Co., each of which is filled with a different kind of infused salt. They’re small enough to slip into even the tiniest of purses, so your salt-loving friend will never be without their favorite flaky finisher.

These adorable scrubbers are great for cleaning grime off delicate cookware, dishes, or glassware. They’re absorbent, fast-drying, and have hooks for hanging—plus they’re incredibly cute.

I recently added these elegant tumblers to my collection thinking they’d be great for dinner parties, and they are—but they’ve also become my new favorite everyday water and iced latte glasses, because while they’re beautiful, they feel sturdy enough for daily use. They bring a smile to my face every time I use them, which is exactly what a great gift should do, isn’t it?

These all-natural firestarters are a chic alternative to the typical firestarter logs, and would make an excellent host gift for the friend who’s lucky enough to have a fireplace or outdoor fire pit.

An olive oil can is the kind of thing that’s meant to live on your counter, so why not upgrade to a beautiful one? This sleek stainless steel model from Seattle-based design studio Holcomb has been in my gifting rotation since it was released. It goes with multiple different home aesthetics and looks equally at home by the stove as it does on a dinner party table.

This snazzy supply of olive oil is a great example of a practical item that’s still gift-worthy. The bold tin (designed in collaboration with Los Angeles-based artist Dave Bowers) makes it a statement kitchen decor piece, and the oil inside is cold-pressed in California by one of our favorite olive oil brands.

Give the gift of cozy hot pot nights at home with this cute and compact appliance by Fly By Jing. You could even pair it with an H Mart gift card, so your giftee can stock up on thinly sliced meats and other add-ins.

Your shoppy shop-obsessed friend will jump at the chance to rep their favorite pantry brand, whether that means donning a “Fish Dad” hat from beloved conservas company Fishwife or throwing on a bright blue Fly By Jing sweatshirt to keep them toasty this winter. And if that sweatshirt looks familiar, it’s because it just so happened to be featured in an episode of Netflix’s Nobody Wants This.

Buttered toast is a perfect food, in my opinion, and anyone that agrees will adore this handblown glass butter keeper from East Fork. Its design ensures your butter can be kept at room temperature for weeks without spoiling, which means it’ll stay perfectly spreadable and ready to be swiped across whatever carbs you so choose.

Give the designated host friend a set of whimsical spiral-tipped serving utensils to use at their next dinner party. And don’t worry, they’re dishwasher-safe.

This tortoise-handled bottle opener from Parisian flatware brand Sabre makes for a handsome host gift, especially when paired with a bottle of your favorite pét-nat or non-alc apéritif.

I’m secretly hoping someone restocks my own supply of this luxurious hand wash this holiday season. It comes in a glass bottle that’s so pretty I took to refilling it with cheaper hand soap after the original soap was long gone, but the scent—a delicate mix of jasmine, geranium, and orange blossom—is what really makes it worth buying.

Any friend who cooks will appreciate receiving this set of ramekins from cult-favorite pottery brand East Fork. At four ounces, they’re a versatile size that works for equally as well for portioning mise en place as it does for serving condiments or sauces.

This stylish pepper grinder looks incredibly cool, but it’s also made with function in mind. That swanky-looking handle? It’s designed to be ergonomic, able to be held and twisted in myriad ways depending on what’s most comfortable for the user. This gift set pairs the grinder with Piper’s 50/50 blend of black and red peppercorns, portioned into four individual packets to ensure the spices stay fresh.

This gift set brings a taste of Richard Christiansen’s Flamingo Estate to your pantry. It’s full of high-quality products you’ll actually use—no weird spice blends or waxy chocolates here.

These stunning wood cutting boards are truly heirloom-worthy, handcrafted by expert woodworkers from sturdy hardwood. They're versatile pieces that are durable enough to be your everyday chopping boards and beautiful enough to serve as serving vessels for cheese and charcuterie.

For the friend who would gladly eat tinned fish for dinner every night, I suggest this 10-pack of greatest hits from Fishwife. It’s got a little bit of everything, from the brand’s smoked salmon collab with Fly By Jing to the fan-favorite Smoked Rainbow Trout with Chimichurri, plus their limited-edition Little Sardines, which are only available as a part of the brand’s holiday sets.

The iced beverage fiend in your life will go gaga for this mini version of our longtime favorite ice maker, the GE Opal. Despite its more compact footprint and lower price tag, it produces the same crunchy nugget ice we know and love—and it’s available in some cute colorways.

You can’t go wrong with a beautiful vase, especially if you fill that vase with a bouquet of fresh flowers. This colorful glass number is sure to earn your giftee compliments, and I love that it’s hand-blown, which means every piece is one-of-a-kind.

Give the latte lover who also values convenience this do-it-all machine from Nespresso, which combines the brand's signature pod technology with an automatic milk frother that'll have them pouring latte art like a pro.

When in doubt, opt for wine. But instead of picking up a random bottle, treat your giftee to a month (or three, or six!) of deliveries from New York City wine bar and shop Parcelle, whose Wine Drop subscription service has been a longtime BA fave. Choose between red, white, rare, or a curated monthly mix, and Parcelle will take care of the rest.

#114. Taylor Swift Made a Subtle Change to Her Wedding Stack—and Wore Her Band on Its Own

The singer switched up her look inside the Academy Museum Gala.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Taylor Swift had two looks at the Academy Museum Gala on Saturday, giving photographers a fresh view of her wedding stack as she posed on the red carpet in a custom blue Dior gown. But inside, she changed into a navy Ralph Lauren dress to perform—and also switched up how she wore her rings.

For the first time at a public event, she wore the rings separately, keeping her contour wedding band on her left hand and moving her old mine cushion-cut diamond engagement ring to her right.

It’s possible Swift wore her rings differently because she played guitar during her performance. She might’ve worn the band on her left hand so she could easily move her fingers around the frets without any big jewelry getting in the way while changing chords. With her engagement ring on her right hand, she could still strum comfortably.

The new photos from the gala give a close look at the sparklers, and jewelers praised the cohesion in Swift’s wedding stack.

It is “a thoughtfully styled bridal stack, with each ring playing a role in the overall design,” Angie Kennedy, senior VP of merchandising at Zales, tells ELLE. “Worn above Taylor’s engagement ring, the wedding band adds sparkle and character while allowing the center diamond to remain the focal point.”

On the band itself, “the diamonds appear to be round brilliant or old European cut diamonds set in a thin, delicate yellow gold bezel setting,” Kennedy says. “Similar to her engagement ring, the band blends classic and contemporary design elements, with the unique diamond shapes adding individuality, while the setting brings a clean, modern edge. The low-profile design allows the rings to sit comfortably together, creating a cohesive and well-balanced look.”

Ali Galgano, founder of Serpentine Jewels, agrees. “What stands out to me most about Taylor’s wedding band is the proportion—the diamonds in Taylor’s wedding band look like exactly the right size to accent her engagement ring without overpowering it,” she explains. “The round stones introduce softness beneath the elongated cushion, giving the eye a change of shape and scale. Each diamond has its own definition, creating a beautiful rhythm across the finger.”

“The delicate yellow gold bezels add a modern, sculptural touch,” she continues. “Bezel-set wedding bands are increasingly popular alongside prong-set engagement rings because the contrast works so well—the openness of the prongs balances the gold outline around each band diamond. There’s also a practical benefit: the surrounding gold helps keep neighboring diamonds from rubbing against one another. Diamonds can scratch other diamonds, so that protective border is particularly useful when wearing rings together every day.”

Galgano points out the shape of the ring as well. “The band looks as though it may contour around the engagement ring, allowing the two pieces to nestle together,” she says. “But it also has enough character to feel complete worn on its own, which is something I love in a wedding band. The overall pairing feels romantic and collected, as though these are pieces she could have inherited and made her own.”

Swift first wore her wedding stack on a red carpet during the MTV VMAs on September 27. She and Travis Kelce got married on July 3 and haven’t yet released wedding photos.
