#115. In Sense and Sensibility, Costume Designer Grace Snell Brings Us Into the Fabric of 1790s Sisterhood

Lived-in dresses, mud-stained skirts, and sisterly hand-me-downs helped make the Dashwoods feel startlingly real

Like many of us, British Independent Film Award-winning costume designer Grace Snell first picked up a copy of Sense and Sensibility as a teenager in English class. Instantly struck by Jane Austen’s “world” and the way “she writes women,” she pored over the novel’s pages before devouring Austen’s sophomore offering, Pride and Prejudice, with similar fervor. Some 20 years later, she has designed the costumes for a new adaptation of Sense and Sensibility, directed by Georgia Oakley and opening in U.S. theaters on October 16. “It’s been one of my career goals—to do a Jane Austen adaptation,” Snell says. “And for that to happen, and to be my first period film, feels quite special.”

Known for her work on The Souvenir (2019), The Outrun (2024), and Pillion (2025), Snell was tapped by Oakley herself to outfit the cast, led by Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles. The novel, written in the late 1790s and published in 1811, predominantly follows the two eldest Dashwood sisters as they adjust to life after the death of their father and subsequent loss of their family estate. For generations, readers have seen themselves in the rational, responsible Elinor Dashwood (the sense) or her emotional, passionate, impulse-driven younger sister, Marianne (the sensibility). And while costuming an adaptation of such a beloved literary classic might seem like a daunting feat for a first foray into period films, it was Snell’s fresh perspective and background in contemporary filmmaking that made her the perfect person for the job.

Less interested in familiar caricatures of late-1790s fashion (if you were hoping for cap sleeves, this won’t be for you) than in what real people wore, Snell turned to the “less documented” elements and “anomalies” of Georgian style. She instructed her on-set team not to steam the dresses in order to preserve wrinkles from the day before and encouraged the cast to wear their costumes out in the mud to create real stains that might result from a day out on the moors. In one scene, the youngest Dashwood sister, Margaret (Bodhi Rae Breathnach), eats blackberries, the juice running down the front of her dress. “There were obviously families in regency England that were completely pristine and pressing and cleaning and doing all that, but I wanted to show that this is a family that now doesn’t have a household looking after them,” Snell explains. “They only have been able to take one maid with them, and they’d normally have so many more. So I wanted to see a family of women learning what that was like to look after themselves for the first time.”

Against a backdrop of muddy fields, heavy downpours, childhood bedrooms, crumbling cottages, and grand ballrooms, Snell imagined the sisters sharing clothes, passing pieces down to Margaret, and experimenting with their individuality through color and styling. Working with a specific palette and picking unusual silhouettes, the team made 85 percent of the costumes from scratch and set up a natural dye room, where they used logwood to dye Elinor’s garments purple and elderflower to dye Marianne’s yellow.

“With our adaptation, I really wanted to bring you all into the room, to knock down the wall and to feel like you are there with those characters. I wanted you to be emotionally invested in those characters because they look like you and they wear clothes how you wear them, and how they style things is how you’ve styled them, and you see your friends and your sisters, and you see yourself in these characters,” she tells me. “I was trying to make costumes that not just looked beautiful. I wanted them to feel very real and very relatable.”

I had studied it very briefly [while at Wimbledon College of Art for Costume Interpretation], as much as you can when you’re studying for your degree. But I think what’s dangerous sometimes about getting those snippets of a period is you just get the highlights. I’m interested in digging deeper into the bits that we might not know about that aren’t as well-recorded. When I approached researching the period, I had to learn a lot very, very quickly. I got the help of a dress historian for about two, three weeks. I gave her specific things to research, and one of those was the unusual, the things that are slightly less documented.

And then myself, I was looking at a lot of fashion plates and portraiture. We’ve got an amazing archive gallery, the Rotherhithe Picture Research Library, that a lot of costume designers use. We didn’t [initially] know [the exact time period] we were going to set our film in. So my research was over a 40-year period for ages. And then I talked to Georgia, our director, and said, “Look, the late 1790s, when the book was first drafted, is actually a really interesting time in fashion history because we’re not quite there yet with the Regency styles that we associate with Austen. We’re in this transition period in history.” It gave me a bit more ambiguity for some of my choices because I did quite openly borrow from some things that are a bit earlier and some things that are a bit later, because they just serviced the characters a bit more. So my approach was to do as much historically accurate research as I could, and then give like this 20% of kind of interpretation.

I think the dye work was really, really interesting—finding out how things were dyed. But the thing that I found most interesting was how much fabric was recycled. It feels completely obvious that, of course, fabric would get recycled. But you’d see the amazing 18th-century Spitalfields silk unpicked and made into a Regency dress with the Empire line and poof sleeves that we associate with the 1800s.

And then our historian had found an example of a mourning cap—such a delicate symbol of grief, a subtle nod. It was one of the first things I latched onto for our chapter in Norland, which is our grief chapter. We see the family alone behind closed doors, and then as guests arrive, the caps go on and the jackets go on.

There was a very specific New York Times article that came out in 2011 about the late Stella Tennant and her husband. They’d relocated from New York to Scotland and they lived in this house with their children. And the photography there is all their children. It’s an intimate portrait of family life. And although that wasn’t of our period, obviously, that kind of attitude inspired me so much. To see these sisters plaiting each other's hair, wearing each other's clothes, having things that were so random (Wellies with pajamas), I wanted to bring that energy into our film.

And then I just love the catwalk shows from the ’80s and ’90s. Romeo Gigli is one of my favorite designers, and he did a collection for Callaghan in the ’80s with these jackets with skirts. I kind of went on this jackets-and-skirts train. I looked at Comme des Garçons, Yohji Yamamoto, and particularly at the styling on the catwalk and how the clothing was just worn by the models.

That was very, very important for me. You need to communicate with your team. I can’t be in so many places at once. When I was communicating with my on-set team, I’d be saying things like, “I don’t want this dress steamed for the day, so that the dress still has the crumples from the day before.” With the staining, we got Bodhi to eat some blackberries and drop some on her and then see where they’d land. And then we had to replicate those stains on two other dresses. And then with the mud, you know, obviously, if you’re going to wear a big dress in the moors with mud, it is going to get muddy. So we just allowed that to happen rather than pinning up the dresses so that they wouldn’t get muddy. They can get muddy. Because that to me feels so real.

For Marianne, I looked at a lot of portraiture from the Rotherhithe Picture Research Library. What’s amazing about portraiture is, at the time, it was often a romanticized version of these costumes and what was happening, so it was very informative for her. For Elinor, some of her dresses have a similar silhouette (round gowns) to her mother’s. I wanted to show she was looking to this female figure in her life and what she wears. But the use of color was very important for the emotional state. One of my favorite duo moments with the sisters is when they’re in the kitchen. I think that’s when I cried. When they have their big argument in the kitchen, we have Marianne in a light color. She was the lightness; she was the optimist. And then we have Elinor in the dark, somber colors. They were light and dark in each other’s lives.

We have Norland, which is very grief-stricken and feels very dark. And then with Barton, we have warmer colors, we’re warming up. We have a lot more burgundy and pink and yellows. And then when we go to London, where the girls feel slightly intimidated. I wanted them to feel that they didn’t quite belong. I chose to make the ball [scene] monochromatic, so it’s all pale for the women and dark tailoring for the men, to feel like this almost dream state that it’s the height of fashion and all the styles that the women are we wearing are becoming progressively more fashionable, that they don’t quite fit in, they’re much more adorned, and our women are much more plain.

It was part of the ethos of the costume design from the beginning. Where can we share the clothes? Where does it feel believable? We don’t want to overdo it. We want to be doing it subtly. We don’t want them to suddenly all be looking like each other. I think Marianne’s pink sash was quite important. Esmé was quite open about that, to her, it symbolized coming of age, first love, innocence, putting your heart on your sleeve. Your pink sash is your heart to the world. And then when her heart gets broken, the sash is disregarded and it’s thrown off in a “Who was I? I no longer want to associate myself with that [mindset].” And she goes into her depression. And then we have Margaret, taking up the sash, ready to go on her journey of love and what that means to her. So that was sort of inspired by Esmé saying, “I don’t want to wear the sash now that I’ve had my heart broken.”

Sharing clothes was a lot about when we could make it work from a practical perspective. It’s all happening very quickly. My on-set team would say, “Now’s a good moment. We can have Margaret in that, and we can have Elinor in that, and we can change.” [One crucial example of this comes towards the end of the film.] For Marianne’s grown-up conversation with [Colonel] Brandon, we wanted her to wear one of Elinor’s dresses. In this pivotal scene, she leans into the rational side of herself, adopting a “sense” we typically see from her sister. So it was important to reflect that in her style. Then we added the frilled scarf so that it still felt a bit like classic Marianne.

Every time we’d make a decision, it would be, “How is this emotionally serving the character?” I didn’t want to ever just dress people to look a certain way or look good. It’s just like, “How is this helping the audience engage with what our characters are going through?”

I do have a really fun story. We were filming the ball scene for two days. Hot room, lots of cast. And Daisy had these white gloves on, and it’s this thin leather that’s so soft, which means that they fit perfectly. So, Daisy had been dancing for like six hours, and she was like, “I need to go to the bathroom.” Obviously, she went to the toilet and washed her hands... with the gloves on. She forgot to take the gloves off. And when you wash leather, it goes hard. So, she washed her hands, and it was only when she stepped away from the bathroom that she was like, “Hang on, my hands are getting smaller.” The leather was tightening. She had these claws. So we had to pull the gloves off and they had to go to a glove hospital and we had to get gloves off someone else and do this glove swap so that she can continue dancing. It is so funny, but it does just show you that your actor is so in this state that they’re not really thinking about anything like that.

It’s such a special experience to look around and see so many women working on a production. And it should just be the norm. There should be equality within filmmaking, and there just isn’t. But I loved having female producers. There’s a nurturing and kindness and sort of understanding that happens that you can really confide in them. I felt like there was an honesty between us all that you really have and an understanding. I felt like I could be very honest with my colleagues. There was no having to put on this shield to be like, “I can do this,” because everybody knew we could do it. You just believe in each other and you really know that you can do it.

Ang Lee’s version is beautiful, and I’m fortunate enough to have worked with John Bright, who, with Jenny Beavan, designed that [1995] Sense and Sensibility. He owns Cosprop, which made costumes for us. And John would be extremely generous with his knowledge and experience and very inspiring. And I felt respected. There is this sort of changing of the guard that happens with new designers coming up. He and Jenny are such a big part of who I am as a designer today, but that doesn’t mean that I have to design costumes like them. I have the utmost respect for them and I’m not going to recreate something that they’ve done.

Reading the new adaptation that Diana Reid wrote, which I think is a more faithful adaptation to the book, personally, and then knowing that Georgia would be directing it... you’re making something different. So I think I knew I had to be approaching this from a different place. So it would always be different. I’m going to bring a fresh, modern, new take, a new version, a new adaptation—inspiring a new audience watching Sense and Sensibility and also avid Austen fans to re-fall in love with the characters and give them an opportunity to see them again.

#117. The Fathers Who Shaped Darth Vader

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

Star Wars Icons: Vader explores the origins of the galactic villain—and the real-life stories that gave him such emotional power.

Darth Vader might have been just another masked villain if not for four words. You know the ones: Luke Skywalker is clinging to a windblown gantry as the masked Imperial monster reaches out and reveals that he did not kill Luke’s father. “I am your father,” Vader intones.

With that revelation in The Empire Strikes Back, the Star Wars galaxy became more than a space adventure about good and evil. It became a metaphor for the age-old conflict between generations. This twist raised a question in the mind of the hero, something also asked by everyone as they grow up and start their own lives: Am I any different?

As I wrote the new book Star Wars Icons: Vader, it became ever clearer that the fatherhood theme was the key factor in the creation and evolution of the most famous screen villain of all time. Fortunately, we had 500 oversize pages to explore the idea. I found that virtually everyone involved in the making of Vader had a compelling fatherhood story that in various ways guided them and shaped their eventual contribution to the character. This is the hidden source of Vader’s strength.

Everyone has a dad, whether you know that person or not, whether they are a force for good or not. It’s a relationship that shapes everyone, which is why Vader resonates so deeply with decades of moviegoers. He is not merely a villain. He is part of the hero’s journey, if only because the hero carries him in his heart, like it or not. We all do the same.

The inspiration for this book goes back nearly 20 years, to when I sat down with George Lucas to talk about dads.

These themes are everywhere in his work. Not only is the Vader/Anakin Skywalker story the emotional core of both the original Star Wars trilogy and the prequels, but fatherhood issues also turn up repeatedly throughout the Indiana Jones series. At the time of the interview, I was at a point in my own life when my wife and I had decided to start a family, so I was eager to talk with Lucas about these storylines, where they came from, and what he thought about them now.

It all traces back to George Lucas. But not the one we’ve already been talking about.

The filmmaker’s father, George Lucas Sr., was born in 1913 and died in 1991. Over the course of his 78 years, he was a loyal son, a devoted husband who raised four children, and a businessman who built a thriving office-supply company. A Depression-era survivor, he was both baffled and annoyed that his only son had zero interest in inheriting it. “He wanted me to go into his business,” George Jr. told me. “I said I’m absolutely not going to do it.”

Instead, young George wanted to make movies. George Sr. objected but couldn’t change his son’s mind. Instead, he started counting the days until his daydreaming son came crawling back. “He thought I was going to fail,” George Jr. said. “Which was reasonable.”

The young filmmaker’s first movie, the dystopian THX-1138, debuted in 1971 and was only a modest success. Then his follow-up, American Graffiti, seemed to be headed toward disaster, with faithless studio executives debating whether to dump it as a TV movie. The teen drama ultimately became a blockbuster and is now a classic coming-of-age tale. That cleared the way for him to make Star Wars, his tribute to the sci-fi fantasies he adored as a kid.

In January 1976, George Jr. flew to London to prep for the shoot. Soon after, their hometown newspaper The Modesto Bee published a business profile on George Sr., announcing he had sold his business and leased his buildings. He was retiring and closing up shop. George Jr. was not coming back.

The father’s empire had ended, just as the son’s was beginning.

“That was his life,” George Jr. told me. “He worked very hard at it. He started out as an errand boy and he ended owning the company, and it was a big deal to him.”

I was gobsmacked. It all suddenly seemed so clear: Join me, and together we will rule the office-supply galaxy of northern California.

Lucas acknowledged the influence, although it may have snuck up on him. Vader did not start out as Luke’s father in the first movie—he was the Jedi who betrayed him. And the early draft of Empire featured Anakin’s ghost. Only later did Lucas decide to make the two father and son. It was obviously something within that was trying to make its way out.

“Both Steven and I do that,” he said, referring to his longtime friend and collaborator Spielberg. “Almost all of our films are about fathers and sons, whether it’s Darth Vader or E.T.”

Let me emphasize: George Sr. was not Darth Vader. He was strict, and like many fathers, then and now, he certainly believed he knew best. He was not maniacal, definitely not a monster. He was like a lot of dads, and his son took their commonplace conflicts and magnified them through the power of myth.

Over and over again, I saw variations on these themes in the people who helped bring Vader to life.

David Prowse, the bodybuilder who played Vader’s physical form. James Earl Jones, who provided the ominous voice. Lawrence Kasdan, the screenwriter of Empire and Return of the Jedi. All of them had complex and dramatic relationships with their fathers, and each ended up where they were through variations on “Join me.”

Some wanted to follow their fathers’ path. Some wanted to avoid it. Sometimes it was a combination. No two stories are alike, but they all have similarities.

George’s father eventually embraced his son’s filmmaking destiny, and by the time he died, his son was a father himself. George Jr. raised three children as a single dad, and he had this advice for me when he heard I was a soon-to-be father.

“The secret is when they turn into the monsters—and you were a monster and impossible, and I was too—don’t do anything or say anything to destroy the relationship,” he said. “Bite your tongue and say, ‘Hey, whatever.’ … They do come back being well-mannered, intelligent people. But if you screw it up early on, you’re never going to enjoy that part when it happens.”

In the ’90s, George Jr. found himself raising teenagers, dealing with the same things he and his father grappled with: expectations, disagreements, clashes with words rather than lightsabers. “Parents try as hard as they can to do the right thing,” he told me. “They don’t want to be Darth Vader. As Luke says, ‘I know there is good in you, and I have faith in you … even though the rest of the universe thinks you’re a schmuck.’ ”

His father had been a hard-charging, work-obsessed president of one company, but after charting a different destiny for himself, he had ended up the head of several massive companies. George Lucas wanted to get back to making movies.

That’s when the prequels emerged, exploring the origins of Vader as young Anakin Skywalker. Even more George Sr. parallels can be found in these movies. The older man grew up in desperate circumstances where dreams were a luxury. Survival was the focus. By his mid-teens, he was caring for his widowed mother in a hardscrabble desert town. Sound familiar?

Then my wife, a librarian and archivist, helped me track down the 1930 census records for Modesto, California. There on Sheet 7B, in the middle of the page, is the entry for 16-year-old George W. Lucas. There was no Sr. at this point. He was the only one.

Under the column marked “Occupation and Industry,” this boy had written: “Mechanic apprentice” in a typewriter repair shop. It still startles me to see that. It’s the same job Jake Lloyd has as the young Anakin, toiling in Watto’s repair shop in The Phantom Menace.

The Vader book explores the full scope of the character, from the original trilogy to the prequels, the comics, the video games, the novels, and the more recent films and TV shows. But throughout the writing, this one census discovery helped me keep focus on the true source of Vader’s power.

I have no doubt that George Jr. loved his father deeply. Otherwise why would he spend his whole life trying so hard to understand him?

#118. I Tried 'Cognitive Reshuffling,' the Viral Trick to Fall Back Asleep Faster

For certain people, the simple technique can help them conk out in minutes.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

EVEN WHEN YOUR sleep hygiene is dialed-in, you're going to have moments where you can't easily fall asleep—or fall back asleep after waking up. You can try to count sheep, but there's a different—and science-backed—technique worth considering: cognitive reshuffling.

It sounds complicated, but it's actually simple. Cognitive reshuffling leans heavily on putting your brain to work to try to crowd out other stuff that may be keeping you from sleeping, like stress, anxiety, or worries. I tried it the other night when my toddler decided to wake me up at 2 a.m., and I managed to conk back out pretty quickly. I do have some notes from the experience, though.

If you're consistently struggling to fall asleep, it's important to rope in a healthcare professional to try to get to the bottom of things. But if you spend a random night here and there trying harder than usual to fall asleep, cognitive reshuffling is a sleep hack worth keeping in your back pocket.

COGNITIVE RESHUFFLING IS a cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) technique to help people fall asleep. "Cognitive reshuffling is essentially a mental distraction technique designed to interrupt the repetitive, emotionally-loaded thinking that often keeps people awake," says Thea Gallagher, PsyD, clinical associate professor at NYU Langone Health and cohost of the Mind in View podcast. "Rather than lying in bed thinking about tomorrow's meeting, replaying a conversation, or worrying about why you aren't asleep yet, you deliberately direct your attention toward random, neutral thoughts or images."

This is essentially another form of counting sheep, according to Christopher Winter, MD, a sleep medicine specialist, neurologist, and author of The Sleep Solution: Why Your Sleep Is Broken and How to Fix It. He says this is a common type of "first step" treatment suggested when someone has insomnia. "Can we reduce the performance anxiety you feel around sleep by getting you to focus on something other than 'I need to fall asleep now, why can't I fall asleep, bad things will happen if I don't sleep?'" he says.

IT IS A fairly simple technique: You pick a word and try to think of unrelated, ideally relaxing or neutral words that start with each letter, before moving on to the next. Picture each word in your mind when you think of it.

"One common version is to pick a word, such as 'bedtime,' and move through its letters," Gallagher says. That means thinking of things like ball, banana, and boat, before moving on to elephant, envelope, and earring.

"The point isn't to create a coherent story or solve anything," Gallagher says. "In fact, randomness is part of the exercise."

The idea is similar to doing things like counting backwards from 1,000 by sevens, according to Winter. "It's all simply a means of distraction," he says. "It's built around helping people stop trying to sleep."

IT CAN. “THINK of it less as a magic sleep trick and more as a way of giving the brain something neutral to do," Gallagher says. When people can't sleep, they tend to get caught in worrying, planning, problem-solving, and replaying things from the day, she points out. "That increases arousal, which is exactly the opposite of what we want when we're trying to sleep," Gallagher says.

A technique like cognitive reshuffling may help because it occupies enough attention to interrupt those loops without giving the brain something overly stimulating or emotionally meaningful to engage with, she says.

I fell back asleep pretty easily when I tried this, but I also usually do anyway. I thought of the word "read" and found myself getting annoyed when I couldn't think of words that started with the letter "r" that weren't aggressive. It took me a while to come up with "raspberry" after things like "rocket" and "race car" and I started to get frustrated when I couldn't think of more words for each letter. In the morning, I tried to repeat it to see what obvious words I'd missed. Ultimately, this exercise tapped into my inner competitor a little too much and may have kept me up for longer while I was trying to top myself.

"Techniques like this are fine, but working with people who can help you understand your sleep better and who can help you manage stress is more likely to create lasting change and confidence in your sleep," Winter says.

Still, Gallagher says this is worth trying. "If someone finds cognitive reshuffling calming, it's a perfectly reasonable tool to have in the toolbox," Gallagher says. "The goal is simply to give your mind a less activating place to go."

She has a master’s degree from American University and lives by the beach.

#119. What *That* Person Was Doing in ‘You Can See Everything,’ Explained As Best We Can

Apple pie and olives and really good hard ciders.

Have you seen You Can See Everything? The film, which was co-directed by Nathan Fielder and Primetime director Lance Oppenheim, is creating buzz for a few reasons. First, the general public did not know the film existed before it premiered at Telluride Film Festival. Second, both the documentarian Fielder and his subject Elizabeth Holmes are fascinating human beings for very different reasons. It’s a narrative match we didn’t know we needed. And there’s this spoiler, this one thing that everybody wants to talk about, but Nathan wanted Telluride and subsequent festival audiences to preserve the experience. We’re going to talk about the mystery person in You Can See Everything, and explain what can be explained.

Spoilers for You Can See Everything ahead! Seriously, try and watch it first if you can. The execution makes the film worth watching even if you happened to get spoiled on this particular thing, but know that if you keep reading it is because you made that choice. Avert your eyes and exit if you don’t want that! Because what you hopefully did not get spoiled before seeing the film is that actress Amanda Seyfried, who won an Emmy and a Golden Globe for portraying Holmes in the 2022 Hulu limited series The Dropout, not only appears in You Can See Everything as herself but becomes an audience surrogate, critic, and participant wrapped up in one.

Fielder visits the actress at several points during the second half of the film, after Holmes herself has been incarcerated in Texas. They meet both at her New York City apartment as well as her farm upstate. At first, Fielder simply shows Seyfried the footage he has so far to get her reaction. He asks a few questions about the research that went into making The Dropout, how she prepared to play Holmes, and whether she considers the limited series to be a work of fiction. She does.

Seyfried then reenacts several unrecorded conversations Fielder had with Holmes before filming began, or after she was behind bars. While other crew members were present in some cases, Fielder transcribed scripts from his own memory. As Seyfried points out, they could have been edited to paint Holmes in a more sympathetic light. Christopher Abbott, who played the husband of Seyfried’s character in The Testament of Ann Lee, plays Holmes’ husband Billy Evans in a few reenactments.

If you’ve seen The Rehearsal you can maybe see why this method was appealing to Fielder as a filmmaker, an artist, and an... I don’t know... investigator? Amateur psychologist? Student of the world? He is no stranger to recreating conversations as verbatim as possible, or playing a facsimile of himself. He’s able to put Seyfried in a fairly unique position as an actress. This is not actually reprising a role, is it? She played a fictionalized version of a real person on screen, saying lines written by Liz Merriweather and a writer’s room, and now gets to play the “real” version.

But is it real, especially if Holmes is lying to Fielder? What is real? Are we not all performing, all of the time? An intro to physics and/or media studies class will teach you about “the observer effect,” i.e. that the act of observation itself tampers with reality. This is the stuff of academic dreams, and right up Fielder’s meta alley.

Fielder stayed with Holmes and her family to document them in spring of 2023, just over a month before Holmes surrendered and began her prison sentence. He resumed filming two years later, and that’s where and when Seyfried comes into play.

As she gets invested in Fielder’s project, Seyfried actually goes with him to meet the real Evans, and his and Holmes’ two children, in a mostly unsuccessful attempt to disarm the husband into revealing information. At that meeting, Evans implies that it has been about 900 days since Holmes’ incarceration, placing it in/around November of 2025. Seyfried would have been beginning press for both The Housemaid and The Testament of Ann Lee at that time.

At one point, the actress insists that The Dropout is (heavily researched) fiction. It does not matter if Holmes actually said the lines in the show, she says, because she actually behaved in a way that supported those lines. Later, she kind of brags about how so many people think The Dropout was a documentary. When Evans unexpectedly puts Holmes on speakerphone in front of Seyfried, the actress anxiously apologizes for taking time away from her children and blurts out “you’re amazing.” She tells Fielder early on that during the making of The Dropout, contact with Holmes was verboten. So that was the first, and only, time they have spoken.

But the moment Evans leaves the room, Seyfried is suspicious of everyone’s motives again. Then, at the end of the film, after reading that Holmes accused her of making her life harder in prison, Seyfried defends herself and the show by saying they were just making television. She holds the line that Holmes is incarcerated because of her own actions, and wonders to what extent Fielder has been manipulated by her.

Why isn’t she consistent? Probably because she is a human being with empathy. Since Seyfried has not been convicted of a crime, I don’t think we need to be concerned by her complicated feelings about a person she portrayed. Multiple things can be true at once. Are you not also a little conflicted after watching the film?

Seyfried is one of at least three people in the film, along with Evans and Fielder, who claim they don’t want to speak for Holmes and then do it anyway. We are all hypocritical, messy, morally grey beings. That’s what makes this film so good. Now it’s in the audience’s hands to unpack, debate and infuse with our own truth.

She was nominated for a Golden Globe and snubbed for an Oscar. She made the a cappella movie musical Octet. She got divorced, or rather the press learned that she got divorced. Is that what you’re asking about? Probably not, right?

Since her large role in Fielder’s film has been kept under wraps, neither has spoken about it in interviews. At the Toronto International Film Festival, Seyfried denied to Entertainment Tonight that she was involved altogether—obviously not true.

At the red carpet for the Academy Museum Gala on the weekend of the film’s release, reporters tried to ask without asking. The Hollywood Reporter’s awkward interaction, which you can watch on Instagram, concluded by asking how Seyfried would like people to engage with her. On the unspoken assumption that she cannot talk about You Can See Everything, THR asked what she would like to talk about.

“I like to talk about the emus,” Seyfried replied. “I like to talk about Halloween. And you can engage with me if you want to talk about all things having to do with apple pie and olives and really good hard ciders.”

When speaking with Variety on the same carpet, she wagged her finger and warned the reporter not to ask her anything. Hopefully, as more people see You Can See Everything we’ll learn more about the film’s surprise tetartagonist—a word that means “fourth main character” that, yes, I Googled just for this sentence. When was she first contacted? How does she feel about Holmes now? Did it hurt to have to mispronounce her own name in a scene? We don’t know! I’ll take any additional insight, at this point. Maybe she could do an Actors on Actors with Primetime’s Robert Pattinson. Just a suggestion!

#121. ‘GBBO’ Fans Are Rallying Behind The Bakers After A Brutal Technical: ‘If The Whole Class Fails…’

Paul Hollywood called it the worst one he’d seen in 17 years.

I’ve watched enough Bake Off Technicals to know they’re supposed to make the bakers sweat. But in this week’s Bread Week episode, when Paul Hollywood asked the remaining contestants to make eight flatbreads stuffed with roasted grapes and blue cheese in one hour, I already had a feeling this one was going to get ugly.

For one thing, the concept itself threw several bakers, and speaking as an American, I understood the confusion. When I hear flatbread, I’m picturing something thin and pizza-adjacent, not dough wrapped around roasted grapes and blue cheese and somehow rolled flat afterward.

By the time judging rolled around, the challenge had gone about as badly as everyone feared. Some of the flatbreads were too large or thick, some had grapes sitting on top instead of tucked inside, and several were raw or undercooked in the middle.

Paul said he couldn’t remember a worse Technical in the show’s 17-year run, and fellow judge Nigella Lawson suggested they “eat them” as punishment for their baking crimes. But viewers quickly started wondering whether the bakers were really the problem.

“If the whole class fails, there was something wrong with the teacher,” one person wrote. Another asked, “If 10 bakers can’t get it right, the problem isn’t the bakers, It’s the method, surely?”

Others had less sympathy for the challenge itself. “This was one of the worst bread weeks ever. And usually bread week is my favorite,” one viewer wrote, while another viewer just wasn’t sold on the flavor combination: “ROASTED GRAPES???? And BLUE CHEESE???? Stuffed in a flatbread???? Horrifying, really.”

Even some former bakers were willing to push back on Paul, too. 2025 finalist Aaron Mountford-Myles wrote, “Some of those were blatantly flat. I will die on this hill,” disputing at least one part of the judging and refusing to let him erase their flatness entirely.

And 2023 contestant Saku Chandrasekara recognized the situation immediately, commenting, “Paul said the same for our steam puddings 😳,” a callback to another Technical where undercooked puddings caused trouble across the tent.

Because apparently nothing bonds generations of Bake Off contestants quite like being collectively roasted by Paul Hollywood.

A couple colleagues returned from a trip to Italy this week. Were they raving about the world-class food? The beautiful views? Their truffle hunting expedition? No, they came into the office chatting about the big wine heist that, according to them, everyone in Italy was talking about.

Basically, a group of men stole 30,000 bottles of wine from a warehouse in Tuscany, estimated to be worth $5.5 million. “Could they simply be passionate oenophiles who plan to drink the 30,000 bottles of Tuscan red themselves?” asks The New York Times. Ever the optimists over there.

Is there a single recipe that you love enough to make your legacy forevermore? That’s presumably the idea behind the recipes people have carved into their tombstones, which, yes, is a real thing that happens quite often. Archivist Rosie Grant has chronicled these recipes online and in her aptly named cookbook To Die For, but in putting the book together she discovered something much more profound about them.

Also in today’s Open Tab: Are GLP-1 supplements just another kind of snake oil? The Michelin scandal unfolding in Texas, new tech from Square that could change restaurants forever, and an essay from Daniel Humm on the frenzy of opening his latest restaurant.

My colleague Nina Moskowitz flagged something to me that caught her eye: A smoothie shop with locations around the country was offering what she called “GLP-1 powder.” Odd, I thought to myself. I investigated and found that it was listed as “GLP-1 Fiber Booster” on the shop’s menu. Naturally, I ordered a scoop in my smoothie; it was $30 with tip.

The powder is made by a company called Supergut, which named it GLP-1 Daily Support. It’s one of many such GLP-1-adjacent powders on the market. On its website, Supergut claims the powder “supports GLP-1 levels”—with an asterisk that notes that the claim hasn’t been evaluated by the FDA.

Babak Orandi, MD, PhD, an obesity specialist at NYU Langone, told me that there’s no evidence these powders can boost the effects or the levels of GLP-1s. “And even if it were to, it is unlikely to have a meaningful effect,” he wrote in an email. “The medications act at concentrations hundreds to thousands of times higher than the body’s own GLP-1 and are designed to last for days, while the body’s own GLP-1 is broken down within minutes.”

In fact, these supplements are something much simpler: fiber.

In an email statement, a spokesperson from Supergut said, in part, that the powder is “not a GLP-1 medication,” but is “designed as companion nutrition for people on GLP-1 medications and anyone supporting their gut health.” The supplement, they said, “may support feelings of fullness and beneficial gut bacteria associated with natural GLP-1 production.”

The $79 billion industry of GLP-1s has changed the way we eat. GLP-1s may even be supercharging nutritional therapy, and along the way they’ve become buzzwords in the weight-loss and wellness space. Slapping the phrase GLP-1 on the label is an easy way to sell more fiber powders (and smoothie supplements), even if it’s misleading consumers. “I think the name oversells it,” Dr. Orandi told me.

It’s telling, too, that the Supergut’s CEO herself has noted that it’s risky to use the term GLP-1 booster. When I first visited the smoothie shop and asked the guy working the counter about the term, he told me, “It’s the same stuff that goes into Ozempic.”

When I returned the next day for another GLP-1 supplement-laden smoothie (might as well see what drinking this supplement for a week does, I’d decided), a different cashier told me the GLP-1 supplement was actually more of an appetite suppressant, but that it wasn’t the same thing as an actual GLP-1.

For what it’s worth, after a week of consuming GLP-1 boosters I feel exactly no difference. Didn’t even keep me full, really.

Dallas landed five new spots on Michelin’s Texas guide this year, part of the guide’s ever expanding remit. But D Magazine’s dining critic Brian Reinhart noticed something strange in the guide’s write-ups. They didn’t read quite right. After putting the text through an AI detector, it looks like the majority of the reviews of the new restaurants were created by AI.

Reinhardt’s reporting points to the overuse of grammatical structures and specific words, such as serene or careful, which LLM’s tend to use more frequently than humans. Michelin denied that AI was used to write the restaurant reviews, and also refused an interview or to review Reinhardt’s findings.

The Michelin guide is known and lauded for its rigor. In a sea of influencers, Michelin’s century of dining expertise and its strict code of secrecy stand out. It is widely considered one of the last international authorities on food and restaurants. But critics have noted that trust has begun to erode as Michelin accepts cash in exchange for coverage, and accusations of AI use would further undermine the rigor and thoroughness on which Michelin has built its reputation.

Do you remember when, seemingly overnight, every coffee place and bakery suddenly had those tablets that would work as cash registers. Point-of-sale (POS) systems, they’re called—the kind that swivel around and ask you if you’d like to add a tip. Those systems are basically made by two companies at this point: Toast and Square.

This week, the latter released the next product in the POS line, simply dubbed Kiosk. It’s an AI-enabled tablet on a stand with microphones and speakers, and it does everything a human working a register would do: take orders, recommend dishes, explain menu items, and upsell, among other things. In short, it seems primed to take a lot of jobs.

Tech optimists would say that Kiosk will help independent restaurants cut costs and stay open, but I’m no tech optimist. I wonder if the idea of Kiosk is built on a fundamental misunderstanding of restaurants. We don’t go out to eat just to satisfy our hunger. We go out to feel like we’re a part of the world, to interact with people, to feel wrapped in and a part of the hum of servers and conversations and disagreements and sly jokes happening all around us. Optimizing that friction out of the restaurant experience with AI isn’t solving for a problem most customers experience. Just as self-checkout machines have made the grocery store experience more lonely, so too might Square’s new devices.

“Opening a restaurant is an insane thing to do,” chef Daniel Humm writes in an essay for Bon Appétit. He’s spent months obsessing over the details—the light fixtures, the perfect shade of red paint—all in service of getting his latest restaurant just right. Read on to see how Humm made it through the madness to open Humm, the first restaurant to bear his name.

#123. The Unlikely Longevity of Longchamp

Across US college campuses, undergraduates are carrying Longchamp’s Le Pliage bag — the trusty, foldable tote that has had teenagers and 20-somethings in a chokehold since its launch in 1993. In Paris, schoolgirls are seen wielding the bag from as young as 13, while in the UK, it’s an undying staple of accessible luxury, associated with royals and it-girls including Lila Moss and Alexa Chung. And in Aaron Sorkin’s new film The Social Reckoning, Mikey Madison’s whistle-blowing protagonist carries the bag as part of her San Francisco tech employee uniform.

On TikTok, creators crow about Le Pliage’s visually and physically satisfying design, produced in workshops across Western France. For many, it’s the perfect first “big girl” bag, priced accessibly at $165 for the classic large canvas iteration — and available in sizes ranging from extra-extra small through XL. “We’ve always had the image of being excellent value,” says CEO Jean Cassegrain. “It’s the history of our brand to always be contemporary, in sync with the times, and to adjust to new customer needs.”

Cassegrain is the third generation in the Longchamp family. His father, Philippe, designed the Le Pliage, while his grandfather (also Jean) founded the brand in 1948, originally selling leather pipe designs. Cassegrain, mustachioed, silver-haired, and smiling, explains that during its early days, the pipes were popular with hip youngsters. Fast forward to now, and it’s birthed another craze, this time with Gen Z and Gen Alpha. While the company doesn’t disclose sales of the Le Pliage, it confirmed the bag is its best-seller.

The classic Le Pliage bag — affordable and trusty — has been a core piece in youth wardrobes since the ‘90s.

For Longchamp, this is a welcome accident. “It’s not something we have manufactured,” he says. “Of course, I see [it] because I have teenagers and younger people around me, and our team members also have teenagers around them, but it’s not a deliberate marketing strategy.” He argues that teenagers make their own decisions. “If you try to market something as ‘for them’, they are not going to like it.”

For other competitors in the accessible luxury market, Longchamp offers a valuable case study in bucking the trend of excessively fawning Gen Z content, at a time when luxury is at risk of losing its hold on youth culture. Longchamp’s passive, product-led approach has won it cool points, but for other bridge brands, such as Coach and Diesel, innovative Gen Z-focused social media strategies helped unlock a sizable audience. Longchamp could risk losing ground to its peers without more social savvy. But for Cassegrain, what’s worked for decades has yet to show any sign of slowing down.

CEO Jean Cassegrain never intended for his brand to go viral.

Roughly 80% of Longchamp’s customers are female, Cassegrain tells Vogue Business. Under-25s and 25-30s are two highly dynamic age segments for Longchamp, and the brand’s median age is around 35-36. In the past three years, the under-35 portion has grown substantially. The age split differs by territory, and in France especially, Longchamp consumers start young.

On TikTok, the #Longchamp Le Pliage features in freshman content, as well as “Longchamp epidemic” videos, which simply showcase the sheer number of women and girls carrying the bag across central London. Some creators recommend the bag, positioning it as the ultimate back-to-school design. Even British Vogue has highlighted its revival, dubbing it the ’00s messy-prep revival piece.

Late last year, Vogue Business and youth culture agency Archrival published a Gen Z report, highlighting that TikTok was indeed the number one social media app for US Gen Zs to find or discover products. Tellingly, one respondent — then a 21-year-old student from Chicago — said TikTok videos influenced her to purchase a blue Longchamp bag. “On the first day of school, literally hundreds of other girls had the exact same bag,” she said. “It was really weird because it’s a specific brand in a specific color. It almost looked dystopian.” Gen Alpha, due to the internet’s flattening of tween culture, are also tapping into Longchamp, drawn in by its bridge brand status.

In the boardroom, the brand is reaping the rewards. France, China, and the US are its leading markets. US sales have accelerated in the past two years to high double-digit growth. China — where many European luxury brands are struggling — remains strong, growing single-digit. In 2025, overall sales were up 10% year-on-year, with all regions and distribution channels contributing to this momentum. North America sales climbed by 40%, accounting for 15% of the total turnover. Digital sales also grew 17% on e-commerce.

Cassegrain forecasts double-digit growth in 2026, outperforming the luxury average. This will more than double its turnover in 2022 — a major four-year jump. A medium-sized player in the market, Longchamp wants to scale in line with growing consumer demand. That way, it can optimize across all channels: service, website, communications, and events. “The goal is also to grow more than the market, so that we can gain market share,” explains Cassegrain, noting that in the past four years, the market for luxury accessories and ready-to-wear didn’t double in size, making Longchamp an outperformer.

One of the most enticing aspects of Longchamp’s offering — and a clear draw for the notably discerning Gen Z consumer — is the custom offering, My Pliage, initiated in 2003. Over the years, this service has evolved and was updated in 2025, allowing customers to select everything from the canvas and monogram details through to hardware finishing. From the outset, more than 20 years ago, Asian customers showed strong demand for this personalizable element, although it’s been a globally popular proposition. The draw? “It’s a product that’s reliable and very well identified, but at the same time, it’s not the same as everyone else’s,” says Cassegrain. “The customer can buy into the safety of the brand, but at the same time, have something totally unique.”

Part of Longchamp’s success lies in it being a family business. Cassegrain is the company’s third-ever CEO, following his father and grandfather. This means Longchamp can invest quietly and discreetly in the brand, think long term, and avoid stock market or private equity pressure to deliver flashy quarterly results.

It’s also a largely women-led company. The workforce is 79% women, the executive committee is 40%, and the international subsidiary of directors is 58%. The creative director and general manager, Sophie Delafontaine, sits across business and creative decisions, giving her a clear view of product performance and strong relationships with the CEO. “So, disclosure: Sophie is my sister,” Cassegrain says, chuckling. “So it makes things easier, and we work together very closely.”

That said, Cassegrain is keen to note that the stability and safety that come with family businesses also mean Longchamp has to self-motivate. “We need to make sure we’re not becoming complacent, so we need to be able to reinvent ourselves — even without outside pressure.” In practice, that’s resulted in an evolving wealth of SKUs across bags, footwear, and ready-to-wear, comprising new releases and updates on brand heroes. Le Cadence, a slouchy, grained leather bag launched in August, sold out 70% of the season’s initial inventory by the end of September. It quickly became a company best-seller.

Longchamp is ready to scale its ready-to-wear offering.

Meanwhile, ready-to-wear serves as a powerful tool in communicating the brand’s image: a blend of Parisian chic and cheery design language. As Cassegrain sees it, Longchamp is an expert in leather goods, but it’s also special because of its strong brand message rooted in color and optimism — key differentiators in today’s luxury market. “A lot of brands feel a little serious, a little dark, a little black, and lack humor sometimes,” he says. “We don’t take ourselves too seriously.”

Until recently, this wing of the business had a very limited distribution, but the plan is to expand that. Currently, around 75% of Longchamp’s sales come from its direct-to-consumer channel, and within that, 80-85% of customers shop in-person rather than online. This is promising. Young people might be infamously influenced online, but clearly they’re heading to stores. If the bag resurgence is anything to go by, the first signs of success will be on TikTok, and then the P&L sheet.

“It shouldn’t be the brand's best-kept secret,” says Cassegrain. “We want it to become more visible, and we feel quite confident in pushing it further.”

#124. Take a Look at the Stunning Italian Estate That Plays a Role on The Diplomat

The 170-acre property once belonged to the Ferragamo family.

For the end of The Diplomat season 4, our favorite characters made their way from the London halls of government to scenic Tuscany, where they attend a G7 summit. One of their particularly camera-friendly stops was the 16th-century Viesca Toscana, which was once the home of Ferragamo founders Salvatore and Wanda Ferragamo and is now a small luxury hotel. Though the Ferragamos, who extensively renovated the home, no longer own it, the family remains involved. Vittoria Ferragamo, the granddaughter of Salvatore and Wanda, oversees the destination.

Viesca Toscana sits on 170 acres, and guests stay either in the original Villa Viesca, the Ferragamo family’s original home, or in the private villas that sprawl across the property. Villa Viesca sleeps up to 18 guests. The hotel’s décor includes meticulously sourced antique pieces, hand-painted frescoes, and custom wallpaper, much of which is original to the Ferragamo family’s own design.

Scenes shot on the property include an al fresco dinner for Ambassador Kate (Kerri Russell), Vice President Hal (Rufus Sewell), first gentleman Todd (Bradley Whitford), and President Grace (Allison Janney) held on the Villa Viesca terrace. We also see both Todd and Grace embracing in the living room, Hal and Kate in the garden, and Todd pantsless in bed in one of the bedrooms, with a brilliant fresco on the wall.

Subtle hints of the Ferragamo legacy can be seen—from sketches of shoe designs to cushions made from Ferragamo fabrics. Villa Viesca has always had a fashion pedigree, but now it’s achieved TV fame, as well.

#127. This Trick Makes Cutting Winter Squash So Much Easier

A little heat makes a big difference when it comes to cutting a stubborn squash.

I love winter squash, but I’ve never been fond of the effort required to get some varieties onto the dinner table. Butternut squash is manageable enough, but a stubborn acorn or Hubbard squash can make even the sharpest chef’s knife feel inadequate. And while I have no objection to a little prep work, I’d rather spend my time cooking dinner than trying to negotiate with a vegetable.

Of course, the reward is usually worth it. Roasted squash is one of fall’s greatest gifts, and there’s no shortage of ways to put it to work in soups, sides and even desserts. But the effort (and fear of accidental finger amputation) is off-putting. Then I came across a video demonstrating a simple way to make cutting winter squash easier, and I put it to the test.

The technique itself isn’t new or complicated. What caught my attention was how little effort it took to dramatically simplify the process of preparing an otherwise stubborn squash.

In the video, the creator places a whole squash in a 400ºF oven for 20 minutes before cutting it.

Afterward, her knife passes through the squash with remarkably little resistance, and she removes the seeds in a single scoop. It’s an impressive demonstration, even though the principle behind it is familiar enough: Heat softens vegetables, and winter squash is no exception.

The question is whether 20 minutes is enough to make a meaningful difference without cooking the squash all the way through.

To find out, I picked up two similarly sized Danish squash—a classic type of acorn squash, recognizable by its dark green, deeply ridged exterior and sweet, golden flesh. Like other types of winter squash, it has a tough rind that can make cutting it in half more challenging than its relatively modest size might suggest.

I left one squash raw and baked the other for 20 minutes in a 400º oven, piercing the skin first to let steam escape. After letting the roasted squash cool long enough for me to handle it, I cut both in half using the same knife.

The difference was immediately obvious. Cutting through the raw squash required much more pressure, while the partially roasted one offered much less resistance. Removing the seeds was easier, too, and the softened flesh was still firm enough to be cut into wedges without falling apart.

Admittedly, putting a squash in the oven before cutting it raises a reasonable question: Why not just roast it all the way through? The answer depends on what you’re making. If you’re planning to scoop out the flesh for soup or puree, you might as well go all the way. But if your recipe calls for wedges, cubes or slices that need to hold their shape and brown in the oven, you need to cut the squash before it’s fully cooked.

Those exposed surfaces are what allow roasted squash to develop its beautifully browned, caramelized edges. And if you’re making a squash gratin, a roasted squash salad or a soup that begins by sauteing cubes of squash with onions and aromatics, the shape and texture of those pieces matter.

This technique doesn’t save time from start to finish. You still have to preheat the oven, roast the squash and allow it to cook before cutting into it. What it does save is the physical effort of cutting through a dense, raw winter squash, which can be complicated if you struggle with hand strength or find vegetables tough to manage. You’ll still want a sharp knife and a stable cutting board, but there’s something to be said about a little less resistance.

Danish squash worked beautifully for me, but the technique certainly isn’t limited to acorn varieties. Other hard-skinned winter squash like kabocha, Hubbard and buttercup can benefit from a brief period in the oven before cutting. Butternut squash is another good option, especially if you’re working with a large one that needs to be halved and cubed.

The size of the squash matters, too. Twenty minutes at 400º may be enough to make a noticeable difference in a smaller squash, but a large variety may need more time. The goal isn’t to cook it until it’s tender; it’s to soften it just enough that your knife can pass through more easily. If I don’t have to test the limits of my chef’s knife, I’ll happily take it.

#128. Could a Human Being Really Survive Whalefall?

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

IN DANIEL KRAUS’S novel Whalefall, a teenage scuba diver is swallowed alive by a sperm whale in pursuit of a giant squid. While that might seem like a farfetched tale, reminiscent of Jonah being swallowed up by a whale in the bible, it actually happens more than you think. In 2025, a kayaker was sucked up by a whale near Chile and in 2021, a lobster fisherman was swallowed while diving to check his traps near Provincetown, Mass. Both survived, having been rather quickly spit back up by their respective seabound captors, but it begs the important question: Is Whalefall’s premise more of a cautionary tale than it is a total fantasy?

That’s certainly one of the questions the creators of Whalefall’s new cinematic adaptation want viewers to ask themselves. Starring the very busy Austin Abrams (who last month appeared in Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil) as poor Jay Gardiner, the diver who ends up in the whale, the film bounces back and forth narratively from the cetacean’s stomach to life with Gardiner’s recently deceased father (Josh Brolin), whose remains Jay was seeking when he was swallowed up.

It’s a complicated story that asks more than just “how will this dude get out of this whale,” and yet, the story and struggle behind Gardiner’s eventual (spoiler alert!) escape is captivating. Could someone really survive being sucked into a whale’s guts and not just their mouths? And what’s actually inside a whale, if not just a big empty cavern and a couple of rowboats, a la movies like Pinocchio?

Ramsey Avery, Whalefall’s Production Designer, has put a whole lot of thought into both questions, mulling over everything from how to accurately depict what a whale’s stomach lining would look like to the mechanics of a whale’s multiple stomach sphincters. (And there are multiples!) Men’s Health talked to him about the practical challenges of building camera-ready whale guts, the realities of life inside a constantly diving sperm whale, and whether he thinks he’s ready to fight his way out of one should a future swim go sideways.

MEN’S HEALTH: Where did your brain go when you first heard you got the Whalefall gig?

RAMSEY AVERY: We dove immediately into a lot of research, and the thing you discover fairly quickly is no one has really stuck a camera down the mouth of a sperm whale to see what that all looks like inside there. We have plenty of photography of porpoises and orcas and dolphins, which gives us something we can compare to, though, and then we reached out to a couple of cetacean experts.

Dr. Joy Reidenberg was our key contact and we just started asking a bunch of questions about size and shape and what happens in each of the stomachs. There are four stomachs in a whale and each has a different function. There are some interesting things about sperm whale anatomy, too, as opposed to say a blue whale or a humpback whale, which make it possible that a human could actually get swallowed and then survive the experience for at least a bit.

Another interesting thing is that sperm whales don't chew. They have teeth, but mostly they're like antlers on an elk. They're for display and dominance battles. Sperm whales kind of suck their food in instead. They create this compression chamber with their tongue that draws squid in.

Also, because sperm whales have evolved to eat giant squid unlike pretty much every other mammal, their larynx has been shifted off to the side rather than in the center so that there’s room for the big squid to go through. That's why, if you look at a sperm whale, its blowhole is on the left side of the head rather than centered like all the other whales and dolphins.

From the autopsies and dissections that Dr. Joy and others have done, we figured out the basic size, shape, and colors of a whale stomach. That meant I looked at a lot of really interesting dissection videos and photography first thing in the morning quite often. That was really how we tried to dive in, because for the director, for the studio, and for the producers, it was really critical that it be believable.

MH: It sounds like you’d have to do a lot of reverse math, like “If we need to fit a six-foot actor inside this stomach, proportionally we’d need a whale that’s this big”?

RA: You are exactly right. For whatever reason, most of the whales that wash up on coasts are either female or juvenile, but we do have a lot of records from whaling days about the sizes of male whales. We were able to take a look at the dimensions of those whales’s internal organs and mouths and project them out. And as it turns out, if you wanted to be able to put a person in a stomach that was about six feet tall and about eight feet long—which was the smallest we felt we could do and actually be able to get a camera inside there with the actor—that meant that the whale had to be about 80 feet long... which is right about the length of the largest sperm whales on record. So, it makes sense!

MH: How many models did you make, and how did you represent the differences between stomachs?

RA: The first stomach, where most of the movie takes place, is where a sperm whale chews its food. There's no digestion going on in there. Because they don't have teeth, their stomach actually does the chewing, so it's a muscular compressive stomach.

We do get into another stomach, which is where digestion starts. That's when you start getting into the acids. For the movie, we had to create part of the outside of a whale and its mouth, which we could put in a tank with water so that we could have both our hero actor and his stunt doubles be able to perform appropriately against a real set piece. We started there and then we looked at how the back of the throat and the esophagus works, how that all connects back in, and what the shape language of that is. We ended up creating a couple of set pieces for that to make it all work.

For the main stomach, we started off with a very simple mockup. We got a bunch of upholstery foam, roughed out the size of what we wanted to do, hung it on a rig, and started to put people inside of it to see how it moved. Is it big enough? What's the shape like? How do we get a camera inside?

A whale’s stomach has two entrances and exits. For the first stomach, there’s an entrance from the esophagus and an exit into the second stomach, and those entrances and exits are called sphincters. I have to say, I've used the word “sphincter” more in the last year than I ever imagined I would over the course of my entire life. But the first thing we figured out is that our sphincters could not sit right behind the actor's head, because you didn't really want the audience looking at the equivalent of a butthole for the entire movie. So we had to figure out how to adjust the anatomy of the stomach, both for the visual of it because we want our audience to be able to go along for the ride, but also to determine the action because when you read the script, it reads like the stomach is a long tunnel with an entrance at the front and the exit at the back. But in a real sperm whale stomach, both of those sphincters are up near the top of the stomach. We ended up going with that because it’s better for the action, better for the visuals, and more real.

But to get all of that to work, we had multiple things that the stomachs had to do, and we had multiple ways we needed to get cameras in there. Sometimes we had to put two or even three cameras in this little tiny space, so we did a whole test process again, carrying on with our mockups. Every time we did a mockup, we did a camera test, and we developed it further and further and further and got more specific with the shape language.

MH: Were all the sets four-walled enclosures?

RA: Yeah, they were 360 degree sets, holding water inside, and you could climb in and out of the sphincters. Those could function as camera ports, too, but we made other camera ports as well to be able to get some shots from different angles. With all the folds inside a whale stomach, you can hide those ports relatively simply, too.

MH: Did the movie already have science experts on staff when you came on or did you have to track down your own?

RA: Because the movie is based on Daniel Kraus's book, he’d already done a lot of that work to make sure everything felt real. So he put us in contact with his experts and then we reached out a little further to other sources. For example, we found a person who was an expert in whale sound to ask what type of sounds a whale would or could make.

We know that the inside of that first stomach is filled with methane and unbreathable gasses, because there have been times—and Dr. Joy actually had this happen to her—when a researcher cuts into a whale’s stomach and it’ll explode because of all the gasses building up inside. So, we know that you couldn't really breathe for any period of time inside that stomach and that's a key element to our story, because it sets a timer. Jay only has X number of minutes of oxygen in his tank—and that's a real thing.

MH: Where did you end up having to stretch the truth?

RA: The whale does a lot of things, and we don’t really know whether or not that’s how a whale would react with something like that in his stomach that he can't seem to swallow. We can make guesses, but we don't know, because that’s not something that can be studied.

The fact is that if you're studying a whale, odds are it's dead or it's on the verge of dying, because that's the only way you can do the work. You can't see a whale’s insides while it's still living in the ocean. There's a lot we can't know.

MH: It’s incredible how much we still don’t know about oceanic creatures. Like, we still don’t know where Great White sharks are born.

RA: It's funny because we’re learning more and more and more now, though, and even in the time that we were doing this project we got the first real imagery of a giant squid.

That's another thing: By the time a giant squid gets to the surface—which happens very rarely—they're dead and they've deflated. How they function is a mystery to us. But just in the last year or so, footage of a whale eating a giant squid came out, so we’re still learning things.

MH: Speaking of giant squid: How did you decide what else to put in your stomachs? What would be inside a hungry whale?

RA: Because of the autopsies that have been done on whales, we know the types of things that are in their stomachs. That second stomach where the digestion happens is where squid beaks get left behind because the acid in there isn't enough to digest them. That’s also where ambergris comes from: The leftover parts and bits of squid that aren't completely digested and that get kind of fused into this weird material.

The water itself was a special effects issue. We had to figure out the right viscosity and the right opacity of the water to make it feel like it would be inside a stomach. Wētā Workshop created a bunch of bits and pieces and flotsam and jetsam, like they built all of the beaks and then did multiples in various levels of digestion. They built the squid as well, which was a practical effect. We did this sequence with Jay fighting the squid that you see in the trailer, and that’s all practical props we then augmented and extended with visual effects.

MH: Having done all this work, how confident are you that, if you got sucked down by a sperm whale today, you could survive? Have you put yourself in the shoes of your lead?

RA: There are a gazillion pictures of me in various components of the stomach, the mouth, and the esophagus, because I didn't want to ask Austin [Abrams] or the stunt doubles to do anything I wasn't willing to do myself. There are even pictures of me crawling in the mouth of the whale in my wetsuit in the tank. In terms of actually surviving inside a whale, though, one of the things we were able to sort out is that Austin [Abrams] is a relatively slight person, so he might fit in with his tanks better than I would fit in with my tanks. I'm not sure I would actually go down the throat, because I'm a bigger guy. But at least I’ve also learned the methodologies that he learned to try and get out.

#129. 10 Pairs of Chelsea Boots You Can Wear in Nasty Weather

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

Style and substance, wrapped into one classic shape.

Nothing in your wardrobe is as targeted as a serious boot. You likely have one pair for when it’s real nasty, real shitty. But, you probably can’t wear them to your desk job, nor could you wear them on a particularly nice date. For that, you need a specialist. We love a Chelsea boot year-round, and there are nice waterproof (or...waterproof-ish) versions for when the weather takes a turn.

Made of supple leather and meant to develop a nice patina over time, Chelsea boots toe (pun intended) that line between stylish enough to wear in more polished settings but also far more functional than your average dress shoe—and there’s that bit of rock ’n’ roll lineage. They make for great commuter shoes on especially rainy days—good cushioning, good shock absorption, great coverage.

The secret to a weatherproof Chelsea boot is two-fold: First, go for rubber soles, not leather. Leather, though the more formal and fashionable choice, is a porous material. It’s fine to walk through a rainstorm in a leather jacket, but on the sole of your foot it’ll soak up water, become soft, and get ripped at by concrete. And once they start spreading salt in winter, keep leather-soled shoes far away. The second key is to care for your leather shoes. You don’t need to shine them weekly, but keep them clean and apply the occasional bit of shine, mink oil, or beeswax-based seal. After that, most of these boots will go the same places your rubber duck hunting boots go.

For any guys who spent their high school years stomping around in a pair of Dr. Martens, do we have some good news for you. While that OG pair you saved up to buy from Hot Topic might not totally fly in all offices, the brand’s Embury Chelsea boot certainly will. The shoe keeps things pretty nondescript—save for that trademark yellow stitching between shoe and sole—making it a familiar shoe to graduate into.

“Over this winter, I realized these boots could replace almost every other shoe I own,” commerce editor Luke Guillory said about these R.M. Williams Craftsman boots earlier this year. They’re made of yearling leather, fine-grained and ridiculously soft. Though they’re not as divine as the classic kangaroo leather R.M. Williams Craftsman boots—kangaroo is classed as an exotic leather, and a specifically divisive one—yearling mimics the soft and sturdy feel.

The thing about R.M. Williams is that it originally made work boots. Don’t get too precious with them, especially when you buy with that comfort sole—which, since it’s rubber, doesn’t wear down like leather when you walk through rain, snow, and salt.

John Lobb is one of the OG names in British benchmade footwear. Its Chelsea boots, particularly the lugged sole varieties, are not only amazing on first wear, they’re made to last.

This boot is for the fellas with the big feet. Allen Edmonds offers sizes up to 15 and EEE width. Again, see the Goodyear-welted rubber sole—great for nasty weather. As long as you take care of the leather, they’re a great pick and a good value.

Blundstones are so damn tough. These things are meant for hikes and are practically begging to be put through the wringer, so a slightly soggy commute is just another day of work to these boots.

Only caveat, they do not look as polished as the options you’ve seen thus far in the list. But that’s because they’re a step above in terms of durability.

Have dreams of living out a cowboy fantasy but aren’t quite ready for the full cowboy boot? Thursday Boot Company comes somewhat close with the different color stitch and the deep brown leather.

We’ll keep it simple: they’re handcrafted in Portugal, they’re polished and sexy, they have memory-foam insoles, and they’ll go with just about everything.

Named after one of the rainiest cities in the country, these L.L. Bean boots feature a thick lugged outsole for hours of easy walking. Combine that with the leather upper, and you’ve got a damn good office boot.

Look, smooth leather’s all well and good, but there’s just no denying the cozy embrace of a suede boot. The only problem is that suede is typically not the biggest fan of anything wet and rainy. Sorel, which specializes in footwear for rain, snow, and slush, balances the lush feel of suede with a waterproof construction to create a sophisticated shoe that can weather (pun intended) just about anything.

#130. Everything to Know About Kylie Jenner's Victoria’s Secret Fantasy Bra—Including the Hidden Detail

Jeweler Jacob Arabo embedded a message to his wife in the design

When the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show returned from a six-year hiatus in 2024, I kept my eyes peeled for one thing—the Fantasy Bra. But while the angel wings were back, the catwalk’s crown jewel was notably absent. Little did I know a record-breaking $50 million bombshell by Jacob & Co. was underway for this year’s extravaganza.

Kylie Jenner wore the piece, which came wrapped in 4,410 natural diamonds that spilled into a full flush of fringe from front to back. A 75.54-carat natural yellow diamond, graded “Fancy Vivid” by experts (the highest designation for color saturation), sat dead-center in the celestial gemscape. Each millimeter contoured to her body like a second skin, without the use of any textile fabrics. Drawing from his Rare Form jewelry collection, founder Jacob Arabo and his team of artisans laid the foundation of the ergonomic structure with articulated segments of precious gold.

“The Fantasy Bras have always stood out to me as a jeweler because they are true high jewelry pieces,” Arabo tells Bazaar. “We wanted to honor their legacy and raise the bar in every way to create the most valuable Fantasy Bra ever made. What matters most to me is the emotion it creates when you see it on the runway.”

I grew up in a family where being the eldest daughter meant no makeup, no reading Twilight, and no exposed belly buttons. So each year, I would plot a visit to my best friend’s house to watch the VS fashion show on live TV. It allowed me to teleport from the confines of tankini life to the land of spray-tanned glamazons with bare midriffs, sky-high stilettos, and vibrant plumes of feathers. I still remember 2006, when Karolina Kurkova emerged like a statuesque snowflake in a negligée made in collaboration with Hearts on Fire featuring 2,000 diamonds, with a 10-carat central stone. To me, it felt both liberating and transporting—an everyday object made magic.

Every year since, the show has brought a new high-carat confection tied to a fantastical theme, ranging in price from $3 million to $15 million. Arabo’s embellished masterpiece is the highest-value Fantasy Bra yet, but its ethereal splendor comes through in considered details, such as proprietary Angel-cut diamonds. Named after his wife, Angela, the cut is defined by 37 facets representing 37 years of marriage. After a two-year development process, the signature design arrived just in time for the making of the most opulent Victoria’s Secret bra yet. The patented stones glistened alongside pear, heart, oval, marquise, and round brilliant diamonds, each hand-placed with specialized settings.

“Each component was cleaned, filed, and pre-polished by hand,” Arabo tells Bazaar. “Fifteen artisans worked for more than 1,000 hours to bring the piece together. I started at the jeweler’s bench, so I have a great appreciation for the skill behind every part of this piece.”

For those intensely discerning coffee drinkers, the ones who have notebooks filled with the outcomes of different coffee-to-water ratios, you can be sure this gift guide will have barista-grade espresso machines and pour-over coffee accessories. If you’re shopping for a Nespresso stan or a programmable drip machine enthusiast, there are things like coffee subscriptions, high-quality mugs, and worthwhile upgrades to their coffee bar that all make great gifts.

East Fork is one of our favorite home goods brands, and their mugs (like the rest of their pottery) come in every color you could possibly want.

Trade is a multi-roaster subscription that sources coffee from independent roasters all over the country. It's great for someone looking for great specialty coffee with an interest in trying a number of different roasters and different roasting styles.

Tester: Chris Morocco, food director This was the easiest subscription I have ever set up, and Trade did such a good job of hitting my preferences right in their sweet spot: medium roast, medium body, medium fruit…just medium all around.
