#133. ‘The Love of Your Life’ Will Make You Cry Your Eyes Out (But It’s One of the Year’s Most Romantic Films)

Margaret Qualley’s new film tells the story of a love capable of changing everything.

There are romantic films that make us dream of fairy-tale love and others that remind us how much it can hurt. The Love of Your Life, available on Prime Video, manages to do both: first, it makes us believe in the possibility of finding someone capable of forever changing the way we look at the world, then it confronts us with one of the hardest questions to face: how do you go on living when you lose the very person with whom you had imagined your future?

Directed by Rachel Morrison and starring a wonderful Margaret Qualley, alongside Gabriel Basso and Aaron Pierre, the film spans the life of Maya, a young nurse who has never truly believed in the concept of family and who, almost by chance, ends up meeting someone capable of making her change her mind. What seems like the beginning of a romantic fairy tale soon turns into a much more complex story, in which fate, grief, and missed opportunities force the protagonist to question everything she thought she knew about love.

The film's strength is that it does not reduce everything to a simple tragic love story designed to make us cry. But the true heart of the story is Maya's journey, a woman who must learn to live with what she has lost and understand who she wants to be after going through a pain capable of profoundly changing her.

The story deals with grief without turning it into something that can be overcome with a single decision or with the arrival of the right person. At the same time, it speaks of second chances and the courage needed to allow ourselves to have them, reminding us that moving forward does not mean erasing what we have lived through. A relationship can end and continue to be important, just as a love can leave an indelible mark without necessarily having to represent the only chance at happiness we will have in life.

It is a message that may seem simple, but that the film manages to make concrete through the protagonist's choices. Maya is not always ready when she should be, she does not necessarily make the easiest decisions, and she does not immediately find the words to explain what she feels. Sometimes she rejects a compromise because she knows it could not make her happy; other times she realizes too late that she is ready to experience something she could not accept before. All this helps make Margaret Qualley's character believable: she is not a perfect protagonist but a person trying to find her way as life keeps changing.

Not all transformations have to lead us to become better people according to a predetermined scale of values, nor should every change be interpreted as a step backward. Sometimes we change simply because our experiences have transformed us, because we need different things, or because we learn to recognize desires we were not able to understand before. And accepting that, especially when it comes to love, requires a good dose of courage.

Holding together a story that spans years, relationships, and profoundly different moments is Margaret Qualley, who is able to accompany Maya through her contradictions without ever making her feel like a distant figure. Her performance lends credibility both to the happiness of the first encounters and to the difficulty of rebuilding oneself after a loss, portraying a protagonist who never stops feeling the weight of the past even when she tries to imagine a different future.

The story is also supported by the cinematography and settings, which accompany the different moments in Maya’s life and help give the story an evocative visual dimension. The landscapes are not merely a beautiful backdrop: they become part of a journey made up of moves, escapes, and attempts to start over, while the passing years allow us to observe how priorities change and how the protagonist’s view of herself evolves.

The film, written by Julia Cox and directed by Rachel Morrison, does not always take the most predictable path, and this is also reflected in its ending. Without giving anything away, it is precisely the way the story reaches its conclusion that makes it even more meaningful: it does not offer a universal answer about how one should love (a life partner or oneself), but leaves room for the possibility that different paths exist, even when they do not match the ones we had imagined.

So get ready to cry your eyes out, not only because of the love story or its most painful turns: perhaps you will be moved because in Maya you will recognize a small piece of yourself, a choice you made, a relationship that changed you, or a part of your life that you have not yet been able to let go of.

#134. Chipotle’s Latest Drop Is A Massive 170-Liter Takeout Bag You Can Actually Win—Here’s How

Chipotle has been making a surprising number of moves into fashion and accessories lately. There was its Béis travel collection, and earlier this year, even hockey jerseys got involved. But apparently none of that was big enough—and I mean that quite literally.

Chipotle has created the Big Ass Chipotle Bag, a comically oversized take on the brown paper bag that usually carries your lunch. It measures 36 inches wide, 24 inches tall, and 12 inches deep, with a 170-liter capacity. To put that into perspective, there’s enough room in there for things like a trumpet, a traffic cone, and even a desk chair.

At three feet wide, you could also probably lose your actual Chipotle order inside it. But there is, technically, a reason the brand decided its usual bag needed this kind of growth spurt.

The stunt is really a very large advertisement for Chipotle’s Family Meals. Previously called Build-Your-Own Chipotle, the online-only order is meant for four to six people, with enough ingredients for everyone to turn dinner into whatever they want—bowls, tacos, salads, nachos, or some combination of the above.

Naturally, Chipotle decided all that food required packaging with roughly the subtlety of a moving van.

“A Big Ass Meal deserves a Big Ass Bag,” Fernando Machado, Chipotle’s Chief Brand Officer, said in a statement. “We took one of the most recognizable parts of the Chipotle experience, gave it an outsized upgrade, and created something that's impossible to miss. It's fun, it's ridiculous and it's exactly the kind of thing we knew our fans would want to get their hands on.”

Unfortunately, you can’t just stroll into Chipotle and ask them to supersize your paper bag. To have a shot at taking one home, U.S. Rewards members need to order a Family Meal through Chipotle’s app or website. That purchase puts them into the giveaway, with more winners picked throughout the promotion.

The Family Meals come in at less than $10 per person, which is a perfectly reasonable price point being used to promote a deeply unreasonable bag.

I just hope whoever wins one has somewhere to put it.

#135. Pumpkin Bolognese

Classic Bolognese, with its multi-hour cook time, can be truly remarkable, if you ever have a stretch to make it. In this version, a scoop of canned pumpkin purée is the head-turning ingredient that gives it full-blown flavor and body, without the wait typical of a nonna-style sauce. Lightly caramelizing the pumpkin in the pot along with tomato paste gives it a nutty, savory edge. Milk is the other surprise ingredient here, especially in the quantity of a full cup. Think of it as a tenderizer, making the final sauce soft and delicate. Pay attention to the order in which the ingredients appear—the milk goes in first with the wine to follow. If you switch the order, the acidic wine will curdle the milk.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Heat 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Add 1 large white or yellow onion, finely chopped, 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. freshly grated nutmeg and stir to combine. Cover pot and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion and celery are very soft, 8–10 minutes. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until onion and celery are golden around the edges, about 5 minutes.

Uncover pot and add 1 lb. ground beef, preferably 20% fat; season lightly with salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until beef is very lightly browned but not crisp (it will still be pink in spots), 6–8 minutes. Pour in 1 cup whole milk and cook, stirring occasionally, until milk has evaporated and fat is pooling on surface of meat, 7–10 minutes.

Pour in 1 cup dry white wine and cook, stirring occasionally, until wine has evaporated, 6–8 minutes. Add 1 cup canned pumpkin purée and 2 Tbsp. double-concentrated tomato paste; season generously with freshly ground pepper. Cook, stirring often and scraping bottom of pot, until combined and pumpkin darkens slightly, 8–10 minutes.

Pour in 1 cup water, reduce heat to low, and cook, stirring occasionally, until mixture is saucy, 12–15 minutes. If meat seems dry, add an extra ½ cup water and continue cooking another 3–4 minutes. Taste sauce and season with salt if needed. Keep warm.

Meanwhile, cook 12 oz. fresh tagliatelle or pappardelle or dry rigatoni, in a large pot of boiling salted water. If using fresh pasta, cook about 3 minutes. If using dry, cook until very al dente, about 2 minutes less than package directions.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to pot with sauce. Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid and 2 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about 1 cup). Increase heat to medium, bring to a simmer, and cook, tossing constantly, until pasta is al dente and sauce is slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.

Transfer pasta to shallow bowls and sprinkle with more Parmesan.

#136. What Will It Take to Fortify Fashion’s Supply Chain?

“We’ve done a lot of talking. Now, it’s time for implementation.” That was the opening gambit from Textile Exchange conference host Samata Pattinson last week, kick-starting three days of programming that said a lot about the state of sustainable fashion, and the frustrations simmering below its surface.

In recent years, sustainable fashion conferences have been dogged by the same sense of frustration. Attendees often pay thousands of dollars to be in the room, only to lament the lack of representation and authenticity on-stage, and the lack of progress outside it. It often feels like the same people saying the same things they have said for the past decade, albeit varied slightly depending on the political zeitgeist.

Organizers have tried to wrangle this frustration into momentum, choosing conference themes like Ambition to Action (Global Fashion Summit, 2023) and The Implementation Era (Textile Exchange, 2026). But sentiment is slow to change, and systems are even slower.

As Lululemon’s senior vice president of sustainability, Noel Kinder, noted in his keynote on day two, corporate sustainability has been through the ringer. The early 2000s were defined by a “reactionary” approach to workers’ rights, hinged on high-profile investigations and crises like the Rana Plaza factory collapse. The late 2010s saw sustainability boom, with values-driven companies like Reformation, Everlane and Allbirds (now an AI company) attracting huge amounts of investment; greenwashing exploded as brands sought to cash in on consumer awareness of the issue.

Now, with political backlash against sustainability and widespread deregulation taking the wind out of corporate sustainability’s sails, the subject is undergoing another metamorphosis. At this year’s Textile Exchange conference, it became clear that the new sustainability buzzword is resilience.

“The reality of the world around us today warrants more discussions about risk and prevention,” says Patrik Frisk, CEO of textile-to-textile recycler Reju, which was the title sponsor of this year’s conference. “It’s all about regulation and geopolitical and environmental risks.”

Exactly what resilience looks like in fashion supply chains is up for debate. Textile Exchange structured the program around two main solutions: regenerative agriculture for natural fibers, and textile-to-textile recycling for synthetics. Both promise to boost supply chain resilience — be that against climate change or geopolitical unrest — but face significant barriers to scale. And many of the people who could unlock progress were not in the room, says Eileen Fisher’s senior director of materials and circularity Inka Apter: “There was a rather glaring absence of sourcing team leaders and CFOs in this space.”

For attendees, organizers attempted to serve up a heavy dose of reality, courtesy of professor Gail Whiteman, Hoffmann impact professor for accelerating action on nature and climate at the University of Exeter and founder of non-profit Arctic Basecamp. She reminded the audience that seven of the nine planetary boundaries have now exceeded the safe threshold; climate-related disasters increased 83% between 2000 and 2019; and wildlife populations have shrunk by 73% in the past 50 years. Meanwhile, sea and land ice — which she called “the biggest insurance system our climate has” — are melting at record rates. “The scale of change is astronomical,” said Whiteman. “The only words that are important right now are implementation and action.”

Against the backdrop Whiteman described, it’s unsurprising that conversation quickly turned to resilience. Around the globe, brands are feeling the impacts of the climate crisis, from raw material sources to shipping and physical retail.

In a session on sourcing strategies in geopolitical unrest, Jordan Lea, vice president of sustainable fibers at leading cotton supplier Olam Agri Americas, noted the devastating effect climate change is having on natural fibers. Cotton Australia has forecast a 40% drop in the country’s cotton harvest this year due to drought, he told attendees, mirroring the effects of flooding on Pakistani cotton in 2022. These wipeouts are becoming increasingly regular, at the same time that disruption in shipping is making it harder to move commodity crops like cotton across the world.

In the same session, VF Corp.’s vice president of global product stewardship, sustainability and government affairs Sean Cady, told the packed-out room how wide-ranging the impacts of continued disruption in the Middle East have been for fashion. The ensuing oil crisis — compounding shortages caused by Russia’s war on Ukraine and the associated sanctions on Russian oil — have sent energy and synthetic material prices soaring. Factories using solar panels and brands using recycled synthetics are somewhat shielded, he explained. Likewise, regenerative agriculture, which outlaws increasingly expensive synthetic fertilizers and pesticides, can help growers keep costs down.

“We are facing levels of uncertainty we have never seen in this industry,” he said. “We have to control what we can, and operate our business strategically instead of managing uncertainty in a reactionary way.”

His is not the only dedicated team shifting its emphasis from sustainability as a moral case to resilience as a business case, leveraging translation and integration skills to make sustainability resonate with executives and help colleagues understand how it relates to their competing KPIs. Just look at the announcements coming out of Textile Exchange this year: Vancouver-based non-profit Canopy presented the business case for scaling next-gen alternatives to forest-based fibers like viscose, hoping to convince brands to start with just 5% recycled content, which it says could save them $40 million over a decade from 2028. Meanwhile, advisory firm Sustainabelle launched its “capitalism-compatible” framework, Shift, which allows brands to make a customized business case for preferred fiber transitions.

In these business cases, “short-term payback is only part of the picture”, notes Jesse Smith, director of land stewardship at US regenerative agriculture hub White Buffalo Land Trust, who wowed attendees with his detail-oriented approach to data, spanning everything from dung beetle diversity to soil health and biodiversity. “Businesses exchange many forms of capital every day, including financial, material, living, social, intellectual, experiential, spiritual and cultural, but few of them are recognized on the balance sheet. Brands that learn to identify and move value across those capitals will likely be the ones that gain momentum in the future of textile and fashion.”

The challenge now is for brands to make this business case in time for innovators to survive, says American Circular Textiles founder Rachel van Metre Kibbe. “The innovators showing up here may not be here next year. They’ve invested their capital, their livelihoods, families, and years of work into solutions your company says it wants. Another year of deliberation may be manageable for your company. It may be existential for theirs.”

Unlike other sustainable fashion conferences, which regularly look to brands for leadership, Textile Exchange puts the emphasis on raw material producers, aka Tier 4 in fashion’s supply change. It was a welcome step-change.

In a roundtable about extreme heat, supplier-led organizations like the Fashion Producer Collective, which have developed clear blueprints for extreme heat adaptation and mitigation, came to the fore. But it’s brands themselves that hold the key to scaling progress. “Most factories don’t have the systems in place to measure temperatures, let alone programs to remediate heat,” said Tiffany Rogers, vice president of research and development in social compliance at the Fair Labor Association.

Similarly, in a session about scaling regenerative agriculture, global sustainability and supply chain strategist Lindsay Humphreys advocated for the industry to move from brand-to-land partnerships (where one brand partners directly with one land manager to transition to regenerative agriculture) to a brandscape-to-landscape model (where collective action stops every brand or land manager starting from scratch and cascades best practices). The best thing a brand can do in this situation — as shared by fellow panelist, H&M Group’s biodiversity impact lead Jennie Granström — is be flexible.

“There was a strong focus on conversations centered around growers, ranchers and producers,” said Theory’s vice president of sustainability Gonzalo Pertile. “Any transition in our industry will depend on bringing the people closest to the land and the product into the conversation, and ensuring they are part of the solutions we are trying to scale. That’s what sets Textile Exchange apart — the chance to connect with practitioners from across the value chain who are actively doing the work every day.”

But, as we heard throughout the week, bridging producers and brands is far from straightforward. In conference rooms and attempts at collective action alike, these two opposite ends of the supply chain often have different agendas and different ideas of success, and many speak different languages — literally and figuratively.

“Working directly with cotton farmers, we experience firsthand how challenging it can be to translate sustainability goals into agricultural practices, particularly when dealing with climate variability, economic pressures, and the complexities of transitioning to regenerative agriculture,” Mariela Calderon Ariz of Peruvian regenerative cotton production company Bergman Rivera said. “At Tier 4, implementation is not a future ambition; it is our everyday reality. The real opportunity is to turn these connections and conversations [at the conference] into meaningful action, ensuring that the people working at the very beginning of the supply chain are part of shaping the industry's future.”

As the conference drew to a close, a handful of key themes emerged: the need to address the investment gap between pilots and commercial scale; the call for closer ties between brands and land managers; and the economic reality of scaling preferred production systems as the existing models collapse. But as the conference dug deeper into highly technical subjects, it was a simple provocation from day one that stuck in people’s minds.

This year’s conference took place in Vancouver, on the unceded territories of the xʷməθkʷəy̓əm (Musqueam), Sḵwx̱wú7mesh (Squamish) and səlilwətaɬ (Tsleil-Waututh) nations. Chief Janice George, master weaver and co-founder of L’hen Awtxw Weaving House, and a hereditary chief of the Squamish Nation, was invited to open proceedings. She spoke about the seventh generation principle, a time-honored Indigenous approach to sustainability. “Mother Earth knows how to take care of herself. It’s humans that need to learn how to work with Mother Earth,” she reminded attendees. “How do we use our resources in an intelligent way that takes care of the next generations?”

#137. Spiderweb Cookies

Preheat the oven to 350°F. Cream the butter, shortening and sugar until light and fluffy, five to seven minutes. Beat in the egg and vanilla until well combined.

In a separate bowl, whisk together the flour, cocoa powder, baking powder and baking soda. Gradually add the dry ingredients into the creamed mixture, beating until a soft dough forms.

In a large microwave-safe bowl, combine the marshmallows and 1 tablespoon of butter. Microwave until melted, 30 to 45 seconds, then stir until smooth. Let the mixture cool slightly so it’s warm but comfortable to handle.

Editor’s Tip: If the marshmallows aren’t completely melted after 45 seconds, continue microwaving in 10-second intervals, stirring after each, until smooth.

​Editor’s Tip: If the marshmallow mixture becomes too firm to stretch, reheat it in the microwave in 10-second bursts. You want it warm and stretchy, but not too hot and overly soft.

Marshmallow creme isn’t a good substitute for whole marshmallows, as it won’t make fully-formed spiderwebs. Spreadable marshmallow cream has a softer consistency and usually doesn’t contain gelatin, so it won’t stretch into the thin, web-like strands that are created by melting marshmallows.

#138. The 9 Best Luxury Gym-Equipment Brands

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

From strength training to low-impact core and recovery—this is how you build a dream gym at home.

Somewhere in this world, there is an element of a gym that would be your Proustian madeleine. Rubber flooring, the smell that metal leaves on your hand, the heat of a poorly ventilated garage—it takes you back to your first junior-varsity summer. Horrible then, captivating now. But nostalgia is a bad reason to rebuild that gym at home. If you’ve spent a huge portion of your savings on a house—and even more making it a place of respite—you want something better. Something fit for your sanctuary. A growing market is betting that you agree. These companies care as much about how a home gym looks and feels as how it performs. They hire well-known designers, show at design fairs, and charge vintage-car money for a Pilates reformer—both, if you ask us, valid ways to spend five figures.

This, though, is a rundown of the latter. If you’re looking to build out a dream gym, these are the brands to know, and for each we give our standout picks.

The Italian brand is the go-to supplier for five-star- hotel gyms, ultra-wealthy clients’ homes, and the Olympics. Which is to say it is, undoubtedly, the leader in this space. Its most recent release, the current crown jewel, is its Pilates reformer in this gorgeous Sand Stone color.

Honestly, this could be a one-brand story. Go to any luxury hotel—we do it all the time, new properties and the long-standing ones—and check out the gym; I’m willing to bet it’s stocked with Technogym. From treadmills, to squat cages, to the new reformer, Technogym is best-in-class. Since it has those high-end partnerships—the Olympics, Formula 1 teams and drivers, and Italian soccer clubs—I could make the “Ferrari of gym equipment joke,” but, well...it would be too on the nose.

It’s not just the high-end machines that Technogym devotes its greatest design and material sourcing to. You could, if you wanted to call and schedule a consultation, get a rack of stunning wood-handle kettlebells and call it a day.

The pinnacle of all NordicTrack’s various technologies. Everything—touchpoint materials, deck cushioning, deck lighting, and even the sound your feet make when you stride—is considered and designed to the highest degree.

Nike only just launched its gym-equipment lineup back in 2023. Where other companies lean toward cardio, Nike bets on the design-conscious strength training customer.

If you’re shopping weight-by-weight, it’s not exactly luxury as you might assume from the other options on this list. The Nike kettlebells look good, and they’re some of my favorite to swing—but they’re still just kettlebells. The luxury comes with the full gym setup, which takes the commercial model and makes it easy for an average consumer to put in an order. When it gets delivered and unboxed, the garage starts to look a little bit like wherever LeBron posts his workouts from.

Natural wood, genuine leather, and full in-house design and production in Poland. This past summer, Pent won a coveted Red Dot award for the design of its Pilates reformer.

Our pick of the bunch would be the manual treadmill. When it comes to actually mimicking the burn of running while staying stationary, it’s our favorite.

The Tonal has dominated as the smart home gym of record, and for good reason. It’s a fully immersive strength and cardio machine. The display is a real game-changer that turns “coaching” into more than just generalized tips. With Tonal, it’s all about form and making sure when you’re spending the time working out, that you’re doing it right. The on-screen trainer will suggest adjustments in real time and let you know when it might be time to adjust your weight load. This helps keep you safe, and at the same time proper form ensures you work the muscles you’re meant to be working.

It’s more affordable than some on this list, but it doesn’t come cheap. Between an annual subscription and some near-essential add-ons, the cost can start adding up quick, but the proof is in the results. Take our reviewer, who stopped going to the gym because of it and said “for a consumer who’s willing to spend, it’s the full-service replacement. More than any at-home fitness gadget, the Tonal makes working out markedly better—much more than lugging all your stuff to a crowded gym after work.”

In our 2026 home awards, we called this the best workout machine of the year. It’s no wonder. With its striking minimalist design, reasonable entry price, and free white-glove installation, there are plenty of valid reasons to go with Amp over these first two systems. You’ll still get real-time workout tracking and coaching, as well as a variety of included workouts ranging across all styles.

The accessory rack will only run you an extra $110 and adds enough variety on top of the core experience. If you get that, then you’ll really be able to go for weeks before you need to repeat any routines.

The newcomer, founded in New York in 2019, Ergatta focuses on U.S.A.-made cherrywood rowing machines that also showed up in this year’s home awards as our new favorite rower.

Ergatta is also big on gamifying rowing workouts, whether that’s via an immersive backdrop or an actual competition. What’s seriously cool is how you can compete in races online by asynchronously racing to beat others’ best times. There are even live races a few times a week that let you compete in real time. All of this with an Ergatta subscription of course.

Okay, look, Joe Rogan bro-science aside, there is a very encouraging trend happening in the world of fitness currently. Recovery is being treated as seriously as the workout itself. Sleep is part of that, but the most one-to-one option for building out the gym is certainly a sauna—plus cold plunge if you are so inclined.

Our favorite maker in this space is Lit Method, who has a near-perfect combination of easy-to-use website, actual quality, and design-conscious look. If you have a corner of the space you can dedicate to recovery, we consider this as essential as any of the other stuff on this list.

#139. The Making of Marie Antoinette, Through Sofia Coppola’s Mother’s Loving Lens

The new documentary Making Marie Antoinette goes behind the scenes of Sofia Coppola’s seminal period film, released 20 years ago, through tender footage shot by her mother, Eleanor

Sofia Coppola’s opulent, candy-colored coming-of-age film Marie Antoinette (2006) hypnotized young audiences, polarized critics, and rewrote the rules of biopics.

Riding the success of her first two films, The Virgin Suicides (1999) and Lost in Translation (2003), Coppola directed the $40 million historical drama with an unwavering commitment to her anachronistic vision, focusing more on the emotions of its titular protagonist (played by Kirsten Dunst) as she grappled with her newfound celebrity than on the grim politics gathering outside the French royal palace of Versailles. For the first time ever, the French government opened the palace to filming, allowing the production to spend 20 chaotic days inside its walls—more than a third of the 57-day shoot. Coppola’s mother, Eleanor, kept her video camera in hand throughout, often pointing it squarely at her daughter. She captured nearly 80 hours of footage, which Sofia has now distilled into a tender feature-length video diary, Making Marie Antoinette, opening in theaters on October 23.

Eleanor had previously captured her family’s love of filmmaking in her documentary debut, Hearts of Darkness: A Filmmaker’s Apocalypse (1991), which chronicled the tumultuous making of husband Francis Ford Coppola’s film Apocalypse Now. But she often prioritized caring for her family over pursuing her own creative projects. Her narrative directorial debut, Paris Can Wait, came in 2016, shortly after she turned 80.

Years later, during the Covid lockdowns, Sofia and Eleanor began stitching the footage together into a film. Eleanor died in 2024 before they completed the project, but Sofia finished the movie, enlisting Diane Lane to voice Eleanor’s journals. The word that best describes the tone of Making Marie Antoinette is affectionate. The tender, intimate film serves as a posthumous time capsule fueled by not only Eleanor’s love of filmmaking but also her unabashed love for her daughter.

The documentary opens in a long hallway filled with makeup designers and costumers preparing countless extras for the shoot. Eleanor slowly walks through the crowded set as Lane reads from her journals: “I’m basically a shy person, and I hate to intrude. It’s counter to my personality to shoot a documentary, but over and over, I do it. … It’s a rare opportunity to see my child at work, to be included in her world.” This opening moment shows Eleanor slinking around the colossal movie set, just out of sight, witnessing both the massive production unfolding around her and her daughter’s most daunting challenge as a director.

Filming Marie Antoinette was, to say the least, ambitious. The budgets of Sofia’s first two movies combined paled in comparison to its $40 million price tag. Within Versailles, Sofia directed hundreds of extras, all wearing glamorized period-appropriate costumes designed by Milena Canonero and six assistant designers, surrounded by intricate feasts and bountiful flower arrangements. The grueling film schedule meant long hours; Eleanor’s camera catches cast members and extras asleep throughout the royal palace.

At one point, Eleanor observes her daughter carrying the stress of the production on her shoulders, a moment that underscores the value of seeing this process through such caring eyes. Her footage doesn’t just show the logistical undertaking that was Marie Antoinette; it also champions how masterfully (and calmly) Sofia directs the production, never once wavering from her vision. Eleanor is equally attentive to the excitement and the joy of the work, from Sofia’s sense of fulfillment when filming wraps to Jason Schwartzman, who plays Louis XVI, exuberantly playing the piano while crew members review the script.

When Marie Antoinette premiered at the Cannes Film Festival in 2006, it drew a swell of boos. Critics lambasted the movie for taking a seemingly frivolous approach to the royal court in the lead-up to the French Revolution. In the two decades since, its reputation has undergone a considerable reversal, with the film increasingly recognized as a masterpiece. Inspired largely by British author Antonia Fraser’s biography, Sofia set out to take a sympathetic view of Marie Antoinette. Instead of centering the looming political disaster, she focused on a young girl unwittingly thrust into the spotlight, subject to the country’s praise and criticism. This was a film told from the young queen’s point of view rather than that of the men who waged wars and plotted political coups.

One scene in the documentary shows how fiercely Sofia fought for this vision. While filming a party scene, Eleanor captures a disagreement between Sofia and her director of photography, Lance Acord, over whether a moment of Marie’s jealousy requires a response from Louis XVI. Acord wants to include the king’s perspective; Sofia insists the film belongs to the queen and the queen alone.

An interview Eleanor conducts with the then-24-year-old Dunst offers another way into Sofia’s affinity for her protagonist. Dunst reflects on the parallels between her own childhood and Marie’s, saying, “I have that relationship that Marie Antoinette did have, starting as a young girl and coming to these movie sets and having all these expectations, all these judgments about you.” By 12, Dunst was acting alongside Tom Cruise and Brad Pitt in Interview With the Vampire. Eleanor sees a similar parallel in Sofia, who also grew up on film sets under the weight of a famous name.

Many of Eleanor’s reflections focus on the generational differences between her and her daughter and the evolution of their relationship. “Sofia’s generation is so different,” Eleanor asserts in her journals. “She and her women friends understand that marriage and family can be parts of a fulfilling life, but they also have career aspirations.” By the time she was Sofia’s age, Eleanor had already given birth to her three children, Roman, Sofia, and Gian-Carlo, and “too often [her] creative self was pushed to last place on [her] to-do list.” She reflects on how she always encouraged her children to pursue their passions yet struggled to give herself the same permission: “At my age, should I be engaged in my own creative process?”

Here lies the deeper poignancy of Making Marie Antoinette. The entire documentary reads like a love letter from Eleanor to her children. At one point, she observes her son Roman joining Sofia as the second unit director. “Their relationship is one of the most profound treasures in my life,” she writes. Witnessing her family’s creative lives, and receiving encouragement from Sofia in particular, eventually inspired Eleanor to pursue the personal project that became Paris Can Wait. In doing so, she became the oldest woman to release a narrative debut.

Twenty years after its release, Marie Antoinette remains an object of fascination, its hyperstylized world endlessly recirculated on social media. A conventional making-of documentary would have plenty to offer its devoted audience, but Making Marie Antoinette offers something far more intimate: a mother watching her daughter claim the creative freedom she had struggled to find herself. Eleanor points her camera at Sofia, proudly observing her own life’s work, even as she begins to imagine what else it might include.

#144. Roasted Brussels Sprouts

Crispy, caramelized edges and tender centers are the hallmarks of perfectly roasted brussels sprouts—and you don’t need much more than olive oil, salt, and pepper to get there. This simple recipe relies on a hot oven and a rimmed baking sheet to turn the humble vegetable into a side dish worthy of both weeknight dinners and the Thanksgiving table.

The key is to halve the brussels sprouts (quarter any especially large ones), then spread them in a single layer so they roast instead of steam. Toss them occasionally as they cook, letting the outer leaves turn crisp and the cut sides develop a deep golden brown color. Serve them straight from the oven, or dress them up with a squeeze of lemon juice, a shower of grated Parmesan, or a drizzle of balsamic vinegar.

How do you make roasted brussels sprouts crispy?

Use high heat (450°F) and spread the sprouts in a single layer on a rimmed baking sheet. Overcrowding traps moisture, causing them to steam rather than roast. Use two baking sheets if necessary.

How long should you roast brussels sprouts?

At 450°F, brussels sprouts typically take 15–25 minutes, depending on their size. Start checking around the 15-minute mark, especially if using a convection oven. They’re ready when the centers are tender and the edges are deeply browned.

Can you make roasted brussels sprouts ahead of time?

They’re best served hot from the oven, when the edges are crispiest. To get a head start, trim and halve the sprouts up to a day ahead and refrigerate in an airtight container. Reheat leftovers in a 350°F oven until warmed through, though they won’t be quite as crisp.

Preheat oven to 450°. Toss 3 lb. brussels sprouts, trimmed, halved, quartered if large, ¼ cup plus 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. freshly ground black pepper on a rimmed baking sheet to coat. Arrange in a single layer and roast, tossing occasionally, until tender and browned, 15–25 minutes.

Once you’ve mastered the basics, there are plenty of ways to change things up. Try frico’ed brussels sprouts with a crispy Parmesan crust; brussels sprouts with warm honey glaze or garlicky balsamic brussels sprouts for a savory-sweet finish; or, for a little heat, make roasted brussels sprouts with gochujang brown butter.

#145. Single-Serve Chocolate Chip Cookie

Preheat the oven to 350°F. In a medium bowl, cream the butter, brown sugar and granulated sugar together until they’re light and fluffy, four to five minutes. Beat in the egg yolk and vanilla.

In another bowl, whisk together the all-purpose flour, baking powder, baking soda and salt. Gradually beat the flour mixture into the creamed mixture. Switch to a rubber spatula and fold in the chocolate chips.

Editor’s Tip: Use a hand mixer or stand mixer to make creaming the butter and sugars easier. Scrape the sides and bottom of the bowl to ensure everything is incorporated before adding the dry ingredients.

#148. I Put the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders’ Beauty Routine to Two Very Sweaty Tests

Big hair, full glam, and a whole lot of setting powder: Here’s how I felt channeling my inner DCC.

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

I haven’t danced since middle school, have never cheered a day in my life, certainly cannot kick my legs anywhere nearly as high as the cheerleaders do in their iconic Thunderstruck dance, and yet I am one of the millions of people who’ve become obsessed with watching America’s Sweethearts: Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders. I love to see women win, obviously, and get quite invested in everyone who makes it through tryouts to training camp. As a beauty editor, I’m enthralled by the perfectly-done makeup and hair that all somehow stays in place through hours of games and practices. I’m also a football fan—my fantasy team is aggressively managed—and watching the DCC is a nice break from the otherwise male-centered Sunday Night Football.

So, it’s safe to say I’ve watched enough of the show to know that being a DCC is basically an Olympic sport. These women are serious athletes whose impossibly high kicks and stamina to get through hours rehearsing perfectly synchronized routines deserve extreme levels of respect. But, again, as a beauty editor, there’s another part of their performances I can’t stop thinking about: How the heck do they keep their hair and makeup looking so good through all that intense exercise?

That question became even more pressing when I recently attended my first-ever Dallas Cowboys home game (as a guest of Charlotte Tilbury, who sponsors the cheerleaders’ makeup). Seeing the DCC in action IRL (and practicing with former DCC Megan McElaney) gave me a whole new appreciation for their signature beauty look: voluminous hair, flawless makeup, bronzed skin, and perfectly polished nails.

So, how much time, money, and effort really goes into maintaining that level of glam? I decided that I needed to find out for myself. I set out to recreate the full Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders beauty routine—or at least, as much of it as I could—before putting the finished look through a long day of my own.

Naturally, the foundation of the whole DCC beauty look is wearing high-glam, long-wear, sweat-resistant makeup that can stand up to a lot of physical exertion. The DCC have partnered with Charlotte Tilbury to make that happen, so I also went with a full face of Charlotte Tilbury makeup, both to get as close to a DCC look as possible and put the same formulas to a real-life long-wear test. for my eyes, I opted for a daytime, cool-toned smoky look with lashes. On my cheeks, plenty of sculpting and bronzer paired with a peachy nude blush. But the products that really helped me channel my inner DCC were the Airbrush Flawless Concealer, Airbrush Flawless Blur Loose Setting Powder, and lip combo Lip Cheat Lip Liner in Pillow Talk Medium paired with Matte Revolution Lipstick in Pillow Talk.

They say everything’s bigger in Texas, and that goes for the hair too. Tangerine Salon is the go-to salon for the DCC, and while I didn’t get to try their services while I was in Dallas, I did get a blowout from another Aveda-affiliated salon in New York City right before the trip. I also got a blowout in Madrid ahead of my friends’ wedding. For both appointments, I asked for a big, bouncy Texas-style (read: very voluminous) ‘90s blowout, just like how many of the DCC do their hair for games.

In all the photos and videos I’ve seen of the DCC, the women always have a fresh manicure. For this experiment, I got a gel French manicure with chrome powder on top, which felt very DCC-esque. Since it was a gel manicure, I wasn’t too concerned about it lasting. (As I write this, it’s still going strong three weeks later, with not a single chip or crack to be found.)

Luckily, there’s one part of my existing personal beauty routine that aligns with at least some of the cheerleaders’: I get regular facials. Though not all the DCC are open about all of the in-office treatments they get, many of them often share pics and videos of their skin post-chemical peels, HydraFacial, and microneedling. They also all have access to neuromodulators, fillers, facials, chemical peels, microneedling, and other skincare treatments thanks to the team’s med spa partner. So, two days before I went to Dallas, I visited the Biologique Recherche New York Residence, where I got a calming facial focused on clearing up congestion, exfoliating my skin, and hydrating my face to get glass skin-like results. This helped turn my skin into a clean canvas for all that makeup to come.

I am a very proud hair color virgin. The most I’ve ever done is a clear gloss for some extra shine and conditioning. It’s pretty common for potential and current DCCs to go through an iconic beauty transformation, and their makeovers are documented on the Netflix show. I’ve seen girls go from blonde to brunette, turn into redheads, and start wearing hair extensions. However, I’m sorry to say I wasn’t ready to fully color my hair for this experiment, even in the name of beauty journalism. I also have thick, medium-length already, so extensions just weren’t super necessary for me.

In the GRWMs I’ve watched from the DCC ladies, almost all of them either self-tan or get a spray tan. While I’ve done both in the past and absolutely loved the results, I am currently dealing with a lot of random skin rashes lately that derms have only been able to categorize as atopic dermatitis, so I’m trying not to expose my skin to too many extra chemicals right now.

In the name of ~science~ I did full glam twice, once with help from a Charlotte Tilbury makeup artist and once on my own.

The day the Charlotte Tilbury makeup artist did my glam, it lasted through very hot, very humid Texas weather (we’re talking over 90°F at the warmest point), a little bit of rain, and quite a lot of walking and stairs in my cowboy boots. Is that the same as a full-blown DCC cheer routine? No, but I did work up a sweat throughout the day. And yet, almost all of my makeup lasted for a full 12 hours: It looked just as perfect at 12 p.m. as it did at midnight. The only thing I had to touch up throughout the day was my lip combo after meals. I attribute the long-lasting wear to the Airbrush Flawless Concealer and Airbrush Flawless Blur Loose Setting Powder especially, which kept my pores invisible all day. It probably helped that I barely had any foundation on—it was mostly concealer and powder—so there was less base product that could have potentially broken or worn off throughout the day.

The day I did my own makeup, I was attending a wedding. My full glam lasted through a very hot subway ride, climbing the subway stairs in heels, happy wedding tears, and hours upon hours of dancing, singing, and general celebrations. I used those same Charlotte Tilbury products for my complexion, which I think is why my beat stayed in place until I got back from the wedding celebrations at 3 a.m.

I also loved that, despite a lot of sweating and wearing allll the makeup, my face didn’t break out. A trusty makeup removing wipe and a solid face wash and skincare routine at the end of some very long days kept my skin in check.

So here’s where I had the most trouble: As great as my makeup looked on both occasions, my hair didn’t last either time. Neither blowout stayed voluminous for very long at all. That was such a bummer for me, but it was also reminder that I already have a pretty good idea of what the best products are for my own hair.

When I’m doing my hair myself, my go-to is the T3 Curl Wrap, which I’ve found keeps my hair in a very nice bouncy DCC-like curl all day. If I were to have done my hair myself, I would’ve used that curling iron paired with the Dyson Airwrap for touch-ups (I’ve seen a lot of the DCC women do this two-step curling-iron-then-Dyson method for their hair routines). Also, I probably need to use a lot more volumizing products. I did some detective work and noticed a few products that routinely pop up in the cheerleaders’ GRWM videos: Sexy Hair Big Spray & Play Volumizing Hairspray, Kenra Professional Volume Spray 25, and Hairitage Magic Dust Texturizing Powder, among others. Their technique seems to be approximately half a can of hairspray on every single curl (I’m only exaggerating a little bit), so it’s clear that their hair routines are made for performance, not real life. The next time I need big hair that really lasts, I’ll be adding a lot more styling product.

Beyond being top-tier dancers and cheerleaders, these women clearly have top-tier makeup and hair routines. After trying my own versions, I’m even more impressed at how well their glam lasts through an entire football game, which ends up being three-plus hours with commercial breaks and all.

In some of the DITL videos they’ve posted on TikTok, I’ve noticed they do touch up their hair and makeup during halftime. I probably could’ve benefitted from some touch-ups throughout the day, but if I’m being honest, I’m trying to have makeup and hair that lasts all day without any extra effort. Too much to ask? I kinda don’t think so, especially given the cost of all these beauty products and treatments.

And on that note, I think it’d be pretty pricey to keep up the DCC look. Makeup is low-key expensive these days! (The total cost of the products Charlotte Tilbury products I used easily surpassed $400.) As are the best hair tools and styling products. And that’s not even getting into professional treatments... A blowout easily costs $50 or more and hair color can set you back at least $150 per appointment. Then, Botox, fillers, facials, and other med spa-related things can add up to hundreds of dollars. And these are just one-time fees; most of these treatments require touch ups a few times per year, so we’re ultimately talking thousands of dollars spent annually just on glam.

That said, being in a full DCC-inspired look made me feel, well, pretty dang fabulous. I felt so confident and truly beautiful with my voluminous hair and smoky eye makeup. Why didn’t anyone tell me I’d feel so grown-up and cool wearing a French manicure? Yes, I got compliments from my friends, family, and my boyfriend about how pretty the glam looked (which was nice, don’t get me wrong!), but what I loved the most is how I felt internally. I felt like I could take on the world, and to me, that’s what beauty is all about. I will say that it took me wayyyy longer to get ready than my usual routine, which is more of a race against the clock.

So, would I do it all again? For a special occasion, absolutely. However, I don’t see myself spending hours on my hair and makeup every single morning. But this experiment taught me that the right products and techniques really can make a full face of glam last through heat, humidity, happy tears, and hours of dancing. My makeup? Ready for game day. My hair? Let’s just say I still have a few things to learn from the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders.

Catharine Malzahn is a contributing beauty writer at Cosmo. She’s covered and tested countless beauty products and treatments, from makeup and skincare to in-office treatments and hair tools.

Catharine Malzahn is a contributing beauty writer at Cosmopolitan and was previously the beauty assistant at Good Housekeeping, Woman's Day, and Prevention.

#149. All of the 2026 Victoria’s Secret Performances

Tate McRae, Megan Thee Stallion, Katseye, and Megan Moroney performed tonight at Sony Pictures Studios in Los Angeles

The 2026 Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show assembled a powerhouse bill of artists. Tonight’s performers at Sony Pictures Studios in Los Angeles include country singer Megan Moroney, pop star sensation Tate McRae, the buzzy girl group Katseye, and the one and only Megan Thee Stallion.

In the two years following its triumphant New York City comeback, Victoria’s Secret has invited stars like Lisa (2024) and Karol G (2025) to join the models on the runway. This year, the show took place in Los Angeles for the first time in 19 years. (Way back in 2007, performers will.i.am and Seal graced the Kodak Theatre stage.)

Models walked the runway during and between the performances, including longtime angels such as Gigi Hadid and Alex Consani. The runway also welcomed the high-profile debuts of models like Kobe Bryant’s daughter Natalia Bryant. The biggest debut occurred during Megan Thee Stallion’s performance, when Kylie Jenner stepped out donning giant white plumed wings.

See all the performers who entertained the 2026 Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show crowd, ahead.

The Georgia-born country singer kicked off the evening with “6 Months Later,” the lead single from her album Cloud 9, taking the stage in giant pink fluffy wings, a bedazzled corset, and silvery high heels. She followed it with “Wish I Didn’t,” a signature tongue-in-cheek song aimed at a man with plenty of red flags. With country music dominating the charts, it’s only right that the show give this Georgia girl some love.

Tate McRae celebrates the release of her new single, “Housewife,” at this year’s Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show. The girls started, as they should, with “Pinky Up,” then jumped to “Animal.” On the pink carpet earlier in the night, the group revealed that one of the two members on temporary hiatus will return soon.

Tina Snow is back. Megan Thee Stallion just dropped a new single, “Tina Tuesday Freestyle,” marking the return of her much-missed alter ego and kicking off the rollout for her upcoming album. Megan didn’t perform the new single, but she took the stage in full Tina Snow flair, with platinum blond hair, a glistening bra, and metallic angel wings. The rapper performed two of her biggest hits back-to-back: “Her” and “Body.” And as she said on X, this performance fulfilled one of her lifelong dreams.

#152. Golf Shoes Are Basically Sneakers Now. These 12 Deliver the Best Comfort and Grip.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Golf kicks have come a long way from the metal spikes your grandfather used to wear.

THE ONLY THING that is almost as important as your golf clubs are your golf shoes. Golf starts from the ground up, and that means you’ll want to have the best golf shoes laced up to maximize your performance. Whether you’re seeking comfort for walking a full round of 18, looking for premium traction to optimize torque, or searching for a pair to be the stylish guy on the course, the best golf shoes should check off most boxes.

Like golf shirts and pants, the best golf shoes are becoming more casual and comfort-driven. Pairs aren't as bulky and heavy as they used to be and certainly don't have scary metal spikes. "Today's golf shoes are more like sneakers; comfortable, cushioned, breathable, and versatile," says Paul Sliva, the head golf pro and tournament director at the historic Van Cortlandt Golf Course in the Bronx. "Technology has gotten better when it comes to traction too, and so you have golf shoes with grippy rubber patterns that are much more gentle on the grass," says Sliva.

Though many golf shoes can blend in with sneakers these days, it's important to wear proper footwear. Why? Well, the biggest risk you pose is injury, especially to the knees and ankles. Golf shoes are designed to optimize traction (and ground force creation) to help keep your feet (and heels) in place when swinging a club. Where sneakers are designed to be comfortable for movement, golf shoes are made to provide a firm foundation and connection to the ground while still being comfortable enough for long days on your feet. It's a tricky line to balance, but there are a ton of brands making exceptional golf shoes these days. Follow us on our testing as we give you the guide to the 12 best golf shoes.

Adidas has some of the best golf shoes around, especially when you consider the value for what you pay. The latest edition of the S2G golf shoes, the 26s cost just over $100 and you get a versatile pair that can be worn with a number of golf outfits and, if you so choose, casual outfits, thanks to their iconic design that looks like a pair of Adidas Boost running shoes. The shoe's upper is made with a soft waterproof leather (we love how Adidas added a toe cap for better reinforcement and water resistance). Our tester also noticed how the deep, sturdy heel adds solid heel protection and stability for feeling locked in.

The Adidas Lightstrike cushioning for the midsole is well-made and very comfortable, but it's not the most cushioned golf shoe you can buy. Instead, the S2G sits somewhere in the middle of supportiveness and cushioning. As for the outsole, it has ample traction with the circular rubber lugs. However, similar to the midsole design, you shouldn't expect the shoe to be the most grippy. The outsole sits somewhere in the middle of grip; just be aware when the tee boxes are slick. Altogether it’s one solid shoe, and takes the crown for best pair overall. And if you want to save even more, the S2G 24s are discounted in lots of places (our previous best overall).

Ecco golf shoes are some of the most comfortable performance kicks you can buy, and the greater golf community loves them. The brand isn't as widely known and played-in on this side of the Atlantic, but the Biom H5 stands out among every shoe we tested.

While they're a little heavier than our tester was used to (though lighter than the leather version), he found that the weight made for a shoe that offered up a ton of stability and support across the entire golf course. "I see why lots of European and U.K. golfers love them—I don’t think I’ve ever felt as locked-in with a golf shoe before," he said, after wearing the Eccos for a few rounds.

Along with the exceptional stability, the mesh upper offers excellent breathability, and the midsole provides ample comfort for long rounds on your feet, whether walking or riding. Our tester was surprised to find that the midsole was not only comfortable for a whole round but also provided some energy return, akin to that you'd get from a running shoe. Walking 36 holes? No problem.

We still can't get over seeing Tiger Woods wearing anything other than Nike, but starting his own brand makes the most sense if he had to move on from The Swoosh. Sun Day Red is the quintessential Tiger brand, full of classic-looking golf gear that puts a premium on performance. The Pioneer Cypress shoes are the perfect representation of that. They're stylish, are a subtle twist on a classic silhouette, and are chock-full of performance features.

I could see and feel the quality from the moment I opened the box (which was very well-made in its own right). The attention to detail is striking. Each shoe comes in its own dust bag, and the pair comes with an extra massaging insole for those looking for something more plush. The materials are stellar, and subtle Tiger-esque touches like tiger stripes on the heel give these a feel that justifies the price without even wearing them on the course.

On the course, though, the function matches the form. The soft spikes are durable and provide exceptional traction across the course, the waterproof leather is supple and actually keeps the wearer dry (even on rainy days). And, where most traditional-style golf shoes aren't comfortable until you've worn them for a few rounds, the Pioneer Cypress were perfect right out of the box.

If you’re not familiar with G/Fore, the brand practically made its name featuring bold prints and loud aesthetics, particularly its solid colored golf gloves. While its golf shoes are a bit more reserved and not too over-the-top, its signature camo printed soles do plenty of talking. With a solid array of options, its waterproof MG4+ O2 golf shoes are the perfect fusion of comfort, athletic design, and genuine performance.

The spikeless option is a bestseller and offers pretty decent traction, even on wet playing conditions, thanks to its unique sawtooth traction pattern. To enhance its locked-in feel even further, its external heel counter provides an even more stable base, which is perfect for even the most aggressive swingers. Though these shoes are waterproof, they feature a perforated and breathable upper which makes them great for hotter days, too. Plus, bonus points for the removable massaging insoles which are also machine washable.

FootJoy makes the best traditional leather golf shoes, but it also makes some pretty awesome modern golf shoes, too. The revamped Hyperflex is a star-studded performer, featuring materials like a breathable knit upper, a supportive foam midsole, and a hidden soft spikes outsole. PGA star Justin Thomas even ditched his traditional FootJoys for a pair of Hyperflexes last season.

Though they're a favorite of the pros, few Average Joe golfers utilize spikes these days, but if you want to play like JT or the rest of the PGA Tour field, shoes with soft spikes are worth a look. Soft spikes mimic metal spikes but are more forgiving to course terrain while still providing incredible traction. I found that with this pair specifically, the chances of slipping and sliding in these bad boys was seriously limited, even when the course was glazed in morning dew.

FootJoy also backs this pair with a two-year waterproof warranty, which adds to our claim that these are some of the best golf shoes for serious players in 2026. You get sneaker-like comfort with premium features, making the shoes great for even subpar weather conditions that you decide to play in anyway.

TravisMathew just has a way of making golf not only look good, but feel good too—especially when it comes to its footwear. One of its latest releases, the Modern Tour golf shoe was designed in collab with PGA Tour pro Akshay Bhatia, and the combo knocked it outta the park with a spiked model that features a modern look and an insanely comfy feel. TM packed it with two of its latest tech: NuRise insoles and NuAge foam cushioning which gives you all of the support and cloud-like feel you could want if you fancy yourself a walker of courses, yet, with its TPU soles you get nine replaceable soft spikes for seriously Tour-level traction. Plus, with a lower profile spike design, if you don’t want to take them off (cause they’re that comfy) immediately after your round, these won’t make you feel like you’re wearing around a pair of football cleats (though be mindful of cleat policies in clubhouses).

The synthetic leather uppers look just as good as the real thing, yet are much more breathable during warner rounds. And they’re water-resistant to help you stay dry during inclement weather. These do take a little bit longer to break-in (and just now are getting them to a comfy spot after a few rounds and additional range sessions of testing) and the heel cup may not be ideal for all. But once broken in, we’re confident they’ll wear like a glove.

NoBull has been on a roll with its golf apparel and golf shoe releases lately. One of our personal favorites (and Tom Brady) is the Ripstop Shoe, a sleek, high-comfort golf shoe that manages to repel moisture with ease while still staying breathable.

The trick to this shoe seems to be how NoBull went with a one-piece ripstop upper that offers one of the highest levels of durability while still remaining breathable enough to not overheat your feet. Unlike older versions that used an extra layer of Gore-Tex, this Ripstop only version remains more flexible yet offers plenty of weather-resistance. Our tester even walked through some puddles intentionally and found no water getting into his socks, and said these shoes still felt light, flexible, and comfortable on the course. And while he did like the upper, he says the real comfort comes from the bouncy Phylon midsole that gave him a pep in his step from hole one to hole 18.

As far as traction goes, you've got a lug pattern (that's not that deep) for staying locked in, though our tester did have a few moments of slippage on extra-damp tee boxes during a couple rain-filled testing rounds.

If you’re looking for a street-cred pick that actually has performance to match, then Nike’s Air Max 90 Gs are the route to go. The latest version of this iconic sneaker ensures that you can even play in wet conditions, thanks to their waterproof design, which also helps you keep them as fresh as can be with an easy cleanup. True to their legendary design, they feature a comfy foam midsole and Air Max unit for premium cushioning, so even if you decide to walk a full round, you can do so in style and comfort.

While they may look like you're typical Air Max 90 sneakers, underneath is where the real magic happens. Nike took the classic waffle soles and redesigned its traction with a slight twist, ensuring optimal grip on any course or playing conditions. While they may not be fully water-resistant, they will allow you to play in crummy weather while looking good doing so.

The golf/everyday sneaker crossover doesn't get much stronger than this. TravisMathew's Daily Pro Hybrid is designed specifically for the guys who have plans after their morning tee time and why we decided to feature another model from TM.

The Daily Pro comes in two versions: hybrid and golf. The hybrid version is virtually the same as the golf version, but made with less traction and a more breathable upper. The golf version utilizes a spikeless golf sole and synthetic waterproof upper to help it stand out from the hybrid.

The Daily Pro, as its name suggests, is a great daily workhorse for the golfer who is constantly on the move from the office to the bar to the range to the first tee—no matter what you're up to on any given day, the Daily Pro has you covered.

A shoe not tailor-made for golf will always leave us a bit suspicious of its ability to perform on the course, but the Daily Pro assuaged those fears with its all-day comfort and solid traction.

Like the Nobull shoes above, the Reebok Nano Golf uses an existing workout shoe silhouette as its foundation. The Nano is one of Reebok's most popular gym shoes, loved by CrossFit hardos and HIIT enthusiasts, so it's not surprising that Reebok tried to recreate that success on the golf course.

After testing, we think the shoe is a big win for Reebok, who rolled out the Nano Golf in 2025 with U.S. Open champ and YouTube star Bryson DeChambeau—a guy who looks like he'd be just as comfortable on the weight room floor as he is on the golf course—so the partnership makes sense.

Wearing the shoe on a suitably soggy spring day in the northeast, our tester's feet stayed completely dry for the whole round, so we're happy to report that the waterproofing works wonders.

He also lauded the traction, which uses raised undulated lugs and a TPU Torsion Shank to provide support and stability across all surfaces, from tee boxes to the rough and sand traps to the green.

Spiked golf shoes are the best option when it comes to providing ultimate traction, and UA’s Drive Pros give you a shoe that is literally engineered and lab tested to, as the brand says, “unlock the power of your natural swing.” Flipping the shoes over, you’ll see how that’s achieved, thanks to its hybrid soft spike system (S3) which utilizes two different spike designs: a hurricane design to improve rotational grip, while the other multi-directional spike enhances stability. This perfect combo of nine cross-diagonally placed spikes helps to maximize power transfer while preventing slippage in any direction. To take it up another notch, these golf cleats are also super comfortable thanks to the conforming uppers that feel like they mold onto your feet, while the brand’s Hovr cushioning not only fully locks in your feet, but also makes walking any course an absolute pleasure. While they’re not the most expensive pick in our guide, they will still run close to that $200 threshold, but most will justify the cost with their excellent performance. Plus, they’re also waterproof.

Don’t sleep on Skechers golf shoes (and running shoes for that matter). The GO GOLF Prestige SL Slip-Ins feature a classic design akin to more traditional styles, as well as waterproof construction and a spikeless outsole. The shoe also boasts another one of Skechers' patented features: Arch Fit technology. This includes podiatrist-certified arch support, as well as a removable, supportive cushioning insole system for a customizable and comfortable walking experience.

Our tester was able to slip into them easily on the pavement, totally hands-free. The insole is springy and molds to your feet, which helps reduce shock and distribute your weight evenly. The comfort was apparent during the first round, and they didn't really require a discernible break-in period. The embedded Heel Pillow helped keep his feet in place and added a layer of much-appreciated comfort. The Arch Fit technology made for a balanced, grounded feel that can go head-to-head with any other shoe in this guide.

Golf shoes are only as good as their outsole. A strong outsole is going to keep you from slipping on your swing, helping to create the conditions for a squared-up ball on every shot you take. Look for durable rubber with some sort of traction pattern on your golf shoes. The traction pattern should be formed well enough to dig into the ground a bit, especially when playing on dewy courses in the morning.

Avoid chunky golf shoes that are made with materials that trap heat. You can usually go by the eye test with this step: If it looks hot and heavy, the chances are it is hot and heavy. Instead, keep an eye out for golf shoes made with durable foams and breathable uppers like mesh. Pro tip: A lot of our editors like to bring a second pair of golf socks to change into when making the turn on a round of 18 on hot days.

Owning a pair of golf shoes with at least a minor level of water resistance is smart, because even when you're playing in dry temps you're likely to encounter fresh dew on the course and/or post-watered grounds. Sliva notes that buyers need to remember water resistance is different than waterproof, as water resistant is only going to minimally keep away moisture. "If you're a more consistent player who will go out when the weather is questionable, then you could probably use a pair of waterproof shoes to have around," says Sliva.

Even though I only get on the links a handful of times a year, the one thing I make sure I do stay consistent with is donning the best golf gear, namely ensuring that I choose picks where style meets performance. As I began my research, I started with this as my baseline criteria before looking at any other considerations. From there, I got some help.

To make our choices for this guide, I consulted with Senior Gear and Reviews Editor Ryan Brower (a mid-handicapper) to determine which shoes we wanted to consider based on our recent testing experiences and general golf consumer consensus. From there, we put over a dozen of the top golf shoes to the test and evaluated each pair's support, comfort, and performance. We did this in rainy rounds, cold winter rounds, and rounds in the stifling heat. We wore the shoes for full 18 holes of walking, for some chipping and putting work, out on the range, and even just for a quick nine holes. We left no stone unturned in determining the 12 best golf shoes for every type of golfer.

*Will Porter provided additional reporting for this story.

Jeff Turbett is a fitness and wellness writer who's based in Miami, FL. His work has been featured in The Manual and FightCamp.

Ryan Brower is the Senior Gear and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, where he tests the best products in outdoor gear, tech, running shoes, and more. He has written about the outdoors for nearly two decades and was previously the Managing Editor, Content Performance at Gear Patrol. He holds a B.A. in Sport Management and is a Certified Beer Server, having previously covered the craft beer industry. Ryan currently lives on the water in New Jersey with his wife and their dog.

From budget multipacks to Celine, these picks make headbands feel chic again.

We’ve all had that moment: a headband that looks perfect on the shelf, then slides back (or front) an inch every time you turn your head. Enter the tiger-tooth headband, the little accessory with a serious bite. Similar to the stretchy black hair bands from the early aughts, this one is lined with a row of small, comb-like teeth that grip your hair. With little effort, this style holds its position from morning commute to midnight, no pinching or constant readjusting required.

The best part is that function doesn’t come at the expense of style. Today’s versions come in everything from sleek black, tortoiseshell, animal print, and other fall-ready and neutral colors.

Headbands can be chic and preppy, but they can also be made for the cool girl. You can dress them up for dinner or keep them low-key for a workout and errands. They work on fine, silky strands that usually refuse to cooperate, and they hold their own on thick, textured hair, too.

Ahead, we’ve curated the best tiger-tooth headbands for every hair type and occasion, from budget-friendly multipacks to a splurge-worthy Celine pick.

An alternative to classic black, this tan and light brown duo is a perfect pick for fall. Crafted from recycled plastic, the headbands put sustainability at the heart of the design.

This marbled amber headband makes everyday styling a cinch, adding a sophisticated touch to any look.

Leave it to Celine to create a luxurious comb headband in timeless tortoiseshell acetate. This is the kind of hair accessory that makes an heirloom-worthy investment.

Give a slicked-back style a fresh, retro-inspired twist next time you’re going out.

At a very affordable price, this two-pack from Scunci will serve you well all through dry, frizzy-hair season.

Handmade in Eastern France from a plant-based plastic alternative, this wide-tooth headband keeps you comfortable and styled all day long.

Lean into the fall ’26 animal-print trend with this two-pack of leopard and zebra prints. The band is flexible, and the teeth are rounded rather than pointed, if that’s something you prefer.

With this six-pack, you’ll have one for your purse, your gym bag, your car, and everywhere in between. The set comes in a fresh selection of fall-ready hues, including cream, espresso, and navy.
