#155. The Best Chocolate Gifts for a Sweet Little Treat (2026)

Here are some of my absolute favorite chocolate gifts, from artist-designed sets of bars to a bundle fit for the best of bakers, for the ultimate Willy Wonkas in your life.

Spring & Mulberry chocolate is notoriously good for gifting—the packaging is gorgeous, and the brand uses direct-trade, single-origin cacao and organic dates for sweetness. This gift set, designed in collaboration with Brooklyn illustrator Phthalo Ruth, comes in watercolor plaid boxes that are almost too pretty to open. It’s special-occasion chocolate at its finest.

The Original Williams Sonoma Peppermint Bark

It doesn’t get more classic than this once-a-year classic Williams Sonoma peppermint bark, so much so that the brand claims it’s the original. Each red tin is packed with layers of white and dark chocolate perfumed with peppermint oil and topped with crushed peppermint candies. The only real question: Should you order one, two, or three (yes, three) pounds of it?

When you taste Beyond Good chocolate side by side with most conventional brands, you’ll immediately notice how fruity and, well, chocolaty it tastes. The brand sources and then produces chocolate right at the source in Madagascar and Uganda, partnering with Direct Trade farmers. You can taste that commitment to quality in the Microbatch Collection with four bars that boast 70% or 72% cacao. There’s candied ginger for those who want something on the sweeter (and spicier) side and sea salt and nibs for a well-balanced, well-textured option.

My loyalty fell strictly in the peanut butter camp until I tried Enzo’s Table’s almond butter and chocolate almond butter. The family-run California-based pantry provisions brand makes almond butter from estate-grown California almonds, and the result is roasty, toasty, and naturally slightly sweet. The chocolate variety takes this already sublime product to the next level with added cocoa powder and just the right amount of confectioners’ sugar. There’s a rich chocolate flavor, but it’s still subtle enough to enjoy any time of day, swooshed on toast, spooned into dates, or eaten straight from the jar.

I was already a loyal fan of Raaka’s chocolate—small-batch unroasted chocolate bars that I love for their fruitier-than-usual taste. This gift box contains eight bars, spanning from 58 to 80% cacao, in flavors like banana foster and green tea crunch for the adventurous and pink sea salt or pure cacao, dates, and vanilla for the purists. Plus, this one comes with a 16-page booklet on craft chocolate so you can learn a thing or two while you indulge.

Tony’s Chocolonely bars scream festive year-round: They’re colorful and vibrant. And it doesn’t hurt that the brand has the powerful, important mission to end all exploitation in the cocoa industry. If buying chocolate means supporting a great cause, why not gift chocolate to everyone in your life this holiday season?

Stellar Eats Grain-Free Fudge Brownie Mix

Stellar Eats makes baking mixes that fit almost every dietary restriction, whether gluten-free or plant-based, and they’re also really, really good. One of my go-tos is the brand’s fudge brownie mix, which has only six ingredients (plus oil and water) and is sweetened with coconut sugar. For an amateur baker like me, this mix makes it easy to have a pan of the fudgiest brownies (with chewy edges, of course) on the table in just 30 minutes. And if you’re not looking to feed a crowd, the brand’s instant treat in a cup means the answer to your craving for a single-serving brownie is just 60 seconds away in the microwave.

This one’s for the chocolate lovers who appreciate a little mythology lesson, too. Hailing from San Francisco-based bean-to-bar chocolate maker Dandelion Chocolate, this advent calendar features handcrafted chocolates from 24 acclaimed chocolatiers, all of whom earned their spot through a series of blind tastings. Along with the chocolate (which is packaged in individual ornament boxes you can hang on your tree), you’ll receive an illustrated storybook full of tales adapted from Nordic mythology, a decorative keepsake star, and daily digital content to be enjoyed along with your treats.

Guittard Chocolate has been in the game for over 150 years, which means it makes a superior product. It’s particularly a favorite of our Test Kitchen team, who love to bake with it. This bundle is for your friend who has a lot of holiday baking ahead of them, with everything from 66% cacao organic baking wafers to cocoa rouge Dutch-process cocoa powder, plus a chocolate tote to carry it all.

Valerie Confections got its start making hand-dipped toffees in Los Angeles over 20 years ago, but these days, everything they make is just as irresistible. I especially love their Chanukah Assortment, which comes with menorah truffles, liquid caramels, champagne truffles, and gilded truffles. It’s the perfect thing to bring to a latke party (yes, I attend one every year) or send to a friend across the country to last all eight nights.

This San Francisco–based confectioner makes chocolates that are literal works of art. My colleague Alaina Chou visited Shekoh’s light-filled studio, where she and her team craft these jewel-like bonbons and caramels. “Each one of the jewel-like bonbons I tried from the 21-piece Hemispheres Collection was delicious, but some favorites were the passion fruit, yuzu, and burnt caramel.”

Kosterina Dark Chocolate Balsamic Vinegar

We’ve written about Kosterina’s cold-pressed Greek extra-virgin olive oil and fruit vinegars, but I have a soft spot for its dark chocolate balsamic vinegar. It’s made with dark cocoa concentrate and is a tangy, slightly sweet treat made for pouring over ice cream like chocolate syrup, baked into brownies, or drizzled over a cheeseboard. It’s a great gift for your friend who can’t choose between savory and sweet.

Jacques Torres understood the assignment of taking the process of making hot chocolate and turning it into a show. Each “bomb” has the brand’s decadent Classic Hot Chocolate Mix in a Belgian dark chocolate shell with mini marshmallows and sprinkles added in. All you have to do to start the party is pour hot milk on top.

Whenever I eat a nut-butter-filled chocolate-covered date (one of my favorite sweet treats), I like to think that I could make it myself. But I could not recreate Gato Dates’s. The Los Angeles–based brand uses organic Medjool dates that are perhaps the fudgiest I’ve ever tasted, 70% organic dark chocolate, organic nut butter and nuts, and sea salt flakes. They’re decadent and indulgent and prioritizing the use of real whole food ingredients in addition to being vegan, gluten-free, and refined-sugar-free. While I usually opt for the pouches, which come in each of Gato’s nut butter flavors (pistachio, almond, cashew, walnut, and now peanut), I dare you to splurge for a gift box for the holidays.

Diaspora Co.’s hot cocoa is delightfully rich and lightly sweetened from jaggery, an unrefined sugar with earthy caramel-like notes. It’s not the Swiss Miss hot chocolate (no shade to them, I still crave those mini marshmallows) that you grew up with. Diaspora’s mix is made with its own Anamalai cacao, and the brand suggests adding spices like cinnamon or chili powder (both of which you can buy on its website) to amp up the flavor.

Alice mushroom chocolates are for the friend who tries every single wellness trend but also loves to indulge in a daily (or nightly) chocolate break. The brand harnesses the power of functional mushrooms in the form of organic dark chocolate sweetened with organic sugar. Alice now has four varieties of chocolate bites: “nightcap” for deep sleep (my personal go-to), “brainstorm” for sharp focus, “happy ending” for the bedroom, and “party trick” for social elevation. The tins, which contain 16 squares or doses of each, are also some of the more chic chocolate packaging one could dream up. If you’re looking to optimize your focus by day and sleep by night, opt for the duo, but if you’re one for experimentation, splurge for the discovery set.

Unreal can do no wrong in my mind. Unreal’s dark chocolate coconut bars got my family through living together during COVID. The brand’s dark chocolate peanut butter cups are superior to any others I’ve tried (sorry, Reese’s). And its milk chocolate gems are like M&M’s but colored with real foods like beet juice and spirulina. This variety pack is the way to go in order to try all the chocolaty delights that Unreal has on offer. Better yet, it’s all gluten-free and soy-free and made with fair-trade ingredients.

#156. Delta Is Seriously Upgrading Its Airplane Food & I Got A First Taste—Here’s What’s On The New Menu

We’ve come a long way from peanuts and a snack box.

On a long-haul flight, I care about two things: Can I get comfortable enough, and what exactly am I going to eat while I’m up there? We’ve come a long way from sad snack boxes and over-salted peanuts, and if an airline is charging premium-cabin money, I want the meal to feel like part of the splurge instead of something I politely move around with a fork.

Delta apparently agrees, as the airline has begun rolling out a major refresh of its Delta One experience, with food and drinks getting a particularly serious upgrade. The new setup launches first on transoceanic Delta One flights leaving Los Angeles this fall before expanding across the global network in early 2027.

I recently got to try a handful of dishes from the new menu, which moves between familiar comfort food and much more restaurant-y territory. My tasting included everything from a soup-and-salad starter, risotto, and lamb to a Wagyu burger and upgraded dessert, giving me a pretty good sense of what Delta is going for before any of it reaches a tray table.

The starter was a nice kickoff, and the meats were tender, but the risotto was probably the biggest pleasant surprise. And if you’ve watched enough Top Chef, you know putting risotto on the menu can feel like tempting fate. The lamb was flavorful, though a little harder to cut than I would’ve liked, especially when the dining surface is approximately the size of a laptop.

I’m also personally not rushing to order fish on an airplane, but the sea bass felt far more upscale than most meals I’ve encountered in the sky.

The meal could’ve ended there and I would’ve been perfectly satisfied, but I have a sweet tooth and Delta is keeping its dessert cart. I didn’t even particularly want a sundae until I spotted the soft doughnut sitting on top of one, alongside chocolate sauce, Amarena cherries, and pecan praline crumble. There’s also a dairy-free sorbet that can get a Champagne Taittinger float, plus a cheese plate featuring Northern California cheeses and crackers.

The drinks are getting an upgrade, too. Blanton’s bourbon joins the menu in December, while the wine list is being refreshed with new bottles and an expanded Champagne Taittinger partnership. And starting in 2027, passengers will also be able to order both boozy and non-alcoholic versions of Hugo Spritzes and Palomas.

It’s tough for any airline meal to make me forget I’m eating somewhere over the Atlantic, but if I’m paying to sit up front, this gets much closer to what I want waiting on the tray table.

#161. ‘Making Marie Antoinette’ Is a Magical Tribute to a Genre-Defining Period Drama

One of the all-time best documentaries centered on the making of a seminal movie is Hearts of Darkness: A Filmmaker’s Apocalypse, Eleanor Coppola’s bonkers account of her husband Francis Ford Coppola’s physical and emotional turmoil as he made Apocalypse Now. Eleanor, an artist, screenwriter, and director in her own right, regularly worked on behind-the-scenes projects that examined the creation of films by those in her family, from her son Roman Coppola’s 2001 comedy drama CQ to her daughter Sofia Coppola’s swoon-worthy 1999 feature debut, The Virgin Suicides. Now, more than two years after Eleanor’s death, her last film is about to be released: Making Marie Antoinette, a privileged peek at the birth of Sofia’s Versailles-set, candy-colored romp about the doomed French queen, 20 years after its release.

Unlike Hearts of Darkness, this is not a dramatic tale of slowly descending madness and narrowly averting disaster—it’s a quieter portrait of a master at work, but just as valuable and perhaps even more poignant for its centering and celebration of the female gaze. In its dissection of the minutiae of filming, from logistical challenges to the numerous costume changes and the intricacies of set decoration and choreography, it’s clearly designed for obsessive fans of Marie Antoinette—if you’re in any way alienated by the froth and fripperies, this won’t convert you. But for those who have watched and rewatched and pored over every single frame of this extraordinary period piece over the past two decades, it’s a one-of-a-kind treasure; an intimate and fascinating look at a revolutionary film which turned an entire genre on its head, and shaped everything that came next, from Bridgerton and The Great, to The Favourite and Wuthering Heights.

Making Marie Antoinette begins by laying out its backstory: during the production of Marie Antoinette in 2005, Eleanor Coppola was on set and captured more than 80 hours of candid footage. Some 15 years later, during the early days of the pandemic, Eleanor and Sofia found themselves in the same COVID bubble and revisited the recordings. Eleanor began stitching it together and, after her death in 2024, at the age of 87, Sofia ensured it was finished. The result is a very much authorized, but still illuminating glimpse at Marie Antoinette’s genesis over its 57 days of filming, from a shy, softly-spoken, then-34-year-old Sofia kicking off proceedings with the crew to a somewhat frenzied race to the finish line while staying on schedule and within budget.

Marie Antoinette devotees who have already scoured the internet for backstage images and anecdotes won’t find much here that’s genuinely revelatory, but it’s an immense joy simply to be in this world—to spot the Uggs peeking out from under extravagant ballgowns; to catch extras in powdered wigs snoozing between takes once shooting days stretched to 11 hours in the final portion of production; and to watch an off-duty Jason Schwartzman, in costume as Louis XVI, going ham on the piano while department heads around him attempt to have serious conversations about the film.

A handful of moments feel like gold dust: in one, Sofia introduces her mother, who is behind the camera, to her then new boyfriend (and now husband), Phoenix frontman Thomas Mars, as he and his bandmates arrive on set to make cameos as a coterie of court musicians at the Petit Trianon. In another, Asia Argento, in the gaudy finery of Madame du Barry, reads the palms of her co-stars during a break in filming. When Sofia asks Asia to read hers, she tells the director that she will have two children. (Romy and Cosima Mars would go on to be born in 2006 and 2010, respectively.)

But where Making Marie Antoinette truly takes off is in its portrait of Sofia. If the film has an arc, it is her evolution from a quiet, marginally less experienced filmmaker to a slightly more assertive one. When we first see her attempting to rally the troops, you almost can’t hear her over the clamour of her colleagues. But then she has to make decisions every single day—to insist on costume changes and order more extras to be brought in and fight for small artistic decisions she believes in. She remains polite, but you can see her coming into her power, however slowly.

This is crystalized in a sequence in which we see her filming the Parisian masked ball scene, in which Kirsten Dunst’s vivacious Marie Antoinette encounters Jamie Dornan’s dashing Count Fersen. Once Sofia has captured their initial spark from Marie’s point of view, her male colleagues insist on getting another shot from Fersen’s. It won’t make sense otherwise, they say. Sofia gently pushes back. This isn’t about his point of view, she says; it’s about Marie’s. There’s confusion and more deliberation, but Sofia eventually has her way. It’s quite something watching her, this slight figure who sometimes seems uncertain and self-doubting, surrounded by this giant, almost all-male team, doing all she can to realize her vision, while also always being herself.

That self is most at ease with Dunst, who, lest we forget, was only 22 at the time of filming. She’s a shy interviewee, giggly and uncomfortable when she’s being observed by Eleanor’s keenly perceptive camera, but also preternaturally poised once Sofia calls “action.” It’s evident that the director and her star, who had of course already collaborated on The Virgin Suicides, have a seemingly cosmic, frequently unspoken connection, a kind of young-woman shorthand that’s joyous to witness. When preparing to shoot Marie’s 18th birthday party, Sofia says to Kirsten: “You know when girls see their friends at a party and they’re like…” She lets out a girlish scream. Kirsten understands perfectly and performs it with precision. It’s silly and hilarious and heartening—a reminder of how rare it still is for us to get to see women making art together and having a great time while they do it.

Making Marie Antoinette’s other star is Eleanor. Like every other documentarian, she feels the push and pull of remaining impassive and strategically intervening. At one point, after watching Sofia cough through a day of filming, Eleanor calls for a doctor without her daughter’s knowledge. It turns out that Sofia has bronchitis and needs antibiotics. Sofia, on the whole, is loving and generous with her mother on set, but there are also wonderful moments when she regresses into a kind of exasperated teenager, as we all do when around our parents for too long. Towards the end of filming, when Eleanor tries to ask a sleep-deprived Sofia more questions about Marie Antoinette, she grimaces. “Maybe I should rest, so I can come onto set fresh and not having done a press junket in my trailer with my mom,” she groans. Touché.

In portions of the film, you can hear Eleanor’s own voice, but in others, legendary actor Diane Lane reads from Eleanor’s journals during the making of Marie Antoinette. It’s a decision that could have felt stilted and false, but is done sparingly enough that it’s quite seamless. This narration is most affecting when it veers into more personal territory—Eleanor’s sorrow at being rejected by Sofia in her adolescence, though she understands that break was necessary for her daughter to become her own person; her recollections of Sofia pretending to direct on the set of Apocalypse Now; and her lingering frustration at having spent so much of her life documenting the rest of her family as they made art, rather than making more of her own.

Marie Antoinette aficionados might leave this documentary wishing for a bit more juice. There’s nothing here, for instance, on Rip Torn’s diva antics in the part of Louis XV, or footage of Sofia and Kirsten partying in Paris on their days off, or an account of the film being booed at its Cannes Film Festival premiere, or any assessment of its reemergence as a cult classic. But that isn’t, in the end, what Making Marie Antoinette is about—it’s a lo-fi, fly-on-the-wall, sometimes meandering return to this magnificent, eye-popping universe; a cultural artefact that functions as a multi-layered love letter to female filmmaking, and one that will likely be obsessed over and rewatched almost as much as the original movie itself.

Making Marie Antoinette will be in theaters from October 23, and streaming exclusively on Mubi from November 6.

#162. Jalen Hurts Has Blood Clots in His Lungs

The Eagles QB is expected to miss the rest of the season. Here’s why.

PHILADELPHIA EAGLES QUARTERBACK Jalen Hurts is out for the rest of the 2026-27 NFL season. Originally, the Super Bowl MVP was diagnosed with a superficial blood clot in the left calf. However, an official statement issued today announced multiple blood clots in his lungs.

While the 28-year-old is “clinically stable” and with a “very good” prognosis, he is not allowed to participate in any contact sports—including football. Hurts is currently undergoing treatment with blood thinners. But what does it all mean to have a blood clot—and can it happen to anyone? We asked the experts to break it down for us.

BLOOD CLOTS, ALSO known as coagulation, are a natural healing process we’ve all experienced. When you cut yourself, blood clots—platelets, proteins, and cells stuck together—over the injury to keep you from bleeding excessively. Once the injury heals, your body naturally dissolves the clot.

A BLOOD CLOT can form anywhere in your body.

Sometimes, blood clots form in your blood vessels or arteries without an injury, and they don’t naturally break down. Blockage of blood vessels and restrictive blood flow can cause a life-threatening condition called thrombosis.

“Thrombosis is responsible for about one in four deaths worldwide,” says Erich De Paula, MD, PhD, vice dean and associate professor of hematology at the University of Campinas School of Medicine in Brazil.

A BLOOD CLOT in your arm and the leg veins is known as deep vein thrombosis (DVT). There are also different types that can appear in your lungs and brain. Each type has its own set of symptoms.

WHEN BLOOD CLOTS in your legs break off and travel to your lungs, it can cause a pulmonary embolism (PE). A PE is “the worst-case scenario” when you have a DVT, says Bibhu Mohanty, MD, cardiologist and associate professor of medicine at the University of South Florida. DVT and pulmonary embolism affect about 900,000 Americans every year.

Symptoms can vary depending on your overall health and the size of the blood clot, but as blood flow to your lungs becomes more restricted, you might experience:

Sometimes PE has no symptoms, says Dr. De Paula. In other instances, “a severe and acute PE can be experienced with symptoms from sudden death to near-fainting, severe chest pain, and abrupt shortness of breath.”

DEEP VEIN THROMBOSIS refers to blood clots that form in your body’s deep veins, usually your legs or arms, according to the National Blood Clot Alliance. Symptoms might include:

“It’s sometimes hard to describe,” says Dr. Mohanty. “It’s like I feel pain that won’t go away, but I didn’t pull a muscle or hurt myself. I feel something that’s tight and just hurts.”

DVT often happens after long periods of being sedentary—such as taking a long-haul flight, lengthy car trip, or sitting for long periods of time, he says. Smoking, being over 60, and being overweight can increase your risk.

BLOOD CLOTS CAN form in the arteries of your heart and block blood flow, causing a heart attack. Symptoms might include:

“It is common that patients do not point to a specific area of the chest, but rather to a more extensive and poorly defined area of the chest when asked to identify the pain point,” says Dr. De Paula.

The symptoms can occur gradually or suddenly. Dr. Mohanty says you might also experience sweating, gas, and bloating, and it might feel like acid reflux or heartburn. Symptoms also vary depending on which artery of the heart is affected and the size of the artery.

BLOOD CLOTS CAN also block blood vessels to the brain, which can cause an ischemic stroke, the most common type of stroke.

A stroke can happen when a blood clot forms within a blood vessel that supplies blood to the brain, known as cerebral thrombosis, according to the American Stroke Association. It can also occur when a blood clot forms in the heart or another part of your circulatory system, breaks loose, and travels through the brain’s blood vessels. This is known as a cerebral embolism.

The F.A.S.T. warning signs can help you spot a stroke:

Numbness, confusion, trouble seeing, difficulty walking, and severe headaches can also signal a stroke.

“Basically, if you're noticing a marked change in your face, your ability to talk and move your hands or arms, one compared to the other, it is extremely important to go to the hospital,” Dr. Mohanty says.

THE INDIVIDUAL SYMPTOMS of different types of blood clots can vary, but anytime you have chest pain or discomfort that’s radiating to the upper limbs or neck, shortness of breath, or a cough, seek medical attention, Dr. De Paula says. Also don’t disregard any unexpected pain or cramping in your leg that’s not related to an injury.

Basically, any time “something isn’t right and is different from your human experience, and it won’t go away, it’s definitely time to seek a professional opinion.

#163. Lowe’s Christmas Tree Review: The Retro, Colorful Lights Are Pure Nostalgia

Forget minimalist holiday decor—this tree brings back the old-fashioned holiday magic we remember from childhood.

Forget minimalist holiday decor—this tree brings back the old-fashioned holiday magic we remember from childhood.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

I’ve always had a soft spot for colorful Christmas lights. Some of my favorite childhood holiday memories involve the big, bright bulbs on Christmas trees and the colorful lights decorating houses around the neighborhood. For me, the bigger the bulb, the better! There’s something about that old-fashioned glow that instantly makes the holidays feel magical.

So when I had the chance to test a prelit Christmas tree from Lowe’s featuring oversized, multicolored bulbs, I was ecstatic. Our team is no stranger to finding the best artificial Christmas trees, but this one caught my eye for a more personal reason: It reminded me of the holiday decor I grew up loving.

Holiday trends have a way of coming full circle, and I have a feeling these nostalgic lights are about to have their moment again. If you love the charm of old-fashioned Christmas decor as much as I do, this is one tree I’d keep an eye on before it sells out.

This prelit Christmas tree features oversized, multicolored bulbs that bring a nostalgic, old-fashioned feel to your home.

The Holiday Living 7.5-foot prelit Christmas tree from Lowe’s puts a nostalgic spin on traditional holiday decor. It features 450 large, multicolored C7 LED lights, giving it a big, colorful look that makes it stand out. With 2,969 lifelike branch tips, a full shape and a 52-inch width, it offers plenty of room for ornaments while making a festive statement on its own.

The tree also features Quick Set technology, which connects the lights automatically when you slide the tree sections together, so there’s no need to connect separate light strands. It comes with a folding metal stand, an on/off foot pedal and replacement lights and parts, plus a two-year limited warranty. Shoppers can also purchase the 5-foot version, as well as an optional Lowe’s Protection Plan, which offers two- or three-year coverage on all their trees.

Shipping was incredibly fast and seamless. My tree arrived less than 24 hours after I placed my order, and Lowe’s provided detailed tracking updates, so I knew exactly when to expect the delivery down to the minute (which was extremely convenient, as I was able to direct the driver to place the box in my garage). The boxed tree arrived in good condition and even had two handles, making it easy for me to lift and carry into my house on my own.

Unboxing was just as simple. Inside, I found the assembly instructions, a few replacement lights and parts, the folding metal stand and the tree itself, which came in three sections. The bottom section also had the power cord and an on/off foot pedal, a convenient feature for turning the lights on and off without bending down to reach the plug.

The tree comes with assembly instructions, though I found setup fairly intuitive without them. I’d still recommend holding on to them for future troubleshooting. The metal stand was easy to unfold and lock into place, and each tree section fit together smoothly, thanks to arrows that indicate how the pieces should align.

The branches feature two needle styles, which add texture and help give the tree a fuller, more natural appearance. Fluffing the branches was straightforward, too, although I learned one helpful lesson along the way: Fluff the top section before attaching it to the rest of the tree. Reaching the highest branches once the tree is fully assembled can be tricky! I ended up removing the top section to finish fluffing it, which was easy enough and gave me confidence that taking the tree down at the end of the season should be just as manageable.

With the press of a button, the tree came to life—and the lights are easily my favorite part. Truthfully, they’re even better in person. Sometimes multicolored LED lights can look a little too uniform or modern, but these have that big, bright, old-fashioned charm I remember from childhood. The oversized bulbs give the tree a cheerful, nostalgic glow that instantly makes the whole room feel more festive.

One thing to know is that the lights have just one setting: a constant pattern with no customization or flashing effects. Personally, I don’t mind this at all, since the classic, steady glow is exactly what I want from this style of tree.

This tree far exceeded my expectations, and I’m genuinely excited to share it with others who love this style of holiday decor as much as I do. Part of what makes the holidays so special is revisiting the traditions we loved as kids, whether that’s admiring colorful lights or counting down to the big day with one of the best Advent calendars. Add in the easy setup and convenient foot pedal for switching the lights on and off, and this tree will be a keepsake for years to come. If you’ve been looking for a tree that brings back the magic of childhood holidays, this one is worth a look.

With its large, multicolored lights, this prelit Christmas tree brings back the cheerful charm of childhood holiday memories.

The Holiday Living Prelit Christmas Tree is available exclusively at Lowe’s in a 7.5-foot size, with a smaller 5-foot version also available. Both options feature the oversized, multicolored lights that give this tree its nostalgic charm.

#164. Hunter Schafer Opens Up About Her Decision to Have Bottom Surgery

In her ELLE cover story, Hunter Schafer revealed she had a gender-affirming surgery last year. “Maybe it’s a good thing to share, for the tension I was talking about between those two worlds [reality and ideology],” she said. “I just had bottom surgery in December, which was amazing, and I love it so much.”

Bottom surgery is a gender-affirming operation that changes a person’s genitals to better align with their gender identity. Schafer, a woman who was assigned male at birth, detailed what led to her decision to have it.

She opened up about queerness generally, saying “the magical thing” about it is that “on an ideological level, it’s about possibility and expansion and growth, and being on that journey and finding yourself.”

She then expanded on her view of her gender identity, saying that while it was expansive for years, it’s “flatter” now. “I’m a woman. I’m a girl,” she said, adding that she reached that point after wrestling with queerness as an idea and philosophy “versus how it applies and works in real life, in the context of the world that we’re living in. I feel like there’s always a tension there.”

Her decision to medically transition reflected her greater journey. “Like I said, for a long time I’ve embraced the gender-expansive part of myself, and I really wanted to try to make that previous body work, because I thought there was something really cool and badass about it,” she said.

As she recovered from the surgery, family and friends came to visit her in the apartment she rented, where she rested. “I think my limit was 150 steps per day, which is nothing,” she said.

#165. 'Changed My Life' Lentil Soup and More Recipes We Made This Week

It’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work. So it should come as no surprise that we cook a lot during our off hours too. Here are the recipes we’re whipping up this month to get dinner on the table, entertain our friends, satisfy a sweet tooth, use up leftovers, and everything in between. For even more staff favorites, click here.

A fried fish sandwich has no season. Also, I’m currently in Tennessee, where it’s hit 90° this week, so it’s basically still summer. I used my colleague Shilpa Uskokovic’s excellent Fritto Misto batter to coat some flounder. After frying, I slid a couple small fillets into top-split hot dog buns with juicy slices of tomato and a quick tartar sauce. It was pure summer satisfaction, even this deep into October. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO and cooking

The days when my husband and I both commute are, to put it lightly, b-a-n-a-n-a-s. That’s when my deep freezer fulfills its destiny. Case in point: this superlative basil pesto, thawed overnight, tossed with hot rigatoni, plus frozen peas thrown in with the pasta for the last few minutes of boiling. It is nourishing and feels purposeful, even if it took less than 10 minutes of effort. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

Andy Baraghani’s Honey-Chipotle Shrimp Tacos are one of my most-made recipes of all time. Last week I decided to change things up and eat the shrimp over some homemade Mexican rice and beans instead of wrapping them in a tortilla. The shrimp are so easy to make (just toss in a two-ingredient marinade and pan-fry) that I ended up cooking fresh batches for lunch on the following days to pair with the leftover rice and beans. The canned chipotles in adobo lend a smoky complexity, and I love how the honey helps the shrimp take on just enough char. A luxurious WFH lunch if there ever was one! —Alaina Chou, commerce writer

Soup on a weeknight? It’s a foreign concept to me. If I’m making soup, I’m committing hours to the cause. But this week I couldn’t quell my craving for a sippable bowl, so I scoured the archive for a quick hit and landed on this Curried Lentil, Tomato, and Coconut Soup. Red lentils break down and create a substantial body, while golden Japanese S&B curry powder adds a mellow earthy kick. After mixing in crushed tomatoes and coconut milk, I went rogue and followed up with a couple dashes of fish sauce for extra umami. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

The ever adaptable rotisserie chicken is one of my favorite emergency dinners. When crunched for time, I’ll grab one on my way home and transform the bird into something unrecognizable. Most recently, I used it to make Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser’s Nuoc Cham Chicken Salad. The pulled meat is tossed with the quickest mayo-lime dressing, then stuffed into lettuce leaves. I like to finish the cups with sliced cucumber, fried shallots, and a flurry of fresh herbs. Don’t bother bringing out plates. I eat this with my hands straight from the platter like nachos. —Carly Westerfield, manager, audience strategy

Whenever I want something more for breakfast, but I don’t want to work for it, it’s a Dutch baby all the way. Heat a skillet with butter, dump a couple of always-on-hand ingredients—eggs, flour, milk, sugar—into a blender, and 20 minutes later, it isn’t breakfast: It’s brunch. Last weekend I tossed the reserved browned butter from Epi’s Take It Easy Dutch Baby into a bowl of sliced Italian plums. I added a glug of maple syrup and a pinch of salt, then let the fruit soak in the flavors while I fiddled over my coffee. Puffed bébé out of the oven, the plums and all their juices went on top, and I sat down to enjoy my morning. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, cooking and SEO

I make lentil soup pretty frequently once the “feels like” temperature dips below 50 degrees. And I was just about to mince up my mirepoix when I stumbled upon senior Test Kitchen editor Shilpa Uskokovic’s Soy-Braised Black Lentils. The promise of salty, tender-but-toothsome legumes on a bed of rice was good enough to shake up my routine. I hauled out my rice cooker, set it to steam, and started a dead-simple simmer of a pack of shiny black Beluga lentils with glugs of soy sauce and thin slices of garlic. Once the liquid was mostly gone, I stirred in glossy agave nectar plus added sugar until they formed a loose, syrupy glaze. We ate half the pot tucked into sheets of toasted seaweed snack along with generous spoonfuls of rice. The next morning, the rest was eaten with crusty bread and fried eggs. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor

Ever since I started working at BA, I’ve seen this single recipe for Bolognese top the charts time and time again. An oldie but a baddie, it’s received over 500 comments that would taunt me on a daily basis, with one overall glaring thesis: Make this! Now! So I decided to hunker down, put on a killer album (Once in a Lifetime), and get comfortable in the kitchen. Yes, this Bolognese takes time—cough cough, three hours—but so do all good things. For those who need immediate gratification, your kitchen will be awash in the savory, primal smells of browned beef and pancetta in just 10 minutes. After adding a good amount of liquid from wine, stock, and milk (in stages), then stirring, dancing, and stirring, it was finally time to serve my meaty sauce tangled with fat pappardelle and a charitable shower of Parmesan. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

When I saw a bunch of bright-eyed leeks at the farmers market from my favorite vendor, I knew just what to do with them: my colleague Rebecca Firkser’s cheesy baked pasta. It was one of those love-at-first-sight recipes for me in the Test Kitchen—somehow minimalist and dramatic at the same time. Save this one for a chilly night when you’re having friends over. The sauce uses a cup of white wine, so there’s most of a bottle left to enjoy with dinner. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

I’ve been making a lot of solo dinners lately, and nine times out of ten that means I’m cooking an omelet. My version with fried shallot, apple, and Fontina cheese is a go-to—I wrote all about it for our series, Me, Myself, and Dinner—but if I haven’t gone grocery shopping, I’ll just cobble together fun stuff from my fridge. Some recent wins: chopped kimchi and yellow cheddar; spinach, feta, and dill; black beans, avocado, and salsa macha. —Rebecca Firkser, Test Kitchen editor

This week I did something I haven’t done in years. I roasted a chicken. And it was revelatory. Not fussy. Easy! Rewarding. Inspired by the method in Kitty Cowles’s cookbook, I sprinkled the bird with salt and let it hang out in the fridge for a few hours. Then I rubbed it with olive oil, threw some lemon and garlic in the cavity, and roasted it as high as my oven would go, convection on. While the chicken was resting, its skin a golden crackle, I deglazed the pan juices with white wine, and let those simmer into a tangy gravy. Served with a salad, it was the coziest supper, even romantic if you ignore my toddler cooing. The next day, the carcass simmered in a pot of water with onion and ginger for a broth I’ll sip for days. The surplus meat has morphed into a rice bowl, towering sandwich, day care lunch box, 3 p.m. snack. And the joy from it all? Incalculable. —E.L.

I’m always on the hunt for a protein-rich, not-too-finicky dinner that I can pull together in a blip. It’s gotta taste good because I’ll probably cook it for five consecutive days, at which point I will tire of it and resume my hunt anew. Like sands through the hourglass, these are the recipes of our lives. This week I settled on customizable Soy-Glazed Salmon Bowls. Cook the salmon in that salty-sweet soy and honey sauce, throw it atop rice, and add whatever vegetables you have. This time, I went with shreddy carrots and cukes, plus some of those crispy sheets of nori that I used to scoop up bite after bite. —Sam Stone, senior editor

My very talented colleague Shilpa Uskokovic forever changed the way I cook ground chicken. She mixes the chicken with baking soda—yes, baking soda—for clusters of bouncy nubbins. Now, anytime a recipe calls for ground meat, I use this hack. This week’s victim: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps. It has a sweet, fiery sauce made from sriracha, brown sugar, soy, and fish sauce that deliberately clings to the juicy meat. I piled the chicken into butter lettuce with a squeeze of lime, and a handful of torn mint for freshness. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

#166. The Legal Proceedings Against Khalid Sheikh Mohammed Have Become an Extended Farce

The alleged “mastermind” of the 9/11 attacks is scheduled for trial in 2028, but we’ll see if that actually happens.

Because of Dick Cheney’s sweet tooth for torturing people and the eagerness of his underlings to satisfy it, the legal proceedings against Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the alleged “mastermind” of the 9/11 attacks, have become an extended farce. KSM has been imprisoned at Guantánamo for 20 years. Now they’re saying he will go on trial before a military commission ... two years from now. What a mess this has turned out to be.

In 2024, KSM and two other suspects struck a deal with the military authorities by which the death penalty would be taken off the table. Then Secretary of Defense Lloyd Austin squashed that arrangement. A military court ruled that Austin did not have the right to do so, but a civilian court reversed that decision, so the three suspects appealed that ruling to the Supreme Court, which this week ruled in favor of the government. This allows the government to keep the death penalty on the table for KSM and his two fellow defendants.

So much of this protracted exercise was directly tied to the fact that the Bush administration made this a country that tortured people. In August, a judge ruled that, in any future proceeding, the government cannot use the transcripts of FBI interrogations of KSM. From PBS:

We also can blame cowardly Republican politicians, especially the late Senator Lindsey Graham, for resisting any plan to try KSM in an American civilian courtroom.

#168. This Unexpected Fruit Will Show Up All Over Coffee Menus In 2027—Here’s Why

Its presence on café menus has nearly doubled in just one year.

Long gone are the days when a cup of black coffee was the only way to get through the day—not because it doesn’t provide energy, but because innovative lattes are being served in cafés around the world.

More and more consumers are looking for ways to dress up their everyday drink, experimenting with everything from classic vanilla to lavender and even banana bread coffee. Fruit used to be a background character in your cup of coffee; now it’s primed to be the main event. And according to Nestlé’s 2027 Food and Beverage Trend Forecast, the future of coffee is looking very fruit-forward.

While these flavors may sound a little out there, fruit pairs well with coffee because the beans themselves can carry subtle fruity notes. And one flavor in particular that’s poised to show up on a lot more menus next year is none other than fig.

Linh Phillips, Director of Consumer Insights & Foresight at Nestlé USA, explains that fruit is moving from a supporting note to a much bigger part of the coffee experience. “In 2027, fruit is showing up in new combinations, formats, and textures, turning coffee and matcha into a source of discovery, customization, and flavor exploration,” she says.

According to Datassential, mentions of fig on coffee menus have grown 98.5 percent over the past year. “As younger consumers look to their coffee cup as a place for new experiences, ingredients like dates and figs will add new complexity to drinks,” Phillips explains. “Date caramel, figs and dark stone fruits bring caramel-like, jammy and toffee notes, while cherries, plums and prunes add a rich, slightly tart sweetness. We’re already seeing this shift on menus.”

Steadfast Coffee, a local shop in Nashville, Tennessee, has seen success with its “Fig Season” drink. And the inspiration came from somewhere unexpected: the charcuterie board.

“We wanted to see how we could highlight our obsession with cheese and jam, minus the salami. So we crafted a housemade fig syrup, topped it with cream cheese cold foam, and sprinkled some pistachios on top and hoped for the best!” shares Sydnie Neumann, the café’s General Manager.

“Fortunately, we can’t keep it in stock!” she continues. “It’s so awesome to see people branch out and try something new. Figs are pricier than other fruits, so making it accessible in an affordable way makes people feel like they get to really treat themselves while enjoying the familiarity of a great cup of coffee.”

Phillips says fruit can also add more than flavor. Cold foam, jellies, and freeze-dried fruit can bring extra texture and visual appeal to a drink, making it feel more premium—and more social-media friendly.

Move over figgy pudding, I’m here for figgy drinks!

#170. Sweet Dreams: 8 Expert-Approved Healthy Bedtime Snacks

For years, the wellness rulebook has treated eating late as a way to guarantee a bad night’s sleep. But the since behind sleep isn’t so black-and-white: It isn't eating at night that sabotages your rest, but instead, what you eat that can lead to restlessness.

The right combination of nutrients (think magnesium, tryptophan, and complex carbohydrates) can actually steady blood sugar through the night, nudging the body towards better melatonin and serotonin production. Here’s what the experts have to say.

The problem was never the snack, nutritionist Prateek Kumar explains. It's the wrong snack eaten at the wrong time. “Eating too close to bedtime, especially something heavy or filled with sugar, will spike blood sugar right when your body is trying to wind down,” he says and that spike is inevitably followed by a dip, which may be the very thing jolting you awake at 2 a.m. But going to bed on an empty stomach isn't the fix either. The goal, Kumar says, is “a small, steady snack, not zero food and not a heavy meal.” General practitioner Swapnil Mehta, MD, adds a sensible caveat onto that thought. “What we eat, particularly when and how much, can influence sleep, although food cannot replace good sleep habits or treatment for an underlying sleep disorder.”

When it comes to selecting a snack, look for these three things. Magnesium calms the nervous system and supports GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid, the important neurotransmitter) production, which helps muscles genuinely relax rather than just feel tired.

Tryptophan is the amino acid your body converts into serotonin and, eventually, melatonin. Your body also needs a bit of carbohydrate alongside it to cross into the brain efficiently, which is why a protein-only snack at night rarely does the job alone. Complex carbohydrates round things out, keeping blood sugar level rather than letting it spike and crash while you sleep.

One of the few natural food sources of melatonin, tart cherry juice gets a fiber and omega-3 boost which you add dry chia seeds (and, if it doesn’t bother you too much, wait a few minutes to let the liquid thicken up). Chia seeds will slow digestion instead of spiking sugar. “Small studies suggest they may improve sleep duration and efficiency,” says Dr. Mehta, though “portions should remain modest, particularly for people with diabetes or insulin resistance.”

Milk delivers tryptophan and calcium, while a pinch of nutmeg brings mild calming compounds. Though, Kumar warns, keep it to just a tiny amount of the spice: “Keep it to a pinch; larger doses aren't safe.”

Kumar's describes pumpkin seeds as "one of the richest natural sources of both magnesium and tryptophan,” while banana lends potassium and a gentle carb to aid absorption.

Yogurt digests slowly overnight because of the type of protein inside, which prevents a blood sugar dip. While honey supports liver glycogen through the night without a sharp spike.

The healthy fats of almond butter paired with a slow-digesting carbohydrate keeps blood sugar stable till morning. The fermentation in sourdough also makes it gentler on digestion than regular bread.

Light enough not to burden digestion, kiwi contains natural serotonin precursors and some research links it to faster sleep onset. “Small clinical studies have reported improvements in sleep onset, duration and efficiency, although the evidence remains limited,” says Dr. Mehta.

Oats bring a complex carb and a small tryptophan hit, while chamomile's apigenin compound has mild calming effects of its own.

Among the few foods that naturally contain melatonin, walnuts also carry omega-3s that support the brain's serotonin pathway. They are calorie-dense, so “a small handful is sufficient,” says Dr Mehta.

Bedtime snacks for better sleep, Kumar says, sit at roughly 150 to 200 calories, with around 10 grams of protein “to prevent an overnight dip without turning it into a full meal,” a little healthy fat to slow digestion and complex rather than refined carbohydrates. Ideally, finish eating 60 to 90 minutes before bed and steer clear of caffeine and alcohol, the latter of which “may make you drowsy, but it disrupts deep sleep later in the night.” Dr. Mehta allows slightly more leeway: “If genuinely hungry, a small snack 1 to 2 hours before bedtime is reasonable, rather than eating immediately before lying down.” Those prone to blood sugar dips, pregnant women, anyone who wakes up hungry and athletes, for whom a little casein overnight supports muscle repair, stand to benefit most.

Caution is warranted, too. Dr. Mehta advises anyone with GERD to “ideally leave 2 to 3 hours between eating and lying down,” while those managing insulin resistance or type 2 diabetes should have their intake timed and portioned individually and anyone with IBS should be mindful of fermentable fruits late at night. Persistent sleep problems, he stresses, “should not simply be managed with food.”

The takeaway? Your midnight snack isn't sabotage. Chosen well, it's simply one more tool in the sleep-hygiene kit.

Enter: Sarah Paulson, whose latest hairstyle might just be the answer to my prayers (and my questionable desk posture).

The actor stepped out at the 6th Annual Academy Museum Gala in Los Angeles this weekend, sporting a glossy, jaw-skimming bob that was slicked back to perfection. Created by celebrity hairstylist Chris McMillan, who dubbed the look a “patent leather slick back,” the hairstyle was all about high-shine lengths, a clean finish, and a sculpted silhouette that frames the face with ease.

Now, I know what you're thinking: a slick-back style sounds like a recipe for exposing every inch of your forehead, but (!!) Sarah's look proves that it can actually have a rather impressive lifting effect. So, if you're after a little extra sculpting without committing to anything invasive, the right hairstyle with some hold can certainly help.

By sweeping the hair away from the face and keeping the sides sleek, the style draws attention upwards, creating the illusion of more defined cheekbones and a sharper jawline. Want to make like Sarah? Add a boar-bristle brush and a handful of hair wax sticks to your shopping list and consider yourself halfway there. We're coming for your look, and your cheekbones, SP!

#173. Cauliflower Piccata

Recipe by Susan Bronson, Rhinelander, Wisconsin

Oven-roasted cauliflower steaks take the place of chicken in this vegetarian riff on chicken piccata.

Back in my vegetarian days, I used to joke to my friends that I was more of a “pastatarian,” as I tended to nosh on pasta dishes rather than elaborate vegetarian entrees. If only I had more recipes like this cauliflower piccata in my repertoire at the time. I would have eaten it all the time! Turns out roasting veggies and adding a flavorful sauce is incredibly easy and flavorful.

This particular cauliflower recipe features a head cut into thick steaks, roasted in the oven until crispy and caramelized before being doused in a bright and buttery lemon-caper sauce. You can serve this dish as a side dish alongside a vegetarian entree, or serve it as a main alongside a quinoa salad or protein-rich dense bean salad.

Preheat the oven to 400ºF. Slice the head of cauliflower through the core into four 1-inch-thick steaks. Place them on greased, foil-lined baking pans. Brush both sides of the steaks with olive oil.

In a small bowl, combine the salt, garlic powder and pepper, then sprinkle them over both sides of the cauliflower. Roast the cauliflower until it’s tender and the edges are browned, 40 to 45 minutes, turning once halfway through the cook time.

Editor’s Tip: Some of the florets may crumble when you slice the cauliflower head into steaks. Don’t worry! Toss extra florets with olive oil and any leftover seasoning. Spread them onto the same baking sheet with the steaks and roast them for the same amount of time.

Heat 1 tablespoon of olive oil in a medium skillet or sauce pot over medium-high heat. Add the shallot and saute it until it’s lightly golden, about one minute. Add the minced garlic and saute it with the shallot for another 30 to 60 seconds. Stir in the vegetable stock, then season the sauce with salt and pepper.

Bring the sauce to a boil, then reduce the heat to medium and simmer it until it’s reduced by half, about 8 to 10 minutes. Add the capers, lemon juice and lemon zest. Remove the sauce from the heat and stir in the butter, 1 tablespoon at a time, until it’s creamy.

To serve, place a cauliflower steak on a plate and top it with the piccata sauce. Garnish it with chopped parsley.

Leftover cauliflower steaks should be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator. Store any leftover lemon-caper sauce in a separate airtight container.

Cauliflower piccata lasts for up to five days when stored properly in the refrigerator.

The best way to reheat the cauliflower steaks is in the oven. Place the steaks on a rimmed baking sheet and reheat them in a 350º oven for 8 to 10 minutes, or until they’re heated through and crispy around the edges.

You can also reheat the steaks in the microwave, but you won’t get the same crispness. Reheat any leftover lemon-caper sauce in a saucepan on the stovetop until it’s heated through, stirring frequently to reincorporate the butter.

You’ll need a sharp knife and a cutting board to cut cauliflower steaks. Begin by slicing off the bottom stem and removing any remaining green leaves. Stand the cauliflower upright on its flattened stem and use long, steady strokes to slice into the cauliflower. I find it works best to first slice the head into two halves, then cut those halves into half to make four evenly sized steaks.

Once cut, be gentle with the steaks; they can easily fall apart. Gently brush them with oil and use a thin spatula to flip them rather than using your hands. Don’t worry if some of the florets crumble as you cut the steaks—you can always roast them alongside the steaks.

If you prefer a thicker lemon-caper sauce, the best way to thicken it is to use cornstarch. Before adding the butter, carefully remove 1 tablespoon from the liquid and stir in 1 tablespoon of cornstarch. Return the cornstarch slurry to the sauce and stir until the sauce is thickened. Add the butter when the pan is off the heat.

Roasting the cauliflower in the oven gives the steaks a perfectly caramelized and crispy texture. If you prefer even more browning and crispiness, pop them under the broiler for a few minutes. Just keep an eye on them—the steaks can go from crispy to charred in a blink of an eye!

#174. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#175. The Launch: October’s Must-Know Fashion News

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Paris Fashion Week may be over, but fashion isn’t slowing down in the slightest. As the runway calendar gives way to a season of shopping and fall wardrobes come into focus, brands are marking October with collaborations, store openings, and investment-worthy staples. To kick off the month, Lié Studio teamed up with Tricot on an understated knitwear capsule; Le Monde Béryl planted permanent roots in New York with its first flagship; Gap unveiled a Roy Lichtenstein collection; and Canada Goose presented its latest Snow Goose offering by Haider Ackermann. Elsewhere, Fendi reimagines its Croissant bag and Banana Republic and Zankov presented a colorful preview to the holiday season. Ahead, the launches to know now.

Where: Online at bananarepublic.com and select Banana Republic stores

Why: Henry Zankov has always had a way with color, and his new Banana Republic capsule turns up the volume. The 27-piece collection brings the knitwear whiz’s signature stripes and saturated hues to brushed-cashmere sweaters, including a sporty striped pullover and a cardigan with a flash of pistachio. Zankov also looked to the brand’s archives, reworking a paneled leather skirt and a burgundy bomber with a signature stripe tucked inside the cuff. “This collaboration with Banana Republic is really an exploration of the visual language I’ve developed through my work, brought together with the brand’s rich sense of craft and heritage,” Zankov said in a statement. “The pieces were created with a spirit of playfulness, but with an enduring, timeless quality.”

What: Capsule collection and limited-edition book

Where: Online at acnestudios.com and selected stores worldwide

Why: It’s been a big few weeks for Hussein Chalayan. After Olivia Rodrigo’s rain-triggered costume change revived his “melting dress” from spring/summer 2016, the designer has teamed up with Acne Studios on a new capsule. The 12-piece collection revisits his early 2000s work through the label’s signature denim, jersey, and leather, with patchwork, layered details, and paint-splatter finishes. Photographed at London’s V&A East Storehouse, the campaign also draws on pieces from the museum’s Chalayan archive. A limited-edition book, Reference: Hussein Chalayan, accompanies the collaboration.

Where: 251 Elizabeth St, New York, NY 10012

Why: Nolita’s latest boutique is designed to feel like the first morning of vacation. At 251 Elizabeth Street, brothers Daniel and Joshua Sitt have opened the first permanent flagship for their New York-born footwear and lifestyle label, Brunch. Studio Jume gives the space a playful, hotel-like feel, from its butter-yellow facade to a check-in counter inside, while a customization bar invites shoppers to add charms, beads, and hardware to their shoes.

Where: Online at fendi.com and Fendi boutiques worldwide starting October 22

Why: Fendi’s Croissant bag has been a deliciously easy arm candy classic since its fall/winter 1999 runway debut. Over two decades later, Maria Grazia Chiuri gave the half-moon shape a fresh update for the brand’s cruise 2027 collection, from paillette embroidery and fringed animal print to crackled leather and FF Zucca jacquard. An adjustable strap and side buckles keep the design ready to move from day to night, while the FF flap closure preserves its signature look.

Where: Online at gucci.com and Gucci stores

Why: Gucci’s latest “Beauty and the Bag” campaign has a new leading lady: Vittoria Ceretti, carrying the Jetset GG Marmont in a look as crisp and all-white as the image itself. The bag is just as much of a star, though, with its soft shape giving the familiar Marmont a more relaxed mood. Its archival Double G—drawn from Guccio Gucci’s initials in the ’70s—meets the house’s Web stripe for a pairing of two unmistakable codes.

Where: Online at apc-us.com and barbour.com

Why: Barbour’s practical approach to outerwear gets a touch of je ne sais quoi in its new collaboration with French label A.P.C. The capsule brings Parisian polish to British country classics, including the Beaufort, Spey, and Sugarlump Bedale jackets. Denim-inspired pockets give the outerwear an A.P.C. signature, while jeans, bags, caps, boots, and clogs round out the collection.

Where: 430 Broadway, New York City through October 18

Why: Good American has touched down in SoHo, drawing plenty of influencers—and Martha Stewart—for its opening night party. Co-founder and CEO Emma Grede also brought L.A.-favorite café Leora to New York City for its official East Coast debut, with an on-site counter inside the store. Stop by through October 18 for one of its signature frozen coffees and, of course, a new pair of jeans.

Where: Online at studiodeve.com, ruadh.com, and modaoperandi.com

Why: Rùadh is beloved for its denim and small-batch, minimalist separates, but the New York-based label is known for jewelry, too. Founder Jac Cameron teamed up with Estelle Dévé of Dévé, her longtime friend, on a capsule shaped by their shared love of thoughtful design. Art Deco architecture informed four sculptural styles, each offered in warm 18-karat gold with red jasper or sterling silver with black onyx. The pieces are made to be worn often and, with time, take on the memories of their wearer. “This collaboration was born out of friendship and a shared desire to create something considered, elevated, and beautiful,” Cameron said in a statement. “A true collaboration from beginning to end, it was a meeting of ideas, perspectives, and a mutual appreciation for thoughtful design and craftsmanship.”

Where: Online at canadagoose.com, Canada Goose stores, and select retailers

Why: Haider Ackermann has never been interested in the obvious, and his latest Snow Goose by Canada Goose collection treats technical outerwear with the same intensity he brings to tailoring. For fall/winter 2026, the designer imagined winter as a state of mind, wrapping the body in sculptural parkas, tactile fleece, and glossy nylons. Earthy neutrals are interrupted by flashes of acid orange, rose, and goldenrod yellow, while an “UNKNOWN” graphic nods to the thrill of venturing into unfamiliar territory. The season also introduces the line’s first leather Chilliwack Bomber and its debut Rainboot, extending Ackermann’s vision beyond the parka. “There is a silence and a stillness to the campaign this season,” the designer said in a statement. “I didn’t want to illustrate endurance. Some things become less powerful when you name them. When you explain it too much, perhaps you lose it. The images evoke a feeling, something almost unspoken.”

Why: Few designers understand the art of a great shoe quite like Bruno Frisoni—and now he's bringing that expertise to Larroudé. For its first-ever designer collaboration, the cult-favorite footwear label tapped the former Roger Vivier creative director to reinterpret its signature blend of glamour and wearability through his distinctly Parisian lens. The result is a tightly edited capsule of pumps, slingbacks, mules, and ballet flats, all infused with the sunny optimism that first drew Frisoni to the Brazilian-born brand. “Larroudé is Brazil in its core, and this was important to me,” Frisoni explained in a statement. “Even for a winter season, I loved the idea that they make you feel in a sunny and lighter spirit.”

Where: Online at goldengoose.com and select Golden Goose stores worldwide

Why: Golden Goose’s latest release comes with some magic—Disney magic, that is. The brand’s new “Mickey & Friends” capsule brings character graphics to ready-to-wear, accessories, and the Super-Star sneaker, reworked in vintage-inspired gray suede with a white leather star. Washed sweatshirts, an oversized reversible bomber, and kids’ styles round out the lineup, while patches and charms offer plenty of room to stand out. That spirit of personalization continues with a worldwide Co-Creation tour, where Disney artists will customize select pieces and sketch live illustrations for guests. The tour begins October 14 at Golden Goose’s South Coast Plaza store, followed by a New York stop on October 15, with more events planned through early December.

Who: Gap and the Whitney Museum of American Art

Where: Online at gap.com and shop.whitney.org, select Gap stores, and at the store in the Whitney Museum

Why: Gap has taken Roy Lichtenstein’s pop art off the gallery wall and into your everyday wardrobe. Created with the artist’s estate and the Whitney Museum of American Art, the 18-piece collection brings his bold visual language to hoodies, sweatshirts, button-downs, tees, and accessories. The launch coincides with “Roy Lichtenstein: Like New,” a major Whitney exhibition featuring more than 130 works spanning six decades that revisits the artist’s fascination with mass media and popular culture.

Why: For the latest edition of DeMellier’s Icons capsule, five women put their own stamp on the brand’s standout designs. Taylor Hill, Lena Mahfouf, Rebecca Donaldson, Grece Ghanem, and Romee Strijd each reworked one of the label’s signature silhouettes—from the sleek Midi Hudson to the celebrity-favorite Stockholm—collaborating with founder Mireia Llusia-Lindh from first mood boards to final details. Beyond style, DeMellier partnered with each woman to highlight their philanthropic and entrepreneurial efforts, from Hill’s work with Alexandria House and Freedom & Fashion to Donaldson’s efforts for Glasgow’s Children’s Hospital. “DeMellier’s dedication to ethical and sustainable craft, timeless style, and their all-female design team drew me to collaborate with them on The Large Siena Bucket—a bag that seamlessly fits into my everyday life,” Hill said in a statement.

Where: 23 East 67th Street, New York City

Why: Le Monde Béryl has always made shoes that feel destined for a New York woman. Now, a decade after its launch, the cult footwear label is putting down permanent roots on the Upper East Side with its first-ever flagship on Madison Avenue. Designed by art adviser Silka Rittson-Thomas with architects Tutto Bene, the space blurs the line between boutique and gallery, pairing mirrored walls, vintage furnishings, and a hidden courtyard with references spanning Renaissance architecture and David Lynch. Rather than a traditional store, founders Lily Atherton Hanbury and Katya Shyfrin envisioned a space that “behaves more like a performance space,” evolving through cultural programming as much as retail.

Where: Available online at lie-studio.com and tricotparis.com and the Lié Studio Copenhagen flagship and Tricot Paris atelier

Why: If anyone understands fall dressing, it’s Copenhagen’s Lié Studio. Now, the Danish label has teamed up with Paris-based knitwear specialist Tricot on a tightly edited capsule that brings together Scandinavian minimalism and Italian craftsmanship. At its center is the kind of effortless uniform the brands do best: a fitted long-sleeve polo, matching midi skirt, and a sleek leather belt designed to slip seamlessly into an existing wardrobe. The knit set is spun from a blend of recycled cashmere and fine wool in black, dark gray, and a rich grape hue, while the belt is crafted from Italian leather.

#176. Anthony Ippolito on Playing Rocky, Wearing Armani, and Meeting Andrew Garfield

The star of the upcoming Sylvester Stallone biopic, I Play Rocky, caught up with Esquire to talk about how he fought to become the Italian Stallion.

“It’s been a crazy couple of weeks,” Anthony Ippolito tells me. The star of the upcoming Sylvester Stallone biopic, I Play Rocky, is at the airport traveling from Saturday night’s Academy Museum Gala in Los Angeles to Monday night’s debut of I Play Rocky in Rome. Over our phone call, you can hear travelers wrangling their kids and flight attendants calling for Zone 3 passengers to head to their gate. But the hectic airport experience is exciting for Ippolito. “I’ve never been to Italy,” the son of two Italian parents from Long Island says. “It’s crazy that it’s taken this long, but at least it’s happening.”

Something very similar could be said about Ippolito’s journey from a child actor in commercials to his role as the Italian Stallion in I Play Rocky—out in theaters on November 6. After appearing in the Netflix teen drama Grand Army with Odessa A’zion (Marty Supreme), the actor moved on from roles like “Blowdried Jock” and “Boy on Subway” to land a part in Paramount+’s The Offer, which followed the making of The Godfather (Ippolito played Al Pacino in the biographical miniseries).

But now the actor’s taking on Stallone, making appearances alongside today’s biggest actors at Academy Museum of Motion Pictures events—and doing it in style. For the Academy Museum Gala, he was decked out in a Giorgio Armani shawl-collar dinner jacket and trousers, and smoking scarf, all black. Ippolito thought the addition of the scarf was an especially nice finishing touch. “Yeah, I was a big fan,” he says.

“I like to try to feel comfortable, especially because this is so new,” Ippolito tells me. “A lot of these events, it’s hard to walk a line between making a statement and having it still feel like it’s an extension of you.”

Luckily, Armani’s looser suit is perfect when you’re meeting fellow actors that you’ve admired your whole life and you’re sweating bullets. “That’s the other thing,” Ippolito says of the breathable look. “I saw some incredible fits last night, but when you take into account the fabrics ... there wasn’t very much air conditioning there.”

Before he jets off to Rome, Ippolito shares more with Esquire about working with Armani, why he wanted to play Stallone, and how he had to live out his own underdog story just to land the role.

“I’ve always been a huge fan of ’80s and ’90s Armani. They have a lot of relaxed fits. Loose. It’s very comfortable. It doesn’t feel incongruent to what you feel like you want to express. At one point it was supposed to be a white blazer and then I changed my mind at the last second. But I just wanted to feel comfortable even though it was an event with a lot of cool people.”

“It was an incredible room. Colman Domingo gave an incredible speech, and seeing John Carpenter was very cool. Andrew Garfield actually approached me and said he was excited to see the film. I couldn’t believe it. I was shocked. Just very, very surreal. It’s kind of like you’re dreaming a little bit in these moments, because I told him—and it’s true of so many of the people there last night—that I’ve looked up to his work for so many years. You never really think you're going to be able to say that to him and then have a moment where he’s actually seen some of my stuff.”

“I think if something fictional happens to come up, I wouldn’t shy away from it at this point. It’s been a pleasure to be able to do this, but there’s a lot of responsibility and weight. The Offer was an incredible experience and I had the pleasure of meeting Pacino. Thankfully, he saw the show and had a positive response. But with Stallone, they’re vastly different people and had incredibly different careers. It was an honor to be in the situation, to play both of them, but I’m also excited to explore some fictional circumstances as well.”

“Nobody was asking me to audition for this, which made it a little awkward. I read an article that Peter Farrelly was doing this movie and I just thought, I’d love to try to get in a conversation for that. I sent in a tape that I recorded in my grandmother’s basement, because it was very much stuck in the ’70s and just felt period correct. Then, when I got my hands on the script, I devoured it and sent another tape. You feel sometimes like you’re sending your stuff into an abyss, especially when nobody’s asking for the thing in the first place. Thankfully, I eventually heard that they were interested in talking more.”

“The raw eggs? Yeah, I did it once by myself and then once on set. I definitely did some interesting stuff. Plus, it was actually pretty funny: When we filmed at the Art Museum in Philadelphia, they actually had to move the Rocky statue the day that we were shooting on the steps.”

“I just hope that the film resonates with people. Rocky was so impactful because it’s the underdog story, and this kind of angle is very much true to his real life. This is what he went through, and it’s pretty remarkable.”

#177. Dutch Apple Snacking Cake

Every autumn the siren song of baking calls bakers home until the volume becomes too much to bear. And at that moment, the only thing that can silence it is a warm-spiced apple cake—the kind that hugs you closer than a knit sweater. This recipe, which keeps things simple, relies on the winning combination of cinnamon and apples to perfume a vanilla cake with pockets of tender fruit. A blanket of cinnamon streusel crowns the cake, giving it a contrasting crunch and a coffee-cake-like character. Feel free to stash the cake on your counter, slicing it throughout the week, enjoying its plush interior as it magically gets better with time.

More cozy bakes this way: Caramel Apple Snacking Cake; Chocolate Olive Oil Cake; and Lemon Poppy Seed Loaf.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lightly coat an 8x8" metal baking pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Line with parchment paper, leaving overhang on all sides. Lightly coat parchment with nonstick spray. Place 1¼ cups (156 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (packed; 200 g) light brown sugar, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1½ tsp. ground cinnamon, ½ tsp. baking powder, and ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter, melted, in a large bowl and mix with your hands, squeezing together as needed, until marble-size clumps form. Set streusel aside.

Toss 1 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 2 large), peeled, cored, thinly sliced, slices halved crosswise, and 2 Tbsp. (16 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl to coat.

Whisk 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1½ tsp. baking powder, ¼ tsp. baking soda, and remaining 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl to combine. Add ½ cup (1 stick) chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until no visible pieces remain. (Mixture should look like lightly moistened sand. Don’t worry about overworking it.) Add 2 large eggs, ⅔ cup buttermilk, 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil, and 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract and stir until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Mix in about two thirds of apples.

Scrape batter into prepared pan and spread into an even layer; smooth surface. Scatter reserved streusel and remaining apples over, letting them organically intermix. Bake cake until a tester inserted into the center comes out clean, 65–75 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan. Using parchment overhang, lift cake out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Dust with powdered sugar and cut into 12 pieces if serving immediately.

Do Ahead: Cake can be made 5 days ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

I’m as susceptible to Reese’s as the next person, no matter what shape they put it in. But staring at 3.25 pounds of peanut butter and chocolate may finally be where my devotion starts to feel overly ambitious.

A 52-ounce Reese’s Milk Chocolate Peanut Butter Pie has been spotted in the wild, and calling it a “pie” feels almost too polite. It’s essentially one absolutely enormous peanut butter cup, with a milk chocolate exterior and peanut butter center, weighing 3.25 pounds and selling for about $40.

Food account @snackolator shared the find on Instagram, noting that Reese’s sold a similar giant version online five years ago and it disappeared almost immediately. This time around, shoppers are actually finding the massive dessert in warehouse stores, and listings have also popped up on DoorDash and Instacart.

The nutrition label really puts the scale of this thing into perspective. Reese’s considers it approximately 48 servings, with each 31-gram serving clocking in at 160 calories. Do that math and the whole thing comes to roughly 7,680 calories.

Forty-eight servings also means whoever is cutting this at Thanksgiving better have the precision of a surgeon. Between its size, the price, and the sheer amount of Reese’s involved, people had plenty to react to on social media once photos started circulating.

“I’ve been imagining this for years. I want this so bad,” one person wrote. Another added, “I neeeeeeeeed this!!!!”

One commenter who bought the earlier version offered some firsthand perspective: “I got the one years ago lasted me a month ate a quarter of it every Saturday.”

Others were more skeptical, particularly about whether it would taste like the Reese’s they remember. “If it isn’t the old recipe they can throw this right in the trash…,” one commenter wrote. Another agreed, writing, “If it tastes like Reese's used to taste, I'd buy it.”

Then there was the one person already thinking about how to get the thing to the holiday table: “I wonder if the TSA would let me bring this with me to Thanksgiving.”

My mouth is already sticking shut just thinking about it.
