#180. Inside the Grand Opening Night of ‘Other Desert Cities’ on Broadway

The star-studded revival of Jon Robin Baitz’s Other Desert Cities drew an equally dazzling crowd for the play’s opening last night at the Hudson Theatre.

Directed by John Benjamin Hickey, the show stars Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Ed Harris, Allison Janney, Lily Rabe, and Joe Keery as the deliciously dysfunctional Wyeth family of Palm Springs—but there was no hint of the piece’s acrimony as friends and family of the cast and creators converged in the gilt lobby beforehand. Sarah Jessica Parker, Matthew Broderick, Bradley Whitford, Ina Garten, JJ Abrams, Michael Kors, Lance LePere, and Annie Leibovitz were some of the guests on hand to see the 2011 play—a Pulitzer Prize finalist—remounted.

“What you think is true…is not quite what you thought at all. And I think that’s fascinating. It’s true of life,” said Louis-Dreyfus pre-show, of the play’s meandering plot and gut-punch twist of an ending. Making her Broadway debut, Louis-Dreyfus plays Polly Wyeth, a vodka-swilling, Goyard-toting, Republican matriarch—more Bush, less Boebert—married to Lyman (Harris), an action star turned right-wing pol. Their two adult children, Brooke (Rabe) and Trip (Keery), converge at the family home—a stiflingly beige Palm Springs fantasia—for Christmas 2004. Joining them is Silda, Polly’s recently rehabbed alcoholic sister, played with devastating bite by Janney. Brooke, a flailing but accomplished writer, arrives home with a bombshell: a soon-to-be-published memoir of the family’s dirty laundry. Merry Christmas, indeed.

“Everyone is right and everyone is wrong,” said Rabe, in a crimson Wiederhoeft gown, on the familial backstabbing and recriminations of Baitz’s drawing-room Grand Guignol. Rabe, fresh off her run in A Winter’s Tale at the Delacorte in Central Park, had one day off before she began rehearsals for this play in September. “Winter’s Tale really did break everything open. It’s a wonderful place to start a new process from…when everything was just wide open.”

Given that the piece hinges on a memoir, what, I wondered, are some personal favorites of the cast’s? For Louis-Dreyfus, it’s Isabel Allende’s Paula, the author’s 1994 bedside recounting of her daughter’s illness and death. Janney just began Lena Dunham’s Famesick, and Keery, also making his Broadway debut, is eyeing Cameron Crowe’s The Uncool. Rabe, true to her character, says Joan Didion’s The Year of Magical Thinking.

As the boisterous crowd packed into the theater, an air of giddy expectation permeated the house. When the curtain finally rose on the Wyeths’ Palm Springs manse, swells of applause for Louis-Dreyfus delayed her first line by several beats. The ensuing two hours lived up to the preemptive praise.

Louis-Dreyfus, as the vinegary and jarringly un-PC desert doyenne, is as perfect a fit for Polly as the Escada suits filling her character’s closet. Sporting a gray-streaked Tulsi Gabbard lob, she deploys her barbs with a breeziness that makes them sting all the more—but not so much that you can’t relate to the pain she masks. If there were questions as to the aptness of revisiting this play—the political stakes of 2004 via 2011 feel quaint by comparison to our current quandaries—the ensemble performance here makes a strong case.

Post-show, the crowd traveled east a few blocks to Cipriani 42nd Street for a grand—even by Broadway standards—after-party. As an army of white-jacketed waiters scurried about, revelers like Andy Cohen and Brad Goreski chatted beneath the towering marble columns and baronial painted rafters. Meanwhile, the faux-metallic palm display at the center of the room nodded to the arid artifice excavated earlier.

At around 10 p.m., Louis-Dreyfus, in a black, ruffle-hemmed Christian Siriano gown, snuck in as Beyoncé’s “Cuff It” echoed through the vastness, the lyric “Have you ever had fun like this?” landing with added meaning on a relieved but merry cast.

#182. Scent and Memory Are At The Heart of Zegna’s First Fragrance Collection in Twenty Years

Memorie is a suite of six scents that tell the story of a fabled textiles master—and how he managed to preserve a special part of Italy.

IN WHAT SHOULD COME as a surprise to absolutely no one, the Italian Alps are breathtaking this time of year. As I soak in the magnificent kaleidoscope of colors (and mind you, the foliage hasn’t even hit its peak yet), I’m in awe of the fact that this very landscape was once barren, nothing but cold, jagged rock. Bled dry by the needs of a country engaged in a massive world war, the area’s natural resources had been whittled down to practically nothing, a far cry from the picturesque landscape I’m currently surveying.

Today, I’m standing in a vast nature preserve called Oasi Zegna, named after the man who restored the area to its wild and wonderful roots when he planted nearly 500,000 trees within the region’s one hundred square kilometers in the 1930s. That man, Ermenegildo Zegna, was born and raised in the nearby town of Trivero, where he founded his namesake textiles and, eventually, menswear brand. The reforestation effort says a lot about Zegna the man and his connection to the land of his birth. He did it knowing he’d never live to see the project reach its full potential. Instead, I’m the one who gets to take it all in.

With this story, this setting, as a backdrop, Zegna the brand has released its first foray into fragrance in nearly 20 years, a six-scent collection called Memorie—that’s ‘memory,’ in Italian. Created with global beauty partnerships agency Give Back Beauty and perfumers Dominique Ropion, Fabrice Pellegrin, and Quentin Bisch, the collection offers a range of scent profiles and accords, some common and accessible, others daring and esoteric.

You’ll be intrigued by this singular blend of Turkish rose, old, and an inkwell accord.

Autumn vibes from start to finish. Sweet vanilla develops into warm suede and sandalwood.

Light and fresh, but with some depth, this is one you’ll wear 24/7.

It’s like bringing the outside in. Earthy hints of carrot seed and patchouli are cut with spicy pink pepper.

The brightest of the bunch, this fougere sparkles with notes of pine, lavender, and vetiver.

It has “date night” written all over it: Woodsy and sweet, with a little hint of smoke.

Memorie is an olfactory ode to Zegna’s founding story and the beautiful part of Italy the company still calls home. Each fragrance tells a different part of that story—from the scent of the ink wafting from the newspaper that Mr. Zegna read every morning to the aroma of the glass of ratafia he drank in the evening—and pays homage to the surrounding area. “Fragrances are probably the first moment anyone in the world can feel the brand, very quickly and with a lot of emotion,” says Alessandro Sartori, Zegna’s longtime creative director. “The ultimate goal is to help people experience the brand through fragrance and we felt like six was the minimum number of scents needed to tell our story.”

It’s a concept rooted in well-established biology: There’s a powerful, visceral connection between scent and memory—if you’ve ever caught a whiff of something that smells a bit rosy and were immediately transported back to your grandmother’s house when you were a child, you already know that. At the same time, it’s a radical departure from how most brands promote and think of fragrance. Rather than focusing on specific notes or fragrance families (woody, sporty, fresh), Zegna is focused on storytelling, creating vignettes around each of the scents. “I hope people will select the one that evokes something for them,” Sartori continues. “I think there is space for a different way of thinking [about fragrance]. We have a vision, which is to create an emotion linked to a memory linked to a scent so that you can really feel these fragrances.”

That storytelling is front and center in the brand’s campaign for Memorie, starring impossibly cool actor Mads Mikkelson and written by Roman Coppola and directed by Boramy Viguier. Mikkelson takes us through each of the six scents by exploring the places and memories associated with each one—reading the newspaper in the original office of Ermenegildo Zegna, taking a drive along Panoramica Zegna, the road that cuts through the heart of the Oasi, sitting back in a well-worn club chair with that glass of ratafia. These vignettes provide a tangible example of how each of the Memorie fragrances are woven into the fabric of the Zegna story.

So, about those fragrances. At the risk of reducing Sartori’s vision to a mundane discussion of notes, I’ll do my best, considering the limitations of this medium, to bring each to life. Ropion’s Il Calamaio is an audacious opener, blending an ink accord with rose absolute and oud to evoke Mr. Zegna’s morning newspaper ritual. To me, it’s the most arcane, a peculiar mix of heady flower and rich oud, with the sharpness from the ink accord. Next, Pellegrin’s Il Lanificio takes us inside Zegna’s famed woolen mills, balancing a suede accord with sweet vanilla and earthy sandalwood. I had the pleasure of seeing the brand’s looms and fabric artists at work in Trivero, and a whiff of Il Lanificio brings me right back to the hustle and bustle of the mill floor.

From there, things veer into more approachable territory. Unsurprisingly, Memorie’s most popular scent is A Trivero, a light, fresh blend of lavender, rose, and myrrh, a classic scent combination known as a fougere. From the mind of Bisch, it’s a crowd pleaser that will resonate with most guys and can easily take you from a day at your desk to an evening date. Pellegrin’s Il Sottobosco is meant to evoke the crispness of the surrounding nature—wet forest leaves, pine, dirt—with pink pepper, carrot seeds, and patchouli. The highlight for this writer is La Panoramica, named after Oasi Zegna’s signature byway. Another fougere, this time by Ropion, it's brighter and more comforting (I think it’s the pine).

The finisher, Saga Del Piedmonte, is as bold as you’d want it to be, taking you inside Villa Zegna, the home of Ermenegildo, after a long day of work. You can almost feel the heat of the fireplace—thanks to smoky cedarwood—and the smooth swallow of his evening cocktail (where a coffee accord meets notes of ratafia). Pellegrin’s second contribution to the project is warm and lush. This one feels perfectly tailored to a chilly autumn evening. It’s worth noting that each scent is refillable.

For a collection so rooted in precise flashes of a particular life, I find all the scents to be so evocative of my own experience. The two fougeres take me back to the summers between my college years, working a day job in an over-air-conditioned mall. Il Sottobosco transports me to the fall I moved to Brooklyn, evoking brisk runs through Prospect Park. And that, of course, is Sartori’s vision for Memorie, to use snippets of Mr. Zegna’s life to create lasting recollections of your own.

And it works. With every spritz of A Trivero, I’m back in Italy, admiring the undulating Alps and my own experience in Oasi Zega.

The Zegna Memorie collection is available in selected Zegna retail locations and on zegna.com.

#184. This Cookbook Author Explores Cemeteries for Recipes To Die For

A recipe quite literally taken to the grave?

That’s the foundation for creator Rosie Grant’s ongoing archival project turned cookbook To Die For. And it’s exactly how it sounds.

Apropos for Spooky Season, the book collects “gravestone recipes” so synonymous with departed loved ones they’re immortalized on their headstones. It celebrates the legacies of ordinary folks who did extraordinary things. They were teachers or coaches, the local dentist, the neighbor everybody knew, and they all showed love through cooking for their communities.

What began as a light curiosity turned into a larger, more emotional realization around identity, place, and what we leave behind.

Over the past five and a half years since starting her TikTok and Instagram accounts under the username ghostly.archive during a digital archives internship at the Congressional Cemetery in Washington, DC, Grant’s travels have taken her across the United States—as far as Nome, Alaska—as well as Nova Scotia, to visit their final resting places and families to learn their stories.

It’s an almost feel-good way to get into the topics of mortality and death, Grant assesses, as sitting around the table to share a meal or stepping into a memory-filled kitchen disintegrates conversational barriers. Though she was raised by parents who gave ghost tours at local cemeteries in Alexandria, Virginia, she says her family was much more comfortable with the idea of hauntings than discussing and planning for the inevitable themselves.

“Something like a recipe feels so life-giving,” Grant expresses, adding that these conversations could also encompass music or travel. “Talking about these many life-filling moments might be an easier way to talk about tough topics.”

The 40 recipes were all approved by family members of the deceased, whom Grant tracked down mostly through internet sleuthing (obituaries and social media) to ask permission to publish.

Initially Grant tried to separate the recipe from its provider and solely focus on the food itself, but the process didn’t feel quite right.

Grant has since cooked with seven families highlighted in To Die For, and has shared her pilgrimages to the gravesites with the goods themselves to pay respect. With her years of research and immersion, Grant notes that burials and grave markers have become so much more personal over the course of time. Granite headstones have allowed for almost any customization after mass-industrialization made the tools to work on it more accessible, and are much more durable compared to the formerly used wood, slate, or marble, making for lasting memorials. Proof cemeteries are beautiful grounds still vibrating with life and knowledge, if you’re open to it.

Her approach to keeping such individual histories alive has deeply resonated, furthering her relationship to the Death Positive Movement: formed by hospice workers, death doulas and other care workers who advocate that discussions around mortality and afterlife planning make for a healthier society; and establishing a more intimate sense of collectivity amongst strangers across the globe.

While she’s gotten her share of detractors for various reasons (mainly self-identified Mediums claiming the deceased, and in one case–one participant still living, didn’t appreciate their culinary secrets being shared), many folks have found inspiration as they consider their own gravestone recipe. Some commenters, meanwhile, express regret around not asking their own loved ones for recipes or helpful tips that most instructions don’t leave nuance for when they had the chance.

“I thought I could just have this on socials and do a PDF format online,” Grant says. “[The families] were like ‘We like the idea of a physical book. Something that’s precious.’ Even the visual style of it is meant to be something you’d inherit from a grandparent.”

The most underrated section of her book offers a thoughtful list of questions to begin documenting one’s own familial food legacies.

“It can feel really morbid to be like ‘Hey mom, can you write down your recipe because you’re gonna die someday?’” Grant says jokingly. “That can look like a lot things. Take pictures of the recipe box and text it to all the cousins or the family group chat and save it to a drive somewhere. Cook with your family member. Teach me how to do it, let’s cook it together. Passing down that knowledge, there’s something very powerful about that shared experience.”

Sentiments from both participants in the book and Grant’s audience echo how revisiting these recipes offers sensory catharsis in addition to talking about their grief. What started as a nerdy food adventure manifested into an exploration of what it means to be remembered for how people made us feel when we were with them; highlighting turn-of-the-century attitudes toward heritage, family and home life, and serving as a “rite of passage” or way to pass the torch to the next generation.

Grant reminds us of observing and maintaining such rituals. “If we don’t do it, nobody else will.”

Dealing with dark spots can be frustrating. Whether they result from post-acne scarring, unprotected sun exposure, or a predisposition to hyperpigmentation, treating dark spots requires patience and, in more severe cases, professional guidance. Dark spots that are particularly difficult to treat often require prescription-strength creams, serums, and even certain lasers, but there’s also a growing assortment of OTC options, too. Ahead, derms unpack the best Rx-free treatments and techniques for fading dark spots.

Before sorting out a treatment plan, know which kind of dark spot you’re looking to treat. Ingredients needed for post-acne marks versus a sun spot may vary. “Freckles, sunspots, melasma, post-acne marks, and flat seborrheic keratoses can look similar but respond differently,” Dr. Kseniya Kobets, director of cosmetic dermatology at Montefiore Einstein Advanced Care, explains to ELLE. “Some improve with creams, others need office treatments, and seborrheic keratoses are benign growths that lightening creams generally won’t remove.” She also notes that shape or color changes, irregularities, or brown spots that bleed should be evaluated to rule out skin cancer.

A dark spot is a general term for discoloration, while a sun spot is a specific type caused by cumulative sun exposure that typically doesn’t fade on its own. “Patients often come to me concerned about post-acne dark spots that are actually red spots, called post-inflammatory erythema,” explains Dr. Rishi Chopra, a board-certified dermatologist at Hudson Dermatology & Laser Surgery in NYC. “These can look darker or purplish in melanin-rich skin and result from blood vessel changes rather than excess pigment, so treatment is different.”

Brown marks after acne are typically post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, which, according to Chopra, is treated by controlling inflammation and reducing pigment production. “True sun spots are more persistent and may require procedures such as lasers for complete removal,” says Chopra.

Kobets notes that historically, Kligman’s formula, a prescription-strength topical cream originally developed in 1975 by Dr. Albert Montgomery Kligman, was the gold standard for treating melasma. Modified versions of the cream, including the controversial hydroquinone, a retinoid like tretinoin, and a steroid, have also been used over the years to treat melasma and other hyperpigmentation, with the strongest evidence for melasma. “These are prescription treatments, and irritation, risks from prolonged hydroquinone use, and skin thinning or visible vessels from chronic steroid use make OTC maintenance options appealing, although OTC doesn’t automatically mean gentler or safer,” says Kobets.

Both Kobets and Chopra say that hydroquinone remains one of our most effective treatments for stubborn pigmentation—but it’s no longer legally available over the counter in the U.S. and should be used under prescription supervision.

Product packaging touting “dark spot remover” is only the starting point. Scan the ingredient list before choosing your treatment cocktail. Some common OTC ingredients include retinol, niacinamide, azelaic acid, kojic acid, cysteamine, topical tranexamic acid, arbutin, and licorice extract.

Chopra prefers four options: thiamidol, tranexamic acid, azelaic acid, and niacinamide, each with different benefits depending on your skin concerns.

Additionally, Kobets says that resorcinol-containing ingredients also have clinical evidence, including 4-n-butylresorcinol (aka rucinol) and thiamidol, the ingredient used in Eucerin’s Radiant Tone line. Newer options include La Roche-Posay’s Melasyl and Mother Science’s malassezin, which Kobets notes work differently. “They don’t all inhibit tyrosinase; Melasyl, for example, captures pigment precursors,” says Kobets.

For an entry-level start to clearing dark spots, alpha hydroxy acids (AHAs) and beta hydroxy acids (BHAs) have also proven to be effective. “Glycolic and salicylic acids can help when texture or acne overlaps, but over-exfoliation can worsen pigmentation,” says Kobets.

There’s been a lot of buzz about vitamin C as a brightener; however, Kobets says it’s a solid antioxidant and supporting ingredient for fading discoloration, but stability and delivery are often inconsistent, making it less effective as a standalone treatment, particularly for clearing stubborn melasma.

Licorice, another common ingredient in OTC creams, has pigment-targeting and anti-inflammatory properties, but, according to Kobets, studies often use combination formulas, so the licorice itself isn’t necessarily doing the heavy lifting. Soy and ferulic acid are also ingredients Kobets says play better supporting roles, as they are not as effective on their own. Turmeric has less convincing spot-fading evidence overall.

For thiamidol, Chopra recommends 0.2 percent (the concentration studied in clinical trials), tranexamic acid at 3 to 5 percent, azelaic acid at 10 percent, and niacinamide around 5 percent. “These concentrations offer a good balance of effectiveness and tolerability, although formulation matters too,” says Chopra. “Higher concentrations aren’t necessarily better, since irritation can worsen pigmentation. Unfortunately, brands don’t always disclose their active ingredient concentrations.”

Kobets adds that formulation, frequency, and tolerance matter as much as percentage. Her starting options include retinol at 0.1 to 0.3 percent, niacinamide at 2 to 5 percent, azelaic acid at 10 percent, and L-ascorbic acid (vitamin C) at around 10 to 15 percent, “although acidic vitamin C can sting and different derivatives’ percentages aren’t interchangeable,” she points out. Kojic acid around 1 to 2 percent, and alpha-arbutin at 1 to 2 percent in facial products; different arbutin forms, she clarifies, aren’t interchangeable. “Glycolic acid around 5 percent or salicylic acid 0.5 to 2 percent can support treatment, especially for clogged pores and post-acne marks, depending on sensitivity. Licorice extracts vary in active components, so extract percentage alone tells us little,” Kobets says.

Cysteamine has evidence at 5 percent, generally as a short-contact, wash-off treatment following product directions. “It’s an option when avoiding or rotating off hydroquinone, but hasn’t consistently outperformed it and can cause burning, redness, and an unpleasant odor,” Kobets also notes.

For Melasyl, thiamidol, and malassezin, Kobets suggests focusing on the tested formula and instructions. Noting that even tranexamic acid’s results depend on formulation, so stronger isn’t automatically better.

Experts agree that most ingredients work across skin tones, but Chopra warns that darker skin is more prone to post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, meaning even mild irritation can leave lasting discoloration. “Redness can also be harder to recognize in darker skin, allowing irritation to go unnoticed,” says Chopra.

Ingredients like azelaic acid and hydroquinone aren't necessarily more irritating in darker skin, but the consequences can be greater. For darker skin, Chopra favors well-tolerated options like tranexamic acid, niacinamide, and azelaic acid.

“Tinted sunscreen with iron oxides is especially important in skin of color because it helps protect against visible light, which, alongside UV exposure, contributes to persistent pigmentation. I consider it a foundational part of treatment, not just prevention,” Chopra adds.

It’s always best to consult with your dermatologist when integrating a dark spot diminisher into your routine, especially when using other actives like retinol. With OTC options, though, both Kobets and Chopra say you can absolutely mix and match ingredients to suit skin type and sensitivity. “Perhaps a morning brightening serum and nighttime retinoid, or alternating days. Introduce one product at a time, check for overlapping acids or retinoids, and include moisturizer,” Kobets recommends, with the caveat that adding OTC retinol to tretinoin usually adds irritation without clear extra benefit.

For acne-related pigmentation, Chopra recommends azelaic acid in the morning and adapalene at night to address both breakouts and lingering marks.

Lastly, since inflammation can worsen melasma, avoid lightening creams that cause redness and irritation, and work against treatment. “Combining prescriptions with gentler, well-tolerated OTC options can help, but OTC isn’t automatically nonirritating. Once improved, I consider non-hydroquinone maintenance and consistent sun protection; melasma is something we manage rather than permanently cure,” Kobets concludes.

Kylie Jenner just got her wings. Tonight, the Khy founder shocked the audience at the 2026 Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show when she made a surprise appearance on the runway, marking her first time ever walking a Victoria’s Secret catwalk—and in a piece of VS history, no less.

For the occasion, Jenner wore a silver studded top, which turned out to be the brand’s iconic Fantasy Bra. #188. Chickpea Saag

This take-out staple is easy enough to recreate at home and fantastic for family dinners. If you’re looking for a comforting vegetarian weeknight meal, this stripped-down version is the ticket—it takes little time to prep, is both budget- and pantry-friendly (thanks to frozen spinach and canned chickpeas), and always goes down a treat. If you have kasuri methi or dried fenugreek leaves, crumble a healthy pinch into the spinach when you’re blending the mixture. It’ll make the saag even more fragrant and delicious. Leftover saag, if any, tastes even better the next day.

Find more delicious vegetarian dinner ideas here: Gochujang-Butter-Braised Tofu; Crispy Tofu With Peanut Sauce; and Sheet-Pan Gnocchi With Soy-Dressed Mushrooms.

Melt 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a medium skillet with a lid over medium heat. Add 1 large white onion, thinly sliced, 8 garlic cloves, coarsely chopped, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, coarsely chopped, 2 tsp. cumin seeds, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and tender, 8–10 minutes.

Uncover pan and add ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ½ tsp. ground turmeric. Cook, stirring often, until yogurt is slightly thickened (it will split into tiny curds), about 2 minutes. Let cool a few minutes, then transfer to a blender; reserve skillet.

Add ½–1 serrano chile (depending on the spiciness of your chile and your heat preference), one 10-oz. package frozen spinach, thawed, and ½ tsp. garam masala to blender; blend until mixture is very smooth, about 3 minutes.

Return purée to reserved skillet and add one 15-oz. can chickpeas, rinsed. Cook saag over medium-low heat, stirring often, until heated through (do not bring to a simmer or saag may split).

Transfer saag to a medium bowl. Serve with steamed rice and/or warm naan, lime wedges, and more yogurt alongside.

Do Ahead: Saag can be made 1 day ahead. Let cool. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Reheat over medium-low heat before serving.

#189. McDonald’s Boo Buckets Are Coming Back for Halloween—Starring the Most Iconic Disney Villains

The Halloween tradition returns to McDonald’s this October with Disney villain Boo Buckets.

As someone who knows her way around a musical theater score, I’ve always argued that Disney villains get the best songs. “Poor Unfortunate Souls,” “Be Prepared,” “Gaston”—I’ll take a theatrical villain plotting someone’s downfall over a lovesick hero singing about their dreams any day. The villains have better lyrics, better entrances and considerably more interesting things to say.

And now it appears they’re getting the better Happy Meals too. McDonald’s is bringing back its beloved Halloween Boo Buckets for 2026, this time with a Disney villains makeover. Five of Disney’s most notorious characters are getting their own collectible buckets, just in time for trick-or-treating.

The Disney Villains Boo Buckets Happy Meal arrives at participating McDonald’s restaurants nationwide on October 20, 2026.

This year’s collection features five characters who have caused their fair share of trouble: Jafar from Aladdin, Ursula from The Little Mermaid, Scar from The Lion King, Cruella de Vil from 101 Dalmations and Maleficent from Sleeping Beauty. It’s a formidable lineup, though I do wonder what Captain Hook did to get himself excluded.

Each collectible bucket features a design inspired by its villain, along with a character-themed lid and stickers depicting familiar faces and details from the films. It’s a departure from the classic pumpkins, ghosts and other Halloween creatures that have appeared on McDonald’s Boo Buckets over the years, but the concept remains the same. Enjoy your Happy Meal, hang on to the bucket, and put it to work collecting the best new candy on Halloween night.

The original Boo Buckets debuted in 1986, so there’s a good chance some parents will be nearly as excited about this promotion as their kids. And with five designs to choose from—or at least hope for—McDonald’s has given collectors another reason to make a few extra trips through the drive-thru.

McDonald’s hasn’t announced an official end date for the Disney Villains Boo Buckets promotion. The buckets will be available for a limited time at participating restaurants, while supplies last.

If you’re hoping to collect all five, I’d recommend getting an early start. McDonald’s hasn’t specified whether customers will be able to request a particular character, so tracking down your favorite villain may require a little luck.

As for me, I’m firmly on Team Ursula. She’s dramatic, resourceful and capable of delivering one of the greatest villain songs in Disney history while conducting business out of an underwater cave. I don’t approve of her methods, but I respect the commitment. And if I can get a Halloween candy bucket out of the deal without signing away my voice, even better.

#190. Watch Alex Consani Get Angel-Ready for the 2026 Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show

With this year marking Alex Consani’s third time walking the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show, it’s safe to say that the top model has officially ascended to Angel status.

During the star-studded show, held in Los Angeles on Sunday night, Consani wore not one but two statement looks down the runway. The first was a classic pink bra and brief combo topped off with a matching sweeping cape with green accents; the second, edgier look was a black lace off-the-shoulder corset finished with golden feathered wings. “The VS Show always makes me feel so empowered,” Consani tells Vogue earlier this morning, fresh off her turn down the catwalk. “There’s something about the energy of it that’s unlike anything else. Everyone is there to have fun, feel amazing, and really own the moment.”

Ever wondered what exactly goes into getting Angel-ready? Before hitting the catwalk, Consani brought Vogue along backstage as she got into hair and makeup yesterday—overseen by legends Guido Palau and Pat McGrath, respectively—and ran through rehearsals.

For Consani, preparing for the show all started with a more internal practice. “For me, preparing is mostly about getting myself into that mindset,” Consani says. “Obviously, you want to feel your best physically—but so much of it is about confidence and going out there ready to have the best time. The second I step onto that runway, the adrenaline takes over.”

A VS look is really about committing to the fantasy, and the second the whole look comes together, you feel completely transformed.

After finding the right headspace, receiving the full Angel glam treatment backstage—from the pro beauty team to the theatrical wings—certainly helped her get into supermodel mode even more. She says all of that excitement and frenetic energy backstage only allows one to get even more into character—especially when she’s alongside friends like Anok Yai or Vittoria Ceretti.

“Walking the runway itself is obviously such a rush, but honestly, some of my favorite moments happened backstage,” says Consani. “Everyone is getting ready together, hyping each other up, laughing, running around. Then suddenly you’re on the runway, and it all goes by in what feels like five seconds.”

I love those final few minutes before walking, when the hair and makeup are done, the look is on, and you see the full thing for the first time. That’s when it becomes real, and you’re like, “Okay, she’s ready!”

How did Consani celebrate the big night, after a successful strut in front of the cameras? The model says she and her fellow model-friends proceeded to hit the town in West Hollywood. “It was truly the best night ever. Everyone was in such high spirits after the show, so we were just dancing, laughing, and celebrating together,” says Consani. “The show itself is such an adrenaline rush that you almost need that moment afterward to let it all out. It was the perfect way to end the night.”

After a busy Fashion Month and the VS show, Consani is now taking some much-deserved and rightfully-earned time for herself. “I love getting back into the rhythm of work, seeing what’s next, and having a little time with the people I love,” she says. “I’m really grateful for everything happening right now, so I’m trying to stay present and enjoy it rather than rush ahead. But obviously, I’m always excited for the next fashion moment.”

Below, see exclusive clips of Alex Consani behind the scenes of the 2026 Victoria’s Secret fashion show. (Come for the morning face mask and extensive hair rollers—stay for her post-show hotel room hang with fellow Angel Paloma Elsesser.)

#193. Ina Garten’s Biggest Cookbook Lesson Started With A Roast Chicken Nobody Wanted

Before Ina Garten became the person I trust to make everything from a fall salad to a very large Cosmopolitan look effortless, she was figuring out the food business one roast chicken at a time. And apparently, even Ina had to serve a few flops before figuring out what people actually wanted.

On a recent episode of The Mel Robbins Podcast, Garten looked back on the earliest days of Barefoot Contessa, the tiny Westhampton specialty food store she bought at 30 despite having zero experience running one. She’d come from working on nuclear energy policy in Washington, D.C., but Garten doesn’t actually see the career pivot as quite as random as it sounds.

“If you’re cooking, you’re testing things,” she told Robbins. “But instead of ending up with, like, gibberellic acid, you end up with roast chicken. So which would you rather have?”

The learning curve was immediate. Garten said she didn’t know how to cash out a register, slice smoked salmon, or scale the 12 brownies she could make for friends into 1,000 for customers. After her first week, she even told Jeffrey, “This is the stupidest thing I’ve ever done in my life.”

Her first day as owner didn’t exactly scream future food empire, either. The register had just $87 in it, prompting Jeffrey to do the math and tell her, “I don’t think you’re gonna make it here.” By the end of the very next day, a busy Friday before Memorial Day weekend, the store was completely cleaned out. Garten and the previous owner stayed up through the night making chocolate cake and chicken salad so they could do it all again. But one of the most important lessons came from food that wasn’t selling.

Garten initially assumed a Hamptons specialty shop called for fancy food, so she made dishes like veal with morels and displayed roast chickens on a huge white platter surrounded by fresh herbs. Nobody wanted them. She eventually moved those same chickens into little red-and-white checkered baskets—and they sold in 10 minutes.

Her takeaway? “People have elegant taste, but they don’t want fancy food at home.” Garten said the realization “totally informed all of my cookbooks.”

That philosophy feels pretty familiar if you’ve ever made her Honey White Bread or Crispy Chicken With Lemon Orzo. When Garten eventually did start writing cookbooks, she said her formula was simple: dependable recipes, beautiful photography, and ingredients you could actually find at the grocery store.

And, fittingly, when Robbins asked Garten for her favorite recipe at the end of the conversation, she didn’t name anything particularly elaborate. She picked a French apple tart with a thin buttery crust, sliced apples, butter, and sugar.

“It’s a very simple recipe,” Garten said. “I just think it’s just gorgeous.”

#194. The 36 Best Movies of 2026 (So Far)

Prior to this month I was beginning to worry there was something wrong with me. In a year of new waves, record-breaking hits, and extreme Anne Hathaway saturation, I was overwhelmingly feeling numb at the movies. Sure, there were plenty of things I liked—even liked very much. But overwhelmingly, my enthusiasm was lacking. Oh, how I yearned to be knocked off my feet, to float out of a theater with a glow that led strangers to ask what drug I’d taken. There were a few films at this year’s New York Film Festival—my go-to fall fest—that provided a solid high. But leave it to Nathan Fielder to really send me soaring into the stratosphere. You Can See Everything, the Elizabeth Holmes doc that Fielder co-directed with Lance Oppenheim, is a surprisingly heartbreaking, utterly staggering work of—yes, I’ll say it—genius.

And part of what’s so thrilling about it is that its genius is not one of invention, but rather of perception. Fielder and Oppenheim take Holmes’s invitation to see everything, and they push “can”—the film’s critical word—to its limit, provoking questions about differences in perception, the value and ethics of depiction, and limits in the pursuit of truth. In a year of moviegoing sensations, this is the one that both feels most deeply of this moment—reflecting what technology has done to us, and also pushing back against its tendency to flatten us—and the one that will most stand the test of time.

At one point in You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder asks Elizabeth Holmes why she enlisted him of all people to document her final days before being sent to prison. Holmes struggles to come up with an answer and her partner mentions that Fielder, like Holmes, thinks differently. Whatever the true motivation, the pairing—and add to it co-director Lance Oppenheim—could not be more perfect. Fielder and Oppenheim’s thematic concerns, aesthetic proclivities, and metafictional methods make for the most intriguing, layered, and complex portrait yet of the disgraced Theranos founder—one that deeply probes ideas around truth, manipulation, human psychology, and artistic portrayal. It’s not just the film of the year; it’s the film of the decade.

There have been countless movies about the making of movies, but there’s one part of the process I’d never seen depicted on screen: location scouting. It makes sense. Location scouts are often siloed off from the rest of a crew, and their jobs aren’t glamorous. But in her debut feature, Paula Gonzalez-Nasser uses a day in the life of a scout to brilliant ends—as a window into the homes and lives of various New Yorkers. Gonzalez-Nasser, who previously worked as a scout, has a keen eye for detail, a knack for creating compelling compositions, and a patience that never verges on indulgence. As the titular scout, Mimi Davila aptly and subtly brings interiority to a person who has to spend most of their time appeasing others.

In his first narrative feature, Lance Oppenheim retains many of his documentary trademarks—an interest in eccentric people with wild dreams, a pull toward the dark and strange goings-on in suburban America, and a kaleidoscopic approach to style and structure. Working off a script from Ajon Singh, Oppenheim depicts the turbulent rise of the early-aughts reality show To Catch a Predator and its host, Chris Hansen. The film boasts a solid ensemble, but Robert Pattinson, as Hansen, commands outsized attention with an indelibly over-the-top performance that Oppenheim has likened to somewhere between Hansen, Jerry Maguire, and Dracula.

Being stuck in a car for a long drive that never ends is among my greatest personal nightmares. While the young filmmaker Alex Ullom squeezes some scares out of that premise, his debut feature is more concerned with reflecting feelings that might be present off the road—malaise, uncertainty, existential despair. That the film also manages to be a good hang is testament to a dynamic young cast and a strong sense of pace.

John Wilson’s first full-length documentary retains all the qualities that made How To with John Wilson such a sensational show throughout its three-season run. It is full of unexpected detours, witty juxtaposition, and genuine curiosity. In turning his camera to the subject of concrete, Wilson encourages viewers to rethink one of the most pervasive materials of modern life, while also illustrating the difficulty of convincing prospective financiers that concrete could be a commercial subject.

Who says libraries can’t be cinematic? Against all odds, one of the most inventive movies of the year was made on a microbudget, stars a real-life academic, and is about a scholarly quest. Kevin Walker and Jack Auen’s debut feature, Chronovisor, follows a Columbia professor as her research into a time-travel device rumored to have been suppressed by the Vatican yields electrifying, mystical results—and they do so with methods of depicting text on screen that are fresh and enchanting.

Hope, from writer-director Na Hong-jin, includes some of the most awe-inspiring action sequences I’ve seen in a movie, and also some of the worst CGI. Whether that latter quality is a feature or a bug is up for debate. Even as he gives the audience what they want, Na provokes the audience, leading to questions about how we watch and how what we watch has impacted our worldviews.

In adapting the Resident Evil video game, Zach Cregger creates a first-person experience that is gnarly, thrilling, and frequently very funny. Austin Abrams is the perfect everyman avatar, constantly muttering through his trip to Hell and not quite back.

In their follow-up to the 2024 documentary No Other Land, which showed the destruction of a Palestinian community in the occupied West Bank, Israeli filmmaker-journalists Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor turn their attention to the post–October 7, 2023, actions of the Israeli Defense Forces as they attempt to eradicate Hamas. Through interviews with twenty-four Israeli intelligence officers and soldiers, conducted on Tel Aviv rooftops, with the subjects’ faces hidden in shadow, we get extensive and detailed testimony regarding Israel’s disregard for civilian casualties. It’s a brutal, terrifying account, and one that, beyond providing information, is an insightful portrait of the complex psychology of the perpetrators.

I can’t include The Odyssey on this list and not include Digger—a film that is equally audacious and full of excellent craftsmanship, but which, similarly, does not quite work. Alejandro González Iñárritu’s layered treatise on climate destruction and human apathy—spoiler alert incoming—spends too much time in the dazzlingly constructed world of its fictitious play, never quite fulfilling the purpose of its meta twist. Still, love the effort, Tom! Keep on taking risks.

With its deep cast of alt-comedy superstars, I was prepared for Maddie’s Secret to be funny. I was less prepared for John Early to dish up such a tonally distinct, pitch-perfect Sirk-meets-Showgirls melodrama—at once a send-up of modern test-kitchen foodie culture and an earnest, emotional account of disordered eating.

When I saw Late Fame at last year’s New York Film Festival, it stood out for the way it captured something I’d noticed but hadn’t yet seen in a movie. In this case, it was the way modern New York literary and art culture can feel like absurd cosplay performed by the rich—with nostalgia for past art-making golden ages distracting from actual art-making. The film, written by Samy Burch and directed by Kent Jones, follows Ed Saxberger (Willem Dafoe), a New York mailman whose old poetry is discovered by a group of young aspiring intellectuals who call themselves the Enthusiasm Society. The high Saxberger gets from the new attention is quickly superseded by what one imagines are the reasons he stopped writing poetry to begin with. Dafoe turns in a tremendous performance as Saxberger, and Greta Lee and Edmund Donovan are equally great in supporting roles.

It feels wrong not to recognize the sheer achievement of Christopher Nolan’s epic. The director and his crew invented new ways to light night exteriors, created spectacular practical effects, traveled to the far reaches of the world, and shot the first commercial feature entirely with IMAX cameras. The results of their efforts are frequently magnificent. And yet, I wished the movie spent more time, or simply went deeper, on the people. It wasn’t until the end of the film that I was truly moved. That said, the highs here are too high to ignore.

The kidnapping in The Kidnapping of Arabella is so whimsical and the movie’s humor so wittily absurd that it caught me off guard when I found myself genuinely affected by the film. But Italian director Carolina Cavalli taps into the adrift anguish of becoming an adult and realizing, as the film’s protagonist says, “It takes so little to keep you from living the right life anymore. And the worst part is you can still imagine it.”

Typically, there’s no type of movie that’s more insufferable than a finger-wagging generational treatise made by an elder statesman and directed toward young people. But while Gregg Araki’s I Want Your Sex is basically that—a plea to have sex and be a little messy—it’s so funny, playful, and balanced that it elides a sense of didacticism. Olivia Wilde gives what may be a career-best performance as Erika Tracy, a controversial modern artist who initiates a turbulent affair with her outrageously horny young underling, Elliot (Cooper Hoffman, also very good). The film doesn’t necessarily approve of Erika’s conduct, but the bulk of its ire is directed at the contemporary art world. And you know what? Fair.

Never underestimate Matt Johnson. I had low expectations for the prolific Canadian director’s seemingly one-for-them Anthony Bourdain biopic after seeing its hokey trailer. But as it turns out, the schmaltz and Bourdain of it all are mainly just a cover to make a solid coming-of-age in a Cape Cod kitchen period piece. Dominic Sessa does his moody young man Holdovers shtick to great effect, and Leo Woodall and Antonio Banderas give lively supporting performances as the devil and angel on young Bourdain’s shoulders.

Much has been made of the ways Jane Schoenbrun’s new film diverges from their previous effort, I Saw the TV Glow. But to me, the two films are flip sides of the same coin—interested in what it means to know yourself, accept yourself, and embrace the things you like. Teenage Sex and Death, the more hopeful and exuberant of the two, centers on hot young queer director Kris’s (Hannah Einbinder) attempt to revive the Camp Miasma franchise. When she pays a visit to the secluded home of original final girl Billy (Gillian Anderson), she gets more than she thought she was looking for—and the film takes great pleasure in muddying reality.

David Wain and his favorite fellow The State alums have put their spoofy spin on camp, rom-coms, and the Ten Commandments. Which leaves … The Wizard of Oz! The Dorothy of this absurd and absurdly funny new film is Gail (Zoey Deutch), a sweet midwestern bride-to-be who flies to Hollywood to find and bed her celebrity sex pass to even the score and save her marriage. It’s perfectly silly, with a deep cast of excellent performers who are down to clown.

Kane Parsons and Curry Barker have been getting all the wunderkind heat for their breakthrough debut features. But another 20-something, Elliot Tuttle, quietly crafted a far deeper and more mature two-hander for his own debut around the same time. In the film, convicted pederast Hank (a superb Reed Birney) hires a cam-boy who goes by Aaron Eagle (Kieron Moore) to pay him a house visit. But his motives are much stranger than sex, and what results is a tense, surprising dark night of the soul.

Kane Parsons’s Lynchian nightmare of infinite strip-mall liminal space haunted me in a deep way, conjuring feelings of pandemic-era time warp, modern isolation, and the discomforting tedium of life online. It’s a remarkably impressive debut—all the more so from someone so young—with tremendous production design, imaginative world-building, and several unbelievable set pieces.

As budgets for original stories continue to shrink, it’s becoming increasingly common for the bulk of a movie to be two characters in a room talking to each other. And you know what? When the two actors are Michaela Coel and Ian McKellen and the dialogue is as snappy as Ed Solomon’s is in Steven Soderbergh’s latest, that’s more than enough.

It’s invigorating when a movie reminds you that the medium is full of possibility. And Sophy Romvari’s debut feature does just that. The film begins as a fairly quotidian story of a Hungarian immigrant family living on Vancouver Island in the late 1990s. The main source of tension for the family is what to do about a misbehaving teenage son. In the second half of the film, Romvari takes a bold swing that transforms the film and expands our understanding of everything that came before. It’s a beautiful, assured, and understated work that’s lingered in my mind long after seeing it.

The hardest I’ve laughed at a scene from a movie this year came in the criminally under-seen first feature from Brandon Daley. The scene involves a beer bong, urine, and a protagonist who doesn’t know what alcohol tastes like. It’s reminiscent, in the best way, of the dumb-guy comedies of the ’90s and early 2000s. The rest of the movie, which revolves around a man with a crypto addiction that threatens to ruin his life, perfectly synthesizes that energy with the unrelenting anxiety of a Safdie thriller.

The first time I saw David Lowery’s Gothic chamber piece about a pop star (Anne Hathaway) reuniting with her original fashion designer (Michaela Coel) I fell deeply under the movie’s spell. The movie struck me as a perfect representation of the mysticism of creative collaboration—as well as a campy showcase for Hathaway’s most earnest instincts. On rewatch, some of the magic admittedly wore off, but there’s no denying the power of some of the film’s key scenes.

Video game adaptations have become Hollywood’s latest IP cash grab. But director Genki Kawamura is clearly after something else in bringing Exit 8 to the big screen. The game he’s adapted was hardly a big hit with widely beloved characters. Instead, it’s an opportunity to send viewers on a journey so repetitive and puzzling it becomes fraught with existential terror. Amid a never-ending, fluorescently lit subway tunnel, Kawamura stages a few dazzling set pieces and sprinkles in plenty of details to ponder—all of which produces concrete feelings and plenty of interpretations.

For the past dozen years, Floridians and some out-of-staters have flocked to the Everglades in hopes of catching and killing the most Burmese pythons. The Python Hunt Challenge was started as a way of confronting an invasive species wreaking havoc on native wildlife. So you might expect Xander Robin’s documentary about the event to be a Tiger King–esque melodrama full of kooky characters and dangerous animals. There are some of both, for sure. But Robin’s film is more soulful and less exploitative. In tracking various participants, he captures the struggle and meaning that can be found in a futile pursuit. And he also suggests that there are probably other, more direct culprits in the destruction of the Everglades.

Lucrecia Martel’s first documentary feature centers around the 2009 murder of Indigenous activist Javier Chocobar. It took nine years for the capitalist raiders who killed Chocobar to be tried in court. And the film shows how the incident was a product of the systematic dispossession of the Chuschagasta people Chocobar represented. Martel’s documentary, which zooms in on the people affected and zooms out to take a wider view of the case, is thorough, revealing, and heartbreaking.

It’s hard to believe that Pillion is director Harry Lighton’s first feature. This opposites-attract, BDSM love story set in London’s suburbs was a highlight of last year’s New York Film Festival. (Pillion also won Best Screenplay at Cannes in May.) After Colin (Harry Melling), a parking attendant who sings in a barbershop quartet, meets Ray (Alexander Skarsgård), a mysterious, leather-clad biker, the two begin a relationship that’s always on Ray’s terms and frequently uncomfortable. Lighton handles this sometimes absurd romance earnestly and with great care. The film avoids any temptation to push for a laugh or judge these characters. It’s apparent what both men are getting out of this relationship, as well as why it can’t work in the long term—a lesson that’s rendered with a little sorrow but also a surprising degree of hope.

This documentary absolutely haunted me. Natchez is directed by Suzannah Herbert, an expert chronicler of the American South, who turns her focus to a small town in Mississippi with a big antebellum-tourism industry. As the town’s sanitized version of southern history is disseminated by white homeowners, her film captures the tension between their antebellum-property tours and the efforts of the local Black residents to correct the record. As the film unfolds, Herbert slowly but powerfully shatters the fantasy of the nation’s past and exposes the malicious prejudices that remain.

Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie is perhaps the all-time high-wire act of indie filmmaking that makes you ask, How’d they do that? The movie is a technical triumph. But more importantly, the extraordinarily playful, idiosyncratic film is simply a really good time at the movies. In Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie, comedians Matt Johnson and Jay McCarrol revive their fictional counterparts from their late-aughts web series, Nirvanna the Band the Show, and send the two characters on a friendship-testing time-travel adventure. The stakes? Comically small. Matt and Jay need to secure a gig at Rivoli, a bar in Toronto. Still, I cared much more about their finding success than I ever have for a superhero’s battle to save the world.

I’ve never had such a smelly theatergoing experience as I did at Grace Glowicki’s imaginative, wacky, and deeply heartfelt new B movie, Dead Lover. The film’s distributor provides downright-nasty scratch-and-sniff stink-o-vision cards at select screenings, containing odors labeled everything from “BBQ Stink” to “Ghost Puke.” But even without the card, the film is so tactile that you will practically smell it anyway. Glowicki plays a lonely gravedigger who finds love, loses that love, and then goes to great lengths to revive them from the dead. Dead Lover is also shot in black-and-white, featuring delightfully handmade sets and costumes. It’s not everyone’s speed, but I had a blast.

There have been a lot—probably too many—movies about sad, failed artists. And yet, Simón Mesa Soto’s new film manages to feel new and original. It’s partially because of how specific and true his Colombian comedy feels. In A Poet, Oscar Restrepo (a brilliant Ubeimar Rios) is a middling poet and divorced father who can’t move forward with his life. He’s captive to his dream of writing a book, but he’s a heavy drinker with a stunted sense of responsibility. Everything changes when he meets a talented teenager, and he sets out to help her reach her potential. The film is very funny and even more cringey, but there’s a lot to appreciate in A Poet’s empathy for its pathetic protagonist.

This shattering docudrama from Kaouther Ben Hania utilizes real phone recordings to depict a traumatizing event during the war in Gaza: when the Israel Defense Forces killed a five-year-old Palestinian girl named Hind Rajab. The child was fleeing Gaza City with her family in January 2024 when their vehicle was shelled by an IDF tank. The drama primarily stations itself inside the emergency aid offices of the Palestine Red Crescent Society. As fictionalized workers at the organization receive calls from Rajab, who was trapped in her family’s car, they wade through maddening bureaucracy and regulations to try and rescue her. Ben Hania employs some controversial gimmickry to prove the film’s verisimilitude, but it’s hard to deny the film’s emotional power.

Few filmmakers are as attuned to the beauty of the natural world as Hlynur Pálmason. The director’s latest film observes an Icelandic family and the rural world they inhabit over many seasons following an event that changes the group’s dynamic. Anna (Saga Gardarsdottir), a sculptural artist, and Magnus (Sverrir Gudnason), a fisherman, have recently split up. What ensues is rarely eventful, but Pálmason imbues the small moments among the family—Anna and Magnus have three children—with so much specificity, truth, and sporadic surrealism that the film never lags. By the end, The Love That Remains winds up feeling momentous.

Miroirs No. 3 begins with a car crash in the German countryside. Although a piano player named Laura (Paula Beer) survives, what ensues feels like a dream. Laura is taken in by Betty (Barbara Auer), an older woman who lives near the site of the crash in an idyllic, sun-dappled cottage. Even after Laura has recovered from her accident, she stays, maintaining a mundane sort of fairy-tale existence. You may figure out what’s going on before Laura does as you watch Miroirs No. 3, but you’ll probably want to maintain the fantasy as Laura does. This slow, quiet little film from German director Christian Petzold is mesmerizing. Beyond its routine pleasures, Laura’s and Betty’s stories serve as an intriguing contemplation on the experience of grief.

It’s the summer of 2003, and 12-year-old Ben (Everett Blunck) is the newbie at a water-polo camp full of adolescent boys who know each other from the previous summer. First-time feature director Charlie Polinger captures the cinematic beauty—and also the brutality—of the sport. But it’s the moments out of the water when the games really begin. Ben is caught between wanting to be accepted among the popular crowd and not wanting to put down an outcast, whom the other boys have labeled as “the Plague.” It’s a nuanced depiction of childhood bullying. Plus, the chief bully, played by Kayo Martin, delivers one of the greatest child performances I’ve ever seen in a movie.

#197. The Under-$100 Gifts That Make Quiet Luxury Feel Effortless

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Luxury gifting doesn’t always have to come with a luxury price tag.

Quiet luxury has emerged as one of the most prominent aesthetics this year. With the viral premiere of FX’s Love Story at the start of the year, we saw a huge resurgence of Carolyn Bessette and her beloved aesthetic. Whether it be through her clean beauty routine or her minimalist wardrobe, it seems everyone has gotten on board with the quiet luxury aesthetic that she lived by.

If you find yourself shopping for the Carolyn Bessette in your life this holiday season, don’t panic; it doesn’t necessarily mean you need a luxury budget. I’ve searched high and low through beauty, home, and ready-to-wear gifts that align perfectly with the quiet luxury lifestyle, all under $100. Shop our favorites below—and don’t forget to give the gift wrapping its own quiet luxury treatment as well!

If you aren’t dry brushing by now, it’s time to add it to your skin care rotation. This luxe option from Tronque is a high-quality way to start.

You can never go wrong with gifting socks during the wintertime. Take this staple a step further with a lavish material like cashmere.

For anyone looking to upgrade their skin care routine, this LED gua sha takes you one step further by helping to promote lymphatic drainage and de-puff the face.

Forget about the large wallet and focus your attention on the card case. This snake-embossed variation from Tory Burch feels timelessly chic and makes for the perfect addition to a going-out bag.

Some luxury beauty staples need no introduction. Masque Vivant from Biologique Recherche is one of them, and for good reason; it leaves your skin with the most refreshing glow.

Perfect for the cooking connoisseur, this flavored olive oil is a great addition to anyone’s kitchen and makes for an easy way to add depth of flavor to any meal.

If you’re looking to add a little bit of luxury to your shower routine, this body oil is a lavish finishing step and leaves the skin feeling lustrous with a soft floral scent.

Candles may seem like a redundant gift, but it’s all about choosing the right ones. Gifting a candle from a luxury fragrance brand like Jo Malone makes for a much more elevated gift, and it also doesn’t hurt that their candles have a long-lasting scent.

This rose quartz crystal eye mask is just as pretty as it is practical. Leave it overnight in the fridge for the perfect way to wake your face up in the morning.

A facial mist is the perfect finishing touch to anyone’s skin care routine. This luxury staple from Augustinus Bader leaves the skin feeling hydrated and refreshed.

For the avid traveler or the skin care addict like myself, this vanity case makes for a glamorous way to store all of your countertop must-haves.

There are only a few routines that feel as luxurious as a deep soak. This honey bath oil from Laura Mercier makes a great complement to your bath time while leaving your skin ultra-soft with a light vanilla scent.

Consider this jewelry book box from Heaven Mayhem your jewelry’s most stylish hiding place.

Guerlain just made application effortlessly chic with this lipstick duo. The mirror compact packaged with the lipstick makes for a seamless application, and more importantly, you can look glamorous while doing it.

When it comes to the quiet luxury aesthetic and jewelry, it’s all about simplicity and attention to detail. This tassel necklace from Lovers and Friends is a perfect example of that, where minimalism makes a subtle statement.

A dazzling pair of hoops is a must for the glamorous woman on your list, and these gemstone-embellished beauties are quite the find.

Consider this the gift of a good skin day. This daily moisturizer from SkinCeuticals is a lavish gift for anyone looking to bring some luxury into their regimen.

The right sunglasses can make an outfit look instantly more luxurious. This pair from Le Specs is the perfect finishing touch that will really complement a chic look.

For those who love a night out, this clutch from Tuckernuck is an effortlessly chic addition to any ensemble.

This lavish home spray from Diptyque keeps a lasting scent that makes a space feel expensive.

#198. Timothée Chalamet Sweetly Cheers on Kylie Jenner As She Makes Her Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show Debut

And mom Kris Jenner has the funniest reaction

Kendall Jenner may not have walked the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show tonight, but another Jenner did: Kylie. The Khy founder made a surprise appearance on the catwalk tonight, joining veteran models like Adriana Lima, Alessandra Ambrosio, and Rosie Huntington-Whiteley, as well as darlings like Bella and Gigi Hadid and Devyn Garcia.

Kylie indeed looked angelic tonight in a silver diamond-covered bra dripping with more diamonds—the iconic Fantasy Bra—and a matching crystal-studded thong. Over the bottoms, she wore a flirty white miniskirt that perfectly coordinated with her massive white feather angel wings. While this is the entrepreneur’s first time walking the VS runway, she has already earned her angel wings—and we’re not surprised.

But even more incredible than seeing Kylie make her runway walk, was seeing her two biggest fans sitting front row to cheer her on: mom Kris Jenner and boyfriend Timothée Chalamet. The actor looked like the absolute sweetest, most supportive partner as he clapped, smiled wide, and excitedly cheered Jenner on. I mean, who wouldn’t? For the evening, he looked cool in a black long-sleeve top and inky sunglasses.

And of course, momager Kris was peak supermom, cheering on right beside him and even filming her youngest daughter with her iPhone. She looked like her fabulous self in a spotted black-and-white scarf look and her sleek black bob.

See their reaction to Kylie’s entrance below:

And while you’re at it, now that the show has wrapped, take a look back at all the fabulous runway looks, and all the stars who were in attendance tonight.

#200. We Tried 70+ Advent Calendars—These Are the Best for Men in 2026

Tested by Paul Rankin, Mary Henn and Daria Smith

Cheese, whiskey and pickles—oh, my! We tested nearly 100 options to find the best Advent calendars for men in 2026.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

If you’ve ever found yourself stumped while looking for the perfect gift for the men in your life, you’re not alone. Shopping for someone we love is often even harder than buying for a stranger. After all, there’s the added pressure of condensing your feelings for them into a single gift! That said, we found a hack that makes it so much easier: Advent calendars for men.

Finding the right Advent calendar for the man in your life is like giving them a whole bunch of gifts that span the season, and it takes surprisingly little effort! The hardest part? Securing the right Advent calendar for him. Sure, you can always gift him a chocolate Advent calendar. A classic is a classic for a reason, after all! But for men who prefer different flavors and hobbies, there are still plenty of options.

These days, there are Advent calendars for every interest. We tested over 70+ calendars for the 2026 season, including luxury Advent calendars and alcohol countdowns. From whiskey to beer, salty to spicy, we found the best Advent calendars for husbands, dads, grandpas and everyone else.

With the perfect mix of elegance and flavor, the Flaviar whiskey Advent calendar is our top pick for folks who frequently enjoy a nightcap. Not only does this luxury Advent calendar offer 24 flights of the world’s best whiskeys, but it also delivers one of the best experiences of all the calendars we’ve tested.

The 2026 theme, Museum of Flaviar, allows you to discover award-winning, curated 1.7-ounce samples of the world’s best drams. Each option comes paired with a work of art for an experience that’s as visual as it is flavorful! And, as if that’s not enough of a reason to preorder, you also get a tasting journal and two high-quality Glencairn glasses you can keep for future flight sampling.

“Whiskey samples include award winners and exclusive new releases,” says product tester Daria Smith. “Some whiskey vials come from bottles worth over $150. Not only does it include two Glencairn glasses, which are ideal for sharing each sample with a loved one, but the education-focused tasting journal includes information on each individual whiskey sample with space for personal tasting notes on each whiskey vial.”

We tried Flaviar’s whiskey Advent calendar in 2023, 2024 and 2025—and can confirm it’s still a stellar deal for serious spirit lovers. While we have yet to taste this year’s pick (it’s currently en route!), we expect it will be equally memorable.

Grab the milk! This 24-Day Fly By Jing Advent calendar is the calendar for you if you’re a spice fiend. Not only do you get to enjoy full-sized offerings of Fly By Jing’s famous flavors (hello, chili crisp), but there are inclusions here that you literally can’t find anywhere else. It’s quite the exclusive calendar for spice lovers!

Contents span spicy instant noodles, Fly by Jing’s original chili crisp and the brand’s signature Sweet & Spicy Zhong sauce. Inclusions hit every tastebud that matters: spicy, swicy and savory. You’ll sample everything from the brand’s sweet shallot sauce, to Sichuan hot honey and a BBQ spice rub. And, as noted before, each option is full-sized, so you can stock your cupboard for the foreseeable future!

While the calendar isn’t cheap at $175, it only includes full-sized jars and packages. I love Fly By Jing’s products (the chili crisp is a staple in my home), and the quality is just as I expect from them. And, considering you get nearly double the products you’d get in one of their gift sets at a similar price point, it’s kind of a steal!

We also tested the 12-Day version and find it a great substitute for budget-focused folks. That said, do note that the smaller version skips a few of the exclusives, like one of the ornaments, fancy chopsticks and a cute little spoon for your chili crisp. If you want to ensure you secure these premium gifts, we highly recommend splurging on the larger version!

Sweet? Check! Salty? Check! Spicy, salty, umami? Check, check, check! The 24 Days of Gourmet Nuts and Snacks calendar is for that friend or family member who’s always munching on something. With a range of flavors and textures that scratch any snacking itch, it’s easily the best Advent calendar for men who love a little treat. Chow down on Smoky BBQ Crunch one day, then enjoy a bag of Buttery Bliss Bites the next. There’s truly something in this Advent calendar for everyone!

Each generous portion of snacks comes in its own little foil pouch, ensuring each bite is fresh and full of texture. Some of my husband’s favorite bites include the spicy Pineapple Heatwave Chips and Truffle Umami Pretzel Pops, though there are also many more to explore. It is worth noting that while he loved most of the snacks, a few weren’t quite to his taste. However, the sheer variety and fun experience of trying new flavors makes it well worth the price.

Calling all brew heads! If bringing breweries from around the country straight to your door sounds better than a typical chocolate calendar, we recommend the GiveThemBeer Advent calendar. Like our favorite wine Advent calendars, this alcohol Advent calendar offers something more spirited than your typical Advent calendar. Plus, it’s designed for everyone, from IPA fans to stout and ale lovers!

This Advent calendar brings a favorite pastime to the comfort of your home. With craft beers from microbreweries across the U.S., it’s truly like a brewery tour—but you don’t even have to leave the couch. Just make sure to keep the box in the fridge to ensure every brew is chilled before opening! We tested the 2023, 2024 and 2025 versions, and pre-orders for 2026 ship early in November. We haven’t had the pleasure of enjoying this year’s assortment, but we’re sure it’s absolutely sip-worthy.

According to tester Pamela Bondurant, for folks who don’t have the time or money to take a tour of the nation’s microbreweries, this calendar is an easy winner.

“I love the diversity of beer included in this Advent calendar. There are stouts, IPAs, ales and more from every coast and some in between,” she says. “There’s no product list, so each day truly is a surprise when you pull your beer from the Advent calendar.”

If your giftee is absolutely obsessed with tangy treats, snag them an Advent calendar dedicated to…pickles?! While it might seem niche, this dill-icious countdown is one of Give Them Beer’s top sellers! The best part is that it comes stuffed with pickle-flavored treats and briny merch galore.

From pickle chips to pickle-flavored lip balm, each pucker-worthy pick inside this adult Advent calendar is bound to bring a smile to fans of the salty snack. Personally, I appreciate that in last year’s calendar not every day was an edible item. Inclusions like pickle-flavored lip balm and a pair of pickle socks helped break up the monotony and ensure that I don’t get sick of my favorite flavor!

Last year, my husband and I enjoyed unpacking pickle-flavored pretzels, mayo and other unexpected snacks like pickle pops and even pickle candy canes. It’s a fun Advent calendar that’s truly unique—I don’t think there’s anything else like it! Shipping for the 2026 calendar starts in late October, and we’re expecting this year’s version to impress just as much as last year’s.

The Cometeer Advent calendar is my absolute favorite for gifting. Not only does your recipient get to enjoy 24 specialty brews, but this one doesn’t require any special equipment—just hot or cold water! Cometeer coffee isn’t your typical stale instant coffee, either. Each flash-frozen capsule is frozen after being brewed, locking in all that delicious flavor. Just mix with boiling water for hot coffee. You can also thaw it and pour it over ice for iced coffee or combine with milk for a latte!

I am a big fan of anything that makes life a little easier during the hectic holiday season. And while I, of course, love to linger over a French press, some mornings call for speed! And that’s exactly what Cometeer coffee capsules achieve without sacrificing freshly brewed flavor. It’s an ingenious solution to instant coffee packets, and the brews actually taste good. We’ve tested this calendar for two years running, and it never fails to impress with its incredible value.

This year’s countdown is still on its way to our tester, but last year served up cozy holiday favorites, top-rated blends and exclusive releases. I enjoyed flavorful brews from brands like Winslow and Klatch coffees. Plus, each calendar comes with a tasting guide featuring information on each brew. The only downside? Since the capsules need to stay frozen, this Advent calendar will take up a bit of valuable freezer space.

Given my husband’s status as the “cheese guy” of my family, it’s no surprise that the Murray’s Advent calendar is a staple in our home year after year. Bursting with two pounds (!!!) of cheese and a number of delicious accompaniments, Murray’s countdown is a delightful pick for fans of pecorino, manchego and everything in between.

Enjoy decadently aged cheeses ranging from mild Gouda to sharp, flavorful English cheddar. Each one arrives in a generous serving, making it a fun experience to share with others. The calendar also comes with a cute cheese-centric Christmas print that makes it highly giftable. It’s packed and shipped carefully with ice packs and insulation, arriving at my door cold and fresh each year.

While the cheese itself is amazing, some days only have crackers or other pairings. Other offerings include Effie’s oat cakes and four sweet and spiced jellies. Because of this, I highly recommend you save some of the previous day’s cheese or wait until the next day to enjoy a pairing. The days with cheese were arguably the best, but finding other delicious accompaniments like jams and crackers broke up the monotony and added a fun pairing element.

Last year’s calendar did not disappoint, and the calendar is largely the same year-over-year, so we expect a similar experience for this year’s option. And, if he can’t wait to enjoy all the accoutrements together, he can always open it all at once for a full spread. Don’t worry—we won’t tell!

If he’s the designated “muddle man” of the house, this whiskey cube Advent calendar is bound to leave an impression. He’ll mix up 12 different drinks inspired by the 12 Days of Christmas carol for a truly immersive seasonal experience!

Unlike your typical alcohol Advent calendar, each of the 12 doors contain a small vial with two mixer sugar cubes. Just add warm water, muddle, pop in some ice and fill the glass with your favorite whiskey for a nice wind-down after the hustle and bustle of the holidays.

Each cube makes one drink, and there are two cubes per flavor, offering a total of 24 cubes to enjoy. Flavors span spiced and sweet, ranging from options like Partridge in a Pear Tree (pear, cinnamon, and lemon with fig and cinnamon bitters) to Calling Birds (cranberry, chocolate, almond, and spiced cranberry bitters). At under $50, this budget-friendly find makes an excellent gift for whiskey lovers!

Great style is all about the details. An interesting texture, an unexpected print, or a particularly good fit can make even the most familiar wardrobe staples feel more considered. And if you’re looking to bring a little more personality to your everyday rotation, Ted Baker’s latest collection is the place to start.

Taking inspiration from London’s historic Victorian buildings, the collection draws on the concept of ornate interiors and rich artistic history. These influences come through in geometric stitching, painterly florals, intricate patterns, and a mix of colors that range from soft neutrals to deeper, moodier shades.

The result is a lineup of modern menswear that feels distinctive without being tricky to wear. From textured polos and printed shirts and knits to versatile outerwear, the seven pieces ahead—available at Bloomingdale’s—offer plenty of ways to update your wardrobe for fall and beyond.

A long-sleeve polo is a fall essential, but this one has a little more personality thanks to its rich olive color and intricate geometric stitching. Wear it with tailored trousers for the office or dark denim and loafers on the weekend.

For days when a basic button-down feels a little too, well, basic, reach for this crosshatch style. The textured finish and weightier fabric make it particularly well-suited to fall, whether you wear it open over a T-shirt or buttoned up with chinos.

A sporty jacket is a great way to make more tailored pieces feel relaxed, and this navy bomber strikes just the right balance between elegance and ease. The quilted sleeves add a bit of structure, while the streamlined cut works equally well with casual weekend clothes or layered over a workday button-down and trousers.

A bold knit is one of the easiest ways to bring some interest to a simple sweater-and-trousers combination. This taupe crewneck features an oversized, dark floral motif that looks great on its own with jeans, but becomes an especially sharp choice with a blazer layered on top for the office or an event.

Lean into the classic country-club aesthetic with this blue polo featuring a contrast collar and ribbed trim. The waffle stitching gives it more depth than your standard short-sleeve style, and the color pairs particularly well with cream, navy, khaki, and other neutrals.

Sometimes, the jacket is the outfit. This black-and-white floral jacquard design certainly makes a case for a statement jacket, especially when the rest of your look stays simple. Try it over a plain crewneck sweater, easy tee, or button-down with dark pants for contrast.

Whether you live somewhere warm enough for short sleeves year-round, or have a sunny getaway on the calendar, this playful duck-print shirt deserves a spot in your rotation. The black-and-white palette makes the whimsical pattern surprisingly easy to wear with simple trousers, chinos, or shorts.
