#202. TIME’s 2026 Best Inventions List Includes 3 Game-Changing Baking Tools

Your sourdough hobby just got a lot easier.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Baking at home is a labor of love. From tending a sourdough starter to meticulously crimping pie crust, each recipe takes finesse and precision. Thankfully, new technological innovations make home baking easier—and many of them appear on TIME’s Best Inventions of 2026.

Each year, the publication rounds up the latest groundbreaking products that make life easier. The 2026 edition spans almost every industry, from tech to healthcare to household goods. But some of the most notable inclusions target home bakers. Here’s what made the list:

Sourdough gets its signature tang from a starter, which needs regular feeding and maintenance to keep the yeast and healthy bacteria alive. And anybody who had a sourdough phase during the pandemic knows how tedious that process can be. That’s where the Sourdough Sidekick comes in.

This compact countertop appliance, made in partnership with King Arthur Baking Company and FirstBuild, automates the process of maintaining sourdough starter. It features a water tank, flour hopper, and mixing paddle that can manage the feeding process for up to a week. The digital display and connected mobile app let you fine-tune settings or choose a preset mode that does the hard work for you.

Since the Sourdough Sidekick debuted in June of this year, home bakers have given it rave reviews, calling it “revolutionary” and “a dream come true.” You can buy it from King Arthur Baking for $179.95.

If you like the idea of baking fresh sourdough but aren’t committed to maintaining a starter long term, Leaven offers a new shortcut. Most store-bought yeast helps your dough rise, but doesn’t bring any unique flavors to the table. Leaven’s Instant Sourdough, on the other hand, offers similar lift with the same live cultures you’d find in a real sourdough starter.

The creators used DNA sequencing to isolate the exact microbes you’d find in a starter and replicated them as a shelf-stable powder—no feeding required. Each pouch can be used for up to eight recipes. While it’s not a 1:1 substitute for store-bought yeast, Leaven offers a detailed guide with conversion charts and a lineup of beginner-friendly recipes for convenient sourdough treats.

Leaven currently sells a three-pack of its Instant Sourdough for $19.99.

After using all of your elbow grease to knead a loaf of bread, the last thing you want to do is spend more time scrubbing bits of dough from the sides of your mixing bowl. Instead of just leaving it to soak overnight (aka procrastinate), you can use this new cleaning product called Dough Dissolve.

Most dish soap is designed to tackle grease and other fat-based residue on dishes. Dough Dissolve is a cleansing gel that instead uses the enzyme amylase to specifically target starches. A few pumps of Dough Dissolve on your dirty dishes, plus a quick 10-minute soak, will dissolve stuck-on stains with little to no scrubbing.

You can get your hands on a bottle directly from Dough Dissolve for $23.39.

#204. Leon Bridges: I’m Still ‘Doing My Thing After All This Time’

Following the release of his new album, Happiness Anytime, we caught up with the musician to hear about his personal style, his performer persona, and the one trick he hasn’t busted out onstage—yet.

If the saying “you’re only as good as your last album” is true, then Leon Bridges is pretty darn good right now. His fifth studio album Happiness Anytime just dropped—a deep blend of soul, Afrobeat, disco, and Brazilian jazz influences—and the musician is making sure his style fits the bill.

“My album is so vibrant and joyous—I wanted my aesthetic to reflect that,” he tells me. “I’ve been trying to challenge myself during this process to incorporate more colors. Even the sneakers are something new. I used to never wear sneakers on stage, but they’re so easy to dance in.”

And boy, can the man move! A few days prior to our chat, I watched him hit a groovy spacewalk across the stage during his album’s launch party at the Music Hall of Williamsburg, hosted by Bulleit Frontier Whiskey—which he nodded to in his song “Light the Way.”

While Bridges might be tearing it up onstage, he’s keeping it pretty low-key when he’s not performing. His upcoming global tour is no easy feat, and learning Bridges is a bit introverted makes it all the more impressive. “Something that’s been helpful is finding moments of solitude,” he says. “These days, I’ve been a little bit more of a recluse. Going out a lot can be really, really distracting. I’m a simple man. In my downtime, I like to watch the ’90s cartoons I grew up on. I still watch the Batman: The Animated Series, Animaniacs—all that stuff.”

We talk about more than cartoons, of course. From his onstage style to his feelings on the new album, here’s what he had to say.

“During this whole run, I’ve been dressing down with a lot of windbreakers, but I’ve also been incorporating dancehall reggae style. Really, anything that’s comfortable enough to move in on stage works for me.

“My stage persona is definitely a different thing. In my personal life, I’m more of a shy, quiet, reserved person. On stage, I really try to be more charismatic and give people a great show. It still feels natural, but I think it’s okay to be able to turn it on and off. When I’m off the stage, I love a simple, Western, ’70s-era fit. And when I’m performing, I’m wearing custom fits and stuff. My favorite fit I wore was at Stagecoach. That was one of my favorite festivals I’ve ever played in. Chrome Hearts made me a custom leather fit, and that was easily the coolest thing I’ve ever worn in my life. I kept the pants, and they also made me some denim sets. I have a black one and a blue one.”

“I still get anxiety before going on stage, but I overcome it by telling myself that I’ve done this a million times. As soon as I step on stage, all of the anxiety goes away. Being there with my band and having that support and the camaraderie really helps. That’s been awesome in general; we’ve been trying to reinvent and change the show, and I really love this new configuration—having Adrian Quesada on the turntables, background singers, and my horn section has been really fresh.”

“Happiness Anytime is a healing album. It’s all about togetherness. It’s a reflection of the space that I was in while I was making it. For the first time, I felt like I wasn’t just creating to survive; I was creating to listen. And I think that’s a testament to working with [producers and musicians] Josh [Lloyd-Watson] and Lydia [Kitto]. It’s a great body of work. I love it, and I just hope everybody who listens to it does, too.

“When I name my songs, I try to find the phrase within the lyrics that I feel is the most encompassing of what the song is about. ‘Tears of Joy’ is probably one of my favorite songs on the album, and it’s really just a celebration of my trajectory and longevity. I’m just grateful to still be here doing my thing after all this time. With this new set, it’s mostly from the new album. In the past, it’s been tough to play the new stuff because people still need time to soak in the music. But with this new music, I feel like the tunes have an undeniable vibe that people are already moving and dancing to. So yeah, it’s been really awesome to see the response to the new music. I feel like it’s catching on pretty quick.”

“One thing I fear is putting out a body of work that doesn’t resonate with people. I guess I’m always chasing an album that has the same effect as my first album. But the awesome thing is that I never really expected those tunes to have the success that they have. I feel like some of my fans are married to my first album, and I think throughout the years, I’ve probably alienated some fans. But I do appreciate that my fans can still grow with me as I’m changing up the music and changing up my sound.

“I still really love ‘River.’ It’s a song that I didn’t even think would make my first album, but it’s really amazing to see how significant it is for people. I just love a good stripped-down moment. I think it shows humanity: none of us are perfect, but it’s always good to strive to put love out into the world and chase things that are meaningful.”

“Man, a lot of people don’t know that I can moonwalk. It’s cliché, so I never do it, but I gotta whip it out one of these days.”

#205. I Indulged in Rare, 135-Year-Old Wine at This Sonoma Resort

In Hotels With Great Taste, we’re pulling back the curtain for a peek at the “special sauce” that hotels use to create memorable, meaningful culinary experiences for their guests.

Look closely at the lodgings that make up Dawn Ranch and you’ll notice they’re actually a patchwork of historic structures in different shapes and sizes. Each building at the luxe 15-acre Russian River resort, which is nestled amongst the towering redwoods in the petite town of Guerneville, California, is linked to a different era of the property’s past.

Built in 1905, it was originally Murphy’s Ranch, a getaway for well-to-do families that operated for seven decades. Later it served for more than 20 years as the pioneering gay resort Fife’s. Today, it’s a refined wine country escape that exists at the crossroads of nature and high-end luxury. The hotel is situated in a floodway, which limits construction for safety purposes, so since 1993 the site’s various owners haven’t been able to build anew; renovating ad infinitum has proven to be just dandy though.

In fact, this limitation turns out to be central to Dawn Ranch’s retro, summer camp-adjacent charm, which feels like a happy throwback even with its modernized facilities and amenities. Spectacularly refurbished in 2023, the current upscale iteration features 81 California-cool rooms, a tremendous spa, a fine-dining restaurant that may very well become impossible to book once word gets out, and a thoughtful, dynamic wine program that highlights some of the world’s most unique bottles.

When it comes to bunking, you have choices that span a hodgepodge of rustic-chic cabins, chalets, cottages, bungalows, and glamping tents. On the main campus, cabins are cozy and compact, while the cottages and chalets offer more space. Most include private outdoor decks, equally ideal for taking in a morning cuppa or an evening tipple. The bungalows are the roomiest accommodation, outfitted for families and large groups with two bedrooms, two baths, a full kitchen, and gas fireplaces. Across the street, the resort’s Grove campus offers more options, which range from snug single-room affairs to spacious two bedrooms.

They’re all scattered amongst the tree-filled property’s sycamores and redwoods, so traipsing to your room feels like a walk in the forest. Inside, the aesthetic is a study in NorCal quiet luxury, with plenty of smooth blonde wood, layered textiles, and eclectic furniture pieces, plus Parachute linens and Le Labo bath goodies.

More adventurous guests will appreciate the smartly furnished glamping tents, situated in Dawn Ranch’s 120-year-old apple tree orchard. The walls may be canvas, but the beds feature the same Bear hybrid mattresses as those in Dawn Ranch’s more conventional rooms. You will, however, have to share a bathhouse—albeit an extremely nice one—with your fellower glampers.

No matter where you sleep, make sure you lay eyes on the resort’s namesake, a 70-year-old pair of rare dawn redwoods located near the pool on the main campus.

The Lodge at Dawn Ranch, which houses the hotel’s main dining, bar, and lounge areas, manages a laid-back vibe that nonetheless feels rarefied and celebratory, with plush mauve-colored banquettes and dim romantic lighting.

But food is the real draw: Co-executive chefs (and husband-and-wife team) Ignacio “Nacho” Zuzulich and Juliana Thorpe center a nine-course, $155 tasting menu informed both by their respective Argentinian and Brazilian backgrounds and their experience cooking in lauded kitchens from Mugaritz in Spain to Napa Valley’s Meadowood resort. A truncated version of the tasting menu is served at the bar for $90.

Seasonal Golden State ingredients take top billing. On a recent visit, corn was a standout, taking the form of a delicate tostada set atop a fire-roasted corn custard. Festooned with the marigold-like flowering herb huacatay, it conveyed an impossibly large, flawless lobe of Santa Barbara uni.

In the morning, don’t skip breakfast at the Lodge, which is best taken on the sprawling outside deck. Soft scrambled eggs with avocado and furikake on homemade brioche are straightforward but deeply effective, while the cinnamon rolls glossed in cream cheese frosting are the perfect excuse to eat dessert before noon.

When drinking, whether in the dining room or bar, vino is the move. This is wine country, after all. The handwritten “Sommelier’s Notebook” dispenses with formality, breaking wines into playful categories like “The Wild Ones,” “Extrovert Whites,” and “Quiet Elegance.” You’ll have plenty of fun ordering by the bottle or glass; if you’re after just a taste, some offerings are available in one-ounce pours.

But for the deep-pocketed, the $400 Decades Wine Pairing is a voyage through time and space, guiding you through wines bottled across generations. The offerings frequently shift, but this past summer, the oldest pour was an intensely molasses-forward D'Oliveiras Verdelho Madeira, first put under cork in 1891.

With its decadent syrup-like texture and vibrant acidity, the Madeira made for a complex complement to the tasting menu’s show-stopping dessert course, which presented local peaches in three manners: a quenelle of peach sorbet; a crystal cupful of peach nectar; and a tart of roasted peach jam and white chocolate ganache, topped with intricately woven, paper-thin peach slivers and served alongside a peach sabayon.

Best of all, returning to my cottage after dinner required only a brief, tipsy walk through the redwoods, the stars lighting my way.

Kylie Jenner may have surprised us with her debut at the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show, but sister Kendall Jenner did not make it after all. The supermodel was notably missing from the runway, which was graced not only by her sister, but also by her besties and fellow supers Gigi and Bella Hadid, as well as many other angels.

A couple of days ago, the lingerie brand shared a list of the models confirmed to be walking the runway, and Kendall was not in it, which left fans thinking that she would be skipping the event once again. And indeed she did.

Kendall walked the show again in 2016, earning her wings, and returned to the VS runway in 2018. As fans know, the show went on hiatus for a few years after that, and when it returned, in its new and improved shape, in 2024, Kendall did not return with it.

This year, the model lineup included the Hadids as well as season angels Alessandra Ambrosio and Adriana Lima, and newer darlings like Devyn Garcia and Barbara Palvin.

#208. Lasagna-Vibes Zucchini Skillet

For years, one of my go-to dinners in the summer was zucchini lasagna, where zucchini is used in place of noodles. It’s delightful, but it’s also very labor-intensive, requiring you to slice the zucchini into long, thin planks, salt each individual plank, wipe each individual plank, and then layer the zucchini “noodles” with ricotta, sauce, and mozzarella. Now I have far too many children to be salting individual planks of zucchini—so I make this. It’s a dump-and-go skillet meal that has all of those favorite flavors in a way, way quicker and easier format.

Read More: Finding My Way Back to the Kitchen After Giving Birth

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. ground turkey and cook, breaking up into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until mostly cooked through with only a little pink remaining, about 4 minutes. Add 3 medium zucchini (about 20 oz.), halved lengthwise, sliced crosswise ⅛" thick, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt; season with freshly ground black pepper. Increase heat to high and cook, stirring often, until meat is cooked through and no longer pink and zucchini is tender, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium and stir in one 14.5-oz. can tomato sauce, 2 tsp. Italian seasoning, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. onion powder, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and half of 1 cup thinly sliced basil leaves. Taste zucchini mixture and season with more salt and pepper if needed. Swirl in spoonfuls of 4 oz. whole-milk ricotta (about ½ cup), then sprinkle 4 oz. mozzarella, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup), over. Reduce heat to low, cover pan, and cook until mozzarella is melted, about 4 minutes.

Top zucchini mixture with remaining basil and crushed red pepper flakes (if using) to serve.

#211. The 10 Best Running Brands, According to Editors and Runners

You can count on these brands for quality gear.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

A HUGE PERK of running is that it doesn’t require specialized equipment like shinguards or sticks to get you out there. But while you can technically go for a run in just about anything, there's a huge difference in logging miles in any old clothes and gear that’s specifically designed for the sport.

The best running brands offer gear with features to support your efforts, including sweat-wicking fabrics, cuts that won’t get in the way of your stride, and strategic air panels to keep you as cool and dry as possible. Go for a run in a plain cotton T-shirt and then later do the same workout in a running singlet—the feel and possibly even your performance will not be equal.

If you’re new to running, it’s easy to get overwhelmed by all the options for running shoes, running shorts, and running jackets out there, and some are admittedly better than others. But slipping into dedicated performance gear created for runners will go a long way toward helping you feel comfortable on the road or trail, ultimately allowing you to push yourself harder and faster.

As seasoned runners, we’ve logged plenty of miles in gear from a range of running brands. Based on our experience, these have proven themselves to be worth your time and money.

To find the best running brands, our fitness and commerce teams have spent years testing some of the most popular running brands. Men’s Health editors and writers have worn gear during intense training sessions, speed workouts, long runs, and race days to see how well they held up to regular use.

We tested shirts for breeziness and sweat-wicking capabilities, along with performance shorts for comfort. Because the right cold-weather gear is crucial during the winter months, we analyzed how well thermal tights and base layers blocked out frigid temperatures without leading to overheating.

After that, we narrowed the field down to the 10 best running brands based on quality, feel, fit, durability, and value. These are the brands that consistently make it to the top of our pile and show up to support everything from training to races.

Seen Above: Lululemon Pace Breaker Linerless Short

Lululemon was a pioneer in the athleisure market, largely thanks to its yoga gear and leggings. But the brand has grown since then, including a thoughtful expansion of its menswear. Lululemon isn’t the first place people think of when it comes to running gear, but there’s plenty in the mix worth considering—especially for daily training.

The brand’s Pace Breaker Linerless Short is a favorite. It ditches the built-in liner found in many running shorts to allow room for your preferred running underwear or compression gear, creating a custom feel. The short is also lightweight and stretchy for a barely-there feel. Lululemon’s Metal Vent Tech Short-Sleeve Shirt is another winner in our book, with its highly breathable construction and refusal to cling to your body, even when you’re dripping in sweat. These will earn a spot in your heavy running gear rotation.

Like other Lululemon gear, the brand’s running clothes can be worn while strolling down the street or to the gym without a second thought. It’s versatile and high-performance, giving you plenty to work with.

Read more: The Best Running Shoes, Tested by Editors

Hoka first grabbed the attention of runners with its footwear. Hoka shoes are max cushioned shock-absorbers with a serious fan base, but the brand has quietly built an arsenal of gear to support more than your feet on runs. Hoka offers a little of everything, including a heavy selection of lightweight gear.

The Race-Day Split Short has a classic semi-split leg and feather-light fabric for a breezy feel when you want to go fast. There’s also the SkyFlow Wind Jacket that’s water- and wind-resistant without weighing you down. But the Everyday Run line shines with its lightweight, breathable FlyLite material and smart side vents to dispel heat.

We’re partial to the EveryRun Short Sleeve, which comes in a slew of matchable shades and features bonded seams that won’t cause chafing, even with high mileage. This is the shirt to grab for treadmill runs, muggy days, or if you just happen to run hot.

Read more: The Best Walking Shoes, Tested by Editors

Seen Above: Brooks Momentum Thermal Hoodie

In an industry of flashy players, Brooks is a solid workhorse. The brand focuses heavily on supportive footwear and gear that will last, only making subtle tweaks and changes to its core offerings over time. Like its shoes, Brooks’ running apparel isn’t showy—it’s comfortable, smartly designed, and matches nearly everything, providing a range that you can hold onto for years.

Take the brand’s Thermal Reflective Tight, with its four-way stretch, brief liner to hold you in, and hidden zip pocket in back with room for your phone and other essentials. The Dash 2-in-1 Short has an internal fitted, breathable liner with a hidden side pocket to keep your phone close to you and out of view.

This season, Brooks launched its Momentum line, including the cozy Momentum Thermal Hoodie. The top feels lightweight on, with a scuba hood and thumbholes for a secure, cold-weather-blocking fit. The built-in odor resistance is a perk you’ll appreciate over time and repeat use, too.

Swiss brand On originally built a name for itself with its lightweight, springy, and highly cushioned footwear. But the company eventually expanded beyond shoes to create a robust selection of gear that’s a solid choice for pounding the pavement and grabbing coffee with your running buddy afterward.

On provides plenty of moisture-wicking fabrics that won’t leave you looking like a running puddle of sweat, along with high-visibility reflective elements for navigating high-traffic areas. On’s aesthetic also crosses over into streetwear, giving you more life out of your gear beyond just running.

Everyday performance shorts, highly breathable T-shirts, and lightweight, waterproof jackets provide plenty to work with. On uses a range of colorways, from basic black to can’t-miss neon, allowing you to choose your preferred aesthetic and visibility. We’re fans of the Performance Long-T, a versatile piece designed for cold weather running. It uses the brand’s proprietary DryTec fabric to pull sweat away from your body while still keeping you warm, with subtle reflective elements all over.

Seen Above: Adidas adi365 Iconic 1/2 Zip Top

You can blow some serious cash loading up on running gear, and the same is true at Adidas. But in addition to some wallet-busters, there’s plenty of inexpensive essentials you can load up on at a fraction of what you’ll spend elsewhere. This gear still offers much of the same high-tech, sweat-wicking fabrics as other brands, just with a lower price tag. The throwback, legacy vibe is nice, too.

A solid example is the adi365 Iconic 1/2 Zip Top, which uses Adidas’ Climacool fabric to wick away sweat while keeping you warm. Thumbholes help keep sleeves in place, and zippered pockets prevent your important stuff from spilling out mid-stride. If you prefer to run in shorts, the adi365 Iconic shorts have a loose, breezy fit with hidden zippered and stash pockets—and they’re just $35.

Running tights, sweat-wicking T-shirts, and more are significantly cheaper than many other well-known brands. If you’re willing to spend a little more, though, the Adizero Running Blaze Jacket has a reflective interior inspired by emergency blankets handed out at cold-weather marathons to retain heat without weighing you down.

Trail running is a completely different animal from road running, making it important to have the right gear. Patagonia answers the call with a slew of Fair Trade products designed to support and protect as you navigate nature and its unpredictability.

Patagonia focuses on minimizing weight while maximizing technical performance to help shield you from things like pop-up storms without weighing down runs. This gear is highly weather resistant to block out wind, rain, and snow—basically, whatever you might encounter on the trail.

The brand’s Houdini Jacket sets the standard for windbreakers, using tough micro-denier ripstop nylon to block out wind and light rain. Still, it only weighs 3.7 ounces and can be folded into its own pockets when it’s not in use. There’s also no shortage of cold-weather tights and technical vests to choose from. Worth noting for budget shoppers: Patagonia offers a “shop used” button on most of its gear to offer similar styles at a reduced price.

Seen Above: Nike Dri-FIT 5" Brief-Lined Running Shorts

Nike has carved out a name for itself in lots of different areas, but it still has no shortage of performance gear. The brand leans heavily into technical fabrics that support all areas of your race, from sprints to marathons.

Nike’s Dri-FIT fabric is specially designed to wick sweat away from your skin to the outer layer of your gear, where it dissipates to keep your clothes from soaking against your skin. But the newer AeroSwift line was specifically created for race day. This line features Dri-FIT ADV technology for ultra sweat-wicking, packaged in ultra-light fabrics with strategically placed mesh panels for extra airflow. Many clothes in the line also have drop-in pockets to hold things like gels and your phone.

There’s a lot to choose from, but we’re also partial to the AeroSwift Men's Dri-FIT ADV Running 1/2-Length Tight as an alternative to looser running shorts. Its second-skin fit is supportive but breathable, with smart details most wouldn’t think of, like a non-reflective finish on logos to protect against race-day flash photography.

Read more: Our Multi-Editor Review Of The Nike Metcon 10

Seen Above: Under Armour UA Base 3.0 Leggings

Most running brands will offer some gear to keep you comfortable in cold weather. But Under Armour has built a cult following with its ColdGear line. These compressive tops and tights use dual-layer fabric to hold in heat without adding bulk. While the interior fabric is warm and brushed, it still wicks away sweat and dries quickly. As a result, you won’t end up freezing in the cold during your cool-down.

UnderArmor has a numbered ColdGear Base line that delivers increasing insulation and warmth as the numbers increase. So, the UA Base 4.0 ¼ zip is one of the brand’s warmest tops for freezing temperatures, while the ColdGear Compression Mock Long Sleeve is designed for the cold, but not the tundra.

We reach for the ultra-warm UA Base 3.0 leggings on below-freezing runs. It has four-way stretch and a secure fit for your comfort, with built-in odor control to keep your bottoms smelling fresh. Layer it under other pants or wear it as-is.

Janji is a brand that’s big on sustainability and social consciousness, appealing to a certain group of runners. But Janji has a wide range of products to suggest you should support this brand for more than just its mission.

Janji is all about breathable materials, with the brand’s incredibly light and airy AFO (“airflatout”) fabric being a favorite. (You can find it in the Middle Running Short, along with plenty of others.) Janji also leans into naturally breathable fabrics, like merino. Case in point: The brand’s Rover Merino Half Zip harnesses merino wool’s natural properties like airiness, thermoregulation, and odor resistance, in a high-performance, versatile top.

Many Janji bottoms offer multi-pocket waistbands to house your phone, gels, and keys, without bouncing all over the place as you run. The brand also gets props for its five-year “run everywhere” guarantee, which promises to repair or replace your gear if anything gets ripped, torn, or broken within five years due to a defect in workmanship or material.

Seen Above: Satisfy AmbientWarp 5" Unlined Shorts

Most running gear provides a certain look and feel that’s immediately identifiable as running apparel. But Satisfy bucks the trend with a range of unique clothes you wouldn’t automatically think were for runners—or athletes at all.

Take the brand’s AmbientWarp 5" Unlined Shorts. While they have a paint-splattered denim look, they’re actually made from Satisfy’s AmbientWarp fabric that’s lightweight, stretchy, and dries fast just like your favorite running shorts. There’s also the AmbientWarp River Shirt, which looks like something you’d wear to a Post Malone show but features the same high-performance fabric as the shorts we just mentioned. It also offers smart features like dual pockets in front to access essentials quickly, along with pockets in back for stuff you want to tote but can deal with later.

Satisfy gear admittedly isn’t cheap, but it offers a unique level of style you won’t see at your average 5K.

There is no set style you need to follow with running gear, but many brands will offer up gear with similar silhouettes: form-fitting tights, vented shorts, singlets and breathable tops, and windbreakers. Each brand has its own aesthetic and go-to colorways, giving you some variation to choose from. If you really want to buck convention, consider tossing in some unique pieces from Satisfy.

This is at the core of what the best running brands can provide. Look for features you can lean on mid-run like thumb holes in long sleeves, zippered pockets, and breathable fabrics. Lightweight fabrics are also a plus, even with cold-weather gear. Ultimately, your running gear shouldn’t cross your mind during training or races.

Fit can be a personal preference. Some people prefer loose-fitting, breezy shorts, while others would rather have second-skin options. However, running gear is often more tightly fitted than clothes designed for other sports for aerodynamics. In general, you may find that you prefer gear that’s tight or offers a weightless feel for your comfort.

It depends. You can get as much life out of a $35 pair of running shorts as you do from something significantly more expensive. Eventually, the elastic in the waistband will wear down or break, signaling that it’s time for a new pair. But while I still have inexpensive running tops I’ve consistently worn for more than a decade, the gear that gets the heaviest rotation tends to be the most expensive. These are the clothes that have thoughtful features like zippered pockets, flat seams that won’t cause chafing, and high-performance fabrics. You can generally expect to spend more ($75 and up) on running tights and cold-weather tops compared to running shorts. And, when you find inexpensive gear you like, stock up.

#213. Tom Colicchio Just Joined The Growing Backlash Against The Michelin Guide

A new report has chefs and diners questioning the iconic restaurant guide.

Pop into any food-related Reddit thread these days, and you’ll find people questioning the relevance of the Michelin Guide. What was once considered the Mount Everest of restaurant accolades seems to be losing its luster in recent years—and it’s now under even greater attack after a report accused the prestigious awards of using AI to write its latest Dallas guide.

For background, Michelin updated its Texas guide last week, adding new restaurants in the Dallas area. D Magazine reportedly conducted an investigation with academic experts and AI detection software and concluded that most of the Dallas additions were written with AI.

While Michelin has denied the allegations, the accusation has reignited the conversation about the guide's relevance today.

“The guide was how you found out about the best of the best back in the day, now you can easily figure out what’s going on in the culinary world...Now we have Instagram and YouTube,” wrote one person on Reddit.

“It’s still relevant. But it’s no longer the Oscars for food,” another person agreed.

“It’s lost some credibility as more people started to find out that it’s a “pay-to-play” marketing process in the cities that are reviewed. As travel [influencer] content has increased over time, people are realizing that Michelin leaves out a lot of great restaurants in cities that don’t participate,” one person said, referring to the fact that tourism boards and destination marketing groups sometimes pay Michelin to bring the Guide to their region. Michelin says those partners don’t control the restaurant selections, though the arrangement has raised questions about independence.

And this was all before the big AI of it all. Even celebrity chef Tom Colicchio thinks the Michelin Guide should be relegated to the past. “It’s time to start ignoring this guide,” he commented on D Magazine’s social media post.

While many people echo Colicchio’s sentiments, others still defend the guide.

“AI detection software is anything but bulletproof...Making accusations based on those is quite literally like calling someone a witch because she floats in water,” one person said on Reddit.

“WHO CARES??? It’s a writing aide…not a controversy. Nothing about the use of AI makes the inspection notes any less real or accurate,” another person commented.

The consensus: People are divided. Many will still consult the Michelin Guide before traveling, whether the AI allegation is true or not, while others look to more modern sources like social media. Time will tell how well the prestigious guide holds up.

#214. The 7 Hottest Watches in the World Right Now

From the Seiko Panda to the Rolex Perpetual Padellone, these are the timepieces that people are really talking about.

It's been a good year in the watch world. Yes, we've had some flops and the usual conveyor belt of minor facelifts launched with the fanfare of royal babies (a slightly lighter blue dial? You spoil us!). But amid the noise, there's been much signal worth tuning into.

The most influential watch of all time? Perhaps. Gérald Genta's masterpiece, the Patek Philippe Nautilus, marked its 50th anniversary with a trio of ultra-thin editions powered by the 240 movement, which is normally found in the dressier Calatrava.

Aesthetically, the anniversary models tack close to Genta's design—any tweaks to the porthole case or integrated bracelet would be sacrilege, mind—but there are some material differences. As in, the materials are different. Where the original ushered in the age of luxury stainless steel watches, here we get the sports style but precious substance; your pick between white gold or platinum. Well, we say take your pick. Good luck finding even one, let alone a choice.

Due in November, but leaked last month, Casio's newest G-Shock hasn't just got us excited because the brand doesn't really do full analogs. That porthole-shaped case, those broad shoulders, they remind us of something…

We're chalking this one up as a birthday tribute to Patek. And we'll also take it as a gift to us, because from around $135, it's a lot of watch for not a lot of money: 200m water resistance, shockproof magnetic hands so it's as tough as any of G-Shock's digitals, a 30-minute stopwatch, and a special battery-saving mode that stretches its runtime to five years (about half the length of a Nautilus waitlist, then). We'll take the resin model in egg yolk yellow, please and thank you.

Rolex is not a surprise-drop brand. So when the Padellone arrived in September, with no hoo and limited ha, collectors sat up (for context, the Crown's last off-cycle release was the Daytona launched at the 100th Le Mans, which got those same collectors rather frothy).

The Padellone is full of collector in-jokes, not least the name, which means “frying pan” in Italian. That moniker was originally bestowed on this watch's inspiration, the 8171, because of its wide case (well, for the 1950s) and domed dial. It also had a moonphase and complete calendar, which is upgraded here to an annual—it automatically corrects for 30/31 months, only needing manual intervention between February and March. An especially neat touch is that all three bits of the calendar jump at midnight. When you first get it on your wrist, you'll spend a few late nights watching that little bit of magic.

Until an official Marmite collab comes along (and considering the watch industry's love of a tie-up, it must be imminent) this is the kind of collector's dream that half the people who see it will think only a mother could love.

Because whatever your thoughts on Jeff Koons's inflatables, a collaboration between the world's most expensive living artist and Switzerland's master of the press cycle was always going to generate heat. Even if it's not a slam dunk for us aesthetically, we do dig the colors and fun details—like the balloon sculpture dog that counterweights the second hand.

We've been suckers for the Black Bay since 2012, when it formed part of the relaunched Tudor's first lineup. We fell even harder in love when the Chronograph dropped in 2017. The only issue was that, as all the other watches in Tudor's catalogue slimmed down to a more modern 39mm, the Chronos refused their Ozempic, staying stubbornly chunky at 41mm.

Some svelte releases finally arrived this year. The reduced diameter is beautifully balanced by a slimmer case and less fussy dial, and the Black Bay's original diver DNA persists with 200m of water resistance. But it's this colorway that we love most; a no-shits-given yellow that makes even the Casio above seem shy, contrasting with that inky bezel in a way that creates a real… buzz [ed's note: see me in my office].

Thought the balloon dog was a bit much? Look, we're nothing if not mercurial in our tastes, and Seiko gets a pass in part because of the price tag, but also because its Power Design Project has long been a skunkworks for its designers' weirder ideas. Few make it to production, but there are 5,000 of these adorably tongue-in-cheek (panda! Geddit!?) watches available.

Our favorite detail is probably that the tachymeter tops out at 30kmh—the panda's top speed. Although we're a little embarrassed that something so lumpy could smoke us in a foot race.

By now these will be tucked in a vault somewhere, but this quartet of one-of-a-kind watches has been churning its way through the rumor mill all year. When they officially launched in September, it turned out they were wilder than anyone had imagined.

These spins on the Rolex Oyster Perpetual Cosmograph Daytona were designed in tribute to the seasons, their natural inspiration a reference to charities founded by two of the brand's ambassadors: the Federer Foundation and Leonardo DiCaprio's Re:wild. The watches raised nearly $50 million for them at auction in September. Though we don't normally like our charity work encrusted in diamonds, we'd happily take the Spring model off the owner's hands, having fallen rather hard for its Wimbledon-like green-and-purple styling.

#217. Nara Smith Regrets Trying to Make Twizzlers

Nara Smith’s internet persona is built on a specific kind of perfection: extravagant gowns, immaculate kitchens, and from-scratch recipes that make artisanal homemade cereal feel entirely reasonable. A true modern renaissance woman, she seamlessly balances cooking, influencing, and motherhood, and is even set to star alongside Charlize Theron and Demi Moore in the upcoming thriller Tyrant, a film delving into NYC’s elite fine dining scene. Her new book, Homemade, balances her campy approach to cooking—the cover features Smith in a dress that doubles as a table—with recipes for homemade cinnamon toast squares alongside more practical, kid-friendly dishes like pork schnitzel and Coconut Cassava Waffles.

In person, she’s far less precious and much funnier. During Smith’s visit to the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen, her relentless pace was on full display. When I ran down a couple of floors to return a pen her producer had left behind, I found her completely transformed, glam fully retouched, already posing for her next shoot for Vanity Fair.

We spoke to Smith about the kitchen slippers hiding beneath her camera frame, the failed homemade Twizzlers that still haunt her, the sudden onset of her egg ick, and the oddly specific way her dad taught her to cut pancakes into tiny squares.

What’s the first thing people get wrong about you?

People think I’m wearing heels. I’m actually wearing slippers. I’m very tall, and if I wear heels the counter is too low and nothing looks proportionate. Also, I’m standing all day and my lower back would never forgive me. So it’s always a really good cushioned house slipper. Comfort first.

You spend so much time making food on camera. Are there recipes that feel especially personal to you?

These German pancakes. My dad made them before school when I was growing up. He’d always make the first one before he woke us up because the first pancake is always bad. When I was writing the recipe for my cookbook, I asked him for measurements, and he was like, “A little bit of this, a little bit of that, maybe two, maybe three eggs.” That's not exactly cookbook language.

Your cookbook is full of from-scratch recipes. Is there anything you’d never make yourself?

Never say never. I tried making Twizzlers once, and they were terrible. Absolutely terrible. I still think about trying again because I love a challenge, but candy is one of those things that can really humble you.

What’s been your biggest kitchen disaster?

The Twizzlers were bad, but sourdough was probably worse. My first few attempts were a complete mess. The funny thing is I often make recipes for the first time on camera, so if something goes wrong, everyone gets to watch it happen in real time.

The Test Kitchen wanted to know: What’s your favorite way to eat eggs?

This is controversial because I have 20 chickens, but I got the egg ick while I was pregnant, and it never fully went away. If I’m eating eggs, I want a fried egg with crispy edges and a runny yolk on top of fried rice. Just don’t give it to me first thing in the morning.

Honestly? My garden is dying. The zucchini is struggling. The cucumbers are gone. All my lettuce died. Between the heat and the rain, everything has kind of given up. It’s my first year, though, so I’m trying to be kind to myself. Next year will be better.

What’s the most specific food habit you have?

I cut these pancakes into tiny squares. My dad used to do it for me, and now it’s the only way I like eating them. I put applesauce on top, dust them with powdered sugar, cut them into little squares, and eat them one by one. Everyone else in my family thinks it’s weird.

Weigh your ingredients. Especially flour. A cup of flour means something different to everyone. Good ingredients matter, too, but if you’re baking, a scale will save you a lot of heartbreak.

#218. Hunter Schafer Has Never Felt More Like Herself

The Blade Runner 2099 star on the art of being human.

Hunter Schafer is good at having a bad time. As Jules in Euphoria, she was thrust into the darkest places as addict Rue’s lifeline; as teenager Gretchen in the movie Cuckoo, she was embroiled in a full-on body-horror conspiracy nightmare; and as assistant Hilda in Mother Mary, she was caught between the drama of two complicated mega-divas. Now, in her first TV role as a lead, she’s a fugitive fighting for the survival of mankind in Blade Runner 2099 (a limited series coming to Prime Video in November). As her character Cora, a human masquerading as a replicant Blade Runner, Schafer tells me, “I smile maybe twice.” It’s an impressive performance in a tough role. “I think a lot of things that portray the future can feel sterile or clean, where everything’s perfect and fascist and robotic,” she says. “The androids in Blade Runner are kind of nuts and artistic and messy, which I think is more accurate.” I’ve previewed the first few episodes when we meet in London, and wonder whether there’s ever any respite for Cora later in the series—a nice bubble bath, perhaps? “Not a chance,” she says with a laugh.

The softness of Schafer’s preternatural beauty as an actress belies the hard-won strength of someone who began transitioning at age 14, and then three years later became the youngest plaintiff in the legal challenge to North Carolina’s anti-trans “bathroom bill.” The contrast makes her Hollywood’s perfect manic pixie trauma girl. She can carry it without it crushing her. Because whatever darkness a script demands, the sweet, funny 27-year-old I meet in London has a way of bringing a special kind of light to the part.

Over our time together, as we’re chatting on a bench in Grosvenor Square in the late summer sun, our conversation spans spirituality, art, freedom, and humanity. I feel relaxed in her easy company. She’s someone you’d bump into at a club and find you’ve lost half the night talking to. I thought she’d be intimidatingly cool, but after I clock the cute little woodland creatures on the socks she wears with her ballet pumps, I readjust the narrative in my head. And when she decides to reveal something pretty major that no one outside her immediate circle of family and friends knows yet, I feel honored to be trusted with helping tell this part of her story.

Schafer grew up in Raleigh, North Carolina. Her parents are pastors, and she says Christianity gave her childhood a structure and purpose. She moved away from the church as a teenager and now isn’t religious, but that sense of “being in service,” as she puts it, or “making things for something bigger than yourself” has continued to be a driving force in her life. Creating art, whether through acting, modeling, or painting (she carries her watercolors with her everywhere), is less about ego and more about a higher purpose? “Exactly,” she says. “I think it’s important to do it for the—oh my God, I’m going to sound like such a pretentious asshole—for the poetry, or whatever. It sounds so annoying, but I do believe that.”

After some difficult teenage years “where I was really angry at the world and at the restrictions I felt growing up in the church and with pastor parents,” Schafer is in a good place with her family, and her younger sisters are following in her footsteps in the entertainment industry. “I can have really beautiful conversations with my parents about spirituality now,” she says. “They might be talking about it through the lens of Presbyterian Christianity, or the house they operate within spiritually, but I feel like we’re talking about the same things.”

Reflecting on her teen years now, she thinks the anger was a result of the “normal teenage thing of waking up to what the world really is versus what you thought it was.” I ask if adulthood turned out how she imagined. “In a lot of ways, I still feel like a teenager,” Schafer says. “I think there’s something about acting where people baby us all the time. On set, we’re being looked after by PAs, coddled, and given all our meals. Sometimes it can make us not great people to be around in real life. So I don’t even know if I feel like an adult.”

She says her early twenties were “kind of a shit show” for so many reasons. “I was just a disaster,” she reflects. “But I don’t feel like a disaster anymore. I think that’s come with entering my late twenties and getting all of that bullshit out.” I wonder if she’s being harsh on herself—after all, she was holding down a major role in one of the most popular TV shows of the decade from the age of 19, and, as a high-fashion model, walked for Dior, Miu Miu, Marc Jacobs, Coach, Rick Owens, Maison Margiela, Helmut Lang, Vera Wang, and others. All while navigating the world of celebrity as a young woman who is trans. It looked, from the outside at least, as if she was thriving?

She thinks for a second, then says, “I do think it’s truthful to say I was a fucking mess for the first chunk of my twenties, up until a few years ago.”

What changed? “I’m getting used to my new life now,” she explains. “It was overwhelming, and it happened really fast. There was a part of me that felt like I needed to resist it, and that was really disorienting.” Now, she says, she’s “okay with riding this very strange, sometimes terrifying, and a lot of the time really delicious wave. Being down for the ride and not trying to push back against it, or self-sabotage.”

As we talk, office workers walk past us on their lunch break, oblivious to the star sitting cross-legged beside me wearing harem pants and a strappy black Prada top. She tells me she’s in town for a friend’s wedding. I later realize the friend she refers to was likely Zendaya, who married Tom Holland at an exclusive hotel in the British countryside in August. Schafer says her Euphoria co-star is “like a sister” to her now. “She showed me the ropes,” she says, adding that she also learned a lot from Zendaya about managing celebrity and reality and “keeping those worlds separate.”

Working with powerful women has been a theme of Schafer’s acting career so far, and she’s grateful for the grace and wisdom they’ve offered her. While filming Blade Runner 2099, her co-star Michelle Yeoh became a mother figure who she says helped “usher me into the world of action.” Schafer did many of her own stunts on the show alongside Yeoh, whom she describes as “one of the best—a master.”

“The reason I like action so much is you don’t have to think that much,” Schafer says. “It’s just being in your body.” She quite literally threw herself into the role. Schafer says that actors who have done action before know how to fall, but as she’d done very little training before being offered the role without auditioning, she’d just flop her body onto the ground as best she could, until Yeoh, tired of watching her hurt herself, explained the art of “layering a fall with your body so the weight gets dispersed.”

We talk more about the freedom that comes from being fully embodied, especially as a trans person who has experienced the knotty discomfort of body dysmorphia—the feeling when your outer shell doesn’t match who you know yourself to be. It’s a theme explored symbolically through the concept of androids and replicants in Blade Runner, and was one of the reasons Schafer signed on to the show, even though she’d vowed to have some downtime to paint and make art. She plays a human pretending to be a robot to survive. But can anyone really hide their truth for long?

I ask Schafer what’s the most human thing she’s done recently, and she tells me about a night she’d had a few days prior with close friends in a nightclub. “We were dancing incredibly hard. There were no cameras out, which was great, so everybody was really letting loose,” she says. “I have little flashes in my head of looking my friends in the eyes and singing the lyrics and feeling completely free.”

Our conversation about feeling free naturally veers into our perspectives on queerness: me as a nonbinary parent in my forties, who came out as a lesbian two and a half decades ago, and Schafer as a woman in her late twenties, who was assigned male at birth. Through the very act of her existence, let alone a growing profile as an actress and model, she became a role model for the queer and trans community, which cast an identity on her from an early age, before she’d really had the chance to explore it for herself.

“I feel like that’s the magical thing about queerness,” she says, taking off her Prada sunglasses so she can look me in the eye. “On an ideological level, it’s about possibility and expansion and growth, and being on that journey and finding yourself.” While she’s had an expansive view of her gender identity for years, where she’s landed now is somewhere she describes as “flatter” in a sense: “I’m a woman. I’m a girl,” she says. To get here, she’s wrestled with queerness as an idea and philosophy “versus how it applies and works in real life, in the context of the world that we’re living in,” she adds. “I feel like there’s always a tension there.”

As we get deep, she suggests we go into a nearby hotel for a drink (and so that she can use the bathroom). It’s probably a good time to tell her about the U.K. law that went into effect earlier this week, which means people should now use the bathroom that corresponds with their birth sex. It’s a ridiculous and unenforceable attack on trans and nonbinary people and their dignity, which everyone sensible is ignoring. She’s shocked, but not surprised by the pendulum swinging backward. “That’s why these laws are so fucking stupid,” she says. “It was the same thing with HB2 in North Carolina. You can make it the law, but are you deploying a little gender policeman to stand outside the bathrooms?”

As we sit down in the glamorous tea room of the hotel, two little girls in face paint dance around as their mother and aunts eat scones with cream. When Schafer settles into the armchair beside me and takes a sip of her Diet Coke, I can feel something has shifted. A steely resolve tugs at the corners of her mouth. She nods, as though silently weighing the pros and cons of a disclosure. “Maybe it’s a good thing to share, for the tension I was talking about between those two worlds [reality and ideology],” she says. “I just had bottom surgery in December, which was amazing, and I love it so much.”

For those who don’t know, what Schafer is describing is a gender-affirming operation that changes a person’s genitals to better align with their gender identity. “Like I said, for a long time I’ve embraced the gender-expansive part of myself, and I really wanted to try to make that previous body work, because I thought there was something really cool and badass about it.” But Schafer describes hitting a wall again and again where this theoretical queer utopia didn’t match up with the world she encountered every day, and the way she personally wanted to show up in it. Medically transitioning was right for Schafer, but every trans person is different. And as a celebrity, she may be judged by both queer and cis people for her decision.

During her recovery at the start of this year, she rented a big apartment and had friends and family visit, while she was forced to lie down. “I think my limit was 150 steps per day, which is nothing,” she explains. Normally Schafer is an all-or-nothing kind of friend—she’s either planning a big adventure, like the one she’s about to go on to watch the solar eclipse in Iceland at a rave hosted by Björk, or chilling out at home. She’s happy being on her own because “there are so many thoughts to think.” She’s different in a romantic relationship: “They defy the introvert because I want to be around them, touching them, all the time. When I’m in love, that’s how I feel. I want to be with you all the time.” She’s previously dated Spanish pop star Rosalía and her Euphoria co-star Dominic Fike, but she notes, “I haven’t had a relationship that’s been longer than two years, and I’ve heard the two-year mark is when it gets more like a partnership rather than some passionate whatever-it-is. Something that feels more sacred and intentional.”

I tell Schafer that I think she would make the perfect goofy, yet adorable, lead in a rom-com, and that, frankly, I want that for her as an actress. Enough scrambling around in the dirt or digging deep into her soul—someone cast her as a big-city girl boss who inherits a chocolate shop in a small town and meets the man of her dreams at Christmas already! “I would just love to see a trans girl rom-com, too,” she says. “I’ve been thinking about that for a while. I would like to make that happen.”

Does she think of herself as cool? Of course not. What genuinely cool person does? “Celebrity is not cool,” she explains. So who is? “Fran Lebowitz, Björk, Patti Smith,” she says. “People who are not thinking about perception at all. And I think about perception all the time. It’s a big part of my job. It’s not cool at all.”

As our conversation winds to a close, Schafer remembers being a young kid at a friend’s birthday party. She was invited to join in with a choreographed dance, but was so cripplingly aware of how she was being viewed, it wasn’t fun. “I was so shy and so scared to dance in front of other kids, I was crying. I was so nervous and scared,” she says. “I still did it, trying to smile, but I kept being like, ‘No.’ I think that’s what I was at my core before this job broke me open.”

She says she was “just a baby” when she first got the role in Euphoria that changed her life. “I was a different person in a lot of ways. I was really introverted and not set on performing in front of people at all. There was this shell that was there that’s not with me anymore.” I like this image of Schafer, like Botticelli’s Venus emerging from her shell, newly born but fully grown, finally in a body that feels like hers and ready to slay.

#219. Tate McRae Out-Angels the Angels at the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show

The 23-year-old singer performed her latest single, “Housewife”

Tate McRae delivered a show-stopping performance at the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show to celebrate her new single, “Housewife.”

The 23-year-old singer performed second in the lineup, appearing in a glistening red lingerie set and scarlet stilettos. Opening with her song Housewife, McRae delivered a razor-sharp dance routine with 10-plus backup dancers, all wearing a similar red lingerie set. Closing out the song, McCrae took the stage alone to sing the melody and introduce Gigi Hadid and the second wave of models. The singer followed this new single with one of her all-time hits, “Dear God,” from her third album So Close to What, bringing back her ensemble of backup singers.

McCrae stayed on stage while the second wave of models walked the runway, now lit with amber lighting. Her flowing, sheer red wings floated behind her as she strutted the runway singing “Sports Car,” the third single off So Close to What.

McCrae released So Close to What on February 21, 2025, before dropping the deluxe edition, So Close to What???, in November 2025. Bazaar spoke to McCrae in February 2025 about the album, and she emphasized that the world still hasn’t seen close to all she has to offer. “I feel like I have so much to share with the world that hasn’t been seen yet, from at least just me and my [dancing] past,” she said at the time. “It just needs to be the right moment.”

“Housewife” dropped on October 15, accompanied by a video directed by Pierre-Ange Carlotti. The video featured McRae as a housewife living it up on a luxury yacht and sitting by a crystal-blue pool on a sprawling estate. In an inversion of the traditional housewife narrative, McRae proclaims that she wishes to be rich enough to be her own housewife. The song is the lead single of the artist’s fourth studio album.

#220. This Is the Only Gluten-Free Flour I’ll Bake With

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

About half of my large family is gluten free, so at holidays and gatherings, almost everything is prepared without gluten. It’s easier and safer that way, preventing confusion or cross-contamination. Dessert is often served with the claim, “You’d never know it’s gluten free.” Perhaps it’s my background as a professional recipe developer, but I can always tell. Sometimes it’s yummy with only a slight textural difference; other times … I just smile politely. Gluten-free recipes—even ones made with the best gluten-free flour blends—can be hit or miss. And that’s frustrating.

My own results using gluten-free flour blends aren’t always great. I’ve tried a bunch, and usually end up with gritty, dense, gummy or crumbly bakes—and sometimes all of those at once. Most of the time, I skip the GF blends entirely and stick with a crowd-pleasing flourless chocolate cake. But recently I saw something new on the shelf from Bob’s Red Mill, a well-known brand I love that sells tons of gluten-free products. The product—Bob’s Red Mill Gluten-Free 1-To-1 Baking Flour—is only kinda new, I should say, because it’s actually an update, with fresh packaging and a new formulation. I decided to put it to the test. And I’m so glad I did!

Gluten-free flour blends are made with a combination of starches, gums, and grain or rice flours. The goal is to have a mixture that absorbs liquid and holds together when baked, mimicking the effect of the gluten in all-purpose flour. Every brand has its own ratios and ingredients, but there are a lot of similarities and overlap between them. White and/or brown rice flour is commonly used as the base. It has a lovely neutral flavor, but the trade-off is that it can be gritty, creating a coarse texture and crumbly interior.

When reformulating, Bob’s Red Mill stuck with its previous base of sweet white rice flour and whole grain brown rice flour, but it adjusted the starch proportions to improve the texture. It also changed one key ingredient. The new formula replaced whole grain sorghum flour with pearled white sorghum flour. Pearled sorghum flour doesn’t include the outer hull of the grain, which gives it a lighter color, finer texture and milder taste. It seems like a small change, but it made a huge difference in my bakes.

One category of recipes to avoid, however, is yeasted recipes. The package specifies this blend is best for recipes without yeast, meaning it won’t work for pizza dough, cinnamon rolls or bread.

One of the best things about Bob’s Red Mill is how widely available it is. My go-to large grocery store, ShopRite, has an entire section just for various Bob’s Red Mill products, including this gluten-free baking flour. I’ve also seen it at smaller neighborhood markets, and it’s widely available from Target, Walmart and Amazon. If you somehow still can’t find it, the store locator on Bob’s Red Mill website is a good resource. I can’t wait to bake up a gluten-free storm at my next family gathering.

#221. I Tested Marmot's Zipperless Sleeping Bag for Months. It's a Game-Changer for Campers Who Toss and Turn.

Marmot’s Wraptor 30 ditches traditional zippers for a clever magnetic flap-and-snap design.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

THE BASIC SILHOUETTE of sleeping bags hasn't changed in decades. It's still basically a slim, zippered fabric "tube" that's exactly as wide as it needs to be, leaving you little room to toss and turn. Most of them prioritize packability over comfort with only two options—zipped or unzipped—with no way to adapt to the temperature. Marmot is looking to change that with the Wraptor 30, a clever new-this-year sleeping bag that replaces old-school zippers with magnetic flap closures that are more versatile than just about everything before it. After months of testing, here's what I found.

I’VE BEEN A fussy (or "hybrid," as the experts call it) sleeper my whole life, flopping like a fish from my back to my side to my stomach—rinse and repeat—all night long. So, traditional mummy-style sleeping bags have always been an annoying but necessary evil facet of my camping gear. I typically "upgrade" to a more plush bedding setup when I rooftop tent or car camp, where Rumpl's Wrap Sack has been my go-to since it debuted last year. But the Wraptor 30 (available in the more affordable synthetic version that I tested or a pricier all-down alternative) hits the sweet spot of comfort, warmth, and portability, making it dang-near-perfect for just about any kind of camping. It's lighter and more pack-friendly than a traditional car-camping sleeping bag, but cushier and roomier than those portable-yet-claustrophobic mummy bags.

The zipperless, magnetic, dual-flap system is dead-simple to use. Just climb inside and layer up however the temperature dictates. That means you can sleep wide-open in the summer, add just one layer in the spring or fall, and close and secure the second layer when temps dip down closer to freezing. It's not unlike peeling off and putting on more or fewer sheets and blankets at home in bed. That system, combined with the roomier shape of the Wraptor 30, makes for maximum comfort for hybrid sleepers. I found it moves with my body and position much more easily than traditional mummy alternatives. It's not nearly as constricting around the legs and feet either.

SWAPPING ZIPPERS FOR overlapping flaps and snaps maximizes versatility, but it also adds bulk and weight. Compared to other 30-degree bags (Nemo's roomier-than-average, spoon-shaped Disco 30 comes to mind), the Wraptor 30 is heavier and bulkier. That's not to say that it's heavy by any means. This is no thick, ultra-plush, car-camping-only bag. But, if you're counting grams or weight is a general concern (say, for longer, multiday backcountry treks), it's something to consider as there are lighter, more packable options on the market.

Speaking of those flaps, there's another trade-off. That added versatility negates the seal you get from a traditional zipper. While I didn't notice any harsh drafts during my testing, there's bound to be heat loss—it's just physics. The same can be said for the envelope-style foot box that ditches the typical zipper closure, giving you the ability to air out your feet and toes in the middle of the night without having to fumble with a zipper in the dark. But this, too, will translate to more heat loss. For those reasons, I think of the Wraptor 30 as a three-season sleeping bag that'll work as a 3.5-season bag in a pinch if you're properly layered up. But, honestly, that's pushing it, and I wouldn't consider this a true winter sleep solution.

Depending on your needs, these are my favorite alternatives to the Wraptor 30:

The Wraptor 30 is a near-perfect, three-season camp sleep solution that should satisfy most car and backcountry campers. I found it reasonably lightweight and packable enough to stuff into a medium to large hiking backpack without it overfilling my pack. Yet it's plush and comfy enough for most of my car-camping trips, even when overnight temps occasionally dipped below freezing. The roughly $200 price tag (in any of the three available sizes) means that it's also approachable even for campers on a budget, especially those looking to buy just one sleeping bag that virtually does it all.

Mike Richard has traveled the world since 2008. He's kayaked in Antarctica, tracked endangered African wild dogs in South Africa, and survived a near-miss great white shark attack in Mexico. His travel advice has appeared on the websites for Forbes, Travel + Leisure, CNET, and National Geographic. He loves the great outdoors and good bourbon, and (usually) calls Tulsa, Oklahoma home. Mike also enjoys speaking in the third person.

He has written about the outdoors for nearly two decades and was previously the Managing Editor, Content Performance at Gear Patrol. #222. Crystal Lake Gives Pamela Voorhees a Story Friday the 13th Never Would

Peacock’s new prequel series shows a grief-stricken mother who searches for any trace of her son.

In the summer of 1982, a young Brad Caleb Kane went to the movies with his big sister, who snuck him in to see Friday the 13th Part III in 3D. For the future actor, TV producer, and singing voice of Disney’s Aladdin, it opened up a whole new world. “My most visceral memory is seeing Jason squeeze somebody’s head and the eyeball flying into the audience,” Kane tells Esquire. “It was a wonky special effect. But everybody screamed, including me. I knew this was something I wanted to do with the rest of my life. It was the gateway drug to my career.”

Decades later, Kane’s magic carpet ride through Hollywood comes full circle as the creator and showrunner of Crystal Lake, a prequel series to the Friday the 13th franchise. Set years before Jason Voorhees picks up his hockey mask and machete, the series follows Pamela Voorhees (played by Linda Cardellini), who grieves for her only son, Jason (Callum Vinson), after he drowns due to negligent counselors who went off to have sex. Over eight episodes, streaming now on Peacock, a grief-stricken Pamela searches for any trace of her son left.

While talk of a Friday the 13th series began as far back as 2003, and a network pilot was produced in 2015, Crystal Lake came to fruition circa October 2022 under a different creative team. After the 2023 strikes, A24 sought new direction. In 2024, Brad Caleb Kane came aboard with his own pitch zeroed in on Pamela. “I was at the tail end of filming It: Welcome to Derry, and we hadn’t been renewed for season 2 yet. I was going, ‘What’s my next job?’ I was scrolling [online], and I noticed that Peacock and A24 were doing Friday the 13th.”

The possibility of creating a Friday the 13th series had Kane begging to try his luck. “I was the kid who had all the novelizations of these movies. This was my jam,” he says. “I knew what I would want to see as an adult fan of TV, which is a deeper dive into character. I made my pitch, and here we are, a year and a half later.”

Like Jason, Kane has long felt out of step with normies. He wasn’t one of the cool kids. He spent weekends watching horror and kung fu flicks, which all seemed “like junk food” to his parents. He was a real-life version of Chainsaw, from the 1987 film Summer School. “All those things that would make you go, That kid’s weird, they all paid off in the end. That’s what I learned as a creator on my first show. All the things you’re doing for fun and trying things out, deep diving into subcultures, that becomes your identity. It becomes grist for the mill.”

In a conversation with Esquire, Brad Caleb Kane unpacks the making of Crystal Lake, what TV can do that multiple sequels can’t, and what the future may hold for Jason Voorhees back on the big screen.

This interview has been edited for clarity.

It’s funny that we can trace a direct line from you seeing Friday the 13th III to recording the Aladdin soundtrack.

The horror part of my life came before Disney. I grew up haunting the grindhouses of New York City in the ’80s. Some of those movies were Disney. The Rescuers and The Great Mouse Detective, and crazy live-action movies you could never make today, like The Devil and Max Devilin. The ones I gravitated towards the most were the janky, low-budget horror movies. Re-Animator and From Beyond, British imports like Xtro. That took me first, then Disney. Careers have long and winding paths.

We know Jason Voorhees’s origins from the very first Friday the 13th. How will Crystal Lake help us better understand Pamela and Jason? What can a TV show do that ten movies can’t?

Show you the connection between mother and son. That’s the thing the first Friday the 13th didn’t, because it was a movie in 1980 and it was a whodunit. Once you hear Mrs. Voorhees’s soliloquy about Jason drowning, that’s it. You don’t have a sense of her and Jason. Jason is just a monster. You don’t see him as a boy. You don’t understand why a mother would haunt the place and kill anybody who steps on it. I think fans would want to see the relationship, how tight it was, and why a mother might go to extremes avenging her son. You’re able to dive into that more in a television show.

Jason’s story is particularly tragic for a slasher villain. It’s a crime and a tragedy that a child died because some teenagers were reckless. If my kid died like Jason, I would want justice. How is Crystal Lake about Pamela’s grief?

The important thing is to feel the justification. She’s trying to tell people, “I still feel my son’s presence.” And there are constant indignities thrown at her. Whether it’s about what her son looks like, or the fact these people are ready to move on when she’s not. A mother wants people to hear her. And when they’re not, they can have a bad reaction. Any parent would understand. When she goes on her killing sprees, you’re with her, because you understand it’s all in service of everything she had to do. It’s for a reason, not for no reason.

Let’s talk Linda Cardellini. She’s done plenty of horror and horror-adjacent projects. What does Linda bring to the table that helps your vision for who Pamela is?

We have an instant connection with Linda. Obviously, there’s Freaks and Geeks. Then all the comedic work, dramatic work—there’s an effortless likability to Linda and you need that feeling with this character, because you have to go on this journey watching her become this killer. There's a shorthand between audiences and Linda where you want to take any ride with her. You instantly like her, even if she's a killer.

She brings a depth of craft that’s critical for this show. A lot of the stuff that's happening with Linda is going on behind her eyes and in her head. Not every actor can do that.

No spoilers, but you’ve cooked up a larger backstory for Jason and Pamela. What compelled you to imagine Jason as more than a haunted mask and machete?

It leans into things I wanted to play with thematically. Creating that backstory for me had to do with the decade these movies came from, the ’70s. The paranoid conspiracy thriller decade. We’re setting the show in ’71, ’72. We’re in Watergate and Nixon; we don’t trust institutions. We’re starting to ask ourselves, if we can’t trust government and elected officials, who are we? I wanted to lean into that paranoid conspiracy thriller feel of it all. I did want to ground it a little bit in real-world situations. There’s something to be said for a revenant boogeyman—this is a twist on that, where Pamela came from and what she’s running from.

Crystal Lake is not the first horror movie with a TV prequel. What are your hopes for the show and its prospects at this moment for streaming TV?

I hope we run for multiple seasons. There’s lots of story to tell in this small town. But I hope audiences enjoy it. Audiences come to the horror genre for catharsis, for pleasure on a Saturday night. We’re doing something that hopefully has a little bit more than you might be used to in these movies, but I want audiences to get to the end and go, “Man, that was a hell of a lot of fun.”

What are your plans for Crystal Lake in relation to the films? Will the show segue into the first movie, or will it follow a new timeline?

The continuity is wonky, anyway. I played it fast and loose. In the original movie, Jason’s drowning was in 1958. Had we gone back to 1958, it would be a whole series in the ‘50s. I wanted Pamela’s grief to feel immediate in the aftermath of Jason’s drowning. I messed around and decided the drowning is ’71, ’72. I want it to feel like a prequel. Later in the season—and I know I’m giving spoilers here—we do shot-for-shot recreations of the first movie. Hopefully audiences make that shift mentally, and can see this running right up into the 1980 movie.

What do you know about the franchise’s future? Do you think this could be a gateway to a new cinematic Friday the 13th?

The Jason Universe people keep stuff close to the chest. I know they’re trying to figure out another Jason movie. I don’t know what decade they’re going to set it in. Obviously, Jason was mowed down by toxic waste in one timeline, went to space in another. I had conversations with them about being involved, and then I got sidetracked with Welcome to Derry season 2. But I know they’re working hard to bring back the Jason everybody loves, with the hockey mask, to the movies. I think they’re in the script stage now, but I don’t know much more.

More than 45 years later, how can this universe stay relevant to audiences?

To me, [Pamela’s story is] about manipulation. You could say [it's about] not listening to women. That’s relevant to the world we live in. That’s the theme I’m playing with, and hopefully audiences see the relevance.

Lately there’s been talk about sex, or lack thereof, in TV and movies. Gen Z audiences are largely averse to watching people have sex in their media. Sex is key to Friday the 13th and the slasher genre. What do you think the aversion to onscreen sex says about audiences today?

That has more to do with technology and isolation. People are immersed in their private worlds, enclaves, in their computers. I lament the fact people are not having more sex. I’m pro-sex and pro-sex on screen. I’m a huge Gregg Araki fan. People on film should keep fucking, and people in real life should keep fucking too. No mask killer is gonna get you.
