#223. All the Gorgeous Locations From ‘Sense and Sensibility’ to Plan Your Next Vacation Around

“I’ve ordered a period costume from Spirit Halloween and I’m going to Dorset”—my current OOO.

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

Sense and Sensibility is the latest in a string of gorgeous Jane Austen adaptations, each of which is dreamier than the next. The Georgia Oakley-directed film follows the Dashwoods, who are forced out of their ancestral home and have to relocate to a sleepy seaside cottage—where they navigate first loves and plenty of misunderstandings. And while there’s no doubt that Elinor and Marianne Dashwood are the central characters, the breathtaking English countryside gets plenty of screen time and there’s a 0/10 chance that you’ll leave the theater not wanting to make a trip. On that note, here’s where Sense and Sensibility was filmed (happy news: plenty of these spots are open to visitors).

Scenes from the Dashwoods’ impressive family home were filmed at Kingston Russell House, which is nestled in the bucolic Dorset landscape. While its a private home (so, sadly, no visitors), the film also used Parnham Park for exterior scenes—including the lake where Elinor and Edward skip rocks (and fall for each other) below some lovely stone steps. Not only can you visit Parnham Park and its “139 acres of parkland, grassland, magical woodland and gardens,” you can even stay there!

The small stone cottage that the Dashwoods move into after being kicked out of their home is known as the Ditsworthy Warren House, and is located in Devon. While the house itself isn’t open for tours, it’s within Dartmoor National Park, which means you can go on a lovely walk and stumble upon it!

This is the stately home of Mrs. Jennings & Co (where the Dashwoods spend a lot of their time socializing, and where Marianne first meets Colonel Brandon). These scenes were filmed in Broughton Castle in Oxfordshire, which is open to visitors and has been used in many film and television productions before—including Shakespeare in Love, My Lady Jane, The Crown, Wolf Hall, and Jane Eyre.

Scenes of the Dashwoods enjoying the seaside (and the moment Marianne hurts her ankle!) were filmed at Mothecombe Beach on the South Devon coast, which is open to the public. The beach is managed by the Flete Estate, which posted a bunch of BTS pics of the movie’s production:

The lively scene—where Marianne and Willoughby have wild chemistry and dance up a storm in front of the whole town—was filmed at Penshurst Place, a 14th-century manor in Kent. It’s also been used in productions like Wolf Hall, The Hollow Crown, and even The Princess Bride.

The interiors were filmed at a Georgian townhouse called Rainham Hall, which is a National Trust property. Meaning yes, you can visit!

This extremely over-the-top London society ball is the backdrop for Marianne finding out Willoughby is engaged. It was filmed inside West Wycombe Park—which was ironically the home of the real-life Dashwood family. The home, and the grounds, are stunning.

Kay, off to book a trip to Dorset if you need me!

#224. I Blind-Tested 9 Store-Bought Pasta Brands—This One Cooked Up Best

What to know before your next trip down the pasta aisle.

Pasta is, and always will be, an ingredient I crave. Take me to the pasta aisle at any market, and I’ll stay there, fantasizing about all the ways I can use it. While fresh pasta is the gold standard, I love and appreciate dry pasta for its texture, accessibility, and long shelf life.

I’m always up for trying something new, but having a go-to brand you know will deliver matters, too. So I set out to test the top budget-friendly and special-occasion-worthy brands. Here’s what I found.

I blind-tested nine pasta brands: five higher-end (Garofalo, Rummo, Sfoglini, Rao’s, and Colavita) and four budget-friendly (Ronzoni, Barilla, De Cecco, and San Giorgio). I kept the water amount, quantity, and pasta type (rigatoni) the same across brands, and I followed the package instructions for al dente. Despite my better instincts, I left out the salt for the sake of the experiment.

I’m thrilled De Cecco is my favorite budget-friendly pasta because I use it consistently at home and when testing recipes for work. It’s bronze-cut (which helps it stick to sauce much better than Teflon-cut), easy on the wallet, and I’m convinced your favorite restaurants use it too, which says a lot!

Rummo was slightly thicker than the other brands. It had a good, chewy texture, with a slight crunch; I love that it cooked al dente in the specified time! It’s also a bronze-cut, slow-dried pasta imported from Italy. You really can’t ask for more.

I always preach that buying and eating a slow-dried bronze-cut pasta is best for you. It produces a higher-quality product, lets sauce adhere better, and is more nutritious. Garofalo took the crown because it’s the only certified al dente pasta, and that’s a hard accolade to beat. According to the brand, the industry-first “Al Dente” certification comes from a testing process that measures the pasta’s ability to maintain its structure and consistency “beyond its optimal cooking time.” That means it should stay firm even if it’s cooked longer than it's supposed to be.

Pasta Garofalo developed this protocol and validated it with Bureau Veritas, which provides food safety, traceability, and organic certification services.

This brand also holds PGI (protected geographical indication) certification, meaning a certain part of pasta production is guaranteed to come from Gragnano, Campania, Italy—the world's most famous pasta-producing city.

#226. A Fifth Fashion Week Capital? Shanghai Makes the Case for Itself

Samuel Gui Yang, spring 2027 ready-to-wear

Fashion insiders like to talk about the next big thing. We’re less adept at looking for it somewhere other than the places we already know. As a first-timer at Shanghai Fashion Week, I can say that the Chinese city offers a fairly persuasive argument for widening the search, and not just because China is a market too large to ignore.

In Shanghai, the scene feels young, interconnected, and unusually close to the people who actually buy the clothes. At Labelhood, the independent platform that has become one of the week’s most compelling showcases for emerging talent, the distinction between industry insiders and the public is refreshingly porous. There’s an audience of editors and buyers, and then there is a second show for everyone else, equally enthusiastic about seeing what comes down the runway.

For Blake Abbie, the Canadian-born EIC of A Magazine Curated By, who has spent considerable time observing the Chinese fashion scene, this proximity is one of Shanghai’s defining assets. Here, he argues, designers are particularly conscious of the market. Elsewhere, that awareness may be left to marketing departments; in Shanghai, designers themselves seem to understand what people want to wear. “I don’t necessarily think that’s the case in Europe or New York, where designers often create clothes based on what they think people should wear,” he said.

The difference, Abbie suggested, has something to do with the fact that designers and customers belong to the same young community. Their relationship is less hierarchical, more of an exchange. Consumers support local labels, designers respond to them, and the resulting feedback loop encourages creativity rather than simply dictating what sells.

Tasha Liu, the founder of Labelhood, sees this consumer engagement as one of Shanghai’s greatest advantages. Shanghai operates on several fronts simultaneously: runway shows, showrooms, retail, and a digital ecosystem that allows consumers to follow new labels almost as soon as they emerge. Domestic buyers come in substantial numbers, she noted, making the city a genuine trading hub alongside its role as a creative showcase. Paris may remain the principal destination for international buyers placing orders, but Shanghai has its own commercial momentum.

That momentum is not accidental. Since 2015, Shanghai Fashion Week has been developing an ecosystem that brings together presentations, showrooms, and business opportunities, explained Landon Du, SWF Projects Director. The main venue generally requires designers to have at least two years of experience, with applications assessed by a committee comprising industry professionals, media, showroom owners, and buyers. Labelhood, by contrast, offers a more open platform for emerging names.

Showing a collection is hardly an inexpensive exercise. Production, models, styling, lighting, and public relations all have to be paid for, and sponsorship rarely covers the entire bill. Many of the designers on the calendar have therefore already established retail businesses in China, with some reaching multibrand stores internationally.

What makes this particularly interesting is that the business infrastructure supports creative independence. Liu pointed to China’s production capabilities and developed e-commerce channels as advantages that allow young labels to reach consumers without first having to build an elaborate international distribution network. Designers can grow through online sales and multibrand retail before opening their own stores. In other markets, that journey can be considerably more arduous.

The commercial awareness does not, however, mean that the clothes are merely an exercise in consumer appeasement. One of the most compelling developments, according to both Liu and Du, is the growing engagement with Chinese heritage, craftsmanship, and traditional techniques. Designers are looking beyond familiar cultural references to explore processes preserved by families and communities, including traditional dyeing and embroidery. The challenge is to bring these practices into the present without turning them into museum pieces.

Liu cited Kinyan Lam, which works with traditional dyeing techniques from rural areas in southwestern China, and Samuel Gui Yang, whose work approaches Chinese aesthetics with a contemporary sensibility. For Abbie, the appeal lies in the way craftsmanship is integrated into clothes that can actually be worn. He spoke of designers devoting months to intricate embroidery, sometimes at a level comparable to couture, while creating pieces intended for everyday life. The distinction matters: these are not necessarily precious objects designed to be admired from a safe distance, but expressions of craft that remain accessible to younger customers.

There is also a shift in attitude behind this exploration. Abbie observed that, after the pandemic, more designers returned to China from their studies abroad and began looking at their own cultural inheritance with renewed interest. Earlier generations had explored Chinese tradition, too, but often without the same everyday sensibility. Now, he suggested, there is a stronger sense of pride in where designers come from, and a desire to make that identity part of contemporary life rather than a decorative reference.

The relationship with international luxury is more nuanced than a simple story of local brands replacing foreign ones. Liu argues that the major fashion houses have helped educate Chinese consumers, introducing them to the importance of design, storytelling, and brand identity. Those same consumers are now developing their own tastes and discovering Chinese labels. A customer can appreciate Hermès or Louis Vuitton and still choose a local designer for reasons that have little to do with price alone.

That distinction is important in a market where consumers have become more selective. As Abbie pointed out, the economic slowdown has affected spending, but it has also created opportunities for younger labels offering a different proposition from international luxury, whose prices in China can be considerably inflated. Local designers may share customers with the established houses, but they are not necessarily competing for the same desires. The question is not simply which logo to buy, but what kind of design identity feels worth investing in.

For Du, another development worth watching is the growing involvement of Chinese designers in the creative teams and hubs of major domestic fashion companies. Rather than limiting collaborations to capsule collections, some groups are bringing designers into their businesses on a more sustained basis. International partnerships are also expanding, as demonstrated by Feng Chen Wang’s work with Under Armour and collaborations involving Chinese outerwear designers and Moncler. The question of whether Chinese talent will eventually lead major international fashion houses is therefore less fanciful than it might once have seemed.

Some names come up as possible candidates. Samuel Gui Yang, for instance, has built an impressive team and a distinctive brand between Shanghai and London. Feng Chen Wang has demonstrated an ability to operate at scale through her extensive collaborations. The artisanal intricacy of the embroidery and handwork of Kinyan Lam, the Hong Kong-based designer, and his sensibility might be translated to a house like Chloé. These are different creative profiles, but they share an understanding of how to develop a coherent identity around their work.

Still, the most resounding argument for Shanghai may be less about exporting a designer to a storied European house than about allowing a local fashion culture to flourish on its own terms. Abbie was struck by how consistently designers attend one another’s shows. The solidarity, he said, feels more organic than performative. People understand that a market cannot be built by individual ambition alone; it requires a network of designers, stylists, photographers, retailers, and customers who show up for one another. “It’s about people,” said Liu.

That sense of community is Shanghai’s most distinctive resource. Its designers are young, its consumers are engaged, and its business infrastructure offers routes to growth that are not always available elsewhere. Not every label will become an international name, nor does every promising designer need to end up at the helm of a Paris fashion house to validate their talent. The more immediate achievement is that a generation of designers is building businesses while developing contemporary points of view.

Fashion’s international conversation has long been conducted from a relatively small number of familiar addresses. Shanghai is making the case that there are other places worth listening to, and that the most promising thing happening here may not be who gets discovered next, but how the system is allowing so many designers to develop consistently in the first place.

#227. Jennifer Aniston Confirms Brown Patent Bags Are Autumn’s Must-Have Accessory

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Could anything feel more perfectly autumnal than shopping for a new handbag? Well, only shopping for a glossy brown bag, perhaps. The polished texture has fast become the choice of the season, and it’s easy to understand why.

Patent leather—be it in black, brown, or vibrant colors—has long been more directional than classic grain or matte leather finishes, and is infinitely smarter than suede. It signals sleek polish with no extra effort, adding an additional texture (the secret to all the best outfits) with just grab-and-go application. It feels perfect for that “back-to-school” feeling that never leaves us, speaking to the elevation that we crave for our wardrobes when we say goodbye to summer’s relaxed silhouettes.

Just ask Jennifer Aniston. The actor was quick to adopt September’s key bag trend on only the second day of the month. She was photographed in New York clutching a brown patent box bag, which, against the contrast of her dark gray dress, stood out with stealth polish thanks to the shining texture of the bag. As is often the case with Aniston’s laid-back approach, it was an effective styling tip that’s easy to adopt.

While Aniston kept her brown patent bag in small proportions for an evening ’do, the best way for the majority of us to carry this trend into the new season is with a tote that can be filled with everyday essentials. Look to Tory Burch’s latest edition of the Romy bag. The style is that perfectly dark, deep chocolate brown that goes with everything. Yes, we’re into the black and brown pairing your mother warned you about.

Fill it with your laptop and desktop water bottle for weekdays, and with gym kits or a copy of The Lion Inside on Saturdays, depending on how your weekends look these days.

Those who prefer a lighter touch should look to Balenciaga’s shiny tan take of its Rodeo bag, which will punctuate dark winter shades well. Or, for something more simple and priced under $50, bags don’t come better than ASOS’s scoop tote.

Simply put: If you’re wanting to invest in a new bag this season or similarly are looking to move your wardrobe on from summer to winter swiftly, then only a brown patent bag will do. Let’s get glossy!

The eldest daughter of the late Kobe Bryant just made her VS debut

Tonight, the 23-year-old model and eldest daughter of the late Kobe Bryant and his wife, Vanessa, walked the Victoria’s Secret runway for the first time at the 2026 Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show. She joined an impressive array of returning stars, like Irina Shayk, Joan Smalls, Alex Consani, Alessandra Ambrosio, Gigi Hadid, and Jasmine Tookes, just to name a few.

On the runway, Natalia was decked out in a look from Victoria’s Secret Pink, including a black bra with the brand’s name emblazoned across the front in leopard letters, which was layered underneath a hot-pink shrug.

The look was completed with a few dazzling accessories, including a mirrorball handbag, silver heels, and jeans bedazzled with multicolor gemstones. Natalia also wore a bow-adorned headband and silver heart-shaped earrings, while her studded belt was strung with mini versions of the Pink stuffed animal dog.

Ahead of her milestone runway moment, Natalia told Page Six that she was “over the moon” about getting to be a part of the event. “I used to watch the show every year, since I was a little girl,” she told the outlet, adding that she prepared for her walk by watching old Victoria’s Secret show clips. “I had the shows on repeat, really trying to get into that mindset.”

Over the past few years, Natalia has been slowly building up her fashion résumé. She made her runway debut at the Versace Spring/Summer 2024 show a few years back, and she has since walked the catwalk for houses like Boss and Off-White. Not to mention, she’s also appeared in campaigns for the likes of Adidas and David Yurman.

This isn’t the first time Natalia has teamed up with Victoria’s Secret, either. She previously appeared in a fall 2024 campaign for the brand’s sub-label, Pink.

#229. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

#230. I Made 3-Ingredient Pumpkin Cake Balls, and I Finally Get the Pumpkin Spice Hype

These easy pumpkin cake balls have me second-guessing my ambivalence toward pumpkin spice. I used store-bought products to save prep time, and you'd never know they were only half-homemade.

Pumpkin spice season is taken very seriously in my house. My husband is fairly reasonable about it, but my kids spend most of fall acting as though cinnamon, nutmeg and cloves are a food group. I’m the outlier. Sure, I like a slice of pumpkin pie at Thanksgiving, but I’ve never understood the annual rush to make everything taste like it.

I do, however, have a soft spot for the pumpkin loaves that start appearing in coffee shops and grocery-store bakeries this time of year. So when I came across an Instagram video from @thefoodarrondissement making cake balls out of banana bread, I wondered what would happen if I gave the idea a more autumnal twist. Instead of baking anything, I picked up a package of frosted pumpkin loaf slices from Walmart, a can of vanilla frosting and chocolate candy melts.

The ingredients and very little work later, I had one of the best pumpkin desserts I’ve made in a while. Unfortunately for my longstanding position as the household pumpkin-spice skeptic, I may have to give this one to the fanatics.

They’re essentially cake pops without sticks, though there’s no reason at all you couldn’t serve them as cake pops as well. They’re made by crumbling cake, mixing it with frosting, rolling the mixture into balls and coating them in chocolate.

The version that inspired me used banana bread in place of regular cake, and pumpkin seemed like a natural swap for the season. You could certainly bake a loaf of pumpkin bread for the purpose, but I was interested in the shortcut version. Walmart sells frosted pumpkin cake slices in its bakery section, which meant most of the work—and even some of the frosting—was already taken care of.

I crumbled the entire package of pumpkin slices into a large bowl, including the frosting on top of each slice. Because the cake was already moist and frosted, I only needed about 1/3 cup of canned vanilla frosting to bring everything together. If you’re using an unfrosted pumpkin loaf, you’ll likely need more, so add it a little at a time until the mixture holds together easily when you squeeze it.

Vanilla worked well because it didn’t compete with the pumpkin and spices, but cream cheese frosting would be a delicious choice here too. Salted caramel or coffee frosting could take them in a slightly less sweet direction.

Once the mixture held together, I rolled it into balls, dipped each one in melted chocolate and sprinkled with a pinch of sea salt. I transferred the cake balls to the fridge to let the coating set. It took about 10 minutes. That’s it!

These pumpkin cake balls have no business being so delicious for how easy they are to make. Pumpkin cake is dense and moist to begin with, so the centers had a richer, softer texture than the standard cake balls I’ve made with regular cake and frosting. More importantly, they weren’t too sweet. The pumpkin and spices were beautifully balanced beneath the vanilla frosting and chocolate shell, and that little bit of warmth kept the whole thing from becoming cloying.

There’s also something particularly wonderful in the contrast between the firm chocolate shell and the almost truffle-like pumpkin center. I may never completely share my family’s enthusiasm for pumpkin spice, but these easy cake balls just got me a lot closer.

#231. This Isn’t Your Dad’s Prostate Test

The PSA screening process got an upgrade. Here’s why it’s worth another look.

IF GETTING A screening test for prostate cancer isn’t on your radar, it’s probably because the government guidelines essentially told you not to bother back in 2012. But prostate cancer rates have continued to rise. It’s now the second leading cause of cancer deaths in men, and it’s particularly lethal for Black men, who are more than twice as likely to die from it as white men. The guidelines have evolved.

The reason to consider the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) test now isn’t any big, headline-grabbing news that there’s a whole new way to test for it (there isn’t yet). It’s not even that PSA testing is now associated with about a 13 percent reduction in deaths from cancer and a 35 percent reduction in metastatic cancer diagnoses. It’s that the entire landscape of what happens after a troublesome result has shifted.

A high PSA number used to fast-track you to an uncomfortable or potentially infection-causing biopsy and hustle you to radiation or surgery. “A lot of men were being exposed to treatments and side effects without necessarily extending their lives,” says Kelvin Moses, MD, PhD, a professor at Vanderbilt University Medical Center who just helped revise the prostate-screening guidelines for the American Urological Association (AUA) and the Society of Urologic Oncology (SUO). Because many prostate cancers grow slowly—which is why doctors say men are more likely to die with prostate cancer than from it—lots of guys underwent procedures that they wouldn’t have really needed.

But now, MRIs and high-tech monitoring can help ID which prostate cancers need to be acted on and which can be left safely alone. “We really need to change the narrative on PSA,” says Yaw Nyame, MD, of the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center at the University of Washington Medical Center. “It’s not whether it works or not. It’s how we can use it as part of a smart screening pathway.”

THE PSA TEST, which measures a protein produced by the prostate, has never been straightforward. High levels indicate something’s off in that walnut-size gland, but they don’t tell you if it’s cancer; it might just be an enlarged prostate or a urinary tract infection.

When the FDA approved the test for cancer screening more than 30 years ago, the message was clear: Get the test! Then in 2012, the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force didn’t recommend it on grounds that there wasn’t enough evidence that the benefits outweighed the harms. Now, the tide is turning back to “get it.” Start at age 40 to 45 if you’re Black, have a family history of prostate cancer (father, brothers, uncles), or if breast or ovarian cancer runs in your family. Start around age 50 if you don’t have a family history or other risk factors. (When to get it again? If your PSA is in a healthy range, then screen every two to four years after that.)

And there’s one test you don’t have to take. If fear of the digital rectal exam (DRE) is keeping you from getting tested, relax. The new guidelines reinforce what people have been hoping for all along: It’s an inefficient way to screen for cancer.

NOW, PSA TEST results are only a starting point. If your PSA is high, you’ll want another test in a few months to confirm that it’s not due to something else—inflammation, irritation, or recent ejaculation can drive up the numbers. In 25 to 40 percent of cases, the second PSA test will be normal. About that “normal”: It shifts with age. “A PSA of 4 has always been a cutoff. If your PSA is 4 and you’re 53 years old, that’s very high. But if you’re 75 or 80, that’s pretty reasonable,” says Dr. Moses.

If the follow-up confirms a high number, doctors dig deeper. You may—depending on your doctor and how clear your case is—be eligible for one of what Dr. Nyame calls a “whole entourage” of urinary and blood biomarkers with names like the Prostate Health Index (PHI), 4K, IsoPSA, and MyProstateScore 2.0 that can help clarify if you’re pointing down a biopsy path.

Even then, the next move should be imaging before anybody comes at your prostate with a biopsy needle. “A prostate MRI can reduce the need for a prostate biopsy by about 20 to 30 percent,” says Dr. Nyame. Yet “only 30 to 40 percent of patients with an elevated PSA are getting an MRI before biopsy,” he says. Part of the issue is access to MRIs, combined with the fact that it’s a relatively new recommendation that some physicians aren’t yet accustomed to following.

If all these checkpoints suggest you do need a biopsy, ask your doc which technique they’re comfortable with and good at doing. Traditionally, these have been done through the wall of the rectum, which leaves up to 7 percent of guys with infections that can land them in the hospital. Research on a procedure that goes through the perineum suggests it may cut the risk of infection. It also requires specific equipment and training, so not every doctor offers it yet. Don’t go off a cliff trying to find this; the AUA/SUO guidelines say that either way is still okay.

ONE OF THE biggest shifts in the new rules of prostate care is what to do if cancer is detected. Often, “keep an eye on it” is the ultimate strategy. “We think that something like 50 percent of cancers don’t need treatment,” says Dr. Nyame. Wait, what?!

“The C-word short-circuits people. There’s this rush to get scheduled for treatment,” says Heather Goltz, PhD, professor of social work at the University of Houston-Downtown and health educator for people with cancer. Skipping right to surgery or radiation carries risks, including urinary incontinence and erectile dysfunction, issues you can avoid when the cancer was never likely to harm you.

Enter active surveillance, a treatment strategy of closely monitoring the prostate with, yes, more PSA tests, as well as with MRIs and biopsies. A multicenter study published in JAMA found that 10 years after guys chose active surveillance, less than 1 percent died of their disease; less than 2 percent developed metastatic cancer; and nearly half saw no progression in their disease at all. “The adoption of active surveillance has increased in the U.S. and has really reduced the harm of PSA-based screening,” says Dr. Nyame.

IF THE WHOLE PSA test thing feels antiquated in this age of cancer blood tests (like Galleri) and whole-body MRIs (like Prenuvo), it’s because these new technologies are still the “someone’s texting you” dots in the screening conversation. They’re a signal, but it’s not clear yet what they’re saying.

Cancer blood tests look for tumor DNA floating around in your circulatory system. “Not every cancer shows up very well in the bloodstream, and prostate is one of them,” says Dr. Moses. That’s because prostate cancer, at early stages, doesn’t shed a lot of DNA into the bloodstream.

But what about MRIs? If you’re going to need one anyway when your PSA is high, why not just start there? Studies are looking at that very thing right now, but even if they are found to be useful, cost and access will still keep them from the front lines, at least for a while.

That means the new tests won’t take over yet, but they don’t have to. The PSA might not have changed, but the protocols around it have made screening easier to opt into, giving the test a better chance to save lives.

Marty Munson, currently the health director of Men's Health, has been a health editor at properties including Marie Claire, Prevention, Shape and RealAge. She's also certified as a swim and triathlon coach.

#232. In Gabe Kavookjian’s Life, Most People Are the Same. But Not Him.

He’s thirty-five years old. Loves movies. Works two jobs. Wants to meet the right person. But because he has Down syndrome, someone told him he’s different.

He wears his blue New Balance sneakers and the black socks with the Nike Swoosh on them, camouflage shorts, and a T-shirt. And his G-Shock watch. Always his G-Shock watch, the kind that’s chunked up with cool functions and you can really beat it up. That is one of Gabe’s hobbies: G-Shock watches.

With his hands in his pockets, he walks along a curve in the road on his way to the farm shop a mile away. They sell coffee and sandwiches and stuff there. Gabe doesn’t drink coffee, and he is not especially hungry just now, but he walks there anyway, like he does most days. Not every day. But most days. It’s private, just him, the way other people do. And it helps make the days go by until the next day, which might be better than this day.

Fwap, fwap. Fwap, fwap. Fwap, fwap. Gabe’s sneakers against the pavement, the only sound except for the singing birds. He’ll order a muffin. They have good blueberry muffins. The women working behind the counter will say, “Hey, Gabe. Howya doing.” It’s nice at the farm shop.

He turns left down a long road with no sidewalks, only bright-green lawns that slope down to the street. Big, mostly older houses. Robins tweet as they peck at seeds in the grass of the big yards. Gabe’s eyebrows are slightly raised and his chin is puckered. He looks a little bored but also receptive to the world around him. He looks ready, in case anything happens, but he knows that it usually doesn’t.

He is the only person walking along the road, so there’s no one to compare himself with, none of the people who are all the same. Most people are the same as one another, which makes Gabe different. On this road he sometimes even forgets, but only for a few seconds. He thinks all the time about the fact that he is different. It’s stuck inside him—that’s how he puts it. He thinks about it in the shower, he thinks about it while he’s watching Indiana Jones movies, and he thinks about it while he’s cooking eggs on the stove, which he is getting better at. “Sssomeone told me that before,” he says, the S sound extending for a syllable. “That I’m different. Down syndrome is not a sickness. There’s no vaccine for it. If there was, I would take it.”

“Can you set up the tripod?” Gabe is in a stairwell at the theater now. For eleven years he has worked two days a week at the Prospector, a movie theater in Ridgefield, Connecticut, a couple towns over from where he lives. Most of the people Gabe works with have some kind of disability because that’s mostly who the Prospector hires, not as a side project but as its main reason for existing. Its mission is to provide meaningful, well-paying jobs for adults with disabilities. Some have Down syndrome. Some have other challenges and aren’t able to walk or talk. But everybody does a job. When you see a movie at the Prospector, disabled people will greet you, sell you a ticket, sell you popcorn and soda, give a short introduction to the film (the audience always claps), and collect your trash on the way out. There’s a commercial kitchen where they make the flavored popcorn for sale in the lobby and online, to raise money.

The employees are called Prospects, and the theater helps them find their “sparkle.” Gabe got the job after he went to see the movie American Sniper here. In his interview, he asked if they offered worker’s comp.

There are different expressions of Down syndrome, different ways of being, different kinds of capacities and limits. Gabe doesn’t talk much about the cans and can’ts. You can’t generalize about it, and why would you want to?

He sees the differences within his differentness at the Prospector. There is a whole language that people like him use, kind of like people in Paris have their own language. Within the language are dialects and accents and nuances. When Gabe speaks, to his ear, his voice sounds like everyone else’s voice. Sometimes he has trouble understanding people who talk the way he does, and other times he understands them as clearly as he can understand his parents, or Matt Damon in a Jason Bourne movie.

In the stairwell, Gabe kneels over a duffel bag of camera cables and extension cords. He does video production for the Prospector. He and his friend and coworker Ian Foss produce and film short movies—ads that play during the previews mostly, starring Prospects talking about their work at the theater and reminding people to turn off their cell phones. Gabe likes working with Ian, partly because Ian is just a great friend and partly because Ian is like most people, different from Gabe.

“Gabe, you wanna set up the tripod?” Ian asks again. “I gotta go grab the card for the FX9, and I have to go get the audio cord because I’m gonna mic you up before we come back up.”

Gabe makes an “mmm” sound and begins unsheathing the tripod’s legs. He sees a birthday party of little girls gather around a balloon bouquet downstairs in the lobby. All the girls are the same as most people. Gabe can look around as he sets up the equipment because he’s done it so many times. A few years ago he took classes in television production at a community college. At home, in his room, he spends hours looking up so many YouTube videos about how his favorite movies were made, behind-the-scenes footage showing how scenes were shot. “Comes to Hollywood, they always shoot more than one shot. They do more than a thousand takes,” he says. “They can spend eight or nine or ten hours for one clip. Here, we do the same thing but it’s a bit different. Here, no way—nnnot a lot of takes.” The Prospector owns Sony Red cameras and all kinds of cinema-grade equipment, and Gabe hopes—and believes, even—that his work might get noticed one day. Sometimes famous actors come to the theater. Ryan Reynolds lives nearby and has been in. Maybe one day one of them will tell Tom Hanks or Steven Spielberg or George Lucas about the preshow videos Gabe Kavookjian shoots for the Prospector and he will get to work in Hollywood.

Sometimes his old friends from New Canaan High School, class of ’11, come to the Prospector with their wives and kids. His buddies. They hug and backslap and laugh. It’s fun to see them, but it’s also hard sometimes. He loves kids, and he thinks about how much he wants the life his buddies have. Sometimes it feels like they’re coming to see him because he works at this place, like he’s on display or something. That’s not the way high school was. In high school, everyone was so good to him, and he didn’t feel so different at all. He was on the football team. The coach put him in for a play in his senior year, and Gabe ran so hard on the field, and all the other players were swirling around him running and tackling, and afterward everyone ran up to Gabe and smiled and slapped his helmet and told him how great he was out there.

Before that, when he was little, school wasn’t always great. Kids can be mean.

“They can call you a ‘puff face,’ ” he says. “For people who have Down syndrome, you have stuff with the way your face looks, or your stomach, right? And for me, I originally had a puff face. And now, I don’t have that anymore. I don’t know how it comes down, but I don’t have that anymore.”

He’s got the tripod set up now. He uncoils one of the cords for the camera.

“I would say half my buddies are married and have children. And I’m not. And I’m still looking,” he says.

“Well, there’s someone I’m trying to find, and I don’t know where it will take me.”

“No. There’s one person. I’m not going to say her name. When you have Down syndrome, it’s so hard to date someone. I’ll keep going at it. I won’t stop or fail. You just want to go for it. I want to meet someone different. When you see someone, you want to go for it. Don’t be afraid when you find someone. It’s hard to go first.”

“I don’t get nervous. The problem is, she might say no to you. She might shoot you down. I don’t drive. That’s tough because you can’t take her places. You can’t go anywhere.”

It’s good that you have that spirit, to not give up.

Are there people who have taught you that?

“Yeah. Tons of them. And the number-one person is Val Jensen.”

“Yyyup. She has pink hair. It’s so easy to find her.”

In his parents’ big white house, he sits in the basement on the overstuffed pink chair by the doors to the backyard with his socked feet on the pink ottoman watching 24. It’s a weekday, and he’s not working today. Gabe owns every season on DVD and has watched all of them. Every episode ends in a cliff-hanger. He also owns The Jason Bourne Collection, every season of Two and a Half Men, every season of SEAL Team, most of the Harry Potter DVDs, all the Pirates of the Caribbeans, Daddy’s Home, Daddy’s Home 2, Grown Ups, Grown Ups 2, American Sniper, the American Pie: 3 Movie Pie Pack, several Fast & Furious DVDs, Jurassic World, and 8 Mile because Gabe is a big nut for Eminem. He is obsessed.

The room is full of gray October light. Rectangles of sun through the windowpanes overlap with Kiefer Sutherland’s face on the flat-screen. Gabe breathes in, then breathes out lazily, the air fluttering his lips. He is half-watching the show and half-holding the remote in one droopy hand. He loves 24, but this is nnnnot that fun. He moves a pillow and pushes himself out of the chair, then thuds up the stairs to the kitchen for a bowl of cereal. Cereal is easy. Milk, that’s all you need.

Gabe loves people, but he’s okay with not having other people around. He likes being alone sometimes. And sometimes being surrounded by people can make him feel lonely. It’s confusing because he’s happy too. With people. Gabe has two parents who love him. He has two brothers and a sister who love him, and they have kids, his nieces and nephews—the loves of his life. He has friends at work, and he has his buddies. He loves and is loved. Maybe tomorrow he’ll meet someone.

The happiness he feels when he’s with the people in his life is real—so real and so happy that it lets him dream about what life would be like if he were even happier.

Maybe he’ll walk down and get a muffin. Say hi to everyone at the shop.

Carhartt is another of Gabe’s hobbies, and he’s head-to-toe right now. He had to get out of the house, but he can’t drive, so he had to get an Uber to Gemstone, the other place he works for pay. Val, who owns the Prospector and has the pink hair, also owns this 160-acre farm with ponds and woods and a rambling mansion. The place was sitting empty for something like forty years, and Val bought it out of foreclosure and turned it into Gemstone, a working farm with chickens, turkeys, vegetable gardens, fish, and a forest that’s been colonized by local wildlife.

“Even on my day off, I come here. Be here when I want and enjoy myself. Before I’m gonna get myself a girlfriend,” Gabe says.

A dozen or so people are working within sight of the mansion, which is the Gemstone headquarters. Val’s here, and Gabe joins the small crew in the kitchen making chicken Caesar wraps for everyone for lunch. This house can feel as much like home as his parents’ house, and these guys are his buddies. Just now they are talking about how to enclose the top of the chicken yard with wire so hawks can’t get at the chickens.

Gabe remembers something and it just comes out, ending the chicken-­wire discussion.

“Someone told me, You’re not gonna date no one because you have Down syndrome.”

His buddies stop grating cheese for a second and look at their friend.

Val scowls. “Who told you that?” she asks.

Gabe shakes his head and says, “Don’t want to say names.” He pauses, looking around the kitchen with his eyebrows up. “That’s a bit hurtful for someone to say that to someone who has Down syndrome.”

Knife chops and the fridge door opening and closing are the only sounds in the kitchen for a few minutes. Gabe opens and closes a drawer, then says, “In 2014, I found someone and lost my chance. She got married and I was waiting, waiting, waited for a while, and in 2022 something interesting happened. I walked into a place and, boom, love at first sight. And I cannot ask her out because she might say no to me. She might shoot me down. Because one, I don’t drive. How can I take her places and I don’t have a car? You think a guy is supposed to take a lady, and she would be in the car.”

“Wwwwell, Uber doesn’t sound sexy on a first date.”

I ask Gabe if having kids of his own is part of why he wants to find someone.

“More people say to me, ‘Gabe, you don’t want to have children.’ I want to have one, because my high school buddies have one. They’re married.”

Val turns to me and says, “We do have a friend at the Prospector who has Down syndrome and is married.”

“And he talks about it nnnon . . . stop,” Gabe says. He groans. “Twenty-­four seven.”

“Gabe can’t stand people with Down syndrome,” Val says. “And my sister, who also has Down syndrome, hates people with Down syndrome.”

“I think because she gets away with a lot, and then when she sees somebody doing her same tricks, she wants none of it.”

Gabe leans against a counter and puts his hands in his pockets.

“Most people don’t understand Down syndrome well,” he says. “It’s ‘down.’ Down syndrome means down. You’re down on yourself.”

“It’s the name of the doctor who discovered it! Doctor Down.”

Gabe folds his arms over his Carhartt shirt and looks over at his boss.

“Well why is your sister so good with me?”

Val smiles, looks up, and shakes her head, searching for the end of the sentence. Gabe, his voice loud and soft at the same time, continues what he was thinking about.

“My whole childhood, I had friends with Down syndrome. You become friends with them when you are little. But eight, nine, ten years old, not really. Comes to the theater, though, it’s different.”

There are people with all kinds of disabilities at the theater, I point out. Does he have friends with disabilities there? Does he fit in?

“I fit in with them because I have it. It’s so hard to get yourself out of that.” He fits in at the theater—but in a way that he doesn’t like to fit in.

Val says, “You’re here, aren’t you? You’re the only one with Down syndrome here, and you get along with everyone. Your Down syndrome doesn’t matter here.”

Gabe says that he likes it best at the farm when there are no other Prospects there, just him and the workers who don’t have a disability.

“Yeah, because we do have Prospects come here sometimes, so they’re mixed in. Today, right now I feel fine because they’re not here.”

They’re not here to remind him that he’s different.

Val turns to me and says, “When we do have a group of Prospects come to the farm, Gabe prefers to be off with his guys and his crew. And I can understand that.”

Gabe cuts in, rewinding the conversation. “And also as someone who’s talked about dating, I’m not gonna say his name—”

“Nobody talks about dating more than you, Gabe.”

After lunch Val assigns him and two other workers to clear some tall grass and brush near one end of the lake so kids who visit can get closer to the water. Gabe likes working with these guys best. They are like everybody else.

Gabe’s parents, Haik and Lynn Kavookjian, heat water for tea in their sunny, open kitchen. Gabe empties two packets of instant hot chocolate into a mug. His parents have been encouraging him lately to think about moving into an apartment with a roommate. There’s a coworker at the Prospector who lives just a few blocks from the theater. Gabe could walk to work.

“He’s a lovely guy,” Haik says. He’s wearing slippers and leaning against the counter. “And he’s looking for a roommate, trying to cover his lease for the next four or five months. He could help with rides, and they’d walk into town—he said just come by and give it a try. Gabe always worries what’s going to happen when we’re not around, which is a natural thing. And although he’s got loving siblings, this is a chance to try and be independent.”

“I really don’t know,” he says quickly, in a monotone.

“And that’s what I said—we don’t know,” Haik says, upbeat. “But I wanted to just go by and see.”

“Having a roommate . . . ” Lynn says, a mother’s hope in her voice. She smiles first at me, then at Gabe, who is stirring his cocoa.

“I think it’s a little overwhelming,” Haik says.

“I tell him half the people in the world have no car and no driver’s license,” Lynn says to me. “It’s no big deal.”

It’s not that they don’t love having their son around. They love having him around. He waters the plants and takes out the trash and does all those things. He makes them laugh. And they can see how he’s doing. (When I first asked Gabe about his relationship with his parents, he sounded like a teenager: “Comes to my parents, it’s not interesting. It’s really nothing to tell there. Yeah. I’ve lived with them for thirty-five years of my life, right? Most people get along with their parents; some people don’t.”) It’s their love for him that makes them want him to be happier—or rather makes them wonder if he could be happier. Gabe wonders the same thing: whether it’s possible for him to be happier.

Part of him worries that if he moved out, he might not see his sister’s kids as much, who live not far from his parents. When they visit he teases them, they back-talk him, he chases them in the yard, they hug him. He is Uncle Gabe, and he loves being Uncle Gabe. “The thing about Gabe himself, he’s amazing,” Gabe says. “I’m a comedian. I can be a goofball. Most people say I’m a comedian, I’m a goofball, I’m great. I have two nephews. I got one little niece.”

Gabe probably spends about half the money he makes at his jobs buying presents for his nieces and nephews. “Every single dime of it, to them and to myself,” he says. He kicks his chin up when he says it. “Comes to Christmas, birthdays, or Easter, you always want to think about the people around you more than yourself. That’s me right there.”

He takes his hands out of his pockets and holds one in the other, in front of him.

They’re coming over later today, in fact. His sister, her husband, and their three kids, including the new baby. His sister and his mom will sit with the baby while everyone else helps his dad with the maple syrup. It’s a family activity Haik started when the kids were little, tapping sugar maples in the yard and boiling the sap for syrup, which they eat, give as gifts, and sell at the farm shop. Gabe and the kids will trudge around the yard, crusted with hard, slippery snow, checking the sap buckets but mostly goofing around. Haik will boost his grandchildren up so they can see into the tall boiler in which the sap cooks down. Gabe will wear sneakers and skate around on the icy yard, looking at his feet, calling out to his niece to be careful or she’ll slide into a tree, threatening to drink all the hot chocolate when they go inside. Wishing he had his own children but loving that he has these.

That’s Gabe right there. Trying every day to love his life and every day wanting one part of it to be different. That’s all of us right there.

“I’m trying to figure out what Gabe wants in life,” he says. “You still want to fight it. You still want to find who you are. It’s like you’re walking into a storm. And you can pick up my hand and we can walk through the storm, warm or cold. You keep going. You always want to keep on going. Just do it. Find who you are. Find your passion. Comes to the Prospector, they say you want to find your sparkle. For me, it’s to find something I love.”

You don’t like being told no, I tell him.

“Some things, I can say no; some things I cannot say no to. If someone’s going through something, I don’t say no, comes to that. Having a bad day? Give him a hot chocolate or something.”

Are you good at knowing when someone needs help? When they’re sad?

“Oh!” His voice jumps, as if he’s been waiting for this question. He looks up, opens his mouth to speak, and takes a second to find the words. There are times when you’re with Gabe when he needs to explain to you something he thinks you can’t understand, and the only way he can say the things he needs to say is to give you a metaphor or to speak like a poet, like a storyteller. “Oh, I’m spot-on with that. You feel what that person is going through in life. That’s me. That’s Gabe right there. Don’t be afraid to guide someone through the storm. The storm doesn’t stop. If it stops, it just finds a new place. You start your day over and over, every, every day.”

In the cold, dim late afternoon, when the yellow streetlights flicker on and the trees look black but the sky is still a little bit blue, his sister’s family will leave, and he will again be with his parents in the big white house. He’ll watch a movie in the basement, then wash up in the bathroom next to his bedroom. He’ll climb into his bed beneath his two framed posters of Eminem, his framed photographs of actors and football players, the G-Shock watches that he has nested in their felted Lucite cases, his team photo of the 2009 New Canaan High School Rams football team. In the photo he’s sitting second-row center, just behind the captains. As he pulls up the sheets, the storm that sometimes enters his mind will quiet, and he’ll sleep until six-thirty or seven. He’ll wake up in the morning the same Gabe he was yesterday, believing in the possibility of his life, over and over, every, every day, the same as us. He’ll shower and get dressed and put on his sneakers and walk to get a muffin. That’s Gabe right there.

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

If Hailey Bieber wears a nail look, it immediately becomes a trend. It all started with her glazed donut nails, and since then, she’s been a mainstay on all of our nail moodboards. The same could go for virtually every step of the It Girl’s beauty routine, from her Rhode blush du jour to whatever haircut and color combo she’s wearing at any given moment.

So when she showed up to the Academy Museum Gala this weekend with a jet-black manicure, I knew it: Everyone’s about to have glossy, black nails this fall.

With a bubblegum-pink Chanel gown, this shiny, full-opacity nail color is reminiscent of a glossy heap of caviar atop a plush blini. And just like a little black dress (and, tbh, caviar), it goes with everything.

Instead of opting for a soft pink or French tip to complement the bright-pink dress, celebrity nail artist Zola Ganzorigt “wanted the nails to stand out against the pink gown.” To create the look, Ganzorigt used OPI’s IntelliGel polish in Black Onyx. “I reach for it every fall, as it’s rich and moody,” she says. “It’s also versatile and can feel sleek on its own or add an edge to something softer, like Hailey’s bubblegum pink gown,” she says. “The contrast against the pink is what made the look so special.”

Nail prep is definitely key here if you’re DIYing. File, shape, and buff your nails to get a smooth canvas first. Ganzorigt went with an almond shape (Hailey’s go-to, but a square or squoval would work here too) to elongate Hailey’s fingers, then applied a few coats of gel polish for a striking finish.

Amid all of the warm, brown nail colors of fall right now (iced latte nails, butter toffee nails, pumpkin pie nails—I could go on), black feels subversive but still so damn chic. A gel polish definitely keeps this looking expensive, adding a smooth, shiny finish that’ll last for up to two weeks (unlike the chipped black manis of your youth). No wonder it looked so good at the Academy Museum Gala, a star-studded event celebrating film, with A-listers like Taylor Swift, Kendall Jenner, Colman Domingo, Inde Navarette, and more.

Zola Ganzorigt is a celebrity nail artist who works with some of the biggest names (and nail lovers) in Hollywood, from Hailey Bieber and Kylie Jenner to Sabrina Carpenter and Jennie.

#235. 6 Fall Boot Trends to Try This Season, From Buckled Styles to Slim Knee-Highs

Great boots and fall weather go hand in hand (or should we say foot in foot?). When summer temps turn into crisp, leafy days, boots are the first thing we’re itching to wear again. Luckily for fall 2026, there are plenty of exciting new boot trends to try out.

On the fall runways, boots appeared with an extra dose of attitude. A favorite of the season is the knee-high slim, which isn’t a new style, per se, but appeared upgraded with a wicked heel, a structured shape, and extra hardware. Speaking of hardware, buckle boots were a hit this season too. The classic workwear style arrived to much fanfare at Dries Van Noten and Dior. Elsewhere, leg-elongating options like second-skin sock boots and extra-tall OTK boots were on view at Celine, Chanel, Chloé, and Balenciaga. Those looking for chic weather-ready options will be eager to shop Miu Miu’s grip-soled stompers and Loewe’s transparent take on the rain boot, while those wanting to add a bit of extra flair might gravitate toward the Western-inspired styles from Valentino and Rabanne.

Whatever your taste, there are plenty of boots to stomp in this season. Shop the top fall boot trends right here.

Knee-high boots, especially with heels with a slim, structured shape, feel fresh this fall. Go for a classic style in chocolate brown or Gucci’s horse-bit style for some extra attitude.

For fall, high fashion houses like Dries Van Noten, Dior, and Ann Demeulemeester put their spin on the tough and humble buckle boot. They’re already flying off the shelves.

Soft leather sock boots acted like a second skin this season at Celine, Chanel, and Calvin Klein. The style looks especially chic when peeking from beneath a midi or a long coat.

Far from your classic Wellies, this season’s weather-ready footwear has fashion-forward appeal. Fit for rain and shine, we’re particularly taken with Miu Miu’s tough grip-sole styles and Loewe’s transparent boots.

Fashion’s flirtation with Westernwear appeared at Chloé, Valentino, and Paco Rabanne. Wear them underneath maxis or over denim and trousers.

If the runways are any indication, extra-tall OTK boots aren’t going anywhere. They appeared over loose trousers and skinny jeans and as a counterpoint to miniskirts.

#236. How to Care for Your Skin on Birth Control

Experts explain why contraception can affect acne, oil, and hyperpigmentation.

Naturally, there’s a lot that goes into the decision to get on birth control. How it affects your skin, for better or worse, may not be top of mind until you notice the changes. Several factors, including age, health history, and the type of contraception you choose, can result in clear skin, breakouts, excessive dryness, and a range of other skin shifts. Experts explain some of the more visible changes your skin may experience—and more importantly, how to care for and keep it healthy and glowing while on birth control.

Birth control can have a pretty significant impact on the skin, particularly when it comes to acne, oil production, and pigmentation. Dr. Chelsea Hoffman, MD, MSc, FAAD, a board-certified dermatologist at Hudson Dermatology and Laser Surgery, explains that the changes vary between combination birth control, which contains estrogen and progestin (OCPs), and progestin-only methods. “Combination pills often improve acne because they work to counteract the effect of androgens—a type of hormone that stimulates oil glands and triggers acne,” Hoffman explains to ELLE. The result, especially for those with oily or acne-prone skin, is less oil production and fewer breakouts. Conversely, Dr. Jennifer Choe, an OB/GYN at Montefiore Einstein Advanced Care, says that while the breakout may subside, this type of birth control can trigger hyperpigmentation like melasma, particularly for those already susceptible to it.

On the other hand, Choe says that some progestin-only methods such as Depo-Provera shots or a Mirena IUD can trigger or worsen acne in some patients. Hoffman agrees, noting that acne is one of the most common reasons people discontinue these birth control methods.

It’s a step that should already be ingrained into your routine, but Choe stresses how crucial regular sunscreen use is while on birth control—especially since melasma and hyperpigmentation can worsen with sun exposure. “Additionally, acne scars can become permanent if they are exposed to the sun,” says Choe.

This last layer is essential, but Hoffman says the rest of your routine doesn’t necessarily need an overhaul. “You generally don’t need an entirely different skincare routine just because you’re on birth control. I recommend keeping the basics consistent: a gentle cleanser, a non-comedogenic moisturizer, and daily broad-spectrum sunscreen with at least SPF 30,” Hoffman suggests.

Additionally, Hoffman says that tinted sunscreens containing iron oxides are especially important for patients dealing with melasma because they also help protect against visible light, which contributes to the condition. Beyond that, she recommends tailoring your routine to what your skin is actually doing. “If your birth control is improving your acne, a simple maintenance routine may be all you need. If you’re experiencing new breakouts, a topical retinoid, benzoyl peroxide, or another targeted acne treatment may help,” Hoffman says. “I always tell my patients to let me know about any persistent or sudden changes, so that we can work with the prescribing clinician to alter birth control if needed, rather than trying to correct everything by adding more products.”

If you do happen to cycle off birth control for any stretch of time, Choe says you may notice some skin changes or the occasional pimple, but you don’t necessarily need to change your skin care routine to follow. “If you notice that you break out during your period, you can opt to skip your menses using birth control pills. Furthermore, topical acne medications are perfectly safe to use alongside birth control,” says Choe.

Talk to your doctor before adding or subtracting products from your regimen. “When you stop a combination birth control pill, you lose its ongoing sebum and acne-suppressing effects, so oily skin and breakouts can return. If you’re prone to hormonal acne, it’s helpful to have a maintenance or treatment plan in place before going off,” says Hoffman. With her patients, she adds that “Sometimes, we will use other anti-androgenic meds to do the work OCPs once did, for example, Winlevi or spironolactone.” One important point Hoffman also notes is that pigmentation doesn’t necessarily resolve when you stop birth control. “If you’ve developed melasma, treating it and consistent sun protection is still super important,” says Hoffman.

Choe says yes; most antiaging-focused ingredients such as retinol are safe to use with birth control. And Hoffman concurs, adding that being on birth control is not a reason to avoid topical retinoids or acids like AHAs. “However, because oral combined pills might be slightly suppressing oil production already, just make sure to start low and go slow when it comes to retinoids to reduce risk of causing irritation and disrupting the skin barrier,” Hoffman advises. She recommends this to everyone, even patients who aren’t on OCPs.

Both experts agree that most treatments are safe while you are on birth control, including Botox, fillers, and many lasers. However, Choe says to be careful with aggressive heat- or light-based procedures like certain lasers, because they can provoke or worsen melasma. Always consult a dermatologist before undergoing any treatments.
