#237. We Tried Home Depot’s Viral Grand Duchess Christmas Tree—Is It Worth It?

Can a $349 artificial Christmas tree really compete with premium models? After a month of testing Home Depot's Smart Grand Duchess, I was surprised by just how much it delivers for the price.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

A realistic (but still artificial) Christmas tree with customizable lighting, smart controls and easy assembly usually comes with a pretty hefty price tag. That’s why I was interested in trying Home Depot’s 7.5-foot Smart Grand Duchess Twinkling Balsam Fir, which promises all of those features for around $350.

I’ve tested plenty of home products and holiday decorations over the years, including artificial Christmas trees costing significantly more than this one. I wanted to see whether Home Depot’s relatively affordable smart tree could really compete with the premium options.

After a full month of testing, decorating, experimenting with the lighting and eventually packing it away, I came away thoroughly impressed. In fact, it held its own against a much more expensive King of Christmas tree I already own.

A smart artificial Christmas tree with app and remote controls and a surprisingly lush look for the price.

The Smart Grand Duchess Twinkling Balsam Fir is a pre-lit artificial Christmas tree from Home Depot’s Home Decorators Collection, available in 7.5-, 9-, 12- or 15-foot size options. It uses both realistic molded branches with 2,250 color-changing micro LED lights and smart controls through the Hubspace app.

At first glance, its biggest selling point is how realistic it looks. The outer branches are made from molded plastic designed to replicate the appearance and texture of natural evergreen foliage. Unlike the flat, papery needles found on cheaper artificial trees, these branches have convincing dimension and structure.

Look a little deeper into the tree, though, and you’ll discover something interesting. The interior uses less expensive, traditional artificial foliage to fill out the branches. It’s a clever cost-saving approach that works really well. The premium-looking tips are what you see from the outside, while the cheaper foliage provides fullness without drawing attention to itself.

The tree also features “Quick Set” technology, which connects the lighting through the trunk as you assemble the sections, along with memory-wire branches that require less shaping. Its integrated lighting can be controlled using the included remote or the Hubspace smartphone app, with adjustable brightness, various lighting effects and customizable schedules.

I set up the Smart Grand Duchess in my home and tested it for one month, evaluating everything from assembly and branch realism to smart features, everyday usability and storage.

Throughout the testing period, I experimented with different lighting modes, decorated the tree, used both the remote and smartphone app, and paid attention to how well the branches maintained their shape. I also compared its appearance and overall quality with my considerably more expensive artificial tree I’ve had for a few years already.

One of the first things I appreciated about the Smart Grand Duchess was how straightforward it was to assemble. From opening the box to getting the tree standing with its lights connected, the process took around 20 minutes. That’s not including any additional time spent fluffing and shaping the branches (which can take hours if you’re anything like me).

The Quick Set design eliminates much of the frustration that can come with assembling a pre-lit tree. Instead of hunting for electrical connections between sections, the lighting connects through the trunk as the pieces fit together. This seems to be a pretty standard feature in modern artificial trees, so I was glad to see it included in this model.

Once assembled, I spent some time arranging the branches to achieve a natural shape and fill any obvious gaps. Thanks to the memory-wire construction, this was relatively easy, and the tree quickly started to look full and balanced.

The metal stand is fairly basic, but it does its job well. I didn’t experience any stability issues during the month I had the tree displayed.

For me, the appearance is where this tree really shines. I’ve seen plenty of artificial Christmas trees that look convincing from across the room but noticeably cheap when you get closer. That wasn’t the case here.

The molded outer branches have an impressively realistic appearance, especially considering the price. They provide the shape and texture you’d expect from a more premium artificial tree, and there’s enough variation in the foliage to keep it from looking overly uniform.

What impressed me most was how effectively Home Depot disguises the less expensive materials inside the tree. The traditional foliage toward the center adds density and prevents the tree from looking sparse, but it’s largely hidden behind the realistic outer branches.

It’s a smart design decision. You’re not paying for premium molded foliage in areas that nobody is likely to see, yet the finished tree still looks full and convincing.

According to Kristin Ilgunas, founder and designer at A Merry Little Kristmas, a luxury holiday design studio, this combination of materials is actually something to look for in a quality artificial Christmas tree. “Then there are trees that are a mix: realistic PE on the outer edges and the PVC on the inside. This makes them full and is generally what a lot of ‘nicer’ artificial trees are now,” she explains. “This is actually what I prefer to use because the inner PVC is easy to manipulate and attach ribbon and other items to.”

The construction on our tested tree also appears to help minimize shedding. Since much of the visible foliage consists of molded plastic pieces rather than individual loose needles, I noticed very little debris during assembly, decorating or disassembly.

I decorated the tree with relatively lightweight ornaments, and the branches held their shape without noticeable sagging. I can’t speak to how well they’d support particularly heavy decorations, but they handled my everyday ornaments without trouble.

Another thoughtful detail is the long, upright section at the very top of the tree. It’s ideal for securing a tree topper and helps keep it standing straight.

Perhaps the strongest endorsement of the tree’s appearance came from friends and family. Several people commented on how good it looked and were surprised when I told them how much it cost.

While the realistic branches were my favorite part of the design, the lighting came a very close second.

The Smart Grand Duchess includes 2,250 micro LED lights, with settings that range from traditional white lighting to colorful displays and animated effects.

I’ve tested trees with multicolored lighting that looks overly bright and almost cartoonish. This one is different. The colors are slightly more subdued and sophisticated, giving the tree a polished appearance rather than an overwhelming display.

My favorite setting was the steady multicolored mode. I loved the way the different colors illuminated the branches without constantly changing or distracting from the decorations. I also found myself returning to the slow-fade version, which adds a little movement while maintaining that more understated look.

Connecting the tree to Home Depot’s Hubspace app was quick and painless. The interface is clean and straightforward, with easy access to lighting modes, timers, schedules and brightness adjustments.

One of the most useful features was the ability to schedule the lights. Rather than switching them on and off manually each day, I could set the tree to light up automatically when I wanted it.

The brightness controls have three settings: low, medium and high. I’d ordinarily prefer a more precise slider, but in practice, these three levels were enough for my needs.

Even with the app working reliably throughout testing, I still found myself reaching for the physical remote quite frequently. It’s simply more convenient when you’re sitting nearby and want to flick through a few lighting options without opening your phone.

I particularly appreciate that the tree doesn’t force you to use its smart features. The app adds some useful functionality, but you can still enjoy the lights without making every adjustment through your smartphone.

Ilgunas says convenience is one of the biggest reasons to invest in a smart Christmas tree. “We don’t need to crawl under the tree to unplug it or switch it off, and we don’t need to worry about resetting the timer after a short power outage. A remote control and/or phone app gives you total control at the tip of your finger.”

Over the course of a month, the Smart Grand Duchess continued to impress. The branches maintained their shape, the stand remained stable and the lighting and smart controls worked without any noticeable issues.

I also didn’t experience the sort of excessive needle shedding that you might find with cheaper artificial trees.

When it came time to pack everything away, the process was as straightforward as it gets.

One detail worth knowing before you open the packaging is that the original shipping box doubles as a storage box. I’d recommend taking a little extra care when unboxing so you have a decent container to use when the holidays are over.

Personally, I actually preferred storing this tree in its original box rather than using a dedicated Christmas tree bag. I’ve dealt with large, floppy storage bags in the past, and they can be awkward to carry, move around and organize in a storage area.

The rigid cardboard box was much easier to handle and fit neatly into my storage space. Of course, you’ll want to keep it somewhere dry, and a dedicated storage bag may be preferable for more demanding storage conditions.

Still, having a usable storage option included with the tree is a welcome bonus, especially considering its price.

I’ve owned and tested artificial Christmas trees across a fairly wide range of prices, including a much more expensive model from King of Christmas.

That’s what made the Smart Grand Duchess such a pleasant surprise. Looking at the two trees, the price difference isn’t nearly as obvious as I expected.

My King of Christmas tree is undeniably a premium product, but the Home Depot model manages to achieve a similarly attractive overall appearance for considerably less money. The realistic outer foliage does much of the heavy lifting, while the interior filling provides the density needed to create a convincing finished tree.

Where the Grand Duchess stands out most is in its combination of price and technology. You get integrated multicolored lighting, app-based schedules, a physical remote and easy assembly without paying the premium that often comes with higher-end artificial trees.

That doesn’t necessarily mean it’s better than every more expensive option. If you prioritize premium materials throughout the entire tree or specialized construction, you may still find a reason to spend more.

But for most people who want a full, realistic-looking Christmas tree with plenty of lighting options, I think the Grand Duchess gives you an excellent balance of quality, features and price.

After a month of testing, I can confidently say that the Home Depot Smart Grand Duchess Christmas tree is one of the better-value artificial trees I’ve found.

Its biggest achievement is making a relatively affordable tree look considerably more expensive than it is. The molded outer branches are convincing, the less expensive interior foliage is cleverly concealed, and the finished result is full and attractive.

The lighting is another highlight. Rather than offering flashy effects simply for the sake of having them, the tree gives you a few beautiful settings that complement its appearance. The Hubspace app is easy to navigate, and the included remote makes everyday adjustments even simpler.

There are a few compromises, including the basic stand and limited brightness controls, but none meaningfully detracted from my experience. Even better, the tree was reliable throughout my testing, drew plenty of compliments from visitors and was easy to pack away afterward.

If you’re looking for a realistic, pre-lit Christmas tree with smart features but don’t want to spend a small fortune, the Smart Grand Duchess would be very high on my list.

A smart artificial Christmas tree with app and remote controls and a surprisingly lush look for the price.

The 7.5-foot Smart Grand Duchess Twinkling Balsam Fir is available at The Home Depot for around $350, and up to around $1,500 for the 15-foot version.

Home Depot also offers other sizes and configurations within the Grand Duchess collection, including slim and flocked versions, so it’s worth comparing the options to find the right fit for your space.

Yes. Based on our testing, realism is one of its greatest strengths. Molded plastic foliage on the outer branches provides a convincing appearance, while less expensive artificial needles toward the center fill out the tree without being particularly noticeable.

Yes. The tree includes a physical remote that lets you to change lighting effects without using your smartphone. The Hubspace app adds features such as customizable schedules and convenient smart controls.

In our testing, assembly took about 20 minutes, not including additional fluffing and branch shaping. The Quick Set design helps simplify installation by connecting the electrical components through the trunk.

We noticed very little shedding during our month of testing. Its molded outer foliage consists largely of solid plastic pieces, which helps reduce the number of loose needles compared with some artificial trees that rely more heavily on traditional PVC foliage.

Yes. We successfully packed the tree back into its original shipping box and found it convenient for storage. Take care when unboxing to preserve the cardboard, and keep the box in a dry location to protect it from moisture.

For this review, product tester and editor Paul Rankin spent approximately one month evaluating the Home Decorators Collection Smart Grand Duchess Christmas tree in his own home. He assembled, decorated and displayed the tree, tested its lighting and smart controls, monitored its performance over time and evaluated how easily it could be packed away.

Paul has years of experience testing and reviewing home products for publications including Family Handyman, Bob Vila and Reader’s Digest. His experience with other artificial Christmas trees, including higher-end models from King of Christmas, provided additional context for evaluating the Grand Duchess’s realism, features and value.

We also consulted Kristin Ilgunas, founder and designer at A Merry Little Kristmas, a luxury holiday design studio specializing in high-end residential and boutique commercial holiday décor. #239. Can You Make Stuffing Ahead of Time? Yes—Here’s How

The key to a breezy Thanksgiving is the same as for any dinner party: Do absolutely everything you can ahead of time. I don’t just mean getting a jump on cranberry sauce, pie dough, or overnight-brining the bird—you should cross every single item, big and small, off your to-do list as far in advance as possible, to free up the big day for last-minute mishaps and (this is going to sound crazy) to enjoy yourself.

Can you make stuffing ahead of time? Absolutely. Many Thanksgiving stuffing recipes can be prepared at least partially in advance. Our make-ahead stuffing recipe uses a two-stage baking process: cook the stuffing through the day before Thanksgiving, then refrigerate it overnight. The next day, all that’s left is to reheat it and crisp up the top while your turkey rests.

If you’re used to throwing together a dish of stuffing from a store-bought mix, this make-ahead stuffing recipe is a very easy, very delicious upgrade. Instead of coating a bag of brittle dried bread cubes with unidentified poultry seasoning, this homemade stuffing recipe builds big flavor with hearty torn sourdough bread, hot Italian sausage, fresh herbs, and a boatload of caramelized onions. It requires minimal day-of labor (without sacrificing taste) by relying on the prep time you’ll carve out on Thanksgiving Eve. The result is a stuffing that’s ready when you are—and plenty of time on T-Day to focus on your turkey recipe and all those other Thanksgiving side dishes.

If you want to make stuffing ahead of time, the type of bread matters. Some classic stuffing recipes call for plain white bread, which will likely absorb too much moisture and disintegrate. A sturdier loaf, like sourdough bread, is more likely to retain its structure as it soaks in the chicken broth, making it the ideal choice for this make-ahead stuffing recipe.

Drying the bread on two baking sheets gives you room to spread the bread cubes into a single layer for even toasting. You’ll dry them in an oven on low heat (250°). Don’t skip this part, even if you’re using a stale loaf (since stale bread isn’t actually dried out), as it helps the sourdough maintain its integrity once submerged into its custardy bath. Transfer the dried bread chunks to a large bowl and prep the rest of the mixture.

True caramelized onions take a long time to break down and become the melty, sweet-savory magic you want them to be. On Thanksgiving dinners past, you would not find a caramelized onion within 100 feet of my table because I absolutely did not have that kind of time. But if I’m assembling the entire stuffing the day before, I can cook spicy sausage, caramelize onions, and create a sage-scented base for torn bread without worrying about the clock.

Sweet, jammy, and totally worth the wait.

Build layers of flavor by sautéing the onions in the same skillet you used to render the sausage fat. Season the onions with kosher salt, add a little extra olive oil, and cook over medium heat until they’re a deep golden brown. If anything starts to stick, add a little water and scrape up the bottom of the pan. Don’t stop cooking the onions until they are certified jammy. Then add in the rest of the aromatics: celery, garlic, and black pepper, plus finely chopped herbs and unsalted butter. Deglaze the pan with white wine and let it simmer before adding it to the bowl with the bread; add the eggs and chicken stock or broth, then transfer the whole mixture to a casserole dish. (Don’t have one? Use a large skillet instead—ovensafe, please.)

Bake the stuffing through its first stage a day or two before Thanksgiving, then let it cool briefly before refrigerating it within two hours of cooking.

On Thanksgiving Day, when your roast turkey is resting, remove the foil and return the stuffing to the oven for its second bake. The recipe calls for another 10 to 15 minutes to warm through and crisp up the top, but go by temperature, not just the clock: The center should reach 165°F before serving.

Yes. Many stuffing recipes can be frozen ahead of Thanksgiving. Our Simple-Is-Best Stuffing, for example, can be baked through its first stage, then frozen for up to six months before the final bake. Let the stuffing cool briefly, wrap tightly, and freeze.

Thaw it in the refrigerator before reheating, allowing at least 24 hours for a large dish. Reheat until the center reaches 165°F, uncovering toward the end to crisp up the top.

How do you reheat stuffing without drying it out?

If your stuffing seems dry, add a splash of chicken or vegetable broth before reheating. Cover the baking dish with foil to help retain moisture, then reheat in an oven set to at least 325°F until the center reaches 165°F. Remove the foil toward the end to crisp up the top.

How long can you keep stuffing in the refrigerator?

According to the USDA, stuffing can be refrigerated for 3–4 days, as long as it’s cooked through and refrigerated promptly. Store it in a covered container, ideally shallow enough to cool quickly, and reheat it thoroughly before serving.

Additional reporting contributed by Zoe Denenberg.

#242. Christopher Ward’s New Watch Is Already Up for an Award. It Only Went on Sale This Week.

The British watchmaker has given its extraordinary Loco a more sophisticated makeover. And it’s already in the running for watchmaking’s biggest prizes.

Anyone with even a passing interest in watches will know that Christopher Ward is on something of a roll. The British brand has spent the past few years producing increasingly ambitious watches at prices that have left some its Swiss rivals looking somewhat, um, punchy.

Its latest is the C1 Loco Classic, a more traditional interpretation of the C12 Loco, introduced last year. It goes on sale today, with prices starting at $5,995, and has already been nominated for one of watchmaking’s most prestigious awards.

The new watch comes in three colors: the previously revealed gold-toned “Oro,” as well as light-blue and black versions unveiled today. All three are available on either a suede strap for $5,995 or on a brand new stainless-steel bracelet for $6,275.

The Loco Classic is one of six finalists in the Petite Aiguille category of the Grand Prix d’Horlogerie de Genève (GPHG), often described as the Oscars of watchmaking, which recognizes watches priced between CHF 4,500 and CHF 10,000. It is the only British-brand nominee in the category.

That matters because Christopher Ward has been here before. In 2023, its Bel Canto, a chiming watch that cost considerably less than most comparable mechanical complications, won the same award. It was the first British watch to win a GPHG prize, bringing Christopher Ward to the attention of collectors who might previously have overlooked it.

The company has since received nominations for its C1 Moonphase in 2024 and the C1 Celestial Moonphase and C12 Loco in 2025. The latter introduced the manually wound CW-003 movement, with its large, exposed balance wheel positioned on the dial side, making the mechanism’s operation a central part of the design.

The Loco Classic uses the same movement but puts it into a completely new setting. Where the C12 Loco had an angular case and integrated sports bracelet, the new model has a rounded 41mm case in 904L stainless steel, individually soldered lugs, and a white ceramic dial with Roman numerals. The lower portion of the dial is finished with a varnish containing powdered mother-of-pearl, which gives the surface a glimmering, changing appearance under different lights.

Despite arriving later, the Classic was not conceived as a straightforward adaptation of the C12. CW says development began back in June 2024, before the original Loco went on sale. Christopher Ward redesigned the movement’s visible bridges with slimmer, more rounded profiles, with each set receiving more than five hours of hand finishing by a specialist in the Swiss Jura.

“The C1 Loco Classic was conceived to evoke an entirely different emotion from the original,” says Christopher Ward cofounder and CEO Mike France. “This is a parallel expression of CW-003 built around the movement-led design and artisanal finishing that we feel has defined the contemporary renaissance in high-end independent watchmaking.”

The case measures a not-insubstantial 14.1mm thick—although more than 5.5mm of that is accounted for by its domed sapphire crystals. Lug-to-lug length is 48mm. The CW-003 movement has an also not-insubstantial six-day power reserve—plus a stated accuracy of between zero and plus seven seconds per day.

The new Consort bracelet, developed for this model, is also made from 904L steel, with alternating polished and brushed surfaces, tool-free link adjustment, and an adjustable clasp.

At $5,995, the Loco Classic is likely to raise more eyebrows in the market.

Its exposed movement, hand-finished components, and unconventional dial arrangement are all features more commonly associated with considerably more expensive independent watchmakers—and now there’s a “classic” version, presumably at least partly intended to appeal to those who found its predecessor’s color options of Frisco Orange, Pasadena Blue, Ursa Black, and Alabaster White a bit much.

The GPHG winners will be announced in Geneva next month. Three years after the Bel Canto’s victory, can Christopher Ward do it again?

#244. Blueberry Protein Pancakes (No Protein Powder)

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week.

Tofu in blueberry pancakes?! Your eyes do not deceive you. Here, silken tofu acts as a binding agent in these protein-packed vegan blueberry pancakes. As there are no eggs in this recipe, you’ll need as much help with leavening as possible to cut through the density of the tofu. This means adding both baking powder and soda—and a lot of it. Baking powder (make sure to use the aluminum-free kind to mitigate any unpleasant flavor) will activate with the water and again when the batter hits the heat; baking soda will react with the water and the acid in the brown sugar. The result is a fluffy, crisp-edged pancake with a slightly chewy, almost mochi-like interior. Small wild blueberries are best, but whatever kind you find at the store will work.

As is the case with most baked goods—even those that technically don’t go into the oven—these pancakes are most successful when the ingredients are measured by weight with a scale. If measuring by volume with measuring cups, it can be easy to pack in a little extra flour. If so, you may need to add about a tablespoon or so more water; you want the batter to be the approximate consistency of pourable whole-milk yogurt (not thick Greek-style).

Discover more Good for You recipes here: Veggie Club Sandwich; Berry Protein Smoothie; Chopped Salad With Sardines and Preserved Lemon

Read More: How I Make Protein Pancakes Without Protein Powder

Whisk 1½ cups (188 g) all-purpose flour, ½ cup (62 g) whole wheat flour, 3 Tbsp. light brown sugar, 2 Tbsp. aluminum-free baking powder, 1 tsp. baking soda, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine.

Blend tofu and liquid from one 16–17-oz. package silken tofu in a blender until very smooth. Scrape down sides and add 1 Tbsp. avocado oil or vegetable oil and 1½ cups water; blend until mixture is very smooth. Scrape into bowl with dry ingredients and gently fold in with a whisk.

Heat a dry large nonstick skillet over medium for 3 minutes. Drizzle in 1½ tsp. avocado oil or vegetable oil. Pour 2 scant ⅓-cupfuls of batter into skillet, leaving space around each. Top each pancake with about 1½ tsp. fresh or frozen wild blueberries. Cook pancakes until tops start to look matte, about 4 minutes. Gently flip and cook until golden underneath, about 4 minutes. Transfer pancakes to a plate or wire rack. (Alternatively, transfer to a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet and keep warm in a 300° oven while you make the rest). Working in 7 more batches, repeat process with remaining oil, batter, and blueberries, adjusting heat as needed to keep pancakes from absorbing too much oil or burning.

Do Ahead: Pancakes can be made 3 months ahead. Let cool, then stack between sheets of parchment paper and place in an airtight container or resealable plastic bag and freeze. Reheat in a toaster or toaster oven until warmed through.

For years, the credit and charge card companies have been fighting tooth and nail to compete with what they could get you: miles, lounge access, a free checked bag here or there. But the most coveted perk today may be a human being who can take things a step further—someone who can find you a suite in a sold-out hotel, or a table at a restaurant that has stopped answering the phone on principle.

That’s the pitch from Atlas, an invite-only charge card with a 24/7 concierge team behind it. “The future of luxury membership isn’t only about maximizing points,” says co-founder and CEO Patrick Mrozowski. “It’s about minimizing friction.”

Friction, as anyone who has frantically tried to book a table at 4 Charles Prime Rib or a hotel room literally anywhere in Paris during fashion week knows, is the real enemy of living well these days. The concierge pitch speaks to a broader shift in luxury: less stuff, more experiences, fewer things to manage, and more time to enjoy them. In the internet age when so much of the world is bookable at our fingertips, having a concierge in your corner has become the new status symbol. Just look at the resurgence of travel agents (sexily rebranded as “travel advisors”).

The trick is knowing what a concierge service can offer beyond the usual booking assistance. Atlas, for instance, draws on relationships with restaurants and hotel groups, along with a team whose members have worked at top hotels and private members’ clubs. The idea is to have someone who knows whom to call when the usual channels come up empty. No concierge can guarantee a table or conjure a room out of thin air—but when you’re vying for a Thursday night table at The Polo Bar, having the right connections in your corner can make a difference.

And the service doesn’t just begin and end with travel or dinner reservations. Here are five ways that having a credit or charge card concierge can really make a difference.

This is the big one. Atlas has personal relationships and dedicated tables at sought-after dining rooms around the world, from New York’s Corner Store and 4 Charles Prime Rib to beach clubs in Ibiza and St. Barth. These are the types of tables that people try to reserve months in advance—but with the right concierge, you can confidently make a reservation with a week or two’s notice. Still, last minute isn’t hopeless—one Atlas member angling for Torrisi landed a same-day table when their concierge learned of a cancellation.

Fashion Week, the Monaco Grand Prix, Art Basel Miami Beach—there are certain peak periods when hotel searches become an exercise in despair. Mrozowski recalls a member heading to Paris Fashion Week when every hotel in the city seemed full—and through one of Atlas’s existing relationships, the team secured a five-star room after a block held for a corporate client opened up. Day-to-day, members get access to more than 2,000 luxury properties, with perks like space-available upgrades, early check-in, late checkout, and property credits.

Anyone can book a flight and a room. The harder job is stitching together a more complicated itinerary with private transfers, after-hours access to places like the Vatican or the Louvre, backstage passes, and front-row seats. Atlas even runs its own jet desk instead of handing you off to an outside broker. Still, every decision is tailored to your requirements—and the benefit is funneling a dozen separate confirmations through a single point of contact.

Concierge services can leverage their relationships for off-menu offerings. When one Atlas member was looking for a memorable reunion dinner at the university they attended, their concierge dialed a Michelin-starred restaurant to arrange a fully catered experience in the dining hall. That’s the distinction between mere booking assistance and the truly bespoke service a concierge can provide: not a mere reservation, but truly individualized moments that you might not be able to realize on your own.

Yes, the benefits of credit or charge card concierge services are most acutely felt when you’re traveling. But increasingly, we’re seeing concierge culture expand beyond vacations and special occasion dinners. Atlas members get partnerships in transportation, wellness, and lifestyle, including Wheely, Remedy Place, and Erewhon. That might mean a car, recovery session, or tickets to something that otherwise might not be on your radar—not the sort of benefits that will transform your life, per se, but what they can do is make an ordinary Tuesday a little bit easier.

#249. So I Tried the Jawline Thing…

This column first appeared in the Men’s Health email newsletter. The Optimized Man is a biweekly series from our editorial director as he tries out the latest, greatest, and weirdest health and wellness innovations so you don’t have to. Sign up here to get the next one.

I feel bad about my jawline, and with apologies to Nora Ephron, it is responsible for roughly 70 percent of my weirdness about getting older—and looking it.

The outer rim of my face began to soften and round in my early 40s, around the time MH contributor Garrett Munce wrote his authoritative guide to jawline preservation and optimization. And as my jaw gradually lost its literal edge, I often thought about the end of Garrett’s opening paragraph:

“Batman, Superman, Thor, the Human Torch. I could draw dozens of their faces from memory even before the Marvel Cinematic Universe began making gods out of guys named Chris. The one thing they all have in common? A jaw that looks like a block of granite.”

My jaw was looking less like granite and more like marshmallow. This is what happens in middle age: Your skin produces less collagen and loses some of its snap; the fat in your face thins in some places and shifts in others, and even the bone underneath subtly changes, leaving the entire lower-face support system a little less…supportive. Doesn’t really matter who you are; the clean lines blur. Next stop—wait for it—Jowlsville.

And I thought: Nope. Not if I can help it.

So over the next five years, I went to a bunch of dermatologists to try the latest and greatest in skin-tightening, collagen-building technology. Sofwave. Morpheus8. Ultherapy. I’ve tried them all. Each creates a slightly different kind of controlled injury to your face and jaw, mostly by heating the tissue beneath your skin. Sofwave and Ultherapy use ultrasound to create tiny zones of heat; Morpheus8 uses tiny needles to deliver radiofrequency energy—and yes, it hurts. The basic idea behind all three is the same: Heat or irritate the tissue enough to bully the body into producing more firmness-inducing collagen over the following weeks and months.

I didn’t dislike any of them, and I’m pretty sure each helped me hold the line on my jawline. But I wished I didn’t have to spend three months waiting for something—anything—to happen, you know? Enter Brian Underwood, the grooming and beauty guru for both Men’s Health and Women’s Health, who recently tipped me off to a new skin-tightening treatment called XERF—from Korea, no less.

XERF—pronounced “zerf”—is not a laser. It is a radiofrequency treatment that heats tissue beneath your skin while using bursts of cooling to keep the outer skin from getting too hot. The treatment head looks like a chunky wand that sends energy through the skin, warming things up underneath. That heat is supposed to do two things. First, it can make some of the collagen already in your face and jaw contract, potentially creating some immediate tightening. Then, over the following weeks and months, it is meant to prompt your body to make more collagen—the stuff that helps skin look firmer, smoother, and less saggy.

The published research on XERF is still early—and so far largely limited to animal studies—but it does support the basic idea that the heat can contract and remodel collagen.

I learn all this when I’m lying in front of David Kim, MD, the founder of Soho Dermatology in New York City, who wielded his XERF wand and described the technology before getting to work on my gel-slicked face.

As he slowly moved the device around my jaw and up into my cheeks, Dr. Kim explained that XERF’s distinguishing feature is its ability to use two radio frequencies to heat tissue at different depths. The idea is to create some immediate contraction while also triggering the slower process of collagen remodeling. At the same time, the device cools the surface of your skin with every pulse—which is probably why, even at the highest intensity, the treatment felt less like a cosmetic procedure than like someone repeatedly pressing a warm washcloth against my face.

About halfway through, Dr. Kim stopped and held a mirror up to my face. The half he had treated looked visibly lifted. My jawline looked cleaner and sharper, and my skin was only slightly redder than usual. He then got to work on the other half, and when I left the office that day, I felt as if I’d gotten a facelift without the redness, swelling, surgery, or trauma of someone actually lifting my face.

And then? Then I got on with my life. I worked. I hung out with my kids. I saw friends. I stopped thinking about the specter of jowls and started thinking about what I was going to have for lunch. Life goes on, and I hate that I even think about my jawline. Honestly, with the world the way it is, who cares? But we all have parts of our bodies that we find weird or annoying or marshmallow-like. And if a next-gen Korean wand can help me forget about my softening jawline for a while—without really hurting or leaving me puffed up and beet red?

Kengo Tsutsumi is executive editor, digital at Men’s Health. Previously, he worked at investigative nonprofit ProPublica and news startup Mic.

#250. Sugar-Free Foods Aren’t Always Healthier—Here’s What A Dietitian Wants You To Know

It’s a little more complicated than the packaging suggests.

If sugar is the ingredient everyone loves to blame, sugar alcohols are the supposed better option waiting in the wings. They show up in protein bars, keto snacks, sugar-free candy, and gum, promising sweetness without the same calorie hit or blood sugar spike. But are they actually better for you, or just better marketed? As a registered dietitian, I get this question all the time, and the answer depends on what you mean by “better.”

Despite the name, sugar alcohols aren't sugar, and they won't give you a buzz. They're a type of carbohydrate called polyols. Their chemical structure looks a bit like sugar and a bit like alcohol, which explains the confusing name.

Some occur naturally in small amounts in fruits and vegetables, but most in packaged foods are made commercially. The big names include erythritol (about 70 percent as sweet as sugar, with almost no calories), xylitol (roughly as sweet as sugar and popular in gum and mints), and sorbitol and maltitol (both common in sugar-free candy and chocolate).

Table sugar (sucrose) breaks down into glucose and fructose, which your small intestine absorbs quickly. Blood sugar rises, your pancreas releases insulin, and your cells pull that glucose in for energy. Sugar provides about 4 calories per gram, and, of course, it tastes sweet. None of that is inherently bad, as glucose is one of your body's main fuel sources.

The trouble comes with the amount. Diets high in added sugars are linked to higher risks of weight gain, type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and cavities. That's why the World Health Organization recommends keeping free sugars under 10 percent of daily calories, and the American Heart Association suggests a maximum of about 25 grams a day for women and 36 grams for men.

For context, one can of regular soda can blow past either number on its own.

This is where it gets interesting. Your small intestine absorbs only some sugar alcohols, so your body gets less usable energy from them. That’s one reason they tend to be lower in calories than regular sugar. Because less is absorbed, sugar alcohols also typically affect blood glucose less than regular sugar, though the effect varies. Maltitol, for example, has a noticeably bigger impact than erythritol.

Sugar alcohols also don't promote tooth decay the way regular sugar does.

The catch? Whatever your small intestine doesn't absorb travels to your large intestine, where gut bacteria can ferment it. That can mean gas, bloating, cramping, and diarrhea, which is why some products carry a warning that “excessive consumption may have a laxative effect.” Erythritol is mostly absorbed and leaves the body through urine, so many people tolerate it better from a GI standpoint.

Not all sugar alcohols behave the same, and knowing the differences can save you a bad afternoon. Here’s a breakdown:

If you're picking a sugar-free product, erythritol-based options may be a gentler starting point from a GI perspective. Maltitol and sorbitol are worth approaching with a smaller-than-usual serving the first time.

Swapping in sugar alcohols can lower a food's sugar content, and often its calories, too. That can help if you're paying attention to blood sugar, but "sugar-free" isn't a health halo. It only tells you about one part of the product, not the whole package.

"Sugar-free" also doesn't mean carb-free. Sugar alcohols are carbohydrates, and many sugar-free foods contain other carbs too. If you track carbs for diabetes, check the total carbohydrate line, not just the sugar line.

Then there's portion creep. Because these foods are marketed as guilt-free, it's easy to eat more than you would of a regular treat. If you end up eating twice as much sugar-free chocolate because it feels "safe," the calorie math stops working in your favor (and your gut may have opinions about it too).

Some research has also raised cardiovascular questions around certain sugar alcohols, particularly erythritol and xylitol, including whether they may affect platelet activity. But the evidence so far does not prove that consuming these sweeteners causes heart attacks or strokes, and more long-term research is needed.

Sugar alcohols aren't a nutritional loophole. Their impact depends on the type, the amount, and the person eating them. The takeaway isn't to avoid them. Treat them as one tool in a bigger picture, not a shortcut that automatically makes a food good for you.

Most people benefit from keeping added sugar in check, but it can be especially important for people with diabetes or prediabetes, anyone managing their weight or metabolic health, those prone to cavities, and kids.

That said, "limit" doesn't mean "never." Birthday cake is allowed, for heaven’s sake!

If you have IBS or a sensitive gut, heads up: Polyols are one of the FODMAPs, a group of fermentable carbs that can trigger symptoms. Sorbitol and mannitol are common offenders, so if you're following a low-FODMAP plan, read labels closely.

And for dog owners, this one is non-negotiable. Xylitol is highly toxic to dogs, even in small amounts. Keep sugar-free gum, mints, baked goods, and other products made with this ingredient far from curious snouts.

Neither sugar nor sugar alcohols are villains, and neither is a free pass. Read past the front label and check total carbs, calories, and the full ingredient list—not just whether something says "sugar-free."

If you're new to sugar alcohols, start with a small serving and see how your body reacts before eating half a bag of sugar-free gummies (ask me how I know). A little added sugar fits into a balanced diet just fine, and fruit, yogurt with berries, or even a square of dark chocolate can satisfy a sweet tooth without much fuss.

If you have diabetes, IBS, or a heart condition, a registered dietitian or doctor can help you figure out what works for your body specifically.

#251. Caroline Chambers on Why Cooking Can Feel Like 'An Absolute Hellscape'

What does Caroline Chambers cook when she doesn’t feel like cooking? That’s what I wanted to ask her after reading her brutally honest and heartwarming essay from our series The Fourth Trimester, all about postpartum meals. In it, Caroline writes about finding herself as a cook after giving birth to her first son. Now she has added three more kids to the mix and is navigating a wild blend of family, work, and life, yet showing up with incredible authenticity and humor. Read our conversation below—and make it to the end for the cover recipe from Caroline’s latest book.

Chris Morocco: Our team loved your first book (for readers who don’t know, we named it one of our favorites of 2024) and eagerly awaited your second. How did you decide on time as the theme for your next title, Make It Fast?

Caroline Chambers: I think that a huge, huge part of why cooking dinner can feel like such an absolute hellscape is that we simply do not have the time. We’re overbooked, overworked, we’re trying to make time to be good parents and good friends and somehow get in a few minutes of exercise in. At the end of the day, cooking yet another meal usually feels like the absolute last thing on earth that you want to do. So knowing exactly how much of a time investment you are going to have to make feels really good. Being able to flip through the 15-minute chapter and think, Okay, I can freaking do this! Or the “walk away” chapter and know that, with under 30 minutes of prep time, you can throw something in a pot to simmer away, or in the oven to slow roast, while you go about your day.

You made the bold choice to incorporate all ingredient prep in your recipe instructions, so your active times actually include how long it takes to chop every onion and shred every carrot. Very few recipes do this! How did you arrive at this practice?

Like Bon Appétit, I have years of hearing directly from my readers via my Substack, What to Cook When You Don’t Feel Like Cooking. When something takes longer to chop than I thought it would take them, I hear about it. And this is a wonderful thing! I can adjust, learn what their pain points are, and help educate them about ways to do it with more ease the next time. But I’ve definitely learned that people do not like to be bamboozled by the prep step being included in the ingredient list. They want to be told exactly when to do it. Plus, when I lay out exactly when they should prep each ingredient, I can help maximize their efficiency in the oven. Mince the garlic while the chicken sears. Chop the herbs while the pasta cooks. Without spelling it out for them in this way, a novice home cook might mise-en-place it all out at the beginning, and that adds a lot of time. And time is of the essence with this book, we ain’t got time to spare!

What are the ingredients you can’t live without that save you time in the kitchen?

I freaking love a bagged salad. I had this series on Instagram once all about how to make bagged salads taste better. I need to bring that back. Taylor Farms Caesar is a regular staple in my household—it’s just an honest-to-God delightful Caesar salad. We’ll have that and steaks for dinner at least a couple of times a month. I know that isn’t really an ingredient, but it sort of is? Other staples: lemons, rice (I cook a huge batch and freeze it in individual portions), those frozen garlic and ginger cubes, Better Than Bouillon (I’m a low-sodium chicken gal but I dabble in the fun ones, too, like “sofrito” and “sautéed onion”). I always have a jar of Trader Joe’s salsa verde (poach chicken thighs in it, shred, dinner is served). I love many types of chili crisp for instant flavor, but Red Clay’s southern chili crisp with peanuts and shallots is king.

During my time in food media, I have seen a trend of the most popular recipes in the zeitgeist getting simpler and easier. Is there any hope for people wanting to roast a chicken again, or has the prevalence of rotisserie chickens in supermarkets made such recipes obsolete?

I have a theory that cooking is really hard for everyone right now, not only because none of us have the time to do it, but also because none of us were taught how to do it. Our mothers and fathers were the first generation of parents where it was really widespread for both parents to be in the workforce. Mom wasn’t home cooking and teaching her daughters how to cook. She was at work! So a lot of people simply never were taught fundamental cooking skills. Like how to cut an onion! If you don’t know how to cut an onion, or mince a garlic clove, you’re instantly pissed. The second you start cooking a recipe, and it tells you to cut an onion, you instantly feel like you suck at cooking and it takes forever.

So…I don’t know, Chris! The irony of my entire brand, What to Cook When You Don’t Feel Like Cooking, is, of course, that my readers do feel like cooking. Instead of ordering DoorDash, they’re willing to give my newsletter and cookbooks a try. They want to want to cook!

I know, and you know, that people feel so proud of themselves when they cook a delicious meal. So I do think that the more people can nail really simple, easy recipes, and learn to cook from those simpler recipes, the more incentivized they are to try things that intimidate them—like roasting a whole bird.

On that note…favorite thing to do with a rotisserie bird?

I have an entire section in What to Cook about what to do with a rotisserie chicken, but the honest answer is that I mostly just eat it straight up! Chop it up for the kids, throw a leg to the baby in his high chair, slice up the breasts and serve them with a salad. I had some leftover rotisserie tonight, in fact, and fed it to the boys with baby broccoli, and made a version of the kale and quinoa salad for my husband and brother and his girlfriend (they live with us!). It’s so good—from the new book!

My other favorite thing to do with a rotisserie chicken is to keep it in the front seat for the drive home from the store and tear it apart with my hands like an absolute animal. If anyone ever sees me eating a chicken leg while cruising on the 1, no you didn’t.

I have two kids with such different tastes in food. Sometimes I think they exaggerate their preferences just to show the world how different they are, which is fine when it comes to hairstyles and shoes, but a bummer with dinner. Is it challenging for you to find meals that all your kids will eat?

Chris. Yes. These kids kill me. I have four boys—7, 6, 4, and 14 months. Those little turds will tell me ribs are their favorite meal, that they dreamed about ribs (!), and then I’ll make the exact same ribs recipe I cooked the last time, and half of them will tell me they’re too spicy. I’m with you—I think kids use food preferences as power. It allows them to have their own opinions and their own say. It absolutely kills me. I recently instigated a very strict and probably absolutely not child-therapist-approved two-bite rule. They have to try at least two bites of dinner, and if they truly do not like it, I’ll make them a PB&J or hummus and veggies. Most of the time, my 7- and 4-year-olds wind up eating the entire thing. My 6-year-old very, very rarely does. That guy is eating a lot of PB&Js right now. And just FYI, the PB&J is: Dave’s Killer Bread 21 Whole Grains, Ground Up Honey Sea Salt peanut butter, Bonne Maman Strawberry Jam. I can’t really blame him, it’s delicious.

After a day working on recipe development, when you have been elbow-deep in pasta and dishes since 9 a.m., do you ever think to yourself when dinner time rolls around, Oh heck no! Is that just me? What do you cook when you don’t feel like cooking? And what’s your go-to takeout?

HELL YES. The cobbler’s kids get no shoes, as they say!!! We live kinda in the country, so our take-out options absolutely suck. My take-out option is steaming frozen dumplings and broccoli florets at the same time in a steamer basket and making a peanut sauce while they’re steaming. Everyone absolutely devours this meal. Except for my six-year-old, of course. But the good news is that the peanut butter is already out for his dinner.

You have two pieces of advice in Make It Fast that I absolutely adore: “Lay corn flat on its side to cut it,” and “salt and pepper are not married.” I guess that isn’t really a question, just wanted to say thank you! And if you have any other sage advice like this, I want to hear it.

Oh my gosh, thanks for noticing those! I’m a self-taught cook, meaning that America’s Test Kitchen and the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen are responsible for so much of my early learning. So that means a lot to hear from you. I read this book called Eight Flavors about the eight major flavors in American cuisine many, many years ago. One of the chapters is about black pepper and to absolutely butcher her beautifully done research and writing—the common use of salt and pepper together, in every single freaking recipe, basically boils down to really good marketing when spice traders first introduced black pepper to America. Salt and pepper are not married!

A few other pieces of advice from the book, for people who do not feel like cooking:

#252. Another Tragic Reminder: Too. Many. Damn. Guns.

Bend has done more than its part watering the tree of liberty.

(Permanent Musical Accompaniment to the Last Post of the Week from the Blog’s Favourite Living Canadian)

We had another unfortunate exercise of Second Amendment freedoms on Thursday, this one in Bend, Oregon. A 16-year old with his mother's pump-action shotgun killed three schoolchildren and a teacher before he was gunned down by a citizen who’d followed him into the school. Silver Rail Elementary School. From Oregon Public Broadcasting:

This was the second mass shooting in Bend since 2022, when a guy walked into a Safeway with an AR-15 style rifle and killed himself and two others. I think Bend has done more than its part watering the tree of liberty.

Now, we will have the usual dialogue. Oregon has relatively tough gun-safety laws, so we will hear from the usual suspects about how those laws don’t work. The guy who killed the mass shooter will get all the run he wants from Fox News and the other, lesser fauna on the wing-nut media savanna. And all of it will obscure, again, the basic problem this country has.

#256. Kylie Jenner Brings the Fantasy Bra Back to the Victoria’s Secret Runway

Adam Selman on nostalgia, spectacle, and bringing the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show into a new era.

“I’m the first one to love nostalgia,” Adam Selman told me ahead of the 2026 Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show. “But I also need to chart [the show] into new territory. A lot of what the fans say they want is 20 or 25 years ago, which culture has moved on from. How do you give it to them in a modern context?”

Tonight, Selman stayed true to his promise with a no-holds-barred fashion-and-entertainment spectacle, bringing together VSFS signatures—lingerie, performances, and, yes, a fantasy bra—with renewed energy. For his second runway show at the helm and the event’s first return to Los Angeles in 19 years, the executive creative director divided the runway into chapters dedicated to each season. “The show is so big that a simple idea is a great starting place,” he noted. “I connected words and emotions to each season as I went to.

To start, Bella Hadid made her long-awaited return to the runway in a see-through petal-green mini skirt and wings sprouting with flora and fauna. Then came Adriana Lima, Ashley Graham, and Alex Consani dressed in everything from rosette-adorned corsetry to a teensy-tiny mini dress engulfed in petals worn by Anok Yai. “Florals for spring, groundbreaking, I know,” Selman joked.

The designer, who began crafting stage costumes for the likes of Beyoncé and Rihanna, excels at theatrical dressing—as evidenced by the extravagant wings and laboriously sequined looks throughout.

The catwalk then segued into “Vintage Victoria,” a run of bias-cut slips in an array of pastel hues. Their silhouettes nodded to the brand’s late-’90s and early-aughts archive. “Fans always say they love that the brand used to do a lot of event dressing and slip dressing and fun, colorful prints,” Selman explains. Now in his second year at the helm, he’s bringing those familiar codes into the present in more ways than one.

The brand brought its devoted fan base, which was out in full force at Sony Studios, deeper into the fun with Angels Among Us, a docuseries following the nationwide hunt for its newest Angel. Solange Omon won the title and made her runway debut to loud applause in black-and-white lace lingerie, gilded wings, and a flowing cape.

While it was easy to lose sight of the clothes amid the spectacle, there was plenty to take in. The more everyday Pink offering featured crystal-embellished low-rise pants, ab-baring bandage dresses in punchy patterns, and playful logo-heavy separates. A crystal-covered mesh dress worn over a skin-toned bra, meanwhile, felt poised to lead the next wave of naked dressing.

The soundtrack was a draw, too: Tate McRae performed her new hit “Housewife,” which played as Gigi Hadid returned to the runway, while Katseye performed “Pinky Up.” Megan Thee Stallion’s hit “Body” felt tailor-made for the occasion. At one point, Adéla’s “Nicole Kidman” came on, prompting a laugh from Kidman herself in the audience.

One of the night’s biggest moments—and a neat summation of Selman’s balance of pop culture and nostalgia—came when Kylie Jenner modeled the Fantasy Bra. The $50 million design, created with jeweler Jacob & Co., marked the showpiece’s return to the runway for the first time since 2018. Jenner’s star power, with boyfriend Timothée Chalamet watching from the audience, made the Fantasy Bra’s return a pop-culture moment in its own right.

“This really is a mashup of fashion, culture, product, entertainment,” Selman explained. “What is the purpose beyond the glitz and beyond the glamour? And for me, this year was a conversation with the fans. I always say internally, ‘Let’s do the thing that only Victoria’s Secret can do. Let’s do the thing that only Pink can do.’ And I say it over and over.”

#257. The Dunkin’ Munchkins Bucket Is Back for Halloween—And It Glows in the Dark

Dunkin's popular Halloween Munchkins bucket is back with 50 Munchkins, festive designs and a spooky surprise!

There are two major decisions that every kid needs to make before Halloween. Primarily, of course, is what kind of costume to wear on fall’s spookiest night. And second, what kind of bag or bucket to tote around the neighborhood collecting all the best new candy of the season.

Growing up, I was the proud owner of a classic orange jack-o-lantern candy bucket. My younger brother usually used a bucket shaped like Frankenstein’s head. Of course, there were always a handful of teens carrying pillowcases around. I mean, that’s certainly very convenient, but where’s the fun in that?

There is probably one candy container that rules all, though: the coveted Dunkin’ Munchkins Bucket. Sure, its primary goal is to serve you a heaping pile of delicious Dunkin’ Munchkins. Once they’ve been devoured, however, it takes on a new life as a trick-or-treating bucket. And this year, it’s got an extra special spooky twist. It glows in the dark!

The Munchkins Bucket is back in stores nationwide beginning now. Per usual, it will be filled with a random assortment of 50 Munchkins doughnut holes—including the brand-new Halloween version that’s covered in sprinkles.

This year’s bucket is purple, which is my personal favorite Halloween color. Why should orange get all the fun? And the bucket is decorated with little cartoon Munchkins wearing costumes.

There are ghosts and bats floating along the bucket, and for the first time ever, the designs actually glow in the dark! Now you won’t have to worry about misplacing your bucket of candy on Halloween. Think of it as a built-in night light.

This will only be available at Dunkin’ retailers nationwide while supplies last. It’s one of Dunkin’s most popular items, so if you have your heart set on trick-or-treating with one of these buckets, you’d better head to your local Dunkin’ soon.

#259. The Key Sleep Metric That Drops for Men After 40

YOU MIGHT STRIVE to go to bed by 9 p.m., hoping to get a good night’s sleep. But if you lie awake for hours before drifting off, your sleep efficiency might be lacking, and it's probably interfering with your ability to get enough rest.

Sleep efficiency refers to the amount of time you spend actually asleep versus the time you spend in bed intending to sleep, says Zachary Strumpf, MD, pulmonary, critical care, and sleep medicine physician at University Hospitals. “It’s different than getting a better night’s sleep and reflects how effective you are at falling and staying asleep,” he says.

One of the biggest factors affecting sleep efficiency is age. Some research points to guys being hit hardest when they reach the fourth decade of life. More on that below.

SLEEP EFFICIENCY STAYS relatively unchanged from childhood to adolescence. Then it starts to decline in adulthood, says Dr. Strumpf.

Research varies on when sleep efficiency takes a dive, but changes seem to occur in middle age (40 to 64). People’s sleep efficiency score tend to decrease from 89 to 79 percent. Sleep efficiency below 80 percent may increase a person’s mortality risk.

One study found an 18.6 percent decline in sleep efficiency between ages 40 and 100. Men specifically ages 65 to 96 were more likely to have an 80 percent or lower sleep efficiency when they were single or had a painful illness. In that study, pain, sleep medication use, and bad dreams were the main culprits for poor sleep efficiency.

Yes, sleep medication lowered people’s sleep efficiency score. Depending on the person, Dr. Strumpf says “certain medications can increase or decrease a person’s sleep efficiency or alter the proportion of time spent in REM sleep.”

SLEEP EFFICIENCY IS the percentage of the time you spend asleep relative to the time you dedicate to sleep, says Nishay Chitkara, MD, director of sleep medicine at NYC Health + Hospitals/Bellevue.

Sleep efficiency scores are expressed as a percentage. To calculate it, divide the total minutes you’re asleep by the total minutes spent in bed trying to go to sleep.

Generally, a sleep efficiency of 85 to 90 percent or greater than 90 suggests that you have little trouble falling and staying asleep, he says. But if it’s lower than 80 percent, you likely have poor sleep efficiency.

If you usually go right to sleep after climbing into bed, your sleep efficiency is likely good, Dr. Strumpf says. Still, that doesn’t automatically mean you’re getting enough sleep.

“A higher sleep efficiency is not the only thing to target for restful sleep,” says Dr. Strumpf. You also need a good sleep duration, meaning getting enough total sleep, ideally at least seven hours. “Ensuring adequate sleep duration and good sleep efficiency will allow your brain to naturally cycle through all the stages of sleep you need,” he adds. These stages are controlled by the systems in the brain and usually can’t be influenced with behavioral changes.

A sleep efficiency score, whether high or low, can tell you a lot about your health. Maybe you’re knocked out when your head hits the pillow because you’ve accumulated sleep debt over the past few days. “If one is sleeping only five hours per night, the sleep efficiency may be great, but the time asleep is not sufficient,” says Dr. Chitkara. Or maybe you’re tossing and turning because your melatonin window for sleep (when your body is prepared for sleep) is off.

“A lower sleep efficiency likely needs improvement, since it could indicate that someone is not sleeping well, has poor sleep habits, or may have a medical condition that interferes with healthy sleep,” says Dr. Chitkara.

YOU CAN GENERALLY improve your sleep efficiency by optimizing your sleep hygiene, Dr. Chitkara says. “Sleep hygiene is the set of practices that are conducive to good sleep.”

SLEEP TRACKER APPS or other devices could help improve sleep efficiency by providing information and insights into your sleep habits, which you can use to make improvements, Dr. Chitkara says.

For instance, they can keep track of light, temperature, noise levels, and other environmental elements influencing your sleep, as well as caffeine intake and stress levels, he says. Trackers can also record health metrics, such as heart rate, movement, body temperature, and blood oxygen levels.

Fortunately, there are a number of ways to keep tabs on your sleep metrics (here are the eight best trackers for optimizing your slumber). You can also track your sleep now without wearing anything.

ANY TIME YOU’RE having trouble falling or staying asleep, waking up several times a night, or feeling excessively sleepy throughout the day, talk to a doctor. Depending on your symptoms, they may refer you to a sleep specialist.

It’s especially important to get evaluated if these symptoms last for more than three months or if your bed partner is complaining that their own sleep is disrupted. Also get checked out if you notice any symptoms of sleep apnea, a dangerous condition where you constantly stop and start breathing when you sleep. These signs include snoring, gasping or choking during sleep, or periods of not breathing when you’re asleep.

#260. Experts Say No One Over 30 Should Still Be Using These Kitchen Items

You're an adult—your kitchen should be, too.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Budget cookware and kitchen hand-me-downs made sense in your twenties, but once you hit 30, it’s time to upgrade—and ditch the kitchen items no one over 30 should still be using.

Spending money on nights out with friends or a vacation was important when you were young. But these days, living life to the fullest is less about slamming $20 tequila sodas and more about investing in a $40 bottle of olive oil. Now that’s an adrenaline rush.

To refresh your cabinets—and make room for better things—here are 11 kitchen items you should finally get rid of, plus what to replace them with.

Dull knives are a leading cause of kitchen injuries, so toss out your old, unsharpened set ASAP. They also make chopping, dicing, and slicing way harder than they need to be.

“A dull knife doesn’t cut; it crushes,” Peter Ki Suk Tondreau, executive chef and co-owner of LenLen, tells Delish. “When a blade lacks an edge, you have to compensate with downward muscle force. The moment that unguided pressure slips off a rounded tomato skin or an onion dome, the blade diverts directly into your knuckles or fingers.” That lack of control is exactly what makes a dull knife more dangerous than a sharp one.

“A razor-sharp knife requires almost zero downward force—it bites the surface immediately and tracks in a straight line,” Tondreau says.

He suggests ditching the 18-piece wooden block set and buying two, maybe three essential blades instead. He says you only need a 10-inch chef’s knife—the “workhorse for 90% of prep,” dicing, slicing, and carving—and a serrated bread knife for crusty loaves, ripe heirloom tomatoes, and citrus peels.

While a glass cutting board might look sophisticated or “grown-up,” it’s just impractical. Users on Reddit agree: “BANG BANG BANG the noise goes right through my brain,” one person wrote.

Another added, “They really are worthless in every way. If you chop on them, they dull your knives. If they’re wet, they get slippery. If you set a hot pan on them, they can crack. If you drop it while trying to wash it, it can break. Why do they even make them?”

You should know better by now: Change your sponges regularly! They're basically a breeding ground for bacteria. For a longer-lasting alternative, consider a dish scrubber, like this OXO one with over 25,000 glowing reviews.

By 30, you must know better than to keep those scratched-up nonstick pans or, as one Reddit user described them, “busted-ass Teflon frying pans.” When the coating flakes off, it can contaminate your food—especially if the cookware contains PFAS, or “forever chemicals,” linked to negative health effects.

“Every home kitchen operates best with a tri-force of materials, because no single pan executes every technique,” Tondreau says. Replace your old nonstick pans with a tri-ply or 5-ply stainless steel skillet, heavy enameled cast iron Dutch oven, and a carbon steel or heavy raw cast iron skillet, and you’ll be golden.

“The single caveat: Keep one small, inexpensive 8-inch nonstick strictly for French omelets and delicate eggs,” he adds. “Treat it like a consumable tool: never use metal utensils on it, and replace it the moment it scratches.”

Keep a couple of plastic plates for emergencies or takeout, sure. No judgment there. But if you're past 30 and still using them regularly, it's time to invest in a proper ceramic set that will upgrade your tablescape tenfold.

Toss ‘em! “The risk far outweighs the benefit of trying to recover the baking pan,” says Dr. Bryan Quoc Le, food scientist and author of 150 Food Science Questions Answered.

You can snag a perfect (brand-new!) set on Amazon for under $20.

One or two for measuring purposes? You're allowed. But your collection from past college spring breaks? Let them go. You don't need the souvenir to remember your visit to Cancun. That's what photos are for.

And if you're buying shot glasses, consider opting for something a little more elevated, like this chic option from Crate & Barrel.

Those takeout containers served you well in your early twenties, but real food-storage vessels are well worth the upgrade.

“Flavor degradation and spoilage come down to two culprits: oxygen exposure and moisture loss/migration,” Tondreau says. “Flimsy takeout plastic warps and allows air exchange, which causes oxidation, refrigerator odors to leach in, and freezer burn.”

So, what should you use instead? Borosilicate glass with snap-lock silicone lids. They’re nonporous, airtight, and resistant to odors. Unlike plastic, glass won’t absorb acidic stains from turmeric, chili oil, or tomato sauces, or leach chemicals during reheating.

“Pro tip for freshness: Press plastic wrap or parchment directly onto the surface of wet foods (guacamole, curries, braises, sauces) before sealing the lid,” Tondreau adds. “Eliminating the headspace pocket of air prevents browning and surface skinning.”

Whether it’s table linens, napkins, or the stove-side hand towel, replace them as soon as they're stained or looking a little ragged. It’s just a matter of polish! You’re old enough to prioritize presentation.

While Tondreau says expired or old spices rarely rot or make you sick, they’re far less flavorful and, in turn, affect the quality of your cooking.

“Ground spices peak within 6 to 9 months. Whole spices (seeds, peppercorns, bark, pods) retain essential oils for 2 to 3 years,” he explains. “Old spices don't season food; they just add colored, gritty sawdust and muted bitterness.”

Luckily, there’s a really simple test to decide whether it’s time to toss it out: Open a jar of cumin or coriander, rub a pinch between your fingers, and if it smells a bit like cardboard instead of how it’s actually supposed to smell, it’s dead.

The solution? “Buy spices in small quantities from high-turnover purveyors or spice markets rather than warehouse club mega-jars,” Tondreau says. “Whenever possible, buy whole spices and toast them in a dry pan for 45 seconds before cracking them in a mortar and pestle or spice grinder—the flavor intensity will be ten times higher than anything pre-ground.”

How often do you really use the Margaritaville frozen drink maker from college or the popcorn machine you thought was such a great idea five years ago? Save yourself the counter space and kick ‘em to the curb.

The temptation is real to store a bag of plastic bags under your sink, but you won’t use them. Really, you won’t. And they’re just taking up space! It’s time to say goodbye and invest in a few solid reusable ones instead.

They’re wasteful and, frankly, not even cute. Invest in some nice table linens that’ll instantly elevate your entire dinner setup.
