#262. The Best Aprons for Home Cooks, Vetted by BA Editors

I recently sent out a Slack poll to find out if and why my fellow staffers wear aprons at home, and the results led me to two conclusions: One, that many home cooks choose to go apron-free. Two, that those who do wear aprons do so in two primary scenarios: when doing messy tasks like frying (duh) and/or when having company over.

To that end, the best apron should be durable and stain-resistant enough for everyday wear, but also chic enough to don for a dinner party, capable of both protecting and complementing your cutest outfit. I must attest that in my personal experience, owning a stylish apron also makes me more likely to reach for one before I start cooking, rather than as an afterthought once I’ve already stained my shirt.

In an effort to figure out which aprons best marry form and function, my colleagues and I put over a dozen options to the test in our own homes. After wearing the aprons for countless weeknight cooking sessions and exposing them to plenty of spills and splatters, these are the 13 that won us over.

Tester: Olivia Tarantino, senior shopping editor

What we love: I own five Hedley & Bennett aprons, which tells you most of what you need to know. The denim one is my grilling and pizza-making apron. It’s durable, and I never worry about staining it, since even red sauce and turmeric either wash out or disappear into the fabric. The cotton one feels substantial enough that I always feel well protected, and that’s my everyday pick. The cotton twill is lighter, so I reach for it when I’m washing dishes or doing something quick that won’t get messy.

The pockets earn their keep. A top pocket holds my instant-read thermometer, and the two on the bottom are big enough for my phone. Some people drape a kitchen towel over a shoulder or tuck it into the waistband, but I like having a dedicated towel loop. The neck strap adjusts, and the fit is flattering. I’m short, so I fold the apron over once at the waist, and it still looks sleek.

What we’d leave: Hedley & Bennett recommends hanging these to dry rather than tumbling them. That’s a small extra step, though it does preserve the fabric.

What we love: I added this apron to my collection two years ago, and it’s since become my most reached-for option (and I say that as someone who owns upwards of 10 aprons). I love the way the vibrant Sweet Pea color pops, that it’s made of sturdy 100% cotton canvas, and that it costs less than $60. But most of all I love the pockets. There are eight of them: three wide ones on the bottom and five slim ones on the top, which are perfect for holding tasting spoons, chopsticks, or plating tweezers if I’m feeling fancy.

The Cargo Crew also washes well. After two years of consistent use and many splatters and spills, my apron still looks good as new.

What we’d leave: While I believe it used to be available in more colors, the Boston Bibb style is only currently available in Distressed Denim, Rose Pink, and Sweet Pea.

Tester: Noah Kaufman, senior shopping editor

What we love: Since I started testing it out this has become my every day apron. The indigo denim looks gorgeous and hides stains incredibly well (not unlike some of the jeans I’ve loved and had to leave over the years); it’s also very lightweight, which I found a pleasant surprise. The pockets are useful; the two small ones at the top are good for holding things like cake testers or thermometers, the big ones lower down I use to hold my phone if I’m cooking from an app. Finally, considering that it isn’t a crossback apron, it doesn’t put any uncomfortable pressure on my neck.

What we’d leave: Gustin has a…different sort of production model. They crowdfund their all their production runs. I totally understand why that is safer than producing in large quantities you aren’t sure you can sell, but it does mean that a Gustin apron (or a pair of Gustin selvedge denim) isn’t always in stock. As I write this, the Selvedge apron is so snap it up while you can. If you miss it you’ll have to sign up to get notified when they produce another round.

What we love: I think it’s still pretty rare that a company focused on making one thing can sell quality pieces that are far removed from that thing. And in the case of Ooni, I’d say putting out textiles like aprons is pretty far from the pizza ovens that made the brand famous. But the pizzaiolo apron a tough canvas piece that holds up to more than a few stray tomato sauce spills. It’s thick, but still pliable and the large pockets can simultaneously accommodate tools like spoons, scrapers, and turners, and a phone if you’re using it as a cookbook. I also used the leather strap on the regular to hold a kitchen towel for cleaning smudges and cooktop spills.

What we’d leave: It pulls on the neck a little. Not so much that it bothers me, because I regularly use this style of apron as opposed to a smock or crossback (I think it’s a little easier to get on and off and hold in place), but I was aware of it while wearing. I think the utility of the rugged canvas more than makes up for that though.

What we love: I never really understood why someone would spend over $100 on an apron until I tried one from WhiteBark Workwear. The brand has been long beloved by professional chefs (including our own Chris Morocco) and it’s easy to see why: their aprons are made from butter-soft blend of organic hemp and cotton and are incredibly comfortable for all-day wear thanks to the cross-back strap design, which limits neck-pulling. Each apron has two deep lap pockets and two skinny chest pockets great for pens or small utensils, and long straps that are meant to be cut to your desired length. WhiteBack also offers complimentary hemming if your apron is too long.

The aprons are available in pretty much every color under the sun, but I went with French Indigo, a purple-tinged bright blue that brings me joy every time I put it on. I’ve been wearing mine nonstop since I got it, and have found that stains wash out with no issue.

What we’d leave: At $124 a pop, these aprons are a bit of an investment. That said, you really do get what you pay for when it comes to the look, feel, and durability.

Tester: Hana Asbrink, deputy food director

What we love: Forgive me if I sound like a broken record here, but the smock apron is the one I'll reach to time and time again. For someone who doesn't care for an apron period on most days, it's the least cumbersome and formal style of apron I can tolerate as you just slip yourself into its criss-crossed (not flailing) arms. They may not be as popular of a style, but I keep tabs on the brands that do them well. Hedley & Bennett's smock apron is the one I turn to at work the most often. After several years of Test Kitchen use, it finally asked to be retired; lucky for me, the latest generation of smock aprons is even sturdier and cuter than its predecessors. The one I've been using is a deep blue shibori-style pattern, beautiful on its own but truly fantastic at hiding stains. It's a nice, thicker weight fabric than the one I used previously, one that takes well to laundering on normal (low tumble for drying to best maintain its shape).

What we’d leave: One potential downside to a smock style apron that I haven't been able to avoid 100% is the occasionally slipping arms. Positioned just right, however, you can manage to spare yourself 90% of the time.

What we love: This apron is so lightweight that I sometimes forget I’m wearing it. The pockets are deep enough to hold my phone and whatever other random things I’m carrying back and forth from the kitchen to the dining table when dinner is almost ready.

Sometimes what keeps me from wearing an apron is the whole process of adjusting the straps, tying it around my back, and then having to undo it when I’m done. I appreciate that I can simply slip this one on and get to cooking. It’s comfortable, stays out of the way, and looks cute.

What we’d leave: I wish it had a strap for a kitchen towel.

What we love: This is one of the sturdiest aprons I’ve tested, and it’s my go-to for grilling. The fabric is thick without being boxy. It drapes rather than hangs, so the fit is flattering. The pockets are the other reason I love it. They’re deep and wide and evenly distributed across the front, so the apron never feels weighed down on one side no matter what I load into it. The top two are especially roomy.

What we’d leave: The top pocket is more spacious than what you'd need for a thermometer, pen, or cake tester, so you may lose small, skinny items up there.

What we love: Made from thick, sturdy cotton (all the better to wipe wet hands on!), this apron feels like a steal at $30. It's a simple tie-back style with an adjustable neck strap and deep pockets in the front, and it comes in a rainbow of colors. It's machine-washable, thank god, because who wants to tackle cooking-grease stains by hand?

What we'd leave: No downsides here! There are more stylish options on this list, but this guy will totally get the job done if you're prioritizing function over fashion.

Tester: Wilder Davies, senior commerce writer

What we love: The aprons from Hawkins New York’s essentials line are made with the same textiles as their table cloths and napkins, so they have a lighter, soft feel than an apron made from performance fabric. I really like the brand’s overall design choices—simple geometric patterns in vivid autumnal hues. This would definitely be more of a fashion apron; you're getting it for the vibes not the design, as it is pretty basic.

What we’d leave: I have reservations about the long term durability. The plating on the D ring fasteners rubbed off very quickly, and the fabric, while beautiful and soft, feels somewhat delicate.

What we love: True to its foundations, this Carhartt apron is unapologetically workwear. The apron is built to take a beating—oils and rogue splashes barely register, practically rolling right off the surface. And even if they did, the design of the apron is casual enough that stains and wear built over time would likely enhance its utilitarian charm. On that note, the apron comes with plenty of pockets, which make it feel useful beyond the kitchen—I could see it easily lending itself to a slew of hands-on hobbies (speaking for myself, I've gone to pottery studio with this happily in tow).

What we’d leave: The heft of the fabric can feel limiting. With my shorter stature, the firm fabric of the bib juts tight at the throat especially when hunched over the counter during cooking prep. After three washes, it's still as tough as it came, so much like a pair of work boots, I suspect this is an apron that begs daily wear to truly break in. In an ideal scenario, this will eventually feel a bit less like protective gear and more like second skin, with how much time I spend in the kitchen.

What we love: East Fork’s Alles apron is constructed of a sturdy linen-cotton blend. It feels well-made and like it will hold up well to longterm use—but let’s be honest, the real reason to opt for this apron is the gorgeous plaid pattern. The blue and orange hues feel very fall-coded, and have me excited to mix up batches of pumpkin bread and cozy braises without splattering any food on my clothes.

What we’d leave: While stains came out with no issue, the apron was quite wrinkled after I machine-washed it and would benefit from ironing.

To test these aprons, each tester brought theirs home and wore it for several weeks’ worth of cooking. We made sure to get plenty of splatters on them (I even smeared gochujang all over mine) before running them through the wash at least once to see how they held up and whether the stains came out.

Aprons generally come in one of two styles: neck strap/halter or cross-back. Neck strap aprons have the benefit of being fully adjustable (usually) and easy to put on, but can weigh down on the back of your neck, particularly if you’re storing things in the pockets. Cross-back aprons can be a bit confusing to put on, but have the benefit of distributing weight evenly across your shoulders.

We tended to like aprons that were made of sturdy canvas, though linen makes for a nice lightweight alternative. Whatever the case, an apron should be made of durable fabric that doesn’t stain easily and can hold up to extensive wear and washing.

Extra design features like pockets and towel straps can take an apron from functional to genuinely useful. That said, we tested some aprons where innovative features we were excited about ultimately fell flat, like a version with towel-lined pockets that proved difficult to actually make use of.

#263. Saucy Pork Chops With Coconut Crisp

If the only pork chops you’ve encountered are dry and leathery, give this recipe a try. Thick-cut pork chops are more forgiving of extended cook times and the generous pour of sauce makes up for any mistakes, should they occur. The buttery pan sauce takes a page from Chris Morocco’s Steak for One, gaining its silky texture from a bottle of oyster sauce. Anything with the word “premium” on the bottle is preferred for flavor, and avoid any oyster-flavored sauces—they are too salty. The coconut crisp is the star of the show. For the best visual effect, you want big shards of coconut flakes rather than shredded here. Doubled up and stored in an airtight container, the crisp will be good for up to five days. Use it over seared tofu or chicken breasts, or buttered white rice with a drizzle of soy sauce.

Find more great pork chop recipes here: Green Chile Puttanesca Pork Chop; Rosemary and Dried Cherry Pork Chops; and Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Cook 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, one 2" piece ginger, peeled, cut into matchsticks, and 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large cast-iron or other heavy skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until scallions and ginger are barely golden and wilted, 6–8 minutes. Add ½ cup unsweetened coconut flakes and cook, stirring often, until coconut is golden, about 5 minutes. Transfer to a medium bowl; reserve skillet. Stir 1 Tbsp. sugar, 1 tsp. garlic powder, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt into coconut crisp.

Do Ahead: Coconut crisp can be made 5 days ahead. Store airtight at room temperature.

Sprinkle two 1"-thick bone-in well-marbled pork rib chops all over with 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and a generous amount of freshly ground pepper. Heat 1 Tbsp. vegetable oil in reserved skillet over medium-high. Cook pork chops, undisturbed, until browned underneath, about 5 minutes. Turn and continue cooking, turning every 2 minutes or so, until pork chops are deeply browned on both sides, 10–12 minutes (an instant-read thermometer inserted near the bone should register 145°). Transfer pork chops to a cutting board and let rest while you make the sauce.

Reduce heat to medium and cook 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan, swirling occasionally, until it foams then browns, about 1 minute. Pour in ½ cup water and bring to a simmer, scraping up any browned bits. Stir in 2 Tbsp. premium oyster sauce and cook sauce until it thickens enough to lightly coat a spoon, about 2 minutes.

Thinly slice pork chops and transfer to a platter; spoon sauce over. Top with coconut crisp and thinly sliced jalapeño.

#264. 6 Drugstore Heat Protectants That Keep Hair Soft, Silky, and Smooth on a Budget

Never scorch your hair again with these protective picks.

I'll never forget when I almost burned my hair off with my flat iron in middle school. (The smell of singed hair is forever etched in my brain.) I've learned a lot about how to correctly heat style my hair since then, and I can tell you that the number one way to prevent any heat-induced hair catastrophe is by using a good heat protectant.

Seriously, ask any professional hairstylist about the number one hair rule, and they'll preach that heat protectant is nonnegotiable. They'll also mention that there's no need to spend a ton of money to get a quality formula. Yep, drugstore heat protectants work just as well—if not better—than all the fancy-schmancy high-end options. Just take a look at some of the stellar (and inexpensive!) options I personally found and tested...

Regardless of your hair type—whether you have fine, straight, wavy, curly, or thick hair—there's an inexpensive yet effective drugstore heat protectant that will keep your strands silky, smooth, and healthy. I know because I tested dozens of formulas and asked three pros for their recommendations. Don't you dare pick up another hot tool until you get your hands on one of these drugstore heat protectants. Your future self (and your hair) will thank you.

This multipurpose spray is the first hair product I EVER remember using...and it's still a mainstay in my hair care routine 20 years later. There's not much this leave-in conditioner can't do. Beyond detangling, minimizing frizz, boosting shine, adding body, and preventing split ends, (oh, and offering stellar heat protection, duh) it simply makes hair look and feel incredibly healthy courtesy of a ton of natural ingredients, including sunflower seed extract, green tea, and silk amino acids. Put this in the hair hall of fame because it deserves a permanent spot, IMO!

Glowing customer review: "I bought this hair product because my hair was very dry from coloring, and this really does the trick! My hair is turning very curly as it’s getting longer and it needs to be maintained. This helps with my frizz, is light weight, & makes my hair very soft. I also like the smell of it:)"

High heat doesn't stand a chance against this weightless spray. Housed inside the psychedelic bottle (side note, isn't it so pretty!?) is a supercharged spray that can protect your hair from temperatures up to 450 degrees. This goes much further than simply safeguarding hair, though. A nourishing mix of argan oil, sunflower seed oil, and vitamin E also repair hair from the inside out, reducing breakage, amplifying shine, diminishing frizz, and just completely reviving hair. Oh, and it works for literally every single hair type. Now that's what I call ✨magic✨.

Glowing customer review: "The older I get the more frizzy and dull I noticed my hair tends to be, and I remedy that with Mane Magic. Just a little spritz makes my hair shiny and smooth. It's literally the best stuff ever."

Coarse hair needs much more than just simple heat protection. It also requires an extra boost of moisture to smooth frizz and keep strands well hydrated, which means you should always use a heat protecting cream, right? Wrong. Pro hairstylist Temur Hamilton swears by this weightless spray for his clients with coarse and curly hair, and ensures it's one of the best options available. "I like that it leaves hair super soft and helps prevent frizz while protecting against high heat damage," he says.

Glowing customer review: "Tresemme Thermal Creations Heat Tamer spray is all I could wish for with thick, coarse hair that is prone to dry ends. Spray it on before using a flat iron and hair comes out shiny and glossy. This product also helps tame the frizzies and banishes static. I say this is good quality for a reasonable price!"

While vitamins and proteins are an important part of your diet, Hamilton explains that your hair also needs them via topical products to be healthy and strong. "These ingredients help hair retain moisture and protect against heat." Spritzing this affordable spray safeguards hair with a mix of bond-repairing proteins and vitamins to make strands more resilient against drying and damaging heat.

One Cosmo expert says: “This spray contains vitamins and proteins to both protect and nourish the hair. It also seals the cuticle so that hair is shinier and more resistant to breakage.”—HAMILTON

I don't know about anyone else, but I absolutely despise layering on a slew of styling products. I want sky-high hair (like, pageant-girl level volume) but my dry, fine hair falls limp when I use a leave-in conditioner, mousse, and a heat protectant. I almost always skip the heat protectant—I know that's bad—but now I don't have to with this multitasker. It also smells like dessert, which makes me want to use it even more!

One Cosmo expert says: "This provides 450-degree heat protection and double the volume while allowing the hair to be easily shaped as you blow dry.”—KIMBERLEE BLAKELY, PROFESSIONAL HAIRSTYLIST

Don't be afraid of heat protecting creams—like this editor-fave—especially if your hair leans dry. While it provides impressive heat protection (up to 450 degrees!) this extra hydrating formula also restores strands with a mix of hydrating argan oil, squalane, and sunflower seed extracts. This mix makes hair softer and shinier, and helps seal split ends. You can use it pretty much any time, too, not just before heat styling. If you want to take a break from the heat (which we all should, tbh) smooth this through your hair and let air-dry to fall in love with your natural hair again.

One Cosmo editor says: "I almost always shied away from cream products because they’d often make my fine hair look greasy. This formula completely changed my view on creams. My dehydrated strands lap this up, and overall, my hair looks more moisturized and healthy when I use this.”—MH

What is the most effective heat protectant?

Ask any expert, and they'll say the most effective heat protectant is the one you'll actually use. However, some formulas will work better on certain hair types.

"Sprays, creams, and serums are all effective," says Rogerio Cavalcante, founder of the Second Floor Salon in New York City. "Sprays work well for fine hair, while creams and serums are better for thicker, coarser textures. It is also a matter of preference—some people prefer spray because they think it is more practical, won’t weigh the hair down as much, and is easier to disperse."

Is spray or cream heat protectant better?

Hamilton reiterates that neither sprays nor creams are inherently better, but one might be better suited for your hair type over the other. "Sprays are lightweight, making them suitable for fine and slightly wavy hair. Creams provide moisture and are ideal for curly or coarse hair types," he explains.

What’s a good heat protectant for fine hair?

Because fine hair has a tendency to fall flat, you're better off selecting a lightweight heat protectant that won't weigh your hair down. Both Cavalcante and Hamilton recommend sticking with sprays over creams or serums if you have fine hair.

How to choose the best drugstore heat protectant:

I may sound like captain obvious saying this, but products that work for fine hair types might not be the best choice for those with thick, curly hair. Those with the former will want to opt for more lightweight formulas, like sprays, that will protect your hair without weighing it down. As for the latter, thicker and curlier hair types need all the nourishment they can get, so our experts recommend opting for more substantial heat protectants, like serums and creams, that will infuse hair with hydration on top of safeguarding strands from high temps.

Beyond the texture (i.e. spray, cream, serum etc.), Blakely urges you to look at the ingredients on the label. "Some ingredients are known to have natural heat-protecting abilities," she explains.

If your heat protectant of choice contains any of the following, Blakely says your hair is in good hands.

Do you regularly blow dry your hair or typically apply heat once your hair is dry? Some heat protectants only work on damp hair, while others can be spritzed on dry hair. Look at the directions before purchasing your protectant of choice to ensure it will mesh with your preferred styling method. (FYI, almost every spray can be used on both wet and dry hair!)

Mary Honkus is a contributor for Cosmopolitan with six years of experience researching, writing, and editing beauty stories, including a deep dive on why your hair gets so oily and making a case for coconut oil for hair. Taylor Swift performed at the Academy Museum Gala in Los Angeles last night—then traveled to Kansas City, Missouri, in time for her husband Travis Kelce’s home game against the Los Angeles Chargers at Arrowhead Stadium this afternoon. Swift was seen wearing a red turtleneck in a suite with Indiana Fever player (and Swiftie) Caitlin Clark and musician Este Haim.

Swift has been at all her husband’s home games so far this season. The couple also spent Kelce’s bye week together in New York City, where they were photographed having a date night on October 9. Swift wore fall’s It color, olive green. She paired a sweater in the hue with brown pants.

While Swift has been in the public eye more frequently promoting the release of The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore, she hasn’t spoken about her and Kelce’s July 3 wedding yet. Her husband has, though. On the September 2 episode of New Heights, he discussed their phone ban and how much it meant to them to see loved ones from all stages of their lives intermingling.

“With no phones comes people not having to be on guard and like feel that something—whatever that feeling is for everyone—it makes everyone be in the moment and be present,” he said. “And it was so cool seeing everyone from my childhood, not only mesh with Taylor and her childhood [group] and her family and friends and people that she works with to who we’ve come [to] encounter over our careers and who we just admire as people and have become good friends with now. It’s just been so cool to see that world come together and hear through person by person after the wedding just how awesome of a time everyone had there. That’s what we wanted it to be. We wanted it to be a beautiful ceremony. And we also wanted to make sure that everybody left there having some fun.”

#268. Can You Eat Sprouted Potatoes?

Those little shoots on your potato don't necessarily mean they are destined for the trash. Here's how to tell when potatoes are still safe to eat.

I’ve pulled some questionable things out of the back of my pantry, but potatoes are particularly good at making me wonder just how long it’s been since I last cleaned the shelves. A few little sprouts are one thing. A potato that’s managed to grow an entire network of shoots while I wasn’t looking is quite another. But is a sprouted potato actually unsafe to eat, or is there still hope for tonight’s mashed potatoes?

Fortunately, finding a few sprouts doesn’t automatically mean you have to sacrifice your dinner plans. There are, however, a few things to look for before you reach for the potato peeler.

Yes, provided the potato is still firm, has only a few small sprouts and hasn’t turned green. You’ll need to remove the sprouts and surrounding eyes before cooking, but a potato that’s otherwise in good condition may still be usable.

The concern is with two naturally occurring compounds, solanine and chaconine. Their concentrations can increase as potatoes sprout, particularly in the shoots and around the eyes. Eating too much can cause nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, none of which are worth risking for a side of loaded baked potato salad.

According to the National Library of Medicine, potatoes that haven’t turned green can still be eaten once the sprouts have been removed. Removing them reduces the risk, although it doesn’t eliminate it entirely.

There is, though, a point at which it’s time to admit defeat. If your potato has developed long or numerous sprouts, feels soft or has wrinkled, shriveled skin, throw it away. The same goes for potatoes with extensive greening, which can indicate increased levels of those potentially harmful compounds.

As inconvenient as it is for those of us who would prefer our potatoes not to turn into science projects, sprouting is perfectly natural. Potatoes are tubers, meaning they store the energy needed to grow new plants. Those little indentations on the surface, called eyes, are buds that eventually produce shoots.

Warm temperatures and prolonged storage encourage sprouting, while exposure to light can cause potatoes to turn green. To keep your potatoes fresh longer, store them in a cool, dark, well-ventilated place. A breathable bag or basket, rather than sealed plastic, works great. Keep them away from direct sunlight and don’t store them with your onions! Onions release ethylene gas, which can encourage potatoes to sprout faster.

Proper storage will buy you some time, but it won’t stop sprouting indefinitely. If you’ve ever bought a 10-pound bag because it was only a dollar more than the five-pound bag, you’ve probably learned this the hard way.

Start by rinsing your potatoes under cool running water, then use a paring knife or the pointed tip of a potato peeler to cut out each sprout. Dig deep enough to remove the entire eye and the surrounding area, rather than simply snapping off the visible shoot. You can reduce your exposure even further by peeling the potato, since these compounds tend to be more concentrated in the skin.

If you’ve caught your potatoes before they’re too far gone, you don’t have to race to use them all at once. Mashed potatoes freeze beautifully, so make a big batch and portion it out for future dinners. You can also bake and freeze whole potatoes or shred and blanch them for homemade hash browns. There’s something deeply satisfying about turning a bag of potatoes you nearly threw away into several dinners’ worth of side dishes.

Or, if you have a green thumb, try planting one! Sprouted potatoes can grow into new plants, and a potato grow bag is a great way to experiment without digging up your garden.

Either way, those little sprouts aren’t necessarily the end of your potatoes. They might even be the beginning of a few more.

#269. The 10 Fall Wardrobe Essentials Every Man Should Own, According to a Style Editor

Think leather jackets, cozy knits, trousers, and shoes you’d wear on repeat.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

FALL IS MY favorite time of the year to get dressed. I love the richer colors and heavier layers that come with sweater season, but it’s also when I spend several mornings staring at my closet, trying to figure out an outfit. Living in New York City, where people dress up even for the grocery store, I’m always looking to switch up my look. But I’ve learned that having more clothes doesn’t necessarily mean having more outfits. I’ve worn the same jeans a few days in a row, so why congest my closet with a bunch of stuff I’ll never grab?

The solution: a capsule wardrobe. It’s a shorthand term that stylists use to refer to a tight edit of perennially great-looking clothes you can mix and match, so you can stack more looks with less garb. You don’t have to be a menswear pro to pull this off. I have my go-to basics and a few standout pieces that sprinkle in a little texture and extra flair. As a style editor (and shameless outfit repeater), here are the essentials I’m keeping in rotation this fall. Take note whether you’re rebuilding your wardrobe or looking to fill in a few gaps.

I’m the knitwear king, so a couple of good crewneck sweaters are nonnegotiable for my fall wardrobe. They’re easy to throw on with light or dark-colored jeans, but look even sharper when I dress them up with tailored trousers and loafers.

When I’m traveling or running around knocking out errands, a hoodie is a warm, comfortable piece to have when the temps dip. I love that it fits under a coat or leather, depending on its fit.

If I’m investing in one statement layer for fall, it’s a leather jacket. It gives even a basic T-shirt and jeans combination some edge, and you can wear it well into spring.

A good pair of jeans is the backbone of this whole capsule. I prefer a relaxed straight-leg fit that gives my thighs room without looking overly baggy. A medium or dark wash will work with just about every sweater, jacket, and shoe in your rotation.

When I need a break from denim and have to attend dressier events, I need a solid pair of trousers in the arsenal. A relaxed or wide-leg fit is my usual go-to for these occasions.

When a crewneck feels too casual but a dress shirt feels like too much, I find that a sweater polo hits the sweet spot. It can be worn casually or dressed up, but the latter is always my go-to. I’d look for one in chocolate brown, navy, or olive.

Henleys have become popular again, and I love the idea of giving my everyday tee a little more character. One with a closer fit through the torso is super flattering, especially when I pair it with relaxed or wide-leg pants, keeping the proportions balanced.

Every fall capsule needs at least one shirt that can handle a work meeting, a dinner reservation, or an occasion that calls for more than a T-shirt. A blue Oxford or crisp white button-down is a good place to start. It’s super versatile, so I can wear mine tucked into chinos or tailored trousers, left open over a tee or layered beneath a crewneck sweater with the collar showing.

Fall is prime time for boots. And I can wear them with denim and dress pants whether I reach for my sleek leather pair or cowboy style.

I’m a loafer guy anyway, but it’s true—sneakers don’t go with a lot of fall looks. Loafers work with relaxed trousers, sweater polos, and even straight-leg jeans, while a classic Derby or Oxford is useful for dressier occasions.

#271. The 25 Best Horror Comedies to Stream Right Now

These “scary” movies will leave you dying. Of laughter.

Are you scared? There ain’t nothing to be afraid of on Halloween, and I can prove it. While October is obviously the month for horror-movie marathons, scaredy-cats who can’t stomach jump scares may be more inclined to watch something that isn’t The Exorcist. (Although Linda Blair’s sardonic Pazuzu is low-key hilarious.) If you’ve already exhausted every possible not-so-scary Halloween movie and plowed through some all-time Halloween-themed TV episodes, fear not: There are still more things to watch, including some of the best horror comedies that are available on streaming.

As you’re preparing your last-minute Halloween costume and trying to get your 12-foot-tall Home Depot skeleton to stand up, here are some lighthearted horror comedies on streamers like Netflix, HBO Max, Disney+, and Tubi. Some are family friendly—of course we mention Hocus Pocus—while others, well, just because it’s funny doesn’t mean it’s suitable for kids. But as with candy, there’s still something for everyone.

Here are 25 horror comedies you can stream right now.

When Barbara and Adam Maitland die in a car accident, they become ghosts. On the bright side, their spirits are tied to their house ... where they plan to remain for eternity. Sounds nice, right? Wrong. Those dreams are crushed when the Deetz family moves in. The Maitlands try to scare them off, but the Deetz clan is unfazed. When all else fails, the Maitlands summon Beetlejuice—a wacky ghost, to say the least—to finish the job. If you’re craving more, the long-awaited sequel Beetlejuice Beetlejuice is also streaming on HBO Max.

The original Ghostbusters—Bill Murray, Dan Aykroyd, Harold Ramis, and Ernie Hudson—work as supernatural exterminators who must save New York City from a spectral apocalypse. Filled with great jokes and remarkable primitive visual effects that hold up after 40-plus years, it’s a classic for a reason. Who you gonna call? If you can’t get enough, all the sequels, including Ghostbusters: Afterlife from 2021 and Ghostbusters: Frozen Empire from 2024, are also on Hulu and Disney+.

Edgar Wright made his directorial debut with this horror spoof, cowritten by its star, Simon Pegg. Shaun (Pegg) spends his mediocre days shuffling to and from work, playing video games with his best friend, and hoping to keep his increasingly estranged girlfriend. But that humdrum life is instantly spun out of control when a zombie apocalypse takes over London, forcing him into action to protect everyone he loves.

Don’t fall for the tricks, or you’ll end up someone else’s treat. From director McG, the Netflix original The Babysitter stars Judah Lewis as Cole, an adolescent boy with a crush on his cool babysitter (Samara Weaving), until she turns out to be a member of a satanic cult. Cole spends the rest of his sleepless night fighting for his life against Samara Weaving’s Bee, who needs Cole’s innocent blood to finish a ritual.

For a moment, Werewolves Within was perhaps the greatest video game movie of all time (until Resident Evil came along). Based on the social deduction VR game, Werewolves Within takes place in a small Vermont town during a freak snowstorm. When the residents realize a werewolf is hiding among them, they descend into pure, utter, and hilarious chaos. Directed by Dropout regular Josh Ruben, Werewolves Within has cultivated a feverish cult audience since its 2021 release.

Bodies Bodies Bodies is a comedic whodunit from A24. A crew of 20-somethings take a weekend trip to their friend’s mansion. When a hurricane hits, they’re forced to stay inside and pass the time with a party game that goes hilariously wrong. Oh, and Pete Davidson is there too.

In this loose adaptation of Mary Shelley’s classic Frankenstein tale, Kathryn Newton plays a quirky teenager who turns a Victorian-era corpse into her boyfriend. Why date regular boys when you can build a man from scratch? Apparently, all it takes is determination, a sense of humor, and a few fresh body parts.

Jim Jarmusch’s The Dead Don’t Die takes place in Centerville—a fictional town with a big problem. The dead have risen from their graves, and they’re hungry for blood. The vicious attacks compel an unlikely group of residents to band together in a hysterical bid for survival. Did we mention that Bill Murray stars as a sheriff turned zombie hunter?

Movie aside, Chucky: M3GAN is here. The film about a cutting-edge robot doll who ends up being a lot more than a little girl bargained for is perfect for those who want a few laughs with their screams. How can anyone forget M3GAN’s iconic dancing to Sia’s “Titanium” right after pushing a preteen boy in front of a car?

We’ve entered an era of fully embracing camp—and we’re better off for it. And what does camp mean nowadays? To me, it’s when you take a real-life story about a bear that accidentally ingests cocaine—dropped by drug smugglers!—and turn it into a tight 95 minutes of over-the-top, hyper-violent, and manic shenanigans. If you want to watch drug dealers, school-ditching kids, and Ray Liotta shine in one of his last roles, this is for you.

Anna and the Apocalypse is the Christmas zombie musical you didn’t know you needed. The madness begins when a high school teenager (Ella Hunt), determined to leave her small town behind, has her plans interrupted by a sudden zombie apocalypse. And at Christmastime, no less! It might be too early for candy canes and sleigh bells, but Anna and the Apocalypse is the best way to smooth the transition from spooky season to cozy holiday warmth.

This 2022 horror comedy from Mimi Cave roasts modern dating and swallows it whole. Having no success with the modern-day horrors of dating (aka dating apps), a young woman (Daisy Edgar-Jones) meets Sebastian Stan’s Steve, who plays a real lady-killer, a man who has an appetite for the exquisite—human meat!

Here’s a spin on the final-girl trope, as a bride tries to make it out alive in a game of hide-and-seek with her new in-laws. Between the laugh-out-loud moments, a strong performance from Samara Weaving as Grace—a newlywed who has the worst first night of marriage imaginable—and a mere 90-minute run time, your mind never wanders as you wait for what gory kill comes next.

Let’s see Paul Allen’s card. Starring Batman (Christian Bale) and the Joker (Jared Leto), this satire will have you laughing at the most serious times. Bale’s legendary performance leaves you wondering if what you just watched actually happened and the characters are too self-obsessed to notice, or if it is all in his imagination, sparked by his inner turmoil.

Sam Raimi, you mad genius. After his Spider-Man trilogy, Raimi went back to his horror roots with Drag Me to Hell, a pitch-black horror comedy about a young woman trying to break free from a curse placed upon her by an angry client. An impressive blend of genuinely frightening scares with some laugh-out-loud hysterics, Drag Me to Hell is an oft-forgotten late-2000s gem that deserves a bigger spotlight.

Call it Freaky Friday the 13th. A mash-up of body-switching comedies and slasher horror, Freaky stars Kathryn Newton as a high school senior who is almost the latest victim of a serial killer called the Butcher (Vince Vaughn). But when an enchanted knife causes them to switch bodies, well, let’s just say hell really breaks loose.

Comic-book writer Scott Lobdell went Hollywood in 2017 with his screenplay Happy Death Day, a genre-blending mix of Halloween and Groundhog Day. After a night of partying, college sorority girl Tree (Jessica Rothe) wakes up in her (platonic?) classmate’s bed, over and over again. She soon realizes she’s become the victim of a masked killer and is stuck in a time loop, and she must figure out how to finally break from the monotony. If you want the sequel, Happy Death Day 2U from 2019, hop over to Netflix.

In 2009, director Karyn Kusama and screenwriter Diablo Cody unleashed a prescient teen horror movie that’s won retrospective praise since its muted release in 2009. After a disastrous night at a local bar to see a popular band, teenager Needy (Amanda Seyfried) learns that her sexy best friend (Megan Fox) has become a demonically possessed succubus and is racking up bodies at their high school. Now regarded as a queer horror classic, Jennifer’s Body is truly so much more than meets the eye.

You’re either really scared or really nostalgic if you’re looking for Hocus Pocus. But we don’t blame you—it’s still a damn fine Halloween classic. In this millennial favorite from director Kenny Ortega, Bette Midler, Kathy Najimy, and Sarah Jessica Parker star as three witches from 17th-century Salem who are accidentally summoned by contemporary teenagers on Halloween night. Despite bombing at the box office in July 1993 (yes, JULY), Hocus Pocus became a cable-TV staple that made it a classic for the BuzzFeed generation. In 2022, the trio reunited for Hocus Pocus 2, which is also streaming on Disney+.

Classic American horror conventions get turned upside down in the unsuspectingly warm Tucker & Dale vs. Evil. Hilarity and horror begin when college students mistake two hillbilly best friends (Alan Tudyk and Tyler Labine) for backwoods murderers. When one of the students gets separated from their friends, well-meaning Tucker and Dale try to help them out, only for the bodies to actually pile high. This festival favorite became a big enough cult hit that a Korean-language remake, Handsome Guys, was released in 2024.

Being a flesh-eating zombie has never been so hot in this hilarious rom-com that retells Shakespeare’s Romeo and Juliet in the zombie apocalypse. Nicholas Hoult stars as a walking undead named “R” who, after biting the boyfriend of beautiful Julie (Teresa Palmer), not only falls in love with Julie but starts to show signs of life.

Sam Raimi’s breakout feature The Evil Dead was a horror movie punctuated by moments of uproarious hilarity. The 1987 sequel Evil Dead II cranks up the volume with Bruce Campbell, back as Ash, who must once again fight off ancient evil spirits. While all the Evil Dead movies are worth marathoning (and I say this as a huge Army of Darkness fan personally), Evil Dead II is a standout.

While it’s a Halloween favorite today, writer and director John Landis actually struggled to secure financing for An American Werewolf in London because no one in Hollywood could square whether it was a horror movie or a comedy. An American Werewolf foresaw the changing moon in its story about an American backpacker who gets bitten by a werewolf in England and recuperates—and then transforms—under the care of a beautiful nurse. The movie’s still-mesmerizing transformation sequence inspired Michael Jackson to ask Landis, and special-effects master Rick Baker, to help bring to life his now legendary music video for “Thriller.”

We really had a thing for horror comedies in the late 2000s, didn’t we? One of the biggest and most successful of the genre blenders was Zombieland, directed by Ruben Fleischer and starring Jesse Eisenberg and Emma Stone right before their rocket to fame. Set against a zombie outbreak, a college student (Eisenberg) joins up with a gun-toting badass and two plucky sisters—and Bill Murray—to make it across the country and see if his family is still alive. A sequel, Zombieland: Double Tap, opened in 2019 and is also streaming on HBO Max.

This bait and switch directed by Drew Goddard (who cowrote it with Joss Whedon) begins as your typical horror flick. Unwitting college students—among them Thor himself, Chris Hemsworth—travel to a remote cabin in the middle of nowhere for a boozy, druggy, sex-filled weekend away, with monsters of varying sorts waiting to off them one by one. But it has a postmodern twist, turning the slasher film into a hilarious horror satire that pays tribute to the genre’s formulaic tropes.

#272. How a Drinks Influencer Balances Diabetes With Dining in 35 Cities a Year

Welcome to The Receipt, a series documenting how Bon Appétit readers eat and what they spend doing it. Each food diary follows one anonymous reader’s week of expenses related to groceries, restaurant meals, coffee runs, and every bite in between. In this time of rising food costs, The Receipt reveals how folks—from different cities, with different incomes, on different schedules—are figuring out their food budgets.

In today’s Receipt, we follow a drinks influencer with diabetes in Chicago who might make anywhere from $50K to $250K. Keep reading for her receipts.

The financesThe dietThe expensesThe diary

What is your occupation? Reluctant drinks influencer/solopreneur

How old are you? The last TV producer I worked with guessed that I am between 36 and 40. I’d say my actual age is considered mature for a California Cabernet Sauvignon, but very young for an Armagnac. Take from that what you will.

What city and state do you live in? Chicago, Illinois

What is your annual salary? Varies with my level of hustle. Since I started my own business, I make anywhere from $50K to $250K a year before expenses.

How often are you paid? Sometimes twice a year and sometimes more, depending on the state of my client roster.

What are your approximate fixed monthly expenses beyond food? (i.e., rent, subscriptions, insurance, bills)

Do you follow a certain diet or have dietary restrictions? I was diagnosed with type 2 Diabetes in 2021, but didn’t admit to myself it was a problem until two years later. That’s when I started listing dietary requests in all of the reservations platforms, only to have them ignored, misunderstood, and refused by even three-star Michelin chefs. One time, a very famous chef served my dining companion a gorgeous 10-piece dessert while plopping a giant wedge of cheese on my plate. Which, he proceeded to tell me, he’d sent a cook out to Whole Foods to buy for me. With no accompaniments.

I try to minimize processed, white-sugar-spiked, and complex carbs at home and when eating out. It’s such a challenge—in this day and age, with diabetes rates on the rise, it makes me crazy that we’re not accommodated.

I should start a charity. Or an action group?

What are the grocery staples you always buy? Apples, berries, and bananas for smoothies. Stone fruits in season. Eggs for easy protein. Greek yogurt, citrus, and herbs (the ones I don’t grow in my Auk hydroponic unit) to make dips and spreads for dinner and, as much good-looking crudités as I can find at my local Mariano’s (Kroger). Wisconsin (support local!) cheese, mostly Marieke Goude and Sartori (the only two women Masters of Cheese in Wisconsin) for snacking and cooking. Rao’s marinara. Pineapple juice to mix with my AG1, coconut water, grapefruit La Croix, and Diet Coke.

How often in a week do you dine out versus cook at home? I visited 35 cities last year, and I have been on the road a lot this year too. Of course, when I am traveling, I eat breakfast out, sometimes two lunches per day out (in order to check out the local restaurant and bar scenes), and sometimes two or three dinners and bar visits. Per day.

When I am at home in Chicago, I try to stay in as much as possible. In this era of my life, I would cook at home every night if I could. Saves money and I can control my dietary preferences, which will hopefully help me stay healthier and live longer. I really wish that chefs and restaurateurs would respect that more.

How often in a week did you dine out while growing up? It was a rare treat growing up. My family lived in Boston, then New Jersey, and then the suburbs of Chicago. My parents’ first choice, even when we were traveling, was any restaurant in a first-rate Chinatown. We were always hosting international students and research assistants of my dad, a PhD research chemist, offering them what was often their first taste of authentic Taiwanese or Chinese food.

And if my little brother or I got straight A’s, we went to Ponderosa or Sizzler Steakhouse!

How often in a week did your parents cook at home? Daily. Three meals a day from scratch. My mom is a graduate of the Fu Pei-mei cooking school in Taiwan. She is the only daughter of her family—my grandfather figured that if she could cook, she’d be easy to marry off. Because what else would you do with a daughter?

My mom is spunky, though, and in addition to graduating from cooking school, she also graduated from college and moved to the US. At first, she lived in a six-person-to-a-room apartment in Queens and worked for the phone company before getting a master’s degree in Library Science.

I will never forget the sound of my mom’s cleaver butchering whole chickens and the sizzle of garlic and chiles in a hot oil-slicked wok. She’d cook at night after returning home from her corporate library job, us kids doing homework upstairs. Our family of four sat down together every day to fresh steamed rice and my mom’s portfolio of Taiwanese classics like beef tendon and noodle soup, whole fish cooked in hot oil with scallions and cilantro, and ’70s American classics like Shake ‘N Bake, pork chops, and meat loaf. My house was my friends’ favorite to visit—hot dog fried rice! Peanut butter and jelly mantou steamed buns! Whole head-on ducks curing in the laundry room!

There were also frequent nine-course dinners with visiting students, research assistants, work colleagues, and neighbors. My mom could have cooked in a Michelin-starred kitchen. I was in charge of setting the table and the special cocktail: my blend of fruit juices and Sprite, made into a slushie.

Week’s total: $1,601.46Restaurants and cafés total: $1,326.46Groceries total: $275Most-expensive meal or purchase: $250 a private club (wine, oysters, and french fries) and The Shipwright’s Daughter (tasting menu and a bottle of Champagne)Least-expensive meal or purchase: 30 for drunk-girl snacks at 7-ElevenNumber of restaurant and café meals: 9Number of grocery trips: 6, including grocery, bakery, bodega, and convenience stores

7 a.m. I re-steam a za’atar bagel from Starship Bagel in Dallas. It’s rock-hard after sitting on my counter for a week, but the old wet-the-bagel-and-bake-in-foil trick worked! I almost never throw out food in an effort to save money, so I will go to great lengths to rescue things.

I top it with Starship’s fermented jalapeño cream cheese and Acme Nova lox, all paired with pineapple juice mixed with AG-1 powder, plus a Diet Coke.

2 p.m. A long-scheduled lunch meeting at an iconic Chicago French bistro is canceled, so I work at home and throw together a cheese plate with Nut Thins Flax Seed Crackers (more fiber to counteract my diabetes!), Marieke fenugreek Gouda (smells like maple syrup but there is NO sugar—sooo good), Sartori Espresso Bellavitano (yes, coffee and Parmesan are delicious together), and some homemade apricot mostarda. I use honey to sweeten it (not white sugar) and use dried apricots that are way past their prime. Like years past their prime. But waste not, want not!

7 p.m.: I make two grocery runs: At Mariano’s (a.k.a. Kroger), I spend $105 on a dozen large eggs (the cheapest ones), two-for-$6 packages of okra (the price is why I bought them), a bunch of fruit and veg, and my drink staples. Then I hit up Jewel-Osco (Albertson’s) and spend another $25. I’ve come for fresh ginger, which I couldn’t find at Mariano’s, hence this second stop. Of course, I also toss some other fun stuff into my cart. I LOVE grocery shopping.

9 p.m. It’s meal prep time, and I cut and chop and cook until I can do no more: roasted okra and red onions; a Tuscan-inspired white bean, tomato, and spinach stew with repurposed breakfast sausage meatballs from the freezer; and a broccoli Alfredo gratin-type thing. I also brunoise and freeze all of the celery, carrots, and onions in my apartment that are about to turn. I don’t eat a proper dinner, but I’m tasting everything as it bubbles and roasts and cooks.

My co-op does not allow dishwashers in my unit, so I am a clean-as-you-go cook: Everything is washed and dried by the time the last dish is completed. I lived in two apartments in NYC with tiny kitchens, in which celebrity chefs cooked multicourse meals with me doing wine service and cleaning up after them. So, yeah—I am very good at this.

7 a.m.: I’m so excited to try the internet-famous “Cleanout Creamy Golden Glow” shot, with turmeric, coconut milk, and juices of a blood orange, lime, and yuzu. I have some amazing Burlap & Barrel New Harvest Turmeric and cans and cans of coconut milk—my mom bought me a lifetime supply from Costco, so I have been looking for ways to use it.

I also slice up the last of the weisswurst I bought last week at Jungle Jim’s in Ohio (a 200,000-square-foot grocery store that is like my Disney World) with an amazing spicy French Pommery Dijon mustard, and a fried egg. Protein is essential!

1 p.m. For lunch, I have the olive-oil-roasted broccoli with a defrosted jar of small-batch Alfredo sauce, which was also purchased on a (different) trip to Ohio, leveled up with a nub of crème fraîche and some Parmigiano-Reggiano butter that was lurking in the fridge. I transform the remains of my no-knead jalapeño cheddar loaf into the most delicious bread crumbs, which I place atop it.

NOTE: I only have dorm-size undercounter freezer and refrigerator units. They are chic stainless-steel Sub-Zero units—so adult in a way, but still very small. And yet, I still manage to lose things in both. I’ll get to them eventually!

6:30 p.m. I add a last-minute clink-and-catch-up with a girlfriend to my schedule. We meet at a new private club in Chicago, and I’m determined to spend as little money as possible in this new era of budgeting and austerity.

I take an Uber Comfort instead of Black. I would have walked, but it was way too windy and rainy. I’ve chosen this bar because I was told their wine markup is very reasonable, and that the wine list is a standout for the city. It’s…okay.

We order all three sparkling wines by the glass, split them, and sip the offerings side by side so I can deliver on a wine primer I’d promised to my friend. We pair the wines with six oysters and an order of black truffle french fries, which we devour over conversations about the care of our aging parents and dealing with our siblings and shitty bosses and clients.

We sample the wines blind: a Crémant de Bourgogne at $18 a glass, a Napa Blanc de Blancs at $28 a glass, and a Champagne at $36 a glass. Lesson: Never be fooled by the price tag. A $36 glass of wine is just not right if it’s not mind-blowing. In all, I plunk down $250, which definitely is not within my budget.

We were surrounded by a handful of bro-looking guys in Arc'teryx vests and Peter Millar quarter zips, mostly drinking beer and whiskey. We were the only two women in the place aside from the women at the host stand. And by the time we left, the place was empty but for us. Crossing this place off of my list for moving forward.

9 p.m. My friend and I are dressed up and cute, so we can’t end the day at the sad club. We try to get past the velvet ropes at Kitty’s Cosmopolitan Club, a brand-new cocktail bar opened by an acquaintance whose other bars we love.

I’m resigned to the fact that my budget is blown for the day. At the host stand, I wave around my friend’s credentials (she’s a news anchor on TV!), and we muscle our way into a table at the four-day-old, 60-seat, reservations-recommended spot. I try to order some dim sum, but the order gets lost in the fun. In the end, we have no food but amazing cocktails served to us by men in tuxedos pushing carts. I spend $150. Whoops.

11:30 p.m. After saying goodbye to my friend, I start to walk home and it begins to rain right in front of a 7-Eleven that I used to go to when I lived in the building right across the street. I dash inside to escape the rain and immediately get the munchies.

I definitely drink a lot less now that I am on a GLP-1. My tolerance is definitely not what it used to be. Upside, my bar tab is generally lower, but the downside is there are more hangovers.

10 a.m. Two Advil, a Diet Coke, and a Tangerine Liquid IV Immune Support later, and OOF. I haven’t felt like this in quite a long time.

Normally, I might order something greasy from DoorDash to speed up my recovery, but I am on a restricted budget until I collect some payments from clients (the joys of being a contractor!). I cancel all appointments, revenue opportunities be damned, and suffer through it.

2 p.m. I heat up one small skillet of the Tuscan bean situation I made on day one, add some BelGioioso burrata, and garnish with the good olive oil. I chase it with some hibiscus strawberry tea.

For the rest of the day, I snuggle up in bed and watch Your Friends and Neighbors, season one.

6:30 a.m. A turmeric shot and a Diet Coke get me out the door into the gray and rainy day. I’m first in line at Chiu Quon Bakery in Chinatown, a weekly ritual whenever I’m doing an errand day with my mom out in the suburbs, where my parents live. I nab $50 worth of steamed mantou, just-fried turnip cakes, rice crepes with shrimp, and eight fresh-from-the-oven egg tarts.

The best Chinese bakery in Chicago also happens to be women-powered. I love watching the women stocking the shelves and practicing my fifth-grade-level Mandarin with whoever’s behind the counter. It is not the best moment for my diabetes, though: It’s all I can do to resist buying all the sweet baked buns, mini mooncake flavors, and sweet cake slices.

Our family's love language has always been food, so I always bring something special every visit. I also tote home a sparkling rosé cherry wine that I discovered on a trip to Michigan and more Starship Bagels from my Dallas trip.

8:30 a.m. The aforementioned bakery haul is enjoyed with my mom and dad at the kitchen table I grew up sitting at, complete with a white board with every color erasable marker for working out chemistry and math equations with Dad.

1 p.m. It is the week of my birthday but I will be out of town on the actual day, so Mom and I go to one of our favorite lunch spots in the burbs, the bar at Wildfire, for a pre-birthday celebration.

Rosé methode Champenoise for me, merlot for mom. We split the whole branzino and sides of creamed spinach and mashed potatoes. For dessert, we share a Key lime pie slice; we bring home slices of the Door County cherry and butterscotch banana pies for Dad. He generally sleeps in most days, but he will get up for sweets! He grew up on a sugar plantation that my grandfather managed and has always had a major league sweet tooth.

The total comes to $150, but I redeem my accumulated frequent diner points and my birthday bonus, so I only spend $30. I leave a $40 tip for our server Sam, who we adore.

8:30 p.m. I get home late after hours of reorganizing Mom’s gardening supplies in preparation for spring planting. I warm up another serving of my Tuscan white bean stew and add the other half of the Belgioioso burrata to it for a late dinner.

3:30 a.m. I start the day with a turmeric shot and Diet Coke. I’m going to see a woman about a bagel at the Cultured in Door County, Wisconsin. It takes four hours to drive there from Chicago, and the bakery is only open Saturday and Sunday from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. (or until everything is sold out). I do not want to miss out on anything, so I’ve got up before the sun to get my hands on their goodies.

5:30 a.m. I stop to fill up gas and get a pre-breakfast bite, but the Hardee’s attached to the gas station was not open. I pop into the Love’s Travel Stop and buy an Olipop Cream Soda (probiotics, right?) and Jack’s Links Smoked Bacon (what does the new food pyramid instruct us to do now?) for $10.

8:30 a.m. I would have been first in line at Cultured but for the local sheriff who I had to crawl behind for 30 miles.

Nevertheless, I get the last parking space in the lot before the locals started parking on the side of the country road. I order one of everything to go: bagels, their signature spreads, marbled rye, and focaccia. To eat in, I get the mushroom toastie plus a mint-and-lemon Spindrift. My total comes to $125.

It’s delicious, but the best part is watching the four-women-strong kitchen team make all of the bagels and crush all of the cooking for the constant stream of locals coming in.

12 p.m. The bagels smell so amazing in my car that I have to pull over and eat the cheddar bagel with elote cream cheese. YUM.

Now I’m onto my next destination: Sway Brewery, a finalist for a James Beard Award, for Outstanding Wine and Other Beverages Program. I am the first customer into the newly reopened space. I was skeptical about this visit, but I am WOWED. I sit up at the counter with the founder and brewmaster, Matt Sampson, sipping and chatting through eight of his artisanal brews. They’re made with local regeneratively grown grains, all pulled from gorgeous Czech taps that do magical things, like pull an entire glass of foam. (They call it the milk tube.)

Do eight 2-ounce beers count as lunch? Matt is a PhD in chemistry, so we chat about CO₂ and calcium and all of the science. My tab (which also includes some merch) comes to $105.

7 p.m. After much consultation with locals, I decide to visit Alexander’s Restaurant, a classic Wisconsin supper club. I’ve never been to one before.

I start with a Wisconsin brandy old-fashioned, sour—a.k.a. spiked with a tart soda or sour mix. (I could have also opted for sweet, which employs a lemon-lime soda, or press, a 50-50 mix of lemon lime soda and club soda). I also order a three-cheese artichoke dip and the lamb chops. The entrée comes with soup (lobster bisque) and a vegetable (haricots verts and potato gratin).

I eat less than a quarter of it and pack it all up for Easter Sunday lunch with Mom and Dad. (It turned out to be plenty for all three of us when I added the tomato, olive, and cheese focaccia loaf I’d purchased from Cultured.)

While I was enjoying the local flavor (both the food and the people), a very well-respected cocktail writer, who recently moved to Milwaukee from Brooklyn, texted me that I was NOT at a proper supper club (oh well!) but that I was .1 miles away from the best classic Wisconsin ice cream drinks. I look up the hours for the spot and realize it closes in 15 minutes. I grab my check and pay—it comes to $113.90—and dash over.

8:17 p.m. The English Inn is like a wacky Disney World for adults who love fine spirits like Pappy Van Winkle bourbon, classic Wisconsin cocktails, a great all-you-can-eat fish fry on Fridays, and medieval suits of armor and paraphernalia. And, of course, ice cream drinks.

I order a Pink Squirrel and a Grasshopper ($62.56) and I am so glad that I did—the bartenders churn cocktail ingredients into local ice cream, one at a time. Both drinks come topped with a giant dollop of fresh whipped cream.

I notice people are grabbing these as takeout, so I have one taste of each, pack them up, and go to sip them in front of the fireplace at my hotel lobby.

7 a.m. It’s a turmeric shot and Diet Coke again. I jump in the car to head to my parents’ house for Easter lunch—I find the bag of smoked bacon jerky I’d previously gotten from the gas station and finish it.

10 a.m. My plan is derailed as I realize I’m about to pass the Mars Cheese Castle in Kenosha, Wisconsin, which, IYKYK, is a mecca for every flavor of Wisconsin cheese (and some others), meats (summer sausage! Kielbasa! brats!), beer, and accoutrements.

I snack on a few samples of cheese I have not tried before and also pick up a bunch of other styles that I never see in my local grocery stores. My final haul includes 18-year-old sharp cheddar, a Tuscan-style fontal, and a hatch chile BellaVitano. It all comes to $55.

12 p.m. Easter Lunch with Mom and Dad features my Alexander’s leftovers. I make us cute plates so none of it looks like leftovers, but like a plated meal at a white tablecloth restaurant. We toast with rosé cherry sparkling wine I brought from Traverse City.

2 p.m. Not only am I dealing with diabetes, I am also going through perimenopause, neither of which were dealt with by my primary care doctor. So, I have to go to specialists and purchase medicines at my own expense.

Our health care system is very broken. I have large medications bills, spend too much time on the phone with the insurance company, and go back and forth with them trying to find coupons and discount pharmacies—all to get my meds at the lowest prices possible. Why are life-prolonging and -saving drugs not covered? These are not vanity medications. Welcome to being a self-employed single woman.

The most recent pharmacy bill might break me. No dinner because I am so depressed about my money challenges and I have to get up at 3 a.m. to pack and travel to Mystic, Connecticut.

3 a.m. I suck down a Diet Coke and turmeric shot, then start packing for my trip to Mystic.

5 a.m. The Admiral’s Club at O’Hare International Airport opens and I beeline for the gratis food stations. I grab a banana, the egg of the day from the hot line, and two sausage links.

12:30 p.m. I check into the Delamar Hotel in Mystic and they give me a glass of prosecco (I love this sparkling wine ritual at all of the Delamar Hotels). I find a chocolate amenity in my room, which I immediately snack on.

3:30 p.m. I meet with chef-partner Renee Touponce and beverage director Jade Ayala, who operate seafood joint The Oyster Club and its attached outdoor dining deck The Treehouse, plus neighborhood bistro The Port of Call and its downstairs bar, The Dive.

These women and their team are AMAZING. I chat with an oysterman from down the street who shucks his oysters and clams for us. We sip on divine women-made cocktails and wines, all while tucking into award-winning Chef Renee’s spins on empanadas, foie gras mille-feuille, oeufs mayo, and larb salad. When the chef is cooking for you, there is no saying no! I spend about $200.

7:45 p.m. I am a little late for the other reason I flew to Mystic, The Shipwright’s Daughter. Its chef, David Standridge, was named the James Beard Award winner for Best Chef, Northeast in 2024, and he was nominated in the national Outstanding Chef category just this year.

This is one of those nights where I have, more or less, three dinners. And a bottle of Champagne. And more cocktails. And some blood orange limoncello at the end! Chef David specializes in supporting regenerative farming and cooking invasive species into fantastic dishes. It costs me $250.

I did not mean to, but I ate every last crumb of the six dishes. I have no regrets.

#273. Pumpkin Butter

A good condiment is always worth having around, and come fall, pumpkin butter earns its place in the fridge. Warmly spiced and sweet, this stovetop version cooks down in 30 minutes and requires no more effort than an occasional stir. Keep a jar on hand for toasts of all kinds, biscuits and quickbreads, waffles and pancakes, or spoon over oatmeal, yogurt, and ice cream. There’s plenty of room to make this autumn favorite your own, and it makes a great gift for the holiday season.

In a medium saucepan over medium-high heat, bring the pumpkin puree, granulated sugar, brown sugar, apple cider, pumpkin pie spice, vanilla, and salt to a boil.

Reduce heat to low and bring the entire mixture to a simmer. Cook, stirring frequently with a spatula, until pumpkin butter has thickened and the desired texture is reached. This should take bout 30 minutes, but could vary depending on your desired texture.

Once done, let it cool, then transfer to mason jars and refrigerate until you’re ready to use.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Allow to cool completely before refrigerating in an airtight container. Keep in the fridge for up to 3 weeks, or in the freezer for up to 6 months.
