#274. The 8 Best Setting Sprays Beauty Editors Swear By for 12-Hour Wear

Whether you like a glowy, matte, or natural finish, these will keep your glam on all day long.

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

Every beauty regimen would be obsolete without a finishing step. What’s the point of painting on a manicure without a glossy, chip-resistant top coat? Or a voluminous blowout without some hairspray to prevent it from falling limp in an hour? And a makeup routine is no different. There’s no point in spending all that time perfecting your glam if it's going to look cakey by noon, or disappear by the end of the day. Luckily, that’s where a good setting spray comes in, locking your makeup in place while keeping it looking fresh, whether you want a blurred finish, extra hydration, or just some added insurance against sweat and humidity.

But let's be real: Some setting sprays are basically glorified water. They might leave your skin looking a little dewier for a few minutes, but the best formulas actually meld your makeup together, prevent fading and creasing, and keep your look intact for hours on end, even on the sweatiest of days.

Don't know which one to choose? We've got you covered. Team Cosmo tested just about every setting spray on the market across different skin types and makeup routines, and we have plenty of opinions. Keep reading for our 12 hour day-approved favorites.

Why we love it: I’m not usually a full-glam girl, but when I do decide to go all out, I need my makeup to stay put—and L’Oréal’s Infallible Setting Mist never lets me down. It’s won several Cosmo beauty awards for its ability to lock everything in place with just a three-second spritz. If I’m doing the whole foundation and contour situation, I’m finishing it off with this.

One Cosmo editor says: "You’ve probably seen an influencer spray this on their face then dunk into water or dabbed their glammed up face onto a wedding dress and wondered if it’s truly effective or not—and I’m here to tell you it’s honestly worth the hype. It keeps my face hydrated while locking my makeup in place during 12-hour days. I also love that you can hold it down for a continuous spritz instead of having to unevenly spray across your face. This budget-friendly pick works better than $30+ setting sprays.”—JASMINE HYMAN, ASSISTANT BEAUTY EDITOR

Why we love it: How could we possibly round up the best setting sprays without this OG? This changed the entire game and still holds up as one of the best setting sprays for keeping my makeup in place all damn day. There's a reason brides have been swearing by this for over a decade, because it instantly sets down your powders and extends makeup wear.

It doesn't mattify my makeup per se, but it doesn't add any dewiness either. Instead, it just takes away some of the excess powder on my face and makes my skin look cohesive. The real shining star is how long it makes makeup last.

One Cosmo editor says: "I've been using this since high school—prom, homecoming, graduations, frat parties, concerts, bar crawls, you name it—and it holds my makeup on for every single one of 'em. Typically, with this on top, I get an extra five or six hours of wear out of my products, which is a strong feat."—BETH GILLETTE, BEAUTY EDITOR

Why we love it: Milani is the blueprint when it comes to drugstore setting sprays, and we didn’t think it could get any better than the original Make It Last formula, but it does. This latest iteration boasts a super fine mist combined with a continuous spray, so you can cover the whole face in just one go. It’s also free of any pore-cloggers, so those with acne-prone skin don’t have to top their makeup off with anything that may break them out.

One Cosmo editor says: “I’ve relied on the original Milani Make It Last Setting Spray for years, but this microfine mist majorly increases my makeup’s longevity. Similar to the One/Size On ’Til Dawn, this claims to make your makeup waterproof, sweatproof, and transfer-proof. I haven’t dunked in a pool wearing this, but it does keep my makeup on even when I’m drenched in sweat on the subway, which is enough for me.”—BG

Why we love it: For those who want a stronghold setting spray without any of the harsh scents or stiffness of a longwear formula, Saie’s is lightweight, super hydrating, and will lock any level of glam into place. It sprays onto the face with a super fine mist (as the name would suggest) and leaves behind a nice natural glow. It’s a big deal when I finish a setting spray, and this is the first bottle I’ve emptied in years. It also comes in a travel-size so I bring it anywhere and everywhere. Beauty director and makeup minimalist Lauren Balsamo is also a major fan.

One Cosmo editor says: "I’ve never really cared about setting sprays. I’m not a huge makeup wearer, and most formulas I’ve tried feel like I’m spritzing hairspray directly onto my face. But Saie founder Laney Crowell promised me her brand’s new setting spray would be different—and she wasn’t kidding. CitySet feels more like a hydrating face mist you’d use in your skincare routine, yet somehow keeps my skin tint and blush looking fresh well into the afternoon." —LB

Why we love it: Beyoncé used this viral formula during the Renaissance Tour to lock in her makeup for a full three-hour sesh of performing. And ya know what? After testing it myself, I genuinely believe I also could perform for three hours on a hot stage in the middle of summer and look like Queen Bey, as long as I had this setting spray on. Because the longevity with this sucker is real.

One Cosmo editor says: "One/Size's formula comes in an aerosol can with an ultra-fine mister that basically feels like I'm spritzing myself with hairspray. And honestly, maybe I am! Because this makes my makeup last longer than any other setting spray on this list. It really nixes shine, thanks to a slew of oil-absorbing polymers in the formula. It makes my makeup completely sweat and waterproof."—BG

If you have sensitive skin and are on the hunt for a setting spray that won’t only keep your makeup in place for hours on end, but will also nourish your skin sans any aggravating ingredients, then Danessa Myricks is our top pick. It’s got niacinamide to soothe, hyaluronic acid to hydrate, and it’s free of pore-cloggers, so you won’t have to worry about breaking out while adding a blurring finish to your glam.

One Cosmo editor says: “This setting spray is sorcery in a bottle. One spritz and my skin becomes velvety perfection. It locks in my makeup, blurs like an IG filter, and somehow still feels weightless. I’m talking all day wear with zero touch-ups.”—JULEE WILSON, BEAUTY EDITOR-AT-LARGE

Why we love it: If you want your face to look like you just came up for some air after gallivanting around the sea like a mermaid, shake this bottle up and spray it all over yourself. Don't worry, it's not filled with chunky glitters. Sure, there are some teeny-tiny shimmers in there, but overall, it offers the most stunning radiant sheen all over my skin (see the pic above of me in Aruba, living my glowiest life). Surprisingly, with all that shine, it actually does extend my makeup a bit too.

One Cosmo editor says: "Iconic London knows a thing or two about making me look glowy as all hell (ahem, their highlighters are my fave), and this setting spray fits the bill. This spray leaves my face illuminated, but still locks down and lasts for a few extra hours than when I don't use any setting spray at all."—BG

Why we love it: I know it's a lil on the nose, but this setting spray really does create the illusion that my makeup was airbrushed onto my face like a painting. A couple of sprays as the last step of my makeup routine, and it helps blur my pores and make my skin look smoother. And it lives up to those 16-hour longevity claims, FYI. I've tested this in hella conditions, including the heat, humidity, and rain, but my makeup stood up to the challenge.

One Cosmo editor says: "This setting spray is my go-to when I want my makeup to look extra dewy. When I spritz this on, everything somehow looks smoother—like you can't tell where my blush stops and my concealer starts. Plus it's super hydrating and doesn't create any patchiness on my dry skin."—JH

If you want makeup that won't budge, choose a setting spray with waterproof or sweatproof formulas. These will help seriously lock down your makeup, often using a mix of oil and sweat-absorbing ingredients. (Dw, we noted the best ones for this above.) But if you would prefer a simpler formula that just gently sets down your makeup and removes any powdery excess from your skin, then focus instead on setting sprays that feature skincare ingredients as well. Which brings us to...

Do you want a matte finish or a glowy finish? That's prob gonna be your most important Q when it comes to setting spray, as most formulas will slightly change the look of your makeup (or enhance whatever you have on). A glowy setting spray will likely be filled with oils and hydrators, making it a great pick for dry skin. Meanwhile, matte formulas are great for keeping shine at bay without having to add layers of powder throughout the day. But if you're not sure, opt for a natural-finish setting spray that'll seal your makeup without changing the look too much.

To test the best setting sprays on the market, we coated our faces in our go-to base routine (foundation, concealer, bronzer, blush, and powder), then doused ourselves in each of the sprays on this list. We tested these mists for months at a time, drawing from years of experience testing setting sprays—to narrow it down to our top picks. We judged each one based on how long it locked in our makeup, how it made our skin look, and how the bottle and mister performed.

Beth Gillette is the beauty editor at Cosmopolitan with six years of experience researching, writing, and editing makeup stories that range from testing drugstore mascaras to reviewing the viral Il Makiage foundation. She's an authority in all makeup categories, but is an expert when it comes to setting sprays after trialing every buzzy formula on her skin over a few months. She regularly tests and analyzes makeup for efficacy, while working with the industry’s top makeup artists to assess new formulas and brands.

Jasmine Hyman is the assistant beauty editor at Cosmopolitan, where she writes about all things makeup and skincare. She's tested dozens of setting sprays in the name of beauty journalism and for personal reasons to see which last the best for long days.

Beth Gillette is the beauty editor at Cosmopolitan, where she covers skincare, makeup, hair, nails, and more across digital and print. She can generally be found in bright eyeshadow furiously typing her latest feature or hemming and hawing about a new product you "have to try." Prior to Cosmopolitan, she wrote and edited beauty content as an Editor at The Everygirl for four years. Follow her on Instagram for makeup selfies and a new hair 'do every few months.

Jasmine Hyman is the Assistant Beauty Editor at Cosmopolitan, where she writes about the latest beauty trends and must-have products. #275. “It’s a Mindset”: Rosie Huntington-Whiteley on Returning to Victoria’s Secret 16 Years Later

Twenty years ago, a 19-year-old Devon native named Rosie Huntington-Whiteley made her Victoria’s Secret runway debut in a polka-dot bra and briefs, carrying a stuffed polka-dot dog, with a polka-dot duvet trailing behind her. This cutesy girl-next-door look helped to catapult Huntington-Whiteley from Teen Vogue favourite to Burberry face, bona fide lingerie designer, beauty entrepreneur and blockbuster movie star. Now, after hanging up her Angel wings in 2010 to focus on building her own Rose Inc empire, she’s back in the Victoria’s Secret fold.

Rosie Huntington-Whiteley’s Victoria’s Secret debut in 2010.

“Delighted” is how Huntington-Whiteley feels now, returning to the runway a decade and a half later. In the back of a cab en route to her fitting in LA, she can’t delve into the details of the feathered, rhinestone-studded tulle extravaganza she might wear as the final look will be a collaboration between the model mogul and executive creative director Adam Selman, who cut his teeth in the underwear business at Rihanna’s Savage X Fenty. What has long been fixed is Huntington-Whiteley’s fitness regime. “It’s really about consistency because I’m a gym girl—I’m always training and taking care of myself,” the model says, who credits strength training (it gets competitive in her home gym with husband Jason Statham) as the backbone of her workout routine. “I’m about to turn 40 next year; I look at my body, and I have so much appreciation for having had two children. For me, it’s really about feeling strong and fit, as opposed to thinking about a number on the scales or on a measuring tape. Competence builds confidence.”

With Izabel Goulart, Selita Ebanks and Miranda Kerr in Times Square in 2009.

There are a few short-term wellness hacks before stripping down on one of the biggest model platforms in the world. Rest, hydration, protein (“Nothing is off the table for me ever with my diet”), lymphatic drainage (via Rebecca Faria), facials (she’s been seeing Shani Darden for 15 years), and cold plunge therapy (the Alo Yoga gym is round the corner from her hotel) all play into Huntington-Whiteley’s belief that “it’s a mindset more than anything”. She knows she’s “put in the best effort”, and after that, it’s up to hair and make-up veterans Guido and Pat McGrath to work their magic.

With Miranda Kerr, Candice Swanepoel and Doutzen Kroes at a Victoria’s Secret “Secrets of a Supermodel” shopping event in 2010.

The electric vibe backstage helps. Despite the brand’s patchy reputation, I’ve never heard a Victoria’s Secret model speak ill of what Huntington-Whiteley describes as “the ultimate iconic American brand.” Rosie is no different: “It’s a show that continues to celebrate everything people have always loved about Victoria’s Secret while embracing a modern perspective on beauty, confidence and individuality—I’m so happy to be here in this new era.” She’s particularly excited to reunite with another returning super (guesses on a postcard!), alongside BFF Candice Swanepoel and industry pals Alex Consani, Paloma Elsesser and Anok Yai.

Her 2010 finale at New York’s Lexington Armory.

It’s this sisterhood that keeps the industry’s most recognizable faces signing on the dotted line (aside from the check.) Prior to flying out to Hollywood, Rosie scrolled all the way back to ’06 on her iPhone, unearthing pictures of “baby-faced, bright-eyed girls with glitter flying everywhere.” Snaps of Rosie and Miranda Kerr, who she was partnered with as a fellow “newbie”, in promo mode on the Hollywood Walk of Fame sit next to selfies with VS veteran Adriana Lima as the “girl from Devon, who’d left school at 17 on the hope of making it big”, got to grips with her new reality in the spotlight.

“It’s a full-circle moment,” reflects Huntington-Whiteley. “My children will wake up on Monday morning and watch it over breakfast with dad—things just feel all the more special now.”

#276. Charlize Theron Made a Rare Red Carpet Appearance With Her Daughters at the Academy Museum Gala

Charlize Theron had her children by her side for a special night out at the 2026 Academy Museum Gala.

The Oscar-winning actress received the Icon Award, which honors artists whose careers have had a significant global impact, while raising funds for the museum’s exhibitions, educational initiatives, and public programming. Sigourney Weaver presented Theron with the honor.

For the gala, Theron wore a striking custom black Tom Ford gown that featured intricate embellishments, sheer panels, and a floor-length skirt with a train for an added flair. She accessorized with statement Boucheron jewelry and styled her bob with sleek, side-swept microbangs, giving the look a modern edge.

Theron posed for photographers on the red carpet solo when she arrived, but was accompanied by Jackson, 14, and August, 12, throughout the evening. Both girls wore black ensembles for the occasion, coordinating with their mother’s glamorous look.

“I’m always a little bit like ‘is it a dream, is it real?’” she said in an interview with The Academy on the carpet, reflecting on her career and the moment at hand. “It’s really lovely.”

Theron has spoken openly for years about adopting and becoming a mother. On National Daughter’s Day in 2020, she wrote: “My heart belongs to these two beautiful powerhouses. I will never be the same.”

In her ELLE summer 2026 cover story, she spoke more about her daughters. “They both have really big, good hearts,” she shared. “It’s not necessarily through my work, but I can tell that they’re thinking outside of their own bubble, and that to me feels good as a mom.”

They also keep her in line, she added: “When I get too big for my britches, they surely let me know that I’m supposed to make lunch for them at 6:00 A.M.”

She shared the advice she gives them as they navigate adolescence: “I tell them, ‘Just you be you.’ It’s so much harder for girls these days, I think, than when I was a teenager. When they get lost in it, I remind them they’re such powerhouses. They just need to remember that. Stay there. That’s probably the daily thing I remind them of—and to unload the dishwasher.”

#278. Sun-Dried Tomato Chicken Salad

A deli classic gets a Mediterranean-inspired makeover with this easy make-ahead recipe for sun-dried tomato chicken salad.

This sun-dried tomato chicken salad is the kind of lunch that gives you something to look forward to when noon rolls around. Taste of Home reader Lorilyn Tenney of Boise, Idaho, puts a flavorful Mediterranean spin on classic creamy chicken salad by tucking in tangy sun-dried tomatoes, nutty Asiago and crunchy pine nuts. It’s high in protein and easy to make ahead, so you can prep a batch on Sunday and tuck it into sandwiches, wraps or salads throughout the week.

In a large bowl, combine the shredded chicken, sun-dried tomatoes, mayonnaise, shallot, shredded Asiago, toasted pine nuts, salt and pepper. Stir until everything is evenly coated and combined. Taste and adjust the seasoning as needed.

Layer fresh spinach leaves onto toasted slices of sourdough bread and spoon the chicken salad over top. Top it with another slice of bread, then serve the sandwiches right away.

Store the chicken salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to four days. Keep it chilled until you’re ready to serve it, then assemble the sandwiches fresh for the best texture.

Absolutely! Sun-dried tomato chicken salad is a great make-ahead lunch. Simply mix the chicken salad at the start of the week or one or two days before serving, then transfer it to an airtight container and refrigerate it until you’re ready to make sandwiches.

There’s no single right way to cook chicken for chicken salad, but poaching, baking or grilling are all great options. Poaching keeps chicken especially tender, while baked and grilled chicken breasts are easy options when you’re already cooking chicken for another meal.

Absolutely! A store-bought rotisserie chicken is an easy shortcut when you’re making chicken salad. Let it cool after bringing it home, then remove the skin and shred the meat before mixing it with the other ingredients. You can use a combination of white and dark meat, or stick with breast meat if you prefer a leaner chicken salad.

This sun-dried tomato chicken salad makes a great sandwich, but don’t stop there. Add a scoop to a green salad, spoon it onto your favorite crackers, or wrap it in a tortilla with fresh spinach. For a hot lunch, turn it into a panini or a toasted Marry Me chicken salad sandwich by layering the chicken salad with fresh basil leaves and cheese, then pressing the sandwich until the bread is golden and the cheese is melty.

#279. The 41 Best Horror Books of 2026

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

A deadly weight loss treatment, a job with a potentially evil corporation, and the late-in-life lure of potential immortality. All premises that feel horrific to us—and that we've already got on our TBR lists for this year.

WE’RE NOW DEEP into the year, and Halloween horror season has arrived. The weather is starting to get crisper, the leaves are turning brown and orange, and there are pumpkins on stoops and windowsills everywhere you look. And there's a slew of new books to read—and even more still coming before the end of the year.

While you're waiting for your flight at the airport or sitting on the beach with a cold drink by your side, why not have an exciting new release in your hands? Last year gave us a lot of good horror to read, like Stephen Graham Jones' Buffalo Hunter Hunter and King Sorrow by Joe Hill. Your TBR is probably piled high with whatever you didn't get to in 2025. But a new year gives you the perfect excuse to put those aside for a moment and turn your attention to what's coming out next.

There's a lot to look forward to. Of what we know about so far, there's a gory book about keeping a marriage afloat, another about a deadly weight loss treatment, and one on voyeurism and revenge. And even if none of those ideas piqued your interest, there's an extensive list below for anyone looking for a book to preorder or even gifts for the next holiday season. And check back throughout the year, as we'll update it as new books are announced. No matter what comes your way this year, at least you know you'll have thrilling horror books to look forward to.

The author behind The Sun Down Motel is back with a new horror novel about siblings forced to return home decades after their brother’s death. His ghost is calling to them, and they’ll have to face their past and the haunted town they grew up in.

This gothic read explores the lives of a mysterious wealthy family known as the Gilberts, whose English manor is now in the hands of a hotelier who plans to renovate. As the house undergoes its transformation, the dark secrets of the family come to light. Reviews liken the book to Shirley Jackson's We've Always Lived in this Castle, and The Addams Family, so expect a fun, haunting read.

Judith fled her childhood home, and thought she'd finally found peace in a home in the woods of Southern Georgia. But a woman arrives at her doorstep, and reignites both desire and an innate urge for violence within Judith. Try as she might to avoid it, Judith is forced to face her ancestry and all its ills.

Set during the Great Famine in Ireland, this novel follows a young woman named Maggie who is saved by a wealthy woman who houses her in her old mansion. The catch? Maggie must impersonate the woman's late daughter to help her gain access to her daughter's widow pension. But as Maggie takes on the persona, she begins to hear mention of curses from the townspeople, and living in the house seems to be digging up difficult memories within her.

Sometimes you want a lighter horror-comedy to break up the darker reads. This novel follows Ivan, a man who has the ability to see people's imaginary friends. He offers a unique service: He'll kill the imaginary friends of adults who have trouble letting go. He would never kill a child's imaginary friend, though. Until he meets eight-year-old Kay and her friend Eddie, who she insists has to go. But Eddie is a tough friend to kill, and it'll take more than the usual ways to get rid of him.

A nurse at a mental health hospital has her own sanity tested when she returns to her hometown for a funeral. Her grandfather years ago deforested the woods and lost a number of lumberjacks in the process. With her grandfather long dead, it's Jasmine the woods are now after, seeking a chance at revenge for her family's crimes.

A gambling addict takes a job as a private chef in a last ditch effort to save himself and his family. But it turns out his wealthy client has a unique appetite. And while the salary is high, it may not be worth the screams he can hear in the distance, or the strange tasks his benefactor bestows upon him.

An A-list actress loses her child in a kidnapping. It morphs her public image into that of a bad mother. A decade later, she works to reinvent herself with the launch of a skincare company with a secret ingredient she discovers after a blogger's death. It kicks off a vengeful-killing spree. But her quest for revenge is threatened when she discovers the truth behind her daughter's disappearance.

A woman fears her marriage, and her life, are under threat in this exciting new read. Years after leaving her family church, Mavis still feels she’s not good enough for her husband. But as she suffers from increasingly bizarre attacks, she finds herself questioning her relationship and herself.

2025’s TheBuffalo Hunter Hunter was a hit. Now Stephen Graham Jones is back with a teen slasher. When a group of kids play a prank—bringing a mannequin to the movie theater—they think it’s all in good fun... until the doll comes to life and starts killing them all one by one.

Claire returns home to care for her dying father and discovers the house is…listening. As the otherworldly danger threatens to come up from the floorboards, she finds an unlikely aid in a woman alive centuries before her.

A nonfiction read for die-hard horror fans, Partially Devoured is Whalefall author Daniel Kraus's love letter to Night of the Living Dead. If you're into frame-by-frame analysis, and want to geek out over one of the best zombie films of all time, this is the book for you.

Space is a classic locale for a horror tale, and Crawlspace is the newest book to feature the cold, dark, and isolating setting. Spacefarers on a mission to expand humanity’s access to the universe find themselves trapped in a ship filled with dangerous mysteries.

In the late 19th century, a scientific illustrator takes a job from a reclusive scientist and moves into his mansion. But once there, she discovers her employer is engaging in awful experiments, and if she can’t escape she’ll be his next test subject.

A experimental weight loss drug helps retail worker Emmett slim down fast, and he notices immediately that his social life improves. One hiccup, though, is the drug’s propensity to cause users to lose stretches of time and gain an immense appetite. When Emmett hears rumblings of a cannibalistic killer on the loose, he worries he might be involved.

What’s worse than being stranded in the woods? Being stranded and hunted by a supernatural threat. While on a camping trip, a group hears a scream, setting off a horrifying journey that puts their lives and their relationships at risk.

In this book, a desperate woman takes a three day job from Craigslist. While a solo trip a house in the Oregon wilderness seems appealing at first, she quickly realizes something evil is lurking, and she’ll have to fight to survive.

A woman’s life is forever changed when she’s the victim of a hidden camera scandal. Her family and boyfriend abandon her, and she begins to see visions of her dead sister. The only way to right what’s gone wrong is to figure out the truth behind the voyeuristic nightmare.

Joe works for The Company and he can't tell anyone what he does there. That's because it's a government facility where they experiment on humans, torturously allowing people to 'intercept' the senses of anyone in the world. It helps catch bad guys, so Joe is willing to overlook the brutal nature of the work. Until one day, when his ex-wife kills herself, and he learns one of the inmates was haunting her. And now, that inmate is haunting his daughter too.

With an introduction from Stephen King, there's not much more to say about why you should pick up this short story collection. But in case you're still on the fence, Nat Cassidy's new book is filled with intriguing horror premises, like a tech millionaire's haunted house, or a yoga retreat in the calming expanse of the desert…made eerie by inexplicable screams.

#281. The 25 Sexiest Horror Movies of All Time

Featuring Obsession, Interview with the Vampire, and other sensual scares to watch this spooky season.

One of my favorite vampire tropes is that they need your permission to enter your house. They must be invited in, technically, before they seduce you. Is it all a trick? Totally. Dracula turns playful neck kisses into feasting on your blood, but sexy vampire fan fiction didn’t rule the Internet during Twilight’s reign.

Sexy situations turning into horrifically violent nightmares are still all the rage in films nowadays. Curry Barker’s indie hit Obsession plays on the crazy-girlfriend trope. Bodies Bodies Bodies filled a house with horny teens that ended up murdering each other, and The Substance contained just as many shots of gyrating asses as it did some of the most horrific body horror onscreen in the past decade.

But if you’re looking for the sexiest horror movies in film history, you’ve been invited to the right place. Below, we also list Brad Pitt and Tom Cruise’s Interview with the Vampire, Megan Fox’s Jennifer’s Body, and thrillers like Darren Aronofsky’s Black Swan. These are the sexiest horror movies of all time.

After Bear (Michael Johnson) wishes on a magical item that his coworker Nikki (Inde Navarrette) would fall in love with him, the girl of his dreams is taken over by a scary new persona that thinks only about their relationship. Navarrette is a breakout performer in Obsession’s reversal of the crazy-girlfriend horror trope, as the girl next door becomes a victim of Bear’s terrible curse.

Under the Skin polarized audiences when it debuted in 2013. In this bizarre Jonathan Glazer film, Scarlett Johansson plays an alien who strips, bathes in a void, and seduces men to kill before presumably consuming them for food. Since its debut, Under the Skin has garnered a cult following.

Are we too desensitized by sex and violence on TV? Probably! But in David Cronenberg’s Videodrome, the Canadian sci-fi body-horror flick explores a world in which snuff films are broadcast to an audience live on air. The 1983 cult classic stars James Woods, Debbie Harry, and Jack Creley as a character with one of the best names in cinema history: Dr. Brian O’Blivion.

Timothée Chalamet reunites with Call Me by Your Name director Luca Guadagnino for this horror romance about two cannibals on a road trip across America. The film also stars Taylor Russell, André Holland, Michael Stuhlbarg, and Chloë Sevigny. Fair warning: Bones and All may not be easy on the stomach. But its stars are certainly easy on the eyes, and the chemistry between them can’t be missed.

In X, a group of fame-hungry actors—including characters played by Mia Goth, Jenna Ortega, and Kid Cudi—decide to make a low-budget adult film. Naturally, they opt for the spookiest location possible: a secluded farmhouse in rural Texas. What could go wrong?

This is your classic teens-in-the-woods horror flick—but with a twist. Bodies Bodies Bodies follows a group of friends (and exes) who reunite at a remote cabin, starring Amandla Stenberg, Pete Davidson, Rachel Sennott, and Industry’s Myha’la. It’s all fun and games until one of them winds up dead.

Everyone understands stranger danger until they meet someone hot. Perhaps that's the takeaway lesson of Stranger by the Lake. This sultry thriller follows Franck (Pierre Deladonchamps), a man who meets (you guessed it!) a stranger by the lake. He’s instantly captivated, but his curiosity leads him down a dark path.

In this early-1980s film, a cheating husband rents a room in a Hollywood Hills mansion from a pair of (unbeknownst to him) serial-killing siblings. He needs a place for his newfound sexual trysts, which opens up an opportunity for his new landlords’ killing spree as well.

This David Lynch–directed thriller, starring Laura Harring as an amnesiac car-crash victim who receives the serendipitous aid of a struggling actress (Naomi Watts), is as haunting as it is intoxicating. The chemistry between the two is palpable as they struggle to uncover the victim’s true identity in this Lynchian version of Los Angeles.

Mila Kunis and Natalie Portman star as rival ballerinas in this brilliant psychological thriller revolving around a production of Tchaikovsky’s Swan Lake. But the tensions run deeper than mere rivalry, or even surface-level attraction, when Portman’s Nina develops a psychosexual obsession with Kunis’s Lily that leads to hallucinatory fantasies.

This South Korean horror romance, directed by the acclaimed Park Chan-wook, is Twilight meets Fleabag meets … something else. Parasite’s Song Kang-ho stars as a devout priest turned sex-thirsty vampire after he comes in contact with a deadly virus. (Yikes.) Then his newfound instincts lead him to a lust-filled affair with a married woman.

Julie Christie and Donald Sutherland star as a married couple who, mourning the recent death of their child, flee to Venice. During their attempt to find respite from grief, the trip turns haunting when they encounter two sisters who claim to have communicated with their child’s spirit. Throughout this grueling journey, the couple try to maintain their connection amid desperate moments of fiery passion.

Delphine Seyrig stars as an ageless countess who inhabits a French hotel along with her young protégée, played by Andrea Rau. The mystery of the two beautiful women unravels when unsuspecting newlyweds find themselves tangled in their web of seduction. This vintage vampire flick is as sultry in its artful, gothic aesthetics as it is in its acts of demented desire.

Catherine Deneuve plays a seductive immortal in early-’80s New York City—a woman as stylish as she is beautiful. When her companion (David Bowie) begins to fade, she sets her sights on a new lover: a doctor played by Susan Sarandon.

Neil Jordan’s adaptation of Anne Rice’s novel is super ’90s, with heartthrobs Tom Cruise, Brad Pitt, and Antonio Banderas playing brooding immortals dealing with the neuroses that come with everlasting life (and a desire for human blood). It’s probably one of the most homoerotic movies ever made, and it introduced the world to Kirsten Dunst, who plays a maniacal child vampire.

Nastassja Kinski stars as Irena, a young woman who is visiting her brother Paul (Malcolm McDowell) in New Orleans. After she falls in love with a zoologist named Oliver (John Heard), Paul reveals to his sister that they are secretly werecats. In this remake of the original 1942 thriller, Irena must mate with another of their species to prevent her ultimate transformation. So begins a deadly game of cat and human as Irena and Oliver need to outsmart Paul—and stop Irena from evolving into a deadly leopard.

Most people remember John Landis’s horror comedy for the fantastic special and makeup effects. A terrifying scene in which the hapless protagonist turns into a werewolf, not to mention the undead Griffin Dunne roaming around with half a face, has kept the cult film alive for the past 40 years. But An American Werewolf in London is also notable for a particular hot shower scene between its stars, David Naughton and Jenny Agutter.

The famed Godfather director’s adaptation of the seminal vampire novel occasionally teeters off the edge into vampire mania, but it’s still a lush, star-studded, deeply erotic version of the classic horror tale. Gary Oldman delivers a tour-de-force performance as the bloodsucking villain in a film that costars Winona Ryder, Anthony Hopkins, Keanu Reeves, Richard E. Grant, Cary Elwes, Tom Waits, and Monica Bellucci.

Megan Fox stars in this pitch-black comedy, from director Karyn Kusama and writer Diablo Cody, as the ultimate mean girl. Jennifer has always been the queen bee in her class—and has spent years tormenting her “best” friend Anita (Amanda Seyfried). But is she just a mean girl, or could she possibly be under the influence of a demonic spirit who uses her body to feast on horny teenage boys?

Have you ever wanted to feel young again? In Coralie Fargeat’s award-winning body-horror thriller, fading Hollywood star Elisabeth Sparkle (Demi Moore) takes an experimental drug that promises to create a younger, sexier version of yourself. Really the other self emerges from your body and sucks your life force, turning this fountain of youth into an absolute nightmare.

Robert Rodriguez directs this cult classic starring George Clooney and Quentin Tarantino (who wrote the script) as the bank-robbing Gecko brothers. When they cross the border into Mexico with hostages in tow, the brothers arrive at the Titty Twister, a strip club in the middle of the desert. Then their hope for refuge is lost after the bar’s patrons and employees reveal themselves as vampires led by a ferocious queen, Santanico Pandemonium (Salma Hayek).

In a picturesque Rhode Island town, three bored women (played by Cher, Susan Sarandon, and Michelle Pfeiffer) discover they have some impressive powers when they accidentally conjure up a seductive—and devious—suitor (played by Jack Nicholson). While he may fulfill some of the women’s desires, he’s also set on destroying their perfect little town.

Guillermo del Toro’s Oscar-winning fantasy-horror-romance hybrid is essentially a cold-war-era fairy tale for grown-ups. Sally Hawkins stars as a lonely mute woman named Elisa who spends her days mopping the floors of a top-secret government facility. Her life is turned upside down when she discovers an amphibious creature, kept hostage by a sadistic colonel (Michael Shannon). What begins as an unlikely friendship turns, surprisingly, into a sexy romp between a woman and a fishman.

While Luca Guadagnino’s remake may have disturbed audiences, you can’t ignore horror master Dario Argento’s bloody, stylish original from 1977. Jessica Harper stars as Suzy, a promising ballerina who moves to Germany to attend a prestigious dance academy. But when other ballerinas start dropping dead in gruesome ways, Suzy begins to unravel a mystery behind the school’s spooky owners.

Taking some thematic notes from Suspiria, Nicolas Winding Refn’s psychological thriller stars Elle Fanning as an aspiring model who moves to Los Angeles to pursue her dreams. Her trip quickly becomes nightmarish when the cutthroat world of fashion reveals a sinister (albeit sexy) underbelly of corruption and destruction.

#282. 3 Excellent Hot Chocolate Mixes, According to Our Taste Test

A good instant hot chocolate mix should deliver everything you want from homemade hot chocolate—deep chocolate flavor, creamy consistency—but, you know, instantly. No chopping chocolate or careful melting required. Just add hot water or milk, stir, and sip. But cocoa mixes vary wildly: Some are milky and sweet; others dark and verging on bitter; and some are closer to thick, velvety drinking chocolate than the stuff you guzzled at that budget ski lodge when you were 10.

To find the best hot chocolate mixes, we sampled 15 supermarket and specialty varieties, including Swiss Miss, Starbucks, Ghirardelli, Guittard, Dandelion Chocolate, Jacques Torres, and Valrhona. We prepared each according to its package directions and judged it on chocolate flavor, sweetness, and texture. Our favorites cover three distinct cravings: Starbucks Classic for quintessential hot cocoa, Guittard for a richer, more luxurious sip, and Dandelion Chocolate’s house mix for complex, splurge-worthy chocolate flavor.

Starbucks Classic Hot Cocoa scratched the nostalgia center of our collective brains, tasting like the hot chocolate we remember drinking at ice rinks or after a snow day spent sledding.

Why it won us over: Tasters immediately recognized this as “classic cocoa,” as senior cooking editor Kelsey Jane Youngman put it. Starbucks’ instant hot chocolate mix delivered satisfying milk-chocolate flavor and silky texture, even when prepared with water—though we recommend using milk or your favorite non-dairy alternative for an even creamier cup. It wasn’t the most complex cocoa we tasted, but its balanced sweetness and familiar chocolate profile made it an easy favorite.

Starbucks Classic Hot Cocoa, 30-oz. canister

Richer and more chocolate-forward than Starbucks’ offering, Guittard’s Grand Cacao Drinking Chocolate is the hot cocoa mix to reach for when you want something a little more indulgent.

Why it won us over: Guittard makes some of our favorite chocolate chips and the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen’s go-to cocoa powder, so we had high hopes for its hot cocoa. It delivered deep chocolate flavor and flawlessly smooth texture. While some premium contenders skewed too bitter, Guittard struck an ideal bittersweet balance with “just enough sweetness to get away with it,” according to food director Chris Morocco.

Guittard & Co. Grand Cacao Drinking Chocolate, 10-oz. canister

Made with single-origin chocolate, Dandelion Chocolate’s House Hot Chocolate Mix produced something closer to drinking chocolate than the hot cocoa packets we grew up with. It was fruity, intensely chocolaty, and slightly bitter, with a thick, velvety consistency.

Why it won us over: Dandelion stood apart from the first sip. While most hot chocolate mixes leaned sweet and milky, this one, as Kelsey put it, tasted like a “melted bar of dark chocolate.” Tasters picked up notes of red berries buried in the deep chocolate flavor—a reminder, per senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewczyk, that cacao is indeed a fruit. Restrained sweetness allowed the intriguingly complex flavors to shine, ultimately luring tasters back for a second (and third, and fourth) sip.

At more than $2 an ounce, this isn’t the hot chocolate we’d reach for when a dozen kids come in from sledding. It’s the one to savor on a cold evening when you’re in the mood for something closer to dessert than an everyday cup of cocoa.

Dandelion House Hot Chocolate Mix, 5.6-oz reusable glass bottle

Dandelion Chocolate House Hot Chocolate Mix, 17.6-oz. bag

We prepared each mix according to its package instructions, using hot water or milk as directed, then portioned the hot chocolate into individual tasting cups and served it warm. Tasters sampled the mixes without knowing which brands they were drinking and evaluated each for flavor and texture.

It sounds silly to say hot chocolate should taste chocolaty, but not all contenders met this basic criterion. We wanted rich cocoa flavor with enough sweetness to balance its natural bitterness, but not so much that sugar overwhelmed the cup.

Texture mattered too. Our favorites were creamy and silky, without the chalkiness, grittiness, or powderiness that knocked other contenders down the rankings.

#285. The Beatles Biopics: Everything We Know

Sam Mendes is directing four films—starring four buzzy heartthrobs—to follow the iconic band’s story.

Director Sam Mendes (who has helmed 1917, Spectre, Revolutionary Road, and more) is creating four films about the legendary British group, in association with Sony Pictures Entertainment and Mendes’s Neal Street Productions. After Deadline first broke the news in February 2024, Ringo Starr tweeted that the films were fully supported by himself and the families of Paul McCartney, John Lennon, and George Harrison.

This is the first time Apple Corps Ltd. and The Beatles have granted a scripted film expansive life story and music rights, making this a major feat. Here’s what we know about the movies, officially titled The Beatles – A Four-Film Cinematic Event, so far.

After much speculation, Sony Pictures confirmed the lead cast of the biopics during CinemaCon 2025: Harris Dickinson as John Lennon, Paul Mescal as Paul McCartney, Barry Keoghan as Ringo Starr, and Joseph Quinn as George Harrison.

The group rang in the news onstage at the Las Vegas event on March 31, 2025.

The official announcement came after months of rumors and reports of the possible cast for this highly anticipated project.

In an interview with Entertainment Tonight, Ringo Starr seemed to confirm that Keoghan had been cast as his youthful doppelgänger. When asked about the actor possibly being a match, Starr replied, “Well, I think he’s great, and I believe he’s somewhere taking drum lessons.” He added that he hopes Keoghan doesn’t take “too many lessons” so he could find his personal groove.

According to The Hollywood Reporter, director Ridley Scott reportedly hinted that Paul Mescal was cast for the role of Paul McCartney during a Directors Guild of America event on Dec. 10, 2024. While also addressing Mescal’s potential involvement in his upcoming project The Dog Stars, Scott noted, “Yes. Well, maybe. Paul is actually stacked up, doing the Beatles next. So I may have to let him go,” suggesting Mescal’s role in the biopic series.

Mescal even addressed the speculation in an interview with Entertainment Tonight, calling the possible opportunity “a dream come true,” but did not confirm any involvement at the time.

In December 2024, Deadline reported that Stranger Things’ Joseph Quinn was likely signed on to play George Harrison, adding that he was seen carrying a guitar on set while filming the new Fantastic Four film.

According to Deadline, Saoirse Ronan will play Linda McCartney, Paul McCartney’s first wife and the mother of their daughter, designer Stella McCartney. Linda was a renowned photographer and musician who sadly passed away from breast cancer in 1998.

The cast also includes Anna Sawai, Aimee Lou Wood, and Mia McKenna-Bruce, per The Hollywood Reporter.

Sawai is set to play Yoko Ono, an artist and musician who married John Lennon and welcomed their son Sean Lennon in 1975. They remained married until John’s death in 1980.

Wood will play Pattie Boyd. Boyd was one of the biggest models of the era and was married to George Harrison. They divorced and she eventually married musician Eric Clapton.

McKenna-Bruce will portray Maureen Cox, Ringo Starr’s wife who also worked as a hairdresser.

“Maureen, Linda, Yoko, and Pattie are four fascinating and unique figures in their own right—and I’m thrilled that we’ve managed to persuade four of the most talented women working in film today to join this amazing adventure,” director Mendes said in a statement.

In December 2025, more casting news was announced. The roles are as follows:

In February 2026, another set of cast members were announced:

Sony confirmed all four films (one from each band member’s perspective) will open in theaters in April 2028. Mendes described the tandem releases as a unique “bingeable moment in cinema,” according to Deadline.

He added that it would take more than a year to shoot all four films. Production List previously reported that filming in London is scheduled for July 2025, but Sony has yet to confirm.

It’s still unclear in which order the films will be released.

Sony’s official logline teases: “Each man has his own story, but together they are legendary.”

Mendes hasn’t been too specific about the plot—the details of the band’s life and history together is pretty well-covered in myriad movies and documentaries anyway, so it is really a matter of style over substance. The Oscar-winning director previously indicated that the films will be interwoven and include one band member’s point of view per movie.

The director explained at CinemaCon, “I had been trying to do a film for years, but I finally gave up,” feeling that the “story was too big for one film.” He also didn’t think a TV series was the right fit. “There had to be a way to tell the epic story for a new generation … I can assure you there is still plenty left to explore and I think we found a way to do that,” he said, per Deadline.

Mendes is directing all four films and producing with Pippa Harris, Julie Pastor, and Alexandra Derbyshire.

In an interview with The New York Times, Ringo Starr explained he met with director Sam Mendes in London to discuss his issues with the script. The Beatles drummer mainly had a problem with how his first marriage to Maureen Starkey Tigrett was depicted.

“He had a writer—very good writer, great reputation, and he wrote it great, but it had nothing to do with Maureen and I,” Starr explained. “That’s not how we were. I’d say, ‘We would never do that.’”

Starr was happy with the changes made, but expressed he’s concerned about Mendes trying to film all four movies at the same time.

“But he’ll do what he’s doing, and I’ll send him peace and love,” he added.

In conversation with Amy Poehler for her podcast, Paul McCartney spoke on the biopics for the first time, and he had one little bone to pick. When Poehler said “it must be strange to have people play you,” McCartney replied “it is.”“And guess what... He’s smaller than the guy who plays John,” he remarked with an expression of shock and confusion. “Sam Mendes is making the film. I said ‘Sam, I got this one thing that I need to say to you,” they laugh. “You know, Paul [Mescal]’s a bit smaller,’” he said, referring to their remaking of the 1969 album cover. “I don’t know how Sam’s going to deal with it but he sent me a picture, a still from the filming they were doing, and they’re crossing the Abbey Road crossing and the Paul character is markedly smaller.”“We were all the same height and you know I’ve got a thing about that,” he told Poehler. “We were all the same height and Ringo was a bit smaller.”

In January 2026, the first official images from The Beatles – A Four-Film Cinematic Event were released through an on-campus postcard distribution at the Liverpool Institute for Performing Arts.

Rather than debuting the images online, Sony printed four postcard-size stills—each featuring one actor in character—and hid them around the school for students to find.

#286. The Best Antiaging Skin-Care Routine, According to Top Dermatologists and Aestheticians

From PDRN and exosomes to growth factors and ectoin, there’s a rapidly expanding array of antiaging skin-care ingredients that are, to quote Wendy Williams, “the moment.” (Well, until it’s time for the next buzzy ingredient to have its moment.) While the innovation is exciting for clinicians and consumers alike, it can be overwhelming to keep up with the latest best practices for an antiaging skin-care routine—even for someone like me, who writes about skin care every day.

During a recent visit to The Spa at the Belgrove Resort & Spa in West Palm Beach, Florida, aesthetician Patricia Conrad helped me to stop spiraling about whether to add peptides to my morning routine, PDRN to my nighttime routine, or exosomes, well, anytime. Conrad assured me that an antiaging skin-care routine needn’t be complicated so much as sustainable—for one’s schedule and one’s skin. “The best routine is consistent and balanced, protecting the skin in the morning and repairing it at night,” she says.

To start, a good cleanser is key. Then a toner or essence can keep the skin luminous and smooth and allow active ingredients to work harder. And speaking of actives, it’s better to know what your skin needs—and to find the right product to provide it—than to hop on the latest ingredient trend. But you don’t have to do the legwork alone.

To help you design a regimen that addresses the needs of aging skin with products that deliver proven results, we tapped the pros. Ahead, see what dermatologists, aestheticians, and other skin experts recommend for keeping skin smooth, supple, and strong at any age, plus which classic and cutting-edge ingredients they actually recommend.

A good cleanse helps other products be more effective—and can also be cost-effective. “The most important thing to understand about this step is that it’s only designed to do one thing: prep your skin for the actives to follow,” says Peterson Pierre, MD, a board-certified dermatologist at Golden State Dermatology in Thousand Oaks, California. “Don’t put too much effort, energy, or money into this step. A cleanser may have wonderful antiaging ingredients, but they won’t be on your skin long enough to do any good.”

Of course, active ingredients will come into play later on, particularly with serums. But for this initial step, Pierre tells mature patients to find a formula that’s gentle, non-irritating, and—if needed—able to remove makeup. Peter Bittar, MD, a double-board-certified dermatologist and Mohs surgeon at Miami Dermatology and Laser Institute, emphasizes the importance of fragrance-free cleansers. “Fragrances often irritate the skin, which can make it harder to use actives such as retinoids,” he says.

Inspired by the longevity of orchids, Guerlain’s Orchidée Impériale collection draws upon research into Vanda coerulea, a blue orchid that can survive for up to 100 years. The firming, plumping cream is a favorite at Vogue HQ—beauty shopping editor Kiana Murden has been raving about this oil-in-gel. Formulated with Orchid Totum Molecular Extract and 40% skin-care oil, it melts into the skin to dissolve dirt and makeup—even waterproof formulas—before transforming into a milky veil upon contact with water. The result? Luminous skin with refined texture and the softness of an orchid petal.

Bittar recommends CeraVe’s fragrance-free cleanser, which exfoliates and smooths the skin as it washes away dirt, oil, and debris. Thanks to its star ingredient—salicylic acid—the formula also helps clarify pores. “If you are dealing with blackheads or want an exfoliating action, a salicylic acid wash can go a long way,” Bittar says.

After cleansing, a toning step can remove any leftover impurities from the pores and balance the skin’s pH level, while essences—which have a slightly thicker texture—tend to be more hydrating. “For aging skin, toners and essences should be alcohol-free and infused with soothing ingredients like hyaluronic acid or peptides,” says aesthetician Nikki Miller, the director of Kohler Waters Spa in Kohler, Wisconsin. “This helps prep the skin for better absorption of subsequent products.” She adds that the lightweight products can also plump the skin.

“I love this concept, and the product seems to live up to its marketing claims,” says Fiona Rahbar, MD, a board-certified dermatologist at Mara Dermatology in South Carolina. “This moisturizer boasts both ceramides and peptides and lists them first in the ingredients, as opposed to many products that talk about peptides in the marketing but then list them last in the ingredients. Red flag!” The green flags in this formula? Multiple ceramides, which help support the skin barrier, as well as two peptides commonly used in collagen signaling.

“I love this product for someone seeking a fragrance-free, natural, plant-based product for skin hydration and plumping,” Rahbar says. Rayva Khanna, MD, a board-certified dermatologist at Schweiger Dermatology Group in New York and Greenwich, Connecticut, notes that the formula combines traditional Japanese botanical ingredients with modern skin-care science. “Green tea contains polyphenols with antioxidant properties that help protect against oxidative stress, a contributor to premature skin aging. Algae-derived components help retain moisture and temporarily plump the skin, softening the appearance of fine lines. This makes it a particular favorite of mine for mature skin,” she says. “ I also like this product for dry, dehydrated skin because it delivers an additional layer of hydration without feeling heavy.”

With the skin thoroughly prepped, it’s time to get active. “Serums are lightweight and designed to absorb deeply, delivering potent antiaging actives where they’re needed most,” says board-certified dermatologist Deanne Mraz, MD. According to aesthetician Audrey Zmigrodski, the director of Spa and Warm Springs Pools at The Omni Homestead Resort & Spa in Hot Springs, Virginia, the best serums for mature skin contain ingredients that target concerns such as wrinkles, elasticity, and uneven tone. “Look for serums with retinol—or bakuchiol for sensitive skin—peptides, antioxidants, and niacinamide,” she says. “Apply the serum after toning and before moisturizer to maximize absorption.” Below, find the best antiaging serums broken down into the benefits they provide.

For aging skin, dermatologists recommend protecting collagen and warding off free-radical damage with a serum that contains proven antioxidants, including the pure form of vitamin C, L-ascorbic acid. “In general, the ingredient L-ascorbic acid is very well studied,” Khanna notes. “Supporting antioxidants are also important in the formula. The classic pairing we see is vitamin E and ferulic acid.” She also recommends seeking out serums with active ingredients like niacinamide or green tea polyphenols—and paying attention to packaging. Because vitamin C can degrade with exposure to light or air, she suggests looking for opaque or airtight packaging.

Loaded with antioxidants and lauded by dermatologists, SkinCeuticals’s CE ferulic serum is one of Bittar’s top recommendations. “This is the gold standard of vitamin-C serums, especially for mature skin,” he says. “It’s one of the original products to stabilize vitamin C with vitamin E and ferulic acid. It carries a substantial price tag, but it is one of the few skin-care products that I believe is actually worth the splurge.”

La Mer’s newly reformulated concentrate is a barrier-focused serum designed to soothe visible irritation and help aging skin withstand environmental stressors. Its formula features Concentrated Miracle Broth, antioxidant-rich Lime Tea Concentrate, and Clarity Algae to help defend against free radicals and improve discoloration. “The formula is rich in silicones, which form a protective layer over the skin to help maintain hydration,” says Khanna, who also highlights its barrier-supporting lipids, including cholesterol and linoleic acid. She considers it a good option for dry or barrier-compromised skin, though its fragrance and aromatic botanical ingredients may be problematic for highly reactive complexions.

“When considering adding a serum designed for firming, you want to set expectations for what your serum can and cannot do,” says May Hall, DO, a double-board-certified dermatologist in Kentucky. She notes that no firming serum can reverse severe sagging or provide long-term skin tightening. “However, can your topical firming serum boost collagen production and support skin elasticity with ingredients like retinol, peptides, and hyaluronic acid?” she asks. “Absolutely!” With consistent use, Hall says that a good firming serum can improve the appearance of skin through surface plumping.

“This serum contains a Tri-Peptide Complex to support better skin elasticity and collagen production,” Hall says. “It also has ingredients like hyaluronic acid to help lock in the skin’s moisture and vitamin C for an overall brightening effect. At this affordable price point, this is a great addition to an antiaging skin-care regimen.”

“This is an ambitious, multi-ingredient formula,” says Nupur Patel, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in Clearwater, Florida. Designed to lift, tighten, and sculpt the skin, the serum “combines amino acids—the building blocks of proteins—with niacinamide, glutathione, adenosine, peptides, and several moisturizing ingredients,” she explains. “I like the intention of addressing multiple aspects of skin quality rather than focusing only on wrinkles. For someone who wants one comprehensive treatment serum, it is an interesting option.”

You don’t have to keep the same hours as your skin care. In fact, some of the most effective products for aging skin work while you’re asleep. SkinCeuticals’s P-Tiox Serum, for instance, is a bedside staple for many Vogue editors, while retinol is the long-reigning MVP of after-hours skin care. “Retinoids have the greatest body of scientific evidence supporting their effectiveness in promoting collagen synthesis and increasing cellular turnover,” says Brandon Richland, MD, a board-certified plastic surgeon and the founder of Richland Aesthetics in California and Nevada. Richland also suggests using barrier-supportive ingredients like ceramides or ectoin at night. These ingredients help maintain hydration and reduce transepidermal water loss, which can make retinoids easier to tolerate and reduce irritation.

According to Pierre, the key to finding a good retinoid for aging skin is to ensure it doesn’t irritate your skin. Medik8’s Crystal Retinal simplifies that process, offering the product in various strengths suited to sensitive skin and those new to retinal as well as experienced retinoid users.

“This is great for a compromised barrier,” Khanna says. “It’s a fragrance-free formula with ectoin, which helps with barrier support, reducing water loss, and may protect against oxidative stress.” She recommends the serum for rosacea- or eczema-prone patients or for general barrier repair overnight.

“The skin around the eyes is delicate and typically shows the first signs of aging,” says Miller. “Choose eye creams with peptides or caffeine to reduce puffiness, firm the skin, and smooth fine lines.” Hydration is also key, she adds, and the ideal eye cream will have a rich yet non-irritating formula. Miller recommends applying eye cream after serum and before moisturizer, day and night—and going about it gently. “Tap gently with your ring finger to avoid pulling the delicate skin,” Zmigrodski instructs.

Designed specifically for the eye area, Blue Lagoon’s BL+ complex uses an advanced system to deliver collagen-boosting microalgae and silica deep into the skin. Also made with ceramides, bakuchiol, and niacinamide, the cream has a rich, melting texture that makes it a treat to apply.

Designed to brighten, hydrate, and de-puff, Tata Harper’s soothing eye gel is one of my morning must-haves—and it’s also dermatologist approved. “Made with vitamin C and Japanese plum, which is known for its antioxidant and antiglycation properties, this formulation is great for dark circles or tired undereyes,” Hall says. What’s more, “the whipped texture feels soothing and smooth on the thin undereye skin.”

“Moisturization is a crucial step in improving the vibrancy and health of mature skin,” Bittar says. “As we get older, our skin gets drier, which leads to a dull appearance.” He says that the best moisturizers for aging skin not only hydrate but also include active ingredients—such as niacinamide, panthenol, or hyaluronic acid—that tend to be common signs of aging. And in this category, it’s okay to double-dip.

“I often recommend investing in a moisturizer with built-in sunscreen to help simplify your morning regimen and buying one without SPF for evening use,” Bittar says. According to Miller, night creams should focus on repair and regeneration, and the best ones help mimic the effects of a restful night’s sleep.

“This is my favorite face moisturizer,” Bittar says. “I keep a bottle at home, in my bag, and even in my car. It has ceramides and glycerin to hydrate and niacinamide to help soothe and brighten tone. The UV version has a built-in SPF 30 that doesn’t pill up and goes on super smooth.”

A firming favorite among Vogue editors, this SkinCeuticals cream targets deep lines, enlarged pores, and uneven texture. Its formula combines peptides, niacinamide, and exfoliating lipohydroxy acid to help skin look smoother and brighter, while keeping it hydrated for hours. “I absolutely love the P-Tiox Serum, and my skin drinks up the P-Tiox cream,” Hall says. “I love how silky the consistency is, and I know my skin is actively benefiting from the high-potency peptide formulation.” She recommends using the cream on its own or layering it with other actives like retinol.

This last step is crucial. “Sunscreen is the single most important antiaging product,” Mraz stresses. “It protects against UV rays that accelerate the breakdown of collagen and elastin.” As collagen and elastin break down, she says, the skin becomes prone to more visible wrinkles, increased skin laxity, and UV-induced hyperpigmentation.

Bittar often tells his patients that sunscreen is “a fountain of youth in a bottle.” Like most dermatologists, he says that a sunscreen with SPF 30 or more is ideal, as SPF 30 blocks 97% of UV light. But he stresses that reapplication is the key to efficacy for any sunscreen.

“What most people don’t realize is that sunscreen only lasts about two hours, so if you put on your sunscreen at 9 a.m., then go out to lunch at noon, your morning application is no longer protecting you,” he notes.

Bittar often recommends tinted sunscreen to streamline a morning routine, since it can double as a foundation. “Almost all of EltaMD’s sunscreens are super-lightweight mineral sunscreens that come with or without tint and go on incredibly smooth,” he says. “This one is specifically designed for sensitive skin and has antioxidants—vitamins C and E—to help with photoaging as well.”

Carte Blanche’s new skin tint is a true multitasker, combining mineral sun protection with ingredients that target hyperpigmentation. “It contains zinc oxide for broad-spectrum UV protection and iron oxides that help protect against visible light,” Khanna says. “This is particularly beneficial for patients with melasma or post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.” She notes that the formula also incorporates licorice root extract, vitamin C, and bakuchiol, which offer antioxidant and potential skin-brightening benefits.

What’s the best skin-care routine for aging skin?

“The best routine is different for each person’s specific needs, but most ideal routines for aging skin are composed of sunscreen, a retinoid, a gentle wash, a solid moisturizer, and a vitamin-C serum—in that order of importance,” Bittar says. “If you have all of these components in your regimen, your routine is already in great shape.” Below, Bittar outlines his go-to routine for aging skin.

Throughout the day:Reapply sunscreen every two hours

In what order should you use antiaging skin products?

“In general, you should use your products from lightest to heaviest,” Bittar says. He typically recommends using a cleanser followed by active ingredients in a toner, serum, and/or cream, and then layering on a moisturizer. “Finally, sunscreen goes on top,” he says.

To keep skin care simple, he also recommends splitting a routine into the morning and evening components outlined above. “Stick with only a few steps in each to make it easier to stay consistent and to make sure that your actives work well together,” he advises.

#288. You Can See Everything You Ever Want to See in a Movie in You Can See Everything

Nathan Fielder’s new Elizabeth Holmes documentary is three hours long. You’ll wish it went on for three more.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

NATHAN FIELDER HAS become one of the greatest arbiters of what is—or isn’t—the truth. Fielder, whose mainstream career unofficially kicked off with his show Nathan for You, a dry, quasi-documentary, quasi-scripted, quasi-spoof of shows like Undercover Boss, has found a way to level up with each project he’s made over the course of his still relatively short career, each step of the way inviting audiences to not only question the reality of what he’s bringing to the screen, but their own stances and ways of thinking about things broadly.

The road for Fielder has included HBO’s The Rehearsal (another often surreal, often Lynchian project that presents as real, but on a subtextual level asks viewers to question whether any of what he’s depicting was really happening as it was shown) and The Curse, a Showtime/Paramount+ series that he starred in and co-created alongside Emma Stone and Benny Safdie. That show was, surprise, surprise, incredibly thoughtful, layered, and, ultimately, surreal when it comes to its underlying themes of sincerity and intention.

In a way, all of this has led Fielder to his latest project, the new A24 documentary You Can See Everything. The subject is a fitting one for Fielder: Elizabeth Holmes, the former Theranos CEO and convicted fraudster who was the subject of books (Bad Blood) and television shows (The Dropout) about her misdeeds. It makes total sense that someone famous for skirting the truth would be of interest for Fielder, a creator who has now spent so much time examining not only the truth, but what audiences might accept as the truth even given some reason not to.

In 2022, Holmes was sentenced to 11 years and 3 months in federal prison. That’s where You Can See Everything comes in: Holmes and her partner Billy Evans invited Fielder (and a film crew, led by co-director Lance Oppenheim) to join them in a home they were renting for complete access during the 34 days before she reported to federal prison in Bryan, Texas, in May 2023. And the film begins there.

And, quite frankly, if you’re considering seeing You Can See Everything, it’s best to leave it there. Fielder gets the access he was promised in the movie, but the joy of the film isn’t only in this exclusive vision of such a notable figure, but how an artist with such a relationship to the truth engages with someone who so notably has, seemingly, bent it. We also get to see Holmes and Evans shot as human beings, removed from any of the prior media circuses that have surrounded them. Fielder and Oppenheim put a fair camera to everything and let the camera do what was promised: See everything.

You Can See Everything has been one of the best-reviewed films of the year, and it lives up to the billing. Just when you think you understand what’s happening and what’s going to happen, you’ll be quickly proven wrong. Just when you think you have a handle on who someone is and what they’re all about… you’ll quickly be proven wrong. The movie is three hours long, which, of course, we know, seems daunting. But by the time it ends, you’ll wish it was going on for three hours more.

Below, we answer some of your questions about You Can See Everything—without spoiling any of the movie’s major twists or turns.

You Can See Everything is, in essence, two movies in one. The first half of the movie is what the trailer and promotional materials for the movie billed: Nathan Fielder joins Elizabeth Holmes (and her new husband Billy Evans) in a home they rented for the 34 days before she reported to federal prison in 2023. This proves to be just as compelling as you’d imagine, as Holmes and Evans are both completely idiosyncratic characters. Moments like when Fielder shows Holmes Abbott and Costello’s “Who’s on First” bit are instant classics.

Eventually Holmes reports to prison in Bryan, Texas, and the movie is not even halfway over. It’s at this point that your eyebrow should raise, and you do the ‘leaning forward in seat’ meme—because this is when You Can See Everything gets truly wild. The timeline jumps forward two hours, and Nathan Fielder gets up to some of his mind-bending, Rehearsal-type business. At this point, we see some people’s true colors, and also meet some other unexpected guests and surprises in the movie. This second part of the movie is what will blow your mind, and leave you thinking long after the credits begin to roll.

You Can See Everything should be an absolute lock for a number of Oscar nominations, including the Best Documentary Feature category. And it should be a strong contender in one of the acting categories for one person whose appearance we will not be spoiling in this story.

Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim are the co-directors of You Can See Everything, and both have been key figures in American film and television culture for the last decade.

Fielder is a Canadian-born actor and director (and childhood friend of Seth Rogen) who rose to fame as the creator and star of Comedy Central’s Nathan for You. He’s dabbled in acting here and there—including a role as a limo driver in Rogen’s underrated holiday comedy The Night Before and in the sensational limited series The Curse—but his real calling has come in mind-bending documentary/comedy series like The Rehearsal. In season 2 of The Rehearsal, for example, Fielder actually got his pilot’s license while exploring the aviation industry. (And that was filmed between part 1 and part 2 of You Can See Everything, which is just bananas.)

Oppenheim, who is only 30, has also established himself as one of the best documentarians in the business. His movies Some Kind of Heaven and Spermworld along with his HBO series Ren Faire are deeply layered portrayals of very real people in very real situations; he shoots these documentaries in styles completely different from anyone else, though, lighting them like cinematic spectacles rather than what you probably think of as a documentary in your mind. (Some of the cinematography in You Can See Everything is unbelievably beautiful.)

Primetime, A24’s film about Chris Hansen and To Catch a Predator that came out last month and starred Robert Pattinson, Skyler Gisondo, and Merritt Wever, was Oppenheim’s scripted feature debut.

It probably helps to have information on Elizabeth Holmes’s case—which we recommend getting from any number of sources: The Dropout was the name of the Hulu series that starred Amanda Seyfried as Holmes, but it was also a well-researched and reported podcast that served as the show’s basis. There’s also an HBO documentary called The Inventor and a book called Bad Blood. Any of this would make for a good source for the crimes Holmes was accused of committing. The movie also includes a very brief recap of her case in the early going—not exhaustive, but enough to get the idea.

It does also make sense to have an idea of who Fielder is, what he does, and how he engages with his subjects. We recommend HBO’s The Rehearsal for that, but it’s not 100 percent necessary to enjoy and appreciate the film.

That’s the question, isn’t it? You Can See Everything explores the idea of truth, lies, perspective, and even documentary filmmaking itself. If it makes the most sense to you to take all of You Can See Everything at face value, then please go for it. If you feel the need to question everything, well, that’s okay too. That’s what makes Fielder’s work so unique and so immersive—you can think about it about 100 different ways, and no understanding or interpretation is wrong. It’s set up to feel like a kaleidoscope. You can understand something one way, but maybe something pops up, and suddenly you can’t think about it that way anymore. That’s the point—and that’s what you’ll go home thinking about.
