#289. God Help Me, I Actually Loved Street Fighter

Stupid, surreal, and a little sexy are the best ways I can describe yet another video game movie.

I try to keep my guard up. As we see the fallout of the successes of Marvel and Star Wars having compelled studios to buy the film rights to whatever IP appeals to millennial men with income, I try not to let my senses get flash-banged by slavish renditions of things I loved at 13. But I’m a cheap date. Jingle the nostalgia keys and I will yearn for when dumb presidents had decorum. Watching Mortal Kombat II, all it took was Liu Kang and Kung Lao fighting in the portal stage to get me clapping like a seal. I loved Masters of the Universe too, to the chagrin of my coworkers who refuse to believe me even now.

I’ve studied Soviet filmmaking and the French new wave and came up during the Indiewood boom of the 1990s and 2000s. I advocate to anyone who will listen to seek out independent and foreign cinema. And I’m a fan of Stephen Chow, whose oeuvre of anarchic cult favorites like Kung Fu Hustle and Shaolin Soccer is an obvious touchstone for what I’m about to talk about. So it’s with a heavy sigh that I admit that Street Fighter, terrible as it is, is incredibly stupid fun.

In theaters now, Kitao Sakurai’s Street Fighter is the latest video game movie of the month, hot on the heels of Zach Cregger’s acclaimed Resident Evil (based on another Capcom property). It’s a remake/reboot/whatever of the seminal arcade franchise about a global martial-arts tournament with competitors who can shoot fireballs, perform 12-foot vertical suplexes, and stretch their limbs. There was a memorably bad movie in 1994, with Jean-Claude Van Damme as the lead and Raul Julia as the evil M. Bison. Street Fighter 2026 is similarly bad, but rather than render a cartoon world into a realistic one as its predecessor did, it doubles down on the hyper-unrealism of martial artists capable of superhuman feats and poor taste in haircuts.

This time, the movie stars a bevy of underrated heavy hitters, like Warrior’s Andrew Koji as main character Ryu, a monk-like champion, and recurring Christopher Nolan/Denis Villeneuve player David Dastmalchian, whose villainous M. Bison comes off as a mad dictator coded with sexual deviancy. (In one scene, he crushes an underling’s head with his bare hands; when blood spurts, his eyes roll back in ecstasy.) There are also familiar faces meant to draw in the Gen Z cohort. Noah Centineo flexes his ab muscles as Ken Masters, Ryu’s former best friend and rival, and controversial comedian Andrew Schulz shows up as Ken’s assistant Dan Hibiki (a joke character in the lore), who winds up the unexpected heart of the whole thing.

There are also noteworthy newcomers that Street Fighter might well turn into stars by Monday: Callina Liang as the iconic Chun-Li, an undercover agent with lightning kicks, and Mel Jarnson as sexy henchman Cammy. (Street Fighter’s strongest assets are, without a doubt, its women, and this movie will inspire a lot of young boys’ first crushes.) Throw in random famous people like 50 Cent and Orville Peck; professional wrestlers Cody Rhodes, Roman Reigns, and Hirooki Goto; and Eric André cashing a paycheck as a grating emcee and Street Fighter is basically a celebrity cosplay group photo at San Diego Comic-Con.

Street Fighter reaches for emotional heft in its story about brotherhood and estrangement. Ryu and Ken came up as fellow students and loved each other like brothers until envy, jealousy, and the murder of their master—carried out by underworld warrior Akuma (a TERRIFYING Roman Reigns)—drove them apart. Years after Ryu’s victory at the World Warrior Tournament, the terrorist leader M. Bison (Dastmalchian) sponsors the next tournament to siphon the powers of its competitors to amass even greater power for himself.

To its detriment, Street Fighter goes out of its way to ensure members of the game’s kooky roster look and feel like their 2D counterparts, to the point it forgets to put on halfway decent fight scenes or tell a legible story. Maybe my standards were raised too high by The Furious, but Street Fighter figuratively and literally loses track of the plot. There are barely any matches in this movie about a martial-arts tournament, and the few fight scenes end with anticlimactic thuds. Say what you want about Mortal Kombat II, but it at least knew how to structure a coherent plot and raise the stakes through winners and elimination.

So what’s actually fun and good about Street Fighter? Everything else. The actors are clearly having a ball playing dress-up—Koji most of all, as his tortured wanderer suggests the British actor was born to play Ryu (and deserving of so much more from here on). Unlike Van Damme, WWE star Cody Rhodes leans into Guile as a lunkheaded hero, delivering his lines with deadpan seriousness (and a touch of homoeroticism). If the volleyball scene in Top Gun were personified into a character, it would become Cody Rhodes’s Guile. When there is action, Street Fighter is almost sublime. Manga-inspired high-impact frames replicate the feeling of decisive blows in arcade matchups, while Shoryuken uppercuts and spinning flash kicks are put to screen with pure elegance. Street Fighter is utterly shameless about its pandering, and it’s allowed to be because it executes on the moments so well.

There’s just an overwhelming sense of unrepentant chaos, as if it’s been made with dollops of juvenile machismo and cheese and even some sex appeal that’s been absent from Marvel’s ascetic superheroes. I can’t stress enough how much the women (and Centineo’s abs) are a draw. Between their formfitting costumes, shapely physiques, and representation as feminine power fantasies, Street Fighter has enough to suggest that sex might finally sell again. There’s no time for any lovemaking in Street Fighter—not even a half-baked romance—but one brief and tasteful shower scene and the sweaty bodies of all the men and women make the movie vibrate with palpable hormonal energy. You don’t miss something until it’s gone, and Street Fighter is a welcome reminder of what we’ve been missing.

I don’t believe in “turn off your brain” movies. You should never turn off your power to think and feel. Popcorn movies like Raiders of the Lost Ark and Back to the Future are classics because, when made with actual skill, it is easy to participate as an audience member. I can’t in good conscience tell you to “turn off your brain” to enjoy Street Fighter, because we should uphold standards and say with sober certainty when any movie, even one based on an arcade game, falls short of its most essential purpose. But I’m only human. Just because I have a brain doesn’t mean I can’t be a little stupid too.

#290. This Specific Hobby Might Ease Your Depression, New Study Finds

Experts have a LOT of theories about why this might be the case.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

For many people with depression, the best treatment involves a combination of therapy, lifestyle changes, and possibly medication. But there's a lot to consider—the lifestyle category alone is massive, for starters—making it easy to get overwhelmed. But the latest research offers a new lifestyle suggestion that might help—and be enjoyable: salsa dancing.

It seems random, but a new Psychological Medicine study found that taking up a salsa dance habit was associated with fewer symptoms of depression. It may also have the added benefit of easing symptoms of social anxiety, as well.

This isn’t a prescriptive study suggesting salsa dancing as a replacement for therapy or medication, but if you're at least open to the idea, psychologists say it's worth considering. Here's why.

Meet the experts: Brennan Delattre, lead study author, international partner dance instructor and psychological researcher at the University of Oxford; John Mayer, PhD, psychologist and author of Family Fit: Find Your Balance in Life; Thea Gallagher, PsyD, clinical associate professor at NYU Langone Health and co-host of the Mind in View podcast; and Hillary Ammon, PsyD, a clinical psychologist at the Center for Anxiety and Women’s Emotional Wellness

For the randomized controlled trial, researchers consulted with a youth advisory group that included participants with depression and anxiety. Researchers screened everyone to see which dance style would be most appealing.

From there, the scientists recruited 121 people between the ages of 18 and 24 who had mild to moderately severe symptoms of depression based on a screening questionnaire. They were then randomly assigned to either an eight-week salsa dance class (which included regular attendees who weren't part of the study) or a waitlist control group. The waitlist group had to wait 12 weeks before they could take the dance class.

During the study, participants completed several questionnaires about their mental health, while the researchers tracked changes in their levels of anxiety, social anxiety, and symptoms of depression. Participants were also asked to rate their happiness daily on a scale of one to 10.

After 12 weeks, the researchers found that those who were in the salsa group reported having lower symptoms of depression compared to those in the waitlist group. Specifically, on the Patient Health Questionnaire, a standard zero-to-27 depression questionnaire, the salsa group's total fell by an average of three points. The waitlist group's total fell by less than one. This drop in the salsa dance group's total was considered clinically meaningful.

Another added perk was that people in the salsa group had a steady decline in social anxiety over the study period.

The study didn't dive into why salsa dancing may help depression and social anxiety—it just found a link. Still, experts have a few different theories.

Social dancing is a "combined intervention" with several aspects that may help, says Brennan Delattre, lead study author, international partner dance instructor, and psychological researcher at the University of Oxford. "In a single class, you can have positive social interactions, moving in sync with other people and to music, laughter, play, light to moderate exercise, a weekly routine, and the deep absorption of learning something new," she says. "Each of these has its own evidence for supporting mood."

Salsa dancing is also a type of behavioral activation, which means engaging in potentially rewarding activities even when your mood makes you want to withdraw, says Thea Gallagher, PsyD, clinical associate professor at NYU Langone Health and co-host of the Mind in View podcast. "A standing class also reduces decision fatigue because there’s already a plan, rather than having to decide each week what to do and with whom," she adds.

Plus, every class can provide people with small, repeated experiences of "social success," like connecting with a partner or getting a certain move right, Delattre says. "For people with difficulties connecting socially, or with low mood, those experiences can quietly challenge the beliefs or experiences supporting the idea that social situations are likely to go badly," she says.

Salsa dancing might also help distract those with social anxiety, says John Mayer, PhD, psychologist and author of Family Fit: Find Your Balance in Life. "The activity of salsa dancing is diverting the brain into thinking about something else besides your social anxiety," he says. "You have to concentrate on your steps and movements, the music, the rhythms [that] divert your mind away from your social anxiety."

Learning with others also gives you all a sense of accomplishment and connection, Gallagher says. "You have a shared challenge, something to talk about, and repeated opportunities to become familiar with one another," she points out.

The study focused on people between the ages of 18 and 24, but experts say it's fair to assume this can extend to others as well. "We don’t think that the beneficial ingredients of social dance are age-specific," says Delattre.

And if you like the idea but are drawn to other forms of dance beyond salsa, this intervention might still be useful. What seems to really matter here is moving your body and learning something new in a group. Leaving with better skills is simply an added bonus.

“A structured class, like salsa dancing, could be beneficial for adults who want to connect with others or try a new hobby,” says Hillary Ammon, PsyD, a clinical psychologist at the Center for Anxiety and Women’s Emotional Wellness. “Look into local classes, as they are often low-cost and in your community.”

But Ammon stresses that this isn’t the only thing you should be doing for your mental health. “If depressive or anxious symptoms are significantly impacting your quality of life, I would also encourage readers to seek out therapy or speak with your primary care physician,” she says.

Carina Hsieh, MPH, is the deputy features editor of Women’s Health. She has more than a decade’s worth of experience working in media and has covered everything from beauty, fashion, travel, lifestyle, pets, to health.

She began her career as an intern in the fashion closet at Cosmopolitan where she worked her way up to Senior Sex & Relationships Editor. While covering women’s health there, she discovered her passion for health service journalism and took a break to get her Masters in Public Health. Post-grad school, she worked as a freelance writer and as The Daily Beast’s first Beauty, Health, and Wellness Reporter.

Carina is an alum of the Fashion Institute of Technology and the Yale School of Public Health. She and her French Bulldog, Bao Bao, split their time between Brooklyn and Connecticut. She enjoys reformer Pilates, (slow) running, and smelling the fancy toiletries in boutique fitness class locker rooms.

#291. The DIY Descaling Solution I Use All Over My Kitchen

If you have an espresso machine, ice maker, combi oven, or other small appliance that requires water to do its thing, you’re likely familiar with descaling. And if you aren’t it means the insides of those small appliances probably look pretty gross. The process uses an acidic solution to remove mineral buildup in order to stop buildup and keep everything running smoothly. But there are a few less obvious spots in your kitchen that would also benefit from regular descaling—and you don’t need to buy a pricey descaling solution to do it.

Descaling solution is an acidic liquid that reacts with—and therefore breaks down—alkaline mineral build ups that happen over time wherever tap water sits or flows. Beyond the inside of tubes and pipes, chalky, crusty alkaline deposits often form around the base of faucets, the outer rims of refrigerator water dispensers, and on the bottom of tea kettles. This kind of buildup is especially prevalent where the municipal water source has a high mineral content (a.k.a hard water), especially if you don’t have a whole-house water filtration system. If you aren’t sure about the status of your water, you can start with this map from the U.S. Geological Survey and get a water test from your local big box store.

You sure can. Now, making your own cleaning products can sometimes be risky business, but descaling solution isn’t really a product you have to worry about. In fact, if you’re buying a bottled version of descaler, you’re wasting your money. You only need two things: acid and water.

For the acid, you can choose either distilled white vinegar or crystallized citric acid. I much prefer citric acid for this because it’s a dry, food-safe powder (takes up less space when bought in bulk) and the comparably faint smell is far more pleasant than vinegar. And while it’s not a true sanitizer or disinfectant, it does have some antibacterial properties.

Tap water is totally fine to use in your DIY descaling solution (I do it in a pinch), but distilled water is an even better option because it doesn’t contain any minerals.

The ratio of acid to water depends on what acid you choose, but since I’m recommending you use citric acid here, I’ll give you that recipe:

If you accidentally add a little more, it’s no big deal, it will just be a more powerful solution. Then, just stir until the crystals are dissolved and voila!: cheap, homemade descaling solution you can use in your small appliances according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

In addition to using your DIY descaling solution for small appliance maintenance, you can use it to remove the chalky film from the bottom of your tea kettle and water bottles.

And remember that white buildup around the base of your faucet? You can descale that away, too. For fairly fresh mineral deposits, simply pour a little of your homemade solution directly onto the problem area (or soak a paper towel with it and lay it on top), let it sit for a few minutes, then wipe it away with a microfiber towel. If you’re dealing with more of a stalagmite situation, you might need to use more solution, more time, and more elbow grease, but I promise I will budge eventually. Just be sure to wear dish gloves, because while citric acid is food safe, it can irritate sensitive skin, especially when mixed with water.

If the base of your faucet has buildup, there’s a very good chance the other end does too. If it’s easy to remove the sprayer head or aerator, you can soak them in your DIY solution. Mine doesn’t detach easily, so I soak the sprayer head of my pull-down faucet by clamping the hose when it’s fully extended, then submerging it in a bowl of descaling solution in the sink. If none of those options work for you, fill a sandwich bag about halfway with the solution and affix it to the sink with a rubber band or twist ties and let it soak for a few hours or overnight; you’ll be amazed at what ends up in the bottom of that bag! You can use this same technique to descale the spout of a refrigerator water dispenser.

If you find descaling as satisfying as I do (and it is so satisfying), you’ll soon be seeking out new spots to clean. Next stop: the dishwasher.

#292. Ben and Erin Napier Just Passed the ‘Home Town’ Torch to a New Duo

The new spinoff takes viewers to the island town of Port Alberni.

The hit HGTV series Home Town, starring the viewer-favorite husband-and-wife duo Ben and Erin Napier, is getting a spinoff focused on revitalizing a small town on Vancouver Island. While the core Home Town ethos will be on full display, the series, which premieres on October 25, will be missing the Napiers’ familiar faces.

Ben and Erin have been building the Home Town brand for a little over a decade, taking viewers into the heart of small-town America, and highlighting the all-too-often overlooked gems, including a maternity ward in their hometown, Laurel, Mississippi, a bowling alley in Fort Morgan, Colorado, and an Art Deco theater in Sebring, Florida, where fans got to see the Napiers tag team with the new hosts, Bryan and Sarah Baeumler.

“Hometown takeover is a lot of work. Bryan and Sarah are incredibly talented. Bryan in Canada is like the Michael Jordan of home renovation,” Ben jokes. “It felt good that we were handing it off to them.”

Bryan and Sarah are hardly strangers to seasoned HGTV fans. Before landing their own hit series, Renovation Island and Renovation Inc., Bryan hosted four shows solo, with Sarah often joining as his design and business partner. Their latest spin-off breaks down the 12-week project into eight episodes, showcasing the small island community, which faces mounting natural disasters including tsunamis and, more recently, forest fires, which have caused quite the economic downturn, closing mills and damaging resources. Despite the physical and economic impact, the small communities and two Indigenous tribes that call the region home have remained close-knit and vibrant.

“It took me back to being a kid in the 80s,” says Bryan. “Everybody knows each other. The community is so supportive of each other. The First Nations that we met are also an incredible asset. The Seshaht and the Hupacasath First Nations, and having the opportunity to meet their elected chiefs, spend time with them, and be involved in their culture was incredible. I wanted to put on a red-and-black checkered jacket and ride into town on a moose. It just felt so it just felt so Canadian.”

Ben and Erin have been forthright in Home Town’s mission to shed a positive light on communities across the country. Home Town Takeover Canada is the first step in taking that mission international. While the hosts and locations may change across episodes, Home Town’s core principle will always remain the same. “Let the townspeople tell their own story,” say Ben and Erin. “That has been something that we learned in Laurel long before TV. You cannot come into a town and make it something it’s not. The goal is to help a town. get a little bit further down the road to rebirth or growth. The only way to do that is to let the town tell the story,” says Erin.

#297. Jordan Roth Recreates His West Village Apartment in a Parisian Hôtel Particulier

In partnership with Design Miami, the award-winning producer debuts a new art installation, “To Think of the Tranquil Life of Things.”

Jordan Roth has seven Tony Awards, an enviable couture collection, and, most recently, an acting credit on Ryan Murphy’s new series The Shards. This week, the Broadway producer is adding his own Parisian art installation to the list.

In partnership with Design Miami and Salon 94 Design, Roth is taking over the Hôtel de Guise, filling the 18th century hôtel particulier with a collection of pieces he created. In this new installation, called “To Think of the Tranquil Life of Things,” Roth transposes his West Village apartment, featured in ELLE Decor in 2016, into this elaborate, Parisian space. Inside an exhibition designed by ELLE Decor A-List firm Charlap Hyman & Herrero, visitors will find 16 images of Roth, each printed on a swath of fabric and draped over an individual piece of furniture.

Roth came up with the idea when he and his husband, Richie Jackson, were moving out of the New York apartment where Roth had spent the past 15 years and where, Roth says, “so much life happened.” He tells ELLE Decor, “I wanted to record this life. It’s about the way in which the objects we live with carry stories.”

When it came time to leave, Roth thought of a novel way to preserve those memories. “The movers were coming to take the furniture away,” when he had an idea: to shoot himself in 16 different looks he had worn while living in the home, he says. The images were photographed all with Roth sitting on various pieces of furniture, printed onto fabric, and draped over the Parisian furnishings. He also recreated the rooms in the exact layout of the New York home, but now in this Paris mansion. The inspiration stemmed from slipcovers but, he says, instead of concealing, “we are revealing something.”

The exhibit’s big moment comes in the form of the “chintz room,” a space where the furniture is covered in a fabric printed with dahlias, the flowers Roth grows and loves. While the installation is personal, Roth hopes his visitors also take with them an opportunity for self-reflection.

“I would be really happy if somebody came to experience this work and then went home and sat on their own couch,” he says, “and started to see their own history and aesthetic evolution and the narrative it holds.”

Jordan Roth’s “To Think of the Tranquil Life of Things” will be on view October 20 to 25, 2026 at the Hôtel de Guise, 72 rue de l’Université. Reservations here.

#298. Put Down the Gas Station Dick Pills

Skip the sketchy sex pills and choose a supplement that helps you rise to the occasion.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

IF YOU GO to a convenience store and see a product behind the counter with a name like "Boner Blaster 5,000," it's a surefire way to know a supplement is not legit. But not all scams are that obvious. That’s because the supplements made of “herbal Viagra” or other natural ingredients don’t always work.

“Even if you buy them at a big retailer, and they seem to be made of ‘natural' ingredients, be cautious,” says Jamin Brahmbhatt, MD, urologist at Orlando Health. “No one is regulating this stuff.”

That's concerning. When it comes to supplements, it’s not clear what you could be putting in your body. There's always the chance it could harm your overall health—and make any erectile dysfunction problem worse. So Men’s Health turned to the experts to get the lowdown on which supplements boost sex drive and/or help with ED. They narrowed it down to five options.

NATHAN STARKE, MD, urologist at Houston Urologist, says his patients ask him about supplements “all the time.” While supplements are usually safe for most people, he urges caution when choosing one. If you’re looking for an extra boost, consider the following expert-backed options:

L-arginine is an essential amino acid that may benefit both heart health and erectile function, says Dr. Brahmbhatt.

One study in the journal Andrology found that patients with severe or complete erectile dysfunction had L-arginine levels that were significantly lower than those of men with milder forms of ED. In guys with mild-to-moderate ED, three months of L-arginine supplementation significantly increased the speed of blood flow to the penis and improved erectile function. One caveat was that L-arginine supplements alone were not as effective in guys with severe ED. However, L-arginine effects may work better when paired with ED medications. An 8-week trial had men ages 50 and older take L-arginine supplements with sildenafil (Viagra) or sildenafil every other day. Those results showed greater erectile function in guys taking the combo treatment than sildenafil alone.

L-arginine is broken down by the body into nitric oxide, a smooth muscle relaxer that allows for more blood flow to the penis, which is important for erections. (Drugs including Cialis and Viagra block the breakdown of nitric oxide in the body, so there are higher circulating levels to help with erections.)

L-arginine is found in most protein-rich foods such as red meat, poultry, beans, and dairy products. The Mayo Clinic marks L-arginine generally safe but cautions people who take blood pressure meds to talk to a doctor first.

This is good advice for any supplements if you’re on blood pressure medications, Dr. Brahmbhatt says. That’s because a product like L-arginine can reduce your blood pressure—which is great if it’s a bit too high, but not if you’re already bringing it down with meds. In that case, you may see a sudden and dramatic drop in pressure that could cause you to faint, or in extreme cases, have a stroke.

If you’re not on those meds and want to try the amino acid, Dr. Brahmbhatt suggests starting at a dose of about six grams a day to see how you tolerate it. In some people, the supplement can cause side effects, including nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and bloating.

In addition to L-arginine, L-citrulline is often recommended to help produce stronger erections. This is because L-citrulline is converted in the body to L-arginine, explains Peter Tsambarlis, MD, urologist at Northwestern Medicine. One review found that taking L-citrulline increased blood levels of L-arginine more effectively than L-arginine supplements did, likely due to higher production of nitric oxide (NO).

“Nitric oxide is involved in vasodilation (widening and opening up of blood vessels), which can begin and maintain the erectile response,” says Michael Eisenberg, MD, urologist at Stanford Medicine. Nitric oxide is considered the main neurotransmitter responsible for causing an erection by relaxing penile smooth muscle.

Omega-3 fatty acids are a lukewarm maybe when it comes to protecting your heart and your erections. The research goes back and forth about whether fish oil supplements are really helpful for the heart. If the scales tip toward them being helpful to your heart, then your erections may benefit as well, says Dr. Brahmbhatt. That’s because heart-healthy changes are geared toward improving blood flow and increasing the size of blood vessels.

Your penis has some of the smallest blood vessels in your body, meaning they are more prone to getting clogged up. Impeded blood flow is bad for erections, so anything that improves blood flow is good.

That’s why, at first, it might not make sense that many blood pressure medications list erectile dysfunction as a side effect. The reason is they modulate the way that blood vessels open and close, which can reduce flow overall, especially in the penis.

By contrast, omega-3 fatty acids can have the opposite effect because they lower inflammation that might be affecting blood vessels, while also reducing blood clotting. That can help boost your blood flow. While you can get your omegas from supplements, getting them from foods such as fatty fish is your best bet.

Some research suggests that men with severe vitamin D deficiencies have a greater risk of erectile dysfunction. That may be because low levels of the vitamin are associated with diseases like hypertension, coronary artery disease, and peripheral vascular disease, says Dr. Brahmbhatt. Basically, blood flow issues that affect your system can also raise your risk of ED.

You can get some vitamin D from foods including salmon and eggs, along with sunshine. However, most people in the US lack the vitamin, especially if you live in the northern part of the country, says registered dietitian Brianna Elliott, RD.

The longer you maintain low levels of vitamin D, the more effects you might see, including potential ED. But how much you should take is a moving target. The National Institutes of Health recommends 15 to 20 micrograms (600 to 800 IU), while the Endocrine Society suggests much higher levels of up to 2,000 IU daily.

Now the one caveat is that the research is mixed on whether further supplementation helps people who already maintain a healthy level of vitamin D. A five-year trial supplemented men ages 60 to 84 with vitamin D, despite a lack of vitamin D deficiency. An analysis at the three-year mark found a lack of improvement or prevention of ED.

ANOTHER SUPPLEMENT THAT is good for overall health and wellness, including erectile health, is folic acid or B9. Some research has linked improvement in sexual performance with folic acid supplementation, which lowered levels of the amino acid homocysteine, says Dr. Tsambarlis. “Homocysteine levels were previously found to be higher in men with ED than their counterparts who were not suffering from ED.”

IN GENERAL, HERE’S the best possible “supplement” you can take for your sex life: lifestyle changes. A healthy diet, regular exercise, good sleep habits, and lower stress levels all go a long way toward improving your health, as you’ve heard a million times, says Dr. Starke.

“Overall health and sexual health are closely related,” says Dr. Eisenberg. "Thus, anything that benefits heart health can also benefit sexual health. A good diet, exercise, and maintaining a good body weight can all help [as well].”

“Diet and exercise have consistently outperformed supplements and have a significant and reliable impact on sexual performance,” says Dr. Tsambarlis. When in doubt, Dr. Starke advises talking to your doctor before taking them if you have heart problems, kidney disease, high blood pressure, or other health conditions.

#300. The 10 Best Lip Balms for Dry, Cracked, and Peeling Lips in 2026, Tested by Beauty Experts

Eadem’s $24 lip balm changed how we treat our lips.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Even if you don’t have an elaborate skincare routine, you probably still use lip balm. Chapped lips aren’t just a winter issue—they can happen year-round. Cranking up my personal space heater creates a warm, dry environment that dehydrates my skin and lips, leaving them dry, flaky, and sometimes painful. While drinking water and not licking lips can help, dermatologists say those aren’t the only reasons they get chapped.

Our lips have a unique anatomy. They have thinner skin, low water retention, and fewer oil glands than the rest of our face. That makes them more prone to dryness, says dermatologist Teresa Song, MD.

A good lip balm hydrates, seals in moisture, prevents cracking, and protects the skin barrier from harsh elements, she says. That’s where the ingredients shine and separate good lip balms from great ones. Once you order one of these editor-tested, dermatologist-recommended lip balms, reapplication is key. Dr. Song advises swiping them on every two to six hours, and once before bed.

The bottom line: You need something that's going to keep your pout hydrated and supple all year long. Thankfully, we tapped four dermatologists to get their input on what to look for in the best lip balms and which ones they recommend to their clientele. Then, we took matters into our own hands and tested them all ourselves, narrowing down our list to the 10 best lip balms for a wide range of different concerns. Before diving into our list, keep reading to discover what to look for when shopping for your new balm.

Dr. Song namechecked three types of ingredients to watch for—humectants, emollients, and occlusives—and shared how they keep the lips hydrated, smooth, and protected.

You’ll want to stay away from alcohol, which causes excessive dryness. Mineral oil may clog pores around the lips, and strong fragrances can lead to irritation and rashes. Though menthol, camphor, and phenol have a cooling sensation, they will irritate and dry the lips over time.

Dr. Song also recommends swapping out lip balms when seasons change and when you're traveling to a different climate. Use lighter formulas such as Rhode’s Peptide Lip Treatment in warm or humid climates and thicker formulas like the Laneige Lip Mask in cold or dry weather.

To find the best lip balms, I reevaluated my collection of 40 products. I considered their ingredients and consistency, as well as their functional and cosmetic benefits. For example, I evaluated how long the hydration lasted and how sticky each swipe felt.

While my favorites range from $5 to $30, I didn’t notice a decline in the quality or feel of more affordable lip balms, nor did pricier picks equate to dramatic hydration.

Additionally, I ensured there was a mix of lightweight formulas for daily wear and heavier balms for overnight use. Because I love experimenting with my lipstick and lip liner combos, I awarded bonus points to balms that come in a variety of tints. I also factored in how vibrant or sheer each hue was on its own and how they layered with makeup. There are clear options for anyone who prefers a more natural look.

To further refine the list, I asked four dermatologists about their go-to picks. I also recruited other WH staffers: beauty director Brian Underwood, beauty editorial assistant Katie Mogg, and associate health and wellness editor Addison Aloian. Beauty contributors Lily Wohlner and Danielle Jackson joined as testers for this story.

When we initially published this story in February 2024, we featured 20 lip balms. For our latest 2026 update, we tried 40 lip balms over a year and settled on 10 tried-and-true recommendations that we’re actually using this fall and beyond. They're all aligned with dermatological guidance and nourish our lips for hours.

Moringa oil provides non-greasy, deep hydration that supports my skin barrier. It also contains a collagen-boosting peptide that smooths the look of my natural lip lines, creating a fuller-looking pout without stinging.

Together, these ingredients keep my lips soft and moisturized for hours. Truthfully, I can go a full day or two without using this balm because the formula is that nourishing. #302. What Gen Z, Millennials, Gen X, and Boomers Are All Hunting for Secondhand

From vintage glassware to chrome-coated sculptures, each generation has its own take on thrift shop treasures.

Every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

You may have heard the news: the golden age of thrifting is upon us. Baby Boomers are downsizing, and storied possessions from the wealthiest generation in modern history are making their way from curio cabinets and mantelpieces to estate sales and antique shops. But with such a trove to browse, how is anyone deciding what to buy? We asked home thrifting experts what each generation is most commonly hunting for on the shelves and in the aisles, and the generational markers are loud, to say the least.

“Thrifting is one of the rare types of shopping that feels like a sport, and it really does feel like you've ‘won’ when you find that special piece,” says Virginia Chamlee, a seasoned antiques dealer and author of Big Thrift Energy. “Then, there's the resale value of some items. Even if you aren't buying to resell, it's nice to buy something that you know might later increase in value.”

No one is immune to the thrill of thrifting, even Gen Z. Known for their commitment to sustainability, Gen-Zers are leading the second-hand shopping category, as a whopping 62 percent of the generation reports shopping thrifted or consignment goods in just the last year and 58 percent browsing pre-owned pieces before they even consider buying brand new. Their commitment to thrifting has even launched a social media movement in the form of #thrifthauls.

Beyond the sustainability and ecological benefits of second-hand shopping, designer Phoenix Grey says the real allure is an air of individuality. “Gen Z thrifts for personality. They’re less concerned with whether something is a ‘good investment’ and more interested in whether it’s fun, strange, or nostalgic. They want something that no one else has because they are so used to seeing everyone with the same items,” says Grey. “They gravitate toward the 70s and 80s: chrome, bold colour, and squiggly, sculptural forms. Grandmacore is a big part of it too, with floral prints, ruffled lampshades, and kitschy ceramics used with a sense of humour, because they want something that's ‘fun.’ Their style is maximalist and eclectic.”

Bargain hunters by trade, potential resale value is a major deal-breaker when Millennials are browsing. The second-hand market is a haven for Millennials, who have weathered the rising cost of living and fluctuating inflation rates for decades, making retail prices harder and harder to justify.

Not wanting to sacrifice beauty or flair, thrifting and DIY culture became a lifeline for personal style to prevail over the often bleak economic landscape. “I think Millennials are also interested in the hunt itself. Finding something amazing for a fraction of its retail price is part of the appeal,” says Katie Zamprioli, a design influencer. “Upcycling, furniture flips, DIY makeovers, and finding creative ways to give something old a completely different look became a huge part of the culture. Instead of seeing a dated dresser or an outdated lamp and passing it by, they saw the potential to paint it, reupholster it, change the hardware, or turn it into something entirely different.”

Millennials championed many of the popular design schemes big-box retailers race to emulate today, particularly midcentury modern sculptural styles and pieces with Victorian-era flair. Original art is also a big hit with the middle-ground generation.

While Boomers may make up the smallest slice of second-hand consumers, their style is pronounced. Like the younger gens, Boomers are chasing nostalgia, but unlike Gen-Zers and Millennials, they aren’t driven by whatever's hot in internet trends. Instead, Boomers are scanning shelves for pieces of their childhoods.

“I think Boomers are drawn to the pieces from their childhood homes as well as brands that made high-quality products in the 80s and 90s. Boomers have a good handle on what things used to cost, too, so they understand practical value,” says Chamlee.

According to Chamlee, their most wanted items include hot-air balloon embossed Pyrex dishes, candy-colored depression glass, and sturdy cast-iron kitchenware.

So, whether you’re shopping estate sales, thrift shops, or consignment, there really is something for every taste hidden on the shelves.

#305. What to Bring to a Dinner Party When the Host Says “Don’t Bring Anything”

Whether you follow instructions or bring a little something, here’s how to be a guest they’ll invite back.

Martha Stewart has a reliable dinner-party gift: “Fresh eggs from my chickens,” she told ELLE Decor. It helps to have a flock, of course, but the rest of us can borrow the principle. Bring something your host will enjoy having around tomorrow, when the guests have gone and there’s no dinner to get on the table.

That’s especially good advice when the invitation comes with a request to bring nothing. There’s no need to arrive with another course or flowers that require immediate attention. If you’d like to bring a small thank-you, the designers and entertaining experts we spoke to have suggestions—and a few reservations about the things guests tend to grab on the way over.

“When a host says ‘don’t bring anything,’ I think they are fairly certain they have enough food and beverage, and probably don’t want excess,” says Amber Mayfield Hewett, founder of event production company To Be Hosted and author of Your Turn to Host. “I wouldn’t bring anything that needs to be served or pressures the host to make accommodations.”

An unexpected dish can put the host in an awkward position, particularly if they’ve planned around guests’ dietary restrictions. Interior designer Christina Nielsen generally avoids bringing food she expects to be served, though she makes exceptions for close friends whose tastes she knows. For them, she might arrive with a freshly baked baguette or pastries. Unless you have that level of familiarity, ask before bringing something for the table.

Nielsen’s suggestions include chocolates, good olive oil, and a bottle of wine intended for another night. Event designer and etiquette expert Hovik Harutyunyan adds coffee, tea, specialty honey, and cocktail olives, as these can all go into the pantry without becoming part of the evening’s preparations.

Choose according to what your host enjoys. Wine is appropriate for someone whose preferences you know, but it needn’t be the automatic purchase for every invitation. Andria Mitsakos, founder and creative director of the brand Anthologist, suggests gifts with a personal connection. She often brings friends things she has found on her travels.

“A gift doesn’t need to be expensive, and it certainly doesn’t need to have anything to do with dinner,” she says. Her other suggestions also include a book the recipient would enjoy or fingerless gloves for a friend who is always cold. “I love gifts that demonstrate you’ve paid attention to someone.”

For a friend whose interiors you know well, Nielsen likes a small vintage object, cocktail napkins, or candleholders. But there’s no need to choose something for the house if you’re less familiar with the owner’s taste—chocolates may be the better bet, she emphasizes.

Flowers seem easy until you’re the one answering the door with a bouquet in your arms and a saucepan on the stove. Nielsen points out that loose stems require a vase, trimming, and arranging while guests are arriving.

Harutyunyan would save them for afterward. Even an arrangement that needs no attention may not suit the room or table the host has prepared. He recommends sending flowers with a handwritten thank-you card one to three days after the dinner.

Arriving empty-handed doesn’t mean you’ve missed your chance. Hewett suggests a handwritten note or a gift card for coffee the following morning. A few specific lines about the evening give your host something they can enjoy without having to unwrap, refrigerate, or arrange it.

While you’re there, be interested in the other guests, enjoy the meal, and offer a helping hand. Hewett says assisting in the kitchen or staying to load the dishwasher can mean a great deal. Take your cue from the host, though—someone who declines help may genuinely prefer you to stay at the table.

“Being a guest is more important than the gift itself,” Nielsen says. “Be engaged and fun!” You can send flowers tomorrow. Tonight, they’ve invited you for your company.

#308. Mark Hamill Makes It Weird: An Exclusive Carrie Interview

The legendary actor reveals that Mike Flanagan pulled him from the brink of retirement.

“Hold up, this was Mark Hamill?!” “Mark Hamill is completely unrecognizable…” “Did you spot him?”

That’s just a sampling of the reactions to episode 6 of Mike Flanagan’s new Carrie series, which closes with a “guest starring” credit for Hamill and sends viewers scrolling back to the beginning to find him. The Star Wars actor is hiding in plain sight in the very first scene, a prologue to the episode that focuses on a phony-baloney fortune teller named Damon Nostra (aka Greg McMurray), who claims to have the power to hear the dead. A grisly scene then plays out as a tearful young woman sits down at his séance table and reveals she can do the same. Or, rather, she can actually do it—and it’s driving her to bloody madness.

Think of it as Hamill dressing up for Halloween. “I remember saying, ‘I want to be as unrecognizable as possible,’ and since he’s sort of this mysterious mystic figure, the sky’s the limit,” Hamill tells Esquire in his one-and-only interview about the role. “I said, ‘I need a nose!’ ”

He initially wanted to go completely uncredited. “I thought it would be more fun if we could try and pull one over on the public,” he says. “Maybe somebody would say, ‘Oh, that’s Mark! I recognize his voice,’ or whatever. And we just wouldn't comment on it. I love stuff like that.”

Being unmasked like the foiled villain in a Scooby-Doo episode is “no big deal,” Hamill says. He’s happy to be associated with the show, developed for TV by his now frequent collaborator Flanagan. “I’m just knocked out by Carrie,” Hamill says. “At first, I thought, Well, why would he want to redo something that’s considered a classic by Brian De Palma? Then you see why, because when he can expand, he can tell you so much more about the friends at school. ... I mean, he just has the luxury of eight hours to tell this story.”

You’d need about the same length of time to walk through all of Hamill’s memorable performances, but this time we decided to focus only on the especially strange ones: the monsters, outcasts, and weirdos he has brought to life in tales of the otherworldly and supernatural. It goes back a long way, to when he was just a little kid.

“Here’s a story I should tell you because this is a turning point in my life,” Hamill begins. “When I was a kid, I had magic tricks and I had a Jerry Mahoney ventriloquist dummy.”

As the middle of seven children, Hamill stood out for his obsession with 1933’s King Kong, puppets, slapstick comedy, and television shows. He didn’t realize it at the time, but his destiny as a performer was beginning to take shape—prompted by his dummy.

“I’d spend hours in front of the mirror trying to learn how not to move my lips,” Hamill says, uttering the last few words through a tight, unmoving mouth. “My brother and sisters, they would laugh, but they’d laugh at me, not with me.”

Then came his big break. “I hosted a sixth-grade variety show in San Diego with my dummy. I didn’t really have an act. I was winging it,” Hamill says. “After the end of this two-and-a-half-hour show, I was addicted to laughter. I thought, Wow, maybe I could be a stand-up comedian.”

Instead he just became a leading man, the epitome of the hero’s journey as Luke Skywalker in the original Star Wars films. Years later, he pivoted to voice acting, becoming the epitome of evil as the Joker in various Batman cartoons. The roles Hamill seems to savor the most are everything in between, the colorful supporting parts and character pieces that subsume who he is and present an entirely different person.

It all goes back to that dummy. “It really made me realize how much I craved laughter and applause and approval,” Hamill says. “It transformed me in a way.”

This is where Hamill entered the so-called Flanagan-verse. For the filmmaker’s 2023 remix of Edgar Allan Poe stories, Flanagan reached out to Hamill for the role of Arthur Pym, the ominous attorney and notorious fixer for the wealthy Usher family. He is inspired by Poe’s only completed novel, 1838’s The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym of Nantucket, a harrowing tale about a stowaway, a mutiny, cannibalism, and madness on the high seas.

The shadowy Pym in Flanagan’s series is said to have a grim and unspeakable history, although these specific points are only alluded to. Hamill plays him as the avatar of inhumanity. “This character is a soulless, evil sociopath and an enabler of evil, because the family is full of terrible people,” he says. “What amazed me was: Why would he think of me?”

As with the ventriloquist dummy of his childhood, Hamill says this was another turning point. “Mike came into my life at a really important time. When I finished the [Star Wars] sequels, I thought maybe this is a good time to, well … to use a word both my agent and my wife hate: retire,” Hamill says. “I probably wouldn’t have announced it. I just didn’t have the drive I had in my earlier years. And then out of nowhere, Mike Flanagan contacted me to do The Fall of the House of Usher.”

On the journey from Los Angeles to the Canadian film set, the actor felt, well … scared. But also invigorated. “I was on the plane on the way to Vancouver with absolutely no idea, I mean zero, how I’m going to play Pym,” he says.

He found the soul—or lack thereof—while in the makeup chair. He felt Pym would shun everything except for his dirty work. “I said to the hair people, ‘He’s dedicated to his job, so the less time spent on grooming, the better. He’s the guy that would want to get out of the shower, rub a towel once, and be done with it,’ ” Hamill recalls. “I said, ‘Make it short.’ Then I found the wardrobe, I found the glasses, I found the hat.”

In his first scene, he found the voice: a low growl. “I wanted to convey that he was sort of dead inside, that he had no soul and no sort of human emotions,” Hamill says. “I wanted him to be somebody that if you’d met him, you wouldn’t want to be around him. So I just started talking in that voice, just that dead voice.”

It was not something he discussed with Flanagan ahead of time. “We were doing the scenes, we were doing different setups, and later in the day when he walked by, just as an aside, he didn’t even stop, he said, ‘Love the voice,’ ” Hamill recalls.

Then Flanagan called again, this time for a feature-film adaptation of the Stephen King novella The Life of Chuck. Hamill’s character of Albie Krantz is the opposite of Arthur Pym. He is a mensch, an elderly accountant who loves numbers, and he’s caring for his orphaned grandchild while enjoying his winter years alongside his kindhearted wife, played by Mia Sara (of Ferris Bueller’s Day Off.)

But there are still dark tidings around the edges. Upstairs in their little Victorian house is a cupola at the end of a dim hallway, and inside you can see things you’d rather not know.

“I love Stephen King, and when Mike called me and said, ‘Oh, I’m doing another Stephen King adaptation, The Life of Chuck, and there’s something in it I think you’d be interested in. Can I send it to you?’ I said, ‘Of course,’ ” Hamill recalls. “As soon as I hung up the phone, I ordered it online, and I think I got it the day after or two days after. Considering Mike’s résumé and Stephen King’s, I’m expecting the ultimate epic supernatural horror film. I was set up in the wrong way, but that made me appreciate it more because it was so life-affirming and so positive.”

This time, Hamill whited out his natural hair and mustache, aging himself to play the rumpled grandpa. “Then I found a pair of wire-rim glasses,” Hamill says. “It wasn’t until I put those glasses on and looked in the mirror that I thought, Oh my God, I’m a dead ringer for the Disney version of Geppetto.”

For Grandpa’s big speech, extolling the certainty of mathematics in a world full of fear and confusion, Hamill was nervous about delivering the entire thing in one take. One paragraph was cut from the final film but provides a window into how he works.

“Here’s how I memorize. I’ll draw cartoons in the margin, write puns, the worse the better, because you’ll remember it,” Hamill says. “There was a point where he’s saying, ‘And math can make you popular. You can go out to dinner and figure out how much it costs for everyone to eat.’ And then the next thought was, ‘It’s good for your brain.’ I was having a real hard time memorizing it. Then I thought, Oh, eat—brains. In the margin, I wrote, ‘zombie.’ ”

In a May 2020 episode of the TV series about vampire roommates, Hamill turns up as an age-old bloodsucking nemesis of Matt Berry’s Laszlo Cravensworth. Like his fake medium in Carrie, this one features Hamill in a wig and colorful gown, speaking in a voice straight out of Transylvania (by way of 1930s Hollywood).

Hamill was a fan of both the 2009 movie and the TV series and tweeted about both several times. The showrunners took notice. “Then my agent calls and says, ‘They want you to do a part on the show.’ I said, ‘You’re kidding. Send me the script.’ I’m thinking I’m going to be playing the high school principal or a neighbor who wants to complain about the odd hours they’re keeping,” Hamill says. “When I got that script and it says, ‘Mark Hamill: Jim the Vampire,’ I just lost it. Even his name epitomizes their kind of humor. It’s not Vlad or Dmitri; it’s this mundane Jim.”

The episode ends with the feud being resolved through the gift of an animatronic Big Mouth Billy Bass, which dazzles Hamill’s ancient vampire until he realizes it’s just a cheap toy. “I’m thinking this deserves a sequel because I want my revenge,” says Hamill, who even had an idea in mind: “He got the best of me, and my idea for the storyline was he comes back in disguise and attempts to seduce Laszlo’s wife. I thought that would be a great idea. I never mentioned it to the writers, and before I could even act on it, they announced that they were going to bring an end to the series.”

Hamill had two other forays into Stephen King country, one very recently, the other long ago. In last year’s The Long Walk—based on the first novel King ever wrote, back when he was 19 years old—Hamill played the sadistic Major, who leads a group of young boys on a televised suicide marathon, meant to instill fear and a sense of grim determination in the nation at large.

Hamill had just wrapped his role when he sat beside King at the Toronto International Film Festival debut of The Life of Chuck. “What surprised me is when I went to meet him, he looks up and the first thing he says to me is: ‘The Major!’ ”

They have continued their social-media friendship ever since, a treat for Hamill, who says he has been a fan of the author ever since he saw a matinee of The Shining in 1980. “I went straight to a bookstore and bought [the book] because I thought, What the hell did I just see?” he says. “There’s so much more detail in the book.”

Once again, the eyes (or eyewear) were a window to what lies within. Along with the Major’s military fatigues and cap, Hamill found a pair of mirror sunglasses that he felt, um, reflected the man himself. “I said to the director, Francis Lawrence, ‘I wonder if we can never take them off,’ ” Hamill says. “So much of a person’s personality is in their eyes. Again, I wanted to dehumanize him. There are no redeeming qualities. He’s just a sadist, and he must hate people.”

The look actually calls to mind Hamill’s very first King role: a cameo as Sheriff Jenkins, investigating a savage killing in the opening of 1992’s Sleepwalkers, based on an original screenplay by King. Hamill put on similar oversize sunglasses and slicked back his hair to play the perplexed investigator, who has stumbled on the bloody trail of two shape-shifting immortals, a mother and son, who feed on the blood of virgins.

Director Mick Garris would go on to direct King’s work again in the miniseries The Stand, the miniseries remake of The Shining, Riding the Bullet, Desperation, and Bag of Bones. But Hamill knew him first through Star Wars, since Garris started out in Hollywood as an office worker at Lucasfilm.

“I don’t call it a favor. I think, if anything, he was probably doing me a favor,” Hamill says. “He said, ‘Hey, I’m doing this thing. Do you want to do such and such?’ And I’m game. I like Mick so much, and I’m so glad that he’s been able to realize his dreams of directing. I just had a great time.”

Hamill’s only regret is that the Sheriff doesn’t follow the trail to the end. “I sort of thought, Well, gee, I wish I had a bigger part. It's like Damon Nostra,” he says. “Having played that character, I don’t want to say goodbye to him, but he’s really not a part of the Carrie universe. He exists on his own.”

Hamill was almost part of a different Carrie universe himself. Back in 1976, George Lucas and Brian De Palma were closer friends, and they joined together to interview the best of Hollywood’s up-and-coming actors for the two films they were about to make.

Lucas was casting for the lead roles in Star Wars, and De Palma was casting the students of Carrie, the very first King adaptation ever made. Most of the actors at the casting call read for both parts, so there’s an alternate history in which William Katt becomes Luke Skywalker and Mark Hamill plays Tommy Ross, the kindhearted but doomed king of the prom.

“On the cattle call for both Luke and Han, I went in and sat down, and basically Brian did the talking,” Hamill says. “He said, ‘Tell us a little about yourself,’ which I did for maybe two minutes. They said, ‘Thank you very much.’ When I walked out, I said to people that were managing the room, ‘Who’s that little guy with Brian De Palma who doesn’t talk? Is that his assistant?’ They said, ‘No, moron, that was George Lucas.’ ”

Hamill shrugs. “I could have been up for the part that William Katt played. Who knows? I think he tested for Star Wars. What struck me was each one of them was perfectly credible had they gotten that part.”

A half century later, Carrie became part of Hamill’s destiny after all. Who could have seen that coming? Certainly not Damon Nostra.

#310. 6 Colors You May Regret Painting Your Kitchen, According to Designers

The design and functionality of your kitchen are integral to the overall language of your home. It’s possibly the most important room—it’s where the meals are prepped and guests gather, which means it’s somewhere you should feel comfortable and content. Something that can greatly affect the happiness you feel in a space? Paint color.

Interior designers have a lot to say about which paint colors look best or most expensive in a kitchen, meaning they can also weigh in on what colors do not look good in this space. Below, find the six colors that these experts think you may regret painting your kitchen, from canary yellow to stark white.

For Shannon Kadwell, the kitchen and bath director at Anthony Wilder Design Build, cool gray is a shade she avoids in the kitchen. “A kitchen is meant to be the warm, welcoming heart of the home where people actually want to gather—not a sterile commercial office or a hospital corridor,” she says. It can be hard to make gray feel anything but cold and uninspiring, and it completely drains the energy right out of a room, Kadwell adds.

While Sharon L. Sherman of Thyme & Place Design loves black, she recognizes that it can be a difficult shade to use in the kitchen. “I know there is an idea that black hides a multitude of sins, but in reality it shows everything,” she says. “Dust can cling to oils that settle on the cabinets from cooking, and it’s easy to ding cabinet drawers when removing heavy pots and pans.” Plus, it’s also hard to touch up. She would prefer a softly distressed finish for cabinetry if her clients want to incorporate the dark shade.

“School bus yellow is often seen as a risky option,” says Darla Bankston May, principal designer of Bankston May Associates. “In small amounts, this bold, saturated shade can make a lovely accent. But when overused, the effect changes. A kitchen painted in bright yellow quickly becomes loud, visually overwhelming, and even stressful to be in.”

“I would not use a stark white,” cautions Kelly Neely, founder of Kelly Neely Interiors. “White kitchens are classic, but going too white can feel cold in a space that is typically the hub of the home.”

“In kitchens, avoid super saturated yellows or reds,” says Marissa Stokes, founder of Marissa Stokes Interior Design. “They can feel overwhelming in a room meant to be welcoming. Kitchens really shine with softer neutrals or muted tones that let the food and life in the space take center stage.”

“I would not choose a color that I need to vacillate on," says Libby Baker, founder of Baker Design Co. “For example, I would never paint a kitchen lime green as it would be too overwhelming and jarring during mealtimes. Don't get me wrong. I love bold colors, and I love to use them unexpectedly, but painting a kitchen lime green would create an overstimulating experience and feel more like commercial design than home.”

#312. The Best Part About the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show Was the Hot-as-Hell OG Angels

Give us glitter, wings, and women of a certain age!

Victoria’s Secret has always understood the power of an OG. Adriana Lima, Alessandra Ambrosio, Heidi Klum—these women became synonymous with the brand, their faces as recognizable as the wings and bombshell bras themselves. For years, keeping a beloved Angel around past the fashion industry’s notoriously short shelf life was less an act of rebellion as it was a smart business decision. They were bankable, iconic, and capable of making a glittery bra and costumey wings into a cultural event. But at the 2026 Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show, the OGs, now all women of a certain age, were the absolute pinnacle of the viewing experience.

It’s one thing to bring back a familiar face for a nostalgia hit; it’s another to embrace the idea that sexiness doesn’t expire. It was absolutely refreshing to see the mix of seasoned faces amid the younger ones.

And VS isn’t the only one hitting this mark recently. Mature models are increasingly appearing on major runways. Designers are revisiting familiar faces, casting cultural icons, and recognizing that a compelling woman doesn’t suddenly become less interesting after 30 or after her kids grow out of the toddler phase. (For what it’s worth, motherhood was a huge theme of the show last year, and this year we did also see a six-week postpartum Barbara Palvin.)

The Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show was built on an almost comically narrow fantasy of femininity: young, thin, and largely white. The Angels who broke through that mold did so largely because they became exceptions—famous enough to outlive the rules. Now, the more exciting possibility is that maybe there don’t have to be exceptions.

There’s something undeniably sexy about confidence that’s experienced a little more life. Especially when so many corners of the internet are focused on femininity through the tight constraints of girlish figures and faces, something as simple as a sprinkle of 40+-year-old women on the runway is a flex. If Victoria’s Secret is still in the business of selling fantasy, the fact that hot has no expiration date is the first one I’ve been interested in in a while.

Aiyana Ishmael is the style editor at Cosmopolitan magazine. In her work, Aiyana focuses on the culture of fashion and how it intertwines and shapes the zeitgeist. She is an award-winning journalist from Miami, Florida, and a graduate of the historically Black university, Florida A&M. She is a 2024 Forbes 30 Under 30: Media honoree, and her debut romance novella PASSING GAME is set to release March of 2027 (831 Stories/Simon & Schuster).

#314. Christie’s Major Upcoming Design Sale Features Lalanne, Prouvé, and Perriand

“Anthology of Design: Masterworks from a French-American Collection” will take place on December 9 in New York.

Above: François-Xavier Lalanne, Important Set of Three “Moutons de Laine,” Exhibited at the Art Institute of Chicago, 1967.

Cross-collecting might be popular these days, but amassing a genre-defying trove of art and design treasures wasn’t always in style. That didn’t stop one prominent French-American collector from acquiring an eclectic group of nearly 150 rare and covetable design pieces starting in the early 2000s. Among his holdings are a flock of Lalanne sheep, a bicycle by Jean Prouvé, and even a Marcel Breuer chair once owned by Peggy Guggenheim.

Now, ELLE Decor can exclusively share that Christie’s will auction off this major collection from the single collector, who is remaining anonymous. Called “Anthology of Design: Masterworks from a French-American Collection,” the sale will take place on December 9 in New York.

“Today, collectors love having the best of everything—they love to mix and match,” Daphne Riou, head of design at Christie’s, says. “But back then, people used to get very deep into just one area. His approach was unique at the time.”

Leading the auction are a trio of sheep sculptures by François-Xavier Lalanne, which are now hitting the block with an estimate between $3 million and $5 million. Originally made in the 1960s, the works are part of the second flock made by Lalanne, who formed half of famed design duo Les Lalanne with his wife, Claude.

“You never find flocks anymore,” Riou says. “This flock always originated together—it wasn’t put together artificially.” These particular sheep once belonged to renowned gallerist Alexandre Iolas and were exhibited at Lalanne’s first American show, staged at the Art Institute of Chicago in 1967.

“Having a Lalanne is like a trophy for a collection,” Riou adds. “And a woolly sheep is probably the most iconic piece that you can get.” She explains that Christie’s is offering the group exclusively as a set. The auction house deployed a similar strategy earlier this year, when they sold a quartet of Lalanne frog fountains as a single lot—and smashed the $3.5 million estimate to achieve nearly $6.3 million.

The Lalanne auction market has exploded as of late. Earlier this year, a single sheep from the Collection of Jean and Terry de Gunzburg at Sotheby’s sold for $2.3 million. “Once you have a Lalanne, you kind of get hooked,” Riou says. “The pieces have such a strong personality, and the older pieces talk to each other when displayed together.”

Other standouts include a rare Charlotte Perriand table created for the first Union des Artistes Modernes exhibition in 1930 (estimate: $600,000—$800,000) as well as one of only two bikes ever made by Jean Prouvé (estimate: $60,000—$80,000). The collector is also parting with the matching trolley that hitches to the back. “To have both the bike and the trailer in the same sale is quite unique,” Riou says.

Also featured will be ceramics by Hans Coper, Lucie Rie, and Georges Jouve; an aluminum Marcel Breuer lounge chair that once belonged to legendary arts patron Peggy Guggenheim; and vases and cabinets by Memphis Milano founder Ettore Sottsass.

Come December, collectors and design buffs alike will be tuning in. “Collectible design has really expanded in the last few years,” says Riou. “The market for design pieces and furnishings is hotter than ever.”

“Anthology of Design: Masterworks from a French-American Collection” will take place on December 9 in New York. Selected works will go on view in Tokyo from November 4–6; in Paris from November 19–24; and finally in New York, with highlights shown during the Fall Marquee Week.

Geoffrey Montes is an associate editor at ELLE Decor with a serious love for all things real estate and design. Before that, he worked at Architectural Digest, Galerie, and Preservation magazines, covering everything from jaw-dropping listings to world-famous architects and design events like Salone del Mobile and Homo Faber.

#315. Hollywood Mourns Presley Gerber After His Sudden Passing

Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber’s son died on Sunday at age 27

Presley Gerber, the son of Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber has died. The 27-year-old passed away at a rehab facility in Los Angeles on September 20.

Sources told TMZ that Presley’s death was the result of an overdose. At the time, the model was living with several people in a separate house on the grounds of the rehabilitation center. A family representative soon confirmed the death to TMZ and said they were asking for privacy during this “very difficult and painful time.”

Presley had previously spoken openly about his struggles with substance abuse, anxiety, and depression.

“Having struggled with mental health, depression and some other things that come along with that, I think that whether I help one person or a hundred people get out of that place that I was in at one point in my life, that's all I need to do,” he said during a 2023 chat on the Studio 22 podcast. He added of his mental health and addiction issues: “It’s a huge part of my life. It’s a 24/7 job and there’s so much to it. That’s what I really want to do: help people get out of whether you're depressed [or] struggling with something that’s having a negative effect on your body. … What I hope I can do is have made the mistakes for some other people, so they don’t have to make the same mistakes that I made.”

His sister, Kaia Gerber, praised him just weeks before to his passing for his openness about his addiction. “When something like that happens in a family, it kind of levels everyone,” the model and actor said in an interview.

“I think that’s also why I started to self-identify as the easy one and never wanted to ask for help. Because it felt like too much to have two children who were needing,” she added.

Kaia also called her brother her “greatest teacher” for showing her “there’s only so much you can hide from the world.”

Since news broke of Presley’s unexpected death, friends of the family have spoken out on social media to voice their sadness and pay their respects. See the tributes below.

Four weeks after her brother’s death, Kaia shared a heart-wrenching post on Instagram that opened with an old video of the two dancing as kids, and was followed by a loving, raw diary entry. “I’ve read all the books and I have none of the answers. My articulation is no match against this, the magnitude of losing you,” she began.

Presley’s parents also shared a loving joint statement as Kaia shared hers. In their post, they included a black-and-white photo of their son holding a pair of white angel wings.

“We are beyond heartbroken to lose our beloved son and brother. We feel so blessed to have had Presley in our lives for 27 years. He is a sweet, beautiful soul who loved and is loved, now and forever. We are so proud of how he showed up in the world, with kindness and vulnerability. We are grateful for the outpouring of love and support from so many who know and love our family and even strangers who feel our pain. Til we meet again our sweet boy. We love you forever, Mom, Dad and Kaia 🪽,” the statement read.

On her Instagram Story this Monday morning, Hilton shared a photo of herself with Presley, and over it wrote a lengthy statement, calling the model “such a beautiful soul,” and sending love to his family.

On his Instagram Story, Beckham posted a photo of himself with his late friend, and wrote: “I am so heartbroken. Presley you were the kindest and we are going to miss you so much x we love you ❤️.”

The reality star commented under Presley’s final Instagram post: “Love you brother.”

#316. 11 Smoky Colognes Perfect for the Cooler Months

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

Add some fire to your fragrance rotation.

You’re in a smoky jazz bar, sunk into a worn leather banquette. A saxophone whines while someone at the next table slowly puffs a cigar. Or, maybe you prefer something softer and more meditative, incense burning in a quiet room. Smoky colognes seek to bottle up those scents.

What makes a fragrance smell smoky in a good way, though? After all, you’re not trying to smell like you just smoked a pack of cigarettes—unless, well, that’s your vibe. Perfumers use notes like olibanum (frankincense) and myrrh, birch tar and cade oil, dark woods, tobacco, and leather to conjure everything from glowing embers to roaring fires. Smoke can form the deep, smoldering base of a fragrance, or it can appear as a light accent in something sweet, earthy, or citrusy.

Whatever your preference, there’s a smoky scent here you’ll love—even if you’re convinced smoky scents aren’t for you, one of these will change your mind.

If you know us, you know we’re absolutely obsessed with Maison Margiela’s Jazz Club from the brand’s Replica fragrance line. Remember that scene in the smoky jazz bar you just read about? That’s this fragrance. With some light citrus notes at the top, smoky tobacco, a bit of boozy rum, and some sweet vanilla bean at its base, it’s the perfect mix of sweet, spicy, and smoky. Oh yeah, and super sexy.

Leave it to D.S. & Durga to create a unique, addictive new scent you’ve never smelled before. We can assure you Cowboy Grass—the fragrance that put the brand on the map—is one of the most interesting fragrances you’ll smell thanks to an intriguing blend of fresh, herbaceous, woody, and dusty notes. The smoke here isn’t a heavy campfire smoke but a crisp, dry smokiness from smoky herbs and vetiver.

Fulton & Roark’s founders were inspired to create their newest fragrance, Cathedral of Ruins, after visiting the City Methodist Church in Gary, Indiana. What once was a lively church filled with people is now in ruins, a relic of the past with no ceiling. This smoky scent is an homage to the site. It features smoldering frankincense—the scent of sacred ritual—along with cypress and black peppercorn, rose oil and saffron, leathered woods and musk.

If you don’t want something too intense and heavy but still want something unmistakably smoky, Belnu’s Incense Antique is definitely for you. It’s actually quite fresh at the top, with lemon and a bright pop of spices, before it moves into a subtly smoky heart of tobacco leaf, incense, and patchouli. You’re left with a lovely blend of smoke, woods, and amber that isn’t too dense.

If you thought a smoky fragrance couldn’t have some fruity notes, or that a fruity fragrance couldn’t have a bit of smoke, this Tom Ford cologne is here to prove you wrong. Like the name suggests, Cherry Smoke is a bold blend of dark cherry and smoked woods. When you add warm florals and frankincense, you get quite the warm, confident scent.

One of our favorite luxury colognes for fall, Dries Van Noten’s Havana Gold is a gorgeous smoky amber scent that balances sweet licorice and smoky tobacco. Add in spicy cinnamon and creamy roasted tonka and you get a deep, warm scent that’s perfect for the colder months.

If you don’t have hundreds of dollars to spend on a luxury bottle, House of Twist has you covered. And if you like Tom Ford’s Tobacco Vanille, you’ll love this more affordable version. It beautifully balances sweet vanilla and creamy tonka bean with smoky tobacco and spices. You’ll want this cologne on your shelf come winter.

Arquiste’s Indigo Smoke is inspired by the traditional smoking of tea leaves in ancient China. The fragrance tells a story as it goes through its top, heart, and base notes—it starts with bright citrus and earthy vetiver, then moves into a heart of juicy apricot, smoky guaiac wood, and sweet vanilla. The base is where most of the smoke comes in with notes of maté tea, pine tar, and incense. If you’ve ever sniffed a box of tea leaves and wondered what it would smell like as a cologne, this is it.

This Villa Erbatium cologne is impossible to categorize into just one fragrance family, since it’s pretty much equal parts fresh, citrusy, smoky, and woody. It’s hard to imagine that all those olfactory families could work together cohesively, but they really do. You get fresh and citrusy notes at the top, then the fragrance takes a woody turn with pine and hinoki. The base brings in a smooth, smoky vibe from oud, incense, and leather.

Oud—a woody note derived from the resinous heartwood of infected Aquilaria trees—is a complex scent that has rich, leathery, and smoky qualities. In Lumira’s Noir d’Oud, the smokiness definitely comes out. Perfect for sweater weather or a cold winter night, it balances powdery florals and soft citrus with the smoky depth of oud.

Kilian’s Smoking Hot is one of our favorite spicy colognes, thanks mostly to its strong, nostalgic notes of cinnamon bark that give it a spicy kick. But aside from being spicy, it’s also beautifully smoky (I mean, it’s in the name) with notes of Kentucky tobacco absolute and literal smoke. But don’t worry, it’s not aggressively spicy and smoky—it also has a sweet side with notes of apple hookah and bourbon vanilla.
