#317. The 8 Best Supportive Slippers for Women, Tested By Editors and Footwear Experts

Our favorite pair on this list is from Vionic.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

The longer I work in style—and the more shoes I test in the name of journalism—the more I care about what’s actually happening underfoot, especially when it comes to slippers. I spend a lot of time on my feet at home, and nothing breaks the cozy spell faster than a cute-but-useless pair that goes flat after a few minutes and leaves my arches aching. These days, the best slippers for me aren’t just cute; they’re thoughtfully designed with real support, structure, and cushion to make all-day wear actually comfortable.

That’s where the best slippers with arch support come in. When choosing a pair, Derek Roach, owner of Orthopedic shoe retailer Flow Feet, says that there are a few key features that will help support your feet to reduce foot pain and properly position your feet for better lower body alignment, including heel pad cushioning, contoured insoles with arch support, heel backing, and a rounded toe box. To learn more about what to look for when shopping, keep reading for expert tips and picks along with editor-tested favorites we’ve personally tried ourselves and recommend for ultimate support.

“My favorite supportive slippers are from Vionic, as they offer a great mix of support and comfort,” says podiatrist Bradley Schaeffer, DPM. This slipper is also a favorite of mine, thanks to its incredible level of cushioning. It keeps my feet pain-free even after walking in it all day.

This style’s claim to fame is the adjustable closure on the upper of the shoe, which makes it feel like your foot is being hugged, and a padded footbed for added comfort. Plus, it features a flexible EVA midsole that provides maximum arch support, helping reduce stress on the feet, ankles, and knees, Roach says. Plus, that adjustable strap on the outside of the slipper offers a customized fit, so your foot doesn’t slide around during wear. It’s no wonder this slipper earned an APMA Seal of Acceptance!

What makes this pair stand out, though, is that it has an open back, so it’s a bit easier to step into than the Kuru pair. However, that means it doesn’t provide as much heel support, but I feel that the extra stability from the deep heel cup helps make up for it.

For an affordable, ultra-cozy house slipper, the Dearfoams Lacey Memory Foam Slipper has quickly become my go-to. At under $30, it’s noticeably plusher, warmer, and more supportive than most budget slippers I’ve tried, and I’ve been wearing them nonstop since I first snagged them about three months ago.

The standout feature is the memory foam cushioning, says Anne Sharkey, DPM, a podiatrist at Solely Podiatry in Austin, TX. It molds to my foot for a genuinely plush, cloud-like feel, paired with a fleece lining that keeps feet warm without overheating. I especially appreciate the heel and arch cushioning after long days on my feet. Plus, the soft knit upper gives it a lounge-all-day vibe that pairs perfectly with pajamas and sweatpants.

While it’s strictly an indoor slipper, the raised heel helps it stay securely on my foot—even while running up and down the stairs—and the durable outsole can handle quick trips to grab the mail or packages.

This moccasin from Kuru is designed specifically for people dealing with foot or body pain, or anyone looking for extra support in a slipper. It offers the support of an orthopedic sneaker while still providing the cozy comfort of a slipper, thanks to its cushy faux fur lining.

The pain relief in this slipper comes from the insole, which features a deep heel cup and built-in arch support. “The heel-holding feature absorbs shock as you move, reducing pressure and easing foot pain,” says Roach. “This is especially beneficial when walking on hard surfaces.” As for the contoured arch support, it’s a game-changer for people with foot issues like plantar fasciitis. Roach says that the deep heel cup and raised arch naturally position your feet for better posture and support. Putting your feet in this position helps distribute weight evenly, relieving strain on the arches and improving lower body alignment.

This shoe is def a bit heavier than other options on this list, so it might feel less light on the feet than some of the other options. However, its supportive features make it worth the chunkier feel.

This stylish mule slipper from Bombas is easily one of the chicest casual shoes in my rotation. The elongated oval toe and allover sherpa give it a cozy-but-polished look that works just as well for couch days as it does for coffee runs. I wear mine with everything from wide-leg lounge pants and leggings to cropped jeans.

Bombas nailed the cushioning here, Sharkey says. Thanks to a plush memory foam footbed that contours to the foot and softens impact with every step, this slipper is super comfortable and also helps it stay put while walking. Though Sharkey says the backless designs can still slip if you’re not careful—something to consider if you need maximum security. “Whether I’m doing housework (ya know, the mind-clearing Sunday deep clean) or getting ready for the day, I can always count on the Sunday Slippers when I’m on my feet,” says style contributor Lily Wohlner. “They’re the first pair I pick up when I’m in need of extra support.”

However, Wohlner wouldn’t recommend getting the lighter color (cream) because it shows dirt really easily, just like any white shoes would. After a few months, hers looked almost grey, so she switched to the dark caramel shade (the pair I own!) and hasn't had any issues since.

I was worried this shoe would make my feet feel super hot if I wore it for too long, but it’s been the opposite. Even though the inside looks like a thick, furry fabric, it's actually a blended fleece made from upcycled wool, which naturally regulates temperature. Wool releases moisture from your skin, and fleece is also moisture-wicking, so my feet stay cool and comfortable no matter how long I wear this cozy slipper.Wohlner also loves this pair, giving it major brownie points for style. “It’s my favorite when I want to feel put together and extra chic—even when I’m just lounging at home,” she says. “But don’t get it twisted, it still has solid support.” The MVP here is the platform sole, which makes it feel more supportive and cushioned. It also has a foam footbed, which keeps your foot in a comfortable position and offers weight distribution, helpful if you tend to feel a bit wobbly walking in a platform shoe.

Plus, if you want to wear it outside, you totally can—the bottom of the shoe is made with a lightweight sugarcane EVA outsole, which, IMO, feels similar to rubber and has awesome traction.

A few months ago, I desperately needed a new house slipper. So I decided to snag this pair from Fulton—and I couldn’t be happier with my decision. While you could totally get away with wearing this slipper outside (it’s super cute and definitely sturdy), I love keeping this pair inside and free from outside germs—IYKYK.

At first, I honestly wasn’t sure this pair would be a winner: the footbed was super uncomfortable the first day that I wore them. It felt like all the raised areas were in the wrong places, which made it a little difficult to walk. Had I known then that the Fulton website explains there’s a 10-hour break-in process, I’d have been way less concerned.

Lo and behold, by the following day the slippers felt much better—and only continued to get more comfortable as the cork footbed molded to the exact shape of my foot. I wouldn’t call this slipper plush by any means (though the wool upper is quite cozy), so if that’s what you’re looking for, the Vionic, Dearfoams, or Orthofeet styles might be better options. But this shoe makes my feet feel so good.

I’ve been suffering from some pretty gnarly foot pain from recently developed plantar fasciitis, but since I started wearing this slipper around the house every day, my feet feel brand new. My arches and heels feel way less achy throughout the day, and it no longer hurts to plant my feet on the ground first thing in the morning.

If you need a slipper with serious arch support, the Orthofeet Charlotte Slipper delivers. Plus, it comes with additional insoles and spacers for days when my feet need extra support.

The Ortho-Cushion system (which includes the removable orthotic insole, ergonomic sole, and fitting spacers) helps to customize the fit and level of cushioning and support. I didn’t realize before selecting my normal size that Orthofeet recommends ordering a half-size down for a more snug fit, but placing the smallest blue fitting spacer (1/16 inch) under the insole kept my foot feeling super secure. Even without any customization, I was impressed by the high level of cushioning that hugs my arches and feels really nice under my heels. The ergonomic sole not only has ample cushioning underfoot, but also the subtle “rocker” design, which refers to a little lift under the heel and toe so those two parts of the shoe don’t touch the ground when standing still, similar to a rocking chair. That shape propels you forward with each step and also helps take some pressure off the joints. Plus, the EVA outsole also has lots of traction patterns to keep every step feeling stable and secure.

I also love the faux fur lining and insole that feels super cozy and keeps my feet warm even while walking outdoors on chilly mornings. The suede outer adds to that cozy vibe and looks super cute. I initially wasn’t sure if this slipper would be my style, but I find myself reaching for it all the time when I leave the house for quick errands and coffee dates with friends. I have the taupe color and often pair it with ankle jeans and sweaters for a comfortable fall fit.

While it does run slightly small, the brand offers half sizes, and the slipper comes with customizable features, so I didn’t find it an issue at all. However, if you’re concerned about fit, I recommend ordering a half size down.

Hearst food producer Tina Martinez is on her feet for eight-plus hours every day, moving around the test kitchen at a rapid pace. But thanks to her Kane Dansko Clogs, her legs never hurt at the end of a long work day. “I started wearing these 15 years ago, and they have made such a huge difference,” she says.

According to Martinez, this slipper-clog hybrid provides just the right amount of style, comfort, and stability for someone who is non-stop and always on the go. “When I don't wear it, I notice a huge difference in how my body feels—aches, stiffness, cramping—and it's just not worth it at the end of the day.”

Where the support comes in is with the Dansko Natural Arch technology, which is an arch stabilizer in the midsole of the shoe that offers support, stability, and shock absorption. This shoe is also super breathable, as it has perforations in the upper. And, because the shoe is mostly made from EVA, a plastic material that's known for being lightweight, flexible, and durable, they feel super lightweight, too.

It only comes in one width—regular—so it might not be the best fit if you have wider feet. And since the material isn't very soft, it doesn't have much stretch, which can make it tougher for people with bunions or wider feet to wear comfortably.

If you struggle with foot pain, Roach says wearing slippers with a contoured insole is essential. These slippers are often equipped with that deep heel cup as well as a raised arch area, which relieves strain on the fascia in the foot and helps anatomically position your feet for improved posture and support. If you have specific foot concerns (like low/high arches or arthritis), consider choosing a slipper that can accommodate a custom insole.

Many supportive slippers have heel pad cushioning, which is an added material (gel or high-density foam) on the underside of the insole of the shoe at the heel area. “This feature helps to absorb shock as you move, reducing pressure on the feet and alleviating foot pain,” Roach says, adding that this is especially helpful when walking on hard surfaces.

Something else to look for is a slipper that has a back, so that the feet stay securely in place. “This feature also helps with ankle stability and reduces strain on the Achilles tendon and lower legs,” Roach says. “It also adds a layer of structure and support that will improve foot positioning and add protection to the heel.”

We found a few backless winners, because everyone deserves a pair of slippers that are easy to slide on. But, we made sure they still had other optimal support features that keep the feet feeling pain-free, like arch support or a platform.

A rounded toe box allows your feet to spread out naturally, which is especially beneficial for those with bunions or swelling, says Roach. Many of the options on this list are rounded, but we made sure the one square-toed option from Kuru runs wide, so it’s suitable for anyone. A wider toe box design gives your toes room to spread out naturally, preventing toe cramping and improving natural foot positioning and weight distribution.

As a style writer who’s been putting shoes through their paces for years, I’ve tested tons of comfortable slippers. To find the best supportive slippers, I consulted three footwear experts, one orthopedic shoe specialist, and two podiatrists to get pro-level intel on supportive slippers. They emphasized that arch and heel support are crucial, as is a roomy toe box. I then put 15 pairs to the test. Additionally, I consulted the WH editor I know is on her feet cooking and testing for eight-plus hours a day, Hearst food producer Tina Martinez, to get her favorite slipper picks for the kitchen, and style contributor Lily Wohlner, who might be the only person to test as many shoes as I do. #318. Don’t Throw Out Your Raked Leaves—Here Are 7 Smart Things to Do With Them Instead

Doing any of these will help your spring garden look so lush.

Golden yellow, vivid red, and bright orange fall foliage is one of the best parts of the autumn season. When the leaves fall off the trees and into your yard, though, they don’t look as charming—especially when it’s time to rake them into piles. Instead of putting fallen leaves into trash bags and taking them to the landfill, use them to your advantage and set your yard up to be beautiful and lush in the spring.

Keep reading to find seven things you can do with raked leaves besides throwing them away.

If your leaf layer is less than one inch thick, you can mow over leaves, breaking them up to add nutrients back to your lawn. Let leaves dry as much as possible, then go over them with a mower. A mulching mower, which keeps grass particles suspended to be recut into tiny pieces, is best. For a non-mulching mower, you can do a second pass at a right angle to chew the leaves up into small particles.

If you aren’t sure what kind of mower you have, search online for your model number. You can also change the regular blades to mulching blades on some mower models.

According to the National Wildlife Federation, you can rake leaves into garden beds to provide winter cover for beneficial insects, spiders, turtles, toads, and small mammals that spend the cold months under leaf litter. Moths and butterflies may also remain in their chrysalis stage in underbrush until they emerge next year. Keep these leaves whole for better coverage.

Use your mower’s bag attachment, or rake the leaves into a pile, then run them over with the mower a few times, as described above. You can then use the shredded leaves as mulch around shrubs and perennials, according to the University of Delaware. A two- to three-inch layer is sufficient to keep down weeds and reduce soil erosion. This mulch can also insulate roots and prevent plants, especially newly-planted shrubs and perennials, from heaving out of the ground with the freeze-thaw cycles that can occur during the winter.

Shredded leaves work best when tilled into garden beds, but you can use small amounts of whole leaves, if necessary. Till into beds in the fall, or spread over surfaces and work into the soil in early spring. You don’t need a tiller; an old-fashioned garden fork or garden spade works fine to turn over the soil a few times and bury the leaves.

You can invest in a composter or start a simple pile in a corner or behind a shed. You can even make an inexpensive composter by using chicken wire or hardware cloth. Then save a bag of leaves, called “browns,” to add to the composter throughout the next growing season to ensure the proper ratio of green and brown materials for efficient decomposition. If you don't have space in your own yard or garden, check with your local municipality; many towns and cities offer free leaf and yard debris pickup, which they turn into compost that's later offered free to residents.

If there’s an area in your garden that’s always muddy, or you want to convert a path from expensive mulch to free leaves, now’s the time to take advantage of the fall bounty. Again, shredded leaves are best. Whole leaves can be slippery, and they tend to mat down too easily.

A thick layer of leaves (either whole or shredded) can extend the growing season of many greens such as Swiss chard and perennial herbs like sage, parsley, and oregano. Simply mound leaves up three to five inches all around and on top of the plants. Keep the leaves in place by making small cages of chicken wire to contain them. You should be able to harvest for much of the winter, even in cold climates.

#319. The 55 Best New Shows of 2026 (and 3 More We Can't Wait For)

We've got murder mysteries, stories of love and lust, and lots and lots of Yellowstone. And that's just the beginning.

THE IDEA OF "new" television shows is a little bit of a tricky one these days. Sure, we do still get a fair share of truly new, exciting, unique ideas each year—just look at shows like Severance a couple years ago and Pluribus last year. Shows like last year's The Lowdown—rich, well-written, character-focused stories—still draw major stars like Ethan Hawke and still hit in a big way for audiences that watch it. If someone was being dramatic and wanted to say original TV was dead, dying, or on life support, there's plenty of evidence out there to throw in their face.

But at the same time, they aren't entirely wrong. For one reason or another, so much of the TV landscape—even shows we're really excited for—are based around something that in one way or another already exists.

Look, we can't beat too much around the bush: People love nostalgia, people love things they recognize and remember, and it can be pretty hard to get anyone to even attempt to give their attention to something new, let alone get really into it in the way we all like to with the very best of TV. Which is why we kind of have two different options here—people need to be really trusting of word of mouth and really aware when something is a really good new, original show (because no one likes to waste their time with a piece of junk), and we just need to really hope that all the remakes, reboots, reimaginings, and re-whatevers are good.

And they should be! HBO's Lanterns is modeled after True Detective, stars Kyle Chandler and Aaron Pierre as the titular Green Lanterns, and counts Watchmen genius Damon Lindelof as a producer. Of course it’s good. Below, we're going to keep track all year. We're charting the shows we already know are good. We're charting the shows we think might be good. And we're charting the shows that may not even come out this year, but if they do... they still might not be good. But, again, say it with us: We're choosing to be hopeful.

Netflix has been really good of late at the pulpy, potboiler, limited series, and His & Hers is the latest in that winning streak. The show follows a detective (Jon Bernthal) and his estranged journalist wife (Tessa Thompson) as they both hunt for answers when a local woman—whom they both have a close connection to—winds up dead. Based on Alice Feeney's book of the same name, His & Hers is exactly how this kind of show should be: Juicy, fun, easy to watch, and filled with really good actors.

In shrinking its story down to a more intimate one that takes place between the margins of major universe events, Game of Thrones takes a page out of the Andor handbook with A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms (based on George R.R. Martin's Dunk and Egg novellas). This short series, which follows a big, humble, anxious hedge knight (former professional rugby playerPeter Claffey)and his little friend/squire (Dexter Sol Ansell) is a true breath of fresh air for Thrones fans on both a story and character level. It's a delight.

Doesn't the premise of Ponies just sound fun? This spy series set in '70s Moscow follows a pair of women working with the CIA who find themselves at the midst of a vast conspiracy when their husbands both die under mysterious circumstances. And those women are played by The White Lotus's Haley Lu Richardson and Game of Thrones queen Emilia Clarke. Sometimes something that sounds like a winner just turns out to be one.

The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins (NBC/Peacock)

This show about a disgraced former football player (Tracy Morgan) and a documentary filmmaker following him (Daniel Radcliffe) comes from the team behind 30 Rock, so you know you're going to get several jokes per minute. Plus, Morgan and Radcliffe are no slouches themselves. The show had a special debut in January and will continue on a regular schedule later in February.

At the very least, Wonder Man is among the best shows Marvel ever made—and you could make a case that it's at the top of the list. Yahya Abdul Mateen II plays the titular hero (aka actor Simon Williams) as the kind of guy we love to love in this sort of story: humble, well-meaning, charismatic, and ambitious. But when he meets fellow actor (and former fake terrorist) Trevor Slattery (Ben Kingsley) and learns that his favorite movie from childhood is being remade by an acclaimed director, everything changes. Wonder Man isn't just a good Marvel show, but a good show about people, movies, and friendship period. Let's hope the MCU takes notes from what worked so well here and keeps the streak going in the future.

One of America's great cultural institutions made its grand return in 2026: The Muppet Show! This version—coming from executive producers Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg—is directly modeled on the original Muppet Show, which means special guests, musical performances, comedy sketches, and lots of fun. The first episode, which featured special guest star Sabrina Carpenter, was an absolute delight for anyone who likes Kermit, Miss Piggy, and friends (or who just likes laughing and having a good time). For now, it's just this one episode, but if the reaction is strong enough (and it seems like it might be), the show will come back in full.

The latest entry in producer Ryan Murphy's American Story universe is called Love Story, and follows the romance and life between Carolyn Bessette Kennedy and John F. Kennedy Jr. The show is, however, much better than that tabloid-y description sounds; Sarah Pidgeon, who plays Carolyn, is a star, coming off her Tony-nominated role in the Fleetwood Mac-inspired play Stereophonic. But Paul Anthony Kelly, who plays JFK Jr., is a real discovery—it's his first role (he was previously a model), and he truly feels like a reincarnation of the late attorney/magazine publisher/dashing public figure. Of course, this is a story that ends in an extreme tragedy—so if you get invested, be sure to have your tissues ready.

This wild documentary series looks at different disputes between neighbors, telling compelling and often escalating true stories that will truly floor you in the depiction of their very-real truth. Think about this less as a story about the legalities of these disputes, and more a look into some larger-than-life characters through an often trippy, absurd lens. The series is produced by Josh Safdie and Ronald Bronstein, coming off of their recent success on the Oscar-nominated Marty Supreme.

The new season of Scrubs brings back almost all of the original cast, including Zach Braff, Donald Faison, and Sarah Chalke. And audiences who love and/or remember that trio and most of the show's original dramedy premise should be pleased with this new version of the beloved aughts sitcom. The last season aired in 2010, so we're OK with calling this 16-years-later revival a 'new' show.

DTF St. Louis follows trio of languishing adults—played by the electric trio of Jason Bateman, Linda Cardellini, and David Harbour—who get involved in a love triangle and general madness that results in one of them winding up dead. You may think you have an idea of what you're getting into with this show based on the cast and that premise, but believe us—all of your expectations will be upended. DTF St. Louis is a tonal balancing act, a show that bounces between hilarious dark comedy, compelling mystery, and gutting, relatable drama. It's one of the best shows of the year.

The second age of Yellowstone begins in earnest with Marshals, a 13-episode drama that airs on CBS (and streams on Parmaount+ either simultaneously or a day later, depending on which tier of subscription you have). The series focuses on Luke Grimes's character Kayce, and how an old SEAL Team leader (Logan Marshall-Green) recruits him into his Marshal squad. There's at least one more Yellowstone spinoff coming in 2026—Dutton Ranch—and so this is the one leading the charge.

One of the busiest men in show business these days—on both the big and small screen—is Guy Ritchie, and his newest endeavor takes him back to a world he's inhabited a couple times before. Young Sherlock follows, well, a Young Sherlock Holmes. And as you can imagine, it follows Arthur Conan Doyle's famous detective as he solves a mystery. Hero Fiennes Tiffin plays the titular character, and Colin Firth is also part of the show's cast. If you're into that, you'll have a fun time! It's an enjoyable show.

The erotic thriller is back! Or, well, juicy erotic character study dramedy? Whatever we want to call it, Netflix's Vladimir is one of the year's most exciting new shows. Based on the novel of the same name, this show follows a longtime literature professor at a college (Rachel Weisz, constantly breaking the fourth wall) who finds herself in the midst of controversy when her fellow professor husband (John Slattery) gets caught sleeping with students. She takes this as an opportunity to switch things up a bit, and so she becomes smitten with her very sexy new colleague (Leo Woodall). It's a fun, zippy, juicy time—and kind of like if Deadpool was actually about a smart woman in academia who's spinning her wheels and maybe just a little bit horny.

From the mold of Ted Lasso and Shrinking comes Rooster, which stars Steve Carell and counts Lasso and Shrinking co-creator Bill Lawrence (who also made Scrubs and Cougar Town) as its showrunner. Carell plays an author who heads to help his professor daughter on a college campus... and becomes enamored with life there. Imagine Back to School but with some middle-age soul-searching and academia at play? Sure! HBO's got another winner on their hands with this one—and maybe Carell can get the Emmy that he somehow never got for The Office.

There are 29 books in the Scarpetta series, and, now, one TV show on Prime Video starring Nicole Kidman and Jamie Lee Curtis. The series follows forensic pathologist Dr. Kay Scarpetta (Kidman) as she solves a crime—but the show is so much more than just that. In a way, Scarpetta is destined to fit into Prime Video's roster of rock-solid procedural murder mysteries, which also includes Reacher, Cross, Bosch, and plenty more. But it's got a little bit of an extra chaotic oomph—helped out by the star-studded cast that also includes Bobby Cannavale and Simon Baker—that make it worth your while and a unique, fun show.

Sunny Nights, which aired in Australia last year, now makes its U.S. debut on Hulu. The premise is simple: A pair of siblings (played by the very funny Will Forte and D'Arcy Carden) want to start a spray tan business, but wind up entrenched in the criminal underworld. Whoops! Forte and Carden have been two of our finest comedic actors for a while—with ability to play depth in addition to that humor—and the show thrives when they're at their strongest. A solid watch for anyone looking for something light but compelling.

This series—from Yellowstone super writer/producer Taylor Sheridan—follows Stacy Clyburn (Michelle Pfeiffer) and her family, as they move from the busy, stressful world of New York City to a more rustic setting out in beautiful Montana after a totally unforseen tragedy. Kurt Russellplays her husband, Preston, with his usual endless charisma, while the supporting cast includes the likes of Matthew Fox and Suits star Patrick J. Adams. Sheridan does his usual zigging and zagging in The Madison—the tone can sometimes shift from very sad to zany and comedic, and, as usual, there's a bit of social commentary speechifying buried in almost every scene. But if you're on board with the writing style he uses in shows like Yellowstone and Landman, you'll probably be OK with it here, especially if you're ready for a heavier and more contemplative tone. This show was originally planned to be part of the Yellowstone connected universe, but those plans have since been changed; It's now a new story, but with that Montana setting, you still get to look at all sorts of beautiful landscapes.

After striking gold a couple years ago with Jury Duty, Prime Video gives its grand Truman Show-esque experiment another try with a second season called Company Retreat. This time around, we follow a regular guy who thinks he’s working as a temp for a hot sauce company and joining them on their annual company bonding retreat. Of course, everyone around him is actually an actor in a scripted, engineered situation. It’s a little goofier than the first season, but seeing how everything plays out is compelling, often very funny television nonetheless. A worthy follow-up, and, honestly, we might just watch these as long as they feel like making them.

Riz Ahmed is the creator and star of Bait, a show about an actor who thinks he's about to get offered the role of a lifetime—James Bond!—and the madness that spirals out of such a revelation. If you're a fan of Ahmed's (and why wouldn't you be?) this will be a fun ride.

Something Very Bad Is Going To Happen (Netflix)

Camila Morrone (Daisy Jones and the Six) and Adam DiMarco(The White Lotus) are set to get married in this horror series from showrunner Haley Z. Boston (who worked on the very underrated Brand New Cherry Flavor) and producers The Duffer Brothers. And not to oversell, but Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen is the best horror show I've seen in quite some time. While the show plays with familiar settings and tropes—you may think of Ready or Not or Midsommar during the show's eight episodes—it's so filled with Ari Aster-esque dread and stunning, striking camera work that it doesn't even matter. Horror fans are in for an absolute treat with this one.

#321. The Diplomat Season 4 Finale Is Shocking, Empowering, and Surprisingly Sad

The series hits close to home...until it doesn’t.

This story contains spoilers for The Diplomat.

It seems in every season of The Diplomat, the U.S. is pushed closer and closer to war, but this time it really feels like it. In season 4 of the Netflix series, all signs point to armed conflict. That’s literally the case for President Grace Penn (Allison Janney), who sent American warships to British shores for questionable reasons. How exactly did we get here?

It’s an issue that’s been snowballing throughout the whole series. At the start of season 4, we know that the U.S. has secretly taken a nuclear weapon, called the Poseidon, from a Russian submarine off the English coast. But Britain and Russia don’t know that—they think the Poseidon is still there. Britain finds out when Vice President Hal Wyler (Rufus Sewell) breaks the news to Prime Minister Nicol Trowbridge (Rory Kinnear) during negotiation talks. This, of course, infuriates Trowbridge, and the Americans worry he’ll rat them out. So, Ambassador Kate Wyler (Keri Russell) plays dirty and blackmails him into staying quiet. It shakes Trowbridge up. He resigns from his post.

The entry of his successor, Prime Minister Bethan Vaughn (Jodie Whittaker), changes things. Vaughn knows that Kate likely caused Trowbridge’s resignation. She understandably wants some space from the Americans. So when Russia tells her it wants to retrieve the bodies of the soldiers who died on the submarine (the one that had the Poseidon), Vaughn lets them. President Penn doesn’t like that. Once Russia sees that the Poseidon is missing, they will surely retaliate. Grace Penn will do anything to make sure they don’t find out. She orders Kate to urge Vaughn to change her mind, “or I will send warships to do it for her.” Grace means it. And as her husband Todd (Bradley Whitford), special envoy to the U.K., later relays, they will shoot at anything that tries to get past. Even civilians.

Grace’s threats give her cabinet pause. Sending U.S. warships to the U.K. and firing at Russian vessels that are simply retrieving their dead will certainly lead to nuclear war. But no matter who tries to reason with her, be it Kate, Hal, secretary of state Miguel Gannon (Miguel Sandoval), or her chief of staff Billie Appiah (Nana Mensah), she won’t budge. Remember, Grace was shot during a trip to the U.K. early in the season. Her harsh stance could be a message to anyone who thinks she’s now fragile; she wants to prove them wrong. Her husband Todd theorizes this much, but she brushes off his assumptions.

Her inner circle continues to try to change her mind as they travel to Italy for the G7 summit. Kate and Hal suggest a fair alternative: that the U.S. and U.K. retrieve the dead for Russia to avoid any possible violence, but Grace doesn’t bite. Stuart Hayward (Ato Essandoh), Kate’s deputy chief of mission and right hand, even files a report in the internal, sanctioned dissent channel to voice his disapproval. The forum was made for situations like this, but Grace believes Stuart took it too far. He is removed from his post in London and sent back to D.C., which means the future of his career—and his relationship with CIA lead Eidra Park (Ali Ahn), who will remain in the U.K.—is now uncertain. The twist only makes an already-scary turn of events even scarier. Now the president is punishing her own staff for exercising the First Amendment. How much farther will she go?

A lot farther, actually. The morning of the G7 summit, Kate learns that President Penn has already launched the warships overnight, without anyone’s knowledge. As the G7 assembly gathers, the president makes a statement to get ahead of the speculation. She reveals that the Brits have allowed the Russians into their waters, which she disagrees with. She admits that the U.S. is “prepared to fire on any country that interferes with our mission.”

It’s the last straw for Kate. In the middle of proceedings, she gets up, faces Grace, and tenders her resignation. She can no longer support the actions of the Penn administration, so she leaves. Moments later, Billie and Miguel follow. Finally, so does Hal—it’s not just a strong show of support from a man to his wife, but also a show of dissent from the vice president to his commander in chief. Together, the four of them face reporters as they exit the premises. The credits roll before we hear what Hal tells the press.

The bombshell raises massive questions for the series: What will happen when the titular diplomat is no longer a diplomat? Will anyone call the president’s ships back? Will a prospective fifth season focus on stopping World War III? It’s also strange to watch as a viewer living in America right now. A president overstepping her power, disregarding the First Amendment, and threatening war on a whim? Where have we seen that before? “It does feel honest to say these events are not happening in a vacuum,” showrunner Debora Cahn told Deadline about season 4.

In The Diplomat, the president’s closest advisers stand up to her and try to hold her to an ethical standard. And when she doesn’t meet it, they walk out. Who is doing that in real life? Somehow, two impeachments don’t feel like a strong enough response for everything that’s transpired.

The last scene of season 4 is meant to play out as an empowering one, and it is. With dramatic pauses and swelling music, Kate and her colleagues exit one by one, leaving behind their powerful jobs and making themselves targets for possible retaliation by the president of the United States. It’s TV. It’s Hollywood. But it’s also depressing to see how far away it is from our current reality. The Diplomat doesn’t have any dragons or magic, but it’s escapist in another way.

#322. Mummy Brie

No Halloween party is complete without fun, festive appetizers, and this one might have a better costume than most of your friends. The best part? This spooky starter takes less than an hour to make! Instead of wrapping our brie in a full sheet of puff pastry (like in classic baked brie), we’re going to cut the puff pastry into 1” strips and layer the strips around your brie to effectively “mummify” it. Enjoy it as a Halloween app at your monster bash, as a post-trick-or-treating dinner accompaniment, or as a spooky snack for your next scary movie marathon.

Recipe tips: While you can choose to stop at the puff pastry wrapping, we like adding eyes (made of sliced olives and peppers) to really amp up the scare factor. Add in the eyes before or after baking—they’re really more for decoration. You can really swap the eyes out for anything; feel free to use candy if you’d prefer this brie to be more of a sweet treat. In that case, we think a little hot honey drizzled on top would be incredible too!

Serving:We love serving this baked brie with crackers for easy sharing, but you can also serve alongside some toasted slices of a baguette to scoop your brie on top of. To amp up your presentation, you can also add some fruit or veggies to the tray.

#323. The Best Victoria’s Secret Angel Hair and Makeup Through the Years

These runway looks prove that Angels didn’t always have spray tans and bombshell waves

Naomi, Tyra, Heidi, Stephanie, Miranda, Gisele—then Alessandra, Adriana, Gigi, Kendall, and Bella. Over the years, every major supermodel has had the honor of walking in the Victoria’s Secret show, but not all of them rocked the signature golden glow and long bombshell waves. Ahead, we trace the history of the hair and makeup looks at the VS show.

Veronica Webb at the first-ever Victoria’s Secret runway show wearing a soft nude lip and natural hair.

Frosty pink lipstick at the first VS show in 1995.

Beverly Peele wearing her signature pixie cut and a shiny nude lip on the 1995 runway.

Rebecca Romijn takes her ’90s, bouncy, layered haircut to the VS runway in 1997.

Naomi Campbell backstage at the 1997 show wearing long curls, pink blush, and major lashes.

Model Stephanie Seymour wearing a voluminous half-up bouffant at the third annual runway show.

The next year, Seymour looked straight out of the ’60s with metallic-and-pink makeup.

Gisele Bündchen looks almost unrecognizable on her first Victoria’s Secret runway wearing minimal makeup (and natural tan lines).

Glossy lips and rhinestone eyes on Tyra Banks in 2000.

Adriana Lima makes a pouty Victoria’s Secret debut with layers of baby-pink lip gloss.

Straight hair was trending in 2001—as seen on Angel Heidi Klum.

Lip gloss and chunky highlights on Banks in 2001.

In the early 2000s, deep side parts reigned, even at the VS show.

Model Alek Wek wearing long, beautiful braids on the 2001 runway.

Klum takes bangs and tons of bronzer for a spin in 2002.

Banks also went with bangs for the 2002 show, paired with white eyeliner, graphic false lashes, and warm blush.

#324. ELLE Decor Checks In: Le Grand Mazarin

The Martin Brudnizki-designed retreat is like an art museum—with croissants.

Rarely does one go to Paris to see a hotel pool, but Le Grand Mazarin, the Martin Brudnizki-designed boutique retreat in Le Marais, is all about the unexpected.

First, there’s the location. Where many five-star hotels stake their claim further west toward the 8th arrondissement, Le Grand Mazarin is perched on a corner of Le Marais, the arty district in the 3rd and 4th. The history of the Marais is unlike anywhere else in Paris. Its first historic building, L’Enclos du Temple, was constructed by the Knights Templar in 1240. Beginning in the Middle Ages, it was a popular home for aristocrats and kept up its society credo through the Revolution. It was then taken up by the city’s Jewish population. In 1913, Hector Guimard, the architect behind many of the city’s most famous metro stations, designed the ornate Agoudas Hakehilos synagogue in the Art Nouveau style, now a landmark of the area. Since the 1980s, it’s been a gathering place for the city’s LGBTQ community and arts scene. Now, there’s a lively blend of historic and contemporary art and culture collaged together. There’s the Centre Pompidou (currently slated to reopen in 2030) and historic department store Le BHV. And the Marais has recently seen a renewed wave of popularity because of its vintage shopping and nightlife scene.

Le Grand Mazarin is an extension of that character. The family-owned hotel group Maisons Pariente brought in ELLE Decor A-List designer Brudnizki to design the space, made up of three historic buildings from the 14th century now connected into one larger building. His MBDS firm has a unique ability to create immersive, kaleidoscopic spaces that never feel overwhelming. Like Brudnizki’s other hospitality projects, including Annabel’s in London and the Cosimo restaurant in Florence, a sense of antique adventure pervades throughout.

Brudnizki was on hand during the renovations, including for the development of the pool, which required building two new subterranean floors. He commissioned contemporary artist Jacques Merle to paint the ceiling mural, which evokes Cocteau to tell the Narcissus myth by way of St. Tropez. There’s also a hot tub and a steam bath adjacent to the pool. The elaborate gym, where treadmills are lit by chandeliers, is across the hall.

If the fantastical lower-level spaces are any indication, the upper floors are a surreal wonder. In total, there are 61 rooms (7 suites and 54 standard) situated across six floors and connected through a serpentine maze of art-covered hallways. Brudnizki’s goal was to echo 19th- and 20th-century Parisian halls of culture, where artists, patrons, and intellectuals met. The art—all 500-plus pieces—punctuates every stay.

Even the beds feature their own masterworks. Each is topped with a canopy made by Art de Lys that resembles an Aubusson-style tapestry. The walls feature hanging art, each piece lit as if it were in a museum. Pastel walls, whimsical lamps, and fabric by Pierre Frey add a sense of play, while plush rugs from Pinton give the space a welcoming touch.

The artistic fixation continues at the hotel’s restaurant Boubalé. Locals, who are just as well represented as hotel guests, seem to step off of the street for a bit of sweet halloumi and creamy lobster linguini.

The special treat, though, as is the case with all great European hotels, was breakfast. The croissants were crispy on the outside, flaky on the inside, and those who wake up early enough are able to watch their preparation. Our recommendation? Start the day with the pastries—end it at the pool.

Dorothy Scarborough (she/her) is the assistant to the Editor in Chief of Town & Country and Elle Decor.

#325. The 5 Best Scalp Serums for Thicker, Younger-Looking Hair

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

Whether you’re looking to prevent thinning or gray hairs, these will help.

So your crown is looking a little thinner than it used to. Maybe your scalp is itchy and irritated—or perhaps you’re simply trying to get ahead of future hair loss or graying. Whatever brought you here, you’re far from alone. Hair supplements and preventative treatments are now firmly mainstream; I personally know plenty of guys in their mid-twenties who already take hair-loss pills, and there’s absolutely no shame in that. But if swallowing yet another daily supplement doesn’t sound especially appealing, or if you’re trying to attack this thing on all fronts, we hear you. That’s where scalp serums come in.

Think of scalp serum as skincare for your head and hair. It’s a lightweight, leave-in treatment designed to support a healthier scalp and create better conditions for stronger-looking hair. Depending on the formula, serums may use ingredients such as peptides, niacinamide, hyaluronic acid, and botanical extracts to moisturize dry skin, calm irritation, or help hair look fuller and more resilient. They’re not miracle cures, and not everyone will have the same reaction to every product, but they can certainly be a useful, low-effort addition to your grooming routine.

Even if you’re already taking a hair-growth supplement, there are serums that work in tandem with those to give your hair that extra boost it needs to look fuller and healthier. In fact, using supplements that work to block DHT (a hormone that shrinks hair follicles) and topical serums hand in hand is a pretty common approach. To help you find the right scalp serum for you, we rounded up the best ones on the market.

Nécessaire’s scalp serum is one of the best things you can use to not only improve the density and strength of your hair but also support your overall scalp health. The serum’s active ingredient is a peptide called Capixyl, which helps your hair grow thicker and more dense, and it also has a bit of hyaluronic acid in there to help keep your scalp hydrated. Plus, vitamins B3 (niacinamide) and B5 help strengthen the scalp’s protective barrier by locking in moisture, reducing irritation, and repairing damage to the skin’s outer layer.

While this serum can’t actually revive dead or dormant hair follicles, meaning it won’t help with hair regrowth, it can successfully reduce shedding and strengthen existing strands. But if you combine this serum with a hair-regrowth treatment, it can make for a successful holistic approach.

Like I mentioned earlier, many hair-growth supplements and other treatments are formulated to block the formation of DHT, the potent androgen hormone that causes hair loss from shrinking hair follicles over time, causing the hair growth cycle to shorten and eventually leading to hair loss. This Anti Hair Loss Spray from Patricks is designed to block DHT, improve hair anchoring, and add nutrition to the hair and scalp using active ingredients redensyl, capixyl, caffeine, and more.

It also works as a styler or pre-styler for other hair styling products and adds texture to your hair, so it’s a really useful product that truly multitasks. Use it in tandem with the brand’s RD2 Anti-Hair Loss Serum to really boost hair density and even target your hair follicles to restart growth pathways. Together, they make a great team.

If going gray (or the prospect of it) is what’s giving you grief, there’s actually a scalp serum that helps prevent—and even partially reverse—graying. Arey’s To The Root serum uses peptides that help with repigmentation, antioxidants that help reduce stress in the hair bulb, and natural extracts that nourish your roots and promote cell turnover. Still skeptical? Arey’s clinical study found that 88 percent of participants who used the serum had less gray hair growth after six months, and three times as many people who used the serum saw fuller, thicker hair as those who didn’t.

Like I mentioned earlier, many scalp serums work hand in hand with other products or supplements, and that’s especially true with Arey. In fact, Arey has its own anti-graying hair-growth supplement that works with the scalp serum to boost hair growth and combat graying. (And if you’re already taking a different hair-growth supplement, Arey’s serum doesn’t counteract any DHT-blocking properties your supplements may have.) You can even complete the set with the brand’s Good Night, Grey overnight peptide scalp serum that promotes hair growth overnight.

Act + Acre’s Stem Cell Scalp Serum uses some pretty amazing science to help revitalize your hair. It uses apple stem cells to help activate scalp cell regeneration and hair growth by protecting hair follicles from environmental stressors, and its active ingredients are retained with Cold Processing so they don’t get destroyed by heat over time. This serum also uses aloe vera and bamboo extracts to hydrate and soothe the scalp, and it’s also rich in phytonutrients that both revitalize hair stem cells and protect the overall scalp microbiome. A hydrated scalp can provide a better environment for hair follicles, which can lead to thicker hairs and less shedding. So if you have issues with both hair loss and an irritated scalp, this serum could be your new best friend.

Our favorite new scalp serum from the past year—awarded in our 2026 Grooming Awards—is this one from Sick Science. It’s a lightweight, non-greasy serum that hydrates the scalp (again, helping provide a better environment for all your hair follicles) and is packed with NX35 Growth Technology plant exosomes that improve overall hair health. Not only does it help with hair thickness and density, but it even has the potential to increase hair volume by reactivating dormant hair follicles. Its main ingredients include niacinamide, caffeine, rosemary leaf extract, sodium hyaluronate, glycerin, biotin, and panthenol, which work together to work on your hair at the molecular level.

#326. This Adjustable Weighted Vest Helped Level Up My Workouts Without the Tactical Bulk

Its body-hugging fit makes light resistance feel surprisingly wearable.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

The best weighted vest is one you’ll actually wear, and the Stakt Adjustable Weighted Vest makes that part easy. Instead of looking like tactical gear, its streamlined neoprene construction fits close to the body and feels more like a weighted garment.

One way I like to use weighted vests in my own training and with my training clients is to increase proprioception, or awareness of the body’s position in space. Because the Stakt vest distributes weight around the torso instead of loading only the shoulders, it can provide helpful feedback for connecting with the core and postural muscles during movement, particularly the transverse abdominis and pelvic floor.

The extra weight provides a physical cue that can help you feel which muscles are working, strengthening the mind-body connection. One of my clients reported that her balance measurably improved after she began wearing a weighted vest on walks and during her bodyweight workouts.

The Stakt weighted vest starts at six pounds, and a two-pound zip-on extension brings it up to eight pounds. I tested both configurations while walking, doing chores around my apartment, doing pushups, and adding it to a functional training workout. It delivered comfortable, evenly distributed weight that fits and feels more like an additional layer than a traditional weighted vest.

The vest hugs the torso rather than hanging from the shoulders, and that close fit makes it super comfortable for walking and functional movements. The aluminum front buckles feel sturdier than the plastic hardware found on many weighted vests.

The shoulder straps use a hook-and-loop adjustment system, so once I found the right position, it was a set-it-and-forget-it situation and the straps stayed put. I didn’t have to interrupt any workout to readjust them.

A porous mesh liner creates a comfortable buffer between the body and the neoprene, which adds some breathability. It also zips out for washing, which is a helpful feature, especially considering that this vest is worn close to the body. The liner can be machine-washed in cold water and should be air-dried. The rest of the vest isn’t machine-washable and can be cleaned with a sponge and water.

The vest also has a mesh pocket for small essentials. Its reflective detailing is minimal though, so you’ll want additional visibility gear when walking in low-light conditions.

The vest isn’t especially heavy. That can be a plus for walking, bodyweight exercise, or anyone new to weighted training, but it limits the vest’s usefulness for people looking to add heavier resistance.

My main issue showed up when I attached the additional two-pound section. Although it zips onto the bottom of the vest, it flapped around a bit during movement. A third buckle or another attachment point would have helped hold the bottom closer to the body. Some excess strap material also hung loose. These are minor details, but they stand out on an otherwise sleek, thoughtfully styled weighted vest.

If you’re looking for a premium weighted vest with a similarly sleek fit, I’d recommend checking out our best overall weighted vest, the Omorpho G Vest. Its weight is adjustable from 6 to 12 pounds, and additional snap-in weight panels can be purchased separately if you want to load up more.

Another option is the über-adjustable Hyperwear Elite Weighted Vest. The fit and weight can be adjusted so incrementally that this vest won our best adjustable weighted vest designation.

If you tend to be hard on your gear and want a weighted vest that fits around the torso and is also extremely durable, check out TRX Hexgrip Weight Vest.

The Stakt Adjustable Weighted Vest is best for someone who wants to add light resistance to walks and workouts without the bulk of a traditional weighted vest. Its body-conforming fit, secure shoulder adjustments, aluminum buckles, and removable liner make it both comfortable and practical.

A maximum weight of eight pounds won’t be enough for everyone, but if you want a sleek weighted vest that feels more like activewear than gym equipment and you’re prioritizing body awareness and light resistance over heavy loading, the Stakt weighted vest is a great option.

#327. Every 2027 Color of the Year So Far, From Moody Greens to Warm Earth Tones

In 2027, the design industry is going green—literally.

Color of the Year season is in full swing as brands continue to unveil their picks before the end of the year. While the 2026 shades focused on bold, passionate reds and creamy, near-white neutrals, this year’s choices, informed by cultural analysis, trend forecasts, and annual sales, are leading retailers across the industry to reach for shades that channel comfort, warmth, and a sense of ease.

For 2027, Earth is the inspiration. That’s right, the data shows that we, as a collective, are practically aching to touch grass. Lush greens, deep browns, ocean blues, and muted clays define the honorees, which make a stunning, nature-inspired palette.

Some brands are still planning their big reveal, and we’ll be here to report as new shades break, but for now, here are the colors of the year so far.

Valspar Color of the Year: Cottage Door (8004-38E)

Cottage Door (8004-38E), Valspar’s pick for 2027, is a cool, mid-toned blue taking the spotlight as a new era neutral. Meant to channel comfort, security, and respite, the slightly grey shade balances warm and cool undertones for an inviting yet versatile feel.

Dutch Boy Paints Color of the Year: Deep Rooted (311-7DB)

In line with the cultural shift toward joy-filled living, Deep Rooted (311-7DB) combines nature’s warmth with red and brown undertones to reveal a bold, earthy orange that pairs effortlessly with classic neutrals, inky blues, and smoky charcoals.

“Our 2027 Color of the Year feels alive with possibility while being rooted in the familiar warmth of nature. Deep Rooted offers a color that feels rich, grounding, and deeply human,” said Lisbeth Parada, Color Marketing Manager, Dutch Boy Paints, in a press release.

Behr Color of the Year: Grounded (T27-01)

Behr’s Grounded (T27-01) is a moss-inspired homage to the beauty of nature.

“It moves between moss and olive, with subtle brown undertones that give the green warmth and weight. There’s something sheltering about that combination, and the moss notes bring life,” says Kayla Kratz, Head of Color at BEHR.

According to data shared with House Beautiful, about 77 percent of Americans report feeling overwhelmed by the demands of daily life. Nature has become a common solace for many looking for a pause in the chaos. Through Grounded, folks can bring the serenity of the outdoors in.

Glidden Color of the Year: Artifact (PPG10-16)

Glidden’s Color of the Year, Artifact (PPG10-16), is a smoky, sturdy blue that’s meant to reset your home and mindset through grey and turquoise undertones. Paired with creamy neutrals, smoky greys, and pastel greens, the hue channels the serenity of a stormy sky, ocean waves, or a babbling creek.

Sherwin-Williams and HGTV Home Color of the Year: Celery (SW 6421)

According to Sherwin-Williams and HGTV Home, Celery (SW 6421) is the new butter yellow. Inspired by the humble garden patch, this organic, earthy, herby, soft hue embraces the growing shift toward the “lived-in” aesthetic and eco-inspired designs.

“Homeowners and designers are increasingly prioritizing wellness at home, seeking soothing environments that support mental health and overall well‑being. This shift has also fueled interest in eco-inspired design, with a greater emphasis on bringing elements of the natural world indoors through color, while a sustainability mindset is shaping preferences for hues that feel enduring,” said Ashley Banbury, color marketing manager at Sherwin-Williams, in a press release.

Clark+Kensington Color of the Year: Vantage Point (38B-4)

Inspired by the beauty of a clear sky, Clark + Kensington’s 2027’s Color of the Year is Vantage Point (38B-4). The serene, sophisticated, slightly dusty shade is a move toward new neutrals that embrace bold expressions of personality.

Little Greene Color of the Year: Marle (355)

Brown is primed for a comeback, and Little Greene knows it. For their Color of the Year, the eco-conscious, family-run luxury retailer selected Marle (355), a hue from the recently launched Colour Scales collection.

“Often dismissed as being a little dull, it’s wonderful to see browns being embraced and recognised as warm, earthy and indulgent shades that are perfect for delivering restful spaces that radiate balance and tranquillity,” said Little Greene’s Creative Director, Ruth Mottershead, in a press release. The complex shade balances bold yellow ochre, black, and red oxide tones to reveal a refreshing neutral filled with warmth.

Dunn-Edwards Color of the Year: French Press Coffee (DEBN07)

Dunn-Edwards Color of the Year is a full-bodied brown with deep plum undertones. French Press Coffee (DEBN07) channels luxury, comfort, and the coziness of routine.

“French Press Coffee is meant to feel like a slow morning: the ritual of a ceramic mug in your hands, warm light, a moment of stillness before the day starts,” says Lauren Hoferkamp, color marketing manager at Dunn-Edwards Corporation. “It's comforting and familiar, but elevated. Culturally, it reflects a real fatigue with the cool, pared-back neutrals that have dominated interiors.”

Minwax Color of the Year: Pickled Oak (MW260)

Minwax, a company specializing in interior wood stains, crowned Pickled Oak (MW260) as its 2027 Color of the Year. Gentle and warm, the ultra-light shade highlights the beauty of natural grain while pairing effortlessly with jewel tones, pastels, and neutrals alike.

Benjamin Moore Color of the Year: Webster Green (HC-130)

Webster Green (HC-130), Benjamin Moore’s 2027 Color of the Year, is a lush shade that channels historical roots. Rooted in an air of storied sophistication, the hue was originally launched in 1976 and was inspired by the 18th- and 19th-century design trends that came to define great North American architecture.

The green color family’s ability to adapt and transform makes it incredibly timeless,” said Andrea Magno, vice president of brand, color, and integrated marketing at Benjamin Moore, in a press release. “Sitting at the center point is Webster Green HC-130, a mid-tone that serves as a reminder of the past but feels right and relevant today.”

#328. The 83 Best Movies of 2026 So Far (and 21 More We Can't Wait For)

With Christopher Nolan, star-studded epic romance, and major Marvel events, this list is a behemoth. And it also features a movie called Behomoth!.

AS A HUGE fan and follower of both movies and sports, the former has one major advantage: There's always something to look forward to. As a fan of the New York Jets, I don't always have that luxury. As a fan of watching films, though, not only is there always something worth my time on the big screen or streaming, but there's always several flicks down the line that will sound great or intriguing for one reason or another. Will they all turn out great? Of course not. But with sports and movies alike, excitement tends to be all about hope.

After a particularly strong 2025—movies like One Battle After Another and Sinners proved to be true standouts—how does 2026 pick up? With strength and energy, that's how. The year has been filled with all sorts of great movies, from horror (like 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple and Obsession) to epics (like The Odyssey), to some pretty great comedies (like Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie and The Invite). It’s been a good year.

But we always like to look at not only what’s been good to date, but also what we can still be excited for—and that includes everything. We’re talking stuff on the calendar already, stuff we suspect could come out this year, and even stuff making noise in places like the Sundance Film Festival. Throughout the year, this list evolves from our most anticpated movies into our favorite movies, and always looks quite different in December than it did in January.

For now, we've got a lot we’ve loved, but still a lot to look forward to as well. Below, we've listed nearly 100 movies on our radar that we think you'll be really interested in seeing.

If you're interested in a killer chimpanzee B-movie slasher, then Primate is for you. The movie delivers what it promises. Ben the chimpanzee does some very terrible things on screen but it makes for quite an enjoyable experience.

28 Years Later: The Bone Temple is a direct sequel to last year's 28 Years Later. And while the great Danny Boyle doesn't return to direct, the movie is helmed by the more-than-capable Nia DaCosta and once again counts Alex Garland as its screenwriter. The real assets, though, are the movie's leads: Ralph Fiennes and Jack O'Connell are sensational, magnetic every minute they're on screen amidst all sorts of post-apocalyptic chaos. Bring on part three.

Here's a quick pitch for The Rip: Matt Damon and Ben Affleck. The longtime friends team up once again for The Rip, a cop thriller in the vein of movies you've probably seen several times before... but done particularly well. This twisty crime story involves a police team finding a ton of money in a stash house (the titular rip), and figuring out who may or may not be corrupt. In addition to our beloved duo, the cast is shockingly stacked: Steven Yeun, Kyle Chandler, Scott Adkins, and One Battle After AnotherAcademy Award nominee Teyana Taylor are all on board.

SAM RAIMI FANS, ASSEMBLE! For the first time since 2009, the master of gross effects and frenetic cameras is back with an original horror story in Send Help. Rachel McAdams plays a Survivor superfan who gets stuck on an island with her dickhead boss (Dylan O'Brien), and then the antics begin. Think Cast Away meets Misery meets Drag Me to Hell. It's great stuff.

Jason Momoa and Dave Bautista are a pair of cool dudes who, with The Wrecking Crew, set out and did exactly what they intended to do: Make a badass buddy action comedy. The movie finds the pair playing estranged brothers who reunite in Hawaii to investigate their father's mysterious death; From there, we get lots of jokes, and a lot of (very violent!!!) action. It's a good time! Honestly, if they want to make a couple sequels to this, I'd be her for it.

Part This Is Spinal Tap, part Josie and the Pussycats, and part Curb Your Enthusiasm, The Moment is Charli XCX's movie for anyone who enjoys her music, persona, or both. A really fun movie about music, stardom, and celebrity in 2026.

Pillion was technically released initially in 2025 (and was also included on our list of favorite movies of that year), but we didn't want to miss an opportunity to recommend it to people once again. This unique film follows a man (Harry Melling) who engages in an unexpected BDSM relationship with a biker he meets at random (Alexander Skarsgård). The movie is quite the tonal balancing act, at times funny, intense, raunchy, and heartbreaking, but it all comes together by the end. A delightful movie, and a great showcase for both leads.

The classic novel comes to life on the big screen once again, this time from Promising Young Woman and Saltburn director Emerald Fennell, and with Margot Robbie and Jacob Elordi in the lead roles. Fennell, an Academy Award winner for her work on Promising Young Woman, has both big fans and big detractors at this point—but her take her, while book purists haven't been thrilled, is a big, visually stunning epic romance. Robbie and Elordi are both up to the task as well, bringing a charged energy to roles that really need it. Alison Oliver, who recently shined on HBO's Task, is another major highlight in a supporting role. An original soundtrack from Charli XCX helps to set the anachronistic mood and feels like a real cherry on top.

This action-thriller, based on a book by Don Winslow, looks like a very solid entry in the genre that we're going to call "Somewhat Resembles a Michael Mann Film." And reviews have confirmed as much—the movie has often been compared to Heat, and while its tough to compare to Mann's 1995 masterpiece, we'll take just about anything in that vein. Look: If someone tells you there's gonna be a crime thriller in the vein of Heat with Chris Hemsworth, Mark Ruffalo, Halle Berry, and Barry Keoghan leading the cast, how could you not be on board?

One of our coolest directors, Gore Verbinski, makes his grand return with Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die—his first movie since 2016's A Cure For Wellness. If you don't know Verbinski by name, you should know several of his movies: the original Pirates of the Caribbean trilogy, The Ring, and Rango are among the standouts. Good Luck follows Sam Rockwell as a man who claims to be from the future and fighting off a rogue artificial intelligence. While the movie takes some pretty tough and labored tangents into on-the-nose satire, Rockwell's performance and the practical effects keep the movie afloat as a fun sci-fi romp.

Despite the title, you don't need to know anything else about Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie before going to see it. Sure, this story of two inept dudes in a band who just want to play music at a bar—and go through all sorts of ordeals, including time-travel, to do it—has existed before in both web series and television series form. But you can just go in and laugh and the absolute madness of the movie. Trust us—you'll have a good time with this one if you're into "madness that makes you laugh." This is a long-term passion project of Matt Johnson, who became well known recently for directing the underrated BlackBerry. His brash talent is again on display here.

We're always in on Glen Powell, and How to Make a Killing marks his first foray into A24's world as a leading man. This black comedy neo-noir comes from Emily the Criminal director John Patton Ford and follows Powell as a man who decides to take out a few members of his family in order to increase his chance at making a whole bunch of money via inheritance. The supporting cast joining Powell isn't too shabby: Margaret Qualley, Jessica Henwick, Ed Harris, and Topher Grace are all along for the fun.

The Napa Boys is a very specific cut for comedy fans. Remember when all those nondescript American Pie direct-to-video sequels were coming out? "American Pie Presents:.."? The Napa Boys imagines itself as one of those: self-impressed raunchy comedy with little tact—crossed, naturally with the wine bro nature of 2004's Sideways. As a result, we get a movie that presents as a sequel to a franchise that both has long been running out of juice, and, in our world, never was. If you get the truly absurd brand of parody being presented here, you're going to get a real kick out of it.

Hoppers feels like a throwback to the golden age of Pixar. Not only is it an original story (at a time when the legendary animation studio has often been leaning into sequels, prequels, and more), but it's a sweet and funny one at that. Following an animal-lover who uses Avatar-style technology to transfer her consciousness into a robotic beaver body that can discover what animals are thinking and saying, Hoppers actually turns into something of a conspiracy mystery story. With a voice cast that includes Jon Hamm, Dave Franco, and Meryl Streep among others, it's a fun one for the whole family.

Look. This is one of those movies that you really don't have to overthink. It's Alan Ritchson—Reacher himself—taking on a giant alien robot monster thing. This is as much of a throwback to '80s-style action filmmaking as we're ever going to get, and it delivers as promised. The fact that the rest of the cast includes staples like Jai Courtney, Esai Morales, and Dennis Quaid is just a bonus.

Undertone has been positioning itself as A24's next huge horror hit—and we'll see how it lands. The filmfollows a supernatural podcaster who gets sent some particularly spooky recordings; Its soundscape has brought tons of hype, with many calling it the scariest experience of the year. A simple premise like that sometimes makes for a very solid horror movie.

Based on the novel by Andy Weir(who also wrote The Martian), Project Hail Mary is a story of space exploration and a regular guy (played by Ryan Gosling) who gets involved. Phil Lord and Chris Miller (who are responsible for the Spider-Verse movies and directed 21 Jump Street) are behind the camera for this one, which has already proven to be a big, big hit. Gosling is basically on his own out in space for most of this, but it also includes a fun little alien guy named Rocky and a nice supporting performance by Anatomy of a Fall star Sandra Hüller. The visuals here are worth seeing on the biggest screen you can find.

2018's Ready or Not was one of the most fun horror films of the last decade, and now eight years later we get to see Samara Weaving's lead sucked back into the same twisted, bloody, violent games. The supporting cast—including David Cronenberg (!!!), March MH Flex star Elijah Wood, Sarah Michelle Gellar, and The Pitt's Shawn Hatosy—is fantastic. The movie kind of keeps with the form of the first Ready or Not, so if you liked that one, you'll certainly have a fun time with this one.

Forbidden Fruits follows a secret coven of witches operating in a shopping mall. Like, guys, some premises you just have to accept for how good they are and see them out. The movie is a campy, fun, twisty turny ride. Understand what you're getting into—a little bit of horror, a little bit of satire, and some fun twists—and it's going to be a good time.

Zazie Beetz (Atlanta, Deadpool 2) gets to lead her own horror/thriller movie with They Will Kill You, where she plays a woman who answers a help-wanted ad for a housekeeper in a luxury apartment building, only to find herself fighting for her life. The movie is pretty similar in tone to fellow horror/comedy Ready or Not 2, which we just talked about. But They Will Kill You leans more into its John Wick-style action and Kill Bill style plot, which sets it apart. The supporting cast, which includes Patricia Arquette, Heather Graham, and Industry star Myha'la, make it extra worth it.

#332. The New Sense and Sensibility Makes Jane Austen’s World Moody and Wild

In creating the sets, production designer Francesca Di Mottola treated the film “as if it were an original screenplay.”

Before filming started on the new Sense and Sensibility movie, director Georgia Oakley and stars Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles had a sleepover. The trio spent the night in the Dorset house that would soon play Norland Park, the estate belonging to the Dashwood sisters and their widowed mother at the beginning of the Jane Austen novel.

It was so the actors “had a feel for the space,” says Francesca Di Mottola, the film’s production designer. They played games in the house’s entrance hall, where a badminton game takes place in the film. “They lived the spaces a little bit,” she notes.

This adaptation of Sense and Sensibility, out in theaters this weekend, is a more wild, rustic take on the world of Jane Austen. As compared to the 1995 film, starring Emma Thompson and Kate Winslet, this version is a bit less polished. The estate’s rooms are somewhat damp and worn; the grass on the grounds is tall and unkempt; the colors are muted and moody, and Barton Cottage, where the Dashwoods move later in the story, seems nearly crumbling. All of that was intentional, as Oakley wanted to create a universe that was “earthy and tonal,” according to Di Mottola, and entirely its own.

Di Mottola read the book many years ago and has seen the previous film adaptations, but she didn’t return to them in preparation for this film. “I wanted to treat this as if it were an original screenplay,” Di Mottola says.

When she first connected with Oakley, Di Mottola, whose past work includes The Great and Mother Mary, was struck by her vision of the film as “almost a coming of age story.” She then put together a lookbook, which mostly featured paintings of nature from Austen’s era. “There’s a lot of gloominess and tonal paintings that’s all reflected in the movie,” she says.

It was paramount to Oakley that they film on location, not on soundstages. “The actors immediately feel like they believe in where they are placed. For Georgia, it was just so important, that approach,” Di Mottola says.

The film’s grandest location is Norland Park, the estate owned by the Dashwood family that they eventually have to vacate due to their patriarch’s death. It’s where the three sisters grew up, played, and spent hours wandering the vast grounds. The movie’s location team found a private house in Dorset, owned and lived in by a real family with three children, that had never been used in a film before. They loved the bones of it: a Jacobean house that had evolved over time, with a Georgian facade added on later.

“We had quite early on made the decision that we wanted it to feel really Georgian rather than other adaptations leaned more into the Regency style of interior decoration,” Di Mottola says. “We wanted to avoid brickwork and red brick.”

Di Mottola and her team redecorated almost the entire interior with antiques and pieces that she had professionally aged. They found and reupholstered Chippendale sofas, rented and hung up vintage tapestries, and even built a library and a courtyard outside. But they left most of the old, worn interior walls alone, as they were a major part of the estate’s appeal to Di Mottola and Oakley.

“When there was damp coming through, we were so happy to show that. We wanted it to feel like the family was wealthy, but not that wealthy that they were always restoring and keeping it perfect,” Di Mottola says. “The fact that the house had a real lived-in and aged feel to it really helped tell the story.”

Di Mottola similarly wanted the grounds to feel natural and unkempt: “We didn't want spaces or gardens or woods that felt manicured or planted. We wanted them to feel like they were wild beings surrounded by nature that they couldn't control.” She needed to be sure to tell the homeowners that, despite the cameras coming, she did not actually want them to touch or clean up any element of the estate.

“It happens to me in every single movie when I choose a location because it's wild and stunning. Suddenly, someone might think, ‘Oh, a film crew is coming. Let me cut the grass entirely,’” Di Mottola says, laughing.

After Norland was settled, the team turned to finding Barton Cottage, the small, dilapidated house where the Dashwood women move after getting booted out of their home. It took a long time to find the right spot: someplace close to the sea but still remote and rustic. They eventually stumbled upon a semi-abandoned cottage in the moors of Dartmoor in Devon. It was certainly untouched—but almost to an extreme. The team had to work extensively to make it safe for filming.

“We had to get rid of mold, and then at one point we almost lost the location because there was a threat of there being a bat living in the roof,” Di Mottola says. But, in the end, it was all worthwhile.

She continues, “It just felt absolutely perfect to tell the story that this family actually leaves this beautiful family house and finds themselves in the middle of absolutely nowhere.”

And it indeed did help the actors transport themselves into Austen’s era. So much so that they may not have wanted to leave it. As Edgar-Jones tells ELLE Decor, “I was obsessed with the interiors of this film.”

Annie Goldsmith is the senior editor and digital lead at ELLE Decor, where she covers design, culture, style, and trends. She previously held positions at The Information, covering technology and culture, and Town & Country, writing about news, entertainment, and fashion. Her work has also appeared in Vogue, Rolling Stone, and the SF Standard.
