#334. How Is Tenzing the Only Film About the Men Who First Climbed Mount Everest?

Seventy-three years after Everest’s first summit, Apple TV finally brings climber Tenzing Norgay’s story to the screen.

On May 29, 1953, a Nepalese Indian Sherpa mountaineer named Tenzing Norgay became the first person in the world to reach the summit of Mount Everest, alongside New Zealand climber Edmund Hillary. It was an amazing feat not just because of its physical difficulty but because of how Tenzing was able to achieve his dream against the force of both the mountain and the racial barriers of the time. Somehow, more than 70 years later, it’s a journey that’s finally been adapted to the screen.

Tenzing is a story about a lot of things, but the film—streaming on Apple TV this Friday, October 16—mostly centers on one man’s spiritual relationship with a mountain. Guided by accounts of Tenzing’s life from his son Tenzing Norbu, who served as an executive producer, breakout actor Genden Phuntsok captures his subject’s quest with true emotional depth. The film portrays the climber as a man who simply sensed his life’s calling from an early age and was compelled to reach the top. Phuntsok’s performance helps the viewer feel the hardships Tenzing faced along the way, thanks to the way he’s able to capture it all on his face. The actor’s pained eyes juxtaposed with his wide smile perfectly mimic the real-life photos of a mountaineer who gave everything to his pursuit of climbing Mount Everest, all just to “know her better.”

Wouldn’t you know it? The mountain makes for a damn good background for a film. You’ll likely ask yourself, How the hell did they film that? multiple times throughout the movie. Though the script is nothing new as far as emotional dramas go, director Jennifer Peedom’s breathtaking views of Mount Everest elevate the picture from the genre’s typical formula to create an intriguing mix of nature documentary and sports biopic.

Before directing Tenzing, Peedom spent the past two decades helming documentaries about Nepal and India’s Sherpa people—a group of Tibetan traders known best for their high-altitude farming and Himalayan tours. Nearly two dozen other Sherpas accompanied Tenzing and Hillary during their ascent. So though Peedom is an expert in the field, this film is her first true narrative work on the subject.

Tenzing covers the climber’s entire life leading up to the 1953 ascent, with the film picking up a year after he helped a Swiss expedition travel farther up the mountain than any group before. He’s living as a Sherpa, carrying hikers’ supplies as they trek for mountain-view picnics. But when British colonel John Hunt (Willem Dafoe) decides that he wants Norgay as his head Sherpa for another expedition, Norgay’s one condition is that he’s part of the main climbing team as well.

So as the crew departs on its journey, Tenzing is forced to split his time between translating for the Sherpas, who are paid a meager wage to carry his fellow climbers’ supplies up the mountain from one base camp to another, and leading the expedition with the Brits. It’s physically and emotionally challenging, as Tenzing straddles the racial divide like it’s a crevice in the ice.

We also travel back in time to flashbacks about how Tenzing became a climber—which aren’t always necessary—even when they display the prejudice he’s faced throughout his life. But instead of focusing only on how Tenzing’s exceptional talents eventually convince Colonel Hunt to allow him to lead the group, Tenzing also takes great care to paint his aims as a sacred act.

Does the climber’s position as a member of both worlds, and also of neither, tell a worthwhile story? Of course. Yet the more compelling narrative comes along once the film introduces his shared worldview with his climbing partner, Hillary, played by Tom Hiddleston.

Unlike Colonel Hunt’s aim to conquer the mountain like an adversary of war, Hillary and Tenzing hit it off over their shared love of the game. Hillary simply feels most alive when he’s climbing. Tenzing, in part, views the mountain as an ally. He calls it by its Tibetan name, Chomolungma, and the words “Mount Everest” rarely ever appear throughout the film. Tenzing understands that the man climbed Everest simply because he respected its power. Unlike the other members of Hunt’s team, who fail to reach the summit, his making it to the top is the only way to fully comprehend the mountain’s might.

You can see it in one of the film’s final images, as Phuntsok’s Tenzing reaches the summit and brandishes a tooth-filled smile. As a Western viewer, you might expect this moment to come with tears running down his cheeks and the bitter-cold winds freezing them onto his face. This stoic yet determined figure, accomplishing a moment he’s lived his entire life for, breaking down in tears and releasing his pent-up pain. Instead, Tenzing just grins—understanding something spiritual and powerful about the world that you can only learn by standing at the top.

#335. Why Weight Regain is So Common After GLP-1 Medications—and What Actually Helps to Avoid It

Nutritionist Kim Pearson shares the habits that can help to maintain weight loss long term.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Weight loss medications have transformed the way many people lose weight. They’ve had the biggest impact of anything I’ve seen in my two decades working in the field. But to me, successful weight loss means long-term weight loss—and maintaining that weight loss after coming off medication can be challenging.

Research shows that weight regain is common after stopping GLP-1s. One landmark semaglutide trial found that people regained around two-thirds of the weight they had lost within a year of ending treatment.

Recently, my hairdresser told me he’d lost 42 pounds on Mounjaro, only to regain it after coming off it. He went back on the medication and admitted he now feels nervous about stopping again—and he’s far from alone.

The good news? If you’re on weight loss medication and don’t want to stay on it forever, maintaining your weight loss naturally is possible with the right habits and support.

Weight regain is common after many forms of dieting—not just after GLP-1 medication.

Many of my clients have lost weight on different diets over the years, only to regain it later. So why does this happen, and how can we prevent it?

First, mindset is key. Whether you’re losing weight naturally or with medication, one of the biggest mistakes is reaching your goal weight and thinking the work is done. It isn’t. Maintenance is the start of a whole new phase, and one that requires its own strategies.

Yes, you’ll usually be able to introduce a little more flexibility compared with the weight loss phase, but key nutrition and lifestyle habits still matter.

From a dietary perspective, I recommend continuing to structure meals in the same way I outline in my new book, The Nozempic Diet. That means prioritizing protein (aiming for around 30g per meal), eating moderate amounts of healthy fats such as olive oil, avocado, raw nuts, seeds, and including plenty of fiber-rich vegetables.

Once you’ve maintained a weight you’re happy with, you can reintroduce moderate portions of carbohydrates such as beans, lentils, chickpeas, oats, potatoes, and brown rice.

I advise continuing to limit sugar, refined carbohydrates, and ultra-processed foods where possible. Many people find these foods less filling and more likely to trigger overeating once appetite returns after medication.

Sleep has a surprisingly significant impact on appetite and satiety. Aim for at least seven hours of quality sleep where possible.

Stress and emotional eating can also sabotage progress, making weight maintenance more difficult. It’s important to recognize when the urge to eat is being driven by emotion rather than genuine hunger.

Strategies such as spending time outdoors, movement, and breathing exercises can all help support nervous system regulation.

Holidays, celebrations and festive periods can all affect our weight. The goal isn’t to maintain perfect habits all year round, but to avoid an “all or nothing” mentality where healthy routines disappear completely.

The magic happens when healthy habits become part of your everyday life. They become so ingrained that they’re simply what you do—and something you naturally return to after holidays or celebrations.

Research shows that a significant proportion of the weight lost on GLP-1 medications is muscle.

While this may mean the number on the scales drops more quickly in the short term, it can make long-term weight maintenance more difficult.

Muscle is metabolically active, meaning the more muscle we have, the more calories we burn—even at rest. Losing muscle can reduce metabolic rate and contribute to the rapid weight regain many people experience after stopping medication.

If you’re currently taking a GLP-1, I strongly encourage you to prioritize protein intake and strength training throughout treatment. This can help preserve muscle mass during weight loss.

Another major factor is the return of appetite. While some people find it comes back gradually, others say it returns with a vengeance.

GLP-1 medications typically reduce both appetite and the desire to eat. Once that changes, it can feel unsettling—but it is normal.

Understanding how to structure meals in a filling and satisfying way, alongside establishing regular mealtimes, becomes especially important.

One thing I strongly recommend when maintaining weight loss is continuing to monitor your weight regularly—once a week works well for many people.

It can be tempting to avoid the scales, particularly if your weight starts creeping up slightly after a holiday or festive period, but staying aware of what’s happening can help you make small adjustments before things escalate further.

This isn’t about obsessing over the number on the scales—small fluctuations are completely normal. It’s about maintaining awareness and being proactive about managing your health and weight.

If you find yourself regaining weight after stopping medication, try not to panic or compensate with extreme measures. Avoid skipping meals, overexercising, or crash dieting. Some fluctuation is completely normal, particularly as appetite returns and your body adjusts.

The goal is to establish a way of eating and living that is realistic, enjoyable, and sustainable long term.

Coming off GLP-1 medication can feel daunting, but with the right strategy, structure and support, maintaining your weight loss is absolutely possible.

Kim Pearson is a nutritionist and founder of the Kim Pearson Nutrition and Weight Loss Clinic. Her new book, The Nozempic Diet (£16.99, Bluebird), is out 4 June.

#336. This Patina-Packed Texas Home Features Handmade Tile in Almost Every Room

See how the founders of Riad Tile decorate their home.

Naturally, this collected look couldn’t happen overnight. Nearly two years before the couple moved in, they started acquiring furniture and decor from artisanal boutiques, antique shows, and international markets. Travel played a huge role in the overall design language; a range of small objects and larger heirlooms they’ve accumulated over the years fill every room. Before breaking ground on the project, the couple and their three children even spent several weeks in Mexico City, a trip which helped reinforce their love of layered and imperfect interiors.

Butcher led the interior design, selections, and documentation for the project, while Kale was heavily involved in sourcing materials through his relationships with makers and suppliers around the world—a benefit that comes with the duo owning Riad Tile. “We spend so much of our lives thinking about materials—where they come from, how they are made, and the people behind them,” Butcher explains. “Building our own home allowed us to use those materials very personally and, in some cases, a little unexpectedly.”

As anyone can imagine for a couple who own a tile company, intentionally sourced stone for countertops as well as layers of handmade tiles can be found in most of the rooms, the unique materiality introducing imperfect dimensionality into each space. They had to think of these architectural details early on in the building process—patina and texture couldn’t solely be added through the furnishings.

“We used reclaimed wood, aged and natural stone, handcrafted tile, wide-plank oak flooring, and materials that inherently have variation,” Butcher says, adding that the entry and living areas specifically incorporate reclaimed fir overhead. These foundational finishes and materials were what Butcher obsessed over the most. “Furniture can move and evolve; those decisions are much harder to change.”

One look inside the home now, and no one would believe it was a new build. It’s a personal haven for the family of five, filled with items and elements that represent the couple’s lives, from their childhoods to their travels and their business. Craftsmanship is held in the highest regard and authenticity reigns, but nothing feels too polished.

“Our children live here. Friends are constantly here—our children’s friends are over a lot,” Butcher says. “Things get moved and worn and used. The house needed to be beautiful, but it also needed to absorb real life. I hope it feels collected, warm, and a little imperfect—because that's how we actually live.”

FAST FACTSDesigner: Aubrey Butcher of Gilded HeightsArchitect: M. Gray ArchitectureLocation: Dallas, TexasThe Space: A five-bedroom, five-and-a-half-bathroom new build spanning 6,490 square feet

The front door opens to the story of the Butchers. Photos, artwork, and objects collected over time and during travels cover the walls, layered atop a warm Phillip Jeffries wallcovering. “I wanted the first impression of our home to really make an impact—and boy does it ever,” the designer says.

Tucked within the vignette is a photo taken by one of Kale’s friends who would trespass into abandoned hospitals and buildings in junior high and photograph the stairwells. Butcher loves the grittiness of the image, now framed and leaning against the wall. Surrounding it are other pieces she found from street artists in Cuba and markets in Mexico, and a Berber necklace sourced in Morocco. The list goes on, all coming together to form a collage of the couple’s life together.

“More than anything, the entry sets up the story of the house. It's collected, personal, and influenced by the places we've been and the things we've brought home with us,” Butcher says. “I love that you understand that almost immediately when you walk through the door.”

Butcher kept the same material richness in this relaxed family room as the rest of the formal spaces in the home, though she chose pieces and fabrics that could handle everyday life with their three children.

“The furnishings are intentionally low and comfortable, and the mix of leather, textiles, art, and vintage pieces keeps the room from feeling overly coordinated,” she explains. It’s a great example of their design philosophy for the home: comfort comes first, but not at the expense of character.

Though the incredible stone mantel by Pittet Architecturals acts as the anchor in the living room, Butcher didn’t want the space to feel like it was arranged around it. She achieved her goal of a layered and sophisticated yet approachable space by choosing furniture, art, textiles, and other natural materials like wood and stone that all have personality of their own.

Surrounded by floor-to-ceiling windows, the dining room feels approachable while still conveying a sense of occasion. The substantial marble dining table is a necessary grounding point since it doesn’t have its own separate space, while the vintage chairs balance out the visual weight with an elegant, airy quality. The final dining spot is still special but doesn’t feel overly precious and can easily be used every single day.

Function was a non-negotiable in this kitchen for the family of five, but Butcher wasn’t about to give up on personality. It needed to “have the presence of a beautifully furnished room rather than read as a purely utilitarian kitchen,” she adds, especially since it’s extremely visible from the surrounding spaces.

With this in mind, she opted for black-stained cabinets and dramatic, timeless marble countertops and backsplash—a moody combination she’s long loved. The dark cabinetry creates depth, adding enough visual weight to ground the room without sacrificing the unique quality of the natural wood grain, whereas the Arabescato Corchia marble gives the kitchen a sense of movement. “Together, the dark wood and marble give the kitchen the weight and permanence I was hoping for, while still feeling warm and very much connected to the living space.”

The smaller footprint of the butler’s pantry allowed Butcher to be more expressive in her design. “I love rooms like this because they can carry stronger material choices without competing with the larger architecture,” she adds.

A countertop made from Arabescato Corchia marble ties this transitional space back to the kitchen, while the checkerboard flooring tile and deep green cabinetry give it more personality. The library ladder provides easy access to the open storage.

This moody, unexpected wet bar is just as perfect when the couple is entertaining as when they’re performing the simple ritual of shaking up a week’s end cocktail on a Friday night.

“The deep, earthy cabinetry and dramatic stone create an almost cocoon-like feeling, while the arched opening, glass shelving, and collected objects give it a sense of discovery,” Butcher says. With the warm glow of the Moroccan pendant light and the artwork they’ve picked up over the years, the bar has a transportive quality.

Inside this tiny room, Butcher chose a transportive theme. Bold, romantic wallpaper depicts an almost abstract Tuscan countryside scene, and a vintage chest—which she converted into a vanity with a marble countertop—gives the utilitarian space a layer of age and imperfection, as does the antique mirror hanging above.

“It's a tiny room, but that's exactly why I felt we could push it,” Butcher explains. “I wanted guests to open the door and feel like they'd stepped somewhere completely different for a minute.”

The serene but warm color palette in the primary bedroom gives it a classic and collected style, while the personal touches and layered textures feel much more relaxing to Butcher than an overly polished space.

The designer recognizes the wall of steel windows as “certainly a choice,” explaining that they bring a strong architectural element to the room, but the hand-dyed, ombré drapery helps to soften this feature and frame the trees outside like a piece of art. “I love how it almost disappears into the room while adding so much softness, movement, and romance,” she says of the curtains. “It completely changed the feeling of the space and creates a beautiful balance against the structure of the windows.”

The soft warmth of the bedroom is translated here as well, with an array of rich tones and natural elements. Opposite the bath is a stained wood vanity with a refined stone countertop, but it’s the tumbled marble floors that ground the space and really add a touch of drama.

“You still get the beauty and refinement of marble, but without the pristine, polished quality that can make a new bathroom feel overly formal,” Butcher says. The soft finish of the marble gives the entire bathroom a sense of age and a lived-in quality.

Butcher wanted something fun and youthful but not childish for her boys’ room. Blue walls serve as a beautiful backdrop for their books, artwork, and items they’ll inevitably collect over the years, and oversize geometric headboards add a playful sense of scale. The bedroom is aged up a bit with the vintage patterned rug.

“I also love the lockers at the foot of each bed—they're practical for two boys sharing a space, but they bring in that slightly industrial element that keeps the room from feeling too polished,” she adds. It isn’t a space they’ll outgrow anytime soon.

“The boys' bathroom was an opportunity to have a little more fun,” Butcher says. She chose a wallpaper covered in little Texas-themed illustrations, giving her boys something new to discover every time they look at it. Dark blue cement tile wainscoting and the warm wood-stained vanity ground the room and balance out all the personality, with refinement and elegance showing up in the marble countertop and brass hardware.

“Like their bedroom, the goal was to find that balance between youthful and lasting,” she explains. “It feels like their space now, but the foundational materials are timeless enough to grow right along with them.”

With layered antiques, bucolic wallpaper, and a beautiful bamboo bed frame, the guest bedroom serves as a little retreat within the home. Butcher wove in more natural textures with a grasscloth-covered nightstand and the woven Roman shade, while the antique artwork and vintage rug give the room some soul.

It feels traditional, but not overly precious; inviting, but not boring. “There are enough interesting details that every time you look around, you notice something else.”

“Nola is fun and full of light, and we wanted her bathroom to reflect that energy,” Butcher says of her daughter. An unexpected patterned tile covers the floor, grounding the room with a playful yet timeless element, while a soft green zellige wraps the shower, giving it a watery effect and creating a natural tension in the space. It’s calming, tonal, and a little bit quirky—a perfect bathroom that Nola won’t outgrow.

There’s no reason a hardworking space can’t be one of the most unique rooms in the house, Butcher says, which is why they used a striped zellige all across the floor and up the wall to give the space movement and intrigue.

The mural above the wainscoting is called Swan Lake, which is a subtle nod to Butcher’s upbringing as a ballet dancer. “It's one of those details that might not mean anything to someone walking in, but it means something to me.”

A room this fun needs some refinement, though, so the designer chose the watery blue hue for the cabinetry, brass details, and a marble countertop to straighten it up a bit. “I love that such a utilitarian space became an opportunity to do something unexpected and personal,” she adds.

Butcher worked with landscape architect studio Terrain Workshop and contractor Original Landscape Concepts on the outdoor aspects of their home, and she says that the custom stone coping and pavers, as well as the checkerboard pool, were an ongoing conversation within the team.

“It was a bit of a risk from an engineering, installation, and shipping perspective because the pieces were incredibly heavy, everything was custom, and the dimensions had to be exactly right once they arrived on site,” Butcher says. “There wasn't much room for error.” Plus, they were quite the investment.

However, the checkerboard tile especially is one of the most distinctive elements of the house and feels designed with the home, rather than a simple add-on.

Aubrey Butcher started her design career in the hospitality industry, working on everything from lobby spaces to the guest rooms. But in 2015, she made a shift to residential interior design and opened Gilded Heights, her full-service interior design studio where she creates authentic and storied homes for her clients. She lives with her husband, Kale, with whom she owns Riad Tile, and her three children in Dallas, Texas.

#337. How to Get Bigger and Stronger With Cluster Sets

Pushing to failure in straight sets isn’t the only way to chase your strength goals.

REP IT OUT, bro! Don’t stop now, keep pushing!

You’ve heard that one before, right? It’s the common refrain in every fitness class ever, and in the majority of the bro-centric, muscle-building gyms out there. It’s not bad, either. It’s a refrain that drips of old-school discipline, of classic ideas of strength and conditioning. The idea of reps upon reps upon reps is the one I grew up with, from classic bodybuilders like Frank Zane, Steve Reeves, and Arnold Schwarzenegger. Push through your set, because the reps are what matters is how it’s always been.

But it’s not the only way. Meet the cluster set, the underutilized training technique that can push you to serious power and strength gains. No, you won’t see a lot of people using this style in your average gym. But powerlifters use it, and top athletes train with it for sports performance. And science is increasingly on board with the cluster set, too.

YOUR MIND WILL take awhile to get used to the cluster set. Typically, you think of a set of 10 reps as a set in which you do one rep, then the next immediately after that, and the next immediately after that—and you keep doing that for the whole set.

With a cluster set, you take a 10- to 30-second rest interval between every rep, or every few reps, in each set. You’re still taking your traditional rest at the end of your set, too. Yes, that’s a lot of rest, but there’s a reason for that.

Cluster sets have been used in a handful of practices, but I believe they should be more widely utilized.

The big benefit of cluster sets: You’ll build serious short-term power—and that can make you stronger and more muscular in the long run. You may not see yourself as a power guy or heavy-duty strength guy, but building power in your one-rep max on, say, the bench press or squat or deadlift, can have more benefits than you think.

Look at the chiseled physique of your favorite NFL player. True story: Most of those guys aren’t training with massive amounts of reps, like the bodybuilding guys at your gym. They’re training with ideas like cluster sets, building power and strength. Power and strength matter, both directly and indirectly. You may not get the same pump from a cluster set on the bench press, but you’re building power that will let you lift heavier the next time you do a “standard” bench press workout.

Improve your metabolic recovery, hormone response, and overall adapative ability and you’ll build the strength and power to make your regular workouts better.

A key advantage of the cluster set over your regular zounds-of-reps sets is all that rest. It keeps you from completely fatiguing your muscles.

It also flies in the face of old-school training. Classic muscle-building tells us it’s all about time-under-tension, the amount of time your muscles actually have to be working instead of relaxing. Time-under-tension is important too, but here’s what’s more important: Quality of movement.

When you do 15 reps of dumbbell curls or bench presses, but your form begins breaking down, it’s not worthwhile. And if you don’t want your form to break down, you have to use lighter weights. Take a little break every few reps, though, and you get to reset and regain focus, hammering the form of an exercise while still using a heavier load.

Quality volume (total load lifted multiplied by total reps, if you’re into the math of it) has always been the critical factor in building strength, power, and mass over time. Cluster sets have shown lower lactic acid accumulation and less neuromuscular fatigue. This means you can use them to pile up much higher volume than you’d get in normal workouts.

THE MAJORITY OF the research has found the main benefits of cluster training around power and high-strength exercises. No, that’s not dumbbell curls and lateral raises. You want to do clusters with movements like squats, deadlifts, bench presses, and power cleans.

Strength and power are a relatively important prerequisite to a solid fatigue. If you’re going for that athlete or bodybuilder look keep this in mind: Those people can move serious weight. Cluster sets will help you move serious weight, too.

You don’t want to use cluster sets on every lift, only your biggest, most powerful exercises. An easy way to start: Build cluster sets in on your leg days, and your chest days. On all other days, train as you normally would.

You’ll only use cluster sets on the first exercise of each day. So on leg days, you’ll start with squats. Instead of doing, say, 3 sets of 10 to 12 reps, you’ll do two-rep clusters for legs.

You’ll do 4 sets of 6 total reps. Do 2 reps at a time. After each pair of reps, re-rack the bar and rest for 30 seconds. Then do another 2 reps. Re-rack it again and do another 2 reps.

Lots of rest? Maybe, but you’ll go heavy in this program. You should use 85 percent of your 1-rep squat max. Rest 3 minutes between sets. Follow that heavy squat with 3 sets of 8 to 10 reps of deadlifts, and 3 sets of 8 to 10 reps per leg of reverse lunges.

On chest day, you’ll also use clusters on the bench press. Make the bench press your first exercise of the day and load the bar with 87 percent of your one-rep max. You’ll do 4 sets on the bench. Each set will include 5 reps, except after every single rep, you’ll re-rack the bar and rest for 20 seconds. Rest for 150 seconds between sets.

Follow that with incline bench presses and close-grip pushups. Or if your training typically has you doing an upper-body day and a lower-body day, do dumbbell rows and pullups after that bench press.

Either way, you’re not simply training with cluster sets all day. You’re using them in small doses to get more out of your workout. It’s the smart way to grow more muscle.

David Otey, CSCS is a fitness writer, NYC-based strength coach, and Men's Health Advisory Board member who specializes in strength and hypertrophy protocols as well as athletic performance. For more on Otey check out www.oteyfitness.com.

#338. Connor Storrie Lets His Accessories Do the Talking at the 2026 Academy Museum Gala

Heated Rivalry’s Connor Storrie has been shooting the show’s second season—but managed to slip away from set to have a glamorous night out in Los Angeles. The star attended the 2026 Academy Museum Gala, wearing a black Saint Laurent by Anthony Vaccarello look featuring a tailored coat, high-waisted trousers, and a silk evening blouse.

But it was his silver accessories from Tiffany & Co. that added extra oomph to his outfit. Per the jeweler, he wore an Apollo brooch, a Tiffany HardWear necklace, Tiffany Lock small earrings, a ring in platinum with a cat’s eye alexandrite and diamonds, and a second ring in platinum with a diamond.

This is Storrie’s first red carpet since the Creative Arts Emmys, which he attended with his mother on September 6:

This has been a year of red carpet debuts for Storrie, who also attended his first-ever Met Gala in May. He spoke to GQ about why he wasn’t really nervous as he got ready for the event.

“I feel like people have explained to me a million times exactly what’s going to happen, and I’m like, I still don’t really know what that looks like,” he said. “I’m excited to see everyone’s looks. I’m excited to meet some people that I haven’t met before. I mean, a lot of people go, right?”

“It’s like 200 people or something,” he added. “So I think it’s going to be a beautiful zoo. It’s going to be some chaos, I can imagine. But yeah, I mean, I feel good. In these rooms, I feel like I’m able to just be myself and flow and move and chat and you just naturally fall into stuff. I’m excited to see everyone’s looks in person because I’ve historically always seen photos at the Met Gala afterwards. But half of these looks and dresses and stuff, you’re like, ‘Oh, I have no idea what that looks like in person.’”

“I feel very lucky,” he continued. “I think a lot of the women have it much harder than I do. I hear stories of girls being in their cars for an hour not being able to sit. I’m sure some of them have started whatever extravagant hair and makeup they have six hours before we even have to get ready to go. So I think comparatively to a lot of other people who are involved, I think I have it pretty easy.”

#341. Is the Kitchen the New Living Room?

Find inspiration for your next kitchen renovation.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE Decor editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Above: Eleven Madison Park chef Daniel Humm’s loftlike apartment blurs traditional boundaries.

Plenty of living happens in the kitchen. It’s a creative comfort zone for the culinarily inclined, the hub of daily activity for many families, and often the most crowded room at a party.

So why shouldn’t the design reflect that? We looked back at some of our favorite kitchens featured in ELLE Decor, from chef Daniel Humm’s to designer Joy Moyler’s, to share what elevates these spaces beyond elegant function and material beauty into inviting destinations. “Where is the kitchen?” Humm asked. “It’s there, but I don’t want it to be all you see.”

Instead, this kitchen—and the rest that follow—make us want to look twice and stay a while.

Gather ’round. No offense to the ever-popular, undeniably functional kitchen island, which, paired with some counter stools, can be a great spot for grabbing a quick breakfast, tackling homework with a snack in the afternoon, or perching with an evening glass of wine. But certain spaces call out for something different. A deftly chosen table with chic, interesting chairs can fulfill the same duties with a welcome lightness and ease, not to mention a ton more flexibility.

Wave goodbye to the island, and vast new design horizons open up. What type of table will you choose? Square or round? Legs or pedestal base? Wood, stone, metal, or another material? Perhaps one with expansion leaves for holiday gatherings or blowout buffets? Whatever style suits your fancy, add the right chairs and it’s a party.

Choose from, say, India Mahdavi’s colorful seating, a structured option from starchitects Herzog & de Meuron, or a classic collectible by Jean Prouvé. Be sure to make plenty of space for stemware, meandering conversation late into the night. Don’t say we didn’t warn you.

Circle: Aqua table by Fabrice Berrux for Roche Bobois

Turn any dinner party into a roundtable chat with this shapely Roche Bobois design—no guest is a corner outcast.

The more space-efficient cousin of the circle table exudes modern grace, as exemplified by this Scavolini table.

Contemporary and crisply balanced, this Antonio Citterio design for Maxalto can be a perfect fit for certain small spaces.

Classic American craftsmanship, warm cherry wood, and elegant midcentury style define this piece by Stickley

Don’t be afraid to play with pattern and palette when it comes to cabinets. “I’m always looking for new materials and putting them together in an unexpected way,” says Elle Decor A-List designer Laura Gonzalez of a Paris project, below. Go for restrained whimsy with Ikea’s -terra-cotta-color wave pattern fronts or Isla Porter’s crafty cutout design. And don’t neglect the backsplash, which can be a statement-making creative canvas unto itself.

Consider trading the parade of industry-meets-farmhouse pendants for something more sculptural, more fabulous to play against the kitchen’s functional identity. There’s no reason you can’t bask in the amber glow of a Saint-Louis crystal chandelier while frying an egg.

Utility doesn’t have to mean boredom. “The brief was to create a gathering place,” says Elle Decor A-List designer Joy Moyler of her project, above. Form and function stylishly blend in faucets such as one by the Danish brand Vola in a -powder-coated pistachio-green finish or a Dornbracht design that has stone handles. For something sleek and understated, Kohler’s minimalist four-in-one faucet offers a choice: still or sparkling?

Out-of-the-ordinary pulls are a savvy way to add personality.

These are stunning fusions of art and technology. Which style suits your tastes?

A selection of irresistibly idiosyncratic kitchen extras that we are longing to live with.

#342. Dietitians Say This Is The Best Breakfast For High LDL Cholesterol

Start your day with a meal that helps lower high cholesterol levels.

If you’re trying to pump up your protein or fiber intake, choosing a breakfast that helps you meet those goals is pretty simple. But if you’re struggling with high cholesterol and you want to start the day with a meal that targets and helps you lower it, the answer is a little more complicated.

High cholesterol isn’t caused by a single thing; it comes from a variety of factors, including stress, activity levels, sleep, and overall dietary patterns. That said, if you’re looking for a breakfast that sets you up for success, experts say oatmeal is one of the best options.

To learn more and get specifics on what to eat and why, we consulted registered dietitian and author Jessica Cording as well as Marissa Karp, registered dietitian nutritionist and founder of MPM Nutrition. Here’s what you need to know.

If you’re looking for a breakfast to support healthy cholesterol, both nutritionists agree that oatmeal is one of the best choices. Oats are high in beta-glucan, which Cording says is “a type of soluble fiber” that helps “reduce LDL (or bad) cholesterol levels.”

Karp agrees, adding that she especially recommends throwing in some chia seeds as an extra bonus, since they contain “even more fiber that will help lower cholesterol.” But for both of the nutritionists, this is just the starting point.

Oatmeal is mostly carbohydrates, and as beneficial as it might be for cholesterol, it’s not the healthiest breakfast on its own. “Pairing (the oats) with healthy protein sources is key for satiety,” Karp shares, and Cording agrees, recommending a “balanced meal” that also includes “protein and healthy fat.”

The best way to do this is to think of oatmeal as the meal's base, a solid starting point to build from. Cording recommends topping it with nuts or nut butter to add healthy fat and some protein, and for an even bigger protein bump, stirring in a scoop of protein powder or a dollop of cottage cheese or Greek yogurt. If you don’t like a sweet breakfast, she suggests making a savory oatmeal bowl with sliced avocado and your protein of choice.

Don’t panic. Oats aren’t the only breakfast food that can help you lower or maintain low cholesterol. Fruits and vegetables high in soluble fiber also help manage cholesterol, so a bowl of Greek yogurt or cottage cheese with lots of berries or banana is a great way to start the day. It might not provide the cholesterol-reducing beta-glucan, but remember: Your cholesterol reflects all the dietary (and exercise!) choices you make throughout the day. In the end, your overall diet pattern matters most.

#344. 'I Did Cardio Every Day for 30 Days—These Were the Surprising Changes to my Mind and Body'

Her stats prove the power of making exercise a daily habit.

If a desk job and evenings on the sofa are leaving you short of the expert-recommended 150 minutes of exercise a week, setting yourself a fitness challenge could help shift your routine. It did for Canadian YouTuber and former athlete Makari Espe. After deciding it was time for a change, she committed to doing some form of cardio every day for 30 days, to see whether moving more could improve her mood, stamina, and boost her VO2 max (the max amount of oxygen your body can use during exercise, and a key marker of aerobic fitness).

Alongside weights and mobility, she tried everything from running and hiking to water aerobics, spin, dance, and tennis, using the month-long experiment as an opportunity to find the forms of fitness she actually enjoys. Thirty days later, she noticed some surprising changes to both her body and mind—all of which were positive, and all of which led to her cementing a sustainable habit she will willingly continue. Here’s what happened.

A caveat: While cardio is brilliant for your heart, stamina and mental wellbeing, it's not the gold standard of exercise in isolation. To reap the full health benefits of movement, experts recommend pairing aerobic exercise with regular strength training and mobility work, like Espe did. Think of cardio as one piece of the fitness puzzle rather than the whole picture.

It didn't take long for Espe to notice a shift in how she felt. Just a few days into the challenge, she said she was feeling “energized, fast, and happy,” adding, “Wow, I feel great.” Even on days when she needed to dial things back, she noticed the difference movement was making, saying a rest day was “so needed” and left her legs feeling “so much better.” She also found herself rediscovering the joy of trying new things, admitting: “I'm having a lot of fun. I haven't tried new things like this in a really long time.”

As the month went on, Espe could feel her fitness improving in real time. “I'm not tired when I'm doing these things. And that feels great,” she said, noting that her aerobic capacity had noticeably improved. She also became stronger on her runs and discovered that walking and running were her preferred forms of cardio. The improvements were reflected in her VO2 max score, too, which rose from 33.76 at the start of the experiment (”good” for her age) to 37.37 (”excellent”) by the end of the challenge.

Running in particular transformed from something challenging into something she genuinely looked forward to. She repeatedly logged her “fastest run yet” and said one guided run was so emotional that she “almost cried.” Another run felt so good that she immediately wanted to do it again, calling it “a good way to start the morning.” By the end of the challenge, she was surprised to find herself declaring running “so hecking fun.”

The benefits weren't just mental. As she continued moving every day, Espe said she was “feeling really strong in the gym” and beginning to see the benefits of regular cardio. That said, she was also candid about the fact that the challenge wasn't always easy, admitting there were “minutes, hours, and days” where she felt “like garbage” and didn't want to keep going.

One of the biggest takeaways was learning that there is no single “best” workout. Instead, the most effective form of exercise is the one you actually want to do consistently. In search of activities she enjoyed, she tried everything from squash to water aerobics, which the latter turning out surprisingly enjoyable: “Nobody told me water aerobics was awesome.” Even workouts she found difficult were often described as “very fun,” and she finished several sessions admitting, “Never thought I'd say this, but I had a lot of fun.”

More broadly, stepping outside her comfort zone gave her a noticeable mood boost. She said she was “having a lot of fun” and found joy in activities ranging from pole dancing to hiking with her parents, adding, “It just feels really good.” After one dance session, she declared, “I feel empowered.”

The challenge also shifted her perspective on what her body can do. On tougher days, she reminded herself how “lucky” she was to have “a fully functioning heart and body” that allowed her to move in so many different ways. By the end, she hoped her experience would inspire others to move more in ways that make them feel “strong, fast, sexy, calm, and alive.”

Doing cardio every day taught Espe an important lesson: recovery is essential. After logging her slowest run, she recognized it as a sign that she needed rest, saying her legs were “so tired.” She also noticed when she was feeling “a little dehydrated” and “a little tired,” making time for stretching because, as she put it, “recovery is super hecking important.”

Perhaps most importantly, the challenge helped her create a sustainable routine. She found that aiming to fit exercise into shorter 20-minute sessions made it easier to get moving and said she had really “hit my stride.” By the end of the month, she saw “no reason” not to keep going, adding, “Only positive things have come out of it.” Her biggest takeaway? “A little bit of movement every day can make a huge difference.”

As Women’s Health UK’s fitness director and a qualified Pilates and yoga instructor, Bridie Wilkins has been passionately reporting on exercise, health and nutrition since the start of her decade-long career in journalism.

After earning a first-class degree in journalism and NCTJ accreditation, she secured her first role at Look Magazine, where she launched the magazine’s health and fitness column, Look Fit, before going on to become Health and Fitness writer at HELLO!

Since, she has written for Stylist, Glamour, Cosmopolitan, Marie Claire, Elle, The Metro, Runner’s World and Red. Today, she oversees all fitness content across Women's Health online and in print, spearheading leading cross-platform franchises, such as ‘Fit At Any Age’, which showcases the women proving that age is no barrier to exercise.

She has also represented the brand on BBC Radio London, plus various podcasts and Substacks – all with the aim to encourage more women to exercise and show them how. Outside of work, find her trying the latest Pilates studio, testing her VO2 max for fun (TY, Oura), or posting workouts on Instagram.

#347. The Meathead’s Guide to Atlantic City, New Jersey

Skip the buffet. Lift, ride, eat, surf, and recover like the locals do.

Meathead’s Guides are Men’s Health’s field manuals for doing a city right—where to train, what to eat, and when to go all out. Built around workouts, great meals, and local intel, these guides are for anyone who’s looking to do more than see the sights and pose for pics. Come hungry, bring decent shoes, and consider this a full-body itinerary.

“THE DAYS OF debauchery have gone by the wayside,” says Sal Spena, 56, owner of the Tennessee Avenue Beer Hall in the Orange Loop section of Atlantic City, New Jersey. Once upon a tide, the seaside town formerly known as the “Nation’s Playground” was best known for boozing, betting, and beaching.

Born and raised in AC, Spena says he’s been through “the bad, the ugly, and the indifferent.” Still, he can’t help but love this island where he and other longtime locals are ushering in a new era, aiming to appeal to younger beachgoers who care less about bottle service and more about bike rides and piglet yoga.

You don’t have to be a “gorilla juice head” from Jersey Shore to feel at home at CrossFit RDT or Island Gym. Heck, you don’t even have to be a “meathead” to enjoy the “Hungry Man” breakfast from Gilchrist Restaurant or a famous Italian hoagie from White House Subs. From PGA-level golf to nighttime volleyball, these days the active traveler is likely to be pleasantly surprised by all the hangover-free options available in Atlantic City and its surrounding areas.

Skip the standard hotel-casino breakfast buffet and start your day at Gilchrist, a beloved bayside breakfast spot frequented by locals and in-the-know tourists. It’s famous for its light and airy blueberry pancakes, the recipe for which Spena jokes he’s been “trying to steal for years.” (Can confirm they are addictively delicious.) Local lifeguard Christopher Pozza, 19, says his go-to order is the Hungry Man, a customizable combo of eggs, pancakes, choice of meat, plus optional home fries or grits and toast—all for $12.95.

Yoga teacher Michell Joga, 30, loves what she calls “gourmet Mexican coffee on the go.” Just make sure to check their Instagram before you go down to the shore to see where they’ll be posted up each week. The mobile espresso trailer frequents farmers markets, food festivals, and local parks. For a brick-and-mortar source of caffeine, Joga also likes Beat the Daily Grind, while other locals recommend HeyDay Coffee.

It may be the obvious item to put on your to-do list, but locals swear a stroll on AC’s historic five-mile boardwalk (the first in the country, FYI) remains a can’t-miss part of anyone’s AC stay.

“I hate running, but I love running on the boardwalk,” says Joga. “The boardwalk makes it worth it for me, especially in the summer.”

Don’t wanna do five miles on foot? Rent a beach cruiser and ride along the boardwalk. While summer might seem like peak seaside biking season, fall is actually the best time to ride. From September 16 through May 14, bicycles are permitted on the boardwalk 24/7. (In summer, you can only ride from 6 a.m. to noon.)

There are multiple beachside bike shops, but locals love North Beach Mini Golf & Bike Rentals. Hourly rentals start at $18 for beach cruisers and $40 for 1920s-style surreys. (North Beach also offers a Putt & Ride special, where you can play a round of mini golf before or after your ride for $5 off.) Pedal through Ventnor to Margate and, while you’re there, make a pit stop at Lucy the Elephant. The 65-foot-high wooden elephant used to be a speakeasy, but is now a National Historic Landmark. (Only in AC, baby!)

Many beachfront hotels offer state-of-the-art gyms, but if you’re renting a house and still want to GLT (“gym, tan, laundry” for the non-Jersey Shore fans), head to Island Gym. Located in Ventnor, DiCioccio describes it as a “very small community gym.” But don’t let the hometown feel fool you. The facility boasts “the largest selection of fitness equipment in South Jersey,” offers free fitness coaching from trainers, and is open 24/7. Plus, the price to join can’t be beat—you can snag a one-day pass for $15 and a one-week pass for $35. All group fitness classes, from traditional strength training to cardio-focused boot camp, are included in that price (the only exception is boxing classes, which cost an extra $10).

Joga recommends Leadership Studio for a sweat and stretch that won’t break the bank (especially good news if your wallet is hurting after a night at the casino). This nonprofit studio offers pay-what-you-can heated power and yin yoga classes starting at $10, as well as free outdoor yoga classes at the historic Absecon Lighthouse. In partnership with Angels in Motion Atlantic City, a nonprofit organization that helps people with substance use disorder, Leadership Studio offers free weekly Yoga for Recovery classes. These sessions are open to anyone in recovery from all addictions, as well as those who would simply benefit from a mindful practice.

High school chemistry teacher Alex Brigden, 49, recommends biking around the Brigantine Island Loop, a flat, 12.8-mile route along the Brigantine Seawall, about a 15-minute drive north of the Atlantic City boardwalk. It’s a smooth path with benches where you can pause and take in ocean views. Joga also likes the Pleasantville to Somers Point Bike Path, an 8.2-mile paved multiuse trail that runs mostly along an old railroad track through Pleasantville, Northfield, Linwood, and Somers Point, about a 10-minute drive inland from the AC boardwalk.

“People that do CrossFit will do CrossFit on vacation,” says Joga, who frequents this locally owned gym in May’s Landing. Sound like you? Expect a warm welcome from the RDT regulars. “They're a really great group if you’re looking for some kind of fitness community,” says Joga. “We've had people come from all over. If they're on vacation, they're still doing CrossFit.”

During the workweek, the gym offers up to 10 daily classes that each last an hour, so you can schedule a $20 drop-in class whenever is convenient for you. A typical coach-led session might include classic strength training exercises like barbell squats and kettlebell swings, as well as some Olympic lifts. Other classes might focus on simple and effective bodyweight movements (pushups, sit-ups, pullups, etc.), or cardiovascular conditioning on rowers and bikes. For the weekend warrior, Saturdays offer three morning classes from 7 to 10 a.m. followed by open gym hours starting at 10:30 a.m., and Sundays are full open gym days. The cost to drop in during open gym hours is also $20, and there’s always a coach on site who can help you get set up.

“A lot of people don't realize we have tons of golf courses in or around the AC area,” says DiCiccio. He, Spena, and Brigden all recommend Seaview Golf Club in Galloway (about a 20-minute ride from Atlantic City proper). It has two 18-hole courses—a “Bay Course” and “Pines Course”—each with a differing terrain that offers a unique challenge.

For a 9-hole course, beach equipment attendant Sean Burke, 17, recommends Hamilton Trails Golf Club in May’s Landing. During the summer, the club offers “Glow Golf” (essentially, normal golf but with a ball that lights up) on Friday and Saturday nights.

For a family-friendly—and refreshingly smoke-free—alternative to another night at the casino, Brigden recommends the Lucky Snake at Showboat. But it’s not just for kids. Adults can grab a bev at the sports bar before taking advantage of classic arcade amusements like pinball and “the world’s largest” Pac-Man game. While you can also drive like Dom Torretto in plenty of racing games, you may want to satisfy your real need for speed zipping around the IRL go-kart track out back.

Most locals fish off the jetties, according to Burke, but if the ocean dwellers aren’t biting, you can always try your luck bayside. In Gardner’s Basin, Highroller Fishing offers family-friendly back bay trips twice daily in the summer.

Come fall, those in the know participate in the Pat Erdman Memorial Atlantic County Surf Fishing Derby, the longest-running public fishing tournament in New Jersey. During the tournament, you’re allowed to drive on the beach and fish, says Nicholas DiCioccio, 30, the marketing manager for Visit AC, with prizes given out for specific species. The 2026 event began on September 28. Stripers, tog, kingfish, and sheepshead were the name of the game.

Find where the sand meets New Hampshire Avenue for “the most beautiful beach in AC,” according to lifeguard Adam Bailey, 21. He recommends the northernmost part of the shoreline for surfing because it’s less crowded than the casino-front beach areas, and it has free parking and showers. Seasoned surfer DiCioccio also likes a beach break called Crystals located near New Hampshire Ave. and the boardwalk, adjacent to the inlet. But he says that at South Carolina Ave., the beach is “particularly good” for catching waves, and Ventnor Pier is another convenient surfing spot.

Channel your inner Top Gun-era Tom Cruise at weekly beach volleyball open play in Ventnor. From May to August, the Ventnor Volleyball League hosts the event every Thursday from 6 to 10 p.m. “You play pickup games all night,” says Joga. “You can bring your kids, your coolers with your drinks, and it's fun.” But the fun doesn’t stop in the fall. From October to April, the league heads indoors and hosts open play nights every Friday from 6 to 10 p.m.. All year round, the cost to play is only $5 per person per night.

AC may be nightclub central, but if you’re looking for a more low-key way to spend your evening, head to the Orange Loop. Just a few blocks from the boardwalk, this up-and-coming part of AC is home to multiple bars and restaurants, including Tennessee Beer Hall. With a big backyard, this classic South Jersey sports bar is home to oversized Jenga, Connect Four, cornhole, and live music every Friday and Saturday night. But it’s not all fun and games—there are some legit (and yeah, still fun) fitness opps here, too. TBH recently hosted a piglet yoga brunch that owner Spena says sold out in less than a day. The enthusiastic response from patrons has him eyeing up potential future fitness-related events.

Bailey says the Italian sub is a must-order from this institution in the heart of Ducktown—AC’s historic “Little Italy” district. White House Subs has been serving fully-loaded hoagies to longtime regulars and visiting celebs for nearly 80 years—and they’ve got the pics to prove it. The small sub shop is covered in wall-to-wall photos of professional athletes, A-list entertainers, and notable politicians.

Another Ducktown staple is Dock’s Oyster House, which boasts the best happy hour in the city, according to Brigden. Every day from 4 to 6 p.m. at the bar, you can get $1.50 oysters on the half shell, as well as $1.75 broiled or fried oysters.

Even if you miss happy hour, you won’t be disappointed. DiCiccio says he usually starts with a corn and crab chowder appetizer, then orders filet mignon or potato-crusted flounder as his entrée. Heck yeah.

However you spend your stay in AC, there’s no better way to end your trip than with a recovery day at this award-winning spa in the Ocean Casino Resort. Spa director Nikki DeMarco, 34, says that men typically get the deep tissue massage, but she also recommends the athletic recovery massage. The spa also offers a specific facial for men that past clients have apparently called “life-changing.”

If you can’t get enough of the beach, you can always experience one of the spa’s “aquatic immersion experiences,” says DeMarco, such as a sea holistic massage and sea body scrub.

#350. Bored of Your Bathroom? Try One of These Four Design Trends

From monastic minimalism to juicy orange tones, here are a few big ideas for the bathroom.

Dive into the most innovative ideas for the bathroom, from the color of the season (it’s seriously bold) to looks that increase light or maximize zen.

First in vogue in the 1930s and then the ’80s, this is a look that loves a comeback (never more so than in the bathroom).

New York-based Darren Jett, founder of Jett Projects, refers to the glass-brick-clad wetroom in this SoHo apartment (pictured top) as a “voyeuristic bathing experience.” The floating marble vanity set against a floor-to-ceiling mirror increases that sensual, peekaboo quality. jettprojects.com

Glass bricks separate this artistic shower space, with its mosaic by Trufle Mozaiki, commissioned by Polish design studio Obiekty. The result is light that appears to dance with the same freedom as the depicted figure. obiekty.studio

Studio Karhard is the design team behind the look of legendary Berlin nightclub Berghain—the club that famously doesn’t have clocks so people won’t know the time of day. Here, it distilled its aesthetic into a more homely setting with industrial elements and curved glass bricks that bring an unexpected amount of light. karhard.de

Colored glass is an exciting take on the look: American design studio Charlap Hyman & Herrero boosted the sunshine in this Silver Lake home with an amber glow. ch-herrero.com

Take a sprinkling of brutalism, add a note of high-end spa chic and you have this pared-back aesthetic.

Belgian architect Nicolas Schuybroek is renowned for his minimalist approach—his studio has designed Aesop stores in Milan and London—so the calm simplicity of this bathroom in an Antwerp office block is true to form, with a font-like bespoke marble basin. ns-architects.com

It was the idea of the tokonoma (a recessed alcove in traditional Japanese homes for displaying art and treasured objects) that was the starting point for the form of this monolithic bathroom design in a Berlin apartment. Carved from Turkish marble, it was conceived by Studio Loes and presents functional bathing areas as moments of discovery. studio-loes.com

Tadelakt walls in a mineral-rich tone lend this compact shower nook in Mosley Thorold’s Clerkenwell project an atmospheric, even spiritual quality. mosleythorold.com

Here, design studio Kerstens chose materials that spoke to the beauty of this home’s French coastal setting. From the fossil-dotted muschelkalk limestone flooring to the Studio Loho bathtub, it’s a quiet reflection on texture. kerstens.be

Love an uplifting shower in the morning? This color will give you the vitamin boost you crave.

When choosing a color as bold as this shade of orange, it can pay to keep everything else simple. In this design by architect Caleb Mulvena from Studio Mapos, the “Isabella” tiles from DDS Tile are arranged in a precise grid and paired with white sanitaryware. studiomapos.com

For this bathroom in London Paddington’s Grand Hotel Bellevue, designer Fabrizio Casiraghi sought to pair a traditionally British style with an unexpected pop of orange. It’s a unique but complementary combination—the black-tiled picture rail bisects the walls, directing the gaze to the elaborately framed still-life painting. fabriziocasiraghi.com

Speaking of unexpected combinations: see this lavender-and-orange guest bathroom by Persistent Objects Interiors. From the lilac grout dividing the crackle finish tiles to the accessories, it’s a pairing that just works. persistentobjectsny.com

Doldam House in South Korea’s Seoraksan National Park by architecture firm One Aftr is a vision in orange that’s reflected in the two-tone Palet tiles that line its bathroom. one-aftr.com

The timber with the highly patterned grain continues its dominance with a takeover of the bathroom.

A collaboration between architects Agathe Lavaud of Agence Volta and Martin Massé, this Parisian home sees the pair lean into the property’s 1970s heritage with their use of materials. In the bathroom, that means travertine-topped, stormy burr wood, whose pattern is reflected in a mirror-clad wall. volta-architecture.com; martin-masse.com

Crafted from elm-root wood (a timber with a naturally intriguing burr pattern) and Chinese marble, the vanity unit in this Madrid apartment by Plutarco manages to marry two very impactful materials deftly. The terrazzo floor continues the pattern-maxing. plutarco.design

This home’s high ceilings are used to their fullest effect with bespoke burr-wood joinery by Bosko Projekty stretching the full height and expanding to form a vanity. A mirrored wall extends the space even further. bo-sko.pl

Created for Polish company Alex Concierge, this office bathroom is more memorable than most, thanks to Skandal Studio’s pairing of dark burr wood with a pop of Yves Klein blue to create a bespoke two-tone vanity unit. skandalstudio.com

#351. Chick-fil-A Is Launching Its First New Sauce In 10 Years—And Fans Already Have One Request

The newest addition arrives nationwide on November 16.

When it comes to fast food signature sauces, few are as iconic as Chick-fil-A sauce. Even with six other dipping sauces available, the eponymous condiment remains the chain’s most popular year after year. But a new sauce is hitting the menu that may unseat the OG.

For the first time in 10 years, Chick-fil-A is adding a new dipping sauce to its permanent lineup: Spicy Chick-fil-A sauce. The condiment has the same sweet, smoky, mustard-forward flavor as the original, plus the kick of spicy peppers. It will roll out nationwide at Chick-fil-A locations on November 16 in both dipping cups and eight-ounce bottles.

The fast food chicken chain rarely makes permanent changes to its menu. Chick-fil-A last updated its sauce selection in 2016, adding Sweet and Spicy Sriracha. So, naturally, fans are very excited about the upcoming menu update.

“Oh yay!! I can’t wait to try,” one Instagram user wrote. Another added, “I just know this is about to be bomb.

But the flavor profile also has plenty of people reviving one of the chain’s longest-running customer requests. “Bruh we just want a spicy option for the nuggets and tenders that’s it,” one Instagram user said. “Everything but spicy nuggets I’m irritated,” someone else wrote.

The chain added the Spicy Chicken Sandwich to the menu in 2010, and aside from a few limited-time launches of spicy chicken strips in select markets, Chick-fil-A hasn’t expanded the seasoning to any other entrees—much to customers’ chagrin.

But who knows? Maybe Spicy Chick-fil-A Sauce will bring us one step closer to turning up the heat across the entire menu.

#353. PSA: Your Yearly Flu Shot Could Also Have Much Longer-Lasting Benefits

There’s never been a better time to stop by the pharmacy and get your annual vaccine.

While we all know that getting a flu shot is good for you, in actuality, the matter of scheduling one and taking time out of your day can sometimes feel troublesome—especially when it seems flu season sometimes ends as soon as it begins. But now, new research suggests that getting a flu shot might offer long-lasting benefits beyond seasonal protection: It could lower your risk of Alzheimer’s.

The observational study, which was published in the journal Neurology, found a link between high-dose flu shots and a lower relative risk of developing Alzheimer's. It's a stretch to say that getting a high-dose flu shot will actually prevent dementia, but the findings join other research suggesting that staying on top of your vaccines—including the flu shot—could help to protect your brain in the long run. Here's what's behind this surprising link.

Meet the experts: Jacinta Anyaoku, MD, family medicine physician and founder of Hibiscus Aesthetics & Wellness in Katy, Texas, and Clifford Segil, DO, a neurologist at Providence Saint John's Health Center

For the study, researchers analyzed data from nearly 165,000 older adults who received either a high-dose flu vaccine or a standard-dose flu vaccine. The high-dose flu vaccine contains four times the antigen (the element that creates an immune response) of the standard-dose flu vaccine, per the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The high-dose flu vaccine is available to adults aged 65 and up.

The researchers found that people who were 65 and older who got the high-dose vaccine had nearly a 55 percent lower relative risk of developing Alzheimer's disease over the two years they were tracked for the study.

It's important to stress that the study didn't prove that getting the flu shot caused the lowered risk of developing Alzheimer's disease—it just found a link. The study also focused on older adults, making it unclear if the potential benefits extend to younger people. Still, doctors say the findings are interesting.

Previous studies have linked the flu shot to a lower risk of Alzheimer’s disease, but this was the first to compare two groups that received different flu vaccine types, points out Jacinta Anyaoku, MD, family medicine physician and founder of Hibiscus Aesthetics & Wellness in Katy, Texas. "This is significant because it helps reduce 'healthy vaccine' bias, the idea that vaccinated people are more health-conscious and engaged in their care, which could influence outcomes," she says. "In this case, both groups were vaccinated, and the group that received the high-dose vaccine showed benefit."

As for what drives this link, Dr. Anyaoku says it could be tied to inflammation. "Influenza leads to inflammation, including neuroinflammation, which could predispose the brain to changes that make Alzheimer's more likely," she says. "Getting the vaccine reduces the risk of influenza infection and therefore the associated inflammation."

The flu vaccine may also change the immune system that impacts a person's predisposition to developing Alzheimer's disease, Dr. Anyaoku says.

But there's still a lot of work that needs to be done to explore this, according to Clifford Segil, DO, a neurologist at Providence Saint John's Health Center. "Prior influenza infection is not a currently accepted pre-Alzheimer’s dementia risk factor," he says. "Most neurologists are not going to advise a flu shot to protect the brain, but will advise a flu shot to protect the lungs and general overall health."

Healthcare providers typically recommend getting your flu shot before Halloween. But flu season started early this year in many parts of the country, making now a great time to get vaccinated.

There are several types of flu vaccines to consider—Dr. Anyaoku suggests looking at CDC guidelines to choose the one that makes the most sense for your needs. "The potential added benefit of reducing Alzheimer’s risk is a nice bonus, but even without it, we already have good reason to recommend the flu vaccine to older adults," she says.

Carina Hsieh, MPH, is the deputy features editor of Women’s Health. She has more than a decade’s worth of experience working in media and has covered everything from beauty, fashion, travel, lifestyle, pets, to health.

She began her career as an intern in the fashion closet at Cosmopolitan where she worked her way up to Senior Sex & Relationships Editor. While covering women’s health there, she discovered her passion for health service journalism and took a break to get her Masters in Public Health. Post-grad school, she worked as a freelance writer and as The Daily Beast’s first Beauty, Health, and Wellness Reporter.

Carina is an alum of the Fashion Institute of Technology and the Yale School of Public Health. She and her French Bulldog, Bao Bao, split their time between Brooklyn and Connecticut. #354. How to Style a Fall Porch That Gives Guests a Warm Welcome

A roundup of outdoor-friendly pieces that set the mood before your guests even step through the front door.

With the backyard barbecues of summer behind us, entertaining moves indoors. Still, there’s one outdoor area that deserves your attention: your porch. It sets the tone for a gathering, creating festive, inviting ambiance before guests even step through the front door.

The four autumnal porch-decorating techniques below work no matter how small or large your space is, and you can put them all into practice after a single shopping trip at The Home Depot. What’s more, through November 3, the store’s Fall Savings event lets you spruce up your porch while spending less.

The best way to make a porch feel like a true extension of your home’s interior is to put down a pretty area rug. Rugs add color and warmth, and they’re an easy fix for covering up weathered floor boards or stained cement. Today’s indoor-outdoor rugs are more stylish than ever, with sophisticated designs such as medallions and florals that would be right at home in a living room. And they’re made with fade- and mildew-resistant materials that can withstand the elements yet still feel luxurious underfoot.

Give your porch warmth and texture by bringing in potted plants—no gardening or yardwork required. Don’t be afraid to use both real and artificial; today’s man-made greenery is astoundingly realistic, and mixing in live plants makes faux versions look natural.

Shorter days mean parties are likely to go until after dark, so be sure your porch has soft, welcoming lights. String lights are cheery and decorative and provide an overhead glow that’s softer than harsh electric or fluorescent lighting. To flank a doorway or light the way up a set of steps, use lanterns with battery-powered candles that will last all night. If you have an open porch, or one that extends to an outdoor patio, consider setting up a gas-powered mini fire pit that encourages moving the party out into the crisp fall air. Many versions ignite with the turn of a knob, so you can add atmosphere instantly.

Get creative with fall-themed embellishments including wreaths, garlands, welcome mats, signs, or wall hangings. The Home Depot carries a diverse assortment of seasonal porch decor, so you can create a rustic vibe, lean a little more modern, or land somewhere in between.

What should I look for in a rug for my porch?

Outdoor and indoor-outdoor rugs made with synthetic fibers such as polypropylene are the most durable, long-lasting options. They’re resistant to fading from UV rays, developing mold or mildew from damp conditions, and showing wear and tear from foot traffic. Look for rugs with a non-slip backing so they don’t shift on smooth porch floors or use an indoor-outdoor rug pad underneath.

What’s the best lighting for entertaining on a porch?

Though many porches have overhead lights installed, softer, indirect lighting sets a cozier, more welcoming mood for parties. Hang string lights around the eaves or along railings to cast an overall glow and use lanterns to gently light up dark corners or guide guests up steps when it’s dark out.

Wreaths and garlands are an easy way to signal the changing seasons or to celebrate specific holidays such as Halloween and Thanksgiving. And year-round, hanging baskets with real or faux flowers or greenery will make a porch look pretty for party guests as well as anyone passing by.
