#356. A Sicko’s Guide to Every Bloody Friday the 13th Movie

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

From summer camp to outer space and now to streaming television with Crystal Lake, this strange saga has taken all sorts of twists and turns.

FOR A SERIES ostensibly about a hockey-mask-wearing, machete-wielding killer, the Friday the 13th series is weird. From the original film, which doesn't really star Jason Voorhees as the killer (a favorite kernel of hack trivia nights nationwide), to fighting a Carrie stand-in to going to space, the slasher franchise has gone through many an identity crisis. Not to mention the wild legal battle over the rights to the names “Jason” and “Friday the 13th.”

For a series born from a cheap, down-and-dirty exploitation film meant to capitalize on Halloween’s success, it’s done quite well for itself. With ten main series entries, a crossover with Freddy Krueger, a remake, video games, and even a TV series, its longevity is nothing to sneeze at. The quality may ebb and flow, and the killer might not always be Jason, but the undead man himself has become a cultural institution. You don’t need to have seen the series to know what that hockey mask means and where it comes from.

As the franchise finds new life in Crystal Lake, a new series now streaming on Peacock and starring Linda Cardellini as Pamela Voorhees, we’ve given you a quick primer. Not all Fridays are created equal, but you’ll never leave an entry mad you saw it. Okay, you might be a little mad, but we’ll get to that.

The film that started it all. Or, rather, copied it all. Yes, Friday the 13th won’t win any points for originality, nor would you call it a “great” film. It’s stuck, though, for a reason, and the lion's share of that goes to its fun hook: A group of campers is stalked by an unseen assailant as the legend of the death of a physically deformed child, the young Jason Voorhees, 20 years earlier looms over them. One might assume the killer hiding in the shadows is Jason, somehow alive and grown up, exacting revenge on a new batch of counselors (including a young Kevin Bacon!), after the carelessness of the previous ones, but it’s not that simple. It’s been 40 years, so forgive the spoiler, but that “Ki-ki-ki-ma-ma-ma” you hear throughout the film? That’s not a fun little stinger on Henry Manfredini’s great score. It’s little Jason’s voice echoing “Kill Kill Kill, Mama” in the deranged mind of his mother as she slaughters her prey. Yes, it’s Mrs. Voorhees (Betsy Palmer) doing the killing in this one. It’s a reveal so iconic that it still surprises new viewers to this day, many assuming that Jason was the killer from the jump. In Crystal Lake, recent Emmy winner Linda Cardellini steps into Mrs. Voorhees’s probably-not-too-comfortable shoes, proving it isn’t just her son who will never die.

Speaking of her son, Jason takes over for his mother in Part II. Not quite the undead zombie he’d become, it’s revealed that the boy never died all those years ago, and now he’s out for vengeance after the death of his mother. It’s like a Russian doll of revenge. As a film, Part II is a touch better than the original, as Steve Miner (Halloween H20) is a better director than Sean S. Cunningham. However, it’s still learning how to become the series it would eventually be, so everything feels just a bit off. With the lowest body count of the series and a Jason who hasn't found his true mask yet, wearing a burlap sack instead, it still has a few tricks up its sleeve. A double impalement of a couple in bed is brutal, but it’s wheelchair-bound Mark who receives the most memorable death in the film. Before John Wick took a tumble down a massive flight of stairs, actor Tom McBride (or his obvious dummy) rolled backward through the rain with a machete sticking out of his head. It’s one hell of an image.

It took only three entries, but Pt. III, or 3-D, is where the franchise finally finds its identity. From the hulking Richard Brooker as Jason, giving him the burly frame he’d have going forward, to that iconic hockey mask, the pieces begin to fall into place. When you think of Friday the 13th, you’re likely thinking of the template set in Pt. III. This begs the question, though: Is it good? Well, that’s all a bit relative. Miner is back as director, giving the film a broader visual palette than the exploitation-heavy first film, but the 3D gimmick creates some unintentionally hilarious moments. The proceedings often stop dead so someone can hold an object, like a baseball bat, dead center in the frame for far too long, just so you really notice it. It’s not all bad, though: Jason lunging at the screen in all his three-dimensional glory is a sight to behold, and his kills leave a lasting impact. In fact, the first time we ever see Jason in his hockey mask on camera is in a very fun harpoon death that makes perfect use of the 3D. Oh, the theme bangs, too.

Oh yeah, now we’re cooking. Widely regarded as the series’s peak (for this writer’s opinion, you’ll have to wait a few entries), The Final Chapter is where Jason fully solidifies into the killer we know today. Kicking off the “Tommy Jarvis” trilogy (played here by Corey Feldman), The Final Chapter introduces the wrinkle that Jason is immortal. While the series always played around with death and what it actually means, here, it’s explicit. Jason, having been “killed” in Pt. III, sits up in the morgue and returns to Crystal Lake to continue his slaughter. Directed by action legend Joe Zito and featuring legendary VFX artist Tom Savini’s return to the series, The Final Chapter is the best the series’s gore has looked to this point, and Jason himself, played by stuntman Ted White, is a terrifying behemoth. It’s Feldman’s performance as Tommy, however, that drives it into all-time great territory. As a frightened child forced to confront the unimaginable, Feldman brings a real pathos to a franchise that had been missing up until that point. His descent into traumatized madness introduces interesting stakes for where the series could go if given the chance. Where it went, however? Well…

Viewed by many as the franchise's red-headed stepchild, A New Beginning is the platonic ideal of a slasher movie, if you can let go of the “Jason” of it all. That’s right, this is the Roy of the series. “Who’s Roy?” you’re asking yourself, and well, (spoilers abound), Roy is the copycat killer unmasked at the end of the film. See, after Jason’s “death” at the hands of Tommy Jarvis and his mother, someone had to pick up the mantle, right? Why not a vengeful father, furious at the death of his son? Derided at the time and still a point of contention for purists, there’s a lot of fun to be had here. Directed by exploitation stalwart Danny Steinmann, A New Beginning brings back an older Tommy (this time played by Jed Shepherd) after a stint in the psych ward. Back at the camp, he and a new batch of deadmeats are stalked by a hockey-masked killer all over again. The trashiest of the series (the nudity is out of control); if you can ignore the Roy of it all, it’s one of the more fun entries in the canon. Garish red blood splatters the screen, teens run for their lives, and the whodunnit is paced perfectly. Think of it as “the best episode of Scooby-Doo, ever.”

In this writer's eyes, the end of the Tommy Jarvis saga is also the best of the bunch. A course correction after Roy didn’t light fans’ hearts on fire, Jason Lives brings our favorite brute back via supernatural lightning. Tommy Jarvis, here played by Thom Matthews, just can’t get over his PTSD and desecrates Jason’s grave in a fit of rage. One metal post and a lightning strike later, Jason is back, better than ever. Proving that some guys would rather bring their arch-nemesis back from the dead instead of going to therapy, Tommy’s gaffe is our gain. Director Tom McLoughlin brings gorgeous atmosphere to the series, calling to mind the great Universal Monsters of the ’30s and ’40s. Jason, here played by C.J. Graham, is an absolute beast. As a superpowered zombie, his size and strength make him nigh unbeatable. The paintball slaughter is a ton of fun as heads roll, but Jason bending the sheriff in half is sickening, both in practical effects and sound design. You’ll immediately want to see about getting that spine of yours straightened out.

How’s this for a logline: “Jason vs. Carrie”? That’s the basic gist of The New Blood, and while it doesn’t quite deliver on that tantalizing premise, the seventh Friday is an underrated gem. Tina Shepherd (Lar Park Lincoln) is our telekinetic Carrie stand-in, a superpowered teen suffering from the guilt of having accidentally drowned her father as a child. The climax between them is a fun bit of telekinesis-vs.-brute-force shenanigans, but if there’s one thing The New Blood will be remembered for forever, it’s the series’s most iconic kill. Ripping a camper out of her tent, sleeping bag and all, Jason slams her repeatedly against a tree until she stops screaming. Fully embracing the cartoon sensibilities of slasher-in-arms Freddy Krueger, The New Blood is the series stretching for something new but definitely running out of gas. The wheels would soon fall off, but before they did, The New Blood also gave us our most iconic Jason, and the man most closely associated with the killer: Kane Hodder.

Or, Jason Takes a Cruise Ship. Here we are, the series’s nadir. With an iconic poster and premise, plucking Jason out of the campground and dropping him into New York City, how could they get it so wrong? Well, to start, most of the action takes place on a cruise ship, where a group of NYC high schoolers is celebrating graduation. Then, when the big man finally gets into the city... the film is largely shot in Vancouver. A real whiff on a great idea, Jason Takes Manhattan also marks the last film in the series produced by Paramount. The killer would soon be shipped over to New Line, losing the Friday the 13th titling in the process. It’s not all bad, though—Hodder’s Jason is a thing of beauty: a massive, dripping-wet horror, and perhaps his best look yet. We’re also given a wonderful shot-on-location moment in Times Square, briefly delivering on the promise of Jason stalking those gritty streets.

The second “finale” in the series, The Final Friday is Jason at his most bizarre. Part of the reason for that is that Jason isn’t really in it. Sure, Kane Hodder shows up for his third straight outing in a few brief scenes as the killer, but in this entry, “Jason” becomes an entity passed from one person to the next. “How?”, you may be wondering. Well, a giant parasitic worm, known as the Hellbaby, of course. Another divisive film in the canon, there’s a lot to like in this one. You can see how Jason fans would be up in arms over their favorite slasher largely missing from the film, but how can you not love the introduction of a demon bounty hunter in the form of Creighton Duke? It isn’t for everyone, but Jason Goes to Hell is the series at its most surreal, silly, and expansive. Fan theories suggest the film is in the same universe as Sam Raimi’s Evil Dead trilogy, and director Adam Marcus has confirmed it. That’s not the only franchise Jason crosses paths with in his “final” outing: As the sun sets on the series, Jason having been defeated once and for all, pleasant music plays over Jason’s mask disappearing in the sand. Suddenly, a famous bladed glove rips through the ground and pulls Jason’s mask into hell. A familiar cackle bellows as the screen goes dark. An exciting tease, but one we’d have to wait a decade to see realized.

Can you really call yourself a long-running franchise unless you’ve gone to space? The Leprechaun did it. A few of Dom Toretto’s “family” members made a brief visit in Fast 9. In Jason’s tenth go-around, after many deaths and finales, where else could he go but to space? Beginning in the “far-off” future of 2010, Camp Crystal Lake is now home to a research facility. To understand the creature that is Jason (again played by Kane Hodder in his fourth and final appearance), the facility holds him under surveillance. As these things are wont to go, Jason breaks free, killing everyone (including the facility’s leader, David Cronenberg) before falling into a chamber that freezes him for almost five hundred years. Thawing out in space, Jason goes on a killing spree around the space station, trading in camp counselors for Sci-Fi Channel rejects. Look, nobody is calling Jason X a “good” movie. Its overwhelming charm, however, is hard to deny. Where else will you find Jason vs. Sexy Android or Jason being upgraded to “Uber Jason”? Sadly, the latter’s leather-clad, silver-masked appearance is all too brief, but don’t let the poor reputation fool you: Jason X is an utter delight.

As promised by Jason Goes to Hell, the Friday series proper finally ends with the main man battling Freddy. Directed by Hong Kong action legend Ronny Yu, Freddy vs. Jason surprisingly blends the two series’ canons into something tangible. Like a perverse Santa Claus, Freddy (now in Hell) has lost his powers because the children no longer believe in him. Invading Jason’s (now played by Ken Kirzinger) dreams, he manipulates the brute into heading over to Springwood, Freddy’s killing grounds, to ramp up the killing again. If Jason can spread fear around town, maybe people will mistake him for Freddy and believe in him again. It’s a foolproof plan. Once resurrected in the real world, all hell breaks loose, and we get less a horror film and more a WWE-style beatdown between the two legends. After two decades in development hell (one version even included Bruce Campbell’s Ash from the Evil Dead series), the hype was nuclear for these two to finally meet. They even had a classic weigh-in in Las Vegas to promote the film. Thanks to its pure, unadulterated fight scenes, FvJ exceeded its lofty expectations. To date, it’s the final entry into the bizarre, nonsensical Jason timeline—but don’t worry, we’re not quite done just yet.

The films—for now—end where we began: Friday the 13th. In the 2000s, Michael Bay had an idea: remake horror classics. This being Bay, they were all filtered through a grimy yet glossy, Maxim Magazine patina. His production shingle, Platinum Dunes, remade everything from Texas Chainsaw to The Amityville Horror and, in 2009, it was Jason’s turn for a makeover. Directed by Marcus Nispel, who made the somewhat successful Texas Chainsaw reboot, Friday the 13th essentially combines the first three films in the series and, in doing so, makes a killer addition to the mythos. It’s a controversial opinion to say you enjoy this one, but if you find the first few entries to be a bit of a slog, it’s not the worst thing in the world to breeze through them with some good-looking kills. Stuntman Derek Mears plays Jason, who looks bigger than ever, and the cast includes CW regulars like Jared Padalecki and Danielle Panabaker along with Party Down legend Ryan Hansen. We run through the hits, sure, with Jason wearing both the burlap sack and the hockey mask, but it does add a fun wrinkle or two—after four decades of machete slashing, it’s at least nice to see him pick up a bow and arrow for a change.

And so we arrive at Crystal Lake, the first official entry in the Friday the 13th franchise in 17 years (a short film, titled Sweet Revenge, was also released in 2025).

Remember when we talked about the original Friday the 13th film, and how Mrs. Voorhees was fueled by revenge due to the carelessness of the Camp Crystal Lake counselors a summer prior—leading to her sweet baby Jason’s presumed demise? Crystal Lake’s story picks up there, with the talented Linda Cardellini putting on Pamela’s signature sweater. The story is kind of fan-fiction adjacent, but what in the Friday the 13th story isn’t? It’s filled with some major gore for all the Slasher-heads out there, and if you’ve made it this far on this list, you’ll probably be pulled in from the very start. Happy streaming, campers!

#358. The One Thing Daisy Edgar-Jones Wishes She Had Stolen from the Sense and Sensibility Set

In honor of the Jane Austen adaptation’s release, the actress, who plays Elinor Dashwood, chats Norland, Barton Cottage, and her own design style.

A crucial plot point in Jane Austen’s Sense and Sensibility revolves around moving. The three Dashwood sisters—the sensible Elinor, the passionate Marianne, and the youngest Margaret—and their widowed mother spend much of the novel concerned about the move, preparing for it, and then coping with the change, as they depart their grand family estate, Norland Park, for Barton Cottage, a disheveled, small house in faraway Devon. The new film version of Austen’s debut novel, out today, brings these spaces—and the Dashwoods’ story—to life.

Daisy Edgar-Jones who, stars as Elinor in the adaptation, and got particular joy working within the film’s intricate sets. In honor of the movie’s release, and this new interpretation of Austen’s spaces, we decided to ask Edgar-Jones some rapid-fire questions about design (“my favorite subject,” she told us).

Below, Edgar-Jones reveals her favorite Dashwood house and what she wishes she had stolen from the Sense and Sensibility set.

ELLE Decor: What house in Sense and Sensibility would you want to live in?

Daisy Edgar-Jones: I love Barton Cottage, and I love what the girls and the women do with it. But it's very, very in the middle of nowhere. It's in the middle of Dartmoor, which is this beautiful moorland in Devon. And I think I would probably ultimately want to live in Norland, which is their first home, because it's so, so beautiful and so homely. And it's in Dorset, which is so beautiful. But, it's a little bit more accessible.

If you could live in any historic or famous house, which would it be?

Is your own decorating style more sense or sensibility?

My taste probably leans more sensibility. I'm not necessarily a minimalist. In a very Marianne-esque way, I love a decorative pillow. I love ribbons. I love lace. I love lots of color and texture.

If you could steal one thing from the Sense and Sensibility set, what would it be?

I wish I could steal more than one thing because I was obsessed with the interiors of this film. Just everything—the vintage pillows, and they sourced the most gorgeous furniture. I did love Marianne's pianoforte. I don't play the pianoforte, but I would like to learn, and an instrument can always make a room feel lived in.

The Dashwood family’s transition from Norland to Barton Cottage is a key part of Sense and Sensibility. What was the biggest move you’ve ever made?

My biggest move was when I was probably 22, and I moved into a flat all on my own, and it was my first time living on my own. It was the first time I really discovered my style and interior aesthetic and what, for me, made a house a home. That felt really formative because it was the first time that I had a space that was completely mine.

Annie Goldsmith is the senior editor and digital lead at ELLE Decor, where she covers design, culture, style, and trends. She previously held positions at The Information, covering technology and culture, and Town & Country, writing about news, entertainment, and fashion. Her work has also appeared in Vogue, Rolling Stone, and the SF Standard.

#359. Having a Supportive Man Is the New Victoria’s Secret Fantasy

Celebrity relationships are officially part of the show, and VS seems to know exactly what we’re watching for.

Victoria’s Secret said your boyfriends better work, too! The 2026 Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show has come and gone, but one thing the internet is still talking about? The unabashedly loving partners in attendance. In the age of parasocial relationships, there’s nothing the online world eats up more than access to the personal romantic lives of our favorite celebrities. It's an easy fantasy, which is why we got a whole five-plus-question interview with Dylan Sprouse on the pre-show pink carpet talking about his Angel wife Barbara Palvin. And it’s why they sat Dylan next to Patrick Schwarzenegger (so we could get a double whammy camera pan to their unceasing adoration). Relationships sell, and it’s clear VS is tuned into that as well.

That’s also why it’s no surprise that when the biggest secret of the night—Kylie Jenner making her runway debut in wings and the $50 million fantasy bra—was revealed, we also got a peek at her boyfriend, Timothée Chalamet. And the screengrabs are already covering the internet. Whether people are asking, “Why is he there?” or saying “Ugh, relationship goals.”

But there’s more to it than just that. When the question of our time has been, “Is having a boyfriend embarrassing?” the answer, according to Victoria’s Secret, is “not when they shout their love from the rooftops.” And that’s the thing: Boyfriends are embarrassing when they belittle their partners, participate in the manosphere, or don’t give their partners the love, attention, or hype they deserve. These men cheering and loving their ladies out loud is refreshing and seemingly rare. Rare enough to become part of the fantasy of the show itself.

The partners in attendance at the VSFS have essentially become WAGS. But where sports has a fair-weather relationship with the supportive women attending games, Victoria’s Secret leaned into the fantasy of it all by giving these men—and specifically their reactions—the camera time they deserved.

We’ve gotten to see sparks of this phenomenon in spaces like the WNBA, but it’s nice to see it on a different field, too. Victoria’s Secret’s entire rebrand has been about women (of all types) being the reigning voice in what’s considered desirable and sexy. Well, now we know a big part of what that may be.

In a world where celebrity relationships are practically their own entertainment genre, VS knows exactly what it’s doing. Give us the wings, the walk, and the boyfriend cam. We’ll be watching all three. (Partners who weren’t there and camera ready, we’ll be watching for you next year. Please come correct.)

#361. GLP-1s May Affect Your Nail Health, According to New Research

If you’re taking a GLP-1, you’ve probably heard plenty about the potential side effects, ranging from nausea and constipation to pancreatitis. And the longer they’re on the market, the more side effects researchers are noticing and exploring, like hair loss and vision changes. The latest addition to the list: Nail changes.

A study presented this month at the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology’s 2026 Congress in Vienna discovered nail problems among GLP-1 users, with two-thirds of them experiencing a nail disorder. Some people are experiencing their nails lifting up from their bed, while others’ nails are changing color. It may sound alarming, but the research is very preliminary.

Here’s what three experts—including a study coauthor—say you should know.

Meet the experts: Bianca Maria Piraccini, MD, PhD, is a dermatologist and coauthor of the study. Dana Stern, MD, is a dermatologist specializing in nail health and an assistant clinical professor of dermatology at Mount Sinai Medical Center. Fatima Cody Stanford, MD, is an obesity medicine physician-scientist at Massachusetts General Hospital and an associate professor of medicine and pediatrics at Harvard Medical School.

The researchers surveyed 575 people taking GLP-1s and 1,329 people with obesity and/or type 2 diabetes who had never taken them. Nearly 40 percent in the GLP-1 group reported that their nails were lifting away from the nail bed, compared with about 10 percent in the other group. Changes in nail color were more common, too, with 46 percent of people taking GLP-1s reporting them, compared with 17 percent of those who weren’t.

“This is an important signal that warrants further investigation, but it does not establish that GLP-1 medications cause nail detachment or discoloration,” says Fatima Cody Stanford, MD, an obesity medicine physician-scientist at Massachusetts General Hospital and associate professor of medicine and pediatrics at Harvard Medical School.

For starters, around half of GLP-1 users said they had nail problems before taking the med. Other health conditions and nutritional deficiencies, like psoriasis and iron deficiency, also explained some of the difference between groups, according to dermatologist and study coauthor Bianca Maria Piraccini, MD, PhD. Psoriasis can cause nails to change color or lift away from the nail bed, while iron deficiency can leave them thin and spoon-shaped, per the American Academy of Dermatology Association.

After researchers accounted for those factors, nail lifting and discoloration were still associated with GLP-1 use, although the links were weaker, Dr. Piraccini says. In a separate analysis that focused only on changes reported to have started after treatment began, neither association was statistically significant—another reason the findings can’t establish that the medication itself caused the problems.

Still, there are reasons to keep examining the phenomenon, Dr. Piraccini says. The survey relied on self-reporting, and there’s always room for error when asking patients to recall symptoms and how they relate to treatment. Having a dermatologist check participants’ nails before treatment and following them over time would help researchers better understand whether the drugs play a role, Dr. Stanford explains.

As for why GLP-1 users might be experiencing nail problems, researchers aren’t so sure. The medications are known to reduce appetite, which can make it harder to get enough protein, vitamins, and minerals, Dr. Stanford explains. Rapid weight loss can also put stress on the body, potentially affecting hair, skin, and nails. But those possibilities don’t necessarily explain nail lifting, which Dr. Stern says isn’t associated with weight loss or not getting enough calories or protein. A direct medication effect is another possibility, she says, although researchers don’t yet understand how that would happen.

When a nail lifts (a condition called onycholysis), it separates from the skin underneath it. One sign it’s happened to you? The white part at the tip might look like it’s creeping back toward your cuticle, says Dana Stern, MD, a dermatologist specializing in nail health and an assistant clinical professor of dermatology at Mount Sinai Medical Center.

And, it’s not so hard for a nail to lift. Even using a tool to clean underneath your nails can loosen their attachment, which weakens with age, Dr. Stern explains. Toenails can lift from repeatedly hitting the front of your shoes during exercise. Psoriasis can cause lifting, too.

Color changes can have different explanations too. When a nail lifts, the separated area can look white, Dr. Stern explains, adding that brown lengthwise bands can also develop when pigment-producing cells in the nail become more active, sometimes after irritation from cuticle picking or aggressive manicures. These bands are often harmless, but any new pigmented band in an adult should be evaluated by a derm, she notes.

Whether your nails are lifting or changing color, take a clear photo, write down when it started, and contact your prescriber or a dermatologist. You shouldn’t stop taking your medication on your own because of a nail change alone, says Dr. Stanford, but do let your doctor know what’s happening so they can help determine the cause and whether you need treatment.

While awaiting evaluation, avoid nail cosmetics, filing, and buffing if your nails are lifting, Dr. Stern recommends. Avoid picking, cutting, or aggressively pushing back your cuticles, too, since that irritation can trigger pigment changes, she explains. Treatment for lifting or discoloration will depend on the underlying cause.

If you notice any pain, swelling, warmth, pus, bleeding, or a rapid change in pigment, contact your provider right away. “A new brown or black lengthwise band should also be checked by a dermatologist,” Dr. Stern says. “Many are harmless, but some need evaluation for nail melanoma.”

It’s tempting to pick up a bottle of vitamins that promises stronger nails and see if it delivers, but there’s no evidence it’ll fix the lifting or discoloration, says Dr. Stern: “Don’t waste your time and money!”

A supplement could help if you’re short on nutrients your body needs—which is something your doctor can help figure out. If you’re struggling to eat because you feel nauseated or barely hungry, mention that to them, too. Your prescriber may be able to adjust your treatment so eating enough feels more manageable. And, yes, they could recommend a supplement if it would be appropriate in your case.

Treatment depends on what’s actually causing the change. Evaluation may include your doctor taking a nail clipping, testing for fungus, or taking blood to check for a nutritional deficiency, Dr. Stanford says.

And, if you’re taking a GLP-1 or considering one, you don’t need to worry too much about this new link. “Patients noticing nail changes should not automatically attribute them to GLP-1 treatment or prematurely discontinue an effective drug,” Dr. Piraccini says.

#362. Psychologists Say THIS Is Why You’re So Drawn to Antique Decor and Old Places

Here's some justification for your flea-market habit.

For many of us, spending an early Saturday morning at an estate sale or touring a historic place such as a house museum is a form of self-care. Feeling immersed in a time-worn setting and among the fixtures of a bygone era is a great comfort, even if it’s hard to put your finger on exactly why.

In a time that feels algorithmically mediated to an excessive degree, it can feel like one must consciously individuate to retain one’s personal style and taste. As a result, we’ve recently seen a renewed interest in tasteful clutter, homes with “old soul,” and even weirdness. Antiques and historic settings, with all of their aged imperfections, are very much an integral part of this shift.

This ineffable feeling of comfort and belonging actually has a name: place authenticity. It’s a socioecological concept that every vintage lover should know about. We asked a psychologist who studies place authenticity what its characteristics are and how we can recreate it in newer settings that haven’t yet been touched by the patina of time.

"Place authenticity refers to the unique essence of a place that makes it feel genuine, alive, and connected to its history, culture, or community," explains Ashley Krause, M.S., a doctoral student in the Department of Psychology at the University of Florida and the co-author of a study on this concept.

Place authenticity intersects with personal authenticity (that is, the sense of being true to oneself), which may account for those feelings of engaged enjoyment in places whose unique look and feel are singular and irreplaceable. After all, they're one of a kind—just like you.

"In one of our studies, we asked participants to recall a time when they felt connected to a particular place. What we found was that the authenticity of the place participants described was linked to deeper emotional and psychological connections," says Krause, emphasizing the interdependence of personal and place authenticity. "A place can become a source of continuity, stability, and identity, offering refuge from the homogenized spaces that often dominate modern life."

Note that place authenticity is also a subjective experience. Krause's paper on the concept posits that two people may have entirely differing views on the assumed authenticity of a place—and the same person may even perceive the place as more or less authentic in differing circumstances. For example, that record store in your neighborhood that you deem the epitome of authentic spirit may be seen by another person as an upstart that replaced the authentic mom-and-pop shop they remember occupying the space previously.

When you experience an innate sense of belonging somewhere—even if you've never stepped foot there previously—it's pretty safe to assume that there's something that feels authentic about the setting to you. Unless you are incredibly conscious of the effect a space has on you, it's easy for this feeling to sweep over you as a general feeling of inexplicable calm. But, in fact, several subtle but identifiable factors contribute to that sense of ease.

"Place authenticity often manifests through a combination of sensory experiences, historical or cultural elements, and community connections," says Krause. She explains how these elements break down categorically:

Our homes, by default, may seem like a guaranteed wellspring of place authenticity. But this may not always be the case if we've just moved into a new build, for example. Just as the concept of slow decorating encourages patience to achieve an aesthetic outcome that is unlike anyone else's, cultivating place authenticity in the home similarly takes time.

"Authenticity arises from genuine connections, history, and emotional resonance, and these can't be replicated by simply mimicking aesthetic elements," says Krause. Luckily, the principles of place authenticity can be translated into the home in three distinct ways.

First, you can incorporate elements with history, which is great news for vintage lovers. "Whether it’s heirlooms, antique furniture, or artwork that reflects your personality or culture, items that carry personal or cultural significance can help your home feel more rooted and authentic," says Krause.

Next, while it's fun to keep up with the latest home decor trends, a place that feels authentic to you is personalized to your tastes and values. Even if you're incorporating design elements and trends that you've admired in other people's homes, Krause recommends that you "include decor that speaks to your identity—perhaps items from local artisans or decor that reflects your cultural heritage or personal experiences."

Finally, make it a priority to create spaces that encourage human connection at home. The memories you make in this convivial atmosphere help to infuse a home with a warmer, more lived-in vibe. "Spaces that facilitate social interaction, like a welcoming kitchen or cozy living room, can foster a sense of community," says Krause. "The more your space feels connected to the people you love, the more authentic it will feel."

#363. Mini Pumpkin Cheesecake Bites

These mini pumpkin cheesecake bites are not only too cute, but they’re so much easier than making an entire pumpkin cheesecake. These no-bake wonders are a godsend for anyone who has ever been personally victimized by a finicky oven. #365. Plaid Gets All Dressed Up

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

This season, the print is elevated in bright colors and rich textures

The biggest plot twist of the fall/winter 2026 runways was the way designers played with plaid. Always a pattern associated with fall, it usually appears in the form of classic cashmere scarves, pleated wool skirts, or the lining of utilitarian jackets. But this season, plaid got an unexpected makeover. Checked pieces in bright new hues and elevated fabrics like chiffon and silk felt light and playful, as opposed to the heavier, more structured looks of the past.

Many designers rethought plaid for day, from Chemena Kamali’s candy-colored chiffon dresses and skirts at Chloé to Matthieu Blazy’s workwear-style shirts at Chanel. Others used plaid to create a dressed-up finishing touch, like Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez’s take on party sandals for Loewe. For evening, Julian Klausner at Dries Van Noten paired checked tops with velvet skirts, while Tory Burch gave us a sheer matching set in the pattern.

Below, I break down three ways to make the pattern feel new and special this fall, whether you’re mixing flannel shirts together for a layered look or investing in a pair of plaid statement shoes. Read on for how to get the look.

Is there anything chicer than a woman in a tuxedo? This fall, tuxedo-inspired accessories like cummerbunds and opera scarves are trending, but a more unexpected twist on the look involves plaid shirts—two of them! Start with a pair of tuxedo pants, then add a plaid button-down, ideally one in a dark color with bright checks. Tie a white opera scarf around your waist to pull it all together, and finish off your look with a lighter plaid flannel tied around your waist. Sling a tuxedo jacket around your shoulders for the coolest interpretation of the trend yet.

Funky sandals are the ultimate starting point if you’re building a statement look for a fun night out. This season, Loewe collaborated with German artist Cosima von Bonin on a collection that included a pair of mix-and-match plaid sandals. Rather than balancing them out with something simple, try pairing them with Dries Van Noten’s mixed-media skirt-pants for a full-body ode to pattern play. Top it all off with a crisp, oversized white shirt to let your shoes do all of the talking.

There’s something so charmingly unexpected about a vibrant plaid skirt in soft chiffon. For true checks and balances, offset the easy silhouette with a structured leather jacket to give your look the edge it needs. A western-inspired boot will make the look feel polished yet laid-back (and a little bit boho). This is a look that can truly take you from day to night with flying colors!

#366. How to Keep Curly Hair Healthy and Hydrated This Winter

Cold air, hot showers, and beanies are no match for these curl-saving winter grooming tips.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

DEALING WITH CURLY hair my entire life, one thing I've learned is that the routine that works for me in the summer doesn't cut it once winter rolls around. I've spent years figuring out how to keep my curls hydrated and defined, but colder temperatures bring a whole new set of problems. Freezing winds and indoor heating can make it harder to keep frizz at bay. Then there’s the issue of deciding when to wear a hat. Curly-haired fellas know keeping our mane looking good can get pretty frustrating.

Curly hair is naturally prone to dryness because scalp oils have a harder time traveling down the bends of each strand. Add all of winter’s problems above, and your curls can become even more susceptible to frizz, tangles, and breakage. Fortunately, a few adjustments to your usual grooming routine can make a noticeable difference in your styling, and here’s what to know.

Whatever you do, don’t over-shampoo... even if you feel like your hair is “dirty” all the time. (It’s more than likely not!) Shampooing too often can strip the natural oils your curls need, especially in winter. That doesn't mean you should stop washing your hair altogether, but it's worth paying attention to how quickly your scalp gets oily or dirty instead of sticking to an arbitrary schedule.

I recommend using a moisturizing shampoo formulated for curly hair and focusing it on your scalp rather than scrubbing your entire head of hair. Also avoid excessively hot showers, which can contribute to dryness.

A regular conditioner for your curls is essential (so please still use that!), but a deep conditioning mask can be especially helpful when your hair starts feeling rough or brittle. Add one to your wash routine once a week, or whenever your curls feel particularly dry, to restore softness and make detangling easier.

Look for formulas with ingredients like shea butter, argan oil, and fatty alcohols, which condition your hair without requiring a dozen extra products. Finer curls generally benefit from lighter formulas, while thicker, coarser textures can usually handle something richer.

I've always considered leave-in conditioner one of the most important parts of my curly hair routine, and winter really proves it. Applying one to wet or damp hair after showering helps maintain softness and makes styling considerably easier. Follow it with your favorite curl cream or gel for definition, but be careful about piling on too many heavy products. You want your curls to look hydrated and bouncy, not greasy or weighed down.

Your regular bath towel might actually be contributing to your frizz. Aggressively rubbing your curls creates friction, which can disrupt their natural shape and increase the likelihood of breakage. Instead, gently squeeze out excess water with a microfiber towel or cotton T-shirt.

And while air-drying is great when you have the time (I quite literally never do), a diffuser on low heat and low airflow, with heat protectant, is especially useful in winter, when walking outside with soaking-wet hair isn't exactly appealing. This is also where you could use an air-dry cream, aka a hair product that is lightweight enough and can “air dry” in a shorter amount of time.

Beanies are practically unavoidable during winter, but certain fabrics can create friction against your curls, leaving them flattened, tangled, or frizzy by the time you take your hat off. Try a satin-lined beanie or wear a silk or satin scarf under your usual hat to cut down on friction. The same goes for sleep, so swapping your regular pillowcase for a satin one can help preserve your curl definition overnight. It’s sort of boujee, but maybe that’s a good thing.

One of the biggest mistakes you can make is assuming your curls need a full restyle whenever they start looking dry. Sometimes, they just need a little water to reactivate the products already in your hair, followed by a small amount of leave-in conditioner to restore their shape.

Gently scrunch everything into place instead of aggressively brushing through your curls. And if the heat is constantly blasting in your apartment, consider using a humidifier to combat dry indoor air. Your hair and your skin might both appreciate it.

You can’t go wrong with styling products in winter. They're the easiest way to keep your curls in shape during windy, frigid weather. After taking note of the steps above, apply gels, creams, pomades, and other products before or after your leave-in conditioner, and always before you dry. #368. Inside Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s Real Estate Portfolio

The couple recently returned to the UK. Here’s where they’re living now.

Since they married in May 2018, hardly a day has gone by when Meghan and Harry, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, haven’t made news. Now that they’ve returned to the UK after six years in Meghan’s native California, that’s gone into overdrive. This week, they made their first formal public appearance together, with a day of events in Nottingham, a city about 100 miles from their new home in the Cotswolds, the idyllic, posh region in Oxfordshire. The rest of their family is living more royally, with King Charles, Queen Camilla, Prince William, and Princess Catherine in palaces and castles in London and Windsor.

But it wasn’t so long ago that they were living right beside them. After their wedding, the couple lived in a cottage at Kensington Palace, where Prince Harry had lived in his bachelor days (when Meghan was still splitting her time between Los Angeles and Toronto). Their worlds collided in 2016, thanks to a mutual friend and a now-legendary Instagram post (Dalmatian filter, if you must know). After a whirlwind of transatlantic dates, Botswana adventures, and a roast chicken proposal, soon the prince and the actress became the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, rewriting royal tradition as they went. After stepping back from official duties, launching new ventures, and growing their family, Harry and Meghan’s journey has been anything but ordinary.

But if you really want to understand the Sussexes, look at where they’ve lived. Each home—quirky, grand, or sun-soaked—marks a turning point in their story.

Before Montecito and million-dollar manses, Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s first home together in 2017 was a far more modest affair: Nottingham Cottage, also affectionately known as “Nott Cott.” Situated within Kensington Palace’s grounds, this 17th-century red-brick charmer designed by Sir Christopher Wren included all the grandeur of a royal shoebox—1,300 square feet, two bedrooms, and ultra-low ceilings. Meghan herself described it as “so small,” and Harry said that the whole cottage was “on a slight lean” in their Netflix documentary, Harry & Meghan.

Yet, what Nott Cott lacked in size, it made up for in intimacy. The checkerboard-tiled kitchen, cozy living room, and petite dining area became the backdrop for the couple’s early romance and Meghan’s transition from Toronto to royal life. It was here that they celebrated their engagement, navigated the end of Meghan’s Suits era, and planned their next chapter. But as their family grew (and perhaps their need for headroom), the Sussexes bid farewell to their first shared sanctuary, relocating just before Archie’s arrival. After they left, Prince Harry’s cousin Princess Beatrice reportedly moved in with her husband, Edo Mapelli Mozzi.

Frogmore Cottage was a wedding gift from Queen Elizabeth II and a testament to the power of a good renovation budget. Situated on the grounds of Windsor Castle, the property was transformed from a five-unit dwelling into a five-bedroom single-family home at a reported cost of $3 million. The upgrades included a yoga studio for Meghan, a sleek kitchen, a guest wing, and a nursery in soothing neutrals for baby Archie. They weren’t always popular.

The move to Frogmore marked a new era—more privacy, more space, and some Windsor prestige. The couple settled in just in time for Archie’s birth, in May 2019, a quiet little family home. But royal life proved less tranquil than the Berkshire countryside, and after stepping back from their official duties, Harry and Meghan reimbursed the renovation funds and announced plans to split their time between the UK and North America. By June 2023, after being asked to vacate, Frogmore was in their rearview mirror.

If Nott Cott was cozy and Frogmore was stately, Montecito is pure California fantasy, at least it seemed that way when the couple moved in 2020. When they first arrived in the U.S., their home was a loan from mogul and friend Tyler Perry, but in July 2020, Harry and Meghan snapped up a place of their own, a Mediterranean-style estate in Santa Barbara County for a reported $14.65 million. Sprawling over 7.4 acres, the mansion includes nine bedrooms, 16 bathrooms, a guesthouse, teahouse, tennis court, swimming pool, rose gardens, and even a chicken coop for those farm-to-table eggs, frequently present in Meghan’s Netflix series, With Love, Meghan (note that they actually filmed the show at the Montecito Orchard Private Estate a few miles away).

The rooms were characterized by wooden beams, sun-drenched rooms, and a palette equal parts Tuscan villa and Napa vineyard. There’s a library, shared office, sauna, gym, games room, arcade, wine cellar, and a five-car garage. The kitchen has undergone a major upgrade, though the couple have kept it mostly private, as Meghan prefers to film her lifestyle series in a lookalike rental to preserve their “safe haven.”

Though it once seemed to be their forever home, they recently left it behind for the UK. However, they still own the house, and Meghan and the children are reportedly returning to spend the holidays there.

Prince Harry’s family has a special connection to the CostaTerra Golf & Ocean Club in southwest Portugal, where it’s believed they own a beachy retreat. The club, which is in the seaside region of Melides, is also home to Harry’s cousin Princess Eugenie and her family. The princess’s husband, British executive Jack Brooksbank, is in marketing for the company that owns the development. The sprawling property, which is reportedly between 700 and 900 acres along the coast, features about 300 units. Harry and Meghan are believed to have bought theirs for £6.3m in 2023.

In the summer of 2026, the couple made headlines by returning to England to live in the Cotswolds. Though the exact location of their new home base hasn’t been revealed, it’s been reported that they are renting or borrowing from a friend. The Cotswolds, located in Oxfordshire, is an area beloved by members of the social set for its natural beauty and privacy. Meghan had her bachelorette weekend at the Soho Farmhouse in the area. Even without specifics, the home seems to reflect that countryside idyll from photos and videos that Meghan has posted on her Instagram.

#370. Street Fighter Star Callina Liang Says She ‘Can’t Stop’ Building Muscle

Here’s how the 26-year-old got strong to play Chun-Li in the action film, out now.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Actor Callina Liang plays a daughter out to avenge her father’s death in the new Street Fighter film (out now). The role of Chun-Li (played by Ming-Na Wen in the 1994 original, starring Jean-Claude Van Damme) required Callina to do something she’d never done before: strength train.

“Before [being cast], I was a Pilates and cardio girl,” she tells Women’s Health in the latest episode of Strong Like. Now, however, the 26-year-old takes pride in pushing herself in the gym—and building major strength. “It's really satisfying to see how much more I can lift as I progressively overload,” she says. “I can't stop. I just want more and more muscles.”

Callina walks us through the routine that helped her get those muscles and kick major butt in Street Fighter.

While training for the film, Callina lifted Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays, in addition to the two hours of stunt training she put in every day.

Her strength routine starts with hip thrusts, typically performed with a Smith or hip thrust machine for easy setup. She cycles through five sets: two at a lighter weight and three at her heaviest weight. “My hip thrust makes me feel the strongest,” she says. “I can do double my body weight.” She supersets hip thrusts with hip abductions. Both exercises, she says, made her kicks that much more controlled and powerful for her fight sequences.

Next comes sumo deadlifts, which she doesn’t superset with any other exercises. Depending on the weight she chooses, she usually aims for six to eight reps per set, for three sets.

Continuing with the leg theme, she finishes her session with cable step-ups, which she supersets with squats. (Alternately, she may also superset the step-ups with weighted back extensions.)

During Street Fighter training, Callina was also super-mindful about her nutrition, especially protein intake. In fact, she ate a dozen eggs each day! “I sneak them into everything,” she says. “If I'm making a protein shake, eggs in there. Oatmeal, eggs in there.” One of her egg favorites—which she still eats today—is scrambled with ground meat, onions, and spinach, on toast with sriracha. If you’re going to eat all those eggs, you might as well make ‘em tasty.

To see Callina’s routine in action, click play on the latest episode of Strong Like above.

#371. See Inside Coastal Nantucket Home Designed by One of Jackie O.'s Favorite Boutiques

She could often be found rummaging through the iconic store’s shelves.

Some stores are grab-and-go spots. Others are inspiration hubs, enchanting customers with curated goods and sparking a full-on design movement. Nantucket Looms is one such spot. Set on the iconic island off the coast of Massachusetts, the weaving studio founded by Bill Euler and Andrew Oates in 1968 evolved into a bustling boutique (Jackie Kennedy Onassis could be found rummaging its shelves) and launchpad for artisans making the island’s famous heirloom blankets, baskets, and rugs.

When Euler and Oates retired, they handed over the reins to their most trusted employee, shop manager and in-house tastemaker Liz Winship, who had worked side-by-side with the duo for more than 40 years. Winship further expanded the business to include an acclaimed interior design studio.

When it was her turn to retire, Winship left her daughter Bess Clarke—responsible for bringing the shop into the digital world—and two longtime employees, principal designer Stephanie Hall and master weaver Rebecca Peraner, to steer the ship. You can read all about the legacy and transformation of this American treasure in their book, Nantucket Looms.

“It’s such a great tribute to all who’ve been a part of our story,” says Clarke. “I really hope people see a side of Nantucket that may be a little harder to find these days.” Keep reading to explore the third home Hall and the Nantucket Looms team have designed and discover a bit of the store’s magic.

FAST FACTSDesigner: Stephanie Hall of Nantucket LoomsLocation: Nantucket, Massachusetts

For many of Nantucket Looms’ design clients, the island is their second home. “They really want to feel like they’re in Nantucket and not anywhere else,” Hall says. One way the designer delivers the coastal aesthetic in an authentic way is by incorporating different shades of blue. “The reflective light out here on Nantucket, because we have so much water and we’re surrounded by the ocean, is so beautiful,” she says. “On any given day, if the sun’s out and the sky is bright blue, the water can be blue or blue-green; those are the colors that you feel you’re surrounded by. I love to bring that to the inside as well.”

To complement the dramatic scale of the living room, an arrangement of sofas and modern wingback chairs is anchored by two coffee tables styled with books and decorative objects that relate to Nantucket’s seafaring history.

Inspired by blown-glass fishing boats, the sculptural chandelier is made of handblown glass “bubbles” bound together with knotted rope. “I just love that piece so much,” Hall says. “It’s a little nod to nautical without doing a red, white, and blue thing.”

A space for playing games and building puzzles, replete with a marble-topped table surrounded by four upholstered chairs, was created adjacent to the living room. A painting by Adam Umbach hangs in the background.

“Our clients have two teenage daughters, so this is a space for the kids to congregate away from the parents,” Hall explains. To keep things fun and cozy, she brought in pops of red with handwoven blankets from Nantucket Looms. Anchoring the room is a large white sectional sofa with bench-seat cushions and two oversized white swivel chairs, all covered in high-performance fabrics. Silk-screened throw pillows add the finishing touch. A painting by Megan Hinton is displayed on the coffee table.

“To me, a space isn’t finished until art is hung on the walls,” Hall says. For its interior projects, the team mixes the clients’ collection with art and decor sourced locally and from Nantucket Looms. “We represent over 70 local artists,” she says. On the bar are two paintings by Kenneth Layman, and a painting by Julija Mostykanova hangs nearby. The comfortable blue armchairs are upholstered in fabric by Peter Dunham.

Rustic vintage finials, matched by a pair of contemporary rattan chandeliers, add interest to the double-pedestal dining room table. A reproduction of a French handkerchief planter is filled with ferns to brighten up the space.

The homeowners are big on wallpaper, but instead of going wild with prints and patterns, Hall took a subtler approach and played with texture on the walls. “There’s a large sitting room in there, which we use for our client’s office,” she explains. To define each space but maintain the flow, Hall used two different types of textured wallpaper. Another reason Hall and her team used textured wallpaper is to add warmth and coziness. “Some of the rooms were quite cavernous,” she says.

A variety of other textures can be seen in the bedroom as well. Rope handles embellish the chest of drawers, and the lamps are white-washed wicker. The bed features a tufted linen headboard with Euro pillows in a bouclé fabric. A kelp green handwoven cashmere throw is draped across the king-size bed. To keep consistency between the two rooms, she used the same painted rattan light fixtures.

Departing from the mostly white walls of the home, a leaf-patterned wallpaper was chosen to make this dressing room stand out. Covering the walls and ceiling is a clever design trick for a space that gets no natural light. The beautiful Schumacher paper adds dimension and makes the room feel brighter and larger. An oversize upholstered bench in a joyful fabric was selected to bring character to the space.

“The clients love modern, very colorful art, and we tried to make the pieces the star of the show,” Hall says. “We kept the walls very white, and a lot of the furniture very neutral so they can incorporate really strong statements through their artwork.”

Barbara Clarke’s photograph “Seafoam” adds depth to the space above an upholstered white linen bed with navy blue welting in the main house, flanked by navy wooden inlay bedside tables. A white chevron wool rug brings comfort underfoot.

#374. Athleticism Is the New Fitness Flex

Guys are sprinting, leaping, and throwing to chase clout instead of just pumping up. Here’s why.

WHAT COMES TO mind when you think of someone who’s really fit? For most people, the end goal of their workouts has been one thing: How they look. The most obvious way to prove you’re serious about fitness has traditionally been to look the part.

But in recent years, the social media arms race to produce the most attention-grabbing content has created a different bar: When your feed is already filled with washboard abs and envy-inducing physiques, those admirable (and hard-earned) gains may not be enough to earn serious fitness clout. And in a world where you have more control over your appearance (partly because weight loss can now be aided by GLP-1s), looking fit is sometimes decoupled from hours spent grinding in the gym or dialing in your diet.

That’s opened the door for a new fitness status symbol: Athleticism, the ability to combine physical qualities like strength, speed, power, agility, and coordination. Guys are now aiming to sprint faster, jump higher, and move more explosively—and they’re doing this largely for its own sake, not because they’re training for the basketball court or the football field.

In some cases, it seems to be about content: biohacking tech entrepreneur Bryan Johnson is attempting to dunk, an athletic feat that marries coordination, serious explosiveness, elite genetics, and years of technical skill development. In other instances, it’s simply about moving better: Since retiring from bodybuilding, six-time Mr. Olympia Classic Physique champion, Chris Bumstead, has shifted his focus to athleticism, posting videos of 60-inch box jumps and treadmill sprints. But no matter what, many fitness feeds are filled with guys who can . . . actually move.

None of this is new, of course. Anyone who played a college sport will be familiar with plyometrics and power development, and strength and conditioning coaches have been training with these principles in mind for decades. What is new is who’s doing it, how they're broadcasting, and, crucially, what's missing—an actual sport that demands these specific physical attributes.

“For a long time, a lot of guys trained with one main goal—to build their body,” says DeVentri Jordan, a performance coach for elite athletes and NFL and NBA prospects and founder of GameFace Training. Now, he says, more guys are asking “what can I actually do with the body that I’ve built?”

DYLAN SHANNON, A fitness content creator and RAW nutrition athlete, started posting on social media about two and a half years ago. His feed is filled with equal parts PR lifts, bounding drills, and max effort sprints. He does all this without looking like a stereotypical lean “athlete”; Shannon is built like a powerlifter. (He says that people often troll his sprinting videos, including one comment with a GIF of the Hulk sprinting.) “I think one of the reasons I've seen some success is 'cause I train this way,” he says. “People see that they can be both jacked and athletic.”

He’s certainly not the only one finding an audience for it. In the last two years, Shannon has noticed a “huge explosion” in athleticism-focused strength coaches or content-creator athletes on social media. Jason and Lauren Pak have amassed more than 1.5 million Instagram followers with an approach that emphasizes strength, mobility, and athletic movement, including videos encouraging people to “train mobility like an athlete.” Online coach Brad Becca racks up hundreds of thousands of views on videos demonstrating agility and explosiveness drills, while Bademba Doumbouya puts everyone from suburban moms to 60-year-old men through mind-bendingly complex coordination drills that look like something a pro athlete might struggle with. These posts rack up views, sure—but Jordan is quick to caution that just because something looks athletic on social media doesn’t mean it’ll actually help you become a better athlete.

The dominance of short form video may also be moving the athleticism trend along: If you only have a few seconds to capture someone’s attention, a display of raw power and speed is going to be more eye-catching than watching someone hammer out biceps curls or maintain their goal pace on a run. (We can only watch so many videos of runners putting up another finger for every mile of their marathon.) “Sprinting or dunking and lifting heavy weights—it looks cool on social media,” says Shannon. “It's easy to sell it that way.”

BOUTIQUE AND BUDGET gyms alike are catering to—and often driving—the growing interest: Tone House, which regularly programs agility drills and sprinting, markets their classes to “unleash the inner athlete” in every New Yorker. And no-frills East Coast chain PureGym recently remodeled some locations to allow room for more athletic training, subbing out rows of cardio machines for turf, which gives aspiring athletes room to run and jump, and more gear that are often perceived as athletic training tools, Ski-ergs and weight sleds.

Juan Herrera-Perla, head coach of Hybrix XT classes at Life Time, says that more and more, their members are calling themselves “athletes”, elevating a trend that started back in the CrossFit era. “And they absolutely are (athletes),” he says. “When they go into a competition setting or when they come into a competitive class, they get a real taste of what being an athlete is.”

The rise of Hyrox has also opened the doors for a host of fitness competitions that bill themselves as testing grounds for athletic movements. Competitions like Life Time Games and ATHX ask participants to merge lifting basics, like a strict press, with conditioning moves like box jump overs or med ball shoulder tosses. Apex Athlete, a new competition blending a 40-yard dash, vertical jump, trap-bar deadlift, and other NFL scouting combine-style tests, lets the most fitness-obsessed compete like football prospects.

For a lot of gym-goers, these competitions have turned the nebulous goal of becoming ‘more athletic’ into a set of skills they have a reason to train. Shannon, who also sells online programs, says he gets a lot of men in their late 20s and 30s who played a high school or college sport and miss training for performance. “They’re getting tired of traditional lifting and not having any larger goals,” he says.

The rise of athleticism training also gives guys a new collection of measurables, many of which can feel more attainable than some classic goals. Some people might be intimidated by the sheer duration of a marathon or half-marathon, but training for a two- to three-second box jump or broad jump can feel far less daunting.

The strict standards of these competitions also force athletes to consider not just how strong they are, but how their movement patterns actually translate, says Shannon. In Apex, male contestants must showcase strength by benching 225 pounds and trap bar deadlift 405 pounds, but power through a 40-yard dash without blowing up a hamstring. Herrera-Perla says many members have gotten serious about mobility after realizing they don’t have the squat depth to get below parallel for their Hyrox wall balls.

WITH ANYTHING THAT garners attention online, there comes the tendency to replicate what you see on viral posts. “One of the biggest misconceptions is if the exercise looks athletic, it must be,” says Jordan. “You see somebody doing, like a ladder drill, jumping on a box, or, combining four or five movements, and it looks impressive.” But he says you’re missing all the boring, behind-the-scenes work that every athlete has to undergo. Much of it—like assessing ankle dorsiflexion or chin posture, or measuring how much force an athlete is applying to the ground—isn’t sexy.

For an athlete who’s training for sport, everything is programmed around the demands of that sport. Football players train acceleration and change of direction so they can evade a tackle; basketball forwards develop power to jump higher; pickleball players practice lateral movement so they can react quickly at the net. So when people train for Instagram athleticism as the end goal, they’re often missing the “why,” Jordan says.

If your goal is to become “more athletic”, Jordan’s first question would be: Well, what do you want to be able to do? While general athleticism includes qualities like speed, strength, power, mobility, coordination, and body control, it also includes “being able to use these different qualities when it matters,” he says.

That “when it matters” will look different when there’s no coach or sport dictating it for you. Maybe you want enough speed to chase after your kid, or balance and coordination to stay on your feet as you get older. That doesn’t mean you need to set wild records in the process. “You may not ever be able to jump on a 60-inch plyo box,” Jordan says. “And you’ve just got to be real—your ceiling may be 25-inch plyo box jump. You’ve just got to be okay with that.”

JUST AS IMPORTANTLY, before you chase that 60-inch box jump (or even the 25-incher), master a few athleticism basics.

The best way to start training like an athlete: Embrace a few types of movement in your workout routine.

Almost every athletic competition has at least one movement that forces you to control your body while airborne, like a box jump, vertical leap test, or broad jump test. If you’re a gym veteran, you could certainly add one of these moves to your training. If you’re new to the gym, start by jumping rope, or add pogos to your routine. To do a pogo, simply bend your knees slightly and hop up and down on both feet. Do this for 30 seconds, then rest for 30 seconds. Repeat for 2 to 3 sets at the start or end of your workouts 2 to 3 times a week.

Athleticism requires you to push your body to, at least for a moment, deliver its maximum force output. Sometimes, that means deadlifting a heavy load for a single rep. Sometimes, it’s a vertical leap. And one of the simplest ways to train that is with a max-effort medicine ball overhead throw. You can do this with any weight of medball: Simply hold the medball with both arms, and either throw it overhead as far behind you as possible or as high overhead as possible. Do 3 sets of 2 to 3 throws. And, especially if you’re throwing as far behind yourself as possible, keep track of your throws. As you get more comfortable, you’ll be able to throw farther.

Whether you love watching football, basketball, or soccer, there’s a good chance you’ve noticed this about athletes: They don’t simply move forwards and backwards on their field of play. Playing sports requires you to twist and move laterally, and too many weight room workouts skip over this. Make sure you don’t by including one lateral component in your training at least twice a week. This can be a classic exercise like a lateral lunge. Or get onto the turf and try lateral shuffles; work for 3 30-second sets back and forth.

Want a full program that can help you train laterally? Check out our Ultimate Athleticism 8-week program, which is a great way to jump (literally!) into athletic training.

#377. What Is a Digital Nomad Visa?

Dreaming of working from Europe? Here’s everything you need to know.

If you can do your job from your kitchen table, it’s tempting to imagine that table somewhere else. Perhaps in an apartment in Madrid or a house outside Florence. A digital nomad visa allows eligible foreign nationals to live in a country temporarily while working remotely for an employer, business, or clients based elsewhere. Programs may accept salaried employees, freelancers, and business owners, though each country decides which types of work qualify.

The term covers several immigration arrangements. Some countries issue a visa, while others grant a temporary residence permit. Each program has its own application process, financial requirements, and restrictions on work. Here’s what you need to know if you’re interested in becoming a digital nomad.

Applicants generally need to show that they can perform their work remotely and that their employment or business meets the country’s rules. This usually means working for an employer abroad, operating a business registered elsewhere, or providing services to overseas clients.

Some programs also require evidence of professional qualifications, relevant experience, or an established relationship with an employer. Employees may need written permission from their company to work remotely from the destination country.

Citizenship can affect eligibility. Before applying, check whether the program accepts people of your nationality and whether you already have the right to live and work in the destination through another immigration arrangement.

The documents vary by destination, but common requirements include:

Programs generally require proof that you can support yourself during your stay. The minimum amount varies by country, and applicants bringing family members may need to show additional income or savings. Depending on the program, financial evidence can include bank statements, employment contracts, or other records.

The length of stay depends on the program and the type of authorization you receive. Some allow up to a year, while others offer longer periods of residence. A country may also have separate visa and residence-permit routes with different time limits.

A digital nomad authorization specifically permits qualifying remote work. A tourist visa or other visitor permission has different conditions and may not allow you to stay in the country primarily to work remotely.

A digital nomad visa does not automatically exempt you from paying taxes. You need to consider the destination’s tax rules as well as any obligations that continue in your home country. Social security requirements may also apply.

Some programs allow qualifying family members to accompany you or join you after your approval. Eligibility varies, as do the application process and the financial requirements. You may need to demonstrate additional resources and provide documents establishing your relationship.

Begin with the destination’s official immigration website or the consulate responsible for your place of residence. The process may be online, in person, or a combination of both. Where you can apply may depend on your nationality and whether you are already legally in the country.

Julia Cancilla is the social media & news editor at ELLE Decor, where she oversees the brand's socials and covers design, pop culture, and emerging trends. She also authors the monthly ELLE Decoroscope column. Her work has appeared in Inked magazine, House Beautiful, Marie Claire, and more.

#378. What Esquire Is Watching This Weekend

Burly brawls, giant whales, and a few cult classics return to streaming.

October is always a tough month for catching up on your watch lists. Football season is in full swing. The autumn leaves start to change colors—and you need to see that before it gets too cold. Then, before you know it, there’s a Halloween party and you don’t have a costume yet. But if you’re looking for something scary to watch, or just need to save a little time scrolling through the tiles on your TV, here are ten movies and TV shows we recommend checking out this weekend.

If I told you a new Street Fighter reboot is actually a ton of fun, would you believe me? Sure-you-can! (Sorry.) Andrew Koji, Noah Centineo, and newcomer Callina Liang star in this hard-hitting, high-energy rendition of Capcom’s arcade phenomenon. Koji and Centineo star as fighters Ryu and Ken, respectively, who enter a martial-arts tournament—hosted by the evil M. Bison (David Dastmalchian)—while secret agent Chun-Li (Liang) works to topple Bison’s operation. Street Fighter is a bombastic bash that feels like Bloodsport meets Kung Fu Hustle in the best way possible. You really can’t ask for much more than Cody Rhodes, as Guile, yelling “Flash Kick!” while doing, well, a flashy kick.

It’s been an amazing year for horror movies, but nothing will scare you more than a movie in which one poor bastard gets caught in a whale’s throat. Whalefall stars Austin Abrams as a deep-sea diver who is swallowed up by a massive sperm whale and races against time—his dwindling oxygen tank—to make it out alive. Whalefall is a sadder movie than you might assume going in, but it’s still one of the gnarliest survival thrillers in recent memory. What, you don’t think the ocean is scary? Let Whalefall show you the real terror lurking in the deep.

Those lucky enough to have seen Nathan Fielder’s documentary about Theranos fraudster Elizabeth Holmes during its festival circuit run last month hailed it as a Best Picture contender with zero hesitation. That’s rare for a documentary—as in, the Academy has yet to nominate one for Best Picture in its nearly 100-year history. The same goes for Fielder, whose awkward and deadpan humor in HBO’s The Rehearsal hit with audiences but has yet to win over mainstream critics. Who knows if it will happen! But I’ll see the film this weekend as it premieres in theaters, and it looks very much like a first-of-its-kind experience.

One of the most in-demand movie-theater tickets of 2026 is for a film that came out in 1971. That should tell you a bit about the quality of Ken Russell’s The Devils, a film about a 17th-century Catholic priest accused of witchcraft in France, as well as the sexually repressed nuns who incite the chaos. The once-banned film received an X rating in the U.S. due to its graphic content, and this latest 4K restoration is also Russell’s original director’s cut. If you’re in for something truly wild this weekend, look no further.

Throughout October, Regal Theaters is screening one-night-only horror classics across the country for just $7.99 a ticket. It’s for an event it’s calling “31 Screams on Screen,” with the schedule including films like Poltergeist, Candyman, A Nightmare on Elm Street, In the Mouth of Madness, and many more. Tickets are selling out fast, but there are still some openings! It’s a great chance to see your favorite horror movie on the big screen.

You don’t need an eight-hour origin story for Jason Voorhees—the first Friday the 13th spelled out his tragic backstory plain as day. But if the streaming era means every franchise gets a series prequel, Crystal Lake on Peacock is a rather impressive effort that gets by on Linda Cardellini as Jason’s mother, Pamela, the first real “villain” of the saga. Set before the first movie (while following a new timeline, set in the 1970s), the films sees Cardellini playing Pamela just after her son Jason drowns at his summer camp due to negligent—and hormonal—teenage counselors. While outrunning the ghosts of her own past, Pamela tries to prove to everyone that her baby boy might still be alive. Months after her outstanding turn in DTF St. Louis, the Cardellini-sance is officially in full swing.

Remember 2016? You know, the mannequin challenge, bottle flipping, the Chainsmokers, Stranger Things season 1, Pokémon Go, and an election we were sure would have a different result? Good times. But that summer also saw a bizarre uptick in, wait for it, evil clown sightings. What was up with that? Was it viral marketing for a Hollywood film, or was it something else? Finally, the stories (plural) behind all those damn clowns are told in Clown Panic, a sordid true-crime documentary from Ed Perkins and streaming on Hulu. While the sightings made headlines nationwide, Clown Panic zeroes in on a small South Carolina town that found the situation anything but funny.

Just in time for Halloween, the cult classic Jennifer’s Body from Karyn Kusama is back on Pluto TV to raise hell. Set against a suburban high school, meek teenager Needy (Amanda Seyfried) learns that her popular, sexy best friend Jennifer (Megan Fox, at the height of her Transformers fame) has become a demonic succubus. While it was dismissed by critics back in September 2009, Jennifer’s Body has enjoyed reassessment as a black-comedy gem and a piece of queer feminist horror that practically foresaw #MeToo.

On Friday, October 16, Pluto TV will stream Jennifer’s Body with the new movie Vampires of the Velvet Lounge as part of its Double Feature Fridays. The movies will play at 8:00 p.m. ET on Pluto TV Spotlight before joining the on-demand collection.

I’ve never seen The Texas Chainsaw Massacre. I know. It’s embarrassing. There’s just something about the combination of chainsaws and massacres that always convinces me to keep on scrolling when I’m looking for something scary to watch around Halloween. But Tobe Hooper’s 1974 slasher is one of the greatest horror movies of all time, and it’s currently streaming on Prime Video. Let’s finally take the plunge together.
