#379. Ugg Cozy Slipper Review: A Style Writer’s Honest Thoughts After 2 Years of Testing

Does the iconic shoe live up to its name?

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Despite my seemingly endless supply of boots and comfortable sneakers, I am deeply susceptible to a good pair of slippers once the weather turns cold. The Ugg Cozy Slipper has been in my rotation since fall 2024, and it's outlasted plenty of other pairs I’ve tested. I wear it around the house, on walks with my energetic Jack Russel Terrier, and anytime I want to throw something cozy on without ruining my outfit.

The sheepskin lining that Ugg is known for makes this slipper especially warm. After two years of near-constant wear, the lining is still plush and cozy, and it’s held its shape extremely well considering I’ve walked approximately more than 20,000 steps in it. Even the sheepskin collar has remained intact. I’m a big fan of the knit outer, which resembles a cable knit sweater and makes the slipper feel right at home with my cold-weather wardrobe. I’ve worn mine with everything from jeans and a henley to matching sweat sets, and I love that it looks more like a “real” shoe than a house slipper.

Packed underneath all the fluff is way more support than I expected from such a plush-looking slipper. The contoured footbed and firm midsole, made with 17 mm of sheepskin, cushion my feet without that sinking-in feeling I get from some ultra-soft slippers. Board-certified foot and ankle surgeon Bobby Pourizaee, DPM, previously recommended it to me for lounging.

The outsole is sturdy. It’s made with dense EVA (ethylene-vinyl acetate) foam and has deep tread patterns for plenty of traction. I regularly wear mine for long walks with my dog around the neighborhood. I’ve even worn it in cold, damp weather and never felt unsteady on my feet. With other slippers, I sometimes worry about slipping or rolling an ankle, but this pair is sturdy enough to wear outside.

Since I don’t wear this slipper as a dedicated house shoe, it’s seen its fair share of dirt and grime. Thankfully, it’s an easy shoe to clean—which I didn’t initially expect due to the fluffy collar and knit material up top. I’ve thrown mine in the washing machine (on a gentle cycle in a mesh garment bag!) at least three times now, followed by air-drying, and they’ve come out looking brand new every time.

The only trade-off I can think of? The open-back design. A closed heel would provide a bit more stability. However, the open-back design lets me kick these on in approximately two seconds when I’m running out the door—or kick them off just as quickly when I get home. I haven’t run into any issues with stability, but I also wouldn’t reach for this slipper for extremely long days on my feet (like a day at the amusement park or a commute to the city). But for grocery runs and walks around the neighborhood, it’s been solid.

After two years of wearing it, I can confidently recommend the Ugg Cozy Slipper to anyone who wants a house shoe that easily crosses over into outdoor wear. The lining has stayed cozy, the outsole still has plenty of grip, and I haven’t run into any need to retire mine just yet. If your ideal slipper is one that’s warm enough for winter and super stylish, this is a very good pair to have by the door.

#383. 3sixteen’s Japanese Selvedge Jeans Are Worth the Hype—Here's What Sets Them Apart

A denim obsessive makes the case for 3sixteen’s jeans.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

NOTHING BEATS FINDING jeans that fit perfectly: The seat is flattering, the length hits your shoes just right, the waistband hugs your hips snug yet ever so gently, and David Bowie’s “Jean Genie” seems to follow you wherever you go. It’s an infrequent find that takes sifting, but damn, the payoff is worth it.

When Style Editor Joseph Cheatham tried over 60 pairs of jeans and named 3sixteen as the best selvedge pair, I couldn’t agree more, though, I’ll admit, they’re my personal pick for best overall.

3sixteen’s heavyweight tees were my gateway drug to selvedge denim. They were much heavier than anything I owned, required a bit more care when washing and drying, and cost more than I was used to. They also quickly became the only tees I wore; nothing compared to the earned comfort. If you’re into raw and/or selvedge denim, this probably sounds familiar.

I finally tried 3sixteen’s jeans when I started working at a men’s shop specializing in raw denim (shout-out Reserve Supply Company—go tell Jason what’s up if you’re in Houston). Between studying Heddels posts, listening to my boss wax poetic on warp and weft, and meeting with brands at trade shows, I learned more about denim than I ever thought I would. I tried pairs from Naked & Famous, Rogue Territory, Pure Blue Japan, Tellason, and Iron Heart, to name a few. After a few hits and a lot of misses, I landed on 3sixteen.

3sixteen’s jeans are sewn in San Francisco using 14.5-ounce Japanese denim from Kuroki Mills. The Japanese have been perfecting selvedge denim for over 70 years now using shuttle looms—a hands-on process that requires tedious skill. That’s why Japanese denim remains revered and costly (but worth it!). 3sixteen perfected the fit.

Immediately, I was struck by the fabric weight. For reference, a standard pair of Levi’s 501 jeans weighs about 11 ounces. You may think three ounces is negligible, but no, 3sixteen CTs feel so much sturdier; heavy without weighing me down, substantial but soft. I always heard raw denim was like wearing cardboard, and that’s true in some cases, but not here. The CT fit—a.k.a. Classic Tapered fit—has a mid-rise that sits comfortably under my belly button and a very slight taper that doesn’t choke out my calf or ankles. I know there’s been recent talk of the return of skinny jeans, but no way am I on that train. If you agree, these are for you.

While I love inky dark indigo denim, my most worn pairs have been the stonewashed CS jeans. They were so good I had to get them in black and the now-sold-out vintage wash. The only difference between the CT and CS is in the leg—CS forgoes the slight taper under the knee for that classic straight fit. It’s not a wide leg per se, nor billowy; I'd describe it as a clean silhouette. The CS jeans were great through summer when I wanted as little fabric on me as possible, though I’ve worn them year-round for the past couple of years.

I’m neurotic about pockets. They’re highly utilitarian but are somehow overlooked on a lot of jeans. Either they’re small, sit too low, or have a brand’s signature stitching. Not to mention, the pocket bags on some might as well be made of tissue; they tear and wear so fast. 3sixteen’s jeans nail my Platonic Ideal of pockets in form and style. They’re well placed, big enough to actually use, and the pocket bags are thick cotton.

The marketing jargon around selvedge denim is verbose but true—they’re more personal than your standard jeans. They also cost more and need a bit more care (i.e., wash in cold water and hang dry), but they're well worth it. Selvedge denim has better construction that lasts longer, but don’t expect to have just one pair for life. Trust me, once you get a pair, you’ll want more. I highly recommend 3sixteen for the selvedge denim afflicted. Also check out their Fall/Winter 2026 available now.

He enjoys thrifting for 90s Broadway tees and vintage pajama sets. His spare time is occupied by watching movies and running to impress strangers on Strava.

#386. The 8 Best Razors That Have Never Let Us Down

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

Get the best shave of your life, starting today.

One of my core memories is my dad teaching me how to shave. I remember standing there in front of the mirror, him using some Gillette, showing me the way he would stick his tongue in front of his top teeth so he could cleanly shave his upper lip. That one quirk aside (and I still don’t know why he did that), I learned everything I could about shaving from him at a young age. I remember the first time I tried to shave on my own and my face was still a bloody mess.

If, as an adult, you find the process of shaving your face irritating or unpleasant, there’s a chance you’re doing something wrong. It could be the shaving cream you use, but I find the razor is what makes the most difference. Maybe you’ve been using electric razors all your life and need to switch to a standard five-blade cartridge razor, or vice versa. Maybe you just need something that will give you a little extra comfort—I promise that exists. Ultimately, it takes some trial and error, since everyone’s skin and shaving process are different. I’ve done what legwork I can for you, though. By trying dozens of razors, shavers, and trimmers, I’ve found the ones that absolutely stand the test of time.

I’ve kept it mostly to cartridge razors, but I’ve thrown in one safety-razor recommendation and two different styles of electric razor in here as well. These are the eight best razors a man can buy.

When Harry’s launched, the company sought to solve a variety of problems plaguing the razor industry—especially high prices for subpar products. The brand did just that, and now, more than ten years later, the Harry’s razor continues to be an Esquire reader favorite and the one I personally reach for often.

The secret lies in the disposable cartridge razors, which are made in Harry’s own German factory and feature five blades that deliver a smooth, close shave with almost no effort on your part. The overall design is simple. Apart from the five blades, there is also a lubricating strip and a trimmer detail blade you can use to shape sideburns and such, and that’s about it. But, again, that is all by design. These are simple to use and effective, which in my book is the mark of a good razor.

Now there are multiple handles to choose from, which are all perfectly weighted and ergonomically designed, but they all fit the classic razor head. (If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it.) Best of all, the price is still incredibly low for the quality, and the subscription service is a must, because I never run out of blades.

It’s generally thought that more blades equal a closer shave, and in the case of the Fusion5, that is true. At the very least, most razor makers agree that five is the sweet spot for a cartridge razor. The five blades glide across your skin effortlessly in combination with the larger lubricating strip, giving you a baby-smooth shave in seconds flat.

Compared with other cartridge razors I’ve tried, especially those with fewer blades, it gives not only a closer shave but also a more comfortable one. Other notable features, like the “channels” that help to clear away shaving cream and work to prevent clogs between the blades, are welcome and add to the experience, but it’s really all about the blades here. Harry’s notwithstanding, I still haven’t been able to find a cartridge razor that gives a closer shave than Gillette’s, even after all these years.

Typically, if you have a problem with ingrown hairs (particularly if your beard is very curly or textured), shaving with a multiblade razor like the two above is not the best idea. Five-blade razors cut so close to the skin that they can lead to more ingrown hairs as your whiskers grow out. In this case, a single-blade safety razor (which we’ve dedicated an entire story to) is a good option.

Bevel takes a traditional razor and updates it for a modern user. Specifically designed for men with textured beards, this easy-to-use safety razor is perfectly weighted to deliver a close shave.

Although it doesn’t shave as close as a multiblade razor, for the reasons above, it’s not like you’re going to have stubble. Shaving with a safety razor takes some getting used to if you’ve only ever used cartridge razors before: You have to go slower and hold it at a specific angle to shave without nicking or cutting your skin, but once you get the hang of it, the shave it delivers rivals one you’d get in a barbershop.

You know that feeling after you get a hot-towel barbershop shave? The warmth and freshness—I mean, is there anything more rejuvenating? This innovative heated razor is the closest thing we’ve ever found to re-creating that feeling on your own. It sounds pretty out-there, but in practice it functions like any other multiblade cartridge razor. The result is one of the most comfortable home shaves you can experience—and one of the closest, as well.

The special cartridges include a bar that heats up when the razor is turned on. The heated bar not only soothes and conditions your skin but also helps to soften hair, making it easier for the five blades to cut through it, minimizing the possibility of nicks and pulls and reducing the risk of irritation. You can even switch between high and low heat settings for your comfort. Truly, it’s a luxury product, with a price point to match, and while the refills are slightly more expensive than your usual cartridges, it just might be worth the investment to get this luxurious of a shave each morning.

If you have sensitive skin, shaving is always going to be a harrowing experience. You’re likely familiar with ingrown hairs, razor burn, and irritation, particularly if you’re using multiple blades. This cartridge razor still has multiple blades, but it’s been thoughtfully designed to minimize irritation on sensitive skin.

The handle is what you’ve come to expect from a Gillette Mach or Fusion razor; it’s the cartridges that are special. With its two lubrication strips (versus the standard one) and a proprietary “irritation-defense bar” situated between the blades, the actual experience of shaving with it is way more comfortable than with many of the other razors at the same price point. It glides over your skin without any drag or pulling, and the additional lubrication strip actually does make a difference. It also shaves at skin level, which means that it helps reduce the risk of ingrown hairs, making it a great option for guys who don’t want to go down the safety-razor track but still want to control ingrowns. It doesn’t shave quite as close as some others on this list, but if you have sensitive skin or problems with razor bumps, that’s a compromise you may be willing to make for a more comfortable, irritation-free shave.

This razor is the next evolution of the Flex 5, which is our disposable razor of choice. Indeed, that really just makes it a standard cartridge razor. The Trim and Shave is a cartridge razor that also includes beard-trimming attachments for making facial-hair adjustments without any batteries. This makes it perfect for short beards and stubble. Each cartridge head has five blades that work to deliver a crazy-close shave, and each trimmer is two-sided to accommodate shorter and longer beards.

The handle has a pivoting head to help make shaving around the contours of your face more comfortable, a lubricating strip, and a precision trimmer blade. The ergonomic design of the handle fits comfortably in your hand and has a rubber grip to keep it from slipping. The addition of the trimming attachments makes it a space-saving alternative to packing a razor and a beard trimmer. If you like to perpetually rock the short stubble beard or five o’clock shadow, this will make it easy to maintain.

For many years, the Braun Series 9 reigned supreme in the pantheon of electric razors. But now it’s time for Nevo to take the throne. The first thing you’ll notice is, yes, it has a screen. Yes, that screen is useful. Before, when your electric razor didn’t work, you had to troubleshoot trial-and-error style. The Nevo will tell you if you need to clean, adjust, or replace your razor head—and you’ll always know how charged the shaver is too.

It’s an investment, but it’s the full package. When it comes to electric, you won’t get a better shave from a lighter device—it’s just not possible. With a travel case and charging stand that also cleans the razor, you (almost) never worry about maintenance. Compared with other electric razors I’ve used, it will genuinely save you time every day you use it. Ten seconds per shave adds up quickly over time.

If that doesn’t sound worth $600 to you, the Series 9 Pro is right there and currently on sale for $350. For something under $200 that won’t compromise on shave quality, check out the Panasonic Arc 5. All good electric razors, but this is the current holy grail.

The Philips Norelco OneBlade 360 is one of the most versatile and easy-to-use grooming tools on the market. The Pro version is loaded with extras, including a precision grooming attachment and a 14-length beard comb. This is the one that has earned permanent icon status in my own grooming routine. From beard trims to mustache touch-ups and, yes, even body shaving when I need to, this is my go-to electric trimmer.

Designed like a traditional razor—but powered up through technological advancements—the OneBlade uses an innovative razor design to mow through whiskers of all thicknesses effortlessly. Since the blade is double-sided, you can use it in multiple directions (unlike a traditional razor), and this upgraded version features a 360 degree swiveling head. You can also use it dry, meaning that without shaving cream your shave is easier and faster.

This is a great tool, one I use most weeks, but it’s not going to replace a razor. For those wanting a close shave, this is more of a way to touch up and maintain existing facial hair.

Gillette Labs with Exfoliating Bar: The idea behind this razor is that it covers two steps in your skin-care routine: exfoliating and shaving. The rough bar physically exfoliates your skin as you move it over the surface, removing buildup and dead skin cells in the process. This helps pave the way for a closer shave by removing things that could prevent the razor from effectively cutting your whiskers.

Gillette Mach3 Razor: If you’re somewhere in the middle and want a closer shave than what a single-blade razor can deliver but find five blades too harsh for your skin, the Mach3 is a good choice. It features three blades that give you a close shave without as much risk of irritation as versions with more blades and deliver a comfortable shaving experience that’s faster and, some might say, easier than a safety razor’s. The long-lasting blades can handle up to 15 shaves before needing to be replaced, which also makes it an economical choice.

Schick Hydro Sensitive Razor: Designed to be used on sensitive skin, this comfortable razor features a very good lubricating strip infused with aloe, and while it still has five blades, each one has a special guard to help reduce potential irritation.

We mentioned all the different types of razor styles up top but wanted to give a quick breakdown for quick reference.

Cartridge Razor: This is the most popular form of razor for shaving. These are sold with replaceable snap-on cartridge heads that you need to change once they’ve dulled. Many have multiple blades, three and five being the most common.

Safety Razor: Safety razors are single-blade straight razors with a guard between the blade and skin. They are easy to use and relatively inexpensive. Blades require a good amount of upkeep and replacement, but the shave you get is very clean and close.

Disposable Razor: Disposable razors are temporary-use blades that (typically) don’t detach from the handle. They tend to come in bulk packs and have a reputation for being cheap and low quality. It’s true that, compared with the others, you won’t get as close a shave.

Electric Razor: It’s not really even a razor. Electric razors use tiny rotating blades to cut through any thickness of hair. They are easy and don’t require force or shaving cream. Electric razors don’t get as close as straight razors do, but they are fast and can cut through bigger beards in the way cartridge razors aren’t built for.

Razors come in all shapes and sizes, so when you’re choosing the right one for you, there are a few factors to think about.

Blades: Generally speaking, the more blades a razor has, the closer it will shave. This can be a good thing if you want a very close shave in a shorter amount of time, but there are a few things to consider. Since multiple blades can sometimes cut so close to the skin that they actually cut the hair below it, the risk of ingrown hairs goes up the more blades you have. More blades may also potentially lead to more post-shave irritation, since you’re dragging more things across the surface of your skin. If you have sensitive skin or problems with ingrown hairs, you may want to use a razor with fewer blades.

Features: Additional features beyond just the blades are welcome but not always necessary. Some common features you’ll find are lubricating strips that help condition skin while you shave and pivoting heads that allow you to shave more easily around the contours of your face.

Refills: Razor blades become dull over time and will need to be replaced eventually. Most traditional razor blades should be replaced after every few uses, though some claim to be good for upwards of ten or more shaves. You’ll want to consider not just how often your razor’s blades will need to be replaced but also how easy it is to replace them.

#387. Crispy Sheet-Pan Black Bean Tacos

The idea for these vegetarian tacos was born when I needed something for dinner that was fast, easy, and cheap. Utilizing only 5 main ingredients, these sheet-pan tacos still manage to bring the party to my weeknights, all thanks to the crunchy, cheesy frico. Featuring refried black beans stuffed inside a crunchy corn tortilla, this irresistible cross between a taco and a sheet-pan quesadilla will make any night feel like a celebration.

The tortillas:Corn tortillas tend to crack when folded, so make sure to warm them until they’re pliable before attempting to assemble on the sheet pan. If they happen to crack anyway, it’s also not the end of the world: You’ve just made an extra place for the cheese to ooze out and create that crunchy cheese crust!

The cook time:How fast your tacos crisp in the oven depends on the way your oven heats and the color of your sheet pan, so be sure to peek at the undersides of the tacos after they’ve been baking for 8 minutes. If they’re still pale, feel free to give them a few extra minutes before flipping. Some of the cheese will have already oozed out by this point, so a metal fish spatula or pancake turner is the best tool for the job. It might get a little messy, but that’s really the joy of this recipe. Roll with it.

The garnishes:These tacos are perfect straight off the baking sheet, but if you want some extra zing, feel free to add a little cilantro or a dollop of sour cream, as well as a squeeze of fresh lime juice.

Storage:Leftovers can be refrigerated in an airtight container for up to 3 days—although, to be honest, you probably won’t have any.

#388. Dune: Part Three: Everything We Know

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

If you’ve already seen Dune: Part Two, a question at the top of your mind (besides where can I find a sandworm popcorn bucket?) might be: So, what comes next?

It’s a fair thought after watching this epic chapter of Denis Villeneuve’s sci-fi saga. Based on Frank Herbert’s ’60s sci-fi novel Dune, Part Two continues the story of Paul Atreides (Timothée Chalamet) with a thrilling sequel that follows him becoming one with the Fremen, falling in love with Chani (Zendaya), avenging his father, and stepping into his role as the Lisan al-Gaib.

There’s still so much to explore on the planet of Arrakis and beyond. Next in line for adaptation is Dune Messiah, the second book in Herbert’s series, on which Villeneuve has already begun pre-production work. Herbert wrote six books in the original series, and there are still dozens more set in the Dune-iverse. However, even in IP-heavy Hollywood, Villeneuve doesn’t want to lead the Dune franchise beyond the third (and supposedly) final film installment, solidifying the chronicle of Paul Atreides’s rise (and fall).

Here’s what we know about a third Dune film so far.

The movie will be released on Dec. 18, 2026. Warner Brothers confirmed the news in March.

Timothée Chalamet is set to return as Paul Atreides, the titular messiah; Zendaya as Chani; and Rebecca Ferguson as Lady Jessica.

On June 17, 2025, Deadline announced two new cast members: Nakoa-Wolf Momoa, the 16-year-old son of Jason Momoa and Lisa Bonet, and Ida Brooke (Silo). Momoa and Brooke will play Leto II and Ghanima, Paul and Chani’s twins.

Robert Pattinson revealed his participation in the series in a Nov. 3, 2025 interview with IndieWire. “When I was doing Dune it was so hot in the desert that I just couldn’t question anything,” and, “it was so relaxing, like my brain actually wasn’t operating. I did not have a single functioning brain cell. And I was just listening to Denis: ‘Whatever you want!'” The Batman star is playing the villain role of Scytale.

By March 17, 2026, several castings were confirmed. Anya Taylor-Joy—who was teased at the end of the second Dune movie—was revealed to be joining the cast as Alia, Paul Atreides’s younger sister. Javier Bardem returns as Stilgar, while Florence Pugh and Momoa will reprise their roles as Princess Irulan and Duncan Idaho, respectively. Isaach De Bankolé joins the cast as Farok.

According to the book’s synopsis: “As Emperor of the known universe, [Paul] possesses more power than a single man was ever meant to wield. Worshipped as a religious icon by the fanatical Fremen, Paul faces the enmity of the political houses he displaced when he assumed the throne—and a conspiracy conducted within his own sphere of influence. And even as House Atreides begins to crumble around him from the machinations of his enemies, the true threat to Paul comes to his lover, Chani, and the unborn heir to his family's dynasty...”

The next potential film seems to be headed in that direction. (Warning: More spoilers ahead!) The end of Dune: Part Two sets up Paul’s reign as emperor. After an epic battle alongside the Fremen, he kills Vladimir Harkonnen, avenging his father, and defeating Vladimir’s nephew Feyd-Rautha in combat for the throne. He offers his hand in marriage to Princess Irulan, the emperor’s daughter, much to the chagrin of Chani, his Fremen love. She’s not the only one upset by his decision; the Great Houses are approaching to attack and reject Paul’s claim for emperor. The holy war he had seen in his dreams is taking shape.

Keep in mind, too, that Paul’s mother Lady Jessica—now a reverend mother—is about to give birth to a daughter. It was also revealed in the film that Lady Jessica is of Harkonnen descent, and therefore so is Paul.

Before the credits roll, Chani appears alone in the desert, ready to hitch a ride on a sandworm, fighting back tears. It’s possible that she might also have a strong role in the resistance to Paul’s authority in the next film, as she already starts to show her disapproval of his rise to power in Dune: Part Two. She tries to warn her people that revering messianic figures is how those in power “enslave us.”

As Villeneuve told Entertainment Weekly, “In [Frank Herbert’s] mind, Dune was a cautionary tale—a warning against charismatic figures. He felt that Paul was perceived as a hero, when he wanted to do the opposite. So in order to correct that, he wrote Dune Messiah, a kind of epilogue that makes it very clear this story is not a victory; it’s a tragedy.” The director added that he “used Chani’s character” to help express Herbert’s intentions with the book. “I gave her a different agenda, and used her to bring a different perspective to the story.”

In an IMAX special reveal event, Villeneuve said that the movie has “a time gap, 17 years, where we see Paul dealing with the consequences of having too much power and him trying to figure out how to get out of this cycle of violence. And of course he’s an emperor who can see the future, so he’s kind of invincible.”

Zendaya also revealed during the event that Chani and Irulan will likely have more scenes together in the new movie. “I want to start by saying I love Florence Pugh—so talented, so wonderful in this role. And we said the last time, on the press tour, we only got one scene together and we were far away. And I was like, ‘I hope we get more.’ So I don’t want to tease anything, but she’s absolutely phenomenal. And you guys will just have to see for yourselves what happens because it’s quite the journey.”

Villeneuve and Zendaya have also offered more insight into the personal stakes of the sequel. In an interview with Empire, Zendaya described Chani’s feelings as including “a deep pain, a deep mistrust, a deep betrayal.” She explained that her character had begun to open herself up to love and “the idea of letting someone in, [and] allowing a space for love or gentleness” in Dune: Part Two before that trust was broken. “That part of her life is not as present anymore,” she expanded.

Villeneuve, meanwhile, said the film explores “the idea of a separation, the idea of a divorce,” as well as the concept of a broken family, which, he said “is something that the book gave me the opportunity to explore.”

During the cast’s appearance at CinemaCon in April 2026, Chalamet said Paul has “become his worst vision and he’s struggling to… figure out how to protect those he loves while becoming the all-powerful dark emperor of the universe,” according to Deadline.

“The years don’t seem to have been kind to anyone in Dune. [It’s been] a really difficult, challenging, ungentle and unkind few years,” though there’s “so much left still to fight for,” Zendaya added. She also noted that Chani is “at a very different place in her life where that youthful outlook is completely gone.”

Villeneuve, meanwhile, explained that the movie is “a very different world” where Atreides’s “nightmares became reality” and he’s left to face “the consequences of his decisions.” He also described the third Dune film as “a redemption story, but still the heartbeat of the film is that love story between Chani and Paul, [albeit] more of a broken love story.”

The director told the crowd that it was “emotional to say farewell to Paul and Chani in the desert. We became like a small family. It’s like 10 years of our lives,” and Chalamet called Villeneuve “the real Paul Atreides.”

Yes! The trailer for the movie arrived on March 17, 2026. In it, Chalamet and Zendaya’s characters excitedly await the arrival of their baby and brainstorm names depending on the sex of the child. The rebellion evolves into an all-out war with new players—including a platinum blonde Pattinson—and new stakes.

With the release of the trailer, Warner Bros. also shared several first-look photos of the upcoming movie.

Deadline detailed the first seven minutes of the film during its April 2026 CinemaCon report, and said it features “Fremen ships sailing through dark, gray, foggy air, crashing down on a planet where it’s raining. They chant and say “God be with us” before heading into battle. Lasers fly at them, obliterating many.”

Another scene in the movie, according to the outlet, features “Momoa’s Duncan Idaho tells Chalamet’s Paul Atreides he’s ‘way beyond redemption’ after becoming a destroyer of worlds.”

Although there are six books in Frank Herbert’s series, and plenty of additional spin-offs, Villeneuve only has a desire to create three films. “Dune Messiah should be the last Dune movie for me,” he confirmed to Time in an interview published in January 2024.

He’d also told Empire in August of that year, “If I succeed in making a trilogy, that would be the dream.” In the time since Villeneuve’s comments, a spin-off series titled Dune: Prophecy, which follows the Bene Gesserit, arrived on HBO Max in November 2024.

Tickets are now on sale for Dune: Part Three via Fandango; the presale began on August 18.

#389. The “3 Homes Rule” Is the Simple Organizing Trick That Makes Decluttering Feel So Much Easier

The key is deciding where each item truly belongs.

Knowing where to put the things you’re keeping—and what to do with the things you’re letting go of—can make decluttering feel harder than it needs to be. But a simple organizing method called the “three homes rule” can help you sort your belongings into clear, manageable categories.

If you’ve ever tried to declutter your home, you’ll know that deciding what to keep is only part of the challenge. You also need to work out where everything should live. Max Wilson, storage expert and CEO and cofounder of Pocket Storage, suggests giving each item one of three homes: somewhere for the things you use regularly, a place for seasonal belongings, or a route out of your home for anything you no longer want.

His “three homes rule” can help you make those decisions one item at a time, so the things you keep are easier to find, and the things you no longer need don’t end up back in the clutter.

Put simply, every item should have one of three homes:

Everyday items should have an easily accessible home near where you use them, Wilson says. This could be school bags, post, gym clothes, or even a loaf of bread.

The easier it is to put something away and find it again, the more likely you are to stick with the system. If returning an item to its everyday home takes several steps, you may be tempted to leave it out instead.

“If putting the hairdryer away means taking out a basket, lifting a lid and untangling three other cables, don’t be surprised when it stays on the dressing table. Something you use most mornings shouldn’t require a small excavation,” Wilson points out.

Your everyday home might be coat hooks by the front door for the jackets you wear regularly, or a bread bin in the kitchen. Choose a clear spot for each item, then make a habit of returning it there.

The second category in Wilson’s “three homes rule” is for items you don’t use all the time but still need to access a few times a year.

“There’s no prize for getting rid of your camping equipment in October if you’ll have to buy it again in June. But these sort of items don’t need to occupy the cupboard you open every morning. Keeping something and keeping it within arm’s reach are two different decisions.”

For items in a seasonal home, Wilson recommends keeping related things together so they’re easy to find when you need them.

“Think about the next time you’ll use these items,” he says. “When you’re packing for a camping trip, for example, you want to find the tent, sleeping bags, and camping kit together. You don’t want to remember that one part is under the bed, another is behind the Christmas tree, and the rest went into a box labeled ‘miscellaneous.’”

Even with a seasonal home, it’s worth being selective about what you keep. Don’t hold on to something simply because you might use it one day. Wilson also recommends choosing a suitable storage spot for each category: hiking equipment may be fine in a garage, while summer dresses need somewhere dry and watertight.

The final category—and arguably the most important—is the “exit home.” It’s for belongings you no longer want or need, which can be difficult to know what to do with when you’re decluttering.

Wilson suggests setting aside a small, clearly defined spot for these items, then making sure they don’t stay there for long.

“Most of us recognize the charity shop bag that’s been sitting by the door so long it’s practically part of the furniture. Deciding to donate something is a start, but it hasn’t freed up any space until it leaves,” he points out.

To stop your exit home becoming another storage spot, decide what you’ll do with the items as soon as you put them there.

“Once you’ve decided something can go, make leaving the easiest option,” Wilson says. “Keep donations together, put a drop-off in your diary, and avoid having another rummage through the bag every time you pass it. Otherwise, you end up negotiating with the same jumper three times.”

Sure, there are plenty of face serums, red light therapy devices, and wrinkle creams to keep your skin glowing all fall and winter, but one not-so-glamorous beauty essential everyone needs this season is a high-quality moisturizer. Face creams and lotions relieve dryness, maintain hydration, and support your skin barrier, which matters most as the weather cools and the air holds less moisture.

My combination skin becomes irritated and develops flaky patches around this time of year, and it only gets worse in winter. To prepare, I beefed up my skincare routine to focus on hydration and barrier protection, so I turned to the best overall moisturizer in our buying guide: Avène’s Cicalfate+ Restorative Protective Cream. Over the past month, I’ve used Avène’s cream in the morning and night. I incorporated it into my skincare routine, applying it after cleansing and toning and before sunscreen in the morning. I also tested it with makeup, using the cream as a face primer, and on other areas like my hands, cuticles, and minor burns.

The Cicalfate+ Restorative Protective Cream has a rich, occlusive texture, forming a protective seal on the skin’s surface to trap moisture. Keep in mind that this product may feel thicker than your typical moisturizer, but my dehydrated skin loves the instantly quenched feel after applying. Avène’s formula contains soothing thermal water, hydrating beeswax, and C+ Restore, a patented postbiotic ingredient that boosts moisture. #392. The Best New Watches of 2026, According to Men’s Health Editors

Whether you're into vintage-inspired designs, rugged sports watches, or luxury timepieces, these new releases deserve a spot on your radar.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

WATCHES HAVE ALWAYS been one of the easiest ways to add a little personality to your wardrobe, and 2026 is giving us plenty of reasons to upgrade what's on our wrists. Some of our favorite watch brands have spent the year revisiting their archives, introducing fresh takes on familiar designs, and releasing new pieces and technology. Whether you're into sleek stainless steel bracelets, old-school leather straps, or sporty digital watches that can keep up with your workouts, there's been no shortage of exciting new releases.

There’s a wide range here in terms of budget, too. You don't need to spend thousands of dollars to get in on the action. Sure, luxury brands like TAG Heuer are continuing to deliver some seriously impressive tickers (and oh, just wait till you see that beaut’), but more affordable watches like Timex and Casio are proving that great design and performance can come at a much friendlier price. I’m especially excited about the resurgence of vintage-inspired designs, plus smaller case sizes and colorful dials, which make some of this year's releases feel true to modern aesthetics.

Below, we're highlighting eight watches on our radar in 2026, including brand-new launches and updated classics. From rugged outdoor watches to sophisticated options, there's something here for just about every guy and every budget.

Timex is keeping the vintage watch trend alive with its latest Marlin Quartz GMT, which debuted in September 2026 with a deliciously handsome chocolate-brown sunray dial. Inspired by the brand's classic 1960s designs, this new version pairs a polished stainless steel case with gold-tone markers and a brown leather strap. A pop of orange on the GMT hand adds personality to the otherwise understated design. It's the kind of watch that looks just as good with a crisp button-down as it does with jeans and a tee. (This is probably the one I’m most excited about.)

We're also fans of the GMT function, which lets you track two time zones at once, making it especially handy for frequent travelers. The leather strap features quick-release spring bars for easy swapping, while the reliable quartz movement keeps maintenance to a minimum.

North Edge is making a strong case for affordable dive watches with its new ABYSS, which packs neat underwater features and a surprisingly stylish design. The standout feature is its glacier-inspired ice-textured dial, which gives the watch a cool, almost frozen appearance. Pair that with a stainless steel case, a ceramic rotating bezel, and luminous markers, and you get a rugged timepiece that looks just as good on dry land.

I’ve been digging solar-powered watches lately, so I appreciate that this can run for up to 180 days on a full charge. There's also an impressive 200-meter water-resistance rating and a durable rubber strap for outdoor adventures. It's a great option for guys who appreciate the look of a traditional dive watch but want something a little more eclectic.

Hamilton has dug into its 2026 military archives. Released exclusively this year to celebrate America's 250th anniversary, this 36mm watch in the Khaki collection draws on a navigator's watch issued to U.S. Air Force crews around 1970. Its matte stainless steel case, black dial, and khaki NATO strap give it a classic military look that never goes out of style.

Inside, you'll find Hamilton's hand-wound H-50 movement, which delivers an impressive 80-hour power reserve. I’m particularly into the smaller case size, which makes this vintage-inspired design feel more wearable for everyday wear. Pair it with your favorite jeans, a chore jacket, or just about anything else in your closet.

G-Shock knows how to make a statement, and its latest collaboration with professional surfer Kanoa Igarashi is easily one of the coolest digital watches I’ve seen this year. Released in July 2026, the GBX-H5600KI-5 features earthy tones and subtle lavender accents inspired by Portugal's coastal cliffs, giving the brand's classic square silhouette a fresh, unexpected look.

It's also packed with technology. This latest G-LIDE introduces heart-rate monitoring alongside its signature tide graphs, making it an especially interesting option for surfers, runners, and other active guys. There's also smartphone connectivity, solar-assisted charging, and 200-meter water resistance. Basically, it's the kind of watch you can beat up during a workout and still feel pretty cool wearing afterward.

Shinola is giving one of its most recognizable watches a serious upgrade in 2026. The new Duck Automatic, which launched in October, swaps the original quartz movement for an automatic one and shrinks the case from 40mm to a more wearable 38mm. It also adds a new textured dial inspired by duck feathers, giving the watch a playful detail without feeling gimmicky.

The real excitement, though, is what's happening inside. Its Miyota 9015 automatic movement delivers approximately 42 hours of power reserve, and a transparent caseback lets you admire the mechanics at work. With its stainless steel bracelet and sapphire crystal, this updated Duck feels like a more sophisticated take on an already great-looking watch.

TAG Heuer is bringing racing energy to 2026 with its redesigned Carrera Chronograph Sport, and the latest version looks better than ever. Unveiled in September, the watch swaps its previous 44mm case for a sleeker 42mm design, making it more wearable without sacrificing its bold, motorsport-inspired aesthetic. Blue might be the color of the year, because this dark water-hued dial version is one of many we’ve seen released this year. It pairs a rich sunray finish with contrasting silver subdials and a matching ceramic bezel.

Of course, there's plenty to appreciate beneath the surface, too. The Carrera runs on TAG Heuer's in-house TH20-00 automatic chronograph movement, offering an impressive 80-hour power reserve. Add a redesigned stainless steel bracelet and sapphire caseback, and you get a luxury watch that looks as good with a suit as it does with a casual weekend outfit.

Casio is having a pretty great year with its vintage-inspired watches, and the MTP-B146D-2AV is a perfect example of why we're paying attention. Arriving in the U.S. in July 2026, this stainless steel watch evokes the understated style of the 1980s, with a gorgeous blue dial and a full day-of-the-week display at the top. It's simple, slightly preppy, and shockingly affordable.

The slim 8mm profile and compact 35mm case make it incredibly easy to wear. The stainless-steel bracelet dresses things up just enough, while its reliable quartz movement keeps maintenance to a minimum. It's an easy everyday option that looks particularly good peeking out from beneath a button-down cuff.

Not every watch needs an elaborate dial or a price tag that hurts your wallet, and Louie Juelen's Easy Reader makes a strong case for keeping things simple. With its minimalist analog design and easy-to-read display, it's a straightforward option for guys who just want a classic-looking watch without all the bells and whistles. That kind of simplicity has a certain charm, especially when so many watches are competing for attention.

Its quartz movement also makes it a practical choice for beginners, since you don't have to worry about winding or complicated maintenance. A watch like this can easily become an everyday accessory, whether you're wearing a casual knit polo, a button-down, or your favorite jeans and tee.

Josiah Soto is a commerce editor and writer at Hearst Magazines, where he covers skincare, grooming, beauty, and style for Men’s Health, Prevention, and BestProducts.com. With a particular passion for skincare and the ingredients behind his favorite products, he keeps readers up to date on the latest beauty launches, grooming essentials, and fashion trends worth knowing about. He also contributes to Runner’s World and Popular Mechanics, covering everything from emerging style trends to running gear and lifestyle products. In another life, Josiah was an editor at ThePioneerWoman.com.

Christian is the Style and Reviews Director at Men's Health and Women’s Health, where he oversees shopping and style content for both brands. He started his magazine career as an accessories assistant at Vogue, and has since held editorial roles at Tatler Asia and The Manual. When he’s not online shopping, you can find him on long walks with his two corgis.

#394. Vhernier's New High Jewelry Collection Evokes Milan's Sleek Cityscape

Crescent shapes and Italian architecture inform Vhernier’s new high jewelry collection.

Top: Ardis Forma d’Eclisse High Jewelry Bracelet, necklace, and ear clips, vhernier.com. Catene espresso set by Gio Ponti for Ginori 1735, $565, ginori1735.com. Architettura tray by Gio Ponti for Molteni&C., $795, molteni.it/us.

Time is ever present in jewelry design. The multitude of pieces with sphinxes and scarabs inspired by the discovery of King Tut’s tomb in 1922 is one example. But what of place? Does where jewelry is made announce itself as clearly? The streamlined contours of Vhernier’s latest high jewelry pieces, Ardis Forma d’Eclisse, suggest the affirmative.

The place, no doubt, is that city of endless inspiration and style, Milan. The movement and modernity of Milan is evoked in each exquisitely crafted layer of black titanium and diamonds. And like the effortless chic of the Milanese locals as they glide through traffic during the annual Salone design fair, these pieces, with their ergonomic modular construction, rest with ease against the skin.

When Gio Ponti, the city’s mid-century master of architecture and design was woking in Milan, he was known for his ability to move between oeuvres. There was furniture and objets d’art (much of which is now produced by Molteni&C), and his much beloved collection for Ginori 1735. All done Italian style. Like Ponti, Vhernier is based in Milan, and as with the best of that city, be it furniture or fashion or saffron-infused risotto, its signature aesthetic translates exceptionally well.

Editor-in-Chief Stellene Volandes is a jewelry expert, and the author of Jeweler: Masters and Mavericks of Modern Design (Rizzoli).

#395. The Indispensable, Exhaustive Guide to Seiko Watches

The Japanese brand offers an almost overwhelming amount of options. We’ve broken everything down so you can find the one that works for you.

Whether you’re just beginning your watch-buying journey or are a seasoned collector, there’s a very good chance that you know—and respect—Seiko.

The Tokyo-based brand makes watches and clocks in thousands of styles, colors, complications, and sizes, all at prices that have proved affordable to millions around the world. From soldiers to students to office workers, athletes to doctors to journalists, people love Seiko for its potent mix of affordability, utility, and variety.

One of the most vertically integrated companies in the watch world, Seiko Group Corporation is a behemoth of a corporation, with more than 11,000 employees across its various business divisions and output estimated in the millions of watches per year. With the ability to manufacture its own mechanical, quartz, and solar movements—not to mention its own cases, dials, and other components—Seiko effectively controls most of its own supply chain in addition to its design and R&D processes. Much like Rolex in this regard, it’s notable for the coherence displayed in its collection through the decades: Take a look at a recent Seiko 5 Sports, for example, and you can easily discern the influence of the original Seiko 5 from the 1960s. That same idea of continuity plays out with the brand’s core dive watches and, of course, its reissues.

Unlike numerous other brands, however, Seiko isn’t a purist endeavor with respect to technology. In addition to conventional mechanical movements of both the automatic and hand-wound variety, it also makes extensive use of quartz and solar-powered movements, and it even pioneered GPS-controlled movements that automatically update the local time as one travels. Aesthetically speaking, Seiko isn’t afraid to experiment with oddball case shapes, fresh complications, and bold colorways—though, to be fair, one could make the argument that the brand’s catalog might benefit from more focus.

From the elegant lines of the vintage-inspired King Seiko collection to the overbuilt quality of the Prospex line, from the affordable good looks of the Presage to the futuristic Astron, from the colorful field watches of the Seiko 5 Sports collection to the envelope-pushing contours of the Power Design pieces, and from the angular design of the Coutura line to the elegant dress watches of the Diamond series, Seiko’s vast assortment of timepieces has every type of buyer covered. And for those who outgrow even this tremendous assemblage of horology?

Seiko’s story begins in 1881, when 21-year-old Kintaro Hattori opened a shop in Tokyo’s Ginza district that sold and repaired watches and clocks. Eleven years later, Hattori established his own factory, Seikosha, beginning with wall clocks and eventually moving into pocket watches. In 1895, the company produced its first pocket watch, the Timekeeper, setting the stage for an even more ambitious project: a domestically produced Japanese wristwatch.

That watch, the Laurel, debuted in 1913, becoming Japan’s first wristwatch. A decade later, disaster nearly wiped out Hattori’s growing enterprise: The Great Kanto Earthquake of 1923 destroyed both the Seikosha factory and Hattori’s store. He rebuilt almost immediately, even replacing roughly 1,500 customer watches and clocks destroyed in the resulting fires. (A genuine glob of these—completely melted together—is on display in Seiko’s museum in Ginza.) In 1924, the company introduced its first watch bearing the Seiko name.

During the Second World War, Seikosha and its newly independent watchmaking arm, Daini Seikosha, shifted much of their production toward the Japanese war effort, producing military watches as well as instruments for aircraft and ships. Among the most notable surviving examples are the small Seikosha military watches and the enormous Tensoku pilot’s watch, a Japanese counterpart to the German Beobachtungsuhr (“B-Uhr”).

Following the cessation of hostilities, Seiko concentrated on precision, producing a succession of increasingly sophisticated watches that culminated in the debut of Grand Seiko in 1960. Designed to compete with the finest watches in the world, this new division demonstrated that Japanese watchmaking could stand toe-to-toe with the established Swiss industry. But there was an even more important innovation to come.

In 1969, Seiko changed watchmaking forever: On Christmas Day, the company released the Quartz Astron, the world’s first quartz wristwatch. Accurate to within five seconds per month—roughly 100 times more precise than contemporary mechanical watches—the Astron helped usher in the Quartz Crisis that would fundamentally reshape the global watch industry. Seiko subsequently opened many of its important quartz-related patents to other manufacturers, ensuring that its technology would spread throughout the industry.

Since then, Seiko has continued to pursue both mechanical and electronic watchmaking, developing everything from LCD watches and sophisticated quartz movements to Spring Drive and GPS Solar technology. The result is one of the broadest catalogs in watchmaking—the history of which is practically a history of wrist-worn horology itself.

The good news: Seiko has one of the most extensive offerings of any watch brand anywhere in the world. The bad news? Seiko has one of the most extensive offerings of any watch brand anywhere in the world. Sorting through this vast oeuvre—which spans dress watches, tool watches, solar-powered watches, and much more—can be complicated, which is why we’ve put together this handy cheat sheet that should, at the very least, help steer you in the right direction. And the best part? While you can certainly spend a few thousand bucks on a Seiko if you’re so inclined, many of the brand’s watches sticker for well below $1,000 and certainly less than $2,000.

Emblematic of Japan’s growth in the postwar era, the King Seiko collection launched in 1961 with a gold dress watch that cost the equivalent of a young graduate’s annual salary. Situated below Grand Seiko in price but finishing at the top of Seiko’s lineup, the collection was reborn in 2022 to much fanfare. From the early-’60s silhouette of the KSK line to the integrated-bracelet funkiness of the VANAC line to the late-’60s architecture of the KS1969 line, it’s full of classically leaning pieces boasting a variety of price points and designs.

For a restrained silhouette—albeit one that is decidedly Seiko—try something from the KSK line. With its round case, sharply downturned lugs with pronounced facets, smooth bezel, and multi-link bracelet or leather strap, it’s an ideal everyday companion. A diameter of 38.6mm promises a comfortable fit on a variety of wrists, while the Seiko cal. 6L35 automatic movement ensures up to 45 hours of power reserve. For a more vintage-leaning approach, the slightly smaller ref. SJE087 features a variety of small touches that call back to the original King Seiko from 1961. The tortoiseshell-like pattern on the regular production models, however, may be even more compelling…

Notable Reference: SJE105Type: Dress/everydayDiameter: 38.6mmMovement: Seiko cal. 6L35 automaticPrice: $3,300MORE INFO HERE

Launched in 1972, the VANAC was unique in several respects: unafraid to use brightly colored dials in interesting fumé-like patterns, it also featured multifaceted cases—and crystals—that quickly separated it from the pack. The relaunched VANAC collection celebrates that heritage with a sharply faceted case and bracelet, a variety of cool dial colorways, and a highly legible dial design that features a date window and plenty of luminous material. Powered by Seiko’s cal. 8L45 automatic movement with 72 hours of power reserve, the VANAC is water resistant to 100 meters and measures 41mm in diameter, making it ideal for someone with a medium to large wrist.

Notable Reference: HKF004Type: EverydayDiameter: 41mmMovement: Seiko cal. 8L45 automaticPrice: $3,300MORE INFO HERE

Based upon the King Seiko 45KCM from 1969, the KS1969 is housed in a distinctive “C”-shaped stainless-steel case that feels distinctly ’70s. At 39.4mm in diameter, it’s significantly larger than a watch from the disco era would have been, though a case height of just 9.9mm keeps it eminently wearable day-to-day. With its simple dial design and smooth bezel, it has a somewhat dressy quality—but the matching steel multi-link bracelet with alternating brushed and polished surfaces adds a welcome injection of sportiness. Powered by an automatic Seiko movement, it’s the right choice for someone whose taste runs classic but who wants 2020s proportions.

Notable Reference: SJE109Type: Dress/everydayDiameter: 39.4mmMovement: Seiko cal. 6L35 automaticPrice: $3,100MORE INFO HERE

Having evolved from Seiko’s long dive-watch heritage, the Prospex Collection now includes all manner of tool watches, from chronographs to field watches to GMTs. Whether you’re exploring a shipwreck underwater or driving a classic car in a rally, there’s a Prospex watch that will provide faithful wrist-worn service for the occasion—and, thankfully, won’t break the bank. Vintage-watch fans in particular are well served by models that recall references from specific years past, such as the 1968 Heritage Diver’s Watch.

Named for the Latin word for light (“lux”), the LX line houses some of Prospex’s quintessential sports watches. Expect to shell out a bit more for these top-of-the-line timepieces—but for good reason. Titanium case construction, Spring Drive movements, extreme water resistance, and useful complications abound here. While the LX line is not the place to search for a more vintage-inspired reference with svelte proportions, it’s certainly perfect for someone on the hunt for a true adventure watch that can stand up to any challenge. The SNR025, with its GMT functionality and compass bezel, is a particularly capable example.

Notable Reference: SNR025Type: GMT/fieldDiameter: 44.8mmMovement: Seiko Spring Drive cal. 5R66Price: $5,500MORE INFO HERE

If the LX line houses chunky, futuristic divers, then the Marinemaster is its spiritual opposite. Currently consisting of riffs on the 1965 Diver’s and 1968 Heritage Diver’s watches, it brings pared-back 1960s aesthetics to bear, combining them with useful features for the ultimate in slightly dressier tool watches. While the 1968 models have oversize 42.6mm cases, the 1965 models are slightly more compact at 39.5mm, with matching steel multi-link bracelets that offer versatility and good looks. The SJE117, with its seafoam-green color and horizontally grooved dial pattern, stands apart from some of the more subdued options.

Notable Reference: SJE117Type: DiverDiameter: 39.5mmMovement: Seiko cal. 6L37 automaticPrice: $2,800MORE INFO HERE

With numerous options priced between $500 and $1,500, the Sea line features a wide variety of attractive dive and dive-style watches for men and women. From no-frills PADI-themed special editions to diamond-slathered pieces with two-tone cases, Sea spans vintage and modern inspiration to offer excellent spec-to-price ratios. Those who travel frequently will find references such as the SPB519 and HBC001 particularly appealing, while veteran divers will no doubt like watches such as the SRPK01 and SRPJ93 PADI Special Editions for well under $1,000. For an excellent mix of features and price, however, the ref. SRPE03 takes the cake.

Notable Reference: SRPE03Type: DiveDiameter: 45mmMovement: Seiko cal. 4R36 automaticPrice: $650MORE INFO HERE

Home to Seiko’s field watches, the Land line is where you’ll find the Alpinist—the slightly quirky adventure watch with an inner rotating compass bezel controlled by an extra crown situated at four o’clock. With both three-hand and GMT editions available, the Alpinist is a fan favorite, though it’s not the only model within the Land line worth calling out: Pieces such as the ref. SPB249 offer no-frills timekeeping with great looks, excellent proportions, and serious water resistance for well under $1,000. The Alpinist ref. SPB503, with its fun teal dial and matching steel bracelet, is emblematic of the Land subcollection.

Notable Reference: SPB503Type: Field/GMTDiameter: 39.5mmMovement: Seiko cal. 6R55 automaticPrice: $995MORE INFO HERE

The through line within the Speedtimer collection is the chronograph, that most utilitarian of timing complications. Those whose leanings skew analog will be happy to know that there are mechanical models within the collection, while those who care more for utility will enjoy the numerous solar-powered references. There are also, however, a few watches without traditional chronograph complications whose internal rotating bezels nevertheless allow for timing of discrete events—and, frankly, these are some of the most fun watches in the lineup. (The SPB513, with its multicolor dial and matching multi-link bracelet, is worth checking out.)

Notable Reference: SPB513Type: RacingDiameter: 39.5mmMovement: Seiko cal. 6R55Price: $995MORE INFO HERE

The Presage Collection houses some of Seiko’s most elegant watches, with the Classic Series in particular drawing from the craftsmanship and traditions of Japan in the manner of numerous pieces from high-end sister brand Grand Seiko. The extensive Cocktail Time line, on the other hand, features more contemporary colorways and adventurous dial colors in numerous sizes and configurations. While there are plenty of pieces paired to leather straps, there are also watches with matching bracelets, which makes a dressier watch more appropriate for everyday wear.

Whether it’s a simple three-handed watch or one with an “open-heart” dial, a GMT complication, or a 24-hour indicator, the Classic series is full of elegant dress watches that can be worn in a variety of settings. Newer references such as those in the HCC series are particularly appealing: With a mix of textured dials in various pastel shades, matching multi-link bracelets, automatic movements, and 100 meters of water resistance, they’re easily able to take you from the office to the pool with finesse. The HCC002, with its pistachio-colored dial in an undulating, concentric pattern, makes a distinctive impression.

Notable Reference: HCC002Type: Dress/everydayDiameter: 38mmMovement: Seiko cal. 6R51 automaticPrice: $950MORE INFO HERE

The colorful, glossy dials of the Cocktail Time line are some of Seiko’s most unusual. Drawing the wearer in with both hue and pattern, they’re paired to hard-wearing steel cases that make these watches excellent everyday timekeepers. Fans of Grand Seiko will no doubt notice a similarity to some of the latter’s high-end timepieces in a watch such as the GMT-equipped SSK049, while others will be drawn to simpler pieces such as the new ref. HCB001, a three-hander with a gorgeous crystalline ice-blue colorway that fades from teal to navy at the periphery. (At 38.5mm in diameter, it’s also the perfect unisex size.)

Notable Reference: HCB001Type: Dress/everydayDiameter: 38.5mmMovement: Seiko cal. 4R35 automaticPrice: $475MORE INFO HERE

Inspired by the Crown Chronograph from 1964, the Style60’s line offers a contemporary dress watch along distinctly sporty lines. Available in several configurations, each features a polished and brushed case with a rounded profile and sloping lugs; a thin, vintage-inspired bezel insert; a box-shaped crystal; applied, faceted indices; and luminous alpha hands. For an evolution of the old Crown Chronograph’s design language, spring for the new ref. SSK009, which incorporates a GMT feature and adds a lovely multitone blue dial and a 24-hour bezel insert.

Notable Reference: SSK009Type: GMT/dressDiameter: 40.8mmMovement: Seiko cal. 4R34 automaticPrice: $650MORE INFO HERE

Consisting currently of just two references, the Inspired by Japanese Gardens subcollection is exactly what it sounds like. Look closely at the dial and you’ll notice a sand-like pattern that mimics that of a Zen garden, while an “open-heart” section displaying the movement’s escapement and a 24-hour indicator provide visual interest and balance. Currently available in forest green and gold tone with a matching two-tone bracelet, these are some of the quirkier designs in the Seiko catalog—especially given their larger diameters and minimal water resistance.

Notable Reference: SSA464Type: DressDiameter: 41.8mmMovement: Seiko cal. 4R39 automaticPrice: $650MORE INFO HERE

Those familiar with Grand Seiko’s zaratsu polishing will notice familiar surfaces on Seiko’s Sharp Edged Series. The mix of polished edges atop brushed surfaces throughout cases and bracelets reflects light, making for handsome silhouettes that any collector would be happy to wear. Furthermore, the Asanoha pattern found on certain dials—which mirrors that of the hemp leaf, a familiar motif in Japanese design—adds a sense of dynamism absent from many watches at this price point. For a particularly useful watch, try this SPB225, whose brown tones and useful GMT complication pair with a matching bracelet and a power-reserve display.

Notable Reference: SPB225Type: GMTDiameter: 42.2mmMovement: Seiko cal. 6R64 automaticPrice: $1,400MORE INFO HERE

In 1969, Seiko debuted its first quartz-powered watch, the Astron. In 2012, it revived the Astron name in the form of a solar-powered collection with GPS technology, which continuously updates local time as you travel. By combining this tech with angular cases, titanium or steel construction, integrated bracelets or straps, and plenty of water resistance, the result is a series of hardy tool watches that frequent travelers would be proud to own. Priced at roughly $3,000, they’re more expensive than many other Seiko models—but the impressive tech more than justifies the added expense.

With a six-month power reserve when fully charged and a two-year power-save mode, the Astron GPS Solar references are designed for longevity, accuracy, and utility. The ref. HAB001, measuring 43.4mm in titanium, has a busy dial, to be sure—but the amount of information at one’s fingertips is staggering. In addition to the local time, the watch features a perpetual calendar, a chronograph, a world-time function, a power-reserve indicator, a time-transfer function between the main and sub-dial indicators, a satellite-acquisition-status display function indicator, and more. Lightweight and water resistant to 100 meters, it’s a true 21st-century tool watch.

Notable Reference: HAB001Type: Travel/everydayDiameter: 43.4mmMovement: Seiko cal. 5X63 solarPrice: $2,700MORE INFO HERE

Born in Japan in 1963, the original Seiko Sportsmatic 5 offered five key characteristics: automatic winding, a day-date display, water resistance, a recessed crown at four o’clock, and a durable case and bracelet. Relaunched in 2019, the Seiko 5 Sports collection ups the ante with a newer automatic movement offering hand winding and hacking, plus a wider variety of case and dial designs to cater to every taste. Consisting largely of diver and field-style watches, the lineup calls back to vintage designs while offering the sorts of specs that collectors have come to expect. Affordable and fun, they’re some of the best watches in the Seiko catalog.

Based upon the beloved SKX watches from the 1990s and 2000s, the modern SKX collection offers dive-style attributes at affordable prices—although unlike their namesake, they’re not ISO-rated dive watches with 200 meters of water resistance. Despite this distinction, a watch such as the ref. SRPL85 is a perfect gateway into mechanical watchmaking. Measuring 42.5mm, its stainless-steel case and matching bracelet are hardy yet comfortable, while the black sunray dial offers plenty of LumiBrite for low-light visibility as well as a handy day-date display. The glossy glass bezel insert, meanwhile, feels like a meaningful upgrade from the old aluminum versions.

Notable Reference: SRPL85Type: Dive-style/fieldDiameter: 42.5mmMovement: Seiko cal. 4R36 automaticPrice: $450MORE INFO HERE

The Field Series is precisely what it sounds like—a subcollection of field watches made for outdoor use. Taking their design inspiration from past models made over the life of the Seiko 5 series, these watches are no-frills tools with automatic winding, day-date displays, steel bracelets or fabric straps, and three-hand displays—though at least one GMT model offers a convenient solution for travelers on a budget. For a bare-bones timekeeper with military inspiration and zero pretense, try the ref. SRPG31, which offers a gray dial with a 24-hour track combined with a matching gray NATO-style fabric strap.

Notable Reference: SRPG31Type: FieldDiameter: 39.4mmMovement: Seiko cal. 4R36 automaticPrice: $315MORE INFO HERE

Like references within the Field Series, the SNXS Series watches take inspiration from vintage Seiko 5 timepieces from decades past, offering good looks, straightforward design, and excellent ergonomics at an approachable price. The SRPK91, for example, swaps out a more typical black or blue dial in favor of a handsome ivory colorway with vintage-colored lume, a bright-orange second hand, and a black day-date display with white printing. A small crown at four o’clock keeps out of the way, while a matching steel bracelet makes its 37.4mm case appropriate for more than just a day outdoors.

Notable Reference: SRPK91Type: FieldDiameter: 37.4mmMovement: Seiko cal. 4R36 automaticPrice: $415MORE INFO HERE

The Seiko Power Design Project is where Seiko stretches out. Offering unconventional wristwatches that spurn more traditional round case architecture and standard bracelets, these pieces skew more toward the type of fare typically found in museum design stores. Currently consisting of a single model, the collection will presumably be populated with new watches as Seiko continues to pair up with younger, forward-thinking designers who favor unisex silhouettes, daring case and bracelet shapes, and funky colorways.

The first (and currently only) model within the Power Design Project is the Collection 1, a limited edition rendered in three different colorways. Based upon the ladies’ TISSE collection from 1984, it features a stainless-steel bracelet consisting of round links in different sizes and finishes. These links are then paired to a small, round watch head with a Hardlex crystal, a simple dial with baton indices and a matching handset, and a snap-on case back beneath which sits the Seiko cal. 4N30 quartz movement. Measuring just 6.7mm thick, the idea is that the jewelry-like Collection 1 watches can be worn by both men and women, making them distinctly versatile.

Notable Reference: SSEH023Type: Dress/everydayDiameter: 20.2mmMovement: Seiko cal. 4N30 quartzMORE INFO HERE

The Coutura line can almost be thought of as Seiko’s own take on the integrated-bracelet luxury sports watch—albeit one positioned as an affordable, largely quartz-powered offering. A curious mix of angular shapes and dressier two-tone accents, Coutura watches are available in a wide variety of configurations, from smaller three-hand references to solar-powered tool watches with a wealth of complications. Priced almost entirely below $1,000, they’re largely available in the American market, where they appeared in the early 2000s.

If you ever wondered what a cross between a Seiko tool watch and an Audemars Piguet Royal Oak might look like, check out the ref. SNE506. Housed in a 42.5mm stainless-steel case with a hard black coating and a matching integrated bracelet, it features gold-tone accents on the crown, on the bezel, and throughout the handset. The dial, meanwhile, uses a guilloché-like motif to achieve a sense of depth, while applied indices and a date window at three o’clock round out the design. Powered by a solar movement, it boasts an impressive ten-month power reserve when fully charged.

#397. Meet the Parfums de Marly Fragrance That's Reinventing Vanilla

Parfums de Marly's latest, Althaïr Exclusif, puts vanilla's sophisticated, masculine side in the spotlight.

Beneath vanilla's layer of velvety coziness lies a complexity that's made it one of the enduring ingredients in gourmand fragrances. Vanilla can be creamy and light, soft and seductive all at once. It is precisely this superpower that's elevated vanilla to become one of modern perfumery's defining signatures.

In a man's fragrance, vanilla can warm up wood notes, deepen amber, or round out the sharpness of citrus. In other words, vanilla isn't simply a passive note within a fragrance; it is the thread that can tie the entire composition together without making it overly sweet.

Althaïr Exclusif leans into this modern versatility while harkening back to a time when vanilla was prized for its rarity and refinement. The Bourbon vanilla used in Althaïr pays homage to the variety brought to France during the reign of Louis XV in the 18th century. In this gourmand-ambery-woody fragrance, Bourbon vanilla serves as one of the three key notes alongside saffron and amaretto. Julien Sprecher, founder and creative director of Parfums de Marly, approaches the harmony of the trio through the lens of another art form from the period: music. "I wanted to dream up a perfume composed like a concerto, an expansive scent with noble materials, but also a quieter, more refined virtuosity," he says. "Each note was crafted to orchestrate contrast, notably with Bourbon vanilla and an amaretto accord, sophisticated ingredients that were already known to the Royal Court at the time."

If Althaïr Exclusif were indeed music, vanilla would take center stage, anchoring the composition with its depth and range. Saffron follows with a quietly leathery edge, adding texture, while amaretto brings in a surprising almond-like chord. Orange blossom, cardamom, praline, and guaiac wood enrich the melody. The result is something that can be many things all at once—bold enough for an evening that calls for making a statement, refined enough to hold its own in the sea of scents at the office, and effortless enough to move between both worlds without missing a beat. Think of it as the bottle on your dresser you'll instinctively reach for knowing that it will seamlessly move with you, no matter where you're actually going.

Althaïr Exclusif's ability to resonate on skin is what makes it so appealing—magnetic, really. Its warmth settles right in, revealing different facets as the fragrance unfolds. And we have the charisma of Bourbon vanilla to thank for making this fragrance not just balanced but bold. That's why Althaïr Exclusif is bound to be a classic—and give vanilla a much-deserved starring role in the process.

#398. How Miley Cyrus Paid Tribute to Her ‘Eternal’ Bond With Dolly Parton at Her Hollywood Bowl Show

Miley Cyrus is holding on to her memories of Dolly Parton. During her concert at the Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles on Friday, October 16, the singer paid tribute to her late godmother in an emotional six-minute speech that included a rendition of one of her most notable songs.

“I only got to see Dolly Parton live in concert one time in my entire life, and it was here,” she told the audience about the significance of the space she opted to host her two-night limited performances of Bass Persuades. It was Cyrus’s first time performing at the iconic venue.

The singer then recalled asking Parton if she could attend that show without performing alongside her, hoping to experience the concert as a regular audience member. Parton agreed, but she had other plans. She opened that show with “The Best of Both Worlds,” the theme song from Cyrus’s Disney Channel series Hannah Montana, before announcing to the crowd that her goddaughter was in the audience.

Cyrus joked that the moment defeated her plan to watch the show quietly. Looking back, however, she said it was worth it. “This memory is gold to me,” she said.

The singer grew more emotional as she reflected on how she continues to feel Parton’s presence following her death in August.

“Me and Dolly, we are eternal,” she continued. “Nothing in this life could ever tear us apart.”

Cyrus then tearfully expressed how much she misses her godmother, telling the audience, “I’m gonna see her again, and I can’t fucking wait ’cause I miss her.”

Before launching into “Jolene,” Cyrus also celebrated Parton’s lasting musical legacy. “Some of the greatest music that we have today was written, produced, performed by my aunt Dolly, and this is one of those songs.”

“She’s right here beside me every day,” Cyrus noted. “All the time more than she could be when she was here. I feel her, more now than ever.”
