#400. Where to Splurge (and Save) When Building a New House, According to Experts

Your future self will thank you for budgeting these upgrades wisely.

Building your dream house is exciting, but costs can add up quickly. By knowing what to pay extra for and which upgrades to skip, you can ensure you’re left with a beautiful, functional space that fits your lifestyle and keeps your budget in check.

“It’s not about spending the most money; it's about spending it in the right places,” says Shandon Barrett, interior designer at Love vs. Design. “Invest in the permanent finishes, craftsmanship, and everyday essentials that will serve you well for years to come. Save on the things that are easy to update, and don't feel pressured to finish every single space at once.”

Whether you’re in the process of building a home or hope to be someday, here’s how to prioritize your budget.

Moving a water or gas line requires breaking concrete slabs and/or cutting floor joists. That’s why you should settle on your ideal layout right off the bat and build with it in mind.

“If you think you’ll want a future basement bathroom, an outdoor kitchen, or an ice-maker, add the plumbing rough-ins now, even if you aren't installing the fixtures quite yet,” says Tammy Crosby, CEO at The House Designers.

Changing window sizes or adding new windows later requires removing siding, changing wall framing, and patching interior drywall. The same goes for doors. Decide on your window plans early so they can be ready to install at the ideal point during construction.

“Many homeowners opt for larger or additional windows in living areas and stairwells to brighten the interior. I also recommend investing in double- or triple-pane low-E glass to save thousands in energy bills over the life of the home,” says Crosby.

Flooring is technically removable, but the labor cost to tear out thousands of square feet of finished flooring, trim, and baseboards makes it one of the most disruptive retrofits you can perform while living in the home.

“It’s a good idea to splurge on continuous hard-surface flooring, like hardwood and LVP throughout the main areas, such as the kitchen, living room, and dining room. If you want a tile floor anywhere, you should also decide that upfront,” Crosby explains.

The exterior of a home protects the entire structure from water, wind, and thermal transfer, making it a critical part of construction. Replacing siding or roofing down the road requires scaffolding, dumpsters, and major labor expenses.

“Don’t be afraid to splurge upfront. High-performance exterior choices yield massive long-term savings,” says Crosby.

There’s often a heavy markup on decorative lighting, plumbing fixtures, and cabinet pulls, but these items are easy to swap out.

“You can choose a simple, builder-grade fixture and upgrade it later when your budget allows. As long as the electrical is planned properly, decorative lighting is one of those elements that can be changed without taking on a major renovation,” Barrett explains.

Appliances are standalone units with an expected 10- to 15-year lifespan, so you’ll have to update them eventually. Accept a standard package or reuse appliances you already own when you build.

“Just make sure the cutouts and utility hookups match your dream appliances so you can slide them in later,” says Crosby.

Custom paint colors, wallpaper, accent walls, wainscoting, and crown molding carry high labor costs from custom builders, but these finishing touches are simple upgrades.

“Stick to a single neutral wall color throughout the build. You or a local contractor can update the walls room by room over time,” explains Crosby.

Rugs, pillows, throws, and smaller decorative accessories are wonderful places to save. You can find beautiful, affordable options, and these are the pieces you can easily switch out as your style evolves.

“Not everything in a room needs to be an investment piece for the room to feel high-end,” says Barrett.

A bonus room gives you the option to create more finished square footage in the future, when needs change and/or your budget allows. That being said, many house plans include a bonus room in the design, so you can frame it out and come back to it later.

“Don’t worry about insulation, drywall, or flooring for this extra space until necessary,” Crosby says.

Follow House Beautiful on Instagram and TikTok.

#401. Every 2027 Color of the Year Announced So Far

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE Decor editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

The 2027 Color of the Year announcements are well underway, and a few common threads are emerging. Across the selections, paint brands are favoring warmth, depth, and colors they say are easy to live with—from softened blues and earthy greens to muted pinks and browns. The shades vary, but the thinking behind them often overlaps: a desire for homes that feel personal and comfortable.

As additional brands unveil their selections in the coming months, here is every 2027 Color of the Year we know so far.

Benjamin Moore has named Webster Green (HC-130) its 2027 Color of the Year, choosing an established shade from its Historical Color Collection. The brand’s senior manager of color marketing, Hannah Yeo, describes it as a “simply quintessential shade of green.” The team specifically sought a color without an obvious association with a particular decade—they wanted something that felt timeless.

Webster Green also anchors Benjamin Moore’s eight-color Color Trends 2027 palette, which pairs soft blues and pinks with rich copper, olive, and burgundy tones. “Webster Green HC-130 reflects this timeless appeal by pairing reassuring stability with optimistic energy,” Andrea Magno, the company’s vice president of brand, color, and integrated marketing, said in the announcement.

Little Greene has named Marle (335), a softened, warm brown from its newly launched paint collection, its 2027 Color of the Year. “The choice comes as brown makes a real comeback in both fashion and interiors,” the paint brand says in a press release. “As our understanding of neutrals has evolved, people have been drawn to brown's comforting appeal. They're also looking for complex, balanced shades that bring color and personality but stay neutral and easy to scheme.”

The brand suggests it for all-over color, including color-drenched rooms, for a cozy, cocooning effect.

Graham & Brown’s 2027 Color of the Year, Rose Earth, is a muted mineral pink with an earthy cast. The British interiors brand points to natural clay pigments as the shade’s inspiration, and positions it as an easy partner for warm neutrals, soft sage, and cooler tones.

Rose Earth arrives alongside the brand’s 2027 Design of the Year, Roselle Grove, a hand-painted floral wallpaper informed by the long history of chintz, and its Mural of the Year, Red Rose County, a painterly take on the Lancashire landscape. “Together, these designs tell our story of craft, color and heritage, each in their own unique ways,” says Iona Graham, Graham & Brown’s brand and marketing controller, in a statement.

Clark+Kensington’s Color of the Year is Vantage Point (38B-4), a rich midtone blue with a slightly softened quality. The shade is available exclusively at Ace Hardware, which developed the selection with the trend-forecasting firm Colour Hive.

“Homeowners are looking for more moments of connection at hoe, and color can have a powerful impact on how a space makes us feel,” Kim Kefko, Ace Hardware’s chief marketing officer, says in a statement. “Vantage Point brings a sense of warmth and character to interiors, offering a versatile blue that feels fresh for 2027 yet timeless enough to live with for years to come.”

Sherwin-Williams and its Lowe’s-exclusive HGTV Home by Sherwin-Williams paint line have named Celery, a soft yellow-green, their shared 2027 Color of the Year. Available as Celery SW 6421 and Celery HGSW6421, the shade was selected from the brand’s 2027 Colormix Trend Forecast, Rewild, a broader collection of dark greens, warm whites, plum browns, blues, reds, and purples. One of Rewild’s 10 “Continuity Colors,” Celery is positioned as a lighter, yellow-leaning alternative to the deeper hues in the forecast.

“Celery was chosen as the 2027 Color of the Year because it reflects today’s priorities: wellness, balance and connection,” Ashley Banbury, Sherwin-Williams’s color marketing manager, says.

Glidden has named Artifact (PPG10-16) its 2027 Color of the Year. The color is a warm, smoky blue—a familiar, easygoing shade.

“When everything feels like a lot, we feel like your space shouldn’t,” Ashley McCollum, Glidden’s color marketing manager, tells ELLE Decor. She describes Artifact as a “very fresh realignment”—a calm, grounded color that can refresh a room without the expense or disruption of a larger renovation. The brand suggests using it on walls, cabinetry, ceilings, and exterior details, though McCollum also pointed to a color-drenched bedroom or study as especially good applications.

Behr has named Grounded (T27-01), a brown-leaning olive green, its 2027 Color of the Year. The newly developed shade sits between moss and olive, with a brown cast that distinguishes it from the gray-green sages that have dominated paint decks in recent years.

“We created a completely new color that wasn’t in our collection before,” Kayla Kratz, Behr’s head of color, tells ELLE Decor. The company tested dozens of olive greens before landing on Grounded, which follows 2026’s smoky jade Hidden Gem. “We wanted this color with depth and dimension that just comes to life,” Kratz says.

Dutch Boy Paints is going all in on orange for 2027. Its Color of the Year, Deep Rooted (311-7DB), is a burnished, earth-toned shade with a terracotta-like cast.

The company shows the color alongside creamy whites and related orange tones, but also with blush pink and bright blue, or a muted blue-gray and forest green. “Deep Rooted offers a color that feels rich, grounding and deeply human,” Lisbeth Parada, Dutch Boy Paints’s color marketing manager, says.

Paint company Valspar has named Cottage Door (8004-38E) its 2027 Color of the Year. The brand describes the shade as a reflective midtone neutral blue, with both warm and cool undertones intended to give it broad appeal across interiors.

According to the brand, the pick reflects consumer interest in spaces that feel honest and grounding. “Cottage Door captures blue’s natural sense of security and trust while serving as a colorful new neutral that layers effortless into the home,” Valspar’s director of color marketing, Sue Kim, says. The company recommends pairing the blue with its warm gray Moon Shot (8005-2B), muted pink Apricot Blush (8003-8A), and light wood tones.

We will continue updating this story as 2027 Colors of the Year are announced, a rollout that typically begins in late summer and continues through December.

Julia Cancilla is the social media & news editor at ELLE Decor, where she oversees the brand's socials and covers design, pop culture, and emerging trends. She also authors the monthly ELLE Decoroscope column. Her work has appeared in Inked magazine, House Beautiful, Marie Claire, and more.

#404. Kim Kardashian Puts a Witchy Twist on Her Classic Skintight Style With This Sculptural Sportmax Dress

Kim Kardashian is ready for the spooky season. Putting a witchy twist on her classic style, she arrived at Los Angeles’s ABC Studios for an October 15 appearance on Jimmy Kimmel Live!, wearing a simple black maxi dress with an unconventional, pointy peplum waist.

The sculptural piece, pulled from Sportmax’s Spring/Summer 2027 collection, featured several markers of Kardashian’s signature style: a deep plunging neckline, a skintight fit, and an hourglass-accentuating silhouette. But unlike many of her wardrobe’s counterparts, which focus on cinching the waist, this dress was all about adding depth to the hips in a playful, funky fashion.

As for the rest of her look, Kardashian kept things pretty simple, leaving her long dark hair down, painting her nails a nude shade, and adding only strappy black heels for accessories.

During the sit-down, Kardashian updated Kimmel and the public about her legal studies (she’s passed the preliminary “baby bar” but not yet the final bar exam) and reminisced on her early-teenage days of “playing investigator.”

At 14 years old, she explained, O.J. Simpson came to stay at her family’s house during his 1995 double-murder trial. Her late father, Robert Kardashian, was serving as his defense lawyer, and the young future-law student got to see “everything from behind the scenes.”

“I just was so into it,” the Skims founder shared. “He had this Louis Vuitton luggage and brought it in the house and I’m seeing what’s going on the news, but I see it in real life at my house, so I’m like, ‘I’m gonna go play investigator, and I want to go through his luggage and see if I can find anything!’”

Shortly after, however, she saw on the news that the bag was going to be seized by investigators as evidence. “I’m like, ‘Oh my God, my fingerprints are all over it,’” she recalled. “And so, it made me realize that people could be involved that aren’t involved, and I need to help them.”

#405. McDonald’s Boo Buckets Are BACK For 2026—And Inspired By Disney’s Most Iconic Villains

Five familiar faces are taking over the Golden Arches this Halloween.

Forget Shamrock Shakes, Monopoly, and McRibs—the best McDonald’s seasonal products are the Halloween Boo Buckets. And this year’s version may be the best yet.

Starting October 20, the fast food chain will roll out five new Boo Buckets inspired by Disney’s most iconic villains: Scar, Cruella, Ursula, Jafar, and Maleficent.

Each collectible bucket features an illustration of its character and comes with stickers to decorate it. Each character’s sticker sheet is unique to their respective movie and includes details “true fans will recognize,” McDonald’s says. The Boo Buckets span a wide range of colors, but they all have the same yellow handle with the chain’s signature Golden Arches.

After 2016, McDonald’s quietly stopped making the annual collectibles. But following years of customer demand, the chain revived the tradition in 2022, and Boo Buckets have been a Halloween staple every year since.

This isn’t the first time we’ve seen pop culture collaborations for Boo Bucket designs. McDonald’s has previously partnered with Mr. Potato Head, Scooby-Doo, Monster High, Minions, and Peanuts. This is, however, the first set of movie-themed Boo Buckets since the 2022 relaunch.

You can get your hands on this year’s buckets with a Happy Meal purchase at participating locations starting October 20. They’ll be available for a limited time, while supplies last, so plan your drive-thru run accordingly before trick-or-treat season.

#406. The 9 Best Hair Thickening Shampoos For Men in 2026, According to Experts

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

The best defense against hair thinning is a good offense—and these are it.

WHETHER OR NOT their hair is actually thinning, most men still want to add a little more oomph to their hair. If you’re one of those guys who spend time in front of the mirror styling, blow-drying, and just trying to get a little more fullness to your quiff (don’t worry, we are too), one of the best things you can do is invest in a quality thickening shampoo. That's because, in many cases, styling starts in the shower, and these hair products help to pump up the volume of your strands even before you towel off.

These days, thickening shampoos are a dime a dozen, most of which contain ingredients like biotin, saw palmetto, caffeine, and a veritable cornucopia of botanical extracts that can help with everything from temporarily volumizing hair, removing scalp buildup to minimize dandruff or dryness, strengthening strands and, in some cases, even address underlying hair thinning and hair loss.

Although, to be clear, the primary agenda of these shampoos is to help hair feel and look thicker, not necessarily reverse thinning, as no shampoo on its own is enough to help you regrow lost hair or prevent balding entirely (you'll have to use a combination of supplements and other treatments for that).

Typically, thickening shampoos accomplish this goal by coating individual strands with ingredients to plump them up and appear thicker. Strengthening hair follicles with ingredients like keratin will also help hair look fuller, while adding moisture can cause hair shafts to swell and present thicker. In short, the healthier your hair is, the thicker it'll look.

Of course, this volume (get it?) of factors is a good thing because it means that no matter what kind of hair you have, there’s a hair-thickening shampoo out there for you. But with all those options, where do you start? After eliciting the counsel of a panel of dermatologists and hair experts on their favorite hair-thickening shampoos and what specifics to look for as a primer, we put a bunch to the test to find which were worth investing in.

When it comes to shampoos that make hair appear and feel thicker (not boost growth), no option scored as high with our testers as this bottle from Kérastase. Not only does this luxe shampoo clean like a dream, but Dr. Kash notes that it's also formulated with ingredients like hyaluronic acid, ceramides, and peptides that help add volume to hair strands, creating a thickening effect.

We can confirm this certainly made our hair look and feel thicker, not to mention the cleansing chops. It’s simply a quality shampoo that we’d recommend even for those with naturally thick locks, especially for men who use a lot of product in their hair. Kérastase packs a powerful lather, strong enough to wipe away the most stubborn grime and sweat, as well as the densest waxes, pomades, or clays.

To be clear, this shampoo is unisex; however, it markets heavily toward women and is designed to withstand the most intense of hair sprays, mousses, or gels. That being said, a byproduct of this is that it has more of a floral scent than you’ll find in most other options on this list.

For us, this scent was subtle enough that it didn’t hinder our ability to use the shampoo regularly as long as you’re using an appropriate amount of it and not overindulging. Still, if you’re 100 percent against floral scents or sensitive to fragrances in general, you might want to look at one of the other options on this list. Dr. Kash isn't the only pro who backs this stellar thickening shampoo either. Dr. Rachel Westbay, MD,, a board-certified dermatologist at Marmur Medical, explains that it not only helps with hair density but also thoroughly cleanses your hair. She adds that this shampoo is enriched with ceramides to promote elasticity and strengthen the hair, along with a dose of salicylic acid, which offers a thorough cleanse.Plus, you barely have to use more than a couple of dabs of this stuff to enjoy the results. We found a nickel-sized amount was more than enough for any man’s hair that sits above the shoulders. So while over $40 is a bit steep for a shampoo, this one lasts long enough to neutralize the cost. Add to the boost in shine we saw after one wash with this shampoo, and it’s easy to justify the price tag.

Read More: Best Shampoos for Thinning Hair

Hims continues to be one of our go-to brands for men's self-care and wellness. This well-reviewed volumizing shampoo offers a deep clean, as well as volumizing benefits, backed by its ability to fortify hair strands, which we saw as soon as the first wash.

The included niacinamide is known to improve blood circulation on the scalp, which in turn helps hair look healthier and also encourages growth. Another hero ingredient in its formula is saw palmetto, which is known to help block DHT (which contributes to male pattern hair loss), so it’s no wonder that our flow was given a boost.

The formula is also free of any parabens, sulfates, silicones, and phthalates, so most of our testers found it to be compatible with their hair without causing any reactions. An extension of this versatility is its subtle but eucalyptus scent, perfect for those who enjoy a scented shampoo, as well as those hoping to rely more on their cologne and other scents for fragrance. Not to mention, at under $12 a bottle, it's a pretty great value.

This Pura D’Or shampoo is highly recommended by William Gaunitz, FWTS, a certified trichologist and founder of Advanced Trichology. He adds that he has seen many clients bring this shampoo to his clinics and say they genuinely noticed improvements in their scalp health while using it.

Like most Pura D’Or products, this shampoo is loaded with botanical and organic ingredients, with none as crucial as its hefty dose of biotin (aka vitamin B7). This nifty vitamin helps support the production of keratin, which is the primary protein that makes up hair strands.

This protein is essential for supporting the structural foundation of hair strands, therefore plumping up locks and potentially helping other growth (though, again, this is not a solution to balding and merely a means of helping hair live up to its fullest potential).

The biggest issue we’ve found with biotin-led shampoos, or even more naturally leaning formulas in general like this one, is that they have a tendency to dry our hair out. However, Pura D’Or avoids this common pitfall, and we found it to give that refreshing feeling without drying out strands. This is likely due to the hefty amount of moisturizing aloe vera (also natural!) in its formula.

Now the downside. Pura D’Or notes that you must keep the shampoo in your hair for two minutes to see the best results; however, we found it’s closer to four or five minutes. Not the end of the world, but certainly a nuisance for those who like to shower quickly (or conserve water).

Beyond that, like many natural ingredient-led beauty products, this has a pretty strong essential oil smell. It’s not overpowering in any way, and we generally dig essential oils anyway, but it could be annoying if you’re especially anti those scents.

Dr. Kash also recommends this volumizing and thickening shampoo because it strikes the perfect balance between effectively cleansing without overly drying out hair or weighing it down. This is a common complaint our fine hair testers have with not just thickening formulas, but shampoos in general, because finer hair generally produces less oil (again, critical for hair health and keeping the scalp moisturized) and is more prone to breakage than thicker or curly hair.

Living Proof combats this with a blend of amino acids, led by amaranth peptides, which help reduce friction between strands and plump finer hair. Plus, it’s also safe for color-treated or chemically treated hair thanks to the inclusion of phytantriol in the formula. This was especially appreciated by our fine-haired testers who dye their gray hair.

Most of the shampoos on this list are intended to merely help hair appear thicker, not battle the process of balding. However, this stellar option from DS Labs is an exception. For board-certified dermatologist Dr. Chris Tomassian, MD, it all comes down to its ingredients.

He explains that shampoo is effective because it contains caffeine, which boosts blood flow to the hair and reduces DHT, a hormone linked to thinning. It also includes procyanidin B2, a compound that research suggests may help promote hair growth, according to Dr. Tomassian. DS Labs' Revita Shampoo is formulated with a collection of DHT blockers, including caffeine, biotin, antioxidants, and amino acids to help battle any incoming hair thinning.

Out of all the shampoos we tested, DS Labs' Revita Shampoo produced the most noticeable boost in both the appearance of volume and genuine hair thickness. That’s because it’s formulated with a collection of DHT blockers, including caffeine, biotin, antioxidants, and amino acids to help battle any incoming hair thinning. It also left our hair feeling soft, without being overly harsh or irritating, reminiscent of some of the more premium daily shampoos we've tried.

Dr. Westbay is a big fan of this shampoo, thanks to the collagen in its formula, which makes hair look and feel thicker and stronger by boosting volume and adding dimension. We also loved the vitamin B7, aka biotin, that helped soothe our dry-scalped testers and left hair feeling silky smooth. Add in a dose of argan oil, and it’s no wonder our scalps were feeling ultra-hydrated after washing with this stuff. Of course, it’s free of any sulfates, parabens, or other common chemicals tossed in shampoos that our dry-scalped testers are sensitive to.

Judging by the bright purple bottle and female-focused marketing, you might expect a strong floral scent, but we found the smell to be minimal and quite nice (more fresh than floral, to be honest). There is some fragrance in the formula; however, we didn’t find it to be enough to aggravate our dry scalps. We have found the dispenser pump to leave a bit to be desired, as it was prone to leakage both in the shipping process and over time from use.

According to Dr. Tomassian, this natural-ingredient-backed thickening shampoo is uniquely formulated to battle the effects of male pattern baldness. He points out that its ingredients are tailored to boost thinning hair and possibly even address androgenic hormonal hair loss (aka male pattern baldness).

In addition to caffeine (beneficial for stimulating blood flow and reducing DHT), it also includes saw palmetto and pumpkin seed. Both of these ingredients are known for their DHT-blocking effects, helping to prevent the hormone from contributing to further hair thinning. Together, these ingredients create a powerful formula designed to support healthier, thicker hair growth, according to the dermatologist.

When using, this shampoo’s no-nonsense, natural ingredient-fronted formula was certainly felt, producing one of the smoothest-feeling lathers on this list. We also dug that it was hypoallergenic for sensitive scalps, despite still being mildly fragranced. Plus, even for our testers who have yet to face any signs of baldness, this shampoo simply made their hair look and feel denser.

Sometimes, if you're just looking to give your hair a bit more volume, all it needs is some TLC. IGK's Extra Love does exactly that with its powerful combination of moisturizing coconut oil and prebiotics, like glycerin and date fruit ferment extract, that help support the scalp's natural microbiome by balancing its oil production.

Plus, there's some biotin thrown in for good measure. It's no wonder Dr. Westbay backs the stuff. Dr. Westbay explains that this shampoo is ideal for those with thinning hair, helping hair look fuller and bouncier overall thanks to its mineral-rich ingredients. One key ingredient, Jeju water, is actually volcanic water that promotes healthy hair, according to the dermatologist. So it came as no surprise that our flow was looking fire after using this stuff.

This ultra-luxe shampoo feels and smells like the top-tier, rich-lathering product it is, but it’s also packed with a proprietary compound of plant-based and scientifically developed ingredients to not only make hair appear thicker and fuller, but also help combat the first signs of hair loss. Sure, it's pricey, but the results we saw were well worth it. To say nothing of the incredible rich, woodsy cologne-quality scent it rocks.

This shampoo is no joke when it comes to claims of thickening, either. We found that after a couple of weeks of use, our hair looked noticeably thicker (and genuinely might have been thicker thanks to the DHT-blocking formula). Plus, you really only need to use a small amount of this shampoo, as the lather is so expansive (which also helps offset the hefty price tag a bit).

When selecting a shampoo to thicken hair, it's essential to consider your specific hair type to achieve both targeted volume results and maintain hair health overall. For example, individuals with finer hair should avoid heavy, ultra-texturizing shampoos, which can make this hair type feel weighed down. Instead, opt for lightweight, volumizing formulas that boost fullness without compromising lift. Alternatively, coarse or curly, as well as color-treated strands, thrive with moisture-rich, sulfate-free shampoos. These will provide much-needed hydration and help prevent dryness.

You'll also want to consider your scalp, as board-certified dermatologist Dr. Natalie Kash, MD, explains that if you have a dry scalp or brittle hair, steer clear of harsh ingredients such as alcohols that can exacerbate dryness, as well as potent surfactants like sulfates. To avoid this, look for gentler shampoos with moisturizing ingredients like shea butter. On the other hand, she says that those with oily scalps should go for a clarifying shampoo to remove excess sebum without irritating the scalp.

Still, Dr. Kash says that not every product will work for everyone, and whether a thickening shampoo works for you largely depends on your hair type, as well as the formulation, concentration, and mixture of ingredients. However, there are a few common ingredients to look for that have been shown to help hair appear thicker and feel fuller.

According to Dr. Hardik Doshi, MD, a board-certified plastic surgeon and lead surgeon at Ample Hair Restoration Clinic in New York City, these are the primary ingredients worth investing in to bolster your hair's thickness or help it at least appear thicker:

When picking a shampoo to thicken hair, the size of the bottle might not be your top priority—but it’s definitely something to keep in mind, especially if you’re on a budget. Many shampoos designed to thicken hair can be pricey, and since you’ll need to buy them regularly, the cost can quickly add up. If you're looking to save a bit, opting for larger bottles can make a noticeable difference in your wallet over time. It’s all about getting the most bang for your buck without compromising on quality.

Over the past two years, I’ve been testing a wide variety of shampoos to see how well they help hair appear and feel thicker. I evaluated how effectively these products cleaned hair, their scents, and their price points. To make sure I covered all the bases, I also consulted with several doctors and one hairstylist on the best hair-thickening shampoos for men they recommend. They helped me narrow down the best products on the market for different hair types, offering valuable insights into what products and ingredients to seek out (and what to avoid).

Based on their expert advice and our extensive testing, I compiled this list of the nine best shampoos that truly deliver when it comes to thickening men's hair.

“Hair-thickening shampoos typically act in two possible ways,” says Gaunitz. He explains that either the shampoo leaves behind some sort of thickening agent after you wash, like protein or a chemical that can help expand the hair shaft, or the shampoo uses topical nutrients like vitamins B12 or B5 to nourish the scalp and strengthen follicles, or ingredients like saw palmetto or tea tree oil to help decrease oil production, depending on the targeted hair type. This is because sebum (aka your body’s naturally produced oil) is key for maintaining a healthy and moisturized scalp. Without it, hair will be prone to breakage and dryness, which will create a thinner appearance.

“You should look for thickening shampoos that act in both ways,” he says. There are a few other ways a thickening shampoo can work, most notably ones that work to block DHT and stimulate hair growth, according to Dr. Doshi. Hair growth claims can be tricky on a product like shampoo, which doesn’t stay on your scalp very long, so most thickening shampoos will use a combination of these mechanisms to achieve thickening and volumizing results.

Important to note, no shampoo will 100 percent reverse thinning or balding. Instead, most of these formulas are designed to either postpone thinning or simply help hair appear and feel thicker.

When it comes to thickening shampoos, what ingredients are not in the formula can be just as important as those that are. Dr. Doshi recommends avoiding sulfates, which can strip your hair of natural oils; parabens and phthalates, which have been linked to potential health risks in some people; silicones, which can build up on hair and weigh it down; and artificial fragrances, which can cause irritation.

Most importantly, keep in mind that not every shampoo is going to work for everyone, says Dr. Doshi, so finding the right thickening shampoo may take some trial and error. Keep at it for a while until you decide, though, because “it can take a while before any noticeable improvement occurs.” And finally, if you’re dealing with “substantial hair loss or thinning,” seek the guidance of a medical professional.

#407. The 9 Best Body Washes of 2026, According to 1 Year of Expert Testing

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

As a beauty editor for over four years, I never gave much thought to the types of body washes I use. But after moving to New York from Florida, I noticed my skin became more reactive to seasonal weather changes. Since a huge part of my job is consulting experts, I chatted with dermatologists about all things body washes for women to figure out how to fix my dry skin. Unlike harsh bar soaps that remove excess oil, these liquid body washes are gentle and made with moisturizing ingredients, says dermatologist Brendan Camp, MD, of MDCS Dermatology in New York. Not to mention, the best ones smell amazing, and lather richly to a spa-like cleanse, making them ideal for women with dry, acne-prone, and bumpy skin, or those who just want to upgrade their shower routine.

So how do they work? Body washes keep skin clean by removing dirt, pollutants, excess oil, and dead skin cells, says Dr. Camp. They can also invigorate the skin, banish acne, soothe irritation, and maintain moisture levels to prevent dryness, making them a holy grail product in my at-home routine.

Body washes aren't a one-size-fits-all pick, but by following guidance from my most trusted dermatologists, you'll learn how to shop smartly for your next game-changing beauty product. And as our resident body wash enthusiast, I tested dozens of cleansers over three months to determine my no-fail picks across all budgets.

The best body wash benefits your skin type by cleansing away impurities without messing up your protective skin barrier, says dermatologist Pooja Rambhia, MD, of Union Square Dermatology in New York. "This balance becomes especially important during seasonal changes when your skin's needs may evolve."

Now it's time to pick a body wash for women that is compatible with your skin type.

Reach for moisturizing body washes infused with humectants like glycerin to hydrate the skin, emollients like jojoba oil or ceramides to support the skin barrier, and occlusives like petrolatum or beeswax to lock in moisture, says dermatologist Hadley King, MD. Also, gravitating toward fragrance-free and unscented soaps helps avoid irritating eczema-prone skin, says Dr. King.

You should avoid comedogenic ingredients like coconut oil that clog pores and lead to zits. Instead, use a salicylic acid body wash because it's an oil-soluble beta hydroxy acid (BHA) that can penetrate pores to exfoliate and remove excess oils gently, says Dr. King. Benzoyl peroxide also effectively dissolves excess oil and penetrates pores to address breakouts without adding extra moisture that could exacerbate oiliness, says Dr. Rambhia.

Dealing with keratosis pilaris (KP)? Chemical and physical exfoliants, a.k.a. the soft, smooth granules in body washes are helpful for removing dead skin cells that leave behind rough patches of skin, says Dr. Rambhia. She likes body washes containing chemical exfoliants like alpha hydroxy acids (glycolic acid) for surface renewal and BHAs (salicylic acid) to clear congested pores.

Harsh detergents like sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS) can strip your skin of oils and leave it drier, says Dr. King. Instead, use gentle surfactants like cocobetaine, isethionates, and glucoside to cleanse and create suds, like the Method Body Wash Hydrating Body Wash. Also, prioritize pH-balanced body washes that fall between five to six and a half to support your skin barrier, dermatologist Blair Murphy-Rose, MD, recently told WH.

For the past year, I’ve tested dozens of the most popular and top-rated body washes for women available on Amazon, Sephora, Ulta, and Dermstore. And because my testing window was so wide, I can accurately weigh in on their efficacy during all four seasons. I used them in the morning to see if they brought an energizing touch to my shower, after exercising to ensure they get rid of sweat and prevent body acne during the spring and summer, and in the winter when my eczema flares up.

And we also considered overall value: my favorite budget buy comes in a three-pack for $32 on Amazon and it can fight acne. Each bottle will last for at least two months, so that’s got you covered for the next six months, or the equivalent of $5.31 a month on body wash. It’s like spending just $0.17 a day to shower. So keep scrolling for more budget-friendly recommendations worth a portion of your hard-earned paycheck.

I've been using Nécessaire's The Body Wash on and off for five years, and it's undoubtedly my all-time favorite. TBH, I only switch it out of my routine when I'm testing products for work, like with this story. #408. The Tenderheart and the Roughneck

There was always an unclosable distance between my father and me. Instead of cutting him off, like so many of my peers have done with their parents, I spent the last year of his life drawing closer to him than ever before.

I lived in the same house from the time I was a small child until I was eighteen years old, but I never noticed the two battered shoeboxes that my father kept in a white wooden cabinet in his bedroom. My parents’ TV sat right in the middle of the built-in shelving. Above it were albums full of family photographs and my dad’s family Bible. Below it were two open-door cabinets. Inside, the shoeboxes. Every child knows there is a zone of privacy in their parents’ bedroom, a place where they keep things that don’t concern you, that pre-date you. So I never noticed them. But I wonder, knowing what I know now, if it’s also the case that some things can’t be found until a person is ready to find them.

It was September 2022, when I was forty-four years old and my father, Victor Plohetski, was seventy-eight, that he told me about the shoeboxes. I arrived at his house—my house, the one I grew up in—and began what was, at that point, becoming our ritual. I met him in the living room in his oversize recliner, a chair he rarely left anymore. I unpacked my recorder and turned it on. I pulled out a yellow legal pad. I composed the questions I wanted to ask.

I am a journalist by training, a journalist in my soul the way my father was a roughneck. For a month, I had been interviewing him, determined to understand more about his life. I wanted to answer a question that had plagued me since I was a boy: Why had there been such an unclosable distance between us?

I grew up in Tylertown, Mississippi, a small dot on the state map with about nineteen hundred people and one stoplight, and spent most of my childhood on forty acres just south of town. I am gay, and as a child I was eager for people to like me, mostly because in that time and place being gay often led to taunts, ridicule, or worse. I remember adults—teachers, friends’ mothers, others in our town—using the same word to describe me: tenderhearted. I was keenly perceptive and deeply curious, and I wanted to understand the people who shaped my surroundings, in pursuit of safety and acceptance.

My father was none of that. He was shut down, closed off, and sometimes easily angered. I was a frequent target. When he thought I was acting like a “sissy,” he added an a to my name: Tonya. When I fell in love with New Orleans, eighty miles to the south of Tylertown, for its spirit of openness and acceptance, he ridiculed me for embracing “the land of fruits and nuts.”

It has become popular, especially among gay men, to cut off your family, to go “no-contact.” I never cut my father off, but for years I did something not far from it. Going no-contact is framed now—and I’m sure on some level, for the two decades that my father and I exchanged only niceties and small talk, that I saw it this way too—as a form of healing or self-protection. I understand that logic, but as a journalist it always sat uneasily with me. What I know how to do is the opposite: to ask questions that push past discomfort and bias and fraught relationships to peer into the complexity of the people underneath.

I became a journalist in part because of my father. I liked that journalism allowed me to ask probing questions, to get at the heart of a person, and his was the most mysterious heart I knew. Behind his layers of emotional insulation, I sensed deep pain. And yet, although I have interviewed many challenging subjects—a grieving father who tragically forgot his eighteen-month-old son in the backseat of a hot minivan; a police officer who accidentally ran over and killed his partner, a young mother—I had never asked these kinds of questions of my father.

But now, here I was. In the last year of his life, I interviewed him properly, like the subject of one of my stories. I wanted to unearth his formative experiences and try to understand how they impacted who he was as a father. I recorded our conversations. I looked through old photos. I turned over my own past anew.

On this day, I decided to ask him about his parents. We had been at it for only a month, and this was one of the first times he warmed to the questioning. He loved talking about his mother, Elizabeth, and his father, Anthony. He loved talking about their love. That is how, almost as an aside, he told me about the shoeboxes.

My journalistic intuition told me I had stumbled upon something important. “What?” I asked.

“I have their love letters,” he told me, gesturing toward the cabinet under the television. And then, almost as soon as that was out of his mouth, he told me that after he passed, I was to immediately burn them.

When I learned my father was dying, I was on my sofa at home in Austin, my dog Calvin at my side and my computer in my lap. It was late July 2022, and I was in the midst of one of the most consequential stories of my career—the bungled law-enforcement response after a gunman slaughtered nineteen children and two teachers in adjoining classrooms in Uvalde, Texas. As I was methodically retracing how officials concocted and disseminated a false story of police heroism after the shooting, my phone pinged with a frantic text from my older sister. Our father had contracted Covid-19 pneumonia. We didn’t know then that this would be his last illness, but we knew it could be bad. He had a long résumé of medical ailments that included leukemia, heart failure, diabetes, and high blood pressure. Doctors were admitting him to the thirty-five-bed hospital in Tylertown.

I had spent the previous two years shielding my father from the virus from Austin, 550 miles away. I shipped masks with the University of Mississippi logo—I knew repping Ole Miss, his favorite football team, guaranteed he’d wear them. And I made sure he was one of the first in the state to get a vaccine, pulling over on the side of a freeway to urgently book his online appointment as rumbling big rigs whizzed past.

Now that my fear of his getting the virus had become reality, I quickly formulated a long-distance care plan. Over the next twelve hours, I negotiated for him to move by ambulance from Tylertown to a bigger hospital along Mississippi’s coast, three hours away, where my brother-in-law was a physician. I abandoned a weekend getaway that I desperately needed in order to decompress from draining Uvalde coverage and raced to see him, cycling through limited visiting hours with my mother and sister. When I left on a hot and humid Sunday afternoon to return to Austin, it was with an unexpected feeling of relief: He was set to go home the next morning.

That night, I shot up in bed at 2:45 a.m. when the phone rang. Our dad’s heart had suddenly stopped, my sister told me through tears, and doctors and nurses were doing CPR.

He had already defied death so many times that I’d lost count. Along with his medical ailments, he had simply lived hard. In addition to spending thirty of his seventy-eight years working on an offshore oil rig through scorching days in the Gulf of Mexico and ferocious summer tropical storms, he worked on towboats in the Mississippi River and managed the family cotton gin in the 1960s. Even after he retired from Shell Oil Company, he kept tending to our family land, sweat dripping from his cap-covered bald head as he steered his beloved John Deere tractor.

So when I got on another plane to Mississippi, I knew my father was beginning an inevitable march to the end. That was when I decided it was time to finally get to know him.

The hospital released him a few days later, but he returned home badly battered, on oxygen and unable to walk without help. He gazed daily from his leather recliner onto our land, determined to return to the Deere.

I staffed my parents’ house with caregivers and visited often, perfecting the routine of a nonstop Friday-afternoon flight to New Orleans, an eighty-mile drive north across Lake Pontchartrain, and two nights in my old room. On Sunday evening, I would return to Austin. In between, we talked every single day.

As a younger man, my father was like a mule in his brute strength. He towered more than six and a half feet, weighed more than three hundred pounds. He drove a series of Ford pickups, and he had a gruff voice that grew raspy from earlier cigarette smoking and years of chewing tobacco. He judged men with office jobs, men like me, as less than.

But in his last year, he grew small. His chair could seem to swallow him up. When I arrived, I would sit on a love seat next to his recliner, plopping down my fully charged recorder on an end table to memorialize his words as I scribbled notes.

I knew that I would need to start slowly, nonthreateningly, and gently began asking him questions about himself. On one of my first visits, he seemed uninterested. I battled for his attention over a blaring rerun of Gunsmoke. The next day, I tried again, even though I often felt forced to ask leading questions for which he would give evasive or incomplete answers.

I began by asking him about one of the key events I already knew about. His response was six words. They were true, but they felt like a stone wall. Did the early loss of your father set the stage for your entire life?

“I reckon you could say that,” he told me.

I left that weekend wondering if my effort to learn about my father would carry on the tradition of our relationship—a constant emotional near miss that would leave me angry, disappointed, and feeling incomplete.

But years of experience had taught me that sometimes, with challenging subjects, you simply have to find the right question. Maybe I was starting in the wrong place.

When I returned a few weeks later, in late September, I arrived to find my father in his recliner drinking a glass of chocolate Ensure with an Ole Miss blanket in his lap. He appeared no worse than before but certainly no better. After a few moments of small talk—“Yes, Dad, it is still hot in Austin,” I said—I started asking him about how his parents had met.

He turned to me and smiled, seeming to relish the opportunity to talk about his parents’ young affair, appearing to love that he was the product of a storybook 1940s romance. This was the day he would go on to tell me about the letters. But first he told me about the people who wrote them.

Elizabeth Brumfield was a college senior, earning her degree at the University of Southern Mississippi in Hattiesburg, and later became a pioneering high school English teacher. My grandfather’s family emigrated from Poland and settled in Brooklyn. Anthony John Plohetski joined the Army as a young man and was a sergeant stationed at Camp Shelby, Mississippi, sixteen miles south of campus.

My father didn’t know exactly when and how they met, but I unearthed an important detail only after he died. I found their wedding announcement in an online newspaper archive. My grandparents married in April 1943, seven months before my father’s birth. My grandmother wore “a becoming pink dress with a sweetheart neckline edged with pinkdyed lace”—details and timing that make me wonder if my father was the result of an unplanned pregnancy. I never got to broach this with him, and I wonder to this day whether he had done that calendar arithmetic.

My father might not have known that, but he knew the basic facts about his father, whom he called “Tony.” One fact loomed larger than all the others: Tony died in Italy in 1944. My father kept the official notice that arrived from the U.S. Department of War folded in his Bible.

The psychological imprint of a young loss was embedded in his earliest memories. He could not bring himself to linger in detail, but he told me about how he was the only child he knew who didn’t have a father and how his elementary school classmates sometimes teased him for it as they raced around the sand-covered playground.

“Dad, I’m really sorry,” I told him. His lip trembled and he turned away.

I know the cruelty of bullies. As a boy I faced repeated attacks from classmates who called me a “sissy” or “fag.” In those times, my father struggled to provide much comfort. His lack of concern was so pronounced that I wondered if he was on their side. Hearing this story changed things for me. I suspect the vision of his son being taunted invoked some of his own memories, memories too painful to bear. We had been bullied on the exact same playground, at Tylertown Elementary School, a generation apart.

The more I spoke with my father, the more the events of his life recontextualized the ones we shared, including one of the most important moments of my life.

My maternal grandfather died in June 1998, between my sophomore and junior years of college, landing me for several days at my parents’ house. The day after his funeral, I sat watching reruns of 1980s sitcoms with my sister. We hadn’t seen much of each other in recent years. I had been in Oxford at Ole Miss—a college I’d chosen to try to earn my father’s grudging respect—and was spending the summer at a journalism gig in Jackson, chasing juicy political scandals and made-for-TV crime stories in the capital city. My sister, five years older, lived in Hattiesburg, the closest town in Mississippi of any real size.

While The Facts of Life flashed across the screen, she began explaining that she suspected that I was gay. Then she simply asked me, point-blank. I had never thought about how I would tell my parents or the rest of my family, but the reality about myself came tumbling out.

With that, I felt boxed in: Once she knew, everyone would need to know, and I was already an experienced-enough journalist to recognize that information is best delivered firsthand, directly from the primary source—not through the rumor mill or dressed up by a PR machine.

I could hear the chug of my father’s tractor outside, and although the timing was terrible, I needed to tell him. He soon came inside for a break, sitting at our round kitchen table with a glass of ice water.

I announced simply and directly: “I’m gay.”

The color drained instantly from his face, which turned to a look of disgust, anger, and shock.

We both sat in silence for several moments before he stood up and walked away. Minutes later, I heard him wailing in the half bathroom, just off the kitchen.

When my mother returned home later that afternoon, I told her too. Without saying much, she called our local preacher, who rushed to our house for what my mother told him was a “family emergency.” When he arrived, I’m sure they both had hoped that he would deliver swift condemnation and a prayer for divine sexual-orientation intervention. Instead, he reminded me that God made and loves each of us. After the minister left that night, my father and I mumbled only a few words to each other.

I’ll never fully understand the intensity of my father’s reaction, but one thing I realize today that I couldn’t fathom then: His response was almost entirely about him. I wonder if it was an affront to his sense of himself, a source of shame that such a tough man could have a gay son.

A couple days later, I packed my red Ford Mustang and returned to Jackson for the rest of the summer and Ole Miss for my junior year. That was the start of a long and low-grade estrangement that would last until he became terminally ill.

In the final months of his life, my father sometimes requested sliced apples served together with milk in a bowl. It was a treat his grandmother, Ethel Brumfield, often made him. He spent a lot of time around Ethel and Claud, his grandfather, after his mother remarried in 1947. His mother—my grandmother—remained family, and I’m still close with her daughters. But my father spent more and more time at the Brumfields, and eventually he went to live with them full-time.

This fatherless boy began calling his grandfather “Daddy.” Dad told me he would follow Claud to the family-run cotton gin as frequently as possible. He admired that many people in the community treated his grandfather with the respect of an upstanding, well-mannered, small-town southern businessman.

A bowl of apples was in front of him one Saturday afternoon in October 2022 when I showed up to talk. As he started telling me about his last years with his grandfather, I could tell something was different. My mother, who often gave us privacy during these conversations, overheard us from the kitchen and suddenly appeared, sitting next to him.

My father told me that when he was thirteen, his grandfather became ill. He didn’t exactly remember what ailed him, but in an echo of my own experience—or perhaps a premonition of it—it soon became clear to my father that Claud was dying. He was terrified of losing another daddy. One day, he told me, desperate to assure himself the two were inseparable, he found a lasso that he used to play cowboy and bound himself to his grandfather.

Claud died days later, in the spring of 1957.

My dad sat quietly in his recliner after sharing that story. My mother had tears in her eyes. Each of us was still for several moments, the only sound the soft whir of my father’s oxygen machine. I decided that I had asked enough for the weekend.

I recall thinking, while driving the winding two-lane roads back to the New Orleans airport the next day, that his grandfather’s death likely cemented who my father became. I had been in enough therapy at that point to know about compounding trauma—that unless a loss is fully processed, the next will stack itself on top and add to the grief. Instead, I surmised, my father hardened any soft edges he had and devised an emotional shield that blocked his pain, the way his respirator had fended off a total and complete silence I’m not sure any of us could have faced.

As the fall passed, winter in Mississippi blew in, and the year turned over. I kept interviewing my father, and a funny thing happened—we reached the domain of my own faint, early childhood memories.

As a boy, I often drove with my father to an area of Tylertown where many Black workers settled—“the Quarters,” people called it—to visit a man named Prentiss Smith. My dad would ease his Ford pickup to the front of Prentiss’s mustard-colored ramshackle house.

“You stay right here,” he’d tell me as I watched from the passenger seat while he and Prentiss exchanged a few words on his screened-in front porch. Several days later, some treat would arrive at our house, usually a chocolate or lemon meringue pie or a steaming pot of chicken and dumplings.

Prentiss worked at my family’s cotton gin for years. Dad shared stories handed down by his grandparents about how Prentiss carried him on a large pillow as an infant. I had already gathered that at the cotton gin all the laborers and customers had adopted my father, whom they called “Little Victor.” But Prentiss became like an older brother, and it was clear that my father elevated him to the position of role-model-in-chief for his strength and work ethic.

It was only during this conversation, there in my parents’ house, that I came to learn the purpose of the repeated trips to see Prentiss that I had witnessed decades earlier: My dad continued supporting Prentiss financially at times, and what seemed like gifts from the kitchen from his wife Lettie were repayments.

The memories were a rare insight into my father’s tenderness but also a window into how he could be emotionally inert. Many southern families at that time employed and had complicated bonds with Black housekeepers or nannies. But my father, even in the final year of his life, even as we were spending so much time digging through his memories, couldn’t seem to muster much introspection.

“That’s just the way we was,” he told me.

My father’s candor, his matter-of-factness about their unconventional friendship, filled me with sadness and anger. In the years after I came out to him, he had not afforded me that level of acceptance.

But then, maybe my father never exactly felt acceptance with Prentiss either. It was certainly unusual for a white boy and a Black man to have such a treasured relationship in an era and place that demanded racial separateness. Maybe this was another memory loaded up with pain. Prentiss, too, was a father figure—one those around my dad would never fully accept.

The last time I remember hearing Prentiss’s name before these conversations was fifteen years earlier, when my mother casually mentioned that he had died. Neither she nor my father made mention of his significance in my father’s life.

A year after I came out to my family, I moved to Austin in 2000 for an entry-level job with the Austin American-Statesman. It was about as far from Tylertown as I could get: much bigger than Hattiesburg, bigger even than New Orleans. Crucially, it was infinitely more open. I began seriously dating but repeated a similar dynamic time and time again for a period of about fifteen years. It was a prolonged “daddy phase” during which I frequently gravitated— “like a heat-seeking missile,” my therapist used to say—to older men with emotional issues.

The trajectory of my personal life changed in the summer of 2016. After a monthslong dating “reset,” I logged back on to dating apps and saw the profile of a handsome Austin lawyer with a name that drew my curiosity: Wroe. We hit it off on our first coffee date. Wroe also was different from the previous parade of men: He was a stable force, three years younger.

In early 2019, we decided to get engaged and marry that fall.

My enthusiasm dampened when I considered my father. He had met Wroe many times and enjoyed his company but did not recognize us as a couple, a reality that he seemed intent on keeping secret from himself.

I planned to attend a Mardi Gras event in New Orleans and divert from my usual trek to Tylertown so I could be on neutral ground when I told my parents the news. I invited them to a favorite spot, one of the easiest to find once they crossed Lake Pontchartrain into the city.

I ate no more than five bites of gumbo, my stomach in knots.

Across the table, my father downed a dozen butter-drenched chargrilled oysters while my mother, to my right, engaged in easy conversation, catching me up on news from our hometown. I went into my well-rehearsed announcement.

“I want to let you know that I have made an important decision,” I said. “Wroe and I are going to get married this year.”

My father’s face instantly turned to stone, transfiguring in a way I’d seen once before: “It is against my wishes,” he declared.

“I’m not really asking about your wishes,” I shot back. “I’m here to inform you. I hope you will support me, but I can’t make you.”

My father shot up from the table, just as he had done twenty-one years earlier when I came out. My mother looked at me and said, “I think you and Wroe will be very happy together.”

There was always a seam of jealousy running through my relationship with my father. He was hypermasculine in a way I could never be, the high school football player, the cotton gin operator, the offshore oil rig mechanic. At the same time, he’s always seemed to resent my achievements. He’d been an average student and, eventually, a community college dropout. I excelled at Ole Miss, the school he idolized, but his attitude toward my education never moved past the way he’d respond when I missed even a single word on a spelling test, despite making an A. “You ain’t as smart as you think you are,” I can still hear him saying.

And marriage? Marriage was an institution he held sacrosanct, one he jealously guarded. He met my mother, Diane Williams, in early 1971 as his life was falling into place. After the cotton gin went under, a casualty of economic change, he’d tried working on the Mississippi before landing a job offshore. Shell hired him, and just as I later understood that journalism perfectly suits me, working in the Gulf of Mexico allowed my father the ultimate tough-guy flex. My mother had gotten a job at the local hospital in Tylertown and rented a tiny apartment behind a home on Magnolia Avenue, just across the way from the white wooden house where my father lived with his grandmother. He recalled her as sweet, soft-spoken, and “mighty purty.” They married six months after they met and stayed that way until he died: fifty-two years.

Could that be the same institution as the one I was about to enter into?

He emerged from the restroom moments later, looked at my mother, and demanded, “Let’s go.”

We barely spoke over the next few months. My mother remained in regular contact, assuring me that she wholeheartedly planned to attend our wedding. I made clear that I wanted my father to come but only if he would support us.

I don’t think he ever got there, but a more profound force in his life changed his mind: the fear of isolation. We had come a long way from the Tylertown of my youth; virtually my father’s entire family planned to attend our wedding. I don’t think he wanted to be alone. One afternoon in September, my mom called to say that she and my father had just returned from a shopping trip. He had bought a new navy suit, a white button-down shirt, and a lavender tie and matching lavender pocket square that he would be wearing to our wedding.

In one of our final conversations, I told my father that I had been thinking that one day I would write about his life. I’m not sure that he exactly knew what that might mean, and until now, until I realized how many people were choosing to run from difficult relationships with their parents, I don’t think I did either. But though he was very ill at that point, he looked up at me and smiled. It was one of the few times I can remember him seeming proud of me.

It was nearly a year after we had started our interviews—a year since my father’s cardiac arrest, a long time since I’d lost count of the number of visits—that his health began free-falling. He struggled even more to breathe and stopped eating. His color changed, and he developed purple splotches on his arms. My mother called especially shaken one morning to say that my father had spent the night semi-delusional, calling out names of his best friends—Buddy, Julius, Floyd, and even Prentiss—who had been dead for years, seemingly having vivid conversations with them.

A strange thing occurred to me when my mother told me that: I felt compassion for my father in a way I hadn’t before. What had been a deep well of resentment was filling, instead, with that compassion. Maybe it was hearing Prentiss’s name again that did it. And I knew the other names that were doubtless passing through his mind—Tony, Claud.

My father made another trip to the hospital to try to get his increasing agitation under control. I now understand his were hallmark end-of-life symptoms.

As July 4, 2023, approached, flights from Austin to New Orleans were oversold. I hit the highway, driving eleven hours across the Louisiana swamps to Hattiesburg.

I have covered plenty of death in my career, but my familiarity came in situations of sudden, traumatic deaths—shootings and car crashes mostly, although I was a media witness for an execution in the Texas death chamber in 2010.

I didn’t know what the process of natural death looked like until I saw the biggest man I had ever known curled into a ball in a drab hospital room.

After months of my asking questions, he turned the tables: Did I think he was dying? My father had spent months being honest, so I tried to offer the same. I told him I thought he might be, but I wasn’t sure. I stayed at his bedside before promising to return after a few hours of sleep.

The next morning, our extended family planned to keep a bedside vigil. Instead, when we walked in, he was sitting up in a blue hospital gown and ready to greet a parade of visitors. I prioritized a few minutes alone with him. I wanted to know whether he accepted that the final chapter of his life was closing and how it felt to be dying.

We shared a sad and uncomfortable laugh when he said his hand was on the doorknob that would take him to the other side. Then he paused and turned serious. “It’s getting late in the evening,” he told me.

I had to return to Austin the next morning, and I vacillated about what to do. Could I really leave? Should I treat my goodbye as final? I realized I was at peace with my father in a way I could never have imagined a year earlier. I settled on a middle ground, a squeeze of my father’s hand and just a few words: “I hope to see you soon.”

He returned home for another night or two, then went back to my hometown hospital once more before we decided to transition him to a nursing facility across the street with a hospice wing. I arrived home from work that same evening, and a nurse called to say that she didn’t think he would survive the night. She called again, just before midnight, to say that he died.

I was on a plane at sunrise, back to New Orleans and on to Tylertown, to the place where I’d grown up. I went about planning my father’s funeral exactly how he had wished. It was to be held at the small-town church, Tylertown United Methodist, where he was a lifelong member. I had assembled the men he requested serve as pallbearers and invited one of his favorite preachers to conduct the service. He also requested that we make sure one particular song was sung, “When They Ring Those Golden Bells.” It was the same hymn he remembered hearing the congregation sing at his grandfather’s funeral when he was thirteen years old.

During the service, the preacher asked people who had crowded into the church to share their memories of him. Several men I had only met in passing rose from their seats.

They were colleagues of his from his time working offshore. They recalled how my father was the dean of the crew on his oil rig and how he had attained elite status among those who worked there. Their remarks gave me a glimpse into that part of my father’s life—how he was the go-to authority when mission-critical machines needed an urgent fix. One described how, when confronted with a problem, my father—they all called him “Vic”—would slide his fingers through the loops of his Carhartt overalls, furrow his brow, then deliver a solution.

In hindsight, I am not the least bit surprised to learn that my father basked in presiding over such a close-knit, man-only club. They saw the version of my father he wanted people to see, and they revered him. But they were seeing only one part of who he was. They could never have understood what I knew now, that he and I shared a wound, that neither of us had the father he needed. It is the kind of wound I now see can be passed, from generation to generation, from father to son. Perhaps going no-contact aims to break that chain. But to my surprise, these wounds can be healed.

My well of compassion had filled up. In the year I’d spent talking to him, I’d replaced my image of my father as one on the oil rig, or in Ole Miss gear, or in the living room the day I came out, or eating oysters the day I announced my engagement. Instead I pictured him in what he was wearing in his casket, the suit I had selected for him: navy blue, white button-down, splashes of lavender down the center of his chest and directly over his heart.

A few months after he died, I went into my parents’ bedroom and opened the cabinet where my father kept his parents’ letters. I had never agreed to burn them, and now I sat on the floor and opened the weathered shoeboxes. The letters were written during the war, not long before Tony, my grandfather, died. There were dozens. I unfolded them gingerly and read them, one by one. They confirmed the young love affair my father had told me about. But they also described the plan his parents had for their life as a family. For him.

April 26, 1943: “I want our baby to be the best looking and smartest kid in Mississippi. I won’t say the United States because that covers too much territory, but if it is as smart as its mother, I will be more than satisfied.”

February 25, 1944: “Dearest sweetheart, You can’t imagine the thrill that I get when you tell me he is growing every day. I sure do miss not being with you and watching him grow.”

In letter after letter, Tony explained his desire to be the best dad possible when he returned home. And then the correspondence ceased.

My grandmother wrote a final letter that Tony apparently never received. It is dated October 1, 1944—after his death. Handwritten on the front of the envelope in black letters is the word Deceased. It was returned to the sender.

“Tonight Victor was in the program at the church. He was so good and afterwards, everyone said to tell you your son performed nicely on his first stage appearance.”

This was what my father found so painful that he could not stand for the letters to outlive him: The father he never had had loved him so, so dearly.

#409. Here’s What the American Dream Home Really Looked Like in the 1990s

Take a tour of the warm, family-friendly showhouse that defined this decade’s style.

Since 2019, House Beautiful’s annual Whole Home project has highlighted some of the best emerging design talent and trends, inspiring a wave of new paint, styling, layout, and organization ideas. In honor of our latest 2026 show house debuting in Charleston, South Carolina, we’re revisiting our archives with a predecessor to today’s Whole Home—the “House of the ‘90s.”

While the 1990s are known for the emergence of mainstream minimalism, à la Calvin Klein and John Pawson, the editors of House Beautiful at the time understood how much the American homeowner really wanted to embrace these trends. Their 1991 show house overlooking the Chattahoochee River in Georgia was a distinctive blend of relaxed traditionalism, family-friendly whimsy, and suburban charm. The whole house is cast in warm, golden neutrals, with flexible seating areas everywhere. Antiques blend in with comfy upholstery (coated in Scotchgard) and beachy white wicker. It’s a home you can really imagine living in.

Read the original story, which ran in our February 1991 issue, and tour the full House of the ‘90s space below.

Story by Mervyn Kaufman, Dara Caponigro, and Susan Zevon

House Beautiful has been talking for almost two years about how we Americans want to live in the ’90s, spelling it out in numerous articles. Finally, we decided to nail our philosophy down literally with boards and shingles, windows and doors. So, with the help of the American Wood Council, this sunny house was built on the banks of a placid river in Georgia, and everything we have been reporting to you was put into it. Our architect was Melanie Taylor of New Haven, Connecticut. Working closely with her were Atlanta interior designer Nancy Braithwaite and the builder, John Wieland Homes.

When HB first began to study what people wanted from their houses in the ’90s, our sources in the design world said, "old-fashioned touches like porches and columns, wedded to contemporary, bright, airy interiors.” They said a home should be “both a refuge and a new frontier... a sheltering, nurturing family center.” They talked about comfort, pared-down traditional styling, classic country details, little hideaway places, romantic bedrooms, pampering baths, big family kitchens.

We said yes to the whole wish list for our House of the ’90s, and you can buy plans to build one of your own.

“The decorating respects the architecture,” says interior designer Nancy Braithwaite. The house has a lighthearted spirit, and in the living room particularly, the accent is on comfort. The beadboard ceiling crisscrossed with rafters is painted off-white, appropriate for an informal space in which sisal carpeting and wicker pieces from McGuire set an easygoing mood.

For the windows, Braithwaite shirred upholstery fabric on a rod, and each room was given a surprise element here. An antique beechwood and shell screen enhanced with a checkerboard of blue art paper. The armoire entertainment center holds a TV and stereo. This is not a room just for guests but for the whole family.

The ceiling of the main bedroom echoes the unusual roofline. The walls’ tent-like stripe, hand-painted by Linda Ridings, was designed by Braithwaite for visual impact. The furniture is a casual mix aimed at everyday comfort. The white damask upholstery is also used for the bed hangings whose borders repeat the linen that makes up the duvet. The same linen print reappears as bands on the Roman shades. Adding to the luxury of the room is a narrow balcony looking out on the Chattahoochee River, “almost like a treehouse," says architect Melanie Taylor.

The main bath is a sumptuous spa under a series of arches, one of which frames the window-wrapped whirlpool tub. It is a space two people can use comfortably, with room for a steam shower. The bath is as airy as the bedroom, creating a kind of three-exposure breezeway in which air will circulate well, even in the hot Atlanta summers.

“People nowadays want warmer, more nurturing environments that support the way they really live,” says architect Taylor. “This house provides a balance between reassuringly traditional values and the demands of contemporary living. At the same time it fulfills our yearning for the new and the surprising.”

House of the ’90s gives major consideration to the needs of the family, and every member is given equal consideration. There are spaces—the living and dining rooms, breakfast room, and kitchen—in which the family comes together. There are private spaces—the conservatory, “secret room,” octagon room and the bedrooms—where it is possible to find solitude or a private conversation or to study, read, relax or do desk work.

“The key to this design is flexibility,” says designer Braithwaite. Each room has a distinct personality, but all spaces flow together, relating to each other and to the total design. “In the ’90s, we have no need for unused rooms,” she adds. “Most rooms in this house can have more than one function and can adapt to a family's changing needs and living patterns. The architecture is strong throughout; the decorating is comfortable and just a little on the playful side.”
