#412. Who Is Elizabeth Holmes’s Partner, Billy Evans?

This story contains spoilers for You Can See Everything.

When Nathan Fielder asked Elizabeth Holmes to document the days leading up to her serving her prison sentence for his new A24 documentary, You Can See Everything, the proposition meant that he would also be spending a large portion of the shoot with Holmes’s partner, Billy Evans.

The documentary spends time delving into Holmes’s public legal scandal with Theranos—the now-defunct biotech company that saw her committing investment fraud—but it also sheds light on Holmes and Evans’s relationship and how they have managed to thrive despite her sentencing.

As the documentary, co-directed by Lance Oppenheim, progresses, Fielder’s focus shifts from Holmes to Evans. “Weren’t you worried she was scamming you?” Fielder asked him at one point, to which Evans responded, “100 percent, but what does she have to gain from me?” When presented with the knowledge of his family’s wealth, Evans defended Holmes and said, “I think there’s a lot of different levels of wealth.” Things only snowball from there.

Evans’s grandparents, William and Anne Evans, own the Evans Hotel Group. Founded in 1953, Evans Hotels consists of three luxury properties, which include The Lodge Terry Pines, the Bahia Resort Hotel, and the Catamaran Resort Hotel and Spa. All three of the properties are located in California.

Evans’s LinkedIn profile revealed that he attended the Massachusetts Institute of Technology between 2011 and 2015. He earned his bachelor’s degree in economics.

Evans’s LinkedIn also revealed that he’s the CEO of Haemanthus, his self-founded AI-driven medical testing startup; he’s held the role since 2022. The company aims to achieve a mission similar to that of Holmes’s Theranos, which sought to provide blood diagnostics through one drop of blood with the Edison machine. Instead of using one drop of blood for diagnostics, Haemanthus is working to create a device that tests blood in addition to urine and saliva for the presence of diseases.

“This is not Theranos 2.0. Theranos attempted to miniaturize existing tests. Our approach is fundamentally different. We use light to read the complete molecular story in biological fluids, seeing patterns current tests can’t detect. Not an improvement. A different paradigm,” the company shared in a statement to Fortune in 2025, following reports of Holmes advising on the project. “Setting the record straight. Elizabeth Holmes has zero involvement in Haemanthus. We’ve learned from her company’s mistakes, but she has no role, now or future.”

In a 2023 joint interview with The New York Times, Evans revealed that he and Holmes fell for each other fast. “To say we immediately fell in love isn’t an overstatement,” he said.

Holmes, however, noted that Evans had some reservations about entering a relationship with her. “It had been two years of all this stuff written about me, and I think you get to know someone in a totally different way when you walk in with that skepticism versus if you meet when everything is sunshine and roses,” she said. “That allowed us to get to know each other in a really deep way.” The couple got engaged in August 2018.

Holmes gave birth to their son, William Holmes Evans, in 2021. By 2023, a court document revealed that Holmes gave birth to her and Evans’s second child, a daughter named Invicta.

Evans attended several of Holmes’s court dates, appearing by her side on the way to and from her hearings. In January 2022, she was found guilty of three counts of wire fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud. She’s currently serving her sentence—which was reduced to nine years from 11 years—at Federal Prison Camp Bryan in Texas. She will be transferred to a halfway house in August 2027.

While Holmes was sentenced, Evans asked the court in November 2022 to shorten her sentence so she could enjoy more special moments with their son. “My heart is broken with the thought of spending any days away from Liz, for a future in which my son grows up with a relationship with his mother on the other side of glass armed by guards,” he said. Evans still visits Holmes regularly, with him telling People in February 2025 that it has been “hell and torture” at the prison facility. The tech CEO added that it “shatters” Holmes when she says goodbye to him and her family.

You Can See Everything makes some shocking revelations about Evans, like that he posts from Holmes’s X account while she’s in prison (for a while, it was without her knowledge), and that he arranged to be paid for his and Holmes’s appearance in the documentary, which he ultimately rescinded. (It’s unclear whether Holmes knew about the deal.)

During a screening of the film in L.A. this month, Fielder said of the couple, “Neither of them have seen the film. Elizabeth is still incarcerated; Billy hasn’t seen it.” He added, according to The Hollywood Reporter, that Evans “started trying to exert a level of control over the process that made it very hard to engage with him, and it was uncomfortable for us and also A24 and everyone. And I think we sort of had to stop—I think communication broke down basically, and we’ve been in that like state for a little bit. So it’s been challenging in that way.”

Evans confirmed that he hasn’t seen the film during an interview with the All In podcast, which was released on October 15. “I haven’t seen it. I might think this is the dumbest thing I have ever done,” Evans said, per Variety. He has seen the trailer and said that Holmes “looks insane” in it. Evans added, “Am I nervous? I have been through so many intense, surreal experiences that it takes a bit to raise my blood pressure. With this, there’s certainly concern, but it’s ultimately our decision.”

On All In, Evans elaborated on why he wanted to make the film ahead of Holmes’s 11-year sentence. “She’s been prevented from speaking publicly in any way, shape or form, and this would come out after that period in which she is now allowed to talk,” he said. “There’s been a lot of media produced on her. There’s been a lot of people who have told her story. That narrative is pretty ossified. The whole idea was: Here she is, see her and make up your own mind. It’s not to re-litigate the case. Practically, at this time she was not allowed to talk about the case, so she was gonna follow the rules and not talk about the case.”

He explained that his own loved ones have thought he was “crazy” for knowing—and now being in a relationship with—Holmes. “And they would meet her and spend time with her and see her in a totally natural environment, like going on a hike or helping a friend. Every opinion of her would radically shift,” Evans said. “That was the intention of the film. To help scale that up and allow other people to sit with her and make up their own minds.”

#413. Don’t Start Over—Here’s How To Get A Stuck Cake Out Of Its Pan

One of the most thrilling moments in a baker’s day is flipping a pan over and hoping that freshly baked cake falls right out. But what if it doesn’t? Is the cake a lost cause, or can you still salvage it without tearing it apart? “If you’ve fallen victim to a stuck cake, don’t fear,” senior food editor Makinze Gore says. “We have a hack to get a stuck cake out of your Bundt pan.” It’s as easy as heating up your pan, running a knife along its edge, and flipping it carefully.

Here’s how to remove a stuck cake from its pan without ruining it.

Aside from a poorly greased pan, Gore says one reason baked goods might get stuck is that they've cooled too long in their pans. She recommends letting a cake cool for about 15 minutes. Then you can take it out of the pan to finish cooling.

“As it cools, the sugar and the fat will start to harden, and that's what will cause it to stick in your pan,” Gore says. She notes that the problem is even worse with a Bundt pan, which you can’t line with parchment paper because of its dips and grooves.

If you let your cake sit in the pan a little too long and have a hard time removing it, the key is to warm it up.

To do this, fill a large pot with hot water and dip the pan in it for a few seconds. You can also wrap a hot, damp towel around the bottom of the pan. “This is going to heat those sugars and fats back up and release them from the pan,” Gore says.

Before flipping the cake over, Gore recommends running an offset spatula or small paring knife along the edges to make sure the cake is loose.

To flip it over easily, place a cooling rack on top of the cake in the pan, firmly grip the pan (if it’s not cool to the touch, use oven mitts) and the cooling rack, and flip. The cake should drop right onto the cooling rack.

“The next time your cake is stuck, don’t start over!” Gore says. “This is the easiest way to get your cake out of your cake pan.”

#414. What Your Knee Pain Is Trying to Tell You, According to Doctors

FAR FROM BEING a simple hinge, your knee is the meeting point for three bones, numerous major tendons, and four ligaments, including the infamous ACL. All day long, your knees endure forces between two and three times your body weight, even during a simple walk. A lot can happen to these complicated, critically important joints. These basics help you avoid trouble or solve it if it’s happening, anyway.

“CrossFit and Pickleball have probably brought us the most patients with meniscus tears out of anything in the past 10 years,” says orthopedic sports medicine surgeon Robert LaPrade, MD, PhD, of Twin Cities Orthopedics. Shuttle runs, lurches for the ball—your meniscus takes the hit when your body moves sideways and your foot doesn’t. Hear a pop? That’s a telltale sign of a torn ACL, the ligament deep in the middle of your knee.

Going from the couch to running 10K in five days, or trying to crush nightly pickup basketball games when you haven’t touched a ball in years—basically, suddenly overdoing volume—can cause swelling and pain in the patellar tendon at the front of your knee. Tendons don’t have a lot of blood flowing through them, so microtears from training take a while to heal—and they don’t if you constantly overload them.

With age, the cartilage that lines the ends of your bones starts to wear down, causing osteoarthritis. Genetics, obesity, alignment issues, old injuries, and sometimes bad luck cause it to degrade faster in some people. “Once it’s damaged, it can’t heal. Even with all the NIH money and everything we have now, we still haven’t figured out a way to make it heal back to normal,” says Dr. LaPrade.

…is painful and so swollen you can’t see the dimples around the kneecap on either side. That’s usually a sign of internal damage, like a meniscus or ligament tear.

…is collapsing or giving out when you’re trying to walk down a flight of stairs or do other daily activities. That could signal a ligament tear.

…locks up or catches and you feel like you can’t straighten it, or it feels as if there’sa pebble in your knee. The meniscus may be in trouble.

Mainly, don’t progress your volume too aggressively. “Maintaining knee stability and neutral knee alignment—keeping knees in line with toes—becomes difficult with increasing weights,” says Brett Toresdahl, MD, an associate professor at University of Utah Health and medical director for US Biathlon. So if your squats and other moves aren’t stable and controlled, back off on the weight to avoid injury.

Less body weight means less stress on the joints.

Your knees do not love a binge workout program. “Our knees do best when they’re consistently loaded and challenged to stay strong and stable,” says Dr. Toresdahl. Both cardio and strength training are essential for healthy joints. Yes, that does mean that running won’t “wreck your knees.”

A PT can assess what to do to strengthen your muscles and keep your knees from hurting. They can also see if anything—including your hips, core strength, or alignment—is contributing to biomechanical alterations that are affecting your knees, says Charles Cox, MD, an associate professor of orthopedic surgery at Vanderbilt University School of Medicine. Sometimes, anti-inflammatory meds can make it possible to start physical therapy.

These compression sleeves might be okay as external reminders to take care with your knee while it heals. “Scientifically, most of the data we have shows that braces probably don’t quite do as much as we think they do,” says Dr. Cox.

“The vast majority of knee pain that starts without a traumatic event can be treated without surgery,” Dr. Cox says. Doesn’t mean DIY’ing it. Check in with a health care provider, of course.

“Knee pain is not like a broken bone, where, if you rest for six weeks, it heals and is strong again. Knees often feel best with regular use, as long as the activity is within the range of what the knee is currently able to handle,” says Dr. Toresdahl. They don’t magically get better with rest; you have to retrain them to work better.

If you have a knee injury and ignore the pain, you may end up putting more stress on your cartilage (not good). Call a doctor and get it sorted out. “Long term, it can lead to arthritis,” says Dr. Cox. “We try to prevent the degenerative snowball from rolling down the hill.”

#416. This Year's Best Classic Watch Remixes

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

Check out the latest riffs on time-tested designs like the Reverso and the Oyster Perpetual.

While innovation drives things forward, there’s nothing quite so appealing as an iconic watch design given a new spin. These six updates are our favorites of 2026.

The Reverso is indisputably Jaeger-LeCoultre’s most famous watch, merging functional performance and elegance in a singular deco design since 1931. You’d think it would be a challenge to reinvent such an outwardly simple watch. But then, in 2025, the house set jaded horological hearts aflutter with a version made almost entirely—from the case to the woven Milanese band and granular dial—from rose gold. This year, JLC added an 18k white-gold edition to the mix. As with its predecessor, the silvery granular dial throws the polish of the case into sharp relief. And the band on its own is something else, requiring 16 meters of tightly woven 18k white-gold wire to create. $52,500

When it was released in 1976, the Patek Philippe Nautilus was a disrupter in every way. It was big for the age, at 40mm, and simple too, with a display of just hours, minutes, and date. It was made of steel (not then considered particularly chic), and its appearance had an almost industrial impudence about it. That, in creator Gerald Genta’s mind, was precisely the point. In an era when the unbeatable accuracy of quartz put mechanical tool watches on notice, the Nautilus created an entirely new language of luxury and remains one of collecting’s most coveted watches. This year’s anniversary version is in white gold, one millimeter bigger than the original, and date-free but otherwise true to the first Nautilus, with a display showing just hours and minutes and a deep-blue sunray dial with distinctive horizontal embossing. $93,774

In 2002, the Roadster emerged for the new millennium as a watch distinct from every Cartier that had come before it. Deeply inspired by 1950s and ’60s sports cars, it featured aerodynamic curves and dashboard-like dials, making it (ironically, perhaps) a bold new step into the future. The original Roadster ceased production in 2012, but after that hiatus it is back in 2026 in steel (as seen here), gold, and gold and steel combined—with its curvy looks fully intact. Yet this is no easy reedition of an old favorite. More than 100 Cartier artisans worked on everything from the case and dial to the movement and strap, refining throughout and leaving nothing unimproved or unevolved. $10,200

It may seem a bit hasty to call this year’s Octo Finissimo 37 a new take on a classic, given it’s based on a watch design that debuted only in 2014. But a record-breaking run of prize-winning complications in the Octo Finissimo family since then has firmly established this unique watch as a pinnacle of contemporary horological design. What makes the 37 compelling to us is that it’s the most wearable version yet. While its predecessors focused on superthin movements doing incredible things, the 37 was conceived to be a daily—if very elegant—workhorse, with a 72-hour power reserve in a movement 20 percent smaller in volume than the model that came before. $17,400

When it landed in 1969, the Heuer Monaco Ref 1133 was unlike anything else in the watch market both inside and out. The first commercially available automatic chronograph, it set the standard for automotive-inspired timekeeping until it ceased production in 1975. Two decades later, TAG Heuer (renamed in 1986) was the first mainstream brand to reissue a classic from its back catalog, and the Monaco was reborn in all its rectilinear glory. But although they looked the part, those ’90s Monacos were very different from the originals. Fast-forward another 30 years and TAG Heuer has introduced an updated Monaco for 2026 that’s much closer to both the spirit and the letter of the original Monaco from 1969, albeit with a 21st-century in-house movement, the TH20-11, inside. $9,350

Nothing has sparked more excitement among Rolex nuts recently than the colored dials of the Oyster Perpetual. They have been revealed, much debated and sought-after, and then selectively discontinued. That array of bright dials led to the “Celebration” dial OP of 2023 (aka “Bubbles”), which brought all the previous colors together in a single watch. Having shown that serious watchmaking and fun can go hand in hand in a modern Rolex, the brand decided to go one step further on the centenary of its groundbreaking Oyster waterproofed case. Updating a relatively rare typographical dial treatment from the past, the “Jubilee” got a pop-art injection of colors (ten, to be precise) painstakingly laid down in successivelayers of lacquer. $6,750

#419. Benjamin Moore Just Revealed Its 2027 Color Trends Palette

The brand’s annual selection brings together eight shades chosen for warmth, character, and lasting appeal.

Green may get top billing, but Benjamin Moore’s 2027 color forecast doesn’t stop at one shade. Released alongside Color of the Year Webster Green HC-130, the company’s annual Color Trends palette brings together eight shades, with an emphasis on warmth, nuanced undertones, and colors that can accommodate differing decorating styles.

Selected from Benjamin Moore’s library of more than 3,500 hues, each shade is intended to work independently or in combination. White Down, Nelson Blue, and Wild Aster are the lighter options, while Shakespeare Tan, Antique Copper, Durango, and Townsend Harbor Brown bring golden, olive, and burgundy tones into the mix.

This broader collection is an established part of Benjamin Moore’s annual announcement. Last year’s eight-color palette accompanied the espresso-brown Silhouette and emphasized detail, craftsmanship, and refinement. For 2027, the brand focused on the balance between fresh inspiration and lasting appeal.

The team began with a familiar problem: keeping up with trends without constantly rethinking. Hannah Yeo, Benjamin Moore’s senior manager of color marketing, tells ELLE Decor that the goal was to find a balance between “something that feels new and exciting” and “something that reassures and endures.”

For Benjamin Moore, that means a more restrained approach to color, not less of it. Yeo sees the 2027 palette as a continuation of the company’s shift from the brighter shades of its 2023 forecast toward softer, more adaptable hues. Even the neutrals have distinct undertones: Shakespeare Tan can read as amber or olive depending on the light, while Durango brings a deeper olive note to the collection. “It feels very lived in, but also has a lot of color and personality,” Yeo says.

The deeper shades also invite some less expected applications. Yeo references the use of Townsend Harbor Brown in a sunroom, where its burgundy tones create a more enveloping atmosphere than the pale colors usually associated with the space. “It is not your typical selection for a sunroom,” she says, noting how comfortable the darker treatment feels. The willingness to reconsider a familiar room runs through the collection: softer colors needn’t be reserved for restful spaces, and deeper ones can work beyond the study or dining room.

The full Color Trends 2027 palette is available to explore on Benjamin Moore’s website.

Julia Cancilla is the social media & news editor at ELLE Decor, where she oversees the brand's socials and covers design, pop culture, and emerging trends. She also authors the monthly ELLE Decoroscope column. Her work has appeared in Inked magazine, House Beautiful, Marie Claire, and more.

#420. Enrique Martínez Celaya’s Monumental L.A. Opera Curtain Is Designed to Transform Before Your Eyes

The artist’s 70-foot work will rise, fold, and later be turned into individual paintings.

Before the lights go down at any opera performance, there is the curtain—the barrier standing between the audience and whatever is about to happen. Tonight at the Los Angeles Opera, that familiar threshold will take on a new life in the hands of the Cuban-born artist Enrique Martínez Celaya, who created a monumental theatrical curtain that will rise and fall before every performance throughout the company’s upcoming 2026 to 2027 season.

A former scientist, Martínez Celaya is best known for a multidisciplinary practice spanning painting, sculpture, installation, and literature that explores questions of perception, memory, and meaning. That interest in how art can change our experience of a place caught the attention of L.A. Opera president and CEO Christopher Koelsch, who invited him to create “The Things We Know,” a 70-foot-wide curtain for the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion. Celaya wanted the piece to do more than serve as a backdrop: As it rose, its image would change, making the curtain’s movement part of the artwork.

“I’m very interested in the idea that anything I do can never be done anywhere else,” the artist told ELLE before the season’s opening performance on October 17. “So I started to think, well, what is special about a curtain that I would never have an opportunity to do in a museum?”

The word curtain feels almost too small for this project: Martínez Celaya’s work is part mural, part moving image. It opens on two children absorbed in their own small worlds—a girl with an aquarium, a boy watching a caged bird. Then stars, flowers, and fractured light come into view, before the scene slips into darkness. For a moment, the opera is still waiting.

“Half of the curtain is folded, so when you sit for 40 minutes, you’re looking at a certain version of the work, and that experience will change as the curtain begins to go up,” Martínez Celaya says. “There’s this evolution, where what you thought you were looking at is recontextualized. It gave me an opportunity to investigate things I could never do in a museum or in the other kinds of institutions I usually work with.”

The work continues Martínez Celaya’s brief but long-running dialogue with classical music: In 2004, he created “Schneebett” (“Snow Bed”), a sculptural installation for the Berlin Philharmonic inspired by Ludwig van Beethoven. “Ever since, I’ve been interested in working with music institutions, because I’m not a good musician at all,” he notes.

Martínez Celaya was also intentional about the curtain’s afterlife. Following the season’s final performance, the plan is to cut it into individual works, which will be sold to support future productions and initiatives. For the artist, the gesture offered a way to give back to an institution he admires.

“When I create my usual exhibitions, all the pieces go around the world and they’re never together again,” Martínez Celaya explains. “To take this curtain, cut it, and create individual paintings, to take this totality and fragment it, and now these pieces go around the world—there’s something very beautiful about that temporary quality of the experience. I also like the idea of giving back and being able to support an institution that I respect and that is doing something great for the city of Los Angeles.”

#421. The Most Beautiful Wallpaper Moments We’ve Ever Published—and How Designers Made Them Work

Wallpaper has a way of changing a room’s entire mood with just a few panels. Across our Whole Home projects over the last nine years, designers have used it to bring pattern, color, texture, and personality to nearly every corner of a space. Some selections make an unforgettable first impression, while others quietly add depth to spaces that might otherwise be overlooked. We’ve seen wallpaper turn ceilings into unexpected focal points, give foyers a dose of charm, and make powder rooms feel transportive. The right wallcovering can introduce a sense of discovery, highlight a home’s good bones, or simply make a space feel more joyful.

And while wallpaper is often associated with maximalist interiors, our favorite spaces prove that this technique can be just as effective when used in a restrained or sophisticated way. From botanical prints to graphic motifs, every wallpapered room ahead offers a different lesson in treating your walls like a blank canvas to showcase your deepest design desires.

See our most memorable Whole Home wallpaper moments—and all the creative ways you can incorporate this accent into your own home.

Everyone loves a good wallpaper moment as soon as they step into a home, and a particularly memorable one came from our 2019 Whole Home. Fourteen designers came together to fill a 6,201-square-foot residence in Nashville, Tennessee, with personality and life. For the foyer, Vern Yip covered the wall with a dragon-themed depiction, complementing the ascending staircase as if the guest, too, were being transported into another world.

A massive living room, like the one featured in our 2021 Whole Home in Fredericksburg, Texas, requires a special eye, which is where Emilie Munroe of the San Francisco firm Studio Munroe came in. She wanted the room to be bold and colorful yet welcoming, which she achieved with vibrant furniture, a variety of textures, and a multicolored wallcovering depicting clouds during a dramatic sunrise. This color scheme was also replicated in the ombré print in the entryway—and the rest of the room’s furnishings.

DuVäl Reynolds wanted to create a transportive feeling in this private lounge for our 2022 Whole Home, located in the Buckhead neighborhood of Atlanta, Georgia. The historic home totaled 11,000 square feet, so a quiet, cozy retreat like this one feels more cocooning and comforting. The 300-square-foot room featured a lush velvet sofa and accent chairs that complemented the moody paint and wallpapered ceiling from Arte. Look closely, and you’ll spot serpents and tigers “roaming” through the clouds.

Some rooms make you stop in your tracks to take in all the details, and such was the case for this guest room, designed by Roxy Owens of Society Social for our 2023 Whole Home in Hinsdale, Illinois. She turned a former beige-and-tan spare space in this David Adler estate into a “traditional meets youthful and feminine” guest room. The focal point centered around her favorite pattern: Chinese Peony, pulled from a mid-19th-century English chintz that had been recolored and introduced as a fabric and wallpaper. She kept the room’s original paneling and painted it in Farrow & Ball's Parma Gray to frame the new wallpaper.

Designers did not shy away from highlighting wallpaper throughout the David Adler estate—they did have 13,000 square feet of space to work with—and another pivotal moment came in the entryway. The damask wallcovering had actually been in this room for decades! Designer Arianne Bellizaire wanted to honor the home’s roots in a fresh way, so she used two shades of blue paint (Hague Blue and Oval Room Blue by Farrow & Ball) to enhance and ground the damask.

The studio apartment overlooking a garden in our 2023 Whole Home project was transformed into this cheerful pink paradise by Jenna Gross of Colordrunk Designs. The designer leaned into bold patterned drapery, rich florals, grassy greens, and tropical blues. Off the bedroom, this small hallway meets an extended getting-ready area that features Morris & Co. wallpaper with roses and birds. The floor is painted in Farrow & Ball's Nancy's Blushes with added details in Rangwali to tie the whole space together.

If there’s one throughline in the 2023 Whole Home project, it’s that many designers chose maximalist vibes for the spaces they brought to life. When Isabel Ladd made over this two-room suite featuring a primary bedroom with an attached bath and walk-in closet, along with a cozy den, she packed it with personality—down to the wallpaper. The Morris & Co. fabric design wraps around the bedroom and complements the other olive, red, and pink elements.

Our 2024 Whole Home project brought us to the Blue Ridge Mountains of North Carolina, situated between Asheville and Hendersonville. Designers got creative with the 4,000-square-foot mountain home, decking out everything from the home gym to outdoor space to the game room, one of our favorite spots. The walls here, including the ceiling, were covered in Morris & Co. botanical motif wallpaper, which created an immersive environment punched up by an eclectic mix of furniture and decor.

Can you spot the genius use of wallpaper in our 2025 Whole Home project, located in Austin, Texas? If your eyes landed on the vintage mirrored folding screen, you guessed right. Designer Kim Lewis layered Sanderson toile fabric onto alternating panels in order to transform the vintage find into a unique piece while also avoiding abrupt stops in the paint and wallpaper of this open-concept living and dining room.

Elsewhere in the same Texas home, designer Kathy Kuo brought her magic to the primary suite. The painterly Vista wallcovering from Phillip Jeffries depicts a serene and muted scene of trees framing a river bend, clouds drifting overhead, and hills fading into the distance. This, of course, tied back nicely to the heart of the room, which is the majestic Wesley Allen bed wrapped in Liberty of London's Wilde Lotus fabric.

For the guest suite in our 2025 Whole Home house, designer Leah O’Connell’s decision to swathe the walls in a bandana-inspired print became the starting point in her treatment for the entire space. She enlarged the paisley design so it stands out, creating a two-tone textured wallcovering, then layered a wide floral border over it on two opposing walls to add intrigue and depth. Velvet sofas, forest green leather, and brass touches complete the room.

#424. A Definitive Ranking of the Most Iconic Whales of All Time

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

In honor of Whalefall, we dredged the depths for the most memorable cetaceans to grace the public consciousness.

THE GLOBAL BOX office is on pace for its best year since the pandemic, buoyed by low-budget breakouts from Gen Z auteurs (Obsession, Backrooms) and the all-powerful Zendaya Cinematic Universe (The Odyssey, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, The Drama). But I’d argue the best is yet to come. No, I’m not referring to Avengers: Doomsday, which feels like it might be spiritually AI slop; nor Dune: Part Three, which, in a just timeline, will prevail on Dunesday. There is another studio release that should be treated as an essential piece of monoculture. May I interest you in the movie where the homeless dude from Weapons gets swallowed by a sperm whale?

This is Whalefall, which dares to ask, “What if 127 Hours covered a much shorter span of time with someone escaping the digestive process of one of the largest species on Earth?” While Whalefall is based on Daniel Kraus’s novel of the same name, this inexplicably happened to someone in real life. In 2021, a lobster diver on Cape Cod was swallowed by a humpback whale and—even more incredibly—lived to tell the tale.

Based on the trailers, Whalefall takes things to a more extreme level: Austin Abrams’s protagonist is swallowed alongside a giant squid, and he has one hour to escape before running out of air. In this race against time, feeble-minded viewers might assume the whale is the villain of this story, but director Brian Duffield has helpfully pointed out that it’s just as much of a victim. “The whale is not a bad guy,” he said in a June interview with Variety. “The whale doesn’t understand that it’s swallowed Austin. It’s trying to swallow its lunch, and Austin is just a byproduct of that.” Noted.

This is why we go to the cinemas. AMC should recreate its iconic Nicole Kidman ad, word for word, except she’s delivering it from inside a whale. There’s no question Whalefall is the moviegoing event of the year—if not our lifetime—and to celebrate the occasion, it’s time to take stock of the most memorable whales in pop culture. From the infamous sperm whale that terrorized Captain Ahab to the majestic Tulkuns of Pandora, we’ve ranked the 15 best pop culture whales. Figuratively and literally, it’s time to dive in.

When Jaws pioneered the summer blockbuster in 1975, it was inevitable that knockoffs would follow. And with all due respect to Piranha, the 1977 thriller Orca got one thing right: killer whales are legit scary. They can coordinate attacks on boats. (Clearly, you’re gonna need a bigger boat.) They kill animals—not only for sustenance, but sometimes for the love of the game. Keeping orcas in captivity is a cruel practice, but let’s not act like they’re gentle giants! Anyway, Orca is interesting in theory—the titular animal is seeking revenge for the death of its mate and offspring—but objectively unhinged in its execution.

Yes, in 1970, this really happened. Because the whale carcass was so heavy and so smelly, officials in Florence, Oregon came up with the ingenious plan of blowing it up with a half ton of dynamite that, in the words of reporter Paul Linnman, “blasted blubber beyond all believable bounds” and even damaged a nearby car. Thankfully, for the event’s 50th anniversary, the Oregon Historical Society arranged a 4K transfer of the segment so that the whalesplosion could be captured in all its gnarly glory.

Local news must be protected at all costs.

As played by the rapper Krondon on Black Lightning, Tobias Whale is one of DC’s most striking villains: a hulking albino crime lord who has a longstanding beef with Jefferson Pierce, a.k.a. Black Lightning. Like Marvel’s Wilson Fisk, Whale’s claim to fame isn’t superpowers but being built like an absolute unit. His weapon of choice is, naturally, a harpoon gun, because the most important thing a superhero villain should do is commit to the bit.

There are all manner of strange humans and sea creatures—and hybrids—in One Piece, an ongoing manga that will probably outlive all of us. It’s only fitting, then, that the series incorporates a giant whale. Laboon is distinguished by all the scars on his head, the result of repeatedly ramming into a mountain because he misses his pirate friends who ventured across the other side of it. (A heartbreaking detail for anyone who’s ever had to leave their pets to go on a long trip.) In a touching gesture, Monkey D. Luffy paints his pirate crew’s symbol on the whale’s head to deter it from further self-harm, and promises to return to him when they complete their journey—assuming One Piece ever actually comes to an end.

Among the weirder sights in Star Wars—even more than Coruscant being home to a 1950s-style diner run by an alien who’s pals with Obi-Wan Kenobi—are the Purrgil. They’re basically giant space whales that, in a twist straight from an ayahuasca retreat, possess the biological ability to travel through hyperspace. (It was through studying Purrgil, you see, that scientists in a galaxy far, far away invented mechanical hyperdrives aboard spacecraft.) Somehow, they’re not the only whales from a storied science fiction franchise to appear on this ranking.

In Star Trek’s long (and mostly revered) history, there might be no premise more goofy than The Voyage Home, in which our intrepid heroes aboard the USS Enterprise must travel back to the year 1986 because an alien probe is disabling power grids around Earth and can only be stopped through [checks notes] whalesong?! You haven’t lived until you’ve seen Spock A) swim with a humpback whale at an aquarium and B) tell the resident cetologist that she is well-liked by them.

For all its silliness, though, The Voyage Home has an endearing environmental message. The probe can’t be stopped because whales have gone extinct, and it’s notable that the film was released in the same year that an international whaling ban went into effect. “Save the whales” has never had such cosmic implications.

For some reason, one of my college courses in sports media was spent reading In the Heart of the Sea: The Tragedy of the Whaleship Essex, which has nothing to do with sports unless you consider surviving a shipwreck an endurance activity. The book is a harrowing account that helped inspire Herman Melville to write Moby-Dick. In 1820, a whaling ship was sunk by an aggressive sperm whale, leaving the crew stranded in the middle of the Pacific Ocean. Most of the crew died; the survivors resorted to cannibalism. Moby Dick is still the OG vengeful whale, but we have to give props to the whale that offered some actual, terrifying historical precedent. The 2015 film adaptation from Ron Howard is an underrated Dad Cinema gem, too.

THAAAANKKK YOUUUUU FOOOOOOOR HEEELLLLPING MARLLIIIIIN FINNND hiIIiiss SONNNNN.

The original #WhalefallChallenge was performed by Geppetto, Pinocchio’s master who was swallowed by the sperm whale Monstro. (Apt name.) Pinocchio risks life and wooden limb to save Geppetto, getting swallowed himself in the process. For proving himself to be brave and unselfish, he’s turned into a real boy. Monstro is all bad vibes, but without him, our little guy wouldn’t have finished his hero’s journey.

The man who helped launch the Universal Monster films, James Whale directed Frankenstein, The Invisible Man, and Bride of Frankenstein in the 1930s, frequently imbuing villains with an air of tragedy. Whale was also one of the rare openly gay filmmakers of his era, at a time when Hollywood (and society writ large) was considerably less tolerant. Maybe that's why he had such an affinity for outcasts—or maybe he was just preternaturally gifted at making rich, thought-provoking horror films. Either way, his name was James Whale, and he made some all-time classics, so he deserves a high spot on this list.

When James Cameron returned to Pandora for an Avatar sequel, it was inevitable that a man who has both made a movie about the Titanic and visited the actual wreck of the RMS Titanic would fixate on the ocean. Your mileage may vary on Avatar: The Way of Water spending half of its runtime as an otherworldly nature documentary, but I was locked in when we were introduced to the Tulkun: pacifist whale-like creatures that, naturally, the evil Sky People are hunting for their special brain goo that stops aging. Is it silly? Yes. Do I wish I could have a best friend like Payakan whose whalesong is conveyed on-screen in the franchise’s beloved Papyrus font? Also yes.

The cruel practice of catching orcas in the wild and keeping them in captivity is brought to light by the documentary Blackfish, which centers on one such orca, Tilikum, who was involved in three deaths. It’s a harrowing subject, but the best way to honor the suffering of these animals is to draw attention to it. The aftermath of Blackfish eventually led SeaWorld to end its orca breeding program and phase out live performances from the animals. Sadly, Tilikum died in 2017. Gone, but never forgotten.

This is a complicated whale to rank. On paper, Free Willy should be the wholesome, family-friendly version of Blackfish: a movie about a bond between a boy and an orca at an ailing amusement park. The film delivers a tear-jerker of an ending, culminating in Willy being released back into the ocean. But the real-life orca that played him, Keiko, was in captivity himself, and while he eventually became the first orca to be rereleased into the wild, he died soon after—never managing to integrate with others of his kind. Still, for any ’90s kid, Free Willy was a cultural phenomenon. It’s just a shame that Keiko didn’t get the Hollywood ending his character did.

I have spent an ungodly amount of time thinking about Pearl Krabs’s parentage. Clearly, her mother was a fellow sperm whale, but that doesn’t account for Mr. Krabs being her dad. If this isn’t an adoptive father situation, why isn’t she a whale-krab hybrid? (In Shrek, Donkey and Dragon birthed donkey-dragon spawns.) Does the world of SpongeBob SquarePants approve of interspecies couples, or is it taboo? Anyway, Pearl is one of the most memorable characters in one of the most iconic animated series of all time, so this was a no-brainer.

Who else could it be? The Michael Jordan of whales (he took Captain Ahab’s vendetta personally), Moby Dick’s reputation precedes him. Herman Melville's 1851 novel delivered the archetypal whale whose imprint is all over this ranking: Orca, Monstro, and even Payakan going Sicko Mode on poachers. He symbolizes the cruel indifference of nature and the futility of humanity’s attempts to conquer it. He’s also just a huge fucking whale that no man should spend their life obsessing over; it’s not gonna end well. Hang his tail fin in the rafters.

Miles Surrey is a Brooklyn-based culture writer who covers television, film, and whatever your dad is interested in. His work can also be found at The Ringer, Vox, Vice, and The A.V. Club.

With notes of cognac, amaretto, and even cachaça, these fragrances are sophisticated—not sloppy.

#426. The 10 Best Deodorants for Women in 2026, Tested by a Beauty Editor

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Real talk: Deodorant isn't a sexy beauty product, but it's arguably one of the most important. Imagine plopping down on your exercise bike, pounding the pavement in your favorite running gear, or even just commuting to the office without one. Scary thought, right? Growing up in notoriously humid South Florida, I was always hyper-aware of body odor and well-acquainted with underarm sweat—and I knew that deodorant was the way to keep me dry and stink-free.

I've no doubt that one of the products below will get the job done beautifully for you (so please, scroll!). But here are a few expert pointers if you want to shop for the best deodorant on your own.

"Keeping underarms fresh involves two main goals: controlling sweat and eliminating B.O.," says dermatologist Blair Murphy-Rose, MD. That's where deodorants and antiperspirants come into play. The only problem? People often use the terms interchangeably, but they're actually very different.

Deodorants help mask or neutralize underarm odor caused by sweat mixing with skin bacteria, while antiperspirants use aluminum to reduce underarm sweat by blocking sweat glands, notes Dr. Murphy-Rose. "One potential downside with antiperspirants is that they can dry out surrounding skin, leading to irritation, itching, and rash for those with sensitive skin," adds Alicia Zalka, MD, a dermatologist and associate clinical professor at Yale University School of Medicine.

Controlling sweat and masking bad odors are both important, but you'll have to be honest to decide which is a higher priority for your needs. If you're a heavy sweater and want to stop underarm wetness, opt for antiperspirants. If excess perspiration isn't as big of an issue for you, stick with deodorants. My daily go-to is deodorant, but I swiped both types to share the full scoop on the best women's deodorants and antiperspirants in the game. And the best part? Everything starts at just $9.

You've probably seen a variety of deodorant and antiperspirant formulations, and Dr. Murphy-Rose says your choice should be based upon personal preference and your unique issues. That said, there are some differences between the different types, so here's a quick rundown to think about.

Solids and sticks typically have a waxy consistency, are generally well-tolerated, and usually are the best for sensitive skin. Dragging on the skin is usually the primary source of irritation with these, so "try warming the stick on your skin first before swiping to minimize friction," advises Dr. Murphy-Rose. They also tend to leave behind annoying powdery white streaks on dark clothes and stickiness on the underarm area, adds Dr. Zalka. (All of these featured solids and sticks did not leave behind any residue on my clothes.)

Gels are convenient roll-ons and are typically light or clear so naturally, they leave behind less residue than solids. The only downside is that they tend to feel wet on skin—so if you're already dealing with excess perspiration, you may not love that sensation.

Creams feel moisturizing and soothing with application, but are a bit more messy and not as easy to apply. They're totally worth using, especially if you're looking to concentrate the application to a specific area or want full-body coverage (think between skin folds or under your breasts). Creams are typically more hydrating than gels and are a good option for those prone to dryness or irritation, notes Dr. Murphy-Rose.

Spray deodorants are quick to use, lightweight, and typically fast-drying, so they're practical for days you're in a rush. "They feel light and dry quickly with fewer ingredients," says Dr. Zalka. However, some may contain alcohol, which can be dehydrating or irritating for sensitive skin. Sprays can also be messy because you can't fully control where all of the deodorant particles land.

In general, you'll want to use deodorants made with moisturizing ingredients like humectants like hyaluronic acid or glycerin for hydration and occlusives like shea butter or beeswax to help protect dry, itchy underarms, recommends board-certified dermatologist Hadley King, MD. There are also deodorants made with bentonite clay, powders, or baking soda to help combat moisture. Important to note: "None of these ingredients blocks sweat ducts—they work by absorbing moisture," she says. Dr. Murphy-Rose is also keen on deodorants made with low concentrations of alpha hydroxy acids (AHAs) to minimize underarm discoloration and baking soda.

That's slightly different from antiperspirants, which use aluminum salts to stop perspiration by creating plugs that block sweat glands, using aluminum, says Dr. Murphy-Rose. She adds that most over-the-counter antiperspirants contain 12 to 25 percent aluminum, while prescription-strength formulas can go up to about 30 percent.

I'm our resident scent-obsessed beauty editor and have tried a slew of deodorants and antiperspirants throughout my nearly decade-long journalism career. For this story, I kept the above dermatologist-approved guidance in mind and carefully researched hundreds of women's deodorants and antiperspirants.

Next, I went to the Women's Health beauty closet and revisited products in my personal collection until I eventually narrowed down my list to 24 potential contenders that seemed promising. I tested these deodorants after showering and, on weekends spent indoors, I delayed showering my underarms to see how these products held up against smell and sweat. I also considered how much odor and sweat protection they provide while exercising, running errands across New York City, and wearing them on special occasions and nights out with friends.

I also considered their ease of use, how they feel on my underarms, whether they leave behind any residue (a major pet peeve of mine), and how frequently I needed to apply to remain confident in how I smell.

With that, I give you: the best women's deodorants of 2026. They are all loved by me, and some are even well-known among the dermatologists I spoke with for this story. Regardless of which deodorant you order, they all earned major snaps from me, a very hard-to-please beauty editor. The best part? They all start at just $9 and don’t leave behind embarrassing white marks on clothing. Sign me up for bulk orders!

When it comes to selecting the best overall deodorant for women, it's tough to find a winner that doesn't include aluminum. As mentioned above, aluminum is the only active ingredient approved to stop perspiration in its tracks—a major consideration. What's more, the powdery texture works double-duty to absorb moisture and leave skin with a silky finish.

And like most Dove products, this stick is chock full of moisturizing ingredients so you can rest assured that this one won't dry out your skin. “I feel like this is a deodorant you can’t go wrong with," says Women's Health beauty writer Danielle Jackson. "I recently switched back to this after using some aluminum-free formulas with more subtle scents, and I’ve just found that I’m much more confident about any sort of odors being blocked when I wear it."

But the ultimate test is, Can this hold up to activity? Jackson says this Dove stick passes that test with flying colors. "I also realized that I don’t have to worry as much about it doing its job when I’m being active or working out," she says. "It lasts all day and has a powdery scent that smells great but isn’t overbearing.”

When it comes to usage, Jackson assures that the Dove antiperspirant stick glides on easily without pulling (a major downside for most other sticks) and won't leave any white marks on my skin or clothes. Talk about an A+!The one potential downside (if you can even call it that) is that some of the other products on our list have a longer-lasting dryness promise (this one will only keep you dry for 24 hours as opposed to say, the 48 or 72 hours promised by some other brands). But if you're like me and shower frequently, that won't be an issue.Read more: Best Natural Deodorants

A Women's Health Beauty Award winner for best deodorant, this heavy-duty antiperspirant leaves me with fresher-smelling pits from the second I swipe and up to 48 hours later. Obviously, I'm not going two days without showering, but I do notice that whenever I wear this antiperspirant while enjoying HIIT exercises or on the treadmill I'm less sweaty. Now that's pretty amazing.

Secret swears their antiperspirant helps camouflage sweat caused by activity, nerves, and heat—and I think it does a solid job, especially for heat. I wore this deo regularly back when I practiced martial arts, swam, rode horses, and attempted to play tennis. I don't normally sweat heavily, but in the summer I'd definitely reach for this antiperspirant especially when commuting underground on the New York subway system. It’s still helpful during the fall and winter season when I’m bundled up in several layers.

The only thing I don't enjoy about Secret is the packaging design. It's shaped like your standard stick deodorant where I twist the bottom to help push up the creamy formula, but I noticed the turn mechanism on mine requires a little more effort than others on this list. But if you're a heavy sweater, that's a fairly minor downside—and you shouldn't let this small con deter you from this one.

I learned about this deodorant years ago through my mom, who has been using Tom's forever. I tried it during the pandemic, but stopped using it in favor of other deodorants. But, I wanted to revisit Tom's for this story—and I'm so glad that I did.

The brand recently reformulated their line of natural deodorants, and I'm obsessed with the chic new packaging and all the incredible new scents available, like Wild Lavender, North Woods, and Mountain Spring. Tom's swears the formula is still as long-lasting as ever though, with this deodorant keeping odor at bay for 48 hours. That's pretty impressive for a natural formula. Like I said earlier, I won't ever skip my daily shower (occasionally twice daily in the summer because it's that humid along the East Coast) but Tom's keeps up with my daily activities. Think long daily commutes to the office, full work days, after work shenanigans, and so much more.

To be frank, this level of protection isn't the norm for natural deodorants, but this stick is formulated with a generous dose of glycerin and aloe to condition my skin. It's also free of artificial fragrances that can irritate sensitive noses like mine.

All this being said, this is not the formula for you if you're a heavy sweater. I'd also say the biggest bummer about this deodorant is that it doesn't glide as easily as other alternatives on this list. There's a light dragging on my underarms, but it's not a huge problem, rather a minor annoyance that shouldn't deter you from enjoying this pick.

Is anyone else flashing back to middle and high school gym class just looking at this deodorant? I know I am, but there are several reasons every girl in my PE classes all used this roll-on antiperspirant—it's so easy to use and it's virtually invisible.

Since it's an antiperspirant, Ban keeps me sweat- and odor-free and embarrassing sweat marks on my clothes are nonexistent when I roll this onto my underarms (its clear formula doesn't transfer or leave behind any marks). What I really appreciate about Ban, though, is how it's lightweight on my skin. Sometimes creamy sticks feel like they're leaving behind a clump of product onto my pits, but that's a non-issue with Ban.

One important thing to note is that this gel roll-on doesn't dry quickly. It's not a huge drawback—the waiting period is minimal—but if you're in a super rush in the morning, keep that in mind. It's also not quite as long-lasting as some of the other formulas at 24 hours, but that's not a problem for me since, again, I shower daily.

I've always preferred stick deodorants and antiperspirants because it's what I'm used to. But this Dove formula makes a compelling case for anyone who's also shopping for weightless odor and sweat protection. So how does it work? “They create a flexible film of active ingredients on your skin and remain dry,” says cosmetic chemist Perry Romanowski. Dove relies on finely milled aluminum for invisible protection, plus a special masking oil to prevent any marks from getting on my clothes.

But similar to spray sunscreens, spray deodorants and antiperspirants can get a little messy and feel hard to control, and this one is no exception. So, it's probably best to skip buying this one for someone who isn’t super clean or a pre-teen who might spray this a little too liberally.

As we've said before: Whole body deodorants are hugely popular right now, with all the major players getting in on this trend. It's a smart idea—just 2 percent of our sweat glands exist in our underarms, so it's clear the need for all-over odor solutions is great.

This formula, with tapioca starch and mandelic acid, works to acidify skin’s pH, preventing odor-causing bacteria from proliferating. Rub a pea-sized amount into smelly areas, including the vulva, under-boob, thigh folds, and underneath the butt cheeks. A little goes a long way here, and you can always add more as needed.

Since its launch, Lume has expanded its portfolio to include stick deodorants, wipes, body creams, body washes, and acidified cleansing bars that are pH-optimized to control odor.

I've spent four years wearing this deodorant on and off and can confirm that evolvetogether hits all of the factors I look for in a deodorant. For starters, it’s made with natural ingredients. Instead of potentially harsh baking soda, aluminum, and talc, this deodorant uses tapioca starch to soak up sweat and moisture. There's also DeoPlex, a plant-based sugarcane that neutralizes bad odors, while glycerin moisturizes and prevents underarm irritation. Panthenol hydrates my underarms and helps the stick glide on easily.

Most importantly, the odor protection is on point! If you are from the South like I am then you know that even if we shave our underarms sometimes it's so hot and humid out that we inevitably get a little smelly. Not the case with evolvetogether. I've worn this deodorant walking 5Ks around my neighborhood, on the treadmill, during long cross-country flights, and I've never felt self-conscious about my smell. (My mom is also very honest and would have told me if I ever have an odor issue, so I know evolvetogether works well for me.)

As much as I love fun colors and prints, in New York I'm almost always wearing something black because it's easy to select an outfit. evolvetogether deodorant glides on clear and doesn't leave behind embarrassing white marks on my dark clothing which is a major relief on laundry day.Bonus: While this doesn't impact the quality of evolvetogether products, I'd be remiss if I didn't highlight that each purchase supports a small, AAPI woman-owned business which I always consider a major win.

As for the cons, it’s really minimal. Heavy sweaters like runners will likely need a traditional antiperspirant to keep their pits truly dry. However, for daily activities this is one of my long-time favorites.

You deserve a deodorant that can keep up with your active lifestyle. Who better than tennis star Sloane Stephens to create a high-performance natural whole B.O.dy deodorant. I’m a huge fan of this spray and previously named it one of the best whole body deodorants of all time.

What impresses me the most is that 24/7 Hustle is made with clean ingredients, but it doesn’t skimp on performance or irritate my skin. I wore it from 5 a.m. to 11 p.m., and was pleasantly surprised that I still smelled fresh and felt clean throughout a long travel day. It keeps up with light and intense physical activity. When I want to touch up I just swiftly spritz on this spray and I’m good to go after workout classes. No obvious residue or clammy coating that sticks to my workout sets. Woo!

So how does it work? The proprietary Deoplex Complex contains enzymes that help neutralize BO, while a botanical blend of goji berry, dragon fruit, chamomile, and ashwagandha prevents environmental damage that causes dry skin. The gentle formula also soothes my sensitive skin.

A bonus: This is the only refillable deodorant worth your hard-earned money. You can purchase a refillable pouch with enough liquid to refill your bottle nearly three times for $35. The combined price of a single refill pouch and the initial bottle is $53, while purchasing four new bottles would cost $72, resulting in a savings of nearly $20.

Meet my favorite deodorant launch of 2026. I recently crowned it the best deodorant of the year in our annual Beauty Awards package. Here’s the TL;DR: They’re travel-friendly wipes that can be used all over the body.And now that the weather has finally warmed up, I’m heavily relying on these dermatologist-developed deodorant wipes to help me win the battle against body odor.

Their genius lies in the trifecta of odor-neutralizing enzymes, soothing aloe vera juice, and exfoliating glycolic acids that don’t sting or tingle my sensitive skin. I’ve tried the spray and love it, but the wipes are my current go-to. Since they’re individually wrapped, I can keep a few in my gym bag, work tote, and carry-on bag so my pits are quite literally covered.

TBH, I genuinely enjoy these deodorant wipes, which is why they took home a big win. However, if I must be nitpicky then it would be cool if these were available in multiple scents. However, that might easily irritate very sensitive skin types and those with sensitive noses. And honestly, the current mild scent isn’t bad—just natural and fresh, which I appreciate. Plus, it won’t accidentally clash with my perfume collection.

If you’re familiar with any of my skincare content at Women’s Health then chances are you’ve likely seen me gush about Nécessaire products. I’m a ride-or-die fan of the brand’s body wash, exfoliator, serum, and deodorant. The line’s genius lies in the simple yet effective ingredient list. Think odor-neutralizing mandelic acid (an alpha-hydroxy acid) paired with triethyl citrate and zinc ricinoleate for odor-protection. The soft and creamy stick deodorant is also infused with soothing vitamin B3, B5, and E for hydration.Another reason I’m genuinely obsessed with this deodorant? The incredible variety of enticing scents that are noticeable enough for me to enjoy but wouldn’t overwhelm my colleagues at work.

The featured Hinoki scent is my top pick—and the one I crowned as the winner in our 2025 Skincare Awards package. Inspired by Japanese hinoki cedar trees, this earthy and woody aroma is a zen dream. It also blends notes of basil, vetiver, and magnolia, adding a spa-like serenity to my morning routine.

Another reason I love this deodorant is that it glides on seamlessly without dragging my sensitive pits. It also doesn’t leave behind white marks on my dark clothing.

TBH, it was super hard to brainstorm a true con. Nécessaire gets so many things right with this formulation. They even have a gel deodorant if that’s more your vibe. If I’m forced to name one area of improvement then it would be that there aren’t any travel-sized versions. The cylinder shape does take up a decent amount of space in my cosmetic pouch, but TBH, the formula and longevity are worth it for me. Still, if you’re a seasoned traveler who keeps things minimal, then you should consider the Anti Odorant pads instead.

Dermatologist Kiran Mian, MD, previously called this one of the best natural deodorants out there because of its impressive ingredients. "It has a blend of probiotics, plant-based extracts, antioxidants, cornstarch for moisture absorption, and soothing ingredients to prevent irritation," Dr. Mian said. It’s also infused with hyaluronic acid to help hydrate my sensitive underarm skin without feeling damp throughout the day.

This is one of the best natural deodorants I’ve used in the last two years. The odor protection is comparable to traditional deodorants even during workouts and unairconditioned subway rides around New York. It definitely keeps up with sweltering summer weather along the East Coast and Euro vacations with ease.

Other reasons I’m a huge fan? It doesn’t leave behind a white cast on my clothing and it holds up nicely after exercising. Since I’m not a runner, I can’t vouch for its efficacy there, but I will say it quite literally has me covered during vinyasa yoga and mat pilates. This deodorant also holds up surprisingly well on the StairMaster and high incline walks on the treadmill.

I’m not the only fan. Tester Brigitt Earley is impressed by the texture of this deodorant, which she describes as almost like a body butter in stick form—and I agree. It doesn’t skip or tug on my skin, which has been an issue with other competitors.

Truly, the only downside with this deodorant is the price but I will say each one easily lasts me at least two months. Technically, I’m only paying $10 a month to have stink-free underarms and that’s well worth the cost to me.

Look, there are studies that have investigated potential links between aluminum-based antiperspirants and breast cancer or Alzheimer’s disease. "To date, no conclusive evidence supports these claims, and aluminum-based antiperspirants are generally considered safe for daily use. There is no clear evidence that they pose a significant health risk," says Dr. Murphy-Rose.

Want more proof? Well, the American Cancer Society says "there are no strong epidemiologic studies (studies in people) that link breast cancer risk and antiperspirant use, and very little scientific evidence to support this claim." Plus, this report in the National Library of Medicine details a study conducted on 130 people regarding the potential exposure to aluminum through antiperspirants, antacids, and Alzheimer's disease (AD). "For all antiperspirant/deodorant use, regardless of aluminum content, there was no association with AD,” according to the study.

#427. This Brand Takes a Haute Couture Approach to Bedding

Millaux’s made-to-order “bedclothes” bring high fashion to bedtime

When was the last time you actually looked at your sheets and felt inspired? Fashion has the power to both inspire and express one’s personality; why not take the same approach to bed? As Harper’s Bazaar’s executive digital director, Lynette Nylander, wrote in her “Why Don’t You...?” monthly column: “Why don’t you… decorate your bed to the standards you would dress yourself for a night out. The same care and dedication should go into sourcing the very best wardrobe for where you spend a third of your life.”

That’s the ethos behind Millaux, founded by Laura Tanzer and Jessica Simpson in 2024. Tanzer’s fashion background includes a Central Saint Martins education, training at Vetements, and haute couture at Balenciaga under Demna. Together with her business partner and wife, Jessica Simpson—who spent her early years globe-trotting as a former professional tennis player (and, in turn, stayed at a number of luxury hotels while competing)—she developed a real sense of what lavish bedding should look and feel like.

“We bring a fashion sensibility to the home, thinking about prints, references, color, and the personality of an object while being equally interested in the intimacy and everyday rituals of domestic life,” share Tanzer and Simpson. “We feel that combination allows us to approach bedding with a little more freedom, taking it seriously as a designed object without taking ourselves too seriously.”

They look for inspiration everywhere around them: “People on the streets, books, magazines, shop windows, museums, a pattern on somebody’s dress, you name it. Everything you see becomes an archive of ideas, which then gets tightly edited down to what feels right for a mood we want to explore. Or, selfishly, a design that is missing in our bedding closet. Some of our main inspirations are vintage wine labels, medieval symbolism, print and fabric archives—and living close to the Met has recently sparked new inspiration too.”

With its Gothic typography and old-world feel, Millaux straddles the line between the linens you’d find inside an old château in the French countryside and a slick modern artist’s loft in Manhattan. The aesthetic is lived-in but still sumptuous, eccentric, and distinct.

Millaux’s prints and patterns give bedding an avant-garde look. And as Tanzer and Simpson put it, “We want our bedding to feel and look delicious.” The collection includes Dalmatian and leopard prints, duvet covers with bold geometric patterns echoing old-world flags, light-sorbet-colored striped linens, and pillowcases decorated with Warholian-style screen-print-like black orchids. The linens are made in Italy from Egyptian-cotton sateen or in Portugal from flax linen and boast an impressive 600-plus thread count. Like couture, every item is made to order and takes about six to eight weeks to produce. Prices range from $180 to $1,420. However, if you’re looking for something completely bespoke, Millaux can do that too. “Haute couture follows this detailed process of design and production; we took this approach especially around personalization,” says Tanzer. “Bedding is often dictated by the sizes, prints, and designs of a brand. We wanted to create a playground for our customers to create products that they are truly excited about and cherish.”

The next time you slip under your covers, consider this: Am I having as much fun getting into bed as I do getting dressed?

#428. 12 Gorgeous Rooms That Prove Bold Color Changes Everything

From high-gloss red to sunset-inspired ombré, these are the hues worth stealing.

From the mountains of Asheville, North Carolina, to the music-filled streets of Austin, Texas, House Beautiful’s Whole Home project has redefined the way we design our homes. Dozens of designers have traded traditional rooms for spaces that help us escape, entertain, and create, all from the comfort of home. And the most important feature in these rooms? The color.

The color palette is the difference between a room that cocoons you and a party pad. Your wall color influences everything from your decor and furniture to your lighting, making it one of the most important design decisions you'll make. Even if you opt for neutral walls, the colors you introduce through accents help define the mood. Blush pink brings a soft, calming energy to a living room, while a bold red can spark lively conversation around the dinner table.

Below, we took a scroll down memory lane to celebrate the very best uses of color over nine years of Whole Home. We have a feeling you’ll get inspired to add some new color to your space.

Modern Remains designer Evan Millard leaned into red as a grounding, activating color for this breakfast room. In the 2019 Nashville Whole Home, he balanced custom gold-framed paintings with a layered red-and-gold rug treatment. The accents of red in the room’s artwork and dining chairs keep it from overwhelming the space.

Marie Flanigan brought a taste of her Houston roots to the Rockies in the 2020 Denver Whole Home. She paid tribute to the Southern tradition of having folks over for tea with a vibrant red tea room, complete with high-gloss wall treatments and a statement plate wall.

The 2021 Whole Home was set in Fredericksburg, Texas, and Dallas-based designer Jean Liu set out to honor the city’s up-and-coming wine scene with a home bar. This tasting room delicately balanced blush and charcoal tones for a space that’s both masculine and inviting. The marbled rug and rosy stool seating encourage both casual and sophisticated cocktail hours.

The design duo behind French & French Interiors turned a tiny guest room into a jewel box in the 2021 Whole Home. Multiple colorful patterns mix effortlessly, from the green debossed diamond trundle bed to multicolored peacock feathers on the canopy drapes. It’s a tropical escape that makes guests feel transported.

Laundry rooms don’t always have to be cold and sterile. Stephanie Sabbe chose a saffron-yellow paint to add warmth to this utility space in the Fredericksburg Whole Home. The blue-black subway tile in the doggie shower makes the built-in shine, and it holds up well to stains over time. Just above the cabinets, a blue-and-white botanical wallpaper adds unexpected contrast.

Ariene Bethea of Dressing Room Interiors brought her love of pattern and African and Asian art to her design of this 2022 Atlanta Whole Home office. While the eggplant-colored walls (painted in Farrow & Ball's Brinjal) add some fun to the office, the eclectic mix of objets d’art is the true showstopper. The built-ins house striking ceramics and trinket boxes, sure to inspire any work-from-home setup.

A tiled backsplash is one of the best places to go bold with color. So when Emma Beryl turned the 2023 Whole Home’s former swimming pool rest area into a warm bar area, she didn’t hold back here. Blue zellige tiles and floating glass shelves nod to the room’s history, while adding a cooling contrast to the paprika-colored ceiling and checkerboard floor.

If we were to pick one word to describe Jenna Gross’s dining area in our 2023 Hinsdale, Illinois, Whole Home, it’d be cheerful. The space feels like it stepped straight out of a chinoiserie pattern, complete with a high-gloss blue ceiling, botanical upholstery, and vibrant details throughout. The cobalt blue fringe on the room’s centerpiece—the tête-à-tête—anchors the sunny yellow walls, creating a look that's both playful and polished.

From the crown molding to the skirted furniture, this living room’s Downton Abbey inspiration is clear the minute you walk in. Caitlin Wilson was inspired by a posh spot to gather, adding feminine touches to the Hinsdale Whole Home. She chose her paint colors to highlight the stunning architecture already present in the historic home. Farrow & Ball’s Pink Ground and Wimborne White both brought the room back to life.

In our 2024 Asheville Whole Home, designer Rajni Alex had the challenge of making a TV lounge feel as elevated as the rest of the retreat. The showstopper of the room is the wallcovering, a metallic ombré that’s reminiscent of a mountain sunset. Soft-glow lighting in the flanking cabinets adds to the sumptuous feel, with a 16½-foot burnt orange mohair sofa bringing the look together. It’s undeniable proof that gray has a place in color-filled homes when used strategically.

Glossy color isn’t just for painted walls and statement ceilings. In 2025’s Austin Whole Home, designer Sara Malek Barney turned the laundry room into one of the most interesting areas in the house. A syncopated combination of sangria red, silk ivory, and algae green tile adds rhythm and fun to a washing station. The three-by-six-inch tiles are less rigid and more playful when paired with Mexican-inspired floor tiles from Clay Imports.

Amber Guyton of Blessed Little Bungalow let the vistas of Austin, Texas, guide the design of this “pause parlor.” The 2025 Whole Home city has a rich music history, so Guyton pulled from that and Texas sunsets for a layered space. Sunset shades shine in the curtains and wood grain shelving. But for a moody spin, Guyton drenched the room in Sherwin-Williams’s Dark Night, pairing the inky blue with a peacock velvet curved sofa. The finished look evokes the night sky that follows the Texas sun.

#429. Benjamin Moore Just Revealed Its 2027 Color of the Year and It Nods to Tradition

Webster Green joins a growing roster of green paint predictions.

Benjamin Moore is going green for 2027—and its choice is already in the archives. The paint company has named Webster Green (HC-130) its Color of the Year, selecting an established shade from its Historical Color Collection. The green has a clear presence without the jewel-toned intensity of emerald or the softness of sage. And, the Benjamin Moore team wanted their selection to feel timeless. “We intentionally chose a green that doesn’t reminisce,” Hannah Yeo, Benjamin Moore’s senior manager of color marketing, tells ELLE Decor.

The choice is also the latest indication that green will feature prominently in the year’s paint forecasts. Sherwin-Williams already selected Celery, a light yellow-green, and Behr chose Grounded, an olive with brown undertones.

Webster Green follows Silhouette (AF-655), Benjamin Moore’s 2026 Color of the Year, a deep brown with charcoal notes. Where Silhouette offered a dark neutral, Webster Green puts a more distinct color at the center of the forecast. Both selections, however, reflect the company’s interest in shades that balance a substantial presence with everyday versatility.

According to Yeo, the 2027 discussions began last winter and repeatedly returned to the speed of trends. The team was drawn to new ideas but found their turnover difficult to keep up with. That led to a consideration of what people might want to keep in their homes, rather than what would simply feel current. The goal, she says, was to balance “something that feels new and exciting” with “something that reassures and endures.”

To explore that idea, the team looked through Benjamin Moore’s archives, including hand-drawn room illustrations, and examined green’s recurring role in interiors. Yeo cited the earthy shades of Arts and Crafts design, Art Deco’s emerald and teals, and the moss, avocado, and olive greens of later decades. Research through trade shows, industry presentations, and travel helped reinforce the selection.

“When we looked across the past, present and future of color trends, variations on green consistently demonstrated remarkable staying power,” Andrea Magno, Benjamin Moore’s vice president of brand, color, and integrated marketing, says in a statement. “Webster Green HC-130 reflects this timeless appeal by pairing reassuring stability with optimistic energy.”

Webster Green anchors an eight-color palette that includes creamy white, pale blue, gray-inflected pink, and deeper earth tones. The collection extends the emphasis on warmth and historically informed color, but the central selection is less about recreating an old interior than reconsidering a familiar shade. As Yeo put it, “this is not a new shade, but it just feels particularly relevant in the way that people want to live today.”

Julia Cancilla is the social media & news editor at ELLE Decor, where she oversees the brand's socials and covers design, pop culture, and emerging trends. She also authors the monthly ELLE Decoroscope column. Her work has appeared in Inked magazine, House Beautiful, Marie Claire, and more.
