#430. The Anatomy of a Great Dress Shirt

Breaking down the details of a 100Hands button-up (not button-down, by the way).

The way we dress has changed immeasurably in the past two decades. That’s a good thing. Liberated from old sartorial expectations at work and social events, we have more freedom than ever in how we express ourselves through our clothes. But that creates its own challenges. The casualization process has also somehow re-mystified certain pieces that once had a clear role and function in our wardrobes.

Take the dress shirt. Once a staple, it’s now a source of anxiety for guys who need to wear one but only on occasion. From collars and cuffs to fabrics and fits, questions about what to look out for—and ultimately bring into your own wardrobe—abound. Never fear: We’re here to dig into what makes a good shirt, well, good.

To do so, we decided to use an example from a brand that’s getting it right: 100Hands. In a clothing industry in which corners are cut but prices frequently aren’t, 100Hands is a bright spot that proves proper shirts can still be done the proper way.

Based in Amsterdam, 100Hands was set up 12 years ago to represent the polar opposite of mass production. The brand makes all its shirts in India, where the significant amount of handwork involved is carefully nurtured. Its name came from the fact that, at the time of its founding, 50 shirtmakers were involved in the making of a single shirt. Now it has 450 full-time artisans. In November, 100Hands opens its first-ever retail space on London’s Savile Row to serve a growing band of customers fond of its no-nonsense approach. In the Americas, the brand is available at Bergdorf Goodman and the Armoury in New York, Harry Rosen in Canada, and Silver Deer in Mexico. And, of course, you can buy it online.

From a distance, most shirts look the same. So you can really recognize a good one only by trying it on and getting a feel for it. When you do at 100Hands, the difference is instantly noticeable. Nailing the fit requires a lot of time. Much of the work at 100Hands involves traditional techniques long lost to economies of scale elsewhere. The sleeves of each shirt, for instance, are deliberately rotated before they’re set into the body, akin to the way an upscale tailor will attach a jacket sleeve to allow for the natural rotation of the wearer’s shoulder. Conveniently, this also provides a cleaner front and silhouette, though surprisingly few luxury brands do it these days. In addition, again much like a Savile Row tailor, 100Hands cuts a relatively high armhole in its shirts, which makes for less bunching cloth at the armpit, allowing the wearer greater movement and comfort.

Dress shirts are traditionally made from cotton, linen, silk, or blends of the three. Cotton is your everyday staple, but better cotton has longer fibers, making threads finer and cloths sleeker.

The most telling hallmark of a superior dress shirt is the collar. For 100Hands, it is the soul of the shirt, and getting it right often takes 30 to 40 percent of a shirt’s production time. Sewing flat pieces of cloth into a curved ergonomic shape around the neck requires skill to ensure it will sit upright and withstand repeated wear and wash cycles.

Many dress-shirt makers don’t bother with pattern matching, the process of lining up the checks or stripes on the cloth so that they appear continuous where seams meet. At 100Hands, it’s something of an obsession. All the various parts of a 100Hands shirt are cut by hand, which means patterns can be matched perfectly. It may not add greatly to the value of a shirt, but it does add time to the process. And for 100Hands, it’s a proof of commitment, a detail that a few years back earned a standing ovation from the buyers at Isetan, one of Japan’s best and biggest department stores.

100Hands shirts generally have 23 separate parts that are largely assembled by hand, with hems sewn to 0.1mm tolerances. This means it takes 36 to 40 hours to make a single shirt. One key area that gets a lot of attention is the bottom hem, which is hand-rolled and sewn to a 2mm width—much like an Hermès scarf but more robust because it must withstand multiple washes. Occasionally threads break in the assembly. Where other makers sew over a broken thread, 100Hands removes it and resews the seam entirely.

1.WEARING One wear, one wash. That’s the rule. A good dress shirt should always be crisp. Otherwise, what’s the point?2.WASHINGInvest in a good-quality washing machine, ideally with a simple wool or shirting program that will protect your shirts from damage. Wash at medium speed in warm water for 45 minutes to an hour. A good laundry will do the same, but avoid dry cleaning, as the chemicals break down the fibers of your shirt with time, shortening its life span.3.DRYINGLike dry cleaning, tumble drying will damage fibers—in this case because of heat and friction. Air drying on a hanger, line, or rack will preserve your shirts longer.4.STORAGEHang your shirts (ideally on wooden hangers) instead of folding, and iron them thoroughly prior to wearing, with plenty of steam. If necessary before ironing, freshen them up in a tumble dryer—but only for a few minutes.5.IRONING Get a good steam iron and always press your shirts inside out. When it comes to the collar and cuffs, press the backside and work your way from the center outward toward the corners or collar points.6.BUTTONS100Hands sews its buttons with a “crow’s-foot” pattern instead of the more common “X” shape. It’s a hallmark of quality shirts and subtly underlines that it was handsewn. But there’s a good reason for it too. The stitch creates a stronger grip and makes losing a button less likely. That said, buttons do pop off occasionally, and learning how to sew on a button is a serious rite of passage for a man. Use the pathetic sewing kits provided by hotels only in extremis. The threads just aren’t up to it.. . . AND A BONUS FACTPeople generally these days refer to any dress shirt as a “button-down” because it has buttons down the front. This is wrong. In fact, a button-down shirt is exclusively one whose collar is buttoned at the tips to the body of the shirt in the preppy style.

#432. People Think There’s ‘Beaver Butt’ in Their Food. The Real Story Is Way Less Gross.

GIVEN THE RECENT rise in food additive scaremongering, it was only a matter of TikToks before “beaver butt” started trending. Yes, beaver butt.

The term was popularized by Vani Hari, aka "The Food Babe," back in 2022 to shine a light on how the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) gives companies leeway with what's marked as "natural flavor" on a food's ingredients list.

"The food industry can use virtually ANYTHING found in nature and label it as 'natural flavors,'" she captioned one Instagram video. "These flavors work against you, getting you addicted to processed food using the best part of a taste or even a smell."

Beaver butt talk is bubbling up yet again, with claims that "beaver booty" shows up in products like instant oatmeal. "The natural flavors comes from beaver ass,” says one ‘gram. Another poster referred to the natural flavor as "juice from a beaver's butthole" to try to steer people toward an electrolyte supplement that presumably doesn't contain this ingredient.

What the hell is going on here? Scott Keatley, RD, cofounder of Keatley Medical Nutrition Therapy, says that online claims aren't quite accurate—and there are two big reasons you don’t really have to worry about any of this.

HARI IS CORRECT that "beaver butt" secretions are an FDA-approved natural flavoring. The flavoring is actually called castoreum, and it's a scent-marking substance derived from pouches called castor sacs near a beaver's anus, Keatley explains.

"The nickname has some geographical accuracy," he says. "The ingredient used in flavoring is an extract of that material.” Castoreum may show up in foods simply as "natural flavor" because it meets the FDA's criteria for natural flavoring. Per the FDA:

The term natural flavor or natural flavoring means the essential oil, oleoresin, essence or extractive, protein hydrolysate, distillate, or any product of roasting, heating or enzymolysis, which contains the flavoring constituents derived from a spice, fruit or fruit juice, vegetable or vegetable juice, edible yeast, herb, bark, bud, root, leaf or similar plant material, meat, seafood, poultry, eggs, dairy products, or fermentation products thereof, whose significant function in food is flavoring rather than nutritional.

Which brings us to a question you may or may not be asking yourself.

ONCE PROCESSED AND DILUTED, castoreum can deliver warm, sweet notes that work well with vanilla flavors, according to Keatley.

"Castoreum gave flavor-makers another way to build that complexity, adding a musky, sometimes slightly smoky character that could round out a sweet flavor," he says. "The goal wasn’t for you to taste beaver, but for the vanilla-flavored dessert to have a fuller, more interesting flavor."

NOT VERY. WHILE castoreum is considered a natural flavor, it doesn’t show up in a lot of foods.

"Castoreum is rarely used in food [but] is recognized as safe for its intended flavoring use," Keatley says. Instead, many companies have resorted to using artificial flavors to get the same taste or they simple use real vanilla.

There is also an animal welfare concern with castoreum. "Commercial castoreum has often been a byproduct of the fur trade, with the castor sacs removed from killed beavers," Keatley says. "Those sacs and their contents are dried, broken down, and extracted with hot alcohol to draw out the aromatic compounds." The extract is then used in small amounts for flavor.

"There's a legitimate animal-sourcing concern, even if the food-safety scare is overblown," Keatley says. But overall, castoreum is not something most people need to worry about in their food, he says.

#433. Can You Really Heal from Trauma in Just a Few Sessions?

A specific kind of treatment promises rapid relief—but is faster really better? Here’s what experts say.

Carol,* 40, was attending a parade when she spotted a few helicopters, triggering instant tears and a tightness in her chest. Helicopters were a painful reminder of the day she watched her son being transported for emergency heart surgery at 2 days old. Oh no, she remembers thinking. Maybe the session didn’t work. The day before the parade, Carol had undergone Accelerated Resolution Therapy (ART), a type of trauma therapy that promises to heal quickly and effectively—in as little as one to five sessions.

But five days later, another helicopter flew overhead while Carol was relaxing at the beach with friends. And this time, she watched it with about as much emotional investment as she would a cloud drifting by.

Carol eventually completed four ART sessions, but she says something had already shifted after the first one. Though it wasn’t immediate, in the days between the parade and the beach, Carol says ART “changed [her] reaction to the memory.”

Since it was developed by Laney Rosenzweig, LMFT, in 2008, ART has drawn plenty of skepticism—but also curiosity. Google Trends data shows that relative search interest started climbing around 2020, roughly quadrupling from its baseline a decade ago, and reaching an all-time high between 2023 and 2026.

The appeal of rapid healing is easy to understand, particularly at a time when access to mental health care remains challenging for many. A recent survey found that 30 percent of U.S. adults who needed mental health care in the previous year weren’t able to get it due to costs or other barriers. According to the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), trauma-focused psychotherapies with the strongest evidence typically take eight to 16 weekly sessions.

Rosenzweig developed ART partly from Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) therapy. Both therapies use eye movements during processing, but ART incorporates a distinctive technique that swaps traumatic imagery for new images of the patient’s choosing. ART is also a proprietary therapy: Medical providers undergo specialized training before incorporating it into their practice and must sign a nondisclosure agreement, which limits what they can share about the technique. Some of these specially trained providers take insurance, while others are self-pay only. And while costs vary, out-of-pocket rates tend to range from around $175 to $400 per session.

The therapy itself involves guiding clients through distressing memories while using bilateral eye movements, says Becca Gregory, LICSW, an ART-trained therapist in private practice. Bilateral stimulation is a hallmark of EMDR and can also be practiced with rhythmic alternating sensory input, taps, or vibrations. Research suggests this technique may make traumatic memories feel less emotionally intense.

Neither EMDR nor ART requires verbally recounting your trauma in detail. However, in EMDR, patients are often asked to identify a core memory to target and share the highlights with their therapist—along with the physical sensations, thoughts, and emotions that arise while processing it. With ART, the therapist can guide you through the memory without needing to know the specifics of what you’re working on. EMDR also involves free association: While noticing what comes up during processing, you might find the original memory triggers a different but related image, sensation, or thought that can lead you to processing something else. Letting your mind wander isn’t part of ART; instead, you stay focused on one specific traumatic memory.

What sets ART apart is what happens after the initial processing: Voluntary Image Replacement (VIR), a technique that involves rescripting the traumatic scene with the imagery of your choice. According to the ART site, the goal is to “delete” or “diminish” negative images in your mind and replace them with positive ones.

For Carol, this meant replaying the scene of her son’s emergency transport under the guidance of her therapist, Laurel Wiers, LMFT, and noticing the emotions and physical sensations it brought up. When certain parts of the memory still felt upsetting, Carol imagined painting over the scene—first in white, then sage green, and eventually with a cartoon snail leaving a trail of silver glitter—to make the images feel less vivid and threatening and to give her a sense of control over a situation she’d previously felt powerless in.

ART is mainly designed to treat PTSD and other trauma-related conditions, but it’s also been used to help patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder, anxiety, depression, and eating disorders. Some women who used ART were trying to recover from a single incident, like a traumatic birth, a loss, or healing from shame. Others were targeting a collection of memories. Complex trauma, or trauma that doesn’t always fit neatly into a single memory, can stem from repeated or prolonged traumatic experiences. This kind of trauma can be trickier to untangle.

“In my clinical experience, ART tends to work best for people who have at least one explicit memory to begin with: a memory that has a beginning, middle, and end, still feels emotionally activating when they recall it, and is affecting the person’s life today,” says Gregory. “Survivors of single-incident trauma are much more likely to benefit from specific-trauma therapies such as ART, EMDR, CPT, and many others, in a shorter period of time, than survivors of complex trauma,” says Emily Haas, MD, a psychiatrist and director of the Triumph Program for complex trauma and dissociative disorders at Silver Hill Hospital.

Still, patients with complex trauma can use ART to target one emotionally charged memory that’s part of a much larger history, and according to Gregory, this can still be helpful, having a “ripple effect” on similar memories.

For Julie,* 52, ART helped her untangle more than a singular memory. She sought out the therapy after struggling with feelings of rejection and abandonment related to being put up for adoption as a child, as well as memories from her adoptive home. During her first two sessions, she worked on painful imagery surrounding how she pictured the separation from her birth mother and a recurring childhood dream in which she desperately searched for her to no avail.

“As an adoptee who had lived with missing information about my own history, truth mattered enormously to me,” she says. “I questioned how creating imaginary scenes could help with real pain.” But she says she found the experience “valuable.” When asked to rescript her triggering memories, she chose to project images of waterfalls and forests onto these scenes, explaining that nature had always been a source of comfort to her. Ultimately, the agency ART provided helped Julie feel better. “I could decide what comfort looked like and create something meaningful over experiences I had never had control over.”

One exercise that felt particularly profound involved imagining the mother she had needed but never got to know. “ART did not undo my separation from my birth mother or change what happened in my childhood,” she says. “It helped me engage with some of that pain and trauma in a way that felt empowering.”

Evidence around ART appears to be limited but promising. A 2024 systematic review published in PLOS Mental Health, which examined five primary studies with 337 enrolled participants, found significant improvements in PTSD symptoms, as well as significant reductions with depression, anxiety, mental distress, and sleep dysfunction, across the board. In a 2013 landmark randomized controlled trial published in Military Medicine, U.S. service members and veterans with combat-related PTSD who received ART experienced significantly greater improvements in symptoms than the comparison group, and those benefits continued three months later.

“These results are encouraging,” says David Storey, lead author of the 2024 systematic review of ART and a clinical psychology doctoral researcher at Memorial University of Newfoundland. Still, he notes that larger, independent, high-quality studies are needed—especially head-to-head trials comparing it with first-line treatments (such as EMDR and CBT). Another critique of existing ART literature is that many of the published studies come from a small pool of researchers, often in collaboration with ART’s creator (including the landmark 2013 trial), Storey notes.

ART’s proprietary nature can also pose challenges for independent research, but that isn’t really a concern to Dr. Haas as a clinician. “I’m less focused on the business model of the intervention than on its ability to offer our patients relief from their suffering and improved health moving forward,” she says.

But properly gauging what “success” looks like in therapy can be tricky. The question isn’t just whether people get better after ART—it’s how we define “better,” says MaryCatherine McDonald, PhD, a research professor at College of the Holy Cross who studies trauma and resilience. Immediate relief is not the same as lasting healing, which is also why studies on ART need longer-term follow-ups. McDonald says that most people focus on symptom reduction, since it means people are experiencing less suffering—but the quality of life after trauma also matters. “You can have symptom reduction and still just be coping rather than thriving,” she says. This might look like sleepless nights, laughing less, and not feeling present with people you love.

For Frank Anderson, MD, a psychiatrist and psychotherapist, another concern about ART is whether creating new images from past trauma could actually be a form of “bypassing” trauma rather than healing. Dr. Anderson believes it’s possible to experience relief in a few sessions—but it depends on the type of trauma and what you’re seeking to heal. “If you’ve been living in a dysfunctional family for your whole life, there’s no way three sessions are going to heal that,” he says. “Will it help a particular part or dimension of it? Sure, possibly.”

So, is faster treatment better? Or the same? The answer is complicated.

Maybe we’ve created two competing myths, says McDonald. “One says healing has to take years of painful work and your job is to power through it,” she adds. “The other says if you’re doing the right therapy, you’ll be transformed almost immediately and with total ease. Obviously, neither is true.” Healing isn’t a marathon or a sprint: There is no award for suffering longer, nor is there one for crossing the finish line quicker. “Trauma treatment doesn’t have to be long to be legitimate, and it doesn’t have to be difficult to be effective,” McDonald says.

Gregory feels that Americans tend to believe that anything worth having must be slow, painful, and hard-earned—an assumption that could deter some people from seeking help. “If someone believes healing means months or years of reliving painful memories in brutal detail, it’s understandable they’d put it off,” she adds. Someone might avoid starting therapy because they’ve heard it takes years, and they don’t have the bandwidth for that right now. Someone else might quit early because they expected fast relief and didn’t get it, and they interpret that as proof it won’t work for them.

The best trauma treatment might not be the one that works the fastest but the one that people are able and willing to finish. Up to one-third of people who pursue therapy don’t return within 45 days after their first visit, according to one study. For some, it may be a cost or scheduling issue. And not seeing results early enough can play a role as well: Research shows that people who fail to improve early in therapy are more likely to drop out. Compared to other established treatments, ART’s early studies show relatively high completion rates—perhaps because so few sessions are required. But it’s not yet clear how much of that difference can be attributed to the therapy itself (versus other factors, like study settings or populations).

Although ART felt transformative for Carol and Julie, it may not work for everyone—and that’s okay. “The important thing to remember is that therapies don’t fail because people fail,” says McDonald. “Sometimes a treatment simply isn’t the right fit for a particular nervous system, history, or moment in someone’s life. Some things will shift quickly. Some things will need to be revisited more than once. That’s just how healing works.”

Healing doesn’t mean someone stops experiencing fear or recalling painful memories—experts all agreed that would be unrealistic. But according to Gregory, it means their reactions become proportionate to what’s happening in the present instead of being amplified by unresolved experiences from the past.

“Can it get better? Yes,” says Dr. Anderson. “Are there ways that healing can be more efficient? Yes. Do we have a good handle on that yet? No. Is it possible that we’re not gonna need everybody to be in 30 years of therapy? I hope so. We have to think outside the box.”

The trauma field used to ask: How do we “get rid” of symptoms? Now, McDonald says, we’ve shifted toward, How do we help someone build a life with more freedom in it? “That’s a much better question, and I think it’s going to keep shaping where this field goes next,” she adds.

*Patients’ names have been changed to protect their privacy.

#435. People Are Paying Up To $200 To Get In-N-Out Delivered

The lengths people will go to for Animal Style.

In-N-Out has a cult following, a famously simple menu, and one pretty major inconvenience: You still can’t order a Double-Double through DoorDash or Uber Eats.

So naturally, people have started finding their own workarounds.

According to a recent report from People, unauthorized “burger brokers” have been popping up on Facebook Marketplace, offering to pick up In-N-Out orders and deliver them to customers for a fee. Some reportedly charge as much as $50, with payments handled through services like Zelle or Cash App.

Facebook Marketplace isn’t the only place this is happening.

Airtasker, an online marketplace where users can post jobs and name a budget, has also become a surprisingly popular workaround for getting In-N-Out delivered. The company now has a dedicated In-N-Out delivery page, and recent listings show people paying anywhere from $10 to $100 just to have someone go through the drive-through and bring the food to them.

One person in Santa Clara offered $225 for two Animal Style cheeseburgers with grilled onions and two orders of Animal Fries.

And some requests go way beyond a quick neighborhood drop-off.

One Airtasker listing offered $200 for someone to pick up an In-N-Out order in Arizona and drive it all the way to Hermosillo, Mexico. The customer said the food needed to be packed in an insulated bag or cooler and kept at a safe temperature for the trip, with food and gas covered separately.

There are even people bringing In-N-Out into major life events. A recent California listing offered $50 for someone to pick up an order and deliver it to a nearby restaurant for a wedding after-party.

The demand makes more sense when you remember that In-N-Out has intentionally resisted third-party delivery for years. The company has said it wants to protect food quality and the in-person customer experience, both of which can take a hit when burgers and fries sit in a car for too long.

Of course, there is a big difference between ordering through a structured marketplace like Airtasker and sending money to a random person on Facebook. People reported cases where customers paid unauthorized sellers and never received their food, with little recourse afterward.

Still, the fact that someone is willing to pay $200 and cross an international border just to get In-N-Out says a lot.

Maybe DoorDash isn’t necessary when the fans are this determined.

#436. An Expert Guide to Going Gray Gracefully

Top hair professionals and friends of Bazaar share their tips on transitioning to your natural roots in style

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Acclaimed producer, writer, and showrunner Mara Brock Akil began going gray slowly, right before she turned 30. Akil first noticed a few gray hairs while working on the set of her hit show, Girlfriends.

“I love telling this story,” the producer tells Bazaar. “I was 29, and there were five of them, literally five, and I used to joke that they were named Tracy, Golden, Persia, Jill, and Reggie. I was producing Girlfriends, and I've since learned I was the youngest showrunner then, and you don’t know sometimes—naïveté—but you jump into this role not realizing how intense it was, what I was really taking on. What it takes to produce these ideas, these stories, and I saw five gray hairs at 29, and I was like, ‘What the heck?’”

No matter your age, when you notice pigment loss in your hair follicles, the shift from your natural brown, blond, or red hair to gray or silver can feel jarring and unexpected. It’s no secret that gray hair often has a negative connotation, with the shade being viewed as a sign of old age and reduced vibrancy, though that isn’t always the case. According to the American Academy of Dermatology, hair typically starts graying in midlife, usually in your 30s and 40s, and is often triggered by stress, oxidative damage, or genetics. “My hair started turning gray in my mid- to late thirties, pretty much after I became a mom,” says celebrity makeup artist Pati Dubroff. “I think there has been, and maybe still is to some extent, a stigma that women with gray hair are ‘over the hill,’ or that going gray is aging and somehow takes away your youthfulness. I don’t believe that.”

Because gray hair is often wiry and fragile, a consistent, effective care routine is key to maintenance, whether you have a few noticeable strands or a full head of silver. Celebrity colorist Kadi Lee, who works with stars like Julia Roberts, Gwyneth Paltrow, and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, as clients, says that when transitioning hair, it’s important to keep strands strong and hydrated, since they likely carry two different textures at once.

“Deep conditioning should be a regular part of the routine, since regrowth is more porous and needs consistent moisture,” she says. “Our Instant Silk Vitality Mask delivers hydration without weighing down newer growth. Scalp care is also vital during transitional periods since healthy regrowth starts at the follicle, so our Root Replenish Active Growth Serum helps support hair through that process.” Lee also advises those transitioning to gray to avoid products with too much protein, as the ingredient can weigh down hair and sometimes even cause delicate strands to snap.

When transitioning from professional or box-dyed hair color to gray or silver shades, experts say you don’t necessarily need a “big chop” to speed it up. “A cut can help remove some of the older color, but each person is different,” continues Lee. “I generally lean toward a gradual approach instead, using regular trims to slowly cut away processed ends while glosses or temporary color ease the visual transition in the meantime.” Temporary color, which deposits pigment on the surface of hair, and hair glosses, like dpHue’s Color Boosting Gloss+ Deep Conditioning Treatment, add a sheer layer of tone and boost shine without lifting or altering the internal structure as permanent color does. “One of my big tips is to be patient with the transition,” notes Dubroff. “When I decided to flip the switch and go from brunette with touched-up roots to gray, it was a long process. Getting that dark, dyed hair lighter without it becoming very, very brassy is tricky, and there can be a lot of damage.” Hair glosses typically last up to six weeks, and temporary color often fades in a couple of washes.

For those who don’t feel quite ready to fully embrace their changing hair tone outright, opting for a treatment, like professional gray blending, is completely understandable. “Hair color can do more than cover gray. It can also support an intentional transition, which is a beautiful option for someone who doesn't want to cut off her hair or let the gray grow in all at once,” says Shvonne Perkins, hair color and trend expert at Madison Reed. “Mostly lowlights in varying shades of her natural color, with a few highlights mixed in (not traditional lightener-only highlights), can help diffuse the demarcation line and blend incoming gray for a softer, more gradual transition.” Perkins adds that to maintain hair color for more than a few washes, demi-permanent dyes can be a longer-lasting option when shifting to gray. “Its translucent deposit respects the natural variation in the hair, can create an almost naturally highlighted effect, and lets some of the gray show through,” she says.

As champions of gray hair, Akil and Dubroff agree that as beautiful and singular as the color can be at any age, a common challenge of owning your gray is a washed-out appearance that may occur without hair pigmentation. Dubroff uses her makeup artist background to incorporate more color in the form of rosy blush, pigmented lip shades, and more to her face. Akil uses her wardrobe—from her eyeglasses to vibrant and even gray-toned pieces—to contrast with her hair color. Ultimately, both women say letting their gray hair thrive has helped them feel more connected to their authentic selves today. “I really love my gray hair journey. I think it really makes you look at yourself,” says Akil. “What I think people might see of me is not just my gray hair, which I do think is beautiful. It's how it's anchored in me—my self-acceptance.”

#437. We Predicted These Kitchen Trends Years Ago—and They Still Hold Up to This Day

These Whole Home ideas proved they were way ahead of the curve.

Because the kitchen is the heart of the home, it's also where some of the most exciting innovations happen. From smart technologies designed to make life a bit easier to experimental layouts that improve the flow and standout design details that elevate the room's style, our annual Whole Home projects have showcased the best in kitchen design.

Since House Beautiful launched the Whole Home showhouse in 2017, each designer has put their unique spin on the kitchen. They’ve created spaces that feel distinct from the rest of the home—and from every Whole Home kitchen that came before. Some of these elements were personal, such as a built-in dog bed beneath an island, while others embraced lighthearted entertaining, like the at-home beer keg displayed on the counter. These creative touches have helped shape kitchen trends that continue to inspire today.

Take a look back at the most memorable Whole Home kitchens that have stood the test of time.

The family pets got special treatment in both the 2019 and 2020 Whole Home kitchens. At the Nashville Whole Home in 2019, kitchen and bath expert Matthew Quinn built a custom dog bed into the side of the island, upholstering the cushion in durable indoor/outdoor Thibaut fabric to stand up to muddy paws and scraps-seeking pups.

The following year in Denver, designer Sarah Robertson of Studio Dearborn reimagined another pet-friendly feature. Rather than installing a pot filler above the range, she placed an Elkay pot filler at a dedicated pet station within the island, making it easy to refill water bowls. The station also included built-in spots for food and water dishes, plus a drawer below for storing toys, treats, and extra kibble.

Anyone who loves their coffee, smoothies, or cocktails recognizes the importance of a drink station in the home. In 2019, Lauren Moore of Modern Remains brought this concept into the media room. But rather than hooking up a simple beer fridge, she made sure the kitchenette was stocked with a personal beer keg, using LG’s sleek HomeBrew to make this space feel extra luxurious. For suds lovers who love to entertain on game day, the unit’s sleek cylindrical build is cool enough to leave on the counter.

Sarah Robertson is known for her incredible kitchen ideas, specifically around storage, so she couldn’t simply stop at a pet station in the 2020 Whole Home. The designer put in a compost bin hidden behind a cabinetry panel in the island to make food cleanup not only easy but beneficial. Any and all fresh food waste gets swiped into this bin to help produce another healthy harvest from the garden.

Even if gardening isn’t an option, getting rid of food this way is an eco-minded way to live, and we can’t help but think Robertson was ahead of the curve here. Notice the drawer also hides a recycling bin, a trash can, paper towels, and a tool drawer.

Stephanie Sabbe of Sabbe Interior Design took inspiration from her grandmother when designing the kitchen in our 2021 Whole Home, located in Fredericksburg, Texas, opting for a dining table in the middle of the action rather than a classic island. “We sat there for hours and experienced life together,” the designer says of her grandmother’s home.

The rest of the cook space feels just as homey, with a charming leaf motif wallpaper, wingback chairs, and a beautiful blue-green paint color to coat the entire space. This idea of forgoing the island for a more furniture-forward piece feels very European and has become a more common practice in American homes as people are opting for more lived-in spaces.

Our 2022 Whole Home in Atlanta was the perfect entertaining space, in part because of Whittney Parkinson’s additions to the already-grand kitchen space. The scullery—a moody, windowless prep space—is decorated with mirrored tile from Ann Sacks and a rich walnut countertop so it still feels intentional within the greater kitchen. It’s equipped with a built-in microwave, dishwasher, and two undercounter refrigeration drawers, making it party-ready and almost as equipped as the main kitchen.

To make it even more obvious that this is a kitchen built for hosting, Parkinson added a wine room, wrapped in a nature-inspired wallpaper for a touch of whimsy and painted in Farrow & Ball’s Hague Blue. There are two Signature Kitchen Suite wine columns to store the precious cargo and a little chest of drawers between them to hold cocktail napkins and other accoutrements.

Would you ever paint your kitchen appliances? Well, Jenna Gross from Colordrunk Designs would and has! When she was tasked with redesigning the in-law apartment in our 2023 Whole Home located in Hinsdale, Illinois, Gross had to infuse as much color into the space as possible, which meant painting the custom cabinetry a soft pink and the vintage, all-in-one Dwyer kitchen unit an even punchier tone, Shallot by Farrow & Ball. It has a depth and playfulness to it that doesn’t take away from the cheeriness of the kitchenette.

As if the highly functional drawers from the 2020 Whole Home weren’t enough, designers Laura McCroskey and Leann Lynn of McCroskey Interiors took the integrated storage to the next level in the 2023 Whole Home main kitchen. The stunning backsplash—an antique turquoise Calacatta marble slab with plum and gold veining—slides to reveal ample shelves flanking the range. They serve as two mini pantries for quick use, holding spices, linens, and cookbooks.

We tasked the designers of our 2024 Whole Home in Asheville, North Carolina, to create a vacation home, an escape where having downtime is the only thing on the itinerary. For Kelsey McGregor of Kelsey Leigh Design Co., that meant designing a cook space that felt more like a hangout, aka the “unkitchen” kitchen.

It’s streamlined yet beautiful, the color palette emphasizing the Blue Ridge Mountains just outside the window, rather than taking from them. Oak woodwork and cabinets paired with floor-to-ceiling zellige tile and a plaster range hood feel natural and fitting with a mountain house, while the double ovens and clever storage remind whoever’s inside that this kitchen means business when it wants to. And you won’t find any small appliances on display on the countertops here—those are all hidden away in the nearby dirty kitchen to keep this space entertaining-ready.

Blurring the line between a dining table and a traditional kitchen island, the statement island brings a more furniture-like feel to the heart of the home. In our 2025 Whole Home, located in Austin, Texas, Sara Malek Barney of BANDD/DESIGN designed an island inspired by the silhouette of a grand piano, pairing a quartzite countertop with a sculptural, curved reeded base.

The result is undeniably dramatic, establishing the island as the room's centerpiece while creating a more inviting, conversational gathering space. The curve “encourages people to look at each other, not just face forward,” Barney says.

#438. Swizz Beatz’s Expansive New Home Line Features an Elevated DJ Booth

The music producer’s collaboration with CB2 takes inspiration from the house he shares with wife Alicia Keys.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE Decor editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Living in an architectural marvel can spark endless creativity. Just ask Kasseem Dean, a.k.a. Swizz Beatz. The award-winning music producer has resided in Southern California’s iconic Razor House, with wife Alicia Keys and their family, since 2019. Originally built by architect Wallace E. Cunningham and revamped by ELLE Decor A-List Legend Kelly Behun, the sculptural residence is perched amid the coastal bluffs of La Jolla, with dramatic concrete-and-glass gestures blurring the line between work of art and functional living space.

So when home brand CB2 approached Dean to collaborate on a full-fledged collection two years ago, he didn’t have to look far beyond his own walls for inspiration. “People are always asking me about our home,” Dean tells ELLE Decor. “For the collection, we wanted to present something that we would actually put in our own house.”

The way Behun approached decorating the space also informed the new collection. “When we first got the house, it was totally Brutalist—you know, Iron Man ready,” Dean recalls. Behun infused warmth and personality through sculptural furnishings and accents that were elevated without being fussy. “We have too much energy, too much love, and too much family to live in a museum,” he says.

Available in stores and online starting October 15, the Casa Dean Collection includes pieces from plush upholstery items with rounded profiles to handsome casegoods with burl-wood fronts. There are also linen lighting pendants, rugs made of New Zealand-sourced wool, vegan leather screens, alabaster vessels, smoked glassware, and works of art by California-born painter Megan Gabrielle Harris.

One of the most personal items nods to Dean’s childhood in the South Bronx, where his grandmother had a credenza equipped with a hidden turntable as well as sliding doors that concealed a record collection. Experimenting with the piece propelled Dean to follow in his dad’s footsteps, as they both got their start as DJs. In honor of that original piece, Dean decided to create his own version, dubbed the Lam-Louie DJ console, named after his father. It features tamboured burl-wood doors, deep green leather surfaces, and a tubular stainless-steel frame—all set atop locking casters, making it a cinch to move when rearranging for a party.

“Having a DJ setup here was important because I wanted the everyday person to be able to entertain themselves, entertain their guests, entertain their pets—or become a secret DJ if they wanted to,” says Dean.

Another of Dean’s favorites is the Brainstorm accent chair, available in a rich caramel suede or olive-hued leather. Evoking the spirit of Brazilian modernism, the seat is nestled within a boxy wooden frame, with an upholstered backrest sporting wide channel tufting inspired by vintage cars. “It was originally named the Think chair,” he says. “I wanted this to be a place where you could write down ideas, unplug from your phone, and reflect on your day.”

To produce the line, Dean worked closely with Evan Jerry, a member of CB2’s Designer Collective and founder of Studio ANANSI. “I wanted to be hands on with this whole thing,” he reflects. “I’m a Virgo, so I’m very particular on details.”

The two-year labor of love even included marathon workdays at the CB2 headquarters in Chicago. “Swizz was a brilliant partner and genuinely passionate about the home we were creating,” says Andrea Erman, CB2’s senior director of design and product development. “Not just how it looked, but how people would live in it.”

For Dean, the hardest part was editing down all of the ideas into one cohesive collection. “The pieces become your babies,” he says. But, he didn’t leave everything on the cutting room floor. “We have some cool things planned with CB2 in the future,” he teases. “Maybe some of those things will get to see the light of day.”

The Casa Dean Collection will be available in CB2 stores and online starting October 15.

#439. At Louis Vuitton, a Century-Old Art Form Is the Height of Modernity

The French fashion house’s latest Objets Nomades collection is an homage to an art deco pioneer.

Louis Vuitton is no dilettante in the world of interior design and furnishings. Its Objets Nomades collection—featuring one-off and made-to-order marvels created by leading contemporary designers, as well as tableware and textiles—debuted in 2012, but its roots in the home sector reach back more than 100 years to a period rich in architectural and aesthetic innovation.

We’re talking about art deco, the thoroughly avant-garde design philosophy that exploded into the world of taste at the 1925 Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels Modernes in Paris. Vuitton was there. And to mark the centenary of this most French of movements, the brand decided to devote much of its new Objets Nomades offering to Parisian artist and craftsman Pierre Legrain, an early deco proponent and a close collaborator of Vuitton’s.

Art deco, which drew its name directly from that 1925 exhibit, was inspired by diverse artistic and industrial movements that emerged in the first quarter of the 20th century. Drawing on everything from futurism and cubism to the mechanized revolutions in aviation and automotives, it was all about the future. For a brand like Vuitton, rooted in the glamour of travel, this brave new world was a good place to be—and one in which the Vuitton family moved easily.

At the time, the maison’s horizons were expanding well beyond the luggage that was its initial raison d’être. That’s thanks to Gaston-Louis Vuitton, the grandson of the brand’s eponymous founder. A polymath designer, collector, and inventor, Gaston added accessories, objects, and furniture to the LV wheelhouse during the ’20s, much of it shown at that fateful exhibition in 1925. Even ahead of that, he had tapped Pierre Legrain in 1921 to create the brand’s first piece of furniture for a Vuitton client: a lacquered red-and-black omega-shaped dressing table that was through and through deco in its curvilinear starkness.

Legrain’s was a world in which every craft discipline bled easily into others. Working in marquetry, bookbinding, and illustration—including advertising materials and drawings for Vuitton as early as 1910—he set the tone for the deco movement before it had a name. And he remains one of its powerhouse figures, despite his death at just 39 years old in 1929.

Fast-forward to 2026 and it was Legrain whom Louis Vuitton turned to once again. For its Pierre Legrain Homage collection, which debuted at Milan’s Salone del Mobile, Vuitton worked with the approval of Legrain’s family to reimagine some of his boldest designs in furniture, textiles, ceramics, and glass. Motifs from bookbinding and marquetry can be found in geometric throws and double-faced cashmere blankets that would look as comfortable mounted on an apartment wall as they would draped over a sofa. And calling on the artisanal skills of hundreds of experts in these fields, the house also re-created some key made-to-order pieces from Legrain himself, including the dressing table from 1921, a folding marquetry screen, and a Riviera Chilienne chair (essentially a deck chair with delusions of grandeur, made from oak and leather with a mother-of-pearl inlay). All of it looks strikingly modern, even a century after it was created.

#440. What Happened to Elizabeth Holmes, the Subject of A24’s You Can See Everything?

Everything to know about the former Silicon Valley darling after Theranos came crashing down.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

It’s been eight years since the unforgettable Summer of Scam. First, there was Anna Delvey a.k.a. Anna Sorokin, who posed as a German heiress to trick New York’s most important—and wealthiest—people out of hundreds of thousands of dollars. Then there was Elizabeth Holmes, former big-time Silicon Valley techpreneur, who duped investors while wearing her signature black turtleneck.

Like Delvey, whose story was dramatized in Inventing Anna, Holmes got the Hollywood treatment. Oscar nominee Amanda Seyfried starred as Holmes in The Dropout in 2021, and now, the Theranos founder is the subject of Nathan Fielder’s new documentary, You Can See Everything—which follows her inviting cameras into her home in the 34 days leading up to her incarceration—out now in theaters. “What begins as an intimate portrait of an enigmatic felon becomes a mind-bending three-year journey into the abyss,” the film’s official logline reads.

In January 2022, Holmes was found guilty of three counts of wire fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud by misleading investors. In November 2022, she was sentenced to 11 years in prison. So how did she get here? The Theranos saga is a twisty one. Here’s everything you need to know.

In 2014, Elizabeth Holmes—then a 30-year-old billionaire entrepreneur—was making history as a bona fide Silicon Valley #GirlBoss. She had dropped out of Stanford at the age of 19, founded a revolutionary biotech company, and landed her first major magazine cover at Fortune. Fitting, given that her blood-testing company Theranos was valued at $9 billion. Some early backers included U.S. Treasury Secretary George Shultz, Rupert Murdoch, and the Walton family.

But by 2016, people began to question Holmes. The Theranos technology simply didn’t work, and Holmes was thought to have lied about her business operations to make money. In 2018, Theranos had all but completely collapsed—and Holmes was deemed a Silicon Valley scammer.

In 2018, Elizabeth Holmes and her former Theranos business partner (and ex-boyfriend) Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani were charged with nine counts of wire fraud and two counts of conspiracy to commit wire fraud. An indictment accused the two of plotting to “scheme, plan and artifice to defraud investors as to a material matter,” according to The New York Times.

On Jan. 3, 2022, Elizabeth Holmes was found guilty of three counts of wire fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud by misleading investors. A jury found Holmes not guilty on four other charges connected to fraud. According to NPR, the jury could not reach a decision on three other counts tied to investor fraud.

Elizabeth Holmes is in a relationship with hotel heir Billy Evans. They first met at a party back in 2017, and got engaged a year later in 2018. On an episode of Inside the Hive With Nick Bilton, Vanity Fair’s Nick Bilton (who covers Silicon Valley) shed light on the inner workings of their relationship, based on what he heard from ex-Theranos employees.

“She doesn’t have any money... he [Billy Evans] is a trust fund baby and has a lot of money, and he is probably helping out with the legal bills, because Elizabeth’s family doesn’t have money either,” Bilton said on the podcast. He added: “Holmes is going to get pregnant before she gets on the stand because she will look very sympathetic as a pregnant woman on the stand.”

In August 2021, it was reported that Holmes and Evans welcomed their first child, William Holmes Evans, in California. Holmes had first informed the court of her pregnancy in March 2021, according to ABC, which delayed her trial.

Before her sentence, Holmes remained free on a $500,000 bond while awaiting her fate and was living in a 74-acre, $135 million mansion in Woodside, California, a wealthier town in Silicon Valley. According to CNBC, the property is called “Green Gables,” and it “evokes the image of an enchanted forest with deer running through the property.”

During her time there, Holmes reportedly moved onto her next venture. Vanity Fair reported in 2019 that she met with documentary filmmakers to talk about telling her “real” story.

She also asked for a new trial after claiming that a key witness came to her house unannounced and allegedly said he felt “guilty” about his testimony, CNN reported in 2022. According to a court filing made by Holmes’s attorneys, Adam Rosendorff—a former Theranos lab director and a whistleblower in The Wall Street Journal’s 2015 investigation into the company—visited Holmes' home on Aug. 8, 2022, and spoke to her husband. Holmes’ lawyers said the impromptu visit counted as new evidence and requested a new trial.

But on Nov. 18, 2022, U.S. District Judge Edward Davila sentenced Holmes to 11 years in prison, which is shorter than the 15-year penalty requested by federal prosecutors. She faced a maximum sentence of 20 years. Holmes must also pay $452 million in restitution from the $1 billion she raised from investors.

Before her sentence was delivered, Holmes read a speech to the courtroom, saying, “I am devastated by my failings. I have felt deep pain for what people went through, because I failed them. I regret my failings with every cell of my body.” After giving birth to their second child, a daughter named Invicta, she reported to prison in May 2023.

In March 2026, Holmes’s prison sentence was reduced to 10 years and 3 months in federal prison; she’s scheduled to be released on Feb. 22, 2030. Holmes is incarcerated at the Federal Prison Camp in Bryan, Texas, but will be transferred to the Austin Transitional Center, a halfway house, in Del Valle, Texas, on Aug. 23, 2027.

According to Fielder, Holmes and Evans have not seen You Can See Everything, which opens in theaters on October 16. But she has watched parts of The Dropout, which is documented in You Can See Everything.

#441. Want to Be Super Fit in Your 50s? This Trainer Has Simple Advice.

Bryan Krahn made this workout mistake so you don’t have to. Here’s how you can age better.

AS YOU GET older, some things have to change. That’s just a fact of life. You wouldn’t want to keep up the same lifestyle as you did in your youth and early adulthood, when you had fewer responsibilities and years on your odometer. But it’s not just about maturing. Some adjustments you make will be more focused on living better and adapting your habits to your body as it ages.

The question is, when should you look into shifting your practices? You might think if you’re not experiencing any issues now, you have no reason to make changes—but that’s not how smart fitness programming works. If you ask Bryan Krahn, the 53-year-old trainer behind MH’s Max Muscle at 50 program, you’ll set yourself up for success if you start sooner.

So if you want to feel good in your 50s, the time to make a change is in your 40s.

“It's not a sexy idea, but I think it's almost a cautionary tale,” Krahn tells MH. ”If you're 40 and you feel great, great—But now is when you actually have to start changing things proactively, because you will have to. Especially if you're doing meatheady stuff.”

Krahn isn’t just falling back on preconceived notions about aging. He’s speaking from his own experience.

“On your 40th birthday, if you stop doing one rep maxes and training like an idiot and start to be more proactive, your 50s will be cake. But I didn't do that,” he says. “When I was 46, 47, I was a mess—I had to rebuild everything.”

What does change look like? More controlled, focused training instead of picking trendy workout programs at random. Fewer one rep maxes and stunt lifts. And much more dedication to recovery.

If you’re not sure exactly how to implement that type of shift to your own routine—or if you’re starting with strength training later in life—Krahn designed the entire Max Muscle After 50 program to give you the blueprint.

Brett Williams, NASM-CPT, PES, a senior editor at Men's Health, is a certified trainer and former pro football player and tech reporter. You can find his work elsewhere at Mashable, Thrillist, and other outlets.

#443. The 10-Minute Daily Habit That Could Help You Sleep Better, According to New Research

And really, what’s ten minutes in the scheme of things?

With everything you've got going on in life, exercise can sometimes fall down your list behind other, more pressing matters. That's completely understandable from a time-management perspective, but new research suggests trying to squeeze in even short bursts of exercise throughout the day can be linked to healthier sleep.

According to a new observational study published in the Journal of Physical Activity and Health, getting at least 10 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous exercise every day could be linked to healthier sleep. "For some outcomes, particularly cardiometabolic health, research suggests that the total amount of activity may be more important than how it is distributed across the week," says Benjamin Baird, PhD, study co-author and research assistant professor in the Department of Psychology at The University of Texas at Austin. "We wondered whether the same would be true for sleep."

If you're currently struggling with getting enough rest or just feel like there's room for improvement, these findings are definitely intriguing. Here's why sleep medicine specialists want you to consider them.

Meet the experts: Christopher Winter, MD, a sleep medicine specialist, neurologist, and author of The Sleep Solution: Why Your Sleep Is Broken and How to Fix It; Benjamin Baird, PhD, study co-author and research assistant professor in the Department of Psychology at The University of Texas at Austin; and Praveen Rudraraju, MD, director of the Center for Sleep Medicine at Northwell’s Phelps Hospital

For the study, researchers asked 69 college-aged adults to wear a Fitbit to measure their physical activity and sleep during two intervals that spanned eight months. The study participants also took electronic surveys three times a week that ranked their energy levels, stress, feelings of contentment, and sleep quality in the morning.

After analyzing the data, the researchers discovered that participants who got at least 10 minutes a day of moderate-to-vigorous-intensity physical activity within a five-day period had a lower rapid eye movement-to-nonrapid eye movement (REM-to-NREM) ratio in the first 180 minutes of sleep. That means they spent a bigger proportion of their sleep in the NREM stages, which include the deepest stage of sleep.

Participants who logged regular exercise also reported feeling more energetic the next day than those who didn't move as regularly.

"Because sleep is organized around a daily circadian cycle, we thought there was a reason to suspect that being active consistently from day to day might matter," Baird says. "That’s essentially what we found: Having more days with at least 10 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity was associated with relatively more non-REM sleep during the first few hours of the night, even after accounting for the total amount of activity."

The study didn't look at why 10 minutes of activity may lead to deeper sleep, but there are a few theories. "Activity creates changes in body temperature, adenosine levels, and other neurotransmitters that result in improvements in sleep," says Christopher Winter, MD, a sleep medicine specialist, neurologist, and author of The Sleep Solution: Why Your Sleep Is Broken and How to Fix It. (Adenosine drives the need for sleep.) "Activity can also serve as a circadian timekeeper as well when people exercise on a schedule and on a daily basis," he adds.

Another leading explanation is likely thermoregulation, says Praveen Rudraraju, MD, director of the Center for Sleep Medicine at Northwell’s Phelps Hospital. "During exercise, core body temperature rises," he explains. "As the body cools during the evening and overnight, changes in temperature regulation correlate with greater slow-wave activity, a hallmark of deeper, more restorative sleep."

Exercise may also increase your "sleep pressure" by helping you burn off more energy, making you more tired when it's time for bed, Dr. Rudraraju says.

But it's important to point out that the findings don't suggest that 10 minutes of movement dramatically change sleep patterns. "Typically, non-REM sleep predominates earlier in the night and REM sleep becomes more prominent later," Baird says. "Our results suggest that regular physical activity may help support that normal pattern."

The researchers found that moderate-to-vigorous activity was the most effective—i.e., breathing harder while still being able to talk. "In everyday terms, moderate activity would include things like brisk walking—activity that noticeably increases your heart rate and breathing—while vigorous activity would include things like running or other exercise that makes it substantially harder to carry on a conversation," Baird says.

He also stresses this: "It doesn’t necessarily have to mean a formal workout."

This study focused on college students, but Baird says it's "plausible" the findings apply to everyone else. "There is a broader literature showing beneficial relationships between physical activity and sleep across adulthood," he says.

Overall, doctors say it's great to incorporate movement into your daily life. The findings "support the idea that there are few things better for sleep than exercise," Dr. Winter says.

#444. Why Is My Brown Hair Always Turning Red?

A hairstylist shares her solutions for this pesky brunette hair problem

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

I began dyeing my hair in earnest two years ago with (gasp!) box dye. My grays were becoming more pronounced, and after I had my son, my natural brown hair felt dull and muted. I didn’t want to go blonder, lighter, or more golden, and I don’t have time to sit in a salon for hours. I wanted a deep, dark brown—with no hint of warmth. So I grabbed a dye off the shelf that promised just that.

Who knew that achieving a cool, ashy deep brown would be so tricky, both in and out of the salon? The problem goes something like this: I color my hair, and it looks amazing. It’s rich, it’s deep, it’s cool-toned. A week or two later, I catch a glimpse of my hair in the sunlight and realize I’m literally a redhead. My hair turned red. Red hair is beautiful, but if I wanted red hair, I would have dyed it that way. What gives?

“Artificial hair color always oxidizes, and it almost always reveals warm tones,” says Jenna Mast, a hairdresser at Bond in Hoboken, New Jersey. “There are things you can do to delay it or minimize it, but regular salon visits are important.” Hair color is both an art and a science. “Simply put, it is oxidation of the color, which reveals the underlying pigment of the hair that was colored,” says Mast. “Artificial color molecules are put into the hair strand, and as the cuticle is opened—whether with heat, chemicals, time—the artificial color molecules escape and reveal the natural underlying melanin in the hair.”

Think of it like painting. The blue color molecule in most dyes is the largest, so it leaches out of the hair first over time. Without the blue toning your hair, the warm pigments (yellows and reds) become more pronounced. This is true for both salon dyes and box dyes, but in the salon, Mast says, your colorist can custom-mix a demi- or semipermanent formula using specific color lines to minimize hair swelling and damage. “A higher amount of peroxide always equals more warmth exposed,” she says.

Our hair’s natural warmth and texture also play a role. “Every person has a different melanin concentration in their hair strands, and it doesn’t correlate to skin color the way we often think of melanin. Somebody who naturally has super dark hair, thick strands with highly concentrated melanin, is always going to have more warmth,” she notes. “Whereas somebody with softer, finer hair that’s also very dark might not have as much warmth.” That’s where a pro colorist can mix the right dye to neutralize your hair’s unique baseline tone. “As a colorist, I always pull from my art background,” she adds. “If I were painting the same tone watercolor over multiple different starting tones, it would look different on each one.” Mast continues: “A lot of people tend to think, ‘I just want cool brown; it should be simple,’ but depending on your unique hair strand, styling, and lifestyle, a formulation is more than choosing a swatch in a color book.”

This in-shower gloss and toner helps boost your hair color and shine and eliminate red tones with a green pigment.

Box dyes, like the ones I use and love, complicate things even more. “Box dye is tricky; it’s meant to be a one-size-fits-most product. The box cannot determine your grey percentage, porosity, environment, etc.,” she says. Box dyes can be harsh, swelling the hair’s cuticle to improve gray coverage but also boosting warmth. They also don’t apply color evenly from your fresh, gray roots to your many-times-dyed ends.

So what can a girl do to keep her cool tone? “Sometimes, a small tweak in your formulation or routine can help prevent the dreaded red from showing through brown color,” Mast advises. “The shower is so important. I think so many people would benefit from shower filters or a water softener.” High chlorine levels (in a pool or at home) or unfiltered heavy metals can fade your hair color—and those blue molecules—prematurely. “You don’t need to get a super expensive filter or own a home or even a wrench… I suggest my clients check out the Aquabliss hair filter. It’s less than $40 and attaches behind your showerhead, so it is very easy and even works for handheld and rain showers.”

Mast’s favorite shower filter, which is easy to install and costs less thn $40.

Then there’s the matter of product. “Personally, my go-to product to maintain colored hair is L’Oréal Metal Detox Spray before the color service. For take-home products, I like to use Redken Acidic Conditioner to maintain hair health.” As for shampoo, she says L’Oréal Vitamino Color Spectrum is fantastic. And be mindful if you’re using a dandruff-fighting shampoo, as it will oxidize your color faster. “Color oxidation is inevitable,” she adds. “The idea is that the products you use should delay it enough until your next touch-up.”

Mast’s favorite color-safe shampoo for dyed hair.

To keep the red out of your hair between dyeing sessions, the best thing you can do, besides minimizing heat damage, filtering your water, and using the right shampoo, is reach for a color-depositing conditioner or in-shower toner. “I have always been a huge fan of Christophe Robin. They have an ash-brown conditioning treatment that not only makes your hair feel amazing but also neutralizes brassy/red tones,” Mast suggests. “IGK makes color-depositing masks in pastel green and blue that you can mix with conditioner to cancel out unwanted tones. Fanola was very popular years back for its potent purple shampoo for blondes; now it makes a green shampoo. And Matrix has a blue shampoo that can neutralize orangey tones.”

Achieving the perfect shade of cool brown is anything but simple, but the right products and routine can help. “Brown hair is not boring, and having tones complementary to your own skin tone can truly elevate your self-confidence in ways a new lipstick or blush would never,” Mast says. “While not everyone can afford to see an experienced colorist or even go to a salon, understanding as much as you can about your own hair and your color goals will help you make the best decisions before you reach for a box.”

#445. How One Designer Turned a 1970s Lake Tahoe Cabin Into a Design-Forward Vacation Rental

The home is just four doors down from a childhood vacation destination.

Anastasia Casey wasn’t necessarily looking to buy a piece of her husband's childhood. But after seven property tours, a handful of rejected offers, and a ballooning budget, that’s more or less what happened. Tucked along Lake Tahoe’s serene West Shore, the 1970s cabin that would eventually become Casey’s latest design project sat just a few doors down from the summer home where her husband, Quinn, spent his childhood swimming off the docks at Chambers Landing and getting into trouble with his cousins. Of all the properties in Tahoe, somehow they'd landed back on the very same street.

The kismet wasn't lost on Casey—the designer and industry multihyphenate behind The Interior Collective site and podcast, who also runs IDCO Studio alongside her husband Quinn and hosts Design Camp with fellow designer Lindsey Borchard—who had been searching for a property to transform into a design-forward vacation rental alongside friends Jennifer Janovetz and Tony Manocchio. The trio had already collaborated on another home for their joint venture, Collective Stays, but this one came with an unusually personal connection—and a decidedly less charming interior. Beneath the promise of a quintessential mountain retreat hid decades of questionable design decisions: mismatched wood tones, faux paneling, and a kitchen that seemed determined to make entertaining difficult. “I wanted it to feel like it had always looked this way,” Casey says of the renovation.

Achieving that thoughtful balance required some inventive maneuvering, though. The kitchen cabinetry, island, and countertops, all from Casey’s line with Unique Kitchens & Baths, were salvaged from her Austin design studio, shipped across the country, and puzzled together to fit into the cabin's quirky footprint. A wicker banquette reclaimed precious square footage, while closing in the staircase made room for a pantry and coffee bar. Elsewhere, retro-inspired wallcoverings from Casey’s Chasing Paper collection disguised unfortunate faux wood paneling, incorporating a spirited mix of plaid, stripes, and 1970s geometry.

Throughout, Casey indulged her affinity for woven textures, leather, mismatched metals, and the occasional oddball antique. Roadside dining chairs, a vintage Levi’s sign, and a 1960s needlepoint now mingle with contemporary furnishings, giving the house the ease and eccentricity of a lakeside retreat assembled over generations, rather than months.

But perhaps the most meaningful detail—besides the cabin’s address, of course—is one Casey didn’t touch: a closet rod in an upstairs bedroom, still divided by handwritten Sharpie notes assigning each child their own hanging space. “I'll never paint over that,” she says. After all, she knows a thing or two about protecting a lakeside legacy.

FAST FACTSDesigner: Anastasia CaseyBuilder: GMK ConstructionLocation: Lake Tahoe, CaliforniaThe Space: A four-bedroom, three-and-a-half-bathroom cabin across 2,244 square feet.

“The kitchen was the biggest transformation in the house,” says Casey. While the footprint didn’t change, the team extended the cabinetry six feet further down the wall and added an island ideal for entertaining a crowd. “The small kitchen now has plenty of storage and works really well for cooking.”

An oversized 72-inch dining table seats 10 with help from a Four Hands x Amber Lewis bench and chairs Casey found on the side of the road and had reupholstered in Schumacher fabric that nods to needlework. “It holds up really well to the commotion of the cabin and is such a fun gathering space,” she adds.

Designed to act as the primary suite, the upstairs bedroom is “definitely the most luxurious,” says Casey. She covered the room’s existing faux paneling in natural grasscloth, then outfitted the space with cozy details, like two generous armchairs and a plush rug from Lauren Liess. “I really wanted to create a cabin that people could stay for extended periods of time, so each of the large bedrooms also has an extra-large desk to accommodate private working areas, perfect for long summer vacations with the kids,” Casey adds.

To skirt the home’s original wood paneling again, Casey wrapped this bedroom in Vintage Plaid wallpaper from her collection with Chasing Paper. “It had the perfect retro feel, and a light enough background that it tied all the wood tones together without making the room darker,” she says. “It anchored the entire color palette—the rust upholstered king bed from Moe’s paired perfectly with the moss green sleeper sofa, making this room feel super cozy and like a place you can retire from the chaos of a busy family stay.”

Casey prioritized expanding the vanity in the downstairs bathroom to two sinks (“It feels quite luxurious in a Tahoe cabin!” she says), finishing the room curtain panels from West Elm that she hemmed and transformed into a shower curtain.

“The fish rug is Moroccan, and a vintage find I knew would bring the level of quirk I was hoping for, while tying into the color palette of the plaid wallpaper in the adjacent room,” she adds.

“The double queen room upstairs is the most whimsical space, with its extreme ceiling angles and dreamy bedding,” says Casey. To help the ceiling shine, she painted the faux paneling in Benjamin Moore’s White Dove, setting a foundation of neutral finishes, including a Lulu & Georgia rug and vintage bedding.

A cozy place to retreat after a day on the lake, the living room feels appropriately rustic and welcoming. To bounce light around the room, Casey hung an oversized mirror on the now-enclosed staircase, finishing the room with a conversation-ready layout of Four Hands furniture. The vintage cypress slab coffee table came from Casey’s personal collection in Austin.

Previously a forgotten room that housed the washer, dryer, and water heater, this oversized bathroom doubles as a spot to toss muddy boots and wet clothes (the washer and dryer now reside behind the door). Penny tile floors and plaid-inspired shower tiles bring playful personality.

“The exterior of the cabin is actually quite misleading—it has a large two-car garage that sits close to the street, and you can only see the original portion of the cabin from the front, so it looks quite small,” says Casey. In reality, the house boasts two spacious front decks, which she outfitted with outdoor furniture from Four Hands for a comfortable place to watch beach traffic go by. “Eventually, we’ll repaint the house a deep green, but for now, we’re loving it in its original form!”

Since 2016, Anastasia Casey has served thousands of interior designers, assembled a team of creative experts, launched an online shop, fostered a thriving online community, founded an industry-first retreat, and cemented her reputation as a tastemaker and invaluable resource in the design world.

#447. Katie Thurston Made a Surprise Announcement at the Breast Cancer Research Foundation Luncheon

Researchers and philanthropists gathered to recognize promising advancements.

In a sea of pink-swathed tables, the mood at the Breast Cancer Research Foundation’s (BCRF) annual Symposium and Awards Luncheon was upbeat. The lunch was held today at the New York Hilton in Midtown Manhattan. Since October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month, it was the perfect time to recognize the world’s most promising research focused on preventing and finding a cure for breast cancer.

William Lauder, chairman of the board of directors of Estée Lauder, kicked things off by speaking about his mother, Evelyn, who started BCRF in 1993. He took a moment to acknowledge how far the foundation has come since its founding. “Today, BCRF is a research powerhouse, supporting a record number of 280 brilliant scientists, including three Nobel Prize winners,” he said. He noted that since its inception, BCRF has had a hand in every major breast cancer breakthrough, and deaths have decreased by 44 percent.

Former Bachelorette star Katie Thurston took the stage with her husband, Jeff Arcuri. “My name is Katie, I’m 35 years old, and I have stage IV breast cancer,” she said by way of introduction. Thurston became visibly choked up onstage while she talked about how, instead of wedding planning, she had to pause her life to figure out treatment when she was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2025. She and Arcuri invited attendees to text donation pledges to a number displayed onstage on screens, where people could watch pledges roll in. “Today I want to donate $610 to represent every day since I’ve been diagnosed,” Thurston said. She then announced that she currently has no evidence of disease, which was met with resounding applause.

BCRF president and CEO Donna McKay presented the Sandra Taub Humanitarian Award to philanthropists Karen and Rob Hale, who committed $50 million to BCRF—the largest private gift ever given to breast cancer research. Other speakers included BCRF founding scientific director Larry Norton, MD, of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, who presented an award to Kornelia Polyak, MD, and Karen Hale and Kinga Lampert, who jointly presented research grants to over 200 grant recipients.

BCRF is the largest private funder of breast cancer research and has supported over 260 scientists who have had a hand in major breakthroughs in the field. It’s raised over $1 billion for the cause. Prior to the luncheon, BCRF hosted a symposium titled “How Studying Early-Onset Breast Cancer Is Helping Women of All Ages,” moderated by Norton and Dr. Judy E. Garber of the Evelyn H. Lauder Breast Center and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and Harvard Medical School.

Katie Berohn is ELLE’s beauty editor. Previously, she held the same title at Who What Wear, where she was promoted from associate beauty editor. She’s written for publications like The Cut, Cosmopolitan, Good Housekeeping, and Mashable. Her interests include fragrance, vintage shopping, hot yoga, food, travel, music, books, and attempting to make every NYT Cooking recipe. She’s on the endless hunt to find the perfect shade of red lipstick.
