#448. Selling Your Home? Here Are the Biggest Mistakes to Avoid

Parting with your home can be a difficult decision tinged with fraught emotions and unrealistic expectations. In today’s economy, luxury homebuyers hold much of the power, with properties taking longer to sell and price cuts appearing with increasing frequency. Looking to dodge that fate? We reached out to brokers at some of the nation’s top firms, asking what mistakes sellers are making—and how to avoid them.

Hands down, overpricing is the most common mistake luxury sellers should avoid, according to real estate experts. They argue that it’s better to set the value appropriately right from the beginning in order to avoid slashing the price later on. “Many sellers say they’re not in a rush to sell, and feel the ‘right’ buyer will come along,” says Etta McLendon of Aspen Snowmass Sotheby’s International Realty. “However, when you lack urgency, so do your buyers, who will happily watch from the sidelines for you to drop the price—three or four times.”

Adds Nicole Hay of Compass, “Every week that listing sits, buyers assume something is wrong.” In Manhattan, where she works, homes entering the market at an optimal price point can set the stage for buyers to swoop in. “The first few weeks on market are your best shot at top dollar, and we always strive to price accurately to garner maximum interest for a quick sale.”

Sellers would do best to set expectations before even reaching out to a real estate agent, according to Lyndsi Armenio, a mid-Atlantic broker with Douglas Elliman. “I completely understand it; if you’ve spent $300,000 renovating your kitchen, you want that investment to show up in the price,” she says. The issue? “Buyers don’t necessarily care what something cost you—they care about what it’s worth to them.”

Sellers should avoid “testing the market,” explains Liza Caminiti, a North Carolina–based agent with Ivester Jackson Christie’s International Real Estate. “When a property launches at the wrong price, it can lose the momentum and sense of exclusivity that are so important at this level,” she says. “You can always create competition around a beautifully positioned property, but it is very difficult to recreate the excitement of a new listing once that initial opportunity has passed.”

It’s no secret that buyers today have a wider array of choices and more room to negotiate than in years past—but some homeowners haven’t gotten the message. “I think the biggest mistake sellers make today is assuming they still control the narrative,” says Cory Weiss of Douglas Elliman in Beverly Hills. “Whether it’s pricing, choosing between buyers, or deciding how much to invest in presentation, the market has shifted.”

He says homeowners can often benefit in the long run by going the extra mile. “Sellers who resist thoughtful cosmetic updates, overlook presentation, or aren’t realistic about pricing can very quickly get lost in the inventory,” he adds. “In this market, character can absolutely command a premium, but dated for the sake of dated generally does not.”

For Helene Barre of Sotheby’s International Realty in Greenwich, Connecticut, the worst transgression involves decor. “The biggest mistake today is refusing to have a house staged if the agent has recommended it,” she says. Douglas Elliman’s Megan Sullivan, also based in Greenwich, zeroes in on the issue. “Too often, sellers either over-personalize the home before listing or, conversely, strip it of the details that make it distinctive,” she says. “The goal should be thoughtful presentation, not genericization.”

Sullivan’s advice? “A well-executed listing needs to tell the story of the house—who designed it, how it has evolved, what has been preserved, and why its design is meaningful,” she says. “Buyers need to envision themselves in the space and how it will work for their family.”

A final note: Be wary of including an overabundance of listing images, which can continue living on the internet long after a property has traded hands. “Many sellers in this market prefer privacy,” says Chicago-based Annika Valdiserri of @properties Christie’s International Real Estate. “For most properties, you don’t need 70 listing photos, and you don’t need pictures of all seven bedrooms and baths.” Her guidance is to stick to a tighter edit. “Include professionally shot photos and video of the main living areas and amenities—enough to get buyers through the door.”

Geoffrey Montes is an associate editor at ELLE Decor with a serious love for all things real estate and design. Before that, he worked at Architectural Digest, Galerie, and Preservation magazines, covering everything from jaw-dropping listings to world-famous architects and design events like Salone del Mobile and Homo Faber.

#450. The Best Work Backpacks, According to ‘Women’s Health’ Editors

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I have come to the tragic realization that my tote bag days are officially numbered. After years of happily throwing my laptop, water bottle, charger, snacks, and approximately 17 more things I don’t need into a tote and hauling it on one shoulder, my body has finally said: enough. I recently suffered a rotator cuff tear, so carrying a heavy bag on one shoulder has been basically impossible. And I’m not the only one on the Women’s Health team who has started questioning the tote life.

The obvious solution is a work backpack. Weight gets distributed across both shoulders, your hands are free, and there’s no awkward bag-sliding-off-your-shoulder situation when you’re running for the train. The problem? Finding one that doesn’t look like you’re heading to a college lecture or a three-day camping trip. I still want to look cute walking into the office.

So, over the past month, I recruited a handful of WH editors to put a bunch of stylish work backpacks through their paces. We carried laptops, gym clothes, water bottles, chargers, lunch, and all the other random stuff that somehow ends up coming with us to work, paying close attention to comfort, organization, durability, and style. The result: a list of work backpacks that are worth breaking up with your tote.

The Troubadour Apex 4.0 has made me a backpack person. I’ve been carrying it almost every day for the past three months, and the biggest surprise is how much better my shoulder feels at the end of a long day. The padded shoulder straps are super comfy and do a great job of evenly distributing the weight across both of my shoulders. Plus, I love the somewhat futuristic look with the structured shape and (vegan) leather details that never clash with my office clothes.

And it holds a lot. The standard Apex is 22 liters and fits laptops up to 17 inches, with plenty of room in the main compartment for lunch, a sweater, shoes, or whatever else I’ve decided to bring to the office that day. There are also two expandable water-bottle pockets (one zips closed), a flat front pocket for smaller essentials, and a bunch of interior compartments for chargers, cords, and other little things that turn into a tangled mess at the bottom of a bag.

I love that the laptop compartment is padded, sits toward the back of the bag, and suspends your computer above the bottom for extra protection. The straps are cushy and curve slightly inward, making it comfortable even when I’ve packed it pretty full. There’s also a padded top handle for carrying it by hand and a luggage sleeve for travel.

It’s worth noting that the standard Apex is a hefty backpack—I’m 5-foot-6, and while I like all that space, it can feel like a lot of bag when I’m not carrying much. For something more compact, there’s also a 16-liter Apex Compact that fits up to a 14-inch MacBook or 15-inch PC. For me, the extra room has been worth it.

For an affordable bag perfect for work and travel, this Amazon pick is your gal. I can’t even keep track of how many times I’ve seen this bag out in the wild (on the streets of NYC, the airport, the train) since I bought it on a whim over three years ago.

For starters, it has so much storage: There are two main compartments, separate sleeves for a 14-inch laptop and 13-inch tablet, a dedicated shoe compartment, and a water-resistant pocket for wet clothes or towels. (Gym-to-office people, this one’s for you.) The padded shoulder straps make it comfortable to carry, and the monochrome design doesn’t scream “I’m going on a backpacking trip.”

It has enough room for work essentials and a change of clothes, so I’ve used it for everything from my daily commute to weekend getaways. The separate compartments are especially handy when you’re trying to keep your sneakers away from your clean clothes or stop your laptop charger from getting tangled. It weighs about 2.2 pounds, so it’s not the lightest bag on this list, but the storage space you get is worth it.

And the real selling point? Mine has been going strong for more than three years with minimal wear and tear. Considering how much I’ve dragged it around NYC and how many airplane seats I’ve stuffed it under, that’s pretty impressive for an Amazon impulse buy. It doesn’t have the luxe materials or refined finish of a pricier work backpack, but it’s functional, roomy, and versatile enough to earn its keep well beyond the office. Plus, in a neutral color (like the beige option I chose), it doesn’t clash with any of my work outfits.

If you’re the kind of person who leaves the house with a laptop, a water bottle, a change of clothes, and approximately 47 other things, the lululemon Everywhere Backpack is for you. It has a roomy 22-liter capacity with tons of compartments to fit everything you need and then some. The durable, easy-to-clean nylon material makes it super practical, while the streamlined shape goes with everyday office wear, says associate editor Olivia Luppino.

Inside, there’s a padded laptop sleeve that fits devices up to 16 inches, plus a spacious main compartment for all your daily essentials (and extras). A front zippered pocket keeps smaller items within easy reach, while side pockets give you a spot for your water bottle. “It’s roomy enough for work necessities and a change of clothes for post-office plans or a workout,” says Luppino.

Even when it’s packed to the brim, the bag doesn’t skimp on comfort. The adjustable padded straps distribute weight evenly, and Luppino found it comfortable for walking around the city and commuting—especially compared to her heavy tote. One small gripe: The straps can be a little finicky to adjust, and at 22 liters, the bag might feel oversized if you tend to pack light.

If your backpack has been leaving your shoulders sore and achy by the time you get to the office, meet the Everlane ReNew Transit Backpack. Fitness & Reviews Editor Natascha Grief noticed a difference almost immediately, thanks to the strap design: “The straps are set closer together at the top so that they sit in a more comfortable place and then flare out, which eliminates the sore and achy shoulders I'd get from my previous backpack,” she says. The bag itself is lightweight, too, so you’re not adding unnecessary bulk before you’ve even packed your laptop. After more than a month of commuting with it, Grief found it durable and super easy to carry.

Don’t let its streamlined design fool you: the backpack holds a whopping 27 liters, including a separate exterior laptop compartment that fits a laptop up to 15 inches. That means you can pull out your laptop without unzipping the entire bag or excavating your lunch and notebook in front of officemates. There are also two zippered pockets, two interior slip pockets, and water bottle holders inside and out. Grief especially loved the flap pocket for stashing sunglasses, keys, and a phone within easy reach, while the discreet zippers add extra security.

Made from smooth polyester, the bag also has a clean look that works well with office clothes and travel fits. Its pass-through strap makes it easy to slide onto a rolling suitcase.

The Calpak Luka might just convert you into a backpack person. Just ask Associate Health and Fitness Editor Addison Aloian, who “used to think backpacks were kind of dorky to wear after high school,” but is now “totally obsessed” with her Calpak after making the switch from a work tote that had been contributing to her back pain.

The Luka is lightweight and made from Calpak’s signature puffy fabric, but it can hold a lot. Aloian regularly packs breakfast, lunch, coffee, a water bottle, workout clothes, and whatever else the day calls for, and somehow, it all fits. The magic? All the compartments.

There’s a dedicated padded laptop sleeve for devices up to 15 inches, plus multiple interior and exterior pockets to keep chargers, mints, hand sanitizer, keys, and other little essentials from becoming one giant jumble. A luggage sleeve makes it travel-friendly, with a hidden zippered pocket for valuables tucked inside. Basically, everything has a home, which is great news for anyone who’s ever had to dump an entire bag onto their desk just to find a lip balm.

One small heads-up: Aloian loved the pink color but notes that lighter shades can show dirt pretty quickly. The scratch-resistant exterior helps with everyday wear, but you may want to opt for a darker color if you’re tough on your bags.

July makes travel gear that looks great well beyond the airport. Beauty Editor Nicole Saunders loves its “sleek design” and “non-bulky appearance,” which makes sense: The 20-liter backpack has a structured shape with a smooth nylon-twill finish, leather-wrapped handle, and gunmetal hardware that feels more “office to drinks” than your average commuter pack. The lightly cushioned straps are comfortable, and Saunders says they don’t dig into her shoulders even when she overpacks.

There’s a padded laptop compartment that fits up to a 16-inch laptop, a smaller interior zippered pocket, a front-access pocket for things you want to grab quickly, and a side zip pocket that fits a water bottle or umbrella. The coolest travel feature by far is the “QuickPass” travel pocket—a hidden, magnetic compartment at the top of the bag for storing a passport or phone. It also has a luggage pass-through strap, so you can slide it right onto your suitcase handle when you’re racing through the airport. Saunders likes having the laptop sleeve and smaller compartments separate from the main 20-liter space, even when she travels light and doesn’t use every pocket.

It has plenty of room for a laptop, travel essentials, and your daily necessities, but it’s more of a medium-size carry than an everything-but-the-kitchen-sink situation. Saunders found it smaller than some of the other backpacks she tried and said it wouldn’t be her pick for weekend trips.

This briefcase-like silhouette sneakily packs a ton of stuff. Copy Group Director Marli Higa put it through an afternoon at the coffee shop with a laptop, two notebooks, two books, chargers, an umbrella, a flannel, two 20-ounce water bottles, and multiple pairs of glasses. Somehow, it all fit. The dual exterior bottle pockets are a big help, freeing up precious room inside, while the padded, fleece-lined laptop sleeve is basically a “comfort blankie” for your computer, she says.

There’s a main compartment with a zippered mesh sleeve, a front compartment with organizers and a key clip, plus a zippered front pocket for quick-access items. There’s even a hidden shoulder-strap pocket for wireless earbuds. Despite all those options, Higa says it has “the exact right amount of internal organization,” meaning you won’t spend five minutes digging around for your keys—or wondering which pocket you put them in.

Then came the real test: an 11-hour flight. The Kaslo worked as an under-seat carry-on, leaving enough room for Higa’s feet while still holding her lunch, headphones, neck pillow, sweatshirt, and a last-minute airport gift. The luggage trolley sleeve made it easy to attach to her rolling carry-on, too.

The Quince Marlow Laptop Backpack is proof that a work backpack doesn’t have to look, well, like a work backpack. Made from 100% top-grain leather with a pebbled finish, it has a handbag-esque look that plays well with dressier office outfits—something WH’s Director of Special Projects Amanda Lucci appreciates.

At $150, this is a steal for a genuine leather backpack—especially since it closely resembles bags from brands like Cuyana and Tumi, which retail for upward of $500.

Inside, the main compartment has four slip pockets and a zippered pocket for keeping smaller essentials organized, while a separate back compartment houses a padded laptop sleeve that fits up to a 16-inch laptop. There’s also an exterior zip pocket for quick-access items and a luggage sleeve on the back for travel.

It has a slim profile—and Lucci found that it isn’t the best choice when she needs to pack a lot. There’s also no exterior water-bottle pocket, so your bottle takes up precious real estate inside the bag. But when she’s traveling light and wants something that looks especially nice with a dressier outfit, the Marlow is the one she reaches for.

I mean, comfort is basically the whole reason you’re considering swapping your tote for a backpack, right? A cute backpack doesn’t make much sense if it digs into your shoulders, slides off one arm, or strains your neck. The biggest pro for backpacks over totes is weight distribution via padded, adjustable shoulder straps. Contoured straps are an added bonus since they are more ergonomic and help distribute the weight more evenly across the chest and shoulders. Beyond straps, look for a cushioned back panel and breathable mesh panels to maximize comfort.

Your work backpack should—gasp—fit everything you need to bring to the office. Before falling in love with a bag, think about what you realistically carry to work every day. A dedicated laptop compartment is a must for most people, while extra pockets for your charger, keys, water bottle, headphones, and other small essentials can keep you from digging around in one giant abyss. And if you regularly bring gym clothes or lunch to the office, make sure there’s enough room for those, too. Most of our testers—women with office jobs who use their backpacks for commuting—gravitated towards a 20L to 22L bag. Testers who prefer a work/travel hybrid backpack often lean toward bags that are 22L or up.

This is a work backpack, not a hiking pack, so there’s no reason it needs to look like you’re about to summit a mountain. If you’re replacing a tote because of comfort, you should still feel good carrying it into the office. Consider a more streamlined shape and neutral colorway, which will look great with the clothes you wear to work and won’t clash with casual outfits.

As a Women’s Health style writer, I’ve tested my fair share of work bags over the years, from roomy totes I once carried everywhere to the backpacks I’ve recently started reaching for instead. For this story, I wanted to go beyond my own closet, so I recruited eight other WH staffers to help me put a range of stylish work backpacks to the test over the past month and a half. We carried them to the office, on commutes, and through all the little daily errands that make a work bag earn its keep, evaluating everything from comfort and storage to durability and, of course, style. After weeks of real-world testing, the above picks are the backpacks we’d actually recommend carrying to work.

Shannen Zitz is the Associate Style & Reviews Editor at Women's Health, where she covers all-things sneakers and activewear. Previously, she was an assistant editor at Prevention. Shannen graduated from the State University of New York at Cortland with a bachelor's degree in English. If she’s not reading or writing, you can probably find her frequenting the skincare and makeup forums on Reddit or hogging the squat rack at the gym.

Christian is the Style and Reviews Director at Men's Health and Women’s Health, where he oversees shopping and style content for both brands. He started his magazine career as an accessories assistant at Vogue, and has since held editorial roles at Tatler Asia and The Manual. When he’s not online shopping, you can find him on long walks with his two corgis.

#452. At 53, Bryan Krahn Is Ripped. He Shares the Smartest Way to Keep Making Gains After 50.

He breaks down his fitness tweaks, supplements, and habits.

AFTER 50, LIFE might look a little different. That doesn’t necessarily mean you have to stop chasing gains. Just look at Bryan Krahn, the 53-year-old coach and creator of the Men's Health Max Muscle at 50 program. Krahn is still 210 pounds and jacked—but he acknowledges that maintaining his physique in this decade of life has required some training adjustments.

“The older you get, it’s strength that slowly filters out,” he says in the latest Strong Talk episode. “But even if you’ve never strength trained—especially if you’re at ground zero at 50—those newbie gains are still there, and they come fast no matter what age you are.”

Building muscle after 50 is all about training smarter, not always harder. For example, Krahn says his biggest priority now is to avoid getting hurt. Since dealing with a shoulder injury, Krahn has shifted to using machines to provide more controlled movements and safe resistance. The goal is to execute the movement well to engage the target muscle.

That doesn’t mean you should train with less focus when you’re older. Instead, train within your known limits. “Not what you used to do, not what you think you could do on a great day,” Krahn says. Take your known limits and subtract 10 percent of the weight. Exercise physiologist and strength coach Dr. Pat Davidson notes training heavy is very movement-specific and individual-specific. At 46, eight to 15 reps of hack squats are a sweet spot in building muscle and minimizing injury for Davidson compared with five heavy hack squats. Meanwhile, he goes harder on press exercises.

Krahn, Davidson, and MH fitness director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., debunk further misconceptions about exercise after 50 in the episode. They also discuss the two muscle-building supplements that work (and what doesn’t), and the absolute minimum Krahn does daily for movement and food.

Jocelyn Solis-Moreira, MS is the associate health & fitness for Men's Health and has previously written for CNN, Scientific American, Popular Science, and National Geographic before joining the brand. When she's not working, she's doing circus arts or working towards the perfect pull-up.

#453. What Did the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show Look Like When It Started?

Funny how a ‘90s lingerie show looks like the ready-to-wear runways of today

With the 2026 Victoria’s Secret Fashion show looming large this weekend, we anticipate another high-octane spectacle that taps into the voyeuristic desire to see perfect women prance around in their underwear. But today, many of these ensembles can hardly be classified as underwear, at least not by average human standards. The lingerie has ascended to a realm that more closely resembles art—diamond-encrusted fantasy bras worth millions with elaborate winged structures at the back. Some of these models have launched highly impressive careers off the back of earning the coveted “angel” title. And the whole production, celebrity musical guests, larger-than-life sets, and all, is televised like the Superbowl, streamed to millions globally. Surely it wasn’t always like this?

The Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show is not that old of an institution relative to the scope of fashion runways; the brand held its first show in August of 1995 at The Plaza Hotel in New York City. It was an industry event, albeit a flashy one. But the purpose remained one of practicality: to show the new lingerie collection to buyers, press, and executives. There were no musical guests or performers. The event was hosted by supermodel Stephanie Seymour, who also walked alongside models including Veronica Webb, Beverly Peele, Frederique van der Wal, Gail Elliot, and more. It was a product of the time: There were no streaming platforms to broadcast the show to millions. No smart phones to post Instagram reels by the minute. (Although it was taped, and I’d recommend a watch on Youtube.)

The first model out wore a thick-strapped T-shirt bra and ‘90s high-rise briefs. (For comparison, last year’s show began with a pregnant Jasmine Tookes in a flesh-toned set with an open-weave, pearl-drop embellished sheath, wearing a Botticelli-esque clamshell cage in place of the traditional wings.) The 1990s look was followed by similar ones with everyday bras worn with full-cut briefs or rolled-over shorts. Then came another “lingerie” look that practically qualifies as streetwear today: a long T-shirt with elbow length sleeves belted at the hip over boy shorts.

It’s funny what came next: a series of bras and bralettes worn with knee-length, lace-trimmed slip skirts, often styled with pumps and ladybags. I’ve spent the past few weeks documenting how the Spring 2027 collections deemed bras the new tops—and often styled them with knee length skirts. (This was Prada’s go-to look of the season.) Another archetypical ensemble came in the form of bras and silk pajama pants, cardigans slung over shoulders and worn undone.

A few looks consisted of a lacy bralette and tap pants—not unlike Maria Grazia’s most recent Fendi collection, no? Even Phoebe Philo showed creamy silk tap pants with a duster coat and kitten heels last season. Then came a series of bustiers that appeared quite simple by today’s standards—the kind we saw at Valentino paired with more mid-length skirts. Bodysuits styled with robes felt reminiscent of Haider Ackermann’s Tom Ford.

The final procession included slinky little slips, cardigans also often tossed over shoulders, and a more robust collection of silky eveningwear alongside a few Chinese-inspired silk adornments. (The cultural appropriation conversation has come a long way in the past 30 years.) But still, the whole thing felt like a swirl of clothing and lingerie that clients could really wear.

Zooming back out, something must have clicked pretty quickly; the theatrics laddered up exponentially in just a few years. By 1998, the first semblance of what we know today was beginning taking shape. The brand was now using the term “angel” to refer to its top-tier models and adorning them as such in fanciful wings. Stars like Jon Bon Jovi were beginning to sit front row. Victoria’s Secret first televised the show in 2001, around the time it began working with the women we now view as OG icons of VS fashion show lore: Gisele Bündchen, Tyra Banks, and Heidi Klum. And in the nearly three decades since, the fashion show has taken a roller coaster ride of ups and downs to become the mega-watt production we know today.

The Victoria’s Secret show has obviously tapped into a collective fascination with fashion’s tendency towards exposure—and capitalized on it. That’s not a new phenomenon in the larger spheres of fashion, but it’s particularly resonant right now. Moving out of the perfectly coiffed era of quiet luxury, a slant towards exhibitionism has made the runways of many major houses look, at least, partially like a lingerie show—perhaps an OG ‘90s VS one.

#454. The Most Underrated Design Trends That Have Quietly Shaped the Last Decade

Think soft curves, sleek minimalism, and wellness-centered designs.

Our homes are constantly evolving. As technology advances and cultural shifts shape the way we live, the design world is always looking ahead—finding smarter ways to declutter, rearrange our floor plans, and, above all, create homes that are as beautiful as they are functional.

That’s always been the mission of our annual Whole Home projects. For the past nine years, we’ve built a show house from the ground up—in locations like Atlanta, Denver, and Nashville—and enlisted top design talent to decorate each room. Ahead, we're diving into the archives of every House Beautiful Whole Home to revisit the most underrated design ideas of the past decade. These are innovations that have quietly transformed the way we live for the better.

Our homes are no longer simply lodgings. They’ve transformed into places where we gather. If you want to earn the title of everyone’s favorite spot, you’ll want your home to feel as fun as it is functional.

This bright, joy-filled Nashville dining room graced the cover of our 2019 Whole Home issue, adding a new level of versatility to traditional purpose. Designed by the team at Chenault James, a single multifunctional piece brings an unexpected element of entertainment to the definitive hosting space, with a height-adjustable table that easily flips from serving plates to ping-pong balls.

For homes with a more minimalist aesthetic, entertainment features tend to stay out of sight. In this ultramodern lounge from our 2024 Whole Home in Asheville, North Carolina, designer Rajni Alex refused to sacrifice sleek style for the visual clutter of a TV. Instead, she created a solution that works for every member of the family: a custom console by Walker Woodworking with a built-in TV lift that conceals the screen when it's not in use.

Alex framed the piece with rich brown drapery and illuminated built-ins, ensuring the room feels just as dramatic during an intense game of chess as it does for the final moments of the Super Bowl. The result is a space that seamlessly balances everyday function with elevated design.

The rise of open-concept homes reinvented columns, changing their reputation from a conscious design choice to an integral structural element. In this paprika-hued sitting room from our 2023 Whole Home in Hinsdale, Illinois, designer Emma Beryl embraced visions of grandeur amid towering seven-foot ceilings and faux marble to transform this circular column from an eyesore into a bespoke sitting area with braid fringe and posh Pomegranate Velvet upholstery by Zoffany.

Another obstacle of the open floor plan is its lack of distinction. High ceilings, rolling hardwoods, and the absence of walls make it almost impossible to give spaces true purpose and definition. When designer Dane Austin took on this “cavernous” home featured in our 2024 spread, he knew he wanted to channel warmth and personality into what could read as a cold and unwelcoming space—the perfect vehicle? Fabric. Austin created division through drapery, defining borders without having to put up a single panel of sheetrock.

Enjoying a coffee or nightcap in bed just got a whole lot easier. Designer Isabel Ladd, featured in our Whole Home in 2023, and Kathy Kuo, a 2024 alum, both built bespoke drinks bars in the master bedrooms, elevating their designs and adding an air of modern luxury.

For designer Anita Yokota, relaxation isn’t just a vacation home perk. It’s also a necessity in your forever home. For Whole Home 2024, she shared her “cocoon room,” an in-house haven for de-stressing. Draped in blue tones, the room also features plush furniture with soft edges in stormy grays and creamy whites to channel levity and mimic her muse, the vast sky.

As it turns out, the English have nailed great literature and great reading room designs. In this “English snug” featured in our 2024 Whole Home issue, designer Anne McDonald used inspiration from the traditional British home to balance expansive windows and vast mountain views. Using mohair club chairs, mossy paint, and delicate drapery, she designed a cozy inlet for settling and solitude.

No windows? No problem. When designer Arianne Bellizaire began working on this bold blue entryway for our Whole Home 2023, she noted one glaring issue: a lack of both natural and artificial light. Not wanting to deviate from the historic roots, she opted to line the ceiling with reflective vinyl to help light flow through the space.

Books and booze both find a home in this 2023 Whole Home library designed by Kate Marker. Working with the original shelves and millwork of this historic home, Marker ultimately decided to flank the functional fireplace with paneled-door cabinets so well-designed they are nearly undetectable to the naked eye. Inside, she installed shelving to stash spirits, mixers, and shakers, creating an in-house speakeasy.

Trellises line the walls of this radiant sunroom, originally featured in our 2022 Atlanta, Georgia Whole Home. Designed by Claire Staszak of Centered by Design, the transitional space marries the indoors to the patio, using the garden structure as a bridge between the two.

Drapery is the star of this 2023 Whole Home bedroom, designed by Mark Williams and Niki Papadopoulos. Embroidered with leaves and acorns, the panels set the tone for the entire room’s palette and connect the home’s interior design with the Georgia landscape just outside.

When designer Zoë Feldman first toured her 2022, Atlanta-based Whole Home project, the pitched ceilings became more than an architectural feature. They became her focus. Working to brighten the dated Gothic design scheme, she deployed creamy white paint to coat exposed beams and rolled out bold variegated black-and-white-striped wallpaper to cover the walls, tent the ceilings, and add a wealth of character to the space.

Designers Mark Williams and Niki Papadopoulos don’t believe in compromising good design for great storage solutions. In their 2022 Whole Home bedroom design, the pair swapped traditional nightstands for a customized desk and a custom storage unit to maximize function and storage potential without infringing on the room’s airy, nature-inspired aesthetic.

Los Angeles designer Linda Hayslett of LH. Designs believes every area of the home deserves a purpose, and she brought that ideology to her 2021 Whole Home project in Fredericksburg, Texas. Taking what would traditionally be an unspecified green space, Hayslett peppered the ground with dice, a ring toss set, and a cornhole board to transform this pool deck into an enviable “party plaza.”

For our 2021 Whole Home, Baltimore-based designer Laura Hodges of Laura Hodges Studio designed a dual-purpose workout and office space to ensure that, no matter your schedule, this space has purpose. She took her wellness-minded scheme a step further by embracing biophilic design, tucking pots and plants into every corner and opting for natural finishes to ground the room with earthy energy. The custom desk is the room’s crowning jewel. Engineered by Grothouse, it easily comes apart to function as a set of aerobic steps. Jane Fonda would swoon.

The husband-and-wife team at French & French are no strangers to a bold palette. Their emerald-hued media room, featured in our 2021 Whole Home issue, is proof. Bathed in lush green and covered in patterns, the space is a watering hole for the client’s family, doubling as a guest bedroom for when their grandchildren visit. With its dual purpose in mind, the pair placed a canopied daybed against the window and stashed a hidden trundle underneath it for additional storage space.

For our 2021 Whole Home, Dallas-based designer Jean Liu saw potential in a space that could have served as a traditional breezeway. At the meeting point between the main house, secondary wing, and garage, Liu transformed what could have been “dead space” into a rustic outdoor dining area, complete with motorized retractable screens to keep buzzing bugs out of dishes and hallways.

Soft edges and storied design schemes define the “hangout” zones designed by Noz Nozawa for the 2020 Whole Home Concept House in Denver, Colorado. Drawing on midcentury silhouettes, 1970s trends, and the importance of face-to-face conversation, Nozawa sourced this custom table and chair set.

For our 2020 Whole Home concept house, husband-and-wife team Brett and Kara Phillips designed a 440-square-foot back house lovingly coined “The WeShed.” Complete with vast windows, a shaded patio, and a cozy lounge space, the build was meant to provide an escape from the stresses and humdrum of daily life, just steps away from your actual home.

For our 2023 Whole Home, designer Jenna Gross of Colordrunk Designs combined her love of vibrant palettes with Victorian flair to dream up this circular, four-seater tête-à-tête arrangement. The storied seating concept offers an opportunity for intimate in-house dining.

It’s often said the kitchen is the heart of the home, so for Whole Home 2025 in Austin, Texas, designer Sara Malek Barney of BANDD/DESIGN gave our concept home an island worth gathering around. Taking the shape of a grand piano, the island is topped with quartzite and sits on a reeded base. The piece easily seats six along its gentle curve, which also encourages eye contact.

For Whole Home 2020, Brooklyn-based duo Cristina Casañas-Judd and General Judd practically wove amusement into this bespoke, eccentric home bar design. Channeling a modern take on the classic Old West aesthetic, the pair installed bold electric-blue cabinetry, basket weave wallcoverings, and a surfboard-shaped sound system. A beer tap and in-counter wine chiller round off the slightly kooky design scheme.

In 2019, the Nashville-based trio behind Modern Remains designed a media room for the Whole Home concept house. They selected a dark, neutral palette for the space, with sand, charcoal, and deep greens setting the tone. Grained wood paneling lined the walls and housed seating, while luxe floor-to-ceiling drapery panels flanked windows for optimal movie-viewing conditions.

#455. How to Look Like a Rising Star This Season

With a little help from comedian Matt Friend.

You’ve probably seen Matt Friend on your Instagram feed impersonating a famous person: Donald Trump, Jennifer Coolidge, Rami Malek, King Charles, Andy Cohen, Howard Stern, Stanley Tucci, Jeff Goldblum, Joe Biden, you name it. Really, they’re uncanny. Close your eyes and you’ll swear you’re hearing the real Bill Gates talk about his relationship with Jeffrey Epstein.

Of course, social-media platforms are awash in funny people doing impersonations of famous people. But Friend, 28, has emerged as one of the most popular from this crowded class, with more than 2 million Instagram followers and nearly as many on TikTok. You can chalk it up to pure talent; he’s better than most. But he’s also an equal-opportunity satirist, punching at DJT and Joe Biden with the same ferocity, expanding his appeal exponentially. A couple years ago, he performed at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner—earning a chilly reception from the D. C. elites and headlines for an off-color joke. (“I am killing this dinner harder than Kristi Noem kills the puppies.”) Still, the event was a milestone, proof that Friend had made the difficult leap from online to IRL entertainer. He has since appeared with a mic in hand at the US Open, Milan Fashion Week, the NHL Awards, and the Oscars. Earlier this year, he hosted America Laughs with Matt Friend for CNN. He’s on tour honing material for his first stand-up special in 2027. Pretending to be other people has worked out very well for Friend.

But when it comes to style, he’s his own man. Unlike most of his fellow comedians, Friend dresses up onstage, opting for sharply tailored suits from brands like Brioni and Zegna instead of tees and hoodies. “I was drawn to this period of show business that has disappeared,” he says. “It’s a different world now; people can make content from their house. But I want to bring glamour back.”

He credits old-school comics like Johnny Carson, Don Rickles, and Rich Little with informing his style—both sartorial and comedic. But his choice of attire is also rooted in the kind of work he does. Celebrity impressions demand a careful balance. Play too hard into the character and you run the risk of losing yourself. “I just did the Mark Twain Prize, but I’m not in costume as Donald Trump,” Friend says. “I’m six-foot-whatever me in a double-breasted suit, coming out of my chair launching into my impression. I’m not using props. That helps retain who I am and become my own thing versus the people I’m becoming.”

A native of Chicago, Friend studied at the legendary Second City as a child. He left for Boston after high school—he was declared “Best Dressed” during his senior year, a period during which he was “wearing J. Crew sweaters all the time”—and logged a year at Tufts before transferring to New York University and immersing himself in the N. Y. C. comedy scene. Then the pandemic hit. Isolated at home like the rest of us, with no comedy clubs to visit, Friend started recording himself doing impressions and uploaded them to TikTok, Snapchat, and Instagram.

By 2023, his efforts on social media were reaching critical mass. People were watching, laughing, liking, and sharing. Among them was actor John Stamos—you know, Uncle Jesse from Full House—who took a shine to the young comedian. Friend credits Stamos with providing guidance and mentorship as his career took off.

Throughout it all, Friend has stayed committed to his suited-up style. After all, his audiences pay good money for him to morph his radio-ready voice to sound like presidents and movie stars. And Friend doesn’t exactly play it clean. When you’re dropping more than a few f-bombs during every performance, looking respectable has a tangible effect.

“There’s something I like about the comedian being better dressed than the audience,” he says. “I should be presentable. I shouldn’t be rolling out of bed in a T-shirt.” There’s a sense of rising to the occasion, clothing-wise. That’s true when he’s hosting on the red carpet too. “Being at these big moments requires a great outfit. You don’t show up to an award show in sweatpants.”

There are still new heights for Matt Friend to reach. He’s waiting for a shot at his own starring vehicle, something that’s not just another podcast. Maybe a gig where he sits behind a desk and interviews some of the stars he impersonates? Something that airs after prime time? Friend won’t say for sure, but he has thoughts on the format.

“Everybody wants to reinvent late night, whatever that means,” he says. “I don’t think you need to reinvent. Old-school talent meeting new tools is a winning formula. I’m trying to think what that will look like.”

He knows what it wouldn’t look like: “In a basement with a bong, interviewing a conspiracy theorist, with Cheeto dust on my T-shirt,” he says. “I’m trying to draw from the past, stylistically, and make it modern. I’m not gonna be that clean, but I like the idea of looking really good.”

#456. True Detective Season 5: What We Know So Far

True Detective: Night Country wrapped in February 2024, with Jodie Foster leading the critically acclaimed HBO anthology show. Night Country, which marked the fourth season of True Detective, received 19 Emmy nominations in 2024, including a win for Foster in the Outstanding Lead Actress in a Limited Anthology Series or Movie category, and nominations for co-stars John Hawkes and Kali Reis.

Fans are eager to see where showrunner Issa López will take the story for the next season’s arc—that is, if True Detective is slated to return. Here’s what we know so far.

HBO confirmed in February 2024 that True Detective will continue for another season, and Issa López, who helmed Night Country, will return as showrunner. (She also landed a new multiyear overall deal to create content exclusive to HBO and HBO Max.)

Upon the renewal news, López said in a statement, “From conception to release, Night Country has been the most beautiful collaboration and adventure of my entire creative life. HBO trusted my vision all the way, and the idea of bringing to life a new incarnation of True Detective with Casey, Francesca, and the whole team is a dream come true. I can’t wait to go again.”

In a separate statement, Francesca Orsi, executive vice president, HBO Programming, head of HBO Drama Series and Films, shared: “Issa López is that one-of-a-kind, rare talent that speaks directly to HBO’s creative spirit. She helmed True Detective: Night Country from start to finish, never once faltering from her own commendable vision, and inspiring us with her resilience both on the page and behind the camera. Alongside Jodie and Kali’s impeccable performances, she’s made this installation of the franchise a massive success. We are so lucky to have her as part of our family.”

Every season of True Detective always starts with a new murder, meaning it’s pretty unlikely the anthology series will return to Alaska to visit Danvers (Foster) and Navarro (Reis). Sure enough, in November 2025, during HBO’s 2026 slate presentation in New York City, HBO boss Casey Bloys shared that season 5 will be based in New York. He also shared that López is still working on the scripts.

In an August 2024 interview with The Hollywood Reporter, López suggested the tone of the new season will differ from season 4. “I’m dying for everyone to know because it’s very different and very exciting,” she said. “It’s even darker and even more twisted. I can’t wait to put it out there.” She had previously shared with Variety that she was “in the writing [process]. And it’s a blast. It’s completely different. Different characters, different setting, different story, and I’m enjoying it like crazy.”

In an interview with Deadline on the Emmys red carpet in September 2024, López teased a little bit more about the upcoming season. “Different characters, different placement,” she confirmed, but teased there will be “a lot of connections with Ennis and Night Country.”

On October 10, Nicolas Cage confirmed that he would be starring in season 5 of True Detective while attending New York Comic Con.

Days later, Variety reported on October 16 that Antonio Banderas will also star in the show. “Banderas will star as Rai García while Cage will play the role of Henry Logan,” the outlet shared, noting that additional details are sparse.

#457. Inside Lucille Ball and Desi Arnaz’s Legendary Homes

In honor of the 75th anniversary of I Love Lucy, see the real-life homes of its central couple.

This month marks the 75th anniversary of I Love Lucy: the legendary sitcom that invited America into the marriage, friendships, and homes of Lucy and Ricky Ricardo. The show made household names of its stars and co-producers, Lucille Ball and Desi Arnaz, who were married during its legendary run. But while I Love Lucy’s nonfiction parallels made millions feel part of the couple’s private world, the life and legacy they built off set took a much different shape than the soundstages we love to revisit.

While their fictional counterparts lived on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, and later in a Connecticut suburb, Ball and Arnaz squeezed three California homes—and three distinct design styles—into their 20-year marriage. From the idyllic homestead where they built the foundations of both their family life and production company, to their eventual Beverly Hills property and glamorous vacation home, their real estate investments and tastes evolved with their growing fame.

But glimpses inside each Arnaz-Ball estate also share a comforting air of familiarity. Though so much of I Love Lucy’s charm is in its detachment from reality, there are glimpses of Lucy’s eccentricities and Ricky’s flair in snapshots of the couple’s actual homes.

Ahead, we rounded up photographs showing Lucille Ball and Desi Arnaz’s life at home—plus a bit more color on the spaces they shared.

Before Arnaz and Ball founded their portmanteau production company, Desilu, the name belonged to their home. According to the Library of Congress, they bought a five-acre ranch in Chatsworth, California, in 1941, shortly after their elopement. They remained at Desilu Ranch for a formative 15 years, using it as a rural retreat through the 1950s while I Love Lucy skyrocketed and the couple cemented their television legacy.

The Chatsworth ranch was designed by prolific Los Angeles architect Paul R. Williams, whose other clients included Frank Sinatra, Cary Grant, and more of Hollywood’s elite. Williams’s architectural style ranged vastly (spanning Hollywood Regency to Space Age futurism over the course of his career), but Desilu ranch was a California classic: its exterior featured white clapboard siding and a sweeping wall of windows, looking out onto an oval-shaped backyard swimming pool.

Interior photos capture Ball’s eclectic, feminine influence in loud floral wallpaper and an abundance of frills: “I decorated it in Early Victorian and Bastard American; with cabbage-rose wallpaper, red plush chairs, white ruffled curtains, trailing ivy and beribboned lampshades," she wrote about Desilu ranch in her autobiography, Love, Lucy.

Desilu ranch was the first home of Ball and Arnaz’s two children, Lucie Arnaz and Desi Arnaz Jr. “[Ball] was a working mom, and when she was home, she was very businesslike about running her house,” Lucie Arnaz said in a 2011 interview. She noted that Ball’s onscreen Lucy was much more “outrageous” and humor-ruled than her actual mother was at home, but she savored the weekends and summers she could slip into the role of homemaker—presiding over dinners, homework, and garage cleaning projects.

The Chatsworth ranch had all the makings of a rural fantasy, with vegetable gardens, avocado and orange trees, a cow (reportedly nicknamed “The Duchess of Devonshire”), dogs, and chickens raised on the property.

Desilu also reportedly saw Hollywood parties, magazine photoshoots, marital fights and reconciliations, and even a Red Scare press conference. But the couple’s scrapbook photos from the ranch capture the same lived-in warmth they conjured on set for millions of viewers.

In 1954., Ball and Arnaz commissioned Paul R. Williams to build a new property for them: a Rancho Mirage retreat. The home, situated on the golf course of the Thunderbird Country Club in Palm Springs, was an example of Williams’s explorations in desert modernism.

A complete departure from the lush landscape and sitcom-worthy interiors of Desilu, the Thunderbird ranch’s open plan and window walls placed its modernist interior in conversation with the sweeping desert and mountain views outside.

Photos of the home from the Getty Research Institute document exposed stone walls, dark wood accents, a party-primed lanai patio space, and a swanky swimming pool. Here, it seems that Ball traded doilies and dusters for sculptural and spare decor elements, while Arnaz was reportedly so involved in the architectural planning that he claimed collaborative design credit with Williams.

The couple used the Palm Springs property as a retreat for five years during the height of their fame, and sold it when they divorced in 1960.

After selling Desilu ranch to former child actor Jane Withers, Ball and Arnaz took primary residence at 1000 North Roxbury Drive in Beverly Hills. The 7-bedroom home was bought by the couple in 1954 for $85,000; today, its estimated value is over $10 million.

According to a Beverly Hills Cultural Heritage Commission Report, the home was built in 1936 by Carleton Burgess in classic Colonial Revival style. Arnaz and Ball lived with their children in the home until their 1960 divorce.

While there are fewer intimate glimpses of Arnaz and Ball’s interior life (both literally and in design terms) at the Roxbury house, the property featured prominently in their public image. The home appeared on a beloved episode of I Love Lucy, centering actor Richard Widmark. According to the Cultural Heritage Commission, Ball’s famous neighbors also recall her handing out Halloween candy from the front door while dressed as a witch. Ball maintained ownership of the Roxbury estate through her second marriage to Gary Morton and until her death in 1989.

Grace McCarty is a freelance Associate Digital Editor at ELLE Decor, where she covers design trends, shopping, and culture. She previously held a staff position at SELF Magazine, where she focused on beauty, style, and wellness. Her work has also appeared in Glamour and Parade.

#458. The 10 Best Workout Tops for Women of 2026, Tested by Experts and Editors

Our fave option on this list is from Beyond Yoga.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I’ve spent years logging miles, reps, and classes in all types of activewear, which means I’ve tested more workout tops than I can count. From Pilates to outdoor runs to heavy lifting sessions, I know exactly what separates a top you forget you’re wearing from one you can’t wait to peel off. For me, the best workout tops for women nail comfort, offer just enough support, and look flattering.

The last thing you want is an overly tight top that clips your movement (especially during yoga!), but it should still provide enough compression to hold you and the girls in, says Rebecca Stewart, CPT, a trainer and mobility coach. While you could make do with a regular cotton t-shirt during your workout sesh, it won't offer the same level of support, mobility, or sweat-wicking capabilities.

But, finding the right workout top all comes down to personal preference. Because there are so many options to choose from—think T-shirts, tanks, and long-sleeve tops—we asked experts and tested tons of options ourselves to find styles we think will fit a wide range of needs and preferences. From lightweight, flowy options to compression shirts great for high-intensity workouts, we’ve highlighted our absolute favorite workout tops below.

Over the last few months, I’ve tested a handful of workout tops, and the Beyond Yoga Spacedye Slim Racerback Cropped Tank topped my list for a few reasons: it’s super comfortable (it won a spot for the softest bra in our Best Racerback Bras story!), has a built-in shelf bra, is size inclusive, and comes in a ton of vibrant and neutral shades.

It's basically the two-in-one bra and workout tank combo you didn’t know you needed. Made from the brand’s signature polyester and elastane blend, it’s the comfiest and most lightweight option I’ve ever worn. It feels like you're wearing nothing at all, but it still keeps the girls in place with a medium-level compression that’s perfect for light to moderate workouts. The cherry on top? It’s moisture-wicking, so it keeps you dry whether you’re working out or just running around on a hot day.

Our only gripe: If you have a bigger chest, you’ll probably want to layer a sports bra underneath for extra support. But if you're part of the itty bitty titty committee, you're good to go wearing this solo pretty much anywhere.

Read More: Beyond Yoga Spacedye Slim Racerback Tank Review

ICYMI, Amazon Essentials Activewear is where it’s at for affordable workout basics that rival the quality of some of the more luxe brands we’ve tried. The cotton, modal, and elastane blend feels thick, substantial, and smooth to the touch. It’s the kind of material that holds up well throughout repeated workouts and wash cycles, so you can keep this workout tee in constant rotation.

We also love the subtle crop length that isn’t too short or too long. It gives you room to move without showing too much skin, and has a semi-relaxed fit that perfectly skims the body. It’s extremely soft, but thanks to the touch of elastane in the fabric, it has ample stretch so you don’t feel constricted during overhead lifts or higher-impact workouts like running or HIIT.

The only con is that the white color can be slightly see-through. We suggest opting for a darker shade or wearing a flesh-toned bra underneath. The color options are also a little limited, but we love the slate grey and light blue options.

WH editors have tried a lot of workout tops over the years and agree that the Lululemon Ebb to Street Tank is a reliable favorite. It’s super soft, seamless, sweat-wicking, and ultra stretchy thanks to a comfortable blend of elastane and nylon. Plus, it offers just the right amount of support and coverage for low-impact workouts like Pilates, yoga, and walking.

The most convenient part: it has a built-in shelf bra, so you don’t have to wear a separate bra underneath (unless you want to for more support!). And, we found that it actually does keep us feeling covered and protected during low-impact exercise, which we didn’t find to be the case with other tanks that have built-in bras. Another pro? The longer length of this top (it hits at the hip) keeps us feeling locked in and covered during workouts where we don’t want a ton of stomach showing.

“I love how versatile this top is, along with its longer length and the buttery-soft blend of nylon and elastane,” says trainer Kristina Earnest, CPT, founder of Kristina Earnest On Demand. This is her go-to top when she's working out at home, and she wears it under a sweater for her cold weather errands. It feels incredibly comfortable thanks to its seamless racerback design—no pesky straps, seams, or tightness to get in the way during your sweat session. However, you should note that because there are no adjustable straps, you can't customize the fit of this tank.We put this tank to the test during a variety of workouts, like HIIT training and running, and found that it’s not the best choice for high-intensity training. We noticed that it didn’t do a great job of holding the breasts in place during high-impact moves and felt the need for more padding and compression. But based on our extensive testing, it's difficult to find a tank with high-impact support. That's why we recommend pairing this with our favorite high-impact sports bra, the Under Armour Infinity 2.0 High Sports Bra.

This tank is meant to be worn over your favorite sports bra as an added layer of coverage. The loose, cropped fit is easy to throw on, and the round neck with the knotted side detail adds a touch of style. Our fave part about this tank? The cotton material is super breathable, so you never feel overheated or constricted like you would with a tighter top.

“I love that this top isn’t too tight,” says Jacqueline Kasen, CPT, trainer and senior director of group fitness at Anatomy. “It’s super comfortable and loose whether you’re running or lifting, but it still stays in place without bunching up.” Plus, it holds its shape after multiple washes and never pills or frays, making it as durable as it is functional.

The tank is made with cotton, but it also has a bit of spandex woven throughout, which makes it stretchy and not too sturdy. This is essential during workouts, as you want your top to move with you instead of against you at the gym.

We noticed that the shirt can look a bit boxy if you go too oversized, so we recommend sizing down for a more flattering, snug fit.

This short-sleeve workout top from Under Armour is a game-changer for high-intensity exercise since it offers both compression and cooling technology. It’s designed as a baselayer to keep you protected under your sports gear (by preventing pinching and chafing), but we love to wear it on its own as a temperature-regulating, sweat-wicking, ultra-lightweight workout top.

This t-shirt has an ultra-tight, compressive fit (which can help with circulation and muscular endurance), but it is super thin and made with the brand's HeatGear fabric to keep you from overheating. It’s made from polyester for a smooth, lightweight feel, plus elastane for a generous amount of stretch. We love that this top is breathable and moisture-wicking, so even though it’s on the tighter side, it doesn’t feel like you’re wearing anything. Whether you’re lifting heavy or doing sprints outdoors, this top is perfect for keeping you cool, dry, and comfortable.

However, this top (like most compressive gear) might not be the best option for lower-impact exercise or workouts that require lots of stretching and bending—like yoga or Pilates. We generally opt for looser, softer fits for these workouts and stick to tighter tops for strength training and cardio.

Listen, I love a cute lil workout set as much as the next Pilates princess, but sometimes I don’t want to bare my entire midriff. That’s where an oversized workout top like this one comes in clutch. I especially love it in white because it's just a touch see-through, so it lets me show off my matching sports bra and workout short combo without feeling exposed. It’s also perfect for those days when I feel a little bloated and just need something loose-fitting that won’t emphasize my stomach.

Unlike the other workout tops you’ll find here, this tee is made from 100% cotton. The natural fiber is not exactly known for its high-performance abilities at the gym (it doesn’t wick sweat very well), but the thinner construction and super boxy fit help keep things super airy. I wore it for an outdoor workout a few weeks ago (yes, in August!) and felt cool and comfortable—well, as much as you can while doing burpees.

It’s also just a really cute shape. I love the sleeves, which, despite being a t-shirt, hit at about the elbow, giving it a really laidback feel. I love it for working out or for throwing on over my skin-tight sets to and from Pilates, but I also find myself grabbing it day-to-day for errands and casual outings. I frequently throw it on over a bright tank styled with some longline biker shorts and comfy sneaks for a cool-girl fit that basically feels like I’m wearing pajamas.

As with any oversized workout tee, it might not be the wisest choice for HIIT workouts or anything super tactical. The billowing sleeves and loose fit could get caught on equipment or flop over your face while bending or jumping.

An open-back top is not only a super stylish choice, but it helps keep you cool as a cucumber during sweaty workouts. I especially love this top for hot Pilates when I want as little fabric against my skin as possible. And since it has built-in padding (that doesn’t shift around in the wash!) I can literally just wear this on its own to yoga, Pilates, strength training, or other low-impact workouts.

I have worn this during my more intense exercise like an Orangetheory class or while running, and it offers enough support for me as someone who teeters between a C cup and a D cup. But if you have a larger chest size, it might be best to reserve this top for low-impact movement or layer it over your favorite sports bra.

Nike’s Dri-FIT tech (a blend of nylon and spandex) is also a major pro. It feels sleek and smooth against the skin but also helps move sweat away from the body. When I leave an intense workout class (even a heated one), it’s noticeable how much less sweat I have sitting between my skin and my workout top when I reach for this one, which is huge for me, since I’ve been struggling with eczema that gets worse with heat and sweat.

The material is also suuuper stretchy and comfortable, and never gets in the way of any kind of movement, whether that’s mat Pilates or an intense upper-body session at the gym. It’s also really lightweight so it feels nearly like a second skin, and never requires adjustments mid-workout.

This tank from Gymshark pairs perfectly with the brand’s bestselling leggings. Like the leggings, this tank is nearly seamless—the only seams are along the bottom hem, but they are super flat and don’t cause any rubbing or chafing when up against the skin.

I love that the stretchy, smooth fabric (made of 96% nylon and 4% elastane) is basically sweat-proof and dries super quickly. That’s because nylon is a synthetic fabric that’s hydrophobic (i.e it resists the penetration of water), so this top is great for wicking moisture away from the body during intense workouts.

Not only that, but it’s super cute, too. I love the square neckline and the length that hits right at the hip bones. It also has a built-in shelf bra to help support and lift the girls for a more flattering shape and a little extra protection against bounce during your workouts. It might not be enough support for larger chest sizes during high-intensity movement, but for smaller chests and moderate activity, it does the trick.

We’ve all been in those super stuffy gyms—when I start overheating during a workout, all I want is to be in a sports bra. But I’m not always comfortable showing my stomach. That’s where the Wild Thing Bra comes in. With its long-line fit, which ends just above my belly button for slightly more coverage than a standard sports bra, while still feeling cool and comfortable at the gym.

And, of course, it’s super cute, thanks to the ruching in the center of the bra. I find this detail really flattering—it gives my stomach a snatched look when I wear it. While it doesn’t offer a ton of support since it’s on the lighter side, it provides decent compression for my higher intensity workouts. Its lightweight design and stylish details make it perfect for pairing with leggings at the gym, but I’ve also seen it styled with trousers or jeans for a sporty yet upscale vibe.

If you’re worried about the lighter colors looking sheer? Don’t be! All styles come with removable cups to cover your girls, which is also helpful because you can take them out when you wash the bra. Speaking of washing, we find that this bra holds up well after multiple washes and never pills or changes in elasticity and shape.

One thing to keep in mind is that the straps aren’t adjustable, which can be a bit frustrating since it means you can’t customize the fit. I also wish it came in more colors.

This tank won the top spot in our Best Workout Tank Tops story for a few reasons: It's super flattering, never rides up, is compressive, supportive, and sweat-wicking.

We tested this ribbed tank across many different workouts—running, yoga, lifting, and HIIT—and we found that it never moves or rides up. And, we love that it’s a tighter spandex tank with high compression, as it holds us in all the right places and doesn’t allow for any boob bounce. It doesn’t have a built-in bra, but it’s tight enough to hold the chest in place.

It's also super moisture-wicking. WH fashion assistant Rose Lauture wore this during an intense workout and said there were no sweat stains, no matter which color she wore, thanks to the soft nylon. Because it's moisture-wicking, it also does a great job at preventing body odor.

This option offers some pretty solid support for not having a built-in bra (it's all about the compression!). However, it is made for medium support, so we like to wear an extra bra underneath this tank from time to time when our workouts get extra intense.

Stewart’s pro tip? For high-impact or high-intensity workouts, look for materials that are shiny and smooth to reduce chafing and wick sweat. For lower-intensity workouts, look for matte fabrics that have a soft, buttery texture for comfort and flexibility.

Should your workout top be loose or tight? While it does come down to personal preference, there are pros and cons to each. Tighter tops don’t get in the way of movement as much as a looser top might: they often feel more secure and supportive. But if you find looser tops more comfortable, they can certainly work for nearly every workout except for those involving a Pilates reformer (where loose fabric can easily get caught) or other equipment like cable machines.

Some workout tops have built-in shelf bras or bra pad inserts, but this can be a “love it or hate it” situation, says Stewart. For bigger busts or high-intensity activities, a built-in bra may not provide enough support, so you might need an extra sports bra underneath. However, for smaller busts, we find that they provide ample support for light and medium intensity workouts. “A built-in bra should feel supportive and not bothersome and shouldn’t be too tight or digging in to restrict your movement,” says Stewart.

There are tons of workout tops out there, so even finding the absolute best options to test was difficult. When I began the August 2026 update of this article, I revisited our original February 2024 story to see which of the picks our team is still wearing. Some of them are still team favorites, but I went back to the drawing board and asked fitness experts and stylists, including style contributors Kristen Saladino, Rose Lauture, and Lily Wohlner, which workout tops they were loving. From there, I removed the picks that we are no longer wearing and added the options we’ve been reaching for the most.

I made sure that the final picks on this list were options that we wear across all sorts of activities, from compressive options perfect for HIIT workout classes to lightweight, flowy tops we like for lounging or lower-impact exercise. Some of the contenders on this list come in tons of different colors and styles, have built-in bras, and are made with the highest-quality materials for their price points

If luxury is what you desire in your bathrobe, Cozy Earth takes the crown for its dual-sided design. The outer waffle-weave exterior gives it a textured finish, while the ribbed terry interior adds a cushioned feel against the skin. The brand uses a blend of cotton and viscose from bamboo that feels light but also warm on chilly mornings when you’re just getting out of bed. The roomy cut is another plus: I could sprawl out on the bed and move around comfortably with no problem.

After washing it before first use, I noticed that the fabric felt even loftier. At $139, you’re paying for more than a basic robe: The two fabric textures help dry you off, while the roomy fit accommodates pajamas. Because the robe runs a little large, consider sizing down if you prefer a closer fit.

The striped broadcloth design of Brooks Brothers’ robe gives it a stylish twist compared to my typical robe. I love this lightweight option because it feels like one of my most comfortable dress shirts, just in robe form. I wouldn’t reach for it when stepping out of the shower, since the cotton broadcloth isn’t designed for drying off like a traditional terry robe. Instead, it’s better suited for draping over pajamas or wearing for show when your close family is visiting. I can even walk my dog or grab the mail without feeling like I’m wearing a towel around your shoulders.

The pockets are deep enough to stash a snack or three in there, and there’s even a chest pocket; a detail you don’t see on most robes. Despite its thinner construction, the robe has neatly finished stitching on the collar and cuffs that helps maintain its crisp shape and structure. It’s cut more tailored than relaxed in the body and sleeves, but I can still move naturally without any tugging in those areas.

You don’t have to shell out a fortune to own a robe that feels at home in a high-end hotel. Quince’s offering is a great option for guys who want a lightweight robe that won’t feel bulky after a shower or at the end of a long workday. This one is made from organic Turkish cotton, which features a waffle-style honeycomb texture that feels airy compared to the thicker terry robes I’ve tested. At 240 GSM (grams per square meter), it’s considerably lighter than Brooklinen’s and Hommey’s offerings, meaning it’s a solid choice if you prioritize breathability over warmth.

The design features a kimono collar and self-tie sash, but what stands out to me is the longer cut. Unlike Onsen’s hooded option and other robes that stop around the knee, this one falls between mid-calf and ankle length on my 5'8" frame. I tested my usual size small, and after four washes, the robe remained soft and kept its shape. Just be mindful of what you wash it with: The honeycomb weave has loops that can snag on zippers, Velcro, hooks, or other sharp hardware, so wash it with similar items to help protect the fabric.

NY Threads’ robe reminds me more of a classic dressing gown than the thick, towel-like robes you typically reach for after a shower. It’s made from a cotton-polyester blend that hits a nice middle ground: It isn’t so heavy that I feel bundled up, but it has enough substance to feel like I’m actually wearing a robe. I like the V-shaped collar and piping along the collar, pockets, and cuffs, which give it a stylish feel. The calf-length cut offers good coverage, whether I’m throwing it on over pajamas, or wearing it while hanging by the pool. I’d recommend washing it before the first wear to soften the fabric. What I like most is that I don’t have to save it for one particular part of my routine. It works whether I’m getting ready for work or preparing for bed.

Some robes feel like towels; this one feels like a teddy bear. Lands’ End’s fleece robe has that fuzzy texture that makes you want to stay wrapped up a little longer, especially when the temps dip. I’d reach for it on slow weekend mornings, after a long day when I’m ready to switch off, or anytime my apartment feels a little too chilly. Unlike a traditional terry robe, which is built with drying off in mind, this one is all about that warm, snuggly feeling. If you want a robe that feels more like your favorite cozy blanket than something you’d grab straight out of the shower, this is a strong contender.

If you prefer a robe with extra room to move and plenty of fabric to wrap yourself in, Hommey’s oversized style is worth a look. Known for Its bold stripes and rich colorways, the lifestyle and bedding brand brings a distinctive look to this espresso pinstripe robe. At 450 GSM (grams per square meter), it has a weightier feel than lightweight styles, making stepping out of the shower a little more indulgent. When I crack the window to let some cool air into my room, I love wrapping myself in what feels like a giant, ultra-plush towel.

Despite its heavier construction, I found that it dried relatively quickly rather than staying damp. The fit is deliberately oversized, with roomy sleeves and plenty of space through the body. If you prefer a robe that feels more like a cozy wrap than a fitted layer, this one delivers. The belt lets you cinch the waist when you want a more secure fit. If you like taking your time getting ready or winding down at home, this robe makes routines feel a little more luxurious. Bonus: its bold pinstripe design also makes it a thoughtful holiday gift for someone who appreciates stylish home essentials.

If you’re looking for a robe that doubles as a bath towel and a hoodie, consider this waffle style from Onsen. It's made with Supima cotton and features a unique honeycomb weave that absorbs moisture like a sponge. If you have dense, curly hair that stays wet longer, the hood is a useful feature to have for quicker, drier hair after stepping out of the shower or pool. It also helps lock in body heat for those who live in cold climates and drafty homes during freezing winter mornings or nights. Most of the robes I’ve tested feel hefty and thick, but this one is much lighter and less bulky. It has an oversized fit, which layers comfortably over pajamas or other loungewear without feeling too tight. Plus, guys with bigger builds get extra room through the shoulders, chest, and body.

I’m 5’8” and on the leaner side, so the robe fits quite generously on my frame, even in its small size. It’s one of the more expensive robes, but at this price, you’re getting premium fabric along with a hood that adds versatility beyond your typical bathrobe. After three washes, I found that it maintained its shape, too. Just be mindful of what you wash it with: The lighter honeycomb weave can be vulnerable to snagging, so avoid washing it alongside garments with zippers, hooks, or other hardware that could catch on the fabric.

L.L. Bean is widely known for its flannel shirts, and the brand channels that same rugged, cozy aesthetic in its Scotch plaid robe. This one is right up the alley for guys who appreciate a classic lumberjack look. Made from Portuguese cotton flannel, this robe is softer and more durable than standard cotton flannel, with a brushed finish on both sides for extra loft and comfort. Unlike Turkish cotton robes, which can feel dense and plush, this one strikes a middle ground: heavier than the Brooks Brothers cotton broadcloth robe, but lighter than the plush 450 GSM Parachute option.

Flannel robes can sometimes feel overly warm, but this one avoids that suffocating feeling—think log cabin by the fireplace while sipping hot chocolate. It keeps you cozy and warm, but it’s not designed for drying off after a shower. You’ll likely want to stick to light layers underneath. Each robe is brushed eight times on each side to create a pillowy, fluffy texture. Plus, you can choose from six colorways that all feel just as comfortable. During testing, it stayed soft after multiple washes and didn’t cling to any jewelry like the waffle robe.

Your bathrobe has to feel comfortable against your bare skin post-shower. That said, we suggest looking for fabrics that are soft, breathable, and absorbent. Typically, cotton is the popular go-to. Three types of cotton used in premium bathrobes are Supima, Turkish, and Egyptian cotton.

It's an American-grown cotton that will give you a luxurious feel. As for stitching, high-quality pieces use tighter, more consistent seams, reinforced edges, and clean finishes—details that keep fabric from fraying or splitting over time. These construction cues are what separate a premium robe from one that starts falling apart after a few washes. And while it's machine-washable, be sure to follow the care instructions to maintain its softness and longevity.

The luxurious and ultra-soft type that’s great for robes, sheets, and bedding when you want that high-end, hotel feel. The stitching is often on point because it's a higher-end material, so it'll last through regular washes. The softness is amazing, and tends to hold its shape better than regular cotton. Like Supima, you want to keep it on a gentle cycle to protect its integrity and softness.

Turkish cotton is a close runner-up to Egyptian cotton in terms of quality. It's soft, absorbent, and surprisingly durable, especially after a few washes. It has this unique ability to get even softer over time, which is a huge win for bathrobes. The stitching tends to be strong, but as always, check the quality of the construction (some cheaper options can skimp on that). Turkish cotton is also machine washable, but, just like the other types, make sure you don't crank up the heat in the washer or dryer so it stays soft and durable.

A bathrobe should allow for easy movement, whether you’re lounging around, reaching for something, or walking around the house. Look for robes with a relaxed or loose fit that doesn’t constrict your shoulders or arms. Or any of the aforementioned actions above. Some styles feature drop shoulders or kimono cuts, which can enhance mobility and comfort.

A bathrobe belt is crucial for keeping your robe where it belongs. There's nothing worse than wrapping yourself in a robe and constantly adjusting it throughout the day. A good belt cinches the robe securely around your waist, so you don't have to worry about it slipping off when you have nothing underneath or moving around the house.

For guys who want a little extra warmth or dry their hair quicker, a hood is the perfect solution. Also, it's great for keeping the chill off your neck when you're getting out of the shower.

Pockets in a bathrobe are more than just a convenient spot for your hands. They're perfect for holding essentials like your phone, TV remote, or even a snack while binge-watching Netflix.

When it comes to sleeve length, it's all about personal preference and comfort. Full-length sleeves are great for cozying up and keeping warm, but if you prefer a bit of airiness or don't want sleeves dragging in your food or drink, a three-quarter sleeve or shorter option might be the way to go. The right sleeve length helps with movement while you're relaxing, cooking, or scrolling through your phone.
