When we revisited this guide two years ago, we retested our original picks to make sure they still held up. Many of them continue to earn their place in our rotation. #461. 30 Gorgeous Coffee Table Books That Double as Conversation Starters

Every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Pretty enough to display and interesting enough to actually read.

A well-styled coffee table can pull a living room together in an instant. There are a few essential accessories: a box to hold your remote controls, a tray to organize everything, and a great coffee table book. The best ones come with beautifully designed covers that inspire you to learn something new, and after thumbing through a few pages, maybe even travel or redecorate. It’s a go-to conversation starter to break awkward silences, and selecting the right one for your home is a careful art.

When curating your coffee table book collection, make sure you choose ones that show off your special interests or knowledge about a topic. It's a seamless way guests can learn about you, and having thoughtful reads (versus books you don't actually care about) makes your space feel more personalized. We’re here to provide some not-so-generic ideas of what to buy.

Of course, at House Beautiful, at the top of our must-have list are books about interior design and architecture. Below, you’ll find reads on how to confidently tackle biophilic design and tablescaping tips from celebrity designers like Shea McGee. You can even learn how to get the Nancy Meyers look through renovation stories from Meyers’s daughter!

They don’t have to be design-focused, though. A cookbook or cocktail guide with striking photography stands well on its own. Or opt for travel books that inspire wanderlust. These books can also accessorize your spot, whether you rest one on top of a media console, a vintage coffee table, or on a side table between two comfy accent chairs. To start curating your coffee table book collection, shop our top recommendations ahead. We found a good mix of selections that will keep both you and your guests occupied any day.

You’ve heard it a million times over: there’s a push for a “collected, lived-in” look right now. Consider this coffee table book your instruction manual. It celebrates every trinket collector and gallery wall lover.

Blessed Little Bungalow designer Amber Guyton’s book celebrates maximalism that’s rooted in history and culture. Find your way towards bold interiors that still tell a story in these colorful pages.

This interior design book centers on the taste and collections you already have, rather than trying to convince you of something new. It’s a great conversation point for guests, featuring guiding questions like: “What do you already love?” “What’s the one thing you really don’t like?” “What do you already have?”

Who says coffee table design books have to focus on interiors? Try a celebration of the spaces outside your front door with this book. It’s packed with inspiration and tips to create your dream patio.

The genius organizing duo behind The Home Edit shares their professional tips in this book. It’s like a Pinterest board come to life, with practical advice for the entryway, garage, and other clutter magnets in the home.

Mercury Stardust is an expert in all things home renovation and repair. Her latest book is the ideal housewarming pick for a first-time homeowner. It gives easy-to-digest advice on all the hurdles you’ll hit, featuring her own success stories. (And her first book, Safe and Sound, is a must-read for any renters.)

If you’ve ever looked at a movie set and thought “that’s my dream home,” this is the coffee table book for you. It combines strategic architectural planning with pop culture references, from a designer who knows how to make “1970s Sofia Coppola in Palm Beach” come to life.

Joel Holland’s city illustrations are a love letter to the stories behind brick-and-mortar institutions. Start with the ones in the Big Apple, from the 18 miles of books at The Strand to Katz’s Deli to When Harry Met Sally fame. Don’t forget to check out his Paris and London books, too.

Anita Yokota, the home therapist, penned this book for anyone who’s ever been confused by the phrase “biophilic design.” It breaks down exactly how to get that nature-inspired feel in your home, beyond buying houseplants.

Few designers have mastered a youthful take on traditional interiors like Corey Damen Jenkins. His second book walks you through ten stunning projects, but the book itself is a work of art. Hiding underneath the jacket are a peacock-feathered cover and gilded page edges.

Babs, the internet’s favorite Grandma, reveals all of her homemaking secrets in this book. It’s all the home hacks your grandma never gave you, from getting stubborn stains out to effortless hosting.

Give your home that subtle aprés-ski look with this book. It features rich ranch design that would be welcomed in a Yellowstone episode. Take the lodge aesthetic well beyond knotty pine cabins.

Shea McGee’s tablescaping tips have already won over House Beautiful editors, and this is a treasure trove of them. Your next dinner party can look 10 times more fabulous with the recipes and design advice waiting inside.

Plant stylist Hilton Carter knows all about melding a houseplant haven with a home that you love. Learn new ways to display houseplants that you never even considered, all through his own Baltimore sanctuary.

This isn’t your everyday cocktail recipe book. It’s a home mixology guide from the pro bartenders behind Death & Co., so you can bring their speakeasy craft cocktails to your own happy hour. Plus, the black debossing makes it a subtle pick for the most minimalist decorators.

Take your design inspiration global with this celebration of Black architecture and heritage. Across the diaspora, from the West Indies to the United Kingdom, peek inside notable homes and the histories their walls hold.

Who better to provide a Nancy Meyers-style guide than her daughter? Annie Meyers-Slayer peels back the curtain on her own renovation story, drawing inspiration from her mother’s iconic set aesthetic. It combines California ease with English sophistication, just like The Holiday came to life.

Who says surf style has to stay on the coast? In this book, California-based interior designer Raili Clasen provides a guide to bringing the beach house aesthetic to your home, no matter where you're located. Flip through photos of colorful, striped, and checkerboard designs to get all the inspo you need for a laid-back home.

For little touches to add to your home that don't feel pretentious, flip through this for inspiration. HGTV's Lauren Liess shares an approachable decorating style full of simplicity. You can even just leave the book out as a reminder to give your abode that TLC when needed.

Joanna Gaines packed her eye for design and expert tips into a coffee table book that is sure to inspire. If you're a newbie to interior design, she walks you through the beginner steps, explaining the difference between farmhouse and modern decor and just what an entryway needs.

#462. Scallion Pancake Quesadillas

Scallion pancakes are always the highlight of a dim sum spread for me. Their golden-brown, crunchy deliciousness is irresistible, but have you ever tried them with a bit of melted cheese (which, let's be honest, makes everything better)? With added gooey cheese and sautéed mushrooms, this already-amazing dish becomes even better as a quesadilla. We promise it’ll become your new appetizer (or late-night snack) obsession.

How to make them:The dough is a simple mix of flour, boiling water, and salt, kneaded by hand and layered with freshly sliced scallions and a sesame oil-flour paste that gives the pancake its signature flaky layers. Once the pancakes are fried to golden-brown perfection, they’re transformed into quesadillas, stuffed with melty mozzarella and umami-packed spiced mushrooms, and paired with a tangy soy-scallion dipping sauce.

Recipe Tip:Using hot water helps make the dough more pliable and easier to roll super-thin, which is key to getting those signature flaky layers.

Make ahead:Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4 days. To reheat, use a skillet on medium heat until the cheese is warm, or place the dish in an air fryer for similar results.

Did you try making these? Let us know how it went in the comments!

#463. Whalefall Is One of the Scariest Movies of the Year

It’s also profoundly sad and beautiful. But damn, isn’t nature terrifying?

Let us agree up top that scary doesn’t always mean spooky. While 2026 has been an unusually strong year for horror cinema, all it takes is a fucked-up situation, and little hope of getting out of it, for fear to bubble to the surface. Twice this year a popular engagement account on X asked, “What is the scariest scene in a non horror movie?” People named the velociraptors in Jurassic Park, the tunnel ride in Willy Wonka, the basement scene in Zodiac. Horror isn’t just possessed girlfriends and eerie shopping malls.

So it stands to reason why, while watching Whalefall, in theaters October 16, I spent all of its 106 minutes squirming in my seat, gripping the armrests as I filled with dread over what midnight-zone monstrosity might show up. I felt everything you should feel from a horror movie, and it’s damning that no actual horror movie from this year has done the same for me. Directed by Brian Duffield and cowritten by Daniel Kraus (adapting his 2023 novel), Whalefall is best known by how it’s been described by your friends: “The One Where a Guy Gets Eaten by a Whale.”

Austin Abrams—starring in his second film in which he endures a profoundly shitty day—stars as Jay, a college student reeling from the death of his deep-sea-diver father (a sun-kissed, dad-bodded Josh Brolin), whose hippie politics came bundled with abrasive child-rearing and a drunken stupor. Jay dives alone, his first mistake, to find any trace of his dad left in order to exorcise the ghosts of their strained relationship. So when a big-ass sperm whale shows up and swallows him whole, it’s a problem. And it thrusts Jay into a harrowing 45-minute (the approximate amount of oxygen in his tank) fight for his life, punctuated by hazy memories of how things fell apart. Think of it as the climax to Pinocchio, stretched out to resemble 127 Hours. That’s Whalefall.

Duffield’s lean and mean undersea thriller is anchored by the complicated grief between an estranged father and son, and it hits those beats effectively, even if it also stretches to the point of incredulity. (No spoilers, but if I told you the whale is a metaphor...) But the real appeal of Whalefall is everything inside the belly of the proverbial beast and watching in real time how the hell this landlubber can make it out alive. That’s what anyone shelling out for tickets and popcorn wants to see, and Whalefall delivers on all the gruesome spectacle of man faced with the depths of nature’s madness.

I can ramble about the movie’s many strong suits—Abrams, mostly—but the most remarkable is the film’s claustrophobic natural horror. Whatever you assume could happen to a guy caught inside a sperm whale’s fundic chamber, Whalefall reminds you in unambiguous terms that it’s so much worse. The air is toxic, there are pools of stomach acid, and there is a 42-foot-long giant squid stuffed inside the same cramped space, whose sole function is to break down organic matter into nutrients. While “body horror” as it’s traditionally understood is concerned with the horrors of physical transformation on the outside, Whalefall—whatever horror you want to call it—is rooted in the terror of what’s inside. It’s neither Cronenberg-esque nor Giger-esque; instead it’s its own thing that will give you pause during your next sushi dinner.

Throughout Whalefall I remembered Underwater, the overlooked Kristen Stewart vehicle from 2020 about scientists whose aquatic facility gets wrecked by monsters. It’s a remarkable creature feature, masterfully marrying ocean-disaster spectacle with horror’s suspense and rhythms. So imagine my delight when I learned that Underwater’s Brian Duffield was its writer. Whalefall is Duffield building upon language shaped by his past pictures in the genre, including 2023’s No One Will Save You and the 2020 teen rom-com horror Spontaneous. Whalefall may not be conventionally scary. There isn’t a single jump scare, and I’ll reiterate that it’s a sadder father-son story than one might expect going in. But watching Austin Abrams crawling in the pitch-black darkness of a whale’s throat and helplessly crying to a boat that can’t hear or see him is terrifying all the same.

I want to be clear that I liked a lot of this year’s horror movies. Backrooms and Obsession were showcases for new talent, while overlooked releases like Hokum, Undertone, and Onslaught brought plenty to the table. And only Sam Raimi could make a movie in which Rachel McAdams looks me in the eye and it’s unnerving. But no horror movie from this year chilled me to the bone and made me wish it was over—not out of distaste or boredom but because I was so enthralled to the point of discomfort—like Whalefall.

In 1975, Jaws promised a movie so scary you’ll “never go in the water again.” Whalefall posits that when you’re swallowed, the horror doesn’t stop.

#464. These Fall 2026 Jacket Trends Make a Case for Going Bold

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Just as the heat of summer distills our wardrobes down to a dress and a dress and a dress (or maybe a skirt!), fall’s brisk bite calls us to thoughtfully layer—puzzling together the pieces of our wardrobe into a cohesive outfit. For some, the most important layer of all is the final one: the jacket.

Creating a perfectly edited outfit, where each piece can stand on its own, takes a practiced eye for style that simply comes with time and practice. However, one can easily create the illusion of the time invested with a good jacket, as it can easily be the centerpiece around which you build the rest of your ensemble—and the specific styles trending for fall 2026 certainly make a statement. On the runways and at our favorite retailers, we’ve seen embellishments and head-turning silhouettes everywhere. Whether it’s in the form of tassel and fringe bags, funky jewelry, or tailored outerwear, the more dramatic or eclectic, the better for this season—and the jackets are no exception.

Military jackets first trickled back into the trend reports this past spring, with the tailored silhouette making appearances on the runways for Alexander McQueen, Balmain, and Ralph Lauren. The style’s only picking up steam, with more recent looks from Dior and Khaite demonstrating a shift into the ornately bohemian realm of Napoleonic military jackets. Now, the jacket’s a canvas for flourishes of detail like braided cords, sharp stand collars, embroidered detailing, and gold buttons.

Every piece in Ralph Lauren’s spring/summer 2027 collection was a study in undone elegance, none more so than the muted teal-blue embroidered velvet duster that floated down the runway and proved that the billowing overcoat is here to stay. This season, the dramatic style invites bohemian and vaguely Victorian touches. While the long length of a duster technically bridges into coat territory, the lightweight nature of a duster gives it a lighter sensibility that makes it a jacket in spirit.

Also known as frog closures, these braided decorative buttons have been slowly appearing on military jackets and blazers for the last few seasons. The gilded jacquard Tilda jacket from Kallmeyer’s fall/winter 2026 collection solidified pankou closures as the jacket detail to look for this year. Typically paired with a stand collar (more on that below), the toggles can add intrigue to more minimalist silhouettes or add to the mosaic of more bohemian styles.

Peplums and nipped waists have been all the rage over the last year, making appearances on dresses, shirts, and now jackets. On outerwear, the style takes cues from the big shoulders and structured lines of ’80s blazers—offering a distinctly femme look for those who prefer a fitted profile.

Collars are coming off this fall, or at least taking a step back in lieu of a more minimalist stand collar. These clean lines create a sharp, sophisticated frame that balances simplicity with a dash of unexpected iconoclasm.

Phoebe Philo might’ve first turned us all onto the funnel neck jacket three years ago, but this season, the oversized silhouette’s reaching new heights. Consider this a more adventurous alternative to your classic bomber—it’s boxy, it’s sleek, it’s a little edgy, and that chimney neck will surely keep you shielded and warm through all the elements.

#465. Apple Debuts Apple HomeView, a New Device for the Home

The product comes in four colors, has a square screen, and might be your next tabletop accessory.

Above: The Apple HomeView in the Starlight color.

When Steve Jobs was 28 years old, photographer Diana Walker captured him at his Woodside, California home. In the now famous image, the Apple founder sat on the hardwood floor, holding a mug and a magazine. It’s a barren space but what illuminates it isn’t a standard light, it’s a towering Tiffany lamp.

Now, decades later, Apple is introducing its own product for the home. And while it bears little resemblance to a Tiffany lamp, Apple HomeView, announced today, is a device made for desks, nightstands, counters, and coffee tables and designed to be both shared and personal.

HomeView features a square screen—that’s 7 inches on the diagonal—and has Apple’s signature curved corners and a black border, giving it a slight retro feel. It’s attached to an aluminum, domed base set on a stainless steel hinge, allowing the screen to tilt forward and back. The whole thing is about the height of a standard martini shaker. And it comes in four colors: Silver, Space Grey, Starlight (a champagne gold), and Rose Pink, a new color for the company. It’s both modern and a little ‘70s, suiting both midcentury houses and high rise apartments.

What Apple calls its Liquid Retina screen displays the HomeView’s main features—it shows FaceTime calls, pulls up recipes, shares household to-dos, manages calendars, and can control any smart home devices. The speakers throughout the display and base allow users to fill rooms with podcasts, music, or audio books. All it takes is a few words to cut the harsh fluorescents and cue up a favorite playlist.

Siri AI is a big part of HomeView. It can recognize up to six people’s voices and personalize the experience based on who is interacting with it. Among other things, users can ask HomeView to respond to texts, call friends or family, remind them of upcoming events, lower the temperature, read an email aloud, and start the coffee maker. And, Apple emphasizes, it’s engineered to keep users’ info and data private.

As far as the design, HomeView is meant to be visible from across the room but unobtrusive. Users can customize the screen’s “faces” to match their rooms—there are analog clocks, modular screens that display chosen widgets (the weather, calendars, music), animated graphics (including a jovial, bouncing Snoopy), and the option to select a personal photo or a shared album slideshow. The clocks in particular can make the HomeView lean modern—sans serif fonts and an almost Nordic look—or classic, with a swooping typeface resembling that on a timeworn Rolex. The display dims and brightens based on its surroundings, so it can be discreet even right next to your pillow.

HomeView comes as a tabletop accessory—meant to sit, plugged in on a sofa side table, kitchen counter, desk, or nightstand—or as a wall-mounted iteration, looking like a high tech A/C control.

Many Apple products are designed to stand out—think the Neo’s bold colors or the AirPod Max’s bulbous shape. But HomeView was built to blend in, to look at home next to Hermès vases or Christofle silver. And, at $299 per device, Apple fans may soon find themselves ordering one for every room.

#466. The 7 Best Compression Socks for Workouts, Travel, and Everyday Wear

Our top picks for travel, workouts, swelling, and everyday wear start at $19.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

As a frequent flier and certified trainer who walks everywhere, I’ve gone through so many pairs of compression socks I’ve lost count. Yeah, they’re pricier than those Hanes tube socks you grew up with, but they’re totally worth the splurge. They’re much tighter around the feet, ankles, and legs to deliver gentle pressure that offers real health benefits, such as blood circulation, soreness, and swelling reduction after sitting or being on your feet for too long.

“The socks essentially assist the body's natural circulatory system by counteracting the effects of gravity on blood flow,” says Mikel Daniels, DPM, a board-certified podiatrist based in Baltimore, Maryland. “Superficial veins lie just under the skin, and without the benefit of muscle contraction, they rely heavily on one-way valves and pressure to return blood back toward the heart.” Simply put, compression socks help blood flow back to your heart by lightly squeezing the legs.

That makes them super handy after a sweat session or a long day at a desk job. Daniels says compression socks can reduce delayed onset muscle soreness in athletes and help prevent blood clots by keeping the blood moving. Before committing to a pair, it’s first important to know what compression level is right for you, which materials are best to help combat sweat, and how to achieve the right fit.

After wearing many compression socks over the years, Physix Gear makes the best pair. I wear these high-cut socks after my weekly seven-mile walks to help relieve leg bloating when I’m on my feet for too long. They have a 20 to 30 mm Hg compression level that doesn't feel too tight after all-day wear, but still provides enough compression to aid with blood circulation and post-workout recovery. Even more impressive: they slip on and off easily, unlike most compression socks I’ve tested. It’s also worth mentioning that these have almost 92,000 reviews on Amazon and a 4.4 rating. They’re a pair that can serve anyone, whether you're an athlete recovering from a long run or someone who struggles with spider veins.

The fabric is a flexible blend of nylon and spandex that wicks away sweat. My feet never feel wet compared to when I wear cotton socks, especially after a workout. While these are great to wear when I’m active, they’re just as useful when sitting for hours. “I wore them during a road trip recently and noticed a pretty significant reduction in swelling in an ankle I injured a few years ago that tends to blow up quite a bit when I sit for too long,” says WH style editor Shannen Zitz.

My only gripes are that these need to be washed in cold water or they’ll shrink, and that the material is thinner. I’d prefer more cushioning in a sock, but the pros outweigh the cons.

A high, wide-calf sock option is hard to come by, but the WH team discovered the Comrad Knee High Compression Socks. Calf circumference depends on your shoe size, but it ranges from 10 to 20 inches. Note that small and extra-large sizes don’t come in wide, so it’s best to size up in that case.

These have moderate compression at 15 to 20 mmHg, so they’re not supposed to fit as tightly as other high-cut socks in this guide. But despite their lower compression, WH beauty editor Nicole Saunders finds they fit just as tightly as medical-grade options. “I’ve owned my pair of pink and navy striped Comrad socks for almost two years, and they’ve come in clutch for minimizing leg swelling on the plane and after I had a slip-and-fall accident,” says Saunders. WH contributor Jennifer Neid, NASM-CPT, agrees that they are a game-changer for long travel days, whether that’s flying, car rides, or even boating. “I realized how effective they were on the return trip when I forgot to put them on after boarding (big mistake) and arrived home with swollen ankles and achy feet,” Neid says.

The fabric is mostly nylon with a touch of spandex, which Nied says is breathable in hot tropical climates. While these do the job of keeping feet cool, Saunders notes that frequent washing causes them to lose their compression power around the year-and-a-half mark, meaning they don’t fit as snugly.

Ankle socks are my favorite for looking sporty with my lululemon Hotty Hot Shorts and Hoka Clifton 11 kicks, and feeling comfortable. The Swiftwick Aspire Quarter Crew Socks look sleek while still providing firm compression. But note these only provide compression to the feet and ankles, so it’s best to go with a high-cut style for ailments like leg swelling and spider veins.

Although a specific compression level isn’t specified, it feels like 15 to 20 mmHg. My feet feel tightened and squeezed by the fabric, especially at the arch and ankle. I specifically recommend these for intense cardio sessions when you’re on your feet, and love wearing them to run or climb the StairMaster. At four inches high, my lower calves feel supported and less sore without the constriction of a high sock. When I’m working up a major sweat, I want minimal coverage. Aside from working out, these are also travel-approved. WH director of special projects Amanda Lucci wore them on a 15-hour flight and experienced no ankle swelling.

These are made with a blend of polyester and olefin fiber (another synthetic material) for absorbing moisture, while the mesh footbed circulates air for proper ventilation. Even during my most heart-pumping workouts, my feet stayed relatively dry and didn’t feel icky when I removed the socks.

I wore different SockWell pairs for a week while logging up to 20,000 steps a day in Germany. This option with a 20 to 30 mm Hg compression level helps a ton with minimizing leg swelling and tightness from intense walking, and a nine-hour plane ride there and back.

The fit isn’t too tight, while the fabric is medium-weight and thin like the Physix Gear Compression Socks. WH associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian is also a fan of SockWell. She says the brand’s quality is top-tier. “Even though I’ve had them for almost a full year, they look just as good as the first day I got them,” she says.

And if foot odor is a concern, this pair is made of merino wool, which is naturally antimicrobial, meaning it’s designed to combat funky smells. And unlike regular wool, merino wool isn’t itchy. I wore this pair when it was 80 degrees, and I didn’t notice any odor after walking all day. Merino wool is also temperature-regulating, meaning it can trap or circulate heat depending on current conditions, making this the perfect compression sock for any season. a.k.a., I plan on wearing these during winter hikes too.

Cotton socks feel plush and cozy, but they often remain wet when sweaty. The Bombas Sport Compression Socks are different. These are made with the brand’s signature Hex Tec Yarn, which is a polyester and cotton fabric blend that helps manage heat. Plus, the socks feel well-cushioned—perfect for anyone who prefers a plush sock while logging miles or sitting on an airplane.

During testing, my feet felt well ventilated. I wore these on a particularly hot day during a one-hour speed walking session and still didn’t experience the looming sweat that I usually get when wearing cotton socks. Moisture evaporated fast, and my feet didn’t feel swampy for more than 15 minutes.

Like the best overall, these have a 20 to 30 mm Hg compression level, but are much tighter. The fit runs smaller and is super snug around the calves, which isn’t my favorite and is tougher to remove. But the trade-off is a plush sock that helps aid recovery. My calves and feet felt less fatigued and sore overall after walking long distances. And you can always size up (sizes are small, medium, and large).

If a low-cut look is your preferred style, the Copper Compression Powerknit Socks are the ideal pick. Compression is targeted specifically to the feet to help relieve fatigue. These only offer moderate compression at 15 to 20 mmHg, but WH executive health and fitness director Jacqueline Andriako still finds that they combat puffiness and swelling when walking. She also loves how the heel pad prevents rubbing and blisters.

Instead of walking, I wore these on runs for a month and can attest that my feet felt well-rested post-workout. The fit is tight but not suffocating, like the Swiftwick Aspire Quarter Crew Socks, so they’re very comfortable for leisure, too. Although these are great, I would only stick to these if you have mild swelling and discomfort. If you need more coverage and support, a high-cut sock is your best bet.

As for fabric, these are made with a sweat-wicking nylon, polyester, and spandex blend that’s infused with copper—hence the name—to help improve fabric durability. It’s held its shape after countless washes. Copper is also a known antimicrobial agent, meaning it helps prevent bacteria from harboring.

Kane is known for the Revive recovery shoes, but the latest edition of its Structured Crew Socks also deserves to be on your radar. I found that the construction of the older style ran way too small and tight, but Kane upgraded these with a perfect fit around the ankle and forefoot. I don’t struggle to remove these, and they’re comfortable for all-day wear. I also appreciate the extra cushioning behind the ankles for blister prevention.

The compression level isn’t disclosed, but it feels like 20 to 30 mm Hg. I’ve been wearing Kane crew socks for almost two years, and my feet are noticeably less achy after long runs of over five miles. They’re also my go-to for hiking. They add a supportive buffer between my ankles and boots, and reduce swelling from walking for hours.

Like the Bombas Performance Compression Socks, these are made with cotton, so they feel plush and cozy. Added nylon and spandex allow sweat to evaporate, so they never stay damp.

#467. Wiz Khalifa's Hard-Hitting, Muscle-Building Workout

The rapper made a commitment to fitness and never looked back. Here's how he trains to achieve his goals.

Wiz Khalifa lies under the weight rack, hands grasping a barbell a few feet above. He tightens his abs and squeezes his glutes, then pulls his chest to the bar. He’s tackling one of his favorite moves—the inverted row, a devastating bodyweight exercise that blasts lats, biceps, and forearms. “I love inverted rows,” says the rapper. “They’re good for my back. I’ve got a really wide-ass back for some reason.”

Khalifa’s been building muscle onto that back—and the rest of his wiry, six-foot-four frame, too—for the past seven years, and in that time he’s come to crave the training process. That’s why the 34-year-old shows up at Unbreakable Performance, an MMA gym in West Hollywood, five or six days a week. And he doesn’t just do the exercises; he studies them.

“I feel like it’s a constant learning process,” he says. “When you’re training, you’re always picking up new methods or techniques, or you’re doing things better, whether it’s months in advance or three months after you start or three years after you start. I love that feeling.”

Along with making and producing music, Khalifa is growing his side gigs: Khalifa Kush, a marijuana brand, and HotBox by Wiz Khalifa, an online delivery-only restaurant. He also churns out regular content for his massive social-media fanbase, which includes more than 35 million Instagram followers and more than 25 million YouTube zealots.

But the moment he hits the gym, he forgets all that. Right now he’s working through a 90-minute session with trainer Zach Goetz. Khalifa starts by hitting the weights and doing bodyweight resistance exercises (like those inverted rows), and he ends the workout by redlining his heart rate with 30 minutes of kickboxing. The sweat forces his mind off his music and businesses, and that actually supercharges his creativity. “I love what it does for me mentally,” he says. “I get to clear my head, come up with different ideas.”

Khalifa also gets to gain size and strength. He’s up to 170 pounds, 30 more than he weighed when he first walked into the gym in 2017. Back then, music was his sole focus and nights partying were the norm. “I’ve been in the studio, smoking weed, and eating pizza for ten years,” he remembers thinking. “There’s no way that can be good for you. Look, it’s time to do something good for yourself.”

So Khalifa strolled into Unbreakable for the first time, aiming to build muscle and get stronger. And a month later, he was training with Goetz, the gym’s director of strength and conditioning.“As slight as he was,” says Goetz, “he was a guy who was serious about his craft. I don’t think he ever does anything without the intention of being great at it.”

Khalifa’s gym focus has led him to devise a strict training plan. He blasts legs and core on Monday, does chest and shoulders or arms on Tuesday, then attacks his back and core on Wednesday. He repeats the entire cycle Thursday through Saturday before taking Sunday off. He forges ahead even when he can’t make it to Unbreakable, bringing equipment with him when on tour, or training in his new home gym when recording sessions go into overtime. “It could be 2:00 a.m. and I just laid down a crazy-ass verse,” but he can still train, he says.“And I just wanted to get it in real fast. It’s right there.”

Somehow, Khalifa says, he has to get his workouts in—if only because they’ll help him reach his new fitness goal: He wants another 15 pounds of muscle.“When it is there,” he says, “I’m going to be built like a house.” And he’ll tell you exactly how he got that far, too.

No equipment? Try this bodyweight blast, which Khalifa uses when he's on the road.

Get in pushup position. Squeeze your shoulder blades. Then spread them and push the floor away. That’s 1 rep.

Stand with your back and arms pressed to a wall, arms bent. Slowly straighten your arms overhead. Return to the start. That’s 1 rep.

Get on all fours. Lift your right knee from the floor and rotate it outward, aiming to get your shin parallel to your torso. Lower. That’s 1 rep.

#469. I Took A Cooking Class With An Italian Nonna—Here Are The Tips I’m Stealing Forever

Turns out, I’ve been doing basil wrong my whole life.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

I went aboard Celebrity Cruises’ Celebrity Ascent expecting a cooking class—I left questioning whether I’m even truly Italian.

Celebrity Cruises invited me to sail on its Celebrity Ascent ship and try one of its hands-on cooking classes, where a real Italian nonna—or grandma—walked us through making gnocchi from scratch. And while I obviously came away with a plate of pasta, I also picked up a surprising number of helpful techniques that I’m absolutely bringing back into my own kitchen.

Gnocchi was the focus of our savory class, and according to our nonna, it’s traditionally the kind of dish you’d make on Sundays. But before we even got to shaping the dough, I was already learning things.

First lesson: Don’t wait to peel your potatoes.

Our instructor explained that potatoes are much easier to peel while they’re still hot. It’s a small thing, but if you’ve ever stood over a potato, aggressively scraping at skin that refuses to come off, this alone is a useful tip.

Once the potatoes were ready, we moved on to the dough, and that's when I learned your hands are arguably your most important kitchen tool.

When making gnocchi, my temporary nonna stressed the importance of working the dough by hand. It’s easier to feel whether it needs more flour or egg when you’re actually touching it rather than relying entirely on a utensil.

She also explained that while some nonnas skip the egg entirely, using some is traditional. From there, the goal is to get the consistency right without overcomplicating things.

Then came the advice I heard repeatedly throughout the class: flour, flour, flour.

Once the dough is ready, roll it into long snake shapes, keeping them as even in size as possible. Plenty of flour keeps everything from sticking while you cut and shape the individual gnocchi.

You can keep your gnocchi relatively simple, but adding texture matters.

We learned the traditional fork method, rolling the gnocchi along the tines to create ridges, but you can also use your finger to make small indentations. Either way, the goal is to give the sauce somewhere to go.

And honestly, anything that results in more sauce sticking to my pasta is a technique I can support.

This may have been my favorite gnocchi lesson of the day because it removes a lot of the guesswork. Drop them into boiling water and watch. As soon as the gnocchi float to the top, take them out.

There’s no cutting one open, no standing over the pot wondering whether another minute will somehow improve things—once they rise, they’re ready.

The sauce portion of the class gave me just as many culinary musings to consider.

One of the biggest: Turn off the heat before adding your basil. According to our instructor, adding basil after you turn off the heat helps preserve its flavor instead of cooking it away.

She also had another basil rule I had genuinely never heard before: Don't use metal to tear it. Instead, use your hands or a ceramic tool. She explained that metal can cause the basil to oxidize, so tearing it by hand is the better move.

And when you’re actually picking basil, go for the smaller, younger leaves near the top of the plant rather than the big leaves at the bottom. Apparently, I’ve been treating basil with nowhere near enough consideration.

This was probably the most controversial lesson of the class for me.

Our nonna told us that, as a general rule in Italian cooking, you use garlic or onion—not both. Her explanation was simple: They “fight each other.”

Considering how many recipes I’ve made that start by throwing both into a pan, this felt mildly life-changing.

My nonna’s tomato sauce recipe uses no garlic at all. Just tomatoes, onion, olive oil, and basil. And that simplicity was kind of the point.

The tomato sauce technique is the one I’m most likely to recreate at home. Start by dropping the tomatoes into boiling water for about a minute. That loosens the skin enough that you can peel it off easily by hand.

Once peeled, put the tomatoes in a bowl and mash them, but don’t purée them completely; leave some chunks for texture. From there, cook them with onion and olive oil. That’s it.

No giant ingredient list, and no throwing every spice in the cabinet into the pot. Once the sauce is finished cooking, turn off the heat and add your basil.

The result was simple, fresh, and exactly the kind of sauce that makes you realize how many unnecessary ingredients you sometimes add at home.

What surprised me most about the class wasn't any single recipe—it was how many techniques simply came down to paying closer attention to the food in front of you.

Feel the gnocchi dough instead of blindly following a measurement. Watch for the pasta to float instead of staring at a timer. Leave the tomatoes chunky. Tear the basil with your hands. Let just a handful of ingredients actually shine.

I went into the class hoping to learn how to make gnocchi. I left with a running list of little rules that will pop into my head every time I cook Italian food from now on (although I'm still emotionally processing the idea that I've apparently been making garlic and onion duke it out my entire life).

#470. Wool vs. Polyester vs. Polypropylene Rugs: This Is the One Experts Say Is Best for Your Home

Experts break down which fibers can handle high traffic—and which feel most luxurious.

Every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

I have to admit: I didn’t do much research aside from taking measurements when I bought my rugs. I cared more about the design and color than anything else, which is how I ended up with two wool rugs that shed nonstop and two washable rugs.

Although I still like all four of my rugs, as I start to host more and babies enter my life—I am a proud aunt—it got me thinking about the pros and cons of wool rugs versus synthetic rugs. Which one is better if I were to have kids in the future? Can I live with the shedding? Should I be worried about microplastics? I know I am not alone in this material-analysis spiral for rugs—plenty of families likely are too.

The more I looked, the more I kept coming back to the same three options: wool, polyester, and polypropylene. They are not the only rug materials out there, of course—cotton, jute, sisal, nylon, and viscose all exist, too—but these were the fibers I found myself seriously comparing. Wool has the natural, luxury appeal, polyester often shows up in colorful and durable styles, while polypropylene is usually billed as the practical, stain-friendly choice.

For families with kids, pets, or a high-traffic home, the “best” rug material is not just about what looks the chicest. It is about what you can actually live with. And as I think about replacing or buying a new rug in the future, I know the wool vs. polyester vs. polypropylene rug topic will keep popping up. I’m sharing everything I learned about the three materials ahead, from performance to maintenance, so you can make a more informed purchasing decision than I did.

Rug materials are often sorted into two broad categories: natural and synthetic. Natural rug fibers include wool, cotton, jute, sisal, sea grass, and silk. Synthetic rugs are composed of polyester, polypropylene/olefin, nylon, acrylic, and sometimes triexta. Depending on which material you choose, it’ll look, feel, and function differently in your home, so it’s important to find the material that’s right for your lifestyle.

When making your purchase, “start with the room, not the rug,” says Asha Chaudhary, CEO and president of Jaipur Living. “Where is it going? How much traffic [will it get]? [Do you have] kids, pets, both? How honest are you about your appetite for maintenance? And how much does the natural character of wool genuinely matter to you, versus how much it just sounds like the right answer?

“Then compare the two rugs as objects: construction, texture, density, craftsmanship, design. At the same price point, you're not choosing between a category and a category. You're choosing between two specific rugs, and one of them is better made. Don't default to wool because it's natural, and don't default to synthetic because it's easier. Buy the better rug for the life you actually have.”

For some parents, there is also the natural-versus-synthetic question. Wool will appeal to families who are trying to bring fewer plastic-based materials into the home, since polyester and polypropylene are both synthetic fibers. Wool, however, requires more care and attention around kids. For families who value convenience and functionality, they may opt for polyester and polypropylene rugs that have also gone through testing and acquired low-VOC certifications or are made with nontoxic dyes.

Rugs can be made from many materials—cotton, jute, sisal, nylon, and more—but I wanted to focus on the three I personally found myself comparing most often while shopping: wool, polyester, and polypropylene. Wool felt like the natural-fiber benchmark, especially for anyone who wants something plush, durable, and elevated, while polyester and polypropylene kept coming up as the more affordable, low-maintenance synthetic options. (I currently own both wool and polyester rugs.)

Wool rugs are primarily made from sheep fleece, though some brands may also use fibers from other animals like alpacas, goats, or llamas. Wool is resistant to water, dirt, and stains, plus it can absorb moisture and dry out without developing mold or mildew.

Polyester rugs are usually made from PET polyester, the same plastic polymer used to make drink bottles and clothes. Polyester is often used when softness, color, or a more decorative look is the priority. Polypropylene (also called olefin), while made from a type of synthetic plastic polymer, is more commonly chosen in a rug for moisture resistance, stain resistance, and indoor/outdoor use.

“Polypropylene is great for heavy traffic wear-and-tear, and it'll hold up to spills better. Polyester is great for a soft touch and underfoot comfort, but better used for lighter traffic areas like bedrooms,” says Munan Xue, CMO of Rugs USA.

While fiber is part of the equation to buying a rug, it’s not the sole factor you should rely on. “Fiber is one input. So is how the rug was made, who made it and under what conditions, how long it will last, what it takes to maintain, and how soon it ends up being replaced,” Chaudhary explains. “Durability is a sustainability question that almost nobody frames that way. A rug that performs well and stays in a home for fifteen years has a completely different footprint than one that's replaced every three years, regardless of what either is made from.”

Her advice to shoppers is to look at the whole product and company. “Fiber is only one part of the equation, but too often it's the only thing considered. Pile, construction, and weight are all important on the label. Practicalities like whether it's spill-proof [for families] are also very important to consider as well,” echoes Xue.

Generally speaking, polyester and polypropylene rugs tend to be more budget-friendly than wool. That does not mean they are automatically the better buy, though. Wool may cost more upfront, but it is beloved for its natural feel and durability; polypropylene is often the most affordable and spill-friendly even compared to polyester, while polyester rugs can offer a softer, more decorative look at a lower price than many wool rugs.

“Wool earns its price. It's naturally resilient, it has a depth of texture and character that's hard to replicate, and a well-made wool rug can stay in a family for generations. But worth it and right for you are two different questions,” says Chaudhary. “In a home with young kids, two dogs and a dining room that gets used every night, a high-quality performance fiber is often the smarter call, not a compromise, just a better match.”

Chaudhary notes that the trade-off is narrowing, though thanks in part to Jaipur Living’s CallaLuxe line. “We engineered a proprietary solution-dyed acrylic fiber to deliver the softness, texture, and rich color people associate with wool, with the cleanability they want from a performance rug.”

If pattern and color are the priority, polyester offers the widest range of stylish options that include washable rugs. Polypropylene can still come in plenty of patterns, though it is usually prized more for affordability, stain resistance, and outdoor practicality than for a high-end designer look. Wool comes in many colors, not so much trendy prints, and will look more luxurious and textural, especially in hand-knotted, hand-tufted, Moroccan, Persian-style, or heirloom-inspired designs.

Wool is generally considered the premium option out of the three because it is a natural fiber that feels richer underfoot and has better texture and depth. Polyester and polypropylene can still be smart choices, particularly for homes with kids, pets, or frequent spills, but they are usually valued more for affordability and easy maintenance than for heirloom-level quality.

Durability depends on what kind of wear and tear you are worried about. A well-made wool rug is usually the strongest long-term investment because wool is naturally resilient and can hold up beautifully over time. However, it does not hold up to heavy stains and aggressive cleaning.

For homes where crumbs, spills, and pet accidents are the bigger concern, polypropylene may be the more practical choice because it is typically more moisture- and stain-resistant. Polyester sits somewhere in the middle: It can be soft, stylish, and budget-friendly, but it is usually valued more for color, comfort, and affordability than for heirloom-level quality.

If easy cleanup is the priority, polypropylene is usually the most low-maintenance of the three. Because it is a synthetic fiber commonly used in indoor/outdoor rugs, it tends to be more forgiving with spills, moisture, and everyday messes.

Polyester can also be a practical choice, especially if you want softer texture, more color options, or a washable rug, though care instructions vary by rug. Wool rugs generally require more upkeep with stains and shed a lot. You also have to be quite careful with the type of vacuum you use on wool rugs (pro tip: do not use a beater bar).

“Shedding is the one [thing] that surprises people most [about wool rugs]. Some shedding from a new wool rug is completely normal, and it is not a defect; it's loose fiber working its way out, and it settles down. How much a rug sheds has a lot to do with construction, not just quality, though,” says Chaudhary.

For stains on wool rugs, she notes people’s first instinct is to attack the spot, but wool responds better to prompt and gentle treatment. “Harsh chemicals and aggressive scrubbing can damage the fiber or pull color,” she adds. “My advice is to understand a rug’s care requirements before you buy it, with the same seriousness you’d give the design.”

The bottom line? Loving how the rug looks and knowing how to live with it should carry equal weight in your purchase decision.

For most families with kids and pets, polypropylene is the easiest material to live with.

“Polypropylene is the practical workhorse. It holds up to sun, moisture, and repeated cleaning. That’s my recommendation for a casual, high-use space: an uncovered patio, a busy entry, a family room where spills are a fact of life, and it delivers that at an accessible price,” says Chaudhary. “Polyester gives you a softer hand and can achieve depth and luster in color, so it's the better choice when comfort and aesthetics are leading—think covered porches, three-season rooms, and spaces where people actually sit on the floor.”

Wool is a solid choice if you want a more premium, natural rug that can last when properly cared for. Place the wool rug in your primary bedroom or somewhere further away from the hustle and bustle of the household, though. “It will give your space that softer, richer feel underfoot and will age beautifully,” says Xue.

#471. William Shatner on Star Trek and the Meaning of Life

“There is this trepidation of life that goes with 95, but also the mysteries of what am I going to see,” Shatner says in a new episode of “What I’ve Learned.”

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

At 95 years old, William Shatner is boldly going—well, who knows, actually? Morbid as it is, the Star Trek icon has been thinking about death lately, including in a new episode of Esquire’s “What I’ve Learned.”

“When you’re 95, you shouldn’t be around. You should be dead,” Shatner tells Esquire editor in chief Michael Sebastian. “There is this trepidation of life that goes with 95, but also the mysteries of what am I going to see. Is there anything after life?”

Sixty years ago, Shatner played Captain James T. Kirk on the landmark science-fiction series Star Trek, leading the starship Enterprise on a five-year mission to explore strange new worlds. On October 9, the documentary The Sixty-Year Mission: How Star Trek Changed Television and the World was released, which included Shatner as both executive producer and one of its primary subjects.

You can listen to Shatner’s “What I’ve Learned” interview below, as well as on Apple and Spotify.

Shatner has done more than Star Trek. He’s been in movies, TV shows, commercials—most notably as the spokesperson for Priceline—and has expanded his public profile to podcasting and leading a heavy-metal band. (Yes, really.) But his work on the seminal sci-fi franchise is still a huge part of why audiences still love Shatner, who in 2024 revealed he and his eldest daughter Melanie Shatner, 61, had simultaneously battled different stage 4 cancers.

So you can’t blame Shatner for thinking a lot about the endless mysteries of the cosmos and what lies beyond this life. He recalls shooting the 1994 movie Star Trek Generations, in which (spoilers?) Kirk dies at the end.

“So here you have this heroic character, and suddenly he realizes that thing in front of him is coming his way and he’s going to die,” says Shatner. “So now Captain Kirk is seeing death. How is he going to react? Well, I forgot what they wrote, but it wasn’t ‘Oh, my.’ So I thought he would react the way he is seeing all these weird things and the planets they visited, all the years of discovering new civilizations and new worlds. And he would react with awe and wonder. My God, here comes a new adventure.”

On the subject of Trek, Shatner tells Sebastian how close he was to costar Leonard Nimoy, who famously played Spock, saying he was “the brother I never had.” But he’s also estranged from his other fellow stars, like George Takei (who played Sulu, the pilot of the Enterprise). “We were very close,” he says about Nimoy. “We went through a lot of experiences together and a great deal of joy together. We would appear onstage and he’d make me laugh to hysteria. So I loved him.”

But George Takei is a different matter. “People like George and Walter [Koenig] would go to these Comic-Cons, and they’d stand on stage and say, ‘I’m Sulu,’ and they’d get applause. And somebody would say, ‘You know, Sulu should have been the lead. You were so good.’ And they began to believe it. That’s what happened. They feel as though they weren’t as well regarded as they felt they should have been. That’s been detrimental to relationships.”

Shatner stops short of calling it a feud. “It’s not a feud. I don’t know him,” he says. “I haven’t seen [Takei] in 20 years.”

The rest of the nearly hour-long conversation spans Shatner’s advice to young men—“Be honest with yourself and do the best with yourself, but do your best”—the story of his metal band, how he feels about artificial intelligence, and the beauty of people changing as they get old. “Is love eternal?” Shatner wonders. “Does love mean you see somebody across a crowded room and you say, I love you? And that remains there for the next 60 years, you die in each other’s arms?”

Then Shatner comes across the most important question: the meaning of life. “Can you imagine what this phone has done to mankind, the good and the bad? The communication between human and that phone has changed everybody’s life. And that change will continue. What is the meaning of life? The meaning of life is the search for the meaning of life.”

Does William Shatner have any regrets? He says only, “I don’t want to go.”

#472. How Luxury Cars Became the Ultimate Expression of Personal Style

Creating your dream vehicle now goes far beyond choosing the perfect paint color.

For many, a car is an extension of personal style—and in the world of luxury vehicles, the possibilities for making one your own have never felt more exciting. Increasingly, buyers are looking beyond what’s readily available on the showroom floor, gravitating toward one-of-a-kind colors, unexpected materials, and bespoke details.

I’ve long been fascinated by the way a car can say so much about the person in the driver’s seat, and often imagine whipping around in something beyond the familiar rotation of black, white, and silver—an ocean-inspired metallic blue, perhaps, a cool matte gray, or even a bespoke two-tone finish. Today, luxury automakers are taking that same spirit of self-expression to the nth degree, inviting clients to shape nearly every detail of their vehicles around their individual tastes.

As the cars become more individualized, so too does the experience of creating them. For the most elaborate commissions, configuring a vehicle can mean sitting down with specialists in private spaces designed to feel less like placing an order and more like commissioning a piece of art.

“I’ve definitely seen an uptick in clients wanting to do something different and special rather than simply sitting in our studio and mixing and matching options,” says Jason Gorman, senior sales executive for exotics and Porsche at Manhattan Motorcars. “There are now dedicated spaces in the city designed specifically for that experience. Lamborghini has the Lamborghini Lounge, which they use for events and product launches, but it also has a configuration space. For a more bespoke build, someone can sit with the client, walk through the possibilities, and make suggestions. Rolls-Royce has a similar space in Manhattan with its Private Office. It’s a beautiful space with a full kitchen where they host events and product launches, but it’s also designed for those really bespoke builds.”

Mercedes-Benz is also expanding its approach to customization with Studio Los Angeles, which opened in Beverly Hills earlier this year. Home to the first dedicated Manufaktur Made to Measure hub in the United States, and one of just two worldwide, the space allows clients to explore an extensive selection of colors, leathers, stitching, and finishes through hands-on material samples and immersive digital visualizations. With specialists on hand to guide the process, every choice, down to the smallest design detail, receives attention.

For Davide Baldini, head of Maserati Fuoriserie, this elevated level of service is fundamental to going bespoke. “The appeal of the program is not only the product, but the experience around the product and the customer,” he says. “At this level of luxury, they’re not simply buying a piece of steel. They’re buying an experience and embracing an entire journey.”

To better understand the growing demand for automotive customization—and what it takes to bring a bespoke vehicle from concept to delivery—I spoke with representatives and design directors from Mercedes-Benz, Bentley, Cadillac, McLaren, and Maserati about the possibilities available to clients, the colors and materials they’re gravitating toward most, and how individual tastes are shaping the cars that ultimately make it onto the road. Here’s how the process works, from start to finish. Who knows? By the end, you may just find yourself dreaming up a custom ride of your own.

Every bespoke vehicle begins with a vision. Maybe it’s a particular paint color you’ve always wanted, an interior inspired by a favorite object or hobby, or details that pay tribute to a meaningful memory, place, or person. The first step is translating that inspiration into a design that can ultimately come to fruition.

For some clients, that process begins with a digital configurator. Bentley, for instance, offers more than a billion possible configurations, according to Maria Mulder, the brand’s head of color and trim. After selecting a model and performance specifications, clients can experiment with exterior paint, pinstriping, interior hides, stitching, dashboard veneers, and countless other details. “The colors themselves often come with a story,” Mulder told me, pointing to Cricket Ball, a rich leather hue inspired by the worn patina of a traditional British cricket ball.

Maserati’s Fuoriserie program also lets clients decide how far they want to take the process. “With Fuoriserie, there are different levels of personalization,” Baldini says. “Clients can begin with the collections available through our configurator. From there, we can move into the bespoke world, where the customer can work directly with our designers and engineers, either remotely or in person, to develop something completely unique.”

“In the bespoke world, we can develop what the customer desires based on their feelings, passions, and the purpose behind the car,” Baldini explains. “If a customer comes to us and says, ‘I want the exact color of a GranTurismo from 1957,’ we can develop it.”

Once the design concept is in place, clients can work alongside designers, engineers, retailers, and customization specialists to determine exactly how their ideas will translate to the finished vehicle.

At McLaren, that’s where McLaren Special Operations comes in. “The Special Operations division is really for clients who have a passion to go beyond what’s available as standard,” says Jonathan Simms, director of McLaren Special Operations. “It’s a very collaborative process. We’ll work with clients to achieve what they want, whether that means a unique or exclusive color, different materials and finishes, brightwork, polished or precious metals, or even a completely unique vehicle.” The process typically begins through a retailer, then evolves into regular conversations about what the client wants beyond the standard palette or specification.

From there, personalization can extend to virtually every detail. “The possibilities really are 360 degrees,” Baldini says. “We can personalize the interior, stitching, exterior badges, rings, brake calipers, leather, and exterior paint. If a customer wants an entirely new leather or paint color, we can develop it specifically for them.”

Cadillac, too, is expanding its bespoke offerings with Curated by Cadillac for the 2027 Escalade IQ. Select clients can work one-on-one with a dedicated Cadillac Design Concierge to explore an expansive selection of exterior colors and finishes, along with an extensive interior palette that spans everything from seating and upholstery to the smallest cabin details.

Once the initial design concept is agreed upon, the fun truly begins: choosing from a seemingly endless assortment of colors, materials, textures, and finishes. And today’s luxury buyers appear increasingly willing to experiment. “The market has moved on,” says McLaren Special Operations director Jonathan Simms. “If you look back five or ten years, there were iconic cars from McLaren’s past that clients were buying even if the specification wasn’t exactly what they wanted. Now, rather than simply accepting that, a good number of clients want to start from scratch and create something that feels entirely their own.”

At Bentley, more than 70 percent of buyers opt for Mulliner customization, opening the door to an expansive palette of statement shades, from fiery Candy Red to Viridian, a rich emerald hue with an appropriately British feel. I put the possibilities to the test myself using Bentley’s online configurator, eventually landing on a Flying Spur S V8 Hybrid finished in dazzling Kingfisher blue by Mulliner with a bold Hotspur red leather interior.

Mercedes-Benz’s Manufaktur program offers an equally impressive range of personalization options, with more than 150 exterior paint colors and 400 interior color choices for the new S-Class. Made to Measure takes customization a step further, allowing for personal touches like custom embroidery, monogrammed cushions, and even family crests. The program’s appeal is clear: In 2025, half of all S-Class vehicles produced featured at least one Manufaktur option, as did nearly every Mercedes-Maybach. Celebrities are embracing the possibilities, too, offering plenty of dreamy design inspiration. Alicia Keys, for one, has given her G-Class a distinctive makeover, pairing an eye-catching Deep Green exterior with Saddle Brown and Black leather upholstery, a walnut wood trim, and 22-inch AMG forged wheels.

Beyond exterior color, materials and finishes play an equally vital role in shaping the final design. Baldini points to the “Cannelloni” leather interior of the Grecale Tributo Il Bruciato, created in collaboration with Marchesi Antinori, one of Italy’s oldest and most prestigious wine-producing families, as an example of the luxe treatments available to clients looking to personalize their interiors.

Once the colors, materials, and finishing touches are decided, attention to detail continues through production. For the most bespoke commissions, the process can even extend beyond the dealership and involve the automaker’s factory teams directly. Gorman recalls a recent bespoke Bentley order in which his team coordinated directly with Bentley’s bespoke specialists in Crewe, bringing a designer into the process to make changes with the client in real time. For truly bespoke orders, he explains, “the factory is involved with their team.”

For another glimpse into the artistry behind these vehicles, step inside Mercedes-Benz’s Manufaktur facilities, where no detail is too small to escape special attention. From precision-cut leather to intricate embroidery, the craftsmanship is nothing short of spectacular. Case in point: Each steering wheel is handcrafted by a single artisan, a process that can take up to eight hours, while the headliner alone requires a sewing pattern comprising 20 individual pieces.

Cadillac, meanwhile, takes a similarly hands-on approach to its 2027 Escalade IQ builds, with artisans painting and assembling vehicles in limited quantities. Individualized touches carry through to the finished product, making each vehicle feel distinctly tailored to the client rather than simply selected from a dealership lot.

#473. A Beginner's Guide to Counting Macros, According To Experts

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Navigating nutrition on a weight loss or body recomposition journey is no easy feat. It involves meticulous meal planning and prep that can leave even the most eager exhausted. Counting macros—a.k.a. macronutrients, including carbohydrates, protein, and fats—can help paint a clear picture of what you’re putting in your body.

In fact, macro counting can beneficial for people with all kinds of goals: body recomp, weight loss, as well as athletes, bodybuilders, and those who thrive on structured eating plans, says Diala Alatassi, MD, a board-certified internal and obesity medicine physician at Endeavor Health Medical Group.

A huge perk of this eating method is that no foods are off-limits. It’s somewhat flexible compared to other restrictive diets like keto and certain intermittent fasting protocols, says registered dietitian and diabetes educator Jessica Crandall Snyder, RDN.

Want more nutrition guidance? Try our Eating for Body Recomp Guide here.

Ahead, experts break down what you need to know about macros for weight loss—plus, the benefits and potential risks of the method.

Repeat after me: Carbs are not the enemy—even if you're trying to lose weight. “Carbohydrates are the most important energy source for almost all human cells,” says Mascha Davis, RDN, a spokesperson for the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics.

When you eat carbohydrates, your body breaks them down into glucose—a form of sugar that enters your bloodstream and gets stored in your liver and muscles as glycogen, says a registered dietitian, Ayla Barmmer, RDN. "This stored fuel powers high-intensity exercise, which is key for building lean muscle and revving up your metabolism," she adds.

Carbs also support brain function and concentration, and they help regulate your mood by boosting levels of serotonin, a feel-good neurotransmitter, Barmmer says.

Some examples of healthy carbs, according to Barmmer:

This macro helps build and maintain your body’s lean muscle, and then some. “Protein makes up the enzymes that power chemical reactions in the body,” Davis explains. “It also makes the hemoglobin that transports oxygen through the body.” And if oxygen doesn’t get where it needs to go, you can forget about having the energy to take the stairs, let alone power through an hour-long run.

When it comes to feeling full on fewer calories, protein is paramount because it triggers the release of gut hormones, “slowing digestion and signaling to your brain that you're full," Barmmer says. "That means food stays in your stomach longer, helping you feel satisfied for hours."

By slowing digestion, protein also slows the release of glucose into your bloodstream to prevent the blood sugar and insulin spikes that can create health issues, says internal medicine physician Alexandra Sowa, MD.

Here are examples of healthy protein, according to Barmmer:

Fat maintains cell membrane integrity, supports brain and nerve function, and helps absorb the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K, “which are key to both metabolic health and effective weight loss," Barmmer says. "While it doesn’t trigger the same satiety hormones as protein, its slower digestion helps stabilize blood glucose, reduce cravings, and enhance overall hunger control."

A few examples of healthy fats, per Barmmer:

When it comes to counting macros versus counting calories, the main difference really rests in the intention. "Calorie counting does not factor in the source of the calories," says registered dietitian Amy Brownstein, RDN. "You can consume an unbalanced diet while staying within calorie targets."

Plus, counting macros can be tailored to be more specific to your weight loss or fitness goals. "Instead of tracking calories, you’re tracking the components of calories that fuel your body," Snyder adds. So, you might add more carbs to your plate when you’re training for an endurance event, like running a race.

First, this is how many calories are in each gram of the three primary macronutrients (you'll need this information later on):

Try our Eating for Body Recomp Guide for more macro guidance

Everyone’s macro goals vary slightly, but for general health, Dr. Alatassi recommends that adults get 45 to 65 percent of their calories from carbs, 25 to 35 percent from protein, and 20 to 35 percent from fat.

When counting macros for weight loss, prioritizing protein is often a key strategy supported by research, says Dr. Alatassi. "Higher protein levels help preserve muscle mass, enhance metabolism, and improve satiety, making it easier to maintain a calorie deficit," she says, adding that you may choose to aim for the upper range of 35 percent protein, or even slightly higher, up to 40 percent. You'd then adjust your carbs and fats accordingly to stay within your target calorie range.

That said, personal preferences, dietary restrictions, goals, lifestyle, activity level, and existing health conditions can influence your ideal macronutrient balance, so consulting with a doctor or registered dietitian can help you nail down your exact numbers, Dr. Alatassi says.

You can use an online calculator like this one from the National Institutes of Health or check out some other ways to find your number here. Once you have that, you can plug it into the below formula:

So for example, if you were to aim for 2,000 calories a day, with a macro breakdown of 50 percent carbs, 30 percent protein, and 20 percent fat, you might go for 250 grams of carbs, 150 grams of protein, and 44 grams of fat. Again, this ratio is general and not an expert-recommended one-size-fits-all plan. It may take some trial and error to nail down the best macro ratio for you.

As you’ve probably already guessed, counting macros involves a good amount of planning and math. “It’s a bit cumbersome to count macros unless you eat the same thing every day,” Angelone says. “But then your diet becomes monotonous and probably not nutritionally adequate.” Still, counting macros gets easier once you get the hang of it, she says.

Setting macro goals too low, for example, might cause energy fatigue, brain fog, and nutrient deficiency, while setting them too high might not give you the health benefits you’re looking for (weight loss, improved workout performance, etc.), says Barmmer.

Counting macros can become rigid or even obsessive when taken to extremes, disconnecting you from your natural hunger cues, Barmmer says, so you'll want to keep an eye out for that along the way. It also might not be beneficial for anyone who finds meticulous tracking stressful or anxiety-inducing, Dr. Alatassi adds.

“For these individuals, focusing on intuitive eating, portion control, or seeking guidance from a nutrition professional might be more beneficial and sustainable,” she adds. Remember: Your macro goals should act as guidelines, but you shouldn't feel obligated to hit them Every. Single. Day.

If you want to test it out before upending your current eating plan, Angelone recommends keeping a food diary to get an idea of what you eat on a regular basis. You can also try incorporating macro-counting in spurts, starting for a week, Snyder says. That way, you’ll "have a really good idea of the kind of foods you’re typically eating and where you need to adjust, and that may give you some really good insights," Snyder says.

Once you calculate and track your macros (per the instructions above), look at your food choices to see what changes you need to make based on those numbers. “Be sure to choose less processed foods, choose whole grains and high-fiber foods, and healthy fats, limit refined sugar, and drink plenty of water,” Angelone says.

While Snyder doesn’t recommend tracking macros forever, checking in with yourself once in a while can be helpful to make sure you’re generally still eating your proper ratio. But if you're looking to count macros for a longer period of time and have some serious weight loss or performance goals you're looking to achieve, consult a dietitian to personalize your plan, says Snyder.

In the free version of the app, you can track how many proteins, carbs, and fats you've eaten for the day. And if you upgrade to premium, you can actually set a target for each macro.

You can track your macros easily on the Lose It! app. Just log your meals and the app will calculate all of your macros consumed under its "nutrients tab."

You can use this app to not only track macros but create meal plans matching your goals. One of the best features about the app is its barcode scanner, which inputs food items directly into your account.

This app gives users a macros countdown, body-weight tracking options, and has a database with over 1.5 million foods.

Remember, just like any other diet, patience is key when you start counting macros, says Dr. Alatassi. This method won’t magically induce weight loss overnight, but with consistency and regular exercise, you’ll hopefully begin feeling better inside and out as you prioritize your nutrients.

#474. Two Stolen Renoir Paintings Have Been Recovered After a French Museum Heist

The works, valued at roughly $10 million, were on loan from the Musée d’Orsay when thieves took them in September.

Local authorities announced that two paintings by Pierre-Auguste Renoir, stolen from his former home on the French Riviera last month, have now been recovered and six suspects have been arrested. The works disappeared during a September 8 break-in at the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer, where the Impressionist painter spent his final years.

The paintings, Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano and Young Woman at the Well, belong to the Musée d’Orsay in Paris and were on loan to the museum. Their combined value was reported at €9 million, or approximately $10.4 million, at the time of the theft.

Two intruders entered the museum before dawn after cutting through its perimeter fence and climbing through a window. They used an electric saw to remove the paintings’ frames from their mountings, taking four works but abandoning two in the garden as they escaped. The burglary lasted less than three minutes, according to the regional prosecutor’s office.

On October 10, a 29-year-old man identified by investigators as the principal suspect was placed under formal investigation for organized theft and criminal conspiracy, his attorney said. Authorities have not publicly detailed how the paintings were recovered.

The museum occupies Les Collettes, the estate where Renoir lived from 1908 until his death in 1919. Set among olive and citrus trees, the property preserves his studio, furniture, and personal belongings alongside paintings and sculptures. Mayor Bryan Masson welcomed the recovery, describing the works as part of the city’s history and cultural heritage.

The paintings will undergo examination before returning to the museum. France’s Culture Ministry said on October 12 that specialists in Marseille would assess their condition and carry out any necessary restoration under the Musée d’Orsay’s scientific supervision. No date has been announced for their return.
