#475. I Lost 203 Pounds Using These 6 Weightlifting Moves

“I can see a bit of loose skin, but to me, that’s a war trophy.”

Zondwa Kula, 43, an auditor in London, would try to lose weight but never seemed to keep it off. His guilty pleasure was sweets, which he ate almost every day without worrying about serving size. The tipping point came when he had to buy a whole new wardrobe for a business trip after weighing an all-time high of 388 pounds. He set off to lose the weight for good. Now at 185 pounds, he reveals how he did it.

I’VE BEEN A big guy all my life. I tried the quick-fix diets, played tennis and even did CrossFit. But whenever I would lose some weight, it would always come back.

My problem is that I have a very sweet tooth. I used to eat dessert almost every day, like a whole slab of chocolate or a massive slice of cake. For meals, I ate junk food and takeout. I paid no attention to portion sizes. There have been times—COVID lockdowns being a prime example—when my weight really skyrocketed because I was sedentary. I’d walk into a room full of people and think, “Do they see me as a fat person?”

Between December 2024 and February 2025, I felt heavier than usual. I remember worrying that I wouldn’t be healthy for my two young daughters. Maybe I wouldn’t be there for them for the long haul.

I’d been on blood pressure medication for about a decade, and while I didn’t have any heart problems yet, a cardiologist told me I needed to lose weight.

The tipping point came before I flew to Egypt for a business trip. I stepped on a scale, and I’ll never forget the number I saw: 388 pounds. I had to buy shirts in a bigger size before the trip, and I said to myself, “I will never buy a bigger size again.” I promised then and there I would lose the weight for good. When I made exercise into a habit, it became second nature to me.

A FRIEND OF mine in South Africa had a personal trainer and saw great results. I found my own personal trainer at Ultimate Performance. I started off with lifting weights, which was completely new to me.

At first, my trainer really focused on doing each and every rep with a slow, controlled tempo, rather than using momentum to swing the weights around. I learned how to go through a full range of motion rather than performing half-reps.

Even at my heaviest, my trainer and I realized I have strong legs. This meant I could really push hard on the lower body exercises, such as the hack squat and the pendulum. Doing those exercises is brutal. To this day, though, the hack squat and the pendulum remain my nemeses! For my upper body work, we prioritized exercises like bench presses and rows.

I enjoyed going to the gym. I chased the feeling of what it’s like when I finished a session. The workouts were tough. I wouldn’t say I enjoyed Bulgarian split squats, but I liked knowing what I could achieve.

Over time, my lifting personal bests included: Hack squat, 374 pounds; bench press (flat), about 176 pounds; and Bulgarian split squat, roughly 136 pounds.

I CUT SUGAR from my diet, except for fruit. My only other carbs came from vegetables. For a typical breakfast, I would eat pineapple, grapes, or strawberries. For lunch, I would have a salmon fillet with a poached egg, avocado, spinach and broccoli. As a snack I’d have a Greek yogurt or protein shake. Then a dinner plate might include a chicken breast, sea bass, lamb with cauliflower, pepper, onions, and vegetables.

I’d eat 160 to 170 grams of protein a day, and about 2,000 calories. As my weight began to come down, my trainer would tweak my calories as the sessions got tougher, because I needed more carbohydrates to fuel my workouts. Gradually, we introduced carbs like oats, which I’d mix with Greek yogurt, protein powder, and berries.

One of the biggest changes I made was to track and log literally everything I ate. I would pre-load my meals into an Ultimate Performance app, so I knew what I was going to eat a few days in advance. That completely took away the guesswork and worry about whether I was eating the wrong things. My trainer and I worked out exactly what meals I needed to eat to hit my macros—my protein levels, my carbohydrate levels, my fat levels—and I would weigh my food to make sure I hit those macros precisely.

At first, it was quite tough. Giving up cake was hard. For the first six months, I didn’t have a single cheat meal. The first time I ate a slice of cake was on my daughter’s birthday, and she jokingly said to me: “Daddy, be careful with that cake! Don’t ruin your diet!”

I ENDED UP losing 203 pounds in a little under 17 months, going from 42 percent to 6 percent body fat.

I feel like a different person. I feel great, and I’m no longer on blood pressure medication.

Once I locked in on my weight loss goal, I achieved it far quicker than I thought I would. I thought it might take two or three years, but it’s taken a lot less than that. My family is very proud of me, especially my daughters. I’m now their “muscly Daddy.”

At the moment, I maintain my weight by eating around 2,500 calories a day. I still enjoy the odd slice of cake on special occasions. On weekends, I’ll indulge in some chocolate. I just log what I’ve eaten, and then adjust my calories over the next few days.

I also run and walk. When I first started my program, getting 10,000 steps a day was hard because I felt as if I had to carve out the time. Now I sometimes wake up at 4 a.m. and go for a walk so I can get my steps in, and still get to work on time.

Because my weight started to come down very quickly, I could see that I was building visible muscle. In fact, when I look at photos of myself now, I can see a bit of loose skin, but to me, that’s a war trophy. It’s a reminder of what I’ve achieved and how far I’ve come. Surgery may be something I might consider in the future, but right now, I am really proud that my body looks real.

The advice I’d give to anyone considering a weight loss journey: Just take the first step. It’s the hardest thing to do, but once you’ve taken that first step, you’re on a journey toward changing your life. Stay consistent and keep showing up. If you can do that, you’ll change your entire mindset and outlook on life.

#476. How to Watch the ‘Friday the 13th’ Movies and TV Shows in Order

Has the new Peacock TV prequel Crystal Lake sparked your curiosity about the Friday the 13th films? Fancy a marathon? There are so many movies about infamous fictional slasher Jason Voorhees and/or his mother. He’s been killed and resurrected again and again and again with increasingly ridiculous and supernatural obstacles. If he wasn’t so scary, you might feel sorry for everything he’s been through. To follow along, here’s how to watch the Friday the 13th movies and television shows in order.

The franchise has inspired video games and novels as well as films. Crystal Lake is technically not the first television series. However, I’m not including Friday the 13th: The Series (1987–1990) on this list because it’s not really connected to the movies. There’s nobody named Voorhees. There’s no Crystal Lake. There’s not even a hockey mask. So let’s stick to the canon, no matter what turns it takes!

The original slasher film about a masked man stalking the teenage camp counselors at a formerly abandoned summer camp on Crystal Lake. Friday the 13th was not only one of the first camp horror movies (camp like sleepaway, not camp like “that’s so camp”) but it also established a lot of the genre tropes that movies like Scary Movie and The Cabin in the Woods spoof.

The second movie in the franchise was the first to officially establish Jason Voorhees as the antagonist instead of his mother, Pamela Voorhees, who had more of a role in the first movie. It takes place only a couple of months after the original film and expands the lore of Crystal Lake.

The third film in the franchise was the first to officially introduce Jason’s hockey mask. Isn’t it interesting how this franchise’s iconography rolled out, one by one? Jason also starts this film injured from the events of the previous film. It is a very direct sequel.

Narrator voice: It was not the final chapter.

The fourth film introduces a nemesis for Jason, aka Tommy Jarvis (not to be confused with the Marvel characters Tommy and J.A.R.V.I.S.) played by Corey Feldman. They think Jason is dead at the beginning of this movie and the end of this movie. Guess what?

Same narrator voice: It was not a new beginning. One year later, the franchise returned like nothing even happened. Jason Voorhees is allegedly dead in this one, but Tommy is haunted by his memory and a copycat killer on a spree of his own. Or was it Jason all along? The twists. The turns.

We know he lives! It’s kind of his thing. The sixth film follows Tommy after he, spoiler alert, resurrected Jason Voorhees at the end of the previous film. It happens. This movie also gets explicitly supernatural in a way that the ones before it do not, and the ones after kinda must.

“New Blood” seems like a fun horror take on “The Next Generation” as a sequel titling convention. More of that, please! Sure enough, the new blood in question is a telekinetic girl named Tina who’s not unlike Carrie White. She accidentally frees Jason while learning how to use her powers. Do they square off, or become murdering besties? Only one way to find out...

It only took eight movies for Jason Voorhees to cross the Hudson River. What did he do next? Four years after The Muppets Take Manhattan, Jason arrived to defy death in even more bizarrely impossible ways. While also killing, of course.

“Evil has finally found a home,” reads the tagline for the film that almost ended the franchise a second time. It’s totally bonkers, involving FBI sting operations, cannibalism, bounty hunters, and a magical dagger. They really went out with a bang, and yet...

Nine years later, the franchise returned in what may be the most 2002 movie of all time. Where does Jason Voorhees go after Manhattan and Hell? Outer space and 400 years in the future, of course! Does this make canon sense? Absolutely not. Don’t worry about it.

For some reason, I thought this movie was made last century. The epic crossover event brings Jason down to Earth for a face-off against another ’80s slasher, the A Nightmare on Elm Street killer Freddy Krueger. It technically takes place “before” the events of Jason X. So if you want to watch in true chronological order instead of release order, flip ‘em.

Six years later it was time for a reboot. Don’t worry about where it fits into the already convoluted timeline. It technically takes place in 2008, the same year that Jason was cryogenically frozen in Jason X, but they’re rightfully not getting into all that. This is just a new, modern, lightly non-canon take on the Crystal Lake classic.

The new series is a different kind of reboot: an origin story for Pamela Voorhees and her son Jason. It takes place before the events of the first film. But you don’t really have to watch it first, you know? Choose your own adventure!

#477. It's Officially "Renter's Regret" Season. Here Are 6 Things to Check Before You Sign the Lease.

The biggest red flags are often hiding above eye level.

Welcome to what I call “renter’s regret” season. After the summer moving rush and the Labor Day weekend chaos, the wave of new leases begins to ebb. You, the renter, start to look at your new home with clearer eyes. And without fail, there’s something annoying you didn’t notice during your tour.

I’ve been a victim of this cycle too many times not to share the tips I’ve picked up. The main thing is to always look up during your apartment viewing. A great agent will spice up the space in front of you, but not above you. The things you’ll notice along the ceiling will tell you a lot.

Learn from my mistakes, and add the six questions below to your tour checklist. It’ll set you up nicely in your new spot, and you’ll avoid renter’s regret.

Our homes all rely on technology, whether you have an intricate movie night setup or a six-in-one air fryer that cooks 99 percent of your meals. So the most important thing? Count your outlets. In every single room, note how many outlets there are. In older buildings, it’s likely there will only be one or two. I can tell you from experience that leads to snaking extension cords through your home and an unsafe reliance on power strips.

It’s just as important to check the placement of each outlet. Are there enough outlets where you want to put your desk? What about for your hair dryer in the bathroom? If you have a reclining sofa or a lamp you want to put in the middle of the room, there needs to be a plug nearby for it.

You may not think to check the level of your floor until you’re placing furniture or hanging art, and then you’re shocked when everything looks crooked. Bring a level tool with you and check your floors, especially on the home’s upper levels.

If bringing a level feels too extra, my go-to is the marble test. I bring a marble with me, put it on the ground, and pay attention to how it rolls. If it immediately heads diagonally, that’s a sign of uneven flooring. How fast the marble rolls will signal how steep the slant is. From there, you can decide if this could be solved with some furniture risers, or if you should skip the unit altogether for one that has better structure.

Many apartment tours happen during the daytime, and leasing agents will leave every window open. If the place gets great natural light, you might forget to look up. This was the case in my current apartment. I didn’t notice there was no overhead lighting in the living room or bedroom until move-in day. I really had to overcompensate with lamps in every corner, and I can’t do anything task-oriented after the sun goes down.

Overhead lighting is hard to miss if it’s a pendant or chandelier, but if it’s recessed, you might not think to look for it. You can change out bulbs if you don’t like the color temperature, but you can’t install lighting if the hardwiring isn’t there. So make sure to flip every light switch, and check that the overhead lighting exists, even if you hate the Big Light.

This one is for all of my fellow plant parents. The direction your window faces will drastically affect your houseplant’s survival odds. If you want big, sprawling houseplants, you’ll need south- or west-facing windows that get a nice balance of bright light and indirect light. North- or east-facing windows still get light, but much lower levels, so your plants would need a little extra care.

This isn’t just for plant lovers, though. It’ll affect your electricity bill. South-facing windows get the most bright light all day, and it’ll heat up your home quickly. Cue higher AC levels and a pricier electric bill. The diffused light from an east-facing window is much easier for temperature regulation.

Seriously, check those hinges and latches. My first New York apartment had a bedroom door that never stayed closed on its own. I had to use a rubber doorstop at all times, removing it whenever I walked through my bedroom door. This became a very annoying part of my home, and a simple open-and-close test could’ve saved me.

Chances are all the doors will be open during your apartment viewing. Make sure to close the door, lock it, and open it again. If you have to struggle with any of those steps, take note. Photograph any faulty latches and ask whether repairs will be completed before move-in. This is especially true with doors and windows that face the exterior of your home. Not only is it a safety issue, but when winter comes, you don’t want to be dealing with that draft.

It’s crucial to catch signs of water damage early on. I’ve lived in three separate houses that experienced some kind of flooding, so I know that bubbling and cracked paint can spell disaster. They’re a sign of unpatched leaks or previous water issues that may have compromised structural integrity. Or, they’re the sign of a landlord who moves slowly to fix things. Either way, watch for puckering paint or jagged and peeled edges along ceilings, around vents, windows, and upper corners.

#480. How to Make Yourself Poop: 14 Doctor-Recommended Tactics for Short- and Long-Term Relief

Let’s be real: Everyone poops. Another universal truth? You’ll probably be constipated at some point or another. In fact, it’s one of the most frequent gastrointestinal complaints in the United States—at least 2.5 million people see their doctor each year for this issue. And understandably, the unpleasant feeling of being backed up (including bloating and stomach pain) will make you look up how to make yourself poop ASAP.

Just to be clear, while everyone’s bowel habits are different (some people poop several times a day while others only poop a few times a week), constipation is typically when you’re passing fewer than three stools a week, according to gastroenterologist Jean Fox, MD.

Meet the experts: Jean Fox, MD, is a gastroenterologist and assistant professor of medicine at Mayo Clinic; Christine Lee, MD, is a gastroenterologist at the Cleveland Clinic; Bharat Pothuri, MD, a gastroenterologist at Memorial Hermann in Houston, Texas; Bryan Curtin, MD, MHSc, is a board certified gastroenterologist and director of The Center for Neurogastroenterology and GI Motility at The Melissa L. Posner Institute for Digestive Health & Liver Disease at Mercy in Baltimore, Maryland; Peyton Berookim, MD, is the director of the Gastroenterology Institute of Southern California in Los Angeles.

Now, to figure out how to get things moving again, you’ll first need to nail down the cause. Constipation can be the result of dehydration, irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), poor diet, or taking various medications, says Dr. Fox. Pelvic floor dysfunction is also a very important (and often ignored) contributor.Below, doctors provide 14 ways that could bring you short- and/or long-term relief. Remember: Always talk to your own doctor for personalized medical advice.

Fiber-rich foods with a high water content, such as raw carrots, apples with the peel on, and avocados, are all great sources of fiber to help get things moving, says Christine Lee, MD, a gastroenterologist at the Cleveland Clinic.

“When consumed, these foods create an osmotic gradient,” Dr. Lee says—that means they force more water to be pulled into the colon during digestion, which then helps ease and prevent constipation by getting things to flow a little more smoothly.

Add more of these fiber-rich foods to your plate if you’re struggling, says Bharat Pothuri, MD, a gastroenterologist at Memorial Hermann in Houston, Texas.

It warrants repeating that a nutritious diet, which should include some natural fiber found in food, is key. If you’re not able to get the daily recommended 20 to 30 grams of fiber through food, you could consider a fiber supplement like one made from psyllium husk, says Bryan Curtin, MD, MHSc, a board certified gastroenterologist and director of The Center for Neurogastroenterology and GI Motility at The Melissa L. Posner Institute for Digestive Health & Liver Disease at Mercy in Baltimore, Maryland. PSA: It’s wise to first consult with your doctor before taking any new supplement.

This is often the first idea that comes to mind when faced with the dilemma of how to make yourself poop. Here’s some welcome news for caffeine lovers: Warm beverages in general, particularly a hot cup of coffee or tea in the morning, can help get things moving, says Dr. Lee. The heat from the coffee can kick your gut into action, but the coffee itself and its high levels of caffeine are also “known to stimulate colon motility,” she says.Be sure to stay hydrated, though. Dr. Curtin says caffeine can act as a diuretic and dehydrate you which could actually worsen the constipation effect. Coffee can work warm or cold. But other cold caffeinated beverages, like iced tea or caffeinated sodas, won’t have the same effect.

Ever been in the middle of a run when you needed a bathroom—STAT? You’re not alone. That’s because “hiking, walking on uneven grounds, jogging, and biking can all increase your metabolism, which in turn increases intestinal motility,” says Dr. Lee.

Also important: If you’ve been busier than usual and have gotten into an exercise dry spell, it might be a clue as to why you’re not pooping as much as you’d like. Making sure to incorporate even short, regular workouts into your routine could be the not-so-secret solution you need, Dr. Lee says.

Polyethylene glycol 3350 (a.k.a. MiraLAX) is made up of compounds that are not digestible and not absorbable, which means they cause a diarrheal effect, says Dr. Lee. At lower doses, it can help prevent constipation, and at higher doses, it can induce diarrhea. So you can adjust the dose if you want to get things moving just slightly, she says.

Dr. Lee also recommends talking to your doctor about trying prescription laxatives if none of the other remedies work. “Prescription drugs are effective, but they can be expensive, so they should generally be left as a last resort after you’ve tried these other methods,” she says.

Another downside to laxatives: Your body can get used to them, so eventually you might not be able to go poop without them if you use them too often.

The squatting position can be mimicked by putting a stool under your feet to raise your knees up, says Peyton Berookim, MD, the director of the Gastroenterology Institute of Southern California in Los Angeles.

Squatting modifies the anatomy by relaxing the muscles in that area while also elevating the part of your colon that makes for easier emptying of the bowel. “The closer you are to a full squat, the easier it will be to poop,” he says.

Applying moderate pressure and massaging your abdomen in a clockwise direction can help you move your bowels, says Dr. Berookim. Colonic massage has been shown to improve constipation, he says.

This can be performed by applying moderate pressure along the horseshoe shape of the colon in your right lower quadrant. Then continue moving up to the rib cage, across the stomach, and underneath the ribs to your left lower quadrant, which is the point where stool is emptied.

“One of the most common causes of constipation is dehydration,” says Dr. Berookim. “When the body is poorly hydrated, it will compensate by withdrawing water from the large intestine (colon) resulting in hard stools.” A good rule of thumb is to drink one ounce of water for every two pounds of your body weight, he says.

Magnesium plays many crucial roles in the body. It supports energy production as well as muscle and nerve function, but it can also help with constipation. “A magnesium supplement (400 to 800 mg daily) is safe for constipation in patients with normal kidney function,” says Dr. Fox. “This works as an osmotic laxative, drawing water into the bowel to provide a soft stool mass and increase bowel action.”

You can also get magnesium from food sources such as almonds, beans, fortified foods, leafy greens, milk, nuts, seeds, and whole grains.

“A stool softener helps ease the passage of stools and can take anywhere from 12 to 72 hours to work,” explains Bharat Pothuri, MD, a gastroenterologist at Memorial Hermann in Houston, Texas. It allows the passage of water and fat into the stool matter and hence allows the stool to pass easier through the colon. He recommends the stool softener Docusate.

You should take it with water and it's generally safe for most people to use. But you may experience abdominal cramping, diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting. Some rare side effects include a rash, shortness of breath, and wheezing. Docusate should not be used on a daily basis, says Dr. Pothuri, as you can become dependent on it.

Foods like dairy products, fatty and fried food, persimmons, and white bread can contribute to constipation. Why? “Generally, foods that are very fatty or very carb-heavy are more difficult for your system to break down and thus can lead to larger more difficult-to-pass stools, resulting in constipation,” Dr. Curtin explains.

You’ll also want to limit red meats because they are low in fiber and generally high in fat, while alcohol can cause both diarrhea and constipation, says Dr. Pothuri. “Patients who drink excessive alcohol tend to be dehydrated and alcohol is also a diuretic, which means we need to urinate more often further compounding the problem,” he explains.

Another common culprit? Chocolate. It contains cocoa, which is a natural diuretic, and most products are rich in fat, milk, and sugar. All three of these ingredients can cause your GI system to become backed up, so if you are a chocolate lover, enjoy it mindfully.

“Many herbal teas have been shown to help with constipation,” says Dr. Pothuri. Senna is the most well-known of these teas. It acts as a stimulant laxative, which encourages the muscles in the intestine to work to have a bowel movement.

FYI: Dr. Curtin notes that senna can actually be more harsh on your system than a laxative such as Miralax, so know that just because something is labeled as “natural” doesn’t mean it’s necessarily “better.” Always talk to your doctor if you're unsure which option is right for you.

Other tea options include ginger, which is best known for treating nausea, but can also help with constipation. Dandelion root contains inulin, which is a dietary fiber, and prebiotics, while chamomile and peppermint can help relax the intestines and keeps things moving. Licorice root also helps keep your intestinal muscles moving. Finally, parsley tea can increase sodium and water within the colon to provide bowel movement, explains Dr. Pothuri.

There are two different types of constipation, occasional and chronic. Though it may seem obvious, the main difference between the two is the length of time. “Occasional constipation is usually constipation in a specific context or setting, such as travel or around the holidays while chronic constipation usually affects a person at least every week and while it may be exacerbated by factors, patients generally do not feel ‘normal’ most of the time,” explains Dr. Curtin.

Although occasional constipation may happen from time to time, you may be wondering when it warrants a trip to your doctor. “Generally, if constipation occurs suddenly without warning or trigger, or if it does not respond to traditional over-the-counter therapies, I would see your doctor,” advises Dr. Curtin.

Bryan Curtin, MD, MHSc, is a board-certified gastroenterologist and director of The Center for Neurogastroenterology and GI Motility at The Melissa L. Posner Institute for Digestive Health & Liver Disease at Mercy in Baltimore, Maryland. Dr. Curtin provides diagnosis and treatment for patients with common and complex digestive health conditions including chronic abdominal pain, GI bleeding, bowel disorders, gastric cancer, and GI motility disorders.

#481. How to Do the Dumbbell Hammer Curl to Build Sleeve-Bursting Biceps

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

BUILDING BIG ARMS is about more than just one move. Yes, the dumbbell biceps curl is the go-to for most guys when they step to the rack looking for a pump—but it's not the end-all, be-all. That’s because your quest for size is also about more than one muscle. To really round out your arms, you'll need to train your brachialis muscle. To train your brachialis muscle, you'll need the dumbbell hammer curl.

The dumbbell hammer curl looks similar to the standard curl at first glance. You grab a dumbbell, raise it up to your shoulder, then lower it back down—but there are some very important nuances between the two exercises. One is fairly obvious: You’ll grip the weights differently, which shifts the focus to that brachialis muscle.

Let Men's Health fitness director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. and Brett Williams, NASM guide you through the move's subtleties, saving you from the bad habits that are keeping you from unlocking your fitness potential. Want to level up your arm training more comprehensively? Once you're ready, check out the holistic Ultimate Arms Recomp program, which provides the plan to build up your biceps (and your whole body) with dedicated workouts and diet tips.

Use this extra insight from Samuel for even more effective reps.

Eb says: This is a curl, but that doesn't mean your body gets to be in anything close to a lazy position. In order to get the most out of this (or any) curl, you need to make sure you're moving only at the elbow joint. To insure that, we need to tighten any point where we might cheat. So tighten your glutes and abs, then squeeze your shoulder blades tight, too. That'll help you erase most of your possible swinging points.

Eb says: Don't just hold the dumbbells during this curl; actively grip them. Think about really tightening your hands around each dumbbell, holding it tightly. This will grant you more control over the dumbbell, and it'll also help insure that your brachialis drives the motion. Added bonus: You'll strengthen your forearms and gripping muscles, too.

Eb says: Curl the dumbbell only as high as it'll go without forcing you to shift your elbow forward, but once you get there, the curl isn't done. Once you're in that position, do your best to squeeze your biceps and arm in general. This little act will force a half-second or so of extra time-under-tension at the top, and it's going to help you develop a stronger mind-muscle connection. It'll also help prevent you from swinging.

Eb says: The most common cheat on any curl is the waist-rocking cheat, where you create motion at your hips to initiate the curling motion. The easy fix to that: Get on your knees.

The position will make you that much more conscious of squeezing your glutes and tightening your abs, which instantly limits your ability to create that waist rock, or other cheats (like arching your back, etc.)

The biggest shift from the standard biceps curl and the hammer curl is in the grip. When you perform a standard curl, you'll use an underhand (or supinated) grip as you raise the weight up. Your biceps will be the main muscle driving that movement. For the hammer curl, you'll adjust your position and use a neutral grip. This shifts the focus to the brachialis, another muscle that sits beneath the biceps and is the primary mover for elbow flexion.

By making this shift, you'll get stronger—and your biceps will pop from any brachialis growth, too. "When we develop our brachialis, it's going to really help push our biceps up and give us a nice 3D look," Samuel says.

There's another big reason to do the hammer curl in addition to the standard biceps curl: You'll be able to train with heavier loads. Standard curls also train biceps supination (rotating the forearm outward), another function of the muscle. Since you're not including that rotation with the hammer curl, you'll have an easier time working with more weight. And as Samuel says: "Bigger weight equals bigger muscles."

Add the hammer curl to your upper body or arm day workouts so you can give your brachialis muscles some focused work.

Start with 3 sets of 6 to 8 reps with heavier weights than you'd use for a standard curl. For extra volume, use lighter weights but more reps—say 3 to 4 sets of 15 to 20 reps.

#483. Everything You've Been Avoiding Is About to Surface Now That Pluto Is in Aquarius

The old ways of doing things are done. Here's what that means for your sign.

Earlier this week, Pluto Retrograde finally ended! Pluto, which is the planet of transformation and destruction, went direct in Aquarius on October 15. And if you've been following Pluto's motions for a while, and you know this last retrograde was intense.

Here's the good news: Pluto doesn't do permanence, it takes what is and remodels it. Even in a sign as traditionally strict and—dare I say—rigidly traditional as Aquarius, innovation and change are coming, because that is simply what Pluto does. Old traditions are dying off, and they're going to have to be revisited.

Aquarius can function as a debilitated sign—even regressive. That is what I think we're about to watch: people refusing the old ways of doing things, looking at their leaders and asking why someone has held the same post for so long. Expect the dissolution of things that run on groupthink—movements that promised meaningful change but turned out to be old power refusing to evolve.

We'll see it in how we innovate, too. Don't be surprised if remote work becomes cool again; once people actually examine why it was shut down, the reasoning won't hold up. It'll look regressive.

So how does Pluto going direct show up in your life? Read your horoscope below, but remember, the changes may not be individual. This isn't your friend changing her morning routine. It's bigger: the communities, workplaces, and organizations around you. The places that held power and resisted new ideas are about to get remodeled. You may find that smaller organizations—or simply new ways of conducting yourself—start to feel normal. If getting ahead used to require arrogance, that playbook is expiring. Let go of the old way of showing up, and make room for something new and meaningful. So ask yourself: what have you been avoiding? Pluto's about to surface it.

You're going to feel this in how community itself is changing—and honestly, that's amazing for you. With the North Node recently moving through your house of community, you've already been asking what it means to have a solid community and how you want to show up in one. You may catch yourself looking back at childhood and spotting the toxic patterns in how people showed up—patterns that served no one. Don't be afraid to walk away from groups or organizations that don't align with your values. Trust this: once you release what's no longer serving you, what you actually need shows up fast.

You're changing how you show up in your career. Maybe you had a boss you felt you had to bow to, or a way of presenting yourself that never quite fit—performing reserve, or keeping people at arm's length until you felt like the odd one out. The tides are turning. You're starting to see that you can thrive by being your authentic self and being a whole lot less critical of yourself. In fact, that might be exactly how you build the lasting relationships that lead to the career you actually want.

You're in a full paradigm shift. Maybe you felt like you'd seen it all and done it all, and you'd gone a little resistant to new ideas. Now you're realizing you don't actually like the old pedagogy—and it's time to revisit some beliefs. A long-distance trip could crack your perspective wide open, showing you the world from an angle you hadn't considered and motivating changes that actually last. Start where the resistance is: the book a friend pressed into your hands, the class you keep postponing, the conversation with someone who sees the world completely differently. That's where the shift lives.

You're transforming the way you see transformation. Funny, right? For a long time, change might have meant disappearing, restricting yourself, or committing to some punishing diet or lifestyle. You're coming to see that none of that is required. Think spiral, not circle: no need to loop. Change one thing here, transform how you do something there, and you get closer to what you're looking for. As they say, insanity is doing the same thing over and over and expecting different results—but doing the same thing with small, deliberate changes? That's evolution.

For the longest time, you thought you knew exactly what you wanted in a soulmate—and in friends. You surrounded yourself with people you trusted. Now you're realizing it's time for something different, and as a fixed sign, admitting that isn't easy. This transit is transforming what you believe relationships and partnerships are. If you thought relationships started with making money together, you may find money matters less than joy—and joy becomes the currency that makes the most sense.

You're changing how you move through your day-to-day life. That health routine you committed to? It might not be delivering what you wanted. If you've been chasing a specific body type or a rigid definition of "healthy," you're starting to loosen your shoulders and widen the lens: there's no one way to be healthy, no one way to have a routine. You may be releasing the way your parents or grandparents set up their lives. Dig a little deeper—it's okay to admit the old way doesn't fit you anymore.

You're changing how you do fun. Fun used to mean the silent retreat or the luxurious event—things that felt impressive but left you a little isolated, since few people could relate. Now you're revisiting pleasure and creativity on your own terms. There's no right way to be imaginative; there's only your way. Pivot where you need to. Take your journal and try something new: if you've always written in first person, try third. See what shifts.

You're changing what home means. Maybe you grew up feeling detached from your environment, so home became just the place you lay your head—or you simply replicated your parents' or grandparents' recipe. This is a new time, and a new way of doing home can make a real difference. Pause and ask what you actually need for a place to feel like home, then start building that. You might even rethink parenthood itself—maybe you don't need a little human. Maybe a puppy heals things you didn't know needed healing.

How you speak and show up is going through changes. Maybe you believed in being loud, boisterous, and blunt—that leading with raw truth meant everyone would understand you. With wisdom, you're realizing that's not how it works. You can hold your beliefs without broadcasting them, and that's not silence—it's discernment. Not everyone needs full access to you. It's okay to sit back, read the room, and open up when there's good reason. Detachment isn't only walking away when people exhaust you; sometimes it's staying unattached until attachment is earned. Try it this week: in your next heated group chat, listen all the way through before you type. You might be shocked what you hear when you're not busy rehearsing your reply.

Your values are shifting. The way your parents or grandparents taught you to live made sense at the time—but the world has changed. Things cost more; what was valuable before isn't valuable, or even attainable, now. And that's okay. Pluto is forcing an honest look at your life as it is now. Staying mindful instead of living in the past is what lets you visualize what you need to build the life you actually want. It's okay to admit things aren't panning out—that's the first step to getting what you need long-term.

You're probably the only sign feeling this one personally—so all my love is being sent your way. You're changing how you perceive yourself. You may have thought you'd built a clear identity from your childhood, your upbringing, your beliefs—but as the world shows you more of itself, you're realizing some of those beliefs were inherited. Some of the issues you've been carrying were never yours to begin with. Many of you are doing real root work now: naming what came from your ancestors and breaking the generational curses you were never meant to carry. You don't have to dissolve who you are—that's not what this transit is about. But becoming who you need to be means accepting that letting go can be part of your identity, too.

Your whole belief system is starting to shift—and I love that for you, even if it feels scary at first. Maybe you committed to a faith-based framework, a set of beliefs you needed for peace. I'm not saying abandon all of it; it may be a genuine protective factor. But this transit wants you to ask an honest question: is your faith driven by fear? Are you using spirituality to detach, to go avoidant? Belief systems can carry us through brutal times—and this one is asking for a little soul work. Did you believe what you believe because you were told to? Some of you will take on new belief systems that actually mean more, stepping away from what your parents and grandparents believed. There's no shame in thinking for yourself. In fact, this transit insists on it.

#484. Protein Powder Prices Are Skyrocketing. Use These Smart Strategies to Save Money and Maintain Muscle.

Whey prices have roughly doubled since 2021. Here's why—and what you can do about it.

MY WIFE AND I use a budgeting app to track our Amazon orders. Last week, we compared three of them.

In five years, whey concentrate has nearly doubled. Now that’s inflation.

Sure, plenty of other things have nearly doubled in that half-decade span, with eggs, electricity, and gasoline hogging the news cycles. Whey protein powder, though, is a more curious case because unlike those aforementioned necessities of life, it used to be totally worthless.

Whey is what's left over when milk curdles into cheese. For most of the 20th century, cheesemakers dumped it into streams or spread it on fields. Federal environmental regulations eventually phased out that practice and so the dairy industry had to find a new way to push whey.

Eventually filtration technology allowed manufacturers to turn whey it into a powder. And not just any powder, but the most complete, most digestible protein-per gram money could buy.

For decades, supplement companies could buy whey cheaply and apply significant markup to what they made with it because the supply was, in effect, free.

Which brings up to today, where demand for whey has spiked and the market expanding well beyond muscleheads. According to a Gallup survey from July 2026, eleven percent of American adults now take a GLP-1 drug, up from 3 percent in 2024. These patients, who find themselves wanting to eat less, are advised to eat lean, easily digested protein like whey powder so they can preserve some muscle while they’re shedding fat. More demand equates to less supply—and it’ll likely get worse.

USDA's benchmark for 34 percent whey protein concentrate averaged 97 cents a pound in January 2024 and $2.14 in August 2026, the highest monthly figure in history. In July, USDA's Dairy Market News put 80 percent concentrate at $12.50 to $13 a pound and isolate near $14, and described bulk buyers as "willing to pay whatever it takes" for available loads.

ONE BULK BUYER knows this "protein math" intimately. "Our cost per kilo is four times higher now than it was four years ago," says Jeff Byers, co-founder and CEO of the supplement company Momentous, who spent four seasons as an NFL offensive lineman, most of them with the Carolina Panthers, before transitioning into the nutrition business. Among the company’s other health and wellness offerings, Momentous sells a single whey product, a 91 percent grass-fed European isolate.

When it comes to why whey prices have soared, Byers points to the case of Glanbia, an Irish dairy cooperative that became the largest producer of American-style cheddar in the United States and the largest milk processor in Idaho. (Glanbia actually bought Optimum Nutrition in 2008 so it could sell its own whey back to lifters in a tub.) But Glanbia, for as massive as it is, still can’t produce enough whey to feed the growing masses.

“[Whey] is expensive because we don't have enough cheese manufacturing to make more whey protein,” Byers says. “You have to have more cheese factories to have more whey protein isolate.” And building cheese factories is slow. "It's hundreds of millions of capital costs. They've got to build buildings, stainless steel filtration systems, dryers. It's not like boom, it's done,” he says.

Brett Massimino, PhD, associate professor and chair of the Department of Supply Chain Management and Analytics at Virginia Commonwealth University and a former bodybuilder himself, calls the root cause supply inelasticity.

"It takes massive amounts of cheese production to yield even modest amounts of whey concentrates,” Massimino says. “If the cheese market does not demand significantly higher output, then whey volumes remain fundamentally constrained."

He cites a cattle problem on top of the cheese problem: With beef prices where they are, "the profitability of beef cows has been much higher than dairy," and farmers with fixed capacity have shifted their herds accordingly.

Despite the efforts of milk-moustache advertising campaigns and raw-milk GOMAD enthusiasts, Americans drink far less milk than they used to, 127 pounds per person in 2024 versus 196 in 2000, and fluid milk has fallen from 46 percent of all dairy consumed in 1975 to under 20 percent. People have kept eating cheese, though.

Per capita cheese consumption was 39.9 pounds in 2024, three-tenths of a pound off the 2023 record, butter hit an all-time high, and total dairy consumption on a milk-equivalent basis sits at 651 pounds a head, up 12 percent over 30 years. The cheese business is on sound footing; it just can't grow fast enough to feed a protein market whose high-protein product launches quadrupled between 2013 and 2024.

"Large food manufacturers such as Pepsi and General Mills utilize massive long-term contracts that provide [those two brands] with cost stability," Massimino says. Supplement companies mostly can't. "Sports nutrition manufacturers rely on spot prices for whey, which are extremely volatile. Those manufacturers have no choice but to buffer against this price volatility by passing price increases on to consumers."

EVEN AS WHEY concentrate costs shoot into the stratosphere, the price of whey isolate—which undergoes extra filtration to remove most of the fat and lactose and is the only type of whey Momentous sells—have remained higher but grown at a less steep rate. Byers explains why: "Because raw prices are so high, brands are putting more concentrate in products than isolate. That's driving up demand for concentrate faster than for isolate, a more premium product. Demand goes up, price goes up."

Whether you should be buying isolate at all is where experts diverge. Richie Kirwan, a senior lecturer in nutrition and exercise physiology at Liverpool John Moores University, has worked with lifters for a decade and tells me, "I've only ever recommended whey isolate to people who have issues with lactose tolerance. If you don't have issues with the amount of lactose in concentrate, isolate is just not worth the extra cost."

Massimino says the same: "For the vast majority of consumers that don't have lactose intolerance, whey protein concentrate provides the exact same muscle-building benefits at a significantly lower price point." Byers, who sells nothing but isolate, argues that a purer input needs fewer flow agents (which prevent the powder from caking), fillers (usually for flavor or to add weight), and emulsifiers (for mixability) to taste right.

Jay Luthar, MD, who runs a longevity practice in Boston and teaches at Harvard Medical School, agrees that such added ingredients can reduce the nutritional value of what you’re buying. He offers a simple shorthand: divide grams of protein per serving by the serving size in grams. "A quality protein powder typically comes in at 70 to 80 percent or higher. If it's lower, you're paying for filler."

Massimino also expects manufacturer corner-cutting and shrinkflation to begin with fillers and other additives. He first advises shoppers to check the unit price, since shrinking the tub is easier than raising the price, then to read the label for "whey blends" that quietly swap in soy or pea, or for manufacturers "substituting non-essential amino acids to artificially inflate protein counts without providing a complete protein source."

His recommendation and Luthar's are the same: Look for certification from a body like NSF Certified for Sport or Informed Sport. "A certified cheaper product is generally more trustworthy than an uncertified expensive one," Luthar says.

BYERS KNOWS THE fitness market and expects that this protein-in-everything fad will pass. "Putting protein in chips doesn't make chips healthier. You can glance at a protein cereal and see that it's three or four grams per serving. This is not protein cereal, guys. They're making a protein claim on three grams."

His hunch is that the buyers propping up those products are the most fickle in the market. When this fad passes, the way the low-fat and gluten-free fads passed, demand for whey will decrease slightly and supply will be loosened, though the golden age of protein pricing is long gone.

Katie Knappenberger, RD, program director for performance nutrition at Northwestern Medicine, isn’t worried about rising protein costs greatly impacting our diets. She tells me that most Americans already exceed the recommended daily allowance of 0.8 grams per kilogram, and that a powder is "generally unnecessary" for anyone who consistently eats dairy, eggs, fish, meat, soy, beans, and lentils.

However, if you’re a lifter trying to hit your 160 grams of protein a day, whey is still cheaper than whole food. Byers's back-of-the-tablecloth math: "Twenty grams of really high-quality whey isolate is still only three bucks a serving."

A meat stick at the checkout is eight grams of protein, a couple grams of fat, and three dollars, and a half-decent rib eye at a grocery store like Whole Foods will cost you $25 to $30 a pound.

Even at its historic high, Byers says, whey "is still the most cost-effective per-gram protein, completely." Physiology professor Kirwan agrees on the muscle science and disagrees on the emphasis on whey, because once you're at 1.6 grams per kilogram, "we don't see any real difference in muscle growth between whey and plant proteins like soy," and if money only covers one supplement, he says creatine, not powder.

Massimino's advice to a broke lifter starting out now: Buy a certified protein and creatine, skip the pre-workouts and largely useless testosterone boosters, and treat your tub of whey as "a convenience tool rather than a dietary staple."

HELP IS COMING. Glanbia is adding 10 million pounds of whey protein isolate at its Clovis, New Mexico joint venture, which will open in 2027. Ireland's Tirlán has €126 million going into a whey plant expected to launch operations that same year. But, as with the power plants opening to feed an increasingly hungry grid, it is too little, too late.

Byers didn’t see any relief whatsoever in his first-quarter 2027 pricing. "The price is not down," he says. "The whey protein I'm buying in January is getting milked probably today."

Cows in the Northern Hemisphere fall off in winter, and some of the European farms Momentous buys from don't milk at all in the cold months. That means next spring's raw material is priced before either of these new plants comes online. "I don't think price relief for whey protein is a six-month or 12-month thing. I think this is a 2028 thing. The price will come back to earth. They will never go back to normal."

The same thing has happened with creatine, the other product Momentous built its name on. "There was zero growth in that market for two decades. All of a sudden, in the last four or five years, after all that research about its cognitive benefits was publicized, boom." One contract manufacturer reported spot pricing on a container of creatine jumping from $85,500 to $630,000 within a year. Byers says the underlying mechanism here is similar to whey: "It's giant factories that take a massive amount of capital expenditure to build, and until those factories come online, suppliers hold the key."

So there you have it: New whey plants come online, cereal companies move on to their next fad (AI-infused corn flakes, perhaps?), the whey price gradually drops from wherever it peaks, and our five-pound tubs settle at $85 or $90 and hopefully remain there for a spell.

Unless you’re willing to switch to soy and pea proteins, five-pound tubs of which can still be found in the $50 range and which a growing body of peer-reviewed research has found to be a viable replacement for whey for most trainees, those increases will take a toll in the long term.

"Ten extra bucks here and there, 20 extra bucks a month, is not nothing for the consumer," Byers concedes. My $54.95 whey isolate was bought at the same time I was still required to wear an N95 mask when I went to grocery stores and gyms—a mere five years ago, yet at the pace everything now moves, it feels like ages.

Oliver Lee Bateman is a historian and journalist based in Pittsburgh. He’s written for The New Republic, Vox, and The Atlantic.

#486. New York City’s Iconic Plaza Hotel Is Closing for 4 Years—Here’s What We Know

The Plaza Hotel has been a New York City icon for over a century. Now, the historic hotel is bracing for a four-year closure to restore its façade. It will shut its doors on January 19, 2027, with a crew scheduled to begin the major, multi-year renovation project on January 20, according to a press release.

The announcement also highlighted the project's complexity, which would undoubtedly hinder the hotel’s day-to-day operations, pose significant safety risks, and disrupt guests if the hotel were to remain open. While the hotel has not announced specific project details, it has noted that careful coordination with stakeholders has been paramount as it considers historic preservation requirements.

The Plaza first opened its doors nearly 120 years ago, on October 1, 1907, quickly becoming a hub for socialites, celebrities, and world leaders, including Nelson Mandela, John F. Kennedy Jr., and practically every U.S. president from William Taft onward. In 1969, the hotel earned New York City landmark status—it was declared a National Historic Landmark nearly 20 years later, in 1986. The Fifth Avenue location has become one of the city’s most recognizable destinations, and it is an architectural masterwork.

Designed by architect Henry Janeway Hardenbergh, who also worked on the Upper West Side apartment complex, the Dakota, the 18-story hotel’s exterior was inspired by the opulence of European palaces. The building boasts dramatic dormer windows, carved stone, terra-cotta veneers, and white brick masonry, all crowned by a sloping green Ludowici tiled mansard roof and soaring chimneys. Inside, a mix of German and Spanish Renaissance Revival styles defines the Edwardian and Oak rooms, while the Palm Court restaurant reflects a neoclassical design scheme.

In addition to its significance to the Big Apple, The Plaza has gained a notable pop culture reputation, appearing in numerous films over the years, including The Way We Were, Sleepless in Seattle, The Great Gatsby, and, of course, Home Alone 2: Lost in New York.

Because of the hotel’s landmark status, the restoration process has to adhere to strict guidelines, which might be the reason behind the lengthy timeline. But as the saying goes, icons never die, and we look forward to seeing The Plaza restored to its true glory.

#487. Garlic Confit

Garlic is already perfect simply cooked into savory dishes (I personally can’t get enough), but can you believe it can get even better? Slow roasting garlic in oil creates a confit, transforming its pungent flavor into something soft, mild, and sweet. You'll get soft, garlicky goodness that can be used in a variety of dishes, from mashed potatoes to garlic butter to spread on your grilled steaks. Plus, you can save the olive oil from roasting the garlic cloves to make a garlic and red pepper–infused oil, perfect for salad dressings or marinades.

Go ahead and preheat your oven to 350°. Grab a 9 x 5-inch loaf pan and toss in your garlic, oil, salt, and red pepper (if you like a little heat). Make sure the garlic is fully covered with oil. Set the loaf pan on a sheet tray, and you're ready to roast!

Pop the garlic in the oven and keep an eye on it. Once the largest clove is soft enough to smash with a fork (usually 45 to 50 minutes), you're good to go. Let everything cool down to room temperature, then place it in a sterilized glass jar, making sure the garlic stays covered with oil. Seal it up tight and stash it in the fridge for up to 2 weeks. When you’re ready to use, spread the softened garlic cloves on toast, or add the oil to virtually any dish.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Time to address the elephant in the room: Is garlic stored in oil at risk for developing the toxins that cause botulism? The short answer is yes. The long answer is that with proper handling and storage, garlic confit is perfectly safe to consume. Since the garlic and oil are cooked at a high temperature for almost an hour, the spores that cause those toxins to develop are killed off, unlike they would be with raw garlic in oil.

Store the cooked cloves in the refrigerator. Storing garlic confit at room temperature is an absolute NO-NO. Let the garlic cool completely, then transfer to a sterilized jar, making sure the cloves are completely covered with oil. Seal the lid tightly and store it in the refrigerator immediately. We'll say it again: This garlic confit should not be stored on the countertop. The refrigerator is the only safe way to store it. For an added layer of protection, you can add a layer of plastic wrap to the top of the oil before closing the jar to keep air out. The oil will solidify as it cools.

#491. 5 Fast-Growing Perennials to Plant in October for a Colorful Small Garden

If you have a small garden, October is a great time to plant perennials that will bring color and fragrance for years to come. They’ll return year after year, making them a lovely investment for flower-loving gardeners.

“October is one of the best times to plant perennials if the borders are looking a bit tired. With the soil still retaining summer warmth and more moisture in the air, roots have time to bed in well before winter sets in,” says Julian Palphramand, head of plants at British Garden Centers.

When space is limited, every plant needs to earn its place. Choosing fast-growing perennials can help you make the most of a small garden, bringing color and fragrance without taking up space for just one season.

We asked the experts which varieties to plant in October. Here’s what they recommend.

“Chrysanthemums come into their own in autumn, and now’s the time to pick them up from garden centers. They like a sunny spot, and regular feeding helps them put on the best show. Many have a classic autumn scent, especially the old‑fashioned and cut‑flower types. It’s worth mulching around the base to help them overwinter,” says Palphramand.

“Caryopteris × clandonensis (bluebeard) is a small deciduous shrub with aromatic grey‑green leaves and dense clusters of blue flowers in late summer and autumn – very attractive to bees and butterflies,” says Palphramand.

“Nepeta (catmint, e.g. ‘Walker’s Low’) is a low, spreading perennial with silvery aromatic foliage and blue‑lilac flowers from early summer into autumn,” says Palphramand. He says the plant is “excellent for edging and scent when brushed.”

“Potted asters can be planted in October if the ground is not frozen or waterlogged,” says Richard Barker, horticultural expert and commercial director of LBS Horticulture. “Although most asters have little to no scent, the foliage of some varieties can release a pine or mint-like scent when crushed.

“As asters are late-season bloomers, they can be used to add color to your garden through autumn, with their flowers coming in shades of purple, blue, pink, red, and white with contrasting yellow centers.”

As with Asters, Barker says geraniums can be planted if the ground isn't waterlogged or frozen. “They can release scent when their leaves or stems are brushed against, and the smell is often described as being herbal or earthy,” he explains. “Hardy geraniums are great for adding colour to a garden as they produce blooms in shades of white, pink, blue, purple, and violet.”

#493. 9 Best Moisturizers for Mature Skin in 2026, According to Dermatologists

Our favorites include Olay, Neutrogena, and Avène.

As you age, your face shows signs of wrinkles, sun damage, and dryness. Getting older is totally normal and, frankly, should be celebrated. Your beautiful expression lines are earned and represent wisdom and happy memories over the years. Dermatologist Brendan Camp, MD, says a gentle cleanser, a moisturizer for mature skin, and sunscreen can keep your skin looking healthy with age.

With fall here, it’s essential to slather on a moisturizer tailored to your skin type and concerns, like perimenopausal acne, a common beauty change for women in their 40s. Face creams and lotions relieve dryness, maintain hydration, and support your skin barrier, says Dr. Camp.

These dermatologist-recommended moisturizers also help prevent your makeup from settling, flaking, and pilling. In just a few weeks, you might need less foundation and concealer because your natural skin becomes a smoother, glowing base. Talk about skincare goals.

There are so many face moisturizers for mature skin available. Amazon has 100 bestsellers alone. Some are geared toward skin types, including dry or acne-prone complexions, while others are more ingredient-focused. That’s where the Women’s Health beauty team comes into play. We’re here to assist with a quick breakdown of how to buy moisturizers for mature skin, according to dermatologists.

First, think about your main skincare concerns and let them guide your shopping.

Are you looking to plump up fine lines and wrinkles? Retinoids, like retinol and retinal, are vitamin A derivatives that promote skin cell turnover, boost collagen and elastin, and minimize discoloration, dermatologist Hadley King, MD, recently told WH in our guide to wrinkle creams. Plus, retinol helps improve the appearance of crepey skin by boosting collagen production and improving the firmness of skin, says Dr. Camp.

Speaking of collagen, your skin naturally loses it and elastin as you age, so slathering on a collagen-supporting moisturizer is helpful. With regular use, you’ll notice a firmer complexion.

If age spots and hyperpigmentation have you down, then choose moisturizers made with brightening ingredients, like vitamin C, niacinamide, and azelaic acid. Glycolic acid, which is naturally found in sugarcane, beets, and pineapple, earned snaps from dermatologist Richard Bottiglione, MD. It’s an alpha hydroxy acid (AHA) that boasts the smallest molecule size, meaning your skin absorbs it easily for quicker results. Notably, it increases collagen production for a smoothing and plumping effect.

Hormonal changes and reduced sebum production make mature skin prone to dryness, says Dr. Camp. He suggests products that improve the skin's barrier function and retain hydration. My favorite is the viral Avène Cicalfate+ Restorative Protective Cream. Your skin will soak up hyaluronic acid moisturizers like a tall glass of water. He’s also keen on ceramides, glycerin, and squalane for moisturizing. Dr. Camp prefers intensely hydrating creams that target fine lines, wrinkles, and dark spots. We’ve got you covered with dermatologist-recommended, editor-tested solutions in this guide.

Forget the myth that face moisturizers for mature skin must be thick and heavy. According to Dr. Camp, the best one for you depends on the formulation.

We’ve covered moisturizers for mature skin since 2021. For our October 2026 update, our beauty team went beyond simple research to find the best moisturizers for mature skin. We began by interviewing four board-certified dermatologists to determine the no-fail ingredients, formulations, and moisturizers that deliver anti-aging and hydrating benefits.

Their suggestions were a starting point for our team—WH beauty director Brian Underwood and me, Nicole Saunders—to test IRL. Together, we bring over 30 years of experience in beauty journalism and hands-on product testing to this guide.

We reevaluated old standbys to ensure they still outperformed the latest drops from 2026. Over the past year, we tested 37 products and narrowed them down to the nine best moisturizers for mature skin actually worth buying.

Testing 37 picks over an entire year allowed us to closely monitor how each face moisturizer applied and how our results evolved. We evaluated their compatibility with various skin types and carefully compared how our results evolved from first impressions to several months of daily use. A few questions we considered include:

During the chilly fall and winter, we checked whether rich face creams left our skin supple and soft. Think gentle, nourishing, and thick formulations that we reply on during retinol recovery nights and during ski trips. We also included lightweight lotions that don’t leave our skin greasy by lunchtime for upcoming warm weather winter destinations.

We tested each moisturizer's performance in different climates, ranging from cool New York falls to trips to the Caribbean. Airplane cabins are notoriously dry, so we also paid attention to how long each hydration level lasts for us while flying. We also wanted to ensure each container didn’t accidentally spill in our toiletry bags—a beauty struggle I know all too well.

Confession time: I’m a beauty editor, and I don’t have perfect skin. Since I’m testing an endless number of skincare products, my face is bound to react. It’s a minor occupational hazard, but one I don’t totally mind to deliver you the most honest product feedback possible.

In addition to their key ingredients and texture, we carefully evaluated their compatibility with various skin types, their performance with wrinkles, dryness, and spots, and how well they layered underneath makeup and sunscreen. In our guide to the best skincare products for your 40s, Dr. Camp and fellow dermatologist Dara Spearman, MD, said that you don’t always have to splurge on products to see results. “A well-formulated drugstore product can work as effectively as luxury creams if it has the right ingredients and consistency,” Dr. Camp said. #497. Building a Fall Wardrobe? Start With These Affordable Uniqlo Staples

These elevated basics bring warmth, polish, and versatility to fall fits.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

I’VE BEEN JONESING for fall since last winter. Winter calls for heavy coats that swallow everything underneath, and summer is just trying to get by with as little on as possible, but fall is the golden ratio of layering: Everything feels balanced, visible, and part of a greater harmonious fit. For this, I go to the mecca of year-round layering staples—Uniqlo.

Uniqlo first evangelized me with its tank tops a couple of summers back. The material feels better than your standard Hanes rib tank: more heft, yet less stiff. I also prefer the fit of Uniqlo’s tanks—perfectly proportioned to wear underneath button-ups and tees, but roomy enough to lounge in. They cost only $10 and last years—I bought a pair when I first moved to New York four years ago, and I still wear them.

Since then, I shop Uniqlo for almost all of my staples. I like that its underwear is comfortable, stretchy, and unbranded, and that it has socks in every color imaginable for either dress shoes or sneakers. They’re cheap, well-made basics, and they come in more colors than I need (but I like knowing I have the option).

Shopping for fall layering pieces is a different dance. Sure, some of them may be hidden under a fleece or sweater, but they’ll still show and should be planned in advance. Case in point: Wearing a tee with a rumpled, saggy collar under a sweater isn’t the polished look I’m shooting for. Uniqlo’s Crewneck Tee has a wide-banded collar similar to vintage tees that holds its shape. The heavyweight fabric adds warmth and helps the tee keep its shape after washes and wear.

Another fall go-to is the waffle henley, which allows me to wear my lightweight jackets well into the season. Waffle—sometimes called thermal—material traps air close to the body for warmth and makes for a solid base layer. The henley placket is also more of a style flex under a flannel or shacket.

Call me neurotic, but I have certain button-ups I wear only under a sweatshirt or jacket in fall and winter. I won’t wear them on their own in the spring or summer because—for me—they don’t carry an outfit; they only facilitate one.

For this, I also look to Uniqlo. I need my layering button-downs to fit closer to the body without feeling constricting, and I want to wash them constantly without being precious with the method. The broadcloth shirt is one of the best white dress shirts out there and costs just under $50. I love wearing it underneath a crewneck sweatshirt or cardigan, and the button-down collar stays in place. I’m also big on flannels under a vest in early fall. Uniqlo has them in the classic buffalo check pattern in a bunch of different colors.

Fall is prime layering season, but it’s also tricky. I’m layering to be seen and want every piece I’m wearing to be noticed without one taking too much from another. Uniqlo saw me through with its summer skivvies, and now it’s time for more elevated basics.
