#498. What the Women in Long-Haul Perimenopause Wish They Knew

For starters: That it can begin as early as your 30s.

When Fiona Byrne entered her 30s, her body started to change. Despite never experiencing acne as a teen, she suddenly had cystic pimples at 32. Then, a few years later, by her mid-30s, her nails became unusually brittle, she started getting dizzy on escalators, her skin itched, and her periods fell closer together. Around 40, she was waking up at 3 a.m. with night sweats, and her hair, which had always been silky, was inexplicably dry. At that point, she started doing some research to connect the dots of this growing constellation of symptoms, and when she finally met with a menopause expert, she got her answer: she was in perimenopause.

“It had been years and years of weird stuff before I had any clue that it was hormone-related. If I knew in my late 30s, I would have been on hormone replacement therapy (HRT) immediately,” says Byrne, now 49—and still in perimenopause.

Most women hit menopause around age 51 or 52, says Mariya Rozenfeld, DO, an ob-gyn and Menopause Society Certified Practitioner (MSCP)—the gold standard certification for physicians who treat patients with menopause—at NYU Langone. Once a woman hasn’t gotten her period for a year, and thus “runs out” of her egg stores, she is considered to be menopausal. Perimenopause isn’t as black and white: it’s the time before you hit menopause marked by fluctuations in hormone levels that cause an array of symptoms. And, they may appear a lot earlier than you’d expect.

Until recently, the median time women spend in perimenopause has been considered to be about four years, but newer studies suggest that the symptoms can last a lot longer and start as early as your thirties. One 2025 study published in NPJ Women's Health on 4,400 American women ages 30 and older found that roughly 55 percent of women 30 to 35 reported perimenopause symptoms that met the criteria for “moderate” or “severe” based on the Menopause Rating Scale. That number rose to just over 64 percent for women 36 to 40 years old. Despite this, most women didn’t seek treatment until they were 56 or older.

“If you think about when perimenopause symptoms really start and when they might start to wane, for most people, that probably takes about 10 years. It's not a short period of time, no matter what,” says Rajita Patil, MD, MSCP, an ob-gyn and director of the Comprehensive Menopause Program at UCLA. In other words, it’s way more common than you might think to be a perimenopause long-hauler.

In the past few years, the conversation around perimenopause and menopause has exploded, fueled, in part, by celebs like Naomi Watts, Penelope Cruz, and Halle Berry sharing their experiences. Social media, too, has allowed women to share resources, stories, and symptoms to better understand this life phase. “People are talking about it. Women are not silent anymore: the demand is there, and it will continue to make care better and make the doctors learn to give the care that these women deserve,” says Dr. Patil.

The age you hit menopause—and perimenopause—is both genetically predetermined by your egg storage, and by each person’s sensitivity to hormone fluctuations. So while some women might start feeling symptoms of perimenopause a few years before menopause in their late 40s, others, like Byrne, can feel it way earlier and more intensely. Here is what women dealing with long-haul perimenopause wish they knew before it started, and what doctors wish more women—and the public at large—knew about perimenopause.

Meet the experts: Mariya Rozenfeld, DO, is an ob-gyn and Menopause Society Certified Practitioner at NYU Langone. Rajita Patil, MD, is an ob-gyn, Menopause Society Certified Practitioner, and director of the Comprehensive Menopause Program at UCLA. Susan Loeb-Zeitlin, MD, is an ob-gyn at NewYork-Presbyterian and director of the Women’s Midlife Center at Weill Cornell Medicine.

A big misconception about perimenopause is that it only starts after periods become irregular. While cycle changes in either direction (more or less frequent; heavier or lighter), are a hallmark sign of perimenopause, there are some more subtle symptoms that can go unnoticed. “In reality, women experience symptoms years before they notice major menstrual changes,” says Dr. Patil. Before anything happens to your cycle, you might notice that you’re not sleeping as well, struggling to cope with stressors, or experiencing more pronounced PMS—that could all be due to perimenopause, Dr. Patil says.

Looking back, Byrne remembers feeling an abnormal amount of rage and irritation at everyday stimuli beginning in her late thirties and early forties; a honking horn from a car on the street would drive her crazy. “It wasn't a normal, logical kind of rage,” she says. “It was just a boiling rage over nothing.” Emma Peterson, 39, noticed similar symptoms in her mid-30s: severe PMS, ovulation pain, trouble sleeping, and increased libido. “I felt like a 14 year old boy a lot of the time,” she says. “I felt so different and kind of feral.”

In their 30s and 40s, most women are hitting their stride in their careers and personal lives—embodying what Dr. Patil calls their “superwoman phase.” So a lot of times, symptoms like fatigue, stress, or irritability are brushed off by women (and their doctors!), as simply being par for the course for this phase of life. But they’re not. When you’re in perimenopause, estrogen and progesterone are fluctuating pretty dramatically, and those fluctuations are what is causing that irritability, increased PMS, and extra fatigue.

Especially right before your period, your hormones’ monthly swan dive can feel way more intense. The PMS you’re used to can suddenly shapeshift into hot flashes, anxiety, fatigue, or even a feeling of “I don’t feel like myself anymore,” says Dr. Patil. “Those rapid hormonal shifts can oftentimes throw the neurotransmitters in the brain off that regulate mood. That's why some people who've never experienced mood symptoms before all of a sudden have mood symptoms.”

Dr. Patil suggests tracking your symptoms of moodiness, anxiety, or irritation and seeing how they fluctuate with your menstrual cycle to help you figure out if your symptoms are hormonal. Having data around your symptoms (like when they happen and how long they last) will also help you work with your doctor to pinpoint ways to alleviate them.

One of the reasons why it’s so hard to pinpoint whether or not you’re in perimenopause is because the symptoms can look so different for everyone. While in perimenopause from age 45 to 56, Laura Standard, now 60, says one of the biggest symptoms was migraines. They were so bad that she’d have to shut herself in a dark room and miss days of work. She had never gotten a migraine before perimenopause, and struggled with them for eight years in her 40s and 50s. (Once she hit menopause, they cleared right up.)

The fatigue of perimenopause was also just completely overwhelming for her: no matter how much sleep she got, it never felt like enough. “One of the worst things for me was bone-crushing fatigue: I felt like someone was pushing an anvil on my head as I was walking around,” says Standard. “I wish I had known it was going to last as long as it did.” In a study of 147,501 symptom logs tracked by women using the MenoLife app, the most common symptom logged for perimenopausal women was fatigue, followed by spotting, cramps, bloating, and headaches.

Perimenopause symptoms can affect so many different parts of your body: some patients may even notice a new onset of heart palpitations (caused by hot flashes), painful joint aches, and irritable bowel symptoms out of the blue, says Dr. Rozenfeld. One of the most frustrating for a lot of patients is brain fog, which comes with unusual forgetfulness, difficulty concentrating, and losing the right words to say mid-sentence.

Looking back, Standard wishes she had more grace for herself and what she was going through—especially because a lot of the time, she didn’t even realize that her symptoms were from perimenopause. When she was experiencing horrible fatigue, maybe it was less important to get everything done at work and at home than it was to listen to her body and take a break.

Upon hitting perimenopause, Byrne realized pretty quickly that alcohol wasn’t going to work for her anymore. A few drinks were all it took to throw a wrench in her sleep and mental health for days on end. She’s not alone: especially in women, alcohol can negatively impact sleep quality and increase feelings of sleepiness, per a 2025 study on alcohol use and menopause in the journal Women’s Health. So the idea that a glass of wine before bed helps you sleep? Not actually true.

Under the surface, the loss of estrogen in your body can impact bone health, muscle mass, the gut microbiome, metabolic health, and more. During the perimenopausal period, women are more prone to developing insulin resistance or weight gain—which can affect their risk profile for diabetes and cardiovascular diseases, says Susan Loeb-Zeitlin, MD, an ob-gyn and director of the Women’s Midlife Center at Weill Cornell Medicine. In this critical time, it becomes all the more important to maintain 150 minutes of exercise each week, avoid smoking and drinking alcohol, stay socially engaged with friends and community members, and ensure you’re keeping up with doctor’s appointments.

Especially since your sleep might be disrupted by night sweats, nailing your sleep hygiene and addressing any sleep disorders (like sleep apnea or insomnia) are going to be key in alleviating your symptoms. “The magic recipe to healthy aging is really in how we live our life: it’s what we eat, how we move, how we sleep, what we employ for stress reduction,” says Dr. Patil. This perimenopausal period of time is a great opportunity to set yourself up for healthy aging in the years to come, and to take a proactive approach in your risk of diseases. “It's a window of vulnerability, but it's also a window of opportunity,” she says.

When she began perimenopause in her early forties, Wendy Wiseberg, 55, was suspicious of HRT. Like many others, she was under the impression that HRT had a large risk of causing breast cancer and heart attacks. (This risk was overstated in a 2002 trial and largely dispelled in a 2017 paper in the Canadian Medical Association Journal. While there is some risk of blood clots and cancers on HRT, it is much lower than previously thought, leading to the FDA’s removal of the black box warning on HRT last year.) Now, at 55, Wiseberg is taking HRT to manage her menopause symptoms. Had she known about HRT and its relative low risk of cancer, she says she might have been open to trying it, or other medications for her symptoms, sooner.

HRT, which usually refers to the use of bioidentical estrogen and/or progesterone, works to treat symptoms of perimenopause by replacing the hormones you’re gradually losing as you approach menopause. It’s FDA-approved to treat hot flashes, night sweats, urinary tract infections caused by low estrogen levels, and osteoporosis. A few studies have even found that HRT therapies help regulate mood and have antidepressant effects in perimenopausal women.

All that said, HRT isn’t for everyone, and it still does carry some risk—the severity of which varies person to person, Dr. Patil says. Luckily, though, HRT is just one of several methods in a toolbox to alleviate perimenopause symptoms. Doctors also use meds like neurokinin-3 receptor antagonists to treat hot flashes, vaginal estrogen for dryness and irritation, psychotropic medications to help with anxiety and depression, and cognitive-behavioral therapy to help with sleep and mood. While there is a lot of room for research and more medications to meet the demand of perimenopause care, talking about treatment options with your doctor might help save you a lot of pain and discomfort.

While Peterson’s primary care provider told her she was in perimenopause, she says her ob-gyn is hesitant to treat her for it because she’s under 40. She feels “gaslit,” and worried about asking for the medication she needs, like cream to treat the vaginal discomfort she’d been dealing with. “I'm just bracing for pushback from professionals. Not getting the treatment that you need feels like a waste of time,” she says.

Menopause and perimenopause are still widely misunderstood in the medical community. One study found that 93 percent of graduating residents in internal medicine, family medicine, and obstetrics and gynecology didn’t feel comfortable managing patients with menopause. This leaves patients in the lurch, with the onus of recognizing perimenopause and finding care falling squarely on their shoulders.

“All of the doctors were saying that perimenopause started around 45, and I just knew that was wrong,” says Byrne. She researched doctors in her area who had experience treating perimenopause, and met with an ob-gyn who told her that perimenopause could very well start closer to 40. Byrne finally felt understood—and finally got her hands on HRT.

The Menopause Society, which is a national organization that trains health care professionals in menopause care, has a search tool you can use to find a specialist in your zip code, or to search for telehealth providers. “There's no one way that women go through this transition,” Dr. Loeb-Zeitlin says. “A trained menopause provider can give you the individualized approach to your own transition.”

Despite the fact that half the population will go through perimenopause, it can feel extremely isolating in the moment—especially when your symptoms start earlier, or feel more intense, than the people around you. “Looking back, I wish I had talked to my female friends earlier about it—I didn't really know what was happening. We could have all supported each other from the beginning,” says Standard.

The biggest issue, she says, is just that people aren’t talking about it. Conversations about perimenopause aren’t happening in mainstream media, at the doctor’s office, in health classes, or even among mothers and their adult children. How do you know what to expect, or even recognize what you’re going through, if you don’t have an example?

After years of being fed up with the lack of information and representation of perimenopause, Byrne took to social media armed with her childhood dolls. She created the Peri Pals, where she acts out skits about perimenopause to spread awareness about the often frustrating symptoms. Since starting the account in April 2026—about six months ago—she’s racked up 132,000 followers and countless comments from women about how they can relate to scenarios about forgetting words in moments of brain fog, increased sensitivity to noises, and mood swings. “I didn't know that many people were feeling like that, too. It's validating,” says Byrne.

This period of life is challenging, and it’s important to let people help you navigate it. That could mean inviting a partner or family member to doctor’s appointments, spending time with friends who are also going through perimenopause, connecting with a practitioner who validates and understands what you’re going through, or even reading books in the ever-growing genre of perimenopause memoirs and guides, the women in this article say. “Building yourself that community with your family, friends, and workplace is the recipe to going through this in a positive way,” says Dr. Patil. “Nobody should just be suffering by themselves.”

#499. The 15 Best Sandalwood Colognes for Men

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

Check the list of scent notes in your favorite colognes and chances are you’ll spot sandalwood lurking somewhere in most of them, whether that’s up top, in the heart, or holding things down at the base. It’s the ultimate chameleon of perfumery, pairing easily with spices, citrus, florals, and pretty much anything else a perfumer can throw at it. Sandalwood can take center stage with its creamy, warm, subtly sweet character, or it can provide a smooth, woody foundation that lets flashier notes be the star of the show.

The ingredient itself comes from trees in the Santalum genus—most famously Indian sandalwood, which has been harvested for more than 4,000 years—and its aromatic heartwood and roots are distilled to produce the essential oils used in fragrance. In recent years, sandalwood has gone from being a reliable supporting player to a bona fide headliner, thanks to the rise of “santal” fragrances. One especially famous bottle on this list has become so ubiquitous that you’ve almost certainly smelled it in a chic hotel lobby or on one of your coworkers (but we’ll let you figure out which one that is).

With so many sandalwood colognes out there, declaring an objective best is basically impossible. Still, we rounded up some of our favorites. These colognes use sandalwood in especially fun, distinctive, and even sophisticated ways we’d urge you to try out.

The bolder version of the original Sauvage, this still has the fresh, blue quality that makes the original so great but dials up the warmth with a lot of sandalwood that gives way to a base note of tonka bean and amber (two notes that really complement sandalwood). The warm, woody quality of sandalwood sticks around on your skin for hours; seriously, the longevity here is something to behold. It’s a welcome take on a classic.

There’s a misleading simplicity to this scent that one could argue is the olfactory version of “quiet luxury.” The pepper in the top note gives it a kick of spice, a double dose of frankincense (olibanum) delivers a luxurious resinous quality, and the smooth base of sandalwood isn’t as apparent as some other sandalwood colognes but still gives it a warm, smooth, woody longevity that sticks around for hours. It’s like a perfect cashmere baseball cap or fur-lined Chelsea boot—a comfortable staple that’s deceptively high-quality.

Say what you will about the ubiquity of Santal 33, but it’s become one of the most popular and distinctive fragrances of our time. It’s instantly recognizable thanks to its smooth, woody, leathery vibe that dries down to reveal more greens and florals without losing the hip, wood-forward aspect that makes it so popular. Think of it as the blue jeans of fragrance—a staple that everyone can wear.

Tom Ford doesn’t do subtle very often, and even with this one, there is a lot going on. The spicy opening, the floral middle notes, and the rich deep base of wood, musk, and oud all sound like they’re going to overwhelm the senses. In practice, however, a deft hand created this, so everything intermingles like a symphony, and the result has surprisingly low projection but is still attention-grabbing enough that people will notice—and want to come in closer for a better whiff.

Everything the House of Creed does is richly layered and exceedingly elegant, and this sandalwood fragrance is no exception. It dials up the warmth of the note with an opening spray of ginger and coriander (along with some fresh citrus to wake you up) before smoothing everything out with sandalwood and lavender. Interestingly, the sandalwood is in the middle note here, which is okay because it sticks around even once the warm, creamy base notes of tonka bean and musk come through. It’s a cozy, inviting cologne that’s perfect for colder weather.

Warm, rich, and resinous is how we would describe Giardini di Toscana’s Christos. With the first spritz, you get a wave of deep amber and smoky incense up top, which set you up for even more amber and incense at the heart. That pair is definitely the star duo here, but sandalwood adds a subtle creaminess at the base that brings out the resinous scent notes beautifully.

Maison d’Etto is a newer fragrance house, but it has already made a huge splash. Every fragrance is inspired by a horse the founder has spent time with, and Durban Jane has become the darling of the brand. Her eponymous eau de parfum is a comforting blend of warm woods, powdery florals, and soft spices, which creates a soft aroma you want to cuddle up with. Hours after you spray this scent, what lingers on your skin is a gorgeous trio of sandalwood, iris, and ambrette.

Oftentimes, sandalwood can read as slightly sweet, which is why it pairs well with other sweet notes like vanilla, as evidenced in Eauso Vert’s Vanilla Ambers. Here, sandalwood and vanilla bean anchor the fragrance with a creamy, warm base, which is sweet but never too sweet, thanks to the sandalwood. Subtle spices at the top and floral undertones make this EDP not just a vanilla fragrance but something more.

D’Orsay makes some of the most sophisticated fragrances out there and always puts a fun twist on whatever scent note a particular cologne focuses on. Nous Sommes Amants M.D. is a perfect example of that: It’s not a super complex fragrance—its base is a simple blend of sandalwood and cedar—but spicy black pepper at the top and smoky Palo Santo at the base provide an interesting contrast to the creamy sandalwood that provides the foundation for the whole thing.

Crack jokes about Old Spice being your grandpa’s cologne all you want, but it doesn’t change the fact that the brand still makes some great fragrances—and for under $20. If you’re looking for a solid sandalwood scent on a budget, this cologne mist will do. It’s a simple blend of citrus water, sage, and sandalwood, and the lasting effect is fresh and woody. It’s reminiscent of the famous Abercrombie Fierce cologne, which we also unironically love.

The sandalwood in the middle note of this very woody fragrance acts as a smooth, warm bridge between the floral top note and the wood-heavy base. The warm sandalwood is a subtle temper to the more distinctive rosewood and cedar but is a welcome addition, along with white musk, to turn what could be a lot of wood into something more wearable. It’s the thinking man’s wood fragrance.

This elegantly masculine scent is all about the clean feeling it gives you. It’s reminiscent of a barbershop, with the soapy lavender and the fresh citrus clearing the way for smooth sandalwood and tonka bean to ground everything. It gives the impression that you’re the kind of guy who gets regular barber shaves and definitely knows his way around a safety razor. It’s traditional and masculine yet modern and subtle at the same time.

There’s an underlying sweetness to this fragrance that amps up the woodiness in an interesting and unique way. Sticky fig, sweet jasmine, and subtle lily-of-the-valley play off the sandalwood and cedarwood in the base to create a push-pull between earthy and airy. Paired with the skin-scent musks, it’s a deeply inviting scent that’s light enough to wear during the day but definitely sexy enough that it can (and should) be worn at night.

This deep, rich, uber-elegant fragrance is not for the shrinking violet. It’s one of the ultimate sexy fragrances, and when you wear it, it delivers a sensual draw that’s unmatched. It’s spicy and warm, with a hefty dash of musk that really amps up the carnal factor. Then, of course, we have the sandalwood, which, along with tonka bean and amber, creates a smooth, warm feeling like silk slipping over skin. Wear it when you want extra swagger.

There’s no denying the citrus factor in this incredibly fresh, “blue” scent that dials it up even further with a dash of spice. But the main difference between this eau de parfum and the original eau de toilette is that this one is more wood forward, which is where the base notes, including sandalwood, shine through. It blends well with the fresh citrus and spices of the top and middle notes and adds a masculine vibe, not to mention longevity, to the entire concoction.

#500. The First Thing Home Buyers Notice When They Walk In, According to Real Estate Experts

Doing so is critical to selling your property fast.

When it comes to selling your home, you might think square footage or high-end finishes seal the deal with buyers. But seasoned real estate pros know that something far more elusive actually sways them: the first impression.

That’s right—the first 10 seconds of walking into a home can determine whether someone sees themselves living there or simply can’t wait to leave. It’s less about the layout and finishes and more about the immediate feeling the space creates.

Catherine Juracich, a real estate advisor at Corcoran, puts it simply: “You can generally tell within the first minute how someone is connected to the home. They show it through their body language, the speed at which they move, and how thoughtfully they look around.”

That initial connection is often so strong that it becomes instantly visible. Karen Feinstein, a real estate advisor at Compass, has seen it happen time and again. “You can tell immediately,” she says. “You see it on their faces and in their eyes the moment they walk in; it’s either 'Oh, wow, this is nice,’ or ‘Oh no, not for me.’”

Jenny Wolf, interior designer and founder of The Huntress New York, says that first impressions go far beyond visual appeal. “The first 10 seconds are the most important, because it’s all about how you feel,” she explains. “Home is a feeling. You want to create an environment that captivates all the senses—smell, lighting, sounds.” And that makes crafting the perfect first impression both an art and a science. Read on for expert-backed tips for how to hook buyers from the start.

Before buyers even set foot inside, your home’s exterior sets the tone. “If the outside doesn’t look inviting, it’s hard to recover from that initial reaction,” says Juracich. “Things like a freshly painted door, clean windows, and well-maintained landscaping can make all the difference.”

Feinstein agrees, noting that small details often matter more than sellers think. “People want to see that a home has been cared for. Simple fixes like power washing the walkway or adding potted plants near the entrance can instantly make the house feel more welcoming,” she says.

Wolf also emphasizes the importance of creating a focal point. “Whether it’s a beautiful wreath on the door or an oversized planter, having one striking element draws the eye and sets an intentional tone from the moment you arrive,” she says.

Smell is one of the most powerful but overlooked elements of a first impression. “Scent is subconscious, but people remember it,” says Wolf. “At The Huntress, we spray a perfume called Isola Rosa and light a Cire Trudon candle in Ernesto. It’s beautiful and creates a nice masculine-feminine balance that everyone responds to.”

She also recommends simple, warm scents that feel welcoming. “A clean house should smell like a clean house, but not like bleach,” she says. “Lighting vanilla or cinnamon candles is also a great choice because they’re subtle but comforting.”

A visually stunning entryway is key, but it’s not just about having the trendiest decor. “The biggest mistake I see is clutter,” says Feinstein. “Get rid of personal items and unnecessary decor. Buyers need to see a space where they can imagine their own lives.”

Juracich agrees that creating focal points can make a big difference. “A styled console, a statement light fixture, or a gorgeous flower arrangement can draw people in and give them something to connect with,” she says.

Wolf highlights the importance of creating vignettes that tell a story. “A welcoming rug, a console with a mirror, a small bench, and a candle can set a mood right at the entryway,” she says. “It doesn’t need to be overdone—just enough to feel inviting and purposeful. It’s about giving people a hint of what’s to come as they move through the space.”

Lighting is a crucial way to set the mood the moment someone steps inside, but it’s not just about having the right fixtures; it’s about balancing natural and ambient light. “Any kind of blue lighting should be avoided,” advises Wolf. “It should just feel warm. I really like a soft, white kind of mood lighting. Nothing over 2700 Kelvin, and dimmable if possible.”

Feinstein agrees, saying that upgrading light bulbs is an affordable way to enhance your first impressions. “It’s a small investment that can change the whole feel of a room,” she says. “Natural light is key," Juracich adds. "It’s one of the most desired features in a home. If the home is bright and airy, it just feels clear, open, and positive. I try not to show it when the sun’s completely down if it’s north-facing. I prefer to schedule showings in the morning to naturally create those elements.”

While visuals and scents play a big role in the ambiance of your home, sound shouldn’t be ignored. “Music can completely change the energy of a space,” says Wolf. “I’ll often put on Carla Bruni or soft jazz. It’s inviting without being distracting, and it just makes the place feel alive.”

Feinstein also sees the value in background music. “I love music in the background,” she says. “Nothing too specific—just something classic. And I’ll keep it on low, so it creates a subtle, comforting atmosphere.”

At the end of the day, creating an enticing home for buyers is not just about designing a beautiful space; it’s about making people feel at home from the moment they walk in. “It’s music, it’s visuals, it’s lighting—it’s magic,” says Wolf.

But it’s not just about mood—it’s also about aspiration. “People are also trying to buy into a lifestyle. And everyone wants a lifestyle that's above what they have,” says Juracich. “You need to think about creating an elevated experience as best you can with what you are given.”

#502. The New Rolex Oyster Perpetual Is Elegantly Exuberant

To celebrate a major milestone, Rolex decided to play with a prime building block: its name.

Rolex is so closely associated with discipline, precision, and deliberate, unhurried evolution that when the brand lets loose, the results can feel almost subversive. And when Rolex has an occasion to celebrate, well, the brakes really come off. The new Oyster Perpetual 36 “Jubilee” dial marks a century of Oyster history not with nostalgia but with kaleidoscopic typography and a sensibility approaching Pop Art. That contrast is the point: Technically, Rolex remains obsessively controlled. Visually, it takes perhaps its most powerful symbol—its own name—and turns it into a painting.

Ten lacquer colors are pad-printed across the dial, which makes the Rolex signature dissolve into a geometric composition. Piet Mondrian is one reference point, with the grid becoming a playground for color and rhythm. But there is something distinctly Warholian about the repetition of the Rolex name. Like soup cans or Marilyns multiplied across a canvas, the familiar logo is repeated until branding becomes pattern and commercial identity becomes image.

Beneath all that exuberance is a direct descendant of the original 1926 Oyster. The 36mm Oyster-steel case is water—resistant to 100 meters, while the three-link bracelet, developed in the late 1930s, includes the signature Oysterclasp and Easylink extension. Inside, the automatic caliber 3230 delivers 70 hours of power reserve. Rolex hasn’t abandoned its codes, it has simply started playing around with them. For a brand famous for rigor, there is something satisfying about occasionally coloring outside the lines.

#503. Everything Previous James Bond Cast Members Have Said About the Next 007

Many actors who’ve previously starred in the franchise have feelings about the big race.

Most people have an opinion about who should be the next James Bond. Gary Oldman is certain it’s going to be his Slow Horses costar Jack Lowden, while the writer of the latest Bond novels isn’t a fan of any of the front-runners. A bunch of people think it’ll be Callum Turner, while Aaron Taylor-Johnson seemed like a dead certainty earlier this year.

However, some people have a better understanding of what it takes to play 007—namely the actors who’ve already had starring roles in the franchise. We’ve rounded up everything that old-school cast members have said about Bond’s rebirth.

Let’s begin with none other than the Bond before Daniel Craig, the legendary Pierce Brosnan: the second non-British Bond and the first Irish Bond. He said that it’s a “given” that the next Bond should be British in an interview with The Telegraph in 2025, though he had said the year before to the BBC that “Cillian [Murphy] would do a magnificent job as James Bond,” at the Oscar Wilde Awards.

Brosnan had previously also endorsed Aaron Taylor-Johnson, whom he acted alongside in 2009, saying on RTÉ Radio the year before: “He was the greatest in [The Greatest]. So, yes, I read the news about his possibilities of being a Bond, so I would definitely tip my hat to the fellow. I think the man has the chops and the talent and the charisma to play Bond, very much so.”

Meanwhile, another Bond, Australian actor George Lazenby, told TMZ that he thought Taylor-Johnson could “handle the stunts” and would be a good choice if he could “do the character justice.”

Jonathan Pryce, who played the villain to Brosnan’s Bond in Tomorrow Never Dies, was also a fan of Taylor-Johnson. Speaking on Good Morning Britain in 2024, he said: “[Taylor-Johnson has] grown into a wonderful actor, and when he was a little younger, he did this extraordinary action film where he played a superhero. [...] Yeah, he’d be a great Bond.”

Daniel Craig’s first Bond outing was made most memorable by the inimitable Mads Mikkelsen, whose first choice for Bond was a favorite for a long time. “I think that Idris Elba was talked about for a while,” he once said. “I think he’s an amazing actor.” However, he did point out that Elba was nearly the same age as Craig, and that may set things back if the production was looking for a younger Bond this time around.

Andrew Scott, who also played a Bond adversary in Spectre, endorsed Paul Mescal, his All of Us Strangers costar, back in 2023 while the filming for Gladiator II was taking place. “He’d probably be a great James Bond,” Scott added.

Meanwhile, Naomie Harris, the actress who last took on the role of Bond’s associate Moneypenny, has a different idea: “I think Regé-Jean Page would be amazing. I’d love Regé to be the next James Bond. But who knows? I don’t know what’s going to happen.” Michael Fassbender, who starred alongside Harris and Page in Black Bag and was also considered a potential Bond once upon a time, agreed with her endorsement.

Rosamund Pike, whose breakout part was as Bond girl Miranda Frost in Die Another Day, picked her Saltburn costar Jacob Elordi, saying: “He’s a fantastic actor. He certainly looks like a great Bond. I mean, why not?” Pike wasn’t the only Brosnan-era Bond girl with a take on who should step into Bond, however, as Michelle Yeoh of Tomorrow Never Dies would like to see someone a little less famous step into the role. “That’s the interesting thing about Bond,” she said. “They always find a very, very good actor but possibly not such a well-known, Oscar-winning actor.”

Not all of them feel so strongly, however. Léa Seydoux recently shared that she doesn’t want to get involved with any of the major Bond speculation but that the actor “needs to be layered.” She also expressed some skepticism about the franchise becoming “American” under the production of Amazon MGM Studios and asserted, “I hope they will keep the British spirit.”

#505. Millions of Women May Have This Painful Condition—and Many Have No Idea It Even Exists

For women living with unexplained pain, swelling, and "stubborn fat," a diagnosis can take more than a decade.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

When Aisha Durham, a professor of communication at the University of South Florida, entered perimenopause in her 40s, she began noticing changes in her body—a not uncommon occurrence for many women at this stage of life as hormone levels shift. But Durham sensed these changes were something else, given the severity of her symptoms.

First came the inflammation: swelling she describes as pervasive and so painful, at times, that she spent days bedridden. Next came the nodules: small, hard bumps that trailed up and down her legs.

Visits to multiple doctors resulted in a litany of diagnoses—and misdiagnoses. One physician suspected the chronic inflammation was due to undifferentiated connective tissue disease (UCTD), a systemic autoimmune disorder, and put her on hydroxychloroquine as treatment. (It wasn’t UCTD.) Another looked at Durham and told her she was simply fat, and that her fat stores were shifting due to perimenopause. (It wasn’t “typical” fat.) A third surmised Durham’s pain was due to fibromyalgia. (It wasn’t fibromyalgia.) The nodules in Durham’s legs were, at turns, diagnosed as a spider bite and an allergic reaction. (Wrong on both counts.)

A dutiful patient, Durham heeded doctor’s orders to overhaul her nutrition and exercise to lose weight. “I hired a dietitian. I did one-on-one pilates sessions, but everything was hurting,” she says. These lifestyle changes did little to relieve her symptoms, and after months of being misdiagnosed or dismissed entirely, Durham was desperate for any clues.

She had a hunch her chronic inflammation might have something to do with fluctuating hormone levels, and after falling down a YouTube rabbit hole, she landed on a scholarly presentation by endocrinologist Karen Herbst, MD. In that video, Durham found her answer.

“She showed pictures, and I said, ‘Those legs look like mine,’ ” Durham recalls.

The photos? They depicted patients who had been diagnosed with lipedema, a chronic, incurable condition that affects mostly women and is characterized by a disproportionate and symmetrical buildup of often painful fat in the lower body and sometimes in the arms and/or lower trunk.

The imagery was a revelation for Durham, who decided then and there that if none of her local doctors would take her seriously, she would fly to Arizona for a consultation with Dr. Herbst herself. About six months later, in Dr. Herbst’s office, she got the diagnosis she’d been relentlessly seeking: stage 2 lipedema.

“I cried,” Durham says of the moment. “I felt lighter. It didn’t get rid of the condition at all. It didn’t make it better. But it was just so relieving to have a doctor confirm what I was experiencing.”

Cases like Durham’s are not unusual. Though it’s estimated that around 5 to 12 percent of women in the U.S. have lipedema, it still takes, on average, about 10 years to receive a diagnosis, according to the Lipedema Foundation, which is dedicated to advancing research and awareness of lipedema. That delay is due to a lack of awareness around the condition as well as frequent misdiagnoses. That’s a decade of doctor visits, patronizing dismissals, and unnecessary pain. And even then, a diagnosis is just the first step in what will likely be a long journey of managing or mitigating symptoms—one that is often emotionally, mentally, physically, and financially fraught.

Despite so many American women walking around with lipedema, few have heard of it or been given any reason to suspect the dimpling on their legs is anything other than cellulite. Though the condition has drawn a few headlines recently—singer Doja Cat speculated on TikTok earlier this year that she may have lipedema—it still remains a largely under-the-radar and underdiagnosed condition.

It might be surprising to learn, then, that lipedema isn’t a new disorder. It was first described by two Mayo Clinic physicians, Dr. Edgar V. Allen and Dr. Edgar A. Hines, in 1940. And researchers say artworks from as far back as 3,000 BC have recorded the telltale pear shape of the lipedema body—slim torsos punctuated by almost cartoonishly large hips, thighs, and butts—suggesting that even bygone civilizations recognized lipedema, even if they may not have had a name for it.

The tag that Dr. Allen and Dr. Hines landed on is a portmanteau of lipid (fat) and edema (swelling). It’s a bit of an unfortunate moniker given its closeness to a separate yet similar condition called lymphedema, which causes abnormal, usually asymmetrical tissue swelling. But they are, in fact, two distinct diseases, so in order to distinguish them, some in the lipedema community have tried brainstorming a new name (none have stuck), while others have leaned into a pronunciation in which the first syllable rhymes with “sky” rather than “skip.” (The American English pronunciation is generally LIP-uh-DEEM-uh, though if you talk to enough people about it, you’ll likely hear it pronounced both ways.) To confuse matters even further? In some cases, lipedema and lymphedema may present as comorbidities in a patient. (More on that in just a bit.)

There’s no known cause for lipedema, though it’s generally considered to have a strong genetic component. It often shows up—or worsens—during periods of hormonal fluctuation. An easy mnemonic device to remember for this is the three P’s: puberty, pregnancy, and peri/menopause. It’s widely believed to be a connective tissue disorder, but that still seems up for debate. It’s also been tentatively (and, in many cases, anecdotally) linked to a host of comorbidities, including hypermobility, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, ADHD, and polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS, formerly called PCOS). Again, more research is needed.

Lipedema is diagnosed by type and in stages. Type indicates where the fat is located on the body. Type I is fat between the belly button and hip. Type II is fat between the pelvis and knee. Type III is fat between the pelvis and ankle. Type IV is fat between the shoulder and wrist. Type V is fat between the knees and ankles. Stage indicates the severity of symptoms. Stage 1 is some accumulation of soft subcutaneous fat with largely smooth skin that might have small nodules under the surface. Stage 2 is more severe dimpling or indentations with larger, more prominent nodules and hardened fat deposits that may be fibrotic. Stage 3 is marked by larger fat deposits that may start to overhang or otherwise noticeably extrude from the body. And then there’s stage 4, which is also known as lipolymphedema, which, as hinted above, occurs when both lipedema and lymphedema are present.

Women may progress all the way to stage 4 or stay fixed in an earlier stage. Some may feel no pain with lipedema; others may feel intense pain during flare-ups. How and why lipedema progresses in some and not others is still one of the mysteries researchers are unraveling. In some cases, the pain and deformities caused by this excess fat accumulation can become so extreme that a woman struggles to walk or go about the daily tasks of life.

“I have several family members who are fully disabled by this disease to the point of being in wheelchairs or having to walk with walkers or walking aids,” says Kasi Grosvenor, a 45-year-old project manager in Richmond, Virginia, who was diagnosed with lipedema at the age of 40. “I’ve watched the progression of this disease through many family members up my dad’s line—that is the line where it came in our family—and I didn’t want to get there too.”

So why does it typically take so long for women (the condition is rare in men, FYI) to receive a lipedema diagnosis? Infuriating stat alert: The average age for diagnosis, per the Lipedema Foundation’s registry, is 48. As in the case with many underdiagnosed and misunderstood women’s health conditions—be it PMOS or endometriosis—much of the delay can be traced back to systemic issues that don’t have a quick or simple solution, says Jonathan Kartt, CEO of the Lipedema Foundation.

“Lipedema really sits at the intersection of two areas that medicine has always been really slow to fund and slow to take seriously, and those are chronic disease and conditions that primarily impact women,” he says.

Indeed, a surprising number of clinicians are as unaware of lipedema as the average Jane on the street. “Medical schools really didn’t historically teach it,” Kartt says. While certain specialties, like vascular medicine, do have relevant training, Kartt says the real gap is primary care—often a patient’s first stop on the road to a diagnosis.

Another barrier to diagnosis is the lack of diagnostic tests for lipedema. Peeing in a cup, swabbing your mouth, or rolling up your sleeve for a blood draw will get you nowhere. Diagnoses are made through a thorough review of the patient’s medical history as well as an exam. Physicians will typically do a visual assessment (checking for signs like irregular fat distribution) and a physical assessment (feeling for nodules or fibrosis, which distinguish lipedema fat from run-of-the-mill cellulite).

If a physician does suspect a patient has lipedema, there’s yet another hurdle: In the U.S., there’s no diagnostic code for lipedema. The World Health Organization has classified lipedema as a distinct disease in the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11), but the U.S. is still using the older ICD-10, which does not. While that might sound like a simple paperwork issue, it’s much more consequential than that. Diagnostic codes are necessary for insurers to determine that they will pay for particular procedures or treatments relevant to the diagnosis. Without a code, the patient may be left to pay for their treatments out of pocket or go without treatment altogether. To get around this, clinicians have had to get creative in their diagnostics, using codes for similar or blanket conditions (such as edema).

“If we want to give a woman a diagnosis of lipedema, we really have to give her six or seven different codes that look like lipedema codes,” says Sarah Whitehead, an advanced registered nurse practitioner and founder of Lumina Vascular Health & Laser Clinic.

Diagnostic codes also help researchers track the prevalence of a disease, which is one reason why estimates of lipedema sufferers always have an asterisk next to them (depending on which study you read, rates vary from the single digits up to 39 percent). But there is some hope: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention have approved a dedicated code for lipedema that should go into effect in October 2027.

“That sounds small, but it changes everything downstream,” Whitehead says. “It lets us count how many women are affected and make a real case for research funding.” She cautions, however, that true change will require updated insurance policies around the code so women can actually access care.

One final (and big) reason many women struggle to get a lipedema diagnosis: A physician untrained in lipedema may conflate the condition with obesity. While the two can coexist and frequently do, lipedema fat behaves much differently than regular fat. It generally doesn’t respond to diet and exercise, meaning there’s no real way to “burn” it off. So dismissing lipedema as simply an issue of needing to lose a few pounds is not only plain wrong (especially given that women at any BMI can have lipedema), but it’s also caused many to needlessly suffer from painful symptoms for decades.

Caroline, a 40-year-old journalist living in Los Angeles, is one such woman. As an active kid who grew up playing soccer and participating in the marching band, Caroline was first told her size was an issue in high school: “My doctor said, ‘We have to do something about your weight or else it will spiral out of control,’ ” she says.

This being the early 2000s, Caroline turned to weight-loss methods many Gen X and millennial women will recognize: She signed up for Curves and started drinking SlimFast. In college, Caroline gained the Freshman 15 and then some, so during her senior year, she joined Jenny Craig. “I’d take my baby carrots and salsa to the movies as a snack,” she says of the restrictive meal plan.

Caroline continued on in much the same way after she graduated from college and moved to New York—to little effect.

“You can only restrict yourself severely for so long before your brain can’t take it,” Caroline says. “That’s when I decided to get weight-loss surgery.”

Bariatric surgery worked—to a point. Caroline lost 140 pounds in the two years following the procedure, largely due to the low-calorie liquid diet she adhered to for three months post-op and an 800-calorie diet for an additional eight months after. But even though she lost a significant amount of weight, her bottom half remained disproportionately large.

“I was working out five days a week. I was eating 800 calories a day,” Caroline says. “I went to my trainer asking, ‘Why haven’t I lost anything in the bottom half?’ and she was like, ‘God, who knows. Let’s focus on your legs.’ ”

As you can probably guess, incorporating a few extra squats and lunges didn’t move the needle. And after weathering a few health issues (including having her gallbladder removed), Caroline started regaining the weight she’d lost. Living in L.A. by this point, she enrolled in a UCLA weight-loss program, which again capped her calories at just 800 a day. For reference, Caroline is 5'11", so this is an incredibly low number for someone of her height.

Indeed, says Caroline: “I have had a doctor-prescribed eating disorder for my entire adult life.”

By around the age of 30, Caroline had had enough. She just wanted to live her life. So for the next half-dozen years, she ate what she wanted and gave little thought to trying to corral her body into a shape it didn’t seem to want to be.

In late 2023, a friend mentioned that she had started taking a GLP-1, and Caroline was intrigued, mostly from a hormonal standpoint. She had long suspected she had what was then called PCOS, but because she didn’t have cysts, she couldn’t get a proper diagnosis. (Caroline has since been diagnosed with PMOS, now that the condition has been reclassified.) Aware of the early research around GLP-1s reducing PMOS symptoms, Caroline asked her doctor if she could go on one. Her doctor agreed to it, saying that, given her BMI, there was a weight-loss case to be made for prescribing the drug. While Caroline’s main focus was hormonal balance, she did lose weight—about 60 pounds in six months. What she didn’t lose? A single pant size.

While scrolling her favorite anti-diet GLP-1 subreddit one night, Caroline stumbled upon the word that would explain everything: lipedema.

“I Googled it and my jaw dropped because I was looking at photographs of me,” Caroline says. It was two decades of confusion and frustration distilled into a single image.

With her newfound knowledge, Caroline moved quickly. She booked an appointment with a doctor who gave her an official diagnosis, and then she began researching surgeons for lipedema reduction surgery.

Because lipedema manifests and progresses differently from body to body, treatment plans also vary widely. Many doctors will opt for conservative therapies that have shown efficacy. This usually includes a compression garment to stave off fluid retention and irritation.

“[Proper] compression will actually stabilize the limb so that it stops that excess movement that can cause a lot of sensitivity,” Whitehead says.

A doctor may also prescribe a pneumatic compression pump that the patient wears (on their upper body, lower body, or both) for a set number of minutes a day to help move lymph fluid around the body. (Picture an astronaut suit.) Anti-inflammatory diets, vibration plates, and lymphatic drainage massages are other go-to protocols. GLP-1s—dual agonists, specifically—are also, at least anecdotally, providing some relief. “A lot of women with lipedema report that their pain gets better when they’re on a tirzepatide,” Whitehead says.

All in all, the Lipedema Foundation lists nearly 70 treatment modalities for lipedema. For some, like Grosvenor, symptom management truly is a part-time job.

“Of those treatment modalities, I consistently use more than 50 things on an ongoing basis,” she says. “On any given day, probably one to two hours of my life is dedicated to the condition.”

Like Grosvenor, Caroline began conservative treatment measures right after her diagnosis, but she knew they wouldn’t be enough to truly tackle her stage 3 lipedema. But the conservative measures serve an important second purpose: They’re needed to prove to insurance that surgery is warranted. This is a hurdle many patients can never clear. And for the ones who do, it often requires a mix of tenacity, privilege, and luck.

Lipedema reduction surgery is, fundamentally, liposuction, albeit a specialized form that is more complicated than a typical cosmetic liposuction procedure, says David Amron, MD, a dermatologic surgeon and lipedema expert in Beverly Hills.

“You’re not only removing the fat, you are decongesting, removing all that fibrous tissue, and improving lymphatic flow,” he says.

The surgery isn’t usually just one procedure but multiple, depending largely on the condition’s progression. It’s often broken down into a few procedures because removing too high a volume of tissue during a single one can be dangerous. But removing more tissue doesn’t necessarily mean more relief.

“Studies have shown that the amount of tissue that’s removed actually doesn’t correlate with symptom improvement,” says Omar E. Beidas, MD, a plastic surgeon at AdventHealth. “That means if you take 2 liters out of a hundred patients and 15 liters of another hundred patients, the hundred who had 15 liters removed don’t necessarily do better than the ones who had 2 liters removed.”

Historically, many insurance companies have hesitated to cover the procedure, deeming it an aesthetic choice rather than a medical necessity. (It also doesn’t help that, again, there has been no dedicated diagnostic code.) Several class-action lawsuits over claim denials have spurred some change, but coverage still varies from plan to plan, and state to state.

“There are a lot of people out there who are like, ‘Forget it. I’m just not even going to deal with this,’ ” Whitehead says. “That’s when it’s really heartbreaking—when someone really does need it, but the process is so cumbersome, so ridiculous, that they can’t even take it on because they’re overwhelmed.”

For others, this is when they unleash their most dogged, determined, and downright stubborn selves, rolling up their sleeves for a fight. Their weapons? Peer-reviewed journal articles, meticulous medical documentation, and sheer grit.

“I worked harder for my insurance than my capstone for my master’s degree program,” says Grosvenor, who has had five surgeries so far—three on her legs, one on her arms, and one on her abdomen. Grosvenor was required by her insurance to undergo what’s called a functional capacity exam (FCE) to prove that her lipedema was negatively impacting her life. (Before her diagnosis and surgeries, Grosvenor could barely walk up a flight of stairs.) Conducted by a trained physical therapist, the exhaustive battery of tests took four hours.

“It was every kind of pushing, pulling, gripping, lifting—all the activities of daily living, including walking, running, even crawling on hands and knees, which was awful,” she says. “At the end, I got a full printed report with the outcomes of all of the modalities.”

The report noted “severe disability” due not just to the pain in Grosvenor’s tissue but also to the positioning of that tissue and the way it impacted her body’s shape.

“My hips were pushed out at angles they shouldn’t. My knees, ankles, and arches were fallen,” she says.

Even with extensive notes from her lipedema therapist and the results of the FCE, Grosvenor continued facing challenges from her insurance provider, especially when selecting a surgeon. They wouldn’t approve any of the lipedema specialists she wanted.

“The specialist that they tried to get me in with is one that specializes in penis surgery,” she says, amusement in her voice. “They were shocked when I did not want to pick that one.”

Grosvenor ultimately landed on a lymphatic microsurgeon, and she’s largely satisfied with the results. “I have a relatively normal shape now, and that is thanks to the surgeries,” she says. “I could have done conservative therapy eight hours a day for the rest of my life, and I could not have gotten rid of that disproportion without the surgery. But this isn’t a cosmetic result, because when you look at it up close and personal, it’s not pretty. There’s loose-hanging skin. There’s discoloration. There’s scarring. But my intent always with the surgery was to regain my capacity to enjoy life and function and work.”

While Grosvenor—who keeps a collection of all of her insurance appeal documentation in annotated binders (yes, she is a Virgo)—eventually won approval for her procedures largely through an unrelenting force of will, Caroline, so far, hasn’t been so lucky.

Caroline’s first surgery was covered by insurance, but she is still waiting for reimbursement on the following three, as her insurance company continues requesting additional documentation. Caroline paid for her procedures out of pocket, utilizing a mix of life savings and credit cards with 0 percent introductory interest rates. Her 2025 total for uncovered lipedema treatments (both conservative therapies and surgeries) is $130,000—and she’s unsure whether she’ll ever get a penny of that back.

But Caroline forges on—just not within the U.S. health care system, because of the cost. Her most recent surgery (and fifth overall) was with a well-regarded surgeon in Cyprus. She took a month off of work to travel to and recover from the surgery, which consisted of abdominoplasty and additional lipedema removal in her torso and flanks. (Skin removal, which is considered a cosmetic procedure, would not have been covered by Caroline’s insurance, so she felt the trip was worth it.) Caroline says she’ll need two more surgeries before the majority of her lipedema tissue has been removed. Over the course of her five surgeries thus far, she’s had about 30 to 40 pounds of tissue and skin removed.

Though she’s not done with her surgeries yet, Caroline is already feeling the positive effects. “This last surgery removed 15 pounds of skin and additional tissue, and my back pain that I have had for, like, my whole life is completely gone,” she says.

While some research indicates that surgery can significantly reduce pain (one method called SMiLE—Softening, Mobilization, Liposuction, Extraction—showed patient pain levels reduced by 74 percent, on average, according to a small study of 62 women), it isn’t a silver bullet, Dr. Beidas says.

“This bad tissue can come back, typically with hormonal spikes or heavy hormonal periods in a woman’s life,” he says. “And you have to do your post-op care just like you did your pre-op care.”

Lipedema may be a physical condition, but it has an enormous psychological impact. Body image frequently plummets. Years—or even decades—of having symptoms invalidated and lived experiences dismissed take a toll on patients, and the effects often linger long after the surgery scars have healed.

“The thing that I felt on January 2, 2025, when I read that subreddit, was mental vindication,” Caroline says. “I knew it. I knew this wasn’t my fault. And I need other women to have that feeling, because even if you can’t get anything done about it—which is actually going to be the case for most women, sad to say—they deserve answers.”

“The mental health toll on people with lipedema is really heavy,” Grosvenor agrees. “I have now occupied both sizes of bodies and seen the amount of fat shaming and fat phobia that is out in the world. The way that people perceived and treated me five years ago vs. the way that they treat me today in the body that I’m living in is palpable.”

The patients Women’s Health spoke with for this story have been galvanized to action by their experiences. Caroline says she would like to dedicate her life to activism, raising awareness of lipedema so other women don’t have to wait as long for a diagnosis as she did. Grosvenor’s advocacy has manifested in a blog called Thriving with Lipedema, in which she documents her experience with the condition. It’s also become her career calling: After working for 24 years in finance, she quit her job and took a position at the Lipedema Foundation. Durham has channeled her frustrations over getting a diagnosis into creating an app called LippyLog. It helps women track their symptoms over time and generate a detailed record that they can share with their health care provider.

“It’s not meant to diagnose but rather to be a communication tool,” Durham says. It’s a tool that no doubt would have come in handy while trying to get her own answers.

Hopefully, through her efforts and the efforts of so many women like her, lipedema will be more widely recognized and prioritized—and diagnosed much earlier, perhaps even during puberty.

“Every young teenage girl should be screened for lipedema,” Dr. Amron says. “We are screening for diseases that are far less frequent than the 10 percent frequency of lipedema.” The aim, eventually, is for scientists to determine what triggers lipedema during puberty and potentially avoid its development altogether.

“We are being advocates for ourselves and almost forcing the medical community not only to take notice but to actually engage in meaningful conversation and do the research,” Durham says. “If it were not for women who live with lipedema and who are advocating, I don’t think this would go anywhere.”

If you suspect you may have lipedema, visit the Lipedema Foundation website (lipedema.org) for a list of providers who can help with diagnosis and treatment.

#506. How Do You Screen Your Kids’ Friends? Apply the “Bob Seger Test.”

It’s a parent’s responsibility to make sure your children are hanging out with the right people. I got help from an American rock ‘n’ roll legend.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

WHEN MY SON and daughter got old enough to start asking if they could hang out with this or that kid, I had no idea what the right answer to that might be. How was I supposed to know if this second-grader or that fifth-grader were good influences or future serial killers?

I knew that interviewing the parents of these potential friends wasn’t the way to go—I’d already been on the other end of those interrogations, probably due to my long hair, necklace, and wallet chain, and knew it was uncomfortable for all involved, and usually didn’t end with a playdate.

So, I came up with a workaround. Instead of vetting the parents, I would vet the kids, but indirectly, with a simple question that would tell me all I needed to know. Whenever my son or daughter came home bouncing with energy to play with a new-to-me kid, I’d ask them, “Do they know who Bob Seger is?”

My assumption here was that you can’t really listen to Bob Seger and not have depth, not be a good person. Listen to Bob’s “Fire Lake” and know that it’s you who’s going to ride that chrome three-wheeler. Try not to nod your head with “Still the Same,” because we all have someone like that in our lives, don’t we? In our lives or sitting right behind us in homeroom. Spin “Turn the Page” and experience the loneliness and anonymity of a different venue every night, whether it’s a tour schedule or parents dragging you along. Or let “Against the Wind” tell you about what it’s like to struggle—in relationships or the line for Jell-O. Bob Seger’s whole catalogue is an education, a guiding light, a set of arms to fall into.

So, when my kids would rush out of school about to burst with needing to play with this or that kid, I’d ask them what I’d ask them, and, each time, they’d look up to me and their shoulders would sag a bit and they’d look around for Mom, because maybe she could override me.

“I don’t think they know him, Dad, no,” they’d say, and I’d shrug, and they’d get it. They wouldn’t like it, but they understood. I was just trying to keep them safe—situate them among quality people.

But, to my kids’ credit, and probably because “Brave Strangers” had always been in the background at home, they never stopped trying.

“Do they know Bob Seger?” I’d ask, down at their level.

“They do now,” they’d tell me, trying to hide their grin. To kids who had never even heard of this songwriter and singer out of Detroit, my son and daughter played “Sunburst” or “Till it Shines” huddled behind a locker, two sets of ears held to one device. And some of those kids are still friends, twenty years later.

No, I no longer ask if the people my kids bring home know who Bob Seger is—it was an arbitrary hoop to get to a playdate—but I know my kids have him in their hearts. As far as I’m concerned, that means they’re out there right now, making good decisions.

Stephen Graham Jones is a novelist. His books include The Buffalo Hunter Hunter, The Only Good Indians, and now Off the Reservation, his latest.

#507. This Art Collector’s Southampton Home Plays by Its Own Rules

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE Decor editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

With an expanding gallery, his first furniture line, and a growing portfolio of interiors, ascending designer Patrick McGrath shows off his mix-master flair.

Above: In the primary bedroom of a Southampton, NY, house updated by designer Patrick McGrath, a Robert Longo drawing overlooks circa 1930 R.C. Coquery lounge chairs and a Marcel Breuer table. Vitsoe shelves host an Andy Warhol Brillo Box and a Jordan McDonald vase.

Some say the world will end in fire/Some say in ice.

Those opening lines to Robert Frost’s apocalyptic 1920 poem “Fire and Ice” provided unlikely inspiration for a line of candles created by interior designer Patrick McGrath that will debut this holiday season. Such a foreboding, intense reference point might seem to belie the confident affability that has endeared McGrath to a range of clients, whether New York City hedge-funders, Hong Kong antiquities collectors, or friends turned collaborators. The latter include fashion designer Francisco Costa, whose brand, Costa Brazil, partnered with McGrath on the new candles. “Patrick has great vision and direction,” Costa says. “He’s great at interpreting style—old and new—and bringing it together effortlessly.”

For one of his latest projects, McGrath injected a heavy dose of sophisticated style into a house on Long Island’s East End for a thirtysomething bachelor and art collector whose Soho apartment he had designed years earlier. Located in the desirable Estate Section of Southampton, the 1970s shingle home featured interiors that were, as the designer puts it, “classic Hamptons floral.” Not exactly compatible with the new owner’s collection of contemporary works by artists such as Rashid Johnson, Vik Muniz, and Nate Lowman.

The client had bought the place after renting it for a few summers, and his plan was to eventually raze the house and build a new one. He even had an architect picked out: McGrath’s life partner, Reinaldo Leandro, co-founder of the firm Ashe Leandro. In the meantime McGrath suggested a refresh to tailor the spaces to the owner’s tastes. “When I did the walk-through, I was like, ‘If you’re having people here, we need to redo the house, and whatever furniture we buy, you can obviously use later.’ ”

Over the course of a year and a half, McGrath outfitted the residence with a sophisticated mix of vintage and new furnishings, repainted walls, replaced the fireplace, and installed carpets in an array of textures, all to give the spaces a more contemporary character. Along those lines, he also updated the kitchen and baths and added a gym and a cold plunge.

In the living room McGrath anchored the space with twin bespoke sofas covered in a textured silk, cotton, and raffia fabric, surrounding them with prize vintage pieces, such as a pair of Jean-Michel Frank end tables, a Pierre Jeanneret armchair, a Jean Prouvé daybed, and a 1930s French cabinet with straw marquetry fronts. The primary bedroom, meanwhile, features a long Vitsoe bookshelf mounted low across one wall, with an Andy Warhol Brillo box perched on top and a graphic Robert Longo wave drawing hung above. Stationed alongside are an industrial-chic pair of R.C. Coquery 1930s lounge chairs in black-and-white checkered upholstery flanking a Marcel Breuer bentwood table. The client was so happy, McGrath says, that he announced, “ ‘Oh, I’m not going to knock down the house.’ ”

As with many creatives, McGrath’s professional path wasn’t linear. He grew up in a Boston suburb and moved to New York in 2005 to attend NYU. After graduation he assisted interior designer Frank de Biasi for a couple of years, developing a fondness for 18th- and 19th-century furniture. In 2014 he was hired by Elle Decor A-List designer Michael Bargo to help oversee the ready-to-wear and accessory displays at Giorgio Armani boutiques across the U.S. (The two became friends and still collaborate, buying pieces from each other for clients.)

In his off hours McGrath began advising friends, typically first-time homeowners, on their decor. “I started by helping out a friend who had bought a house upstate, and then another friend, and at one point I had, like, three jobs,” he says. “I was using my PTO to do installs.”

It was around that time that McGrath became romantically involved with Leandro, who nudged him to leave Armani and start Studio McGrath in 2015. “Rei was super-encouraging,” McGrath says. “I also think he was tired of listening to me bitch about doing visuals.”

Business was steady from the jump, and a decade in, most of McGrath’s clients are repeat customers or friends of friends. Last year he opened a showroom and gallery in downtown Manhattan, partly to expand his clientele. “Obviously, the market is not huge for young people buying 18th-century furniture,” he says. His second exhibition reunited him with Bargo. For “Icons: Antiquities, Jean Prouvé and Bruce Weber,” the two juxtaposed photos from Weber’s archives with midcentury French design pieces and antiques.

This month McGrath moves into a new gallery space in Noho with a show based on the Seven Deadly Sins. Next year he’ll release his first furniture line, a six-piece collection inspired by 19th-century Biedermeier.

“Patrick has the most incredible vision and sense of style,” says Aerin Lauder, who recently purchased a 19th-century French nursing chair and ottoman from him. “I love making discoveries at his showroom, seeing his antique finds and custom products.”

Also in the works, McGrath and Leandro are starting renovations on their new apartment in a prewar building on the Upper East Side. The previous owner was none other than the legendary decorator and renowned maximalist Mario Buatta. McGrath, while an admirer of Buatta’s, favors a more restrained kind of flair. “I’m interested in how to make the mix feel sexy,” he says. “It can very easily drift into pastiche, but to live with museum-quality pieces, that is really cool.”

Sarah Cristobal is a writer, editor, and creative consultant. She is currently editor-at-large for 10 Magazine USA, among other freelance projects.

#509. Lava Lamps Are Having a Moment—Here's How Designers Style Them in Modern Spaces

Experts are on board with this groovy trend.

Every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

As older design styles are getting a revamp—think postmodernism and traditionalism—decor pieces that are synonymous with certain eras are getting their moment in the spotlight too, such as lava lamps.

This psychedelic relic of the 1960s has had its ups and downs in the zeitgeist since it was first created, becoming popular again in the late ‘90s and early aughts as the style we now call whimsigoth became popular. However, this current resurgence isn’t just nostalgia bait; lava lamps have their place in the home, according to many designers, and they can really elevate a room.

Read on to find out why designers believe lava lamps are becoming popular again, and find their tips on styling these groovy pieces, as well as others like them.

The revival of the lava lamp isn’t surprising if you’ve been paying attention, according to Vanessa Larsson, an interior designer at Planner 5D.

“Maximalism never really left, and the Gen Z aesthetic—color, neon, a bit of glow, and above all personality and nostalgia—has made room for objects that are expressive and unapologetic,” she explains. “The lava lamp fits that mood perfectly: it is warmth, motion, and a wink of the ‘60s and ‘70s, all in one piece.”

However, just because something brings up feelings of nostalgia doesn’t mean it’s going to rise in popularity—it has to resonate. People are embracing homes that reflect their personalities more than resemble a showroom, and the most interesting spaces are layered with vintage finds, unique treasures, and thoughtful investments. Lava lamps fall right into this category. They’re playful and humorous, and every home could use a bit of humor.

“For millennials, there's definitely a nostalgia factor. For Gen Z, it feels like this cool vintage object they've discovered for themselves,” explains designer Marisa Wilson. “Either way, people are looking for pieces with personality instead of perfection.”

Lava lamps used to feel more like novelty items, and maybe they still do for some, but Wilson says she’s been adding them and seeing them in rooms that feel more collected and intentional. She says to commit to this intentionality if you’re adding a lava lamp to your home, but don’t make it the loudest piece in the room.

“I love one tucked into a bookshelf with vintage books, brass candlesticks, ceramics, and framed art,” she says. “It also works on a credenza or in a cozy reading corner where it's adding ambient light instead of competing with the rest of the room.”

Before going out and buying one, though, Wilson suggests finding a vintage one because their proportions and finishes tend to hold a lot more character than new ones today.

Larsson likes to see a lava lamp treated like a sculpture. She says to give it attention; set it on a table in the corner of the room and keep the surroundings monochromatic so the lamp “becomes the only source of color and movement in the frame.” Or you can embrace the dopamine decor aspect and design your color scheme to complement the colors of the lamp. Either way, respect the actual light.

“A lava lamp does its magic in a low-lit setting where its glow can actually do something. In a bright, busy room, it disappears,” Larsson adds.

For even more personality and an emphasis on the sculptural vibe, maybe a regular lava lamp isn’t what you need at all. Artist Shae Hickey of Studio Shae started making her Groove Tubes in 2023 after finding that modern lava lamps tend to be poorly made. Her lamps, some of which are pictured above, sit on uniquely shaped bases with equally as fun toppers that come in many different colors and patterns—some are even skirted—and they’re both amusing and mesmerizing.

Rosectra is another artist who makes lava lamps that are objectively more interesting than the ones you can find in your local mall. She customizes hers with 3D-printed bases or different-colored wax (that’s the goo inside). She’s even been making ones out of old gumball machines.

Though these are harder to obtain than a mass-produced one, these and others like them transform the lava lamp into a one-of-a-kind art piece that’s sure to get attention and add a magnetic layer to any space.

If lava lamps still feel a bit juvenile for your space, there are other ways you can enjoy that ethereal, glowing vibe without sacrificing sophistication.

For Wilson, she captures this warmth through layered lighting rather than relying on a single statement piece. “Table lamps, sconces, candles, and reflective objects all help create a home that changes throughout the day and feels inviting at night,” she explains.

Specific pieces would be Noguchi’s Akari lamps, adds Larsson. “No color theatrics, just an organic sculptural form and a soft, even glow,” she adds, like in the homes below.

If color is what you’re after, Larsson likes artist Sabine Marcelis's resin work, specifically her pieces that trap light inside so the sculptures glow from within. A more accessible option would be IKEA’s doughnut lamp, which creates the same radiant vibe.

Larsson reaches for Oskar Zięta's steel sculptures to capture movement. “It's as if you extracted only the lava itself, froze it, and hung it on the wall,” she says. “Liquid metal that never stops moving even though it's completely still.” However, if this isn’t within your budget, try a convex mirror or a less expensive abstract light sculpture.

It’s definitely possible to capture the allure of a lava lamp without having to commit to one for your home. No matter your style, your interiors can likely benefit from some movement and warmth.
