#511. Just FYI, This Year’s Flu Season Is Even Earlier Than Expected

While you normally only hear about a surge of flu cases during the deep winter months, it’s still early fall and the U.S. is already seeing flu at higher-than-usual rates.

A recent report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) notes that seasonal flu activity is “increasing” in many parts of the country, though it is still generally low. Based on the latest data, 3.6% of Americans tested for a respiratory issue were also positive for the flu.

“Flu season is happening much earlier than usual,” says Thomas Russo, MD, professor and chief of infectious disease at the University at Buffalo in New York. “The beginning of influenza season is always unpredictable—this is another example.”

What's driving this increase in cases and, more importantly, how can you stay healthy? Here's what you need to know.

Meet the experts: Asefeh Faraz Covelli, PhD, APRN, researcher and associate professor at The George Washington University School of Nursing and Thomas Russo, MD, professor and chief of infectious disease at the University at Buffalo in New York

The flu doesn't hit the country at the same level, at the same time. Right now, for example, the CDC points out that the highest flu activity is happening on the West Coast. California's test positivity rate for influenza currently sits at 8.8 percent, based on state data, while Alaska's public health department noted that flu cases started to "increase noticeably" in mid-August.

“There isn't one clear explanation for why it's happening earlier this year,” says Asefeh Faraz Covelli, PhD, APRN, researcher and associate professor at The George Washington University School of Nursing. “We need to keep watching the data to understand whether this early rise will translate into an earlier or more severe flu season overall.”

The earlier-than-usual season is largely driven by an H1N1 variant of the flu, with a D.3.1.1 HA subclade. That may be more immune-evasive than other strains, leading to the rise in early infections, Dr. Russo says.

But Covelli includes this important caveat: “An earlier start doesn't necessarily mean the flu is stronger.” Flu viruses change every year, and some of those changes may make it easier for the virus to spread in people who have some level of immunity already. "Researchers are watching the strains circulating this year, but it's too early to know whether these changes will make this flu season more severe," she says.

If you’re worried you have the flu, keep the following in mind. Flu symptoms don't really change from year to year, and these are the biggest ones to be aware of, per the CDC:

Public health agencies usually recommend getting vaccinated by Halloween. But given the season's early start, healthcare providers say you're fine to get the vaccine now. “If you haven't gotten your flu shot yet, I'd get it now rather than wait,” Covelli says. “September and October are generally the best time to get vaccinated, and it takes about two weeks for your body to build up protection.” Getting vaccinated now can help to protect you throughout the season, she says.

Also, while it's easy to assume an early start to flu season means it might also end sooner, that's not guaranteed. “Sometimes we have two waves due to influenza A and then influenza B," Dr. Russo says. "We will have to see.”

#512. How You Can Use the Spoto Press to Crush Your Bench Goals

This variation will power up your bench to new heights.

SOMETIMES THE SMALLEST changes can deliver the biggest results in the gym. Sure, it’s important to switch up your routine by swapping in new exercises occasionally, but it’s also well established that little tweaks often work just as well (if not better). Subtle adjustments like altering your grip, stance, or even the pace of each rep can be the springboard that launches you out of a training rut and reinvigorates your gains.

Nowhere is that truer than in the barbell bench press. There’s a reason it’s a mainstay of most men’s training programs and a card-carrying member of strength training’s “big three” lifts: Few other upper body exercises mobilize as much muscle or build as much lean mass. But a consequence of its storied status is that it can be overused, with lifters performing it the same way set after set, week after week, month after month, and year after year.

Eventually, guys stuck in the same cycle will hit a plateau. They might look to all kinds of wild approaches for a fix—which is a shame, because a possible solution to their struggle can be simple. By stopping the bar before it reaches their chest and pausing before finishing the rep, lifters can elevate their pushing (and muscle-building) power.

That “hold and hover” transforms the standard bench press into the Spoto Press, named after elite powerlifter Eric Spoto. He used it as the cornerstone of a training regimen that helped him crush a 722-pound raw bench press in competition. Follow his lead to maximize your push.

UNLIKE A TRADITIONAL barbell bench press, which involves lowering the bar all the way to your chest, the Spoto Press entails lowering the bar until it’s an inch or two above your pecs and then holding it there for a beat (one to two seconds) before pressing back up to the starting position. Everything else about the exercise is the same as a standard barbell bench press. That brief hold at the bottom makes all the difference.

Pausing the lift when your pecs are almost fully lengthened eliminates the stretch reflex, which is the natural tendency of a muscle to store energy briefly when stretched (much like a rubber band). During a standard bench press, the stretch reflex helps you drive the bar out of that bottom position. Removing it makes that job a lot harder. You’re going to struggle through the last couple of reps of each set. That’s a good thing; the harder your muscles work, the faster, stronger, and bigger they’ll grow. It’s also why most trainers recommend that you reduce your typical bench press load by at least 10 percent when performing the Spoto Press (more on that in a bit).

The “active suspension” (as kinesiologists call the pause) at the bottom of each rep will also increase your time under tension (TUT), a key hypertrophy stimulus, as well as prevent you from bouncing the bar off your chest (an all-too-common form faux pas) while helping to eliminate a sticking point that plagues many men: The transition off your chest when your mechanical advantage is the lowest. By taking away the inclination to bounce, and you’ll put more of the onus on your triceps, too.

And as you’re reaping these benefits, the Spoto Press will also force you to control the bar through its entire trajectory, helping to ensure you execute the movement with perfect form. That demand also makes this variation slightly different than a board bench press, another technique used by powerlifters to help hone their lockout power.

YOU CAN SWAP the Spoto Press in for the standard bench press in your strength programming when you’re looking to bust through a plateau, or if you’re aiming to ramp up your reps to a new goal. But because you’re pausing at the bottom of each rep, you’ll want to reduce the load a bit, tailoring the amount of the reduction to your primary training goal.

First, learn the lift. If you’ve never done it, start with a load you can control; think of doing three to five sets of six to eight reps with 50 percent of your one-rep max. Then, you can get more nuanced.

If the skill you’re targeting is strength, shoot for three to five sets of three to five reps at 75 to 85 percent of your one-rep max (1RM). You should also rest three to five minutes (notice a pattern?) between each set to allow sufficient recovery for peak performance in every rep.

Hypertrophy requires a slightly different approach. If your focus is muscle growth, perform three to four sets of six to 12 reps. As the rep count increases, the weight on the bar should decrease slightly, so load it with 65 to 75 percent of your 1RM. That will allow you to crank out all of your reps with proper form and maximize your growth potential.

You’ll follow most of the same cues for the Spoto press as you would a standard barbell bench press rep. Check out the video below to get set, then adjust for the shift in range of motion and the pause.

Trevor Thieme is a Los Angeles-based writer and strength coach, and a former fitness editor at Men’s Health. When not helping others get in shape, he splits his time between surfing, skiing, hiking, mountain biking, and trying to keep up with his 10-year-old daughter.

#514. Esquire First Look: The Greatest Goes Beyond the Ring to Show Muhammad Ali’s Family

You’ve watched the documentaries and seen the photographs. A new Prime Video series will reveal even more about the sports icon.

Few people have lived a life like Muhammad Ali’s. The certified Greatest of All Time has had umpteen books, documentaries, and biographical dramas that told and retold of his years as a heavyweight champion and a political activist. Hell, there is a movie about Muhammad Ali starring Muhammad Ali. (Not to mention an iconic Esquire cover featuring the legend.) But a new Prime Video series, simply titled The Greatest, aims to be more than another boxing biography. The Greatest isn’t just about the man who was born Cassius Clay; it’s also about the family who raised him to be a legend.

“Most things you’ve seen or read, they don’t go into his childhood much,” says Lonnie Ali, the wife of Ali and the interim president and CEO of the Muhammad Ali Center, in an interview with Esquire. “The Greatest is his pathway to growth, at home with his brother and his parents. It’s a granular deep dive into Muhammad’s life, to understand who he was, how he started, and how he progressed to become one of the most beloved icons.”

Created by Ben Watkins, with Lonnie Ali among its executive producers, The Greatest stars newcomer Jaalen Best as Muhammad Ali in the years from his gold-medal victory at the 1960 Olympics in Rome to his championship bout against Sonny Liston in February 1964. Between these hard-fought wins, Ali lives in Louisville—where his godlike status collides with Jim Crow—and trains to turn pro with the support and tough love of his family: father Cassius Clay Sr. (Omari Hardwick), mother Odessa “Bird” Clay (Dana Gourrier), and brother Rudy, later Rahaman Ali (Kai Parham). The series will begin streaming on Prime Video on November 4.

You can watch the trailer below, along with exclusive images only at Esquire.

In conversations with Esquire, Watkins and the stars describe the series as a coming-of-age family drama that happens to follow the footsteps of an icon. That meant putting an equally big spotlight on the people who surrounded Ali in his most formative years—and being truthful to who they were. “It’s an interpretation of real life and a real person,” says Watkins, who adds that there was a “feeling-out period” where he sought to gain the trust of Lonnie Ali and the Ali family.

“I had to gain their trust, but they also had to give me leeway to tell the story the real way. That means you’re going to see parts of Muhammad Ali that aren’t always flattering. And it shouldn’t be. We shouldn’t do something where he’s perfect.”

At the same time, Watkins and his team knew they were treading familiar ground. Throw a rock at your Roku and you’ll hit a documentary about Ali. And his mythical boxing matches? They’re on YouTube, upscaled to 4K. So Watkins, whose previous work in television includes Burn Notice and Cross, imposed a rule (albeit loosely) for his writers room. “The rule was: Anything that’s in a documentary will not be in the show,” he says. He admits it’s an exaggerated rule—so much of Ali’s legend unfolded in the public eye—but it was about setting “intention.”

“We need to be excavating, looking for details that give us a better understanding of who this is. The Crown is a recent example, where some of the best episodes are about things no one ever knew about. That’s what I wanted to do.”

Which is what made Ali’s family members compelling subjects for a streaming series. You can quiz sports scholars and historians on Ali’s stats or what his conscientious objection meant to the anti–Vietnam War movement and to future athletes who use their platforms for protest. But ask them about Ali’s family—the way he doted on his mother, the way his father built dollhouses as a hobby—and you might stump them all.

“That’s what you see here,” says Omari Hardwick, who plays Cassius Clay Sr. in The Greatest. “You get to see how the person we know as Muhammad Ali is created. How is he able to think the way he thinks? Who are the folks around him who shaped his thoughts? The backdrop is the boxing, the things we know that we don’t have to read about. The forefront of this story is the family members around him.”

If you think The Greatest is all feel-good warmth, think again. Set against the segregated South, the home life of the Clays was as turbulent as it was supportive of his lofty ambitions. Resentment, greed, suspicion, and infidelity sit at the same dinner table as love and compassion. “The reality is you could never be as powerful as Muhammad Ali if your greatest opponent was not your father,” adds Hardwick.

But the main event of The Greatest is still bearing witness to the rise of Ali’s legend. Jaalen Best, in his first-ever lead role, stars as the young champ when he still went by Cassius Clay. Best tells Esquire that he studied other onscreen Alis—namely Eli Goree in Regina King’s One Night in Miami—before figuring out his own voice through repeat listens of Ali’s real interviews. “I would watch these again and again, and I would find the little pieces that I think I could change,” he says. “Listening to his voice constantly and repeating it so many times until I felt like I can do a voice memo [in his voice]. It was repetition, repetition, repetition.”

An athlete before he became an actor, Jaalen Best says he could never get enough playing time to show off his stuff. “I could never showcase how great I knew what my potential was,” he says. “Taking this opportunity, I was like, ‘I’m gonna show y’all how great I am.’ Proving to myself how great I could be, proving to people how great I could be, while also bringing to life the greatest Muhammad Ali—”

Best catches himself. “That was a rhyme. I didn’t even try to rhyme.”

Oddly enough, learning how to box was the easier part. “I remember getting the role in April 2024. When I met with the trainer, the goal was [to train] from June all the way until we went to film the next year. So for eight months, I had to run every single day, Sundays off. I would report that time in and weigh myself every morning.”

Though a natural athlete, Best had never boxed before. Quite literally, he had to be shown the ropes. “[My trainer] would be like, ‘This is the proper way to throw a hook,’ because if you can understand the proper way, then you can understand how Ali broke the laws to create his own.”

Adds Best, “We would do three hours training doing the Ali routine. He’s putting me in the ring—I’m dancing around, throwing punches. At night he would send me clips of Ali and he’d say, ‘Break this down for me, punch by punch.’ That’s how I started learning the way he floats, his shoulder relaxation, how natural his face was. In that routine of studying it, it allowed me to really bring it to life.”

For as much as the team strove to tell Ali’s story from a new angle, The Greatest inevitably comes across some of his greatest hits. Like his climactic battle with Sonny Liston (played in the series by Amin Joseph). Other moments are still up in the air in potential future seasons. Ben Watkins tells Esquire he has a three-season plan in mind. This first season, which he’s titled “I Shook Up the World,” is all about Cassius Clay becoming Muhammad Ali. Should the series see a renewal for season 2, it would be titled “I’m Ready to Die,” covering Ali’s ban from professional boxing due to his refusal to be drafted into the Vietnam War.

As for season 3? It’s called “I Am the Greatest.” “It takes place in the mid-’70s. Of course it includes Rumble in the Jungle,” Watkins says. When I ask if it would also include his infamous (and disastrous) match against Japanese pro wrestler Antonio Inoki, Watkins says it might. “I would love for folks to see that wrestling match, because not only does it make a huge statement about how the world was at the time, but he [Ali] sustained injuries that he never really recovered from.”

Sadly, Watkins skips Ali’s legendary meeting with the Beatles entirely, which took place weeks before his fight against Liston in 1964. “Imagine the challenge we have in terms of casting,” he says, “You have to get four legends right. I had to, unfortunately, let that moment go.”

But The Greatest isn’t about re-creating episodes of Ali’s life in period-accurate cosplay. It is about how one man changed the world with his people at ringside. “Before he was a legend, he was a man, a brother, a father, a son,” says Watkins. “We admire him for accomplishing things that are almost superhuman, and it’s easy to forget he had the same fears and flaws. Once you are reminded that he’s human, you admire what he did even more, because you know how hard that is to do.”

#515. This West Palm Beach Home Features a Shell-Encrusted Powder Room

Classic Old Florida design references emerge in every room.

T here are certain design liberties afforded to a beach home that other projects just can’t carry as naturally. A coral bedroom? Obviously. A dining room that doubles as a tropical garden? Of course. A sailfish cresting over a velvet sectional? Practically a requirement. When a family of Texas transplants enlisted Mimi Maddock McMakin and Peyton Urbanek of Kemble Interiors to transform their West Palm Beach home, they came with a Florida-approved appetite for color, a collection of beloved possessions, and very little interest in playing it safe.

For the Maddock McMakin and Urbanek, the brief turned out to be an exercise in creative restraint, though you wouldn’t know it from the results. Having downsized from a significantly larger home, the homeowners needed every inch of their new residence to earn its keep. “We wanted the spaces to feel comfortable, charming, and thoughtfully layered, so every inch had to work without feeling crowded,” says Urbanek. Rather than gutting the property, the team worked with Rothrock Construction to rethink its proportions, repurposing overlooked corners and unused nooks, and coaxing new character from existing details.

Some of the cleverest interventions made were also the smallest. A former closet beneath the stairs became a powder room, enveloped in pink grasscloth and finished with a Sailor’s Valentine shell display by Kellie Leighton. In the kitchen, the existing cabinetry was lacquered in Farrow & Ball’s Green Blue, while cane and bamboo trim gave the original coffered ceiling new charm. Elsewhere, pecky cypress ceilings, intricate latticework, and exuberant wallcoverings provide the type of Old Florida charm that has become so beloved in the area.

Delightful decorative elements aside, the home's smartest play may be its pacing. In the entry, the designers narrowed a long hallway and introduced archways to create a more deliberate progression between rooms. "We believe a home should offer a sense of the unexpected as you enter, revealing itself room by room rather than showing you everything at once," Urbanek explains. And it does just that, with each room offering a new reason to linger, a fresh color combination to admire, and proof that a change of address can be an excellent excuse to have a little fun.

FAST FACTSDesigner: Kemble InteriorsBuilder: Rothrock ConstructionLocation: West Palm Beach, FloridaThe Space: A three-bedroom, three-and-a-half-bathroom home across 4,000 square feet.

Designed to feel like “a garden perched at the water’s edge,” the sunroom is wrapped in lattice on the walls and ceiling, creating an enveloping backdrop. A bench swing and rattan swivel chairs invite you to settle in, turn toward the water, and linger over morning coffee or cocktails as the light changes.

Reminiscent of a tropical garden, the dining room is framed in rich turquoise trim and outfitted with a lively mural from Clake & Clark. Instead of traditional window treatments, the team opted for custom micro-lattice shutters that filter the sunlight and cast dappled light throughout the space.

“The kitchen shows how much character can come from reimagining what is already there,” says Urbanek. Farrow & Ball’s Green Blue brought new life to the existing kitchen cabinetry, while cane and bamboo trim on the coffered ceilings nods to classic Floridian style. “We wanted the kitchen to feel as layered and personal as the rest of the house, with materials that grow more charming over time.”

“The client wanted the living room to feel like a natural extension of the sunroom by day, then take on the mood of a cocktail lounge for evenings spent entertaining friends,” says Urbanek. To achieve that balance, the pair started with the P. Kaufmann print on the sofa, which the client fell in love with, and allowed that to guide every design decision that followed.

Tucked beneath the stairs, this petite powder room makes the most of a small footprint. “Almost every element had to be customized to suit its proportions and meet code requirements, including a sink made entirely from pink stone,” says Urbanek.

Though the client’s sailfish draws the eyes in this cozy space, there are plenty of other elements to love. “The deep blue velvet sectional sets the scene for a family room with plenty of comfort,” says Urbanek. “Its dramatic silhouette plays off the sofa’s scalloped back, while a bone-inlay coffee table adds another layer of pattern and surprise.”

Unexpectedly bright for a bedroom, this coral-clad space boasted just the right amount of fun for the clients. “Deeper than a familiar Florida coral, the wall color brings warmth and richness that beautifully complement the verdigris on the ceiling,” says Urbanek. “In the center, a rope-wrapped canopy bed is dressed in sheer verdigris-striped curtains, creating a breezy enclosure with a little romance.”

“We wanted the bathroom to have a personality of its own,” Urbanek says of the colorful space, which features a grass green vanity and wallpaper from House of Harris. “Each room tells a different story.”

“The client fell in love with the patterned wallpaper, and we felt its exuberance deserved to extend beyond the walls,” Urbanek says of the room’s pink and green palette. “We wanted guests to feel immediately transported to Florida through the room’s freshness, color, and playful spirit, a sense of place that comes from its atmosphere rather than familiar coastal motifs.”

Kemble Interiors, Inc. was founded in 1982 by Palm Beach native Mimi Maddock McMakin. She has over 40 years of experience consulting and working under the direction of licensed architects and contractors to bring comfort and beauty to her clients' homes across America. She now runs the firm alongside her daughter and partner, Celerie Kemble, in the New York office of Kemble Interiors, with designer Peyton Urbanek on the team.

#518. Is BetterDays Rebound Cream Worth It? I Put VicBlends' New Leave-In Conditioner to the Test

I've tested plenty of curly hair creams, but this $20 formula has quickly become one of my favorites.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

I’VE TESTED A lot of curly hair products over the years, and so I was excited to try the new Rebound Cream Leave-In Conditioner from BetterDays, the haircare brand founded by celebrity barber VicBlends (Victor Fontanez). The cream promises to hydrate, define, and soften hair without weighing it down, which sounds great in theory, but as someone with tight, type 3B and 3C curls, I've learned to be skeptical of those claims.

Some creams leave my curls flat, while others control frizz but make my hair feel stiff or greasy a few hours later. Finding something that gives me the volume I want while keeping my curls soft and defined is a bigger challenge than it probably should be.

That's partly why I was so interested in trying the new BetterDays line. VicBlends has built a massive following through his haircuts and the conversations he has with the people sitting in his chair. His new haircare line aims to bring that barber-shop experience into everyday grooming, and I was curious whether the products could live up to the hype.

The brand also launched its Grip Powder, a texturizing styling powder designed to add volume and hold, particularly for guys with straighter hair. But it was the Rebound Cream that caught my eye. After putting it through its paces in my morning routine, I can confidently say that it delivers. In fact, it's quickly become one of my favorite curly hair products I've tested, and I don't say that lightly.

BetterDays Rebound Cream is a leave-in conditioner designed to hydrate, soften, and improve hair manageability while helping maintain its natural texture. Unlike a traditional rinse-out conditioner, it's meant to stay in your hair all day, providing conditioning benefits while also acting as a lightweight styling product.

The formula features ingredients like shea butter and coconut oil, commonly used to soften and condition hair, along with panthenol, a form of vitamin B5 that helps improve moisture retention and hair feel. Together, these ingredients aim to combat dryness and frizz without the heavy, greasy finish some richer curl creams leave behind.

What's particularly interesting is that BetterDays markets the Rebound Cream for a wide range of hair textures, from straight and wavy to curly and coily. While I can't speak to how it performs on every hair type, I can vouch for how well it's worked on my own curls.

SHOP THE BETTERDAYS LEAVE-IN-CREAM ON AMAZON

The first thing I noticed about the cream was the smell. BetterDays uses a custom fragrance called Scent No. 26, and the best way I can describe it is that it smells like stepping into a really good barbershop. It's fresh, with that familiar grooming-product scent that immediately reminds me of getting a haircut.

The application is another thing I appreciate. The pump makes it easy to dispense the product without scooping anything out of a jar, and the cream spreads smoothly through my hair. I typically use three to four pumps and work the product through my curls with my hands. One important detail I've learned, though, is that my hair needs to be damp, not soaking wet. When I apply it right after getting out of the shower, my curls tend to fall a little flat, which defeats the whole purpose of using a styling product.

Instead, I let my hair air-dry until it's damp, which is also how the bottle recommends applying it. Once I work the cream through, the difference is almost immediate. My curls look fuller, more defined, and noticeably less frizzy, without the heavy feeling I get from many other curl creams. Volume matters to me because I like my curls to have lift, and this product delivers that without making my hair feel coated.

Another thing I love is that it doesn't leave behind much of a crunch. Anyone with curly hair knows what I mean. The Rebound Cream leaves my curls feeling relatively soft, though I still like to scrunch my hair a little with my hands once everything has dried.

That helps break up any slight stiffness and gives my curls a more natural appearance. That said, I’ve received more compliments than ever on my curls once I started using this cream. From friends to literal strangers, too.

But the biggest selling point for me is how well the results hold up throughout the day. My curls stay defined and practically frizz-free from when I leave my apartment in the morning until I get ready for bed.

Even better, the cream is water-reactivated, which makes touch-ups easy. If my curls get flattened or frizzy, I can head to the bathroom, wet my hands, and work a little water through the sections that need attention. Within about 30 seconds, my curls are looking refreshed again.

SHOP THE BETTERDAYS LEAVE-IN-CREAM ON AMAZON

For $20, I think BetterDays Rebound Cream is absolutely worth trying, particularly if you have curly hair and struggle to find styling products that offer definition without sacrificing volume. It checks nearly every box I look for in a curl cream: It smells fantastic, applies easily, controls frizz, and leaves my curls full and defined without feeling stiff or greasy.

This is my experience with my own type 3B and 3C curls, so results will vary by hair type, but I know BetterDays markets this for guys with all curl types.

I've tested enough hair products to know when something deserves a permanent spot in my routine, and this one has. With all-day curl definition, easy touch-ups, and that ridiculously good barbershop fragrance, BetterDays Rebound Cream has become a product I genuinely look forward to using every morning.

#519. Chanel's New High Jewelry Collection Takes Its Cues From Coco's Paris Apartment

How volumes on a bookshelf, botanicals in a Riviera villa, and the mosaics of a French abbey find themselves in a necklace.

“There are things we live among,” the Pulitzer Prize–winning American poet George Oppen wrote, “and to see them is to know ourselves.”

Oppen, a man who organized for workers’ rights and was investigated by the House Un-American Activities Committee, might be a surprising reference in a story about high jewelry, but stay with us. For there are things Gabrielle “Coco” Chanel lived among, and to see them is to know her jewelry. The first Chanel High Jewelry collection, presented in Paris in 1932 and the only one Coco designed herself, featured a series of diamond comet and star pieces. Those designs were direct translations of the comets she witnessed streaking across the Aubazine night sky and of the stars carved into the mosaics of the abbey she was raised in.

Almost a century later those motifs remain, joined in Chanel’s 2026 High Jewelry collection by the lions of her birth sign (the beasts adorned multiple furnishings in her Rue Cambon apartment) and by the camellias inspired by Alexandre Dumas’s 1848 novel La Dame aux Camélias, one of the many volumes that lined her bookshelves.

If there were any doubt of the impact meaningful objects have on the design of Chanel jewelry, the name of the latest collection makes the case irrefutable: Signes & Symboles, an 85-piece array that includes turquoise lion rings, diamond and onyx star cuffs, and a pink sapphire camellia. Necklaces featuring a new lozenge shape called Talisman often combine all three. The Talisman Graphique necklace bears amulets pavé set with yellow sapphires and engraved stars punctuated by a camellia flower set with a 3.57-carat -emerald-cut rare diamond. The Talisman de Symboles necklace is on a tubular chain with hanging plaques bearing a camellia, a star, a sun, and a lion in pink gold and pink sapphires.

But there’s more here, notably a presence of color not often found in Chanel High Jewelry. The use of stones like onyx, carnelian, turquoise, chrysoprase, and spessartite garnets is a marked departure from past patterns dominated by white diamonds. And since we’re in the Chanel universe, where everything is a symbol—where, as Coco herself put it, “every jewel represents an idea”—what could we make of these stones of color and mystery? The answer, it turned out, was coming from inside the house.

Signes & Symboles was presented to press and clients earlier this year at La Pausa, the 10-acre Mediterranean estate in Roquebrune-Cap-Martin that Coco Chanel purchased in 1928 and was bought back a decade ago by the company, which recently commissioned a restoration by ELLE Decor A-List architect Peter Marino.

The villa, which now hosts select company events as well as artist residencies, is surrounded by gardens that include jasmine-laced stone walls, fields of lavender and iris, and 250 ancient olive trees. Gazing up at the villa’s shutters, painted a custom blue to match the original color, and then looking at a necklace of emerald beads fastened with a turquoise clasp, makes the signs and symbols of inspiration perfectly clear.

Editor-in-Chief Stellene Volandes is a jewelry expert, and the author of Jeweler: Masters and Mavericks of Modern Design (Rizzoli).

Measuring 12.6 inches high and 5.9 inches wide, this vintage-inspired set of cordless lamps is bright enough to cast a soft glow on the table and not so big as to get in the way of conversation between you and the other person. It has three lighting modes, allowing you to adjust the ambiance as desired.

Let’s add some playfulness, perhaps? While the personality-packed lamp speaks for itself, we’ll add that Pooky has a reputation for its luxurious yet relatively affordable designs. The base is available in clear, amber, and green, and you can choose from an abundance of lampshades to customize your lamp’s look. And a battery life of 15 hours proves this beauty is as functional as it is fabulous.

Created in collaboration with acclaimed chef Marcus Samuelsson, this contract-grade table lamp is as pristine as it gets. Available in antique brass and matte black, its layered design offers a distinctive touch that truly sets it apart.

If you’re always on the lookout for patio essentials for your outdoor gatherings, or if you enjoy evening strolls, this portable lantern is the perfect investment. With a battery life of up to eight hours and a weatherproof exterior that can withstand dust and splashes, it’s designed for durability. Weighing just two pounds, it’s easy to carry, but you might also consider adding a matching stand if you prefer to hang it.

Who said we had to stick to traditional lamp shapes? For a more modern take on lighting, consider this rechargeable accent globe designed by Sean Lavin. Crafted with hand-rubbed antique glass, this head-turning design adds some oomph to any space and features built-in three-way dimming for customizable ambiance.

Having a couple of portable table lamps on hand is a fantastic idea for your kitchen. In powder-coated aluminum, this Serena & Lily table lamp can certainly stand the test of time indoors as you cook and outdoors if you take dinner into the garden. Despite its sleek, simple design, this beauty can last you up to nine hours of an inviting glow–making it a reliable choice on the list.

This lamp may be petite, but it’s sure to stand out on any console, table, or surface you display it on. Its high-style design and aged-brass finishes aren’t the only selling points—it’s worth noting that you can use this mini lamp while it charges, which takes up to 3.5 hours.

#522. The Afterlife of Jane Doe

For decades, I kept my sexual assault a secret. Finally telling the truth helped me understand how silence had shaped my self-worth, my relationships, and even my health.

I climbed onto the treatment table in the home office of my new pelvic floor therapist, settling under the worn, floral sheets. Naked from the waist down, except for my socks, I relaxed my hips and exhaled, steadying myself for the appointment.

I’d gone there seeking relief for pain during sex, brought on by menopause, medically induced by adjuvant breast cancer treatments at 37. “The Change” happened practically overnight, bringing with it an onslaught of symptoms: mood swings, fatigue, hot flashes, brain fog, and genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM) that caused pain—terrible pain—during intercourse.

After a few minutes, the practitioner, an older, petite woman with a soothing voice and soft hands, knocked on the door. I told her it was okay to enter, and she did. After taking a seat in the chair beside me, she quickly reviewed my medical history. Then, she asked for my consent to perform a physical exam, using a pelvic wand. I closed my eyes and nodded. I watched her move to the end of the table, push the sheet up to my waist, and help my legs into a butterfly pose.

“Hold on,” she said, reaching for two small throw pillows to place on either side of my thighs.

“Yes,” I said, grateful for her concern. “Thank you.”

The space felt different than the countless other exam rooms I’d found myself in over the nine years since my breast cancer diagnosis. I noticed my body softening, letting go of the vigilance I carried into most medical settings.

“I'm going to start by using a small vaginal dilator to stretch the tissue,” she said.

A few moments later, I felt the pain, like shards of glass breaking inside me. I must have let out a sound because she stopped immediately.

“I’m so sorry,” she said. “Did that hurt?”

“OK, we’ll stop there,” she said, slowly removing the dilator. She spent the rest of the appointment gently massaging my lower abdomen and working through trigger points in my pelvis.

Before leaving me alone to get dressed, she turned and said, “Don’t worry. It gets easier over time.”

Her words, meant to reassure, landed like a weight. I thought of all the prior moments in my life I’d been told something similar—to push through my discomfort, endure the pain until it receded or became easier to ignore. Suddenly, panic gripped my chest, and I jolted upright.

Dressing hurriedly, I shoved my bra into my purse. As soon as the practitioner came back, I made up an excuse to leave and ran to my car.

When I got home, the house was empty. I crawled into bed and buried myself under the covers. Everything between my legs felt numb, as if I’d left part of myself behind on the exam table. Beneath the ache, a memory began to surface, one I’d spent decades trying to press down. It was as if my body and my brain were finally connecting the dots, drawing a throughline between a long-buried adolescent trauma and the pain I was experiencing in midlife.

When I was a teenager, I was sexually assaulted at a house party. For many years, I kept the experience monitored, contained, separate from the rest of my life. It never came up during any medical intake, counseling appointment, or even in conversation with my best friend. Up until recently, I hadn’t even told my husband. I’d never told anyone.

And yet, I remember everything about that night. The drive to the party seemed endless. I rode shotgun in my boyfriend’s jeep, drinking two and a half warm Coors Lights, which didn’t seem like too much, but enough to blur everything outside my window. All I could see was the narrow road lit by our high beams, two yellow lines pulling us deeper into the woods.

When we finally pulled up to the lake house, glowing like a giant paper lantern against the shadowy landscape, I felt drunk. I opened the passenger door and fell straight to the ground. Surprisingly, it didn’t hurt. Nothing did. That was the revelation: Alcohol didn’t just soften the hurt; it numbed it. It smoothed over the goosebumps and insecurities. The restlessness that prowled my chest like a caged animal, the new unease I couldn't quite name. That was the summer everything changed. The summer I started to see myself through the male gaze, lost my virginity to my first real boyfriend, watched my childhood disappear in the rearview mirror.

My boyfriend dropped to the ground beside me, laughing, taking my hand in his, tracing constellations overhead. Then he hauled me upright and steered me down the stone path to the front door. Inside, the house was warm and smelled like a campfire. People I didn’t recognize were staring at us, cheering and shouting things from the kitchen.

Upstairs, my boyfriend found an empty bedroom, pulled off my brown leather J.Crew boots, and helped me under the quilt. He stayed for a while, tickling my back and singing me songs until I drifted off, then went back downstairs.

I was half asleep when I heard the door creak open. I thought it might be my boyfriend, coming back to check on me, but then I heard the sound of a belt buckle dropping to the floorboard, and felt a strange body pressed against me. I could tell the boy was naked from the heat and softness of his shape. I tried to push him off, tell him to stop, but he was too big. I went completely still—I was silently screaming, drowning in that bed. When it was over, he got dressed and left without saying a word.

Eventually, I swung myself over the side of the mattress and sat upright. I found my underwear, twisted between the sheets at the foot of the bed, and got dressed. When my boyfriend came back, I told him I felt sick and needed to leave. He looked genuinely concerned, which only made me feel worse.

On the drive home, I stared silently out the passenger window, remembering my mother’s warning to keep watch for leaping deer at night. How she’d taught me to scan the rural roadside for flashing eyes reflecting in the darkness, lithe bodies poised to jump. When we pulled up to my parents’ house, I swung the car door open while the vehicle was still in motion.

I kept my secret for three decades—a hot coal, burning in my chest. My thickened skin kept me protected and functional, or so I thought. Over time, I learned to push down discomfort and carry my burdens without complaint. Telling the truth would mean disturbing Pandora’s box, letting out the ancient feelings of shame, disgust, and unworthiness.

Instead, I treated what happened to me like something survivable. So long as I didn’t disturb the memory, I could triage the symptoms. Work around the wound. Consider myself healed. But in the end, pain doesn’t care how prepared or vigilant you are; it arrives whether you’re watching for it or not.

“Sexual trauma can have lasting effects on how the brain and body respond to perceived threats, even years after the traumatic experience,” says Elizabeth Beverly, PhD, a professor and behavioral health researcher who has studied the neurobiology of sexual assault. “Traumatic experiences affect how memories are processed and stored in the body. These memories may remain outside conscious awareness until a specific sensory trigger unexpectedly brings them to the forefront of the mind. When this happens, survivors may feel as though they are reliving aspects of the traumatic experience.”

During treatment and follow-up care after cancer, I became practiced at compliance: stay still, endure the pain, let someone else decide what should happen to my body. After years of being told what I could and couldn’t do, something long dormant inside me began to awaken. Lying on the exam table at the pelvic floor therapist’s office, the vaginal dilator burning like a torch inside me, I was right back in that room at the top of the stairs, trapped in a moment I couldn’t run from. For the first time, locking the memory away began to feel less like protection and more like being devoured from the inside out.

When I started sharing the truth about my sexual assault with my closest friends and family members, I began to understand how many women were carrying their own version of the same story. The details were different, but the emotional architecture was always familiar: the shame, dissociation, fear, estrangement from the body. The way a traumatic event can rewire a human brain. How even after years of therapy, healthy partnership, and achieving various metrics of success, survivors can still feel broken. How you can close the wound, and still bleed out.

It took me a few months to muster up the courage to tell my husband. Voice shaking, I explained how the assault had braided sex and shame together in my body, how even in good relationships—this one, our marriage—there was still a dark undertow, a sense that sex was dangerous, wrong, or impossible to enjoy without inhibition. My husband listened, and cried. In the end, I felt as if a weighted vest had slipped off my shoulders, due to the simple fact that I no longer had to carry it alone.

I told my doctors, too. For my entire adult life, every medical intake I completed seemed to circle a different piece of me. Not one doctor held my entire story, and I wanted that to change. I spoke to my primary care provider and my oncology nurse practitioner about how my adolescent trauma impacted my experience with GSM, along with my relationship to my sexuality and desire. How GSM triggered the shame I had tried to keep hidden all these years. Saying what happened out loud helped loosen shame’s grip, making the story less powerful. Once it was out in the open, my care changed, too. There was more attention to what my body might be responding to beyond the symptom itself.

It made me wonder if this was true for other women, too. What would a medical intake look like if it included trauma-informed care? If it considered the whole person, our entire lived experience? Not because every detail belongs in every exam room; it doesn’t. But context matters.

I never disclosed what happened to me, in part because I was never asked to during a medical intake. Trauma-informed care is designed to close the gap between patient and provider by building safety, choice, consent, and patient control into the medical encounter—principles that can shape everything from a GSM intake to the pacing of a pelvic exam.

During past pelvic exams, my body often reacted before my mind did, tensing, clenching, as though some old part of me was still keeping watch. This is a common reaction, Beverly says, which is why trauma-informed care is so important: “Health care professionals need to understand how sexual trauma affects the brain and the body, so they can recognize these responses and provide compassionate, supportive care to minimize re-traumatization.”

The reporting around the Cornell Seven has stirred up a rush of memories. It has also created an online movement: I Am Jane Doe. Thousands of survivors are speaking out, sharing their own experiences, and demanding change. These different yet familiar stories have flooded my Instagram feed, touching a part of me I worked hard to keep hidden. Watching women speak out, then watching their words get picked apart, made clear to me how little had progressed, even after the #MeToo movement. In the end, I decided to come forward because I no longer wanted silence to be the price of feeling safe. If we don’t speak out, nothing will ever change.

Women do not owe anyone the gory details of their sexual assaults. Disclosure is not a requirement for healing, nor should a medical appointment become an interrogation. “Many of our patients have a history of sexual trauma, and most won’t tell us at intake,” says Kelly Casperson, MD, a urologist and sexual-medicine and menopause specialist. “So, I don't make disclosure the price of good care. I ask one simple question: 'Is there anything that would make this exam easier for you?’”

Sometimes we choose to keep certain experiences private because solitude is what allows us to survive them. Yet privacy and isolation are not the same thing. Shame isolates us and convinces us to contain what happened, bury it, and keep it separate until we live in verticals.

Sharing my story with other people, absorbing others’ stories—the witnessing, the exchange—is what helped me heal. Shame loses its power when we tell each other the truth. Being honest with myself, speaking openly about my sexual assault offered me a kind of life recalibration. Once illuminated, the shame I carried for years became a pharos, showing me a new way forward.

Eventually, I opened up to my pelvic floor therapist, too. Telling her what happened to me as a teenager informed the way we worked together. There was more conversation before touch, more attention to what made me tense or pull away, more permission to stop.

In our sessions, I learned how to stay present in my body rather than leave it, how to relax instead of going rigid. I learned how to work with my pelvic floor muscles, how to engage them and release them. For most of my life, those parts of me had remained detached, remote, almost unknowable—a place as mysterious as the ocean floor. I began to understand that treating my physical symptoms meant acknowledging everything my body had carried into the room. Forgiveness, I realized, was not only about what had been done to me. It was also about forgiving myself—for the silence, for the shame, for all the years I believed my body was at fault for what happened to me.

It took me a long time to understand that healing was never about “fixing” myself. It was about learning how to return to myself, again and again. My body was never the enemy—it did not betray me. Not even when I buried the traumatic memory deep in my cells. It had only done what bodies do. Survived, endured, and asked—sometimes begged—to be listened to.

Anna Sullivan is a writer, speaker, and licensed mental health therapist. Her work has appeared in The New York Times, Vogue, Women's Health, and more. She is the author of These Bones Are Real: A Memoir of Menopause, Motherhood, and What Remains, forthcoming in March 2027.

#523. Thierry Henry’s Massive NYC Penthouse Lists for $25 Million—Plus 5 More Luxury Homes for Sale

The soccer star’s sprawling SoHo condo leads this week’s luxury real estate listings, alongside homes tied to Diane Keaton, Dolly Parton, and Taylor Swift.

French soccer superstar Thierry Henry, who played for both U.K.–based Arsenal and FC Barcelona, is parting with his glass-walled Manhattan penthouse. The decorated athlete and his partner, Bosnian model Andrea Rajacic, just listed the 5,600-square-foot SoHo aerie for $25 million. It’s not the only property making waves this week: the former Los Angeles home of Dolly Parton, who died in August at age 80, is also now for sale, though it’s been totally reimagined since she lived there some 40 years ago.

Also in Southern California, Sharon Osbourne is cutting the price of her longtime home in Hancock Park, Tyler Perry is bidding farewell to his custom Beverly Hills mansion, and Taylor Swift’s onetime hideaway is newly on the market, for sale by the couple who bought it directly from her. Check them all out below.

Perched atop a cast-iron Soho landmark built in the 1870s, the glass-walled penthouse owned by soccer star Thierry Henry and model Andrea Rajacic just hit the market for $25 million. It’s the second time the couple has tried offloading the sprawling five-bedroom home, which they first put on the market in February 2025 for $26.75 million. Now listed with Sotheby’s broker Joshua Judge, the 5,600-square-foot condo has 4,600 square feet of private outdoor space thanks to a network of terraces across four different floors. Other perks include 14-foot ceilings, two deeded parking spaces, and an indoor bamboo garden.

From a one-bedroom cabin in rural Tennessee to a 63-acre Nashville compound, Dolly Parton’s homes reflected her humble beginnings and subsequent rise to the top of the entertainment industry. In the mid-1980s, a few years after the country music legend starred in her first Hollywood film, 9 to 5, she and her husband Carl Dean bought a property in Southern California. Now, just weeks after Parton’s death at age 80, their Los Angeles estate, which was rebuilt in 2009, according to the listing, just hit the market for $8 million.

Sharon Osbourne just slashed $1 million off the price of her Los Angeles estate, which she shared with her late husband, Ozzy Osbourne. Back in April, less than a year after the Black Sabbath singer’s death at age 76, Sharon listed the Hancock Park home for $17 million. It represented a renewed attempt to offload the 1929 mansion, which the Osbournes had first tried selling in 2022. Now, six months later, the nearly 11,600-square-foot property has a new price of $16 million, a discount of roughly 6 percent.

Add this to your “Wi$h Li$t.” Taylor Swift’s former Beverly Hills bungalow just hit the market for nearly $8 million—and it’s brimming with pop star lore. Swift acquired the mini-compound in 2011, fresh off releasing her third album, Speak Now, when she was just 22 years old. At the time, she had a pair of Nashville residences to her name, though her property empire has since expanded exponentially.

Tyler Perry’s sprawling Beverly Hills mansion—where Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex lived as they transitioned out of royal life—just hit the market for $57 million. The Tuscan-style villa features palatial proportions, with nine bedrooms and 15 baths across nearly 24,600 square feet, while the grounds span 22.5 acres. It’s one of the most expensive properties for sale within the coveted 90210 zip code.

The final home that Hollywood star Diane Keaton put her stamp on is now for sale. Perched atop a bluff in Laguna Beach with postcard views of the Pacific Ocean, the four-bedroom house just hit the market for $10.3 million.

Originally built in 1976, the Southern California retreat belonged to the Pinterest-loving late Oscar-winning actress from 2021 to 2022, during which time she updated the internal systems, installed a new roof, and revamped the fireplace. The interiors adhere to the black-and-white color scheme favored by Keaton, with the kitchen sporting industrial-style lighting pendants—a flourish that became one of her signatures.

Geoffrey Montes is an associate editor at ELLE Decor with a serious love for all things real estate and design. Before that, he worked at Architectural Digest, Galerie, and Preservation magazines, covering everything from jaw-dropping listings to world-famous architects and design events like Salone del Mobile and Homo Faber.

#524. The 10 Best Fitness Trackers, Tested by Our Fitness and Tech Experts

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Our fitness team recommends trackers from Garmin, Apple, and Suunto.

NOT SURE WHAT fitness tracker is right for you? You've come to the right place. We've been wearing and documenting fitness trackers as far back as 2015, when we reviewed the very first Apple Watch. We started cross-comparing fitness trackers as early as 2017, when we broke down the best fitness trackers for activities like strength training, running, hiking, golf, and more. Now in 2026, we're more dialed into the state of fitness trackers than ever before as nearly all our editors are wearing some sort of device on a daily basis.

On the most basic level, the best fitness trackers offer GPS connectivity to help you stay on your training course and basic activity tracking. Newer iterations of fitness trackers include advanced smartwatches that can do anything from tracking your archery workout to detecting a heart attack, as well as (our personal favorite) smart rings. Smart rings pack a ton (no literally, an absurd amount) of sleep/stress stats and workout/health information into a tiny package you wear on your finger 24/7.

Depending on what your health and fitness goals are (like losing weight, improving your sleep, or cutting time off your mile PR), the best fitness trackers can help you identify where your training is lacking, optimize your stress levels, improve your recovery time, and streamline your training sessions and daily wellness habits.

As the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, it’s my job to test the latest and greatest fitness trackers. I am supported in this effort by my fellow editors like Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., Grooming Editor Sean Zucker, Senior Gear Editor Ryan Brower, and Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM. We have put countless fitness trackers through the gauntlet and evaluated models on accuracy, design, durability, and price. We also paid close attention to comfort, ease of use, syncing with our favorite apps, and their ability to meet our standards for any activity.

We update our lineup of fitness trackers often, so you can expect up-to-date information that takes into account the latest fitness tracker releases.

If you want a basic level fitness tracker, the Whoop PEAK membership with its new 5.0 band may be your answer. Men’s Health Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. backs this device for that reason. “Simplicity is what works here, because it's reliable, has great battery life, and I don't need to think about it,” he says. The Whoop 5.0 Band is a fitness tracker band, which means though it’s still decently functional, it does not have a display like most wrist devices. It tracks all of your data in the corresponding phone app, but it’s worth noting, you cannot see the data directly on your wrist.

If you like the no-frills appearance, the Whoop 5.0 can definitely accomplish most of your tracking needs. “Whoop's activity sensing has improved over the years and continues to take steps,” says Samuel. It can track anything from running, cycling, and rowing to weightlifting, yoga, soccer, and even massage therapy. From our personal experience with Whoop, we love how it fits on the wrist. It is one of the more comfortable fitness trackers we’ve worn—the strap has a soft back, is woven with microfilament yarn, and can also be easily adjusted.

Unfortunately, Samuel had some qualms with the heart rate monitoring. “The device isn't tremendously accurate in terms of tracking heart rate, which is important to note,” he says. “In general, note that whatever [Whoop] is telling you about heart rate, it's almost always overshooting.” This can be an issue because a lot of the other tracking metrics (calories, activity, etc.) are based around heart rate. However, if you just want something basic to wear on your wrist, count your steps, and give you a general look into your health and workouts, Whoop 5.0 Band with the Peak membership will do just that.

Oura was a pioneer in the smart ring space, and it’s still the best smart ring we’ve tested to date (and we’ve tested a lot). Multiple editors have been wearing an Oura Ring for the last ten years and can attest that each new iteration outkicks the competition. This particular release updated a few physical features: Oura shifted to a fully titanium build (vs. a titanium exterior, epoxy interior), added smaller and larger sizes, and ditched its three-nodule sensor design. This latest model eliminates the nodules that used to be on the inside of the ring and pinch into my finger on the Oura Ring 3. Those aren't required anymore with the new tech, so that is a huge improvement over the past model.

The battery can also last up to eight days now, instead of just seven. And the updated software is available on all models, new and old. While Oura has always offered heart rate monitoring, the new software now features automatic heart rate monitoring, allowing you to detect and track your workout stats without hitting the “Record HR workout” button. This automatic detection feature also lends itself to workout monitoring for over 40 activities (a new capability compared to the past, solely cardio-focused tracking that Oura offered).

The daytime stress features have also gotten an improvement—one of our favorites is illness detection. The Oura Ring 5 can detect changes in your stress stats and body temperature that may indicate an illness before you feel the entirety of the symptoms. A couple of months ago, one editor felt a slight earache when they woke up, and Oura called out they may have a cold coming on. The next day, that cold had arrived. It’s not always entirely accurate like this—there have been a few times the Oura Ring has said we were getting sick when it was actually just a hangover (oops).

Even as Oura lovers, we’d be remiss not to call out one of the downsides to the product: In order to attain full use of the Oura Ring, you need to pay a monthly subscription fee of $5.99 (or $69.99 per year). There are other smart rings in the space that don’t require any fee (shout out to our second favorite product, the Ultrahuman ring), but with the updated technology and consistent top-of-the-line features, we deem the extra $69.99 per year a pretty minimal price to pay.

For the most style-conscious users, the company also released a Ceramic version of the Oura Ring 4, which offers a unique look and additional color options.

Read More: Our Hands-On Test of the Oura Ring 5

Adventurers, look this way. We’re not exaggerating when we say this is the most rugged fitness tracker we have tested. The Garmin Instinct 3 AMOLED is packed with technology and has a thick face made for trail hikes, rock climbing, and even swimming (it’s water rated up to 100 meters). According to Men’s Health contributor Korin Miller, this Garmin can take a beating. “I accidentally banged it into several doorways and even scraped it against a kettlebell during a clumsy gym moment—it still looks brand new,” Miller says.

In addition to its outwardly masculine look and durable design, the technology here is super simple to navigate, which can’t be said for all fitness trackers. Though there’s no touchscreen, Miller had the five buttons figured out within just a few minutes of receiving the product. And while you can track up to 30 different workout types, Miller praises the display for the easy-to-digest layout outside of workout mode. “The 390-by-390-pixel AMOLED display resolution is sharp and bright, allowing Garmin to jam a lot of stats on the home screen. At a glance, you can see your step count, heart rate, weather, date, time, and more. It’s arranged smartly in a way to deliver plenty of information without feeling overwhelming,” she says.

But one of our favorite features? Garmin prioritizes a wind-down time, switching from a jam-packed interface to just a clock during the time you are typically sleeping (which you note during set-up). It’s worth mentioning that in order to be this rugged and durable, the Garmin Instinct 3 is also quite heavy at 53 grams. But if you’re going hard on the trails, there’s no better wrist partner.

Read More: Our Hands-On Test of the Garmin Instinct 3

At this cost, you’d expect a simple appearance, no touchscreen, and limited functionality. However, the Google Pixel Watch 5 has a beautiful, easy-to-navigate touchscreen, a smooth design, and almost all the metrics you’d get on a more high-end device.

Google puts a big emphasis on overall wellness rather than just fitness tracking, focusing on breathing and stress management. “This is a very underrated device and it's gotten more accurate with the third edition,” says Samuel. “The breathing exercises don't reinvent the wheel, but the presentation is solid and the timing is good. Overall, in this market, there's a lot we don't fully understand about stress levels, and some of the algorithms are simplistic. But Google has smartly gotten us thinking about how we feel, and that's a good thing.”

If this watch tracks stress, readiness, and sleep, what are the limitations of this budget-friendly device? Well, it doesn’t offer as many workout modes as most other fitness trackers, clocking in at just 41 options. You also have to charge it every day, and it’s only compatible with Android devices. But for such a clean, aesthetic appearance and great individual wellness metrics, we definitely consider this fitness tracker a steal.

Most fitness trackers carry a hefty price tag, so if you’re in the market but not looking to sell out on this particular accessory, the Suunto Race S is the best value you’ll find. With a high definition AMOLED touchscreen, over 95 sport modes, and a water rating up to 50m, the specs here are just as good as you’ll find on many high-end fitness trackers. The AMOLED display on this watch is fantastic for its compact design. And personally, I think the Suunto Race S is superior to the larger model.

A lot of fitness trackers in this price range (around $350) offer only more basic tracking, like steps and calories burned. That’s not the case here, there is more to this fitness watch than just a run tracker—there are workouts and other great fitness insights, like HRV, sleep monitoring, activity tracking and race pacing. Sure, it's not as powerful as a top-of-the-line Garmin, but it gets the job done and brings great value.

Let’s chat about some of those features. Sleep tracking is having a moment and the Suunto Race S can track your sleep duration, timing, deep sleep, light sleep, heart rate, REM and HRV from sleep. One downside here? Wearing a watch to bed isn’t for everyone. Another cool feature worth digging into is race pacing. If you’re training for an upcoming marathon (or just life), the Race Pacer can help keep you on track when the mid-long run rut strikes. Overall, this is a great budget-friendly find—just note that if you opt for the titanium version over the stainless steel version, that will hike the price up by $120 (which makes it not as budget-friendly).

Apple fans already know how great the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is. It features a large, durable aerospace-grade titanium body built for outdoor adventure. It’s water-rated up to 100m and boasts dual-frequency GPS. What’s that do for you exactly? It offers much more accurate tracking in tough environments (like densely populated cities, mountain terrain, and forests)—great for trail runners and climbers.

Apple has always been at the top of the game for fitness tracking. The Ultra 4 offers all the typical metrics of the older Apple Watch models—activity rings, over 60 workout modes, blood oxygen, ECG, etc. But the Ultra 4 can be used as a dive computer, an emergency siren, and a compass that retraces your steps (ideal for those prone to getting lost mid-hike).

A watch that can do this much won’t look dainty on the wrist, though. Men’s Health Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM wrapped everything up nicely here. “The new design overhauled the sensor, which is on the rear of the watch and sits against the wearer’s wrist. Even though the casing is still the same 49-millimeter size as previous versions of the device and the sensor takes up the same amount of space.” Williams continues, “There’s now more surface area for device-to-skin contact for ECG readings, a new, circular optical sensing array, and larger, more efficient LEDs for heart rate sensing.”

For us, the only real downside is that it’s a bit chunky on the wrist, but we’ll take it—the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is truly the full package for all iPhone users.

Read More: Our Hands-On Test of the Apple Watch Ultra 4

If you’ve ever been big into running, you’ve likely considered a Garmin watch. But the Garmin Fēnix 9 isn’t just great for run tracking—it tracks over 100 different types of workouts and can last up to 29 days on one charge. In addition to its functionality, the Garmin Fēnix 9 also boasts a high-end design. One of the thinner offerings in the way of chunky Garmins, this is the perfect fitness tracking watch for anyone who doesn’t want to wear anything too cumbersome on the wrist (plus it now comes in a 43mm size). This watch has everything that fitness tracking powerhouse Garmin has to offer packed into its low-profile casing.

One of the coolest offerings? Garmin has both an AMOLED and a solar-powered option. The solar-powered watch can extend the battery life even further, but the screen is not quite as bright as the AMOLED option. The solar watch also does not have a touchscreen like the AMOLED one, making it a bit less convenient to have to click through the features via buttons.

While the Garmin Fēnix 9 has the capabilities to track pretty much any metric you want tracked, the charging experience falls a bit short. While the battery can last up to 24 days in low-power mode, turning on GPS drops that to just under 24 hours of charge—a stark difference. Additionally, the charging cord is a bit short, so you might want to keep these USB-C charger extension cords on hand to charge your Garmin.

Overall, this is a sleek, all-in-one package with a unique (and modern) solar-powered option. If you don’t mind a bit of a sub-par charging experience, you can’t get more premium than the Garmin Fēnix 9.

No iPhone? No problem. The Galaxy Watch9 can go anywhere thanks to a large scratch-resistant screen and a strong titanium case. One of our favorite features is the advanced sleep coaching that analyzes your sleep habits, suggests what you can do to improve, and is even FDA-approved to detect sleep apnea. We also appreciate the body composition reader—in just a few seconds, the Galaxy Watch9 works to tell you your vitals, and even provides a body fat estimate. These stats are prone to inaccuracy (few home devices can accurately track body fat), but we give props to Samsung for trying to push metrics to another level.

The Galaxy Watch9 also delivers the features you expect in high-end smartwatches. That means accurate dual-frequency GPS specs and voice navigation. Nailing these (as Samsung does) is extra-critical, partly because the Galaxy Watch9 has some new competition for Android users (namely, from Google's Pixel Watch).

Thanks to several generations of trial and error and new AI health insights, the Galaxy Watch gets the edge as our preferred pick for Android owners. There are more health insights and data in this watch than most competitors. Once you grant the device access to your health insights on your phone, it will make recommendations on sleep, exercise, and overall health, after you choose what your own personal goals are. I appreciate the design as well, which looks more like a classic watch than other smartwatch options.

The array of features available and the materials used to craft the watch have been optimized a few times over, thus producing a seriously strong, long-lasting fitness tracker (and everyday smart watch) most users will be happy adding to their training arsenal.

When you’re just starting out, you probably want a no-fuss fitness tracker to help get your bearings. The G-Shock Move is easy to navigate and offers just enough tracking to get you started. Men’s Health Grooming and Commerce Editor Sean Zucker tested it out for himself and likes how easy it is for newbies. “Thankfully, where the watch really excels is where it’s most meant to be used—when you’re working out or going for a run,” Zucker says. “Its face has a simple design and navigating it was a breeze, even for someone as technologically challenged as myself. It was easy to switch between lap/route times, heart rate/zone, homepage, etc. while I was running with only a couple of clicks (the watch itself only has 4 buttons so I appreciate the simplified design).”

The G-Shock Move tracks all your basic needs: steps, running, walking, heart rate, blood oxygen, and even sleep recovery. Zucker also found it quite comfortable. “[It’s a] super comfortable watch, and handles sweat/rain with ease,” he says. “It doesn’t move around at all or get greasy after a long run/workout.” Though he did have a couple qualms with the functionality.

“Now, I’m not someone who likes to wear a watch, let alone a fitness watch, all of the time but I will if I have a few minutes or I’m planning out a run,” says Zucker. “I’ll check in on what I’ve done that week and unfortunately, the app doesn’t let you access any of that info unless your phone is currently connected, which is, in my professional opinion, quite annoying.” Another small downside, Zucker did mention he had a tough time with initial setup.

“It’s important to note that I am generally 100 years old and grumpy about this type of stuff, [but] still, the set up on this watch was a bit of a pain,” says Zucker. “There were a lot of ads (this extends to the app itself after you start using as well, very muddy).” If you can get past the setup and are okay with only being able to check past stats when you’re connected to the phone app, this is a great beginner-friendly tracker offering all the basic functions you need to kick off your fitness tracking journey.

Fitbit is back, with a vengeance. The Fitbit Air is the brand’s smallest and lightest tracker ever, weighing just 12 grams and featuring a design 25 percent smaller than the discontinued Luxe. Setup is simple through the new Google Health app, and the Air’s tracking features, including 24/7 heart rate, HRV, skin temperature, and sleep, run seamlessly in the background, with automatic workout detection and a reliable seven-day battery life.

What truly elevates the experience is the integration of Google’s Health Coach AI, available through a Google Health Premium subscription, which is included for those who already have Google One. Food logging is a surprise standout—you can snap a picture of your meal, and the app accurately breaks down the macros. While the core tracking functions are available without a subscription, the real value comes from the Premium features like AI coaching, deeper analytics, and adaptive plans. But you don’t need the membership for the basic features.

Some trade-offs to consider: The Air is screenless, so you can’t check notifications or your heart rate on the go, which may take some getting used to for smartwatch users. The default band can feel a bit stiff, and you charge it off-wrist. Still, the Fitbit Air is a compelling option for those who want minimalist, screenless health tracking without a hefty commitment.

At $99 with no required subscription, it’s an accessible entry point for anyone who wants comprehensive health data and a genuinely helpful AI coach, especially those seeking a distraction-free, streamlined alternative to full-featured smartwatches.

Read More: Our Full Review of the Google Fitbit Air

Fitness trackers started as mostly wrist devices—from step counters like the Fitbit to the original Apple Watch. Now, you can choose from an array of fitness tracking watches or smart rings, all of which track far more than just your fitness. While most of these devices offer similar capabilities, the design you choose—watch or ring—will depend on your own personal aesthetic.

Do you prefer the look of a fitness tracker watch? Do you find it more convenient to navigate all your stats on your wrist? Or do you like the look of a ring better and prefer the sleeker, more compact design? If so, are you also agreeable to the fact that you will need to visit your phone app to view all of your stats? Only you have the answers to these personal questions.

Fitness trackers don’t just track fitness anymore. Sure, your workouts are still a key part of what these devices do, but in addition they’re also tracking your sleep, heart rhythm patterns, blood oxygen levels, HRV, stress, and even caffeine consumption. Fitness trackers are more of an overall wellness tool than ever before.

That said, the type of fitness tracker you choose should weigh heavily on the way you intend to use it. If you’re just looking for insights into your sleep cycle, you’ll probably want a smart ring that’s fairly comfortable to wear to bed each night. If you’re training for a marathon, you may want a watch with a touchscreen that’s easy to navigate mid-run. This last part may be especially important: If you’re already using certain tracking apps that you love (let’s say, Apple Fitness for instance), you’ll want to make sure you find yourself a fitness tracker that is compatible with that app in particular.

The accuracy of a fitness tracker begins and ends with how precisely it tracks your heart rate (most other stats, with the exception of new hydration tracking features, are derived from this baseline data). This mark is as much about pure accuracy as it is about consistency of accuracy, which is key in helping you understand your own fitness trends. While some trackers tend to be more accurate than others, all of the trackers we included here were consistently accurate.

With the exception of the Apple Watch Ultra 4 and the Samsung Galaxy Watch9 (two fitness trackers that are equal parts smartwatch but have seen improvement in their battery life), the fitness trackers we tested are all designed to run for days (even weeks) on a single charge. We love a fitness tracker that needs minimal charging, and we also love a fitness tracker that can run for a long time when running its GPS mode. Two fitness trackers that surprised us when testing battery life include the Suunto Race S (up to 13 days on a single charge) and the Garmin Instinct 3 (21 days on a single charge when set to its most basic mode).

All fitness trackers are made to take a beating, but some are better designed than others. Look at case construction, screen construction, and for smart rings, material. The most advanced fitness trackers (smart rings included) are typically made with stainless steel, titanium, or another type of quality metal. For screens, sapphire glass is a premium spec to look for thanks to its high scratch resistance and strength.

Sometimes the most durable fitness tracker is unnecessary, though, especially if you are using it for pavement running. In fact, a plastic construction fitness tracker can be a much better choice for cardio-intensive activities like running and biking, since the material is going to be much lighter than stainless steel or titanium. On the flip side, if you are using your fitness tracker for strength training (or hiking or trail running), it would make sense to look for stronger materials.
