#525. The Year's First Frost Can Kill These 3 Popular Plants. Here's How to Save Them.

Don’t let one cold snap end your garden’s season.

Every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

The first frost can catch gardeners off-guard—and leave vulnerable plants struggling to survive the cold. It’s worth protecting them before temperatures drop.

Spring and summer may be the showiest seasons in the garden, but autumn is the time to prepare plants for winter. Here’s what to look out for and how to help your flowers weather the first frost.

“The first autumn frost often catches gardeners off-guard because it arrives while your garden still looks full of life,” says Eflorist flower and garden expert David Denyer. “Many plants have been putting out new growth after a warm summer and wet September, but that growth is full of water and has soft cell walls. When frosty temperatures arrive, the water inside your plants freezes and expands, rupturing those cells and leaving them blackened and unable to recover.

“Later in winter, most plants naturally harden off and become more resilient, but the first frost usually arrives before they’ve had the chance to do that, which is why it can cause so much damage.”

So, which plants are most at risk? Begonias, dahlias, and cosmos can all suffer in the first frost if they aren’t protected.

“Half-hardy bedding plants, like begonias, are usually among the first to suffer because they can’t tolerate freezing temperatures,” Denyer says.

“Dahlias are another one to keep an eye on. Their fleshy tubers store water, and once that water freezes, the tuber walls burst, which means the plant won’t regrow next year.”

And the same applies to cosmos. Monique Kemperman, horticultural expert at Plants & Flowers Foundation Holland, says, “Cosmos are particularly vulnerable to the first frost because they are tender annuals that originate from warmer climates. As with dahlias, frost damages the water within their cells, causing stems, foliage and flowers to quickly blacken and collapse.

“Unlike hardier autumn plants, they don't have the natural resilience to withstand freezing temperatures, so even a light frost can bring their flowering season to an abrupt end.”

There’s no need to panic as temperatures drop: a few simple steps can help protect dahlias, begonias and cosmos from frost. Denyer recommends covering vulnerable plants when a cold night is forecast.

“To protect your plants from frost overnight, you need to slow down how quickly they lose the warmth they’ve absorbed during the day,” he says. “Covering your more vulnerable plants with fleece, cloches, or even an old sheet will trap a thin layer of warmer air around them and stop it escaping overnight.”

Be sure to remove the covers the next morning so air can circulate. Leaving them on during the day can trap moisture, Denyer warns, increasing the risk of rot and mold.

Potted plants and hanging baskets need a slightly different kind of protection. If a frost is forecast, move vulnerable containers close to a wall, where they’ll be sheltered and can benefit from the warmth stored in the brick or stone.

“Brick and stone walls hold onto warmth during the day and release it slowly at night, which can help raise the temperature around your plants by a few degrees, which is often enough to stop frost forming,” Denyer explains.

You can also help protect plants by insulating the soil around them. “Adding a mulch of compost, bark, or even fallen leaves around the base of your plants helps to insulate the soil and keep moisture and temperature levels steady,” Denyer suggests. “By protecting your soil, you’re also protecting your plants’ roots by preventing damage from constant freezing and thawing, which means they’ll stay stronger and recover more easily in spring.”

#526. How Many Steps Should You Walk a Day for Maximum Health Benefits? Experts Weigh In

Pretty much everyone has an opinion on how many steps you should take in a day. My Oura Ring sets a goal based on how much rest I got the night before, while influencers online always seem to be peddling the magical 10,000-step count.

And it’s not just influencers. At this point, we’ve all heard about the 10,000-step rule, whether it’s something your mom’s walking group aims for, your high-achieving friend hits like clockwork, or a goal you feel internal pressure to hit.

But this number is more arbitrary than you think. Though the 10,000-step rule of thumb—which shakes out to about five miles—has been around since the 1960s, there’s little evidence to support that it should be your target, according to a 2022 review in The Lancet.

Luckily, there is some newer research that helps clarify what an ideal step goal is, and spoiler alert: It’s lower than 10,000 per day. Here’s how to determine how much you should actually walk per day, according to experts.

Meet the experts: Alexander Rothstein, CSCS, ACSM-EP, is an exercise physiologist and instructor for the exercise science program at the New York Institute of Technology. Laura A. Richardson, PhD, is a professor of applied exercise science and movement science at the University of Michigan School of Kinesiology.

On the low end, anything above 2,200 steps (which is roughly over a mile) was associated with lower mortality and cardiovascular disease, according to a 2024 study in the British Journal of Sports Medicine. Remember: Any movement is better than nothing, and for people who are just starting out, the payoffs of shorter distances can be huge.

But, if you want a step count to aim for, the most recent research suggests it should be around 7,000. Per a 2025 meta review in the The Lancet Public Health that analyzed data from 88 different studies, 7,000 steps every day is enough to reduce your risk of dementia, cancer, type 2 diabetes, and depression, particularly when compared to people who walk 2,000 steps a day. Even more interesting? Additional steps beyond 7,000 only saw marginal benefits. (Basically, don’t let anyone make you feel bad for not hitting a full 10K steps.)

One thing to keep in mind is that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that adults get 150 minutes of moderate- to vigorous-intensity exercise per week, so if walking is your main form of exercise, you want to make sure that you’re hitting this number of minutes—no matter what the step count is, says Alexander Rothstein, CSCS, an exercise physiologist and instructor for the exercise science program at the New York Institute of Technology.

This might mean walking for about 22 minutes every single day or for 30 minutes, five days a week. Since time is what matters and everyone walks at a different pace, there’s a range of how many steps and miles this would shake out to.

Another thing that’s non-negotiable is making sure your walks fall into that moderate- to vigorous-intensity range. Your heart rate should be elevated and your breathing should be a little heavy to make sure you’re really getting the cardio benefits of a walk instead of just taking a leisurely saunter.

Join WH+ to Get the 4-Week Walking Plan That Burns Fat and Builds Muscle

Something else experts want you to consider is that when it comes to walking for better health, frequency is also super important. “With walking, you’re looking for this to be as many days of the week as you can,” says Laura A. Richardson, PhD, a professor of applied exercise science at the University of Michigan. It’s all about finding a step count that’s sustainable—as in, it won’t leave you dreading going on your daily walk—which will be different for everybody based on their fitness level. Start with fewer miles and then increase over time.

Aim for: anywhere between 2,000 and 7,000 steps per day—which is between one and three and a half miles. Keep in mind that the total time, intensity, and frequency of your walks are also important.

Fat loss requires a calorie deficit, meaning you’re burning more calories than you're taking in (more on how to calculate that number, here). So, answering this question really comes down to energy expenditure, both experts agree. Increasing distance or intensity are both ways to turn up the amount of energy you’re using on a walk, so it's critical to take those factors into account if you want to maximize the weight loss potential of your walk. One 2018 study in Obesity found that 10,000 steps did enhance weight loss, especially if 3,500 of those steps were performed at a higher intensity.

Keep in mind: So many other factors like genetics, nutrition, and environment significantly contribute to someone's ability to lose weight, so it's not as simple as adhering to a step count. You can always reach out to a doctor or dietitian to provide tailored guidance about what will work best for you. One benefit of walking for weight loss is that it's a low-impact option that's gentle on the body, making it a more sustainable option.

Aim for: closer to two miles (and up to five) at a higher-intensity speed. But remember that walking alone might not be enough to see weight loss results, and strength training and nutrition are key.

You don’t need to hit your step goal in one fell swoop. In fact, it may be best to break it up throughout the day with walking breaks. Focusing on breaking up sedentary time, or the time that you spend not moving, has important health benefits that might be more important than your total distance walked per day, Rothstein says. One small 2024 study in Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise found that people who got up and walked for just 5 minutes after 30 minutes of sitting were more likely to have lower blood pressure and lower blood sugar.

Plus, “micro-walks,” or walking in short bursts throughout the day, were found to use more energy than walking the same distance all at once in a 2024 Proceedings of the Royal Society B study. They demand more of your metabolism and can improve circulation, mental health, and digestive health when spaced out, per previous WH reporting.

I know what you may be thinking: Why would you want to make a walk more challenging? Well, you want all the heart health benefits, don’t ya?

Walking too casually could mean that you’re not working your cardio system hard enough to improve it, and well, then you may have spent time thinking you’re working out—but not quite doing as much as you could. Remember: Ideally, you should feel like you’re working. Your heart rate should be slightly elevated, and you may breathe a bit harder.

At the end of the day, the science is clear: Any number of steps is something to celebrate. There are ways to fine-tune your walks for sure, but just getting out there will make a difference.

#527. Chicken Caesar Smash Tacos

I could eat chicken Caesar salad every day of the week, but unfortunately my family won’t let me get away with that, so these chicken Caesar smash tacos are a perfect compromise. Crispy smash chicken patties are topped with mounds of Caesar-dressed romaine, Parmesan, and croutons for a playful mash-up that takes “taco Tuesday” to a whole new level.

My top tips:Medium heat and a well-oiled pan are key to getting the perfect cook on these smash tacos. Ground chicken can easily dry out, but in testing I found that cooking the tacos chicken-side-down on a medium heat for just two minutes gave them a beautifully caramelized crust and allowed them to cook through while still keeping them plenty juicy. If you happen to have a large flat-top cast iron griddle, this is the perfect time to use it; otherwise, a cast iron pan will work just as well!

Make ahead & storage:I don’t recommend making these tacos ahead (they tend to be soggy once refrigerated!), but if you don’t want to eat all eight at once, you can scale down the amount of ground chicken and salad and only season, assemble, and cook the number of tacos that you want at one time. Fortunately, it doesn’t take long to make them fresh.

#528. Deli Meat Has Long Been Linked to Health Problems. Inside the Race to Make Cold Cuts Healthier.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

One company swears its cracked the code on “clean” lunchmeat.

My daughter loves the stuff, though. With a slice of white American cheese and a squiggle each of Kewpie mayo and yellow mustard, there’s nothing she’d rather eat between two slices of bread. But when I remove that glistening pink pork slice from its plastic wrap, I do so with two pinched fingers, as if I were transferring something questionable. Because, in essence, I guess I am.

Even though the deli meat category is worth an estimated $217 billion globally—and projected to grow further, fueled by the demand for quick, protein-rich options—nutrition researchers have long known that cold cuts are awful for us.

The World Health Organization has, since 2015, classified cured meats as a Group 1 carcinogen. Research over decades has linked a diet heavy in the food additives found in processed meat to a slew of health problems beyond cancer, too, including type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

And now a whole bunch of influencers online are decrying cold cuts as an ultra-processed food while they toss packs of lunch meat into garbage cans. “They’re packed with nitrates, nitrites, preservatives, and emulsifiers. Lunch meat is like rocket fuel for inflammation. Start cleaning your fridge now,” says Pete Sulack, a chiropractor and holistic influencer with 960K followers on Instagram.

There’s a #MAHA bent to all these claims, too. “To Make America Healthy Again, we must return to the basics,” reads the latest Dietary Guidelines for Americans, which the secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., helped to formulate. “With a dramatic reduction in highly processed foods laden with refined carbohydrates, added sugars, excess sodium, unhealthy fats, and chemical additives, this approach can change the health trajectory for so many Americans.”

The mounting social media and political pressure have the lunch meat industry shook. Deli counter sales have been trending downward, according to recent data from the market analytics firm Circana.

Yet at least one of America’s largest producers of cold cuts believes it can innovate its way out of worrying trends. The company is close to reaching a goal that has taken it roughly a decade to achieve: a near-complete product line of “clean” cold cuts, redesigned for the wellness age.

It’s a meat feat that goes well beyond your typical “uncured” products at the grocery store, the company says. And its team was so proud of that fact that they invited me down to their facilities to experience it for myself.

THE HEADQUARTERS OF Dietz & Watson sits just north of the Delaware River in an industrialized area of northeast Philadelphia, a city that might well be called the deli meat capital of America. Philly is so dedicated to its hoagie culture (don’t you dare call them “subs”) that, in 1992, then mayor Ed Rendell publicly declared the hoagie—not the cheesesteak—the official sandwich of the city. At Wawa, a gas station and hoagie shop chain proliferating throughout the metropolitan area, it’s not uncommon to see a Philly dude sporting a tattoo of a flying goose, the company’s logo.

To tour Dietz & Watson’s 350,000-square-foot production facility is to look very closely at ham. Nearly everywhere you step in the factory, there is the smell of smoked meat; a color palette of pink, beige, and brown; brick floors glistening with sodium bicarbonate cleaning solution. The processing floor is bracingly cold, and everyone is wrapped in hygienic/protective casing of some kind. I myself sport a fashionable beard-and-hair net, polyester-blend lab coat, and stretchy booties.

Past the rooms of workers shuttling racks of swaying sausages, beyond massive plastic tubs filled with shrink-wrapped hunks of beef, and separate from a Dr. Seussian contraption casually referred to as the “hot dog roller coaster” sits the company’s research and development kitchen.

It’s in this room that Dietz & Watson has worked to engineer and deploy what it claims is a revolution in deli meat processing. Its executives say the method significantly reduces, if not eliminates, the potential formation of nitrosamines—the technical name for the unstable compounds that have been linked to cancer, heart problems, and diabetes.

Through a combination of what the company calls “alternative curing methods” and controlled cooking temperature, Dietz & Watson will soon sell a nearly complete line of “clean” deli meat products engineered to mitigate the formation of nitrosamines.

Louis Eni Jr., president and CEO of Dietz & Watson, told me during my visit that his company overhauled its curing process because of growing consumer demand. Eni, too, is wearing a lab coat, but no booties over his dress shoes. He’s worked for the company for more than 50 years and is the kind of guy you imagine would make an excellent grandfather—dark brown eyes behind thin-rimmed glasses, always ready with an anecdote. He’s almost jovial. And very convincing.

“There’s a big push—and I agree with the push—[against] processed foods. You know, highly processed, ultra-processed foods,” Eni says. “We need to desperately make sure that we message properly so that consumers don’t associate what’s been for years called processed meats as ultra-processed foods.” Eni says that, instead, what Dietz & Watson makes is “multistep prepared meats.” That phrase doesn’t really roll off the tongue either, but as I tour the facility, I begin to understand what he’s talking about.

Early in Dietz & Watson’s history, the company used synthetic nitrates and nitrites to cure its meats, and the link between those lab-made ingredients and dangerous nitrosamines has become a frequent target of health research and the anti-cold cut cabal. Now the company uses all-natural additives to preserve the shelf life of the product and prevent bacterial growth, including botulism. (Natural curing agents may produce nitrosamines, too, but more on that soon.)

Dietz & Watson’s curing process begins with raw, pre-butchered cuts of meat, like the kind you might find at the butcher shop. Those cuts undergo a marinade stage, in which hundreds of microneedles inject the meat with a salt solution that contains its natural curing ingredients: celery juice powder and acerola cherry powder.

“We found adding cherry powder helps stabilize color a lot, and it helps in controlling the nitrous elements that come out of the cure,” says Gregory Yingling, operations and procurement at Dietz & Watson. The celery powder, which is naturally high in nitrites, helps cure the meat, ensuring food safety and quality, he says. Neither ingredient tastes like anything that would throw off the flavor of a ham sandwich. The ocher-colored celery powder is earthy, almost like cumin. The cherry powder is faintly tart.

Other deli meat manufacturers use natural curing agents—and even celery and cherry powders—but Yingling says his team has discovered the ideal minimal amounts to cure products that have few to no nitrites remaining in the final product.

The salt in Dietz & Watson’s marinade cures the meat too, but it also acts as an abrasive. That’s important because after the meat marinates for at least 24 hours, powerful vacuums transport the cuts into cement truck–like drums that tumble everything until tenderized. The abrasive salt, through tumbling, creates a slightly tacky texture on the meat. “We call [that texture] ‘meat glue,’ ” says Yingling, pointing to a plastic tub of semi-macerated marinated chicken breasts. “That tackiness—that’s myosin. That’s the protein that the salt has brought to the surface.” The production line then takes that sticky meat and bundles everything together in a net, which helps mold deli meat products into the uniform shape consumers have come to expect.

“Some competitors grind up the meat, suck it into [a tumbler], put a bunch of marinade in it, and spin it for 30 minutes,” says Yingling. Unlike synthetic curing ingredients, which dissolve in a salt solution, natural ingredients like celery powder can require longer marinating periods. That extra time means less efficiency, says Yingling, but it’s critical for ensuring a safer product. Translation: less risk of nitrosamines in the final product.

But heat, too, may lead to the formation of nitrosamines—even in deli meat processed with natural curing agents. Nitrogen compounds are unstable and combust when temperatures rise. (This is also why you’ve likely heard that grilling or frying cured meats like bacon is especially dangerous.) Although scientists haven’t yet pinpointed the exact temperature at which nitrosamines start to form, they agree that lower temps are less risky. Yingling’s team has found the same: Controlling the heat also helps prevent nitrosamines from showing up in cooked meat.

Eni guides me into a cavernous room that houses what can only be described as a metal bathtub the size of a shipping container. “The water’s about 175, 180 degrees,” he says. “It’s this very even cooking medium where the temperature comes up evenly.” As soon as the meat is done, off it plunges into an ice bath to prevent overcooking.

After chilling, and depending on the product, Dietz & Watson’s meats are dispersed elsewhere around the facility. Some go into a slow-smoking chamber, others undergo further seasoning, and some fly off for slicing and packaging. And, at some point, some products find their way to the meat lab, where Yingling and his team will run tests to ensure that the meat contains as few residual nitrites as possible.

Dietz & Watson isn’t the first company to swap synthetic curing agents for natural ones. In fact, in the early 1990s, Eni’s company actually helped create uncured deli meats and hot dogs for Applegate Farms, which was then an organic-focused boutique brand. (Quick but important side note: Deli meat labels in the U.S. can carry the word “uncured” as long as no synthetic curing agents were used in the processing. And yes, even though they are still technically cured.)

Back then, Dietz & Watson used a vegetable-based natural curing agent, Yingling says, but not cherry powder, which has the ability to prevent nitrosamine formation in the final product. Eni says the consumer response to Applegate products was exciting. In the early 2000s, Dietz & Watson began experimenting with—and eventually launched—its own brand of uncured ham.

Plenty of competitors followed. In 2006, Hormel launched its Natural Choice line of cold cuts, free of preservatives, artificial colors, and artificial flavors. (The line was relaunched in 2015, and it includes ham, chicken, turkey, and salami.) Oscar Mayer expanded its Deli Fresh line, with no artificial preservatives or flavorings, in 2014. Applegate (now owned by Hormel Foods) still sells uncured bacon, breakfast sausage without added nitrites or nitrates, and uncured ham deli meat.

All these brands use some type of alternative curing method—often a form of celery and sea salt. Many of them tout language like “uncured,” “no artificial flavors or preservatives,” and the ever-present “no nitrates or nitrites added.” Yet despite their health halo, “uncured” deli meat contained a similar amount of potentially carcinogenic compounds when compared with traditionally cured products, revealed third-party tests from Consumer Reports.

Dietz & Watson insists that its new products are different. Yingling says that they’ve learned since 2022 to use just enough of their natural curing agents to minimize and, in some cases, eliminate the potential nitrosamine conversion. By next year, 99 percent of Dietz & Watson’s deli meat will follow its new standards. The goal: “as clean a label as possible,” Eni says. I asked Eni whether it was okay for my daughter to eat their ham every day. “Every day,” he told me with a smile and a nod.

I was still torn over whether Dietz & Watson’s “clean” ham was lipstick on a pig or a viable healthy choice for my family and myself. I’ll admit that I was feeling better about deli meat, but I was still leaving it off the weekly shopping list because I had more questions—ones I knew only scientists who studied this stuff could answer.

WITHIN THE PAST decade, scientists have started to unpack something interesting about nitrosamines: They’re always in you. “Nitrosamines don’t only form in the factory or the frying pan—they also form inside your own body,” says Norman Hord, PhD, RD, the director of the School of Human Environmental Sciences at the University of Arkansas. “When you swallow nitrate from any food, some of it is converted into nitrite, and the acid in your stomach turns that into the same reactive chemicals that build nitrosamines.”

This is true even of vegetables, especially arugula, spinach, beets, and, yes, celery, which are all loaded with nitrate. Consider that researchers have even found nitrosamines in dairy products and booze, and you may want to start swearing off anything processed.

But hold up: “We’re still pinning down how much dietary risk [nitrosamines] carry at real-world amounts,” Hord says. “That argues for sensible moderation now, not panic.” While the science unfolds, experts say there’s a simple way forward to better health.

Gunter Kuhnle is a professor of food and nutritional sciences at the University of Reading in the U.K. He’s studied nitrosamines extensively, and he told me there’s a two-pronged approach we can take to reduce risk.

The first prong, obviously, is eating deli meat that contains few to no nitrates or nitrites—or eating less of the stuff that does. What’s more, if you’re cooking deli meat, like sizzling ham for a breakfast sandwich, doing so over low heat can help prevent nitrosamines from forming.

The second is eating deli meat along with fruits and vegetables. Because there’s also a decent amount of science behind how certain antioxidants can prevent the formation of nitrosamines, both during food production stages and in the digestive system, says Kuhnle.

A 2025 study found that people who were overweight or had obesity and ate a diet high in nitrite-rich vegetables (again: arugula, spinach, celery, beets) reduced their risk of cardio-metabolic health problems, likely because of the vegetables’ favorable effect on blood pressure, fasting glucose, and cholesterol levels.

“The same thing is true if you consume high amounts of nitrite with high amounts of fiber. It also reduces the amount of nitrosamines that form,” Kuhnle says. (It probably goes without saying, but deli meat contains no fiber and paltry amounts of antioxidants.) “So even without changing the products, changing the diet can already do a lot of good,” he says. Think of pairing deli meats with high-fiber fruits and vegetables as a sort of “nitrosamine offset,” like how rich people who fly private purchase “carbon offsets,” such as funding tree planting, to ease their guilty consciences.

While I reported this article, I wasn’t buying ham or eating hoagies. On my trip down to Dietz & Watson headquarters, I briefly considered stopping by DiCostanza’s for an Italian hoagie, but the itinerary was tight and it also felt antithetical. Nitrosamines had scared me off. Plus, the USDA does not currently set limits, nor does it test for amounts of natural curing agents—like celery juice powder or cherry powder. This leaves deli meat companies to largely self-police the safety of their uncured products.

But to hear from Kuhnle that I could occasionally enjoy deli meat, and even give it to my daughter if we were eating a fiber-rich diet—well, that seemed like a fine compromise.

“I always think that the big problem in nutrition is trying to find sort of the magic bullet,” he says. “The only dietary recommendation I know that most people in nutrition can agree on is the idea of a balanced diet”—which, Kuhnle stresses, is a varied diet: fruits and vegetables, beans and legumes, fish and seafood, and, yes, even some deli meat now and then. “This is very, very boring—the one thing which will never get you any headlines,” Kuhnle says. But a balanced and varied diet works.

Dietz & Watson’s reformulated products won’t start hitting grocery stores until around the time this article comes out and, fine, okay, I’ll eventually make the switch to its ham for my daughter. But when I pack her a ham and cheese sandwich, I’ll also swap our usual whole wheat sandwich bread for a brand that has more fiber per slice. And instead of Ritz crackers, I’ll pack her some kind of fruit—raspberries, grapes, blueberries—on the side. Maybe someday I’ll even throw in a beet and see what happens.

But I’m not sure when I’ll eat a hoagie again. That’s blasphemy coming from a guy who lives deep in Wawa country, I know. Instead, next time a craving strikes, maybe I’ll make my own hoagie at home. With just a few slices of deli meat, a ton of vegetables, and a great big salad on the side.

Paul Kita is a Deputy Editor at Men's Health, where he has covered food, cooking, nutrition, supplements, grooming, tech, travel, and fatherhood at the brand for more than 15 years. If you’re looking to bring an air of storied sophistication to your home, look no further than Benjamin Moore’s 2027 color of the year: Webster Green.

“For 2027, our focus centered on the green color family,” says Andrea Magno, vice president of brand, color, and integrated marketing at Benjamin Moore. “When we looked across the past, present, and future of color trends, variations on green consistently demonstrated remarkable staying power.”

Interestingly, greens appear to be ruling the design industry right now, with other paint brands announcing their own verdant shades for their 2027 color of the year. Benjamin Moore’s 2027 pick is quite a departure from its 2026 honoree, Silhouette AF-655, an elevated neutral with deep charcoal undertones.

“Webster Green HC-130 reflects this timeless appeal by pairing reassuring stability with optimistic energy. Its composed nature feels both rooted and forward-looking, while enhancing spaces that feel distinctive, collected and continually new,” says Magno.

The shade comes from the brand’s collection of historical colors. Originally launched in 1976, the year of America’s bicentennial, the assemblage of hues was inspired by 18th- and 19th-century design trends that came to define North American architecture. Describing the lush tone now as the “quintessential shade of green,” the team at Benjamin Moore hopes to channel a feeling of timelessness while reading bold enough to make a statement.

In their lookbook, the team at Benjamin Moore pairs the almost jewel-toned green with watery Nelson Blue, powdery Wild Aster, and rich Townsend Harbor Brown, highlighting the adaptability of the shade, thanks in part to its rich olive and deep blue-gray undertones.

“The green color family’s ability to adapt and transform makes it incredibly timeless,” says Magno. “Sitting at the center point is Webster Green HC-130, a mid-tone that serves as a reminder of the past but feels right and relevant today.”

#531. The Surprising Mid-Race Fuel Runners Are Using Instead of Energy Gels

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Training for a race can get expensive. New running shoes, clothes, running belt, and race fees add up fast. Factor in the energy gels and chews runners use to fuel long runs, and the cost can push a budget to its breaking point—and cause some unwanted G.I. problems, too.

Instead, some runners on TikTok are sharing cheaper, simpler alternatives. Peanut butter and jellies, chewy candy, applesauce packets, and even maple syrup are replacing the name-brand energy gels and chews on high-mileage training days.

But can candies, syrups, and other everyday foods fuel you as effectively as specialized sports nutrition products? And when do runners need to be fueling in the first place? We asked dietitians and run coaches when fueling matters, which everyday, accessible foods can get the job done, and what to consider when experimenting with a new fueling strategy.

During exercise, the body relies largely on carbohydrates, which are converted to glucose and stored as glycogen in the muscles and liver. “Your body only has so much stored carbohydrate to burn, and it starts running low somewhere around 60 to 90 minutes into a run, depending on where your fitness is,” says Kelly Roberts, certified run coach and founder of Badass Lady Gang.

Hitting that wall can cause a load of side effects, including fatigue, brain fog, stomach issues, mood swings, or a slow running pace. “Mid-run fuel keeps you ahead of that, so you're feeding your body before it asks,” she says.

How many carbs you need depends largely on your fitness level and the length and intensity of your workout. For runs lasting over 90 minutes, Roberts recommends consuming 40 to 60 grams of carbs an hour, though some athletes may need closer to 60 to 90 grams. It’s recommended to start taking in carbs about 30 to 45 minutes into a run.

For runs longer than 90 minutes, you’ll want to consume at least 40 to 60 grams of carbs per hour, starting about 30 minutes into your run, Roberts says.

Fuel is a performance tool, Roberts says. “The longer you're going to be out there or the harder you plan to run, the higher your carb needs may be. Running is already really hard. Fueling runs—both before and during—actually makes it easier.”

You’re not necessarily missing out by skipping specialty products, Roberts says.

Gels can be useful because they are fast-digesting and convenient to carry and consume, but they’re not automatically more effective at fueling than regular foods. “Real food usually gives you more sustained energy and tends to be easier on the stomach,” Roberts notes.

The best choice comes down to personal preference and what your body can tolerate. “Oftentimes familiarity and comfort are the most important variables when the body is pushing hard,” says Leslie Bonci, RD, sports dietitian for the Kansas City Chiefs.

Bonci and Roberts recommend trying options such as:

Don’t feel like you need to be snacking up a storm during your run, either (last time I checked, eating while running is no easy feat). “A little goes a long way,” Bonci says. Eating small amounts every hour or so can help you work toward your carbohydrate target.

The key is to find a fueling strategy that will work for you, without surprises, on race day. “Treat every long run like a dress rehearsal, because nothing new should show up on race day,” Roberts says.

It takes time to adjust to taking in the amount of carbs most people need for marathons and half-marathons, so slowly start by working your way up to 40 to 60 grams per hour, including your sports drinks.

Practice chewing and swallowing while running, Roberts says. Take a walk break until you get used to it if you need to.

If you are on a budget but appreciate the convenience of pre-packaged gels, you can always start with real food for the first several weeks of training. Then, slowly incorporate more gels once you get about six to eight weeks out of your event, Roberts says.

This approach gives your body time to adjust to gels without requiring you to buy them throughout an entire 16- to 20-week training period. Whatever fuel you choose, test it during training to make sure it works for your stomach, pace, and race-day needs.

#532. Prime Video’s Carrie Covers All of Stephen King’s Book. Here’s Why Season 2 Could Still Happen.

Mike Flanagan has talked about a potential three-season arc for this new version of the story.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

IT’S ALWAYS INTERESTING to see how different creative people decide to adapt classic, iconic stories that have been adapted before—and how audiences then react to those adaptations. The latest story to find itself under the microscope in that way is Carrie, which first entered the world as Stephen King’s debut novel in 1974 before being adapted into a film three separate times, a stage musical in 1988, and now, in 2026, a television series for Prime Video created by Mike Flanagan.

If someone wanted to see a pretty close adaptation of King’s novel—and a masterpiece of a film—then look no further than the Brian De Palma–directed Carrie, which first hit theaters in 1976. The two other film adaptations, which were released in 2002 and 2013, were not quite as highly revered.

Flanagan’s TV series, then, operates on three different levels: bringing the ’70s-set source material into our 2026 world, expanding on characters and subplots from the book that had to be cut from a film but that an eight-episode series has time for, and, finally, doing something entirely new altogether.

It’s always going to be the case that some people aren’t going to like that last part. But in Carrie, Flanagan goes for it, making some major changes to the source material in his adaptation (like keeping Carrie White alive at the end of the story) and bringing things like a cult/coven into the mix.

When it comes to making Carrie the TV show, these new aspects to things were kind of the whole point, especially when it came to getting Stephen King on board. “The changes were what excited him, because I think he loved De Palma's movie. It'd already been done,” Flanagan told Men’s Health about working with King, who is also an executive producer on the show. “Changes were the thing that got him to sit forward and be like, ‘Oh, well, this could be actually really interesting. This could be really different.’”

And while the first season of Carrie covers the entire arc of the novel—including, of course, the iconic prom night massacre and its aftermath—it does keep Carrie alive, and introduces a host of powerful new characters who have never been included in the Carrie lore before. (Although we will note that the end of the Carrie novel does suggest that there are others out there with Carrie’s abilities, and that the rest of the world is just going to have to deal with it.)

So, does that mean Carrie will continue on for a season 2?

Flanagan has said that in an ideal world, his Carrie show would have three seasons. “I think it’s three seasons,” he told Collider. “In my dream scenario, I think Carrie has a wonderful three-step arc. It’s a trilogy, really.”

He’s done something very smart in that regard. The Carrie show, as is, exists as a wonderful retelling and adaptation of King’s original story. But he’s also planted these seeds that allow the Carrie character to continue on with her own story, while also teasing some future characters—including cult leader Adelaide (played by Kate Siegel) and others—who could absolutely figure into things should the story continue.

He told Men’s Health that his focus has been exclusively on getting this first season out and rendering it as well as possible. But that doesn’t mean he hasn’t begun to speculate about what could be fun for the future, either, and that seems to point toward the cult/coven that was teased throughout the season. “There's so much richness just in the Carrie White that we got to explore in this season,” he said. “That character has so much more potential to see where she goes from here. We only got to see the tip of the iceberg of her place in this legacy of other gifted women, and I think that's where the focus would be. But I've worked in television long enough to know that I shouldn't think too much about that until it's time to.”

There’s also the Amanda character as well, played by The Mandalorian and Battlestar Galactica star Katee Sackhoff, who was revealed to be both Emmaline’s mother and some kind of assassin of powered people. That could be a strong villain should the show continue.

There are a lot of possibilities going forward, should Carrie move toward a second season. But for now, we’ll just have to wait and see what happens.

#533. 8 Signs You Secretly Think Like an Interior Designer, According to Experts

This profession takes more than just having good taste.

Pictured above: A kitchen designed by McCroskey Interiors in our 2023 Whole Home.

Many people assume that helming a successful interior design firm is all about having impeccable taste. And yes, while an instinct for color or the ability to effortlessly pick the perfect rug size for any room certainly come in handy, they’re only one part of what it takes to thrive in the profession.

According to Neal Beckstedt, founder of Neal Beckstedt Studio, the best designers often possess qualities that seem to contradict one another. “Creative yet practical, free-thinking yet organized, and being a great listener yet opinionated are my top three must-haves,” he says. Balancing these traits is essential, especially while juggling deadlines, budgets, contractors, clients, and the inevitable surprises that come with every project. Success in interior design depends as much on problem-solving and organization as it does on artistic vision.

We spoke with experts across the industry to learn the essential traits all exceptional designers possess. Here’s what they said.

Recognizing that a manicured garden or a museum-quality painting is beautiful isn't hard, but it's seeing beauty in the everyday moments that helps designers make the most of a room.

“Having an innate appreciation of beauty allows you to see potential in every space,” says Cheryl Luckett, the founder of Dwell by Cheryl. “When you naturally appreciate beauty, you’re able to recognize the little details that make a room feel truly special,” she adds. “This deep sense of beauty guides you in designing spaces that not only function well but also inspire and bring joy to the people who live there.”

Many designers have an innate sense of inquisitiveness that fosters their desire to push beyond the expected. “From an early age, successful designers tend to be curious about their surroundings,” says Linda Hayslett, the founder of LH.Designs. “They have a heightened awareness of how spaces feel and function, and they notice details others might overlook. This attentiveness allows them to instinctively understand what elements make a space cohesive or disruptive.”

It takes time to develop a discerning eye; designer Michelle Gage of Michelle Gage Interiors recommends seeking out opportunities that stretch you beyond what you typically see and experience. “Take yourself to museums and home shops,” she adds. “Get out and travel. Be around other people who do the same. You must put in the time.”

On a tight budget? Flip through magazines, books, or browse design stores instead. “Scrolling on social media has its purpose and can be inspiring, but you have to get out from behind the screen if you want to really hone your eye and become the person with ‘the gift,’” Gage adds.

Developing and understanding your own personal style is the difference between recognizing what looks good and creating a great space yourself.

“Having a defined sense of style brings clarity and confidence,” Luckett says. “When you know your style, it helps you create spaces that are cohesive and true to your vision, while also allowing your clients to trust in your direction.” Of course, one doesn’t want to become too rigid. “It’s not about sticking to one specific look but having a strong foundation that guides your choices, making it easier to blend your expertise with what your clients need.”

That said, being able to choose a nice couch or pretty pillow is all well and good, but having a sense of how all the different components will come together is a crucial trait. “It’s more than just knowing what looks good; it’s understanding how colors, textures, and layouts can create harmony and evoke emotion,” says Luckett. This means also having a strong understanding of scale, proportion, and flow, she explains.

Confidence is also key when it comes to being able to resolve problems that emerge during the design process.

“No design project goes 100 percent smoothly,” Hayslett says. “Whether it’s an unexpected layout issue, sourcing difficulty, or budget constraint, skilled designers are adaptable and thrive on problem-solving. They view obstacles as challenges to overcome with creativity.”

Sarah Lederman, the founder of Sarah Lederman Interiors, agrees. “At the end of the day, it's a client-centric business,” she says. “Even if [clients] understand your aesthetic, they are all looking for different outcomes, so being open and willing to try different approaches will take you far.”

Interior designers know how to quickly make—and feel confident in—their decisions. “I have always had a strong gut instinct,” says Amy Studebaker, the founder of Amy Studebaker Design. “I follow that feeling often, whether I am selecting fabrics, navigating clients, building my team, or determining what’s next,” she adds. “That trust and confidence in myself and others tends to lead me in the right direction and keep me on track as a designer and business owner.”

“The trait that has pushed me further in my career as a designer is being empathetic to my clients and their wants and needs,” says Phil Norman, the founder of Norman Design Group. “Being a good listener and picking up on things they may not be telling you is what sets good designers apart.”

Designers need to be able to look at an empty room and picture a world of potential. “Looking at a space, you can quickly envision in your mind exactly what it’s going to look like before you even get started,” Nayak says. However, having the ability to sell that vision to others is equally important, says Sarah Fleischer, the founder of SRF Interiors. “You can have the best design sense and style, but without the confidence to communicate that vision or opinion to a client, it likely won’t get you very far,” she says.

In some cases, executing one’s vision may require pushing clients beyond their comfort zones, which requires excellent communication skills, says Cheri Etchelecu Martin, the founder of Cheri Etchelecu Interior Design. “Without solid communication skills, a project will be unsuccessful, no matter how wildly creative you may be,” she says.

Those who appreciate order and direction will feel right at home in the design world. “Many skilled designers have Type A personalities, which means they thrive on precision and control,” Hayslett says. “It’s not just about noticing the big things—like a room’s layout or color scheme—but the smallest details that others may overlook, like whether screws match a fixture’s finish or if a light bulb looks wrong or out of place.”

I’ll be honest—working out in shorts was never really my thing. I’ve always been more of a leggings girl. I used to think flowy shorts felt too exposed and compression shorts weren’t flattering. But since I'm a style writer who lives a pretty active lifestyle, I figured it was time to give athletic shorts a real shot. Now, after testing over 20 pairs of workout shorts over the past year and a half, I can officially say I’m a convert.

Alongside stylists and other WH editors, I tested the internet's most popular workout shorts. Over the past two years, we evaluated them based on coverage, moisture-wicking abilities, comfort, size range, and fit. The result? A list of six fantastic pairs that we recommend for all types of workouts, including running, HIIT training, yoga, Pilates, and more.

I’ve tested a wide range of athletic shorts, but the Gym People High Waist Short topped my list for a few reasons: it’s super soft, has nice compression, comes in a ton of colors, and has many different pockets to store your belongings. Plus, said pockets don’t add any bulk to your legs—a rare find in a short.

My biggest pet peeve with athletic shorts is when they feel way too tight and restrictive. But this pair, made from a polyester-spandex blend, has four-way stretch that makes it feel breathable, light, and easy to move in. “The fit is a bit more compressive around the stomach, which gives a nice smoothing and lifting effect—something I actually appreciate since super stretchy biker shorts can sometimes feel a little shapeless around the hips,” says style contributor Lily Wohlner.While this short does offer some compression, it leans more on the stretchy side than super form-fitting, so it might not be the best pick for high-impact workouts. It feels supportive, but I wouldn’t wear it for running or burpees since it doesn’t hold me in quite enough. That said, the fabric is buttery soft—like, ridiculously comfortable—so it’s perfect for walking, yoga, and Pilates. I also love that it’s not see-through, so I felt totally fine stretching and bending without worrying. The only downside? The moisture-wicking could be better. Wohlner says she wore it to hot yoga once, and the sweat stains were definitely noticeable.Read More: Best Leggings For Working Out

So many WH editors love this short from lululemon, especially for running. "I hadn't bought a pair of running shorts in years, but given that I've taken up running as a hobby, I knew I needed some for moving in hot weather," says associate health & fitness editor Addison Aloian. This extremely lightweight short, made from polyester and elastane, stood out to her because it's light and airy and comes in a ton of colors. Plus, there's a little side pocket where you can store your keys while logging miles.

Fast forward to today, she has logged hundreds of miles in this short and says it’s her all-time favorite pair for hitting the pavement. But, she also loves its versatility because she can wear it paired with a big sweatshirt for running errands, to a yoga class, or during her weekly strength training sessions. It never chafes or rubs against her legs, even when things start to get sweaty. Plus, she says the four-inch inseam offers excellent coverage so her cheeks are fully covered while she’s out and about. “They never ride up or move around, which is hard to find in a running short,” she says.

Stylist Rose Lauture is also a mega fan of this short, but she actually prefers the shorter, 2.5-inch inseam option—it’s the shortest option on this list—for its super airy feel. Despite the shorter inseam, she never feels exposed, but opt for the longer pair if you want to feel more covered. However, both shorts have a built-in panty liner for added coverage, so you never have to worry about anything slipping out (IYKYK).Both testers commented on how quickly this short dries. After a run, Aloian says there were some sweaty spots, but they were completely dry by the time she was ready to shower.

When I reach for a flowy workout short, it’s usually this pair from Beyond Yoga. I’ve been wearing it a ton to heated Pilates classes (my latest hyperfixation), and the lightweight breathability is unmatched. It’s made from a lightweight, woven fabric comprised of polyester and elastane. Woven fabrics, as opposed to knit fabrics, tend to be super breathable—and the vented back panel and perforated material at the sides give this short an extra airy feel. I never overheat while wearing it, whether I’m sweating it out on the mat or running miles.

Speaking of, this short is the epitome of versatile—I love it for strength training when paired with the Spacedye Slim Tank (my #1 workout top!), but it’s also a great running short. Despite the non-stretch material, the waistband offers plenty of give (and is adjustable!) and the leg openings are wide enough to keep things comfortable without chafing or riding up at the inner thighs—IYKYK.

It’s also really flattering, especially for a short that lacks compression. The body-skimming, flowy silhouette somehow makes my lower belly look super snatched. I love wearing it for regular days running errands, paired with a matching tank or zip-up sweatshirt. My only small complaint is that I wish it were available in more core colors. Right now, you can get it year-round in two shades, but there are usually lots of fun seasonal options depending on when you’re browsing.

Read More: Beyond Yoga Spacedye Slim Cropped Tank Review

Have you seen a cuter pair of workout shorts? I love the retro design with colorblocking and contrasting trims along with the mesh panels at the sides and hem. It’s one of the few workout shorts I wear just as frequently outside of the gym as I do to break a sweat. Pair it with a simple white tank (or top in any other color featured in the short) and flip-flops, and you have the perfect vintage activewear fit.

I’m also a big fan of the length: The approximately 5-inch inseam and roomy leg openings with notched hems at the sides give a leg-slimming effect and are also just super comfortable. It also makes sure I don’t accidentally show too much skin while running in my neighborhood or picking up weights at the gym. An added layer of protection there is the built-in brief, which, unlike many I’ve encountered, doesn’t feel like it's giving me a constant wedgie (I’ve literally cut them out of my shorts before, but I barely notice it in this short).

Another bonus? The mesh paneling I mentioned earlier is as stylish as it is breathable. Even when I throw it on for a run on a hot August afternoon, things stay feeling light and airy.

I only wish this short came in more colors—I would genuinely purchase them all. Right now, you can snag it in two color combos, but I’d love to see a few more and maybe even a neutral option.

If you're looking for a buttery-soft workout fit, this biker short from Beyond Yoga is your best friend. The brand itself is a favorite among our fashion team, and that's because the fabrics, which are made from super soft polyester and elastane, are never tight and constricting, always smooth and soft (yet still contouring and flattering!).

Yes, the short is awesome for all sorts of workouts, but we also love it for running errands and, dare we say it, lounging, as it looks so cute with every outfit and feels so comfortable for all-day wear. Plus, it's moisture-wicking during sweaty workouts or super hot days. Speaking of sunny days, the short also has built-in UV protection, because we're all about staying protected from the sun here.

The Spacedye Biker Short is also one of the longest options on this list, so it's a solid choice if you're looking for something with a bit more leg coverage.

I often wear this short to yoga, but it's compressive enough that it doesn't budge when I wear it for a run or to higher intensity classes. According to stylist Kristen Saladino, the high-waisted fit makes you feel super tucked-in and secure without feeling constricted. And, if you need a larger size, this short goes all the way up to a 4XL.

I do wish there were more colors to choose from. As of now, the brand only offers two core colors in this short.

Sure, we love the lululemon short for running, but the Norvan Short from Arc'teryx is built for the trails—and that’s exactly what we use it for. Lauture gives this fitted short a big thumbs-up for feeling super light and breathable, especially on long runs. It’s made from 100% polyester, so it’s airy and helps keep you cool by letting moisture escape and regulating your body temp. And if things do get sweaty, the built-in moisture-wicking brief (with anti-microbial treatment) helps manage odor—so you don’t have to stress.

Got loose keys or headphones? There's a discreet zippered back pocket that fits the essentials, like gels, electrolyte packs—you name it. It also has a reflective logo to help with visibility if you're running after dark. Another plus: the split side hem gives you a full range of motion, which is great for picking up the pace.

Our only real gripe is that we wish the waistband were a bit thicker for more tummy support. It’s also low-rise, which might not be everyone’s thing—but Lauture said she was surprised by how comfortable it felt and that it stayed put during her runs.

In my experience, it's difficult to find flowy workout shorts that don't show too much skin, but this option from Alo shifts that paradigm. It's light and airy with its woven material, but it doesn't have any open seams, so you don't have to worry about the wind catching it in the wrong way (IYKYK). Plus, it has a built-in brief, which is awesome for added protection.

I also love the thick elastic waistband, which not only adds a fun design element, but hits at the perfect height on our stomach to offer a nice contouring effect. There's also an invisible side pocket to store all your small essentials while on the go.My favorite part about this short is that it's never clingy, so it doesn't ride up the thigh or need constant re-adjusting while you're working out. I’ve owned it for months and recently tested it during a 45-minute strength and HIIT workout as well as an hour-long cross-training workout, and I never felt over-exposed or uncomfortable in it. It's roomy, but also holds you in. Plus, the fabric dries super fast, so you're in good hands if you get super sweaty.It does run one size big, which you should note when adding to cart. However, if you like shorts that are roomier, I can confirm that this one still gets high marks even when it's a size too big. In my experience, it still felt full-coverage, airy, and lightweight.

Patagonia’s Baggies Short is a warm-weather favorite among our editors—especially the ones who love spending time outdoors, like myself. I recently took this short on a trip with me to hike Utah’s Mighty 5, and it was perfect for a hot, sunny day hiking in Arches National Park.

It’s easy to throw on, thanks to its comfy fit that completely avoids any unwanted cling (no camel toe here, thank you very much). Plus, it’s made from quick-drying, breathable nylon, so I never have to worry about feeling weighed down. I’m personally stoked to wear this short again while hiking in Cotopaxi National Park in Ecuador.

While it definitely has a sporty vibe, it’s versatile enough to wear around the city, too. In black, it feels laid-back and low-key—perfect for running errands without looking like you just left the gym. Toss on an oversized sweatshirt or a longline sports bra, and you’ve got an effortless, off-duty look. And if you get caught in the rain or decide to take a dip? No stress—it’s water-repellent, so it won’t stay soaked.

The 5-inch inseam is another win: not too long, not too short—just the right amount of leg without worrying about coverage. Prefer something shorter? The Baggie also comes in a 2.5-inch version, which is great if you want a more cropped fit.

Fabric is everything when it comes to workout shorts—look for lightweight, sweat-wicking materials that move with you, not against you. According to Saladino, it's best to steer clear of cotton when looking for athletic shorts, as it doesn't wick away moisture as well as materials like polyester and nylon. After all, you want to make sure you're staying totally dry in your workout shorts (because who wants sweat stains down there?).

Most shorts on this list are high-rise, which we found to have the most coverage and look the most flattering during our workouts, as they offer flattering tummy control. Many high-rise shorts also have a drawstring, which helps you customize the fit so it doesn't slip down or ride up while you're getting a sweat on. Some of the options we tried were low-rise, but we ended up ditching most of them because we didn't love the fit. However, the Arc'teryx pair on this list is low-rise, and we actually love that it sits nicely on our hips and looks flattering.

When it comes to the best length for workout shorts, you want to think about the inseam length, AKA the distance between the crotch area and the bottom of the short. There are some longer options for those who prefer more leg coverage (ideal for burpees and squats!), and super short options on this list if you like a lightweight mini short for running or walking. After testing, we prefer something right in the middle that makes us feel nimble but also provides coverage, like our favorite of the bunch, The Gym People High Waist Shorts.

After testing, we found that some shorts are better for specific activities. For example, the Beyond Yoga pair is great for yoga because it’s super stretchy and buttery soft, so it’s easy to move in, whether you’re in downward dog or trying to master crow pose. On the other hand, the Arc'teryx pair is low-rise, super light, and has a snug fit, making it ideal for running since it feels weightless and doesn't slow us down.

#535. On the Couch with Gucci Westman

The celebrity makeup artist and beauty founder shares her design takes and what’s next for her mega brand.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE Decor editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Gucci Westman is best known for making her celebrity clientele look (even more) flawless, primping Hollywood’s most famous faces ahead of their biggest events. She worked her magic on Anne Hathaway throughout the Devil Wears Prada 2 press tour, Cate Blanchett for the Emmys, and, just this week, Nicole Kidman for Chanel’s Spring 2027 runway show. In 2018, she launched a namesake beauty line, Westman Atelier, alongside her husband and business partner, David Neville. Her products quickly grew a devoted following of “It” girls, contouring and airbrushing with Westman’s signature makeup. In August, the brand debuted one of its biggest launches yet with Suprême Bio-Complex Liquid Foundation, their first liquid foundation.

Now, Westman is expanding her world beyond face makeup. Last month, she hosted a New York City activation with ShopMy called Good Foundations. There, in a Soho space designed to look like her own closet, she curated a collection of her favorite products and brands beyond her own, from Helen Kaminski hats to TWP shirts to Flamingo Estate candles. She’s also building a new Manhattan headquarters in Flatiron in collaboration with her friend Lyndsay Caleo of The Brooklyn Home Company.

“Seeing our office come to life through her lens and sensitive touch has been amazing to watch. It feels like a new chapter to have a new place to call home for our brand, and seeing our team working together in person is so rewarding,” Westman says.

But she’s not stopping there. What could be next? She gave us a hint: “Something I'm tremendously passionate about, and I do love fragrance.”

Below, we asked Westman to share a bit more about the people, places, and products she loves in our On the Couch survey. She divulges her favorite hotels, restaurants, and how to really handle a hostess gift.

Greatest influences: My mom, David, and my closest friends. I’d also have to say some of the people we work with inspire me and teach me to want to be better and dig deep!

Favorite eras of design: I really love following Coco Chanel's evolution. What she started with, where Chanel is today. Design is in a really cool place at the moment. Fashion feels very desirable.

Most beloved buildings: The Louvre, the Grand Palais, the Chateau de Versailles, the Eiffel Tower, and the Arc de Triomphe

Architect you admire: Bolle Tham and Martin Videgård

Vintage piece of your dreams: Les Lalanne’s sheep or Rhinocrétaire

Favorite getaway: EPI Baie de Pampelonne in Ramatuelle, France

Hotels to check into: Hacienda Alta Gracia in Costa Rica, Collegio alla Querce in Florence, Hȏtel de Crillon and Le Bristol in Paris, The Surrey in New York City, Ett Hem in Sweden, and Cashel Palace in Ireland.

Best host/hostess gift: Little in size and impactful! Anything that feels like there’s thought put behind it around who the host or hostess is. Something you know the person loves. If it’s a glass or a coffee cup, something specific to the person. Those are always my favorite gifts and I try to do the same!

Entertaining tips: I need some! I love having people over and cooking, but I also get overwhelmed and find myself leaving the table too many times to check on things. I’m trying to improve that. I think it’s nice when it feels as if there’s less effort. My mother-in-law is the best host. She makes it seem so easy and effortless. It’s an art.

Style icons: Harry Styles, Coco Chanel, Katharine Hepburn

Fashion designers: Matthieu Blazy, Phoebe Philo, The Row, Khaite

Cocktail of choice: Champagne, always. No prosecco ever!

Favorite restaurant: Le Voltaire in Paris, Polo Bar, Kappo Masa, and Frenchette in New York, the restaurant at Ett hem in Sweden and Il Baretto in Milan

Must-have accessory: A good belt, shoe, and a watch

Watch of choice: A chunky men’s Rolex in rose gold or gold with a white face. I also love the Petite Cartier Tank watch.

#536. How a Madrid Apartment Got the History It Always Deserved

When a family bought a bland home in a former office building in Madrid, they turned to Spanish firm Casa Muñoz to conjure up a Belle Epoque home from scratch.

In search of a base in Europe where their family and friends could gather, a couple from Mexico finally settled on an unlikely site: 5,000 square feet of former office space in Madrid. The property happened to be in a grand 1920s building in the city’s tony Salamanca district, with views of the American embassy. To create a livable apartment, complete with period character, they turned to ELLE Decor A-List designers Mafalda Muñoz and Gonzalo Machado. The couple, founders of the Madrid design firm Casa Muñoz, relished the chance to work with a blank slate.

“It’s not their primary residence, so there were no heirlooms or art collections we had to incorporate, no workspaces or school routines to consider,” Muñoz says. “They wanted a place to unite as a family and celebrate. The rest was up to us.”

The owners had been drawn to the sophisticated but confidently unfussy ambience Muñoz and Machado bring to their interiors. Since its launch in 2012, Casa Muñoz has become synonymous with a pedigreed version of authentically Spanish design and lifestyle. The firm was tapped to create the first Forbes House private club, which opened in Madrid in late 2024. Other recent projects include homes in Miami and Rome, and the elegant restaurant at the Fondation Beyeler in Basel, the contemporary art museum in Switzerland designed by Renzo Piano.

Muñoz and Machado, both Madrileños, have known each other since childhood and now have three kids of their own. She is local design royalty, the daughter of the late designer Paco Muñoz, who is credited with modernizing Spanish decor in the midst of the dreary Franco dictatorship. But she has cut her own path with refined, thoughtfully functional design rooted in tradition with contemporary flair.

For his part, Machado studied industrial and interior design before spending two decades as a photographer. His port-folio includes portraits of prominent figures, including King Juan Carlos I, as well as fashion, interiors, and lifestyle stories for virtually every Spanish publication. “Having spent 20 years looking through a viewfinder and telling a story without words—just through faces, fabrics, and objects—comes in handy when creating smart design,” he says.

“Mafalda and Gonzalo have a real understanding of the nuance and feel of quality, the sense of solidity and permanence a home should have,” says Spanish model and actress Eugenia Silva, a longtime friend and client. “I hired them precisely because I didn’t want anything hippie-chic about my home in Madrid.”

The duo’s combined talents are on full display in the Salamanca apartment, where they completed the entire renovation in a breathtaking 10 months. “We invented the layout from scratch. Every single wall, floor, and ceiling is new,” Muñoz says. It’s now what she calls “a proper Madrid apartment,” a place that might be grand or dramatic or even a little sexy, but always practical and solid. “From our own backgrounds and experiences growing up, Gonzalo and I have a clear view of what makes a home, especially in the Spanish way of understanding home as the place where so much of life happens. Spaces that are well lived in and loved are what everyone wants.”

The designers started with a welcoming entry hall and a bar tucked discreetly into a nearby passageway. A series of flexible entertaining rooms unfold graciously from there. About a third of the home is given over to the primary suite, with another third housing smaller family and guest bedrooms, a kitchen, and other service rooms.

A focal point of the apartment is a round library that doubles as a home cinema (pictured top). “The owners are fanatics for sound quality,” says Machado, who notes that the room integrates 20 speakers and a video projector into the custom boiserie and bookshelves. A benefit of the property’s origins as office space is that state-of-the-art 21st-century systems could be built into what appears to be a Belle Epoque interior.

An elevated mix of objects and textures is layered against a muted palette of grays and browns throughout. Contemporary ceramics that riff on ancient Greek red-figure vases sit atop burnished wood columns, and polished marble obelisks adorn sleek glass cocktail tables. Bronze griffins and other 19th-century Grand Tour objects share space with works by contemporary Spanish artists like Jacobo Castellano, Antonio Ballester Moreno, Carlos León, and Alvaro Negro. In the primary bedroom an ornate gilded 18th-century mirror hangs next to a matte 1990s riveted aluminum folding screen by Swedish designer Mats Theselius.

For all the apartment’s grandeur, Muñoz and Machado paid close attention to how their clients actually live. Case in point: the “clean kitchen,” an open-plan cooking and dining area where simple, casual meals can be shared with friends. Tucked at the back of the house, the “dirty kitchen” handles intensive cooking and cleaning for formal dining or entertaining.

“Everyone loves the laid-back vibe of sipping wine in the kitchen while the host dresses a salad,” Muñoz remarks. “But pull a roasted turbot out of a hot oven and your guests get a blast of fishy odor and a dirty pan to look at. It can break the spell.”

#537. The 7 Best Microcurrent Devices of 2026 Tested By Women’s Health Editors

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

We’re living in the golden age of high-tech skincare devices—and as our beauty editor, I couldn’t be happier. Red light therapy devices, including LED face masks, provide excellent anti-aging benefits from the comfort of our couch, while face steamers have replaced my need for pricey spa facials. Laser hair removal devices are becoming more inclusive by offering technology safe enough for deeper complexions. Face massagers also help de-puff skin after a hangover. However, when it comes to lifting saggy skin, microcurrent devices are the ultimate MVP skincare tool deserving of a spot in your beauty arsenal.

Think of them as a sculpting workout for your face without the sweat. “Microcurrent devices use low levels of electrical current to stimulate facial muscles, helping to boost collagen and sculpt and lift the face,” says dermatologist Marisa Garshick, MD. And don’t worry: These aren’t painful. You’ll notice more of a temporary tingling sensation that’ll disappear within minutes of using the device.

While these at-home machines aren’t as powerful as the ones used by professionals, they’re a more cost-effective option for achieving subtle improvements, says dermatologist Bradley Glodny, MD. You’ll just need some patience to find a weekly cadence and intensity level that works for you. (More on that in a bit.) And if you’re getting seasonal in-office microcurrent treatments, these at-home machines help enhance and sustain your professional results over time, says Dr. Garshick.

What was once a closely guarded secret among my fellow beauty editors and plastic surgeons has now become increasingly popular and readily accessible across our most trusted sites, such as Sephora, Ulta, and Amazon. But an influx of hundreds of options can be overwhelming, which is where I come in. My years of reporting and research have informed this shopping guide. I also consulted the pros about what to look out for when buying at-home microcurrent machines. Ahead are a few non-negotiables to keep in mind, which helped inform the devices we tested and ultimately featured in this story.

Most devices on this list have a range of microcurrent levels—some, like Foreo, even go up to 10. The higher you go, the more intense the microcurrent will feel. If you're accustomed to microcurrent and prefer a device with more power and customization options, opt for one that offers multiple microcurrent levels.

On the other hand, if you're a beginner, you might only need to purchase a device with a few microcurrent levels, such as the NuFace Trinity.

Dr. Garshick advises using your microcurrent device at least three times a week for four to six weeks before you can expect to see results, although some devices recommend daily use. “While much of the initial benefit may only be noticed for hours to days, with consistent use, the results will continue as collagen production can take six or more months,” she says.

After the initial treatment period, you can decrease the frequency of treatments to two to three times per week to maintain your results. Always refer to the specific instructions for use of your microcurrent device.

Many microcurrent devices come with additional features, such as interchangeable attachments, smartphone app connectivity, and even instructional guides.

An added bonus for your microcurrent device is FDA approval, which means that the government organization has determined that the device is safe and effective for its intended use. This is not a necessity when purchasing a microcurrent device, but it's definitely a solid addition if you're looking for something that has been rigorously tested.

You’ll also want to order a microcurrent device that either includes a priming gel or purchase one separately. They’re conductive and allow the electrical currents to be transmitted from the device to the skin. They also help the device glide easily across the skin and help prevent irritation.

Unlike bulky in-office machines, at-home microcurrent devices are about the size of a closed fist. Someone who travels often might prefer the Solawave Facial Wand, a slim option that resembles a T-shaped salad fork. Regardless of which of these featured options you order, they won’t take up too much space in your medicine cabinet or cosmetic bag.

At-home microcurrent machines aren’t exactly cheap. Entry-level models cost around $150, while high-end options can easily go for upward of $500. However, you’ll save money over time because you get multiple uses out of a single device. And if it helps ease the burden, I spent $275 for a pro microcurrent facial, which costs $60 more than the WH Skincare Award-winning Laduora Lumeo and conductive gel.

With the above dermatological guidance in mind, I began whittling down our list of contenders. The Women’s Health beauty closet was my first stop, along with my at-home collection of skincare devices. Of course, because I’m inquisitive and love knowing what the pros actually use IRL and recommend to their patients, I asked both Dr. Garshick and Dr. Glodny for their fail-safe picks. Next, I tapped our team of skin-obsessive editors and writers, including Brian Underwood, Lily Wohlner, Maridel Reyes, and Cristina Montemayor. And because we prefer only spotlighting products we actually tested, we put them all through a vetting process, which includes:

I eliminated anything that was cumbersome. For example, anything with a short cord or an extra-long one that easily tangled was cut. Were the cordless devices easy to charge quickly if I was in a crunch? Were there any other buttons or features that are easy to accidentally hit while rolling the device across my face?

These aren’t exactly short treatments. We’ll need at least a few minutes per treatment session, so caring for an entire face can easily take 15 minutes or more. I prioritized lightweight, but durable devices that easily slide across my skin. Anything that made my wrist tired after a few minutes was docked points. Was the tingling too intense for beginners or best suited for novices? Are there enough levels for both beginners and experienced users?

This was particularly important because everyone wants a lifted appearance. I evaluated if I noticed any improvements after the first usage, and kept checking in over the last six months. How do the results improve over time?

This was determined based on how each device scores in relation to the above factors. Plus, I asked myself and our team if these are products they’d be willing to repurchase or gift to loved ones because they stand behind the quality of the devices. Ultimately, each of these featured picks met those requirements; here are the results of our labor.

This NuFace device ticks all the boxes on my microcurrent wish list. The lifting effect smoothens the appearance of wrinkles and contours my cheekbones and jawline, even without makeup. The Trinity+ Starter Kit includes accessories to enhance my routine, such as a conductive gel that helps the NuFace glide smoothly across my skin. The device also comes with a lip and eye attachment, allowing me to target smaller problem areas, such as the 11 lines between the brows and smile lines.

This palm-sized powerhouse fits comfortably in my hands, and the five-minute treatment time was quick and easy. It doesn’t sting, and the tingling is mild as long as I use enough conductive gel. The Trinity also beeps, indicating when to move onto a new area of my face. I noticed results after just a few uses, which continued to improve after several months of consistent treatments.

Dr. Glodny and Dr. Garshick also both recommend this device. "This microcurrent device is FDA-cleared, helps to tone facial muscles, and improves the overall contour and appearance of the skin," says Dr. Garshick, adding that it can help rejuvenate the skin and improve skin laxity and the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles.

Honestly, the worst thing I can say about this is the upfront cost. However, I’ve had my device since 2020, and it still performs well six years later. For that reason alone, the NuFace is a long-term investment that delivers fast results that continue to improve over time.

Given its capabilities, the Solawave is comparable to devices that cost twice as much, including the TheraFace Pro.
