Yes, this is the priciest option, but the capabilities are next-level great. This is, by far, the smartest microcurrent machine on this list. The Bluetooth-capable device has a smartphone app that allows you to choose from seven different facials, all ranging from four to 14 minutes long. Some focus on sculpting, while others zap acne, brighten your complexion, or smooth out fine lines. To unlock all available treatments, simply sync your device with the app.

Setting up the account on iOS or Android is straightforward, and it includes FAQ tutorials that guide you on how to use the device correctly. Each step of the Ziip device is broken down into easy-to-follow clips that remind you when to move onto a new section of the face for anti-aging benefits. One of my favorite treatments is called “Energize,” which starts at my neck and works its way up to my forehead in about 12 minutes.

It is also unique because Ziip combines microcurrent and nanocurrent technologies. Microcurrent amplifies the lifting effect of jowls and stimulates collagen and elastin for major anti-aging benefits. Meanwhile nanocurrent is a low-intensity, sensitive skin-friendly way to reduce fine lines and enhance skin radiance.

Reyes also adores her ZIIP. "I used it every night, and after a few days, my husband noticed that my face looked more contoured," says Reyes. "The day after I use it, my skin looks smoother and glowier." She relies on it right before important events for more chiseled cheekbones, a sharper jaw, and a slightly lifted brow because it provides instant gratification and is "way less spendy than getting a microcurrent facial at a spa."

I’ve been using the Laduora Lumeo device since it was first released in 2025—and I’ve adore it so much over the past year that I named it the best new microcurrent tool in our 2026 Beauty Awards

TBH, it’s so effective and seamless to use that I’ve ditched my other bulky microcurrent devices and LED face masks in favor of this 4-in-1 device.

Microcurrent gently lifts and defines my cheekbones, while electroporation helps my face serum and cream penetrate more effectively. It also taps into red LEDs to soften my fine lines and wrinkles, while near-infrared light penetrates beneath my skin's surface, helping it feel firmer. Instead of splurging on multiple devices, I can easily get away with just using this single tool.

It’s a kit that includes the conductive gel, so there’s no need to make a separate purchase. I have oily, acne-prone skin, and it has never caused breakouts.

Still, the functionality is on point, and it costs less than other devices on this list, including the TheraFace. And for that, Laduora will have a permanent spot in my beauty stash.

When you’re short on time, you’ll want to reach for this top-rated Foreo tool. I like to concentrate on my cheekbones for an extra lift. It’s great for travel, and I found myself using this device more regularly than other devices because the treatments are so quick. The Bear doesn’t feel like a chore, and it's something I can easily use during commercial breaks on TV or while on the phone.

Both Dr. Garshick and Dr. Glodny recommend this cute palm-sized device, which firms and tones skin with microcurrent and massaging T-sonic pulsations that help with sagging skin, reduces puffiness, smooths wrinkles, and relaxes muscles. When I saw that this device offers eight treatments in one, I was initially skeptical that the microcurrent attachment wouldn’t be up to par with some of the other devices I tried. I was pleasantly surprised by how effective it was; I saw a difference after using the microcurrent for just a few minutes. But what really sold me was the combination of a powerful microcurrent skin toning device to lift the jowls, along with several magnetic attachments that amplify my skincare routine.

Pesky adult acne and redness have been cosmetic concerns for Wohlner, but the TheraFace Pro has helped solve her skincare woes. She saw some initial glowy finish, but achieved the most visible anti-aging results after a few weeks of regular use.

While some microcurrent devices also relieve jaw tension, when using the percussion attachments in conjunction with the microcurrent, Wohlner found that her jaw muscles felt more relaxed and looked more toned than ever. The combination of those treatments in this single device truly sets it apart in terms of effectiveness. “I also struggle with jaw pain from grinding my teeth, and the percussive therapy this device offers is a major game-changer when I wake up with a sore jaw," says Wohlner.

You can’t go wrong with this tool, but if you won’t realistically incorporate at least a few of these modalities into your routine, it’s probably best to save some money and stick with a more affordable alternative. That said, we’re big fans and have gifted some to our lucky loved ones, including our moms, who are fine-tuning their mature skincare routines.

NYC eyebrow guru Joey Healy created the ultimate microcurrent for lifting the delicate skin around your eye area. This microcurrent device is made specifically to target the eyebrow area and tighten the skin around the browbone, giving hooded eyes a lifted, more awake appearance.

Montemayor gave this device a solid five stars because she noticed a noticeable difference in her eyebrows after using it. Even after her first go, her droopy eyebrow was even with her other one. She tells us that this device is super powerful; she can't even fathom using the highest level. Another reason to love this device? It automatically powers down after 15 minutes of use, preventing skin overstimulation and accidental battery drain.

The only downside of this device is that it uses batteries. While we wish it were rechargeable, this device is cordless, which is particularly helpful for anyone with limited outlets in their home.

Microcurrent devices aren't exactly cheap—the most affordable ones are still over $100, though the best ones tend to be around $300. Just be sure to use your device consistently at least three times a week, as Dr. Garshick mentioned.

If you're hesitant, she recommends chatting with your dermatologist about your skincare concerns and goals. They can help you come up with a treatment plan to supplement the use of your microcurrent device, optimizing the benefits of it.

#538. These Are the 6 Most Expensive Celebrity Homes of All Time

The record-breaking buys in this list have redefined luxury living.

Boasting some of the most luxe amenities, gorgeous design details, and over-the-top features, A-list celebrity homes are total showstoppers. But when your budget is seemingly endless, how do you decide when and where to buy?

These homes are located in some of the most elite neighborhoods imaginable, from Miami’s “Billionaire Bunker” to California’s “Billionaires’ Row” and the stucco-lined streets of London’s Chelsea neighborhood. Ahead, we’ve rounded up the six most expensive celebrity home purchases to date.

In 2024, David and Victoria Beckham decided to ditch the penthouse lifestyle for mansion glamour, trading their ultra-luxe penthouse for a mega-mansion overlooking Biscayne Bay. Described in its original listing as one of "Miami Beach's most significant estates," the 14,270-square-foot property boasts 124 feet of private waterfront real estate, a Gatsby-style dock, and panoramic views of the city, including Nu Stadium, where his team, Inter Miami CF, plays. In addition to its nine bedrooms and nine bathrooms, the home features a spa, a rooftop fit for entertaining, and towering 12-foot floor-to-ceiling windows to let in the Florida sunshine. The mansion was originally listed for $80 million, but the couple snagged a deal, paying $72.3 million and setting the record price for a home on North Bay Road.

Drake may now be eager to part ways with his Beverly Hills mansion, but the singer originally paid $75 million to add the 20-acre property to his real estate portfolio. The Tuscan-style estate sits on 20 acres of land with 24,800 square feet of living space, 10 bedrooms, 13 bathrooms, a whopping 11-car garage, a wine cellar, a tennis court, a screening room, and a private gym. The home features towering French doors throughout and nine functional fireplaces.

In 2024, designer Tom Ford took his real estate portfolio across the pond to London’s posh Chelsea neighborhood. There, he purchased a white stucco-front mansion just a short walk from Hyde Park and the River Thames. The home’s amenities remain private, but the sale was one of the most expensive residential transactions in the United Kingdom that year, bringing in the equivalent of $140 million.

When Jeff Bezos went house hunting, he wasn’t just searching for prime views and vast square footage. He was hoping to find a home with character, charm, and a decent dose of history—and in February 2020, he did. The business mogul now owns the illustrious Warner Estate, a historic nine-acre compound in Beverly Hills, with only two previous occupants: Jack L. Warner, the cofounder of Warner Bros. Studios, and David Geffen, the cofounder of DreamWorks Records. Bezos paid $165 million for the storied Neo-Georgian mansion.

Mark Zuckerberg’s “Billionaire Bunker” Abode

Mark Zuckerberg holds the record for the most expensive home sale in Miami-Dade County ever. The tech tycoon and his wife, philanthropist and pediatrician Priscilla Chan, dropped $170 million on their waterfront mansion on Florida’s Indian Creek Island, a well-known enclave for the ultra-rich. Their estate boasts 200 feet of Biscayne Bay frontage accompanied by a private dock. Inside, the massive mansion accommodates nine bedrooms, about 15 bathrooms, and features a private hair salon, jazz lounge, and an opulent Himalayan salt-wall sauna.

Beyoncé and Jay-Z’s Brutalist-Style Malibu Home

Topping off the list is celebrity power couple Beyoncé and Jay-Z. The pair broke California price records with the purchase of their brutalist-style Malibu mansion on “Billionaires’ Row,” just off the Pacific Coast Highway. Outfitted in minimalist flair, the glass-and-concrete home clocks in at 30,000 square feet, with seven bedrooms, 11 bathrooms, and eight acres of oceanfront bluff. As for amenities, the property features a private beach, a basketball court, and a climate-controlled art gallery. Bey and Jay dropped a cool $200 million on the home. California ranks second in the nation for the most expensive real estate market, with a median home value of $780,000 to $809,000.

#539. Dolly Parton’s Former Los Angeles Home Is Now on the Market for $8 Million

The late music icon lived in the now-rebuilt Bird Streets estate in the 1980s.

From a one-bedroom cabin in rural Tennessee to a 63-acre Nashville compound, Dolly Parton’s homes reflected her humble beginnings and subsequent rise to the top of the entertainment industry. In the mid-1980s, a few years after the country music legend starred in her first Hollywood film, 9 to 5, she and her husband Carl Dean bought a property in Southern California.

Now, just weeks after Parton’s death at age 80, their Los Angeles estate, which was rebuilt in 2009, according to the listing, just hit the market for $8 million.

Parton and Dean acquired the residence in December 1985 for $750,000, per Robb Report. It was set on a third of an acre in the celebrity-heavy Bird Streets enclave, perched above the Sunset Strip. The couple, who wed in 1966, reportedly sold the home just five years later, in March 1990, for $1.2 million.

On the market for the first time in 25 years, the property has since undergone a total revamp, rendering it virtually unrecognizable from what it looked like when Parton and Dean lived there. The current owner, Eric M. Shore, reimagined the property in 2009, according to the listing, which also notes it has been refreshed since then.

Originally dating to the 1970s, the two-story structure is now a modern mansion. It’s still christened the Dolly Parton House, but it’s outfitted with top-of-the-line finishes and appliances. Spanning nearly 4,700 square feet, the five-bedroom home comes with five baths, a wood-paneled library, an expansive primary suite, and a chef’s kitchen.

Outside, a pool and spa are highlights of the manicured gardens, while a separate terrace features an above-ground hot tub. There’s also a two-car garage on the property.

9196 Thrasher Ave. is listed for $7.95 million with Edward Tinney of Nourmand & Associates and Kurt Rappaport of Westside Estate Agency.

Geoffrey Montes is an associate editor at ELLE Decor with a serious love for all things real estate and design. Before that, he worked at Architectural Digest, Galerie, and Preservation magazines, covering everything from jaw-dropping listings to world-famous architects and design events like Salone del Mobile and Homo Faber.

#540. This Los Angeles New Build is Filled With Antique Finds and Living Trees

Designer Sierra Fox of Studio MTN brought vintage character into this new build.

Designing a home often requires finding balance—with color, with furniture, with proportion. In this 11,330-square-foot new build, the latter proved to be one of the biggest challenges for Sierra Fox, principal designer at Studio MTN. Her clients—who had already moved into the sprawling Los Angeles abode at the start of the project—wanted to use as much of their current furniture and decor as possible, but in a house of this size and with rooms this expansive, their existing pieces didn’t fit the scale or language of the spaces.

“There was a delicate balance between honoring what they loved while gently guiding them toward pieces that better suited the home,” Fox tells House Beautiful. And for her clients, those pieces had to make their newly built home feel layered, collected, and soulful from the outset.

Fox relied heavily on antique finds and aged materials, choosing items with a good patina—vintage rugs, sculptural treasures, and future heirlooms—to keep the rooms from feeling overly polished. Rich mohairs, thick linens, plaster finishes, and other natural textures added warmth and softness, while large-scale greenery brought a soulful yet energetic element inside. The designer also worked closely with Inner Gardens in L.A. to integrate living trees throughout the interior in a way that felt unified with the home’s architecture, rather than simply decorative.

Walls coated in Roman clay add an earthy depth and subtle movement, catching the light and creating dimension in a quiet, understated way. “Even when we incorporated color, we approached it through an earthy lens,” Fox adds. Red became oxblood, bright yellow became muted mustard, cobalt blue became oceanic hues. “It became a really beautiful balance between the husband wanting more color and personality while the wife wanted the home to still feel calm and organic.”

Much of Fox’s time went to the styling, as she and her team went through “multiple rounds of sourcing and in-person mockups with local Los Angeles vendors to really study how everything worked together in the space,” she explains. But it paid off by the end of the installation, as the home feels intimate and livable despite its vast size, balancing out the luxury pieces with aged finds that ensure the house doesn’t feel overly precious. “Relaxed, layered, inviting—it’s very cinematic, very Nancy Meyers in spirit, but with a little more depth and moodiness.”

FAST FACTSDesigner: Sierra Fox of Studio MTNLocation: Los Angeles, CaliforniaThe Space: A six-bedroom, eight-bathroom new build spanning 11,330 square feet

Fox and her team collaborated with Bananas & Hammocks, a collective of custom furniture builders and designers out of Ventura, California, to create the striking marble fireplace surround. The original felt flat and developer-grade, so they opted for a patinated brass surround for depth, warmth, and character. “It became such a strong focal point and brought a level of dimensionality the space was missing before,” Fox says.

They layered textures, warm earthy tones, and a mix of vintage and modern furnishings throughout the rest of the room, giving it a collected and timeless feel without feeling too formal.

A warm, tonal palette grounds the dining room, making it feel intimate and understated, even with a jewelry-like statement light fixture. Windows draped with ethereal fabric allow natural light to shine in, while the sculptural seating and simple wooden table add contrast.

“Wrapped in rich, moody tones, the den feels intimate and inviting from the moment you enter,” Fox says. The deep oxblood plaster coating the walls is a custom hue they created with Portola Paints to emphasize the cocooning feeling inside this gathering space, while the circular layout of the oversize shearling chairs encourages undistracted conversation. Anyone in need of a break can make their way to the connected wine room or play some tunes on the piano.

As part of the primary suite, Fox designed this sitting room to feel as serene as the main area, anchored by large floor-to-ceiling windows that flood the space with natural light and frame the surrounding greenery. “Soft, tonal furnishings and understated wood accents keep the room feeling calm and refined, while the subtle marble detailing adds a quiet architectural polish,” she adds.

“The hallway is defined by its sculptural black iron balustrade, whose rhythmic, looping lines introduce a sense of movement against the crisp, paneled walls,” the designer explains. Warm wood flooring softens the architecture while open sight lines create an interplay between depth and light.

The custom sculptural desk, paired with the large oceanic artwork on the navy paneled wall, gives this workspace a warm organic feel, leaving quite an impression. Along with the BDDW captain’s credenza, a generational piece, it feels polished but not lacking personality.

Clean architectural paneling and layered neutrals define this primary suite, giving it an undeniable sense of calm. Fox introduces texture and shape through the sculptural lighting and soft curved seating on either side of the bed, resulting in a bedroom that still feels thoughtfully designed and quietly elevated.

With help from the neutral palette and natural sunlight, the burl wood desk serves as the focal point in this second workspace. “Sculptural forms, oversized paper lighting, and touches of greenery give the space an easy warmth.”

Sierra Fox is the principal designer of Studio MTN, a full-service interior design studio based in Sun Valley, Idaho, and Los Angeles. The studio specializes in high-end residential design, layering rich materials, rustic warmth, contemporary elegance, and earthy tones into their clients’ homes.

#541. The 6 Best Electric Razors for Women in 2026, Tested by Beauty Editors

It's time to ditch the disposable this summer.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

My interest in hair removal started in elementary school when I snuck into my mom's medicine cabinet and dragged her razor across my leg like I was coloring with my favorite box of markers. Needless to say, I've learned the right way to shave since then (namely to apply shaving cream and gently glide my razor toward the grain with light pressure).

I've had a lot of help perfecting my technique—as a beauty editor with a decade of testing experience, I have access to the best dermatologists and aestheticians. Yet, no matter how on-point my new shaving technique is now, most women's razors never get my legs quite as smooth. And other hair removal methods are super painful, ripping strands out at the root. Ouch!

But then, I upgraded to electric razors—and I've never turned back.

“A closer shave can feel nice, but because the surface of our skin is not perfectly smooth, it inevitably results in removal of some skin cells,” says dermatologist Caroline Robinson, MD. This can lead to microscopic nicks and irritation. “Electric razors can help avoid this. They’re typically less sensitizing,” says Dr. Robinson, because the shave they provide is not as close. At-home laser hair removal devices, waxing, sugaring, and threading are all great options for hair removal if you’ve got the time (and the coin), but if silky-smooth skin sans irritation is what you’re after, the answer is electric.

Over the past year, Women's Health editors have been testing popular electric razors to determine which seven are worth the investment. Ultimately, we found that the Philips Beauty Series was the best multi-use product due to its five-blade razor and dual-sidedness that allows for a super close shave. Meanwhile, the Remington Smooth & Silky On-the-Go Shaver delivers on quality for quick touch-ups while being budget- and travel-friendly. Read on to see our other winners from our testing process.

A favorite of our editors, this hair removal device hits all of the targets we're looking for when buying an electric razor. For starters, it literally has 40 micro-grip tweezers in its motor to provide a super close shave, keeping your skin smooth for weeks at a time. While that might seem intimidating, it upgraded my in-shower shaving routine in a major way.

You can hit even the trickiest spots on your body. From your underarms and belly down to your ankles, this electric razor has you covered quite literally from head to toe. And with an impressive 50-minute runtime you can eliminate all of my unwanted hair with this device at least a couple of times before recharging it for just an hour. You’ll also appreciate that it's lightweight but not flimsy like it'll slip out of your grip. Plus, it's waterproof so you can shave in the shower without worrying about your new razor cranking out mid-shave.

An upgrade from the original Braun model, the more expensive but higher-tech Flex comes with a flexible head (hence, the name) that can uniquely adapt to your body's curves and contours—even the complicated corners of your bikini line. In addition to the epilator, the bundle also comes with a body exfoliation brush, skin contact cap for additional comfort, and more—definitely a bargain.

"The face and body brushes are especially useful, and I love how you can interchange the heads depending on what type of cleansing you want to do," says Women's Health contributor Isabel McMahon.

She credits the device’s built-in light, called the "smartlight," as a great option for women who like dimmer lighting while showering but still want to see what they're doing.

Read more: Best At-Home Laser Hair Removal Devices

We previously tried and enjoyed the Philips Lady Shaver Series 6000, but it's no longer available. Thankfully, the brand upgraded to the 9000 model—and we love the changes.

You're paying $30 more, but it's worth the upgrade. The new model is a more powerful device that has two speed settings for faster plucking. It also features a quicker two-hour recharge time and can be used cordless for up to an hour.

The 9000 is equipped with eight attachments, including a floating foil head that glides across the skin. The different blades of the Philips electric razor are designed to target specific areas of your body, like the more compact bikini trimmer comb and head versus the larger trimming comb for your legs. It does an excellent job of trimming coarse body hair without any irritation or tugging.

Regardless of which attachment you employ, they all ensure that you can shave safely, even in the tightest contours of your legs and underarms. Whether you shave wet or dry, the ergonomic handle design will make sure nothing slips through your fingers. For this reason, we think the Philips is an incredible value. There are five interchangeable heads that target everything from the bikini area and legs to underarms and face. If you’re dealing with rogue hairs in hard-to-reach areas use this one for touchups. It comes with trimmers and traditional razor heads so you can snip longer hairs to about the length of a rice grain before shaving. Offering IPX7 waterproof protection, you can confidently shave in the shower with this device or use it dry if you prefer.

Our favorite Philips model is no longer being sold, but we found a much cheaper alternative that doesn’t skimp on quality. After all, it can be nerve-racking to take an epilator or electric razor to the face, but this compact model was made just for that.

It’s shaped like a lipstick tube and features a hypoallergenic head that glides over rogue chin hairs and your upper lip with ease. Though it lacks a built-in mirror or LED light so you can conveniently see and remove even the smallest facial hairs, this device is only $20 compared to $47 Phillips model. Pro tip: You should try using it before your skincare routine to help your products to really penetrate the skin for a major glow. Just don't use anything with too many active ingredients like retinol right after as that can cause sensitivity.

Looking to stay silky-smooth on vacay? Then click "add to cart" on this extremely travel-friendly razor and then toss it in your carry-on or gym bag for quick, simple touch-ups. It's compact, so it won't take up precious room in your cosmetic bag (you could even stash it in your office drawer to ensure that you're hair-free for any impromptu after-work activities like happy hours and date nights). And yep, this little shaver is super lightweight to carry which is always a win.

Despite being battery-powered, you'll be shocked by how durable it is compared to something cheaper. This dual trimmer lifts and guides the blades for smooth results whether you're shaving wet or dry. It does a great job for the price, but you might notice that it seems to work best when the hair is longer, so it may not be ideal for targeting stubble. (It's totally NBD though because you can just shave less often and ultimately who doesn't love that?)

It's also not waterproof or durable for daily, consistent use so you wouldn't want to consider this your primary hair remover, but for a quick trip—brilliant! No wonder it earned an impressive 4.1-star average from more than 14,430 Amazon reviews.

This razor, which is specifically designed for the bikini and underarm areas, can be used both inside and outside the shower, no matter your hair type. It's ideal for thick, coarser hair, though, because it has a sharp blade that trims them on the first attempt. Additionally, this cordless device has rounded edges to prevent accidents. Anyone who's shaved knows hair removal can get messy, but the head on this shaver opens up for easy rinsing, too.

You’ll appreciate how beginner-friendly the Phillips razor is. The instructions are so clear and easy to follow, which make your experience a breeze. The electric razor is relatively small and very easy to get a secure grip on, so anyone with butterfingers can rely on this device.I tried this razor and think it's pretty sweet, especially when cleaning up my bikini line. At first I was nervous that my longer hairs would get caught in the razor (it was winter, please let me live), but I was pleasantly surprised that it was a nonissue. It actually gets down quite low, especially when I don't use the comb attachment.

I enjoyed my bikini line shaving experience enough to use this device on my underarms and that's when I realized it heats up relatively quickly, which may be something to keep in mind if you're going for a longer shave sesh. With the multitude of options available on Amazon, Ulta, and Dermstore, there are a couple of features to consider the next time you're in the market for a fresh shave:

More is not always better. In fact, a larger number of blades can sometimes increase irritation, says dermatologist Lauren Ploch, MD. On the other hand, fewer blades mean more passes over the skin, which can also cause irritation. It's about finding a happy medium that works for you. This may take some testing, so remember to try out your razor on a small patch of skin to see how you react before going all in.

Think about how well a razor feels and fits in your hand. You want something that’s well-balanced and not too heavy for the most comfortable shaving experience. Also consider if it will shave wet or dry. Not all electric razors can be used in the shower, Dr. Ploch points out. So, if you're a shower shaver, make sure to grab something waterproof and cordless.

You also want to make sure your razor head can contour to your body's curves, especially when you're targeting areas like the bikini line, underarms, toes, and even legs. Some of the razors on this list, like the Panasonic Close Curves Electric Razor, can uniquely adapt to the body's curves with their rotating heads.

If a razor is rechargeable (big plus already), make sure to check how long it takes to charge and the battery life. If you don't want to deal with a cord or annoying charge time, some of the options on this list—hi, Philips Series 5000 Electric Facial Hair Remover—are battery-powered, which may be more convenient while traveling.

Some razors come with trimmers, blade guides, and changeable blade heads for different areas of the body. If you're looking for more of a Swiss Army knife-type, multi-tool situation, take a look at the available attachments. Then, see if those are compatible with the parts of your body you want to tackle.

Believe it or not, many razors have a warranty, so if you're unsatisfied with your purchase, you can most likely return it for a longer period than you might think. Most razors on this list have a 30-day warranty, which gives you ample time for testing.

Our team tests a wide range of products and services to provide our readers with reliable, honest, and trustworthy information. It's our belief that our readers deserve the best, which is why our recommendations have been thoroughly tested and vetted by our very own editors. For the past year, Women’s Health editors, including myself, and contributors Jasmine Gomez and Sabrina Talbert, tested the bestselling, most popular, and top-rated electric razors. Our team also consulted four dermatologists, and then evaluated thousands of customer reviews and ratings to narrow down the six best electric razors for a wide range of needs and preferences.

Ready for smooth, bump-free skin? Look no further than these editor-tested and expert-approved electric razors for women, below.

If you struggle with bumps and irritation, an electric razor might be your new best friend. Of course, you still need to make sure you use that electric razor properly. Dermatologists say you should follow the below best practices for a smooth shave every time.

Make sure your skin is well hydrated before shaving because using an electric razor over dry, irritated skin can make matters worse, says dermatologist Joshua Zeichner, MD. Dr. Robinson adds that you should also use a gentle cleanser prior to shaving. And, avoid fragrance or products known to cause irritation immediately before and after shaving, she says.

And please, do so in the direction of the hair growth, says Dr. Zeichner. Repeated strokes over the same area increase the likelihood of irritation and ingrown hairs.

Hydration is key. "I advise patients that they do not need a dedicated post-shave or aftercare lotion—a gentle moisturizer is just fine in these areas," says Dr. Robinson, who likes light, fragrance-free formulas. Aside from that, Dr. Robinson recommends making sure you follow any specific instructions on the product package—in other words, you should actually read the directions.

At the end of the day, everyone's going to have their personal preference, and it's not worth, ahem, splitting hairs if you prefer one type of razor over another. That being said, if your skin is prone to irritation, it might be time to ditch the traditional razor. With an electric razor, you’re not scraping against the skin really hard like a traditional razor does, says dermatologist Cameron Rokhsar, MD.. This means that you won't see a lot of the cuts and burns that sometimes result from a manual blade, says Dr. Rokhsar. There are also areas of the body that might be better suited to shave with an electric razor. "Most women's electric razors are designed for our curvy areas," says Dr. Ploch. "I prefer electric razors around the ankles because manual razors cut this area easily."

Keeping your electric razor clean is incredibly important, says Dr. Rokhsar. Many derms will recommend changing a manual razor every time you shave, but you can't do that with an electric one, which makes running the blades under warm water after use a crucial step. This will keep it free of hair, shaving cream, and other residues.

Dr. Rokhsar also recommends swiping over the blades and the outside of the razor with a rubbing alcohol-soaked cotton ball regularly. "Especially if it sits in your bathroom moisture, bacteria will accumulate on the blades," he says. "It's an easy entry point for bacteria to go down the hair follicle." That's a big no-no if you want to stay free of irritation or infection.

Our team of editors follow Dr. Rokhsar's advice and it hasn't led us astray. And despite evaluating some of these razors for close to a year, we are pleased that we haven't noticed any rusting after using the alcohol-soaked cotton ball.

Another tip is to actually read and follow the maintenance instructions of your device. (Admittedly, we threw ours away since we've been using these for several months and like to keep the limited space of our beauty closet as streamlined as possible.) You can also prioritize using devices like the Philips Series 5000 Electric Facial Hair Remover that's easy to clean, as the head can easily be removed so you can dump shaved hair and dead skin cells straight into the garbage.

#542. An Exclusive Look Inside Barack and Michelle Obama’s Private Offices

In the new presidential center on Chicago’s South Side, A-List designer Michael S. Smith creates a place of purpose and promise for the former president and first lady.

Above: The seminar room of the Obama Presidential Center in Chicago, designed by Michael S. Smith, with architecture by Tod Williams Billie Tsien Architects. A site-specific painting by Lorna Simpson is above the mantel. Sofas and armchairs by Anees; custom daybeds by Luteca; rug by Elson & Company with artist McArthur Binion.

I have a crystal-clear recollection of how all this began. It was late afternoon on a cold, gray day during the first week of December 2008, just after Thanksgiving, and I was in Chicago to be introduced to Michelle and Barack Obama, then the president-elect. It had been a whirlwind few days: a recommendation to them through a serendipitous connection, an interview scheduled, and then the news that after reading my design books the Obamas had chosen me to be their White House decorator before we had even had time to meet.

That first visit to Chicago was impactful. I vividly remember the Obamas’ friendly welcome, as well as the remarkable warmth of their home. It was inviting, personal, and full of character—airy, spacious rooms with a thoughtful mix of elegant furnishings, objects from their travels, and shelves overflowing with books.

This was the beginning of an incredibly important part of my creative life—as well as a deep friendship with the Obama family—which in many ways culminated with the grand opening of the Obama Presidential Center (OPC) on a dazzling June morning 18 years later. The design trajectory in between included eight White House years focused on far more than decorating the family quarters and the Oval Office. The constant conversation regarding decisions large and small ranged from a request for better lighting over the desks of their daughters, Malia and Sasha, so they could do their homework, to overseeing the display of a diverse cross-section of American art in their residence.

I found artisans to craft official gifts for foreign leaders and prominent guests, such as hand-blown glass jars to hold the White House honey and jewel-like boxes sculpted by artist Nancy Lorenz. And when I was asked to help design the presidential china, I chose a color I called Kailua Blue, the blue of the ocean off Oahu, a place dear to the Obamas. It was an extraordinary experience to contribute to such decisions and to distill them, much later, into the DNA of the OPC’s interiors—down to the Kailua Blue tile cladding the café walls.

There was also a dictate I received early from Mrs. Obama, which became the brief for everything I did at the White House and beyond: There was an understanding that the Obamas were merely guardians of a bigger idea, taking inspiration from the past but always looking forward.

The first meetings about the OPC started midway through President Obama’s second term. There were conversations about what this might be and where, and I learned that the president wanted my participation and help. I volunteered immediately and helped lead a small advisory committee—longtime Obama advisors joined by creative leaders—that was charged with compiling a shortlist of architects to consider for the project. Prominent international architects submitted proposals, and the list was gradually culled after visits to their offices and studios.

We sought a distinguished talent who could design a center that would reflect President Obama’s vision of what a reimagined presidential center could be. He didn’t want it to be a static tribute to his presidency but a place that would continually generate new ideas while reflecting his and Mrs. Obama’s commitment to public service.

Eventually a few firms were selected to meet the president and first lady, though it was clear to me that Tod Williams and Billie Tsien were standouts. A then-married couple who had balanced each other for decades, they created elegant, humane buildings—a softened International Style, modernist yet tactile. It felt like an exact fit. I had realized in the White House years that the president’s aesthetic was a kind of modernist classicism, shaped in part by his school years in Hawaii spent in buildings designed by noted modernist architect Vladimir Ossipoff. And it mattered enormously to me that Tod and Billie had a portfolio of homes in addition to their celebrated museums and civic buildings. They designed spaces that draw you through them—something I do not know how to do—with windows that frame views as powerfully as any painting on the walls.

My job, as I always saw it, sometimes in heated discussion, was to protect the Obamas’ vision—to find the magic crossover point where everything I knew of the Obamas’ taste fused with Tod and Billie’s architecture so that neither was diluted. Because the building, in the end, is a home-coming. It’s on the South Side of Chicago, blocks from where Michelle Obama was born and raised. It’s the same city where a young lawyer arrived to do community work, met her, and began the series of steps that led to the presidency. The Obama Center is a testament to what has come out of the South Side: Mrs. Obama, the president, and generations of artists from the culturally rich, deeply connected community.

President Obama, who has said that he once wanted to be an architect, was very involved in the selection process, as well as in every decision that followed—the location, the materials, the form of the buildings. And his mandate was explicit: He said the center was not to be a monument to the past but a living destination; not a reliquary but a place where things are meant to happen.

And so it is. People who watched a tall granite structure rise from a muddy construction site could not have imagined how friendly it would become—the centerpiece of a living campus, brimming with color, art, and joy. Located within a restored Jackson Park, the campus includes gardens, public art, an athletic center, a huge plaza for concerts, a Chicago Public Library branch, playgrounds, and even a sledding hill, because Mrs. Obama always wanted one as a child, but the local terrain was too flat. Access to the majority of the property is free; tickets to the exhibitions in the Museum Tower are sold in advance.

The tower’s private presidential suite is where I was most deeply involved from the beginning, and it is the culmination of my institutional knowledge. The seminar room’s ceiling oval takes its proportions from the iconic Yellow Oval Room—the Obamas’ public-private living room in the family quarters at the White House. I chose koa wood to clad these rooms, a wood almost spiritual in Hawaiian tradition, so it’s connected to the president’s childhood yet perfectly at home in a city that understands modernism. The carpets and furnishings were made by artists and craftspeople, many Chicago-based, many whose work was featured in the Obama White House. The dining chairs in the seminar room, based on a Paul Dupré-Lafon form, are replicas of chairs I made for their house in Hawaii.

Borrowing a concept from Jean-Michel Frank’s 1930s collaboration with Henri Matisse, we built art into the architecture itself, with a Lorna Simpson work that surrounds the seminar room’s fireplace form. Throughout the OPC the art program was led by longtime curator Virginia Shore and includes many works by artists who became friends of the Obamas’ over the years—including a stained glass window by Julie Mehretu flanking the escalators and a Mark Bradford mixed media work that reads as a love letter to Chicago.

Within this strong, outward-facing building, I wanted Mrs. Obama’s office to feel like a retreat, so I used soft creams and pinks that are as impactful and dynamic as she is. I knew that someone who exudes so much light and energy in every meeting needed a place to regroup and take a breath.

I thought of the late hours the president had spent each night in the White House’s Treaty Room, which served as his study in the family quarters. His office at the OPC is also a study, with his books at hand, a table for meetings, and places to read and reflect. A Susan Rothenberg canvas hangs on one wall, an echo of an iconic horse painting that was displayed in the Treaty Room. Familiarity, for both of the Obamas, is a kind of strength.

There is a golden hour on the presidential floor, especially in the seminar room and president’s study, when dappled light moves through the space as if it were a sundial, highlighting the frieze of four-foot-tall words that wrap the tower’s corner and spell out part of the president’s historic Selma speech. Later in the evening the exchange reverses: The tower becomes a lantern, a beacon with light emanating outward through cast stone text visible for miles—so right for a president who is, above all, a writer who understands how words lift people up. This building does not just stand; it speaks.

#543. The "One Weird Thing" Rule Is the Designer Secret to a More Personalized Home

Don’t overthink it—the best conversation starter might already be in your home.

Pictured above: This bedroom, designed by Alicia Savin, is chockful of eye-catching features, including a white rabbit figurine holding court on the nightstand.

Once upon a time, not so long ago, interior design was fairly…predictable. All-white kitchens. Gray everything. Some farmhouse touches for good measure. Then came a revolution within interior design, a creative revolt against the expected. Nowadays, everyone wants character, personality, and surprises within their spaces. They want homes with warmth and a story to tell.

Enter: the “one weird thing” rule. It’s an interior design concept that’s increasingly coming up on social media, and it can actually benefit a wide array of spaces. Here’s what designers want you to know about it.

But first of all, what makes an object “weird”? Justina Blakeney, artist, designer, author, and founder of Jungalow, says that an object might appear to be completely ordinary, but it can become unexpected because of how or where you use it, such as hanging a rug on the wall as art.

Lily Walters, interior designer and founder of Elter Studios (who’s known for her “Your Home Isn’t Weird Enough” reels on Instagram), says that a “weird” object possesses one of three qualities.

“It is something so random that it immediately draws your attention, something that has a story attached to it, or something that has no meaning at all, just made you smile, and you knew you wanted to bring it home,” she defines.

If you want to bring some oddities into your home without totally throwing off your vibe, read on to learn how designers do it right.

Fawn Galli, founder and principal designer of Fawn Galli Interiors, says that the “one weird thing” rule means integrating something in a room “that doesn’t make sense, that’s wacky, that’s unusual.”

“I love it when it’s personal, especially something you found on your travels, something that relates to you or your family, something with a story,” she adds.

Alicia Savin, creative director and owner of Alicia Savin By Design, puts it even more plainly: “It’s the one thing in a room or a home that makes your guests say, ‘Wait. What is that?!’

Although you may be keeping conversation starters in mind as your guests enter your home, it can also be helpful if you come up with your own definition of “weird.”

“I think the question, ‘What does ‘weird’ even mean?’ is worth asking,” Blakeney says. “An object that feels weird to one person might be completely ordinary to someone else. So, I like to think of ‘weird’ as something that challenges convention, or uses something in a new or unexpected way.”

What are the benefits of getting a little adventurous and “weird” within your interiors? Well, there are actually quite a few, which all center on creating visual appeal.

“When everything matches, your eye slides right through a room—nothing holds it,” Galli remarks. “The unexpected piece does.”

Within this same vein, and eschewing perfection, Walters says, “The ‘one weird thing’ rule gives you permission to be human. To share the parts of your soul that make you who you are. We spend so much of our time at home. It should reflect who you are and tell the story of the person who lives there.”

Blakeney additionally believes that a “weird” object or two creates notable juxtaposition, saying, “Contrast and tension are really important in design. They help create visual interest. I like to think of it kind of like music. The room has a steady beat, and then the unexpected element works as a kind of syncopation. It breaks up the rhythm and makes the room really sing.”

What are some “weird” objects you can consider bringing into a space (or more than one space)? Well, you can start somewhat small with “a massive piece of horse art” or “as small as a seashell you picked up on a walk,” as Walters says. Or you can go big or go home, with Savin recommending things like a “framed cocktail napkin from the bar where a couple met” or “a taxidermy squirrel wearing a tiny cowboy hat that they picked up on a ski trip to Jackson Hole.”

You might be wondering: how can you add this level of personality without throwing off your aesthetic? You might want to start without thinking about your aesthetic at all.

“Don’t worry too much about aesthetic,” Galli recommends. “If you love it, there’s a way to make it work.” She does add that it can be helpful to pay attention to the scale of the “weird” object—if it’s too small, it doesn’t have the same effect; if it’s too big, it overwhelms. But she’d rather overwhelm than underwhelm.

Blakeney advises starting with something you genuinely love or that has meaning for you.

“Maybe it doesn’t match anything else in the room color-wise,” she says. “Maybe it’s from a different era or made of a wildly different material. Don’t overthink it! Find a good spot for it and see how it feels.”

Savin believes that when seeking out weird objects, you should begin with things you already have on hand, saying, “Don’t go shopping for ‘weird.’ That defeats the whole purpose. Start with a childhood photo. One that borders on making you cringe but is filled with good memories. Or display the rattlesnake skull you found on the side of the road in Mexico after your car broke down. Put it right on top of one of those enormous coffee table books.”

When it comes down to it, being “weird” in our homes can come down to gumption.

As Blakeney says, “I think we could all stand to be a little less afraid of being weird in our homes. Your home is one of the few places in the world where you get to be as weird as you want! It doesn’t have to make sense to anyone but you—and honestly, it doesn’t even have to make sense to you. And if you think one weird thing feels good…try two.”

#544. The Best Thing You Can Do for Your Brain This Week Might Actually Help Someone Else

Giving back might do more than lift others up.

Living a long, physically healthy life isn’t enough—you want to be mentally sharp along the way, too. There are many everyday habits that can improve your brain health, but there's one that benefits you as well as those around you: helping others.

Both volunteering and offering informal help to neighbors and friends may slow down cognitive aging, which can impact your ability to think, learn, remember, and make decisions, suggests one study published in the journal Social Science & Medicine.

Here’s what the researchers found, plus how to put this knowledge to work for your gray matter.

Meet the experts: Sae Hwang Han, PhD, is the lead study author and associate professor in the Department of Human Development and Family Sciences at The University of Texas at Austin. Faye Begeti, PhD, is a neuroscientist at Oxford University Hospitals.

For the study, researchers analyzed data from more than 30,000 U.S. adults over 20 years using data from the Health and Retirement Study.The researchers discovered that people who volunteered their time or regularly offered less formal help to neighbors, relatives, or friends had 15 percent to 20 percent less cognitive decline linked with aging than those who didn’t help others.

When they dove a little deeper into the data, they discovered that people who spent around two to four hours a week giving back saw the biggest benefit.

There are likely a few things going on here. “Volunteering and helping others engage both the brain and body in ways that protect against cognitive aging,” says Sae Hwang Han, PhD, lead study author and associate professor in the Department of Human Development and Family Sciences at The University of Texas at Austin. “These activities provide social connection, a sense of purpose, and often an environment that can be cognitively stimulating—all of which are linked to better cognitive health.”

Mental stimulation is paramount, says Faye Begeti, PhD, a neuroscientist at Oxford University Hospitals. “The key factor to prevent cognitive decline is to continue challenging our brains throughout life,” she says. “I often see people who slow down after retirement, and I always encourage them to stay cognitively active. Volunteering is a wonderful way to do that.”

Helping others may even reduce stress and inflammation, two factors that are linked with cognitive decline, Han adds.

In-person seems to be the ideal way to go, Han says. Think: offering a hand at a soup kitchen or reading to kids. “Face-to-face engagement likely strengthens the social psychological rewards that help promote cognitive health,” he says. “That said, remote or virtual volunteering could still offer benefits if it’s cognitively stimulating or provides a meaningful human connection.”

And don't forget, you don't necessarily have to sign up for a formal volunteer opportunity—the study found that offering informal help to others was just as effective. So, why not agree to water a neighbor's plants or pick up their mail while they're out of town? Or if cooking is more your thing, making a lasagna for a friend recovering from a surgery could be your way of showing love and support. (And, while not scientifically proven, we'd imagine you'd get bonus brain points for dining together, too!)

Ultimately, Han recommends doing what you can. “Even modest levels of helping—about two to four hours a week—can make a real difference for long-term cognitive health,” he says. And really, any amount of helping is better than none, according to research. "There’s just robust evidence that around two to four hours a week is the sweet spot where the benefits become most pronounced," Han says.

At the end of the day, a small time investment has potentially large returns, especially compared to how much time many of us spend in front of screens each day, Han says. "The key message is that meaningful engagement with others isn’t just good for the community—it’s good for your brain.”

#547. Experts Say Weight Lifting Is The Fountain Of Youth. Here's How To Get Started At Any Age

If you want to haul groceries, get up the stairs with ease, play with your grandkids, and conquer all of life’s adventures with confidence as you age, here’s the science-backed secret: lift weights. Yep, those dumbbells in the gym aren’t just for young buffs (you know this!)—and they’re your ticket to keep doing the things you love most.

Getting older doesn’t have to mean getting weaker. In fact, senior weight lifting—that is, doing resistance training with machines and/or free weights in your 60s and beyond—offers physical and mental benefits that make it a vital part of aging well.

Women start losing muscle after 30, and this speeds up after menopause due to dramatic changes in your hormone levels. This change impacts both muscle and bone health, but strength training can help maintain bone density, promote preservation (and even addition!) of muscle, and set your body up for an active, independent life, according to the International Osteoporosis Foundation.

Here, we share all the fundamentals you need to understand why weight lifting and strength training are so important as you age, and how you can (safely!) get started.

Aging gracefully isn't just about staying active; it’s about choosing the right kind of activity to support your health. Resistance training (such as bodyweight, free weight, and resistance band exercises) is one of the best ways to counter the effects of aging, helping you build up muscle to support daily activities and prevent conditions like osteopenia and osteoporosis that can lead to bone fractures. And even if you've never lifted a weight before, it's never too late to start.

“Weight training is the fountain of youth,” says Abby Bales, PT, DPT, CSCS, founder of Reform Physical Therapy. “Not only does it help increase and maintain bone density to prevent fractures, but the muscle mass that weight training builds also helps to regulate our blood sugar and metabolism.” Weight lifting can even improve balance and coordination, decreasing the frequency, severity, and likelihood of falls.

On top of the physical benefits, resistance training has shown promise in staving off neurological conditions like Alzheimer’s and dementia, according to a 2023 study published in Frontiers in Neuroscience, making it a multi-benefit tool for aging well. You can think of lifting weights as your body’s best tool to promote resilience, energy, and independence through the aging process.

Want to gain serious strength? Try our Strong After 50 4-Week workout plan.

Starting with small, manageable steps—such as incorporating resistance bands or light weights into your routine—can help you gain confidence and momentum while reaping the long-term benefits.

The best exercises for women over 60 are weight-bearing and promote strength, posture, and/or balance (sometimes all at once!). While the best exercises for each individual depend on factors including medical history, fitness level, and personal preference (a personal trainer or physical therapist can help you design a more personalized plan!), it’s always great to start with fundamental exercises that incorporate movements used in daily life.

To help get you started, here are a few exercises that Bales recommends older women incorporate in their weekly routine.

Instructions: Select five to seven of the exercises below, mixing two to three upper body exercises, two to three lower body, and one or two core. Start with two to three sets of 10 reps of each. If you’re new to strength training, begin by doing the routine once a week and gradually work up to three times per week. Choose a weight that feels heavy enough to make the last two to three reps of each set feel tough, yet achievable.

Time: 15-20 minutes | Equipment: Dumbbells, kettlebells, stair or step-up platform | Good for: Full-body

Why it rocks: The air squat mimics many daily activities, such as getting up and down from a toilet seat, standing up from a chair, and bending down to pick something up. All of these activities are important as we age, so make sure you’re doing some form of squatting as you get older to help stay independent and capable of all these tasks and more. This move is also great because it can be done using your body weight alone, although adding a weight to up the intensity is always encouraged.

Pro tip: If getting down low enough or balancing feels too challenging, try doing this with a chair or couch behind you. At the bottom of the move, tap your bum to the seat or briefly pause there before standing back up.

Why it rocks: This exercise helps with strength and mobility in the shoulder joint, which will allow you to reach items in upper cabinets or even put on/take off a t-shirt for years to come.

Pro tip: If this is too challenging with weights, start by trying it without weights. Doing the move seated as opposed to sitting can also help. Focus on slow, controlled movements to protect the shoulder joint and get the most muscle engagement out of this move.

Why it rocks: As we age, simple things like stepping up onto a curb, walking on uneven surfaces and going up and down stairs can become challenging and increase the risk of tripping or falling. For this reason, it’s important to practice fully picking up the feet and clearing them from the floor. This exercise focuses on just that.

Pro tip: If this is challenging, start by doing it somewhere that you can hold onto a railing or fixed surface with one hand for support. You can also start with a low step or platform—something that’s six inches high or less—and eventually increase the height as the move becomes easier.

Why it rocks: Your biceps help you bend your arm and make it possible to perform daily tasks such as doing your laundry, lifting a heavy pot or pan, and more. Biceps curls are a great way to keep this muscle strong.

Pro tip: If moving both arms at once feels too challenging, do one at a time. Once the seated version of this exercise feels easy, try doing it standing up.

Why it rocks: Good posture is important for preventing things like stress fractures, which can occur in women with low bone density due to osteoporosis. This move targets the shoulders, upper back, and biceps all at once, helping to improve posture and strength.

Pro tip: Rows can be done in an upright or bent-over standing position. The angle at which you hinge forward will impact the workload: the more forward you lean, the more intense the exercise will feel. Modify this angle or try a more upright position to find a variation that works for you.

Why it rocks: Reverse lunges build strength in the glutes, hamstrings, and quads, while also improving balance and stability to help prevent falls as we age.

Pro tip: This can be a challenging exercise for many people because of the balance aspect, so try holding onto a stable object or countertop with one hand at first.

Why it rocks: Incline pushups are a gentler version of regular pushups, perfect for building arm, shoulder, and chest strength without straining your wrists or shoulders.

Pro tip: Begin with a higher surface to reduce intensity and pressure on the wrists. You can even use a wall! As you improve with this move, gradually lower the incline to make your body more parallel to the floor, which will make the exercise feel more challenging.

Why it rocks: This move is truly a full-body functional exercise that is great for improving balance, strength, and mobility to help older adults get up and down from the floor.

Pro tip: This is a complex move, so it’s best to break it down into smaller parts first. Try it first without weights and start by practicing just one or two pieces of the movement before putting it all together.

Why it rocks: Your triceps are important for extending your elbow, making daily movements possible like pushing yourself up from the ground or supporting your bodyweight with your arms (like in a plank).

Pro tip: Because the triceps are a tiny muscle, they don’t need much resistance to “turn on.” Start with no weights and only a small lean forward to see how it feels, then gradually increase the resistance by adding light weights. For extra support, try this move seated or using a single arm at a time for better focus on form.

Why it rocks: This squat variation has all the perks of a classic squat, but widens the stance to target the inner thighs, glutes, and quads from a slightly different angle.

Pro tip: As always, start with a lighter weight or body weight only to master form. If stability is challenging, try holding onto a support for extra balance.

Why it rocks: The farmer’s carry prepares the core for real-life activities such as carrying heavy things by your sides. It strengthens the core by making you resist the urge to bend, improving stability and balance.

Why it rocks: This exercise recruits your abdominal muscles to maintain balance and stability. A resistance band offers an added challenge for the core and lower body.

There really aren’t any exercises that are completely off-limits for older women, says Bales—as long as you’re comfortable. If an exercise causes pain, skip it. If it feels too challenging or confusing to get the hang of, try tweaking it to better suit your needs.

That said, depending on your fitness level, bone density, and current mobility and stability level, high-impact, single-side, and twisting exercises should be approached with caution, and may be best left behind for certain people, she says.

High-impact moves like jump squats and box jumps—while great for building up and strengthening your bones—put extra strain on joints, and therefore may not be a good idea for those who already experience joint pain or have arthritis, says Bales. If balance is an area of improvement for you, single-leg exercises are a great tool to rely on, as long as you’re using a stable platform to stabilize yourself and avoid ending up on the floor. Similarly, rotational exercises involving twisting of the spine are great for core strength and mobility, but can increase the risk of spinal compression fractures for those with advanced bone density issues, she says.

For beginners, it’s best to stick with slow, controlled resistance and bodyweight exercises that build strength without unnecessary strain, like bodyweight squats, resistance band work, or moderate weight lifting, says Bales. Above all, prioritize good form over the amount of weight you’re lifting, and don’t let fear stop you from getting started.

Bales’ bottom line: “Move as much as possible.” If you’re not sure which exercises are appropriate for you, consider seeing a physical therapist to get a full assessment and discuss your preferences and goals.

Building a strength training routine doesn’t have to be complicated—it just needs to be consistent. “Start small, build gradually, and stick with it,” says Bales. She recommends starting with two or three sessions per week, focusing on five to six exercises from this list for three sets of 10 reps. Try selecting an equal number of upper body, lower body, and core exercises to keep things balanced.

Progress takes time, so be patient. “Results usually show in six to eight weeks,” Bales explains. The key is to keep showing up and enjoy the process—your future self will thank you.

#550. Chanel Gets a Bird’s-Eye View at Paris Fashion Week

Matthieu Blazy chooses avian sets for a collection with freedom at its core

Yesterday at Paris’s Grand Palais, Nicole Kidman’s voice played over speakers, echoing through the cavernous space. To open Chanel’s Spring 2027 show, she recited a passage from Virginia Woolf’s 1928 novel, Orlando. "What's life, we ask, leaning on the farmyard gate; Life, Life, Life! cries the bird, as if he had heard, and knew precisely, what we meant by this bothering prying habit of ours of asking questions…”

It’s a pivotal moment in the novel: the titular Orlando is questioning the meaning of life, which leads him to consult his surroundings, including a nearby starling bird. As artistic director Matthieu Blazy presented his newest collection during Paris Fashion Week, he also asked his audience to look around—and above. Over celebrity attendees like Dua Lipa and Pedro Pascal were not just one but many birds—gull-like, white with orange beaks, and massive, lit from within and suspended mid-flight.

Since beginning his tenure at Chanel in April 2025, Blazy has worked to merge the house’s larger-than-life legacy with a contemporary, forward-looking vision. His set design in particular has exemplified this new, youthful take on Chanel, constructing spaces like an enchanting, mechanical garden for his Fall 2026 Haute Couture show, made in collaboration with ELLE Decor A-Lister Martin Brûlé, and a mushroom-filled wonderland for his Spring-Summer 2026 Haute Couture debut.

This season, Blazy turned to avian motifs, enlisting the help of celebrated French scenographer Richard Peduzzi. A flock of 95 birds cascaded across the cavernous hall of the Grand Palais in a reference to migration and freedom. Made of wooden frames covered in a semitranslucent tracing paper, their forms took inspiration from storks, geese, mallards, cranes, gulls, and more. Beneath them, the floor was painted with colored resin in an almost impressionistic style, resembling a rippling body of water seen from above. The glowing gulls’ reflections sparkled in the mirror-like surface.

As the Orlando voiceover faded into Tchaikovsky’s “Valse Sentimentale,” models moved beneath the birds in looks from the Spring 2027 collection. Titled “La Conversation – Part Three – Different Faces of the Same Coin,” the pieces also reference the brand’s matriarch. The first look included Gabrielle “Coco” Chanel’s own archival 2.55 handbag, and the rest of the collection spotlights Coco Chanel’s life and history, from her early career as a seamstress through to her fashion world success. “It’s about one woman, Gabrielle, who then became Chanel,” said Blazy in the show notes.

But, in showcasing the evolution of Chanel, Blazy also brought back that theme of freedom. He debuted lighter, movement-friendly variations on the classic Chanel tweed suit, including “smocked tweed,” as the fashion house referred to it in the show notes, a new version of a classic made more malleable and comfortable for the modern woman. It’s a design that draws from both Coco and the brand’s heritage and from 2026. Much like the flocks of birds soaring overhead, Blazy presents a vision of joyous freedom.

“It’s a collection about Gabrielle Chanel’s layered stories,” said Blazy. “Ultimately, Chanel took off, and each step she took led to her being free, like a bird.”

#551. 'After Brain Surgery, I’m Back to Training Five Days a Week—and Building Muscle'

“Getting stronger isn’t a destination—it’s the process of improving little by little, day by day.”

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

When the COVID-19 pandemic hit, my usual routine came to a halt. Aside from the occasional walk with my family, I became pretty sedentary, and it didn’t take long before nightly charcuterie boards and a glass or two of wine were the norm. At first, it didn’t seem like much, but over time, I stopped taking care of myself the way I used to.

Those habits stuck with me for the next few years, but by 2022, when I was 51, I knew something needed to change. I’d been active up until the pandemic, and I missed what it felt like to feel strong. I had gained weight, lost a lot of muscle, and just felt lost overall. I wasn’t sure where to begin.

As I was scrolling Instagram one day, I came across a post of a woman who had gone through an incredible strength transformation. She shared how she had gone through The Wonder Women Official program—a virtual training program focused on mindset, macro-based nutrition, and resistance training—and seeing what she achieved was so inspiring. It made me want to take that same step, so I decided to apply to the program myself. A few months later, I was accepted and ready to do whatever it took to get stronger.

I had never tracked macros or followed a structured weight training plan, so there was certainly a learning curve, but I stayed committed to the process. I followed a high-protein diet and went to the gym seven days a week. I was strength training five times a week and did cardio every day—paying close attention to proper form and gradually increasing the weight over time whenever I could. I worked with my coach virtually, but we had regular check-ins to review form, track progress, and set new goals, which helped keep me accountable and motivated.

Overhauling my lifestyle wasn’t easy at first, but after a few weeks of adjusting and fine-tuning my routine, things started to click and I felt great. Each week, I noticed myself getting stronger, more capable, and more in-tune with my body. I was building visible muscle, my clothes were fitting looser, and I genuinely enjoyed having a consistent routine. After years of feeling lost, I appreciated the structure and discipline this new lifestyle gave me.

My doctors had been monitoring a small cancerous mass in my brain for some time. In early 2023, it started growing again, requiring surgery. I was, surprisingly, not nervous going into the procedure—I was strong, powerful, and in the best shape of my life, which gave me a lot of confidence in my ability to recover. And it really paid off.

While doctors originally expected I’d be in the hospital for five days, I was up and walking shortly after surgery and able to go home after two. Naturally, I had some discomfort, but I believe the strength and endurance I built from consistent resistance training played a significant role in my recovery process.

I couldn’t go to the gym for two months after surgery, but with the support of my doctor and coach, I stayed focused on getting back my strength. The first few weeks were hard since I had very little energy and spent most of my time in bed, but by week six, I felt ready to start moving more. With the guidance of my same Wonder Women coach, I began walking about 2,000 steps a day, gradually rebuilding my stamina and endurance from there.

Once I was cleared to return to the gym, I kept things simple. My doctor said as long as I felt good, it was safe to exercise, so I started with three days a week, focusing on bodyweight exercises and light dumbbells. My coach also checked in daily to make sure I felt okay and wasn’t overdoing it. Slowing down wasn’t easy, but I constantly reminded myself that progress takes patience. Within a few weeks, I was lifting a 95-pound barbell again. By eight months post-surgery, I had worked my way back to lifting the same weights I was before.

Today, at 54, I still train virtually with The Wonder Women program five days a week: three days focused on upper body and two on lower body. The number of exercises varies, but I usually do three sets of 10 to 15 reps per exercise, depending on the weight. I also do 30 to 45 minutes of cardio on my Peloton a few times a week.

These days, my goal is to keep building muscle, so progressive overload remains a priority, even if it’s an incremental amount. I’m also working toward a new 200-pound bench press goal. Before surgery, I was benching 135 pounds, and now I’m up to 163 pounds.

These incremental weight plates are perfect for progressively overloading barbells when the next jump in weight feels too heavy.

I love my lifting straps because they add extra grip support to prevent slipping when I’m holding heavy weight.

Good music is a must for my workouts, so I always have my AirPods with me.

To be honest, I don’t think I would be where I am today without the incredible support of my coach and community.

Even while recovering from brain surgery, when I could barely walk for more than five minutes, my coach stayed right there with me—checking-in, celebrating every small win, and pushing me just enough to safely keep moving forward. Having a teammate who truly believed in my ability and worked with me to rebuild my strength was invaluable, and her encouragement made all the difference.

Plus, the whole Wonder Woman Official community is such a tight knit group—the support is unbelievable. And of course, my family have always been my biggest fans, and have supported me every step of the way. I never felt alone in any portion of my journey—I always had a whole community rooting for me. I couldn’t have done it without any of them.

I’ve always believed in the power of mindset, but it’s gratitude that really keeps me grounded. I’m so thankful for my health, my body, and the amazing people who have supported me every step of the way. Life has definitely thrown me some curve balls, but I’ve learned that being grateful doesn’t mean ignoring challenges or pretending that everything is perfect. It’s about recognizing and celebrating resilience, determination, grit, and strength, even in the face of setbacks.

There have been days, or even weeks, when life gets in the way and progress feels slow. In these moments, I remind myself that moving my body is a privilege. I understand it’s easier said than done, but I truly believe that gratitude can turn even the smallest wins into something big. It reminds me that every challenging moment is part of a journey I’m lucky to be on.

One of the biggest lessons I’ve learned through everything is that fitness isn’t linear. Some weeks, walking just 2,000 steps felt like a victory, while other weeks, picking up a barbell seemed impossible. But through every up and down, I reminded myself that progress doesn’t happen in a straight line because every small step forward matters.

Returning to the gym and gradually rebuilding strength after brain surgery wasn’t about hitting PRs or pushing to extremes. It was about proving to myself that I could recover, adapt, and keep moving forward. After all, getting stronger isn’t a destination; it’s the process of improving little by little, day by day.

#553. 5 Paint Color Trends to Try for Fall

This season’s hottest tones take their cues from the 1970s.

Now that the weather has finally started to turn, our focus is shifting back into the home. Autumn is the ideal time to consider a decorative refresh, and the most effective way to do it is with a change of paint color.

In recent years, muted palettes and the so-called “quiet luxury” look have reigned across interiors. This year, however, there’s been a shift. Designers are pulling inspiration from the 1970s, from opulent decorative techniques to hedonistic homeware, like ashtrays and caviar spoons. Color palettes, too, are being influenced by this retro revival with warm, earthy tones cropping up in contemporary homes. Consider these five colors a way to bring a touch of the ’70s to your space.

If any color defined 1970s interiors, it had to be avocado. A little punchier and a lot less murky, consider olive green an update on the verdant shade that works everywhere from powder rooms to kitchens. “The Botanist” by Paint and Paper Library is a classic olive with a reddish undertone.

More characterful than beige and not as saccharine as pastel pink, dusty rose colors like “Freudian” by Edward Bulmer are an excellent neutral for living spaces and bedrooms. These colors are subtle enough to not overwhelm a space and act as a natural canvas for layered artwork and textiles.

Tangerine has been the zippy color of choice for bathroom design recently, while muted shades like Little Greene’s “Ashes of Marigold” work for larger spaces like living rooms. An elevated take on the brand’s punchier “Marigold” color, creative director Ruth Mottershead says, “This alternative orange has a muddier undertone, containing more black pigment to create a shade that feels gentler and more subdued.”

A 1970s palette wouldn’t be complete without a modern play on maroon. To prevent your home from becoming a pastiche to the past, aim for a deeply pigmented color with black undertones like Lick’s new “Red 07.” Ideal for reading nooks and snugs, this dramatic color delivers instant atmosphere.

This rich, warming yellow is a sophisticated way to introduce the decade’s mustard colors into the modern home. “Amber Earth” by Graham & Brown is subtle yet uplifting and makes for a striking accent color on doorways and in alcoves.
