#554. Trail Running Is Growing at an Exponential Rate—This Is Why Women Are All In

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

More women are taking to the path less traveled in pursuit of feeling free and leaving PRs behind. (Plus, here’s how to jump into this world if you’re a total trail newbie.)

When Taylor Abrams hit her mid-30s, she started getting serious about road running. She worked diligently to run a sub-three-hour marathon in 2024 but had a hard time repeating the magic in 2025. Stressing about her paces and splits, she started feeling burnt out and unmotivated. On a mission to make running fun again, Abrams took to the trails in Marin County, California, where she’d been living for two years.

Today, at 39, the mom of three leans on the sport to explore, be adventurous, and feel like a kid again as she zooms down the hills. She’s rejuvenated her relationship with running—and many others are doing the same, for similar reasons.

Running in general has boomed over the past three to five years, and trail running is no longer hiding in the shadows of glamorous road races—it has fully entered the mainstream. The sport is growing annually by 8 percent, with more people entering races like the Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc, which has 2.4 times more participants now than it did in 2022. The fan base is growing as well: The 2026 Cocodona 250-mile race amassed over 1.4 million total views on its livestream, compared with 841,000 in 2025. Those are extreme ultra-based examples, yes, but there’s also this: The number of athletes who uploaded trail runs on Strava increased when comparing the first half of 2025 with the first half of 2022, with female users logging twice as many trail runs in 2025 as in 2024. Over on the AllTrails app, trail running has gone up by 11 percent since August 2024. And the entire trail running market is worth over $14 billion—even everyday fitness brands like Lululemon and Alo are now dropping trail-specific shoes.

Women like Abrams are gravitating to the sport because we’re “looking for a different relationship with running,” says Alysha Flynn, a Road Runners Club of America–certified running coach specializing in performance, sustainable training, and the realities of women’s lives, and the founder of What Runs You. By nature, trail running requires you to let go of pacing and PR pressure (and comparing yourself to others) and instead just enjoy the challenge. Here’s what else is behind the boom.

Being in nature does wonders for your mental health, research shows, and those benefits increase tenfold with trail running. It requires you to drop your speed, concentrate on the terrain, and stay present, which can feel almost meditative. “The focus is really on the now,” says Noel B. Salazar, PhD, a professor of social and cultural anthropology and the founder of the Cultural Mobilities Research (CuMoRe) cluster at KU Leuven in Belgium. “It triggers a kind of mental re-pacing.”

This process can help take your mind off life pressures. (Finances! Scary headlines! Uncertainty about the future!) “Trail running is seen as a meaningful activity in a world where people feel increasingly overwhelmed,” Salazar adds. “People seem to be craving activities where they are in direct contact with their bodies in the environment.”

This feeling is something Megan Gorsky, 24, experienced on her first trail run in college. Subconsciously focusing on the nature and environment around her, she was shocked at how the time passed. “You’ll hit five miles before you thought you were at three—it goes by so much quicker,” she says.

On the trails, women are able to reframe running. Relationships become “built around effort, exploration, and adventure, rather than constantly chasing pace or comparing themselves,” says Flynn. We get the chance to ask ourselves questions like “How do I feel today?” “Can I stay calm as the terrain is changing?” “Can I adapt?”

These days, it’s almost unheard of to run without a wearable or not upload a run to Strava. “We’re getting burnt out by chasing metrics,” says Flynn. However, trail running is naturally less of a data-driven sport. Because you run at an inconsistent pace, many runners leave wearables (and music or podcasts) at home, Salazar adds.

Instead, you’re dialed in to your next step. “Notifications, music, and constant watch checking disappear,” Flynn says. “It’s almost like permission to let go and allow the terrain to dictate your effort.” As such, the stakes are lower and you don’t have to worry about shaving a minute from your mile time. You can just listen to your body, adds Stefanie Flippin, DPM, a run coach with over 15 years of coaching experience, a foot and ankle surgeon, and a professional trail and ultrarunner for Lululemon based in Pine, Colorado.

Abrams notices she’s less stressed on the trails because she’s just trying to have fun. “I put a lot of pressure on myself about running for a hobby,” she says. “It takes the pressure off, to not feel like you have to be hitting certain paces when you’re bouncing around in the woods.”

When Dr. Flippin started trail running 15 years ago, there weren’t many opportunities to livestream races. “Now you can follow races in real time,” she says. That’s changed the game for trail running’s exposure. This year, over a million people watched Rachel Entrekin become the first woman to win the Cocodona 250-mile race. “That’s a really inspiring aspect for women, too, just to see that, ‘Oh, you know what? She’s doing this. She’s at the front of the pack here,’  ” she adds. “We can’t really see that in any other sport that’s endurance-based.”

With more exposure comes more money from major brands, especially following the 2021 decision to permit collegiate athlete name, image, and likeness (NIL) deals. So, in addition to pros, college athletes are being offered contracts for cross-country, steeplechase, mountain running, and track and field. “We’re definitely going to be seeing more and more of that with trail brands stepping in,” says Dr. Flippin. (Particularly for athletes whose main goal is to go from the NCAA into professional trail running.)

As visibility increases, many long-held beliefs are falling away. Historically, women have been told that our bodies can’t handle running, especially long distances. (Women weren’t allowed to run marathons until the 1970s.) However, research shows that female runners actually have greater durability and physiological resilience than our male counterparts, per a small recent study in the Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. “There’s something really empowering about being able to summit mountain peaks and take on more intimidating terrain,” says Dr. Flippin.

That’s part of the reason Gorsky was hooked on trail running almost instantly. “When you start to see how your body is able to climb so much elevation and go far, it’s insane to see how you adapt,” she says. “You get to know yourself pretty well.” With the right fueling, she has learned to go higher and longer than she ever thought possible.

The solo endeavor payoff is great, sure, but the community one might be even better: “Trail running tends to be more relaxed and community-focused” than road running, says Dr. Flippin. You might get judged for walking on an uphill stretch during a road race, but not on trails: Slowing down to hike up a hill is a real strategy. “The community emphasizes sharing the experience rather than proving yourself,” Flynn adds.

Yssis Davis, 30, loves spending time outside and has been running for over a decade, but she doesn’t feel safe doing so in her current neighborhood in Los Angeles. However, when she found Hike Clerb, a local outdoor collective for women of color, on Instagram, she decided to take the plunge and finally start trail running. She was intimidated, but having that crew by her side helped her feel more confident, she says. And as more women go trail, those communities are poised to grow in the U.S.—and around the world.

Trail running is “a totally different type of running” than road running, says Salazar. You’re working on your core stability and ankle and foot strength as you constantly land in different positions; there’s also less impact. “It’s less repetitive on the body, so there tends to be less of an injury risk,” says Dr. Flippin. Adapt your technique from pavement to path:

Social media is full of misconceptions about trail running, says Flynn. (Hint: It’s not always running 100 miles up a mountain in your most expensive gear!) To make it feel more accessible, run just a few miles in a grassy field or a local nature preserve. “Go out there with the expectation that you are not trying to run the trail the same way you do roads,” she adds. Her number one tip: “Leave your pace expectations at home.” Stay open-minded and become a student again.

You have to “be more intentional” with trail than road running, says Dr. Flippin. “You can’t just be daydreaming and looking out at the terrain or else you might risk a fall.” Keep your focus several yards ahead to anticipate upcoming rocks or trees, and look down if you need to.

“New trail runners tend to struggle with descending on more technical trails because there’s a greater risk for falling,” says Dr. Flippin. “The natural inclination is to lean back and tense up the quads in order to ‘brake.’  ” The better option: Lean into the downhill and allow gravity to assist you.

Before you hit the trails, run a downhill stretch on the road. “Practice picking up your pace and running a little bit quicker on a non-technical downhill first so that you’re reinforcing good mechanics,” says Dr. Flippin. “Then, start building in faster efforts on more technical downhill terrain.” Over time, you’ll build confidence—and speed. (On the flip side, if you need to slow down and hike an uphill climb, that’s part of trail running, too, and doesn’t make you any less of a runner, she adds.)

“We usually see more elevation gain and more descent with trail running,” says Dr. Flippin. (Also: fewer flat stretches.) So make sure you’re doing lower-body strength work during the week to build up quad and calf strength. Also throw some plyometrics into your routine, which will help you navigate more technical terrain.

The right shoe is key. For beginners, avoid max-cushion sneakers—you’ll feel more stable on the ground, Dr. Flippin says. Also, look for shoes with pronounced lugs on the bottom to provide grip. A few of our favorites:

This hybrid road-trail shoe is versatile and will support your feet through routes that alternate between pavement and trails.

The grip is solid on wet rock and mud, all while keeping your feet dry.

These feel stable on rocks and secure on your feet even when you’re descending, per Flynn, who wore them for 48 miles on the Grand Canyon’s rocky trails, loose sand, and steep climbs.

The ultra-plush, thick cushioning will spare your feet on tough terrain while stopping them from underpronating—which is common as you cruise over sticks and tree trunks.

Size Matters Experts recommend going down a half-size in trail shoes compared to road ones. “That tends to take away the potential element of catching your toe on rocks and roots,” says Dr. Flippin.

“Some people equate trail running to ultrarunning,” says Dr. Flippin. But “you can run a trail 10K, 5K, or half-marathon, and that is 100 percent still trail running.” A few groups to help you find your match…

#558. Former Royal Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor Takes Legal Action Over Home Search

The brother of King Charles III had two properties raided in February.

In February, British authorities made global headlines when they arrested Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, the younger brother of King Charles III, and searched multiple properties on suspicion of misconduct in public office. Now, the disgraced former royal has responded by taking legal action.

The New York Times reports that the erstwhile Duke of York, who lost his royal titles last October and was forced to leave his longtime home in Windsor, has asked a court to review the basis for the police searches of two properties: Royal Lodge and a residence at Sandringham.

The Thames Valley Police, who made the arrest, obtained search warrants from England’s Central Criminal Court in February as part of the investigation into whether the former Prince Andrew improperly shared classified information with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, who died in 2019. Mountbatten-Windsor has long denied any wrongdoing in connection with the scandal. In addition, he was released without charge following the arrest.

The local police force arrested Mountbatten-Windsor on February 19 on the grounds of the royal Sandringham Estate, when he was living at a temporary residence there called Wood Farm. After the arrest, the Thames Valley Police raided Marsh Farm, also at Sandringham, where he was in the process of moving.

Previously, Mountbatten-Windsor had lived at Royal Lodge, near Windsor Castle, for more than two decades. King Charles ordered him and ex-wife Sarah Ferguson to relocate off the property’s grounds last fall, although Mountbatten-Windsor didn’t end up vacating until February 4.

In the wake of the arrest, officials also descended upon Royal Lodge. The BBC obtained aerial photos showing more than 20 unmarked police vehicles outside the home.

Now that Mountbatten-Windsor has questioned the legality of the search warrants in court, a private hearing will take place on Thursday in the U.K., per the Times.

#560. The 5 Best Acupressure Mats for Relaxation and Sore Muscles

I rolled my eyes at acupressure mats—then I tried one.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Working out regularly is how I stay emotionally regulated, even though it feels like I’m constantly trying to fend off stress. But when I can’t fit in a standard workout, spending a few moments on my acupressure mat can feel like the next best thing.

I’ll be honest: I secretly rolled my eyes when a friend gifted me the mat and said it would help me relax. But after weeks sitting in my closet, I decided to try the mat out—and I was hooked. It felt uncomfortable at first, but I found that the mat’s sensation gave me a feeling similar to a runner’s high when I could zone out and just go with it.

Not familiar with an acupressure mat? They’re not totally mainstream, but they’re building up a following with health-conscious people who need help chilling out (me, hi). Acupressure mats are foam mats that are covered with thousands of small, sharp plastic spikes, explains Dayna McCarthy, DO, an osteopathic and sports medicine physician at Parsley Health. Those spikes are designed to stimulate pressure points on your body, with the ultimate goal of lowering stress. The mats may even help relieve muscle aches and pains by targeting pressure points, says Jamie Bacharach, a licensed acupuncturist.

When you lie or stand on an acupressure mat, those spikes create a firm pressure on hundreds of points across your skin, McCarthy says. It’s important to get this out of the way: There isn’t a robust body of research to support the use of acupressure mats. Still, plenty of people swear by them. “Although there is limited evidence in regards to their overall benefit, the best-documented physiologic effects are acute pain reduction, relaxation, and improved sleep quality,” McCarthy says. “But the evidence is still limited, and they’re not a miracle cure.”

An acupressure mat isn’t made to be a cure or substitute for medical care. So, if you’re dealing with back pain that won’t quit, go get that checked out with a doctor instead of lying on a spiky mat hoping things will improve. But if you like the idea of a naturopathic way to ease muscle soreness and de-stress, there’s really no reason not to try one of these mats. They’re budget-friendly and an interesting way to try to manage minor health issues.

Bacharach says to avoid using acupressure mats to treat sudden acute conditions (such as a sprain, strain, or broken bone), while pregnant women and those with skin or heart disorders need to consult a doctor before use. Once you’re in the clear, figure out what size, material, spike density, and accessories are best for you before choosing an acupressure mat.

Each option on this list includes something for everyone, whether you want something less intense or with a budget price tag. Ready to relax and release tension? Keep reading for the best acupressure mats based on your specific needs.

After sifting through dozens of acupressure mats, the ProsourceFit Acupressure Mat deserves the top spot. Besides being highly rated (and affordable!), Bacharach loves the durable design, thousands of spikes, accessible sizing, and effective support, with enough stimulation to treat things like muscle tension and headaches.

Not impressed yet? The thick cotton and linen are breathable, while the plant-based eco foam provides ultimate comfort and mid-level support for frequent use. Large and extra-large sizes are available, so if you're tall, you're in luck! The mat is washable and comes in five shades, in case you want to match your wellness tool to your decor.

The one con? Testers say the pillow feels flimsy, but we still think it enhances support and the overall experience.

Tension doesn’t take a vacation just because you’re on the road. While some mats can be tricky to maneuver into a suitcase, the Sivan Back and Neck Acupressure Mat has plenty of features to make it easy to tote on the go, like a compact size and included travel bag. Just roll it up and slide it into the bag for acupressure away from home.

This mat has a slightly gentler touch than other, more intense mats. The thick, one-inch padding contrasts nicely against the hard spikes to support balance. Bacharach specifically recommends this mat for stress relief and sleep support.

The mat provides thousands of nontoxic plastic stimulation points for pain relief to help increase circulation. The mat and pillow are slightly wider than other options if you want extra room, while the removable cover is washable. We also found that the durable materials are made to sustain countless uses.

If you’re an acupressure newbie, it’s best to keep scrolling. This ShaktiMat is a level 2 mat, which means that it has fewer spikes for a more intense feel. That can be a good or bad thing, depending on your level of comfort with these health tools.

ShaktiMats have been around for ages, to the point where some people use the brand name synonymously with acupressure mats. This particular mat uses 6,000 spikes to ease tension but, just a heads up, it will leave a (temporary) mark on your skin afterward. Testers note that it can feel more uncomfortable at first. But many people swear that you get used to that quickly.

The ShaktiMat is also available in level 1 (read: less intense) and level 3 (super intense) versions, so there’s something in the mix for everyone.

There’s a wide range of materials used to fill and cover acupressure mats, but the WTHN mat delivers a premium feel from the inside out. This memory foam mat is covered in a blend of coconut fiber and linen, creating an airy, moisture-wicking feel as you rest. It has more than 8,000 spikes to create a noticeable, but not intense, feeling.

WTHN added thoughtful details, like a matching linen carrying case and included pillow to help you with all-over tension release. There’s also a handy how-to guide with step-by-step instructions on how to use the mat, along with acupressure points to try to hit. Just be aware that this mat is on the smaller side, which means it’s not the best choice for taller users. But if you’re just looking to target your shoulders and back, it’s a solid choice.

Whether you’re new to acupressure mats or just prefer a softer touch, Gaiam’s acupressure mat is worth a look. This mat delivers gentle pressure to give you the perks of an acupressure mat, just in a more subtle way. The mat feels high-quality and doesn’t lose its shape over time, even with regular use.

The mat comes with an included pillow that feels supportive under your head and neck. The set is also lightweight, so it’s easy to lift and store away when it’s not being used. This isn’t the largest acupressure mat you’ll find, but it’s also not the smallest. Overall, it delivers enough coverage area for your shoulders and low back, which is all most people need. Just keep in mind that the milder feel may not be enough for more seasoned acupressure mat users. If that’s you, consider the level 2 ShaktiMat instead.

Since you’ll be lying down, you want a mat that covers the designated areas you wish to target, says Bacharach. Larger sizes typically cover the upper and lower body, while smaller sizes are great for travel and targeting specific pain areas like your neck and shoulders. Some models also come in extra-long lengths for taller folks. As a general rule of thumb, find a mat that fits at least the length of your back.

Most mats on this list are made of high-quality cotton and non-toxic plastic spikes. Medical-grade ABS plastic (meaning, it’s reliable enough to use in the medical field) is preferred, according to McCarthy. Bacharach says to seek out cotton or linen given its breathability and high durability. Many options we chose also have sturdy foam padding for extra comfort and support. If you want to regularly wash the acupressure mat, find an option with a removable hand-washable cover.

Mats in our guide range between 8,000 and 12,000 lotus-shaped spikes, so choose a suitable mat depending on your preferences. “More spikes usually means less intense pressure per spike and greater comfort,” McCarthy says. “Very low spike counts—under 4,000—can feel excessively painful and increase bruising risk.”

If you’re new to acupressure mats, it’s best to start with a mat with a higher spike density. Otherwise, it may feel too intense for you. “Start with five to 10 minutes, use a thin T-shirt if needed, and stop if pain increases or you feel dizzy,” McCarthy says.

Many mats come with extra accessories such as a pillow, carrying bag, or storage strap for additional support and convenience when traveling, so Bacharach says to consider what add-ons are important to you. A carrying bag and storage strap are especially great for travel, while a pillow or crescent wedge can add support and comfort to your head and back during a session.

To find the best acupressure mats for all preferences, the WH team consulted with an acupuncturist and osteopathic physician to learn more about what makes a great mat. From there, we researched bestsellers and relied on our personal experience with these mats, combing through extensive testing notes to narrow down the top picks. Because every person’s experience is different, we analyzed reviews and only included products with overwhelmingly positive feedback.

#563. The 10 Best Sports Bras, Tested by Fitness and Style Editors

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Finding the right sports bra is crucial. That’s because a well-fitted one keeps your girls locked in and comfortable during jogs, stretches, and squats, so you don’t have to worry about spillage or bounce.

To find the best of the best sports bras, our fitness and style editors tested more than 50 options—from high-impact sports bras designed to minimize bounce to softer options from our fave activewear brands that prioritize comfort. We evaluated each pick for support, fit, comfort, and performance across a range of workouts and body types.

This bra is a 2026 Fitness Awards winner, and basically “the holy grail of sports bras for high-intensity workouts,” Andriakos says. It’s ultra-comfortable with adjustable straps for a customizable fit that works for all sorts of exercises.

The Performance Flex Bra offers medium support, but we’ve found it minimizes bounce without restricting movement, thanks to a higher neckline and light built-in padding that helps me feel secure while I train. In testing, it felt just as comfortable during slower sessions like yoga and Pilates as it did during higher-intensity workout classes. The hold is supportive without feeling overly compressive, so the girls stay in place without that squeezed-in feeling some medium-support bras can have.

One of our favorite details is the padding. “It’s built in—so you never have to deal with shifting, scrunching, or fishing pads out of the laundry,” Andriakos says. That means the bra keeps its shape wash after wash and eliminates the annoyance of removable inserts. The padding also stays comfortable through body changes—Andriakos says it even supported her during pregnancy and postpartum. The only potential downside is that the padding isn’t removable, which might not appeal to those who want less coverage.

The wide adjustable straps are another favorite feature of mine. They distribute weight evenly across my shoulders without digging in or creating pressure points during longer workouts. Even better, the straps adjust from the front, so it’s way easier to adjust than traditional bras.

And for my sweaty gals, the fabric is perfect for keeping perspiration under control. It’s made from a breathable, sweat-wicking blend of recycled polyester and elastane, which feels soft and flexible while maintaining shape. It keeps me cool and comfortable—even in heated classes—and the full mesh racerback panel adds tons of ventilation. That open, breathable design helps release heat during workouts. It also gives the bra a streamlined silhouette that sits smoothly under all my workout tops.

Read More: On Performance Flex Bra Review

This bra is a favorite among four (!) WH editors—myself, Andriakos, Wohlner, and Lauture. We love its support during high-impact workouts, durability, value, and stay-in-place cups that move like a second skin.

Andriakos says that this bra is great for medium-sized busts. It has a slight compressed feel, which keeps everything secure and minimizes bounce during plyometric moves and running, but it’s not so tight that it restricts movement. It also has a high support option, which has more compression and an adjustable band, and a low-support option, which is looser with gentle hold. We picked the medium support bra for our number one choice because it’s the most versatile option. We’ve worn it during runs, pilates, walks, yoga, and HIIT and found that it offers solid support with minimal boob bounce, but it’s not too tight that we want to rip it off after our workouts.This bra is also moisture-wicking, so it doesn’t get super wet and sweaty during workouts, which we appreciate. The 100 percent polyester material has a super slippery feel, which we like for its ability to stay breathable, but we find that it tends to chafe under the breasts during long runs. I wore this bra a ton during my half-marathon training last year and found that it would irritate my skin after about five miles. I found the solution should be to level up to the high-impact bra for my runs, so there’s less room for movement and chafing.Back to the pros: This bra handles the wash super well. Every time we wash and air dry it, the bra comes out looking good as new and never pills or comes unsewn. Andriakos has owned hers for two years and says it still looks the same as when she first bought it. Since then, she’s purchased multiple in different colors.“My ideal sports bra doesn’t have any hardware or fastening, or removable pads that get lost in the dryer,” says Andriakos. This one easily pulls on over the head without any adjusting and it’s a breeze to take on and off. It has a minimal silhouette with super wide armholes, so you can rip it right off after a workout without playing around with straps or closures. Plus, Lauture and I love that the cups are sewn in place, so they don’t move around during your workout.

The first time I pulled on the Forme Power+ Bra, I instinctively rolled my shoulders forward like I usually do at my desk—except this time, they didn’t stay there. Within seconds, the bra gently guided them back, opening up my chest and lifting my upper spine so I stood noticeably taller without consciously trying. It’s a subtle shift, but one you feel immediately: less hunching, more length through your torso, and a sense that your upper body is quietly being coached into better alignment.

The Power+ is made from a compressive blend of polyester, nylon, and spandex and features multiple tension fabrics with strategically placed, double-layered support panels throughout the back and shoulders. Together, they create a gentle pull that encourages your shoulders to stay back and your chest open. The result feels supportive without restricting movement, and I love wearing it for all my workouts.

Despite its posture-focused design, the Power+ also functions as a solid sports bra. The compression keeps everything comfortably locked in during strength sessions, cardio workouts, and high-impact movement, while the breathable fabric prevents that heavy, trapped-in-sweat feeling some compressive bras create. Wide straps, generous arm openings, and a full-coverage back also help smooth things out and give the bra a flattering, secure fit.

Another unexpected perk: It’s just as helpful during everyday wear as it is in the gym. Whether you’re sitting at a laptop for hours or driving to a workout class, the bra keeps your shoulders from rounding forward and helps reduce some of that end-of-day neck and upper-back tension I know too well.

The only downside? That supportive compression makes the bra a bit snug—especially when you’re pulling it on for the first time. And after a particularly sweaty workout, taking it off can require a little extra effort, too.

If you’re a fan of Lululemon, then chances are you’ve tried this OG Energy Bra, which has been around for years. And, even after all of the brand’s launches, it remains one of our all-time favorites. Why? It’s super lightweight, breathable, sweat-wicking, soft, and it’s easy to take on and off. It slides on like a dream and feels super lightweight and comfy the whole time it’s on.

“This is my go-to bra for Pilates, yoga, or barre,” says Saladino, who adds that it provides medium support. “The straps don't dig in and there is a good amount of coverage so when I go into downward dog I don't have to worry about my girls popping out.” She also likes that it’s suuuper stretchy, soft, and easy to take off after a sweaty workout. Plus, I find that I forget I’m even wearing it hours after I leave the gym because it’s not overly tight.

Wohlner owns this bra too, and she finds it runs a bit large. Personally, she likes a tighter fit with more compression since it makes her feel more supported, so we’d recommend sizing down if you feel the same. But if you prefer a looser fit, stick with your usual size.

If you need a high-impact sports bra that can handle any type of workout, this option from Under Armour will keep you locked in. According to trainers Nellie Barnett, CPT, an online fitness and wellness coach, and Taylor Beebe, a kettlebell coach and two-time USAPL (USA Powerlifting!) National Qualifier, the Infinity 2.0 High Sports Bra is the best of the best for intense workouts—no matter your chest size.

Not only do the encapsulated cups keep everything in place, but the bra is comfortable to boot. It’s still flattering, and not overly compressive (no pancake chest here!). The Infinity 2.0 also has fully adjustable straps, both in the front and back, which makes putting it on and taking it off (even after a sweaty workout) a breeze. It has a streamlined fit that’s not too tight or too loose, making it great for staying secure and moving freely during high-impact workouts. Plus, the cups have strategically placed molded padding for an aerodynamic, lightweight feel that doesn’t skimp on support. Also impressive is the bra’s moisture-wicking band that keeps underboob sweat at bay.

This bra performed amazingly well during strength training, cardio, and explosive movements like burpees and high knees. It even kept Beebe feeling supported and secure throughout the entirety of a cardio kickboxing class (IYKYK). “No adjustments needed for the full hour,” she says. If that’s not impressive, we don’t know what is.

Just be aware that the bra does run a bit small, so if you’re unsure which to pick, definitely size up.

Read More: Best Sports Bras for Large Breasts

Another 2026 Fitness Awards winner for best longline sports bra, this is the rare piece that blurs the line between workout and casual clothes. The extended cut gives it the look and coverage of a cropped tank while still functioning like a supportive sports bra—making it an easy pick for everything from studio workouts to running errands.

The versatility is exactly why it’s become a “mainstay” in Luppino’s rotation. “It’s long enough where it’s a proper top, yet also a sports bra,” she says. “The material is thick and supportive enough, but still totally moves with you, making it functional for any workouts without compromising on style.” We also love the flattering scoop neckline, which adds a slightly elevated feel compared to more traditional sports bras.

The silhouette makes it especially easy to style. You can wear it on its own with leggings or biker shorts, or layer it under an oversized tee, zip-up hoodie, or lightweight jacket. The racerback design is both flattering and functional—it allows full range of motion during workouts and sits smoothly under tanks and tees.

Performance-wise, this bra delivers high compression with medium support, offering a sculpted feel that holds the girls in place without feeling restrictive. It’s made from a sleek blend of polyester and elastane, which has a smooth, slightly shiny finish that looks super polished. The bonded (aka seamless) construction helps it lie flat and disappear under clothing, which I love when wearing beyond the gym. Another pro? The removable cups, which give you the option to customize the level of shaping and coverage.

The only caveat is that the bra is super snug. The brand recommends sizing up if you have a fuller cup size, which I agree with based on testing.

This bra provides great support—we never have to worry about the girls moving out of place during wear. While this bra is made for medium impact, the cups and adjustable straps make it versatile enough for high-impact workouts. I wore it during a HIIT workout and noticed some bounce, but it’s perfect for strength training and mobility workouts that don’t involve much jumping.

A lot of the high-impact sports bras we tested have hardware that digs in. That's why we love this one from Alo. When I’m in need of that extra support, the adjustable straps add more compression without digging into the skin. The removable cups can shift in the wash, but you can take them out and pop them back in for extra chest support. My one downside is that tightening the straps can put a lot of pressure on your shoulders.Plus, Lauture says this bra is one of her all-time favorites because of the fit. “It’s so flattering and it looks good on—no gaping or bunching in sight.” That’s because this bra is made with Alo’s most compressive fabric, Airlift, which offers the tightest fit of all the brand’s materials, but I found that it still has plenty of stretch that moves seamlessly even while jumping and running. With a blend of 82% polyester and 18% elastane, it’s incredibly soft, yet has a nice, tight feel to keep you supported.

Read More: Alo Airlift Suit Up Bra Review

A high-neck top with a built-in light support bra, this is the perfect top when you don’t feel like layering a shirt on top of a bra but you want more coverage than a bra alone. I love that this top hits at the top of my fave high-waisted leggings because it creates a seamless look. And, if you want a matching fit, it pairs perfectly with the Spacedye At Your Leisure High Waisted Midi Legging.

I like to wear this on days when I’m doing yoga, pilates, or walking, because it provides light compression to hold the girls in place while still being comfortable enough to wear long after the gym. It’s extremely soft, as it’s made with a high polyester percentage, but the stretch comes in with the addition of elastane. I even went to brunch in this top and didn’t feel constricted at the table at all. Plus, it’s moisture-wicking to keep you dry when things start to heat up. If you’re working out outside, the shirt is treated with UV protection to protect your chest and upper waist from the sun (big ups!).

My one con: I wish that there was more coverage on the sides of the shirt to prevent the breasts from spilling out.

The Rhone Revive Longline Bra stands out for one very specific reason: It’s actually odor-resistant. The bra is made with the brand’s specialized GoldFusion anti-odor technology, a fabric treatment that uses gold-infused particles to help tamp down on odor-causing bacteria. Whether I’m heading into hot yoga or a sweaty strength class, I appreciate that the fabric doesn’t cling to post-workout funk like others do—a small but major win.

I’ve mostly worn this bra for yoga and pilates, and it keeps everything secure, even during upside-down poses like shoulder stands (no awkward shifting or spillage, thank you!). I also wore this bra on an 85-degree day in NYC after a sweaty hot yoga class and a packed subway ride home, and somehow still felt (and smelled) fresh. I’ve never had a sports bra handle sweat this well.

In terms of support, it also holds up well on short runs—but we’re not sure those with larger chests would share that experience. I mostly recommend it for low-impact workouts since the support level may not cut it for all bodies during HIIT or long runs.

I also love how easy it is to wear solo or layer under a workout tank top or T-shirt. The elastane blend is buttery soft, breathable, and moves with you. It gives just enough support without feeling overly tight or restrictive. Our only gripe? Because it’s so stretchy, you might want to size down for a snugger fit.

All in all, this bra nails comfort and performance for most workouts. Bonus points for built-in sun protection if you’re taking your workout outdoors.

If you need an ultra sweat-wicking, odor-neutralizing sports bra, choosing one made from Merino wool is surprisingly the move. “I don’t know about you, but when I thought ‘wool,’ the first thing that came to mind was an itchy winter sweater—not exactly what I’m going for when I’m shopping for a sports bra,” says fitness and reviews editor Natascha Grief, NASM-CPT. But Branywyn’s Essential Busty Bra (and really everything we’ve tried from the brand) has been everything but itchy or uncomfortable.

Merino wool as a technical fabric has been a “revelation” for Grief, because it’s one of the few natural fibers that performs well in activewear. It comes from the coat of sheep and other animals, is naturally antimicrobial, and wicks away and absorbs sweat rather than letting it sit on the skin. If you run hot during your workouts, you can trust this bra to dry quickly and even wear it straight from the gym to brunch or errands if needed.

Grief says the bra doesn’t chafe or feel scratchy in any way, which is partially due to the fabric and partially due to the (nearly) seamless construction. The bottom band is a raw edge with no underwire, so it feels weightless and smooth, but also doesn’t ride up. It provides medium support, so it’s great for all workouts except HIIT classes. But it handles strength training, incline walks, casual jogs, and yoga or Pilates with ease.

You want to make sure your sports bra is made from high-quality, breathable fabrics, such as the ones below.

When looking for a sports bra, you should know the difference between compression and encapsulation in your bra. Compression, which can be found in the Nike or Lululemon sports bras, offers the feeling of your boobs being so supported that they’re a bit squished and pushed down. Encapsulation lifts, cradles, and separates your girls while still eliminating boob bounce. It can be found in the Beyond Yoga bra. #568. On Performance Flex Bra Review: A Fitness Editor’s Honest Take

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

As a fitness girlie with a particularly large bust, finding sports bras can feel like a sport in itself. Every few years, I wear out the ones I own, hunt high and low to find a style I like, buy several, and wear them into the ground—then the cycle repeats itself. It’s always been a particularly frustrating part of shopping for me and my 38DDs (DDD, depending on the brand).

Recently, I found myself once again on the hunt for my next emotional support bra. This time, I decided to try my luck with the Women’s Health 2026 Fitness Award winner and best sports bra overall: the On Performance Flex Bra. Here are my honest thoughts.

As a fitness editor and trainer, I’m constantly changing up my workouts. I tested this bra during heavy strength-training sessions, runs, and some athletic conditioning workouts including box jumps, kettlebell swings, and hurdle bounds. I wore it to coach some of my strength classes, and I also ran some errands around town with it to see how it handled everyday activities.

One of the biggest advantages of this bra is the adjustable straps. For high-impact activities, like running and athletic conditioning, I could tighten it up for extra support. When I was only lifting or running errands, I could loosen it a bit to give myself some more flexibility and comfort. The best part: the straps stay put no matter what you’re doing—no loosening during jumps or runs.

My only complaint about the fit of this bra is that it runs a bit tight around the ribcage. I have a particularly wide ribcage—again, I’m roughly a 38DD—and the underband was a bit snug in the size XL, the largest size they offer. It wasn’t so unbearable that I couldn’t wear it for long stints of time, and the fabric’s stretch definitely helped. Still, I felt some relief taking it off at the end of the day.

One complaint I often have with sports bras for larger busts is that they tend to have super restrictive necklines. Where they score points for proper coverage and avoiding wardrobe malfunctions mid-workout, they lack in comfort. Those ultra-high necklines often feel super limiting during upper body workouts and can dig into my shoulders or underarms.

The On Performance Flex Bra provides enough coverage and makes everything feel secure without feeling like it’s closing in around my neck. I also appreciate the lower scoop and cutout in the back, which makes the bra feel more relaxed (and stylish!) for everyday wear.

It also has built-in padding, which is a huge plus. You don’t have to worry about it shifting on you mid-workout or it scrunching up in the laundry. It keeps its shape after several washes and wears.

This bra is made of a combination of quick-drying polyester and super-stretchy elastane, so it feels performance-ready. It also has mesh paneling in the back of the bra, making it super breathable and airy, which I appreciate when working out at a high intensity.

That said, the fabric isn’t particularly soft. It feels a bit more like performance, quick-dry material. It’s not itchy or uncomfortable; it just doesn’t exactly have the same feel as a pair of leggings might. So if you prefer a smooth, buttery texture from your activewear, know you won’t find it here. But if you prioritize function over feel like me, the material dries quickly and stays relatively cool—even during the sweatiest workouts.

For me, the Performance Flex Bra’s only major con is the limited size range. In a perfect world, I would go up just one more size and not deal with the tightness of the underband. If you have a ribcage larger than 38 inches, this might not be the bra for you.

If it is available in your size, I highly recommend this bra for just about any workout. The adjustable straps let you customize the level of support, while the breathable, quick-drying fabric stands up to even the sweatiest sessions. It also provides plenty of coverage without restricting any of my workouts.

Needless to say, I think I just found my new go-to sports bra.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

As a registered dietitian, I recommend getting most of your nutrition from a well-balanced diet. But a meal replacement shake can be an efficient supplement to help fill in the gaps. Whether you’re looking for a high-protein meal but have a low appetite or need something on the go after a gym session, meal replacement shakes can be literal lifesavers (and these ready to drink options are easier than using protein powders!).

The best meal replacement shakes provide calories, protein, carbohydrates, and a mixture of vitamins and minerals to mimic what’s found in a meal—just crack open a bottle and sip. They're substantial enough to provide you with the energy you need until your next meal. I often recommend them to clients who skip breakfast if they’re not hungry enough to eat. I advise thinking of meal replacements as a convenient supplement to, not a substitute for, a balanced diet.

However, there are many other factors to consider when choosing the right one for you. If you have diabetes or are watching your carbohydrate intake, choosing one that’s low in carbs and sugar is best. But if you’re active, planning a workout, or replenishing from one, you may want a shake higher in carbs. Calories, protein amount and type, and sweeteners are also worth evaluating.

The Huel Black Edition drink takes the top spot with its complete, plant-based formula. It contains 400 calories, 35 grams of protein, and 27 essential vitamins and minerals per bottle, so it’s built to do more than just tide you over.

It’s made with a blend of pea protein and faba bean powder, which provides a more complete amino acid profile. That means better support for muscle growth and recovery and satiety. Each bottle also delivers six to seven grams of dietary fiber, plus healthy fats. The added micronutrient blend of iron, zinc, calcium, vitamin D, and B-complex vitamins covers your daily needs.

Huel is also a Certified B Corporation, which means it meets rigorous standards for environmental impact, social responsibility, and ethical sourcing. If you care about what goes into your shake and how it’s made, that’s a meaningful bonus.

At $6.04 per bottle or $4.83 with a subscription, it’s one of the pricier options, but for a genuinely complete, no-prep, plant-based meal on the go, Huel Black Edition delivers.

If you’ve tried your fair share of pea protein shakes, you know the texture can be chalky and that it’s an acquired taste. So, I was genuinely surprised by how smooth and satisfying Evolve turned out to be. I tested the double chocolate and chocolate caramel flavors. Both were rich, creamy, and had no weird aftertaste.

It’s important to notes that with 140 to 150 calories, 20 grams of protein, and 10 grams of fiber, Evolve straddles the line between snack and supplement. It isn’t technically a meal replacement shake, but it’s great as early morning pre-workout fuel—especially blended into coffee when my appetite is slow.

Nutritionally, Evolve earns extra credit for its micronutrient profile of calcium, iron, zinc, and B12—nutrients that are often hard to get on a plant-based diet. And while pea protein is technically a complete protein, it’s a little low in methionine, which is important for tissue repair and metabolism. A simple fix is to pair it with methionine-rich foods like nuts or seeds to round out your intake.

At $2.79 per bottle, it’s one of the more affordable ready-to-drink options. Plus, it’s free from artificial flavors, colors, and GMOs.

Short for “Only What You Need,” OWYN delivers clean, high-quality nutrition without fillers, artificial additives, or common allergens. Every product is free from the top nine allergens, including dairy, soy, gluten, eggs, peanuts, and tree nuts.

Each shake uses a blend of pea protein, organic pumpkin seed protein, and organic flax oil, which all help deliver 26 grams of plant-based protein. This combination supports a broader amino acid profile than pea alone, helping to promote muscle repair, satiety, and overall recovery—all without relying on dairy or soy.

The drink also includes 23 essential vitamins and minerals that support bone health, immune function, and energy metabolism. It’s a well-rounded shake that offers more than just protein.

With fewer than 200 calories, it’s not a full meal replacement, but it’s perfect as a post-workout shake, mid-day snack, or on-the-go boost. Blend it with fruit, oats, or nut butter for a more filling option, or pair it with breakfast to help round out your morning.

Among all the options I tested, Koia stands out as the best almond milk-based for its smooth texture and rich, nutty flavor.

I tried cacao bean, cold brew coffee, and vanilla bean, and each one delivered a creamy, balanced sip that felt more like a treat than a supplement. Accardi is obsessed with the chocolate banana flavor and loves using it to make lattes. “Besides tasting like a creamy treat in my coffee, it’s an easy 20 grams of protein, which makes it easier to hit my macro goals,” she says.

Each bottle comes in at 180 calories with 20 grams of plant-based protein, six grams of fats, and six grams of fiber. The protein blend—made from brown rice, peas, and chickpeas—offers a more complete amino acid profile than single-source proteins, supporting both muscle recovery and satiety.

While it’s important to note that it’s not high enough in protein and calories to replace a full meal, Koia is a satisfying option if you need something quick to hold you over until your next meal. Or, simply blend into a smoothie or pair with a piece of fruit and nuts for nutritional balance. And if you want an energy boost, the cold brew coffee flavor includes 100 milligrams of caffeine.

Koia uses a combination of organic cane sugar (adding three grams of sugar) and monk fruit extract to sweeten the shake, resulting in a smooth flavor without an overly sugary or artificial taste.

Ka’Chava is one of the best powder-based meal replacements thanks to its blend of whole-food ingredients.

Each serving provides 25 grams of plant-based protein from yellow pea and brown rice, covering all nine essential amino acids. You’ll also get six grams of fiber, omega-3s, MCTs, antioxidants such as turmeric, adaptogens like ashwagandha, probiotics, and digestive enzymes—a full-body formula in one scoop.

I tried all five flavors—vanilla, chocolate, coconut acai, matcha latte, and chai—and was surprised by how smooth and drinkable they were. No grassy aftertaste or chalky texture. My favorite combo? Vanilla, almond milk, and coffee for a creamy, energizing breakfast that held me over for hours—rare for a shake IMO.

At 240 calories, it may need a boost (like fruit or nut butter) to fully replace a meal. It’s also gluten-, dairy-, and soy-free, though it does contain coconut and sesame. It also has 450 milligrams of sodium per serving, which might be a consideration for some.

It’s a premium product at $4.66 per serving or $3.99 with a subscription, but it’s a balanced product with all three macros and nutrients to support your wellness. For those who want a nutrient-dense, plant-based powder that delivers on both flavor and function, Ka’Chava is as complete as it gets.

With 320 to 330 calories per 11-ounce bottle, and up to 400 calories in the larger 14-ounce version, this one’s a solid option for fueling.

Each 11-ounce serving provides 16 grams of protein from soy protein isolate, a complete plant-based protein containing all nine essential amino acids. The 14-ounce bottle bumps that up to a more ideal 20 grams of protein. With 19 grams of fat (primarily from high oleic sunflower and canola oils) and 28 to 32 grams of carbohydrates, Soylent offers a well-balanced macronutrient profile that makes it more than just a snack. Accardi likes them for breakfast when she’s not in the mood for a heavy meal. “These are ideal when I don’t want a full meal weighing me down, but still want an energy boost to start my day,” she says. “Plus, some flavors taste quite decadent, such as the chocolate and vanilla, so it’s easily enjoyable, although I will note some flavors leave a chalky aftertaste.”

Soylent’s flavor lineup includes both seasonal and staple options such as pumpkin spice, gingerbread, chocolate, vanilla, and strawberry, making it easy to find a favorite (or three).

As for sweeteners, Soylent uses a combination of allulose and sucralose. Allulose is a naturally occurring low-calorie sweetener, but sucralose is artificial and may cause digestive discomfort in some individuals.

At $2.50 per bottle (when purchased in a 12-pack), Soylent stands out as one of the most affordable and nutrient-dense high-calorie meal replacements.

Whey-based: Whey protein is derived from dairy and is a complete protein, meaning it contains all nine essential amino acids necessary for muscle repair, immune support, and overall health. The three main forms—concentrate, isolate, and hydrolysate—differ in processing, digestion speed, and lactose content. Whey concentrate is the least processed and contains more fats and carbohydrates, while whey isolate is more refined, lower in fat, and typically better tolerated by those with lactose intolerance. As for hydrolysate, the protein is broken down into smaller peptides for easy digestion.

Plant-based: Plant-based proteins are sourced from ingredients such as peas, rice, soy, and hemp, which makes them a great option if you’re avoiding animal products. While some single-source plant proteins may lack one or more essential amino acids, blends can offer a complete amino acid profile. Plant proteins are naturally lactose-free and often higher in fiber, so they’re ideal if you’re sensitive to dairy or following a plant-forward diet.

While a sedentary adult only needs 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight for basic functions, you likely need more than that, especially if you’re active or looking to lose weight. Whether you're a recreationally active woman or a competing athlete, you'll want to aim for around 1.2 to 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight, according to current research and recommendations.

Protein helps build and repair muscle, supports the immune system, and is needed for almost all chemical reactions that take place in the body. It also helps you feel fuller and slows your digestion down when you eat meals. A meal replacement shake that provides a quarter of your protein needs, or at least 20 grams per serving, is ideal.

If you’re looking for a true meal replacement shake, choose an option with a minimum of 300 to 400 calories. Even then, you may need to supplement it with something else, like a handful of nuts, a piece of fruit, or some veggies and hummus. I've included shakes with fewer calories in our guide, and these would make a great snack or breakfast if you’d otherwise skip the first meal of the day. Remember that a shake with fewer than 200 calories won’t supply your body with enough energy.

Some meal replacement shakes have a lower amount of carbohydrates and added sweeteners, while others may contain anywhere from 15 to 30 grams of carbohydrates. Added sugars can range from cane sugar to fructose, but natural sweeteners such as stevia, monk fruit, or allulose are more common. Artificial sweeteners such as sucralose, aspartame, or sugar alcohols like erythritol or sorbitol can also be found, but it's best to limit your intake. They can cause stomach pain, gas, and bloating in people with sensitivities.

I’m a St. Louis-based dietitian with nearly a decade of experience in nutrition writing and editing. I also have an M.S. in nutrition and dietetics from Saint Louis University. After carefully researching and evaluating dozens of meal replacement shakes for a month, I came across these top eight. I focused on calories, protein type and amount, and sweeteners when making my decisions.

Meal replacement shakes are generally safe for most people, but individual needs and health conditions should be considered. For example, individuals with kidney or heart disease may need to limit protein or sodium intake, making some shakes unsuitable. Those with severe food allergies should also use caution, as many shakes contain common allergens or carry a risk of cross-contamination. As with any supplement or dietary change, it's best to consult with a healthcare provider, especially if you’re managing a medical condition, taking prescription medications, or are pregnant or breastfeeding, to ensure a shake is safe and appropriate for you.

It’s generally safe to drink meal replacements daily, especially if they’re the most practical option in your routine, but they should only make up a small portion of your overall diet. To support long-term health, it’s important to prioritize whole, nutrient-dense foods that provide a wide range of macronutrients (protein, carbohydrates, and fats) and micronutrients (vitamins and minerals). Think of meal replacements as a convenient supplement to, not a substitute for, a balanced diet.

#571. This Is the One Mistake You Might Be Unknowingly Making When Touring New Homes

Imagine bringing someone along to tour a house for sale—the place is nice, but your companion isn’t a fan of it, criticizing the maintenance and raising concerns about some water issues. They even declare that they wouldn’t take the house even if someone gave it to them for free. But despite their protestations, you decide to make an offer on the home anyway... only to be immediately rejected.

It turns out that the private chat you were having wasn’t so private after all. Because the homeowner had security cameras installed, they could hear every word. This is a scenario that Kori Sassower, a principal agent at Compass, is all too familiar with—because it happened when one of her clients brought their parents to a showing.

“A seller’s emotional attachment to their home can be just as powerful as their interest in the offer,” Sassower tells House Beautiful. “The parents thought they were having a private family discussion; the seller felt they were insulting a home they loved.”

In an age where Ring doorbells, Flock cameras, and general neighborhood surveillance are becoming the norm in cities and towns across the United States, this has become the reality of homebuying. Before even pulling into the driveway, real estate agents are warning their clients not to say anything about the house—not the good, bad, or ugly—until they all get back into the car in case someone’s listening or watching.

“The two sentences I never want a seller to hear are ‘This is the one’ and ‘We could go higher,’” explains luxury Palm Beach real estate advisor Greg Forest. “Those are the most expensive words in real estate, and the front step is exactly where they get said.”

While the act of home buying has always been methodical, Forest says you now have to treat it like a game of poker: Don’t ever talk about the negotiation strategy, don’t announce your maximum, and never wax poetic about a home. And if you do have something to say, write it down or text it to your realtor for later.

That’s what Denver-based licensed realtor Tamara Mattox-Kabat tells her clients to do.

“I treat every showing as though a camera could be present.” And she’s right to: over 60 percent of U.S. households have at least one security camera, according to SafeHome.org. This is up from 52 percent in 2024 and 42 percent in 2023. “A video doorbell is standard now. At the top of the market, a full system with its own room is the norm rather than the exception,” adds Forest.

As these devices become more common, real estate agents are having to adapt their practices. Sassower requires all buyers to sign an audio disclosure acknowledging the possibility that someone is likely listening, while Mattox-Kabat contacts the listing agent prior to the walkthrough to verify whether there are any recording devices or cameras present.

In certain states, though, a disclosure that someone’s being watched and listened to is legally required, such as in Florida where Forest and other luxury agent Allison Freeman are based.

“Florida requires consent from everyone in a private conversation before it is recorded, so a seller listening in is taking on real exposure,” Forest explains. “Every seller should ask their own attorney about their own setup.” For Freeman, who mostly shows vacation rentals, cameras aren’t allowed inside the home at all, but when she’s showing a primary or second home, she has to assume there are cameras watching.

“I was once showing a house and mentioned to my client that I'd spotted cameras. He loved the house, so I was surprised when he made a point of loudly announcing that it was overpriced, and by exactly how much,” Freeman says. “That number was really just what he hoped to get it for. I don't think that approach serves a buyer well.”

None of these professionals, however, are anti-camera, and they wouldn’t tell a client who’s selling a home to take them down or turn them off if they’re outside.

“If a home is vacant, I’m comfortable with sellers keeping security cameras on for protection. The key is transparency,” Mattox-Kabat explains. “Security is one thing; using surveillance as part of the negotiation is another.”

Once the cameras and audio devices are on the inside, though, that’s where they draw the line. Not only can a seller get their feelings hurt, which will likely affect negotiations, but it’s extremely invasive for the potential buyers and can hurt the pace of the sale.

“Buyers who feel watched move fast, and a buyer who rushes does not fall for a house,” Forest says.

It’s easy to feed into our innate curiosity, especially when the tools are in place, but in instances like these, these experts feel it really doesn’t do anyone any good.

#573. Designers Love "Tasteful Horse Decor." Here's How to Pull It Off Without Looking Tacky

Make the equestrian trend work—without becoming a cliché.

Every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Pictured above: The bar area of Carson Kressley's Pennsylvania home is the epitome of horse decor done tastefully.

According to the Chinese zodiac, 2026 is the Year of the Horse—the fire horse to be exact. This element, coupled with the strength the animal represents, signifies rapid change and bold risks. As design editors, we're choosing to view this as yet another excuse to lean into the tasteful horse decor trend that's been percolating over the last year.

"Horses have always been a popular subject in the art and design world, going back to early cave drawings in the Lascaux Cave, France. It is so fun to see them back in the spotlight in interiors," designer Maria Burke says. "We have definitely seen a resurgence in layered, British interior style, so I think it is fitting that all sorts of equestrian subjects and patterns have also seen a rise in popularity."

While several designers we spoke with mentioned the influence of British style in homes right now, others link the uptick of equestrian decor to a yearning for a different time.

“We're seeing a major shift back to traditional, cozy, old-world design. I think it's everyone's desire for comfort and reassurance during these rocky political and technological times. It's the antithesis of AI," interior designer Lindsay Gerber Northart says.

“The resurgence [of horse decor] seems to stem from a deep-seated yearning for connection with nature and a romanticized notion of freedom and open horizons," L.A.-based designer Jennifer Miller adds. “Horses embody both untamed beauty and a sense of serene strength in their powerful yet graceful presence. This inherent duality resonates with contemporary desires for authenticity and a touch of the organic within our living spaces."

In a world where we scroll endlessly on TikTok, check work emails while on vacation, or are spammed with fake phone calls daily, returning to a slower seems idyllic. Designers everywhere, from Los Angeles to Virginia, are seeing an uptick in client requests for equestrian decor in their homes. Burke notes that, in one of her projects, they used the client's collection of riding crops and turned them into a gallery on their second-floor hallway. Meanwhile, Jeanne Hayes, founder of Camden Grace Interiors, recalls a client in the New York City suburbs asking them to adorn her husband's office in oil paintings featuring hunts and horses.

As you can tell, there are plenty of ways to capture their essence in your home. “There's a romanticism to equestrian imagery that evokes both rustic countryside charm and old-world luxury, making it incredibly versatile across styles, from modern farmhouse to classic traditional and even minimalist spaces,” designer Katie McCaffrey says.

Tasteful horse decor is here to stay, so check out the expert styling tips ahead on achieving the look seamlessly in your home.

Mixing new pieces with vintage finds is a tried-and-true furnishing method that gives your home its character. Even though this takes time, we're firm believers in slow decorating. When it comes to horse decor, Burke recommends employing the same method by merging "old master-style oil paintings with horse subjects above more modern pieces of furniture."

If you already have such works of art, you're one step ahead of everyone else. However, if you're sourcing art from scratch, Burke says, "These works can easily be found on auction sites and even consignment stores if you are up for the challenge, and they make for a wonderful mix with newer pieces." We suggest checking out places like Chairish, 1stdibs, LiveAuctioneers, and Everything But the House.

Besides framed artwork, designers suggest adding horse sculptures to your space, whether that's a small statue of a stallion nestled on your bookshelf or a giant horse head that commands attention near your staircase. The best part about these pieces is that you can move them around the house anytime without dealing with annoying photo hooks or adhesive strips.

“In my own home, I have a large, cast-iron horse head that meanders through my house, depending on my mood,” Hayes says. “Lately, he's hanging out on our porch bar, greeting guests with a cocktail.”

Whether you dabble in photography or follow a National Geographic photographer who shoots the most amazing wildlife, if this is your art medium of choice, incorporating a stunning visual of a horse in your space is a no-brainer.

"Professional equine photographers are increasingly producing some spectacular large-format images in both black and white and color. These can be striking statements alone or as a collection, and really set a sophisticated, luxurious vibe to any space," says designer and passionate equestrian Megan Winters.

If you're not into the animalcore look, you can instead hint at your love for them through horse-adjacent decor. "I think horse decor needs to be more of a nod and hint rather than literal...otherwise you're very easily getting into a tacky decor situation," Gerber Northart says. "Introduce patinated old leather pieces and brass accent pieces, which hint at the look and feel of horse tack. Wool and plaids hint at a fox hunt."

Similarly, McCaffrey suggests using checks, plaids, and natural materials, such as woven baskets, to evoke equestrian style without “being too literal.”

All the designers we spoke with agree on one thing when it comes to making your horse decor feel tasteful: moderation is key. "I like to try to limit the use of a 'themed' element to one or two items per room," Burke says. "Instead of layering all sorts of prints with an actual horse on it [throughout the home], we will use one and then draw inspiration from other sorts of horse-related items, such as leather, thick wool blankets, and dark iron [for the other spaces]."

"The key is to ensure the execution feels intentional and contributes to the overall narrative of the space," Miller adds. "In our Sun Valley project, we incorporated a few horse drawings and a red horse painting I created myself, which felt especially fitting for the setting and served as a nod to the Western heritage and natural beauty of the area. The artwork reflects the landscape’s rustic spirit while adding a personal layer of storytelling."

#575. All of the Duke and Duchess of Kent’s Royal Homes

Tour the stately residences owned by one of the Royal Family’s most discreet couples.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE Decor editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

In the year since Katharine, Duchess of Kent passed away, her widower, Prince Edward, now 90, has maintained a public presence at family weddings, Wimbledon, and, just last week, a memorial concert for his wife. The Duke of Kent—a first cousin of the late Queen Elizabeth II—and the Duchess, born Katharine Worsley, married in 1961. They later had three children: Lady Helen Taylor, Lord Nicholas Windsor, and George Windsor, the Earl of St. Andrews, all of whom maintain an active presence alongside the royal family.

For decades, the couple were frequently seen on the Buckingham Palace balcony, waving and smiling next to the Princess of Wales during the Trooping the Colour and Royal Ascot. Given their working royal statuses, they were given use of various royal residences around England, the first of which was Coppins, a 19th-century country house in Buckinghamshire, England, following their wedding.

Below, take a look at the stately residences the pair have called home over the years, including one later used by Prince William and Kate Middleton.

After their 1961 wedding, the Duke and Duchess of Kent moved into Coppins, a 19th-century farmhouse built by John Mitchell. They lived here until 1972 when they moved to York House at St. James’s Palace, and later sold it in 1977. Formerly the home of Princess Victoria, the estate was left to Prince George, Duke of Kent, and was the home of two generations of the Kent family.

Completed in the 1730s for Frederick, Prince of Wales (and father of the future George III), York House is a Georgian wing attached to St. James’s Palace in London. It served as the residence of several royals including King George V and King Edward VIII. The Kents used the estate as their base in London starting in the early 1970s through 1997, when the couple moved to Wren House at Kensington Palace. Following their departure, then-Prince Charles, along with Princes William and Harry, lived in York House. Today, though, it is no longer a home for senior working royals.

The couple used Anmer Hall, a ten-bedroom Georgian manor, as a country home between between 1972 and 1990. In his book, A Royal Life, the Duke said, “I regret ever having left” the stately home, though he also claimed that the house, which is located on the grounds of the royal Sandringham estate, was “too big” for the pair. Since 2011, when Queen Elizabeth II gave Prince William and Kate Middleton the home after their wedding, it has served alternately as their country house and primary residence (today, the family mostly lives at Forest Lodge in Windsor). They also oversaw a $2 million renovation by designer Ben Pentreath and architect Charles Morris, during which a glass-lined conservatory with a pergola and an outdoor swimming pool were added.

After leaving Anmer Hall, the couple used Crocker End House in the Oxfordshire countryside as a retreat. Built in the mid-19th century, the Victorian Gothic Revival manor features steep gables, pointed windows, and sits within roughly 30 acres of woodland. They put the house up for sale in 1996 and sold it in the late 1990s.

In 2002, the Duchess of Kent purchased the Old Forge in the Oxfordshire village of Brightwell Baldwin. She reportedly paid £540,000 for the three-bedroom, Grade II-listed estate, a former metal workshop. The Duke and Duchess spearheaded a renovation to modernize the property, which they sold in 2017.

Designed by architect Sir Christopher Wren, Wren House is one of the 20 private residences on the grounds of Kensington Palace and served as the main home of the Duke and Duchess of Kent beginning in 1997. The two-story, five-bedroom dwelling has a traditional brick exterior, sash windows, and a white-picket fence. As of 2026, it remains the primary residence of the Duke of Kent.

#576. How Two Friends Turned a Timeworn Connecticut Garage Into a Vintage-Inspired Barnhouse

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE Decor editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

The new wing designer Ryan Lawson added to restaurateur Rose Bonura’s 300-year-old Colonial feels like it's always been there.

The graceful barn beside restaurateur Rose Bonura’s 300-year-old Connecticut farmhouse may appear as if it’s been there for a century. But in reality, just three years ago it was a sagging, foundationless garage—the kind of structure nobody mourns. “It was old, but not historic,” says designer Ryan Lawson, who tackled the renovation of Bonura’s Colonial. After three years, Bonura decided to add on, transforming the barn into a greenhouse and enlisting Lawson to help. But, after a few conversations, she wound up with an entire second wing of her house, one in such easy conversation with the original that it now feels more like the home’s missing half.

Lawson and Bonura’s relaxed rapport came through in the design process. She would propose something sensible, Lawson would push it a bit further. She pitched a place to winter her plants; he countered with a custom post-and-beam barn from Country Carpenters in Hebron, Connecticut. “Ryan’s always right,” Bonura says now, a refrain that’s become a running joke between them.

The project was right in Lawson’s wheelhouse. The New York City-based designer, who founded his firm in 2005, has become known as a confident mix-master, someone who can layer centuries and continents in one room and make it feel effortless rather than contrived. He and Bonura have been friends for 18 years, and he drew on that longstanding relationship for the design. The two have traveled together, cooked together, and shopped at flea markets and antique fairs side by side for so long that Lawson can anticipate Bonura’s wants. For example, when the contractor suggested brightening the space with another window, Lawson steered Bonura toward vintage stained glass. He knows that she craves soft, quiet light at home after a day in her bright restaurant, Rosie, in New Canaan, Connecticut. And Bonura calls the result a “perfect decision.”

Bonura trusted Lawson in other ways, too. He talked her into repainting the original house in Benjamin Moore’s Jamesboro Gold, which both she and his partner, Sean Robins, had initially written off on sight as resembling “baby poop.” One test patch later, they’d changed their minds.

Inside, Lawson gave a pair of 17th-century Venetian sconces, found at Parma’s famous Mercanteinfiera antiques fair, new life with custom shades of his own design. An Ingo Maurer fixture, still wearing the original wine labels from the Los Angeles restaurant where it hung, is suspended nearby. Across the room, a pair of bright red vintage Italian chairs face a claw-footed 1980s mosaic table, the very first thing Lawson and Bonura bought for the space. In the living room, a Suzani textile on a simple curtain rod slides open to reveal a television no one would otherwise guess was there. Out in the glass-walled walkway connecting the two houses, a bobbin étagère holds ceramics alongside gourds from Bonura’s garden. Upstairs, a needlepoint-covered American chair sits beside an Italian bed.

Bonura compares living here to walking through a museum. Working with Lawson, she notes, taught her to embrace the unexpected. And, most of all, to let a room hold “lots of curiosity,” she says, “and a bit of magical thinking.”

Special Projects Editor William Li is the founder of art consultancy Armature Projects and the Emmy-nominated co-host of Lucky Chow, a series about Asian food and culture on PBS.
