#577. The Kitchen Work Triangle Is Officially Out, According to Designers

Kitchens are shape-shifting for maximum productivity.

Pictured above: The deVOL kitchen in Lee Thornley’s English cottage strikes a balance between beauty and everyday function.

A well-designed kitchen starts with a layout that makes cooking and entertaining easier (and more organized!). While the exact layout will depend on the size of your space and your home’s architecture, one of the most enduring design principles that often comes up is the kitchen work triangle, a classic concept centered on efficiency.

The idea connects the sink, stove, and refrigerator—the three most frequently used areas of the kitchen—into a triangular arrangement to encourage natural movement throughout the space. When generous counter space separates at least two of these workstations, it creates a practical zone for prepping meals with minimal interruption.

"The kitchen triangle is almost like breathing," says Rebekah Zaveloff, cofounder and creative director of Imparfait Design Studio. "The concept is based on avoiding hard turns—ideally, you take one step and pivot rather than walking multiple steps. Fewer steps equals less time, which equals more efficiency."

While the kitchen work triangle has helped dictate kitchen design for decades, it's no longer the only approach designers look to when laying out a cook space. Every home has different demands, and many designers are moving beyond this traditional framework to create kitchens that better suit modern lifestyles. Below, we explore the limitations of the kitchen triangle and hear from design experts about how today's kitchens are evolving to be even more flexible and functional.

For households that love to cook, the kitchen triangle may be the apotheosis of floor plans. Why mess with perfection? “It's basically about taking fewer steps to get from one task to the next,” Zaveloff says. “If you're going from the fridge to the sink to the cooktop, and you're walking across other work zones or around obstacles like islands, it's less efficient than having these three main areas laid out in an unobstructed triangle.”

That said, the plan cannot end there. If you're working with a designer on reimagining your kitchen layout, you should consider additional factors to ensure you create a cook space that makes sense for your household.

“The kitchen work triangle is a consideration, but definitely just the starting point for us,” says designer Sarah Robertson of Studio Dearborn. “Beyond the work triangle, we consider who is using the kitchen, cooking style, traffic patterns, the household makeup, their ages and abilities, entertaining styles, natural light, access to the outdoors…and then we also want to consider how all of that may change over time!"

The kitchen may be a workhorse space, but it's also a hub that draws family members and guests to congregate, relax, or perhaps steal a snack from the pantry. How you accommodate everyone's needs beyond just those of the home cook will make for a kitchen that feels less builder-grade and more bespoke.

The kitchen work triangle is by no means going away; if you're cooking a major holiday dinner for a house full of guests, you'll be happy to have that basic foundation locked in. But designers working on kitchen renovations today are less concerned about the triangle, per se, and more interested in creating functional "zones" that support every step of the cooking process.

"We tend to think about the overall kitchen space in terms of zones, and how those zones interact, overlap, and work together," Robertson says. She explains that primary zones can be broken down by purpose: food prep, cleanup, cooking, and dry food storage.

"Beyond these, we often include a coffee bar, drinks bar, baking area, dining/hangout zone, and a desk/drop zone," Robertson adds. These secondary options make more sense for how we live today, and can be added as they are deemed appropriate for a household's shifting needs. Strategic placement of these discrete zones should allow multiple people to move through the kitchen without creating a traffic jam.

"For example, if a parent is cooking while kids come home from sports looking for snacks, those snacks should be positioned away from the cook's workspace," Zaveloff says. "Similarly, if one person is cooking while another is cleaning and loading the dishwasher, the dishwasher should be positioned on the side of the sink closest to dish storage, ideally without crossing the cook's path," Zaveloff says.

If you're embarking on a kitchen renovation, talk with your architect and interior designer about prioritizing the work zones that will see the most daily foot traffic. From there, it's time to break out the tape measure.

"Every kitchen is different, but we will measure clearances and distances between major appliances and have clients measure in real life what that feels like. If the larger footprint feels too spread out, we will move the major zones closer together, and leave peripheral spaces for secondary zones such as coffee, baking, or a drinks/snacks area," Robertson says.

Instead of adhering to a default layout, think critically about whether certain kitchen features or appliances are truly worthy of center-stage status. "We will often consider moving less-used appliances, such as the freezer or a second oven, to a more peripheral location if that helps us solve a layout challenge," Robertson adds.

Any way that you can save yourself some steps in the kitchen is a good thing, even if that means your setup is a little unconventional. "We usually carve out a walk-in pantry for food storage (sometimes even putting a freezer and secondary fridge in the pantry) and create dedicated zones for specific tasks, like breakfast prep with all necessary food and small appliances in the same area, so you're not walking across the kitchen," Zaveloff says.

Ultimately, having dedicated zones outside of the kitchen work triangle allows us to enjoy the at-home rituals we love—such as making a morning matcha at a drinks station or whipping up loaves of banana bread in our baking zone—without needing to haul out heavy appliances and gather supplies from faraway corners of our kitchen each time. The way we live today in our homes is changing, and rethinking the kitchen's layout helps to allow for as much flexibility as possible.

"It's really quite logical," Zaveloff says. "It just takes thoughtful consideration and planning."

#578. Here’s Exactly How to Start Strength Training in Midlife, According to a Trainer

Get ready to invest in your long-term health.

As you get older, you may notice you have more pesky aches and pains in your joints, find that you're not as mobile as you used to be, or feel that your strength isn’t quite what it once was—and that’s normal. But that doesn’t mean you have to feel that way. Through consistent strength training, you can move pain-free and feel strong for the rest of your life, and it’s never too late to start.

“Strength training in midlife is an investment in your long-term health,” says Patricia Greaves, CPT, WH Strength in Diversity alum and the founder of StrongHer Personal Training, a virtual and in-person coaching service. “It builds muscle, strengthens your bones, and helps you stay strong, mobile, and independent for longer.”

But throwing around weights when you’re, say, 50, may feel different than it did at 20. After all, you can start losing muscle mass and bone density in your 30s, and without training, you may lose strength, stability, mobility, and overall resilience over time. In other words, your body changes in midlife, so your approach needs to as well.

But starting a strength training routine—at any age—is easier said than done. Here’s how to move freely and easily in midlife and beyond, according to Greaves.

Starting out, your goal should be “about learning movement patterns, not proving anything,” Greaves says. Starting lighter builds confidence, protects your joints, and allows you to focus on proper form while gradually building a solid foundation of strength. Depending on your current ability, Greaves recommends beginning with bodyweight exercises or light dumbbells around 2 to 3 lbs for upper body, and 5 to 8 lbs for lower body. (The smaller muscles of your upper body, like your biceps, triceps, and shoulders typically can’t handle as much weight as the bigger muscles of your legs, like your glutes and quads.)

That said, the key to getting stronger over time is progressive overload—gradually increasing the weight, reps, or sets to consistently challenge your body—so Greaves suggests upping your dumbbells by 2.5 to 5 lbs once you can easily complete 10 to 12 (or more) reps of an exercise. (If you can’t get 10 to 12 reps with the new weight, aim for 6 to 8 reps at first.) For example, if you’ve been squatting with 5-lb dumbbells for a few weeks, and all 12 reps feel easy while your form is solid, it’s time to step it up to 7.5- or 10-lb dumbbells.

“The goal is to create a routine that actually feels doable, so I usually recommend [starting with] three 30-minute strength sessions a week—one lower-body day, one upper-body day, and one full-body day,” Greaves says. However, if that feels like too much, even just two sessions a week—one upper-body and one lower-body workout—can still make a difference in your overall strength and endurance, she adds.

Greaves also suggests starting with three moves per session (with three sets of 10 to 12 reps each). To get the most bang for your buck, she also recommends sticking with compound exercises (movements that target multiple muscle groups at once), like split squats, deadlifts, overhead presses, push-ups, and bent-over rows.

Remember: It’s consistency that changes your body and improves strength. “Strength training works best when you stick to a plan that’s simple, effective, and something you can actually keep up with long-term,” Greaves says. As your body adjusts and grows stronger, you can always tack on an extra training day or add more moves.

Resting “isn’t optional, because recovery is where strength actually builds,” Greaves says. To set yourself up for success, Greaves recommends aiming for seven to nine hours of sleep each night. On days you aren’t lifting, she also encourages gentle activity like walking and stretching to boost circulation, support recovery, and keep your body moving.

Nutrition matters too, and protein and fiber should become your best friends. “Protein helps build muscle and keep you full while fiber supports heart health, digestion, and satiety,” she explains. Specific protein needs will vary person to person, but a good rule of thumb is aiming to eat 20 to 30 grams of protein per meal, with a few protein-heavy snacks throughout the day. Go for eggs, chicken, turkey, tofu, lean beef, Greek yogurt, and cottage cheese, paired with fiber-packed fruits and veggies.

For recipe ideas, check out the WH Ultimate Protein + Fiber Guide.

Building strength in midlife isn’t about going to extremes or chasing perfection. It’s about starting smart, keeping it doable, and choosing what feels good for your body so you can stick with it and make real progress over time.

When in doubt, the key is “listening to your body, respecting your limits, and understanding that what strength looks like now might be different than before, but that’s not a bad thing,” Greaves says. “It’s how you stay consistent and keep improving over time.”

Andi Breitowich is a freelance writer who covers health, fitness, relationships, beauty, and smart living. #579. Taylor Swift’s “Blank Space” Castle Heads to Auction—Plus 6 More Luxury Homes for Sale

This week’s top listings include homes linked to King George III, Diane Keaton, Julia Child, Meghan Markle, and Jackson Pollock.

It’s been a dizzying week in the luxury real estate business. High-profile properties around the world are hitting the market, from an observatory built for the British royal family that has since been converted into a lavish residence to the final renovation project completed by late Oscar-winner Diane Keaton to the longtime Cambridge home of Julia Child.

Also turning heads? Two estates linked to Taylor Swift. The pop superstar’s first property in Los Angeles just hit the market for nearly $8 million—and it’s where she reportedly wrote her blockbuster album 1989. The other is Long Island’s enormous Oheka Castle, which clocks in at over 100,000 square feet and was the setting for Swift’s “Blank Space” video. The Jazz Age landmark is heading to auction this month. See below for what else caught our eye this week.

Got a blank check? The massive Jazz Age estate featured in Taylor Swift’s “Blank Space” video—to say nothing of its appearance in Citizen Kane—will hit the auction block on October 27 with Concierge Auctions. Built in 1919 by Delano and Aldrich, Oheka Castle on New York’s Long Island spans a whopping 109,000 square feet, making it the nation’s second-largest residence, behind the Biltmore. A popular event space and wedding venue, the 23-acre landmark property is anchored by a French chateau-style manor equipped with 34 guest suites and a ballroom, all surrounded by formal gardens designed by the Olmsted brothers. It’s worth an estimated $92 million, per People.

Tyler Perry’s sprawling Beverly Hills mansion—where Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex lived as they transitioned out of royal life—just hit the market for $57 million. The Tuscan-style villa features palatial proportions, with nine bedrooms and 15 baths across nearly 24,600 square feet, while the grounds span 22.5 acres. It’s one of the most expensive properties for sale within the coveted 90210 zip code.

The final home that Hollywood star Diane Keaton put her stamp on is now for sale. Perched atop a bluff in Laguna Beach, with postcard views of the Pacific Ocean, the four-bedroom house just hit the market for $10.3 million.

Originally built in 1976, the Southern California retreat belonged to the late Oscar-winning actress from 2021 to 2022, during which time she updated the internal systems, installed a new roof, and revamped the fireplace. The interiors adhere to the black-and-white color scheme favored by Keaton, with the kitchen sporting industrial-style lighting pendants—a flourish that became one of her signature touches.

Jackson Pollock’s onetime Manhattan loft is hitting the market for the first time in more than a decade. The light-flooded West Village penthouse listed on October 1 for $1.99 million with agent Shane Boyle of Compass. Perched atop a Federal-style brick townhouse at 46 Carmine Street, the roughly 690-square-foot unit was home to the late Abstract Expressionist painter in the early 1930s, when he moved in with his brother, Charles, and sister-in-law, Elizabeth. The brothers apparently used the unit not just as a living space, but also as a studio, per historian Tom Miller.

Add this to your “Wi$h Li$t.” Taylor Swift’s former Beverly Hills bungalow just hit the market for nearly $8 million—and it’s brimming with pop star lore. Swift acquired the mini-compound in 2011, fresh off releasing Speak Now, when she was just 22 years old. It’s where she reportedly wrote her fourth album, 1989. At the time, she had a pair of Nashville residences to her name, though her property empire has since expanded exponentially.

Julia Child’s pegboard-covered kitchen might be in the Smithsonian, but her longtime Massachusetts home—where the famed cooking space was once located—can now be yours. The late chef’s former Cambridge house just hit the market for $6.475 million.

A lavish astronomical observatory—not just fit for a king but actually built for one—just hit the market in London for $24 million. The monarch in question was King George III, who ruled over Great Britain and Ireland between 1760 and 1820, famously losing the American colonies during the Revolutionary War.

#580. The 6 Best Brooks Shoes for Walking, Tested By Style and Fitness Editors

The Adrenaline GTS 25 and the Ghost 18 topped our list.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I’ve been known to have questionable standards in some areas of life—like my preference for boxed wine post-grad or my ability to convince myself that cereal counts as dinner. But when it comes to what I put on my feet, the bar is high. I used to think a good walking shoe just meant something that didn’t give me blisters. Now, as a style writer with a pile of sneakers so high it rivals Everest, I expect a lot more. I’m talking support, tons of comfort, and yes, style. That’s exactly why Brooks has become my go-to. The brand’s secret sauce: a perfectly balanced, firm-yet-plush cushioning that makes long days on my feet feel like a walk in the park.

Brooks has been around for over 100 years, and the brand has perfected its walking (and running) shoes. It’s no wonder that Brooks sneakers also come highly recommended by our team of active editors and podiatrist Brad Schaeffer, DPM. “Brooks has always been one of my go-to shoes, especially for walking,” says Schaeffer. That’s thanks to their ideal balance of comfort and support, extensive sizing, secure laces, and breathable, sturdy mesh uppers. You need a shoe specifically for walking because it offers the necessary cushion to take the impact off your joints and give your foot the support it needs to propel forward. These features help prevent aches and injuries.

There’s a seemingly endless amount of sneakers to choose from, but don’t stress: I’ve put in the work to try out the best Brooks shoes for walking. I log (at least) 10,000 steps per day between walking my energetic Jack Russell terrier all around Long Island and commuting into Manhattan for work. Our team of editors also tested every Brooks sneaker through power walking, long days at the office, and leisurely strolls. Our favorite shoe of the bunch is the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25, but many others came close for their cushion and stability.

After testing dozens of shoes, the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 takes the crown as my go-to for walking (and tbh, everything else). The latest Adrenaline GTS iteration still nails the balance between cushion and support, keeping my stride steady without feeling stiff or squished—which is exactly what I loved about the 24.

What really seals the deal? The firm-yet-cozy midsole hugs the foot just right, offering a secure, locked-in feel that still stays comfortable mile after mile. The 25 has a bit more cushioning than the previous version without sacrificing stability (something I was nervous about). Add in the breathable mesh upper that keeps things cool without sacrificing structure, and you’ve got a sneaker that truly goes the distance. I also love that Brooks reduced the heel-to-toe drop from 12 mm to 10 mm, which helps reduce the potential for strain in the hips and knees. In the past two months, I’ve racked up 40+ walking miles and 15 running miles, pain-free with these.

A few other WH editors have also taken the Adrenaline GTS 25 for a spin and came back equally impressed. In our 2026 Fitness Awards, the Adrenaline GTS 25 took the top spot for walking shoes for its near-perfect balance between cushioning and stability. “It offers just the right amount of cushioning for a bouncy step without compromising on support for my flat, wide feet," says beauty editor Nicole Saunders.

I’ve had the same experience, and credit that to the shoe’s GuideRails tech, which uses firm foam on either side of the heel to keep feet locked in. The foam is infused with nitrogen, making it super comfortable and lightweight without being overly plush. Bonus: The breathable mesh upper keeps things comfy without too much stretch (key for stability while walking), Schaeffer says.

One heads-up: the Adrenaline GTS 25 is a bit heavier than the 24 at 9.5 oz., so if you like a super lightweight shoe, you may want to consider the Glycerin Flex. However, I barely notice a difference in weight and chalk it up to the increased foam in the midsole.

Read More: Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 Review

If versatility is your priority, the Brooks Ghost 18 delivers. With its nitrogen-fused cushioning, the latest version of the shoe packs in the same amount of plush padding that we loved in the Ghost 17 (it was a 2025 WH Sneaker Award winner for a reason!). Impressively, the moderately high stack height at the heel doesn’t feel too squishy or wobbly. It’s a great do-it-all shoe for long walks, standing all day, and running.

Upgrades from the previous version include a new sockliner that makes for a comfy, snug fit and a flat tongue (the old one was a more classic padded option). “It does a good job of hugging the shape of your ankle without rubbing or chafing,” says fitness writer and WH contributor Korin Miller. “I like the smooth, seamless feel it creates, but I noticed that the edges start to curl in with repeated use.” I’ve noticed the same, but it’s definitely not an issue once your foot is in the shoe—just something to double-check when you slide your foot in.

I’ve worn these for long walks with my pup, all-day errands, a Costco shopping spree (IYKYK), and a full day on my feet at a music festival—and my arches stayed happy through it all. The soft midsole offers that just-right level of give that absorbs impact without feeling too soft or marshmallowy. The knit mesh upper is even more breathable than in the last version, adding to the barely-there feel, as does the plush ankle collar, which doesn’t chafe or rub at all.

One of my only gripes about the Ghost 17 was the slightly narrow toe box, but thankfully, the Ghost 18 solved this issue for me. It’s much more spacious now, both in terms of width and height.

If you’re after a walking shoe that’s super cushy, the Brooks Glycerin 23 is it. I’ve tested these on nearly 10-mile walks through nature preserves and standing for hours at the DMV (ugh). I never once felt like my feet were sore or that I needed to rush to sit down—these things felt like walking on pillows.

But the cushioning isn’t the only win here. The Glycerin 23’s knit upper gives this shoe a sock-like feel that hugs your foot without squeezing. It’s smooth, stretchy, and breathable, making it one of the most comfortable shoes I’ve worn on long walks. The shoe has a mild heel drop that helps distribute pressure evenly across the foot and reduces foot fatigue, which I sometimes experience with other walking shoes. While I wouldn’t quite describe the shoe as sleek or minimalist, it balances its plush cushioning with a more understated silhouette (aka it doesn’t veer into chunky dad shoe territory).

I also appreciate how well this shoe performs on uneven surfaces thanks to its wide platform and ample traction. The durable outsole covers plenty of ground, and the traction has a complex, winding tread pattern. I never feel like I’m going to slip, even on slick pavement.

So far, the Glycerin 23 does a great job of keeping my feet locked in despite its super thick cushioning—but it’s not designed for max stability. Those with specific foot problems, like plantar fasciitis or issues with overpronation, may want to pick a slightly less cushioned, more supportive shoe, like the Adrenaline GTS 25.

Read More: The Best Shoes For Standing All Day

The Brooks Ghost Max 3 took home the top spot in our guide to the most comfortable sneakers for its perfect balance of maximum support and cushioning. It keeps my feet comfortably locked in, even after hours of wear, and my ankles never feel wobbly, which often happens with plush shoes like this one.

“Out of all the sneakers I’ve tried, I find myself wearing the Brooks Ghost Max 3—it’s the newest addition to the Ghost Max series—the most when I want to feel comfortable during walks or runs (yep, it can do both!),” says style contributor Lily Wohlner. I agree. That’s because the rocker bottom sole, which has a slight curve to it like a rocking chair, helps propel my foot forward with less energy. Wearing it almost feels like walking on a moving runway at the airport.

Even for a max cushioned shoe, it’s super stable thanks to its signature Guardrails tech (the same found in the Adrenaline GTS 25). The outsole also has a broad base, which reduces rolling of the foot inward and outward and cradles the foot in place without interfering with your stride. Fitness contributor Talene Appleton says these features are great for high arches. After hours of walking, she doesn’t feel one ounce of pain or discomfort. And if you have wide feet or bunions, you’re in luck—this shoe comes in both wide and extra-wide options.

During testing, we did notice some wear and tear on the upper pretty early on (after a few months). While it was a bit of a bummer, the elite combo of cushion and support keeps this kick high on my list of Brooks sneakers.

Think of the Glyceric Flex as Glycerin 23’s lighter, more flexible counterpart. The upper and outsole are both made from super bendy materials that give the shoe an almost barefoot feel.

I’m a big fan of this shoe for walking, long periods of standing, running, and plyometric workouts. It's incredibly versatile, thanks to ample nitrogen-infused cushioning and a flexible midsole. The FlexZone technology—a strategically placed groove in the center of the shoe’s outsole—helps enhance the shoe’s flexibility and allows the foot to move naturally. Combined with the pods under the front of the foot (which reminds me of On’s signature CloudTec system you see on most of the brand’s outsoles), the shoe has a super bouncy feel without feeling wobbly.

Bonus: at only 8.0 ounces, it's the lightest shoe on this list, so your feet won’t feel bogged down. But it still falls in Schaeffer’s recommended weight range (eight to 10 ounces), so it's hefty enough to keep your foot locked in. Plus, the flat knit upper is super soft, breathable, and—yes—flexible, which adds to its airy feel.

But the shoe’s lighter weight means it offers less heft and a less supportive feel. If you need more structure or have specific stability needs, these might not be your best bet. But, if you’re into a flexible, responsive shoe that doesn’t weigh you down—this one’s tough to beat.

The Brooks Ghost Max L offers a super plush, easygoing stride. The high-stacked cushioning is next-level—soft but stable, like walking on a marshmallow. It has an outsole with a curved bottom, like a rocking chair, to help propel you forward so each step takes a bit less energy.

I didn’t expect to notice the rocker bottom that much, but I totally get the hype. Schaeffer says he actually prefers rocker-bottom shoes for walking, especially as we get older, because they help take pressure off joints. That said, the same rocker technology makes me feel a little off-balance when I try to run or power walk in them, so I keep these strictly for leisurely walks and casual wear.

Looks-wise, I’m team Ghost Max L all the way. Some might say the stacked foam gives grandma shoes, but I think it strikes that perfect balance of chunky and cool—especially when styled right. I like to wear mine with a wide-leg pant and a blazer on top. It’s got just the right amount of bulk to feel trendy without being clunky, and pairs well with everything from athleisure to workwear.

However, this shoe runs small. Definitely size up if you’re in between sizes or like a little wiggle room. I could have used a half size larger than what I wear in the rest of my Brooks shoes for a little more comfort, but I still get a lot of casual wear out of them regardless.

First things first, you want a good mix of comfort and stability in your walking shoe, says Schaeffer. He recommends looking for a pair that cups your heel in a way that isn’t too snug or too loose. This feature will keep your feet from wobbling with every step you take. That sort of stability keeps your foot aligned as you walk, which is key for overpronation (foot rolls in too much) or underpronation (foot rolls out), helping prevent strain on your joints and maintaining balance. You want a shoe that’s comfortable on your feet, but Shaeffer says to avoid any that are overly cushioned, and instead look for a shoe that is a bit sturdier to keep your feet in neutral alignment to avoid foot fatigue and prevent sprains or strains.

The front of your sneaker (aka toe box) should never be too snug because it can pinch the nerves and inflame the ball of your foot (aka metatarsalgia). One way to know if your toe box is wide enough? Make sure your foot lies one thumb width from the side of the shoe and one thumb width from the front of the shoe. Tip: If you have a longer second toe, a larger toe box is even more important, Schaeffer says.

Brooks is famous for its incredible arch support, which is exactly what Schaeffer says to look for in a walking shoe. However, if your arches need a little extra TLC, Schaeffer suggests getting insoles that cater to your specific foot needs. He recommends Dr. Scholl’s Multipurpose Insoles or custom orthotics. "The insoles help with alignment and keep you balanced," he says, which is especially important if you suffer from chronic pain, plantar fasciitis, or issues with your feet rolling inward or outward while you walk. If this sounds like you, we def recommend scheduling a visit with a podiatrist to make sure your feet get the care they need.

A heel-to-toe drop, sometimes called a midsole drop, is the difference in height between the heel and forefoot (toe area). Schaeffer says to look for a walking shoe with a heel-to-toe drop that puts your foot in a neutral position, which will be different for everyone’s unique foot and step pattern.

Schaeffer says most people love a lightweight shoe since it's nice to feel like there's nothing down there. Just make sure the shoe has a supportive feel, and it holds your foot with every step you take. "In this case, I'm okay with the shoe being light," he says. "But, if the shoe is too light (under four ounces), you sacrifice function and stability." All of the Brooks sneakers on this list are between eight and 10 ounces, so they're the perfect weight in Schaeffer's book.

Over the past two years, the Women’s Health team has undertaken a comprehensive approach to curating the ultimate guide to the best Brooks walking shoes by testing nearly every new pair as it drops. Along with insights from Brad Schaeffer, DPM, board-certified foot surgeon and owner of Central Park Sole in New York City, we’ve put more than 30 Brooks sneakers through their paces.

As the associate style and reviews editor, I led the testing process with support from fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi, NASM-CPT, associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian, NASM-CPT, and fitness and reviews editor Charles Thorp, NASM. Our evaluation involved multiple phases, consulting runners and walkers on the Women's Health team, and most importantly, testing the shoes firsthand. We subjected each shoe to everything from fast walks to long travel days to leisurely strolls. The narrowed-down list above includes the six shoes we were most impressed by

#581. We Slept on Thuma’s Luxury Sheets for Weeks to Find Out If They're Worth the Splurge

They feel just as soft now as they did on night one.

Every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

When it comes to bedroom furniture, I was already a major fan of Thuma’s pieces. Their walnut nightstands, cushioned bed frame, and soft-close dresser are the grounding pieces in my bedroom. The brand’s reputation for high-quality furniture that’s built to last rings true in my book. When they launched bedding, I, of course, had to give them a try in order to complete my whole Thuma bedroom setup.

The brand’s main entries into the bedding game are two weaves: a linen and a percale. I tested out the percale, but I’m not the biggest fan of linen, so I tagged in my linen-loving colleague, Senior Commerce Editor Marina Liao. We spent weeks sleeping on the sheets in our respective homes to see if they earned the House Beautiful stamp of approval. So how did it go? Scroll on to find out.

Best For: The percale sheets are best for sleepers who want cool, crisp hotel-style bedding. The linen sheets are great for linen skeptics who want a softer alternative.

Not ideal for: Budget-minded shoppers or those who prefer colorful bedding.

Price at review (Queen-size set): $205 for Cotton Percale; $315 for Linen set.

Bottom Line: These sheets provide luxury sleep with low-maintenance care, and they maintain their day-one softness after weeks of use.

Great percale sheets are like a glass of Sauvignon Blanc: crisp and refreshing. It’s what you usually encounter in a freshly made hotel bed. Not designed to be cooling, but easy to slip into, and it feels high quality. It’s a delicate line between crisp and stiff, and Thuma’s Cotton Percale Sheet Set walks that line effortlessly. The sheet set strikes a balance of that cool feeling with a soft hand-feel, so it’s still lightweight and smooth when I drape it over me at night.

The sheet set is also sized well, so there isn’t a bunch of extra material I have to tuck into my bed frame. The lighter color means you can see through it to a patterned pillow or mattress. Thuma’s percale sheets have a thread count of 270, which falls well below the 400 TC threshold that starts to bother hot sleepers.

Of course, Thuma’s bedding pairs well with my Thuma bed frame, but the four neutral colors and lightweight weave would truly work on any bed. I’d gladly use these as my main sheets, or as guest room sheets. They have that all-star appeal. Not so pretentious as silk or cashmere sheets, but not a pilly microfiber set.

Senior Commerce Editor Marina Liao loves sleeping on linen sheets year-round, so she also has high standards for them. She’s tested sets from viral bedding brands like Quince, Hommey, Parachute, and Brooklinen. Liao is also a proud owner of Thuma's bed frame, but has yet to give the brand’s linen sheets a test drive. After weeks of sleeping on it, she noted that they’re the softest right out of the package of any brand she’s tried. It’s rare that linen sheets don’t need to be broken in.

“I washed them and slept on them the same night, noticing how they regulated my temperature well during the summer months,” Liao says. “Now that it is cooler, they still feel nice and keep me warm in 65-degree morning weather. Sometimes I can feel hot even when sleeping on linen sheets, but I have had zero issues with these.”

There’s really only one thing Liao would change about the sheets: have them come in a few more colors. The only options right now are six neutral shades, which will suit any bedroom, but variety is on her mind.

“While I don’t think I would buy these again for my bed specifically simply because they don't fit my mattress that well—the saggy look around the sides vs. tightly pulled and taut look bothers me—I think these linen sheets are perfect for deeper pocket mattresses. I think these will fit my taller mattress in the guest room better, and in the process convince a friend or two sleeping there that non-scratchy linen sheets do exist!”

Though Thuma’s bedding comes with a luxury price tag, its care instructions are not precious. The Percale sheet set is made from 100 percent cotton, and the Linen set is 100 percent European flax linen. Both sets are pre-washed for extra softness upon arrival. And they have the same wash instructions: machine wash with warm water and tumble dry on low heat. Easy to do, no trip to the dry cleaners needed. Two things to note: the percale sheets wrinkle easily, so make sure to fold those as soon as they come out of the dryer. And the linen sheets shed quite a bit, even after a few washes, but they won’t shrink in the dryer.

Yes, Thuma bedding is worth the investment. It follows the brand’s trend of high-quality pieces, without the high-maintenance care routine. You can launder these sheet sets right at home, and they’ll maintain their day-one softness. If you’re a linen skeptic, the linen set just might be soft enough to change your mind. But if you have a slimmer mattress, or you’re trying to recreate a hotel room in your bedroom, the percale sheets will offer a refreshing sleep.

#583. Protein Shake or Meal Replacement? A Dietitian Explains the Differences

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Protein powder and meal replacement powder can look like twins perched upon the shelf. Both come in tubs, both can be mixed into smoothies, and both can be high in protein. But despite the family resemblance, they’re designed to perform different functions.

Protein powder is primarily meant to add more protein to your diet. Meal replacement powder has a bigger assignment: providing more of what you’d typically get from a meal, including protein, carbohydrates, fat, fiber, and vitamins and minerals.

So while you can absolutely use protein powder to build a meal, the two aren’t interchangeable straight out of the tub. Ahead, we’ll break down the differences, what to look for in each, and which one makes the most sense for your needs.

Protein powder is a concentrated source of protein designed to help you get more protein without cooking or preparing yet another protein-rich food.

It can come from many sources, with whey and casein among the most common. Whey comes from milk, digests quickly, and is rich in the essential amino acids that build and repair muscle. Casein also comes from milk and provides all nine essential amino acids, but it digests more slowly than whey. Both are solid options unless you have a milk allergy or avoid dairy.

Prefer plant-based? Soy is a complete protein, meaning it provides all nine essential amino acids. Other plant-based powders may use pea, rice, hemp, or a blend of different proteins. These can all be good options if you avoid dairy or animal products, though the amount of each essential amino acid varies by protein source.

You don’t have to be a gym regular to use protein powder, either. While it’s long been popular among athletes and people looking to build muscle, it can also come in handy when you’re busy, have a low appetite, follow a vegetarian or vegan diet with limited protein intake, or struggle to get enough protein from food alone.

It’s versatile beyond the standard shake, too. Blend it into a smoothie, stir it into oatmeal or yogurt, or simply mix it with water or milk for an easy protein boost.

Just keep in mind that, regardless of the source, protein powder isn’t necessarily a meal replacement. It’s primarily there to provide protein, so on its own, it may be pretty light on calories, carbohydrates, fat, fiber, and other nutrients you’d get from a balanced meal.

Our best overall pick Promix Whey Protein Powder packs 30 grams of whey protein isolate into a short, simple ingredient list, with just 0.5 grams of fat and 2 grams of carbs per serving. Because whey isolate undergoes additional filtration to remove much of the lactose, it may also be easier to digest for people with lactose intolerance.

Meal replacement powder is designed to do more than provide protein. Nutrition varies by product, but most combine protein with carbohydrates, fat, fiber, vitamins, and minerals to provide more of what you’d typically get from a meal.

That can make it a convenient option when you don’t have the time, appetite, or ability to sit down to a regular meal—or when you simply need something portable enough to come along for the ride. Literally.

There is one catch: The words “meal replacement” on the label don’t guarantee you’ll get what a balanced meal provides. Some are too low in calories to realistically stand in for one, while others provide plenty of protein but very little carbohydrate, fat, fiber, or certain vitamins and minerals.

Rather than taking a meal replacement at face value, flip that tub around. The Nutrition Facts panel can tell you much more about whether it actually has what you need from a meal.

Our best overall meal replacement shake Huel Black Edition Ready-to-Drink actually delivers what you’d expect from a meal—and it’s not just a hefty dose of protein. Each bottle provides 400 calories, 35 grams of plant-based protein, six to seven grams of fiber, healthy fats, and 27 essential vitamins and minerals. The pea and faba bean protein blend also provides a more complete amino acid profile, making this one of the most nutritionally well-rounded, grab-and-go options we tested.

Taste-wise, chocolate is the standout—it’s rich, smooth, and not overly sweet—but the variety box is a great way to sample other flavors and shake things up. The bottles are shelf-stable for easy grab-and-go convenience, and we think they taste even better chilled.

Shop Huel Black Edition Meal Replacement Shake

The biggest difference comes back to what each product is designed to do. Protein powder concentrates on, well, protein. A meal replacement has more to cover: enough energy and a broad enough mix of nutrients to replace what you’d otherwise get from a meal.

Meal replacements generally provide more calories than protein powders, since they’re meant to replace the energy you’d get from a meal. Protein powder, on the other hand, is usually something you add to a meal or snack.

How much you need at a meal depends on your overall energy needs and what the rest of your day looks like. Still, it’s worth looking at whether a product provides enough calories to serve as a meal. A 150-calorie shake may work well as a snack, but for many adults, it won’t provide enough energy on its own.

You can get plenty of protein from either product. The difference is what comes along with it.

With protein powder, protein makes up much of the nutrition in each serving, with many products providing around 20 to 30 grams. A meal replacement may provide a similar amount, but protein should be just one part of its overall nutrition.

Protein powders tend to be relatively low in carbohydrates and fat because their primary purpose is to provide protein.

A meal replacement should generally provide both, since carbohydrates and fat contribute energy and other nutrients you’d typically get from a balanced meal.

Many protein powders contain little or no fiber. Whey and casein naturally contain none, while plant-based powders may provide some depending on the source and how the product is processed.

Fiber is more important in a meal replacement because the product replaces foods that might otherwise contribute fiber to your day. Fiber supports digestive health and can help the meal feel more satisfying.

Protein powders don’t typically offer many vitamins and minerals, but they may provide some depending on the protein source. For instance, dairy-based powders may contain calcium, while plant-based powders can be a source of iron.

Meal replacements are more likely to provide a broader range of vitamins and minerals because they’re meant to take the place of a meal. Many are fortified with nutrients such as vitamin D, iron, calcium, and B vitamins.

There isn’t one vitamin or mineral that’s a must-have in every meal replacement. Look for a variety of micronutrients, along with enough calories, protein, carbohydrates, fat, and fiber to make it a well-rounded meal.

Protein powder can be part of a meal, but a scoop mixed with water usually isn’t enough to count as one. You might get 20 or 30 grams of protein but very little carbohydrate, fat, fiber, or overall energy.

If you want your protein shake to replace breakfast or lunch, give it a little more substance. Blend the powder with milk, frozen fruit, and peanut or almond butter to add carbohydrates, fat, fiber, and calories. Or keep the shake simple and have it with something like a banana and a handful of nuts or whole-grain toast with nut butter.

What makes a good protein powder isn’t necessarily what makes a good meal replacement. But one thing I like to see on either is third-party testing. The FDA regulates dietary supplements, but it doesn’t approve them or verify their contents before they reach the market. Third-party testing provides an independent check of a product’s contents and, depending on the certification, may also screen for certain contaminants.

Look for certifications from organizations such as NSF Certified for Sport, Informed Choice, or Informed Sport. If you’re an athlete subject to drug testing, look specifically for a sport certification that screens for banned substances.

Around 20 to 30 grams per serving is a useful range to look for in a protein powder, though how much you need depends on your overall diet and what you’re using the powder for. The guidance here is the same for meal replacements, too.

Choose one that fits your dietary needs and tolerance, whether in a protein powder or a meal replacement. For muscle building or maintenance, look for a source that provides all the essential amino acids, such as whey, casein, soy, or a well-formulated plant protein blend.

Check the sweeteners and other ingredients if certain sugar alcohols or additives tend to bother your stomach. When it comes to sweeteners, remember that current dietary guidelines recommend no more than 10 grams of added sugar per meal, so check how much you’re getting per serving.

And pick a flavor you’ll actually want to finish. If you’re on a budget, compare the cost per serving rather than the price of the container alone.

When it comes to carbohydrates and fat, look for both. A product that’s mostly protein with a handful of added vitamins and minerals may be more like a fortified protein shake than a full meal.

At least 3 grams of fiber per serving is a reasonable benchmark I look for, along with a mix of micronutrients. Just know that you don’t need 100 percent of the Daily Value for each one in one shake.

Compare the calories per serving with what you’d typically get from a meal. There’s no single amount that works for everyone, but a 150-calorie shake may be closer to a snack for many adults unless you add other foods.

The choice mostly depends on what’s missing: protein or an entire meal. If you’re eating regular meals but struggle to get enough protein, protein powder can help fill that gap. Mix it into oatmeal or a smoothie, have a shake alongside a meal, or use it when you need a protein-rich snack.

A meal replacement makes more sense when the meal itself is what’s missing. Maybe you have back-to-back meetings, you’re traveling, or your appetite is low, and a plate of food sounds like… a lot. In those cases, look for something that provides enough calories and a mix of protein, carbohydrates, fat, fiber, and micronutrients.

#585. Diane Keaton’s Final Home Project, a Laguna Beach House, Is Now on the Market for $10.3 Million

The Southern California retreat was the last renovation the interior design-loving movie star spearheaded.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE Decor editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

The final home that Hollywood star Diane Keaton put her stamp on is now for sale. Perched atop a bluff in Laguna Beach with postcard views of the Pacific Ocean, the four-bedroom house just hit the market for $10.3 million.

Originally built in 1976, the Southern California retreat belonged to the Pinterest-loving late Oscar-winning actress from 2021 to 2022, during which time she updated the internal systems, installed a new roof, and revamped the fireplace. The interiors adhere to a black-and-white color scheme favored by Keaton, with the kitchen sporting industrial-style lighting pendants—a flourish that became one of her signatures.

The current owners purchased the 2,700-square-foot residence directly from Keaton, who died last October, for $7.9 million, according to data from real-estate platform Redfin. They have kept nearly all of Keaton’s design decisions intact and are only selling to give their growing family more space.

Among the standout features of the property are its sun-drenched interiors, bar-equipped lofted lounge, beamed ceilings, and numerous fireplaces. The house also comes with a network of terraces, including one equipped with a barbecue and al fresco dining area.

The structure sits on a sharply angled, 0.4-acre plot perched directly above Table Rock Beach in the coastal community of South Laguna. A staircase at the rear of the property leads directly to a secluded, cove-like stretch of sand.

The Book Club actress had a well-documented passion for home renovations, spearheading a series of thoughtful makeovers throughout her life. Among her best-known projects was her Brentwood estate, which she masterminded using Pinterest as the main source of inspiration. Keaton even wrote a book chronicling the painstaking process called The House That Pinterest Built. She also flipped two homes by Frank Lloyd Wright’s son, Lloyd Wright, in the 1990s and 2000s.

31595 Table Rock is listed for $10.3 million with Brooke Wainwright and David Koffs.

#586. ‘I Started Consistently Lifting Weights at 90. Now, I’m Training for My First Hyrox Race—Here’s How’

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

“You’re never too old to get stronger or discover what you’re capable of.”

When I was 83, I had a tough decision to make. My husband of 62 years had just died, and I needed to decide what to do with the rest of my life. I could give in to the enormous loss and let it swallow me, or I could move forward and take on some of his responsibilities. I chose the latter, and for the first time, I started mowing our lawn, hauling heavy bags of mulch around the yard, and taking care of the household chores.

I was always recreationally active and had walked a few miles a day for most of my life, so I was comfortable on my feet. But I hadn’t done any organized exercise consistently in decades, so taking on this kind of physical work at 83 was challenging. People told me I should hire someone so I wouldn’t get hurt, but the truth was, I enjoyed it. I felt strong and capable, and it was empowering to know that I could still take care of business. That sense of independence became a way of life for the next several years.

Then, shortly after my 90th birthday this past spring, my daughter-in-law, who is a serious athlete, saw me casually lift a 40-pound bag of mulch. She decided I was ready for something bigger: Hyrox, a fitness competition that combines running with functional workout stations like sled pushes, wall balls, and ski ergs. (She’s competed in numerous Hyrox races around the world.) I had never heard of Hyrox, but I’ve always been competitive, so I was immediately up for the challenge. We signed up for a race in Dallas this November, deciding to compete as a relay team, meaning we’d split the events and race together as a pair.

Within a few days of signing up, I was in the gym and ready to train. I’d done a little weightlifting here and there in my 30s and 40s, so I was generally familiar with the gym, but I knew I had a lot to learn. Luckily, I had the perfect teammate and coach, as my daughter-in-law programmed my workouts and began training with me three days a week.

Each workout lasts about an hour to an hour and a half, and I always start with 15 minutes of walking on the treadmill to warm up. From there, we move through different exercise stations, focusing on the events I’ll encounter in the Hyrox relay: ski ergs, sled pushes, sled pulls, burpee broad jumps, rows, farmer’s carry, sandbag lunges, and wall balls. The number of reps and sets varies from workout to workout, but I typically train three or four exercises during each session.

I’ve already noticed a big difference from staying consistent: I’ve built visible full-body muscle, my everyday house chores have become even easier, and I have more energy throughout the day. Plus, it’s been really rewarding to see how much progress I’ve made in only a few months: Sled pushes and wall balls have become my favorite challenges, and when I started about four months ago, I could push a 60-lb sled. Since then, I’ve made a point of increasing the weight at least once a week, and I can now push 200 lbs, which I’m extremely proud of. I’ve come a long way with wall balls, too. At first, I couldn’t do a single rep because I struggled just to toss the ball above my head. Now, I can do 10 reps with a 10-lb ball.

However, burpee broad jumps are by far my most challenging event. I can do the burpee, but I hadn’t jumped in years, so getting comfortable with the movement has taken time. To build my confidence, I’ve been practicing small, controlled jumps and working on exercises like step-ups to strengthen my legs and build explosive power.

On top of that, I walk four to eight miles with short bursts of jogging three days a week. The days I’m not in the gym training with my daughter-in-law, I also do 15- to 20-minute upper-body strength sessions at home with 10-lb dumbbells for exercises like overhead presses and biceps curls. These shorter workouts help me build strength and stay familiar with Hyrox movement patterns without overtraining.

I don’t track macros or focus too much on nutrition, but I’ve definitely become more intentional about getting enough protein to build muscle and support recovery; chicken, fish, and protein shakes are my go-tos. I’ve also noticed that I have more energy when I prioritize fresh, whole foods like fruits, vegetables, nuts, and seeds. I’m not overly strict about what I eat (I still love and enjoy sweets!), but I’ve learned to choose foods that help me feel strong and energized.

Grab-and-go protein shakes make it easy to eat enough protein throughout the day, and I especially enjoy the vanilla flavor.

Nike leggings are my favorite for training. The comfortable, supportive material holds up through even the most challenging workouts.

I love practicing wall balls at home, so investing in a durable medicine ball that’s easy to hold was a must.

I don’t always feel like working out, especially on the days when I’m tired or sore. But I don’t have to feel motivated to show up. Instead, I lean on my determination to get stronger by reminding myself that every workout is another opportunity to improve. Once I start moving, I almost always feel better, and by the end of a workout, I’m glad I did it. Motivation comes and goes, but determination is what keeps me showing up and striving to become better.

My family is a huge part of why I keep living life to the fullest. My daughter-in-law saw something in me that I didn’t see in myself and encouraged me to take on a challenge I never would have imagined at 90. Sharing this journey with her has become one of the most joyful parts of my life. My granddaughter has joined us for workouts too, making our time at the gym even more special.

Having both of them by my side keeps me motivated, but more than anything, they make the experience fun. We laugh, encourage each other, celebrate the small victories, and push one another when things get hard. Knowing they’re waiting for me at the gym is often all the motivation I need to keep showing up and giving it my all.

I’ve never been someone who sits on the sidelines and watches life happen around me, and turning 90 didn’t change that. If anything, it made me even more curious about what I could still accomplish. My body may have changed with age, but my mindset hasn’t. I’ve never believed getting older should mean putting limits on yourself. From pushing a 200-lb sled to tackling burpees and jumping again for the first time in years, I’m putting that belief into action.

If there’s one thing this experience has proved so far, it’s that you’re never too old to get stronger or discover what you’re capable of. Today, my sights are set on November, when I’ll step onto the Hyrox course and put all my hard work to the test. I’m excited, determined, and ready to see just how far I can go.

#590. Look Inside Tyler Perry’s Beverly Hills Mansion, Where Prince Harry and Meghan Markle Hid After Leaving the Royal Family

The movie director’s 22.5-acre compound just hit the market for $57 million.

Tyler Perry’s sprawling Beverly Hills mansion—where Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex lived as they transitioned out of royal life—just hit the market for $57 million. The Tuscan-style villa features palatial proportions, with nine bedrooms and 15 baths across nearly 24,600 square feet, while the grounds span 22.5 acres. It’s one of the most expensive properties for sale within the coveted 90210 zip code.

The Madea filmmaker custom built the gated estate after acquiring the parcel of land for $4.3 million in 2004, per The Wall Street Journal. Construction on the massive residence wrapped up in 2012. The interiors feature ornate molding, coffered ceilings, wood paneling, and a dramatic entry hall with a curving double-staircase.

Lavish amenities include a 24-seat home cinema, a music hall, a massage room, a wine cellar, and a state-of-the-art fitness studio. The manicured grounds, meanwhile, feature a separate guest cottage, staff quarters, and a pool court with sweeping mountain vistas.

In 2019, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex announced they were leaving the United Kingdom, along with their official royal duties, in a high-profile departure that became known as “Megxit.” After a brief stint in Canada, the pair relocated to Meghan’s home state of California, where Perry offered his lavish estate as a temporary landing pad.

The former Suits actress revealed she had never met Perry in person prior to moving to the property. But in 2018, the filmmaker had gotten in touch to offer his support—and his security detail.

The couple stayed at the home for several months before buying their own residence in Montecito, a celebrity-favorite enclave near Santa Barbara. Now with two young children, they recently announced a move back to England.

For his part, Perry is trimming his property portfolio after announcing a planned move to Puerto Rico. Not only is he parting with his Beverly Hills estate, but he also just put his woodsy Wyoming retreat on the market for nearly $40 million.

10 Beverly Ridge Terrace is listed for $57 million with Santiago Arana of The Agency.

#591. What Is the Pyro Method? How Celebrity Trainer Kirsty Godso Builds Functional Strength

The trainer behind Hailey Bieber's workouts says strength, repetition, and consistency—not endless cardio—are key.

To say Kirsty Godso’s resume is impressive would be an understatement.

Alongside a stint as a Nike Master Trainer, her 15-year career in fitness has seen her partner with athleisure brand Vuori and train clients including Olivia Rodrigo, Hailey Bieber, Maddie Ziegler and Kaia Gerber.

During that time, she's also developed her own training philosophy—a strength-Pilates hybrid with “micro-doses” of HIIT known as Pyro—which she now uses with many of her celebrity clients.

Pyro incorporates everything from resistance bands and dumbbells to bodyweight exercises, but its foundations are simple: consistency, repetition, and gradually lifting heavier.

“The body wants to learn something and get better at it, then you can be more confident, increase your weight load and improve your skill,” she explained in a recent interview with The Financial Times.

“I get a little evil in workouts,” she added of her coaching style. “But instead of talking about burning calories, I talk about why it’s important to do hard things. I find their goal beyond aesthetics and champion that.”

Signature Pyro exercises include the “hot-sauce burpee,” which combines a tuck jump with a traditional burpee; switch climbers, a dynamic variation of the mountain climber that involves jumping between lunge positions; and typewriter planks, where you shuffle horizontally while holding a high plank.

However, Godso is quick to point out that Pyro isn't prescriptive. When working with clients, she adapts sessions to suit the individual—something she previously told Women's Health.

“To me, a quieter, more intuitive approach is really at the heart of how I train my clients and myself,” she explained. “In an industry that always has a new training trend and a lot of outside noise, I always focus on putting the personal in personal training. It’s about focusing on the specific needs of each client and not getting distracted by the latest and greatest things that the algorithm is serving you.”

Preparation is another key part of her philosophy. Godso says she always spends five to 10 minutes before training on foam rolling and activation work to ensure her clients are ready for the session.

Although she deliberately keeps her client roster small, Godso shares many of her workouts through the Pyro app and regularly posts training snippets on Instagram.
